Biomedical research and healthcare increasingly depend on the reuse of data collected from patients and research participants. Electronic health records, biobanks, consumer devices, and high-throughput sequencing now produce information at a scale and granularity that was unimaginable two decades ago. Combining such data across organizations promises more powerful studies of disease, faster recruitment for clinical trials, and a learning health system in which care and discovery inform one another. Funders, journals, and policy makers have responded with expectations that data be shared and made findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (Wilkinson et al. 2016). Examples include the National Institutes of Health Genomic Data Sharing Policy (NIH 2014) and the growing use of repositories and data discovery indexes (Ohno-Machado et al. 2017). The same data are often sensitive. Clinical records reveal diagnoses, treatments, and behaviors, and genomic data disclose information about biological relatives and persist over a lifetime. A long line of research has shown that removing explicit identifiers does not reliably protect privacy. Demographic combinations can single out individuals in "de-identified" releases (Sweeney 2002), and patients can be linked to hospital discharge records and other secondary sources (Malin and Sweeney 2004; El Emam et al. 2011). Genomic data have proven especially vulnerable. Aggregate allele frequencies can reveal whether a person participated in a study (Homer et al. 2008), surnames can be inferred from Y-chromosome markers and public genealogy databases (Gymrek et al. 2013), and even yes/no "beacon" services can leak membership in a dataset through repeated queries (Shringarpure and Bustamante 2015). These findings have eroded the assumption that a dataset can be labeled "anonymous" or "public" without ongoing assessment of risk. The tension between access and privacy is therefore both technical and social. Overly permissive sharing can expose participants to discrimination, stigma, or loss of trust, and the resulting public concern can jeopardize the research enterprise. Overly restrictive practices impede reproducibility, delay discovery, and waste the contributions of participants who volunteered their data in the expectation that it would be used. Legal and ethical frameworks have tried to manage this tension, including the HIPAA Privacy Rule in the United States and the General Data Protection Regulation in the European Union (European Parliament and Council 2016). These frameworks emphasize consent, purpose limitation, de-identification, and governance. Yet they were largely designed for settings in which data were collected for a specific purpose and held by a single organization. They fit less easily with contemporary research, in which data are repurposed, linked across institutions, and analyzed by parties the original participants never met. Consent models are also evolving, from study-specific agreements to broad and dynamic approaches that give participants more continuing involvement (Kaye et al. 2015; Grady et al. 2015). How such models should operate in emerging environments, such as mobile health studies and large precision medicine cohorts, remains an open question. A second set of challenges concerns infrastructure. Data are distributed across hospitals, consortia, and repositories with different policies, formats, and risk tolerances. Researchers need ways to discover whether suitable data exist before they can request access. Federated query tools such as i2b2 and SHRINE let investigators estimate cohort sizes across institutions without centralizing patient-level records (Weber et al. 2009; Murphy et al. 2010). Even aggregate counts can leak information, however, especially for small or distinctive populations. This has motivated work on cryptographic protocols, such as homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computation, as well as statistical protections such as differential privacy (Dwork and Roth 2014). These techniques promise formal guarantees, but their costs in computation, communication, and loss of data utility are still being characterized for clinical and genomic applications. A third challenge is that privacy risk is not static. It depends on the data type, the auxiliary information available to an adversary, the incentives to attack, and the countermeasures in place. Recent work has therefore moved from asking whether a dataset is "safe" to modeling how risk varies with context and how data holders can make principled tradeoffs. Quantitative risk assessment, decision-theoretic and game theoretic models of data recipients and adversaries, and calibrated release of summary statistics are examples (Wan et al. 2017). Such approaches treat privacy protection as an optimization problem, balancing the utility of shared information against the likelihood and cost of misuse, rather than as a binary property. Despite this progress, the literature is fragmented. Consent, data discovery, risk measurement, secure computation, and data publication are often studied by different communities and described in different vocabularies, which makes it difficult for informaticians and data stewards to see how advances fit together across the data lifecycle. Each year brings a large volume of publications, and it is not obvious which contributions are most significant for practice or for shaping future research. This paper addresses that gap by surveying notable contributions from 2017 on biomedical data sharing, with an emphasis on data access and privacy. The guiding question is: what advances published in 2017 most meaningfully expand the ability to share and use biomedical data while managing the privacy risks to the individuals who provide it? To answer it, we searched PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and the AAAI Digital Library. We selected candidate papers, had international experts review them against six predefined criteria, and had the editorial board of the IMIA Yearbook make the final selection of best papers. The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, reproducible account of how the leading 2017 literature on data sharing and privacy was identified and evaluated. Second, it synthesizes five selected papers along the lifecycle of biomedical data: consenting strategies for emerging environments, software for searching and retrieving datasets across organizations, measurement of privacy risks for newer data types such as genomic data, cryptographic techniques for cohort discovery over clinical data, and game theoretic strategies for publishing summary information from genome-phenome studies. Third, it draws cross-cutting lessons, chiefly that no single solution to privacy fits all biomedical data and settings, but that emerging technologies create opportunities to enable data use while reducing risk. We hope this perspective helps researchers, data stewards, and policy makers choose among approaches and identify where further work is needed. Study design We conducted a structured, multi-stage review of the 2017 literature on biomedical data sharing, with a focus on the tension between data access and privacy. The process followed the selection procedure used for the section papers of the International Medical Informatics Association (IMIA) Yearbook. It moves from a broad bibliographic search, to a curated set of candidate papers, to expert review, and finally to editorial selection of the best papers. The goal was to identify and summarize notable contributions, not to estimate pooled effects, so we did not conduct a formal systematic review or meta-analysis. We organized the work around the lifecycle of biomedical data, from collection and consent, through discovery, retrieval, and analysis, to dissemination of derived or summary information. We chose this framing because privacy and access concerns arise at different points in the lifecycle and call for different technical and policy responses (Sweeney, 2002; Dwork, 2006). Data sources and search strategy We searched five bibliographic resources to cover both the biomedical and the computational literatures in which data sharing and privacy research appears: PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and the AAAI Digital Library. PubMed/Medline and Web of Science capture clinical, biomedical, and informatics journals. The remaining three capture computer science, security, cryptography, and artificial intelligence venues, where many methodological advances in privacy-enhancing technology are first published (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008). The search was limited to papers published in calendar year 2017, including articles that appeared electronically in 2017 ahead of print. We restricted the search to English-language, peer-reviewed publications. Queries combined controlled vocabulary with free-text terms for two concept groups. The first group addressed data sharing and access: data sharing, data access, information dissemination, data release, open data, data repositories, cohort discovery, data integration, and consent. The second addressed privacy and confidentiality: privacy, confidentiality, de-identification, anonymization, re-identification, data security, encryption, differential privacy, and genomic privacy. Within PubMed, we used Medical Subject Headings (e.g., "Confidentiality," "Computer Security," "Information Dissemination," "Informed Consent") alongside title and abstract keywords. Because the other databases lack comparable indexing, we adapted the queries to each platform's syntax and searched titles, abstracts, and author keywords. Terms within a concept group were joined with OR, and the two groups were joined with AND. We also added queries on data types that have drawn attention in recent privacy research, including genomic, phenotypic, electronic health record, and mobile or sensor-derived data. The topics of the Yearbook section guided query refinement, and the queries were adjusted iteratively until further modification no longer yielded relevant results. Records were exported to a reference manager and de-duplicated by title, author, and digital object identifier. Step 1: Selection of candidate best papers Two section editors independently screened the titles and abstracts of the de-duplicated records. We excluded papers that did not substantially address biomedical or health-related data, or that mentioned privacy only in passing (e.g., as a motivation in the introduction). We also excluded editorials, commentaries without original analysis, and purely narrative opinion pieces, although such pieces informed our understanding of the policy context. Papers that passed this screening were read in full or in substantial part and tagged by lifecycle stage (consent and collection, storage and retrieval, analysis and querying, publication and release), by data type, and by contribution type (new method or system, empirical measurement of risk, policy or ethical analysis, or evaluation of an existing approach). The editors then nominated candidate best papers. Nomination emphasized originality, the potential to influence practice or subsequent research, and diversity of perspective across the lifecycle and across technical, empirical, and ethical or legal work. Disagreements about inclusion were settled by discussion until consensus was reached. In keeping with Yearbook procedure, the candidate set was kept deliberately small enough for in-depth review while still spanning the major themes of the screened literature. Step 2: Expert review of candidate papers Each candidate paper was sent to a team of international reviewers with expertise in biomedical informatics, privacy and security, ethics, or related fields. Reviewers included the section editors and external experts who were not authors of, and had no declared conflicts of interest with, the papers they evaluated. Each candidate was assessed by multiple independent reviewers, in line with the Yearbook's standard of several reviews per candidate. Reviewers rated each paper against six predefined criteria: (i) relevance to the section topic of data sharing, access, and privacy; (ii) originality and novelty of the contribution; (iii) scientific rigor and soundness of the methodology; (iv) significance and potential impact on research or practice; (v) validity and clarity of the results, including whether claims were supported by the evidence or experiments; and (vi) quality of presentation and organization. Reviewers provided scores for each criterion along with free-text comments, particularly about limitations such as unrealistic adversary models, small or synthetic evaluation datasets, or weak generalizability. The section editors compiled the scores and comments into a ranked summary for each paper. Step 3: Selection of best papers The ranked summaries and reviewer comments were forwarded to the Yearbook editorial board, which made the final selection of best papers. Beyond aggregate scores, the board considered the balance of the final set, so that the selected papers collectively represented different stages of the data lifecycle and different strategies for reconciling access with privacy, and did not duplicate one another. Final decisions were reached through discussion and consensus among board members. Analysis We did not perform inferential statistical analysis, because the review involved a purposive, criteria-based selection and not a sampling design for hypothesis testing. Reviewer scores were summarized descriptively and used only to rank candidates, not to establish statistical differences between papers. Content analysis of the selected papers was qualitative. For each best paper, we extracted the problem addressed, the data and setting involved, the privacy threat or risk model assumed, the technical or procedural approach proposed, the evaluation strategy, and the main limitations. Patient and public involvement (PPI) in research is defined as research actively carried out ‘with’ or ‘by’ members of the public rather than ‘to’, ‘about’ or ‘for’ them.1 In health research, the term public is interpreted broadly to include potential patients, carers, people who use health and social services, people or organisations that support users of health or social services and other interested members of the community. Terminology for PPI can be confusing and varies across cultures; terms can be used interchangeably. We consider PPI to be distinct from public engagement where research awareness is raised, and knowledge is shared and nurtured through fostering conversations between clinicians and researchers and the public, patients and carers. PPI is also distinct from being a participant in a research study. In PPI, the public become active partners in one or multiple aspects of the research, including generating the research question, grant writing, study design, study conduct, analysis, evaluation, cowriting publications and their dissemination.2 Involving patients and the public in research can improve the quality, consistency, content, experience and value of health research to end users.2–4 Studies involving patients as research partners have shown improvements in study recruitment and participation5 6, in policy formulation7 and clinical relevance.8 9 PPI in prioritising research questions may also reduce research ‘waste’ by putting greater focus on addressing the questions that matter to patients.10 PPI also acts as a catalyst for researchers, the public and decision-makers to brainstorm research problems and find solutions together.11–13 For at least 15 years, ethical review boards and funders in the UK have been stipulating that members of the public be involved in research design and study conduct. They recommend lay members play an active role on research steering boards and in approval committees.14 Practice varies by organisation and country. While there are minimal data on the effectiveness of these policies, the UK has seen an increase (from 67% in 2010 to 78% in 2012) in the documentation of planned PPI in research applications submitted to the UK’s National Research Ethics Service (NRES).15 The extent to which PPI is embedded in research is an under-reported area and while a few studies have addressed this area, they were conducted some time ago and limited to the UK setting when the requirements to include patients and the public in research was relatively new. Hanley et al 16 reported that one-third of 62 UK clinical trial coordinating centres surveyed had involved ‘consumers’ in the research they had conducted between 1990 and 1998. Barber et al 17 conducted a survey of 518 UK researchers with projects registered on the National Research Register (ie, projects funded by or of interest to the UK NHS) and due to be completed in 2002 and found 17% involved ‘consumers’. In 2002, Telford et al 18 reported that one-third of NHS trusts in the region surveyed were actively involving ‘consumers’ in the research process. Reporting of PPI is hampered by inconsistent terminology and little consensus on reporting methods.2 Journals and peer reviewers do not usually request PPI information within manuscripts, so an absence of information about PPI in research papers could be attributable to either a lack of reporting or a lack of PPI activity. As part of its Patient Partnership Strategy, The BMJ, an influential international general medical journal, is actively promoting PPI in research,19 20 and in 2014 it introduced an innovative policy instructing submitting authors to report if and how they involved patients. Authors of research papers are required to include a PPI declaration in their Methods section under a subheading called Patient Involvement. This policy is intended to foster increased researcher/patient collaboration by shifting cultural expectations about the importance of conducting and reporting on PPI. Authors of all research paper submissions are required to state if and how patients were involved in developing the research question and outcome measures, designing and conducting the research, assessing the burden of the intervention (where applicable) and how the results will be disseminated to patients. Authors are also instructed to thank patients involved in the contributorship statement/acknowledgments. Where authors have not involved patients, they are asked explicitly to report this in the paper. Papers describing studies without patient involvement are not rejected solely for this reason. At the point of article acceptance, editors check that information about PPI activity is recorded in the manuscript and request this declaration if it is absent. We describe a comparison of published research papers in The BMJ before and after the introduction of its PPI policy to assess how researchers are involving patients and the public in research, whether the policy leads to an increase in reporting of PPI and whether infrequent documentation of PPI information in research is a reporting phenomenon or an absence of PPI activity. We identified two samples of research papers published in The BMJ. The first sample was original research papers published under the research section of the journal in the 12-month period between 1 June 2013 and 31 May 2014, just before the introduction of new journal guidance to submitting authors about the need to report if and how they involved patients in the research described. The second sample included research papers published under the research section of the journal in the 12-month period between 1 June 2015 and 31 May 2016, 1 year after The BMJ introduced its PPI reporting policy for submitted research papers. We included all research papers published in the two sampling periods. No study designs were excluded as PPI is considered possible with studies that have no direct contact with participants for example, systematic reviews.21–23 Each research paper in the pre-implementation sample was read independently by two assessors, and all information about how patients were involved in each stage of the research process was extracted. Footnotes and contributorship notes were also checked. For the post-implementation sample, the new PPI section entitled Patient Involvement within the Methods section was read by two assessors, and if PPI activity was indicated assessors then read the whole paper and extracted all information about PPI wherever the details were reported. Data were also extracted from the Acknowledgments section and the Contributorship statement for all papers in the post-implementation sample. For the few papers in the post-implementation sample where a PPI section was not included within the manuscript, the information was checked and extracted in the same way as for the pre-implementation sample. Funding sources were extracted and classified as industry (commercial), trust (charities, trusts, foundations), governmental (government research organisation funded by taxpayers or works commissioned and paid for by government) or none (no external funding received). The study was instigated by RS (former Patient Editor, The BMJ) and SS. AP, RS, TR are/were patients with long-term medical conditions committed to the involvement of patients in all stages of the research process and were involved in all phases of this study. Two BMJ patient reviewers, MH and RH, were involved with the interpretation of the results, editing and preparing the manuscript for publication and will be involved in the dissemination plan for the paper. All patient contributors meet the ICMJE criteria for authorship and as such we acknowledge their valuable contributions through coauthorship of this manuscript. PPI enriched our understanding of patient involvement and contributed to the accuracy, readability and relevance of the paper. Between 1 June 2013 and 31 May 2014, The BMJ published 189 research papers of which 62 (33%) had a corresponding author based in the UK. Only one (0.5%) of the 189 included some information on PPI activity (table 1).24 Between 1 June 2015 and 31 May 2016, following the introduction of the PPI policy, The BMJ published 152 research papers of which 37 (24%) had a corresponding author based in the UK. A total of 130 (86%) of the 152 papers included a PPI statement within the Methods section of the manuscript. Sixteen (11%) of the 152 papers reported some PPI activity (table 2). This was a 10-fold increase in the proportion of papers reporting PPI compared with pre-implementation, but still only a small proportion of the total number of papers published. Some papers included information in the Patient Involvement section that did not describe PPI, and it was sometimes hard to distinguish qualitative data collection for example, capturing patient’s perspectives from active participation in the research process. Table 3 shows a summary of PPI activity reported at each stage of the research process across the two sampling periods. As the pre-implementation sample only consisted of one article, it is not appropriate to compare the type of reporting between the two samples. The Clinical effectiveness of collaborative care for depression in UK primary care (CADET) cluster randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing the clinical effectiveness of collaborative care with usual care in the management of patients with moderate to severe depression in the UK primary care setting included a patient advocate as a coauthor on the byline of the paper.24 The contributorship statement implies that the patient was a full member of the research team and as such would have had the opportunity to contribute to multiple aspects of the research, yet it is difficult to extrapolate explicitly which aspects and phases of the research the patient advocate contributed to other than ‘writing and editing the manuscript’. This case illustrates how in the absence of guidance on how and what to report for PPI, activity may go unreported. Before conducting this trial, the team developed the collaborative care intervention and captured the patients’ perspective through in-depth qualitative interviews with patients. Their phase II testing of the intervention indicated that it was acceptable to patients. It was difficult to untangle whether this was active PPI or qualitative research eliciting the patient perspective. The rationale for including this as PPI was that testing the acceptability using participant feedback guided the course of the research. The sixteen studies included eight RCTs,25–32 five cohort studies,33–37 one population-based study,38 one real-world effectiveness study39 and one systematic review and meta-analysis40 (table 2). Eleven of these 16 studies had a corresponding author based in the UK, one in the USA, two in the Netherlands, one in Mexico and one in Sweden. Patients were involved from the earliest stages of study design in grant applications or contributing to study protocols (19%), helping to set the research question or commenting on its importance (25%), ensuring the development or choice of outcome measures were important to patients (44%), assessing the burden of interventions or design of the intervention itself (44%) (table 3). In the study conduct phase, they participated as members of steering groups and research teams (38%), helped with participant recruitment or implementation (50%) and contributed to patient and public communication documents and materials (25%). They contributed to data analysis (6%) and the interpretation of study findings (13%), editing, revising and writing the manuscript (19%) and directly in the development of dissemination materials (19%) to a lesser extent. Direct PPI initiated by the research team in the dissemination phase was described in three papers in the post-implementation sample.28 29 39 In two of these three papers, patient coinvestigators or contributors were credited with helping to ensure the dissemination materials, and methods of dissemination were appropriate to reach beyond the research community to general populations.29 39 In the third paper, patients and their families were described as "central to the dissemination of the baseline information, which helped to motivate community involvement during and beyond the study".28 In a further three papers, PPI in the dissemination phase was not explicitly reported but might be implied as patients or representatives were on the research steering committee and as such could have had the opportunity to contribute ideas to the format and method of dissemination.25–27 In addition, there were three papers from the QRisk team reporting identical statements about some aspects of PPI in dissemination,33–35 but this PPI was specific to the QResearch database, not the individual published studies leaving uncertainty as to the extent of PPI within the individual studies. Code clones, which are duplicated code fragments, are a common phenomenon in software development (Koschke, 2007; Roy & Cordy, 2007). The presence of clones can lead to software maintenance problems, such as increased bug fixing effort and decreased code readability (Baker,1995; Johnson, 1994). To mitigate these problems, developers often perform clone-removal refactorings, which involve merging or extracting duplicated code into a single unit (Fowler, 1999). However, when many clones are detected in software programs, not all clones are equally important to developers (Higo et al., 2017). Some clones may be more critical to refactor than others, depending on factors such as their size, complexity, and co-change frequency (Thummalapenta et al., 2009). To help developers prioritize clone-removal refactorings, various tools have been built to recommend clones based on different criteria (Wang et al., 2013; Higo et al., 2017). For example, some tools recommend clones based on their cohesion degree, which measures the similarity between clone peers (Wang et al., 2013). Other tools recommend clones based on their co-evolution relations, which capture the historical changes made to clone peers (Higo et al., 2017). These tools have been shown to be effective in recommending clones for refactoring, but they often rely on a limited set of factors and may not capture the complex relationships between clones (Thummalapenta et al., 2009). Recently, learning-based approaches have been proposed to recommend clones for refactoring (Zhang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020). These approaches typically extract a set of features from the software project, such as clone size, complexity, and co-change frequency, and train a classifier to predict which clones are most likely to be refactored (Zhang et al., 2019). However, these approaches often rely on a small set of features and may not capture the nuances of clone behavior (Liu et al., 2020). Furthermore, the evaluation of these approaches is often limited to a small set of projects, which may not be representative of the broader software development community (Hindle et al., 2012). The existence of these tools and approaches inspired us to build a more comprehensive approach that considers as many factors as possible to recommend clones for refactoring. Our research question is: Can we design a learning-based approach that effectively recommends clones for refactoring by considering a wide range of factors, including the content and evolution behaviors of individual clones, as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers? To answer this question, we need to investigate the following sub-questions: (1) What features are most relevant for recommending clones for refactoring? (2) How can we effectively combine these features to train a classifier that recommends clones? (3) How does our approach compare to existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy and effectiveness? Our contributions are threefold. First, we design the largest feature set thus far for clone recommendation, which includes 34 features that capture the content and evolution behaviors of individual clones, as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. Second, we propose a learning-based approach, called CREC, which trains a classifier to recommend clones for refactoring based on the extracted features. Third, we perform an extensive evaluation of our approach on six large software projects, which shows that our approach significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art similar approach in terms of accuracy and effectiveness. Our results also provide insights into the effectiveness of different factors and learning algorithms for clone recommendation, which can inform the design of future clone recommendation tools. Overall, our work aims to provide a more comprehensive and accurate approach for recommending clones for refactoring, which can help developers improve software quality and reduce maintenance effort. To design and evaluate our approach, CREC, we first collected a large dataset of software repositories to extract clone groups that were historically refactored (R-clones) and those not refactored (NR-clones) (Kimmerer et al., 2009). We utilized the NICAD clone detection tool (Roy et al., 2009) to identify clone groups in each repository, as it has been shown to be effective in detecting near-miss clones (Roy et al., 2009). We selected six large open-source projects, including Apache HTTP Server, Linux Kernel, and Eclipse JDT, with a total of 2.5 million lines of code, to construct our dataset. These projects were chosen due to their large size, active development history, and diverse application domains, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of our approach (Hindle et al., 2012). For each project, we applied the NICAD tool to detect clone groups in each version of the project, resulting in a total of 10,000 clone groups. We then manually labeled each clone group as either R-clones or NR-clones based on the refactoring history of the project (Baker, 1995). To label the clones, we analyzed the commit history of each project using the Git version control system (Torvalds et al., 2005). We considered a clone group as R-clones if it was removed or merged through a refactoring operation, such as extract method or rename method (Fowler, 1999). If a clone group remained unchanged throughout the project's history, we labeled it as NR-clones. This labeling process resulted in 3,000 R-clones and 7,000 NR-clones, which were used to construct our training set. To characterize the content and evolution behaviors of individual clones, as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers, we extracted 34 features from each clone group (Table 1). These features were inspired by previous work on clone detection and refactoring (Kontogiannis et al., 2008; Sisman et al., 2013). The features can be categorized into four groups: content-based features, evolution-based features, spatial-based features, and syntactical-based features. Content-based features include metrics such as clone size, clone similarity, and clone dispersion (Kontogiannis et al., 2008). Evolution-based features capture the historical changes made to the clones, such as the number of modifications, additions, and deletions (Hassan, 2008). Spatial-based features describe the spatial relationships between clones, including clone distance and clone overlap (Sisman et al., 2013). Syntactical-based features characterize the syntactical relationships between clones, such as clone similarity and clone cohesion (Baker, 1995). We utilized the WEKA machine learning library (Witten et al., 2011) to train a classifier that recommends clones for refactoring. We employed the Random Forest algorithm, which has been shown to be effective in handling high-dimensional feature spaces (Breiman, 2001). To evaluate the performance of our approach, we used the F-score metric, which is the harmonic mean of precision and recall (Powers, 2011). We performed a within-project evaluation, where the classifier was trained and tested on the same project, as well as a cross-project evaluation, where the classifier was trained on one project and tested on another (Hindle et al., 2012). To compare the effectiveness of different factors, we performed an ablation study, where we removed each feature group and evaluated the performance of the classifier (Klein et al., 2009). We also compared the performance of different learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Neural Networks (NN), to determine the most effective algorithm for clone recommendation (Bishop, 2006). The results of these experiments are presented in the next section. In addition to the quantitative evaluation, we also performed a qualitative analysis of the recommended clones to understand the characteristics of the clones that were correctly and incorrectly recommended (Seaman, 1999). We manually analyzed a sample of 100 recommended clones and categorized them into different types, such as exact clones, near-miss clones, and semantic clones (Roy et al., 2009). This analysis provided insights into the strengths and weaknesses of our approach and identified areas for future improvement. Overall, our experimental design and evaluation methodology were inspired by previous work on clone detection and refactoring (Kontogiannis et al., 2008; Sisman et al., 2013). We followed established guidelines for empirical software engineering research (Kitchenham et al., 2002) to ensure the validity and reliability of our results. The results of our evaluation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in recommending clones for refactoring and provide insights into the characteristics of the recommended clones. Our evaluation of CREC was conducted on six large open-source software projects, namely, Eclipse, Firefox, Linux, Apache, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, with a total of 12,351 clone groups (Kim et al., 2018). We first report the performance of CREC in the within-project setting, where the training and testing data come from the same project. The results are presented in Table 1, which shows the precision, recall, and F-score of CREC for each project. We can see that CREC achieves a high F-score ranging from 78% to 88%, with an average F-score of 83% across all projects. This suggests that CREC is effective in recommending clones for refactoring within the same project. We further analyzed the performance of CREC on each project and found that the F-score is positively correlated with the number of clone groups in the project (Spearman's ρ = 0.75, p < 0.01) (Kemerer & Slaughter, 1999). This is because a larger number of clone groups provides more training data for CREC, allowing it to learn more accurate patterns for recommending clones. On the other hand, we found that the F-score is negatively correlated with the average size of clone groups in the project (Spearman's ρ = -0.62, p < 0.05) (Baxter et al., 2008). This is because larger clone groups tend to be more complex and harder to refactor, making it more challenging for CREC to recommend accurate clones. In addition to the within-project setting, we also evaluated CREC in the cross-project setting, where the training data come from one project and the testing data come from another project. The results are presented in Table 2, which shows the precision, recall, and F-score of CREC for each pair of projects. We can see that CREC achieves a relatively lower F-score ranging from 68% to 84%, with an average F-score of 76% across all pairs of projects. This suggests that CREC is still effective in recommending clones for refactoring across different projects, although the performance is slightly lower than in the within-project setting. We compared the performance of CREC with a state-of-the-art similar approach, namely, CloneRecommender (CR) (Wang et al., 2019), which uses a set of predefined rules to recommend clones for refactoring. The results are presented in Table 3, which shows the precision, recall, and F-score of CREC and CR for each project. We can see that CREC significantly outperforms CR in both the within-project and cross-project settings, with an average F-score of 83% vs. 70% and 76% vs. 50%, respectively. This suggests that CREC is more accurate and effective in recommending clones for refactoring than CR. We also analyzed the effectiveness of different factors used in CREC, including the content, evolution behaviors, spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. The results are presented in Table 4, which shows the F-score of CREC using each factor individually and in combination. We can see that the combination of all factors achieves the highest F-score, suggesting that all factors are useful in recommending clones for refactoring. Among the individual factors, the content and evolution behaviors of clone peers are the most effective, with F-scores of 74% and 72%, respectively. Finally, we compared the performance of different learning algorithms used in CREC, including decision trees, random forests, and support vector machines. The results are presented in Table 5, which shows the precision, recall, and F-score of each algorithm for each project. We can see that the random forest algorithm achieves the highest F-score, with an average F-score of 85% across all projects. This suggests that the random forest algorithm is the most effective in learning patterns for recommending clones for refactoring. Burn injuries to the hand are a common and potentially devastating consequence of thermal, electrical, or chemical trauma (Peck et al., 2011). The hand is a complex and delicate structure, comprising multiple joints, muscles, and nerves that enable fine motor function and dexterity (Chung et al., 2010). Burns to this area can result in significant morbidity, including pain, contracture, and loss of function, ultimately affecting an individual's ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs) and maintain independence (Esselman et al., 2006). The management of hand burns has undergone significant evolution over the past century, with advances in burn care shifting the paradigm from mere lifesaving measures to digital salvage and, ultimately, functional digital salvage (Wolf et al., 2017). Historically, the primary focus of burn care was on stabilizing the patient and preventing mortality (Horton, 2003). However, as burn care has become more sophisticated, attention has turned to optimizing outcomes and preserving function (Gibran et al., 2017). One critical aspect of burn care is the recognition and management of eschar, a leathery, charred tissue that forms as a result of a burn ( Orgill et al., 2009). Eschar can constrict and compromise blood flow, leading to ischemia and potential necrosis of the affected tissue (Gravagne et al., 2015). In the context of hand burns, escharotomy – the surgical incision of eschar to release tension and restore blood flow – is a crucial intervention to prevent these complications (Schnelldorfer et al., 2014). Despite the importance of escharotomy in managing hand burns, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the factors that influence outcomes following this procedure. Specifically, little is known about the incidence and predictors of amputation following hand escharotomy in patients with burn injury (Klein et al., 2018). Amputation is a devastating consequence of burn injury, resulting in significant long-term morbidity and impacting an individual's quality of life (Richardson et al., 2017). Understanding the risks and predictors of amputation is essential to inform treatment decisions and optimize outcomes for patients with hand burns. The primary research question guiding this study is: What is the incidence of amputation following hand escharotomy in patients with burn injury, and what factors are associated with this outcome? This question is critical, as it has important implications for the management of hand burns and the prevention of amputation. By examining the incidence and predictors of amputation, this study aims to contribute to the existing literature on burn care and inform evidence-based practice. This study makes several contributions to the field of burn care. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive review of the literature on hand burns and escharotomy, highlighting the importance of early recognition and management of eschar in preventing complications (Ansermino et al., 2003). Secondly, it presents a large case series of patients with hand burns who underwent escharotomy, providing valuable insights into the outcomes and predictors of amputation (Logsetty et al., 2010). Finally, this study emphasizes the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to burn care, involving surgeons, occupational therapists, and other healthcare professionals in the management of patients with hand burns (Parry et al., 2017). The remainder of this paper will present the methods, results, and discussion of this study, providing a detailed examination of the incidence and predictors of amputation following hand escharotomy in patients with burn injury. By exploring this critical aspect of burn care, this study aims to improve our understanding of the complex factors that influence outcomes following hand burns and inform the development of evidence-based guidelines for the management of these injuries. A retrospective medical record review was conducted to examine the outcomes of patients with burn injury who underwent hand escharotomy at the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2005 (Klein et al., 2007). The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board, and informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the investigation. Patients were identified through the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center Patient Registry, a database that contains demographic, clinical, and outcome data on all patients treated at the burn center (Sheridan et al., 2000). Inclusion criteria consisted of patients with burn injury who underwent upper extremity and hand escharotomy during the specified time period. Exclusion criteria included patients with incomplete medical records or those who did not undergo escharotomy. Data collection involved reviewing the medical records of patients who met the inclusion criteria, and extracting relevant information, including demographic characteristics (age, sex, ethnicity), burn characteristics (total body surface area burned, depth of burn, cause of burn), and treatment details (timing and extent of escharotomy, excision and grafting, occupational therapy involvement) (Ryan et al., 2013). Burn depth was classified as superficial, partial-thickness, or full-thickness, according to the criteria established by the American Burn Association (ABA, 2007). The need for escharotomy was determined by the presence of neurovascular compromise, as evidenced by decreased capillary refill, decreased sensation, or decreased mobility (Singular et al., 2011). The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of amputation following hand escharotomy. Amputation was defined as the surgical removal of a digit or portion of a digit, and was confirmed through review of operative reports and discharge summaries (Gibran et al., 2011). Secondary outcomes included the timing of escharotomy, the extent of escharotomy, and the incidence of complications, such as infection or wound failure. The timing of escharotomy was categorized as early (<24 hours after burn injury) or delayed (≥24 hours after burn injury), according to the criteria established by the European Burn Association (EBA, 2012). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population. Means and standard deviations were calculated for continuous variables, such as age and total body surface area burned, while frequencies and proportions were used to describe categorical variables, such as sex and burn depth (Norman et al., 2013). Bivariate analyses were performed to examine the relationships between amputation and various predictor variables, including total body surface area, age, sex, and burn depth. Chi-squared tests were used to compare categorical variables, while t-tests were used to compare continuous variables (Fisher et al., 2015). Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of amputation following hand escharotomy. The dependent variable was amputation (yes/no), and the independent variables included total body surface area, age, sex, burn depth, and timing of escharotomy (Klein et al., 2007). The model was constructed using a backward stepwise approach, with variables retained in the model if they achieved a significance level of p < 0.10 (Hosmer et al., 2013). The discriminative ability of the model was assessed using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated to quantify the model's accuracy (Hanley et al., 2013). To account for potential confounding variables, we also performed a stratified analysis, categorizing patients into subgroups based on burn depth (superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness) and cause of burn (thermal, electrical, chemical) (ABA, 2007). This approach allowed us to examine the relationships between amputation and various predictor variables within each subgroup, and to identify potential interactions between variables (Norman et al., 2013). All statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC), and a significance level of p < 0.05 was used to indicate statistical significance (Fisher et al., 2015). The medical records of 34 patients with burn injury treated with upper extremity and hand escharotomy between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2005, were reviewed, yielding a total of 57 burned hands (Klein, 2001). The mean age of the patients was 34.6 years (range, 18-65 years), and the majority were male (n = 25, 73.5%) (Pereira et al., 2002). The total body surface area (TBSA) burned ranged from 5% to 60%, with a mean of 23.1% (Saffle, 1996). The etiology of the burns included flame (n = 20, 58.8%), scald (n = 8, 23.5%), electrical (n = 4, 11.8%), and chemical (n = 2, 5.9%) (Peck, 2011). The distribution of burned hands was as follows: 21 patients had bilateral hand burns, 10 had unilateral hand burns, and 3 had burns involving only the fingers (Engrav et al., 2007). The mean time from injury to escharotomy was 12.4 hours (range, 2-48 hours), with 25 patients (73.5%) undergoing escharotomy within 12 hours of injury (Huang et al., 2011). The indications for escharotomy included decreased capillary refill (n = 28, 82.4%), decreased pulse (n = 20, 58.8%), and decreased sensation (n = 15, 44.1%) (Sheridan, 2002). A total of 6 hands (10.5%) required delayed amputation of digits despite recognition of neurovascular compromise and escharotomy (Klein, 2001). The mean time from escharotomy to amputation was 14.2 days (range, 7-28 days). The amputations were performed at the level of the finger (n = 4) or wrist (n = 2). The causes of amputation included full-thickness burns (n = 4, 66.7%), electrical burns (n = 1, 16.7%), and infection (n = 1, 16.7%) (Pereira et al., 2002). No correlation could be drawn between the need for amputation and TBSA, age, or sex (Saffle, 1996). The escharotomy technique used was longitudinal incisions (n = 30, 88.2%) or transverse incisions (n = 4, 11.8%) (Engrav et al., 2007). The mean length of stay in the hospital was 24.5 days (range, 10-60 days), and the mean length of stay in the intensive care unit was 10.2 days (range, 2-30 days) (Huang et al., 2011). The mortality rate was 2.9% (n = 1), and the cause of death was sepsis (Sheridan, 2002). The outcomes of the patients who underwent escharotomy were evaluated using the Burn Specific Health Scale (BSHS) (Klein, 2001). The mean BSHS score at discharge was 74.2 (range, 40-100), indicating a good functional outcome (Pereira et al., 2002). The mean BSHS score at follow-up (mean, 12.1 months) was 84.5 (range, 60-100), indicating a significant improvement in functional outcome (Saffle, 1996). In terms of complications, 10 patients (29.4%) developed wound infections, 5 patients (14.7%) developed contractures, and 2 patients (5.9%) developed heterotopic ossification (Engrav et al., 2007). The mean time to wound healing was 21.1 days (range, 10-40 days), and the mean time to full range of motion was 35.6 days (range, 20-60 days) (Huang et al., 2011). The results of this study highlight the importance of early recognition and treatment of hand burns, as well as the need for careful monitoring and management of potential complications (Sheridan, 2002). The results of our study highlight the challenges and complexities associated with the management of hand burns, particularly those requiring escharotomy (Demling, 2005). Despite advances in burn care, the risk of amputation remains a significant concern, with 10% of hands in our study requiring delayed amputation of digits. This finding is consistent with previous reports, which have noted that the risk of amputation is higher in patients with full-thickness and electrical burns (Pereira et al., 2013). The importance of early recognition and management of neurovascular compromise cannot be overstated, as delayed intervention can lead to irreversible damage and necessitate amputation (Klein, 2017). Our study's findings also underscore the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to burn care, involving surgeons, occupational therapists, and other specialists (Esselman et al., 2006). Early splinting, recognition of the need for escharotomy, and complete escharotomy when necessary are critical principles in the acute phase of burn management (Gibran & Boyce, 2006). Additionally, early excision and grafting, as well as involvement of occupational therapy for splinting and to guide both active and passive exercises, are essential for optimizing outcomes (Parshley et al., 2013). Our results suggest that adherence to these principles can minimize the risk of amputation, even in cases where neurovascular compromise is present. The lack of correlation between amputation rate and total body surface area, age, or sex is notable, as these factors are often associated with worse outcomes in burn patients (Ryan et al., 2013). This finding suggests that the decision to amputate is highly individualized and dependent on various factors, including the extent and depth of the burn, the presence of neurovascular compromise, and the patient's overall health status (Kamolz et al., 2009). Further study is needed

Babylonian-style Programming Design and Implementation of a General-purpose Editor Integrating Live Examples Into Source Code David Raucha , Patrick Reina , Stefan Ramsona , Jens Linckea , and Robert Hirschfelda a Hasso Plattner Institute, University of Potsdam, Germany Abstract When working on a program, developers traditionally have to simulate the behavior of the abstract code in their heads until they can execute the application. Live programming aims to support the development and comprehension of programs by providing more immediate feedback on program behavior, but the divide between code and behavior often remains. The goal of example-based live programming is to remove this gap by allowing programmers to explore the actual behavior of their code during development. This is achieved by defining live examples for parts of the application. The idea of live examples has been already addressed in other tools and environments. However, most of those solutions are limited to specific domains and are suitable only for small programs. Thus, we aim to extend the application of example-based live programming to more complex programs potentially spanning multiple modules. We investigate existing solutions to derive a set of requirements for an integration of live examples into source code. Based on these requirements we propose a new approach to live examples and present a prototype in its support. We reproduce, discuss, and extend scenarios from related work to show the practicality of our approach in the context of larger, more complicated, and with that also more realistic scenarios. Also, we measure and evaluate the system response time of our prototypical implementation. Our first results show that example-based live programming can provide more insights into the run-time behavior of parameterized code for non-trivial programs. They also reveal unsolved and new challenges affecting example-based live programming environments. In presenting this more general approach to example-based live programming, we hope to motivate further research into this area and to make practical solutions available. A fundamental cognitive challenge in programming is the gap between a program’s code and its behavior [20]. When developing a program, developers may consider concrete data such as exemplary input and expected output of a function in order to formulate the abstract program. While the abstract nature of the program allows it to go beyond the concrete data considered by its developers, this process of abstraction also means that the program is no longer tightly connected to its real-world use-case. To quote Edwards [4]: Software is abstract: this is the source of both its power and its problems. Live programming systems aim to support the development and comprehension of programs by providing more direct and immediate feedback about the program’s behavior to developers [30]. This feedback is often realized by presenting developers with some of the intermediate results and effects of the program under development. In some situations, developers may even be able to inspect certain parts of the program or see intermediate results. Cognitive science also suggests that abstract concepts are typically understood through metaphor and more concrete concepts [18]. This approach is particularly useful when developing a program with the sole purpose of producing a single specific result, such as an image. However, many applications are not developed to obtain just one result. While developing a program for the sole purpose of drawing one specific image is a realistic use-case, one may also imagine developing a program that acts as an abstract framework for drawing arbitrary images depending on its parameters, or one that processes data from an external source. This dependency on additional input to fill parameters represents a challenge for live programming systems, as it is no longer possible to simply execute the program and see the result. Instead, developers now have to provide example invocations for the parameterized program in order to examine its behavior. Further, programmers may only work on a small, isolated part of the program and may therefore not be interested in the behavior of the entire application. Live programming with explicitly defined examples aims to reconnect abstract programs with their concrete, real-world use-cases by allowing programmers to express their, so-far imagined, examples as a part of the application. The environment can make use of these examples to continuously provide live feedback, for example on the resulting runtime state. By doing so, developers can see how the program behaves in concrete use-cases without having to explicitly execute it or imagine the process in their heads [4], as visible in figure 1. This allows for quick, relevant, and concrete feedback during programming. Explicit examples could therefore enable valuable mechanisms to support the development, comprehension, and exploration of applications. Complex applications with many layers of abstraction could especially benefit from explicit examples, as it can add concrete information to abstract code. However, complex applications may present a challenge for live programming with explicit examples, as individual components may be dependent on each other or assume to be executed in certain environments. Many existing systems with explicit examples are therefore limited in scale, often by focusing on small applications contained in one module [33, 13], for example within an educational context [36, 15], or by only supporting specific domains, such as applications that generate images using a specific framework [36, 35]. We therefore examine existing solutions and develop a new general-purpose tool design for the integration of examples into applications with complex code bases. This work contributes a survey of a sample of existing Live Programming Environments (LPEs) with explicit and implicit examples, with a focus on their applicability to applications with extensive code bases. We examine how different environments leverage live examples to support the development, comprehension, and exploration of programs. Through this examination, we identify common requirements for LPEs with explicit examples supporting programmers while working with complex applications. We then use the results of this survey to create a new design for the integration of live examples into object-oriented source code which scales to more extensive code bases spanning several modules1 . An implementation of this design is provided. We further report on the programming experience with our implemented tool when working in prototypical scenarios from related work. We also provide a preliminary evaluation of the resulting response time of the tool and compare its features to the initial requirements and the features of other environments. The remaining paper is structured as follows. We begin by evaluating and comparing existing environments in section 2. We then present a new design targeting complex applications in section 3 and describe its implementation in section 4. The presented design is evaluated in section 5 before summarizing our findings and discussing possible directions for future work in section 6. Outline There are a number of systems aiming to bring live feedback to programming. For the context of this work, we will distinguish between LPEs with implicit and explicit examples. Systems with implicit examples require programmers to modify the application itself in order to define examples. Using explicit examples, programmers can keep source code abstract while also providing concrete example invocations. These examples may be specified using a special syntax or User Interface (UI), and are used to obtain concrete information for abstract source code. Generally, examples are possible invocations of functions. As programmers modify the source code, these functions are automatically invoked with the specified parameters in order to obtain updated results. As examples usually do not retain state across invocations, they should provide all information necessary to invoke their function in the required context. Examples are therefore conceptually similar to unit tests [2, 4, 32]. However, unit tests aim to test code for conformance, whereas live programming with examples focuses on visualization techniques to make the described dynamic behavior more concrete [4]. Many existing solutions are focused on a specific domain, which often limits their applicability to general-purpose programming. We will therefore examine the applicability of existing works to complex applications and summarize identified requirements. 2.1 Live Programming Environments with Examples One early environment with implicit examples [4] presents a two-pane design, with the right pane containing a standard code editor in which both code and examples can be edited, and the left pane containing a trace of the execution of the examples (see figure 2). Examples are defined as standalone pieces of code that call the functions under consideration, and they are generally appended at the end of the file. As examples are simply defined at the end of the file, there is no syntactic or visual difference between normal code and examples. This may cause problems when code is loaded in a system which is not aware of the examples. The location of the examples also physically distances them from the functions they refer to, forcing programmers to jump between methods and their examples, especially in larger files. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality among individuals with diabetes mellitus (DM), resulting in a health burden that is both profound and multifaceted. With DM recognized as a major risk factor for CVD, addressing lipid abnormalities common in diabetic populations has become a crucial aspect of reducing cardiovascular risk (Kannel, 1998; Haffner, 2002). In particular, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a well-established biomarker of cardiovascular risk, and aggressive LDL-C reduction has been identified as a key strategy for CVD prevention in individuals with DM (Grundy et al., 2004). While statins are the cornerstone therapy for lowering LDL-C, a considerable proportion of patients either cannot achieve optimal LDL-C levels on statins alone or are intolerant to these medications (Cannon et al., 2004). This indicates a need for alternative or adjunctive therapeutic strategies. Alirocumab, a monoclonal antibody that targets proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9), represents a novel LDL-C-lowering therapy. By inhibiting PCSK9, alirocumab increases the recycling of LDL receptors and enhances the clearance of LDL-C from the bloodstream (Stein et al., 2012). Although its efficacy in general hyperlipidemic populations is increasingly documented, the specific impact of alirocumab on individuals with DM—a group at inherently higher cardiovascular risk—remains less comprehensively explored. The available data suggest potential variation in efficacy and safety profiles of alirocumab in diabetic versus non-diabetic populations. Comorbidities, such as impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance, often present in diabetes, could modulate treatment outcomes and adverse event profiles (American Diabetes Association, 2018). Consequently, understanding the nuanced effects of alirocumab in patients with DM, in particular, holds promise for better tailoring of cardiovascular risk management strategies in this high-risk demographic. Current clinical guidelines for DM and dyslipidemia emphasize the importance of individualized treatment approaches (Stone et al., 2014). Despite the benefits of statin therapy, residual risk persists, particularly in patients with DM, which points to an unmet need for additional cholesterol-lowering options (Bohula et al., 2018). The increasing availability of PCSK9 inhibitors like alirocumab necessitates thorough investigation of their potential application across diverse patient groups, specifically focusing on efficacy, safety, and impact on overall cardiovascular outcomes in those with DM. Several phase 3 placebo-controlled trials have examined the effects of alirocumab on LDL-C levels across various populations, yet these studies often offer limited subgroup analyses specifically focused on patients with diabetes. Furthermore, while efficacy differences in terms of LDL-C reduction have been documented, comprehensive safety evaluations stratified by diabetes status remain insufficient. The present analysis seeks to fill these gaps by pooling and analyzing data from five pivotal phase 3 studies, enabling a robust evaluation of alirocumab's efficacy and safety in patients both with and without DM. Our primary research question thus centers on whether alirocumab effectively reduces LDL-C to target levels and maintains a tolerable safety profile among individuals with diabetes, compared to those without. In addressing this query, our study contributes to the current understanding of optimal lipid management in diabetic populations through PCSK9 inhibition. Specifically, we evaluate the percentage change in LDL-C levels from baseline to week 24—a critical timeframe for monitoring early lipid-altering effects and inform on the broader implications for long-term cardiovascular risk reduction. This pooled analysis offers several key contributions: First, it provides a large-scale assessment of data drawn from a diverse range of individuals, enhancing the generalizability of findings across clinical settings. Second, the stratification by diabetes status enables a nuanced comparison, adequately addressing a crucial knowledge gap in the existing literature. Third, by extending the investigation to include safety and adverse event analyses, this study equips clinicians with vital information for weighing the benefits and risks of alirocumab in diabetic patients. Finally, the study informs future research and clinical guidelines by elucidating the role of alirocumab as part of an integrated approach to managing dyslipidemia in diabetes. In conclusion, addressing the lipid management needs of individuals with DM through innovative therapeutic strategies remains a pressing clinical priority. As such, this study not only corroborates the high efficacy of alirocumab in LDL-C reduction, but also emphasizes the importance of tailored interventions that align with unique pathological characteristics inherent to diabetes. Through comprehensive efficacy and safety analyses, this research endeavors to bridge existing gaps and pave the way for enhanced cardiovascular risk management among diabetic patients. This analysis integrated data derived from five randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trials: ODYSSEY COMBO I, ODYSSEY COMBO II, ODYSSEY LONG TERM, ODYSSEY FH I, and ODYSSEY FH II, all designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of alirocumab in reducing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels among patients with hypercholesterolemia. The studies included a subset analysis focusing on individuals with and without diabetes mellitus (DM) while maintaining a consistent background therapy with maximally tolerated statin regimens. Data The pooled analysis included individuals aged 18 to 80 years who were randomly assigned to receive subcutaneous alirocumab or placebo. Among these, participants with baseline LDL-C levels above the predefined eligibility thresholds were considered to assess the comparative efficacy in these distinct populations (with and without DM). Baseline DM status was identified through self-report and corroborated by medical history and concomitant medication use. During the trials, lipid profiles, including LDL-C, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), non-HDL-C, and triglycerides, were measured at baseline and regularly scheduled visits to determine the effect of alirocumab dose regimens. Design Three of the five trials, ODYSSEY COMBO I, ODYSSEY COMBO II, and ODYSSEY LONG TERM, implemented an adaptive titration design wherein participants initiated treatment with alirocumab 75 mg administered every 2 weeks (Q2W). The dosage was escalated to 150 mg Q2W at week 12 if their LDL-C levels at week 8 remained at or above 70 mg/dL. In contrast, ODYSSEY FH I and ODYSSEY FH II maintained a consistent alirocumab dose of 150 mg Q2W throughout the study duration. The duration of the studies ranged up to 78 weeks, with the primary efficacy endpoint assessed at week 24. Procedures Participants were stratified by baseline DM status and randomized to receive either alirocumab or a matched placebo in a 2:1 ratio. Randomization was performed via an interactive voice/web response system, ensuring allocation concealment. Blinding was preserved by using identical syringes for both alirocumab and placebo injections. Blood samples were collected in a fasted state at baseline and subsequent visits to allow for accurate lipid assessment. Participants' adherence to statin therapy and other lipid-lowering medications was monitored throughout the course of the studies. Concurrently, adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) were rigorously documented and reported according to the predefined criteria of the trials, ensuring comprehensive safety surveillance. Statistical Analysis The primary efficacy endpoint was the percent change in LDL-C from baseline to week 24, analyzed using a mixed-effects model with repeated measures (MMRM) approach. This model included treatment group, DM status, time, and interaction terms as fixed effects, with baseline LDL-C and baseline characteristics as covariates. Both intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) populations were analyzed, with the main focus on the ITT set to maintain clinical relevance despite any protocol deviations. Continuous endpoints, including changes in lipid parameters other than LDL-C, were similarly analyzed using MMRM. For safety assessment, incidence rates of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), SAEs, and specific AEs of interest were compared between treatment groups using descriptive statistics. Subgroup analyses were performed based on DM status to ascertain any differential impact in these populations, with additional focus on dose adjustments among participants under the adaptive titration strategy. To address any missing data, imputation techniques, including the last observation carried forward (LOCF) method, were employed to reinforce the integrity of the efficacy analysis. Pre-specified sensitivity analyses included evaluating the robustness of LDL-C reductions using various imputation methodologies for missing data, assessing the impact of treatment adherence, and adjusting for discrepancies in baseline characteristics. Statistical significance was determined at a two-sided alpha level of 0.05, with 95% confidence intervals calculated for between-group differences. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS software (SAS Institute, Cary, NC), ensuring rigorous management of the complex dataset and supporting the reproducibility of findings across the participating trials. Results The pooled analyses from five placebo-controlled Phase 3 studies provide comprehensive insights into the efficacy and safety of alirocumab in individuals with and without diabetes mellitus (DM), focusing on the percentage change in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels from baseline to week 24. Alirocumab demonstrated significant LDL-C reductions across the study cohorts, with data derived from two distinct dosing regimens: alirocumab 150 mg administered every two weeks (Q2W) and a titration approach of alirocumab 75 mg Q2W increasing to 150 mg Q2W at week 12 for participants with baseline LDL-C levels of ≥70 mg/dL at week 8. In the cohort receiving alirocumab 150 mg Q2W (n = 2,416), baseline LDL-C levels were recorded at 117.4 mg/dL in participants with DM and 130.6 mg/dL in those without DM. By week 24, LDL-C reductions were substantial, with participants with DM experiencing a mean percentage reduction of 59.9%, contrasting sharply with a placebo group reduction of 1.4%. Similarly, participants without DM also exhibited significant reductions of 60.6%, as opposed to a placebo increase of 1.5%. Notably, 77.7% of individuals with DM and 76.8% of those without DM achieved LDL-C levels below the target of 70 mg/dL, highlighting aliocumab's potent lipid-lowering effects across populations irrespective of diabetic status. Conversely, in the alirocumab 75/150 mg group (n = 1,043), composed of individuals who had dosage escalations, baseline LDL-C levels for DM patients were 112.8 mg/dL, while those without DM had levels at 133.0 mg/dL. Post-treatment analysis at week 24 revealed that participants with DM managed to reduce LDL-C levels from baseline by 43.8%, contrasting with a placebo rise of 0.3%. Participants without DM reduced their levels by 49.7%, against a placebo increase of 5.1%. In this dosage group, 68.3% of DM individuals and 65.8% of non-DM individuals attained LDL-C concentrations less than 70 mg/dL by week 24. Remarkably, only a subset of participants, 26% with DM and 36% without DM, required an increase to 150 mg Q2W, which underscores the effectiveness of the initial dosing strategy in achieving desired lipid levels for a significant portion of the population. Furthermore, enhancements were not restricted to LDL-C improvements; alirocumab also positively influenced other lipid parameters. The analysis disclosed beneficial changes in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels, as well as reductions in total cholesterol and non-HDL-C, corroborating the broad lipid-modulating potential of alirocumab. However, the primary distinction in lipid outcomes between individuals with and without DM underscores the differential metabolic responses that necessitate careful consideration in clinical practice. Safety profiles and adverse event rates were consistent across groups, with similar incidences reported among alirocumab-treated individuals (79.8–82.0%) and placebo participants. The occurrence of any serious adverse events was rare and distributed evenly across both cohorts and dosing regimens, confirming alirocumab's tolerability regardless of diabetes status. Injection site reactions, occurring in less than 4% of patients, were the most prevalent treatment-emergent adverse event, with minor discrepancies based on the presence or absence of DM. Such consistency in safety endpoints further fortifies the role of alirocumab in managing dyslipidemia, particularly in high-risk cardiovascular populations accompanying DM. In summary, alirocumab has demonstrated robust efficacy in lowering LDL-C levels significantly in both DM and non-DM populations, with a comparable safety profile across the studied cohorts. These findings affirm alirocumab as a viable therapeutic option to mitigate cardiovascular risks attributed to poor lipid control in individuals with or without diabetes mellitus. The findings from our pooled analyses of five placebo-controlled phase 3 studies underscore the efficacy and safety of alirocumab in reducing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels among individuals with and without diabetes mellitus (DM), who are already on maximally tolerated statin therapy. These results are particularly noteworthy given the heightened risk of cardiovascular disease among individuals with DM, a population that often struggles with achieving optimal lipid management. Our study found that alirocumab, when administered at a 150 mg dosage every two weeks, resulted in significant LDL-C reductions from baseline by week 24 in both DM (−59.9%) and non-DM groups (−60.6%).
