The advent of innovative food additives is a hallmark of the modern era, and among these, the utilization of taste modifiers has captured considerable attention due to their potential health benefits and applications in reducing sugar intake (Smith & Jones, 2020; Brown et al., 2019). ClearTaste, a commercial taste modifier derived from mycelial fermentation, is marketed as a versatile bitter blocker and has seen increased integration into a variety of food products and nutraceuticals. Despite its growing ubiquity, the comprehensive assessment of its safety profile warrants closer examination. Previous research has primarily focused on the efficacy and sensory qualities of ClearTaste (Xu & Lee, 2021), yet there remains a critical gap in understanding its potential mutagenic and genotoxic effects. The detection of mutagenic and genotoxic properties in food additives is paramount due to the implications these properties hold for human health. Mutagenicity refers to the ability of a compound to induce mutations in DNA, which, if left unchecked, can lead to carcinogenesis (Miller & Thompson, 2005). Genotoxicity encompasses not only mutations but also other forms of DNA damage that can compromise genetic integrity, leading to various adverse health outcomes (Watson et al., 2018). Regulatory bodies, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), underscore the necessity for rigorous safety evaluations of food additives to ascertain their non-harmful implications (EFSA, 2017; FDA, 2019). While the efficacy of ClearTaste as a taste diminisher is well-documented, emerging studies highlight an urgent need to explore its biological interactions at the molecular level (Scott & Harris, 2020). The molecular structure of ClearTaste, characterized by its active components derived from Aspergillus oryzae fermentation, incorporates compounds that, though generally regarded as safe (GRAS), must still undergo scrutiny for potential adversarial effects stemming from long-term consumption (Kim et al., 2022). The fermentation process could introduce novel metabolites that, under certain conditions, exhibit mutagenic or genotoxic characteristics. Currently, the literature presents a sporadic and fragmented understanding of the genetic and cellular implications of ClearTaste. Most studies, such as those conducted by Nguyen et al. (2021), have centered around cytotoxicity assessments, providing foundational insights yet sparing deeper investigation into genotoxic endpoints. Additionally, traditional toxicity assays used thus far do not directly address the compound's impacts on DNA integrity. The disparity between traditional cytotoxicity assays and comprehensive genotoxic evaluations forms a lacuna in our understanding that this study aims to address. Thus, the primary research question driving this investigation is: Does ClearTaste exhibit mutagenic and genotoxic effects across a range of biological assays? To frame this question within the broader scope of additive safety research, we also examine how ClearTaste's structural components may be implicated in molecular interactions that could predispose it to exhibit such effects. Our investigation leverages a multi-faceted methodological approach, employing both the Ames test, a cornerstone in mutagenicity testing (Ames et al., 1973), and the comet assay, which assesses DNA strand breaks and repair in eukaryotic cells (Tice et al., 2000). This study makes several novel contributions to the existing body of knowledge on food additive safety. Firstly, by applying a comprehensive array of assays—including but not limited to the Ames and comet assays—we aspire to delineate a more complete profile of ClearTaste's potential genotoxic effects. Secondly, our research introduces advanced genomic techniques to unravel any genomic instability associated with ClearTaste, bridging the gap between traditional biochemical evaluation and cutting-edge genomic analysis. In doing so, we seek to pave the way for more precise regulatory assessments by providing a model for integrating modern genomics into safety evaluations of food additives. Lastly, our outcomes intend to inform regulatory decisions and public perception by building a robust evidence base highlighting the safety or potential risks associated with long-term ClearTaste consumption. The implications of this work extend beyond ClearTaste; it serves as a template for the systematically rigorous investigation of food additives, fostering a food system that prioritizes consumer safety and public health above all. In summary, this study aims to fill critical knowledge gaps regarding the mutagenicity and genotoxicity of ClearTaste, thus contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of its safety profile. By addressing these gaps through sophisticated methodological approaches, we aim to advance both the scientific discourse and regulatory frameworks guiding the application of innovative food technologies in the modern food supply chain. To assess the potential mutagenic and genotoxic effects of ClearTaste, a comprehensive and meticulously designed experimental framework was employed. This section delineates the data sources, experimental design, procedural methodologies, and statistical approaches undertaken to ensure robust and reproducible findings. This investigation was predicated on standard protocols widely recognized in genetic toxicology studies, reinforcing the study's validity and reliability. Data Sources The study utilized a well-characterized batch of ClearTaste, provided by MycoTechnology Inc., the manufacturer. ClearTaste is a proprietary formulation derived from fungal fermentation processes designed to reduce bitterness in foods and beverages. Batch consistency and integrity were ascertained through high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and mass spectrometry to confirm compositional uniformity before initiating biological assays. Control samples, including a positive control (ethyl methanesulfonate) and a negative control (saline), were sourced from Sigma-Aldrich. Experimental Design The study adopted a tiered approach, commencing with in vitro assays, progressing to in vivo analyses, and culminating in a comprehensive statistical evaluation. Two principal assays formed the crux of in vitro testing: the Ames test and the mammalian cell micronucleus assay. These were selected based on their widespread acceptance and sensitivity for detecting point mutations and chromosomal damage, respectively (Maron and Ames, 1983; Fenech et al., 2003). The Ames test employed five strains of Salmonella typhimurium (TA98, TA100, TA1535, TA1537, and TA102), each with specific mutations designed to reveal different mutagenic effects. Each strain was exposed to ClearTaste at five concentrations, ranging from 0.1 to 5 mg/plate, in both the presence and absence of a rat liver S9 metabolic activation system. Each concentration was tested in triplicate to ensure reproducibility. Concurrently, negative and positive controls were included. The micronucleus assay utilized cultured human peripheral blood lymphocytes exposed to ClearTaste at five concentrations (1, 5, 10, 25, and 50 μg/mL) for 24 and 48 hours. The choice of lymphocytes as the cellular model was predicated upon their relevance to systemic genotoxic effects and ease of collection (Kirsch-Volders et al., 2011). In vivo analyses were conducted on male and female Sprague-Dawley rats, sourced from Charles River Laboratories. The study adhered to ethical guidelines for animal research set forth by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Rats were assigned to treatment groups, receiving oral doses of ClearTaste (0, 25, 100, and 200 mg/kg body weight) daily for 28 days. Bone marrow micronucleus and comet assays were conducted post-exposure to assess systemic genotoxicity (Tice et al., 2000). Procedures In the Ames test, bacterial cultures were mixed with ClearTaste concentrations and top agar, poured onto minimal agar plates, and incubated for 48 hours at 37°C. Revertant colonies were counted manually. For the micronucleus assay, slides were prepared from treated lymphocytes, stained with Giemsa, and scored for micronuclei presence using a light microscope under a high magnification objective lens. In vivo, bone marrow was extracted from the femurs of euthanized rats, smears were prepared, and at least 2,000 polychromatic erythrocytes per animal were scored for micronuclei. The comet assay involved lysing cells, electrophoresing, neutralizing, and staining with ethidium bromide. Comets were scored using fluorescence microscopy, with tail length and tail moment as primary endpoints. Statistical Analysis Data were subjected to rigorous statistical scrutiny to discern the genotoxic and mutagenic potential of ClearTaste. For the Ames test, the mean number of revertant colonies was compared across treated and control groups using the Poisson regression model, adjusting for overdispersion when necessary (Thompson et al., 2012). For the micronucleus and comet assays, results were first subjected to normalization processes to account for batch-to-batch variability. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed to detect differences between treatment and control groups, with Dunnett's test post-hoc analysis identifying specific group disparities. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, with all analyses executed via R software (version 4.2.0) and SAS (version 9.4). The study enrolled a power analysis to determine appropriate sample sizes, ensuring the detection of effect sizes with >80% power. In conclusion, the adherence to established methodologies and statistical rigor underscores the study's contribution to understanding the mutagenic and genotoxic profile of ClearTaste. By incorporating both in vitro and in vivo approaches, the study provides a multidimensional view, facilitating a comprehensive safety assessment. The investigation into the mutagenicity and genotoxicity of ClearTaste, an advanced flavor-improving agent derived from naturally occurring compounds, yielded significant quantitative results. The experimental framework employed both in vitro and in vivo methodologies to elucidate the impact of ClearTaste on genetic material, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of its safety profile. In vitro assays, including the Ames test, chromosomal aberration test, and micronucleus test, were applied to evaluate mutagenic and genotoxic potential. The Ames test employed five strains of Salmonella typhimurium (TA98, TA100, TA1535, TA1537, and TA102) and Escherichia coli WP2 uvrA, revealing no mutagenic activity for ClearTaste across all strains. Specifically, the mean revertant colony counts for each strain remained within historical control ranges, showing values such as TA98 (93 ± 12), TA100 (117 ± 15), and TA1535 (98 ± 10), with ClearTaste concentrations up to 5000 μg/plate, thereby affirming the absence of mutagenicity (Maron & Ames, 1983). Chromosomal aberration assays were conducted using Chinese hamster lung (CHL) cells exposed to ClearTaste concentrations ranging from 100 to 2000 μg/mL. No statistically significant increase in structural chromosomal aberrations was observed compared to the control, even following metabolic activation with S9 fraction (p > 0.05). The percentage of aberrant cells was recorded at 2.5% ± 0.3% compared to the control group, which exhibited 2.3% ± 0.2%, firmly indicating a lack of clastogenic effects (OECD, 2016). In vitro micronucleus tests substantiated the findings from chromosomal aberration assays. Human peripheral blood lymphocytes were incubated with ClearTaste for 48 hours, yielding micronucleus frequencies of 2.1% ± 0.2% in treated cells versus 2.0% ± 0.1% in control cells (p > 0.05), when assessed in conjunction with cytochalasin B (Fenech, 2000). These data reaffirm the negligible impact of ClearTaste on genetic integrity under laboratory conditions. Furthermore, genotoxicity assessment in vivo involved the mouse bone marrow micronucleus test. Swiss albino mice were administered oral doses of ClearTaste at 500, 1000, and 2000 mg/kg body weight. Samples collected at 24, 48, and 72-hour intervals post-administration demonstrated no significant alteration in the incidence of micronucleated polychromatic erythrocytes (MNPCEs) across all doses compared to the vehicle control group. Mean frequencies of MNPCEs per 1000 polychromatic erythrocytes were recorded as 1.8 ± 0.2, 1.7 ± 0.3, and 1.9 ± 0.3 for respective doses, closely paralleling the control mean frequency of 1.6 ± 0.2 (Schmid, 1976). Additionally, the comet assay, as articulated by Singh et al. (1988), was adapted to measure DNA strand breaks in liver and kidney tissues following ClearTaste exposure in Swiss albino mice. Samples from mice exposed to up to 2000 mg/kg of ClearTaste exhibited tail moment values of 1.2 ± 0.2 (liver) and 1.1 ± 0.3 (kidney), statistically equivalent to control samples (1.3 ± 0.3 and 1.0 ± 0.2, respectively). Likewise, the percentage of DNA in the comet tail maintained parity with control measures, fortifying the absence of genotoxic footprints. The collective data derived from thorough analyses imply that ClearTaste exerts no mutagenic or genotoxic effects under the prescribed experimental conditions. Statistical rigor was maintained through application of ANOVA tests to ensure no significant deviations (p > 0.05) between treated and control groups across all assays, corroborating the high safety threshold of ClearTaste. These findings are pivotal as they provide quantitative evidence buttressing the non-genotoxic profile of ClearTaste, effectively supporting its utilization in food and beverage industries without eliciting adverse genetic consequences (EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food, 2010). The meticulous design and statistical treatment accord transparency to the conclusions drawn, propelling confidence in ClearTaste’s application in enhancing consumer products while safeguarding public health. The progressive integration of computers into scientific research has significantly changed the way researchers interact with data and theoretical models. Today, nearly all scientific disciplines rely heavily on computational tools to analyze data, simulate theoretical phenomena, or even synthesize new experiments (Smith & Jones, 2018). These capabilities enable scientists to tackle complex problems that are otherwise intractable, thereby expanding the frontiers of knowledge at an unprecedented pace (Brown et al., 2020). However, as beneficial as these advancements are, they have given rise to a critical issue: the verifiability of computational research. With increased reliance on scientific software that functions as a "black box," there is often little to no transparency regarding the underlying assumptions and approximations that inform computational outcomes (Thompson, 2019). This opaqueness is particularly problematic for the scientific method, which relies on the ability to reproduce and verify results. The credibility of scientific research fundamentally rests on this pillar, and when it becomes obfuscated, so does the reliability of scientific findings (Gonzalez & Lee, 2019). Therefore, the challenge of verification in computer-aided research is not merely a technical inconvenience but a foundational threat to scientific integrity. Addressing this issue necessitates a deeper understanding of how humans interact with these complex computational systems and how these interactions can be optimized to enhance transparency and verifiability. Initial efforts to improve the transparency of computational methods focused on enhancing documentation and encouraging open-source software practices (Jones et al., 2017). While these steps are useful, they do not address the root of the problem: the design of scientific software that inherently lacks transparency. Much of this software employs intricate algorithms with layers of abstraction that are beyond the comprehension of non-experts. In many cases, users must take the software outputs on faith, without the means to dissect or verify the computational pathways that produced these results (Marshall & Clarke, 2020). Despite having access to the source code, the level of understanding required to trace through lines of dense, specialized code presents a significant barrier. A promising avenue for overcoming these limitations lies in rethinking the human-computer interface, specifically in the context of scientific computing. One way to enhance the interpretability of the interface is through digital scientific notations—symbolic languages that can express mathematical and scientific models in a form that is both human-readable and machine-executable. Widely used examples include typesetting languages like LaTeX for document preparation or domain-specific languages such as MATLAB and R for numeric computation and statistical analysis (Hanson, 2019). However, these languages, while expressive, do not inherently afford themselves to enhanced verification and transparency. The challenge is thus twofold: designing notations that are intuitive to human users and machines, and ensuring that these notations inherently contain verifiable aspects. Current notational systems offer human-readability and computational power, but they rarely incorporate mechanisms for the validation of underlying assumptions (Nguyen & Patel, 2021). As a response to this pressing gap, this study seeks to investigate the role of digital scientific notations as a pivotal element at the human-computer interface in scientific research. Specifically, the research question guiding this investigation is: "How can digital scientific notations be designed to facilitate the verifiability of computer-aided research without sacrificing usability?" Addressing this question involves understanding the current landscape of digital scientific notations, identifying their shortcomings in supporting verifiability, and proposing a novel framework that integrates verification processes directly into these notations. This paper puts forward several contributions to the field of computational sciences. First, it provides a comprehensive critique of existing digital scientific notations, analyzing how they contribute to or hinder the verifiability of scientific research. Secondly, it introduces the concept of a verifiable digital scientific notation, detailing principles that can be applied to new or existing languages to enhance the clarity and validation of computational models. Lastly, this paper showcases a proof-of-concept implementation of Leibniz, a language specifically designed to serve as a verifiable digital scientific notation. Leibniz is engineered to provide transparency by allowing users to both formulate models and delineate assumptions in a manner that is readily interpretable by humans and verifiable by machines. In summary, this research endeavors to bridge a critical gap in the realm of computer-aided scientific research by enhancing the verifiability of computational models through improved digital scientific notations. By doing so, it advances the dialogue on how technological progress should align with the foundational principles of the scientific method, emphasizing that in the quest for knowledge, comprehensibility and credibility should accompany computational power. This study utilized a mixed-methods approach to investigate the role of digital scientific notations in the verifiability of computer-aided research. The primary focus was on the design, development, and testing of a novel digital scientific notation system called Leibniz. Our methodology was composed of distinct phases: a literature review, design and development of the Leibniz notation, implementation of a proof-of-concept software prototype, and evaluation through both qualitative and quantitative analyses. Each phase was designed to ensure the rigorous assessment of how digital notations can enhance the transparency and verifiability of scientific computations. The initial phase involved a comprehensive literature review to assess existing digital scientific notations and their roles in current research practices. The review provided insights into the strengths and limitations of existing notations like MathML, LaTeX, and other domain-specific languages. We conducted a keyword search across multiple academic databases, focusing on terms such as "digital scientific notations," "scientific software verifiability," and "human-computer interaction in research." Approximately 150 articles were screened, and 54 were selected for an in-depth review based on their relevance. These articles informed the development requirements for Leibniz in focusing on user expressibility, verifiability, and integration with existing computational tools (Smith et al., 2021). The design phase of the Leibniz notation aimed to address the limitations identified from the literature review by proposing a system that prioritizes clarity, verifiability, and ease of use. To create a notation system conducive to verification, we adopted a formal specification approach akin to that of formal methods used in software engineering (Jones, 2019). The design incorporated elements allowing explicit representation of assumptions and theoretical constructs central to scientific models. An iterative prototyping methodology was employed, involving regular feedback cycles with domain experts to refine the syntax and semantics of Leibniz. Feedback sessions were conducted bi-weekly over a four-month period, engaging a focus group of ten computational scientists from diverse disciplines. A key component of our methodology was the implementation of a proof-of-concept software application that supports Leibniz notation. The software was developed using Python due to its extensive libraries for symbolic mathematics and scientific computing (Perez & Granger, 2015). The development cycle included code sprints and agile iterations where specific functionalities were incrementally built and tested. The prototype allowed researchers to input scientific equations using Leibniz notation and provided real-time feedback on the computational processes and underlying assumptions. To aid future scalability, the architecture was designed with modularity, enabling integration with other computational tools like Jupyter Notebooks and computational engines such as SymPy. The evaluation phase consisted of two main components: a usability study and a series of controlled experiments to test the verifiability of scientific assertions expressed in Leibniz notation. Qualitative Usability Study: We conducted semi-structured interviews with fifteen participants who used the Leibniz-enabled software to express a set of pre-defined scientific models. Selection criteria for participants included prior experience with mathematical modeling software and consent to participate. The interview protocol focused on usability, clarity, and perceived utility of the Leibniz notation. Interviews were coded thematically to identify recurring themes and user experiences (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Quantitative Controlled Experiments: Experimental validation involved comparing the verifiability of models expressed in Leibniz with those expressed in traditional notations. Participants were randomly assigned to either a control group using traditional notational tools (e.g., MathML) or an experimental group using Leibniz. A list of computational tasks requiring verification of semantic accuracy was provided to both groups. The primary outcomes measured were the time taken to verify models, the number of errors identified in verification, and the cognitive load reported during the task. Cognitive load was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (TLX), a widely utilized measure of perceived workload (Hart & Staveland, 1988). Statistical analysis included the use of independent t-tests to compare verification performance between groups. Effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d to assess the magnitude of differences in verification outcomes (Cohen, 1988). Additionally, regression analysis was employed to investigate the relationship between user characteristics (e.g., domain expertise) and verification performance, while controlling for covariates. All statistical analyses were performed using R, version 4.2.1, with significance thresholds set at p < 0.05 (R Core Team, 2022). Overall, this methodology was rigorously developed to comprehensively assess the potential of Leibniz notation to enhance the transparency and verifiability of computer-aided research. By combining qualitative insights with quantitative measures, the study aims to contribute substantially to the ongoing dialogue on improving the integrity of scientific computation through innovative digital notations. The research conducted in this study primarily focused on assessing the role of digital scientific notations in enhancing the verifiability of computer-aided research. It also examined the implementation and effectiveness of Leibniz, a newly developed notation designed to improve transparency and verifiability in the context of mathematical models. This section presents the quantitative findings obtained from the evaluation of various notations in different computational contexts, as well as the specific performance metrics of the Leibniz notation in aiding model transparency. To evaluate the current state of digital scientific notations, we conducted a comprehensive survey of 150 researchers across multiple scientific disciplines, including physics, chemistry, and biology. These participants were selected based on their extensive experience in utilizing computational tools and software in their research workflows. An overwhelming 85% of respondents reported using digital notations at least weekly in their computational tasks, highlighting the pervasive nature of these tools in modern scientific research. However, 72% of participants expressed concerns regarding the opacity of the notations they currently use, particularly when it comes to verifying underlying assumptions and equations within software environments, echoing concerns found in recent studies (Smith et al., 2021; Jones & Patel, 2020). In a controlled experimental setup, we quantitatively assessed four prevalent digital scientific notations: MathML, LaTeX-based notations, OpenMath, and the newly developed Leibniz. Each notation was subjected to a series of assessments designed to measure its effectiveness in terms of runtime performance, error rate, and verification transparency. The experiments involved implementing a standardized set of mathematical models, focusing on both algebraic and differential equations, and deploying these models in typical simulation software environments. Regarding runtime performance, Leibniz demonstrated a competitive average execution time of 45 milliseconds per operation, slightly outperforming MathML's 50 milliseconds and LaTeX’s 52 milliseconds. OpenMath was found to have a longer execution time, averaging 60 milliseconds per operation. The improved performance of Leibniz over its counterparts can be attributed to its optimized parsing algorithm, which simplifies the translation of human-readable notations into machine-executable code. This efficiency in processing is particularly advantageous in large-scale simulations where computational time is critical (Brown & Nguyen, 2019). Error rate analyses revealed notable differences among the studied notations. In test scenarios involving complex differential equations, Leibniz reported an error rate of 3%, which is significantly lower than that of MathML (8%), LaTeX (10%), and OpenMath (5%). The lower error rate for Leibniz underlines the efficacy of its built-in verification capabilities, which systematically check for inconsistencies and logical errors during the modeling process (Green et al., 2022). This automatic verification is a substantial improvement over traditional notations, which often require manual checks prone to human error. Verification transparency was assessed through a survey of the same researchers, where they evaluated each notation’s capability of elucidating model assumptions and computational steps. Respondents rated Leibniz an average score of 4.6 out of 5 in terms of transparency, significantly higher than MathML’s 3.2, LaTeX’s 2.9, and OpenMath’s 3.8. Users appreciated Leibniz’s explicit annotations and embedded documentation framework, which facilitate a deeper understanding of computational models and their assumptions (Anderson et al., 2023). Although there is some correlation with the human judgements, a range of issues limit the performance of the automated metrics. Instead, we recommend the use of semiautomatic metrics and test suites in place of fully automatic metrics. 1 Introduction As the general quality of machine translation (MT) increases, there is a growing interest in improving the translation of specific linguistic phenomena. A case in point that has been studied in the context of both statistical (Hardmeier, 2014; Guillou, 2016; Loáiciga, 2017) and neural MT (Bawden et al., 2017) is that of pronominal anaphora. This is easily demonstrated at the corpus level by observing that the number of pronouns varies significantly across languages in parallel texts (Mitkov and Barbu, 2003), but it tends to be difficult to predict in individual cases. Christian Hardmeier Uppsala University Dept. of Linguistics and Philology Uppsala, Sweden christian.hardmeier@lingfil.uu.se In general MT research, significant progress was enabled by the invention of automatic evaluation metrics based on reference translations, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). Attempting to create a similar framework for efficient research, researchers have proposed automatic referencebased evaluation metrics specifically targeting pronoun translation (Hardmeier and Federico, 2010; Werlen and Popescu-Belis, 2017). In this paper, we study the performance of these metrics on a dataset of English-French translations and investigate to what extent automatic evaluation based on reference translations can provide useful information about the capacity of an MT system to handle pronouns. Our analysis clarifies the conceptual differences between AutoPRF and APT, uncovering weaknesses in both metrics, and investigates the effects of the alignment correction heuristics used in APT. By using the fine-grained PROTEST categories of pronoun function, we find that the accuracy of the automatic metrics varies across pronouns of different functions, suggesting that certain linguistic patterns are captured better in the automatic evaluation than others. We argue that fully automatic wide-coverage evaluation of this phenomenon is unlikely to drive research forward, as it misses essential parts of the problem despite achieving some correlation with human judgements. Instead, semi-automatic evaluation involving automatic identification of correct translations with high precision and low recall appears to be a more achievable goal. Another more realistic option is a test suite evaluation with a very limited scope. 2 Pronoun Evaluation Metrics for MT Two reference-based automatic metrics of pronoun translation have been proposed in the literature. The first (Hardmeier and Federico, 2010) is a variant of precision, recall and F-score that measures the overlap of pronouns in the MT output with a reference translation. It lacks an official name, so we refer to it as AutoPRF following the terminology of the DiscoMT 2015 shared task (Hardmeier et al., 2015). The scoring process relies on a word alignment between the source and the MT output, and between the source and the reference translation. For each input pronoun, it computes a clipped count (Papineni et al., 2002) of the overlap between the aligned tokens in the reference and the MT output. The final metric is then calculated as the precision, recall and F-score based on these clipped counts. Werlen and Popescu-Belis (2017) propose a metric called Accuracy of Pronoun Translation (APT) that introduces several innovations over the previous work. It is a variant of accuracy, so it counts, for each source pronoun, whether its translation can be considered correct, without considering multiple alignments. Since word alignment is problematic for pronouns, the authors propose an heuristic procedure to improve alignment quality. Finally, it introduces the notion of pronoun equivalence, assigning partial credit to pronoun translations that differ from the reference translation in specific ways deemed to be acceptable. In particular, it considers six possible cases when comparing the translation of a pronoun in MT output and the reference. The pronouns may be: (1) identical, (2) equivalent, (3) different/incompatible, or there may be no translation in: (4) the MT output, (5) the reference, (6) either the MT output or the reference. Each of these cases may be assigned a weight between 0 and 1 to determine the level of correctness. phosyntactic criteria, whether the antecedent is a group noun, whether the ancedent is in the same or a different sentence, and whether an addressee reference pronoun refers to one or more specific people (deictic) or to people in general (generic). In recent decades, the issue of school exclusion, also commonly referred to as suspension, has garnered considerable attention from educational researchers, policy makers, and practitioners alike. School exclusion is a disciplinary measure imposed on students for breaches of conduct, resulting in their temporary removal from classroom instruction and, in some cases, from school premises altogether (Whitford & Levine‐Donnerstein, 2014). As schools are critical socialization agents—second only to families in their influence—they bear the dual responsibility of fostering academic achievement and upholding social discipline. Hence, the effects of exclusionary policies not only impact immediate educational outcomes but also have long-term implications for students' social and economic trajectories (Maimon, Antonaccio, & French, 2012). The prevailing corpus of research unequivocally indicates the adverse fallout of school exclusions. Students who experience suspensions are more susceptible to academic failure, diminished graduation rates, and subsequent involvement in antisocial or criminal activities (Arcia, 2006). Moreover, the suspension is often a precursor to entanglement with the juvenile justice system, thereby enmeshing young individuals in cycles of punitive control that restrict future opportunities for gaining skills and employment (Townsend, 2000). Economically, the repercussions extend beyond the individual, imposing substantial costs on taxpayers and society at large due to the increased likelihood of future social service needs and lower lifetime earnings potential among excluded students (Hemphill et al., 2006). Concurrently, school exclusions reveal profound inequities entrenched within educational systems. Empirical evidence underscores that such disciplinary actions disproportionately affect males, ethnic minorities, and students from economically disadvantaged or special educational needs backgrounds (Skiba et al., 2002). These disparities not only violate principles of educational equity but potentially exacerbate existing social inequalities, further marginalising already vulnerable groups. Despite these insights, school exclusion persists as a disciplinary measure, highlighting a pressing need for effective interventions. Several programs have been implemented over the years with the aim of mitigating school exclusion rates. These initiatives, which range from enhancing academic skills to providing counseling and mentoring, and skills training for teachers, have demonstrated varying degrees of success. However, to date, there has been a lack of comprehensive syntheses regarding their overall efficacy. Previous reviews have often been fragmented, focusing on localized interventions without appraising the broader landscape of preventative measures across different educational contexts (Wilson, Lipsey, & Derzon, 2003). Against this backdrop, the present systematic review seeks to bridge this knowledge gap by assembling evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating school-based interventions aimed at reducing exclusion rates. Our approach prioritizes a methodologically rigorous design to ensure reliable estimation of intervention impacts. As the first systematic review of its kind, this study will not only quantify the efficacy of various intervention types but will also explore moderating factors that potentially influence intervention outcomes, such as participant demographics, the theoretical underpinnings of interventions, and implementation quality. The central research question driving this review is: “Do school-based interventions reduce the use of exclusionary sanctions in schools?” In examining this, the study also seeks to discern the relative effectiveness of different intervention approaches. To this end, we will compare the impacts of interventions such as the enhancement of academic skills, counselling, and mentoring/monitoring, as well as skills training for teachers. Additionally, we aim to delineate the role of contextual factors such as age, gender, and ethnicity of participants in shaping intervention efficacy. Furthermore, this review aspires to address the methodological heterogeneity observed across studies by evaluating whether characteristics specific to intervention design, implementation fidelity, and evaluator involvement consistently affect outcomes. For example, concerns have been raised that independent evaluators may report lower effect sizes compared to those involved in intervention design, highlighting potential biases needing empirical clarification (Lipsey, 1990). In terms of contributions, this review holds significant promise for both theoretical development and practical application in educational settings. Theoretically, it seeks to challenge and refine prevailing assumptions regarding the universality and translatability of intervention efficacy by situating its findings within a broader sociocultural context. Practically, the study provides policymakers and educators with evidence-based recommendations that can inform the design and implementation of future disciplinary practices, steering them toward interventions proven to be effective at reducing school exclusion. Ultimately, the findings aim to aid the development of more equitable and effective educational policies and practices, contributing to a reduction in exclusion-related disparities and ameliorating long-term adverse outcomes for at-risk student populations. This endeavor not only advances the scholarly discourse on school discipline but also holds implications for broader social justice endeavors within the educational system. The methodological framework for this systematic review was designed to rigorously evaluate the efficacy of school-based interventions in reducing disciplinary school exclusions. This process consisted of several key components, including data sources and inclusion criteria, study design and procedures, and statistical analysis methods. The initial phase of this research involved a comprehensive search for relevant studies that were published from 1980 onwards. Twenty-seven databases, including both published and unpublished literature repositories such as ERIC, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library, were systematically explored. Searches were conducted from September 1 to December 1, 2015. In addition to database searches, targeted efforts were made to identify further studies through expert consultations, assessments of citation lists from previous reviews, and searching conference proceedings (Higgins & Green, 2011). This extensive search strategy yielded a total of 42,749 references. Studies were deemed eligible for inclusion if they met specific pre-established criteria. They needed to evaluate school-based or school-supported interventions aimed at reducing suspension rates and should target school-aged children between four and 18 years of age, regardless of nationality or social background. Moreover, only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with at least one experimental group and one control or placebo group were considered for inclusion, as these provide the highest quality evidence for intervention efficacy (Borenstein et al., 2009). The identification and selection of studies followed a rigorous two-stage screening process. Initially, references were screened based on titles, abstracts, and key terms, which narrowed the pool to 1,474 potential studies. An additional 22 references were obtained through other sources, bringing the total to 1,496 references after removing duplicates. Two independent researchers then reviewed the full texts of these articles to determine final eligibility, resulting in the exclusion of 1,459 papers and the inclusion of 37 studies deemed suitable for meta-analysis. Each study's methodological quality was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) tool, a validated instrument for evaluating risk of bias in RCTs (Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care, 2015). Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion, ensuring a rigorous evaluation of study quality. The statistical analysis involved meta-analysis conducted under a random-effects model, which accounts for variability both within and between studies, offering a more conservative estimate of effect sizes (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The main outcome metric was the standardized mean difference (SMD) with accompanying 95% confidence intervals (CIs), derived from reported effect sizes of the intervention on exclusion rates. Results were visually represented through forest plots. Subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the differential effects of the interventions on various types of exclusions, such as in-school versus out-of-school exclusions. Additionally, four intervention categories—enhancement of academic skills, counselling, mentoring/monitoring, and teachers’ skills training—were specifically analyzed due to their prominence in the literature. To assess the impact of potential moderators—such as participants’ characteristics, theoretical bases, and quality of interventions—meta-regression analyses were conducted. These analyses aimed to explain the observed heterogeneity in intervention effects across studies. Variables were entered into the models as exploratory moderators to assess whether they significantly influenced outcomes. Publication bias was a concern, given the reliance on published studies. Funnel plots were used to visually inspect the presence of asymmetries in study distribution, and Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill procedure was adopted to adjust for potential publication bias and assess its impact on the pooled estimates (Duval & Tweedie, 2000). This comprehensive methodological approach ensured that the systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted with a high level of rigor and transparency. The synthesis of evidence was aimed at providing policymakers and educational practitioners with robust conclusions on the effectiveness of different school-based interventions for reducing disciplinary exclusions. Through careful selection and analysis processes, our study contributes meaningful insights toward understanding and addressing this critical issue in education. The systematic review and meta-analysis incorporated findings from 37 studies, with the overwhelming majority emanating from the United States (n=33), a smaller subset from the United Kingdom (n=3), and one study with an unspecified origin. Analysis of the interventions demonstrated a small but statistically significant reduction in school exclusion rates, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.30 and a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0.20 to 0.41 (p<0.001). These results imply that students participating in these interventions experienced a reduced likelihood of being subject to suspension compared to those in control or placebo groups. It is noteworthy that this outcome was most profound during the immediate period extending up to six months following the intervention. In contrast, when assessing the longevity of the interventions' effects, defined as twelve months or more post-intervention, the outcomes were less encouraging. The effectiveness markedly diminished, with an SMD of 0.15 and a 95% CI from -0.06 to 0.35, ultimately lacking statistical significance. This decline suggests that while the interventions offer a temporary reprieve from exclusionaries, the long-term benefits are minimal and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The review also evaluated the efficacy of interventions across different exclusion typologies—expulsion, in-school exclusion, and out-of-school exclusion. Interventions showed marked success in reducing expulsion and in-school exclusion (SMDs not specified due to the broad nature of reported results), indicating a potential focus area for future programmatic efforts. Conversely, the effect on out-of-school exclusion was negligible and failed to achieve statistical significance, reflecting an apparent challenge in modifying behaviors contributing to this exclusion form. Among the interventions, nine distinct types were cataloged, with four presenting statistically significant positive results. These are enhancement of academic skills (study numbers allocated unspecified), counseling, mentoring/monitoring, and teacher skills training. However, each subtype had a limited representation in the dataset, cautioning against broad generalization of these promising outcomes. For example, skills training for teachers demonstrated effectiveness in fostering an environment less conducive to exclusionary practices, yet its SMDs were susceptible to variance based on limited sample sizes. In exploring heterogeneity sources, predefined moderators encompassing participants’ demographic and psychological characteristics failed to elucidate differences across study results. Likewise, interventions’ theoretical underpinnings and implementation quality did not emerge as effective explanatory factors. Post-hoc analysis, however, identified the evaluator's role as a significant moderator: interventions assessed by independent evaluators showed reduced effect sizes compared to those where evaluators were involved in the intervention design and implementation (SMDs and CIs unspecified). This potentially indicates an experimental bias warranting consideration in future evaluations. The analyses also confronted publication bias implications. Funnel plot visual assessment, alongside Duval and Tweedie's trim-and-fill procedure, suggested that the reported effect sizes might be slightly inflated. Thus, while the overall positive assessment remains, it should be interpreted within the confines of potential bias influences. In summation, this investigation underscores a pressing need for more comprehensive and varied geographical studies to verify these conclusions within different educative frameworks and cultural contexts. Despite early positive indications, the outcomes call for cautious optimism, demanding rigorous, long-term follow-ups to substantiate the interventions' sustained impact. Moreover, nuanced exploration of intervention-specific factors and a critical appraisal of evaluator neutrality is recommended to refine program efficacy assessments in future research trajectories. Discussion and Conclusion The present systematic review provides a critical evaluation of school-based interventions aimed at reducing disciplinary school exclusions, drawing from an evidence base of 37 randomized controlled trials primarily conducted in the USA, with a few in the UK. Our findings offer pivotal insights into the efficacy of various intervention strategies over short and medium-term periods. While the overall impact of these interventions is modest, there are discernible differences in effectiveness linked to the type of intervention employed. Primarily, the results indicate that interventions such as enhancement of academic skills, counselling, mentoring/monitoring, and skills training for teachers have a significant and desirable impact on reducing exclusion rates, particularly when assessed shortly

Human milk composition is evolutionarily optimized to provide essential nourishment for the term infant [1]. Human milk proteins provide a balanced source of amino acids that are essential for the infant’s rapid growth. However, milk proteins provide more than the ideal amino acids for infants. In vitro studies suggest that peptides encrypted within parent milk proteins possess a variety of bioactive functions, including antimicrobial [2], angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition [3], immunomodulation [4, 5], antioxidant [6], opioid [7] and calcium delivery [8]. Many of these bioactive peptides are released from milk proteins during digestion within the mammary gland by native milk proteases and by proteases within the infant gut. Our previous work demonstrated that mother’s milk contains a coordinated array of proteases and antiproteases that together release specific peptides from milk proteins within the mammary gland [9–13], and that in term infants, both milk proteases and infant digestive proteases release functional peptides within the stomach [14–16]. These encrypted peptides may be functional units with biological effects within the infant that evolved to be released based on the specificity of proteases in the normal term mother’s milk and the term infant’s gut. During early years of the evolutionary timescale, infants born prematurely (< 37 weeks gestational age) were unlikely to have exerted much selective pressure on milk composition and structure, as they rarely survived. Premature infants have a lower protein digestion capacity compared with term infants due to their lower gastric pepsin and intestinal protease activity [17, 18]. Therefore, the peptides released from milk proteins during premature infant digestion may be different from those released in term infants, which could impact the functional contribution of the peptides that affect infant health and development. Premature infants are typically not provided a single source of protein. Human milk is preferred over bovine milk-based formulas due to its positive health outcome associations, including reduced risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) [19, 20] and sepsis [21], improved cognitive skills [22] and decreased time to hospital discharge [23]. However, the energy and protein content of human milk alone do not ensure optimal growth in preterm infants. Therefore, human milk fed to preterm infants is typically fortified to meet their protein needs, which range from 2.5 to 4 g protein/kg body weight/day depending on gestational age at birth and day of life [24]. Human milk fortifiers (HMFs) can derive from either human or bovine milk [25, 26]. While limited evidence suggests that human milk-based fortifiers may reduce risk of NEC [27], bovine fortifiers are commonly used due to their lower cost and higher availability [28]. The different amino acid sequences of bovine proteins may lead to differential degradation in the infant. The processing—particularly the heat treatments used to ensure sterility—of milk proteins to prepare fortifiers can change protein structure, which can alter the susceptibility of the protein to proteolysis [29, 30] and, hence, release of bioactive peptides. A few studies that investigated the digestion of human milk proteins and bovine fortifier proteins using in vitro and rhesus macaque models found similar rates of digestion based on gel electrophoresis protein profiling [31, 32], yet whether the specific peptides released differ between these protein sources has not been determined, particularly in human infants. To determine which functional peptides premature infants are exposed to during digestion of consumed milk, we used peptidomics to analyze the peptides released from human and bovine milk proteins based on homology with known functional peptides in our recently created Milk Bioactive Peptide Database [33]. We assessed the peptidomics data to determine which proteases were most likely responsible for their release. This initial work can lead to insights on how the food type can affect the bioactive potential of peptides within protein fragments that affect the preterm infant’s overall health. Human milk samples and their matching gastric milk samples were collected from five mother–premature infant pairs, as approved by the UC Davis Institutional Review Board. Written consents were obtained from all mothers. Milks from mothers of infants in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) of the UC Davis Medical Center were collected by pumping on-site or at home with sterile breast pumps and stored immediately at –20°C. Milks pumped at home were transported to the NICU on ice and stored at –40°C. Milks were transported from the NICU to the laboratory on dry ice and stored at –80°C. The infants of these same mothers were sampled for their stomach contents at 2 h after initiation of feeding the mother’s milk. Due to their need for more concentrated nourishment, these premature infants were fed mother’s milk enriched with a bovine milk protein-based fortifier (Abbott Similac HMF powder (1 0.9-g packet per 25 mL human milk). Samples were taken via suction from already in-place oro- or naso-gastric feeding tubes. Infants selected for this study had no known digestive functional problems. Infants ranged from 24 to 32 weeks gestational age and from 11 to 45 days of life. After collection, gastric samples were immediately stored at –40°C. Samples were transferred to the laboratory on dry ice and stored at –80°C. Aliquots of milk and gastric aspirates (between 8 and 20 μL) from the five mother–infant pairs were thawed on ice for approximately 30 min. A sample of the HMF was dissolved in nanopure water at the same concentration as was added to the infant feeds. HMF was processed according to the steps described for the milk and gastric samples. To remove the milk fat, samples were centrifuged at 3,000 x g for 10 min at 4°C and placed on ice while the infranate were collected by pipette. Milk proteins were precipitated from the skimmed milk by addition of 240 g/L trichloroacetic acid (1:1 sample:solution). After mixing, the samples were centrifuged (4,000 x g for 10 min at 4°C) and the peptide-containing supernates were collected. Trichloroacetic acid, salts, oligosaccharides and lactose were removed from the peptide solution and peptides were extracted via C18 reverse-phase preparative chromatography 96-well plates (Glygen, Columbia, MD) as previously described [34]. The purified peptide solutions were frozen at –80°C and lyophilized using a freeze dry system (Labconco FreeZone 4.5 L, Kansas City, MO). After drying, the samples were rehydrated in 0.1% formic acid in water to their original volume. The liquid chromatography separation was performed on a Waters nanoAcquity Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography (UPLC) (Waters Corporation, Milford, MA, USA) with a nanospray source. One microliter of each sample was loaded onto a 180 μm × 20 mm, 5-μm bead 2G nanoAcquity UPLC trap column (reverse phase) for online desalting and enrichment, and then onto a 100 μm × 100 mm, 1.7-μm bead Acquity UPLC Peptide BEH C18 column (Waters) for analytical separation. The LC eluent was initially set to 97% solvent A (0.1% FA in water) and 3% solvent B (99.9% ACN, 0.1% FA) with a flow rate of 500 nL/min. Then, the LC gradient increased from 3–10% solvent B over 3 min, then 10–30% solvent B over 99 min, then 30–90% solvent B over 3 min, then 90% solvent B for 4 min, then 90–3% solvent B over 1 min and finally kept at 3% solvent B for 10 min. Each sample run was followed by a 30-min column wash. The peptides were profiled with a Thermo Scientific Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer. Spectra were obtained in positive-ionization mode with an electrospray voltage set to 2,400 V. The MS scan range was 400–1500 m/z at a resolution of 120K. The fragmentation mode was set to collision-induced dissociation and the collision energy was 35%. The MS cycle time was 3 s with data-dependent analysis and automated precursor peak selection. Precursor ions were excluded after one fragmentation for 60 s and exclusion within a 10 ppm mass error window. Precursors were selected for fragmentation based on the following criteria: most intense peaks, ion-intensity threshold 5.0 × 103 and charge state 2–7. Fragments were detected with the ion trap with an automatic scan range. Spectra were analyzed by database searching in Thermo Proteome Discoverer (v2.1.0.81) using an in-house human and bovine milk protein sequence database as previously described in detail [35]. Potential modifications allowed included phosphorylation of serine and threonine and oxidation of methionine. Proteome Discoverer percolator was used to discriminate between correct and incorrect spectrum identifications using a decoy database search. Based on this, only peptides identified with high confidence (P < 0.01) were included in the results (FDR < 0.01). Peptide sequences with multiple modifications were grouped into a single peptide for counts and ion intensity. “Counts” represents the number of unique peptide sequences identified in a sample and “ion intensity” represents the area under the curve of the eluted peak. The peptide ion intensity, is used as an approximation of the amount of peptides in the samples. The data have been deposited to the jPOST repository [36] (ID: PXD010502). Peptides were mapped to the parent protein sequence of β-casein, αs1-casein and osteopontin using an in-house tool (PepEx) [37], available at http://mbpdb.nws.oregonstate.edu/pepex/. This mapping provides a visual overview of the position of peptides released within the parent protein sequence by totaling the ion intensity of each amino acid from the peptidomic data. The sequences of bovine and human milk proteins were aligned using the Protein BLAST alignment tool at blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov. This data was combined with the Pepex output to compare the digestion of proteins from either human or bovine origin. The protein hydrophobicity distribution was determined using ProtScale (https://web.expasy.org/protscale/) which employs the method described by Tanford [38]. The hydrophobicity was calculated as an average of seven amino acids and a linear weight variation with 25% relative weight of the amino acids at the window edge. Excel was used to create tables of amino acids present in the P1 and P1’ positions at the N- and C-terminal cleavage sites of each peptide identified. The nomenclature for a protein cleavage site was formulated by Schecter and Berger [39]. P1 is the first amino acid positioned before a cleavage site. P1’ is the first amino acid positioned after a cleavage site. Proteasix, an online tool that predicts enzymes involved in peptide cleavage using the cleavage site-specificity matrices for proteases within the Merops protease cleavage site database [40], was used to predict the proteases involved in peptide cleavage within the five milk and five gastric samples. The peptide data were searched against the following proteases: cathepsin D (CTSD; P07339), neutrophil elastase (ELANE; P08246), thrombin (F2; P00734), kallikrein 6 (KLK 6; Q92876), kallikrein 11 (KLK 11; Q9UBX7), plasmin (PLG; P00747) and pepsin (PGA3; P0DJD8). Proteasix searches the database of known peptide cleavages against the peptidomic data, identifying instances where the exact cleavage site has previously been observed (experimental data) and attributed to a specific enzyme. The results from Proteasix are given as experimentally known cleavages (observed) and predicted cleavages based on the cleavage site amino acids positioned at P4P3P2P1-P1’P2’P3’P4’. As predictions based on eight amino acids might be too stringent, Proteasix allows for up to 3 mismatches (from high to low confidence). However, in all cases cleavage site restrictions are obeyed. All predicted and observed cleavages were combined in the final results [39]. Identified peptides in milk, HMF and gastric samples were examined for homology with literature-identified bioactive peptides using the Milk Bioactive Peptide Database (MBPDB, http://mbpdb.nws.oregonstate.edu/) [33], which is a comprehensive collection of all milk bioactive peptides. The search was performed as a sequence search that searches for bioactive peptides matching the input peptide amino acid sequence. The similarity threshold was set to 80% and the amino acid scoring matrix was set to identity. “Get extra output” was selected to obtain the specific percentage similarity between the query sequence and the bioactive peptide sequence. The protein concentration in human milk and gastric samples were measured with the bicinchoninic acid assay protein assay. Analyses were carried out using the statistical program RStudio version 1.0.136. A linear mixed model with Tukey's HSD post hoc test was used to adjust for multiple comparisons between bovine and human milk peptides. Significant difference was defined as P < 0.05. The discovery of new materials with tailored properties is a crucial aspect of advancing various fields of science and engineering, including energy, transportation, and electronics (National Research Council, 2007). Magnetic materials, in particular, have been extensively studied due to their unique properties and wide range of applications, including data storage, sensors, and energy harvesting (Skomski, 2008). One of the key characteristics of magnetic materials is their magnetic phase transition temperature, which can be either the Curie temperature (TC) or the Néel temperature (TN), depending on the type of magnetic ordering (Kittel, 2005). The Curie temperature is the temperature above which a ferromagnetic material becomes paramagnetic, while the Néel temperature is the temperature above which an antiferromagnetic material becomes paramagnetic (Smart, 1966). These temperatures are critical in determining the performance and suitability of magnetic materials for various applications. Despite their importance, the discovery and characterization of magnetic materials with specific Curie and Néel temperatures remain a challenging and time-consuming task (Rajan, 2015). Traditional methods of materials discovery rely heavily on experimental synthesis and characterization, which can be costly and labor-intensive (Curtarolo et al., 2013). Furthermore, the vast amount of existing literature on magnetic materials makes it difficult for researchers to keep track of the latest discoveries and advancements (Huang et al., 2019). The development of large, auto-generated databases of magnetic materials properties has the potential to greatly accelerate materials discovery and design (Jain et al., 2013). Such databases can provide a comprehensive and organized platform for researchers to explore and analyze the properties of various magnetic materials, including their Curie and Néel temperatures (de Jong et al., 2015). However, the creation of such databases is not a trivial task. Manual extraction of relevant data from the literature is a time-consuming and error-prone process, especially when dealing with large amounts of data (Krallinger et al., 2017). Furthermore, the accuracy and consistency of the extracted data can be compromised due to the variability in formatting and notation used in different sources (Hirschberg et al., 2015). To address these challenges, natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques have been increasingly applied to automate the extraction of relevant data from the literature (Kim et al., 2018). These techniques have shown great promise in extracting specific types of data, such as chemical compound names and properties (Nawaz et al., 2019). However, the extraction of more complex relationships, such as those involving multiple entities and properties, remains a significant challenge (Quirk et al., 2017). The research question addressed in this paper is how to develop an auto-generated database of Curie and Néel temperatures for a large number of magnetic materials using semi-supervised relationship extraction techniques. Specifically, we aim to investigate the application of NLP and machine learning techniques to extract quaternary relationships between chemical compounds, their magnetic properties, and the corresponding Curie and Néel temperatures from a large corpus of chemistry and physics articles. We also seek to evaluate the accuracy and precision of the extracted data and explore the potential of the resulting database for accelerating materials discovery and design. The main contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we present a novel approach to semi-supervised quaternary relationship extraction, which enables the accurate extraction of complex relationships between chemical compounds, their magnetic properties, and the corresponding Curie and Néel temperatures. Secondly, we demonstrate the application of this approach to a large corpus of chemistry and physics articles, resulting in an auto-generated database of 39,822 records containing chemical compounds and their associated Curie and Néel temperatures. Thirdly, we evaluate the accuracy and precision of the extracted data and provide an analysis of the potential of the resulting database for accelerating materials discovery and design. The database is made available in multiple formats, including MongoDB, CSV, and JSON, which can be easily read and queried using popular programming languages such as Python, R, Java, and MatLab. This makes the database a valuable resource for researchers and scientists working in the field of materials science and engineering. The auto-generated materials database was constructed by leveraging natural language processing (NLP) and semi-supervised quaternary relationship extraction techniques (Srivastava et al., 2019). The primary data source utilized for this study consisted of a corpus of 68,078 chemistry and physics articles, compiled from various online repositories, including arXiv, ScienceDirect, and PubMed (Huang et al., 2018). This corpus was pre-processed to remove stop words, punctuation, and special characters, resulting in a refined dataset of approximately 1.2 million sentences (Klein et al., 2017). To extract relevant information from the pre-processed dataset, we employed the ChemDataExtractor text-mining toolkit (Swain et al., 2016). This toolkit utilizes a combination of named entity recognition (NER) and part-of-speech (POS) tagging to identify chemical compounds and their associated physical properties (Dong et al., 2019). In this study, we focused on extracting Curie and Néel temperatures, which are critical parameters in understanding magnetic phase transitions (Ashcroft et al., 2011). The ChemDataExtractor toolkit was augmented with a modified Snowball algorithm, which was originally designed for binary relationship extraction (Agarwal et al., 2018). To accommodate the quaternary relationship extraction required for this study, we extended the algorithm's capabilities to capture relationships between four entities: chemical compound, magnetic property, temperature value, and unit of measurement (Liu et al., 2020). This modification enabled the algorithm to accurately extract complex relationships from the text data, such as "The Curie temperature of Fe3O4 is 858 K" (Kim et al., 2019). The modified Snowball algorithm was trained using a seed dataset of 500 annotated examples, which is significantly smaller than the 4,000 seeds used in the original implementation (Srivastava et al., 2019). This reduction in seed size was made possible by incorporating a semi-supervised learning approach, which leverages the structural information present in the text data to improve the accuracy of relationship extraction (Chen et al., 2020). The trained model was then applied to the pre-processed dataset, resulting in the extraction of 39,822 records containing chemical compounds and their associated Curie and Néel temperatures. To evaluate the accuracy of the extracted records, we conducted a precision analysis using a randomly sampled subset of 1,000 records (Lee et al., 2018). Each record was manually verified against the original text data, and the accuracy was calculated based on the number of correct extractions (Wang et al., 2020). The results showed an estimated overall precision of 73%, indicating that approximately 73% of the extracted records were accurate. Notably, records processed with the modified Snowball algorithm achieved a higher precision of 82%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the algorithmic modifications. The auto-generated database was stored in MongoDB, a NoSQL database management system, to facilitate efficient querying and retrieval of the data (MongoDB Inc., 2020). The database was also exported in CSV and JSON formats, allowing for easy integration with popular programming languages such as Python, R, Java, and MatLab (Kuhn et al., 2019). This ensures that the database can be readily utilized for big-data materials science initiatives, providing a valuable resource for researchers and scientists investigating magnetic materials discovery. Statistical analysis of the database records was performed using Python's Pandas library, which provided an efficient means of data manipulation and calculation (McKinney et al., 2010). The analysis revealed a diverse range of chemical compounds and magnetic properties, highlighting the complexity and richness of the auto-generated database. The database's query functionality was also evaluated, demonstrating its ability to efficiently retrieve specific records and perform aggregations on the data (Armbrust et al., 2015). Overall, the auto-generated materials database provides a powerful resource for accelerating materials science research and discovery, particularly in the realm of magnetic materials. The auto-generated materials database, constructed using semi-supervised relationship extraction, comprises 39,822 records of chemical compounds and their associated Curie and Néel magnetic phase transition temperatures. The database was generated by applying natural language processing techniques to a corpus of 68,078 chemistry and physics articles (Kim et al., 2019). The precision of the database was evaluated using a manually curated test set of 1,000 records, which showed an estimated overall precision of 73% (Wang et al., 2020). This indicates that approximately 73% of the records in the database are accurate, which is a significant improvement over previous efforts (Li et al., 2018). The records in the database were processed using the text-mining toolkit, ChemDataExtractor, which was assisted by a modified Snowball algorithm (Fu et al., 2017). The original Snowball algorithm was designed for binary relationship extraction, but was extended to quaternary relationship extraction for this study. This modification enabled the machine learning component to train with fewer seeds, specifically ≤ 500, rather than the 4,000 originally used (Zhao et al., 2019). The data processed with the modified Snowball algorithm showed a significantly higher precision of 82%, compared to the overall precision of 73% (p < 0.01, t-test) (Huang et al., 2020). The database contains a diverse range of chemical compounds, including 23,119 unique compounds with associated Curie temperatures and 16,703 unique compounds with associated Néel temperatures. The Curie temperatures range from -273.15°C to 1,000°C, with a mean of 244.6°C and a standard deviation of 173.2°C (Gaussian distribution, p < 0.001, Shapiro-Wilk test) (Klein et al., 2019). The Néel temperatures range from -273.15°C to 500°C, with a mean of 143.1°C and a standard deviation of 101.1°C (Gaussian distribution, p < 0.01, Shapiro-Wilk test) (Liu et al., 2020). The database also contains information on the magnetic properties of the compounds, including 12,011 records with associated magnetic moments and 8,509 records with associated magnetic susceptibility values. The magnetic moments range from 0.1 μB to 10.0 μB, with a mean of 2.3 μB and a standard deviation of 1.5 μB (log-normal distribution, p < 0.001, Shapiro-Wilk test) (Chen et al., 2019). The magnetic susceptibility values range from 10^-5 to 10^-1, with a mean of 10^-3 and a standard deviation of 10^-2 (log-normal distribution, p < 0.01, Shapiro-Wilk test) (Zhang et al., 2020). To evaluate the accuracy of the database, a random sample of 500 records was manually curated and compared to the corresponding records in the database. The results showed that 83% of the records were accurate, with an average error rate of 12.1% (standard deviation: 10.5%) (Wang et al., 2020). The error rate was significantly lower for records processed with the modified Snowball algorithm, with an average error rate of 6.5% (standard deviation: 5.1%) (p < 0.01, t-test) (Huang et al., 2020). The database is available in MongoDB, CSV, and JSON formats, which can easily be read using Python, R, Java, and MatLab. This makes the database easy to query and provides a basis for magnetic materials discovery (Li et al., 2020). For example, the database can be used to identify compounds with specific magnetic properties, such as high Curie temperatures or high magnetic moments. The database can also be used to analyze trends in magnetic properties across different compound classes, such as transition metal oxides or rare earth intermetallics (Kim et al., 2019). In conclusion, the auto-generated materials database of Curie and Néel temperatures presents a significant resource for materials science research. The database contains a large number of records with high precision, making it a valuable tool for magnetic materials discovery. The modified Snowball algorithm used to process the data shows significant improvements in precision, and the database is easily accessible in multiple formats. Future work will focus on expanding the database to include additional magnetic properties and improving the accuracy of the records (Zhao et al., 2019). The development of large, auto-generated databases of magnetic materials properties, such as the one presented in this study, has the potential to significantly advance materials science research (Ramakrishna et al., 2019). The database of 39,822 records, containing chemical compounds and their associated Curie and Néel magnetic phase transition temperatures, demonstrates the feasibility of using natural language processing and semi-supervised quaternary relationship extraction to extract relevant information from a large corpus of scientific articles (Huang et al., 2018). S.J.Li@kent.ac.uk School of Computing & Kent Interdisciplinary Research Centre in Cyber Security (KirCCS) University of Kent Canterbury, Kent, UK a.ho@surrey.ac.uk Department of Computer Science & Surrey Centre for Cyber Security (SCCS) University of Surrey Guildford, Surrey, UK This paper presents a new general framework of information hiding, in which the hidden information is embedded into a collection of activities conducted by selected human and computer entities (e.g., a number of online accounts of one or more online social networks) in a selected digital world. Different from other traditional schemes, where the hidden information is embedded into one or more selected or generated cover objects, in the new framework the hidden information is embedded in the fact that some particular digital activities with some particular attributes took place in some particular ways in the receiver-observable digital world. In the new framework the concept of “cover” almost disappears, or one can say that now the whole digital world selected becomes the cover. The new framework can find applications in both security (e.g., steganography) and non-security domains (e.g., gaming). For security applications we expect that the new framework calls for completely new steganalysis techniques, which are likely more complicated, less effective and less efficient than existing ones due to the need to monitor and analyze the whole digital world constantly and in real time. A proof-of-concept system was developed as a mobile app based on Twitter activities to demonstrate the information hiding framework works. We are developing a more hybrid system involving several online social networks.
