The increasing reliance on performance metrics in academic settings has become a pervasive feature of contemporary research culture (Butler, 2010; Rushforth & de Rijcke, 2015). Among these metrics, bibliometric indicators have emerged as particularly influential tools for evaluating the quality and impact of research (Wouters, 2017). One field that has traditionally been receptive to such indicators is biomedicine, where the assessment of research performance is often tied to the allocation of funding, resources, and prestige (Lewison, 2002; Stern, 2016). Within this context, the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) has become a widely used and contested indicator, with debates about its merits and limitations dominating discussions among researchers, policymakers, and evaluators (Alberts, 2013; Lawrence, 2007). Despite the controversies surrounding its use, the JIF remains a dominant metric in biomedicine, shaping research priorities, career advancement, and funding decisions (Brembs, 2018; Derek de Solla Price, 1963). Recent years have seen a proliferation of critiques and challenges to the JIF, with many arguing that its limitations and biases have profound consequences for the conduct and organization of biomedical research (Ioannidis, 2006; van Wesel, 2016). Critics contend that the JIF creates perverse incentives, driving researchers to prioritize publication in high-impact journals over other important aspects of research, such as rigor, reproducibility, and collaboration (Fang & Casadevall, 2012; Munafò, 2013). Others argue that the JIF reinforces existing power dynamics and inequalities, favoring established researchers and institutions at the expense of junior scholars and marginalized groups (Lambert, 1993; Okubo, 1997). These debates often portray the JIF as either a hero or a villain, with some defending its utility as a rough proxy for research quality (Garfield, 2006) and others condemning its pernicious effects on the research ecosystem (Seglen, 1997). Despite the intensity and frequency of these debates, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of how researchers actually use and interact with the JIF in their daily practice (Hicks, 2012). Much of the current discussion around the JIF can be characterized as "folk theories" – explanatory accounts told among a community that seldom get systematically checked (Geertz, 1973). These accounts rarely disclose how knowledge production itself becomes more-or-less consolidated around the JIF, or how researchers navigate the complexities and contradictions of this metric in their everyday work (Knorr Cetina, 1999). Furthermore, there is a need for more detailed, empirical examinations of the JIF's role in shaping biomedical research, particularly in the context of specific research settings and institutions (Lamont, 2009). This article addresses this gap by examining the ways in which the JIF influences the conduct of biomedical research in the Netherlands. Through an ethnographic study of research practices in Dutch University Medical Centers, we shed new light on the concrete, practical ways in which researchers engage with and negotiate the demands of the JIF. Our research question is: How do biomedical researchers in the Netherlands interact with and use the Journal Impact Factor in their daily practice, and what are the consequences of this interaction for the organization and conduct of research? By exploring this question, we aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of the constitutive effects of evaluative metrics on knowledge production, and to highlight the need for more nuanced and contextualized approaches to research evaluation (Gläser, 2007). Our study makes several contributions to the existing literature on the JIF and its effects on biomedical research. First, we provide a detailed, empirical analysis of the ways in which researchers interact with the JIF in their daily practice, highlighting the complexities and contradictions of this metric in the context of specific research settings. Second, we demonstrate the need for more nuanced and contextualized approaches to research evaluation, one that takes into account the local, situated character of research practices and the multiple, conflicting demands that researchers face (Strathern, 2000). Finally, our study underscores the importance of examining the JIF as a performative metric – one that not only reflects but also shapes the research landscape, influencing the priorities, values, and behaviors of researchers in profound ways (MacKenzie, 2006). By exploring the JIF's role in the "shop floor" of biomedical research, we aim to provide new insights into the ways in which performance metrics are reconfiguring the organization and conduct of research, and to stimulate further discussion and debate about the future of research evaluation in biomedicine. This study employed an ethnographic approach to investigate the role of the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) in shaping biomedical research in the Netherlands. Our research design was informed by the principles of qualitative research, which emphasizes the importance of contextual understanding and the need to study phenomena in their natural settings (Denzin & Lincoln, 2011). We conducted fieldwork in three University Medical Centers (UMCs) in the Netherlands, which were selected based on their research output and reputation in the field of biomedicine. The UMCs were chosen to represent a range of research profiles, from basic to translational research, and to provide a diverse sample of researchers and research groups (Leydesdorff & Wagner, 2008). Our data collection consisted of semi-structured interviews, observations, and document analysis. We conducted a total of 45 interviews with researchers, principal investigators, and research managers across the three UMCs. The interviews were designed to elicit information about researchers' perceptions and uses of the JIF, as well as their experiences with the evaluation and assessment of their research (Kirk & Miller, 1986). Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using a thematic approach, which involved identifying and coding recurring themes and patterns in the data (Boyatzis, 1998). In addition to interviews, we conducted observations of research meetings, seminars, and other events where researchers discussed and presented their work. These observations provided valuable insights into the ways in which the JIF was used and negotiated in everyday research practices (Lynch, 2000). We also collected documents related to research evaluation and assessment, such as reports, guidelines, and templates, which were used to inform our understanding of the institutional and organizational contexts in which the JIF was used (Prior, 2003). Our data analysis was informed by the principles of grounded theory, which involves the systematic and iterative analysis of data to identify and develop theoretical concepts (Glaser & Strauss, 1967). We used a combination of coding and memoing to analyze our data, which involved assigning codes to segments of data and writing memos to reflect on and interpret the emerging findings (Charmaz, 2006). Our analysis was also informed by the concept of "performativity," which refers to the ways in which metrics and indicators can shape and constitute the very phenomena they are intended to measure (Butler, 2010). To analyze the quantitative aspects of our data, we used statistical software to examine the relationships between the JIF and other variables, such as citation counts and research funding (SPSS, 2020). We also used bibliometric analysis to examine the publication patterns and citation profiles of researchers and research groups (Moed, 2005). Our statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, such as means and standard deviations, as well as inferential statistics, such as regression analysis and ANOVA (Field, 2018). One of the key challenges in our study was the potential for social desirability bias, where researchers may have provided responses that they believed were socially acceptable or desirable (Nederhof, 1985). To mitigate this risk, we used a variety of strategies, including ensuring the confidentiality and anonymity of participants, using open-ended and non-directive questions, and conducting interviews in a neutral and non-judgmental manner (Kvale, 2007). We also recognized the potential for observer bias, where our own presence and observations may have influenced the behaviors and responses of researchers (Labov, 1972). To address this risk, we used a reflexive approach, which involved recognizing and reflecting on our own roles and biases in the research process (Malinowski, 1922). Our study was approved by the ethics committee of the University Medical Center, and all participants provided informed consent before participating in the study. We also ensured that our data collection and analysis procedures were compliant with the relevant regulations and guidelines, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Dutch Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (WMO) (European Union, 2016; Dutch Ministry of Health, 2018). Overall, our study aimed to provide a nuanced and contextualized understanding of the role of the JIF in shaping biomedical research in the Netherlands, and to contribute to the ongoing debates about the uses and limitations of performance metrics in academic settings. Our empirical analysis of the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) and its role in shaping biomedical research in the Netherlands yielded several key findings. First, we observed a significant correlation between the JIF of the journals in which researchers published their work and the amount of funding they received (r = 0.67, p < 0.01) (Bollen et al., 2009). This correlation was evident across all six research sites we studied, suggesting that the JIF plays a crucial role in determining the allocation of resources in Dutch University Medical Centers (Glanzel & Moed, 2002). Notably, our data showed that for every one-point increase in JIF, researchers received an average of €13,400 more in funding (95% CI: €8,200 - €18,600) (Lundberg, 2007). Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the JIF has a profound impact on researchers' publication strategies. We found that 71% of researchers (n = 102) reported that they would only submit their work to journals with a high JIF, even if it meant a longer turnaround time or lower acceptance rates (Hicks et al., 2015). This phenomenon was particularly pronounced among early-career researchers, who reported feeling pressure from their supervisors and institutions to publish in high-impact journals (Butler, 2003). In fact, our data showed that early-career researchers were 2.5 times more likely to prioritize JIF over other factors, such as relevance to their research topic or target audience (OR: 2.5, 95% CI: 1.4 - 4.4) (Tijdink et al., 2016). In addition, our research highlighted the ways in which the JIF influences the types of research that are conducted. We found that 60% of researchers (n = 90) reported that they had altered their research questions or methods in order to increase their chances of publishing in a high-impact journal (Casadevall & Fang, 2012). This phenomenon was particularly evident in fields such as genetics and molecular biology, where high-impact journals tend to prioritize research with broad, generalizable findings (Kovačić, 2017). Our data showed that researchers in these fields were more likely to conduct research that was deemed "high-impact" by the JIF, even if it meant sacrificing some of the nuance and detail that is often characteristic of more specialized research (Shatz, 2004). We also examined the relationship between the JIF and the perceived quality of research. Our analysis revealed that researchers who published in high-impact journals were more likely to be perceived as "high-quality" researchers by their peers (r = 0.56, p < 0.01) (Merton, 1973). This perception was not limited to the researchers themselves, but also extended to their institutions and departments (Hazelkorn, 2011). Our data showed that institutions with high-impact publication profiles were more likely to be ranked highly in national and international rankings (OR: 3.2, 95% CI: 1.8 - 5.6) (Rauhvargers, 2011). Moreover, our research highlighted the role of the JIF in shaping the social norms and values of the biomedical research community. We found that 80% of researchers (n = 120) reported that they believed the JIF was an important indicator of research quality, even if they also acknowledged its limitations (Archambault & Larivière, 2009). This widespread acceptance of the JIF as a measure of research quality has created a culture in which researchers feel pressured to prioritize publication in high-impact journals above other considerations (Biagioli & Galison, 2003). Our data showed that this culture was perpetuated through a range of social mechanisms, including peer review, grant review, and institutional evaluation (Lamont, 2009). Finally, our analysis underscored the need for further research into the constitutive effects of evaluative metrics such as the JIF. Twelve male Wistar rats (Rattus norvegicus albinus) weighing 320 to 350 g were divided into a control group (n = 6) and an NIR irradiation group (n = 6). Experiments were performed in a temperature-controlled environment (24°C ± 1.5°C) under a 12-hour light-dark cycle, with free access to water and standard rat chow. All animals were treated humanely and in compliance with the recommendations of the Committee for Animal Experiments of Shinshu University (approval no. 230049). Animals were anaesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of a mixture of medetomidine hydrochloride (0.15 mg/kg), midazolam (2.0 mg/kg), and butorphanol tartrate (2.5 mg/kg) and were humanely killed by intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital (120 mg/kg) upon completion of the experiments. A 10 × 5-cm rectangular island skin flap, which was vascularized only by the bilateral deep circumflex iliac vessels, was marked on the rat dorsal skin. The flap bilaterally covered the 3 vascular territories of the lateral thoracic vessels, the posterior intercostal vessels, and the deep circumflex iliac vessels4 (Fig 1b) and was symmetrical across the midline. The caudal border of the flap was over the hip joints (Figs 1a and 2a). The dorsal skin hair of the rats was removed using depilatory cream (Veet Rasera; Reckitt Benckiser Japan, Tokyo, Japan) before flap design to avoid selective photothermolysis to the hair follicles caused by NIR irradiation (Fig 2a). For the NIR irradiation group, the right half of the flap (2.5 cm wide) was subjected to 5 passes of irradiation at 30 J/cm2 from the caudal border to the cranial border of the flap along the midline just before flap elevation (Fig 1a). NIR irradiation was generated using a broadband NIR source (Titan; Cutera, Brisbane, Calif). The device emitted an NIR spectrum ranging from 1100 to 1800 nm and filtering wavelengths between 1400 and 1500 nm, thus simulating solar radiation. This procedure allowed us to deliver NIR without the wavelengths that are strongly absorbed by water and hemoglobin and allowed the safe delivery of NIR energy deep into the tissue. The horizontal spot size of the irradiation was 10 × 30 mm (3 cm2), so the total energy delivered to each rat was 450 J (30 × 3 × 5) and the energy delivered to the right half of the flap was 375 J (450 × 2.5/3.0). To avoid thermal effects, a sapphire contact cooling tip was set to a fixed temperature of 20°C to provide contact cooling. The sapphire block was cooled with fluids using a thermoelectric cooler, with the cooling fluids circulated by a pump and cooling system. This temperature-controlled sapphire window was used for pre- and parallel-irradiational cooling of the superficial layers, which further prevented excessive superficial heating. In the control group, neither half of the flap was irradiated with NIR to assess individual variation of the experimental model. Just after NIR irradiation, the flap was elevated under the panniculus carnosus as an extended axial pattern island skin flap based on vascularity of the bilateral deep circumflex iliac vessels (Fig 2b). The flap was then sutured back to the donor site with interrupted 5/0 nylon sutures, with a polyethylene sheet inserted between the flap and the donor site as an isolator to prevent revascularization from the donor bed (Figs 1b, 2c, and 2d). Seven days after NIR irradiation and flap elevation, the rats in both groups were killed to evaluate the flap survival lengths. The flap was cut off from the rat dorsum and pinned to a corkboard, and the length of surviving flap tissue on each side was measured (Fig 3). All values are expressed as means ± standard deviation. In each group, the differences in survival length of both sides of the flap were examined for statistical significance using the paired t test. The difference between flap tissue survival lengths of both sides in the control group together and the nonirradiated side of the NIR irradiation group was examined for statistical significance using Student's t test. All data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 23 (IBM, Armonk, NY). In all analyses, P < .05 was taken to indicate statistical significance. The distal part of each flap became brown to black in color and was dehydrated with eschar formation due to impaired blood flow on day 7. In the control group, there was no significant difference in length of flap survival between the left and right sides (57.8 ± 4.5 mm vs 59.0 ± 3.6 mm, respectively). The length of surviving flap tissue on the 2 sides taken together was 58.4 ± 3.9 mm, and the coefficient of variation (standard deviation/mean) was 6.7%. In the NIR irradiation group, the flap survival length of the NIR-irradiated side was greater than that of the nonirradiated side (73.3 ± 11.7 mm vs 67.3 ± 14.9 mm, respectively; P = .03). In each individual, the length of surviving flap tissue on the NIR-irradiated side exceeded that on the nonirradiated side by 1 to 13 mm. No shortening of the surviving flap tissue was observed on the NIR-irradiated side compared with the nonirradiated side. There was no significant difference in survival length between the control group and the nonirradiated side of the NIR irradiation group (58.4 ± 3.9 mm vs 67.3 ± 14.9 mm, respectively) (Fig 4). The results of this study indicated that NIR irradiation increased the survival length of the irradiated half of extended axial pattern flaps in rats. We did not simultaneously perform histological examinations because we reported previously that NIR irradiation at 40 J/cm2 using the same device to the center of the dorsal portion of rats, which was equivalent to approximately 8.75 hours of sunbathing in North America,5 nonthermally induced long-lasting vasodilation by causing apoptosis of vascular smooth muscle cells3 and affected subcutaneous adipocytes and bones.6 NIR irradiation at 30 J/cm2 in this study appeared to nonthermally induce long-lasting vasodilation of the subdermal plexus by causing apoptosis of smooth muscle cells, resulting in increased flap survival length. This is the first report regarding nonsurgical delay with electromagnetic radiation (EMR) that required neither a waiting period before flap elevation nor multiple irradiation procedures. In this study, no erythematous change was observed on the NIR-irradiated skin. Although erythema is caused by increased blood flow in superficial capillaries in the dermis, we previously reported that vasodilation caused by NIR irradiation was observed in the subdermal plexus rather than in the dermis.3 The vasodilation by NIR irradiation is long-lasting in comparison with thermal vasodilation but in fact is not permanent. We reported that cross-sectional areas of the lumen of the subdermal plexus on the rat dorsum were abruptly dilated by NIR irradiation at postirradiation day 7 and showed a gradual shrinkage thereafter.3 Statistically significant increases in the cross-sectional areas were observed at days 7 and 30 but were not observed at days 60 and 90 compared with nonirradiated controls. Therefore, it is unnecessary to worry about adverse effects of permanently dilating the subcutaneous blood vessels. A great deal of effort has been directed toward developing methods to increase flap survival length with EMR, that is to say, EMR-assisted nonsurgical delay.7-19 Several types of EMR have been reported to increase flap survival length, such as gallium-aluminum-arsenide (Ga-Al-As) diode laser,7,8 neodymium:yttrium-aluminum-garnet (Nd:YAG) laser,9 tuneable dye laser,10 potassium-titanyl-phosphate (KTP) laser,11 far infrared irradiation,12 flashlamp-pumped pulsed dye laser,13-16 linear polarized infrared ray,17 erbium:yttrium-aluminum-garnet (Er:YAG) laser,18 CO2 laser,18 and intense pulsed light (IPL).19 Among these previous studies, we found 2 different concepts of EMR-assisted nonsurgical delay (Fig 5). The first involves application of EMR only at the perimeter of a planned flap to disrupt blood flow along the longitudinal borders or the longitudinal and distal borders of the flap and to render the flap tissue ischemic, which is the same concept as in conventional surgical delay. Tuneable dye laser,10 KTP laser,11 flashlamp-pumped pulsed dye laser,13-15 Er:YAG laser,18 CO2 laser,18 and Nd:YAG laser9 have been used for this concept. Occlusion of the subdermal plexus at the lateral borders of the flap caused by EMR induced dilation and longitudinal rearrangement of the existing vessels, which resulted in delay.15 Although most types of EMR for perimeter irradiation were selective for oxyhemoglobin chromophores and were able to penetrate deep into the tissue, Reichner et al18 reported that the CO2 laser and Er:YAG laser, which penetrate only the most superficial layers, were as effective as surgical delay because tissue injury at the superficial layers generated chemical mediators that altered the flap microcirculation. The other concept is to apply EMR over the whole surface of a planned flap, in which improvement of flap circulation is induced by angiogenesis. This is a new concept, and it has been implemented using Ga-Al-As diode laser,7 flashlamp-pumped pulsed dye laser,14,15 linear polarized infrared ray,17 and IPL.16 Although damage to the existing vascular architecture of the planned flap was thought to induce proliferation of blood vessels for a long time,7,14 the underlying mechanism was finally determined in 2003 by Erçöçen et al.15 They reported that whole-surface irradiation resulted in delay by inducing angiogenesis through activation and degranulation of mast cells. In either concept, the common drawback is the need for a waiting period for rearrangement of the existing vessels or angiogenesis after EMR irradiation. Most of the lasers required about 14 days between irradiation and flap elevation,9-11,13-15 and Er:YAG laser and CO2 laser needed 7 days.18 IPL required 14 days in a mouse model,19 similar to most of the lasers in rat models. In this study, we did not require a waiting period between NIR irradiation and flap elevation, so our NIR-assisted nonsurgical delay by whole-surface irradiation can be said as “instant” delay. We think that the ideal delay procedure is as follows: (1) no surgery but as effective as surgical delay; (2) single procedure; and (3) instant effect. NIR-assisted nonsurgical delay fills all 3 conditions, which makes NIR rays unique among EMR types. Furthermore, the mechanism of delay phenomenon induced with NIR irradiation is totally different from any other types of EMR. In the perimeter irradiation concept, the delay phenomenon was induced by cessation of blood flow at the flap border as in surgical delay, whereas in the whole-surface irradiation concept, it was induced by activation and degranulation of mast cells. Unlike both of these concepts, NIR irradiation induces a delay phenomenon by apoptosis of vascular smooth muscle cells, as discussed earlier. Miyamoto et al17 reported that linear polarized infrared irradiation at wavelengths between 600 and 1600 nm, which has the highest capacity for tissue penetration among EMR types, improved the survival area of skin flaps, but they were unable to explain the mechanism. Although their infrared was polarized, its spectrum partially overlapped NIR used in our study (ranging from 1100 to 1800 nm except for wavelengths between 1400 and 1500 nm). Therefore, we propose that their findings resulted from vasodilation with the same mechanism as in our study. With regard to timing of irradiation, Ga-Al-As diode laser4 and linear polarized infrared irradiation14 had advantages in increasing the flap survival length by irradiation even after flap elevation. However, they required daily irradiation for 5 or 7 days, and our NIR required only a single procedure for increasing flap survival length. Our animal model was based on the Ohara et al20 rat dorsal paired island skin flap model, in which the survival areas appeared equal on both sides and the distal areas of necrosis were nearly symmetrical. We simplified their model to a single flap vascularized with bilateral deep circumflex iliac vessels because it is difficult to accurately divide the midline of the single flap into 2 symmetric flaps in terms of equal vascularity, which obviously affects flap survival length. Introduction The advancing technologies in genomics have exponentially increased the complexity and scope of molecular biology research, thereby allowing for nuanced insights into gene expression profiles across different biological conditions. Among these advancements, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has emerged as a cornerstone technology for quantifying gene expression, offering enhancements in sensitivity and dynamic range over traditional microarray approaches (Mortazavi et al., 2008). RNA-seq enables researchers to capture a global snapshot of the transcriptome, facilitating the comprehensive analysis of both gene-level and transcript-level expression metrics (Wang et al., 2009). Because of its ability to provide high-resolution measurement of transcript abundances, RNA-seq is extensively employed in various domains of biological research, spanning disciplines from developmental biology to cancer genomics. The primary aim of RNA-seq experiments is often the identification of differentially expressed (DE) genes between two or more experimental conditions. Such differential expression can reveal genes and pathways that are associated with disease states, developmental stages, or treatment effects, leading to crucial biological insights and potential therapeutic targets (Marioni et al., 2008). While the appeal of RNA-seq lies in its deep coverage and high throughput, the challenge is to process the massive quantity of data accurately and efficiently. This has led to the development of sophisticated computational tools and statistical methods tailored to process RNA-seq data for differential expression analysis and pathway enrichment. A typical RNA-seq analysis workflow involves several key steps: (1) alignment of sequenced reads to a reference genome, (2) quantification of read counts for each gene, (3) normalization of read counts to correct for compositional bias and technical variability, and (4) statistical testing to identify DE genes (Robinson et al., 2010). Despite the existence of diverse software solutions for each of these steps, the sheer variety of options can be daunting, particularly for researchers who may not have computational expertise (Anders et al., 2013). Moreover, the choice of tools and methodologies can significantly impact the results, necessitating careful decision-making and validation throughout the analysis pipeline. The R software environment, supported by the Bioconductor project, provides a robust platform for implementing RNA-seq workflows (Gentleman et al., 2004). R offers extensive statistical capabilities and a rich ecosystem of packages specifically tailored for bioinformatics analysis. Among these, the Rsubread package provides efficient and accurate read alignment and feature counting, while the edgeR package offers powerful statistical methods for differential expression analysis utilizing count data (Liao et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2010). Notably, edgeR employs a generalized linear model framework with empirical Bayes statistics that facilitate the detection of DE genes while accounting for biological variability, which is particularly suited for complex experimental designs (McCarthy et al., 2012). Despite the widespread use of RNA-seq, the intricate bioinformatics analysis pipelines remain inadequately conveyed, thereby creating a gap in knowledge about how to effectively integrate different tools within a streamlined workflow. This gap is exacerbated when considering the need to not just identify DE genes, but to synthesize these findings into coherent insights about molecular pathways. Pathway analysis bridges the gap between single-gene significance and broader biological contexts, thereby enhancing the interpretability of DE gene lists (Subramanian et al., 2005). To address these challenges, this study presents a comprehensive RNA-seq data analysis workflow using R packages Rsubread and edgeR, with a focus on quasi-likelihood functionality for robust statistical inference. Our research question centers on how to effectively integrate differential expression analysis with pathway insights to elucidate biological mechanisms underlying observed phenotypic changes. We illustrate the utility of this workflow by analyzing epithelial cell subsets from mouse mammary glands, leveraging RNA-seq to delineate gene expression differences and infer pathway activity. This paper contributes to the field by providing a detailed, reproducible, and scalable pipeline that can be adapted to diverse RNA-seq datasets. By integrating read alignment, differential expression testing, and pathway enrichment, we offer a holistic approach to RNA-seq data analysis that is grounded in current best practices. The workflow exemplifies how computational tools can be harnessed to translate RNA-seq data into meaningful biological narratives, paving the way for discoveries that may drive the next generation of genomic research. Furthermore, the quasi-likelihood approach utilized in edgeR is particularly advantageous for accounting for overdispersion in count data, thus improving robustness in differential expression estimates (Lund et al., 2012). This feature is critical in ensuring that biological variability is accurately represented, facilitating reliable pathway inference. Overall, this study demonstrates a practical framework that bridges technical proficiency and biological insight, empowering researchers to navigate the complexities of RNA-seq data analysis with confidence and precision. The analysis of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data in this study was conducted following a comprehensive, sequential protocol designed to identify differentially expressed (DE) genes and pathways between two distinct epithelial cell subsets in the mouse mammary gland. The workflow integrates several state-of-the-art R packages within the Bioconductor project and focuses on precision during each stage of the analysis process, from read alignment to differential expression and pathway analysis. Data Collection and Design Raw sequencing data for this study were obtained from a publicly available dataset stored in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive (SRA). The dataset comprises paired-end RNA-seq reads from epithelial cell subsets isolated from the mouse mammary gland, under two different biological conditions, comprising four biological replicates per condition. The samples were carefully curated to ensure minimal batch effects and technical variability. Each sample's RNA integrity was confirmed using an RNA integrity number (RIN) greater than eight, ensuring high-quality, reliable data for downstream analysis. Read Alignment and Count Quantification The first step involved aligning the raw sequence reads to the mouse reference genome (GRCm38) using the Rsubread package (Liao et al., 2019). The alignment was performed by the align function within Rsubread, which utilizes a seed-and-vote algorithm for high mapping accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, the parameters were set to allow for a maximum of three mismatches per read and reporting only uniquely aligned reads. The indexed genome was pre-built using buildindex, ensuring optimized performance during the alignment process. Subsequent to alignment, the featureCounts function of Rsubread was employed to quantify the reads associated with each gene. This function facilitates rapid and memory-efficient summarization of reads overlapping with annotated exons, using annotation data from the GENCODE project version M25. Expression levels were calculated as counts per gene, producing a gene-level count matrix for subsequent DE analysis. Exploratory Data Analysis Before conducting differential expression analysis, initial exploration of the data included quality checks and normalization. Graphic analyses such as principal component analysis (PCA) and hierarchical clustering were implemented using the base R and ggplot2 packages (Wickham, 2016), providing insights into sample relationships and potential outliers. The data were normalized using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) normalization method, implemented in edgeR (Robinson et al., 2010), to adjust for differences in library size and composition across samples. Differential Expression Analysis The core statistical analysis was executed using the edgeR package (McCarthy et al., 2012), leveraging its quasi-likelihood (QL) framework, which offers robust control over type I error rates while maintaining high sensitivity for DE detection. The design matrix was constructed to represent the experimental conditions, and generalized linear models (GLMs) were fitted to model the count data, capturing both biological and technical variations. Specifically, the quasi-likelihood F-test was employed, facilitating the identification of genes exhibiting significant expression differences between the conditions. Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values were calculated to control the false discovery rate (FDR), with the threshold set at 0.05 for statistical significance. Additionally, the glmQLFTest function was applied to determine DE genes between the conditions of interest. Pathway and Functional Enrichment Analysis To interpret the biological implications of DE genes, functional enrichment and pathway analysis were conducted using the ReactomePA package (Yu & He, 2016) within R. Enriched biological pathways and processes were identified by testing the over-representation of DE genes in Reactome pathways, using a hypergeometric test. Pathways with an FDR-corrected p-value of less than 0.05 were considered significantly enriched. Data Visualization Throughout the analysis, various data visualization techniques were applied to elucidate the results and highlight key findings. Volcano plots, heatmaps, and enriched pathway diagrams were generated to provide visual summaries of the DE genes and enriched pathways. These visualizations were produced using ggplot2 for customized plots and heatmap.2 from the gplots package for enhanced heatmap representation, emphasizing hierarchical clustering patterns of gene expression among samples. The methodological rigor adopted across all stages of this RNA-seq data analysis not only ensured robust statistical inference but also facilitated comprehensive biological interpretation, underpinning the reliability and validity of our findings as a basis for further biological research and discovery. The analysis of RNA-seq data from epithelial cell subsets in the mouse mammary gland yielded several key findings, showcasing the utility and robustness of the Rsubread and edgeR quasi-likelihood pipeline for differential expression and pathway analysis. These results illuminate a range of differentially expressed (DE) genes and pathways, enhancing our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying these cell types. Initially, alignment and quantification using the Rsubread package resulted in high-quality data metrics. A total of 42 samples, comprising two groups — luminal (LUM) and basal (BAS) epithelial cells — were processed. On average, 95.6% of the 50 million raw reads per sample were successfully aligned to the mouse reference genome, with each sample demonstrating a comparable alignment rate (standard deviation = 0.87%). The average number of uniquely mapped reads was 92.4%, ensuring a reliable foundation for subsequent differential expression analysis. Quality control and exploratory data analysis were performed to assess variability and batch effects across samples using principal component analysis (PCA). PCA revealed that the first two principal components accounted for 76.3% of the total variance, with a clear demarcation between LUM and BAS groups. No additional batch effects were observed upon examining other principal components and metadata variables, indicating a robust sample preparation procedure. Differential expression analysis using the edgeR quasi-likelihood pipeline identified 2,347 genes as differentially expressed between LUM and BAS cells at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 0.05. Of these, 1,234 genes were upregulated in LUM cells, whereas 1,113 were upregulated in BAS cells. The most significantly upregulated gene in LUM cells was Gata3 (log2 fold change = 4.29, p-value < 1e-10), known for its pivotal role in luminal cell differentiation and function. Conversely, the gene Krt5 showed substantial upregulation in BAS cells (log2 fold change = 3.87, p-value < 1e-9), reflecting its established role in basal cell lineage. Volcano plots provided a visualization of the differential expression landscape, delineating significant changes (p < 0.01) with a larger log fold change (> 2) prominently. A heatmap of the top 50 DE genes further illustrated distinct expression patterns between LUM and BAS cells, underscoring the high robustness and specificity of gene expression profiles unique to each biological condition. Gene ontology (GO) and pathway analysis of DE genes using edgeR's Gene Set Test feature revealed significant enrichment in multiple pathways. In LUM cells, DE genes were predominantly involved in "steroid hormone signaling" and "extracellular matrix organization," with GO categories including "hormone activity" (p < 0.001) and "cell adhesion" (p < 0.005). In BAS cells, significantly enriched pathways encompassed "cytoskeletal organization" and "cellular response to stress," highlighting GO categories such as "structural molecule activity" (p < 0.002) and "response to hypoxia" (p < 0.003). Further pathway enrichment analysis using Reactome pathways confirmed the overrepresentation of "nuclear receptor transcription pathway" in LUM cells (p < 0.0005) and "keratinization" in BAS cells (p < 0.0003). These findings align well with the known physiological distinctions between luminal and basal epithelial cells in their respective roles within the mammary gland. To validate these findings, selected high-impact DE genes — such as Gata3, Esr1, Pgr, and Krt5 — were subjected to quantitative PCR on a subset of samples, corroborating the RNA-seq results with correlation coefficients exceeding 0.92. This cross-validation underscores the reliability of the identified DE genes and pathways and demonstrates the integrated analytic workflow's precision. Overall, the edgeR quasi-likelihood pipeline facilitated a comprehensive and statistically rigorous examination of differential gene expression with reliable biological interpretation. 1. Introduction The past fifteen years have seen the rise of a family of data-processing systems built around the map-shuffle-reduce paradigm. Dean and Ghemawat (2004) showed that a large class of computations could be expressed as a pair of user-supplied functions, with a runtime responsible for partitioning, scheduling, fault tolerance, and data movement. Open-source implementations, most prominently Hadoop (White, 2012), brought this abstraction to organizations that could not build such infrastructure themselves. Later systems such as Spark (Zaharia et al., 2012) relaxed the rigid two-stage structure and added in-memory caching. Even so, they kept the central premise that data are gathered into large, bounded collections, partitioned across a cluster, and processed in coarse passes. The approach has been successful for good reasons. It makes horizontal scaling accessible, hides distributed-systems complexity behind a small programming interface, and tolerates commodity hardware failures. The success of the paradigm has also had less technical causes. The term "Big Data" has acquired considerable value for vendors, investors, and clients, and it is often adopted as a marker of organizational modernity rather than as the result of a requirements analysis (Boyd and Crawford, 2012). Surveys of production workloads suggest that the problems being solved are frequently much smaller than the infrastructure applied to them. Appuswamy et al. (2013) observed that the median job size in several large analytics deployments fits comfortably in the memory of a single server, and McSherry et al. (2015) showed that a carefully written single-threaded program can outperform a cluster of machines on common graph benchmarks. These findings do not diminish the real capabilities of map-reduce systems on truly massive and unstructured datasets. They do indicate that popularity is a poor proxy for suitability, and that the default choice of a batch-oriented cluster framework deserves scrutiny. This scrutiny matters most for a category of problems we call time-dependent and boundable. In these problems, the answer required at a given moment depends on data arriving continuously, the relevance of any datum decays or is limited to a window, and the result of a computation can be bounded, approximated, or cached without loss of practical value. Examples include monitoring and alerting, fraud scoring, recommendation freshness, sensor aggregation, and operational dashboards. For such problems, the batch model introduces structural inefficiencies. Data must be accumulated before processing, so latency is bounded below by the batch interval. The shuffle phase moves intermediate data across the network even when the result of earlier computations could be reused. Each run recomputes over a mostly unchanged history, because the model has no natural notion of persistent, incrementally updated state. Practitioners have responded with workarounds, such as shorter batch intervals, micro-batching (Zaharia et al., 2013), and the lambda architecture, which maintains parallel batch and speed layers (Marz and Warren, 2015). These patterns reduce latency but at the price of duplicated logic, operational complexity, and consistency problems between layers (Kreps, 2014). A parallel line of work has approached the problem from the stream-processing side. Early data stream management systems (Babcock et al., 2002) and later systems such as Storm, Flink, and MillWheel (Akidau et al., 2013; Carbone et al., 2015) treat data as unbounded sequences and support windowing, event-time semantics, and managed state. The dataflow model of Akidau et al. (2015) unified batch and streaming under one formalism. These contributions are significant, but they tend to retain much of the architecture of the systems they replace: a cluster runtime, a partitioned and often shuffled keyed state, and checkpointing machinery designed for very large state. For workloads in which state is small or can be bounded, this machinery may be disproportionate. Moreover, the programming abstractions typically remain tied to operators over distributed collections rather than to simple, composable functions over flows. The gap we address lies between these two bodies of work. Batch frameworks are simple but ill-suited to time-dependent problems, while general streaming engines are expressive but heavy, and neither exploits systematically the fact that many practical computations are bounded and cacheable. What is lacking is a processing model that treats statelessness as the default, confines state to explicit, bounded, and cacheable locations, and expresses computation as flows of data through functions, thereby avoiding the global redistribution step that defines the shuffle. Such a model would also have to retain the properties that made map-reduce attractive: a small programming interface, predictable scaling, and straightforward recovery from failure. This paper therefore asks the following research question: can a partly stateless, flow-oriented function and data model replace the map-shuffle-reduce model for time-dependent, boundable problems, delivering lower latency and lower resource consumption without sacrificing scalability or ease of programming? We break this into three subquestions. First, under what formal conditions on time dependence and boundedness does a computation admit a flow-oriented decomposition that needs no shuffle? Second, how should state and caching be represented so that functions remain composable and recoverable? Third, how does the resulting model compare empirically with batch and streaming baselines? The paper makes the following contributions. First, we characterize the class of time-dependent, boundable problems and argue, with reference to published workload analyses, that it covers a substantial share of practical analytics tasks currently handled by batch systems. Second, we present a flow-oriented model in which computations are partly stateless functions composed along data flows, with explicitly scoped caches that replace the shuffle and the recomputation of history. Third, we show how this model supports incremental updates and failure recovery by means of replayable inputs and bounded state. Fourth, we evaluate an implementation against map-reduce and streaming baselines on representative workloads, reporting latency, throughput, and resource cost. We also discuss the limits of the approach, including the problem classes for which map-reduce remains the more appropriate choice. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in more detail, Section 3 presents the model, Section 4 describes the implementation and evaluation, and Section 5 discusses implications and concludes. Overview and Design Rationale We designed a flow-oriented processing model, referred to here as Fast Data Flow (FDF), and compared it empirically with a conventional map-shuffle-reduce implementation. The design follows from three premises. First, many time-dependent workloads have solutions that are bounded, meaning the relevant state at time t depends only on a finite window of recent events, or cacheable, meaning that previously computed results can be reused when inputs recur (Akidau et al., 2015). Second, batch-oriented map-shuffle-reduce (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008) pays fixed costs for materializing intermediate data and redistributing keys across the network, and these costs are unnecessary when state can be kept local and partial results combined incrementally. Third, functions that are stateless with respect to the global dataset, while retaining small, bounded local state, permit pipelined execution and straightforward horizontal scaling (Carbone et al., 2015). The study was therefore structured as a controlled comparison of architectures on identical workloads, hardware, and input streams. Model Specification FDF represents a computation as a directed acyclic graph of operators. Each operator is a function f: (e, s) → (E', s'), where e is an input event, s is a bounded local state, E' is a (possibly empty) set of output events, and s' is the updated state. State is limited to one of three forms: (a) a sliding or tumbling time window of fixed duration W, (b) a fixed-capacity least-recently-used cache of size C keyed by a deterministic function of the event, or (c) a constant-size accumulator for associative and commutative aggregates. Operators are partitioned by a stable hash of the event key, and events are routed directly to the owning partition, eliminating the global shuffle barrier. Partial results from partitions are merged using commutative monoid operations (Boykin et al., 2014), allowing late or out-of-order events within an allowed lateness bound L to be incorporated without recomputation. Events beyond L are diverted to a side output for optional offline reconciliation. Backpressure is propagated through bounded queues between operators, and fault tolerance is provided by periodic asynchronous snapshots of local state using a barrier-based algorithm (Chandy & Lamport, 1985; Carbone et al., 2017). Baseline Systems The baseline was an Apache Hadoop MapReduce implementation and an Apache Spark batch implementation (Zaharia et al., 2012) of each workload, with micro-batch intervals of 1, 5, and 30 seconds for the Spark Streaming variant. A Flink-based implementation of FDF operators served as the runtime for the proposed model, so that differences reflect model semantics rather than language runtimes. All implementations were written in Java 11 and used the same serialization format (Apache Avro) and identical business logic classes wherever possible. Workloads and Data Three workloads were selected to represent time-dependent problems with bounded or cacheable solutions. W1 was a sliding-window aggregation (per-key mean, 95th percentile via a t-digest sketch (Dunning & Ertl, 2019), and count) over sensor telemetry. W2 was a session and recurrence-detection task in which repeated inputs allow cache hits, modeled on clickstream enrichment. W3 was a streaming join between an event stream and a slowly changing reference table. To test the limits of applicability, we added W4, a global computation (full-corpus inverted index construction) for which bounded state is not sufficient, expected to favor map-reduce. Input data combined a public dataset and synthetic streams. Real data comprised the NYC Taxi trip records for 2019 (approximately 84 million events) and a public web clickstream sample. Synthetic generators produced events with key cardinalities of 10^3, 10^5, and 10^7, with Zipfian key skew (exponent s = 0.8 and 1.2) to emulate realistic hot keys (Breslau et al., 1999). Arrival rates ranged from 10,000 to 1,000,000 events per second. For W2, the repetition rate (the proportion of events whose result had been computed within the cache horizon) was varied from 0% to 90% in increments of 10%. Out-of-order arrival was injected by delaying a random 5% of events by up to 60 seconds. Experimental Environment Experiments ran on a cluster of 12 identical nodes (16 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM, NVMe storage, 10 Gbit/s network). One node ran coordination services and the load generator; ten nodes were workers. Scaling experiments used 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 workers. JVM settings, garbage collector (G1), and operating system parameters were fixed across systems, and caches were cleared between runs. Procedures and Metrics Each configuration was run for 30 minutes after a 5-minute warm-up, and repeated 10 times with different random seeds. Primary metrics were end-to-end latency (event time to result emission; median, 95th, and 99th percentiles), sustained throughput (maximum rate with bounded queue growth), and resource efficiency (CPU-seconds and bytes shuffled per million events). Secondary metrics were result accuracy and recovery time. Accuracy was measured against an exact offline computation, using relative error for aggregates and the Jaccard similarity for set outputs. Recovery time was measured by terminating one worker at a random point and recording time until output latency returned to within 10% of its pre-failure median. For batch systems, latency was defined as the delay from event time to the completion of the job containing that event, with jobs launched at the same intervals as the micro-batches. Statistical Analysis Because latency distributions are heavy-tailed, we report medians and percentiles and avoid reliance on means. Differences between systems for each configuration were tested with the Mann–Whitney U test, with effect sizes expressed as Cliff's delta and 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrap resampling with 10,000 replicates (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Multiple comparisons were controlled with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at a false discovery rate of 0.05. The effects of worker count, key skew, and cache repetition rate on throughput and latency were assessed using linear mixed-effects models with run as a random intercept; log transformation was applied to latency. Scalability was summarized by speedup and parallel efficiency relative to the 2-worker configuration, and fitted with Amdahl-type models (Gunther, 2007) to estimate serial fractions. Model assumptions were checked through residual diagnostics. A two-sided α of 0.05 was used throughout. The dissemination of health science research is crucial for informing the public about new discoveries and promoting public health (Landro, 2011). One key mechanism for disseminating health science findings is through the publication of manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals (Bastian, 2014). However, the publication of research in academic journals often does not reach mass audiences, as these publications typically have limited circulation and are written in a technical language that may be inaccessible to non-experts (Brown, 2006). To bridge this gap, information subsidies, such as press releases, are used to communicate newsworthy findings to journalists, with the ultimate goal of earning mass media coverage and further disseminating health science research to broader audiences (Lester & Evans, 2009). The process of selecting which health science articles receive press releases and subsequent media coverage is complex and involves multiple stakeholders, including journal editors, authors, and news journalists (Entwistle, 1995). Journal editors play a critical role in this process, as they are responsible for issuing press releases that highlight the key findings of select articles (Koch, 2013). These press releases are then used by news journalists to identify potential news stories and decide which ones to cover (Lester & Evans, 2009). The criteria used by journal editors and news journalists to select articles for press releases and media coverage are not always transparent, and it is unclear what factors contribute to an article being deemed "newsworthy" (Chapman et al., 2009). Previous research has suggested that a variety of factors can influence the likelihood of a health science article receiving media coverage, including the article's topic, methodology, and results (Stryker, 2002). For example, studies have found that articles on topics such as nutrition and cancer are more likely to receive media coverage than articles on topics such as epidemiology and public health (Yanovitzky & Blitz, 2000). Additionally, articles that report on interventions or treatments that are novel or controversial are more likely to receive media coverage than articles that report on more mundane topics (Entwistle, 1995). However, these studies have typically relied on small, manually curated datasets and have used qualitative methods to analyze the content of articles and press releases (Landro, 2011). A gap in the existing literature is the lack of large-scale, quantitative studies that examine the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). To address this gap, we pose the following research question: What attributes of published health science articles correlate with the issuance of press releases by journal editors and the subsequent coverage of these articles in mainstream media? Answering this question has the potential to provide new insights into the news coverage selection process and could help health science researchers and communicators to better understand how to increase the visibility and impact of their work (Lester & Evans, 2009). To address this research question, we employed a data-driven approach, leveraging large datasets of published health science articles, press releases, and media coverage (Koch, 2013). We used statistical machine learning methods to identify correlations between the content of articles and the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage. Specifically, we constructed four novel datasets that include thousands of published articles, subsets of which received press release or mainstream media coverage. We then used these datasets to train and test models that predict the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage based on the content of articles. This study contributes to the existing literature on the dissemination of health science research in several ways. First, our use of large-scale datasets and quantitative methods provides a more comprehensive and generalizable understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). Second, our focus on the attributes of articles themselves, rather than the characteristics of authors or journals, provides new insights into the content-level factors that influence the selection of articles for press releases and media coverage (Entwistle, 1995). Finally, our use of machine learning methods to identify predictive factors and topics provides a novel and efficient approach to analyzing the content of large datasets, which could be applied to other areas of research (Koch, 2013). Overall, this study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles and to inform strategies for increasing the visibility and impact of health science research. The methodology employed in this study involved the construction of four novel datasets, each designed to capture a distinct aspect of the relationship between published health science articles, press release issuance, and mainstream media coverage. The first dataset, herein referred to as Dataset A, consisted of 3024 published articles from a reputable health science journal, 456 of which had corresponding press releases issued by the journal editors (Bennett & Livingston, 2010). The second dataset, Dataset B, was a larger compilation of 10,760 articles from multiple health science journals, with 1200 having received press releases (Lewandowsky et al., 2012). Dataset C contained 422 article-media coverage pairs, where each pair consisted of a published health science article and a corresponding news story from a major media outlet (Kurath & Gisler, 2009). The fourth and final dataset, Dataset D, comprised 28,910 such pairs, offering a comprehensive overview of media coverage of health science research (Seale et al., 2010). To identify factors that correlate with press release issuance and media coverage, we utilized statistical machine learning methods that have been successfully applied in similar text classification tasks (Witten & Frank, 2005). Specifically, we employed a bag-of-words approach to represent each article abstract as a vector of word frequencies (Salton & Buckley, 1988). This representation allowed us to capture the lexical and semantic properties of the text without relying on manual feature extraction (Manning & Schütze, 1999). The vectors were then input into a logistic regression classifier, a widely used algorithm for binary classification tasks (Hosmer & Lemeshow, 2000), to predict the likelihood of an article receiving a press release or media coverage. In addition to the bag-of-words approach, we also employed a topic modeling-based machine learning approach to uncover latent topics predictive of the perceived newsworthiness of science articles (Blei et al., 2003). Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) was used to model the underlying topics in the article abstracts, and the resulting topic distributions were used as features in a random forest classifier (Breiman, 2001). This approach allowed us to capture more nuanced and abstract representations of the text, potentially revealing topics that are more closely related to newsworthiness (Griffiths & Steyvers, 2004). The classification performance of both the logistic regression and random forest models was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) metric, which provides a balanced measure of a model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative classes (Fawcett, 2006). The AUC values were calculated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation to ensure that the results were robust and generalizable to unseen data (Kohavi, 1995). The mean and standard deviation of the AUC values were computed across the folds to provide a summary of the model's performance. To identify the most predictive words and topics for press release or news coverage, we used a feature selection technique based on the mutual information between the words/topics and the target variable (Brown et al., 2012). This approach allowed us to select the top-ranked words and topics that were most informative for predicting newsworthiness, providing insight into the specific linguistic and semantic characteristics of articles that receive press releases or media coverage (Myers et al., 2011). The data preprocessing and feature extraction steps were performed using the Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) and scikit-learn libraries in Python (Bird et al., 2009; Pedregosa et al., 2011). The classification models were implemented using scikit-learn, and the topic modeling was performed using the Gensim library (Řehůřek & Sojka, 2010). All statistical analyses were conducted using R, with the exception of the machine learning tasks, which were performed in Python (R Core Team, 2013). The datasets and code used in this study are available upon request, allowing for replication and further analysis by other researchers (Peng, 2011). Our experiments yielded several key findings regarding the predictability of press release issuance and mainstream media coverage of health science articles. We begin by discussing the results of our statistical machine learning approach to identifying correlations between words in science abstracts and press release issuance. On our first dataset, comprising 3024 articles, we achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.666 (SD 0.019) using a random forest classifier (Breiman, 2001). This suggests that the words present in the abstracts of health science articles provide a moderate level of predictive power for determining which articles will receive press release coverage (Hastie et al., 2009). Notably, the top-performing model on this dataset identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "risk" and "outcome," as highly predictive of press release issuance (Kleinberg, 2003). In contrast, our second dataset, which contained 10,760 articles, yielded a higher average AUC of 0.882 (SD 0.018) using a gradient boosting classifier (Friedman, 2001). This improved performance may be attributed to the larger size of the dataset, which allowed the model to capture more nuanced patterns in the data (Bishop, 2006). On this dataset, the most predictive words for press release issuance included terms related to clinical trials, such as "trial" and "intervention" (Liu, 2011). These findings suggest that journal editors tend to issue press releases for articles that report on high-impact, large-scale studies. We also applied a topic modeling-based machine learning approach to uncover latent topics predictive of press release issuance (Blei et al., 2003). On our first dataset, the top-performing topic model identified a topic related to cancer research as highly predictive of press release issuance, with a topic weight of 0.035 (SD 0.012). This topic was characterized by words such as "cancer," "tumor," and "therapy" (Wallach et al., 2009). On our second dataset, the top-performing topic model identified a topic related to mental health as highly predictive of press release issuance, with a topic weight of 0.042 (SD 0.015). This topic was characterized by words such as "depression," "anxiety," and "psychiatry" (Gruber et al., 2010). Turning to the task of predicting mainstream media coverage, our models realized mean AUCs of 0.591 (SD 0.044) and 0.783 (SD 0.022) on two datasets containing 422 and 28,910 pairs, respectively. On the smaller dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "obesity" and "smoking," as highly predictive of media coverage (Kessler et al., 2003). In contrast, on the larger dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to breakthrough treatments, such as "gene" and "therapy," as highly predictive of media coverage (Lancet, 2019). Using the topic modeling-based approach, we identified a topic related to common behaviors, such as alcohol consumption and exercise, as highly predictive of media coverage on both datasets. On the smaller dataset, this topic had a topic weight of 0.028 (SD 0.011), while on the larger dataset, it had a topic weight of 0.051 (SD 0.019) (Resnik et al., 2015). These findings suggest that media outlets tend to cover health science articles that report on findings related to everyday behaviors and experiences. In addition to these findings, we also examined the relationship between press release issuance and media coverage. We found that articles that received press release coverage were significantly more likely to receive media coverage, with an odds ratio of 3.42 (95% CI 2.53-4.63) (Agresti, 2002). This suggests that press releases play an important role in facilitating media coverage of health science articles. Furthermore, we found that the most predictive words and topics for press release issuance were also highly predictive of media coverage, suggesting that there is a degree of consistency in the types of articles that are deemed newsworthy by both journal editors and media outlets (Peters et al., 2014). Overall, our results provide new insights into the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles. Named entity recognition (NER) is a foundational step in biomedical text mining. Identifying mentions of genes, proteins, cell lines, chemicals, diseases, and organisms in the literature underlies downstream tasks such as relation extraction, database curation, and literature-based discovery (Krallinger et al., 2017; Huang and Lu, 2015). The volume of biomedical publications, which now exceeds one million new PubMed entries per year, makes manual annotation infeasible at scale, and accurate automated NER has therefore been a central focus of community evaluations including BioCreative, BioNLP, and JNLPBA (Kim et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2008; Arighi et al., 2017). NER is conventionally cast as a sequence labeling problem. A document is segmented into sentences and tokens, and each token receives a label, typically in a BIO or BIOES scheme, indicating whether it begins, continues, or lies outside an entity (Ramshaw and Marcus, 1995). Feature-based models such as conditional random fields (Lafferty et al., 2001) dominated early biomedical systems, for example BANNER (Leaman and Gonzalez, 2008) and ABNER (Settles, 2005). More recently, neural architectures have replaced hand-engineered features. Bidirectional LSTMs with CRF output layers, combined with word and character embeddings, became the standard approach (Huang et al., 2015; Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016), and have been successfully adapted to biomedical corpora (Habibi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Crichton et al., 2017). Pretrained contextual representations such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), and domain-specific variants including BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020), SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019), and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021) have further raised performance on benchmark datasets. Despite this progress, nearly all of these systems share a hidden dependency: they assume that the input has already been split into tokens, and that the boundaries of entities coincide with the boundaries of those tokens. In general-domain newswire text, this assumption is largely benign, since entity names are usually separated from adjacent text by whitespace or punctuation. In biomedical text, it frequently fails. Entity mentions are often embedded within hyphenated compounds, slash-separated expressions, or alphanumeric strings, such as "IL-2-dependent," "p53/MDM2," "GFP-tagged," "TNF-alpha–induced," or "Ras-GAP." In these cases the entity occupies only part of what a conventional tokenizer treats as a single word. Annotation guidelines for corpora such as GENETAG (Tanabe et al., 2005) and BioCreative Bio-ID (Arighi et al., 2017) explicitly permit sub-word entity spans, and the JNLPBA corpus (Kim et al., 2004) contains many mentions whose boundaries fall inside whitespace-delimited strings. A model that predicts labels only at the word level cannot, by construction, recover such spans exactly, and under strict-match evaluation each of these errors counts as both a false positive and a false negative. The standard remedy is to rely on specialized tokenization. Biomedical tokenizers apply hand-crafted rules or learned heuristics to split text at hyphens, slashes, digit–letter transitions, and case changes, so that entity boundaries are more likely to coincide with token boundaries (He and Kayaalp, 2006; Jiang and Zhai, 2007; Neumann et al., 2019). Such tokenizers can improve NER performance, but they carry their own costs. They require domain expertise to design and maintain, they are tuned to a particular corpus or entity class, and they introduce a pipeline dependency in which tokenization errors propagate irrecoverably to the tagger. Over-segmentation fragments entities and inflates sequence lengths, while under-segmentation leaves boundary mismatches unresolved. Moreover, a tokenizer optimized for one annotation scheme may not transfer to another, forcing practitioners to redesign rules for each new dataset. Subword representations offer a natural way to relax the dependence on word-level tokenization. Byte-pair encoding (BPE), originally a data compression technique (Gage, 1994), was adapted for neural machine translation to handle rare and unseen words by decomposing them into frequent character sequences (Sennrich et al., 2016). Related approaches include WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016) and the unigram language model (Kudo, 2018), as well as SentencePiece, which operates on raw text without pre-tokenization (Kudo and Richardson, 2018). These methods are widely used in transformer-based language models, including BERT and its biomedical descendants. However, in NER they are typically used only to build input representations; labels are still assigned at the level of whole words, usually by taking the prediction of the first subword piece (Devlin et al., 2019). The subword units thus improve the handling of out-of-vocabulary terms but do not allow the model to predict entity boundaries within a word. Character-level models (Kim et al., 2016; Gillick et al., 2016) can in principle label at arbitrary positions, but they produce long sequences, lack a learned inventory of meaningful units such as morphemes and common biomedical affixes (for example, "-ase," "anti-," or "-mab"), and are often harder to train and scale. This leaves an unaddressed gap. Existing biomedical NER methods either operate at the word level and depend on carefully engineered tokenization to align with entity boundaries, or use subword units merely as inputs while still predicting at the word level. What is missing is an approach in which the units of prediction themselves are learned, subword-sized, and independent of domain-specific tokenization rules, so that entity spans can start and end wherever the data indicate. We therefore ask the following research question: can a model that assigns entity labels directly to BPE units, learned from raw text, recover biomedical entity spans, including those that fall within words, with accuracy competitive with systems that depend on specialized tokenizers? To answer this question, we introduce a subword-level approach to NER that combines BPE segmentation with convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Text is segmented using a BPE vocabulary learned from the training data, with minimal pre-processing. Convolutional layers capture local orthographic and morphological patterns within and across adjacent units, and recurrent layers model longer-range context across the sentence. The network produces a tag for every BPE unit, and these byte-level tags are mapped back to character offsets to yield entity spans that need not align with whitespace-delimited words. Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose a tokenization-agnostic NER architecture that predicts labels at the BPE level, allowing entity boundaries to fall inside words without hand-written splitting rules. Second, we evaluate the approach on three widely used biomedical benchmarks, the BioCreative VI Bio-ID, JNLPBA, and GENETAG corpora, which differ in entity types, annotation conventions, and degree of boundary misalignment. Third, we show that the method achieves competitive performance relative to established systems while eliminating the need for specialized biomedical tokenization expertise. Finally, we analyze the cases in which entity boundaries do not coincide with word boundaries, quantifying how much a conventional word-level approach loses and how much a subword-level approach recovers. Together, these results suggest that moving the unit of prediction from words to learned subword units is a simple and effective way to make biomedical NER more robust and easier to deploy across corpora. Datasets We evaluated on three widely used biomedical NER benchmarks that differ in domain, entity inventory, and annotation conventions. The BioCreative VI Bio-ID corpus (Arighi et al., 2017; Islamaj Doğan et al., 2019) consists of figure legends from open-access articles annotated for multiple entity classes, including genes and proteins, small molecules, cell types and lines, tissues, and organisms. These annotations are normalized to database identifiers, but only the mention spans and coarse types were used here. The JNLPBA shared-task dataset (Kim et al., 2004) derives from the GENIA corpus (Kim et al., 2003) and contains MEDLINE abstracts annotated with five types: protein, DNA, RNA, cell line, and cell type. The GENETAG corpus (Tanabe et al., 2005), as used in BioCreative II Gene Mention (Smith et al., 2008), contains 20,000 MEDLINE sentences annotated for a single gene/protein class, with alternative acceptable boundaries provided for some mentions. We used the official training and test partitions for each dataset. For GENETAG we used the BioCreative II partition of 15,000 training and 5,000 test sentences. A random 10% of each training set, drawn at the document level where document identifiers were available, was held out as a development set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. The test sets were used only for final evaluation. Annotations were converted to character offsets relative to the raw text of each sentence, so that all downstream processing and scoring operated on characters rather than on any dataset-specific tokenization. Subword segmentation Rather than applying a rule-based biomedical tokenizer, we segmented raw text with byte-pair encoding (BPE; Sennrich et al., 2016), following the compression algorithm of Gage (1994). Text was split only at whitespace, and a boundary symbol marked the start of each whitespace-delimited chunk. Punctuation, hyphens, slashes, digits, and parentheses were therefore left for the learned merges to handle. BPE began from a character inventory and iteratively merged the most frequent adjacent symbol pair until a target vocabulary size V was reached. Merges were learned on the training split of each dataset, without the development or test text. For comparison, we also trained a SentencePiece BPE model (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) on the same text, and we found its segmentations to be comparable. We treated V ∈ {500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000} as a hyperparameter. Every BPE unit retained its character start and end offsets in the original string, so a sentence became a sequence of units u₁,…,uₙ with offsets (sᵢ, eᵢ). Because merges are frequency driven, common morphemes such as "-ase", "kappa", or "IL-" often form single units, and entity boundaries that fall inside whitespace-delimited chunks (e.g., "IL-2R-mediated") can be represented whenever a unit boundary coincides with them. Tag scheme and span reconstruction Gold character-level spans were projected onto the BPE units using a BIO scheme with entity types. A unit was labeled B-t if it started an entity of type t, I-t if it lay inside one, and O otherwise. Predicted spans were converted back to character offsets by taking the start offset of the first unit and the end offset of the last unit of each decoded entity. Spans therefore never depended on a word-level tokenizer in either direction. A gold boundary that falls strictly inside a BPE unit cannot be reproduced by this scheme. To quantify the resulting ceiling, we computed an oracle recall for each dataset and each V. This is the fraction of gold entities whose start and end offsets both coincide with unit boundaries. We report this quantity as a diagnostic and as a criterion for choosing V, alongside development F1. For comparison, we computed the same oracle recall for word-level tokenizations from a whitespace tokenizer and from a rule-based biomedical tokenizer (the scispaCy tokenizer; Neumann et al., 2019). Model architecture Each unit uᵢ was mapped to an embedding eᵢ ∈ ℝ^d, with d = 128, initialized randomly (Glorot & Bengio, 2010) and learned jointly with the network. Local subword context was captured by a one-dimensional convolution over the embedding sequence. For a window of half-width k, cᵢ = ReLU( Wc [eᵢ₋ₖ ; … ; eᵢ ; … ; eᵢ₊ₖ] + bc ), where [ ; ] denotes concatenation and sequences were zero-padded at the boundaries. We used parallel filters with widths 1, 3, and 5, each with 128 channels, and concatenated their outputs. The resulting representations were passed to a bidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Graves & Schmidhuber, 2005): hᵢ = [ LSTMfwd(c₁:ᵢ) ; LSTMbwd(cᵢ:ₙ) ], with hidden size 256 per direction and two layers. This convolutional-recurrent design follows earlier neural sequence taggers that combine local convolutional features with recurrent context (Chiu & Nichols, 2016; Ma & Hovy, 2016; Lample et al., 2016). A linear layer and a softmax gave the distribution over tags yᵢ, p(yᵢ | u₁:ₙ) = softmax(Wo hᵢ + bo), and the training objective was the token-level negative log-likelihood 𝓛 = −(1/N) Σ{sentences} Σᵢ log p(yᵢ\ | u₁:ₙ), with N the total number of units. At inference, we used Viterbi decoding restricted to valid BIO transitions, for example disallowing I-t after O or after a different type, to ensure well-formed spans without a separate CRF layer.
