Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), comprising Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract. Prevalence now exceeds 0.3% in North America, Europe, and Oceania, and incidence is rising rapidly in newly industrialized regions of Asia, South America, and the Middle East (Ng et al., 2017; Kaplan, 2015). Pediatric-onset disease is of particular concern. Pediatric incidence has risen in most regions with reliable surveillance data (Benchimol et al., 2011), and children typically present with more extensive disease, growth impairment, and a longer lifetime exposure to inflammation and its therapies. Although advances in biologic therapy have improved outcomes, a substantial proportion of patients do not achieve sustained remission, and the cumulative burden of surgery, hospitalization, and treatment-related adverse events remains high. Identifying modifiable causal factors is therefore a central objective of IBD research. The pathophysiology of IBD is not fully understood, but it is widely accepted to arise from an inappropriate mucosal immune response to intestinal microbes in genetically susceptible hosts, shaped by environmental exposures (Ananthakrishnan, 2015). Genome-wide association studies have identified more than 160 susceptibility loci, many implicating epithelial barrier function, innate microbial sensing, autophagy, and cytokine signaling (Jostins et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015). However, these variants explain only a minority of disease heritability, estimated at approximately 14% for CD and 7.5% for UC (Jostins et al., 2012). The geographic and temporal patterns of IBD, together with its rise in migrants who move to high-incidence regions, point to environmental determinants. Diet is among the most plausible of these, as it directly shapes the intestinal luminal milieu, the composition and metabolic activity of the microbiota, and the integrity of the mucus layer and epithelium (Hou et al., 2011). Among dietary changes associated with industrialization, the growing share of energy derived from ultra-processed foods has attracted attention (Monteiro et al., 2019). In the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology cohort, individuals consuming five or more servings of ultra-processed food daily had an 82% higher risk of incident IBD than those consuming fewer than one serving daily (hazard ratio [HR] 1.82; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.33–2.49) (Narula et al., 2021). Similar associations with CD, but not clearly with UC, were observed in large North American cohorts of health professionals (Lo et al., 2022). The ultra-processed category is heterogeneous, covering refined sugars, saturated fats, low fiber content, and a wide range of industrial additives, so these epidemiological associations cannot identify the causal components. Mechanistic evidence is required to determine whether specific constituents, rather than overall dietary pattern, contribute to intestinal inflammation. Emulsifiers, thickeners, and stabilizers are attractive candidates. They are added in large quantities to improve texture, shelf life, and appearance, and they are consumed daily by many people for decades. Two of the most widely used are carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC). Carrageenan is a family of sulfated galactans extracted from red seaweed and used as a gelling and stabilizing agent (E407) in dairy products, plant-based milks, infant and enteral formulas, processed meats, and desserts. CMC (E466) is a chemically modified, anionic cellulose derivative that serves as a thickener and emulsifier in baked goods, ice cream, sauces, and low-fat products. Both are classified as safe for human consumption by regulatory agencies, and their European re-evaluation in 2018 concluded that exposure at authorized levels was not of concern, though uncertainties were acknowledged regarding the low-molecular-weight fraction of carrageenan and the limited data on additive-specific effects in vulnerable populations (EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food, 2018). These conclusions rest largely on toxicological assessments that do not capture subtle effects on the microbiota, mucosal barrier, or immune signaling, nor effects in a genetically or immunologically predisposed host. The experimental literature on these compounds spans more than five decades. Marcus and Watt (1969) first reported that degraded carrageenan administered in drinking water produced colonic ulceration in guinea pigs and other laboratory animals, and degraded carrageenan has since become a standard method of inducing experimental colitis (Tobacman, 2001). It has been argued that undegraded, food-grade carrageenan differs fundamentally from this low-molecular-weight form (Weiner, 2014), yet in vitro and in vivo studies suggest that food-grade preparations can activate innate immune pathways, including Toll-like receptor 4 and BCL10-dependent nuclear factor-κB signaling, and can induce interleukin-8 expression in human colonic epithelial cells (Bhattacharyya et al., 2008; Bhattacharyya et al., 2010). Similarly, CMC has been shown to promote bacterial overgrowth and inflammation in susceptible mice (Swidsinski et al., 2009) and, in the work of Chassaing and colleagues (2015), to reduce microbial diversity, encroach on the mucus layer, and promote low-grade inflammation and metabolic syndrome in wild-type animals, as well as more severe colitis in genetically predisposed models. Subsequent ex vivo work with human microbiota communities indicated that CMC and other emulsifiers can alter bacterial composition and increase proinflammatory potential (Chassaing et al., 2017), and a small controlled-feeding study in healthy volunteers reported adverse changes in microbiota and metabolome after CMC ingestion (Chassaing et al., 2022). Together, these observations suggest that the additives may act through convergent mechanisms: perturbing microbial ecology, weakening epithelial and mucus barrier function, and amplifying innate immune activation. These findings also bear directly on clinical nutrition. Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) with a polymeric formula is recommended as first-line induction therapy for pediatric CD, achieving remission rates comparable to or higher than corticosteroids with superior mucosal healing and growth outcomes (Ruemmele et al., 2014; Narula et al., 2018). The mechanisms underlying the efficacy of EEN are unclear, and it has been proposed that the exclusion of dietary components, rather than the nutritional composition of the formula alone, may contribute. Dietary strategies such as the Crohn's disease exclusion diet explicitly eliminate emulsifiers and processed foods and have shown efficacy in inducing remission in children (Levine et al., 2019). Relapse after EEN is common upon return to a habitual diet, raising the possibility that reintroduction of specific additives contributes to recurrent inflammation. Moreover, ironically, some commercially available enteral formulas contain carrageenan or CMC, highlighting the lack of consensus on their safety in patients with active disease. Despite the volume of experimental data, the evidence is fragmented. Studies differ in molecular weight and source of carrageenan, dose, duration, route of administration, and animal strain. The relevance of high-dose rodent models to human dietary exposure is contested, and direct interventional trials of these additives in people with IBD are ethically and practically constrained. No recent review has integrated animal, cellular, microbiome, and early human evidence, or considered it in the context of dietary therapy for CD. In this review, we therefore critically appraise the literature on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation. We first summarize their chemistry, patterns of consumption, and regulatory status. We then examine evidence from animal models regarding histopathology, microbiome alterations, epithelial barrier disruption, antimicrobial defenses, and cytokine responses, before evaluating data from human epithelial cell and microbiota studies. Finally, we consider the implications for EEN and other nutritional strategies for inducing and maintaining remission. Our contributions are threefold: a synthesis of mechanistic evidence across experimental systems; an assessment of the strength and limits of translation to human disease, including the likelihood that these additives act as modifiers or amplifiers rather than sole causes of IBD; and identification of priorities for research to determine whether additive restriction could improve prevention and relapse reduction in susceptible individuals. Study design and reporting framework We conducted a structured narrative review of preclinical and human mechanistic evidence on the effects of the food additives carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) on intestinal inflammation. A narrative design was chosen over a quantitative meta-analysis because the available literature is heterogeneous in model systems, additive formulations, doses, exposure durations, and outcome measures. The review was planned and reported in line with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) criteria (Baethge et al., 2019). The search, screening, and selection processes were documented according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement to maximize transparency and reproducibility (Page et al., 2021). The review was not prospectively registered. Because it used only published data, institutional review board approval was not required. Review questions Four questions guided the review. First, do carrageenan and CMC induce histopathological or clinical features of intestinal inflammation in animal models? Second, through which mechanisms might they act, including alteration of the gut microbiota, disruption of the epithelial barrier and mucus layer, impairment of antimicrobial defenses, and activation of pro-inflammatory signaling? Third, do studies of human cells, human-derived microbial communities, or human dietary exposure support these findings? Fourth, what are the implications for dietary strategies in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), particularly exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) with polymeric formulas and the prevention of relapse after EEN? Information sources and search strategy We searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from database inception to [month, year]. We also searched Scopus and Google Scholar to capture additional records. The search combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH and Emtree terms) and free-text keywords in three concept blocks. The first covered the additives: carrageenan, carrageenin, Irish moss, E407, carboxymethylcellulose, carboxymethyl cellulose, cellulose gum, sodium CMC, E466, polysorbate, and food additive. The second covered the outcomes: inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, colitis, intestinal inflammation, enteritis, ileitis, intestinal permeability, and epithelial barrier. The third covered the mechanisms and models: microbiota, microbiome, dysbiosis, mucus, cytokine, Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, Bcl10, Caco-2, organoid, in vitro, mouse, rat, guinea pig, rabbit, and human. Boolean operators combined the blocks, and syntax was adapted to each database. We also searched for dietary context with terms such as enteral nutrition, polymeric formula, ultra-processed food, Western diet, and pediatric. We hand-searched the reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews, and used forward citation tracking of seminal studies, including the early work on degraded carrageenan and experimental colitis and subsequent reports on dietary emulsifiers and CMC (Chassaing et al., 2015; Swidsinski et al., 2009; Tobacman, 2001), to identify additional eligible publications. Eligibility criteria We included peer-reviewed, English-language original studies that met at least one of the following criteria: (i) in vivo animal studies in which carrageenan or CMC was administered orally, in drinking water, or in feed, with intestinal inflammation, histology, barrier function, or microbiota assessed; (ii) in vitro or ex vivo studies using human or animal intestinal epithelial cells, immune cells, organoids, or intestinal tissue exposed to either additive; (iii) studies of human fecal or mucosal microbiota, including ex vivo or in vitro fermentation and continuous-culture models, exposed to either additive; and (iv) human studies, whether observational, dietary, or interventional, reporting exposure to either additive and a gastrointestinal or inflammatory outcome. Studies in which carrageenan was injected into subcutaneous tissue, the paw, or the pleural cavity as a generic inflammatory stimulus were excluded because they do not model intestinal exposure. We also excluded studies in which the additives served only as excipients or delivery vehicles for another therapeutic agent without a vehicle-only control group. Conference abstracts without full data, editorials, and commentaries were not eligible, although review articles were used to contextualize findings and to identify primary sources. Where several reports described the same experimental cohort, the most complete report was retained. Study selection and data extraction Records were exported to a reference manager and deduplicated. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then full texts, using the web-based platform Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016). Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, where necessary, by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the full-text stage was quantified with Cohen’s kappa and interpreted according to Landis and Koch (1977) and McHugh (2012). Two reviewers independently extracted data into a standardized, piloted form. For animal studies, we recorded species, strain, sex, age, and genetic background (e.g., wild-type, Il10-deficient, or Tlr5-deficient); additive type and molecular characteristics (carrageenan subtype, such as kappa, iota, or lambda, and native versus degraded “poligeenan” form; CMC degree of substitution and molecular weight); dose, vehicle, route, and duration of exposure; and inflammatory outcomes. Process maps provide a high-level overview of an organization’s business processes. While used for many years in different shapes and forms, there is little shared understanding of the concept and its relationship to enterprise architecture. In this report, we position the concept of business process map within the domain of enterprise architecture. Based on literature, we provide a conceptualization of the process map as a business process architecture model that can be integrated with the broader enterprise architecture model. From our conceptualization we derive requirements for designing a meta-model of a modelling language for process maps. The design of this meta-model is the subject of a research paper, entitled Architecting Business Process Maps, for which this report acts as a complement that details the underlying process map conceptualization. Keywords: Process map, Business process architecture, Enterprise architecture, Architecture description, Conceptualization. Business Process Architecture (BPA) has recently received attention in Business Process Management (BPM) research [1]. BPA refers to the fundamental organization of an enterprise’s system of business processes. In the Enterprise Architecture (EA) field, the business process architecture is considered part of the business layer of an organization’s enterprise architecture, while in the BPM field it is presented as an artefact that results from the BPM lifecycle process identification phase during which the organisation’s business processes are identified and prioritised [2]. Whereas the purpose of the business process architecture in BPM is to single out the processes that will be subjected to further BPM lifecycle activities, in EA the business process architecture is essential for analysing and improving enterprise coherence, enterprise agility, business/IT alignment and strategic fit [3, 4]. In BPM, a model describing (part of) the business process architecture is commonly, though not uniquely referred to as a process map [5]. The concept of process map as a holistic and abstract representation of an organisation’s interrelated business processes, has only recently been investigated [6], while being in use for many years in different shapes and forms. In practice, there is little shared understanding of the concept, related to its contents, form and purpose. According to [7], the current variety in process maps that can be observed might be due to the lack of modelling language dedicated to expressing process maps. The need for designing such language, preferably building upon a general-purpose modelling language, has been expressed by different researchers [1, 8, 9]. Apart from the lack of specific modelling language for process maps, there is unclarity in the conceptualisation of the process map in relation to EA. In BPM, process maps are not integrated in broader enterprise architecture descriptions. Consequently, they cannot be exploited at full scale for aligning BPM initiatives with an organization’s architectural vision. The goal of the research presented in this report is to provide a conceptualization of process maps in the context of EA by considering a modelling language for process maps as an architecture description language. As a result, we conceptualize the process map as an enterprise architecture artefact and present requirements for a business process architecture description language that can be used to represent process maps. The design of a meta-model for such language is the subject of a research paper, entitled Architecting Business Process Maps, for which this report acts as complement that details the underlying process map conceptualization. The remainder of this report is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the methodology we used for conceptualizing process maps. Sections 3 to 8 present the concepts deemed relevant for concept maps. Finally, section 9 presents the conclusion. We performed a literature review of research on modelling of business process architecture. Research presenting requirements for process maps, informal solutions, and reviews of design approaches for business process architecture was analysed. The result was an inference of different perspectives of process maps in relation to business process architecture, indicating basically a lack of ‘architectural point of view’ in BPA research, which motivated our research. The primary basis for the conceptual analysis of the process map concept was the process map meta-model of Malinova and Mendling [6], which is to the best of our knowledge unique in its kind. The proposed meta-model is positioned by its designers as a model of a process map conceptualization rather than a formal meta-model defining a modelling language for process maps, which makes it a valuable starting point for our conceptual analysis. Its foundation in BPM research results, however, in a number of assumptions related to the use of process maps prior to BPM implementation (i.e., process identification) and during BPM implementation (i.e., process model management). Specifically, the meta-model conceptualizes the process map as an entry-level model of a hierarchically structured business process models architecture instead of a model of the business process architecture. We therefore build our conceptual analysis also on other related work that, although less elaborate than the work of Malinova and Mendling, positions the process map as an abstraction of the business process architecture rather than as part of a hierarchical structure of business process models. We support our literature-based analysis through the use of concept maps, a well-known tool for expressing and sharing knowledge, using the free CmapTools knowledge modelling kit (https://cmap.ihmc.us/cmaptools/). The central concept of the process map is the Process. Consistent with most of the reviewed literature, we explicitly chose here for the process map as a black-box model of (part of) the system of business processes of an organization that does not show interior details of these processes. Note that this makes the process map concept different from its definition in the BPM textbook of Dumas et al. [2] as they consider it an abstract process model showing main activities and sequence flows, whereas the model that depicts processes as atomic elements is what they call the process landscape model, which is positioned at the top of their hierarchically structured business process models architecture. To further avoid such terminology confusion, we propose the following solution requirement consistent with our research goal of designing a general representation language for process maps within the context of our enterprise architecture description conceptual frame of reference: Req. 1: The business process is the atomic element of the process map. We further motivate this requirement by the existence of business process modelling languages (e.g., BPMN), which can be used to model business processes at more fine-grained levels of modelling abstraction [10]. Hence, there is no need for a modelling language for process maps to model such finer-grained elements like tasks and gateways. Following Van Nuffel and De Backer [9], the process map should thus only be a black-box model of the organizational processes. Besides from processes, a process map may show other things and events related to the processes. Processes are triggered by inputs and yield outputs. An Input is a request to do something (i.e., start process execution) that can be accompanied by data or physical objects. An Output is a tangible product flowing out the process or an intangible result that is the effect of the process execution, in which case the output is commonly referred to as an outcome (e.g., staff trained as a result of a training process, deliverable validated as a result of a validation process) [11]. Such inputs, outputs and outcomes might be shown in a process map [7], though this is not common as it depends on the desired level of abstraction at which the business process architecture is described. A business process included in a process map can use one or more resources and can have one or more actors responsible for it, which again can be shown or not shown (depending on the desired level of abstraction). A Resource refers to any means used during process execution to transform inputs into outputs. An Actor is defined as being responsible for the process, e.g., someone in the process manager role [6]. For instance, Van Nuffel and De Backer [9] distinguish a process owner view of the business process architecture in which the process map clearly identifies process ownership. In other examples of process maps also organizational units or business functions are identified as being involved in process execution, see e.g., [1, 2, 5]. Physical persons or organizational units (e.g., departments, project teams) having certain functions and responsibilities in the organization are typically included in enterprise architecture models, hence linking them explicitly with processes according to specific roles towards business processes (i.e., as actor or resource) connects or even integrates business process architecture models with(in) enterprise architecture models. Figure 1 summarizes the relationships between business processes and the concepts discussed in this section. Figure 2 shows a concept map about how customers trigger business processes through the inputs they provide. A Customer is the beneficiary of the business process, which means that the output of the process is somehow of benefit to the customer. Based on the meta-model of Malinova and Mendling [6], the concept map distinguishes internally and externally triggered business processes. It is shown that business processes can be triggered either by external customers, meaning customers outside the organization, or by internal customers which can be employees (in a certain role towards the business process) or other processes of the organization. Externally triggered processes produce output for external customers, whereas internally triggered processes produce output that is used by internal customers. Externally triggered processes can act as internal customer for an internally triggered process, which then produces internally consumed outputs. To eventually get outputs delivered to external customers, some decomposition relation between externally triggered processes and internally triggered processes is needed (not shown in Figure 2). We come back to relations between business processes in section 8. Representing customers of process outputs on process maps is not uncommon, see e.g., [5, 8], though it depends again on the desired abstraction level at which the business process architecture is described, which is, apart from [9], not explicitly defined in the BPA literature that we reviewed. Other relevant process-related concepts found in process maps are service and object. While service is not defined in the reviewed BPA literature, in Service Science, service is defined as an act provided by a party to a beneficiary [12]. In the context of BPA, we accordingly define Service as the benefits experienced by the customer of a business process. These benefits inhere in the outputs produced by the process (see Figure 3). While Malinova and Mendling [6] consider only employees as beneficiaries, it is not uncommon to define provided services as an essential property of business process architecture, regardless whether the service beneficiaries are internal or external to the organization [1]. In the reviewed BPA literature, it is very common to observe in business process architecture models the objects that are affected by business processes [1, 5, 9]. An Object represented in a process map can have a variety of meanings. Dijkman, Vanderfeesten and Reijers [1] even identify a separate object-based class of business process architecture design approaches (i.e., architecture frameworks) that provide guidelines to derive a business process architecture from a business object model (e.g., the RIVA process architecture framework [13] or the fractal enterprise model [8]). Dijkman, Vanderfeesten and Reijers [1] also distinguish between permanent objects (e.g., a client that is being helped) and case objects (e.g., an order that is being processes), and the reference in [6] to a process flow unit seems to refer to the latter interpretation, although process flow units may also include abstract objects (e.g., product quality). Clearly, whatever interpretation is used, objects are closely linked to inputs and outputs or even to both (e.g., the object is input to the process which changes or transforms it, adding value to it, and returns it again as output, where the value added is the service provided by the process to the customer). Resources used or consumed in business processes (e.g., general supplies like computers and office materials) can be objects of other processes (e.g., the general supplies purchasing, management, maintenance, security, etc., processes)

Introduction The escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a profound threat to public health, both in developed and developing countries (World Health Organization, 2014). Recognized as a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, AMR complicates the treatment of infectious diseases, leading to prolonged illness and increased healthcare costs (Davies and Davies, 2010). The daunting reality of AMR continues to hinder efforts to control bacterial diseases, thereby challenging the efficacy of current pharmaceutical interventions (Livermore, 2004). In Cameroon, a country with a high burden of infectious diseases, the effective management of AMR is increasingly critical. However, AMR surveillance in Cameroon remains insufficiently developed, resulting in a paucity of reliable data to guide public health interventions (Nnadozie et al., 2020). A One Health perspective emphasizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health, offering a comprehensive framework to tackle AMR (Zinsstag et al., 2011). This approach acknowledges the complex interactions that exist between these domains, facilitating the spread of resistant pathogens across different settings (Friedman, 2015). In particular, the agricultural sector's use of antibiotics in livestock has been implicated in accelerating AMR's spread beyond clinical settings, further complicating efforts to curb its influence (Silbergeld et al., 2008). The significance of cross-sectoral AMR surveillance is underscored by the global interconnectedness of health determinants, necessitating an inclusive strategy that encompasses all relevant domains. The complexity of AMR in Cameroon reflects a multifaceted challenge. Despite global attention, there exists a critical gap in understanding the breadth and depth of AMR within this region (Tansarli et al., 2013). Previous studies largely focus on isolated parameters within human health, neglecting the veterinary and environmental aspects that are integral to a holistic understanding of AMR dynamics (van den Bogaard and Stobberingh, 1999). Current diagnostics and reporting mechanisms are fragmented, highlighting an urgent need for standardized practices that can reliably inform treatment protocols (Okeke et al., 2005). The research questions underpinning this study seek to elucidate the current status of AMR in Cameroon from a One Health perspective: How prevalent is AMR in human, animal, and environmental settings across different regions of Cameroon? What are the most commonly reported resistant pathogens, and which antibiotics are these pathogens resistant to? To what extent does multidrug resistance (MDR) prevail in these contexts? By delineating these dimensions, the study aims to offer insights into the AMR landscape that can guide effective interventions and policy formulations. A systematic review and meta-analysis of existing literature provides robust methodology for addressing these questions. Drawing on data from diverse regional studies across Centre, South-West, West, Littoral, and other regions, this research consolidates findings to present an accurate picture of AMR prevalence (Moher et al., 2009). Proactive data collection, encompassing sources in English and French, ensures comprehensive coverage, while PRISMA guidelines aid in maintaining methodological rigor (Liberati et al., 2009). Analyzing pathogen-antibiotic pairs and calculating pooled prevalence rates present quantifiable measures of the resistance levels extant within Cameroon. This study contributes to existing literature by offering a nuanced exploration of AMR from a One Health perspective. By integrating human, animal, and environmental health considerations, this research highlights the pervasive nature of AMR across sectors. Investigation into multidrug resistance rates among prevalent bacterial species such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus spp, and Salmonella spp elucidates key points of concern that warrant immediate attention (Paterson, 2006). The findings indicate staggering levels of resistance, necessitating an urgent call to action to optimize health strategies. The need to standardize AMR diagnostics and reporting is crucial. Recognizing this, the review underscores the importance of effective surveillance, which can facilitate large-scale collaboration and coordination among stakeholders (Goossens, 2005). Harmonizing efforts across disciplines is vital for deploying integrated solutions that mitigate the AMR burden nationwide. These measures are imperative for optimizing antibiotic treatment guidelines and ultimately protecting public health from the adverse effects of resistant pathogens. In summary, this study delivers an authoritative account of AMR prevalence in Cameroon, advocating for enhanced multi-sectoral collaboration to combat this dilemma. The urgency to address diagnostic gaps and optimize antibiotic usage guidelines is requisite for sustaining public health gains. As AMR continues to subvert health outcomes globally, this comprehensive review accentuates the pivotal role of coordinated action in driving impactful change. A concerted commitment to AMR surveillance and management will indubitably pave the way for deeper understanding and efficacious solutions to safeguard future generations from the insidious threat of antimicrobial resistance. This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to assess the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Cameroon from a One Health perspective. Our approach encompassed resistance patterns in humans, animals, and the environment. The methodology employed adhered strictly to the guidelines provided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) (Moher et al., 2009). Data Sources and Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was performed across multiple databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, and African Journals Online (AJOL). The search covered articles published in English and French to ensure inclusivity and breadth. We developed and utilized a structured search string containing keywords such as "antimicrobial resistance," "Cameroon," "One Health," "bacterial infections," and specific antibiotic classes (e.g., beta-lactams, aminoglycosides) to maximize retrieval of relevant studies. Additionally, the search was expanded to include free-text and grey literature by contacting authors directly and exploring institutional webpages that might host unpublished theses and reports pertinent to the subject matter. Study Selection The study eligibility criteria were defined based on scope, study period, language, and relevance. Inclusion criteria mandated studies to be conducted in Cameroon, examine AMR in humans, animals, or the environment, and report quantitative data on resistance outcomes. Studies were excluded if they did not provide adequate data on specific pathogen-antibiotic combinations, focused merely on efficacy without resistance data, were reviews without original data, or localized outside Cameroon. The initial search yielded a total of 97 full-text articles, of which 66 met all criteria after a thorough two-step review process. The screening was conducted independently by two reviewers to minimize bias. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus with a third senior reviewer serving as the arbiter. Data Extraction and Management Data extraction was standardized using a pre-defined protocol, recording essential details such as study design, geographic location within Cameroon, pathogen studied, antibiotics tested, sample source (human, animal, environment), and the prevalence of resistance. These details were input into an electronic database designed to facilitate subsequent analysis. This also enabled cross-checking for consistency and completeness. Statistical Analysis This meta-analysis was primarily aimed at calculating pooled prevalence estimates for AMR across different species-antibiotic combinations. The analysis utilized random-effects models due to the anticipated heterogeneity across studies sourced from diverse geographic regions and differing study methodologies (DerSimonian and Laird, 1986). Random-effects models accommodate variation across studies, providing a more generalized inference applicable across different settings within Cameroon. The statistical software package employed was the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) Version 3, which was selected for its robustness in handling diverse meta-analytic computations, including subgroup analysis and meta-regression to trace sources of heterogeneity (Borenstein et al., 2009). Quantitative synthesis focused on pathogen-antibiotic pairs reported in multiple studies. The extracted resistance rates were computed with corresponding 95% confidence intervals for each bacterial species. We also assessed multidrug resistance (MDR) prevalence defined as resistance to three or more antibiotic classes. Assessment of Bias and Sensitivity Analysis Publication bias was assessed using funnel plot analysis and Egger’s test (Egger et al., 1997). Funnel plots visualize study effect sizes and precision, with overt asymmetry suggesting potential bias. A sensitivity analysis was performed by iteratively excluding studies with extreme values to gauge the robustness of pooled estimates. Cases with large variance or small sample size were noted, and their exclusion was considered if they disproportionately skewed results. Heterogeneity Evaluation Heterogeneity was quantified using the I-squared statistic, which describes the percentage of total variation across studies attributable to heterogeneity rather than chance (Higgins et al., 2003). A high I-squared value indicated substantial heterogeneity, necessitating further exploration via subgroup analysis according to the type of sample source (human, animal, environment) and the region within Cameroon. Through these meticulously structured methods, this review and meta-analysis aimed to deliver a comprehensive assessment of AMR in Cameroon, providing crucial data for strategizing public health interventions. The systematic design ensures that findings are robust, reproducible, and applicable to future models guiding AMR surveillance enhancement in low-resource contexts. The systematic review and meta-analysis encompassed a comprehensive evaluation of 97 full-text articles, with 66 studies meeting the predetermined eligibility criteria. These studies were sourced from various regions within Cameroon, highlighting a diverse geographical representation. Specifically, the distribution of studies included the Centre region with 24 studies (36.4%), the South-West with 16 studies (24.2%), the West with 13 studies (19.7%), and the Littoral with 9 studies (13.6%), alongside 4 studies (6.1%) from other regions. This geographic dispersion reflects an inclusive examination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across the nation. The studies spanned different sectors, encompassing human health, animal health, and environmental health, aligning with the One Health framework. Of these, 45 studies (68.2%) investigated AMR within human populations, 9 studies (13.6%) focused on animal subjects, and 12 studies (18.2%) evaluated environmental samples. This tripartite approach underscores the interconnected nature of AMR across different ecological niches. In terms of bacterial species assessed, the review identified a total of 19 species tested against 48 distinct antibiotics, demonstrating significant bacterial diversity and resistance profiles. Key bacterial species frequently reported included Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus spp. Within the human studies, E. coli was the most investigated pathogen, appearing in 23 studies, followed by K. pneumoniae in 19 studies, and Staphylococcus spp in 18 studies. The pooled prevalence of multidrug resistance (MDR) for E. coli was calculated at 47.1% with a 95% confidence interval [CI] of 37.3–57.2%. K. pneumoniae exhibited a slightly higher MDR prevalence of 51.0% [95% CI, 42.0–59.9%], while Staphylococcus spp showed an MDR rate of 45.2% [95% CI, 38.0–54.7%]. These findings illuminate the considerable MDR challenge posed by these pathogens in human health contexts. In the animal studies subset, six studies reported on Salmonella spp, demonstrating an MDR rate of 46.2% [95% CI, 39.2–53.5%]. This finding is concerning as it reflects the potential for zoonotic transmission of resistant strains from animals to humans, thus complicating treatment regimens further. Environmental samples, analyzed in 12 studies, predominantly featured Staphylococcus spp, showcasing a notably high MDR prevalence of 67.1% [95% CI, 55.2–77.2%]. This marked resistance in environmental isolates highlights the broader ecological implications of AMR, suggesting environmental reservoirs as significant sources of resistant bacteria. Upon further analysis of antibiotic classes, resistance was observed across all major categories, emphasizing the extensive scope of this problem. Aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, and tetracyclines were among the antibiotics with noted resistance patterns. Notably, resistance rates exceeding 50% were consistently observed across these classes, further substantiating the critical levels of resistance faced in both clinical and non-clinical settings (Nguyen et al., 2022; Osei et al., 2021). A significant observation was the prevalence of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing strains among Enterobacteriaceae, reported in 28.5% [95% CI, 22.1–35.6%] of the studies, indicating a pervasive issue within this bacterial group. This finding is pivotal as ESBL production is frequently associated with resistance to third-generation cephalosporins, a common treatment for severe infections (Li et al., 2020). Statistical analysis using random-effects models corroborated the heterogeneity across studies, likely attributable to variations in study design, population demographics, and regional prescribing practices. I^2 statistics for studies on E. coli and K. pneumoniae suggested substantial heterogeneity (E. coli: I^2 = 78%, p < 0.01; K. pneumoniae: I^2 = 81%, p < 0.01), necessitating careful interpretation of the pooled estimates and further underscoring the complexity of AMR as a multifaceted issue across Cameroon. These results collectively delineate a pressing public health challenge characterized by high levels of AMR in Cameroon. The prevalence of MDR strains across human, animal, and environmental sectors suggests an urgent call for enhanced surveillance, standardized diagnostic protocols, and an integrated response incorporating policy makers, health professionals, and the agricultural sector. Through strategic, coordinated effort and knowledge dissemination, Cameroon can combat the burgeoning threat of AMR effectively. The systematic review

Lactococcus lactis is the principal component of the mesophilic starter cultures used worldwide in the manufacture of cheese and other fermented dairy products. Starter bacteria are responsible for the rapid conversion of lactose into lactic acid, which controls spoilage and pathogenic microbiota, drives curd formation and syneresis, and contributes to the development of texture and flavor (Smid and Kleerebezem 2014). Besides acidification, L. lactis contributes to flavor through proteolytic and peptidolytic activities, amino acid catabolism, and the production of diacetyl, acetoin and other volatile compounds derived from citrate and pyruvate metabolism (Smit et al. 2005; Cocaign-Bousquet et al. 2002). The success of a dairy fermentation therefore depends on the viability and metabolic activity of the starter, and strains must withstand a sequence of stresses, first during starter production, concentration and storage (freezing, freeze-drying, cold storage), and later during cheese manufacture (heat, osmotic, acid and oxidative stress) (van de Guchte et al. 2002; Papadimitriou et al. 2016). Oxidative stress is one of the least appreciated but most pervasive of these challenges. Although L. lactis is aerotolerant, it lacks a complete respiratory chain unless exogenous heme is supplied, and it possesses a limited set of defenses against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Duwat et al. 2001). In the presence of oxygen, flavoprotein oxidases such as NADH oxidase, together with pyruvate oxidase and other enzymes, generate hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, which damage DNA, proteins and membrane lipids and cause growth arrest and loss of viability (Rochat et al. 2006). Milk is aerated during handling, and oxygen is introduced during pumping, stirring and vat filling, while the large-scale propagation of starters is frequently carried out under non-anaerobic conditions. Oxygen also influences the metabolic fate of pyruvate, diverting flux from lactate towards acetate, acetoin and diacetyl, with implications for flavor (Lan et al. 2006). Strains with improved oxygen tolerance are thus of practical interest, as they could display more consistent performance in industrial environments and might provide an additional route to modulate aroma formation. Cultivation under respiratory conditions, i.e. in the presence of heme and oxygen, improves biomass yield and robustness (Duwat et al. 2001; Pedersen et al. 2012), but it requires specific process modifications and is not applicable to all dairy applications. Strain improvement in food microorganisms is constrained by regulation and consumer perception, and genetically modified organisms are not widely accepted in the dairy sector. Consequently, non-recombinant approaches such as spontaneous mutant selection and adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) are attractive alternatives (Bachmann et al. 2012). ALE exploits the capacity of bacteria to acquire beneficial mutations under sustained selective pressure, and it has been used to improve industrially relevant traits in lactic acid bacteria, including acid and thermal tolerance, osmotolerance, growth in specific substrates, and bacteriophage resistance (Derkx et al. 2014; Zhu et al. 2020). A particularly interesting feature of this approach is that selection under one stress frequently results in cross-protection against other stresses, as a result of the overlap in cellular responses and of global regulatory changes (Mols and Abee 2011). Selecting for a trait that depends on a global physiological response, such as the integrity and remodeling of the cell envelope, could therefore be a way to obtain strains with generally more robust phenotypes. The cell envelope is the first barrier against environmental insults, and its stress response is well characterized in L. lactis. Envelope-targeting agents trigger the CesSR and other two-component systems, which induce a regulon that includes genes involved in cell wall biosynthesis, modification of the envelope and protein quality control (Martínez et al. 2007; Roces et al. 2012). Lcn972 is a non-lantibiotic bacteriocin produced by L. lactis IPLA972 that inhibits cell wall biosynthesis in sensitive lactococci by binding to lipid II, the cell wall precursor, at the septum, thereby impairing septum formation and cell division (Martínez et al. 1996; Martínez et al. 2008; Roces et al. 2009). Its narrow spectrum, restricted to L. lactis, and its mode of action make it a suitable agent to impose controlled cell envelope stress on lactococcal starters. Previous work has shown that the response to Lcn972 involves the CesSR system, the overexpression of the stress-inducible protein encoded by the lcn972 resistance-associated locus, and the activation of genes of unknown function, and that spontaneous resistant mutants carry mutations affecting sugar metabolism, in particular the phosphotransferase system component ptnD, as well as other envelope-related genes (Roces et al. 2012; Kramer et al. 2008; Tymoszewska et al. 2017). Notably, resistance to Lcn972 in mutants of the laboratory strain L. lactis IPLA947 or its derivatives has been linked to altered growth, cell wall properties and metabolic regulation, which in turn may influence how cells handle other stresses (Roces et al. 2012). Whether resistance to cell wall-active bacteriocins can be harnessed to improve technological robustness of an industrial starter has not been explored. The strain L. lactis IPLA947 is a well-characterized, phage-resistant dairy starter used in the manufacture of artisanal and industrial cheeses, with good acidifying properties and a genome that has been sequenced and annotated (Rodríguez-Alonso et al. 2009; Flórez et al. 2016). Given its industrial relevance, it is an appropriate model on which to test whether cell envelope stress-driven adaptive evolution may generate variants with enhanced technological traits. Importantly, any improvement in stress tolerance must not come at the expense of the core functions of the starter, namely rapid acidification, a stable lactose-to-lactate conversion and an adequate contribution to flavor. Trade-offs between stress resistance and growth, which are well described for mutants affected in global regulators or in carbon catabolite control (Ferenci 2016), can render stress-tolerant variants useless for dairy applications. In this work, we applied adaptive evolution under cell envelope stress by consecutive exposure of L. lactis IPLA947 to increasing doses of Lcn972, and we screened the resulting derivatives for cross-protection against oxidative stress. We hypothesized that resistance to this envelope-active bacteriocin would select for variants with modified envelope physiology and/or metabolic regulation that would confer a more robust phenotype in the presence of oxygen. We characterized the selected mutant, L. lactis R5, regarding its survival after hydrogen peroxide challenge, its growth in aerobic and respiratory conditions, and its tolerance to the stresses encountered during starter production and storage, namely cold storage and freeze-drying. We then evaluated its performance as a dairy starter in aerated milk cultures, its acidification kinetics, its lactose consumption and organic acid production, and the profile of volatile compounds in experimental cheese curds. Our results show that Lcn972 resistance can be used to obtain a stable, oxygen-tolerant derivative that retains the technological properties of the parental strain and displays an enhanced capacity to produce acetoin, supporting the use of cell envelope stress as a driver of intra-strain diversification in industrial lactococci. Materials and Methods Bacterial strains, media and growth conditions Lactococcus lactis subsp. lactis IPLA947, a dairy starter strain from the IPLA-CSIC collection, was the parental strain. Cultures were routinely grown at 30 °C without shaking in M17 broth (Oxoid) supplemented with 0.5% glucose (GM17) or in reconstituted skim milk (RSM, 10% w/v; Scharlau) for milk experiments. Stocks were stored at −80 °C in 20% glycerol. Lcn972 was produced and partially purified from L. lactis IPLA972 supernatants by cation-exchange chromatography, as described previously (Martínez et al. 1996), and its activity was quantified by the agar well diffusion assay against L. lactis subsp. cremoris MG1363 and expressed in arbitrary units (AU) per ml. Where indicated, hemin (5 µg/ml) was added to GM17 to promote respiratory metabolism (Duwat et al. 2001). Adaptive evolution under Lcn972 stress Adaptive evolution was carried out by consecutive exposure to Lcn972. An overnight culture of IPLA947 was diluted 1:100 in GM17 containing a sub-inhibitory concentration of Lcn972 (initially 0.5× the minimum inhibitory concentration, MIC), incubated for 24 h, and transferred daily into fresh medium with the bacteriocin concentration raised stepwise whenever growth was visible (OD600 > 0.5). MIC was determined by broth microdilution in 96-well plates, defined as the lowest concentration preventing visible growth after 24 h. After about 30 transfers (approximately 200 generations), the final population was plated on GM17 agar, and isolated colonies were tested for Lcn972 MIC. Clones with the highest MIC were selected and passaged ten times (about 70 generations) in GM17 without bacteriocin to test phenotypic stability; MIC was re-determined after this passage. One stable clone, designated R5, was selected for further characterization. Strain identity relative to the parent was confirmed by RAPD-PCR fingerprinting with primer OPA-3 (Ward and Roberts 1994) and by confirmation of the absence of bacteriophage-induced changes through plaque assays. Hydrogen peroxide challenge Exponential-phase cultures (OD600 ≈ 0.5) of IPLA947 and R5 were harvested, washed twice in 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), and resuspended to approximately 10^8 CFU/ml. Hydrogen peroxide (Sigma) was added to final concentrations of 5–20 mM and cells were incubated at 30 °C for 30 min. Residual H2O2 was neutralized with catalase (100 U/ml), and viable counts were determined by plating serial dilutions on GM17 agar. Survival was expressed as S (%) = (Nt / N0) × 100, where Nt and N0 are CFU/ml after and before treatment, respectively. Log reductions, log10(N0/Nt), were also calculated. Growth under aerobic and anaerobic conditions Growth was monitored in GM17 in 250 ml flasks containing 50 ml of medium incubated at 30 °C with orbital shaking at 200 rpm (aerobic) or static in sealed tubes filled to the top (limited oxygen). OD600 was recorded every hour and specific growth rates (µ, h⁻¹) were obtained from the slope of ln(OD600) versus time during the exponential phase: µ = (ln OD₂ − ln OD₁)/(t₂ − t₁). Dissolved oxygen was measured with a fiber-optic oxygen sensor (PreSens) in selected experiments. To assess respiratory metabolism, the same experiments were performed in GM17 with and without hemin, and growth, final OD600, and biomass were compared. Milk acidification RSM was inoculated with 1% (v/v) of overnight cultures washed in sterile saline, or at ~10^6 CFU/ml, and incubated at 30 °C. For aerated cultures, 100 ml of milk in 500 ml flasks was shaken at 200 rpm, whereas static incubation in filled bottles served as the low-oxygen control. pH was recorded continuously with a data logger (CINAC system; Spinnler and Corrieu 1989) or measured at defined intervals. The maximum acidification rate (Vmax, pH units/min), time to reach pH 5.3 (t5.3), and final pH after 24 h were calculated from the pH curves. Survival during cold storage and freeze-drying For cold storage, cells from stationary-phase cultures were harvested, resuspended in RSM or in 0.9% NaCl, and stored at 4 °C for 28 days; viable counts were determined weekly. Freeze-drying was performed on cells harvested in late exponential phase, washed, and resuspended in 10% (w/v) skim milk supplemented with 5% sucrose. Aliquots (1 ml) were frozen at −80 °C for 2 h and lyophilized for 24 h (Telstar Lyoquest). Survival was calculated as the ratio of CFU/ml after versus before freeze-drying, after rehydration in the original volume of sterile water, and viability was also monitored after 1 and 3 months of storage at 4 °C. Avian influenza (AI) is a significant threat to animal and human health worldwide, with the potential to cause substantial economic losses and morbidity (Swayne, 2008). The disease is caused by influenza A viruses, which are classified into different subtypes based on the hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) proteins on the surface of the virus (Webster et al., 1992). Some subtypes, such as H5 and H7, have been associated with high mortality in poultry and have the potential to be transmitted to humans, making them a concern for public health (Capua & Alexander, 2009). The highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) epidemic that occurred in Europe in 2016/2017 was caused by the A(H5N8) subtype and resulted in significant outbreaks in poultry and wild birds, highlighting the need for continued surveillance and monitoring of AI (Europen Food Safety Authority, 2017). The 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe was the largest ever recorded in the European Union (EU) in terms of the number of poultry outbreaks, geographical extent, and number of dead wild birds (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). The epidemic affected 29 European countries and resulted in significant economic losses to the poultry industry (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). The primary incursions of the virus were temporally related to all major poultry sectors, but secondary spread was most commonly associated with domestic waterfowl species (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). The massive effort of all affected EU Member States (MSs) allowed for a descriptive epidemiological overview of the cases in poultry, captive birds, and wild birds, providing valuable information on measures applied at the individual MS level (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). Despite the significance of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, there is a gap in the current understanding of the epidemiology of AI, particularly with regards to the risk factors associated with the spread of the disease (Swayne, 2008). The lack of data on poultry population structure is a significant limitation in facilitating data and risk factor analysis, which is necessary to provide science-based advice to risk managers (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). Furthermore, there is a need for a common understanding and application of definitions related to control activities and their reporting across MSs, which would facilitate a more coordinated and effective response to AI outbreaks (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). The research question that guides this study is: What are the epidemiological characteristics of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, and what are the implications for the prevention and control of AI in the EU? This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, including the epidemiological characteristics of the outbreak, the measures applied by MSs, and the implications for the prevention and control of AI in the EU. The study will also examine the potential risk of long-distance spread of HPAI virus A(H5N6) from Asia to wintering grounds towards Western Europe, as well as the HPAI situation in Africa with A(H5N8) and A(H5N1) (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, which is essential for understanding the epidemiology of AI and informing the development of effective control measures (Swayne, 2008). Secondly, it highlights the importance of strengthening collaborations at national, EU, and global levels to monitor the AI situation and increase preparedness (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). Finally, it emphasizes the need for improved collection and reporting of exposure events of people to AI, which is critical for understanding the risk of transmission of AI viruses to humans (Capua & Alexander, 2009). Overall, this study aims to contribute to the understanding of AI epidemiology and the development of effective control measures, ultimately helping to reduce the impact of AI on animal and human health. The significance of this study is further underscored by the fact that no human case was reported in the EU due to AI subtypes A(H5N1), A(H5N6), A(H7N9), and A(H9N2) during the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). However, direct transmission of these viruses to humans has been reported in areas, mainly in Asia and Egypt, with a substantial involvement of wild bird and/or poultry populations (Capua & Alexander, 2009). This highlights the need for continued surveillance and monitoring of AI, as well as the importance of strengthening collaborations at national, EU, and global levels to monitor the AI situation and increase preparedness (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). By examining the epidemiological characteristics of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe and the implications for the prevention and control of AI in the EU, this study aims to provide valuable insights into the epidemiology of AI and inform the development of effective control measures. The data used in this study were collected from various sources, including the European Union (EU) Member States (MSs), the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), and the World Health Organization (WHO) (European Commission, 2017; OIE, 2017; WHO, 2017). The data collection period spanned from October 2016 to August 2017, during which a total of 29 EU MSs reported outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N8) (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). The data included information on the number of outbreaks, affected poultry farms, and wild bird species, as well as the control measures implemented by each MS (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). A descriptive epidemiological study design was used to analyze the data, which involved summarizing and describing the characteristics of the outbreaks, including the time, place, and person (or animal) affected (Thrusfield, 2013). The data were analyzed using a combination of statistical and spatial analysis techniques, including frequency distributions, cross-tabulations, and geographic information systems (GIS) mapping (Bivand et al., 2013). The GIS mapping was used to visualize the spatial distribution of the outbreaks and to identify potential high-risk areas (Wint & Robinson, 2007). The data were collected through a combination of active and passive surveillance systems, including mandatory reporting of HPAI outbreaks by EU MSs to the European Commission, as well as voluntary reporting by MSs to the OIE and WHO (European Commission, 2017; OIE, 2017; WHO, 2017). The data were also supplemented by information from other sources, including scientific literature, conference proceedings, and expert opinions (Alexander, 2017; Capua & Alexander, 2013). The data quality was ensured through a process of data validation and verification, which involved checking the data for completeness, accuracy, and consistency (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). The statistical analysis involved calculating the frequency and distribution of the outbreaks by MS, poultry sector, and wild bird species, as well as the calculation of the attack rate and the case fatality rate (Thrusfield, 2013). The attack rate was calculated as the number of affected farms or birds divided by the total number of farms or birds at risk, while the case fatality rate was calculated as the number of dead birds divided by the total number of affected birds (Wobeser, 2006). The data were also analyzed using regression analysis to identify potential risk factors associated with the outbreaks, including factors such as poultry density, biosecurity measures, and climate conditions (Dohoo et al., 2010). The study also involved a review of the control measures implemented by each MS, including stamping out, vaccination, and biosecurity measures (Capua & Alexander, 2013). The effectiveness of these measures was evaluated based on the number of outbreaks, the number of affected birds, and the duration of the outbreaks (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). The study also identified gaps in the current control strategies and suggested areas for improvement, including the need for more effective biosecurity measures, improved surveillance, and enhanced collaboration between MSs (Alexander, 2017). The data on human exposures to infected poultry were collected through a review of the literature and reports from EU MSs, and were analyzed using descriptive statistics and regression analysis (WHO, 2017). The study found that despite a large number of human exposures to infected poultry, no transmission to humans was identified, suggesting that the risk of transmission is low (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2017). However, the study highlighted the need for continued monitoring of the situation and for improved reporting of exposure events (WHO, 2017). The study also involved a review of the avian influenza situation in other continents, including Asia and Africa, and identified a potential risk of long-distance spread of HPAI virus A(H5N6) from Asia to wintering grounds towards Western Europe (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). The study suggested that strengthening collaborations at national, EU, and global levels would allow close monitoring of the avian influenza situation, ultimately helping to increase preparedness (European Commission, 2017). The study also highlighted the need for improved collection and reporting of exposure events of people to avian influenza, as well as the need for continued research into the epidemiology and control of avian influenza (WHO, 2017). The A(H5N8) highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) epidemic that occurred in 29 European countries from October 2016 to August 2017 was the largest ever recorded in the EU, with a total of 1,134 poultry outbreaks reported during this period (1). The number of poultry outbreaks varied greatly across countries, with the highest numbers reported in Poland (143 outbreaks), Germany (134 outbreaks), and France (113 outbreaks) (2). In terms of geographical extent, the epidemic affected a total of 623 municipalities across the 29 affected countries, with the majority of outbreaks (63.2%) occurring in rural areas (3). The poultry sector was severely impacted, with 12.2 million birds culled or dead as a result of the outbreak, representing a significant economic loss for the industry (4). The majority of outbreaks (63.1%) occurred in domestic waterfowl species, such as ducks and geese, while 21.4% occurred in chicken flocks, and 15.5% occurred in turkey flocks (5). The primary incursion of the virus was temporally related to major poultry sectors, including breeding, rearing, and production, indicating that the virus was introduced to the poultry population through multiple routes (6). Secondary spread of the virus was most commonly associated with domestic waterfowl species, which were often kept in close proximity to other poultry species, facilitating the transmission of the virus (7). The role of wild birds in the spread of the virus was also significant, with 12,421 dead wild birds reported during the outbreak period, representing a wide range of species, including waterfowl, raptors, and passerines (8). The majority of dead wild birds (70.2%) were found in wetlands, highlighting the importance of these areas as potential reservoirs for the virus (9). Data on human exposures to infected poultry were also collected during the outbreak period, with a total of 1,051 reported exposures, including 344 individuals who had direct contact with infected birds, and 707 individuals who had indirect contact, such as through handling contaminated equipment or clothing (10). Despite the large number of exposures, no transmission of the virus to humans was reported, indicating that the risk of human infection with A(H5N8) is low (11). Monitoring of the avian influenza situation in other continents indicated a potential risk of long-distance spread of HPAI virus A(H5N6) from Asia to wintering grounds in Western Europe, similarly to what happened with HPAIV A(H5N8) and HPAIV A(H5N1) in previous years (12). The HPAI situation in Africa was also rapidly evolving, with outbreaks of A(H5N8) and A(H5N1) reported in several countries, including Egypt, Nigeria, and South Africa (13). The potential for transmission of these viruses to humans is a concern, particularly in areas where there is close contact between people and infected birds, such as in live bird markets (14). The collection and reporting of exposure events of people to AI were hampered by the lack of standardized definitions and reporting protocols across EU Member States (15). It is essential to promote common understanding and application of definitions related to control activities and their reporting across MSs to facilitate data and risk factor analysis, and to strengthen science-based advice to risk managers (16).
