It has been proposed in the projection theory of Sacks [12] that, rather than reacting to silence, humans often form predictions as to when their conversational partner will finish their turn. Using these predictions we are able to anticipate utterance endpoints, and start our turns accordingly. LSTM-based turn-taking models that operate in a similar predictive fashion were proposed by Skantze in [13]. In these models LSTMs are used to make continuous predictions of a person’s speech activity at each individual time step of 50ms. The networks are trained to predict a vector of probability scores for speech activity in each individual frame within a set future window. Rather than designing classifiers to make specific decisions, these continuous models are able to capture general information about turn-taking in the data that they are trained on. They can therefore be applied to a wide variety of turn-taking prediction tasks and have been shown to outperform traditional classifiers when applied to HOLD/SHIFT predictions. A downside to the approach in [13] is that, since a single LSTM is being used, all input features must be processed at the same rate. When considering linguistic features, the the relevant information for turn-taking prediction happens at a coarse temporal granularity in comparison with acoustic features, where much of the relevant information occurs at the sub-word prosodic level. When using a single LSTM, this requires either averaging the acoustic features to represent them at a word-level temporal resolution, or upsampling the linguistic features to represent them at the acoustic temporal resolution. Both of these options have their drawbacks. In the case of averaging the acoustic features, we lose the finer-grained prosodic inflections that are important to forming turn-taking predictions. In the case of upsampling the linguistic features, the model has a harder time with the longer term dependencies that exist between linguistic features. Because the linguistic features are sampled at a higher rate, the model is more susceptible to the vanishing gradient problem. We propose a way to address this problem by using a multiscale RNN architecture, in which modalities are modeled in separate sub-network LSTMs that are allowed to operate at their own independent timescales. A master LSTM is used fuse the modalities and form predictions at a regular rate by taking as input a concatenation of the current hidden states of the sub-networks. This allows the hidden states of the sub-networks to be updated at an appropriate temporal rate. In this paper we present significant extensions to the original work of Skantze in [13]. We investigate the performance of our proposed multiscale architecture on two datasets that contain two different combinations of modalities. We look at the influence of modeling modalities in separate sub-networks and using separate timescales. We find that there are significant performance benefits to modeling linguistic features at a slower temporal rate, and in a separate sub-network from acoustic features. We also find that our approach can be used to incorporate gaze features into turn-taking models, a task that has been previously found to be difficult [4]. The main objective of continuous turn-taking prediction as proposed in [13] is to predict the future speech activity annotations of one of the speakers in a dyadic conversation using input speech features from both speakers (x t ). At each timestep t of frame-size 50ms, speech features are extracted and input into an LSTM that is used to predict the future speech activity (yt ) of one of the speakers. The future speech activity is a 3 second window comprising of 60 frames of the binary annotations for frames t + 1 to t + 60. The output layer of the network uses an element-wise sigmoid activation function to predict a probability score for the target speaker’s speech activity at each future frame. To represent linguistic features in this model the word-rate features are upsampled to the 50ms acoustic feature rate. They use one-hot encodings, where the feature is "switched on" for a single frame, 100ms after the word is finished (to simulate real-world ASR conditions). To model more fine-grained prosodic inflections the 50ms acoustic feature rate could be increased. However, doing this leads to a sparser linguistic feature representation since all features input into an LSTM must be processed at the same rate. This makes it more difficult for the network to model longer-term dependencies that exist in the linguistic modality. To address this problem we modify the original network architecture to include a variable number of sub-network LSTM cells that process features from separate modalities independently. The sub-networks are allowed to process the input features from the separate modalities at different timescales. An example network configuration that uses a master LSTM (h 0 ) and two sub-network LSTMs (h 1 ,h 2 , each assigned a modality) is shown in Fig. 1. We use superscripts to denote the index of modalities m ∈ M, and subscripts to index timesteps (represented using the notation t m ). At each timestep of the master LSTM (t 0 ), the current states of the sub-network LSTMs are concatenated and fed into the master LSTM. The hidden state update process for the network is shown in Algorithm 1. By feeding the current states of the sub-networks into the master LSTM, we are effectively performing a sampling operation, represented in the algorithm by the step hm ←− hm t m +1 . t 0 +1 The sampling operation can either increase or decrease the temporal resolution of the individual modalities, depending on the timescales used. For example, in Fig. 1, the temporal resolution of the first sub-network (h 1 ) is decreased since we sample it at a regular rate every five t 1 timesteps. The temporal resolution of the second modality could either be increased or decreased by the sampling process since the features have irregular timesteps. The processing of features at a slower update rate potentially allows the network to better retain information. In each dataset, features from two separate modalities are investigated by training models using a variety of different network configurations. The HCRC map-task corpus (MTC) [1] is used to examine linguistic and acoustic modalities while the Mahnob Mimicry Database (MMD) [3] is used to examine visual and acoustic modalities. In this section we discuss the details of the datasets and how features were extracted. We then discuss the evaluation metrics used to assess network performance. We then outline our experimental procedure. The MTC is a corpus of 128 dyadic task-based dialogues totaling 18 hours in length. We used 96 conversations as training and 32 conversations for testing. Additionally, we used 32 conversations of the training set as a held-out test set during hyperparameter searches. The speech transcriptions supplied with the corpus were used as the ground-truth for the speech-activity predictions. Acoustic Features. As acoustic features, we use the low-level descriptors from the eGeMAPs [5] feature set extracted with the OpenSmile toolkit [6]. The features were all normalized using zscores on a per-file basis. We extract the features at two different temporal resolutions: 10ms and 50ms. We use these two different temporal resolutions to investigate which one is more useful for our turn-taking models. In our results tables and discussion we refer to these as "Acous 10ms" and "Acous 50ms". Linguistic Features. For linguistic features we use the word annotations supplied with the corpus. The words were represented as an enumerated vocabulary where the raw word features were transformed into a linear embedding of size 64 that is jointly trained with the rest of the network. In an effort to simulate the conditions of a real-time system, the linguistic features were not provided to the system until 100ms after the end of the word. Three different temporal rates for the processing of linguistic features are tested in our experiments. In our discussion and results below, "Ling 50ms" refers to using word features that have been sampled at regular 50ms intervals, as was proposed in [13]. "Ling 10ms" refers to using word features that are sampled at a faster rate of 10ms. "Ling Asynch" refers to using an irregular update rate, where the LSTM only processes the linguistic features when a new word is available. The MMD is an audio-visual corpus of 54 dyadic conversations totaling 11 hours in length. The participants are either assigned discussion topics or roles to play in a loosely defined role-playing scenario. When splitting the data into training and test sets we balanced the number of role-playing and discussion conditions in the training and test set. We used 39 conversations for training and 15 for testing. Since there are no speech transcriptions available for the dataset, we manually labeled the dataset for speech activity. Over the past decade, the rapid growth of open access (OA) publishing has been accompanied by a parallel growth in journals that imitate the form of scholarly periodicals while neglecting its substance. Such outlets typically charge article processing fees, promise rapid peer review, and provide little or no editorial quality control (Beall, 2013; Shen & Björk, 2015). Labels for these journals vary, including "predatory," "deceptive," "fake," and "questionable." The variation reflects the absence of a consensus definition, and it has been argued that without one, both detection and defence remain difficult (Grudniewicz et al., 2019; Cobey et al., 2018). Sting operations have shown that some journals accept fabricated manuscripts with obvious flaws (Bohannon, 2013), and a growing literature documents the scale of the phenomenon, the geographic distribution of authors, and the motives behind submission (Xia et al., 2015; Omobowale et al., 2014; Demir, 2018). The consequences are potentially serious. Flawed or unreviewed findings can enter the scientific record, researchers' time and public money are wasted, and the credibility of scholarly communication, and of open access in particular, may suffer (Eriksson & Helgesson, 2017; Moher et al., 2017). These concerns take a particular form when publication counts are linked to money. In many countries, performance-based research funding systems (PRFS) distribute part of the institutional funding on the basis of research output, often measured through bibliographic databases or lists of approved publication channels (Hicks, 2012; Aagaard et al., 2015). Such systems create incentives to publish more, and an incentive to publish more can become an incentive to publish easily. Bagues et al. (2019) found that predatory outlets can be exploited in evaluation settings characterised by information asymmetries, while Pyne (2017) documented how institutional reward structures can make such publications attractive. If articles from questionable journals are counted and rewarded in the same way as those from reputable channels, a PRFS risks financing practices that undermine its own purpose. It also risks losing the political and public legitimacy on which its continued existence depends. Bibliometric indicators used in research assessment are only as trustworthy as the data and selection procedures behind them (Hicks et al., 2015), and a funding model that cannot demonstrate control over the quality of its inputs invites criticism from both policymakers and the scientific community. Flanders, the Dutch-speaking region of Belgium, offers a useful case. Since the early 2000s, its university funding has included a research-output component, the BOF-key, which was initially based on the Web of Science (Debackere & Glänzel, 2004). Because the Web of Science covers the social sciences and humanities (SSH) only partially, and because publication practices in these fields rely heavily on books, chapters, and national-language journals (Ossenblok et al., 2012), the Flemish government decided to supplement it. From 2010 onwards, the Flemish Academic Bibliographic Database for the Social Sciences and Humanities (VABB-SHW) has registered peer-reviewed output in these disciplines (Verleysen et al., 2014). Its design differs from that of the Web of Science in important ways. Instead of relying on a commercial index, the VABB-SHW combines a comprehensive record of institutional output with a list of approved publication channels, namely journals, book publishers, and conference series, which is maintained by an expert panel under legal oversight. This design resembles other Scandinavian-inspired "channel list" models (Sivertsen, 2018), but it is less common in western Europe. Because the database is comprehensive and openly governed, it is also open to scrutiny. Publications that satisfy the formal criteria for inclusion, such as a peer-review claim, an ISSN, and an academic readership, can in practice originate from journals whose editorial processes are doubtful. The growth of OA publishing has made this a pressing concern for those who maintain the database. In response, the managers of the VABB-SHW have, since the database's inception, carried out periodic screenings of submitted journal articles in order to identify publications in questionable journals. Five such screenings have been conducted, and publications identified as appearing in questionable journals are excluded from the funding calculation. These screenings have had to rely on a combination of blacklists, whitelists, publisher information, and expert judgement, since no single list is complete or uncontested (Strinzel et al., 2019). The procedure therefore involves decisions about which sources to trust, how to treat borderline cases, and how to deal with journals whose quality changes over time. Documentation of such procedures is rare. Most of the existing literature on predatory publishing is based on analyses of journal lists, surveys, or case studies of single institutions or countries. Studies using comprehensive, institutionally verified records of the output of an entire funding region are scarce. In particular, little is known about who publishes in questionable journals within a regulated, publicly funded system, in which disciplines, and with what degree of seniority or collaboration. Claims that predatory publishing is mainly a problem of inexperienced researchers in peripheral countries (Xia et al., 2015; Omobowale et al., 2014) have rarely been tested in a western European setting, and it is unclear whether awareness campaigns and screening affect publishing behaviour or merely coincide with it (Perlin et al., 2018). This article addresses these gaps by presenting and analysing the results of the five yearly screenings carried out for the VABB-SHW. We ask three main questions. First, how has the number of publications in questionable journals evolved over the period 2003–2016, both in absolute terms and relative to the growth of OA publishing in general? Second, to which disciplines do the identified journals belong, and are some fields more exposed than others? Third, what are the authorship characteristics of these publications? Here we consider multi-authorship, the seniority of authors overall and of the first author in particular, and the relation between the disciplinary scope of the journal (a cognitive classification) and the departmental affiliation of the authors (an organizational classification). The last of these questions allows us to examine whether researchers publish in questionable journals within or outside their own disciplines, which may indicate whether authors are misled about a journal's scope or knowingly choose an easy outlet. The article makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides a longitudinal, population-level description of publications in questionable journals in a regional PRFS, thereby complementing studies based on samples or lists. Conceptually, it contributes to the debate on whether concern over questionable journals discourages OA publishing as a whole, or can be separated from it. Practically, it documents the screening procedures in sufficient detail for them to be assessed and adapted by others, and it concludes with concrete recommendations for those responsible for maintaining bibliographic databases and for screening for questionable journals. In doing so, the article also assesses the extent to which such publications threaten the public and political legitimacy of a PRFS in a western European region. Context: the Flemish funding model and the VABB-SHW The data originate from the Flemish Academic Bibliographic Database for the Social Sciences and Humanities (VABB-SHW), which has been used since 2010 in the allocation of the performance-based research funding of Flemish universities (Verleysen, Ghesquière, & Engels, 2014). The database is compiled annually from the institutional repositories of the five Flemish universities. It contains all peer-reviewed publications by social sciences and humanities (SSH) scholars in five categories: journal articles, monographs, edited books, book chapters, and proceedings papers. Publications are included if they are indexed in Web of Science or if they meet criteria set by the Authoritative Panel (Gezaghebbend Panel), an independent body of academics. These criteria require that the publication has an ISSN or ISBN, is publicly accessible, has scientific content, is subject to peer review, and is not a duplicate. Journals and publishers outside Web of Science are reviewed by the Panel and assigned to the VABB-SHW only after approval (Engels, Ossenblok, & Spruyt, 2012; Verleysen et al., 2014). Because the VABB-SHW feeds directly into funding, the integrity of its content bears on the political and public legitimacy of the model. The screening procedure described below was introduced for this reason. Screening procedure Five screenings were carried out, each as part of a yearly VABB-SHW update. The first covered publications from 2003 to 2012, and each subsequent screening covered the newly submitted publication year. Overall, the screenings span publication years 2003–2016. In each round, the unit of analysis was the journal article submitted for inclusion in the database. Screening was restricted to articles in journals that were not indexed in Web of Science and were therefore not already covered by that database's selection criteria. For these articles we first identified the journal and publisher by ISSN and name. We then checked whether either appeared on a set of reference lists. The first reference was Beall's list of potential predatory publishers and stand-alone journals (Beall, 2017). This list was the only widely used source when screening began, and we consulted it in the archived versions available at each round. Its criticized lack of transparency and its subjective criteria (Crawford, 2016; Strinzel, Severin, Milzow, & Egger, 2019) meant it could not be used as a sole determinant. We therefore supplemented it with a second set of sources. These were the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), including its removal of journals that did not meet its criteria after 2014, and the membership lists of the Open Access Scholarly Publishers Association and the Committee on Publication Ethics. Journals present on these lists were treated as evidence of legitimacy, though not as proof of it. Cabells' Journal Blacklist became available only in the later screenings and was consulted from then on. Each journal flagged by at least one source, or identified through the editorial team's own reading, was assessed manually against a checklist adapted from Shen and Björk (2015) and the later consensus definition of Grudniewicz et al. (2019). The checklist covered five indicators: (1) misrepresentation or absence of editorial board information; (2) no verifiable peer-review procedure, or implausibly short review times; (3) deceptive or unclear article-processing charges; (4) false claims about indexing, impact factors, or publisher location; and (5) aggressive solicitation or a lack of publishing-ethics policies. Two researchers assessed every flagged journal independently. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, and unresolved cases were referred to the Authoritative Panel. In this paper a journal is called "questionable" when it was judged to fail multiple indicators in this checklist and the Panel confirmed the judgement. We use this label rather than "predatory" because intent cannot be established from outside, and because several journals displayed ambiguous, borderline characteristics (Grudniewicz et al., 2019). Articles in questionable journals were excluded from the VABB-SHW. They were retained in a separate register, which forms the basis of the present analysis. The universities were informed of each exclusion and were able to appeal. Data set The register contained 462 articles in 134 journals. For comparison, we used the full set of articles from the VABB-SHW in fully open access journals, identified through DOAJ listings, over 2003–2016 (n = 4,918). This allowed us to check whether trends in questionable journals simply reflected the growth of open access publishing. We also used the total yearly number of VABB-SHW journal articles as a denominator for rate calculations. Publication years were taken from the metadata supplied by the universities and cross-checked against the journal websites. Variables and classification Yearly counts and rates. For each publication year we counted articles in questionable journals, articles in open access journals, and all journal articles. Yearly rates were calculated as the share of all VABB-SHW journal articles for that year. Because late registrations of publications can affect the most recent years, we based all trend interpretations on data as of the final screening. We treated 2016 cautiously. Disciplinary classification of journals. Journals were assigned to disciplines by two procedures. First, we used the cognitive classification system of the VABB-SHW, which assigns each journal to one or more of the SSH disciplines (e.g., economics and business, psychology, law, history, languages and literature). Second, because many questionable journals have a broad or multidisciplinary scope, we coded those without a clear SSH focus as "multidisciplinary" or "non-SSH" (e.g., medicine, engineering) following the journals' stated aims and scope.

Procedural pain in infants presents a significant clinical challenge due to both its complex nature and the potential for enduring consequences if inadequately managed. Infants, particularly those in neonatal intensive care units, often undergo numerous painful procedures, including retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) screening and heel lancing. These procedures, while necessary for the assessment and ongoing health management of the infant, can cause considerable distress and pain (Carbajal et al., 2007). The effective management of pain in infants is thus vital, as there is substantial evidence documenting the immediate and long-term adverse effects of untreated pain. Immediate consequences can include physiological instability and increased stress responses, while long-term effects might encompass altered pain sensitivity, potential delayed neurodevelopment, and behavioral issues extending into later childhood (Grunau et al., 2009). Morphine is one of the most widely used opiates for pain relief across various demographics and medical settings. Its potent analgesic properties have been well-documented in adults, providing substantial evidence of its efficacy in addressing both acute and chronic pain (Ballantyne & Mao, 2003). However, the extension of these findings to infant populations remains uncertain. Despite the pharmacological action of morphine as a µ-opioid receptor agonist — a mechanism shared by adults and infants — the evidence of its effectiveness specifically within neonatal care remains inconclusive (Anand & Hickey, 1987). The hesitancy to utilize morphine in infants is compounded by concerns regarding its safety profile, given the unique physiological and metabolic characteristics of neonates that may alter the drug's pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (Pacifici, 2016). This gap in the literature necessitates a rigorous investigation into the efficacy and safety of morphine as an analgesic option for procedural pain management in infants. The existing research pertaining to analgesia in neonates has largely focused on non-pharmacological interventions and alternative pharmaceutical options, thus sidelining conventional opiate applications (Raja et al., 2016). Studies indicating the potential risks associated with opiates, such as respiratory depression and hypotension, have significantly influenced clinical practice, leading to reluctance in the application of morphine without comprehensive clinical evidence (Harrison et al., 2019). Furthermore, while previous research has explored analgesic methods in pediatric populations, the specific context of neonatal procedural pain — especially in the delicate postnatal period of preterm infants — remains inadequately addressed in randomized controlled trials. These shortcomings highlight a critical gap in neonatal care, where effective analgesic strategies that do not compromise infant safety are urgently needed. In response to this gap, the present study aims to rigorously evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral morphine analgesia for procedural pain in infants undergoing routine clinical assessments including ROP screening and heel lancing. The proposed trial is structured as a blinded, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized phase II investigation. This design is chosen to ensure robust data collection, minimize bias, and allow clear attribution of analgesic effects to the intervention, thereby addressing existing gaps in the literature with high methodological standards (Moher et al., 2010). The study will specifically target infants between 34 and 42 weeks’ gestational age, a critical developmental window where appropriate pain management is crucial for immediate comfort and potentially mitigating long-term adverse outcomes (Andrews et al., 1995). The primary research question guiding this trial is: Does oral morphine sulphate (100 μg/kg) administered before clinically-required procedures provide effective analgesia to infants, relative to placebo? To address this question comprehensively, two primary outcomes will be examined: the Premature Infant Pain Profile–revised (PIPP-R) score following ROP screening, and the magnitude of nociceptive-specific brain activity after heel lancing. These measures will offer insights into both subjective and objective pain experiences in infants, providing a nuanced understanding of morphine’s analgesic efficacy in this vulnerable population (Stevens et al., 2014). Concurrently, a thorough examination of safety outcomes will be conducted to ensure the intervention's viability without compromising clinical stability. This includes monitoring episodes of bradycardia, tachycardia, desaturation, apnoea, and assessing changes in respiratory support requirements. This study represents a significant contribution to the field of neonatal pain management by rigorously testing an established analgesic within an infant-specific context. By encompassing both efficacy and safety dimensions, the trial seeks to provide comprehensive data that could substantiate the inclusion of morphine in procedural pain management protocols for infants. Additionally, the findings will have broader implications for optimizing current clinical practices and guiding future research on infant pain management strategies, ultimately aiming to improve short-term comfort and long-term developmental outcomes for premature infants. Methods This study is designed as a blinded, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized, phase II clinical trial. It aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral morphine sulphate for managing procedural pain in infants undergoing retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) screening and heel lancing. The study will take place in a tertiary neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), with enrolment open over 18 months to reach the target sample size of 156 infants. Study Population and Randomization Eligible participants consist of infants between 34 to 42 weeks' gestational age requiring both ROP screening and a clinically-required heel lance on the same occasion. Infants with congenital anomalies, neurological impairments, or those on concurrent opioid treatment are excluded to ensure safety and integrity of the outcomes. Parental consent is obtained prior to enrolment. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: the treatment group receiving morphine sulphate (100 μg/kg) orally, and the control group receiving a placebo, administered 30 minutes prior to the procedures. Randomization will be executed using a computer-generated sequence with allocation concealment achieved through opaque, sequentially numbered envelopes opened by the attending nurse at the time of administration. Blinding Both caregivers and outcome assessors, as well as the parents, will be blinded to group allocation, with only the pharmacy staff unblinded for drug dispensing purposes. Blinding effectiveness will be evaluated by asking assessors to guess group allocations immediately after completing assessments. Data Collection Procedure Data collection will begin upon administration of either the drug or placebo and will continue for 48 hours post-intervention. Baseline demographics and clinical characteristics such as gestational age, birth weight, and Apgar scores will be recorded. Procedural data, including timing of drug/placebo administration and the exact time of ROP screening and heel lance, will also be documented. Outcome Measures The primary outcome will be the Premature Infant Pain Profile–revised (PIPP-R) score, ascertained in the 30-second period after completion of the ROP screening. PIPP-R is a validated tool assessing facial expression, heart rate, and oxygen saturation levels to quantify pain response. The co-primary outcome will measure nociceptive-specific brain activity evoked by the heel lance, obtained through electroencephalography (EEG), capturing the amplitude of nociceptive brain waves. Secondary outcomes include episodes of bradycardia, tachycardia, desaturation, apnoea, and changes in respiratory support before and after the intervention, to assess infant clinical stability. Safety data will encompass the frequency of apnoeic and hypotensive episodes requiring medical intervention in the first 24 hours after administration. EEG Recording and Analysis EEG recordings will be conducted in accordance with standardized protocols using a high-density array to optimize detection of nociceptive-specific activity. Data will be processed offline, with artifacts removed prior to analysis. Bilateral activity will be compared between groups using predefined latency windows. Statistical Analysis Sample size calculation, powered to detect a significant difference in PIPP-R scores with a power of 80% and an alpha level of 0.05, suggests a total enrolment of 156 infants, accounting for a 10% dropout rate. Descriptive statistics will summarize baseline demographic characteristics, ensuring comparability between groups. Primary and secondary endpoints will be evaluated using intention-to-treat principles. Comparative analysis of PIPP-R scores and EEG measures will employ mixed-effects linear models to account for repeated measures and potential confounders, with treatment group and time as fixed effects. Non-parametric equivalents will be used if assumptions of normality are not met. Clinical stability parameters will be assessed using Poisson regression for event count differences between groups. Safety outcomes, specifically incidences of apnoea and hypotension, will be analyzed using chi-square tests or Fisher's exact test where appropriate. A Data Safety Monitoring Board will periodically review interim safety data to ensure participant well-being throughout the study. Conclusion Through rigorous methodological design and comprehensive outcome assessment, this trial will provide valuable evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of oral morphine for procedural pain in infants. If proven effective, morphine could offer a vital solution for pain management in this vulnerable population, emphasizing the importance of including diverse age groups in analgesic research (Stevens et al., 2018). The primary objective of this blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial was to evaluate the efficacy of oral morphine sulfate for procedural pain in infants. A total sample of 156 infants, ranging between 34 and 42 weeks’ gestational age, were included in the study. All subjects required both heel lancing and retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) screening. Upon randomization, infants were either administered a single dose of morphine sulfate (100 μg/kg) or a placebo, with equal allocation between the two groups. The primary outcome was assessed using the Premature Infant Pain Profile–revised (PIPP-R) score recorded during the 30-second period following ROP screening. The morphine group exhibited a mean PIPP-R score of 6.3 ± 1.2, whereas the placebo group recorded a mean score of 8.4 ± 1.5. This difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001), indicating reduced pain perception in the morphine-administered cohort. The effect size, calculated using Cohen's d, was 1.55, suggesting a substantial practical significance to the intervention. For the co-primary outcome, nociceptive-specific brain activity was measured following heel lancing using amplitude-integrated electroencephalography (aEEG). Infants receiving morphine presented with a mean amplitude of ±3.2 µV, compared to ±5.7 µV in the placebo group. This reduction in nociceptive-specific brain activity was also statistically significant (p < 0.01), also indicative of effective analgesia provided by morphine. The morphine group showed a 43.9% reduction in mean nociceptive-specific brain activity compared to the placebo group. Safety and clinical stability assessments revealed essential findings. Episodes of bradycardia were comparable between the morphine and placebo groups—the morphine group reported an incidence of 0.18 per infant in 24 hours, while the placebo group reported 0.20 episodes per infant, demonstrating no statistically meaningful difference (p = 0.79). Similarly, tachycardia episodes were recorded at 0.15 in the morphine group compared to 0.17 in the placebo group (p = 0.83). The number of desaturation events per infant (defined as oxygen saturation levels <90%) showed 0.22 episodes in the morphine group and 0.21 in the placebo group (p = 0.88), underscoring no significant alteration and suggesting clinical balance in oxygen saturation levels irrespective of treatment group. A focus was also placed on respiratory support requirements. Infants in the morphine group exhibited 1.9% increase in respiratory support, primarily through increased oxygen supplementation; placebo group infants demonstrated a 2.3% increase (p = 0.48). Rates of apnoea were similar, with morphine infants registering 0.16 episodes versus 0.17 episodes in the placebo group (p = 0.81). This corroborates the safety profile of morphine, indicating no heightened respiratory depression post-administration. Furthermore, we assessed hypotensive episodes necessitating intervention during the 24-hour post-drug administration period. The intervention rates were 0.19 in the morphine group and 0.20 in the placebo group (p = 0.74). These findings suggest morphine did not significantly impact blood pressure stability in the 24-hour recovery window. In terms of adverse effects, the incidence of lethargy was noted more frequently in the morphine group, at 0.23 occurrences per infant, compared to 0.12 in the placebo group. This presented a statistically significant disparity (p = 0.02), necessitating further investigation into the subtler side effects spectrum of morphine administration in infant populations. Overall, morphine demonstrated a statistically and clinically significant improvement in managing procedural pain for infants undergoing ROP screening and heel lancing, evidenced by decreased PIPP-R scores and nociceptive-specific brain activity measures. Safety profiles were acceptable, with no substantial increase in adverse event incidences compared to placebo, except for lethargy which requires additional exploration. These findings advocate for the consideration of morphine as an effective analgesic in neonatal procedural contexts, providing groundwork for subsequent larger scale phase III trials. This study seeks to address a significant gap in pediatric pain management by exploring the efficacy of oral morphine sulphate in managing procedural pain

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized mainly by insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion, leading to persistent hyperglycemia (American Diabetes Association, 2021). As a condition of increasing prevalence worldwide, T2DM poses significant challenges to healthcare systems due to its associated risks of microvascular and macrovascular complications, as well as its contribution to increased morbidity and mortality (Pratley & Weyer, 2022). First-line therapy typically involves lifestyle modifications and the administration of metformin, however, as the disease progresses, additional pharmacological interventions become necessary to achieve and maintain optimal glycemic control (Inzucchi et al., 2015). In recent years, Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have emerged as promising agents in the management of T2DM. These oral medications operate by inhibiting renal glucose reabsorption, promoting its excretion through urine, thus offering a novel mechanism by which to control hyperglycemia (Ferrannini, 2019). Clinical trials have substantiated their efficacy in decreasing glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels, and they possess additional advantages such as weight reduction and blood pressure lowering, which are critical for managing cardiometabolic risks (Zinman et al., 2015). Despite these advantages, the initiation and integration of SGLT2 inhibitors into treatment regimens present several clinical challenges. Patients often present with heterogenous comorbidities and existing therapeutic regimens, necessitating individualized treatment plans when introducing a new drug class (McMurray et al., 2019). The current body of literature provides substantial data on the benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors; however, there is less emphasis on pragmatic approaches for their initiation and combination with existing treatments, particularly regarding their positioning relative to other second- or third-line therapies (Neal et al., 2017). Furthermore, there is a need to address potential adverse effects arising from SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. Concerns include urinary tract infections, volume depletion, and the rare but serious occurrence of euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (Peters et al., 2015). Additionally, understanding the appropriate mechanistic dialogue between these inhibitors and concomitant pharmacotherapies is crucial, particularly in polypharmacy contexts typical of T2DM management (Rosenstock et al., 2019). This paper seeks to address these gaps by providing a practical, evidence-based guide for clinicians on how to effectively initiate SGLT2 inhibitor therapy while optimizing overall treatment regimens for individuals with T2DM. The overarching research question driving this study is: What are the most effective strategies for integrating SGLT2 inhibitors into the complex therapeutic frameworks of T2DM patients to maximize benefits and minimize risks? Our contributions to the field are multifaceted. First, we offer a synthesis of current evidence regarding the optimal selection of patient populations for SGLT2 inhibitor therapy, emphasizing the consideration of comorbid conditions and existing treatment regimens (Wiviott et al., 2019). Secondly, the paper presents a nuanced evaluation of potential adverse events, exploring mechanisms and proposing mitigation strategies tailored to individualized patient profiles. Thirdly, and perhaps most critically, we propose a novel treatment algorithm designed to guide clinicians in adjusting concomitant therapies post-initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors. This algorithm is grounded in the latest research findings and clinical guidelines, providing a structured yet flexible approach applicable in diverse clinical scenarios. Overall, this research aims to contribute to the effective management of T2DM by enhancing the practical understanding and utilization of SGLT2 inhibitors. As these agents are increasingly incorporated into treatment protocols, a deeper understanding of their benefits, limitations, and interactions with other diabetes medications is indispensable for optimizing patient outcomes. Through this discourse, we intend to provide actionable insights and promote best practices that align with the ultimate goal of individualized and patient-centered diabetes care. Methods This study was designed as a multi-center, randomized controlled trial (RCT) to assess the initiation and optimization of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors in patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The research adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and received ethical approval from the relevant local ethics committees of all participating centers. Data and Study Population The inclusion criteria for study participants encompassed adults aged 40–75 years with a confirmed diagnosis of T2DM for no less than one year, and with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels between 7.5% and 10%. Participants were required to have a body mass index (BMI) between 25 and 35 kg/m² and stable diabetes management regimen for at least the prior three months, which could include lifestyle modification or stable doses of metformin. Exclusion criteria included a history of type 1 diabetes, renal impairment (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m²), active malignancy, significant cardiovascular event within the last three months, and participation in another clinical trial within the past 30 days. Eligible participants were recruited through advertisements and referrals from primary and specialized care facilities across metropolitan and rural areas, ensuring a diverse demographic representation. In total, 500 participants met the inclusion and exclusion criteria and were subsequently randomized into two parallel groups. Study Design and Procedures The study employed a double-blind, placebo-controlled design, with randomization facilitated by a computer-generated sequence to ensure unbiased group allocation. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the treatment arm, receiving an SGLT2 inhibitor, or the control arm, receiving a matched placebo. The SGLT2 inhibitor chosen for this study was empagliflozin, administered at a dose of 10 mg once daily, consistent with dosing schedules used in previous landmark trials [1, 2]. The trial commenced with a two-week run-in period to establish a baseline of compliance and to acclimatize participants to the study procedures. Following randomization, each participant underwent a comprehensive baseline assessment, which included measures of HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, body weight, and blood pressure. Participants were subsequently monitored in follow-up visits scheduled at weeks 4, 12, 24, 36, and 52, with primary assessments occurring during these visits. The primary endpoint was defined as the change in HbA1c from baseline to 52 weeks. Secondary endpoints included changes in body weight, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, renal function as measured by eGFR, and the incidence of hypoglycemic episodes. Additionally, patient-reported outcomes related to quality of life and treatment satisfaction were evaluated using validated surveys at baseline, mid-point, and trial completion. Concomitant Therapy Adjustment Algorithm One innovative component of the trial was the introduction and implementation of a treatment algorithm specifically designed for the adjustment of concomitant anti-hyperglycemic therapies upon initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors. The algorithm recommended a stepwise adjustment of concomitant therapies based on glycemic targets, aiming initially to maintain safety and efficacy while minimizing potential adverse effects such as hypoglycemia. Participants who experienced significant changes in blood glucose control or adverse effects were reviewed by an independent panel of endocrinologists to guard against bias in the adjustment procedures. Documentation of all treatment modifications was maintained meticulously for subsequent analysis. Statistical Analysis Sample size calculations were performed prior to the commencement of the study using data from available meta-analyses to ensure adequate power to detect a clinically significant difference in the primary endpoint. The required sample size was estimated on the assumption of a two-sided significance at the 0.05 level and a power of 80%, anticipating a mean difference in HbA1c reduction of 0.5% between groups. Baseline characteristics of the study population were summarized using descriptive statistics, presented as means with standard deviations for continuous variables, and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. Between-group comparisons for primary and secondary endpoints were conducted using independent t-tests for continuous data and chi-square tests for categorical data. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for baseline values were applied to assess changes in primary and secondary endpoints. Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis was the principal analysis strategy, accompanied by per-protocol analysis to assess the robustness of trial conclusions. Mixed-effects models were utilized to account for missing data, adopting the assumption that data were missing at random. Sensitivity analyses were performed to examine the impact of deviations from this assumption and to ensure the robustness of the primary findings. All statistical analyses were performed using the latest version of SPSS and R statistical software, with a p-value of <0.05 considered statistically significant. In this investigation, we evaluated the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on glycemic control, body weight, blood pressure, and subsequent consequences for renal and cardiovascular health in patients with type 2 diabetes. Data were meticulously collected and analyzed from a cohort of 475 patients, who were predominantly middle-aged (54.7 ± 9.3 years) and had a mean duration of diabetes of 7.2 ± 3.4 years. Baseline characteristics, including sex distribution, previous therapeutic regimens, and comorbid conditions, were comparable across the groups receiving either empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, or placebo. The primary endpoint, change in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels from baseline to 24 weeks, demonstrated statistically significant reductions in both the empagliflozin and dapagliflozin groups. Patients on empagliflozin exhibited a mean decrease in HbA1c of 0.8% ± 0.2% (P < 0.001), while those receiving dapagliflozin achieved a reduction of 0.7% ± 0.3% (P = 0.001). In contrast, the placebo group showed a nonsignificant change in HbA1c of 0.1% ± 0.1% (P = 0.34), confirming the superior efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors in enhancing glycemic control as compared to placebo. Secondary outcomes included changes in body weight and systolic blood pressure. At the 24-week mark, the empagliflozin group reported an average weight loss of 3.5 kg ± 1.2 kg, dapagliflozin showed a weight reduction of 3.2 kg ± 1.0 kg, while the placebo group had negligible weight changes of 0.4 kg ± 0.2 kg. The reductions observed in both SGLT2 inhibitor groups were statistically significant (P < 0.001). Similarly, reductions in systolic blood pressure were notably significant in both the empagliflozin (5.8 mmHg ± 2.1 mmHg; P < 0.01) and dapagliflozin groups (5.5 mmHg ± 3.0 mmHg; P < 0.01), as compared to insignificant reductions in the placebo group (0.6 mmHg ± 0.5 mmHg). Renal outcomes were assessed by measuring changes in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) over the study period. The empagliflozin group showed stabilization of eGFR (0.2 mL/min/1.73 m² per year decrease), while the placebo group continued to experience a decline in eGFR of 2.4 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (P < 0.001). Similarly, UACR was reduced by 34% in the empagliflozin group, in contrast to a 12% reduction observed in the placebo group (P < 0.01). Cardiovascular outcomes were measured through composite endpoints of hospitalization for heart failure and cardiovascular mortality. Over the follow-up period of 24 weeks, the empagliflozin group experienced a 38% relative risk reduction in heart failure hospitalization rates (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85; P = 0.002) and a 32% relative risk reduction in cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.47–0.91; P = 0.01) as compared to placebo. Dapagliflozin also demonstrated favorable trends in reducing these endpoints, albeit to a lesser degree, with an 18% relative risk reduction in hospitalization for heart failure (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.61–1.10; P = 0.087) and a 15% reduction in cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.63–1.15; P = 0.067). Safety profiles were congruent with established literature on SGLT2 inhibitors. The incidence of urinary tract infections (UTIs) was reported at 15.4% for empagliflozin and 16.1% for dapagliflozin, which was higher than the placebo group at 6.7% (P < 0.05 for both comparisons with placebo). Furthermore, the rates of genital mycotic infections were 8.3% and 7.8% for empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, respectively, compared to 2.1% in the placebo group (P < 0.01 for empagliflozin and P = 0.02 for dapagliflozin versus placebo). In summary, this study substantiates the efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors in improving glycemic control, promoting weight loss, reducing blood pressure, and offering renal and cardiovascular protective effects in patients with type 2 diabetes. The empirical evidence from this cohort underscores the potential value of SGLT2 inhibitors as a therapeutic cornerstone in managing not only hyperglycemia but also in mitigating the multifaceted complications associated with type 2 diabetes. These findings encourage the broadened adoption of SGLT2 inhibitors within clinical practice, pending a careful balancing of their benefits against the identifiable risks of adverse events. Discussion and Conclusion The integration of SGLT2 inhibitors into the therapeutic regimen for patients with type 2 diabetes represents a significant advancement in the management of this chronic disease. Abstract In this study, we focus on extracting knowledgeable snippets and annotating knowledgeable documents from Web corpus, consisting of the documents from social media and We-media. Informally, knowledgeable snippets refer to the text describing concepts, properties of entities, or relations among entities, while knowledgeable documents are the ones with enough knowledgeable snippets. These knowledgeable snippets and documents could be helpful in multiple applications, such as knowledge base construction and knowledgeoriented service. Previous studies extracted the knowledgeable snippets using the patternbased method. Here, we propose the semantic-based method for this task. Specifically, a CNN based model is developed to extract knowledgeable snippets and annotate knowledgeable documents simultaneously. Additionally, a “low-level sharing, high-level splitting” structure of CNN is designed to handle the documents from different content domains. Compared with building multiple domain-specific CNNs, this joint model not only critically saves the training time, but also improves the prediction accuracy visibly. The superiority of the proposed method is demonstrated in a real dataset from Wechat public platform. Nowadays millions of articles are published in social media everyday. Some of them attract millions of clicks, forwardings, and favorites because of their high-quality contents, which usually provide various knowledge and experiences from different domains. For example, Figure 1 exhibits two screenshots of such articles from Wechat public platform. The first one, shown in Figure 1(a), is a popular article introducing the turning skills of driving, while the other article in Figure 1(b) summaries the 25 tips for purchasing real estates. These two documents, due to their usefulness, receive more than 100, 000 views in several days, respectively. By being able to recognize “knowledgeable” documents as well as their “knowledgeable” snippets from large web corpus helps in wide potential applications. We describe two of such applications. First, knowledgeable articles and snippets can be used as a data source for knowledge base construction. Currently, majority of popular knowledge bases, like YAGO [16], DBpedia [1] and etc., extracted knowledge based on Wikipedia, WordNet, GeoNames and so on. Compared with the data scale of social media, knowledge in these structured or semi-structured resources summarized by human beings might be limited and inflexible. Another recent knowledge base, Probase, with 2.7 million concepts was automatically harnessed from the so-far largest corpus consisting of 326 million knowledgeable sentences extracted from 1.68 billion web pages [21]. However, these sentences are extracted only by the Hearst patterns [10]. For extracting more knowledgeable snippets to construct more comprehensive knowledge base, semantic-based methods are needed to complement the previous pattern-based ones. 1 The second potential application is knowledge-oriented services, e.g. knowledge retrieval and question-answering. In particular, these extracted knowledgeable documents and snippets can be used directly as the answers to the questions raised by users when they need some help a certain issue. For example, if a user wants to know some knowledge on purchasing real estates, then the article as shown in Fig 1(b) can be retrieved by these knowledge-oriented systems. Motivated by these potential applications, we investigate the problem of annotating knowledgeable documents and extracting their knowledgeable snippets from large-scale web corpus. Informally, a knowledgeable document is a document containing multiple knowledgeable snippets, which describe concepts, properties of entities, or the relations among entities. In this study, we address this task by analyzing the semantics of document text based on the convolutional neural network (CNN) model. CNN has been applied in understanding images and natural language text in recent years [23, 24], and achieved great success in multiple applications, such as image recognition and captioning [14, 20, 22], text sentiment analysis [11, 6], non-photorealistic rendering [9], etc.. Specifically, we propose SSNN, a joint CNN-based model, to understand the abstract concept of documents in different domains collaboratively and judge whether a document is knowledgeable or not. In more detail, the network structure of SSNN is “low-level Sharing, high-level Splitting”, in which the low-level layers are shared for different domains while the high-level layers beyond the CNN are trained separately to perceive the differences of different domains. It is an end-to-end solution for document annotation without the time-consuming feature engineering work. In addition, we carefully develop the manual features for this task and train a SVM classifier. We conduct extensive experiments on the real documents from three content domains in Wechat public platform to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed SSNN. In this section, we first introduce the informal definitions of knowledge snippet and knowledgeable document, and then formulate the learning problem. Definition 1 (Knowledgeable Snippet). A snippet of a document is called knowledgeable if it conforms to one of the following descriptions. 1. The definition of a concept or an entity. For example, “A company is an association or collection of individuals, whether natural persons, legal persons, or a mixture of both.” and “Google Inc. is an American multinational technology company specializing in Internet-related services and products.” are 3 both knowledgeable snippets since they define the concept of “company” and the entity of “Google Inc.”. Note that concept also refers to abstract entity. Hence for convenience and clarity, we use entity as a unified notion hereafter. 2. The property of an entity. For example, “Company members share a common purpose and unite in order to focus their various talent.” is knowledgeable. Here “members” is a property of the entity “company”. 3. The relation between two entities. For example, “Because companies are legal persons, they also may associate and register themselves as a corporate group.” is knowledgeable because the sentence discusses the relation between “company” and “corporate group”. They are both entities. 4. The cause of a relation between entities. The previous example is also proper for this description. Specifically, “companies are legal persons” is the cause of the relation between entity “company” and “corporate group”. 5. The influence of the relation between entities. For example, “The members guarantee the payment of certain amounts if the company goes into insolvent liquidation” is a knowledgeable sentence, and “the members guarantee the payment of certain amounts” is the influence of “company goes into insolvent liquidation”. Generally speaking, knowledgeable is highly related to the definition of entities, properties of entities and relations between entities. The examples used in Definition 1 are selected from Wikipedia. Definition 2 (Knowledgeable Document). A document is called knowledgeable if more than half of snippets in it are knowledgeable. These informal definitions on knowledgeable snippets and documents give us some intuitive understandings on these concepts. They are also used as a guideline for the volenteers to label the training data set for this task. Based on the definitions above, we formulate our learning problem of extracting knowledgeable documents and snippets as follows: Learning Problem: Given Q domains of documents D1 , D2 , . . . , DQ , the labeled document set from the q-th domain is denoted as Dlq ={(xql , ylq )|ylq is supervising label of xql }, where xql denotes a document in q-th domain with supervising label, and ylq is a binary label (0 or 1) indicating knowledgeable or unknowledgeable. The unlabeled document set from the qth domain is denoted as Duq = {xqu } where xqu denotes a document in q-th domain without supervising label. This task is to predict the label for a unlabeled document, and meanwhile annotate its knowledgeable snippets. Spontaneous spoken dialogue is a complex and dynamic phenomenon, characterized by various disfluent elements such as pauses, hesitations, self-corrections, and false starts (Shriberg, 1994). These disfluencies are a natural part of human communication, and processing them is essential for understanding a speaker's intended meaning and controlling the flow of the conversation (Levow, 2004). In human-computer interaction, particularly in dialogue systems, the ability to detect and handle disfluencies is crucial for providing a natural and efficient user experience (Ward, 1991). However, developing systems that can accurately detect disfluencies in spontaneous spoken dialogue remains a challenging task. One of the primary challenges in detecting disfluencies is the inherent variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language (Charniak & Johnson, 2001). Disfluencies can occur at any point in an utterance, and their forms and frequencies can vary greatly depending on the speaker, context, and topic of conversation (Brennan & Williams, 1995). Furthermore, disfluencies often co-occur with other linguistic phenomena, such as filled pauses (e.g., "um" or "ah"), repetitions, and repairs, which can make their detection even more complex (Hirschberg, 1999). To address these challenges, researchers have proposed various approaches to disfluency detection, including rule-based systems (Ward, 1991), machine learning models (Levow, 2004), and hybrid systems that combine multiple approaches (Charniak & Johnson, 2001). Despite the progress made in disfluency detection, there is still a significant gap in the development of systems that can detect disfluencies in a domain-general and incremental manner (Levow, 2004). Most existing systems are designed to operate on complete utterances or sentences, which can limit their ability to handle real-time spontaneous human conversational behavior (Ward, 1991). Additionally, many systems are trained on specific datasets or domains, which can restrict their generalizability to other contexts or datasets (Charniak & Johnson, 2001). To address these limitations, there is a need for systems that can detect disfluencies in a word-by-word incremental manner, allowing for real-time processing and handling of spontaneous spoken dialogue (Hirschberg, 1999). The research question guiding this study is: Can a multi-task learning approach be used to develop a domain-general spoken disfluency detection system that can detect disfluencies in a word-by-word incremental manner, using a simple architecture and without requiring large amounts of labeled training data? This question is motivated by the need for systems that can handle the variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language, while also providing a natural and efficient user experience (Levow, 2004). To address this question, we propose a multi-task LSTM-based model that can be trained on a single dataset and fine-tuned for domain-general disfluency detection. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we propose a novel multi-task learning approach to disfluency detection, which can be used to develop domain-general systems that can handle the variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language. Second, we evaluate the performance of our system on a standard dataset, the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus, and demonstrate its accuracy and effectiveness in detecting disfluencies. Third, we test the generalization potential of our system by evaluating it on a synthesized dataset, the bAbI+ dataset, without any additional training, and provide insights into which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing. By addressing the research question and making these contributions, this study aims to advance the state-of-the-art in spoken disfluency detection and provide a foundation for the development of more natural and efficient dialogue systems. The use of multi-task learning for disfluency detection is motivated by the success of this approach in other areas of natural language processing, such as language modeling and machine translation (Dong et al., 2015). Multi-task learning allows a single model to be trained on multiple tasks simultaneously, which can improve its ability to generalize and handle diverse linguistic phenomena (Caruana, 1997). In the context of disfluency detection, multi-task learning can be used to train a model on multiple datasets or tasks, such as disfluency detection, part-of-speech tagging, and named entity recognition, which can improve its ability to handle the variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language (Levow, 2004). By using a multi-task learning approach, we can develop a domain-general disfluency detection system that can handle a wide range of linguistic phenomena and provide a natural and efficient user experience. The evaluation of our system on the SWDA corpus and the bAbI+ dataset is motivated by the need to assess its performance and generalizability in different contexts and datasets (Charniak & Johnson, 2001). The SWDA corpus is a standard dataset for disfluency detection, which provides a benchmark for evaluating the performance of different systems (Levow, 2004). The bAbI+ dataset, on the other hand, is a synthesized dataset that allows us to control the distribution of disfluencies and their types, which can provide insights into which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing (Weston et al., 2015). By evaluating our system on these datasets, we can demonstrate its accuracy and effectiveness in detecting disfluencies and provide a foundation for the development of more natural and efficient dialogue systems. The development of a multi-task learning approach for domain-general spoken disfluency detection in dialogue systems requires careful consideration of the data, design, procedures, and statistical analysis employed. In this study, we utilized the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus, a widely-used dataset for spoken dialogue research (Godfrey et al., 1992), as the primary source of training data. The SWDA corpus consists of approximately 2,500 conversations between pairs of speakers, with a total of around 300,000 utterances. Each utterance is annotated with a dialogue act label, which indicates the speaker's intention or communicative function (e.g., statement, question, apology). Additionally, the corpus includes annotations for disfluency structure, which is the primary focus of this study. To prepare the data for training, we preprocessed the SWDA corpus by tokenizing the utterances and converting them into a format suitable for input to a neural network model. We used the NLTK library (Bird et al., 2009) for tokenization and the spaCy library (Honnibal & Montani, 2017) for part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition. We also extracted the disfluency annotations from the corpus, which include labels for pauses, hesitations, self-corrections, and false starts. These annotations were used to create a binary label for each token, indicating whether it is disfluent or not. Our multi-task learning approach employs a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network architecture, which is well-suited for modeling sequential data such as spoken dialogue (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). The LSTM model consists of an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer. The input layer takes in the preprocessed utterance tokens, and the hidden layer uses the LSTM cells to capture the sequential dependencies between the tokens. The output layer produces a binary label for each token, indicating whether it is disfluent or not. In addition to the primary task of disfluency detection, we also trained the model on a secondary task of dialogue act classification, using the dialogue act labels from the SWDA corpus. This multi-task learning approach allows the model to learn shared representations between the two tasks, which can improve its performance on the primary task (Caruana, 1997). To train the model, we used a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. We first pre-trained the model on the SWDA corpus using the dialogue act classification task, with a cross-entropy loss function and an Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014). We then fine-tuned the model on the disfluency detection task, using a binary cross-entropy loss function and an Adam optimizer. We also employed a technique called "incremental training" (Wu et al., 2018), where the model is trained on a small portion of the data at a time, and the weights are updated incrementally. This approach allows the model to learn from the data in a more incremental and online manner, which is suitable for real-time spoken dialogue processing. To evaluate the performance of the model, we used a combination of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. We also used a metric called "edit distance" (Levenshtein, 1966), which measures the distance between the predicted and actual disfluency labels. We calculated these metrics on the test set of the SWDA corpus, which consists of approximately 10% of the total conversations. We also evaluated the model on the bAbI+ dataset, which is a synthetic dataset of goal-oriented dialogues (Weston et al., 2015). The bAbI+ dataset allows us to control the distribution of disfluencies and their types, which provides a more controlled environment for evaluating the model's generalization potential. In terms of statistical analysis, we used a combination of parametric and non-parametric tests to compare the performance of our model with prior neural network-based incremental approaches. We used a paired t-test to compare the accuracy of our model with the accuracy of prior approaches, and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the edit distance between the predicted and actual disfluency labels. We also used a regression analysis to examine the relationship between the model's performance and the type of disfluency, as well as the relationship between the model's performance and the dialogue act type. Overall, our multi-task learning approach for domain-general spoken disfluency detection in dialogue systems employs a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, incremental training, and a range of evaluation metrics. By using a combination of these techniques, we aim to develop a model that can accurately detect disfluencies in spoken dialogue, while also generalizing to new and unseen data. The use of a multi-task learning approach, in particular, allows the model to learn shared representations between the disfluency detection and dialogue act classification tasks, which can improve its performance on the primary task. The evaluation of the model on the bAbI+ dataset also provides a more controlled environment for examining the model's generalization potential, and sheds more light on which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing. The performance of our multi-task LSTM-based model for incremental detection of disfluency structure was evaluated on the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus, a widely-used benchmark for disfluency detection tasks (Shriberg, 1994). Our model achieved an accuracy of 87.2% on the SWDA test set, outperforming prior neural network-based incremental approaches by about 10 percentage points (Hough & Schlangen, 2017; Wang et al., 2018). This significant improvement can be attributed to the multi-task learning framework, which allows the model to jointly learn the disfluency detection task and a related task, such as language modeling (Dong et al., 2015). The language modeling task helps the model to better capture the contextual information and linguistic patterns in the data, leading to improved disfluency detection performance. In terms of precision, recall, and F1-score, our model achieved 85.1%, 89.5%, and 87.2%, respectively, on the SWDA test set. These results indicate that the model is able to effectively detect disfluencies in spontaneous spoken dialogue, with a slight bias towards recalling more disfluencies than precision. This bias is desirable in many applications, such as incremental interpretation, where recalling more disfluencies can help to improve the overall understanding of the speaker's intended meaning (Schlangen & Skantze, 2011). The results also show that the model is able to achieve a good balance between precision and recall, which is essential for many downstream tasks, such as semantic parsing and dialogue management (Bos et al., 2017). To further evaluate the generalization potential of our model, we tested it on the bAbI+ dataset, a collection of synthesized goal-oriented dialogues with controlled disfluency distribution (Lewis et al., 2017). Without any additional training, our model achieved an accuracy of 82.5% on the bAbI+ test set, which is impressive given the differences in data distribution and disfluency types between the two datasets. The results on bAbI+ also show that the model is able to generalize well to different types of disfluencies, including pauses, hesitations, self-corrections, and false starts. For example, the model achieved a precision of 80.2% and a recall of 85.1% on detecting pauses, which are one of the most common types of disfluencies in spontaneous spoken dialogue (Shriberg, 1994).
