Array-intensive programs are central to scientific simulation, signal and image processing, linear algebra, machine learning, and many other compute-heavy domains. Their control flow is dominated by nested loops, and their data is held in multidimensional arrays accessed through index expressions that are often affine in the loop iterators and program parameters. This regularity makes them well suited to parallel execution, both across the cores of a single machine and across the nodes of a cluster. It is therefore no surprise that array-intensive programs have been studied extensively in high-performance computing (HPC) and in compiler research (Feautrier, 1992; Kennedy & Allen, 2001). To reach good performance, such programs usually pass through a pipeline of transformations. Loop transformations, such as interchange, skewing, tiling, fusion, fission, unrolling, and peeling, restructure the iteration space to improve locality and expose parallelism (Wolf & Lam, 1991; Kelly & Pugh, 1995). Arithmetic transformations, such as algebraic simplification, common sub-expression elimination, strength reduction, and the exploitation of associativity and commutativity, reduce the cost of the computation or reshape it for vectorization. Parallelizing transformations then map the restructured computation onto threads, vector units, accelerators, or distributed processes, typically through OpenMP, MPI, or CUDA. Polyhedral compilers have automated many of these steps (Bondhugula et al., 2008; Grosser et al., 2012), and domain-specific systems such as Halide and TVM separate algorithm from schedule so that optimization choices can be explored systematically (Ragan-Kelley et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018). Despite this progress, automatic parallelizing compilers remain limited in practice. Dependence analysis is conservative in the presence of irregular accesses, pointer aliasing, or non-affine subscripts. Profitable transformation sequences are hard to find with static cost models. Performance-critical code is often tuned for a particular architecture, memory hierarchy, or interconnect. For these reasons, experienced programmers continue to apply hand-optimized transformations, often combined with compiler-generated ones, and then iteratively tune the result through profiling and experimentation. The final optimized program may differ greatly in structure from the original sequential version: loop nests are reorganized, temporary arrays are introduced or eliminated, expressions are rewritten, and computation is distributed over many threads or processes. This flexibility comes at a cost. Manual or semi-automatic transformation is error-prone, and bugs introduced during optimization, such as an off-by-one error in a tiled loop bound, a violated dependence after fusion, an incorrect reduction rewrite, or a data race in a parallel region, are notoriously difficult to detect. Testing is rarely sufficient. The input space is huge, failures may appear only for particular problem sizes or thread interleavings, and floating-point nondeterminism makes output comparison unreliable. Even trusted compilers have been shown to contain defects in their optimization passes (Yang et al., 2011). It is therefore essential to establish that the optimized program is functionally equivalent to the original sequential specification, so that the pursuit of performance does not compromise correctness. Two broad families of approaches address this need. The first is to verify the transformation engine, proving once and for all that a compiler pass preserves semantics, as in CompCert (Leroy, 2009). This is powerful but expensive, and it cannot cover transformations applied by hand or by external tools. The second is translation validation or equivalence checking, in which each (original, transformed) program pair is checked separately (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000). This approach treats the transformation as a black box and is thus well suited to the mixed human–compiler workflows common in HPC. For general programs, equivalence is undecidable, and early techniques such as regression verification and relational program logics rely on strong structural similarity between the two programs (Godlin & Strichman, 2008; Benton, 2004). Array-intensive programs, however, have a restricted structure, namely static control flow, bounded loops, and affine index expressions. This enables more specialized and more complete methods. Over the past two decades, a body of work has emerged on functional verification of array-intensive programs. One line models programs as systems of affine recurrence equations and decides their equivalence using polyhedral techniques (Barthou et al., 2002). Another represents programs as array data dependence graphs (ADDGs) and checks equivalence through synchronized traversal and reasoning over the iteration domains and dependence mappings, handling loop and algebraic transformations (Shashidhar et al., 2005; Karfa et al., 2013). Subsequent work extended these ideas to recurrences using widening (Verdoolaege et al., 2012), to code-motion transformations through value propagation (Banerjee et al., 2014), and to the verification of loop-parallelizing transformations and parallel program models (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2015). Complementary work verifies concrete tiled or parallel code using symbolic execution, model checking, or deductive verification (Blom et al., 2017). Together, these efforts define a rich but fragmented landscape that spans compiler theory, polyhedral mathematics, program logics, and automated reasoning. For a newcomer, this literature is difficult to enter. The relevant papers appear across venues in electronic design automation, programming languages, formal verification, and HPC, and they use different program representations and assumptions, such as affine versus non-affine subscripts, sequential versus parallel targets, and static versus recurrent dependences. To our knowledge, no concise introduction organizes this material around the transformations a practitioner actually encounters and the verification techniques that address each. This paper addresses that gap. Our guiding question is: which techniques exist for verifying that an optimized array-intensive program, produced through loop, arithmetic, and parallelizing transformations, is functionally equivalent to its sequential original, and what are their scope and limitations? We make three contributions. First, we describe the class of programs and transformations of interest and explain why they challenge conventional verification. Second, we survey and relate the principal approaches, covering recurrence-based, ADDG-based, and translation-validation methods, as well as those for parallel programs, and we compare them by the transformations they handle, their assumptions, and their guarantees. Third, we identify open problems, including non-affine accesses, floating-point semantics, and scalability, to guide further research. We intend this as a quick but rigorous starting point for readers entering the field. This paper is a narrative survey. It is not a systematic review with exhaustive meta-analysis, and it reports no new experiments. The goal is to give a newcomer an ordered entry point into the literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs. The methodology therefore covers four things: how we scoped the field, how we found and selected the literature, how we organized the selected work into a classification framework, and how we compared techniques qualitatively. No statistical analysis was performed. The works surveyed report heterogeneous benchmarks, tool chains, and hardware, and these cannot be pooled meaningfully. Scope and problem definition. We define an array-intensive program as one whose computation is dominated by loop nests that read and write multi-dimensional arrays. Typically the array subscripts and loop bounds are affine functions of the enclosing iterators and symbolic parameters. This is the class studied under the polyhedral model (Feautrier, 1991; Bondhugula et al., 2008). It includes the dense numerical kernels, stencils, and signal- and image-processing pipelines common in high-performance computing and embedded systems. The verification problem is as follows. Given an original sequential program and a transformed program, decide whether the two compute the same input–output relation. We treat this as equivalence checking and exclude the verification of properties of a single program, such as assertions, absence of out-of-bounds accesses, or termination, except where those properties support an equivalence argument. The transformations of interest fall into three groups: (i) loop transformations such as interchange, fusion, fission, skewing, tiling, unrolling, and bumping; (ii) arithmetic and data-flow transformations such as algebraic simplification, expression propagation, and operator reassociation or commutation; and (iii) parallelizing transformations, including those that produce multithreaded, vectorized, or GPU code. We treat translation validation, where the verifier checks each compilation instance (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000), and verification of hand-optimized code as two settings of the same problem. In the second setting no compiler provides hints about which transformations were applied. Literature identification. We searched the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and DBLP, and used Google Scholar for forward and backward citation tracking. Queries combined terms for the object of verification ("array-intensive," "affine programs," "data-dominated," "loop nest," "static control programs") with terms for the task ("equivalence checking," "translation validation," "regression verification," "program equivalence," "verification of loop transformations," "verification of parallelizing transformations"). We also added transformation-specific terms such as "code motion," "tiling validation," and "recurrence." We began from a small seed set of foundational papers on equivalence checking of data-dominated programs (Samsom et al., 1995; Shashidhar et al., 2005; Barthou et al., 2002) and followed citations in both directions until no new relevant work appeared. We also read the principal venues for compiler verification, program analysis, electronic design automation, and formal methods, including PLDI, POPL, CAV, TACAS, CC, DATE, DAC, and IEEE TCAD, for the period from the early 1990s to the present. Inclusion and exclusion criteria. A paper was included if it met all of the following conditions: (a) it addressed equivalence or refinement between two programs, or between a program and a specification in program form, where arrays are first-class data; (b) it handled at least one of the three transformation groups above in a way that goes beyond scalar-only programs; and (c) it presented a technique with enough detail to assess its soundness conditions and its limits. We excluded work whose main contribution was a transformation or optimization framework without a correctness-checking component. We also excluded purely testing-based or fuzzing-based validation without a formal argument, bounded model checking limited to tiny fixed array sizes, and domain-specific hardware verification that does not operate on program-level array semantics. Several adjacent areas were handled selectively. These are data-race and deadlock detection for parallel programs, such as GPU kernel verification (Betts et al., 2012), and general relational verification and product-program constructions (Benton, 2004; Barthe et al., 2011). We included these only where they clarify how equivalence of array programs differs from, or reuses, their ideas. When an extended journal version superseded a conference paper, we cite the journal version and mention the earlier paper only when it introduced a distinct idea. Classification framework. We read each selected paper against a fixed set of dimensions and then grouped the papers by the main modeling formalism. First, we recorded the program representation, such as array data dependence graphs, finite state machines with datapath, systems of affine recurrence equations, or polyhedral and integer-set representations. Second, we recorded the equivalence-checking strategy. The strategies we distinguished are synchronized traversal of dependence graphs with slice-based comparison (Shashidhar et al., 2005; Karfa et al., 2013), cut-point or bisimulation-style correspondence between control states (Kundu et al., 2009; Churchill et al., 2019), and direct comparison of closed-form or recurrence-based input–output mappings (Barthou et al., 2002; Verdoolaege et al., 2012). Third, we recorded the decision machinery, such as Presburger arithmetic and integer-set libraries (Pugh, 1991; Verdoolaege, 2010), SMT solvers, and normalization of arithmetic expressions. Fourth, we recorded the transformation coverage across the three groups above, including whether recurrences and data-dependent control flow are supported. Fifth, we recorded the guarantees, namely soundness, completeness for stated program classes, and the way each method fails. Sixth, we recorded the assumptions about the input pair: whether the loops are statically controlled, whether single-assignment form is required, and whether the transformations must be known in advance. Comparative analysis. For each group we assessed qualitatively three properties: expressiveness, meaning the range of transformations and program features handled; scalability, meaning whether the method depends on loop bounds or array sizes or is parametric in them; and automation, meaning the degree of user guidance, annotations, or proof effort required. Where papers report empirical results, we extracted the benchmark families, typically PolyBench-style kernels and multimedia or signal-processing codes, together with the reported verification times and the instances on which a method failed or returned an inconclusive answer. We did not rerun tools or normalize these numbers across papers. We cite them only as indications of practicality. Throughout, we separate claims established by proof in the original papers from claims supported only by experiments. Limitations of the method. The digital revolution of the late 20th and early 21st centuries has transformed numerous sectors, among them the field of academic publishing. This transformation has been characterized by the widespread adoption of open-access (OA) publishing, which removes financial, legal, and technical barriers to accessing academic materials. Several factors, including technological advancements, the demand for democratizing knowledge, and the push for transparency and repeatability in research, underpin the rise of the OA movement (Suber, 2012). Furthermore, global initiatives, such as the Budapest Open Access Initiative and the more recent Plan S, have exerted significant pressure on publishers to adapt to models that ensure scientific outputs are freely accessible to all (European Science Foundation, 2019). Despite the evident progress, the transition from subscription-based to open-access publishing has not been without challenges. One primary concern is the sustainability and quality control of OA publications (Van Noorden, 2013). The open-access landscape is diverse, comprising numerous platforms and models, including gold, green, and hybrid OA, each with its own merits and limitations. The fluctuations within these models highlight the complexity of fully operationalizing a universal OA framework (Harnad et al., 2004). Furthermore, quality assurance remains a concern, given that the barrier to publication in some OA platforms can be lower, potentially facilitating the dissemination of unverified research (Beall, 2016). Additionally, while OA publishing is now more prevalent, significant gaps exist in indexing and discoverability. Platforms such as the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and PubMed Central serve as repositories for OA literature. Still, their capacity to keep up with the growing volume of publications and to ensure seamless integration with search engines are areas needing improvement (Laakso et al., 2017). Particularly, non-Western countries, such as China, Japan, and Russia, are keenly investing in upgrading their indexing systems to ensure wider dissemination and visibility of their scholarly outputs (Ren, 2015). Another critical consideration is the role of identifiers in scholarly communications. Unique identifiers like ORCID (Open Researcher and Contributor ID) and DOI (Digital Object Identifier) play a fundamental role in enhancing transparency and ensuring that contributions are accurately attributed. These identifiers facilitate the accurate tracking of scholarly output and peer review processes, making academic contributions more transparent and accountable (Haak, Fenner, & Paglione, 2012). Social media channels further complicate the OA ecosystem by serving as both platforms for dissemination and discourse regarding academic work. The scholarly community’s increasing engagement with platforms such as Twitter, ResearchGate, and Academia.edu signifies a shift toward more interactive and publicly accessible scholarly communications. The scholarly discourse on these platforms, coupled with traditional media, provides immediate metrics of impact through Altmetrics, offering real-time indicators of how research is being used and disseminated beyond traditional citation metrics (Priem, Taraborelli, & Groth, 2010). Given these considerations, several research questions arise: What constitutes a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing that balances accessibility, quality, and sustainability? How can indexing services evolve to better meet the needs of a diversified global research community? What frameworks and strategies can enhance the integration of alternative metrics with traditional citation-based evaluations to assess the impact of scientific work comprehensively? This study aims to address these questions by proposing a model for open-access publishing that encompasses total accessibility, integrity adherence to ethical publishing standards, and the diversification of evaluation metrics. Specifically, the article contributes to existing literature by providing a detailed analysis of various OA models and tools, evaluating the efficacy of current indexing platforms, and offering strategies for integrating traditional and alternative metrics. Furthermore, it highlights the initiatives taken by countries beyond the traditionally dominant Western academic hubs, emphasizing the dynamics and contributions these regions bring to the OA sphere. Through this comprehensive analysis, the study seeks to provide researchers, publishers, and policymakers with a nuanced understanding of the OA landscape and practical recommendations for its enhancement. By exploring these dimensions, this study not only contributes to the ongoing discourse on OA but also provides a roadmap for future developments in making academic research more accessible, equitable, and impactful across various disciplines. Methods To investigate the comprehensive approach to open access publishing, a mixed-methods research design was employed, integrating both quantitative and qualitative components to ensure robust and comprehensive outcomes. The study was structured to provide a broad understanding of current platforms, tools, and techniques utilized in open access publishing. The quantitative component involved a systematic review of publishing practices across a selection of open access journals from various indices. Data were extracted from the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and PubMed Central, which represent ubiquitous and multifaceted sources of open access content. A sample of 200 open access journals was selected using stratified random sampling to ensure representation across disciplines, geographical locations, and publishing models. This stratified sampling technique was necessary to account for potential biases arising from regional disparities and discipline-specific practices in open access publishing (Smith et al., 2021). Data points included journal visibility, indexing status, adherence to ethical publishing standards, use of digital publishing tools, and metrics for evaluating scholarly communication impact. Data extraction was performed using a web-scraping algorithm developed in Python to systematically collect and store information from the journal websites and associated platforms. This automated approach reduced human error and increased efficiency in data collection. Journals were categorized based on their compliance with Plan S standards, participation in initiatives to improve transparency and ethical standards, and integration with social media channels and alternative metrics systems such as Altmetrics (Piwowar et al., 2018). Statistical analysis was carried out using SPSS Version 27. To evaluate the prevalence and diversity of platforms and tools in open access journals, descriptive statistics were first employed, providing central tendencies and dispersion metrics for variables of interest. Bivariate analyses, specifically chi-square tests, were utilized to examine associations between journal characteristics (such as geographical location or publishing model) and their adoption of open access tools and practices. Furthermore, a logistic regression model was developed to predict the likelihood of a journal integrating social media metrics based on its indexing status and adherence to ethical standards (García et al., 2020). The qualitative component comprised semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders in the academic publishing ecosystem, including authors, editors, and librarians. A purposive sampling technique was used to identify participants with extensive experience in open access publishing, aiming for a diverse sample representing different academic disciplines and regions. Interviews were conducted virtually, recorded with consent, and transcribed verbatim. Anonymity and confidentiality of participants were assured to foster openness and depth in responses. The thematic analysis approach was employed to analyze qualitative data, identifying recurring themes related to the perceived challenges and benefits of various open access platforms and tools (Braun & Clarke, 2022). Codes were developed iteratively and reviewed by multiple researchers to ensure reliability and reduce bias. These themes were cross-referenced with quantitative findings to provide nuanced insights into the scholarly community's needs and preferences regarding open access publishing. Integration of the quantitative and qualitative data occurred through a process of connecting the data sets in a synergy that allowed for a comprehensive overview of the investigated domain. The triangulation of data sources ensured a more detailed and accurate depiction of the current state and future directions for open access publishing (Creswell, 2014). Throughout the research design, ethical considerations were prioritized. Participants in the qualitative study provided informed consent, and ethical clearance was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB). Data handling and analysis adhered to the confidentiality agreements and GDPR compliance for international participants. In summary, the detailed methodological framework adopted in this study provided a multifaceted understanding of the mechanisms and dynamics of open access publishing platforms and tools. The integration of diverse data sources and types enabled an in-depth analysis of the open access landscape, addressing the research questions comprehensively and generating findings with implications for policy makers, publishers, and the academic community at large. This study investigates the implementation and effectiveness of open-access platforms and tools, underscoring their roles in enhancing the visibility, accessibility, and impact of scholarly communications. Our findings are categorized into themes aligned with transparency enhancement, ethical standard adherence, evaluation metric diversification, and improved indexing. An analysis of 200 open-access journals indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) revealed that 80% of these journals have implemented policies mandating authors to disclose conflicts of interest and have established strict guidelines conforming to the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) standards (Smith et al., 2021). The adoption of digital object identifiers (DOIs), a critical step in ensuring transparency and traceability of scholarly work, was observed in 92% of the sampled journals. This implementation facilitates seamless citation tracking and usage analytics, contributing to greater transparency in scholarly publishing. The emergence and proliferation of alternative metrics (Altmetrics) were evident from our study. Analysis from a sample of 500 articles published across disciplines showed that 68% received significant attention on social media platforms, with an average Altmetric Attention Score of 55.3 (Johnson & Lee, 2023). Articles with moderate traditional citation counts (<20) displayed Altmetric scores exceeding 70 in 40% of cases, indicating that these alternative metrics capture dimensions of impact not visible through citation counts alone (Anderson et al., 2022). Utilizing ORCID (Open Researcher and Contributor iD) as a persistent digital identifier showed that 75% of researchers in our study sample linked their ORCID to publications, enhancing the precision of author attribution and contributing to more accurate impact assessments. This linkage is essential for recognizing and rewarding peer review activities and was facilitated through platforms like Publons, where reviewers in our sample accrued an average of 2.1 credits per review (Harris et al., 2023). Significant advancements in open-access journal indexing have been recorded, most notably within Asia, as evidenced by initiatives from China, Japan, and Korea (Li et al., 2023). In these countries, a 25% increase in the number of journals indexed in PubMed Central and DOAJ was identified between 2020 and 2023. Furthermore, these journals experienced a 40% surge in article downloads, reflecting improved availability and discoverability due to enhanced indexing protocols. The revamping of institutional repositories in Russia led to a 35% increase in submitted scholarly outputs, reflecting the enhanced confidence and reliance on open-access platforms (Ivanov & Petrov, 2023). Concurrently, free indexing services such as Google Scholar saw usage rise by 30%, underscoring the necessity for adaptive indexing mechanisms that meet the evolving demands of researchers. The breadth of tools fostering scholarly interaction and post-publication discourse was exemplified by the widespread adoption of platforms like ResearchGate and Academia.edu. Our findings indicate that 60% of researchers utilized such platforms to share preprints and post-publication versions, facilitating academic discussions that attract an average of 1200 views and 250 downloads per document shared (Müller & Schmidt, 2022). Moreover, the integration of open-access publications into educational resources has seen significant growth, with educators incorporating open-access content in 40% of university curricula within our study's scope. This inclusion has led to heightened student engagement and retention, observed through course performance data where students accessing open-access resources scored an average of 6% higher than peers reliant on restricted materials (Garcia et al., 2023). In summary, our results outline significant advancements in open-access publishing ecosystems, echoing a trend towards increased transparency, accessibility, and diversified impact assessment methods. These improvements suggest a robust trajectory of growth and adaptation in open-access publishing, positioning such systems to meet the nuanced demands of contemporary scholarly communication efficiently. Discussion and Conclusion The drive towards open-access (OA) publishing represents a transformative shift in scholarly communication, promising expanded accessibility and dissemination of research findings globally. This discussion centers around the various strategic elements inherent in a comprehensive approach to OA publishing, emphasizing transparency, ethical standards, and diversified evaluation metrics. Our findings indicate that while these components offer significant advantages, several challenges must be addressed to fully realize their potential. Firstly, increased transparency in scholarly communication emerged as a fundamental promise of OA publishing. Transparency facilitates the democratization of knowledge and ensures equitable access to research outputs (Suber, 2012). Over the past 15 years, the U.S. has witnessed a general decline in overall rates of youth homicide (David-Ferdon, Dahlberg, & Kegler, 2013). Nonetheless, youth violence rates remain high in this country, with homicide being the third leading cause of death among persons aged 10–24 years (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2011). While the negative consequences of youth violence are experienced most directly by individuals and families, communities and society also experience the negative effects. Youth violence can affect communities by substantially increasing the cost of health care, reducing productivity, and diminishing property values (Mercy, Butchart, Farrington, & Cerda, 2002). In 2005, it was estimated that the medical care and lost productivity costs associated with youth violence were roughly $17.5 billion (WISQARS, 2010). Given the public health importance of preventing youth violence, it fits with the overall mission of CDC, which seeks to put science into action in order to protect America from health, safety, and security threats. Broadly, the Division of Violence Prevention (DVP) at CDC is committed to the primary prevention of violence. DVP’s work addresses violence at all stages of the public health model: monitoring violence-related injuries; conducting research on risk and protective factors for violence; developing and evaluating the effectiveness of violence prevention programs and strategies; conducting research on and promoting the widespread adoption and dissemination of evidence-based prevention programs and strategies; and helping state and local partners plan, implement, and evaluate prevention programs and strategies. Despite DVP’s many state and local partnerships, it is still the case that a majority of the efforts to reduce youth violence in communities are limited as to their intended audience or their approach. The intended targets of youth violence interventions are frequently violent offenders. The strategies used frequently involve identifying, incarcerating, and/or rehabilitating known juvenile offenders to prevent them from committing violent acts again. Although such criminal justice efforts are important, evidence-based primary prevention strategies have the potential to prevent youth violence from occurring in the first place. Many interventions are also limited by an approach that focuses solely on individual- or relationship-level factors. Research indicates that prevention activities should attend to the accumulation of risk factors across multiple levels of the social ecology, as youth with multiple risk factors are more likely to become violent than those exposed to only one risk factor (Herrenkohl et al., 2000). While it is important to pay attention to individual- and relationship-level factors (e.g., early aggressive behavior, social problem-solving skill deficits, negative parental influences, exposure to violence, and affiliation with delinquent peers), attention to the roles that larger sociocultural, economic, and community factors play in the development of youth violence is also important, particularly when attempting to generate a community-wide impact on reducing youth violence rates. Unfortunately, most evidence-based prevention strategies tend to focus on addressing individual- and/or relationship-level risk factors for youth violence. A multifaceted prevention approach is needed to reduce risk factors and to enhance protective factors at the individual, relationship, and community levels. A multifaceted prevention approach includes complementary components (e.g., programs, policies, and strategies) that are designed to work at multiple levels of the social ecology to address identified needs within a community. Moreover, a prevention approach designed to have a community-wide impact on youth violence needs to provide an adequate exposure to the prevention components to a sufficiently large number of people to have the level of saturation necessary to achieve desired preventive effects. The type and intensity of the components provided are likely to vary according to the risk factors present in the groups involved in the program. By including universal components (i.e., delivered to all youth, regardless of risk) as well as components that focus on selective subgroups of youth or families at elevated risk, a multifaceted approach can have a pervasive reach within a community, thereby increasing the likelihood of community-wide reductions in youth violence. However, few studies have utilized rigorous methodologies to evaluate comprehensive and multifaceted efforts to prevent youth violence in specific communities. The National Centers of Excellence in Youth Violence Prevention (YVPCs) are filling some of these critical gaps by partnering with communities to prevent violence. The YVPCs were established in 2000 through a Congressional mandate in response to the 1999 Columbine school shootings, and they represent DVP’s largest investment in youth violence prevention (www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/ACE; see Table 1 for a list of all current and former YVPCs). In 2000–2005, CDC funded ten centers (then known as the Academic Centers of Excellence [ACE] Program; David-Ferdon & Hammond 2008) across the U.S., with the primary goals of: (1) building the scientific infrastructure necessary to support the development and widespread application of effective youth violence interventions; (2) promoting interdisciplinary research strategies to address the The advancement of robotic-assisted surgery has revolutionized the field of minimally invasive procedures, capitalizing on the precision and dexterity offered by surgical robots. Robotic systems, such as the da Vinci Surgical System, have enhanced surgical outcomes by providing surgeons with enhanced visualization, precision, and control within the operative field. Despite these advancements, a critical limitation of current robotic surgical systems is the lack of direct haptic feedback—specifically, the ability to sense and interpret forces applied to and by surgical instruments in real-time (Rucker et al., 2019). This absence of tactile sensation can lead to excessive force application, potentially causing tissue damage, or insufficient force application, inhibiting effective tissue manipulation. Thus, an accurate and reliable method for force feedback remains a significant unmet need in robotic surgery. Efforts to incorporate haptic feedback in surgical robotics have primarily focused on designing complex hardware systems capable of simulating the sense of touch (Passenberg et al., 2014). However, these systems are often costly and difficult to integrate into existing surgical workflows due to their sensitivity to sterilization processes and potential interference with the surgeon’s tactile capabilities (King et al., 2014). To circumvent these limitations, an alternative approach involves leveraging visual cues to infer force information, thereby avoiding the complexities associated with direct hardware feedback systems. The human visual cortex has an innate capacity to intuitively interpret environmental forces based on visual information. This intrinsic ability to perceive forces through observation of object movements and deformations has inspired our pursuit of utilizing visual data to approximate force feedback in robotic surgery. Video sequences from endoscopic cameras offer a rich source of visual data that can be leveraged to discern mechanical interactions between surgical instruments and biological tissues (Li et al., 2019). This passive sensing approach not only capitalizes on existing video feeds integral to surgical procedures but also promises a non-invasive, cost-effective solution to the haptic feedback problem. Current methodologies utilizing visual information for surgical force feedback have largely focused on static images for force estimation (Papazov et al., 2018). However, these approaches generally neglect temporal dynamics and the potential insights about forces that can be gained from motion cues during tissue deformation. Moreover, traditional methods often rely on handcrafted features, which may not capture complex patterns indicative of force interactions adequately. In recent years, deep learning techniques, particularly Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs), have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in modeling sequential and temporal data across various domains (Bai et al., 2018). These architectures are adept at capturing long-range dependencies and have shown promise in tasks that require understanding of temporal dynamics, such as action recognition in videos and sound classification. TCNs provide an end-to-end learning framework that can effectively model the progression of tissue deformation over time, offering a potential pathway to infer surgical forces directly from dynamic visual cues. Given these considerations, this study introduces an innovative methodological framework that marries RGB video data with 3D point cloud information, processed through a Temporal Convolutional Network. This approach harnesses the spatial and temporal representations of tissue interaction to predict forces during robotic-assisted surgery. Our method introduces a novel application of TCNs specifically tailored to understand the temporal sequences inherent in surgical video data, contributing to the growing body of research on perception-based force estimation. This study builds upon existing literature in several critical ways. First, our approach integrates depth information via point clouds, enriching the force prediction model by providing 3D spatial context to the RGB data. Prior studies have predominantly focused on 2D video data, whereas our model leverages the added dimension of depth to reveal more intricate details of tissue manipulation. Second, by employing a TCN architecture, we transform the concept of endoscopic video analysis from static image classification to dynamic sequence analysis, thus enhancing the temporal sensitivity of force estimation. Finally, our work demonstrates the utility of this method in practical settings, validated through experiments conducted on phantom models and ex vivo liver organs to assess the accuracy and potential translational impact of our approach. The central research question driving this work is whether temporal visual cues, derived from RGB and point cloud data, can accurately predict interactive forces during surgical tasks in a robotic surgery setting. By addressing this question, the study seeks to evaluate whether a purely vision-based system could complement or even replace current haptic feedback methodologies, which are largely reliant on hardware sensors prone to physical constraints and integration challenges. Our findings aim to provide meaningful insights into the potential integration of video-based force prediction systems in robotic surgical applications, potentially reshaping the approach to haptic feedback in minimally invasive surgery. This paper presents our comprehensive approach to this challenge. We describe the design and implementation of an RGB-Point Cloud Temporal Convolutional Network, detail its ability to translate endoscopic video data into actionable force estimation, and evaluate its performance on both a controlled phantom setting and an ex vivo liver model. Through this work, we envision contributing to the development of more intuitive, cost-effective, and efficacious tools for robotic surgery that enhance surgeon capabilities and patient safety. In this study, we aim to develop a robust deep learning framework to predict surgical forces using RGB-point cloud data captured from endoscopic procedures. Our approach involves a series of methodical steps including data acquisition, model design and architecture, training procedure, and statistical analysis. This section provides a detailed description of each of these components. Data Acquisition The data collection was executed in both phantom and ex vivo settings to ensure the robustness and applicability of the model across different scenarios that mimic real surgical environments. We utilized the da Vinci Surgical System in a controlled laboratory environment equipped with an OptoForce force sensor to capture true force measurements alongside visual data. The data acquisition system was set to operate at a synchronized rate of 30 Hz, which is the standard frame rate for most video captures in surgical settings, aligning the force data with the visual frames effectively. For the phantom setting, a silicon-based synthetic tissue model capable of mimicking the heterogeneities and mechanical properties of actual human tissue was employed. This model was subjected to a variety of instrument-tissue interactions such as poking, grasping, and pulling. In the ex vivo setting, porcine liver segments were selected due to their anatomical and biomechanical similarity to human liver tissue. The liver samples were prepared within 24 hours of slaughter to preserve tissue integrity and maintain physiological relevance (Gibson et al., 2019). All procedures involving ex vivo tissue adhered to ethical guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). The dataset consisted of visual data captured in the form of RGB images and corresponding point clouds, with the latter constructed using stereoscopic imaging techniques to derive depth information. Model Design and Architecture The core of our predictive framework is the RGB-Point Cloud Temporal Convolutional Network (RPCTCN). This architecture leverages the temporal nature of both the visual and depth data to analyze and predict the interaction forces. The RPCTCN is composed of three principal components: a feature extractor, temporal convolutional layers, and a regression output layer. The feature extractor processes RGB images and point clouds separately. The Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture, based on ResNet-50 pre-trained weights (He et al., 2016), is utilized for extracting rich features from the RGB images. Meanwhile, the point cloud data are processed using a Pseudo PointNet++ structure, known for its effectiveness in capturing geometric information through multi-scale grouping layers (Qi et al., 2017). The temporal convolutional layers, utilizing dilated convolutions, are designed to capture temporal dependencies over multiple time frames. By increasing the receptive field with dilations, the model effectively considers the temporal evolution of deformations, a critical factor for accurate force prediction. The fusion of RGB and point cloud features is achieved through a late fusion strategy to allow the model to learn complementary features before the final regression layer predicts the contact forces. Training Procedure Data augmentation techniques, including geometric transformations and photometric alterations, were applied to reduce overfitting and enhance the generalization capabilities of the model. Additionally, we employed a real-time data backpropagation strategy to make optimal use of GPU accelerative computations provided by NVIDIA’s CUDA platform. The model was trained using a Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function, with the Python-based PyTorch framework facilitating the model development. An Adam optimizer, known for its efficiency and adaptability, was chosen with a learning rate initialized at 1e-3, gradually decreasing with a schedule based on validation loss plateauing (Kingma & Ba, 2015). The batch size was dynamically adjusted based on the available GPU memory, with an epoch size that considered the entire data cycles fivefold. A train-validation split of 80%-20% was utilized, with stratification to ensure all force ranges were represented in both datasets. Statistical Analysis To evaluate the performance of the RPCTCN model, statistical techniques were employed to compare predicted forces against ground truth measurements. The primary metric was the mean absolute error (MAE), computed as follows: \[ \text{MAE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \left| Yi - \hat{Y}i \right| \] where \( Yi \) represents the actual force measured by the OptoForce sensor, \( \hat{Y}i \) denotes the predicted force, and \( N \) is the total number of test samples. A secondary evaluation metric, the Pearson correlation coefficient, was calculated to assess the linear relationship between the predicted and actual forces, providing insights into the model’s ability to preserve force trends (Benesty et al., 2009). Cross-validation techniques with K-fold (K=5) ensured that model performance metrics were stable and generalized across unseen data. Results were statistically analyzed using a paired t-test to determine the significance of the difference between predicted and true forces, with a significance level set at α = 0.05 (Rosner, 2016). In summary, the methodological framework established here provides a comprehensive blueprint for implementing and assessing a deep learning approach for predicting surgical forces from RGB and point cloud data, potentially filling the gap for haptic feedback in robotic-assisted surgery. The results from our study demonstrate the capacity of the proposed RGB-Point Cloud Temporal Convolutional Networks (PC-TCN) to accurately predict surgical forces from visual data in both phantom and ex vivo settings. Our experimental setup, which included the da Vinci Surgical System augmented with OptoForce sensors for ground truth force data capture, revealed significant findings concerning the feasibility and precision of using video-based methods for surgical force prediction. To establish baseline performance, we initially conducted experiments on a phantom tissue model designed to mimic the mechanical properties of human tissue. The OptoForce sensors, providing highly reliable force data, were used to benchmark the predictions of our PC-TCN model. Over a set of 150 experimental trials, the data captured was used to train the network, yielding a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.582 N (SD = 0.156). This level of precision highlights the network's capacity to accurately predict force application based solely on temporal visual features. A broad range of force values were tested, with the model consistently producing errors within the range of human perceptual sensitivity, which, according to Visell et al. (2017), can typically discern force changes of approximately 1 N. Extending our study to more biologically relevant conditions, we applied the PC-TCN model to an ex vivo liver tissue environment. In these trials, designed to simulate real-world surgical conditions, the system demonstrated its robustness across different levels of tissue compliance and anatomy complexity. The ex vivo trials comprised 120 experimental runs, capturing varied interactions with the tissue and dealing with complex deformation dynamics. The advent of high-throughput sequencing technologies has ushered in a new era of medicine centered around genomics and precision healthcare. This paradigm shift is profoundly altering how diseases, particularly oncological conditions, are understood, diagnosed, and treated. Genomic data have emerged as integral components in developing targeted therapies, refining disease classification systems, and tailoring treatments to individual patient profiles (Collins and Varmus, 2015). Despite the transformative potential of genomic information, significant challenges remain regarding the integration and utilization of this data within clinical workflows and research environments. A formidable obstacle in realizing the benefits of precision medicine is the fragmentation of data across disparate systems and the complexity inherent in harmonizing clinical and genomic datasets (Manolio et al., 2017). One central issue is the siloed nature of data storage in healthcare institutions, where clinical data reside in electronic medical records (EMR) and genomic information is often stored in separate research databases or within specific laboratory information management systems (LIMS). The divergence in data storage formats, coupled with privacy and security constraints, complicates efforts to craft holistic and integrative views of patient data that could accelerate translational research (Kho et al., 2012). Furthermore, the sheer volume and complexity of genomic data necessitate advanced computational tools for effective data mining and interpretation, a capability not typically embedded in conventional EMR systems (Kohane et al., 2012). The need for an integrative approach that seamlessly combines clinical and genomic data into a singular and accessible platform has been recognized as a critical priority in advancing the practice of personalized medicine (Tenenbaum et al., 2016). The goal is to enable researchers and clinicians to efficiently query, extract, and leverage comprehensive datasets to facilitate research initiatives and optimize patient management strategies. While various genomic databases and bioinformatics tools exist, these are often limited in scope and operational efficiency, failing to adequately bridge the translational gap between research settings and clinical applications. Current solutions typically offer fragmented functionalities, lacking comprehensive integration with EMR systems or focusing exclusively on either genomic insights or clinical outcomes without duly considering the interplay between the two (Hamburg and Collins, 2010). Additionally, many existing systems are limited by challenging user interfaces, scarce interoperability features, and non-compliance with privacy standards, which collectively hinder their utility in real-world clinical settings (McCarty et al., 2011). Given the limitations and hurdles identified, our primary research question centers around the development of a robust, secure, and efficient platform that integrates clinical and genomic data comprehensively, facilitating translational research and enabling precision medicine. Our contributions aim to address these gaps by emphasizing several key areas: 1. Data Integration: Developing a platform that seamlessly aggregates clinical and genomic data from heterogeneous sources into a unified model accessible for both retrospective analyses and cohort identification for prospective trials. 2. User Accessibility: Crafting an interface that supports non-technical users in navigating complex datasets, thereby democratizing access to data for researchers and clinicians without extensive bioinformatics expertise. 3. Privacy and Compliance: Ensuring robust data security measures aligned with regulatory standards such as HIPAA, thereby safeguarding patient information while facilitating research advancements. 4. Scalability and Flexibility: Building a scalable infrastructure capable of accommodating a growing volume of diverse data types and ensuring adaptability to future technological advancements. 5. Enabling Research Queries: Allowing customizable data retrieval functionalities that facilitate hypothesis-driven research and data exploration, thus accelerating scientific discovery and clinical application. 6. Clinical Translation: Emphasizing toolsets that directly aid in clinical decision-making processes by providing actionable insights derived from integrated datasets, which support improved patient outcomes through tailored therapeutic strategies. In response to these needs and challenges, we introduce the Synergistic Patient and Research Knowledge Systems (SPARKS) and the suite of tools encompassed within the Oncology Data Retrieval Systems (OncDRS). OncDRS represents a significant stride towards creating an integrative informatics framework that redefines how clinical and genomic datasets are utilized within healthcare ecosystems. By addressing the complexities of data integration and focusing on practical functionality within clinical and research domains, OncDRS sets the groundwork for the next evolution of precision medicine. This paper details the design, development, and deployment of the OncDRS platform, examining its capabilities in facilitating translational research and enabling precision health interventions. By leveraging OncDRS, we aim to provide an indispensable resource for catalyzing research initiatives and driving innovation in personalized healthcare, potentially transforming patient care paradigms and enhancing clinical research outcomes. Methods The development and deployment of the Oncology Data Retrieval Systems (OncDRS) were designed with a focus on creating an integrative and scalable platform that effectively bridges the gap between disparate clinical and genomic data, ultimately facilitating translational research and precision medicine initiatives. This Methods section delineates the data sources, system architecture, user interface design, data integration procedures, and statistical analysis protocols employed in OncDRS. Data Sources OncDRS aggregates data from multiple repositories including electronic health records (EHR), laboratory information management systems (LIMS), and genomic sequencing databases. The EHR data includes patient demographics, procedural history, diagnosis codes, medication records, and clinical notes, sourced from a network of participating hospitals and clinics. Genomic data is acquired through partnerships with national genomic sequencing efforts and in-house sequencing cores that provide detailed information on genomic variants, expression profiles, and methylation patterns. Metadata from relevant open-access genomic databases, such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), are also incorporated to enrich the contextual understanding of genomic variations (Smith et al., 2020). System Architecture The system is built on a robust, cloud-based infrastructure to support the complex demands of data processing and retrieval. It utilizes a three-tier architecture comprising the presentation, application, and data layers. The data layer is underpinned by a hybrid storage model that leverages both relational databases for structured EHR data (e.g., MySQL) and NoSQL stores (e.g., MongoDB) to manage unstructured genomic data (Johnson et al., 2019). This hybrid approach permits scalable storage and rapid retrieval of high-throughput genetic information. The application layer is developed using a service-oriented architecture (SOA) that supports modularity and reuse of key functionalities, such as data preprocessing, security authentication, and query handling. APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) are used extensively to ensure compatibility and interoperability with existing institutional systems and external data sources (Chen and Clark, 2021). User Interface Design The OncDRS user interface is designed with usability and accessibility in mind, allowing researchers with varying levels of technical expertise to navigate the system effectively. The interface employs a dashboard-driven approach where users can visually explore data sets, refine queries using a series of filtering tools, and generate customized reports. An advanced query builder tool enables users to construct complex queries using a combination of clinical and genomic data attributes. This is achieved through an intuitive drag-and-drop panel and natural language processing capabilities that allow users to query the system in plain language (Martinez et al., 2022). Data Integration Procedures A critical component of OncDRS is its ability to integrate and standardize data from heterogeneous sources. Data integration procedures are carried out in four principal stages: data extraction, transformation, normalization, and loading (ETL process). During extraction, data is pulled from source systems using automated scripts and APIs. Data transformation ensures that disparate data formats are converted into a common schema, employing standards such as HL7 FHIR for clinical data and VCF for genomic variants (Ramanathan et al., 2020). Normalization involves resolving coding discrepancies across data sets—for example, mapping various diagnostic codes to a unified ontology such as SNOMED CT. Furthermore, the integration pipeline employs controlled vocabularies and ontologies to annotate genomic data with relevant phenotypic information. Loading involves ingestion of the standardized data into the unified database where it is indexed and made available for querying. Statistical Analysis A suite of statistical tools is embedded within OncDRS to facilitate data analysis and visualization. Descriptive statistics are routinely generated to provide summary insights into patient populations, treatment outcomes, and genomic variant distributions. Advanced analytics, such as survival analysis, regression modeling, and machine learning algorithms, are implemented to support hypothesis-driven research. Kaplan-Meier plots are used for visualizing survival data, while Cox proportional hazards models facilitate the identification of prognostic factors within genomic and clinical datasets. Machine learning applications utilize both supervised and unsupervised approaches. Predictive modeling for patient stratification employs algorithms such as random forests and support vector machines, enabling the identification of potential biomarkers for therapy responses (Lee et al., 2021). Unsupervised clustering methods, such as hierarchical clustering and k-means, assist in the discovery of novel subgroups within high-dimensional genomic data. The statistical computations are conducted using integrated libraries from R and Python, with computational tasks being orchestrated through a distributed framework to enhance processing efficiency. Visualizations are produced using tools like ggplot2 and D3.js, ensuring that the output is both interpretable and publication-ready. In summary, OncDRS represents an advanced platform designed to promote seamless integration and analysis of clinical and genomic data, thereby empowering the translational research efforts and supporting personalized medicine applications. The implementation and application of the Oncology Data Retrieval Systems (OncDRS) platform have yielded significant outcomes in terms of research facilitation, data integration, and precision medicine advancements. The platform's operational performance was evaluated over a period of one year, during which it demonstrated remarkable efficiency and effectiveness. First, the adoption rate of OncDRS within our institution was quantitatively assessed. Within 12 months of its deployment, OncDRS facilitated a total of 1,532 research queries, reflecting an average of 128 queries per month. This high query volume signifies the platform's pivotal role in supporting oncological research initiatives and highlights its utility in streamlining data retrieval processes (Smith et al., 2023). In addition to query volume, the system processed requests at a median response time of 4.2 minutes per query, indicating a high throughput and robust data handling capacity (Johnson et al., 2023). In terms of data integration, OncDRS successfully amalgamated clinical and genomic datasets from 14 distinct data repositories across multiple institutions, encompassing over 1.2 million patient records. This integration effort enabled comprehensive data congruence, allowing for the retrieval of harmonized datasets. Notably, genomic data coverage was extensive, with complete genomic profiles available for 85% of the integrated patient cohort. This comprehensive data amalgamation substantially augments the granularity and breadth of datasets available for research, providing more nuanced insights into oncological diseases (Miller and Chou, 2023). Further, OncDRS demonstrated substantial efficacy in cohort identification for retrospective and prospective studies. The cohort retrieval capability of OncDRS was validated by its application in identifying patient subsets for 54 different research studies, of which 38% were initiated as multicenter collaboration efforts, leveraging the platform’s interoperability features (Chen et al., 2023). Importantly, the system supported the precise identification of patient cohorts based on specific genomic and phenotypic characteristics, facilitating highly targeted research studies that are pivotal for advancing precision medicine. Quantitative analysis of OncDRS's impact on research outcomes revealed tangible benefits. For instance, studies utilizing OncDRS-retrieved datasets reported a 30% increase in statistical power attributed to enhanced sample size and data specificity. Furthermore, there was a reported 24% reduction in time to data acquisition compared to traditional data retrieval methods, underscoring the platform's efficiency in expediting research workflows (Nguyen et al., 2023). In the realm of precision medicine, OncDRS has been instrumental in advancing patient-specific treatment strategies. Among the clinical applications, OncDRS facilitated the identification of pathognomonic genetic mutations in 27% of patients analyzed, which subsequently informed and altered therapeutic decisions in 81% of those cases. This exemplifies the direct impact of integrated clinical-genomic data on improving patient outcomes by tailoring treatment interventions to individual genetic profiles (Brown and Patel, 2023). To assess user satisfaction and system usability, a survey was conducted among researchers and clinicians who utilized OncDRS. Feedback from 312 respondents indicated a 92% satisfaction rate regarding the platform's user interface and data retrieval capabilities. Qualitative comments highlighted the system's intuitive design and robust query capabilities as significant factors contributing to user satisfaction (Kim et al., 2023). Overall, the results substantiate that OncDRS is an effective, efficient, and essential tool for oncology research and clinical applications. In the dynamic landscape of health-related settings, the role of Knowledge Brokers (KBs) has gained significant attention as an integral component for facilitating Knowledge Translation (KT). Knowledge Translation, defined by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), involves a dynamic and iterative process that includes the synthesis, dissemination, exchange, and ethically sound application of knowledge to improve the health of Canadians, provide more effective health services and products, and strengthen the healthcare system (CIHR, 2015). KBs serve as pivotal intermediaries who engage with various stakeholders to bridge the gap between research and practice, thereby enhancing the uptake and utilization of evidence-based practices in healthcare settings (Bornbaum et al., 2015). Despite the acknowledged importance of KT, the empirical evaluation and theoretical exploration of KBs' roles remain underdeveloped. Particularly, there is a noticeable gap in the literature concerning the effectiveness of KBs in health-related environments and the specific factors contributing to their success or failure in facilitating knowledge exchange (Lomas, 2007; Phipps et al., 2012). KBs often operate as multifaceted agents performing tasks such as knowledge management, linkage facilitation, and capacity building (Ward et al., 2009). However, the breadth and depth of these roles may vary significantly across different contexts, influencing how effectively they can translate knowledge into practice. The ambiguity surrounding the effectiveness of KBs can be attributed to several factors, including the lack of standardized metrics for assessing KB performance and the complex nature of health systems where these brokers operate. Health sectors are typified by intricate interactions among diverse stakeholders, ranging from researchers and policymakers to clinicians and patients. The absence of a universally accepted framework for evaluating KBs complicates efforts to quantify their impact on KT outcomes (Dobbins et al., 2009). Moreover, while anecdotal and descriptive accounts provide insight into the practical activities conducted by KBs, rigorous empirical evidence focusing on their direct influence on knowledge, attitudes, skills, practices, and health policy changes is limited (Gagnon et al., 2011). This systematic review and thematic analysis aim to address the existing gap by exploring the nature and function of knowledge brokering within health-related settings. Our primary research question seeks to determine whether KBs effectively contribute to KT and to identify the factors that influence their success in various health contexts. Specifically, we investigate the operational roles of KBs and map the diverse activities they engage in to facilitate KT processes. Additionally, this review evaluates evidence from a subset of studies to ascertain measurable changes in knowledge, skills, and policies or practices attributable to knowledge brokering efforts. The contributions of this study are multifold. First, by systematically gathering and synthesizing empirical data, the review provides a comprehensive overview of the existing evidence regarding KB roles, responsibilities, and methodologies across different health settings. This evidence can inform stakeholders and guide future research directions in exploring effective strategies for knowledge brokering (Lavis et al., 2003). Second, the thematic analysis categorizes KB functions into distinct roles, offering a clearer conceptual understanding of their potential impact on KT. Such categorization is essential for developing standardized evaluation frameworks that stakeholders can utilize to measure KB effectiveness reliably (Van Kammen et al., 2006). Moreover, this review highlights the inadequacies in current research methodologies and stresses the need for enhanced rigour in evaluating KB effectiveness. By identifying the gaps in methodological approaches, the study sets the stage for developing robust research designs that can yield more conclusive evidence regarding KB impacts. Our findings suggest an urgent need for long-term, outcome-focused studies incorporating diverse methodologies to assess the effectiveness of KBs across various dimensions of health systems. Ultimately, by clarifying the roles and effectiveness of KBs, this research endeavors to contribute to improving the integration of KT processes within health systems. Enhanced understanding and application of KB strategies can significantly impact education, practice, and policy, leading to better alignment between research outcomes and real-world health practices. This alignment is crucial for optimizing healthcare delivery and fostering an environment where evidence-based practices become integral to continuous quality improvement processes within health sectors (Grimshaw et al., 2012). Overall, this review underscores the significance of knowledge brokering as a critical element in bridging the 'know-do' gap in health-related settings. By addressing current knowledge deficiencies and proposing pathways for future inquiry, our study endeavors to cultivate a more profound appreciation of KBs' potential to catalyze meaningful change in healthcare systems worldwide. Methods This systematic review was designed following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to ensure methodological rigor and transparency (Moher et al., 2009). The review aimed to identify, evaluate, and synthesize available evidence on the function and effectiveness of knowledge brokers (KBs) in health-related settings. Data Sources A comprehensive search strategy was developed in collaboration with a health research librarian to capture a wide breadth of relevant literature. Eight electronic databases were searched, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Scopus, SocINDEX, and Health Business Elite. The search strategy combined keywords and MeSH terms related to knowledge brokering, knowledge translation, and health settings. English language restrictions were applied due to resource and expertise limitations. Additionally, grey literature was sought through OpenGrey and relevant organization websites to supplement published data and mitigate publication bias (Adams et al., 2016). Study Selection and Eligibility Criteria Two independent reviewers participated in the screening process. The primary focus was on studies conducted within health-related settings that reported on the application of KBs and were available in English. Inclusion criteria encompassed empirical studies with primary data, involving any design that documented KB activities explicitly in a health context. Exclusion criteria filtered out studies unrelated to health settings, those without explicit KB involvement, non-English studies, and secondary research not directly relevant to our topic. The initial search yielded 7,935 records. Deduplication using EndNote software was followed by the independent screening of 6,936 abstracts. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussions or consultation with a third reviewer. The screening process led to the selection of 240 full-text articles for detailed review. The final inclusion comprised 29 articles representing 22 unique studies, embodying a diverse range of methodologies, including qualitative (n = 18), quantitative (n = 1), and mixed methods (n = 6) designs, plus pertinent grey literature sources (n = 4). Data Extraction and Quality Assessment Data extraction was uniformly executed by the two reviewers using a pre-defined template, covering study characteristics, KB activities, observed outcomes, and influencing factors (O’Brien et al., 2018). To assess study quality, adapted versions of the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) checklists for qualitative and quantitative studies and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) for mixed-method studies were employed (Hong et al., 2018). Thematic Analysis Approach A confirmatory thematic analysis was conducted to synthesize findings across different study designs (Nowell et al., 2017). This approach allowed for categorization and interpretation of the data, elucidating recurring themes and patterns regarding the functions and perceived effectiveness of KBs. The reviewers followed Braun and Clarke’s six-step framework, consisting of data familiarization, initial code generation, theme searching, theme review, theme definition, and narrative writing (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Statistical Analysis Quantitative data, although limited, were subjected to descriptive analysis to support thematic findings. The absence of comparable quantitative data precluded meta-analysis. However, studies meeting high methodological rigor standards (n = 2) were highlighted to assess any measurable impacts KBs had on policy or practice. The mixed-methods studies contributed valuable triangulated data, ensuring a rich understanding of the multifaceted KB role across different contexts (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2017). Inter-rater Reliability Inter-rater reliability was assessed during abstract and full-text screening processes using Cohen’s kappa coefficient (McHugh, 2012). Kappa values reflected substantial agreement, indicating consistent and reliable selection and analysis processes. Reviewer interpretations of complex qualitative themes were cross-validated through frequent consensus meetings and methodological triangulation with grey literature insights. In summary, this thorough methodological process ensured a comprehensive understanding of KB activities in health-related settings. By employing diverse analytical approaches and upholding rigorous quality standards, this review provides insights into the potential of KBs in facilitating effective knowledge translation, despite current limitations in conclusively appraising their effectiveness. Further robust studies are necessary to clarify the role of KBs and identify contextual factors influencing their impact. The systematic review identified 7935 records from eight electronic databases and grey literature, with 6936 abstracts screened after removing duplicates. Subsequently, a total of 240 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, leading to the inclusion of 29 articles representing 22 unique studies that qualified for thematic analysis. The analysis included qualitative studies (n=18), a quantitative study (n=1), mixed methods studies (n=6), and grey literature sources (n=4). The synthesis of these data provided insights into the roles and functions of knowledge brokers (KBs) within health-related settings, although conclusions regarding their effectiveness in knowledge translation (KT) remained inconclusive. Qualitative studies highlighted the multifaceted roles of KBs, particularly emphasizing their functions as 'knowledge managers', 'linkage agents', and 'capacity builders'. The role of KBs as knowledge managers was evidenced across 15 studies, wherein they were instrumental in tailoring information to fit the specific needs and contexts of diverse stakeholders. As linkage agents, KBs facilitated connections between various healthcare professionals and organizations in 14 studies, enhancing collaboration by bridging gaps in communication and understanding. Additionally, in 10 studies, KBs acted as capacity builders, engaging in activities that contributed to the skill development and empowerment of healthcare teams. Quantitative findings were scarce, with only one study providing numerical data on the impact of KBs. This single study reported a 15% increase in evidence-based practice implementation rates in health settings where KBs were actively engaged (p < 0.05). However, the limited sample size and scope of this study preclude broad generalizations about the overall effectiveness of KBs. Mixed methods studies contributed further insights, such as the integration of KBs in multidisciplinary teams. Among the six mixed methods studies, four reported perceived improvements in knowledge sharing and collaboration efficiency, with qualitative feedback highlighting how KBs facilitated better understanding across clinical teams. However, these studies did not provide numerical support to solidify claims of increased effectiveness or efficiency due to the integration of KBs. Outcome data from eight studies explored changes in knowledge, skills, and policies or practices attributable to the KB role. While all eight reported at least some positive shifts, only two studies employed methodologies meeting high methodological standards. For instance, one study portrayed a 20% improvement in policy adherence related to patient care protocols following the introduction of KBs, demonstrating potential policy influence (p < 0.05). Conversely, the other rigorous study found no significant change in the overall outcome measures of practices, though it noted qualitative benefits in stakeholder engagement. This juxtaposition of findings underscores the heterogeneity in reporting and the challenges in measuring KB outcomes quantitatively. Despite the qualitative enrichments offered by KBs in facilitating knowledge dissemination and uptake, the lack of consistent, rigorous quantitative metrics limits definitive claims about their effectiveness. Moreover, qualitative evidence suggests that KBs are positively perceived as pivotal constructs within their organizations, mitigating barriers and fostering environments conducive to sustained KT practices. Grey literature reinforced the findings from peer-reviewed sources, describing case examples where KB interventions reportedly led to organizational changes favoring evidence-based practices. Still, these accounts primarily relied on anecdotal evidence or descriptive reporting rather than robust evaluative frameworks to substantiate claims. Ultimately, the outcome data suggest that while KBs are integral to fostering environments that support KT through their dynamic roles, robust evidence quantifying their impact remains limited. The inconclusive nature of the findings, driven by methodological variations and a paucity of high-quality quantitative data, highlights the necessity for further rigorous research. Such investigations should focus on standardized measurement approaches to delineate the quantitative impacts of KBs on knowledge, practice, and policy transformations in health-related settings (Catan et al., 2015; Nyström et al., 2016).
