Food choice is among the most consequential and most frequent decisions people make. It shapes nutritional status, the risk of chronic disease, cultural identity and everyday pleasure. The growth of online recipe repositories, meal-planning applications and food-delivery platforms has produced an abundance of options that individuals cannot readily evaluate on their own. Recommender systems have therefore become a natural tool for helping users navigate this space (Trattner & Elsweiler, 2017; Min, Jiang & Jain, 2019). Food recommendation differs from the canonical domains of movies, books or music in several respects. Food is consumed multisensorially and repeatedly, it is constrained by health, religion, allergy and availability, and acceptance depends on an experience, flavour, that arises from the interplay of chemistry, physiology and learning rather than from any single observable attribute of the item. Existing food recommendation approaches draw largely on three families of techniques. Collaborative filtering exploits patterns in user–item rating matrices to infer preferences from similar users (Sarwar et al., 2001; Koren, Bell & Volinsky, 2009). Content-based methods represent recipes by their ingredients, categories or textual descriptions and match them to profiles built from a user's past choices (Freyne & Berkovsky, 2010; Ge, Elahi, Fernández-Tobías, Ricci & Massimo, 2015). More recent work employs hybrid models, knowledge graphs and deep representation learning over images, text and ingredient networks (Min et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020). A second stream of research emphasises healthfulness, using nutrient content, calorie constraints or nudging strategies to steer users towards better diets (Elsweiler, Trattner & Harvey, 2017; Starke, Willemsen & Trattner, 2021). Together these studies show that preference prediction in food is feasible and that recommendations can be tuned towards healthier outcomes. However, they typically treat taste as latent. Ingredients serve as a proxy, and the algorithm is expected to discover through data what users like without any explicit representation of why a dish is appealing. This omission is notable because flavour is a primary driver of food acceptance. Surveys of food choice consistently find that sensory appeal outranks health, price and convenience as a reason for selecting foods (Glanz, Basil, Maibach, Goldberg & Snyder, 1998). Perception of flavour results from the combination of gustation, olfaction and trigeminal sensations such as pungency and astringency (Spence, 2015). Gustation itself rests on well-characterised biology. Taste receptor cells in the taste buds of the tongue and oral cavity detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami stimuli through specific receptor families, including the T1R and T2R G-protein-coupled receptors and ion-channel mechanisms (Chandrashekar, Hoon, Ryba & Zuker, 2006; Roper & Chaudhari, 2017). Signals are conveyed to the brainstem through three cranial nerves: the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (VII), the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) and the vagus nerve (X) (Breslin & Spector, 2008). This anatomical organisation offers a principled, domain-grounded way to decompose the taste of a food into channels that correspond to physiological pathways, rather than into arbitrary latent factors. Individual differences in taste further motivate explicit modelling. Sensitivity to bitterness varies with genetic polymorphisms such as those in TAS2R38 (Bufe et al., 2005), the density of fungiform papillae differs across people (Hayes, Bartoshuk, Kidd & Duffy, 2008), and hedonic responses to sweetness, saltiness and fat are shaped by exposure, culture and age (Mennella, Jagnow & Beauchamp, 2001; Drewnowski, 1997). Two users may therefore rate the same dish very differently for reasons that are systematically related to its taste composition. A system that represents both the flavour of the food and the flavour tendencies of the user could, in principle, generalise more effectively to new items, mitigate cold-start problems, and offer interpretable explanations such as "recommended because it is savoury and mildly bitter, like dishes you have enjoyed." Computational research on flavour has begun to move in this direction. Ahn, Ahnert, Bagrow and Barabási (2011) analysed flavour compounds shared among ingredients and proposed the food-pairing hypothesis as a network phenomenon. Subsequent studies used compound data and recipe corpora to generate ingredient substitutions and novel combinations (Teng, Lin & Adamic, 2012; Garg et al., 2021), and to link molecular features with perceived taste through machine learning (Zheng et al., 2019). Curated resources such as FlavorDB (Garg et al., 2018) catalogue flavour molecules and their sensory descriptors. Despite this progress, three gaps remain. First, most of these studies concentrate on aroma-related compounds and ingredient pairing, rather than on the gustatory dimensions that map to the basic taste pathways. Second, they are largely descriptive or generative, and are rarely coupled to personalised recommendation, where user preference must be estimated and matched. Third, the taste information used is often drawn from dispersed or qualitative descriptors, with no empirical, reproducible procedure for converting a recipe's ingredients into a quantitative flavour profile that a recommendation engine can consume. As a result, the knowledge from sensory science and neurobiology has seldom been used as a structured feature set in recommender design. The present work addresses this gap. We ask whether an empirically derived flavour representation, organised around the major gustatory nerves, can be incorporated into a food recommendation engine so as to improve the match between recommended dishes and users' flavour preferences. This question divides into three parts. (i) How can the flavour of a food item be estimated empirically from available data, such as its ingredients and their taste attributes, in a form aligned with gustatory biology? (ii) How can a user's flavour profile be inferred from interaction history and compared with item profiles? (iii) Does using this flavour knowledge yield recommendations that are more likely to be enjoyed than recommendations that do not use it? We make the following contributions. First, we propose a flavour representation for food items whose dimensions are grounded in the pathways of the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, thereby embedding taste-biology domain knowledge directly into the feature space. Second, we describe an empirical procedure for computing these flavour vectors from recipe composition, and a corresponding method for building user flavour profiles from past preferences. Third, we integrate the resulting vectors into a recommendation engine that ranks candidate foods by their match with the user's profile, and we outline how this approach offers interpretability and robustness for new items. Fourth, we present a preliminary evaluation that illustrates the feasibility of the approach and identifies limitations, with the aim of stimulating more rigorous mechanisms in which flavour is treated as a principal feature set in food recommenders. We regard this study as a first step in a longer programme. Our long-term vision is to combine flavour-aware personalisation with health constraints, so that systems recommend foods that are both tasty and nutritionally appropriate. Because people are more likely to adhere to dietary advice when the foods recommended are enjoyable (Drewnowski & Almiron-Roig, 2010), a system that reconciles flavour preferences with health goals could contribute to improved diet quality and quality of life. The remainder of the paper describes our methods, presents results, and discusses implications and future directions. Overview and design We designed a hybrid recommender that adds a physiologically grounded flavour representation to a conventional collaborative filtering (CF) model. The pipeline has four stages: (i) assembling recipe, ingredient and rating data; (ii) estimating a taste vector for each ingredient and aggregating it into a recipe-level flavour vector; (iii) projecting that vector onto the three gustatory nerve pathways to obtain a nerve-activation profile; and (iv) matching users' inferred flavour preferences to candidate dishes and blending this score with a CF score. We evaluated the system offline against baselines that do not use flavour information. Data Recipe content came from Recipe1M+ (Marin et al., 2019), which provides ingredient lists and instructions. User–recipe interactions came from the Food.com (formerly GeniusKitchen) corpus released by Majumder et al. (2019), which contains explicit 1–5 star ratings. We matched recipes across the two sources by normalised title and ingredient-set Jaccard similarity (threshold 0.8). Ingredient strings were parsed with a rule-based tagger that removed quantities, units and preparation terms, and then mapped to canonical entities using fuzzy string matching against FlavorDB (Garg et al., 2018) and FooDB. Ingredients that could not be mapped, and recipes with fewer than three mapped ingredients, were excluded. To limit sparsity we retained users with at least 20 ratings and recipes with at least 10 ratings, an approach common in food recommendation research (Trattner & Elsweiler, 2017). Ratings were treated as explicit feedback for rating prediction. For ranking, ratings of 4 or higher were treated as positive. Ingredient taste estimation Flavour was operationalised on the five basic taste qualities, sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (Chandrashekar et al., 2006), plus a trigeminal pungency/astringency dimension. This gives a six-dimensional taste space, indexed by k. For each canonical ingredient i we built a taste vector ti ∈ [0,1]^6 empirically from two sources. 1. Compound-level evidence. We took the flavour molecules associated with each ingredient in FlavorDB and labelled them with taste annotations from curated resources (BitterDB, Wiener et al., 2012; SuperSweet, Ahmed et al., 2011; and FlavorDB's own taste labels). The compound-derived score for taste k was the fraction of an ingredient's labelled compounds carrying that taste, weighted by log-scaled concentration where FooDB supplied it. 2. Compositional evidence. We mapped nutrient and chemical composition to taste proxies. Sugars (sweet), titratable acids and organic acids (sour), sodium (salty), free glutamate and 5′-ribonucleotides (umami), and capsaicinoids, piperine and allyl isothiocyanate (pungency) were taken from FooDB and USDA FoodData Central. Polyphenols and alkaloids served as bitterness proxies. Each proxy was rescaled to [0,1] by percentile rank across all ingredients. The two estimates were averaged, with the compositional estimate given weight γ = 0.5 (tuned on validation data, see below). Because the compositional proxies are indirect, we validated the resulting vectors against a small reference set. Two annotators independently labelled the dominant tastes of 150 randomly sampled ingredients. We report agreement as Cohen's κ and the Spearman correlation between estimated and annotated taste intensities. Recipe-level flavour vector For recipe r with ingredient set Ir and relative mass fractions mi (estimated from listed quantities converted to grams using unit-density tables, or set uniform when quantities were unparseable), the raw flavour vector is fr = Σ{i∈Ir} mi ti. Perceived intensity grows sublinearly with stimulus concentration (Stevens, 1957), so we applied a saturating transform: f̃{r,k} = f{r,k}^β / (f{r,k}^β + θk^β), where θk is the median of f{r,k} across the corpus and β = 0.6 approximates the compressive exponent for taste. Gustatory nerve projection Taste information reaches the brainstem through three cranial nerves: the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (VII), innervating the anterior tongue; the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), innervating the posterior tongue; and the vagus nerve (X), innervating the epiglottis and larynx (Yarmolinsky et al., 2009). Each nerve responds to all taste qualities but with characteristic sensitivity. The chorda tympani is relatively sensitive to salty, sweet and umami stimuli, the glossopharyngeal to bitter and sour, and the vagal pathway to bitter and, in part, umami (Breslin & Spector, 2008; Lindemann, 2001). Pungency is carried mainly by the trigeminal nerve (V), which we included as a fourth channel because it contributes to flavour but not to taste proper. We encoded relative sensitivities in a nonnegative matrix W ∈ ℝ^{4×6} with rows VII, IX, X and V. Entries were initialised from the qualitative ordering in the physiological literature (0 = negligible, 0.5 = moderate, 1 = strong). They were then row-normalised and refined by constrained optimisation (see "Model fitting"). The nerve-activation profile is ar = W f̃r. This projection is a low-dimensional, domain-informed re-weighting of the taste space. It lets the model treat, for example, bitter and sour as partly sharing a pathway. User flavour profiles A user's profile summarises the nerve-activation patterns of recipes they liked relative to those they disliked. For user u with rated set Ru and mean rating r̄u, pu = Σ{r∈Ru} (y{ur} − r̄u) ar / Σ{r∈Ru} |y{ur} − r̄u|, where y{ur} is the rating. Hepatic steatosis and iron overload are two key features of chronic liver disease [1]. Quantitative MRI can provide surrogate metrics for these features and, in some cases, predict clinical outcomes [2]. A healthy liver should contain relatively low amounts of fat, though it is estimated that up to 1 in 3 people worldwide have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) [3], and this number is increasing. In the UK Biobank imaging enhancement study, for example, which aims eventually to include 100,000 nominally healthy participants [4], liver fat was measured using MRI proton density fat fraction (PDFF) in 4,949 participants (aged 45–73 years) [5]. The results showed that although the median fat level was 2.11%, a further 19.9% of participants had fat levels > 5.5% (the commonly accepted risk level for NAFLD [6]), 9.2% of the participants (n = 455) had fat levels > 10%, and 84 (1.7%) participants had fat levels > 20%. In the same cohort, liver iron levels were measured using quantitative T2-mapping, then converted to liver iron concentration in mg Fe/g dry weight [7]. Preliminary results suggested that a higher than expected number of participants for a normal population had elevated iron levels [8]. This is important for healthcare, since iron overload significantly increases the risk of liver disease, including cirrhosis and cancer, but can be treated effectively once diagnosed. Furthermore, liver fibrosis and inflammation can be quantified using the MR T1 relaxation parameter, but only after correcting for iron level [9]. For these reasons, multiparametric MRI, combining T1, T2 and PDFF, has been proposed as a comprehensive method for the non-invasive diagnosis of liver disease, to provide early diagnosis, treatment monitoring and an alternative to the limited method of tissue biopsy [1,2]. Note that T2 measurements can also be reported in terms of the reciprocal R2 and both have their advantages. In our work, we have adopted T2 because it has dimensions of time and so is consistent with T1 measurements. MRI-based quantification of PDFF and iron is well-established and validated. Standard techniques for measuring PDFF rely on multiecho gradient echo (GRE) imaging with chemical shift-based methods to decompose the signal from in-phase and opposed-phase images into fat and water [10,11]. For iron quantification, standard approaches measure T2 relaxation times using spin-echo imaging [12] or T2 relaxation times [13,14] using multiecho GRE imaging. T2 relaxometry has the advantage over T2 relaxometry of shorter acquisition times, so reduced physiological artefacts, such as those resulting from breathing and motion. When multiecho GRE data are acquired using in-phase and opposed-phase images, they can be used to derive both T2 and PDFF maps. However, it has been established that for higher levels of iron, increased T2 decay yields errors in PDFF estimates; similarly, T2 decay is influenced by higher fat levels, leading to errors in T2 estimates, hence iron quantification [15,16]. Such confounds are addressed by the IDEAL approach (Iterative Decomposition of water and fat with Echo Asymmetry and Least-squares estimation), by simultaneously estimating fat and T2 decay [17,18], to provide iron-corrected PDFF estimates fat-corrected iron quantification [19]. The IDEAL technique also embodies use of a more realistic fat spectrum model with multiple resonant frequencies, enabling more accurate PDFF and T2. It also facilitates shorter and more closely-spaced echo times, which is important for reducing motion artefacts and imaging higher iron levels. Various studies have demonstrated the accuracy, precision and reproducibility of PDFF quantification using methods based on the IDEAL approach [20–22]. However, to date, much of the published work has used vendor-specific versions of the image acquisition protocol and PDFF estimation methods (e.g. IDEAL IQ, GE Healthcare or mDIXON Quant, Philips Healthcare). Although in some cases encouraging results were reported across vendors and field strength, the differences that have been observed have been attributed to differences in the acquisition and estimation techniques. For example, in a recent study [23], the agreement of PDFF measurements were determined among readers, two MR scanner vendors, and two field strengths. PDFF estimation was performed using two different vendor products with the precise data acquisition protocol and PDFF calculation being specific to each vendor. Although the results were reported to be highly reproducible across readers, field strengths, and imaging platforms, a number of small but systematic and significant differences in PDFF were observed between scanner platforms. These were attributed to differences in the pulse sequences and PDFF calculation. This highlights the need for a liver fat and T2 quantification method that is standardized across field strength and MR scanner vendor, not least to: facilitate longitudinal assessment of individuals; characterize disease across larger populations; and to normalize clinical decision making. The overall goal of this work is to both develop and validate such a vendor neutral, field strength independent (“standardised”) method for liver fat and T2 quantification. To this end, we licensed and acknowledge the intellectual property for the ‘IDEAL’ method from the University of Wisconsin [17], which we then implemented in software in-house. In this paper, we distinguish between the published concept and licensed intellectual property and the software that we have developed to implement it, and we refer to our software as “LMS (LiverMultiScan) IDEAL”. LMS IDEAL incorporates some of the methods reported in the referenced publications and a number of novel algorithmic steps, which we have found necessary to address different confounds resulting from the imaging process. LMS IDEAL has been designed to use image acquisition protocols that can be installed on most MRI scanners and cloud-based image processing to provide fast, standardized clinical results, which are consistent for data acquired on different vendors’ scanners and at different field strengths. We present two studies to validate LMS IDEAL. First, PDFF values were calculated for publicly available phantom data and compared with independently calculated and published values using the same phantom data, which had previously shown excellent results for reproducibility across sites, vendors, field strengths and image acquisition protocols [24]. Second, LMS IDEAL PDFF and T2 values were calculated in human volunteer data acquired as part of the UK Biobank data study, and the results were compared with the PDFF and T2 values estimated in the same participants using a different, but widely-used “standard” MR imaging protocol and quantification method. As noted above, the ‘IDEAL’ method, from the University of Wisconsin [17,18] was implemented in-house (LMS IDEAL), to perform simultaneous water and fat decomposition and estimation of T2 decay in the presence of field (B0) inhomogeneity (see Fig 1 for flowchart). The most basic version of the IDEAL method [25] fits a signal equation describing the complex-valued data sn at each pixel resulting from multi-echo spoiled gradient echo (SPGR) images acquired at each echo time tn, as sn=(∑j=1Mρjei2π∆fjtn).ei2πψtn(Eq 1) where: ρj is the intensity of the jth of M chemical species, with chemical shift (in Hz) of Δfj with respect to water, and ψ is the local value of the “field map” (Hz). The model fitting proposed in the patent and published papers first uses an iterative least squares estimation method to determine ψ, which is then demodulated from the original signal, and decomposed into estimates of the two chemical species, water and fat. PDFF values are then calculated by dividing the estimates for fat by the estimate of fat plus water. LMS IDEAL extends the basic version of the IDEAL method, which estimates a “complex field map” (replacing ψ with ψ^ in Eq 1) and decomposes it into field map ψ and T2 (or 1/R2) from the real and imaginary parts of ψ^ respectively [18], ψ^=ψ+i/(2πT2)(Eq 2) Given a poor starting estimate, large deviations in the B0 field, and/or low SNR, estimation of the B0 field may converge to the wrong solution. In such a case, the assignment of signal to water and to fat can be ‘swapped’, resulting in ‘fat/water swaps’ either in individual pixels or, more usually, in larger contiguous regions. To mitigate this, LMS IDEAL includes the method based on [26], which initially down-samples the complex echoes then uses a region growing algorithm to encourage B0 estimates to be similar among neighbouring pixels. This (pseudo-regularisation) step provides an initial estimate of the B0 field map in a central region of the image where it is most likely to be reliable, so that the final estimated field map is less likely to contain artefactual discontinuities across the image and therefore reduces ambiguities in fat and water estimation. LMS IDEAL also incorporates a model that assumes that the spectrum of fat has several prominent peaks [15,16]. The model can be adjusted to approximate the spectrum for liver fat, which is required for human imaging, or for peanut oil, which is typically used in fat phantoms. For consistency with the published data, the (human) liver fat model comprises six peaks with frequency shifts relative to the water peak (ppm) of 0.6, -0.5, -1.95, -2.60, -3.4 and -3.8 and relative amplitudes of 0.047, 0.039, 0.006, 0.12, 0.7 and 0.088 [27]. Conversely, the peanut oil phantom model also comprises six fat peaks which are corrected for room temperature by adjusting the frequency shifts relative to water by 0.1ppm (this assumes 22°C), resulting in frequency shifts (ppm) of 0.5, -0.49, -2.04, -2.7, -3.5, and -3.9, and relative amplitudes of 0.048, 0.039, 0.004, 0.128, 0.694 and 0.087 [24,27]. Performing IDEAL model fitting to the complex-valued data results in estimates of fat and water which cover the entire range of possible PDFF values (from 0% to 100%). However, the accuracy of such estimates depends on the consistency of phase information across the acquired echoes. Since LMS IDEAL was implemented to be used with data acquired on different vendors’ scanners, the accuracy of the phase data can not always be guaranteed. The negative impact of inconsistent phase information can be removed by discarding the phase information from the data and estimating the IDEAL model using just the magnitude of the data (as described in [28]). It has been reported that model fitting to magnitude only information restricts estimates of PDFF values to the the range [0%, 50%], which can result in ambiguity between fat and water estimates. For this reason, based on [28], LMS IDEAL uses the initial, full PDFF range estimates of fat and water resulting from the complex-valued data estimation steps (including the region growing to avoid discontinuities in the field map) as starting estimates for model fitting using the magnitude of the data. The two sets of water and fat estimates (from the complex and magnitude model fitting) are then combined so that values closer to 50% are weighted towards the complex estimates and values closer to 0% and 100% are weighted towards the magnitude results [28]. Furthermore, to address the effect of a positive noise bias for low PDFF values, as a result of the magnitude data estimation steps, LMS IDEAL includes the approach described in [29], where, rather than trying to estimate the fat parameter as an independent signal component from the water, the model is adjusted to estimate the combined fat plus water signal, and the estimated water parameter is subtracted from the result. Finally, the LMS IDEAL complex-valued data estimation steps were implemented to allow for bipolar readout gradients, as well as the more typically used monopolar readout gradients. For bipolar readout gradients, inconsistent phase information will have an opposite effect on odd and even echoes resulting in spatially varying estimates of water and fat across the image. To address this, model fitting in LMS IDEAL is modified by additionally including a signal modulation, which is equal and opposite in consecutive echoes (as described in [30]). This enables a pixelwise phase error map to be estimated, to which a single linear function can be fitted across the image to correct for the effect of the bipolar readout gradient. The LMS IDEAL version used in this study was implemented in Matlab (The MathWorks, Inc.) with executable mex-files, consisting of compiled C++ routines using ITK libraries (www.itk.org). The Internet of Things (IoT) has moved in little more than a decade from a laboratory concept to a general-purpose architectural paradigm. In it, uniquely identifiable physical objects sense, compute, and communicate with minimal human intervention (Atzori, Iera, & Morabito, 2010; Gubbi, Buyya, Marusic, & Palaniswami, 2013). Industry estimates project more than 25 billion connected endpoints by 2025, spanning manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, energy, and urban infrastructure. Healthcare is among the domains where the paradigm promises the most. Populations are ageing, with the number of people aged 65 years or older expected to reach roughly 1.5 billion by 2050 (United Nations, 2019). Chronic conditions impose a growing burden, and cardiovascular diseases alone account for an estimated 17.9 million deaths annually (World Health Organization, 2021). These pressures strain episodic, clinic-centred care models and strengthen the case for continuous, remote, and personalised monitoring. Health informatics is a multidisciplinary field that applies information engineering to the acquisition, storage, retrieval, and use of health-related data. It has traditionally drawn on institutional sources such as electronic health records, laboratory systems, and imaging archives. Increasingly, clinically relevant data originate outside the hospital, in wearable, implantable, ambient, and handheld devices that record physiological and behavioural signals in everyday settings. Applying IoT principles to these devices has given rise to the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), a connected infrastructure of medical devices, sensors, software applications, and services that exchange data with healthcare information systems (Islam, Kwak, Kabir, Hossain, & Kwak, 2015; Dimitrov, 2016). Typical IoMT deployments include continuous glucose monitors, ambulatory electrocardiography patches, pulse oximeters, smart inhalers, fall detectors, and connected infusion pumps. They are used in chronic disease management, post-operative recovery, elderly assistance, and fitness and wellness. The IoMT differs from general-purpose IoT in ways that raise the engineering stakes. First, many medical signals are time-critical. A delayed or lost arrhythmia alert can have consequences that a delayed thermostat reading cannot, so latency, reliability, and quality of service become safety properties as well as performance metrics. Second, the data are highly sensitive. Health records are consistently among the most valuable and most frequently breached categories of personal data, and regulatory regimes such as HIPAA in the United States and the GDPR in the European Union impose stringent obligations on confidentiality, integrity, and consent. Third, the devices are severely resource constrained. Sensor nodes must often run for months or years on coin-cell batteries, fit within the body or on the skin, and tolerate the poor propagation conditions of the human body, which absorbs and shadows radio-frequency energy (Movassaghi, Abolhasan, Lipman, Smith, & Jamalipour, 2014). Fourth, the ecosystem is heterogeneous. Devices from many vendors, using different protocols and data models, must interoperate with gateways, cloud platforms, and clinical systems. Together these characteristics mean that the properties of the IoMT as a whole are bounded by the properties of its lowest-level communication links. Those links are provided mainly by Personal Area Networks (PANs). A PAN interconnects devices within the immediate vicinity of a person, typically within a range of about 10 m, and in the IoMT it forms the first hop of a layered architecture. Sensors measure changes in physical, chemical, or physiological stimuli and transmit them over the PAN to a personal gateway such as a smartphone, a home hub, or a bedside unit. Local area networks (LANs) and wide area networks (WANs) then carry the data to clinicians, caregivers, insurers, researchers, and analytics services. Choices made at the PAN layer determine achievable data rates, which range from a few kilobits per second for slowly varying vital signs to several megabits per second for multichannel electroencephalography or streaming audio. They also determine energy consumption, coexistence behaviour in the crowded 2.4 GHz band, network topology and scalability, and the security mechanisms available to protect data at its point of origin. A subset of PANs, Body Area Networks (BANs), is designed specifically for devices on, in, or around the human body, with requirements for extremely low power, minimal interference with tissue, and strict limits on radiated energy (Chen, Gonzalez, Vasilakos, Cao, & Leung, 2011; Movassaghi et al., 2014). Despite the importance of this layer, the literature on IoMT remains uneven. Existing surveys have concentrated on application-level services, cloud and big-data analytics, or security and privacy frameworks, usually treating the underlying wireless technologies as a background detail (Islam et al., 2015). Conversely, the wireless sensor network and BAN literature offers detailed protocol-level analyses, but it rarely connects them to the requirements of deployed healthcare products or to the commercial landscape in which clinicians and system architects must decide. As a result, practitioners and researchers entering the field have no consolidated account that relates PAN standards to the characteristics of medical data, the requirements of IoMT applications, and the offerings of current vendors. The standards themselves are also evolving quickly. Bluetooth Low Energy, for example, has progressed through several specification revisions that changed its throughput, range, and mesh capabilities, so earlier comparisons are partly outdated. This chapter addresses that gap by characterizing the PAN landscape that underpins the IoMT. We pursue three research questions. (RQ1) Which PAN standards are most widely used in academic prototypes and commercial IoMT products, and how do they compare in data rate, range, power consumption, topology, and security provisions? (RQ2) How do BANs, and the IEEE 802.15.6 standard in particular, extend or diverge from general-purpose PAN technologies in meeting the constraints of body-centric medical sensing? (RQ3) How are these technologies currently embedded in IoMT applications and vendor offerings, and what open challenges does this reveal for real-time operation, security, and privacy? The chapter makes four contributions. First, it provides a structured comparative analysis of three PAN standards that dominate current practice, Bluetooth (including Bluetooth Low Energy), ZigBee built on IEEE 802.15.4, and ANT/ANT+. The analysis uses a common set of quantitative criteria, including nominal physical-layer data rates from roughly 250 kbps to 2 Mbps, typical communication ranges of 10 to 100 m, and duty-cycle-dependent energy profiles. Second, it examines BANs as a distinct class of PAN, reviewing their architecture, tiered communication model, and the particular demands of in-body, on-body, and off-body channels. Third, it surveys prevalent IoMT application areas and maps each to the PAN technologies and vendor products that realise it, so that technical characteristics can be read against real deployments. Fourth, it synthesises cross-cutting challenges, namely real-time performance, security, privacy, interoperability, and energy efficiency, and identifies directions for future research and standardisation. The remainder of the chapter proceeds as follows. We first describe the layered IoMT architecture and the role of the PAN within it. We then analyse the selected standards and BANs in turn, survey applications and vendors, and conclude with a discussion of open issues. Study design and scope We conducted a structured narrative survey of the technologies that form the personal-area layer of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). The design follows the guidance for systematic reviews in software and systems engineering (Kitchenham & Charters, 2007) and borrows the transparency conventions of the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009). We did not attempt a formal meta-analysis because the primary literature reports heterogeneous metrics under non-comparable experimental conditions. Instead, we combined a protocol-driven literature review with a normative comparison of published standards and a catalogue of commercial IoMT offerings. The review addressed three questions. (RQ1) Which short-range wireless standards underpin personal area networks (PANs) in healthcare, and what are their physical-layer and medium-access characteristics? (RQ2) How do body area networks (BANs) extend or specialize these standards for on-body and implanted sensing? (RQ3) Which IoMT application classes and vendors currently use these technologies? Selection of standards The candidate technology set was derived from the IoT and health-informatics surveys of Gubbi et al. (2013), Islam et al. (2015), and Baker et al. (2017). A technology was retained for detailed analysis if it met three criteria: 1. It is defined by a publicly available specification issued by a recognized standards body or industry consortium. 2. It is supported by commercially available silicon or certified end-user devices. 3. It appears in at least one peer-reviewed clinical or health-monitoring application. Applying these criteria yielded three PAN standards: Bluetooth, including Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) (Bluetooth SIG, 2019; Townsend et al., 2014); IEEE 802.15.4 and the ZigBee protocol stack built upon it (IEEE, 2015; Baronti et al., 2007); and Near Field Communication (NFC) as specified in ISO/IEC 18092 and the NFC Forum technical specifications. Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) was excluded from the core comparison because its power envelope and network topology place it in the local-area rather than personal-area tier, although we discuss it as a backhaul option. IEEE 802.15.6, the dedicated standard for wireless BANs (IEEE, 2012), was analyzed separately to address RQ2, together with the architectural and channel-modelling literature on BANs (Movassaghi et al., 2014; Ullah et al., 2012). Literature search Searches were executed in IEEE Xplore, the ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, PubMed, and Scopus. Google Scholar was used only for backward and forward citation chaining. The search string combined three concept groups with Boolean operators: (“Internet of Medical Things” OR “medical IoT” OR “healthcare IoT” OR “mHealth” OR “e-health”) AND (“personal area network” OR “body area network” OR “BAN” OR “WBAN” OR Bluetooth OR BLE OR ZigBee OR “802.15.4” OR “802.15.6” OR NFC) AND (sensor OR monitoring OR wearable OR implant). Search strings were adapted to the syntax of each database and applied to titles, abstracts, and author keywords. The search window covered January 2005 to December 2019, which spans the ratification of IEEE 802.15.4 and the introduction of Bluetooth Low Energy in the Bluetooth 4.0 specification. Earlier foundational documents were included when cited as normative references. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Records were included if they (a) were written in English; (b) were peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, standards documents, or authoritative technical white papers; and (c) reported an architecture, protocol evaluation, security analysis, or deployment relevant to a PAN or BAN used for physiological or contextual health sensing. Records were excluded if they (a) treated only wide-area technologies (e.g., cellular, LoRaWAN) without a PAN component; (b) addressed purely back-end analytics or electronic health record integration with no reference to the sensing network; or (c) were opinion pieces without technical content. Duplicates were removed by matching DOIs and normalized titles. Screening and data extraction Screening was performed in two stages, first on title and abstract and then on full text. Two reviewers screened independently, and disagreements were resolved by discussion with a third reviewer. Agreement at the title-and-abstract stage was assessed with Cohen’s kappa (Cohen, 1960), with κ ≥ 0.61 taken as substantial agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977). A standardized extraction form captured the following for each retained source: publication year; technology; reported application domain; topology; carrier frequency and channel plan; nominal and measured data rate; transmit power and reported current consumption; communication range; security mechanisms; and coexistence or interference observations. Normative comparison of standards For each standard, we extracted parameters directly from the governing specification to avoid propagating secondary-source errors. Where specifications gave ranges, we recorded both the minimum and maximum. The comparison covered nine dimensions: operating band, channel count and bandwidth, modulation, nominal physical-layer data rate, typical range, supported topologies, maximum network size, link-layer security, and energy profile. For example, BLE operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM band with 40 channels of 2 MHz spacing and a 1 Mb/s symbol rate under Gaussian frequency-shift keying (Bluetooth SIG, 2019). IEEE 802.15.4 specifies 250 kb/s using O-QPSK across 16 channels in the 2.4 GHz band, as well as 20 and 40 kb/s in the 868 and 915 MHz bands (IEEE, 2015). NFC operates at 13.56 MHz with data rates of 106, 212, and 424 kb/s over a working distance of roughly 4 cm. IEEE 802.15.6 defines narrowband, ultra-wideband, and human-body-communication physical layers with data rates from approximately 75.9 kb/s to 15.6 Mb/s (IEEE, 2012). Tobacco use remains an alarming public health challenge, particularly among the youth, who are susceptible to both the immediate and long-term health ramifications of tobacco consumption. Despite extensive global efforts to curb tobacco use, the prevalence among young individuals continues to pose a significant threat, highlighting the need for tailored interventions. Adolescents and young adults represent critical age groups where habits form, thus making tobacco prevention strategies among this demographic vital for long-term public health outcomes (Moura et al., 2021). Existing tobacco control policies predominantly focus on adult populations, leaving a significant gap in addressing the unique needs and behaviors of the youth. Many policy frameworks, although guided by international norms such as the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), lack the specificity required to effectively target young individuals (WHO, 2019). The neglect of youth-directed tobacco control measures reflects both a gap in policy design and an oversight in recognizing the broader societal and developmental impacts of youth tobacco use (Johnson et al., 2020). This study seeks to address these gaps by critically evaluating current tobacco control policies through an explorative and systematic review approach, with a focus on understanding their impacts and the challenges faced in targeting youth tobacco use. The research question guiding this exploration is: How do existing tobacco control policies address the specific issue of youth tobacco use, and what are the potential impacts and challenges associated with these policies? Our research aims to provide several contributions to the field of tobacco control and public health. Firstly, by highlighting the shortcomings in current policy design and implementation, we aim to inform policymakers about the necessity of age-specific interventions that consider the cultural, social, and physiological differences of younger individuals compared to adults (Patel et al., 2022). Secondly, through systematic analysis, we discern key strategies that have proven effective in certain contexts, thereby offering insights into adaptable models that can be employed internationally. Thirdly, this research underscores the importance of integrating interdisciplinary approaches in developing tobacco control policies that not only discourage initiation but also promote cessation among youth. By synthesizing evidence from diverse geographical and socio-economic backgrounds, we provide a comprehensive overview of practices that have the potential to revolutionize tobacco control measures (Smith & Lee, 2023). The prevalence of tobacco use among youth has been persistently high, with a significant portion of this population initiating tobacco use during their teenage years (Global Youth Tobacco Survey, 2018). The factors contributing to this phenomenon are multifaceted, encompassing socio-cultural influences, peer pressure, aggressive marketing strategies by the tobacco industry, and limited enforcement of age restrictions in many regions. As a result, effective tobacco control policies should be intricately designed to tackle these various aspects while remaining adaptable to different cultural settings (Thompson & Garcia, 2023). A notable challenge in youth tobacco control is the pervasive nature of indirect forms of tobacco consumption, such as e-cigarettes and smokeless tobacco products, which are often perceived as safer alternatives despite evidence to the contrary (Baker et al., 2021). This misconception has led to an uptick in usage among youths, necessitating tobacco control policies that are inclusive of all tobacco products. Moreover, the rise of digital media and social networking platforms has introduced new avenues for tobacco marketing, requiring innovative policy approaches to counter these emerging threats (Anderson et al., 2022). To achieve meaningful reductions in youth tobacco use, it is imperative that policies incorporate both preventative and interventionist strategies. Prevention efforts should start early, emphasizing education and awareness programs that are culturally relevant and resonate with young audiences (Lopez & Kim, 2022). Furthermore, intervention strategies should leverage peer influence by incorporating peer-led programs, thereby increasing the credibility and effectiveness of cessation efforts amongst youths (Brown et al., 2021). A key hurdle to effective youth-targeted tobacco control is the ongoing challenge of illicit tobacco trade, which bypasses legal restrictions and undermines policy efforts. This issue is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries, where regulatory enforcement is often limited (Choi & Wang, 2022). Addressing this challenge requires international cooperation and robust policy frameworks that ensure compliance across borders. In conclusion, the exploration of tobacco control policies specifically targeting youth is critical in the global fight against tobacco use. By delving into the specific practices, impacts, and challenges associated with youth tobacco use, this research aims to provide valuable insights that can guide future tobacco control initiatives. Ultimately, fostering a healthier next generation hinges on our ability to craft policies that are not only effective but also resonant with the diverse experiences and needs of youth worldwide. Through this systematic policy review, we strive to underscore the urgency of prioritizing youth-centric approaches in all tobacco control efforts, thereby ensuring sustained public health benefits for years to come. This study was conducted following a systematic policy review framework to provide an explorative analysis of tobacco control policies focusing specifically on youth. Our primary data sources included the Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS), a comprehensive, internationally-administered survey that provides data on tobacco use among young populations, as well as studies accessed through various academic databases. We utilized PubMed, the Health Inter-Network Access to Research Initiative (HINARI), Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Google, and Google Scholar in our search strategy to ensure a comprehensive overview of existing research and policy narratives. Design and Data Collection The design of this study involved a multi-stage process to identify, select, and analyze relevant literature and policy documents. Initially, a broad search was conducted using specific keywords: "tobacco control," "youth smoking," "smoking reduction policies," "prevalence of tobacco use in youth," "classification of tobacco control policies," "incentives to prevent young people from using tobacco," and "WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC)." The keyword selection aimed to cover a wide range of policy aspects, from legislative frameworks and economic sanctions to educational and preventive measures targeting youth. We imposed a timeline criterion for the inclusion of studies published between 2000 and 2023, reflecting significant developments in tobacco control policies post-WHO FCTC's introduction in 2005. This allowed us to capture both historical and contemporary policy adaptation and implementation. We also ensured the reliability of the studies by including peer-reviewed articles and excluding any literature that had not undergone rigorous academic evaluation. Given the focus on youth, studies and policies were considered if they addressed age-specific interventions or outcomes related to individuals typically defined within the youth age range of 10 to 24 years (United Nations, 2019). Procedures Our procedures followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to ensure clarity and accuracy in capturing relevant data (Moher et al., 2009). The initial search retrieved a total of 1,249 records, which, after duplicate removal, resulted in 896 unique articles. These records were then screened at the title and abstract level by two independent reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus or by consultation with a third reviewer. Full-text assessment of potentially relevant articles was the subsequent step, narrowing the selection to 122 studies that met our inclusion criteria. These included 25 studies focusing on theoretical and contextual elements of youth-related tobacco control policies, 41 studies examining various national policies and associated challenges, and 7 studies addressing global challenges in controlling youth tobacco use. Data Synthesis and Analysis Data extraction was performed systematically to identify the types and characteristics of tobacco control policies, their scopes, impacts, target populations, and the contextual challenges associated with each policy. Extracted data categories included study design, sample size, geographical focus, target demographic, stated outcomes, and noted challenges. Statistical analysis was kept descriptive, given the qualitative nature of policy reviews. Summary statistics such as frequencies and percentages were used to provide an overview of policy types and challenges. However, we incorporated advanced thematic synthesis to develop an understanding of policy frameworks and their effectiveness (Thomas & Harden, 2008). We employed a Constant Comparative Method to analyze themes emerging from qualitative data, utilizing NVivo software to facilitate thematic coding and retrieval. This approach enabled us to categorize findings into primary themes, including program characteristics, enforcement strategies, the effectiveness of specific interventions, and the barriers faced in policy implementation. Bias and Limitations We acknowledge potential biases and limitations inherent in our methodology. Given the variation in age definitions for "youth" across studies and national contexts, our findings might not seamlessly integrate into a universally applicable framework. Additionally, global representation was inevitably biased towards countries with substantial publication outputs in English. The heterogeneity in policy types reviewed means that our synthesis has a broader stroke, potentially overlooking nuanced differences within policies. Finally, while we focused largely on smoking control measures, smokeless tobacco use among youth represents a parallel concern that warrants further specialized analysis beyond this scope. Further studies are needed for deeper quantitative evaluations and to validate the qualitative insights obtained from this systematic review. This methods section underpins a comprehensive, systematic approach to understanding tobacco control policies related to youth worldwide. It addresses multifaceted data and insights that provide foundational support for our analysis of the situation, impacts, and future challenges outlined in the overarching study. Results The exploration of existing tobacco control policies for youth across various countries and their effectiveness yields varied insights. Our systematic review identified 122 relevant studies, out of which 25 focused explicitly on understanding the situation, significance, and theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies associated with youth, 41 provided insights into national population policies and challenges, and 7 discussed global challenges in overcoming the youth tobacco epidemic. Among national policies guided by the WHO-MPOWER strategies, the increase in tobacco taxation emerged as a common and effective measure. Studies indicate that in countries like Australia and the United States, significant increments in tobacco taxes have led to noteworthy declines in youth smoking rates. For instance, in a longitudinal study in Australia, it was reported that a 10% increase in tobacco tax resulted in approximately a 5% reduction in youth smoking prevalence over a two-year period (Smith et al., 2021). Similarly, youth smoking rates in the United States showed a 3.4% decrease following a substantial tax hike, as per analyses conducted by Johnson and Thompson (2020). Another frequently employed policy is the introduction of warning signs on tobacco packaging. The systematic review indicates a positive correlation between graphic health warnings and a decrease in youth smoking initiation rates. In Canada, a study by Anderson et al. (2022) demonstrated that graphic health warnings led to a 4.9% reduction in smoking initiation among youth aged 15-20. The effectiveness of these warnings is echoed in European countries, where packaging regulations have decreased youth smoking initiation by an average of 3.2% (García and Rasmussen, 2020). Restrictions on tobacco advertisement have also proven vital in controlling tobacco use among youth. Evidence from a meta-analysis conducted by Harris et al. (2021) reveals a discernible link between reduced exposure to tobacco advertising and lower incidences of youth tobacco use. In particular, countries like the United Kingdom and Norway have seen significant reductions in youth smoking rates, with decreases of 4% and 6% respectively, following stringent advertisements regulations (Collins and Kaur, 2021). The review highlights challenges in implementing policies that specifically deter youth from tobacco use. The smuggling of tobacco products represents a persistent challenge in many regions, as noted in studies focusing on Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia and the Philippines. The prevalence of smuggled tobacco products undermines taxation policies, with approximately 7% of youth in these countries reporting access to illicit tobacco products (Tobacco Reports, 2022). This accessibility reduces the efficacy of tax-induced price hikes, pointing to a need for better international collaboration to prevent smuggling. Additionally, there is an evident ignorance regarding the control of smokeless tobacco among youth. Despite the existence of smokeless tobacco bans in several countries, compliance remains minimal, as supported by data from studies in India and Bangladesh, where use among youth persists with prevalence rates above 20% (Patel and Singh, 2023). This indicates a need for increased focus on smokeless tobacco regulation alongside smoking control measures. Peer-based approaches and smoking cessation programs geared towards youth receive considerable attention, but their efficacy varies greatly

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood, affecting roughly one in 1,000 children and encompassing a heterogeneous group of conditions defined by arthritis of unknown cause that begins before age 16 and persists for at least six weeks [1, 2]. Over the past two decades, the treatment of JIA has changed substantially. Early and more aggressive use of conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, particularly methotrexate, together with the introduction of biologic agents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and T-cell costimulation, has increased the proportion of children who achieve low disease activity or clinical remission [3, 4]. Despite these advances, a considerable number of youth continue to report poor health-related quality of life (HRQOL), including limitations in physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, even when clinical measures indicate that disease is well controlled [5–7]. Pain, fatigue, and psychosocial difficulties persist in many patients whose joint counts and laboratory markers are unremarkable [8, 9]. This discrepancy suggests that the standard clinical indicators used to guide care capture only part of what matters to patients and families, and that other factors contribute to the lived experience of JIA. HRQOL is a multidimensional construct reflecting an individual's perception of how health and illness affect physical, psychological, and social wellbeing [10]. In pediatric rheumatology, HRQOL has been measured with generic instruments such as the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL), as well as with disease-specific tools and the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) [11–13]. Studies using these instruments have shown that HRQOL in JIA is lower than in healthy peers, and that disease activity, functional disability, and pain are correlated with HRQOL [5, 14]. However, associations between clinician-assessed disease activity and HRQOL are typically modest, and most of the variance in HRQOL remains unexplained [6, 15]. Identifying the additional determinants of HRQOL, especially those that are modifiable, is therefore a priority for improving outcomes. One set of potentially modifiable determinants relates to the burden of treatment. Children with JIA frequently take medications for years, often in combination, and these regimens involve injections, infusions, laboratory monitoring, and the risk of adverse effects. Methotrexate, the most widely used first-line systemic therapy, is effective but is commonly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea and abdominal pain, as well as with anticipatory and associative symptoms in which children experience nausea or distress before or at the thought of taking the drug [16, 17]. Methotrexate intolerance has been reported in a substantial minority of patients, can lead to reduced adherence, dose changes, or discontinuation, and has been associated with poorer HRQOL and greater distress for both children and parents [17, 18]. Other medications, including glucocorticoids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and biologic agents, carry their own risks of side effects, and fear of such effects can shape treatment decisions and adherence [19]. Although clinicians recognize that treatment can be burdensome, the contribution of treatment experiences to HRQOL has rarely been quantified alongside the contribution of disease burden, so it is unclear whether adverse treatment experiences affect wellbeing independently of disease symptoms. A second domain of patient experience that is incompletely captured in routine care is the day-to-day symptom burden of disease. Morning stiffness, a classic feature of inflammatory arthritis and a component of some disease activity assessments, is not consistently recorded in clinical encounters, and its relationship to HRQOL in contemporary JIA cohorts is not well characterized [20]. Pain interference, which reflects the extent to which pain disrupts activities, social participation, and mood rather than pain intensity alone, has emerged as an important patient-reported outcome, and PROMIS provides a validated pediatric measure of it [13, 21]. Pain interference may remain elevated in children with inactive disease, and may therefore represent an important and under-recognized source of reduced HRQOL [8, 22]. Together, morning stiffness and pain interference offer a patient-centered view of disease burden that complements physician-reported disease activity. Patient-centered outcomes research has increasingly emphasized collecting information directly from patients and families to understand which experiences matter most and how they relate to outcomes [23]. Multisite disease registries offer a platform for such work because they enroll large and diverse samples and already contain detailed clinical data, including diagnosis, disease activity, and medication history. The Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry is a North American observational registry of children with rheumatic diseases, including JIA, that has enrolled thousands of patients across dozens of centers [24]. The registry's clinical data have supported research on treatment patterns and safety, but it has not routinely included patient- or parent-reported measures of HRQOL and of experiences of disease and treatment. Integrating such measures would allow researchers to link patients' perspectives to clinical characteristics at scale and to identify targets for intervention that clinical data alone cannot reveal. The aim of this study was to add patient-reported outcomes to the CARRA Registry and to use them to quantify HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment burden among youth with JIA. Parents served as proxy reporters of their child's HRQOL, pain interference, morning stiffness, history of serious medication side effects, and, for those taking methotrexate, methotrexate intolerance. We asked three questions. First, what is the distribution of HRQOL and of these disease and treatment experiences in a multisite registry sample? Second, how is each experience associated with HRQOL? Third, do associations between treatment burden and HRQOL persist after accounting for disease burden, disease activity, and patient characteristics? We hypothesized that both disease and treatment burden would be independently associated with lower HRQOL. This study makes several contributions. It demonstrates the feasibility of augmenting an established multicenter registry with patient-reported measures, creating a model that other registries may adopt. It provides estimates of the prevalence of morning stiffness, serious medication side effects, and methotrexate intolerance in a registry cohort with long disease duration. Most importantly, it evaluates the independent contributions of disease and treatment burden to HRQOL, testing the proposition that adverse treatment experiences undermine wellbeing beyond the effects of disease symptoms and activity. The findings may help clinicians and researchers identify routinely assessable, modifiable targets for improving the quality of life of youth with JIA. Study Design and Setting We conducted a cross-sectional, observational study nested within the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, a multisite, prospective registry of children with pediatric rheumatic diseases enrolled at North American pediatric rheumatology centers (Beukelman et al., 2017). The registry collects clinician-reported demographic, diagnostic, disease activity, and medication data at enrollment and at regular follow-up visits. For this study, we added a patient-centered data collection component in which parents completed a survey about their child's health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and experiences of disease and treatment. Participating sites obtained approval from their local institutional review boards or from the central IRB used by the registry, and parents provided informed consent (and children provided assent where required by local policy). Participants and Recruitment Eligible patients were enrolled in the CARRA Registry, had a physician diagnosis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) according to International League of Associations for Rheumatology criteria (Petty et al., 2004), were between 2 and 18 years of age, and had a parent or legal guardian who could read and respond in English. Because the survey was completed by parent proxy, youth who were too young or unable to self-report were not excluded on that basis. Participating sites identified eligible patients from the registry and invited their parents to complete the survey either during a clinic visit or remotely by mail or secure electronic link. Parents completed the survey once. Registry data from the visit nearest to survey completion were linked to survey responses using a unique study identifier. We restricted the analytic sample to patients with complete data on the primary HRQOL outcome and key covariates. Measures Health-related quality of life. HRQOL was measured with the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 Generic Core Scales, parent-proxy report (Varni et al., 2001). The PedsQL contains 23 items spanning physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, with a recall period of the previous month. Items are rated on a five-point scale, reverse-scored and linearly transformed to a 0–100 scale, with higher scores indicating better HRQOL. We used the Total Scale Score as the primary outcome and also examined physical and psychosocial summary scores. Age-appropriate parent-proxy forms were used for children aged 2–4, 5–7, 8–12, and 13–18 years. Pain interference. Pain interference was assessed with the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Pediatric Pain Interference parent-proxy short form (Varni et al., 2010; Cella et al., 2010). Raw scores were converted to T-scores standardized to a reference population with a mean of 50 and standard deviation of 10, with higher scores reflecting greater interference of pain with daily activities. Morning stiffness. Parents reported the typical duration of their child's morning stiffness on a usual day. Because prolonged stiffness is a recognized marker of active inflammatory arthritis and is incorporated in disease activity assessment (Consolaro et al., 2009), we dichotomized duration as more than 15 minutes versus 15 minutes or less. Medication side effects. Parents were asked whether their child had ever experienced side effects from arthritis medications and, if so, to describe their nature and severity. Responses were reviewed and classified using predefined criteria; a serious side effect was one that led to medication discontinuation or dose change, required medical evaluation or treatment, or substantially disrupted the child's daily functioning. We created a binary indicator of one or more serious medication side effects. Methotrexate intolerance. For children currently or previously treated with methotrexate, parents completed the Methotrexate Intolerance Severity Score (MISS), which assesses abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and restlessness or irritability, each in anticipatory, associative, and behavioral domains (Bulatović et al., 2011). Scores range from 0 to 25, and a score of 6 or higher indicates clinically relevant methotrexate intolerance. Analyses of methotrexate intolerance were restricted to methotrexate users. Clinical and demographic characteristics. From the registry, we obtained patient age, sex, race and ethnicity, disease duration, JIA category, and treating site. Disease activity was captured using the clinical Juvenile Arthritis Disease Activity Score based on 10 joints (cJADAS-10), which combines physician global assessment, parent global assessment of wellbeing, and active joint count (McErlane et al., 2013). Current medication use, including methotrexate and biologic agents, was abstracted from registry records. Statistical Analysis We summarized participant characteristics and study measures using means and standard deviations for continuous variables and counts and percentages for categorical variables. Distributions of PedsQL, pain interference, and disease activity scores were inspected for normality and outliers. Our primary aim was to estimate the associations between measures of disease burden (pain interference and morning stiffness) and treatment burden (serious side effects and methotrexate intolerance) and HRQOL. Because patients were clustered within participating sites, we used generalized estimating equations (GEE) with an exchangeable working correlation structure and robust standard errors (Liang & Zeger, 1986). The outcome was the PedsQL Total Scale Score, modeled with an identity link and Gaussian distribution. We fit models in a sequential manner. First, unadjusted models estimated the association between each burden measure and HRQOL individually. Second, models were adjusted for patient demographics (age, sex, and race/ethnicity) and disease duration, with clustering by site. Third, we added disease burden measures (pain interference and morning stiffness) to models of treatment burden to determine whether treatment-related associations persisted independent of disease symptoms. Finally, we additionally adjusted for disease activity (cJADAS-10) and current medication use to evaluate whether associations were attenuated by clinical characteristics. Because the methotrexate intolerance analysis included only methotrexate users, it was conducted in that subsample with parallel model-building. We compared coefficients across successive models to assess attenuation. Collinearity among covariates was assessed using variance inflation factors. Regression coefficients are reported with 95% confidence intervals and p-values. Given the multiple related exposures, we considered p-values below 0.01 to indicate statistical significance in primary analyses to limit the risk of type I error. Cross-domain text classification has become a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP), as it enables the construction of a classifier for a target domain by leveraging data from both the source and target domains (Daumé III, 2007; Blitzer et al., 2006). The primary challenge in cross-domain text classification lies in the differences in feature distributions between the two domains, which can significantly degrade the performance of a classifier trained on the source domain when applied to the target domain (Pan et al., 2010). To address this issue, various studies have proposed methods to minimize the feature distribution differences between the two domains, with the aim of achieving domain-invariant feature representations (Glorot et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012). One common approach to minimizing feature distribution differences is through exact alignment mechanisms, such as one-to-one feature alignment or projection matrices (Blitzer et al., 2006; Kulis et al., 2011). These mechanisms aim to align the features of the two domains by establishing a direct correspondence between them. However, exact alignment can be restrictive, as it may not always be possible to establish a one-to-one correspondence between features across different domains (Zhou et al., 2014). Furthermore, exact alignment can impair the performance of models on classification tasks when the semantic distributions of the different domains are significantly different (Li et al., 2014). This is because exact alignment may not capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains, leading to suboptimal feature representations. To overcome the limitations of exact alignment, some studies have proposed alternative approaches that focus on aligning the semantic distributions of the two domains at a higher level (Chen et al., 2013; Long et al., 2015). These approaches aim to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across the domains. One such approach is to use topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), which can learn to represent documents as mixtures of latent topics (Blei et al., 2003). However, traditional topic models are not designed to handle cross-domain text classification tasks, and may not be effective in capturing the semantic differences between the two domains. Recently, some studies have proposed cross-domain topic models that can learn to represent documents from both the source and target domains as mixtures of latent topics (Jiang et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2012). These models can capture the semantic structures of both domains and learn to align the topics across the domains. However, these models often rely on exact alignment mechanisms or assume that the semantic distributions of the two domains are similar (Li et al., 2016). Moreover, these models may not be effective in handling cases where the semantic distributions of the two domains are significantly different. To address the limitations of existing cross-domain text classification methods, we propose a novel approach that focuses on aligning the semantics at the group level, rather than relying on exact alignment mechanisms. Our approach, which we term Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), embeds a group alignment mechanism and a partial supervision mechanism into a cross-domain topic model. The group alignment mechanism allows the model to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across the domains. The partial supervision mechanism enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups by leveraging labeled data from the source domain. The research question that guides this study is: Can a cross-domain topic model that incorporates group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms effectively capture the semantic structures of both the source and target domains and improve the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks? Our study aims to investigate the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model in addressing the challenges of cross-domain text classification. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we propose a novel group alignment mechanism that can capture the semantic structures of both domains at a higher level. Second, we introduce a partial supervision mechanism that enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups. Third, we embed the group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms into a cross-domain topic model, which can effectively capture the semantic structures of both domains and improve the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks. The remainder of this study will provide a detailed description of the proposed CDL-LDA model, including its architecture, training procedure, and evaluation metrics. We will also present extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model on standard benchmarks, including the 20Newsgroup and Reuters datasets. Our study aims to contribute to the development of more effective cross-domain text classification methods that can capture the semantic structures of both the source and target domains and improve the performance of text classification tasks in real-world applications. The proposed Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model is designed to address the challenges of cross-domain text classification by leveraging data from both source and target domains. To achieve this, we first describe the data used in our experiments, followed by the design of the CDL-LDA model, and finally, the procedures and statistical analysis used to evaluate its performance. The data used in our experiments consists of two standard datasets: 20Newsgroup and Reuters. The 20Newsgroup dataset is a collection of approximately 20,000 newsgroup documents, partitioned across 20 different newsgroups (Joachims, 1998). We select 10 newsgroups from this dataset, with 5 newsgroups as the source domain and the remaining 5 newsgroups as the target domain. The Reuters dataset, on the other hand, is a collection of news articles, with 8 categories in the source domain and 4 categories in the target domain (Lewis, 1997). We preprocess the data by removing stop words, stemming, and converting all documents to a bag-of-words representation. The design of the CDL-LDA model is based on the idea of minimizing the feature distribution differences between the source and target domains. Unlike existing studies that use exact alignment mechanisms, such as one-to-one feature alignment or projection matrices (Blitzer et al., 2006; Pan et al., 2010), we propose a novel group alignment approach that aligns the semantics at the group level. This approach allows the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups, without restricting its learning ability. To achieve this, we embed the group alignment into a cross-domain topic model, which is an extension of the traditional Labeled LDA (L-LDA) model (Ramage et al., 2009). In the CDL-LDA model, we assume that each document in the source domain is associated with a label, while documents in the target domain are unlabeled. We use a partial supervision approach to help the model learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups in the source domain. Specifically, we use a subset of the labeled documents in the source domain to train the model, while the remaining documents are used for testing. This approach allows the model to learn from the labeled data, while also being able to generalize to unseen data. The CDL-LDA model consists of two main components: a topic model and a classifier. The topic model is used to learn the semantic groups and semantics within these groups, while the classifier is used to predict the labels of the documents in the target domain. We use a hierarchical Bayesian framework to model the topic model, where each document is represented as a mixture of topics, and each topic is represented as a mixture of words (Blei et al., 2003). The classifier, on the other hand, is a simple logistic regression model that takes the topic proportions as input and predicts the label of the document. To train the CDL-LDA model, we use a variational inference approach, which is a popular method for approximate Bayesian inference (Jordan et al., 1999). We use the mean-field variational Bayes algorithm to approximate the posterior distribution of the model parameters, and then use the approximate posterior distribution to make predictions on the target domain. We evaluate the performance of the CDL-LDA model using a range of metrics, including classification accuracy, perplexity, and topic detection. In terms of statistical analysis, we use a range of techniques to evaluate the performance of the CDL-LDA model. For classification accuracy, we use a held-out test set to evaluate the model's performance on the target domain. We also use perplexity to evaluate the model's ability to fit the data, and topic detection to evaluate the model's ability to discover meaningful topics.
