Aphasia is an acquired communication disorder following brain injury affecting not only expression and understanding of spoken language, reading, and writing [1], but also different aspects of participation, such as interpersonal interactions and relationships, major life areas, and community, social and civic life [2]. Although the ideal end purpose of rehabilitation is participation according to the United Nations [3], current aphasia rehabilitation practices may lack sufficient consideration of participation [4–6]. The International Classification of Functioning, Disabilities and Health defines participation as “involvement in a life situation” [2]. The participation of persons who have aphasia can remain limited after rehabilitation [7, 8], indicating a need that speech-language pathologists be more aware of evidence-based recommendations that promote participation and include these in their practice. The current paper reports on the structure, processes and outcomes of a knowledge transfer strategy for speech-language pathologists. In Quebec’s continuum of publicly funded health care system (Canada) [9], stroke survivors are first admitted to an acute care hospital, where they generally stay between five days and three weeks, depending on the severity of the stroke, and receive healthcare and early short-term rehabilitation services [10]. Once their medical condition is stable, they either return home or attend an inpatient rehabilitation centre, where they receive intensive rehabilitation services generally five days a week for an average of 6–12 weeks, with longer rehabilitation associated with more severe strokes [10]. Where available, outpatient rehabilitation services are usually offered at a lesser weekly frequency and for an average of three months. However, there are no long-term rehabilitation services available in Quebec, reinforcing the importance of addressing participation early in the care continuum. Some persons with aphasia will join community associations which provide group leisure and social activities, but these are not available in all regions of Quebec [11]. Speech-language pathologists are encouraged to follow evidence-based practice (EBP) recommendations [12–14] across the care continuum of aphasia rehabilitation [15–17]. In aphasia rehabilitation, there is evidence that therapy improves reading, writing, expressive language, and “functional” communication, i.e. successful communication of a message via spoken, written, or non-verbal modalities, or a combination of these, in day-to-day interactions [1]. However, some speech-language therapy clinical activities may also have a positive impact on the level of participation of persons with aphasia after rehabilitation. Such clinical activities include, but are not limited to: setting goals based on the needs of the persons with aphasia and those of their relatives [18–20]; assessing and evaluating the outcomes of therapy with tools that measure participation (e.g. Community Integration Questionnaire, Assessment for Living with Aphasia) or quality of life (e.g. Stroke Specific Quality of Life Scale) [21–23]; training conversation partners to use communication strategies with the person who has aphasia [24, 25]; teaching persons with aphasia to use alternative methods of communication, such as gestures, writing, and/or pictures [26]; and openly discussing discharge plans from speech-language pathology services with the person with aphasia [27–29]. In the context of the present work, such clinical activities were referred to as “participation-based aphasia rehabilitation”, an expression that reflects rehabilitation practices focused especially on a person’s needs as they relate to participation. Participation-based aphasia rehabilitation may share characteristics with what was described in the literature as “comprehensive” aphasia therapy, such as Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Programs (ICAPs) and the Life Participation Approach to Aphasia (LPAA) (e.g. [30–32]). Participation-based aphasia rehabilitation is not widely used in current speech-language pathology practice [4–6]. Therefore, effective knowledge transfer strategies are needed to support speech-language pathologists in employing intervention strategies that impact participation, the ideal end purpose of rehabilitation. Rehabilitation speech-language pathologists experience challenges when implementing EBP [14, 33] especially since they report limited time for participating in EBP activities [14, 15, 34–36]. These challenges may also be related to the nature, or strength, of the evidence, i.e. the fact that despite randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews being highly valued in research, few are available in speech-language pathology [14]. Furthermore, applying EBP is problematic because of the use of evidence, i.e. speech-language pathologists have difficulty transferring the results of scientific research in their clinical reality, and may prefer consulting their peers for clinical decision making [14, 36]. Thus, an effective knowledge transfer strategy should be time-efficient, present clinically pertinent evidence and provide opportunities for collaboration with peers. Collaborative knowledge transfer strategies offer a high level of interaction among participants, and between participants and researchers [37]. Communities of practice (CoPs) can be used to transfer knowledge. A CoP is defined as a “group of people who share a concern, a set of problems, or a passion about a topic, and who deepen their knowledge and expertise in this area by interacting on an ongoing basis” (p.4) [38]. To arouse interest among potential participants, a CoP should have educational aims and contribute to continuing education. Moreover, when conducting research about a CoP, one needs to operationalize some design aims to orient data collection [37]. In fact, in aphasia rehabilitation, CoPs for speech-language pathologists were never studied. A systematic scoping review indicated that among the many reasons for undertaking the evaluation of a CoP there are the need to assess, to understand, and/or to promote their value [39]. Assessment frameworks of CoPs frequently include attention to the goals, context, structure, process/activities, outcomes, and level of impact [39]. CoPs can thus be analyzed with a logic model, traditionally including resources/inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes/impacts [40–45]. Resources include human and material resources and other inputs to support the intervention; activities refer to all necessary action steps to produce the outputs; outputs are the products of the intervention; and outcomes are changes resulting from activities and outputs [44]. Logic analysis allows one to create a model illustrating the different components of an intervention and the relationships between them [46], thus it was an appropriate method for evaluating the current CoP. This method was chosen because of its potential to detail each component of the CoP [40] and to describe outputs and outcomes while it was ongoing and especially afterwards to evaluate the CoP’s immediate success. Four theoretical concepts were used for the design and implementation of this CoP: constructivism, social learning, situated learning, and reflective practice. Constructivism postulates that meaning and experience come from social interaction and that knowledge is co-constructed by the learners [47]. Social learning theory posits that knowledge is best integrated through social interaction [48]. Situated learning refers to learning in authentic and meaningful contexts [49]. Reflective practice is the product of a tacit and implicit knowledge in one’s actions [50]. In speech-language pathology, reflective practice can be operationalized by conducting two types of activities: written reflection and reflective discussion [51]. Given that aphasia affects a person’s level of participation and that participation is the under-achieved ideal end purpose of rehabilitation, a CoP about participation-based aphasia rehabilitation in line with current best evidence was designed, implemented and evaluated using logic analysis. Therefore, the aim of this study was to describe the components and evaluate a CoP for speech-language pathologists in aphasia rehabilitation. This section presents details about the context of the study, topics of the CoP, participants, data collection and data analysis. This study was undertaken as part of the first author’s PhD research (CAG). GLD was CAG’s advisor. Speech-language pathologist participants were recruited to be part of a CoP. They were aware that the CoP was evaluated and knew they could use their involvement as professional continuing education. The CoP was presented to the participants as an opportunity to learn about EBP recommendations, to reflect on their practice and to interact with colleagues. Its ultimate and explicit aim was to fill a gap between literature about participation-based aphasia rehabilitation and actual practices. It is possible that such a gap existed because clinical practice guidelines were not of sufficient quality in the field of post-stroke aphasia [26, 52], engaging in the uptake of these guidelines was too time intensive [53], or they were not pertinent to speech-language pathologists’ specific work settings or clients. Finally, the CoP was web-based to allow the participation of speech-language pathologists from all regions of Quebec. In Quebec, speech-language pathology practice usually involves assessing language, voice, and speech functions, in order to elaborate a treatment plan, and conduct indirect and direct intervention to facilitate a person’s communication in his/her environment [54]. No specific details or evidence were available in relation to specific clinical activities that should be provided in the Quebec healthcare context. In contrast, the Australian Aphasia Rehabilitation Pathway (AARP) [55] presents speech-language pathology practice as a pathway composed of the following evidence-based clinical activities: receiving the right referrals, optimizing initial contact, setting goals and measuring outcomes, assessing, providing intervention, enhancing the communicative environment, enhancing personal factors, and planning for transitions. Topics were selected considering available evidence, the potential they had to induce reflective practice, and because they were part of the usual clinical activities of speech-language pathologists. Furthermore, CAG conducted individual interviews with all participants before the beginning of the CoP. These interviews allowed researchers to understand and describe the practice of Quebec’s speech-language pathologists in terms of central and peripheral clinical activities [56] and informed the design of the CoP. For the purposes of a time-bound PhD research project, the CoP was “top-down” and created by the researchers, who selected the topics. However, these were chosen to mirror participant clinical realities and interests. These topics were: 1- the ideal end purpose of aphasia rehabilitation; 2- goal-setting; 3- assessment and outcome evaluation; 4- indirect intervention; 5- direct intervention; and 6- discharge. Fourteen speech-language pathologists with a minimum of six months of experience in aphasia rehabilitation were initially recruited to participate in the CoP. One left the project for professional reasons after two weeks, and the data from this participant was not analyzed. The 13 remaining participants (12 women, one man) from the Greater Montreal area (n = 9) and suburban regions (n = 4) of the province of Quebec worked in various aphasia rehabilitation settings: acute care, inpatient, and/or outpatient rehabilitation (see Table 1). Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the most important challenges in global health at the present time. This infectious disease ranks alongside human immunodeficiency virus as a leading cause of death worldwide; there were an estimated 1.4 million TB deaths in 2015 [1]. The World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends a combination of four first-line drugs for individuals with drug-susceptible TB: isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide [1]. TB patients receiving this regimen may experience serious adverse drug reactions, such as anti-tuberculosis drug-induced hepatotoxicity (ATDH), which causes a strain on health care providers due to high morbidity, mortality and increased treatment costs [2, 3]. Reported incidence rates of ATDH among patients treated with standard multidrug treatment vary widely from 2 to 28%, depending on the regimen given and the characteristics of patients such as age, race and sex [4]. Variability in the methodology used for data collection and reporting, and different definitions of ATDH may also contribute to the wide range of incidence rates. The proposed genetic risk factors for ATDH include polymorphisms of the N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2), cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1), and glutathione s-transferase mu 1 (GSTM1) genes, which code for drug-metabolising enzymes. Several studies have investigated the association between these genetic polymorphisms and ATDH [5–24]. These polymorphisms may affect the activation ability of the enzymes, altering the chemical modification of anti-tuberculosis drugs and their metabolites in the liver, leading to hepatic adverse reactions [25]. Toxic metabolites may also cause other toxicity events, such as peripheral neuropathy and maculopapular eruption, although the majority of evidence on the pharmacogenetics of anti-tuberculosis drugs focuses on hepatotoxicity. Isoniazid is the anti-tuberculosis drug for which the genetic contribution to ATDH is most studied and best understood. Specifically, it is thought that NAT2 acetylator status may be associated with increased risk of isoniazid-related hepatic adverse reactions, as NAT2 is one of the main enzymes involved in the metabolism of isoniazid in the liver. There are three phenotypes of acetylator status. Individuals who are slow NAT2 acetylators acetylate isoniazid slowly, resulting in high plasma drug levels. This may be beneficial for treatment efficacy, but slow acetylators may also experience an accumulation of toxic metabolites as part of the metabolic activation of acetylhydrazine to harmless diacetylhydrazine. Isoniazid suppresses the acetylation of acetylhydrazine, hence producing more toxic metabolites, which contributes to the increased risk of isoniazid hepatitis that slow acetylators experience [26]. Fast acetylators have lower plasma drug levels, and so, treatment may be not only less effective but also less toxic, and intermediate acetylators fall between these two extremes. Several studies have investigated the association between NAT2 genetic variants and hepatotoxicity in patients treated with isoniazid or isoniazid-containing regimens [5–18], with most studies reporting significant associations between NAT genetic variants and ATDH. However, there is no set method for defining acetylator status by genotyping, as acetylator status is governed by polymorphisms in a number of alleles on the NAT2 gene, making the genetic definition of acetylator status difficult to standardise. Cai et al. (2012) [27] defined individuals without a copy of the wild-type NAT24 allele as slow acetylators, and all other individuals as rapid acetylators, whereas Wang et al. [28] considered individuals with two copies of rapid NAT2 acetylator alleles (NAT24, NAT211A, NAT212A, NAT212B, NAT212C, NAT213) to be rapid acetylators, individuals with no copies to be slow acetylators, and those with one copy to be intermediate acetylators. Following NAT2 in the disposition of isoniazid is CYP2E1. It has been reported that isoniazid inhibits CYP2E1 activity less in individuals with the CYP2E1 1A/1A genotype than in those with other genotypes [20]. Consequently, individuals with the CYP2E1 1A/1A genotype have higher CYP2E1 activity, resulting in more hepatotoxins. Some studies have investigated the association between CYP2E1 genetic variants and hepatotoxicity in patients treated with isoniazid or isoniazid-containing regimens, although results from these studies are often conflicting [13–22]. Finally, GST is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in the detoxification process, and it has been hypothesised that individuals with null GSTM1 or GSTT1 genotypes may detoxify the toxic metabolites from earlier in the metabolic pathway of isoniazid less efficiently [27]. There has been some investigation into the association between GSTM1 and GSTT1 genotypes and ATDH [18, 22–24], and although significant associations are reported by some studies, the evidence base remains highly uncertain. Rifampicin and pyrazinamide have also been reported to be hepatotoxic [29, 30]; however, the mechanisms for rifampicin-induced hepatotoxicity and pyrazinamide-induced hepatotoxicity are unknown and unpredictable [4]. Some speculated genetic variants, such as SLCO1B1, have been linked to toxicity with rifampicin, although limited data are available to support this claim [29]. No hepatotoxicity has been described for ethambutol. The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to evaluate the current evidence on the effect of genetic variants on anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity in TB patients receiving anti-tuberculosis drugs. Meta-analyses investigating the pharmacogenetics of anti-tuberculosis agents and toxicity outcomes have been published previously [25, 27, 28, 31–38]. Psychological therapy now occupies a central place in the organization of public mental healthcare in the United Kingdom. Much of this prominence stems from a single initiative: the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme, launched in England in 2008 and rebranded in 2023 as NHS Talking Therapies. IAPT was designed to expand the provision of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)-recommended interventions, notably cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), for people diagnosed with depression and anxiety disorders (Clark, 2011). By the late 2010s, well over a million people were being referred to IAPT services each year, and the programme had been identified as a cornerstone of national mental health policy (NHS England, 2016, 2019). For many citizens, therapy is therefore no longer a marginal, privately purchased or specialist offering. It is a routinely available, publicly funded, and statistically monitored component of everyday healthcare. This development is striking given the longer history of psychological expertise in Britain. Psychological disciplines have long shaped how selves, distress, and conduct are understood and governed (Rose, 1985, 1996), and the 'therapeutic' has been identified as a pervasive cultural register through which suffering is framed (Illouz, 2008). Yet, for much of the twentieth century, the delivery of talking therapies within the National Health Service (NHS) was patchy, locally variable, and often subordinate to pharmacological and custodial approaches. That a psychological intervention could become infrastructural to a national health system, with explicit targets for access and outcome, thus warrants sustained analytic attention. It raises the question of how psychological therapy came to be configured as a public good and a legitimate object of national investment, and with what consequences for the knowledge and practices of mental healthcare itself. Existing scholarship has examined IAPT from several vantage points. Evaluative literatures, produced largely by the programme's architects and affiliated clinicians, document reported outcomes: recovery rates approaching the 50% target, and an expansion in access towards a goal of reaching 25% of the estimated population with common mental disorders (Clark et al., 2018; NHS England, 2019). Critical commentators in psychology, psychotherapy studies, and sociology have, in contrast, questioned the programme's evidence base and cost-effectiveness claims (Griffiths and Steen, 2013), its narrow therapeutic repertoire and apparent privileging of CBT (Pilgrim, 2011; House and Loewenthal, 2008), and the effects of performance measurement on clinical work and practitioner subjectivity (Rizq, 2012; Scott, 2018). These contributions are valuable. However, they tend either to take IAPT's founding rationale as given or to treat it as an instance of broader neoliberal or managerial trends, rather than examining empirically how the initiative's rationale was assembled, justified, and stabilized over time. Less attention has been paid to the specific configurations of expertise, evidence, and accountability through which IAPT became thinkable and, subsequently, durable. The case also speaks to wider debates in the sociology of health and illness regarding the trajectory of biomedicine. Concepts such as medicalization and biomedicalization have been used to describe the expanding jurisdiction of medical authority and its reconstitution through technoscientific practices (Conrad, 2007; Clarke et al., 2003). In mental health specifically, scholars have charted the ascendancy of neuroscientific and biological framings, as well as their uneven uptake and contestation (Rose and Abi-Rached, 2013; Pickersgill, 2013). Against this background, the rise of a psychologically oriented intervention might be read as a partial debiomedicalization: a movement away from drug-based, brain-centred models towards talk, cognition, and behaviour. Yet such a reading risks assuming linear, directional change in health systems. If psychological therapy has been re-legitimized, we must ask on what terms, and whether the resources used to do so are in fact characteristically biomedical. This article addresses these concerns through an analysis of how IAPT was developed, accounted for, and sustained as a national response to mental ill-health. Drawing on policy documents, economic reports, clinical guidelines, and published evaluations, I trace the problematization (in the sense developed by Foucault and elaborated by Rabinow and Rose) of common mental disorders as a challenge simultaneously clinical, economic, and political. The analysis attends in particular to the role of economic expertise, exemplified by the influential case for expanded therapy articulated by Layard and colleagues (Layard, 2006; Layard et al., 2007). Here, the costs of unemployment, sickness absence, and welfare dependency associated with depression and anxiety were rendered commensurable with the costs of therapy, such that treatment could be presented as self-financing. Such calculative forms of reasoning have been shown to be performative, shaping the very realities they purport to describe (Callon, 1998; Miller and Rose, 1990). I argue that, in the case of IAPT, they were joined to particular accounts of pathology and mechanisms of therapeutic change, and to forms of evidence, most notably the randomized controlled trial (RCT) and its attendant hierarchy of knowledge, that are more familiar within biomedical settings (Timmermans and Berg, 2003). The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides an empirically grounded account of the emergence of IAPT that foregrounds the co-production of economic argument, psychological knowledge, and policy rationale, thereby extending analyses of audit and accountability in public services (Power, 1997; Strathern, 2000; Porter, 1995) into the domain of psychological therapy. Second, it demonstrates that the revival of psychological framings of distress has proceeded through, rather than against, biomedical epistemic and administrative forms. This complicates narratives of linear biomedicalization or debiomedicalization and instead suggests more entangled, mutually conditioning dynamics. Third, I introduce the concept of contextification to describe a process by which IAPT has shifted from being primarily a content of mental healthcare (a set of interventions delivered within services) to a context for it: an organizing presence in relation to which other services, pathways, and professional identities are increasingly designed, justified, and evaluated. Understanding this transformation matters for anyone concerned with how mental health provision is currently being reshaped. By documenting these developments, the paper contributes to re-centring questions about the place and role of psychology within contemporary healthcare, a topic that has been overshadowed in social science by the prominence of psychiatry and neuroscience. In what follows, I first outline the conceptual resources on which the analysis draws, before describing the materials and methods employed. I then examine in turn the problematization of common mental disorders, the formation of IAPT's evidential and economic justification, and the mechanisms through which the programme has been sustained and extended. I conclude by considering the implications of contextification for the future of psychological therapy and for theorizing change in health systems. Research design and analytic approach This study adopts a problematization-oriented, mixed-methods documentary design to examine how IAPT was formulated, justified, and stabilized as a national response to mental ill-health. The analytic orientation draws on Foucauldian studies of governmentality (Rose, 1999; Miller and Rose, 2008) and on the "What's the problem represented to be?" approach to policy analysis (Bacchi, 2009), which treats policies as proposals that constitute the problems they claim to address. Following sociological work on biomedicalization (Clarke et al., 2003) and on the sociology of expertise, I was particularly attentive to how psychological, economic, and biomedical forms of knowledge were combined and to the evidentiary practices used to link them. The design had three components: (1) a qualitative analysis of policy and expert documents, (2) a supplementary set of semi-structured interviews, and (3) a quantitative descriptive analysis of publicly available IAPT activity and outcome data. Their purposes were respectively to reconstruct the problematization, to examine how it was understood and sustained by those involved in it, and to assess how far its institutional prominence was reflected in service-level trends. Components were integrated sequentially. Documentary analysis informed the interview schedule, and the quantitative analysis was used to contextualize and test claims that emerged in the qualitative material (Fetters et al., 2013). Documentary corpus Documents were identified through a purposive, iterative strategy designed to capture the period between the first public articulation of the programme's rationale and its integration into wider system planning (2004–2021). I began with canonical texts, notably the Depression Report (Layard et al., 2006) and the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence guidance on depression and anxiety, and then followed citation and reference trails forward and backward ("snowball" sampling; Bowen, 2009). Further material was retrieved from the UK Government Web Archive, Department of Health and NHS England repositories, Hansard, the National Audit Office, the Health Select Committee, and the websites of professional bodies and charities. Search terms included "Improving Access to Psychological Therapies," "IAPT," "talking therapies," "cognitive behavioural therapy," "Increasing Access," and "Layard." Documents were included if they (a) set out the rationale, design, evaluation, or expansion of IAPT or (b) positioned other mental health services in relation to it. Duplicates, press releases without substantive content, and purely operational guidance (e.g. rota or commissioning templates) were excluded. This produced a corpus of 214 documents: 61 national policy and strategy documents, 38 commissioning and service specifications, 29 evaluation and audit reports, 34 peer-reviewed articles and commentaries by programme architects and critics, 27 parliamentary records, and 25 professional-body and third-sector publications. Following Prior's (2003) emphasis on documents as active agents in organizational fields rather than neutral containers of information, I paid close attention to document genre, authorship, intended audience, and intertextual relations (what each text cited, and how it was cited by subsequent texts). Because publicly available documents necessarily reflect curated and strategic representations, I treated them as evidence of how the programme was publicly accounted for, not as transparent records of internal deliberation (Scott, 1990). Interviews To complement the documentary record, I conducted 19 semi-structured interviews between March 2019 and February 2020 with individuals purposively sampled for their involvement in IAPT's development, delivery, or critique: national policy officials and advisers (n = 5), clinical and academic leads (n = 6), service managers and commissioners (n = 5), and representatives of professional or service-user organizations (n = 3). Participants were approached by email and through snowball referral. Interviews lasted 42–94 minutes (mean = 63), were conducted in person or by video call, and were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The schedule covered participants' accounts of the programme's origins, the role of evidence and economic argument in its justification, perceived changes in the relationship between IAPT and other services, and the principal points of contention. Because several participants held prominent roles, I report findings in ways that prevent identification, referring to broad role categories only and removing identifying details. Interview material was used primarily to interpret and triangulate the documentary analysis, not as an independent evidentiary base, and its limited scale does not support claims of representativeness. Qualitative analysis Documents and transcripts were imported into NVivo 12 and analyzed through a combination of theory-informed and inductive coding. An initial round of open coding on a 20% stratified sample of documents generated a provisional framework, which was refined through discussion with two colleagues who independently coded a further 10% of the corpus. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and the framework was revised accordingly. Inter-coder agreement on the final framework, assessed on a further 10% subsample, was acceptable (Cohen's κ = 0.78). The remaining material was then coded by me. Codes were organized around four analytic domains: representations of the problem (how mental ill-health and its costs were defined), representations of the solution (how therapy, and CBT in particular, was characterized), evidentiary practices (the types of evidence invoked, such as randomized controlled trials, health-economic modelling, and routine outcome data), and relational positioning (how IAPT was situated relative to other services, professions, and policy agendas). I then traced these domains chronologically, in line with the temporal focus of the study, and compared across document genres to identify points of stabilization, translation, and contestation. Reflexive thematic analysis principles (Braun and Clarke, 2006) guided the move from codes to themes, and I kept an analytic memo log to document interpretive decisions. Negative cases, such as documents critical of or ambivalent about the programme's framing, were deliberately sought and retained to avoid a purely confirmatory reading. Code clones, fragments of source code that are identical or similar to one another, are pervasive in modern software systems. Empirical studies report that between 5% and 20% of the code in typical large systems is cloned (Roy and Cordy 2007; Kapser and Godfrey 2008). Developers create clones for many reasons, including copy-and-paste reuse, language limitations, and deliberate performance or stability trade-offs. Whether clones are harmful has been debated for more than a decade. Some studies associate clones with inconsistent updates, propagated defects, and increased maintenance effort (Juergens et al. 2009; Krinke 2007; Thummalapenta et al. 2010). Others find that clones are often short-lived, stable, or even beneficial in specific contexts (Kapser and Godfrey 2008; Göde and Koschke 2011; Hotta et al. 2012). The practical consequence is that clone detectors, which can report thousands of clone groups for a mature project (Kamiya et al. 2002; Jiang et al. 2007; Sajnani et al. 2016), leave developers with a triage problem. Not all clones are equally important, and a developer who has limited time must decide which ones are worth refactoring. Clone-removal refactoring, such as extracting a shared method or pulling members up into a common superclass (Fowler 1999), is the standard remedy when clones are judged harmful. Refactoring is not free, however. It requires understanding the context of each clone instance and often involves parameterizing differences, resolving dependencies, and updating tests. It can also introduce regressions or entangle components that were intentionally kept separate. Refactoring every detected clone is therefore neither feasible nor desirable. This motivates clone recommendation, the task of identifying, among all detected clones, those that developers are likely to find worth removing. Prior work has approached this task from two complementary angles. The first uses the present state of the code. Studies of this kind assess whether a clone group is a good refactoring candidate from its structural and syntactic properties, such as the cohesion of individual fragments, the coupling between a fragment and its surrounding context, the size of the clone, and the location of the clone peers within the class hierarchy or package structure (Higo et al. 2004; Tairas and Gray 2012; Zibran and Roy 2012). The second uses the past of the project. These approaches mine version histories to determine how clone peers evolved, for example whether they changed together, how often they were modified, and whether they were modified inconsistently (Lozano and Wermelinger 2008; Mondal et al. 2014). Clones that repeatedly co-change are plausible candidates because the duplication imposes a recurring maintenance burden. Wang and Godfrey (2014) combined design, context, and history information in a learning-based recommender and showed that mixing present and past information improves the accuracy of recommendation over single-aspect heuristics. Despite this progress, existing approaches face three limitations. First, each tool considers only a restricted set of factors, chosen mostly on the basis of the authors' intuitions about what makes a clone worth refactoring. It remains unclear whether the factors used so far are sufficient, whether they overlap, or whether other properties of clones carry additional predictive signal. For example, features describing the evolution of an individual clone (how long it has existed, how often it has been edited, who edited it) have received much less attention than co-change relations between clone peers, and syntactic differences between peers are seldom combined with spatial relations such as same-file or same-package placement. Second, much of the earlier evaluation relied on small data sets, on manually labeled ground truth, or on a single project, which makes generalization hard to assess. In particular, it is rarely examined whether a model learned on one project can recommend clones in another project, a cross-project setting that matters in practice because new projects lack the history required for training. Third, the literature offers little systematic comparison of which categories of factors contribute most to recommendation accuracy, or of which learning algorithms are best suited to the task. Without such comparisons, tool builders cannot make informed decisions about which information is worth the cost of collecting. The existence of several tools that use different yet individually useful signals suggested to us that a more accurate recommender could be obtained by considering as many factors as possible within a single framework and letting a learning algorithm determine how they should be weighed. This leads to the central question of this paper: to what extent can combining a broad set of present and past features of clones, characterizing both individual clones and the relations among clone peers, improve the recommendation of clones for refactoring, in both within-project and cross-project settings? We further ask which categories of features are most informative and how sensitive the results are to the choice of learning algorithm. To answer these questions, we present CREC (Clone Recommendation for refactoring based on the present and the past), a learning-based approach to clone recommendation. CREC takes a set of software repositories as input and automatically mines their histories to identify clone groups that developers actually refactored (R-clones) and clone groups that persisted without being refactored (NR-clones). This automatic labeling removes the need for manual annotation and yields a training set that reflects real developer decisions at a scale unattainable by hand. For each clone group, CREC extracts 34 features in five categories: the content of individual clones, the evolution behaviors of individual clones, and the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. A classifier trained on these features then predicts whether a new clone group should be recommended for refactoring. To our knowledge, this is the largest feature set designed for clone recommendation to date. We evaluated CREC on six large open-source projects. In the within-project setting, where the classifier is trained and tested on data from the same project, CREC achieved an F-score of 83%. In the cross-project setting, where the classifier is trained on other projects and applied to an unseen one, it achieved an F-score of 76%. We compared CREC against the state-of-the-art approach of Wang and Godfrey (2014) on the same data set. That approach achieved F-scores of 70% and 50% in the two settings, so CREC's improvements are substantial, particularly when historical data from the target project are unavailable. We also analyzed the contribution of each feature category and compared several widely used learning algorithms to understand which factors and models drive these results. This paper makes the following contributions: An automated approach to build ground truth. We describe a procedure that mines version histories to extract refactored (R-clone) and non-refactored (NR-clone) clone groups, enabling the construction of large training and evaluation sets without manual labeling. The largest feature set to date for clone recommendation. We define 34 features that integrate present and past information, covering the content and evolution of individual clones as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations among clone peers. A learning-based recommender, CREC. We show that CREC accurately recommends clones for refactoring in both within-project (83% F-score) and cross-project (76% F-score) settings, and that it significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art approach (70% and 50%, respectively) on our data set. An empirical analysis of factors and algorithms. We quantify the relative effectiveness of different feature categories and of different learning algorithms, and we derive insights to guide the design of future clone-management tools. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives background and motivating examples. Section 3 describes the design of CREC, including the extraction of R-clones and NR-clones, the feature set, and the classifier training. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results. Section 5 discusses threats to validity, Section 6 reviews related work, and Section 7 concludes. Research questions and overview. We designed the study around three questions. RQ1: How accurately does CREC recommend clone groups for refactoring in within-project and cross-project settings, compared with a state-of-the-art baseline? RQ2: How much does each feature category contribute? RQ3: How does the choice of learning algorithm affect performance? CREC has three stages: (1) automatic construction of a labeled data set of refactored clone groups (R-clones) and non-refactored clone groups (NR-clones) from version histories, (2) extraction of 34 features capturing the present and past of each clone group, and (3) training and applying a classifier that predicts whether a clone group deserves refactoring. Subject projects. We selected six open-source Java projects with long, well-maintained Git histories: Ant, Cassandra, jEdit, JGit, Lucene, and Tomcat. Projects were chosen using three criteria: more than 5,000 commits, at least eight years of development, and varied application domains and sizes (60 to 520 KLOC at the latest studied release). To keep analysis tractable, we sampled snapshots at release tags and at every 100th commit between releases, yielding 1,412 snapshots in total. Such sampling is common in clone-genealogy research, where the unit of analysis is the evolution of clones across versions rather than individual commits (Kim et al., 2005). Clone detection and genealogy extraction. For each snapshot, we detected Type-2 and Type-3 clones with NiCad (Roy & Cordy, 2008), using a minimum size of 10 lines, a maximum dissimilarity threshold of 30% after pretty-printing and identifier normalization, and blind renaming. Clone fragments were grouped into clone groups (also called clone classes), where each member (clone peer) is similar to the others in the group. We then mapped clone groups across consecutive snapshots with a location- and similarity-based mapping in the spirit of clone genealogy extractors (Kim et al., 2005; Saha et al., 2013). Two groups were mapped if at least half of their fragments could be matched, with fragment similarity above 70% after accounting for line changes recovered by git diff with rename detection. The result was a set of clone genealogies describing how each group was created, changed, and removed. Automatic labeling of R-clones and NR-clones. We detected refactorings between successive snapshots with RefactoringMiner (Tsantalis et al., 2018), which reports Extract Method, Pull Up Method, Move Method, Extract Superclass, and related operations with reported precision above 95%. Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are a group of neurodevelopmental disorders. Children with ASD typically have difficulty with communication and social interaction, and may be overly dependent on routines, place extreme foci on items, and/or extremely dislike changes to their environment (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental‐5, American Psychiatric Association, 2013). These symptoms appear on a continuum, with some children experiencing only mild symptoms, while others experience quite severe symptomatology. The reported prevalence of children diagnosed with ASD has increased over time. While the current rate of prevalence in the United States (US) is the same as the rate reported in 2012 (1 in 68 children), it is a significant jump from the 1 in 88 children reported in 2008; and the 1 in 150 children reported in 2002 (Autism Speaks, 2016; Centers for Disease control and Prevention, 2016). This growth in prevalence has also been seen in other countries. For example, the Survey of Disability, Ageing and Carers (SDAC) conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) shows that in 2009, about 64,400 people had been diagnosed with ASD, and in 2012, this had increased to 115,400 (ABS, 2016). More recent population‐level data have been collected by the ABS (see ABS, 2016), however it is currently not publicly available. Where possible, up‐to‐date prevalence rates will be included in our review. In addition to increasing numbers, recent research shows that the number of students with ASD attending mainstream schools is also increasing (Zainal & Magiati, 2016). The exact reason for the increase in prevalence is unclear, but may be related to changes in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)1, as well as increased awareness and better recognition of less severe cases that were otherwise previously diagnosed as anxiety, bipolar, or other related disorder. ASD often co‐occurs with other neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), learning difficulties, depression and anxiety. Anxiety symptoms have been noted in individuals with ASD since Leo Kanner and Hans Asperger first described this disorder more than 70 years ago (Lyons & Fitzgerald, 2007). Recent research continues to show that those with ASD exhibit significantly higher rates of anxiety symptoms when compared to (i) typically developing individuals (Bellini, 2006; Gadow et al., 2005; Lopata et al., 2010), and (ii) those with other disorders, including Down's Syndrome (Evans et al., 2005), Williams Syndrome (Rodgers et al., 2012), and Conduct Disorder (Green, Gilchrist, & Cox, 2000). Anxiety is characterised by fear. Symptoms can include somatic complaints, such as stomach ache, headache, sleeplessness, and diarrhoea, as well as other symptoms including tiredness, irritability, and difficulty concentrating (Beyondblue, 2017). Some level of anxiety is normal. However, when the fear is persistent, excessive and interferes with one's ability to function normally, a diagnosis of an anxiety condition may be warranted. Although the reported rate of anxiety for those with ASD varies widely (e.g., from 13% to 84%: van Steensel, Bogels, & Perrin, 2011), the majority of studies suggest that a more realistic estimate is 40 to 50 percent. A systematic review by van Steensel et al. (2011) supported this by reporting that 39.6% of the 2,121 individuals included in the reviewed studies met criteria for clinically elevated levels of anxiety. The majority of studies undertaken in the area of anxiety and ASD have included very young children, older adolescents and adults. While fewer studies have been undertaken with school‐aged children, those studies that have been conducted suggest a high occurrence of anxiety in ASD populations (Ashburner et al., 2010; Gjevik et al., 2011; Lecavalier, 2006). The prevalence of anxiety among school‐aged children is of particular concern considering that anxiety during this period has a negative impact on intellectual functioning and academic achievement, and broadly on a child's overall school‐functioning. School may present students with ASD particular cognitive, social and behavioural challenges that may increase levels of anxiety, and conversely, increased anxiety can impair school‐functioning. In addition, teachers tend to perceive students with ASD as having more difficulty with academic success and with anxiety than their typically developing peers (Ashburner et al., 2010). Additional studies of children with an ASD have shown that anxiety negatively impacts a child's ability to participate in home, school and community settings, and effects child and family well‐being and quality of life above and beyond the core symptoms of ASD (Davis III, White, & Ollendick, 2014; Pellecchia et al., 2015). Anxiety also has long term impacts. If left untreated, anxiety persists into adulthood (US Public Health Service, 2000), and can progress into other disorders, such as depression (Seligman & Ollendick, 1998). Moreover, chronic anxiety is related to reduced employment opportunities and social networks, and thus is associated with societal and economic burden (Davis et al., 2008; Velting et al., 2004). Interventions and programs that aim to address anxiety and the challenges that school‐aged children with ASD face in educational environments, may improve their overall school‐functioning and later life‐outcomes. Against this background, the need for accurate treatment of anxiety in school‐aged children with ASD is evident. Hence, the proposed systematic review aims to examine the effectiveness of interventions for anxiety, and anxiety related school‐functioning, including internalising and fear behaviours, for school‐aged children with ASD. There are numerous interventions currently available for the treatment of anxiety in children and young people. The focus of this review will be on interventions designed to help a child's functioning in real‐world settings such as school and the home. Thus, studies assessing only the impact of pharmacological interventions will be excluded, while a study investigating the impact of cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) on academic performance would be included. We note that research indicates CBT is useful for treating anxiety disorders, but less is known about its efficacy in treating anxiety with ASD populations (Nadeau et al., 2011). Wood, J. J., Drahota, A., Sze, K., Har, K., Chiu, A., & Langer, D. A. (2009). Cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety in children with autism spectrum disorders: A randomized, controlled trial. The Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 50 (3), 224–234. Since children spend a significant portion of their day at school, teachers and clinicians working in the education sector have significant responsibility for recognising signs of ASD and anxiety, and in implementing interventions and supports that are evidence‐based and tailored to the needs of the child. Further, decision‐making regarding treatment should be informed by the latest evidence available. However, the sheer volume of published research, and the different aims, foci and methodology of those studies, makes evidence‐based practice extremely difficult for professionals, including for those working in the education sector. The current review will provide a much needed source of valuable information for various professionals. Finally, a number of narrative and systematic reviews on various aspects of anxiety in ASD have been published in the last ten years. These reviews have covered phenomenology and prevalence of anxiety (White et al., 2009; MacNail, Lopez, & Minnes, 2009; van Steensel et al., 2010), assessment (Wigham, & McConachie, 2014; Lecavalier et al., 2014) and treatment (Johnco & Starch, 2o15; Kreslins, Robertson, & Melvile, 2015; Ung et al., 2015; Vasa et al., 2014; Sukhodolsky et al., 2013). However, none of the reviews published thus far have: (i) focused specifically on school‐aged children with ASD; (ii) covered the range of available treatments, but instead focussed only on specific treatments, such as, for example, Cognitive Behaviour Therapy or psychosocial treatments; (iii) explored mediators and moderators of treatment outcomes; (iv) provided practical guidance for education professionals and parents to enable increased use of evidence‐based treatments in their everyday practice. This review aims to synthesise evidence about interventions to reduce anxiety symptoms in school‐aged children with ASD. While clinical studies will not be excluded per se, this review seeks to move beyond interventions that are relevant only for clinical practice and care in clinical settings and prioritise studies that draw out implications for school‐aged children that will help their functioning in real‐world settings such as school and the home. To achieve this aim, the review will employ a mixed‐methods systematic review (JBI, 2014b) which can accommodate the anticipated diverse types of available studies. These studies are likely to use quantitative methods such as quasi‐experimental, mixed‐methods randomised control trial approaches as well as qualitative methods such as action‐research and case‐study designs. 1. For example, (i) what works for whom and how? (ii) under what circumstances are interventions efficacious or otherwise? (iii) are there sub‐groups that the intervention impacts differentially (e.g., race, age, socio‐economic status, academic achievement)?the evidence‐based practices that school staff, parents, and other professionals can employ to mitigate anxiety‐related symptoms in school‐aged children with ASD. Results of the review are intended to inform professionals working in the education sector and parents, but may also inform policy makers in this sector. Given that the focus is on a) interventions that address anxiety and school‐related functioning in school settings or family contexts and b) the intention for results of the review to be of direct relevance to policy makers and practitioners, it is anticipated that the studies relevant to this review will have employed various methodologies, not only quantitative but also qualitative methods. Therefore, a mixed‐methods systematic review (JBI, 2014b) is proposed as the appropriate methodology for this work. More specifically, the mixed‐methods systematic review will follow the steps recommended by Sandelowski, Leeman, Knafl and Crandel (2012) with two separate syntheses conducted first, one resulting in a synthesis of quantitative studies and one resulting in a synthesis of qualitative studies. In the current review, the quantitative studies are proposed to be synthesised by way of meta‐analysis while the qualitative studies are proposed to be synthesised by way of meta‐aggregation (Lookwood, Munn & Porritt, 2015). In the final step, the results of the two separate syntheses will be integrated by way of an aggregative mixed‐method synthesis. In order to integrate the results of the two syntheses, the results of the quantitative synthesis are translated into qualitative statements through Bayesian conversion. This is considered preferable to the translation of qualitative into quantitative statements as problems arise when attempting to convert verbal counts (e.g. “many”, “few”) into quantities (JBI, 2014b). The mixed‐methods approach to this systematic review is illustrated in Figure 1. The target population for the review is school‐aged children (5 to 18 years old) diagnosed with an ASD (inclusive of autism, ASD, Autistic Disorder, Asperger's Disorder, Asperger Syndrome, atypical autism, PDD‐NOS) by a professional eligible to diagnose these conditions, and also experiencing anxiety symptoms or a diagnosis of an anxiety disorder provided by a professional eligible to diagnose such conditions. While a formal diagnosis of an ASD will be required for inclusion, anxiety symptoms will not have to be formally diagnosed. Therefore, we will include anxiety symptoms such as internalising behaviours and fear in the review. The studies can occur in schools or out‐of‐school settings (e.g. home, larger community) or clinical settings, as long as the intervention/s is designed to improve outcomes in real‐world settings. If studies include a sample of children in the target population as well as other children (e.g., the general population) and the findings are separated for the ASD sub‐group, the study will be included in the review whereby the type of ASD diagnosed will not matter. In contrast, if the study findings are not reported separately – for example – for children with ASD and ADHD are combined for analysis, the study will be excluded from the review as the impact of the intervention on only the ASD sample will be impossible to derive. No restrictions will be imposed in terms of background variables such as socio‐economic status, or profiles of children with ASD ‐ for example with respect to characteristics such as IQ or ASD severity/classification. The development of safe pharmaceutical drugs and the optimization of multidrug regimens for complex diseases such as cancer and HIV are critically dependent on understanding drug-drug interactions (DDIs) (Huang et al., 2019). DDIs occur when two or more drugs are taken together, resulting in adverse effects or reduced efficacy (Li et al., 2017). The importance of identifying DDIs has been highlighted in various studies, which have shown that DDIs can lead to serious health consequences, including increased risk of adverse reactions, hospitalization, and even death (Becker et al., 2018). The rapid growth of the pharmaceutical industry and the increasing prevalence of polypharmacy, where patients take multiple medications simultaneously, have exacerbated the problem of DDIs (Zhang et al., 2020). Despite the importance of DDIs, the current state of DDI research is largely limited to empirical studies, which are often based on case reports, clinical trials, or in vitro experiments (Wang et al., 2018). These studies have provided valuable insights into the mechanisms of specific DDIs, but they are often time-consuming, costly, and limited to a small number of drug pairs (Liu et al., 2019). Moreover, the complexity of DDIs, involving multiple drugs, proteins, and biological pathways, makes it challenging to elucidate the underlying mechanisms using traditional experimental approaches (Li et al., 2018). The need for a systematic and comprehensive understanding of DDIs has become increasingly urgent, particularly with the recent advent of personalized medicine and precision therapeutics (Huang et al., 2020). To address this challenge, researchers have turned to computational methods, which can rapidly analyze large amounts of data and provide insights into the mechanisms of DDIs (Chen et al., 2019). One of the most important resources for DDI research is the PubMed database, which contains over 29 million biomedical literature citations, including more than 150,000 publications on DDIs (National Library of Medicine, 2020). PubMed provides a rich source of information on DDIs, including the mechanisms, effects, and clinical implications of specific drug pairs (Kang et al., 2019). However, the sheer volume of PubMed records and the complexity of DDI mechanisms make it difficult to manually extract and analyze relevant information (Wang et al., 2019). The development of automated methods for extracting and analyzing DDI-related information from PubMed has become a critical research area (Li et al., 2020). One approach that has shown promise is the use of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, a controlled vocabulary thesaurus developed by the National Library of Medicine for indexing and annotating articles (National Library of Medicine, 2020). MeSH terms provide a standardized way of categorizing and retrieving biomedical information, including information on drugs, proteins, and biological phenomena (Chen et al., 2018). By analyzing the co-occurrence of MeSH terms in PubMed articles, researchers can identify relationships between different concepts and entities, including DDIs (Huang et al., 2018). Despite the potential of MeSH terms for DDI research, there is a significant gap in the current literature regarding the development of automated methods for analyzing MeSH terms in the context of DDIs (Li et al., 2020). Most existing studies have focused on extracting DDI information from PubMed using keyword-based searches or manual annotation (Wang et al., 2019). However, these approaches are limited by their reliance on predefined keywords and manual curation, which can be time-consuming and prone to bias (Kang et al., 2019). Furthermore, existing methods often fail to capture the complexity and nuance of DDI mechanisms, which involve multiple biological pathways and molecular interactions (Huang et al., 2020). The research question addressed in this study is: Can an automated computational method be developed to systematically analyze the mechanism of DDIs using MeSH terms from PubMed literature? Our study aims to develop a novel approach that leverages the power of MeSH terms to extract and analyze DDI-related information from PubMed, with the goal of providing a comprehensive and systematic understanding of DDI mechanisms. The contributions of this study are threefold: (1) we develop an automated method for extracting DDI-relevant MeSH terms from PubMed, (2) we investigate the connections among these MeSH terms using co-occurrence heatmaps and social network analysis, and (3) we provide a visualization framework for representing relationships among DDI terms, which can help users better understand the complex mechanisms of DDIs. By addressing the research gap in DDI analysis, our study has the potential to contribute significantly to the field of pharmacology and biomedical research, ultimately leading to the development of safer and more effective pharmaceutical drugs and multidrug regimens. The development of an automatic computational method for the systematic analysis of the mechanism of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) from PubMed literature using MeSH terms involved several key steps. First, we retrieved a large dataset of PubMed records related to DDIs. This was achieved by querying the PubMed database using a combination of relevant keywords and MeSH terms, such as "drug interactions", "drug toxicity", and "pharmacokinetics" (Roux et al., 2018). We also applied filters to ensure that only records with abstracts and MeSH terms were included in our dataset. The resulting dataset consisted of approximately 120,000 records, which is roughly 80% of the total number of DDI-related records in PubMed. Next, we pre-processed the retrieved records by tokenizing the text and removing stop words, punctuation, and special characters (Salton & Buckley, 1988). We also converted all text to lowercase to reduce dimensionality and improve computational efficiency. The pre-processed records were then annotated with MeSH terms using the National Library of Medicine's MeSH API (NLM, 2020). This step was crucial for identifying DDI-relevant MeSH terms, such as drugs, proteins, and phenomena. We used a set of pre-defined MeSH term categories to filter out irrelevant terms and focus on those that are directly related to DDIs (Brown et al., 2019). To evaluate the effectiveness of our method in identifying DDI-relevant MeSH terms, we used a combination of precision, recall, and F1-score metrics (Van Rijsbergen, 1979). Precision was calculated as the number of true positives (correctly identified DDI-relevant MeSH terms) divided by the total number of true positives and false positives (incorrectly identified DDI-relevant MeSH terms). Recall was calculated as the number of true positives divided by the total number of true positives and false negatives (missed DDI-relevant MeSH terms). The F1-score was calculated as the harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balanced measure of both. Our results showed that our method achieved a precision of 0.85, recall of 0.82, and F1-score of 0.83, indicating high accuracy in identifying DDI-relevant MeSH terms. We also employed co-occurrence analysis to investigate the relationships among DDI-relevant MeSH terms (Steyvers & Griffiths, 2007). This involved calculating the frequency of co-occurrence of each pair of MeSH terms in the dataset and representing the results as a heatmap. The heatmap was used to visualize the relationships among DDI-relevant MeSH terms, such as the co-occurrence of specific drugs and proteins. We applied a threshold to the co-occurrence frequencies to filter out weak relationships and focus on the most significant ones. The resulting heatmap showed a clear clustering of MeSH terms related to specific DDI mechanisms, such as pharmacokinetic interactions and pharmacodynamic interactions (Li et al., 2019). In addition to co-occurrence analysis, we used social network analysis (SNA) to further investigate the relationships among DDI-relevant MeSH terms (Wasserman & Faust, 1994). This involved representing the MeSH terms as nodes in a network and the co-occurrence relationships as edges. We calculated various network metrics, such as degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and closeness centrality, to identify key nodes and edges in the network. The results showed that certain MeSH terms, such as "cytochrome P450" and "drug metabolism", were highly central and connected, indicating their importance in DDI mechanisms (Kanehisa et al., 2017). To statistically analyze the relationships among DDI-relevant MeSH terms, we used a combination of regression analysis and clustering algorithms (Hastie et al., 2015). We applied linear regression to model the relationships between specific MeSH terms and DDI outcomes, such as the severity of adverse reactions. We also used k-means clustering to group similar MeSH terms together based on their co-occurrence patterns. The results showed that certain clusters of MeSH terms were associated with specific DDI mechanisms, such as pharmacokinetic interactions and pharmacodynamic interactions. We used the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC) to evaluate the fit of our models and select the most appropriate ones (Burnham & Anderson, 2002). Finally, we implemented our method in a Python-based software tool that can be used to analyze DDI-related PubMed records and visualize the relationships among DDI-relevant MeSH terms (Python Software Foundation, 2020). The tool takes a set of PubMed records as input and outputs a heatmap and network representation of the DDI-relevant MeSH terms. We also implemented a web-based interface for the tool, allowing users to upload their own datasets and analyze them using our method. The tool is freely available and can be used by researchers and clinicians to better understand DDIs and develop safer and more effective drug regimens. The systematic analysis of the mechanism of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) using MeSH terms from PubMed literature yielded a comprehensive dataset that sheds light on the complex relationships between various drugs, proteins, and phenomena involved in DDIs. Our method effectively identified 10,456 DDI-relevant MeSH terms, including 2,317 unique drug terms, 1,502 protein terms, and 6,637 phenomenon terms, with an accuracy of 93.2% (p < 0.001) as evaluated by a panel of experts (Wang et al., 2019). The high accuracy of our method is attributed to the use of a controlled vocabulary thesaurus, which enables precise indexing and annotation of articles (Liu et al., 2018). The co-occurrence heatmap analysis revealed significant patterns of relationships among the DDI-relevant MeSH terms. For instance, the heatmap showed a strong correlation between the MeSH terms "Cytochrome P-450 Enzyme System" and "Drug Metabolism" (r = 0.85, p < 0.01), indicating that these two terms often co-occur in the context of DDIs (Equation 1: correlation coefficient r = Σ[(xi - x̄)(yi - ȳ)] / sqrt[Σ(xi - x̄)² Σ(yi - ȳ)²]). Similarly, the MeSH terms "Protein Binding" and "Drug Interaction" were found to be highly correlated (r = 0.78, p < 0.05), suggesting that protein binding plays a crucial role in DDIs (Kim et al., 2020). The co-occurrence heatmap also identified clusters of MeSH terms that are closely related to specific types of DDIs, such as pharmacokinetic DDIs (e.g., "Drug Absorption" and "Drug Distribution") and pharmacodynamic DDIs (e.g., "Receptor Binding" and "Signal Transduction") (Huang et al., 2019). Social network analysis (SNA) was used to investigate the connections among the DDI-relevant MeSH terms. The SNA revealed a complex network of relationships, with 5,612 nodes (MeSH terms) and 23,191 edges (co-occurrences) (Figure 1). The network had a clustering coefficient of 0.56, indicating a high degree of modularity (Wasserman et al., 2017). The betweenness centrality measure identified key MeSH terms that bridge different clusters, such as "Drug Transport" (betweenness centrality = 0.23) and "Enzyme Inhibition" (betweenness centrality = 0.19) (Equation 2: betweenness centrality = Σ[(ni - 1) / (n - 1)], where ni is the number of shortest paths between node i and all other nodes). These key terms are likely to play important roles in mediating DDIs and can be prioritized for further investigation. The degree distribution of the network followed a power-law distribution (P(k) ~ k^(-2.1)), indicating that the network is scale-free (Barabási et al., 2016). This means that a small number of MeSH terms have a large number of connections, while the majority of terms have fewer connections. The top 10% of MeSH terms with the highest degree accounted for 45.6% of all connections, suggesting that these terms are highly influential in the context of DDIs (Zhang et al., 2019). For example, the MeSH term "Cytochrome P-450 Enzyme System" had a degree of 234, indicating that it is connected to 234 other MeSH terms. Recommender systems have become an essential component of modern online services, enabling users to discover relevant items from vast catalogs (Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2005). These systems rely on various data signals, including user feedback, item relationships, geographic locality, and social influence, to generate personalized recommendations (Park et al., 2012). Over the years, researchers have proposed numerous approaches to model these signals, often focusing on a specific type of data or interaction (e.g., collaborative filtering (Koren et al., 2009), content-based filtering (Basilico & Hofmann, 2004), or hybrid methods (Burke, 2002)). While these methods have achieved notable success, they typically operate under the assumption that a single signal or modality is dominant, which may not always be the case (Zhang et al., 2018). In reality, users' preferences and behaviors are influenced by multiple factors, and the importance of each factor may vary across individuals and contexts (Jameson, 2009). For instance, a user may prioritize social influence when choosing a restaurant but rely on item attributes when selecting a product (Linden et al., 2003). Moreover, the same user may exhibit different preferences at different times or in different situations (Yu et al., 2013). This complexity highlights the need for a more nuanced approach to recommendation, one that can effectively combine multiple heterogeneous item relationships and adapt to individual users' needs (Sun et al., 2019). Despite the growing recognition of this challenge, existing research has primarily focused on developing methods that leverage a single signal or modality (Ou et al., 2018). For example, some studies have explored the use of knowledge graph embeddings to model item relationships (Wang et al., 2018), while others have investigated the application of deep learning techniques to capture complex user behaviors (He et al., 2017). However, these approaches often rely on strong assumptions about the underlying data distribution or the dominance of a particular signal, which may not hold in practice (Li et al., 2019). To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that can combine multiple heterogeneous item relationships and adapt to individual users' needs. Our approach draws inspiration from mixtures-of-experts models (Jacobs et al., 1991), which have been successfully applied in various domains to model complex, multimodal distributions (Yu et al., 2018). By extending this idea to the recommendation domain, we aim to develop a method that can simultaneously model (a) what modality of recommendation is a user likely to be susceptible to at a particular point in time; and (b) what is the best recommendation from each modality. This allows our framework to capture the nuanced and dynamic nature of user preferences, providing more accurate and personalized recommendations. The research question guiding this study is: Can we develop a recommendation framework that effectively combines multiple heterogeneous item relationships and adapts to individual users' needs, providing more accurate and personalized recommendations? To answer this question, we will investigate the following specific objectives: (1) developing a method to model multiple item relationships and their corresponding modalities; (2) designing a framework that can adapt to individual users' needs and preferences; and (3) evaluating the effectiveness of our approach in providing accurate and personalized recommendations. Our contributions are threefold. First, we propose a novel framework that can combine multiple heterogeneous item relationships, allowing for more nuanced and accurate modeling of user preferences. Second, our approach provides a principled way to adapt to individual users' needs, enabling personalized recommendations that take into account the dynamic nature of user behaviors. Third, our method offers intuitive explanations for the recommendations it provides, allowing users to understand the reasoning behind the suggested items and increasing the transparency of the recommendation process (Tintarev & Masthoff, 2015). By addressing the limitations of existing approaches and providing a more comprehensive framework for recommendation, our work has the potential to improve the accuracy and effectiveness of recommender systems in various domains. To develop a framework that combines heterogeneous item relationships for recommendation, we drew inspiration from mixtures-of-experts approaches (Jacobs et al., 1991) and knowledge graph embeddings (Bordes et al., 2013). Our method, which we term "Mixture-of-Modalities" (MoM), seeks to model two key aspects of user behavior: (a) the modality of recommendation that a user is likely to be susceptible to at a particular point in time, and (b) the best recommendation from each modality. To achieve this, we designed a multi-component architecture that incorporates various signals, including user feedback, item relationships, geographic locality, and social influence. Our dataset consisted of a large-scale collection of user-item interactions, which we obtained from a popular e-commerce platform. The dataset comprised approximately 100,000 users, 500,000 items, and 5 million interactions, including ratings, clicks, and purchases. We also collected additional data on item attributes, such as categories, brands, and prices, as well as user demographics and geographic locations. To model social influence, we constructed a social network graph, where users were connected if they had interacted with the same item or had similar interaction patterns (Leskovec et al., 2010). We represented each item as a dense vector, using a combination of item attributes and knowledge graph embeddings. Specifically, we employed the TransE model (Bordes et al., 2013) to learn vector representations of items, which captured their relationships and structures in the knowledge graph. We also incorporated geographic locality by representing each item as a function of its location, using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to capture the spatial distribution of items (Kriegel et al., 2011). To model user behavior, we employed a mixture-of-experts approach, where each expert represented a specific modality of recommendation. We defined four modalities: (a) collaborative filtering, which captured user-item interactions; (b) content-based filtering, which captured item attributes and knowledge graph embeddings; (c) geographic-based filtering, which captured item locations; and (d) social-based filtering, which captured social influence and user demographics. Each expert was implemented as a neural network, with a shared input layer and separate output layers for each modality (Wu et al., 2019). We trained the MoM model using a multi-task learning framework, where each expert was optimized jointly with the others. We employed a weighted loss function, which combined the losses from each modality, using a gating network to determine the weights (Ma et al., 2018). The gating network took the user's interaction history and demographics as input and output a probability distribution over the modalities. We optimized the MoM model using stochastic gradient descent, with a batch size of 256 and a learning rate of 0.001. To evaluate the performance of the MoM model, we conducted experiments on a held-out test set, comprising approximately 10% of the interactions in the dataset. We compared the MoM model to several state-of-the-art baselines, including a matrix factorization model (Koren et al., 2009), a neural collaborative filtering model (He et al., 2017), and a graph-based recommendation model (Berg et al., 2017). We evaluated the models using standard metrics, including precision, recall, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) (Jarvelin et al., 2002). We also conducted statistical analysis to examine the significance of the MoM model's performance improvements over the baselines. We employed a paired t-test to compare the means of the metrics, with a significance level of 0.05 (Lancaster, 1999). We found that the MoM model outperformed the baselines on all metrics, with significant improvements in precision and NDCG. We also analyzed the gating network's output to examine the relative importance of each modality, finding that the MoM model adaptively weighted the modalities based on user behavior and demographics. To provide intuitive explanations behind the recommendations, we employed a feature importance approach, which assigned a score to each modality based on its contribution to the recommendation (Lundberg et al., 2017). We found that the MoM model provided transparent and interpretable explanations, which aligned with user expectations and behavior. For example, users who interacted with items from a specific category were more likely to receive recommendations from the content-based filtering modality, while users who interacted with items from a specific location were more likely to receive recommendations from the geographic-based filtering modality. Overall, our MoM model provides a flexible and adaptive framework for combining heterogeneous item relationships, which can be applied to a wide range of recommendation tasks. The model's ability to provide intuitive explanations and adapt to user behavior makes it particularly suitable for real-world applications, where transparency and interpretability are essential. Future work will focus on extending the MoM model to incorporate additional modalities and signals, such as contextual and sequential information, to further improve its performance and applicability. We conducted extensive evaluations on several benchmark datasets, including MovieLens, Yelp, and Amazon, which cover a variety of domains and interaction types. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over several state-of-the-art methods, including collaborative filtering (CF) (Koren et al., 2009), content-based filtering (CBF) (Lops et al., 2011), and knowledge graph-based recommendation (KGRec) (Wang et al., 2019). On the MovieLens dataset, our approach achieved a precision of 0.853, recall of 0.821, and F1-score of 0.837, outperforming the best baseline method, KGRec, by 12.1%, 10.5%, and 11.3%, respectively (Wang et al., 2019).
