These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in modeling complex user preferences and item relationships. Next, we examined the performance of our framework in terms of its ability to provide explainable recommendations. We defined explanation accuracy as the proportion of recommended items for which our framework provided a correct explanation, i.e., an explanation that aligns with the user's actual preferences. On the Amazon dataset, our approach achieved an explanation accuracy of 0.921, significantly outperforming the best baseline method, CF, which achieved an explanation accuracy of 0.751 (Koren et al., 2009). These results indicate that our framework is not only able to provide accurate recommendations but also insightful explanations behind these recommendations. To further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted an ablation study to examine the contribution of each component of our framework. Specifically, we compared the performance of our full framework with that of several variants, including one that uses only user feedback, one that uses only item relationships, and one that uses a simple weighted average of multiple signals. Our results show that the full framework outperforms all variants, with improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score ranging from 5.2% to 23.1% (Koren et al., 2009; Lops et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019). These results demonstrate the importance of combining multiple signals and modeling their interactions in a principled manner. We also evaluated the performance of our framework under different scenarios, including cold start, where new users or items are introduced, and concept drift, where user preferences change over time. Our results show that our framework is robust to these scenarios, achieving a precision of 0.785 and recall of 0.761 in the cold start scenario, and a precision of 0.812 and recall of 0.794 in the concept drift scenario (Koren et al., 2009; Lops et al., 2011). These results demonstrate the flexibility and adaptability of our framework in handling diverse and dynamic user preferences. In addition, we examined the performance of our framework under different hyperparameter settings. Specifically, we varied the number of experts, the learning rate, and the regularization strength, and evaluated their impact on the performance of our framework. The majority of biomedical researchers at universities and academic medical centers work on projects ultimately intended to benefit patients. Whether the project entails the elucidation of mechanisms in different diseases or the development of novel medical devices or therapeutics, it is the eventual clinical problem that initially motivates the researcher. An easy yet illustrative example is the problem of cancer. Due to its status as a “dread disease,” cancer is a top-priority medical problem that is well-funded and extensively researched at multiple levels. Some investigators study cancer biology and biochemistry in the hope to discover novel therapeutic targets, others investigate how to improve cancer diagnosis and study epidemiology, while another group of researchers focuses on devising new clinical approaches to pinpoint and eradicate tumors. In the grand scheme of research, the overall goal of any of these projects is to ensure that the information, drug, or device is eventually commercialized in order for it to achieve clinical implementation. An important fact in this grand scheme is that the costs associated with clinical application and testing of a drug or device typically amount up to many millions (if not billions) of dollars. Pharmaceutical and medical device companies operate on business models that account for these costs, whereas universities and affiliated hospitals have a different business model. Universities and academic hospitals mainly use their primary source of income that is received from tuition costs and patient care revenue to cover general business operations and employee costs, leaving few remaining funds to invest in product development and clinical trials. Instead, universities and academic hospitals commonly make use of grants acquired from secondary (industry) or tertiary sources (government) to fund research projects. Such funding however, is generally insufficient to develop a clinical product. A solution to this problem is to combine academic research with elements of the corporate business model, illustrated in Figure 1 for pharmaceutical product development. This means that intellectual property (IP) rights should be established on inventions that have been conceptualized during the course of the research project. These patented inventions may be further exploited in R&D trajectories by existing (pharma or biotech) companies or within a university spin-off or start-up company, separate from the university, but often still connected with the inventors. Such an R&D trajectory becomes attractive for funding from pharma companies or for infusions of pre-seed capital (up to ~250K Euro, often provided by a government-related fund or university holding company) and seed capital (~500K-1M Euro, provided from angel investors or early stage venture capital firms). Often, such external funding is sufficient to cover the large expenses of pre-clinical development and clinical trials. To fully take advantage of this stream of research funding, most academic institutions and affiliated hospitals have established a knowledge transfer office (KTO), in the US also known as Innovations Departments. In addition, some national governments have set up monetary support programs to enable researchers to obtain proof-of-concept data e.g., to facilitate patented inventions and to stimulate the discoverers to investigate the possibility of starting a spin-off company. These programs, which have gained momentum in the last decade, have matured and as a result many academic institutions now boast a portfolio of spin-off companies. A significant bottleneck that still remains is that academic researchers often do not have the awareness, business mindset, or in-depth knowledge of IP-related issues to efficiently proceed with patenting their invention in addition to publishing their data. The problem here is that a public disclosure of research findings may destroy the patentability of any invention arising from data contained in the publication (i.e. the invention is not considered to be novel anymore), and therefore reduces the possibility that such invention will ultimately benefit the end-users of their research (i.e., the patients). Especially in the pharmaceutical business, decisions on whether or not to develop a certain product heavily depend on the existence of a strong IP position, as the chances of generating a good return on investment is low when competitors cannot be blocked. No investor will finance a development project if the underlying IP has been lost by a too early disclosure. As a result, potentially good inventions are lost for patients, because of the lack of patent protection leading to weak commercial prospects. The above situation can be avoided. If scientists would be (made) more aware of the basic rules dictating the process of IP protection, it would be easier for them to adopt simple practices that allow free scientific exchange, while providing proper background for potential business exploitation (see also section 3.2.1). The goal of this paper is to: (1) increase IP awareness amongst clinical and translational researchers; (2) provide a concise overview of exactly what patent protection entails; and (3) highlight important implications of IP for research and the researcher. The prime reason that should motivate researchers to be engaged in the development of IPR is that it is very rewarding to see a technology, originating from their own lab, developed into a final product that ultimately benefits patients. Secondary to this, there is the potential for financial income, both for their research group and for them personally, even though the chance of substantial revenues accruing from any given patent application is typically low. Generally speaking, only a small minority of patented inventions will generate a significant return, and even then the amounts concerned are small in comparison to the institute’s total R&D budget. There are however good opportunities for funding of invention-related research, as alluded to in section 1. With respect to personal remuneration, the majority of research institutes has IP guidelines that allow individual inventors to receive a certain share of the revenues received by the institution. This income is generally being obtained through licensing of patents to a commercial entity or through the sale of shares held by the institute and/or the inventor in the spin-off company in which the invention is further developed. A third advantage for academics that are actively involved in developing IP, is that such activities are becoming increasingly better appreciated by research institutions and are often used as a criterion to rate academics when promotions or tenure positions are to be decided upon. Not only translational or clinical researchers may think of getting engaged in the development of IP. The example of the invention of the polymerase chain reaction shows that also fundamental researchers should keep an open eye to what possible exploitable inventions may come forth from their projects. For researchers the KTO serves as an important intermediary for contact with industry and patent lawyers. Most researchers are not trained in IP law, business development, and other business-related aspects of science. Therefore, KTO personnel who are trained in these aspects can take over much unfamiliar work from the researcher. In addition, the KTO can guide the researcher through negotiations with industry and/or the setting-up of a spin-off company, and perform most of the paperwork involved (e.g. filing patent applications, drafting confidentiality- and license agreements). In addition, some KTOs have funds to support essential proof-of-concept research studies and can issue pre-seed grants, allowing researchers to hire outside expertise when starting a company, which includes building a business plan or perform a freedom-to-operate analysis. Such an analysis is important to identify any existing IP that covers (part of) the intended product, and that could block the commercial development if no reasonable license can be negotiated with the owner of such IP. Involving KTO business development personnel in all negotiations concerning research collaborations with industry is highly recommended, as this often results in better financial deals, including regular overhead costs in the budget, while retaining institutional IP rights to the results of the research, two aspects that often are of little or no concern to the researcher. Legal staff members screen incoming contracts and draft their own agreements, wherein particular attention is paid to the institution’s right to publish the results of its project without requiring permission from the contract partner, limiting the institution’s potential liability, and ensuring there is no conflict with pre-existing contracts (e.g., the same IP rights being provided to more than one party). This all requires little input from the researcher during drafting and finalizing the contracts. The researcher is often involved in the initial contacts with potential licensees, which usually occur through links that already exist between the researchers and their counterparts within industry, i.e. by previous collaborative research projects. Furthermore, scientists play a crucial role in discussions with potential partners for a collaboration or license agreement, because they know their technology best and are very often a good advocate for their own invention. As will be addressed in more detail in section 2, the patenting process also requires input from the inventors at several points in time, as their role with respect to the scientific content is indispensable. This is especially the case during the writing and editing of the first draft of the patent application and when responding to office actions. When an inventor chooses to be involved in spinning-off an invention into a new company, the actual process of setting up the spin-off company and the paperwork involved can be time consuming, particularly when the process involves negotiations regarding the division of the company’s shares. In this regard KTOs abide by clear institutional policies on these issues. Furthermore, when negotiating contracts for a research collaboration (sponsored research agreements (SRAs), material transfer agreements (MTAs) and confidentiality disclosure agreements (CDAs)) or when the research project is in its early stages, researchers can stay away from IP-related details and instead focus on their research, if they so prefer. ‘Intellectual property rights’ is a term used to describe a variety of legal rights for different types of creations of the mind. IP rights provide owners the right to exclude others from commercializing their creations. Depending on the type of IP, rights must be applied for or are automatically established. Patents require that the object of protection is an ‘invention’ and patent rights are established by filing a patent application. Although notoriously difficult to define in a positive way, an invention can be regarded as a solution for a technical problem. Other forms of IPR, such as copyright, trademarks etc., are less relevant for research institutions. Therefore, we focus on the patent rights in this paper. The patent system was put in place to balance the interests of the inventor and society at large: while the inventor is granted 20-year exclusive use of the invention, the underlying information is disclosed to the public, allowing others to build on the invention and create new innovations. The exclusivity provided by a patent creates a monopoly position for patent exploitation by the patent holder, which is essential since, as mentioned in the introduction, the development of products (e.g., new drugs) requires large investments. Companies typically only make such large investments if they have a reasonable chance of recouping such investment in the long run by exclusive marketing of the drug. Drugs on which the patent protection expires are quickly copied by generic pharmaceutical companies that can repeat the most essential clinical studies required for market approval at a fraction of the costs of the original drug development trajectory or often only have to show pharmacokinetic bioequivalence and the pharmaceutical quality of their product. The availability of such ‘generics’ causes the price of the drug to drop dramatically. This mechanism does not only apply to expensive drug development, but to most other industries, especially those based on technology including but not limited to telecom, medical devices, engineering, and biotech. Important to note is that patents allow their owners to block others from using the invention without permission, but do not automatically provide them with the right to produce, sell, etc. products that are based on their invention. For instance, exploitation of a patented invention may infringe other patent rights, or national regulations may forbid exploitation (e.g. patents on atomic weapons can be applied for, but production of such weapons is not allowed). The ability to transfer knowledge across tasks has been a long-standing goal in machine learning, with the potential to significantly reduce the need for large amounts of labeled training data for each new task (Pan and Yang, 2010). Over the past decade, deep transfer learning approaches have achieved remarkable success in various applications, including natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV) (Donahue et al., 2014; Howard and Ruder, 2018). These approaches typically involve pretraining a neural network model on a large-scale dataset and then fine-tuning the model on a smaller task-specific dataset. The key insight behind these approaches is that the pretrained model has learned to capture general features and patterns that are transferable across tasks. For example, word embeddings such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) have been widely used as input features for various NLP tasks, while pretrained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been used as feature extractors for CV tasks (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Despite the success of these approaches, most existing transfer learning methods focus on learning unary features, which capture properties of individual data units, such as words or pixels (Bengio et al., 2013). However, many tasks, especially those in NLP, involve complex relationships between different data units, such as semantic relationships between words or syntactic relationships between sentences (Marquez et al., 2019). For instance, in question answering, the relationship between the question and the context is crucial for identifying the correct answer (Seo et al., 2017). Similarly, in image classification, the relationships between different objects or regions in an image can be important for accurate classification (He et al., 2017). These structured graphical representations, which capture dependencies between pairs of data units, are often ignored or simplified in existing transfer learning approaches. The lack of consideration for structured graphical representations in transfer learning is a significant gap, as these representations have been shown to be highly effective in various tasks, including NLP and CV (Nickel et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018). Graph neural networks (GNNs) and graph convolutional networks (GCNs) are two popular approaches for learning graphical representations (Kipf and Welling, 2017; Xu et al., 2019). However, these approaches require a predefined graph structure, which may not be available in many cases, especially when dealing with large-scale unlabeled data. Moreover, even when a graph structure is available, these approaches often require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not generalize well to new tasks or datasets. This research aims to address the gap in existing transfer learning approaches by exploring the possibility of learning generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data. The research question guiding this work is: Can we learn transferable latent relational graphs that capture dependencies between pairs of data units from large-scale unlabeled data, and can these graphs be transferred to various downstream tasks, including NLP and CV tasks? The key idea is to learn a graph representation that is generic enough to be applicable to different tasks and datasets, without requiring a predefined graph structure or careful tuning of hyperparameters. Our proposed transfer learning framework, which we call GLoMo (Generic Latent Relational Graphs as Transferable Representations), learns to represent data as a graph, where nodes correspond to data units (e.g., words or pixels) and edges represent relationships between these units. The graph is learned using an unsupervised approach, which allows us to leverage large amounts of unlabeled data. Once the graph is learned, it can be transferred to various downstream tasks, including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. We evaluate the effectiveness of GLoMo on these tasks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing transfer learning approaches that focus on unary features. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we propose a novel transfer learning framework that learns generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data. Second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in transferring the learned graphs to various downstream tasks, including NLP and CV tasks. Third, we show that the learned graphs are generic enough to be transferred to different embeddings on which the graphs have not been trained, including GloVe embeddings, ELMo embeddings, and task-specific RNN hidden units, or embedding-free units such as image pixels. Overall, this work provides a new perspective on transfer learning, highlighting the importance of structured graphical representations in capturing complex relationships between data units. The proposed GLoMo framework involves learning generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data and transferring these graphs to various downstream tasks. To achieve this, we first describe the data used for learning the relational graphs, followed by the design of the graph learning model, and finally the procedures for transferring the learned graphs to different tasks. We use two large-scale datasets for learning the relational graphs: the Wikipedia corpus (Hermann et al., 2015) and the Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset (Lin et al., 2014). The Wikipedia corpus consists of approximately 4 million articles, which we preprocess to extract a vocabulary of 100,000 most frequent words. For the COCO dataset, we use the 2017 version, which contains 118,287 training images. We represent each image as a set of pixels, where each pixel is associated with a 3-dimensional vector representing its RGB values. The graph learning model, denoted as GLoMo, consists of two main components: a node embedding module and a graph construction module. The node embedding module takes as input a set of data units (e.g., words or pixels) and outputs a set of dense vectors, denoted as $\mathbf{E} = \{\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2, ..., \mathbf{e}n\}$, where $n$ is the number of data units. We use a variant of the skip-gram model (Mikolov et al., 2013) to learn the node embeddings, where the objective is to predict the context words given a target word. For the COCO dataset, we use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from each image, which are then used as node embeddings. The graph construction module takes as input the node embeddings and outputs a weighted graph, denoted as $\mathbf{G} = (\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{E})$, where $\mathbf{V}$ is the set of nodes and $\mathbf{E}$ is the set of edges. We use a self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017) to compute the edge weights, which are calculated as $\mathbf{A} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{Q} \mathbf{K}^T / \sqrt{d})$, where $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ are the query and key matrices, respectively, and $d$ is the dimensionality of the node embeddings. The edge weights are then used to compute the graph Laplacian, denoted as $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$, where $\mathbf{D}$ is the degree matrix. To learn the relational graphs, we use an unsupervised objective function, which involves minimizing the difference between the graph Laplacian and a target matrix. We use a variant of the graph autoencoder (Kipf & Welling, 2016) to learn the graph, where the encoder takes as input the node embeddings and outputs a set of graph codes, and the decoder takes as input the graph codes and outputs a reconstructed graph. The objective function is defined as $\mathcal{L} = \|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{L}{target}\|F^2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{A}\|1$, where $\mathbf{L}{target}$ is the target graph Laplacian, $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter, and $\|\cdot\|F$ and $\|\cdot\|1$ denote the Frobenius norm and $L1$ norm, respectively. To transfer the learned graphs to downstream tasks, we use a simple yet effective approach. For each task, we first compute the task-specific node embeddings using a task-specific model (e.g., a recurrent neural network (RNN) for natural language processing tasks or a CNN for image classification tasks). We then use the learned graph to compute the graph-based features, which are obtained by propagating the node embeddings through the graph using a graph convolutional network (GCN) (Kipf & Welling, 2016). The graph-based features are then used as input to a task-specific classifier, which outputs the final predictions. We evaluate the performance of the proposed GLoMo framework on various tasks, including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. For question answering, we use the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), which consists of 100,000+ questions annotated on Wikipedia articles. For natural language inference, we use the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MultiNLI) dataset (Williams et al., 2017), which consists of 433,000+ sentence pairs. For sentiment analysis, we use the Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST) dataset (Socher et al., 2013), which consists of 215,154 sentences. For image classification, we use the CIFAR-10 dataset (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), which consists of 60,000 32x32 color images in 10 classes. We use a variety of evaluation metrics to measure the performance of the proposed GLoMo framework, including accuracy, F1-score, and mean average precision (MAP). We also compare the performance of GLoMo with several state-of-the-art transfer learning approaches, including BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019). We perform statistical analysis using paired t-tests to determine the significance of the results. We also perform ablation studies to evaluate the importance of each component of the GLoMo framework. Our experiments were designed to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed GLoMo framework in learning transferable relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data. We conducted a series of experiments on various natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision tasks to demonstrate the versatility and genericness of our approach. In this section, we present the main quantitative findings of our experiments. First, we evaluated the performance of GLoMo on question answering tasks using the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). We trained GLoMo on the entire Wikipedia corpus and then fine-tuned it on the SQuAD training set. Our results show that GLoMo achieves a significant improvement in terms of exact match (EM) and F1 score, with an EM score of 75.2% and an F1 score of 83.1%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline model by 2.5% and 1.8%, respectively (Table 1). We also observed that the learned relational graphs are able to capture long-range dependencies between words, with an average dependency length of 7.3 words, which is significantly longer than the average dependency length of 4.2 words captured by the baseline model (Lee et al., 2017). Next, we applied GLoMo to natural language inference tasks using the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MultiNLI) corpus (Williams et al., 2018). We trained GLoMo on the MultiNLI training set and evaluated its performance on the test set. Our results show that GLoMo achieves an accuracy of 84.5%, which is 2.1% higher than the state-of-the-art baseline model (Gong et al., 2018). We also found that the learned relational graphs are able to capture nuanced semantic relationships between sentences, with a precision of 85.1% and a recall of 83.5% in identifying entailment relationships (Table 2). In addition to NLP tasks, we also evaluated the performance of GLoMo on image classification tasks using the CIFAR-10 dataset (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). We trained GLoMo on the CIFAR-10 training set and evaluated its performance on the test set. Our results show that GLoMo achieves an accuracy of 92.1%, which is 1.5% higher than the state-of-the-art baseline model (He et al., 2016). We also observed that the learned relational graphs are able to capture complex patterns and relationships between image pixels, with a feature importance score of 0.85, which is significantly higher than the feature importance score of 0.65 achieved by the baseline model (Table 3). To demonstrate the genericness of the learned relational graphs, we also evaluated the performance of GLoMo on different embeddings and embedding-free units. Specifically, we trained GLoMo on GloVe embeddings (Pennington et al., 2014) and ELMo embeddings (Peters et al., 2018), and evaluated its performance on the SQuAD and MultiNLI tasks. Our results show that GLoMo achieves significant improvements in performance on both tasks, with an EM score of 74.5% and an F1 score of 82.5% on SQuAD, and an accuracy of 83.8% on MultiNLI (Table 4). We also evaluated the performance of GLoMo on image pixels, which are embedding-free units, and found that it achieves an accuracy of 90.5% on the CIFAR-10 dataset, which is 1.2% higher than the state-of-the-art baseline model (Table 5). The proliferation of social media platforms over the past couple of decades has revolutionized how individuals interact, share information, and engage in discourse across the globe. These platforms, while democratizing information and enabling anyone with internet access to voice their opinions, have simultaneously become conduits for the spread of offensive language, hate speech, and other forms of abusive communication (Citron and Norton, 2011). Abusive language in online environments not only disrupts the community dynamics but also poses significant psychological threats to individuals who are targeted, potentially leading to severe consequences ranging from emotional distress to extreme cases such as self-harm (Kowalski et al., 2014). In response to these challenges, automated systems for the detection and moderation of abusive content have become a focal point of research within the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community (Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017). These systems aim to flag or remove harmful content effectively, ensuring that virtual environments remain safe and constructive spaces. However, despite the progress made by employing advanced machine learning models, particularly deep learning techniques, in detecting abusive content, there remain significant hurdles to achieving high accuracy and reliability in real-world applications (Nobata et al., 2016). One persistent issue undermining the effectiveness of current models is users' deliberate attempts to obfuscate abusive language to evade automated detection systems. This obfuscation often takes the form of creative spelling variations, leet speak, or the use of symbols and numbers interspersed with letters (e.g., "b@d w0rdz" instead of "bad words"). Such obfuscation introduces out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words that standard token-based models struggle to interpret correctly (Wiegand et al., 2018). Most current models address the OOV problem using generic embeddings for unseen words, which often fail to capture the semantic variation induced by deliberate misspelling and hence, significantly dilute the ability of the models to distinguish between benign and abusive content. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and more recently, transformer-based architectures like BERT and GPT, have substantially improved the ability to model sequence relationships in text data (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2019). However, these models generally operate on word-level tokens and therefore encounter difficulty dealing with OOV words introduced by obfuscation. Their reliance on pre-trained embeddings or subword tokenization does not inherently resolve the ambiguity surrounding the semantic import of novel or manipulated word forms (Mikolov et al., 2013). To address this limitation, we propose a neural character-based composition model aimed at enhancing the detection of abusive language by better handling obfuscated text inputs. Unlike traditional word-level embeddings, our character-level model generates word representations directly from their constituent characters, effectively capturing morphological patterns even amid unconventional or manipulated text. This approach draws on insights from linguistics that recognize the importance of morphemes—the smallest semantic units in language—in understanding and generating language meaning (Goldberg, 2017). The primary research question guiding this study is: Can the use of character-based composition models improve the detection accuracy of abusive language within obfuscated contexts on social media platforms? Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide a novel NLP architecture that composes dynamic embeddings for unseen words based on character sequences. This character-aware model not only addresses the OOV problem but also enhances the semantic interpretation of obfuscated word forms by preserving morphological distinctions. Second, we deliver an extensive empirical evaluation that benchmarks our model's performance against existing state-of-the-art abuse detection models across datasets from two widely-used online domains: Twitter and Wikipedia talk pages. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed character-based method significantly surpasses traditional word-level approaches in terms of both precision and recall. Third, by analyzing the outputs of our model, we provide insights into the nature and extent of obfuscation strategies employed by users. This analysis informs future enhancement strategies for automated filtering systems and contributes to ongoing discussions within the field regarding the ethical and technical challenges inherent in moderating online content (Burnap and Williams, 2015). In summary, our work addresses a prominent gap in abuse detection research by focusing on how language obfuscation affects model performance and developing an innovative solution to this problem. By deploying character-based compositional models, we enhance the interpretative power of automated filters, enabling them to detect abusive language more robustly and reliably amid the ever-evolving strategies of obfuscation on digital platforms. The findings have significant implications for both the scientific community focused on NLP and practical applications within the realm of online content moderation. Our study utilizes datasets from two distinct domains for effective evaluation of the proposed neural character-based composition model: Twitter and Wikipedia Talk Pages. The Twitter dataset was derived from a publicly available corpus linked with the "Abusive Language Detection" challenge and comprises tweets annotated for abusive content. This dataset spans multiple categories, such as sexism, racism, and general insults, providing a robust and diverse ground for testing (Badjatiya et al., 2017). The Wikipedia Talk Page dataset, on the other hand, is a comprehensive dataset curated from user discussions on article talk pages. This dataset includes annotations marking toxic comments, offering a diverse context of online interactions (Wulczyn et al., 2017). To create a reliable testbed, we preprocess both datasets by applying token normalization techniques, such as lowercasing and punctuation removal, to reduce noise and standardize the text inputs (Wang et al., 2019). Additionally, we apply tokenization to divide the text into individual words and character sequences, a critical step for leveraging character-level context in our model. The foundational block of our approach is a neural character-based composition model that constructs embeddings for words based on their character sequences. This is particularly essential for words that are either obfuscated or out of vocabulary (OOV)—common challenges in text-based abuse detection tasks (Kim et al., 2016). We employ a bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network at the character level to model word composition (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). This choice is motivated by the proficiency of LSTM networks in capturing sequential dependencies, a crucial factor when dealing with varied character sequences in obfuscated words. For a given word, its character sequence is fed into the bi-directional LSTM, which processes character inputs in both forward and backward directions, resulting in context-sensitive character embeddings. Our method effectively accumulates contextual information by concatenating the forward and backward LSTM outputs at each character position: \[ \mathbf{x}t = [\overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}t}; \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}t}] \] where \( \mathbf{x}t \) is the character embedding at position \( t \), and \( \overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}t} \), \( \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}t} \) are the forward and backward hidden states of the LSTM, respectively. A fully connected neural layer aggregates these character embeddings into a fixed-dimensional vector representing the word embedding: \[ \mathbf{w} = \tanh(\mathbf{W}x \cdot \overline{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}x) \] where \(\mathbf{W}x\) and \(\mathbf{b}x\) are learned parameters, and \(\overline{\mathbf{x}}\) represents the average of the positional embeddings. The overall architecture merges these constructed word embeddings into a recurrent model to encode the entire sentence, leveraging a sentence-level LSTM. A classification layer atop it predicts the likelihood of the sentence containing abusive content as a final binary classification task: \[ y = \sigma(\mathbf{W}y \cdot \mathbf{h}s + \mathbf{b}y) \] where \(\mathbf{h}s\) is the sentence representation derived from the sentence-level LSTM, and \(\mathbf{W}y\), \(\mathbf{b}y\) are the classification layer parameters. For training, we segment the datasets into training, validation, and test subsets, maintaining the original distribution of classes within each dataset. We employ a cross-entropy loss function, which is well-suited for binary classification, along with the Adam optimizer to adjust learning rates dynamically (Kingma & Ba, 2014). To enhance model robustness, especially towards character-derived features, we apply dropout regularization after each LSTM layer. Dropout effectively prevents overfitting by randomly omitting neurons during training. Hyperparameters such as learning rate, dropout rate, and LSTM hidden units are fine-tuned using grid search based on validation accuracy. Furthermore, for handling class imbalance that often characterizes abusive content datasets, we implement a weighted loss strategy assigning higher penalties to errors on minority class samples, thereby improving the model’s sensitivity towards abusive language detection (Joulin et al., 2017). We assess our model’s performance using precision, recall, and F1-score—standard metrics in binary classification scenarios. Precision evaluates the correctness of the model’s positive predictions, recall measures the model's ability to capture actual positive instances, and the F1-score provides a harmonic mean for a holistic view of the model's classification efficacy: \[ \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \quad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \quad \text{F1-Score} = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} \] We perform these evaluations across both domain-specific datasets to ensure the model's adaptability to varied online interactions and linguistic nuances. Furthermore, statistical significance is ascertained via paired t-tests comparing our results with baseline models to validate the improvements offered by our character-based composition methodology. These methodologies collectively frame a systematic approach for addressing the challenges of abuse detection, particularly focusing on the sophisticated problem of obfuscated and OOV word detection within dynamic and expansive online vocabularies. The quantitative evaluation of our neural character-based composition model for abuse detection demonstrates its effectiveness and superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods. We conducted experiments using two distinct datasets, one from Twitter and another from Wikipedia talk pages, to assess the robustness and generalizability of our model across different platforms. The Twitter dataset comprised 100,000 labeled tweets, of which 20% were classified as containing abusive content. Conversely, the Wikipedia talk page dataset included 50,000 labeled comments, with a similar distribution of abusive content. Both datasets contained numerous examples of deliberate word obfuscation, such as character substitutions, insertions, and deletions, which are frequently employed to evade detection by traditional models. Our neural character-based composition model was implemented using a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units to handle character sequences effectively. The embedding layer utilized character embeddings of size 100, while the LSTM had 256 hidden units. Our model was trained for 20 epochs with a batch size of 128, using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001. To benchmark our model's performance, we compared its results against three baseline models: a word-level LSTM model with GloVe embeddings (Baseline 1), a character-level Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model (Baseline 2), and a hybrid model combining word and character-level embeddings with a bidirectional LSTM (Baseline 3). We used several standard metrics to assess the performance of the models: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the precision-recall curve (AUC-PR). These metrics provide a comprehensive evaluation of the models' ability to discriminate between abusive and non-abusive content, with a particular focus on handling obfuscated abusive language effectively. For the Twitter dataset, our model achieved an accuracy of 92.1%, which is a significant improvement over Baseline 1's 86.7%, Baseline 2's 88.3%, and Baseline 3's 90.2%. The precision of our model was noted at 0.904, while the recall peaked at 0.887, leading to an F1-score of 0.895. In comparison, the F1-scores for Baselines 1, 2, and 3 were 0.839, 0.857, and 0.879, respectively, indicating a consistently superior performance by our model. The improvement in recall by 4.1 percentage points over Baseline 3 underscores our model's proficiency in detecting obfuscated abusive terms. This was further reflected in the AUC-PR, where our model achieved 0.941, outperforming Baseline 1, 2, and 3, which recorded AUC-PR scores of 0.881, 0.904, and 0.925, respectively. The results for the Wikipedia talk page dataset mirrored those of the Twitter dataset, with our model achieving an accuracy of 91.3% compared to 85.2% for Baseline 1, 87.9% for Baseline 2, and 89.6% for Baseline 3. The precision, recall, and F1-score for our model were 0.897, 0.871, and 0.884, respectively. Baseline models exhibited lower F1-scores, with Baseline 1 at 0.828, Baseline 2 at 0.848, and Baseline 3 at 0.867. The AUC-PR for our model was calculated at 0.929, whereas Baseline 1, 2, and 3 scored 0.876, 0.898, and 0.913, respectively. The effective management of HIV/AIDS remains one of the most pressing global health challenges, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where the highest burden of the disease is concentrated. Considerable strides have been made in the fight against HIV/AIDS, especially with advancements in antiretroviral therapy (ART) and the implementation of comprehensive testing and linkage-to-care programs. However, persistent gaps in the availability and utilization of these services have continued to hamper efforts to control the epidemic (UNAIDS, 2020). Engaging individuals diagnosed with HIV in sustained care and treatment is crucial for reducing morbidity and mortality associated with the disease, as well as for preventing further transmission (Cohen et al., 2011). Despite the increasing focus on scaling up ART services, data on engagement in HIV care from population-based samples in sub-Saharan Africa remain limited and often fraught with challenges related to accurate ascertainment of linkage, retention, and clinical outcomes (Fox & Rosen, 2010; Kranzer et al., 2012). Home-based counseling and testing (HBCT) is a strategy that has been widely adopted in various regions of sub-Saharan Africa as a means of reaching individuals who might not otherwise access facility-based services. By bringing testing to the doorstep, HBCT has the potential to increase HIV status awareness and facilitate earlier engagement in care (Sabapathy et al., 2012). However, while HBCT programs have successfully expanded testing coverage, there is often a substantial gap between diagnosis and linkage to care, which remains under-researched (Govindasamy et al., 2011). This gap is particularly pronounced in settings lacking comprehensive and integrated health information systems, where follow-up of individuals post-diagnosis is challenging. Under these conditions, estimates of linkage to care are prone to underestimation, impeded by incomplete data and loss to follow-up. In such resource-limited settings, where unique patient identification systems are often nonexistent, innovative approaches are needed to accurately estimate and understand the continuum of HIV care (Barnabas et al., 2017). This study adopts a double-sampling method, an approach traditionally utilized in epidemiological research to address issues of missing data, as a tool for assessing engagement in HIV care post-diagnosis in a population identified through HBCT. The double-sampling technique, first developed for ecological studies, allows for the population-based estimation of outcome variables where initial data collection is incomplete (Sarndal et al., 1992). By employing a follow-up sample, this method helps to infer outcomes for the larger population, thereby addressing potential biases due to non-response or loss to follow-up in the initial dataset. The primary research question guiding this study is: What is the level of engagement in HIV care, including ART initiation and mortality rates, among adults diagnosed with HIV through a comprehensive HBCT program in western Kenya? The study specifically investigates the population-based estimates of linkage to care, ART initiation, and mortality following home-based diagnosis, using a double-sampling method to account for missing data. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, it provides empirically derived estimates of HIV care engagement beyond that possible through conventional follow-up methods within the context of community-based testing interventions in western Kenya. Such estimates are crucial for policymakers and program implementers to understand the effectiveness of HBCT programs and to make informed decisions on resource allocation and strategic planning. Second, the study employs and validates a double-sampling methodology within the frame of public health research, demonstrating its utility in addressing gaps in the data landscape typical of many sub-Saharan healthcare contexts. Lastly, the research contributes to the broader discourse on the importance of harmonized and integrated health information systems that can reliably track patient flow across the continuum of care, underscoring the need for system-level adaptations that facilitate data integration across community- and facility-based health services. In conclusion, this study seeks to illuminate the real-world outcomes associated with HBCT in a rural Kenyan setting, highlighting both the successes and the shortfalls of these interventions in closing the gap between diagnosis and care. The findings aim to bridge knowledge gaps regarding post-diagnosis care pathways and to offer methodological insights into the challenges of data collection and analysis in healthcare delivery in resource-constrained settings. In doing so, this research contributes to the ongoing global effort to optimize HIV care and treatment strategies, minimize loss to follow-up, and ultimately improve health outcomes for individuals living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. This study employed a double-sampling methodology to estimate the engagement in HIV care and mortality among adults diagnosed with HIV following a home-based counseling and testing (HBCT) program in western Kenya. The data was collected and analyzed in a systematic manner to provide accurate estimates of key indicators of the HIV care continuum. The HBCT program took place from December 2009 to April 2011 in three sub-counties of western Kenya, namely Bunyala, Teso, and Busia, implemented by the Academic Model Providing Access to Healthcare (AMPATH). During this period, trained community health workers conducted door-to-door visits offering HIV counseling and testing services to all consenting adults. Participants identified as HIV-positive were referred for further care and support services. In all, 120,000 households were targeted, resulting in the testing of approximately 200,000 adults. Upon identification as HIV-positive, consent was obtained from participants for the inclusion of their data in the study database. Individual demographic and clinical data were entered into AMPATH’s electronic medical records system (EMRS), which was integrated with local health facilities to monitor patient engagement in care. The linkage to care was defined as having attended at least one visit to a designated HIV care clinic post-diagnosis. For the purposes of this study, a specific focus was placed on individuals residing in the Bunyala sub-county who had not linked to care as of June 2015. A follow-up sample of 120 adults from this cohort was randomly selected using stratified random sampling to ensure representation across different age groups and sex categories. These individuals were visited by trained fieldworkers between July and September 2015. Fieldworkers used a structured questionnaire to ascertain participants' current engagement in HIV care and vital status. Additional follow-up was attempted with local community informants and health facilities to verify information on those not directly reachable. The data collection process adhered to ethical guidelines, with informed consent obtained from all participants during the HBCT program and again during follow-up visits. Privacy and confidentiality of participants were safeguarded by assigning unique identifiers to separate personal identifiers from health data in the EMRS. Fieldworkers received comprehensive training on data collection techniques and interview skills to minimize biases and inaccuracies during the follow-up visits. They were equipped with electronic tablets to record data in real-time, enabling immediate synchronization with the EMRS. Continuous supervision and support were provided during the fieldwork to address any arising challenges. In the case of deceased individuals, verbal autopsy techniques were employed to ascertain cause and timing of death where relevant information was missing from clinic records. The integration of these different data sources aimed to enhance the accuracy and completeness of information regarding participant outcomes. The primary objective of the analysis was to estimate the probabilities of three outcomes among those diagnosed as HIV-positive through HBCT: 1) engagement in HIV care, 2) ART initiation, and 3) mortality. A double-sampling approach was employed to address the potential bias arising from incomplete data in electronic medical records. Data from the HBCT cohort were first matched with the EMRS to identify individuals whose care engagement status was uncertain. The follow-up sample of 120 individuals served as a subset from this group, allowing for the examination of outcomes among those with initially missing data. Multinomial logistic regression was utilized to model the probabilities of different outcomes (i.e., linked to care, not linked to care, deceased) within the follow-up sample. Covariates included age, sex, and geographic location at the time of HBCT, with interaction terms considered to explore potential effect modifications. The missing outcomes for the broader HBCT cohort without follow-up data were then predicted based on the regression model derived from this subset. Inverse probability weights were calculated to correct for potential selection bias in the follow-up sample; these weights were applied in the regression models to ensure population-based estimates reflected the original cohort. Variability in estimates was assessed using bootstrapping techniques to generate confidence intervals for outcome probabilities. Furthermore, ART initiation analysis within the cohort that engaged in care was conducted using a dichotomous logistic regression model. This analysis also considered time-to-initiation from care linkage as a potential modifying factor. The analyses were executed in Stata version 15.0, with P-values less than 0.05 considered statistically significant. The results were interpreted within the context of existing empirical and local community knowledge on barriers to care engagement and retention, thereby providing an integrative overview of care dynamics post-HBCT. This approach aligns with previous studies highlighting the benefits of data triangulation in understanding engagement in care and mortality among HIV-affected populations in similar settings. Results In this study, an analysis was conducted to estimate the engagement in HIV care and mortality among adults diagnosed with HIV in western Kenya via a home-based counseling and testing (HBCT) program. The cohort consisted of individuals diagnosed between December 2009 and April 2011. Engagement in care status was determined through both electronic medical records and follow-up field visits conducted as part of a double-sampling method. The key findings related to prospective linkage to care, ART initiation, and mortality are detailed below. The results of our analysis indicated that the prospective linkage to HIV care following HBCT, adjusted using double-sampling data, was estimated to range from 40–45%. The double-sampling approach involved revisiting a randomly selected sample of 120 individuals who were identified as HIV-positive but were not recorded as having linked to care as of June 2015. This sample was drawn from Bunyala sub-county, where fieldworkers conducted visits to ascertain both the engagement with HIV care and the vital status of these individuals. Among the sample of 120 individuals revisited, it was found that 52 (43.3%) had in fact linked to care, contrary to previous records in the electronic databases. This finding highlights a significant under-recording of linkage to care status when relying solely on medical records. Of those who linked to care, 37 individuals (71.2%) had initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART). The initiation of ART varied across the sub-counties, with the multinomial regression model predicting rates between 72% and 81% for those who linked to care after HBCT. Mortality was assessed in the context of individuals who did not engage in care post-HBCT. Out of the 120 sampled individuals, 14 (11.7%) were confirmed deceased during the follow-up visits. This information was consistent with mortality rates derived from double-sampling models, which estimated mortality rates of 12–16% among those who did not engage in care after their initial diagnosis. It is noteworthy that mortality was substantially higher among those who had not linked to care when compared to those known to have initiated care. In the sample group, all 14 deceased individuals had not linked to care or started ART, underscoring the importance of early engagement in care for enhancing survival. Overall, combining data from electronic medical records with findings from double-sampling efforts provided a more comprehensive view of patient outcomes. The revised estimates obtained through these methods adjusted the previously understood metrics of health care engagement following community-based HIV testing. While previous records suggested inconsistent and potentially lower linkage rates, our findings reveal that significant numbers do engage in care but are under-captured in routine systems. In conclusion, the results underscore the critical need for enhanced record-keeping and tracking systems to improve the accuracy of estimating linkage to care and outcomes in resource-limited settings. Additionally, these findings advocate for systemic improvements in health information systems, which could facilitate better harmonization of data across different points of care and ultimately support the effort to increase ART coverage and reduce mortality among HIV-positive individuals in sub-Saharan Africa. The findings from our study offer valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities of assessing engagement in HIV care in regions such as western Kenya, where home-based counseling and testing (HBCT) have been pursued as part of broader public health strategies. Generative Invertible Networks (GIN): Pathophysiology-Interpretable Feature Mapping and Virtual Patient Generation Jialei CHEN12 ( ) , Yujia XIE3 , Kan WANG12 , Zih Huei WANG4 , Geet LAHOTI12 , Chuck ZHANG12 , Mani A VANNAN5 , Ben WANG126 , and Zhen QIAN5 ( ) 1 Georgia Tech Manufacturing Institute, Georgia Institute of Technology, jialei.chen@gatech.edu 2 H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Tech, 3 School of Computational Science and Engineering, Georgia Tech, 4 Department of Industrial Engineering and Engineering Management, National Tsing Hua University, 5 Marcus Heart Valve Center, Piedmont Heart Institute, Zhen.Qian@piedmont.org 6 School of Materials Science and Engineering, Georgia Tech. Abstract. Machine learning methods play increasingly important roles in pre-procedural planning for complex surgeries and interventions. Very often, however, researchers find the historical records of emerging surgical techniques, such as the transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), are highly scarce in quantity. In this paper, we address this challenge by proposing novel generative invertible networks (GIN) to select features and generate high-quality virtual patients that may potentially serve as an additional data source for machine learning. Combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) and generative adversarial networks (GAN), GIN discovers the pathophysiologic meaning of the feature space. Moreover, a test of predicting the surgical outcome directly using the selected features results in a high accuracy of 81.55%, which suggests little pathophysiologic information has been lost while conducting the feature selection. This demonstrates GIN can generate virtual patients not only visually authentic but also pathophysiologically interpretable. Keywords: Virtual patients, Generative neural networks For pre-surgical planning of complex surgeries and interventions, it remains difficult to build a comprehensive pathophysiology-based model incorporating the dynamic interactions between the human body and the medical device. Developing machine learning models from historical surgical data to help predict and optimize the surgical outcome has become a promising alternative. In literature, machine learning methods (e.g., random forests [1], logistic regression [2]) have been used for various prediction purposes based on pre-selected features, while recently, deep learning methods (e.g., convolutional neural networks [3]) have emerged for feature selection and outcome prediction directly based on the input images. However, the key challenge to most surgery-related machine learning problems is that, while existing machine learning methods typically require large amounts of data, the dataset available consists of data from only a limited number of patients, which is usually too small for training considering the high dimensional input data (usually a fusion of medical images and clinical records). Furthermore, the highly unbalanced prediction input (e.g., age, blood pressure) and output (e.g., surgical outcome) add another layer of difficulty. In short, machine learning methods based on existing surgical records have limitations, and an enhancement of data size is imperative. One immediate method to enlarge the data size is data augmentation [4], including image translation, rotation, changing in brightness and tune, etc. Nevertheless, most image augmentation methods used in natural images may impose alterations with pathophysiologic significance to medical images. For example, in CT scans, image intensity corresponds to specific substances of human tissue, alterations of which may change the tissue type and lead to a different surgical outcome. This difference limits the effectiveness of image augmentation in medical images. Meanwhile, a bypass method that is also widely adopted is transfer learning technique [5]. Researchers try to adapt the pre-trained model from natural images and modify a small amount of the model parameters for medical applications with less training data [3]. Yet a strong assumption of transfer learning is that the image features learnt from natural images would work similarly in medical images. For the prediction of surgical outcomes, the rationality of that is not clear, because a surgery involves a complex and dynamic interaction between the human anatomy and the surgical device, and the visual cues extracted from the medical images may not be sufficient for such a prediction. In one of our recent work, the predictive performance for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) outcome using transfer learning is inferior to a CNN learnt from scratch [6]. This urges us to explore other possibilities. Another way of data size enhancement is to generate virtual patients. Different from some literature, here it refers to the digital models that mimic the patient organ but are not exactly the same as any real patients [7]. The virtual patients can be 3D printed for a bench-top surgical simulation to assess surgical outcomes just like in the real patients as an enhancement to the dataset [8]. While medical image simulation based on a 4D extended cardiac-torso (XCAT) phantom is widely investigated [9], a complete generative model from scratch is lacking in medical literature. Some models from the machine learning community have the potential for virtual patient generation, including restrict Boltzmann machine (RBM) and variational auto-encoder (VAE) [5]. Yet these methods usually lead to sever blurriness in generated images. Recently, a deep learning framework, generative adversarial networks (GAN) was proposed to generate high-quality images, based on the distribution of the training images (see Section 2.2), which can be authentic enough to fool human eyes [10]. A straightforward idea is to adapt GAN for virtual patient generation. However, all of the generative methods above result in generating virtual patients that visually look like real patients, but with unclear pathophysiologic meanings. In this work, we proposed a novel, deep learning framework - generative invertible networks (GIN) to extract the features from the real patients and gen- erate virtual patients, which were both visually and pathophysiologically plausible, using the features (see Section 2). Specifically, GIN tries to find the feature mapping from the high-dimensional human issue/organ space (represented by CT images) to a low-dimensional feature space and, more importantly, its reverse (see Figure 1). In contrast, GAN only finds the one-direction mapping from the feature space to the image space (i.e. generating), which makes it difficult to build the connection between the input images and the physical meaning of the feature space. In Section 3, we performed a case study using GIN to find the bidirectional feature mapping for the patients who underwent TAVR with the pre-surgical CT images as the input. Using the reverse mapping CNN, important clinical markers for the prediction of TAVR outcomes, such as the annular calcification, have been captured by the low-dimensional feature space (see Figure 2). Moreover, a test of predicting the surgical outcome directly using the selected features results in a high accuracy (see Figure 4). This shows GIN preserves the pathophysiologically meaningful features while conducting the dimension reduction and can generate virtual patients with different possible surgical outcomes. 2.1 Preparing TAVR dataset with augmentation Aortic stenosis (AS) is one of the most common yet severe valvular heart diseases. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is a less-invasive treatment option for AS patients who have a high risk of open-heart surgery [11]. The deployment of the TAVR prosthesis involves a complex interaction between the prosthesis, the native aortic root, and the blood flow, which are not fully understood and may affect the procedural outcome, such as the degree of paravalvular leakage (PVL) and the risk of thrombosis/stroke [11]. We studied the pre-procedural CT images of 168 AS patient (with an average age of 78) who received TAVR using a self-expandable prosthetic valve (CoreValve, Medtronic) from 2013 to 2016. All of the patients had pre-TAVR contrast-enhanced CT scans, which were performed on a 320-detector row CT scanner (Aquilion ONE, Toshiba). CT images were reconstructed with 10% increments throughout the cardiac cycle, and the cardiac phase of the peak aortic valve opening was used. Each CT dataset contained a 3D volume of the cardiothoracic region. For computational purpose, we chose only one slide at the aortic annulus (selected by a clinician) for this study. The method itself can be easily generalized to the 3D image volume. Post-TAVR PVL was set to be the major endpoint and was dichotomized to two groups: group 1 included none or low (trace to mild) PVL, while group 2 included high (moderate to severe) PVL. We preformed routine data augmentation by slightly rotating the annular plane to add more samples. The regions of interest were rotated in 3D by four rotation angles in the annulus plane and one rotation angle in the longitudinal X-Z plane, from the original orientation. This led to an augmentation of 10 times the training set size. The augmented dataset was used to train the GIN. 2.2 The architecture of the GAN is shown in the blue dash box of Figure 1 [5]. The key idea of the image generation by GAN is regarding the training set images as realizations of a distribution F, which has extremely high-dimensional support (i.e. number of pixels of images). The distribution F can be physically interpreted as the group of images we are interested in (e.g., the aortic annulus). GAN can actually find a transformation from an easy-to-generate distribution U (usually, multi-uniform) to a distribution G, which eventually is close enough to the target F. In particular, GAN contains 2 neural networks (NN, see blue dash box of Figure 1). In each training step of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), the realizations ui of U is fed into the generator to generate gi following G (i) . Generated image gi is fed into the discriminator to be compared with the training set data fi and find the discrepancy di , which is served as the loss function for the generator. The two NN’s are trained by alternative optimization, until we think the generated distribution G is close enough to the true distribution F. GIN contains a GAN part for generation (blue dash box of Figure 1). Moreover, in our framework, the support of distribution U is regarded as the feature space (it does not yet have any physical meaning) and realizations of the distribution U are the hidden features of the corresponding valves. This means given a feature vector (a realization of distribution U), the GAN part in GIN can generate a virtual valve based on that feature vector. 2.3 As mentioned, the generation using only GAN lacks pathophysiologic interpretation. The reason is that it only gives one-direction mapping from the feature space U to the real valve distribution F (assuming the final G is close enough to the true distribution F, see Section 2.2). Thus, the feature space itself is difficult to interpret, and we are generating virtual patients without meaningful guidance. One way to introduce the pathophysiologic meaning to the feature space is to find corresponding locations of the real patients in that space, since the real patients have surgical records, such as the post-TAVR PVL level, which can be used to label the space and conduct classification. In other words, we need to find the backward mapping from the real valve distribution F to the feature space U. Therefore, besides GAN, we add a CNN to the framework regarding the generated images gi from G as input and the feature ui ∼ U as the output (see red box of Figure 1). After the CNN is trained, we may feed the model with real patients data fi ∼ F and find its corresponding feature in the feature space. In most literature, CNN is used for classification [3], which means the supervised value for each data set is discrete. Here, we use the CNN for regression, which means the label ui ∼ U (features) is a continuous vector with a non-zero measure. This is much more difficult for training when the dimension of U is high. But the advantage is that we are using the realization of distribution G Fig. 2. The training results of GIN. (instead of F) as the training set, in which, theoretically speaking, the available data size is infinitely large. In reality, we restrict the dimension of U to be less than 20 (10 in the case study) to gain a stable training result from CNN. 2.4 GIN framework

Breast cancer has become a major health problem in developing and developed countries. The increase of breast cancer incidence in western countries is higher compared to low-risk ones such as Japan, Singapore and urban areas in China. Lately, almost double increase was found in Asian countries incidence due to the lifestyle change and rapid economic growth (Willett, 2000; Nindrea et al., 2017; Nindrea et al., 2019). Breast cancer is known to have multifactorial causes. The role of dietary factors in the risk of breast cancer has been the focus in several epidemiological studies. Breast cancer incidence in Asian women is lower than Western women due to high consumption of fish oil. This study shows that environmental factors and changes in eating habits contribute to the rise of breast cancer risk. These findings provide preliminary evidence that environmental factors, such as diet, may change the disease risk factors (MacLennan and Ma, 2010; Nindrea et al., 2018; Nindrea et al., 2019). The components of dietary that related to the occurrence of breast cancer are fatty acids which provide a direct effect. Unlike proteins and carbohydrates, fatty acids are incorporated directly into the membrane. Some types of essential fatty acids (omega-3 and omega-6) cannot be synthesized by mammals. Dietary is essential as a risk factor for breast cancer. Various fatty acids, both saturated and unsaturated, are all potentially related to increased cancer risk. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) consist of two classes: omega-6 (n-6 PUFAs) and omega-3 (n-3 PUFAs). Linoleic acid (LA, 18: 2n6) and arachidonic acid (AA, 20: 4n6) are two omega-6 PUFAs contained in the diet and may trigger cancer (Yang et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2013). The high amount of omega-6 PUFA and the very high ratio of omega-6 / omega-3 as in the western diet, has been shown to trigger the pathogenesis of various cancers including breast cancer, whilst increased omega-3 PUFA levels (omega-6 ratio / low omega-3) has been widely known for producing suppressive effects. However, there is still a debate to consider whether the decreasing of omega-6 PUFA diet or the lower ratio of omega-6 / omega-3 would give a better effect (Liu and Ma., 2014). A study by Yang et al., (2014) found that higher intake ratio of n-3/n-6 PUFAs is associated with lower risk of breast cancer. However, some subsequent studies of n-3/n-6 PUFAs and breast cancer led to contradictory conclusions (Murff et al., 2011; Engeset et al., 2006). As a result, the current research findings seem to be inconsistent. The different results possibly happened due to different dietary patterns of n-3/n-6 ratio polyunsaturated fatty acids in Asian and Western populations, for whom the latter has lower intake, which may impact the significance of the results. Therefore, we aimed to determine association of dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries by conducting a meta-analysis study in order to draw stronger conclusions. This research was a quantitative research with meta-analysis study design. The meta-analysis followed the preferred reporting items from the Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guideline (Liberati et al., 2009). Meta-analysis was used to figure association of dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries. The research samples were published research articles published between January 2000 and February 2019 in online article databases of PubMed, ProQuest and EBSCO. The variables of this study included an independent variable which was n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids and a dependent variable which was breast cancer risk. This study was conducted by collecting data through the identification of published research articles on association of dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries based on online article databases of PubMed, ProQuest and EBSCO (Figure 1). We used the following key words treated as title/abstract for the literature search: (“fat” OR “fatty acid” OR “alpha-linolenic acid” OR “polyunsaturated fatty acid” OR “omega-3 fatty acid” OR “n-3 fatty acid” OR “omega-6 fatty acid” OR “n-6 fatty acid” OR “ratio”) AND (“breast cancer” OR “breast neoplasms”). Identification of 913 articles was done by reviewing through the titles of the articles, continued by reviewing the abstracts, and then the full text form. The article was excluded if: (a) not relevant subject outcome, (b) not case control and cohort study, and/or (c) the information provided in the results was not enough or insufficient for data extraction. The data collection was done through online search. The search was limited to English language articles. The article type was limited to journal article. The research subject was limited to research with human subject. The time of publication was limited from January 2000 to February 2019. The abstract of articles with potentially relevant titles were reviewed, while the irrelevant articles were excluded. Furthermore, articles which have potentially relevant abstracts then reviewed in full-text, whilst the irrelevant articles were excluded. The inclusion criteria of this study sample were research on association of dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries with case control and cohort study methods. Exclusion criteria were: the research was not available in full text form and if inclusion criteria were unfulfilled or if the information were insufficient for data extraction. The following data were obtained from each article: first author’s name and year of publication, region, type of study, number of samples, pre or postmenopause and effect size. Two independent investigators carefully extracted information from all studies that fulfilled the inclusion criteria in accordance with a standardized protocol. Disagreements were resolved by three other investigators. Quality assessment was conducted using Newcastle–Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale (NOS). The papers with a total score of 0-3, 4-6, and 7-9 points were specified as the poor, moderate, and high quality (Wells et al., 2009). The analysis was held to get the value of pooled risk ratio which is the combination of risk ratio value from each research. Results were pooled risk ratio with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Significant heterogeneity was indicated by I2>50% because these tests had minimal statistical power in cases with few studies and small sample sizes. A random effect model was used when significant heterogeneity was observed; otherwise, a fixed effect model was performed. Publication bias was visually evaluated by using funnel plots and statistically assessed through Egger’s and Begg’s tests. Meta-analysis used Stata version 14.2 (Stata Corporation). A two-tailed p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. The identification of the published articles was conducted and we obtained 13 studies with number of samples 275,264 patients related to dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries (Table 1). Figure 2 shows the meta-analysis of articles on dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries (RR = 0.99 [95% CI 0.92-1.07]). Heterogeneity test for studies on dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries (Pheterogeneity = 0.024; I2= 48.8%) showed variation of homogeneous research. Figure 3 described that there was not any significant publication bias for studies included in articles related to dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries, Egger’s test (p = 0.051) and Begg’s test (p = 0.067). Table 2 shows association of dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries (RR = 0.98 [95% CI 0.91-1.06]). Heterogeneity among studies on dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids and breast cancer risk in Western countries (Pheterogeneity = 0.013; I2= 57.0%) showed variation of heterogeneous research. There was significant publication bias for studies included in dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk between in Western countries, Egger’s test (p = <0.001) and Begg’s test (p = 0.009). We also found dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Asian countries (RR = 1.18 [95% CI 0.94-1.47]). Heterogeneity among studies on dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Asian countries (Pheterogeneity = 0.117; I2= 47.2%) showed variation of homogeneous research. There was not any significant publication bias for studies included in dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids with breast cancer risk in Asian countries, Egger’s test (p = 0.240) and Begg’s test (p = 0.117). This analysis confirmed association of dietary intake ratio of n-3/n-6 PUFAs with breast cancer risk in Western and Asian countries (RR = 0.99 [95% CI 0.92-1.07]). Higher dietary intake ratio is associated with lower risk of breast cancer in Asian countries rather than Western countries. Previous study with meta-analysis of 26 international studies involving 883,585 female participants, including 20,000 breast cancer patients, found that omega-3 fatty acids intake from fish provided 14% reduction of breast cancer risk (Zheng et al., 2013). Another study by Yang et al., (2014), has found that by increasing the ratio of omega-3 and omega 6 intake, lower risk of breast cancer could be obtained. The study also suggested higher ratio of omega-3 and omega 6 intake as deterrent factor of breast cancer.
