Graph-Based Decoding for Event Sequencing and Coreference Resolution Zhengzhong Liu and Teruko Mitamura and Eduard Hovy Language Technologies Institute Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA {liu, teruko, hovy}@cs.cmu.edu Abstract Events in text documents are interrelated in complex ways. In this paper, we study two types of relation: Event Coreference and Event Sequencing. We show that the popular tree-like decoding structure for automated Event Coreference is not suitable for Event Sequencing. To this end, we propose a graph-based decoding algorithm that is applicable to both tasks. The new decoding algorithm supports flexible feature sets for both tasks. Empirically, our event coreference system has achieved state-of-the-art performance on the TAC-KBP 2015 event coreference task and our event sequencing system beats a strong temporal-based, oracle-informed baseline. We discuss the challenges of studying these event relations. Events are important building blocks of documents. They play a key role in document understanding tasks, such as information extraction (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2011), news summarization (Vossen and Caselli, 2015), story understanding (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016). Conceptually, events correspond to state changes and normally include a location, a time interval, and several entities/participants. In a text, events are realized as text spans, normally as verbs and nouns that indicate state changes (Vendler, 1957). The text spans are often referred to as event mentions or event nuggets (We use the term event mention in this paper.). The textual mentions of events have rich relations among them, and collectively convey the meaning of one or more related documents. In this paper, we study two different types of relation: Event Hopper Coreference (EH) and Event Sequencing (ES). Event Coreference: There is a rich literature on the Event Coreference problem (Liu et al., 2014; Cybulska and Vossen, 2014; Lu et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2016; Lu and Ng, 2017; Araki, 2018). By analogy to entity coreference, the “same” conceptual event may be realized by multiple text spans (event mentions). The coreference problem aims at identifying these relations to recover events from the text spans. The Event Hopper Coreference task in the TAC-KBP evaluation campaign defines coreference links as follows (Mitamura et al., 2018): Two event mentions are considered coreferent if they refer to the conceptually same underlying event, even if their arguments are not strictly identical. For example, mentions that share similar temporal and location scope, though not necessarily the same expression, are considered to be coreferent (Attack in Baghdad on Thursday vs. Bombing in the Green Zone last week). This means that the event arguments of coreferential events mentions can be non-coreferential (18 killed vs. dozens killed), as long as they refer to the same event, judging from the available evidence. Event Sequencing: The coreference relations build up events from scattered mentions. On the basis of events, various other types of relations can then be established between them. The Event Sequencing task studies one such relation. The task is motivated by Schank’s scripts (Schank and Abelson, 1977), which suggests that human organize information through procedural data structures, reassembling sequences of events. For example, the list of verbs order, eat, pay, leave may trigger the restaurant script. A human can conduct reasoning with a typical ordering of these events based on common sense (e.g., order should be the first event, leave should be the last event). Red lines are coreference links; solid blue arrows represent Subevent relations; dotted green arrows represent After relations. The ES task studies how to group and order events from text documents belonging to the same script. Figure 1 shows some annotation examples. Conceptually, event sequencing relations hold between the events, while coreference relations hold between textual event mentions. Given a document, the ES task requires systems to identify events within the same script and classify their inter-relations. These relations can be represented as labeled Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). There are two types of relations1 : After relations connect events following script orders (e.g. order followed by eating); Subevent relations connect events to a larger event that contains them. In this paper, we focus only on the After relations. Since script-based understanding is built in the ES task, it has some unique properties comparing to pure temporal ordering: 1) event sequences from different scripts provide separate logical divisions of text, while temporal ordering considers all events to lie on a single timeline; 2) temporal relations for events occurring at similar time points may be complicated. Script-based relations may alleviate the problem. For example, if a bombing kills some people, the temporal relation of the bombing and kill may be “inclusion” or “after”. This is considered an After relation in ES because bombing causes the killing. For structure prediction, decoding — recovering the complex structure from local decisions — is one of the core problems. The most successful decoding algorithm for coreference nowadays is mention ranking based (Björkelund and Kuhn, 2014; Durrett and Klein, 2014; Lee et al., 2017). These models rank the antecedents (mentions that appear earlier in discourse) and recover the full coreference clusters from local decisions. However, unlike coreference relations, sequencing relations are directed. Coreference decoding algorithms cannot be directly applied to such relations (§3.1). To solve this problem, we propose a unified graph-based framework that tackles both event coreference and event sequencing. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the event coreference task (§4.4) and beats an informed baseline on the event sequencing task (§4.5). Finally, we analyze the results and discuss the difficult challenges for both tasks (§5). Detailed definitions of these tasks can be found in the corresponding task documents2 . Many researchers have worked on event coreference tasks since Humphreys et al. (1997). Recent advances in event coreference have been promoted by the availability of annotated corpora. However, due to the complex nature of events, approaches to event coreference adopt quite different assumptions and definitions. Most of event coreference researches are conducted on the popular ACE corpus (Chen and Ji, 2009; Chen et al., 2009; Sangeetha and Arock, 2012; Chen and Ng, 2013; Chen and Ng, 2015). Unlike the TAC KBP setting, the definition of event coreference in the ACE corpus requires strict argument matching. Work on the Intelligence Community (IC) Corpus (Hovy et al., 2013; Cybulska and Vossen, 2012; Liu et al., 2014; Araki et al., 2014) considers event relations on a restricted domain (i.e., terrorist events). Works on the ECB corpus (Lee et al., 2012; Cybulska and Vossen, 2014) focuses on both within-document and cross-document coreference. Our work follows the line of work promoted by the TAC-KBP event nugget tasks (Mitamura et al., 2015). There is a small but growing amount of work on conducting event coreference on the TAC-KBP datasets (Lu et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2016; Lu and Ng, 2017). For event sequencing, there are few supervised methods on script-like relation classification due to the lack of data. To the best of our knowledge, the only work in this direction is by Araki et al. (2014). This work focuses on the other type of relations in the event sequencing task: Subevent relations. There is also a rich literature on unsupervised script induction (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Cheung et al., 2013; Rudinger et al., 2015; Pichotta and Mooney, 2016; Ferraro and Durme, 2016) that extracts scripts as a type of common-sense knowledge from raw documents. The focus of this work is to make use of massive collections of text documents to mine event co-occurrence patterns. In contrast, our work focuses on parsing the detailed relations between event mentions in each document. Another line of work closely related to event sequencing is to detect other temporal relations between events. Recent computational approaches for temporal detection are mainly conducted on the TimeBank corpus (Pustejovsky et al., 2002). There have been several studies on building automatic temporal reasoning systems (Uzzaman and Allen, 2010; Do et al., 2012; Chambers et al., 2014). In comparison, the Event Sequencing task is motivated by the Script theory, which places more emphasis on common-sense knowledge about event chronology. In the Latent Antecedent Tree (LAT) model popularly used for entity coreference decoding (Fernandes et al., 2012; Björkelund and Kuhn, 2014), each node represents an event mention and each arc a coreference relation, and new mentions are connected to some past mention considered most similar. Thus the LAT model represents the decoding structure as a tree. This can represent any coreference cluster, because coreference relations are by definition equivalence relations3 . In contrast, tree structures cannot always fully cover an Event Sequence relation graph, because 1) the After links are directed, not symmetric, and 2) multiple event nodes can link to one node, resulting in multiple parents. Optimization in Software Engineering A Pragmatic Approach Guenther Ruhe Abstract Empirical software engineering is concerned with the design and analysis of empirical studies that include software products, processes, and resources. Optimization is a form of data analytics in support of human decision-making. Optimization methods are aimed to find best decision alternatives. Empirical studies serve both as a model and as data input for optimization. In addition, the complexity of the models used for optimization trigger further studies on explaining and validating the results in real world scenarios. The goal of this chapter is to give an overview of the as-is and of the to-be usage of optimization in software engineering. The emphasis is on a pragmatic use of optimization, and not so much on describing the most recent algorithmic innovations and tool developments. The usage of optimization covers a wide range of questions from different types of software engineering problems along the whole life-cycle. To facilitate its more comprehensive and more effective usage, a checklist for a guided process is described. The chapter uses a running example Asymmetric Release Planning to illustrate the whole process. A Return-on-Investment analysis is proposed as part of the problem scoping. This helps to decide on the depth and breadth of analysis in relation to the effort needed to run the analysis and the projected value of the solution. The famous Aristotle (384 to 322 BC) is widely attributed with saying It is the mark of an educated mind to rest satisfied with the degree of precision which the nature of the subject admits and not to seek exactness where only an approximation is possible [43]. Applying Aristotle’s saying to software engineering means that we need to understand the problem first, its nature and degree of uncertainty, before we start running any sophisticated solution algorithm. In this chapter, we explore the usage and usefulness of optimization techniques in software engineering. We take a pragmatic perspective and propose a model looking at the Return-on-Investment and provide directions for future research in this field. The purpose of optimization is insight rather than numbers [26]. What counts is utilizing insight for making decisions. Software development and evolution are full of decisions to be made on processes, resources, artefacts, tools and techniques occurring at the different stages of the life-cycle. Some of these decisions have a strong impact on the success of the project. However, the information available for doing that is typically incomplete, imprecise, and even contradictory. The paradigm of software engineering decision support [53] emphasizes the decision-centric nature of software engineering. It outlines how different methods including modelling, measurement, simulation as well as analysis and reasoning, can be used to support human decision-making. Optimization is another piece of that decision support agenda. Looking for the best possible item, artefact, process, action, or plan is tempting and a natural desire, but it is not automatically clear what that actually means. Part of the difficulty is that decisions typically are in the space of multiple criteria: Improving in one direction typically requires compromising against another criteria. In other cases, the data and information available are vague or even contradictory. Finally: To what extent decisions are based on rationality? Software development is a creative and human-centered process, and humans do not necessarily act based on rational arguments. So, another question arises: How valuable and how practical is optimization for the area of (Empirical) Software Engineering? The chapter shows all the many opportunities of optimization in the various areas of software engineering (Section 9.2) and how to avoid pitfalls in its application. Optimization is not something that creates value automatically and easily. It is data intensive and requires time and effort investment. Optimization includes the whole process starting from the problem analysis, followed by modeling, running solution algorithms, understanding and interpreting data, likely modifying data and/or the underlying model, and re-running algorithms. In this chapter, we take a process view and provide a checklist for how to perform this process (Section 9.3). Its implementation is illustrated by a case study addressing asymmetric release planning (Section 9.4). Usage and usefulness of optimization is the key concern of Section 9.5. The chapter is completed by recommendations for further reading (Section 9.6) and conclusions on the future usage of optimization in the context of software engineering (Section 9.7). 2 Optimization in Software Engineer ing - Where? The Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI) [13] characterized companies with the highest maturity CMMI level as Optimizing. This highest level of maturity refers to the application error analysis and process monitoring in order to optimize the current processes. While optimization is applicable to all types of questions, in software engineering it is primarily related to structured and semi-structured decisions on all technical and managerial aspects of software development and evolution. The Software Engineering Body of Knowledge SWEBOK [1] lists technical and managerial areas to describe the field of software engineering: • Software requirements • Software design • Software construction • Software testing • Software maintenance • Software configuration management • Software project management 1 • Software engineering process • Software engineering models and methods • Software quality Decisions are made during all stages of the software life-cycle. Depending on their type of control and impact, decisions are classified into operational (short-term), tactical (mid-term), and strategic (long-term) decisions [4]. As another dimension of their classification, decisions are classified, based on their input, into structured, semistructured, or unstructured decisions. The emphasis of optimization is on tactical and strategic decisions based on structured or semistructured information. In Table 1 (see Appendix) we present a list of publications using optimization methods in software engineering. As it is impossible to present a complete list, we only selected papers published since 2000. Among the many papers found, we picked those having highest number of citations in Google scholar (as of September 4, 2019). 1Replacing Software Engineering Management as used in SWEBOK Figure 1: Word cloud for publications devoted to optimization in software engineering since 2000 Using the keywords of 84 optimization related papers published since 2000, a word cloud was created and is presented in Figure 1. We found a diversity of algorithms and concepts. Overall, the highest number of publications is in testing, requirements engineering, and design. This does not imply that there is nothing to optimize in the remaining areas. Lack of proper data might be one reason, and uncertainty in formulating explicit objectives and constraints another one for these current deficits. Optimization is a form of prescriptive analytics, aimed to propose actions to the decision maker. Different models for the process of data analytics (or data mining) exist, see the survey of Kurgan and Musilek [38]. We adapted the widely accepted CRISP data mining process introduced by Shearer [59] and integrated ideas of the engineering and the empirical cycle described by Wieringa [68]. The process model shown in Figure 2 establishes a link between (i) iterative software development (object of study), (ii) empirical studies (as a means to improve problem understanding, to create valid data, or to validate the research design), and (iii) existing model and data repositories. For iterative development, two sample iterations k and k+1 form the optimization context. Each iteration is assumed of having design, coding, and test activities, which result in a release version of the software product. Different parts of these processes might be optimized for higher efficiency. For example, there might be the problem of how to perform re-factoring, to finding best test strategies and test cases, to perform scheduling and staffing, or to decide about the functionality of the upcoming releases. For any of these questions, optimization helps to find a good or even the (formally) best answer. The process to find these answers is composed of eight steps that are further outlined in Section 3.2 by providing checklist questions to each step. Checklists are proven to be a means to facilitate the proper application of the overwhelming amount of existing knowledge existing in a field [25]. Similar to tools, applying checklists are no guarantee for success, but hopefully serve as filters or recommendations. They need continuous adaption to accommodate all the new directions and developments. Checklists have been used in software engineering, e.g., for case studies, project risk analysis, and performing inspections. Here, we propose a checklist for the usage of optimization in software engineering. The checklist questions follow the key steps recommended in Section 3.1. The questions are classified in terms of their usage. M(andatory) questions need to be answered with ”yes” to make optimization a valuable effort. C(larification) questions (What?) are aimed to qualify the setup of the whole process. TMTB questions (How? How much?) are the ones that benefit from ”the more the better”. 1 Scoping and ROI analysis: Scoping defines the problem context and its boundaries. At this stage, performing an analysis of the potential Return-on-Investment (ROI) helps to determine the depth and the breadth of the investigation. Questions How important is the problem? How much time and money can be invested to solve the problem? Can the problem not be solved easily without optimization? What are alternative solution approaches? How much is the optimization problem aligned with business objectives? How much impact has an optimized solution in the problem context? What is part of the investigation, what is not? Who are the key stakeholders and decision-makers? 2 Modeling and problem formulation: Modeling and formulation of the problem is the phase where the variables, constraints, and objectives of the problem are formulated. The formulation needs to be verified against the original problem statement. Questions What are the key independent problem variables? What is a reasonable granularity for problem formulation? What are the dependent variables? What are the human resource, budget, and time constraints? What are the technological constraints? 3 Solution design: The design step includes an analysis of what? and how much is enough? Exploring possible solution alternatives and its related tools depends on the scope selected. The design depends on the size of the problem (and its subsequent computational effort), the nature of the problem (linear, integer, convex, non-convex), and its projected impact. The design also decides between the use of traditional methods (linear, integer programming), and one of the many existing bio-inspired algorithms [7]. Questions What baseline solution exist to compare with? What are possible solution method alternatives and which ones have proven successful in similar context? Which related tools exist? What are the expectations on optimization solutions (heuristic vs approximation vs exact)? Is it search for just one (optimized) solution or for a set of solutions? What scenarios are planned for running the algorithms? How much would the optimization process benefit from interaction with the decision makers? 4 Data collection: Collect and prepare data needed to run optimization. While data is seldom complete, empirical studies can be used to improve the amount and quality of data. Goal oriented measurement [63] is the established technique to guide the data collection and analysis. Questions Is all necessary information available? Is all available information also reliable? Is there a need for data cleaning? Is there agreement between stakeholders on the data? 5 Optimization: Specify parameters for the tool and algorithm to execute optimization. How robust is the solution against changes on the input? What is the impact of adding or changing constraints? Questions Type Which parameter settings are made and why? C Should the parameter settings be varied and if so, C how? For randomized algorithms (e.g., bio-inspired algorithms), how many replications are needed to make C sound conclusions? Is there a time constraint for running the solution alC gorithm? What are the termination criteria for the optimization C algorithm? 6 Validation: The solution of the mathematical optimization problem needs to be validated. How do the results compare to apply- ing alternative algorithms? What do the results mean for the original problem? Possibly, the scope, the problem formulation or the solution design need to be adjusted. Questions How much do the generated solutions make sense in the problem context? Bibliometrics has been defined as the use of statistical methods to analyze a body of literature to reveal historical development through the scientific and quantitative study of publications (Young & Belanger, 1983). Applications of bibliometrics are numerous: determining a library purchasing policy (Garfield, 1972), studying the structure of the network of a scientific field (Wallace, Larivière & Gingras, 2012), and mapping the literature related to a research field such as health literacy (Kondilis et al., 2008) or cancer research (Glynn et al., 2010). Bibliometrics can also evaluate the speed of publication of manuscripts in journals (Chen, Chen & Jhanji, 2013), allow one to recognize new topics in the literature (Boudry, 2015), or even evaluate research and researchers (Hirsch, 2005). Viewed as an objective and quantifiable assessment of research output, such bibliometrics are inextricably linked with research funding, and an investigator must possess a strong publishing background to obtain the financial grants necessary for further work (Geisler, 2000). Few bibliometric studies have appeared in the literature in the field of ophthalmology. Although some analyses have been done on specific countries, (Kumaragurupari, Sieving & Lalitha, 2010; Katibeh, Moein & Javadi, 2011; Schlenker, Manalo & Wong, 2013) continents or territories (Ugolini et al., 2001; Sweileh et al., 2015), sub-specialties (Zhao et al., 2011; Gupta, Bala & Gupta, 2014; Boudry & Mouriaux, 2015), or production of a selection of ophthalmologic journals (Kumbar & Akhtary, 1998; Guerin et al., 2009; Kumar, Cheeseman & Durnian, 2011; Liesegang, 2011), no attempts have been made to describe the field “eye diseases.” The main purpose of this paper is to provide a report on scientific production in the field of eye diseases. For this, core journals have been identified, and frequency and distribution of MeSH terms in articles calculated. Furthermore, the geographical distribution and the temporal trend of papers published between 2010 and 2014 have been investigated with ad hoc geographical analyses evaluating literature production and weighted according to major socioeconomic variables, i.e. population size and Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Data were downloaded from PubMed in Extensible Markup Language (XML) and were processed through developed Hypertext Preprocessor language (PHP) scripts, then were imported to Microsoft Excel 2010 (Microsoft, Redmond, USA) for data processing. The search for papers to be included in this study was carried out on January 16th 2015, using the PubMed database (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed), developed by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) at the National Library of Medicine (NLM). PubMed was chosen because it is the most widely used in medicine (Falagas et al., 2008). The search strategy was the following: eye diseases [MH] AND journal article [PT] AND 2010:2014 [DP] where MH stands for “Medical Subject Headings,” DP “Date of Publication,” and PT “Publication Type.” “Journal Article” includes the following publication types: journal articles, introductory journal articles, and reviews. MeSH is the National Library of Medicine’s controlled vocabulary thesaurus (http://www.nlm.nih.gov/pubs/factsheets/mesh.html) and consists of sets of terms named “MeSH terms” arranged in a hierarchical structure (called a MeSH tree) with more specific terms arranged beneath less specific terms. In the indexing process, 2 to 50 MeSH terms are assigned to PubMed documents by a team of trained experts (indexers) to properly identify the content, and indexers always index as specifically as possible (MEDLINE Indexing Online Training Course, 2015). It is worth mentioning that it is not obligatory for author’s keywords to be taken into account by indexers to determine MeSH terms of an article (Boudry, 2015, personal data). The MeSH term “Eye Diseases,” the definition of which in the NLM-controlled vocabulary thesaurus is “Diseases affecting the eye,” was chosen because it covers all diseases of the eye when used in a PubMed search. Indeed, when using a MeSH term in a PubMed search, articles that carry the specified MeSH term are retrieved, but so are all of the articles that carry any of the more specific MeSH terms located beneath it in the tree structure. Thus, searching with the MeSH term “Eye Diseases” automatically includes all the MeSH terms located beneath “Eye Diseases” corresponding to diseases of the eye in general. As done in other studies (Ugolini et al., 2007, 2010; Ramos, González-Alcaide & Bolaños-Pizarro, 2013; Neri et al., 2015), an analysis of the MeSH terms used by PubMed indexers to classify the articles was done by calculating their frequency in the retrieved articles. Check tags, i.e. MeSH terms obligatorily used by indexers to describe recurrent patterns in medical articles, were excluded from this frequency analysis because of their compulsory and recurrent character. They are shown in Supplemental Table S1. The co-occurrence is the simultaneous association of two identical MeSH terms in different articles. The frequency and the percentage of co-occurrence of the MeSH terms located beneath the MeSH term “Eye Diseases” in articles has been calculated. Likewise, the frequency of all other MeSH terms not situated beneath the MeSH term “Eye Diseases” retrieved has also been calculated. The average yearly growth rate of the literature related to eye diseases was calculated as the mean percentage of annual growth rate for the period studied using the equation: Annual Growth Rate = Current Year Total Number of Articles – Previous Year Total Number of Articles/Previous Year Total Number of Articles (Deshazo, Lavallie & Wolf, 2009). The average yearly growth rate was also calculated for the whole PubMed database for the period 2010–2014. Bradford’s law has been used extensively in the information science literature to describe the dispersion of articles in any scientific field (Goffman & Warren, 1969), or to identify “core journals” of serial titles (Deshazo, Lavallie & Wolf, 2009; Venable et al., 2014). Bradford’s law states that “If scientific journals are arranged in order of decreasing productivity of articles on a given subject, they may be divided into a nucleus of periodicals more particularly devoted to the subject and several groups or zones containing the same number of articles as the nucleus.” To identify the core journals containing articles dedicated to eye diseases, Bradford’s law was applied by dividing the journals ranked according to publication output frequency into three groups with each group representing approximately the same number of articles. The 2013 Journal Citation Reports (JCR) (Thomson Reuters, New York, USA) was used for Impact Factor (IF) determination and for the ranking of the journal in the category “Ophthalmology” of the JCR. Language of publication was determined using the “Language” field for all articles retrieved. The percentage of papers published in English in the entire PubMed database between 2010 and 2014 was also calculated using the following search strategy: Medline [sb] OR publisher [sb] OR pubstatusaheadofprint AND 2010:2014 [DP] AND journal article [PT] where sb means “subset.” A quantitative evaluation of the scientific production related to eye diseases was done by evaluating the total number of articles published for each country. To implement a qualitative evaluation, each article was related to the corresponding journal manually in the JCR 2013 to determine the Five-Year Impact Factor (5-Y IF). If a journal did not have an 5-Y IF, the value zero was assigned to the article. For each country, the cumulative 5-Y IF was calculated as the sum of the 5-Y IF of all articles. The mean Five-Year Impact Factor (m5-Y IF) was calculated as the cumulative 5-Y IF divided by the number of articles. For the quantitative and the qualitative evaluation, we calculated the number of publications and the cumulative and m5-Y IF according to countries and continents. The country of affiliation of the first author was determined by the address in the “Affiliation” field. When the country was absent in the address, it was determined from the city or email address using an Internet search engine if necessary. If the name of a country no longer existed (e.g. Yugoslavia), the city was used to find the name of the existing country in 2015. England, Scotland, Northern Ireland, and Wales were grouped into the United Kingdom. Hong Kong was considered as part of China. The GDP is the market value of all officially recognized final goods and services produced within a country in a given period. GDP per capita is often considered an indicator of a country’s standard of living (World Bank Group: http://www.worldbank.org/). For each country and each continent, the 5-Y IF GDP index (cumulative 5-Y IF per 1 billion US dollars of GDP) and the 5-Y IF population index (cumulative 5-Y IF per million inhabitants) were calculated using the World Development Indicators from the online databases of the World Bank (http://data.worldbank.org/). The 5-Y IF GDP and the 5-Y IF population index were calculated using the mean GDP and mean number of inhabitants from 2010 to 2013 (data for 2014 were not available). Countries were clustered by their continent according to the United Nations classification (United Nations Statistics Division- Standard Country and Area Codes Classifications: http://unstats.un.org/unsd/methods/m49/m49regin.htm). The search in PubMed resulted in a total of 62,123 articles over the period 2010 to 2014. We calculated that the average growth rate of literature related to eye diseases was 4.27%. We also calculated that the average growth rate for the whole PubMed database was 6.59% for the same period. Thus, the difference in growth rates between the growth rate of eye diseases and all scientific production in the PubMed database is equal to −2.32 (4.27 − 6.59), which indicates a moderate interest of the scientific community for eye diseases for the studied period, and a stabilization of publication rate (Michon & Tummers, 2009). The 62,123 articles found in the present study were published in 3,368 different journals over the period 2010 to 2014. Fifty-four journals of 58 belonging to the category “Ophthalmology” in the JCR were found in the 3,368 journals retrieved. These 54 journals published 29,183 articles of the 62,123 (46.98%) that we found in the present study. According to Bradford’s law, the total number of articles compared to the number of journals in order of decreasing productivity was divided into 3 zones containing approximatively the same number of articles. The first third of the total number of articles (n = 20,779) represented the journals (n = 19; 0.56%) that published between 3,619 and 589 articles (Table 1). The middle third (n = 20,637) corresponds to the journals (n = 118; 3.5%) that contained an average number of articles (between 290 and 579 articles), and the last third (n = 20,707) includes the “long tail” of journals (n = 3,231; 95.9%) that published the fewest articles (less than 114). It is important to note that 1,428 journals (42.4%) published only 1 or 2 articles related to eye diseases over the 5-year study period. Thirty-one different languages were identified in the 62,123 articles retrieved. The five predominant languages were English (n = 55,829; 89.87%), German (n = 1,401; 2.26%), French (n = 1,132; 1.82%), Chinese (n = 927; 1.49%), and Japanese (n = 641; 1.03%). All other languages amounted to less than 1%. The percentage of articles in English in the entire PubMed database was 93.49% for the same period. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease and cancer, account for roughly 70% of deaths worldwide, and the burden is increasingly concentrated in low- and middle-income countries (World Health Organization, 2018). Primary care is widely regarded as the setting best placed to deliver the continuous, coordinated and person-centred care that chronic conditions require, and it is central to global strategies for universal health coverage (Starfield et al., 2005; Kruk et al., 2018). Consequently, a large number of interventions have been developed to improve the detection, management and long-term support of people with NCDs in primary care. These include structured self-management education, decision support for clinicians, task-shifting to nurses and community health workers, audit and feedback, and multicomponent models of integrated care (Wagner et al., 2001; Coleman et al., 2009). Many of these have been evaluated in randomised controlled trials (RCTs), and systematic reviews of such trials suggest that effects are frequently modest and heterogeneous, with similar interventions producing markedly different results in different settings (Smith et al., 2016; Tricco et al., 2012). This heterogeneity is not surprising. Interventions in primary care are typically complex: they contain several interacting components, target multiple levels (patients, providers, practices and organisations), require tailoring to local circumstances, and depend on the behaviour of many actors (Craig et al., 2008; Hawe et al., 2004). Their effects are shaped by the context in which they are delivered, including the structure and financing of the health system, workforce availability, and local social and cultural norms (Pfadenhauer et al., 2017). A conventional trial that reports only whether an intervention "worked" on average cannot explain why an effect was or was not observed, whether the intervention was delivered as intended, which components were responsible for any change, or how the findings might transfer to other settings. Null results are particularly difficult to interpret without this information, since they may reflect a flawed intervention theory, poor implementation, or an unsuitable context (Oakley et al., 2006). Process evaluations (PEs) have been advocated to address these limitations. The UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions defines their purpose as examining implementation (what is delivered, and how), mechanisms of impact (how delivered activities produce change), and contextual factors that shape both (Moore et al., 2015). By answering questions of for whom, how and why interventions have an impact, PEs help distinguish implementation failure from theory failure, identify unintended consequences, and provide the information needed to refine interventions and support scale-up. Earlier frameworks for describing implementation, including those of Steckler and Linnan (2002), Baranowski and Stables (2000) and Grant et al. (2013), and widely used theory-based approaches such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (Damschroder et al., 2009), normalisation process theory (May and Finch, 2009) and RE-AIM (Glasgow et al., 1999), have similarly emphasised the need to examine reach, fidelity, dose and adaptation alongside outcomes. The MRC guidance further stresses that PEs should be underpinned by a clearly articulated intervention theory or logic model, so that data collection and analysis are directed at the hypothesised causal pathway rather than being purely descriptive (Moore et al., 2015; De Silva et al., 2014). Despite this guidance, there is concern that PEs are inconsistently conducted and reported. Reviews in other fields, such as school-based health promotion and public health, have found that PEs often lack explicit theoretical grounding, apply inconsistent definitions of constructs such as fidelity and context, and rely on convenience samples or purely descriptive data (Oakley et al., 2006; Bonell et al., 2012; Grant et al., 2013). Where theory is absent, it is difficult to judge whether the right processes were examined, and findings from one PE are hard to compare with, or build upon, those of another. Improvements in reporting have been proposed, including the Standards for Reporting Implementation Studies (StaRI) and the TIDieR checklist for describing interventions (Pinnock et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2014), but it is unclear how far these have influenced practice in primary care. Several existing syntheses bear on this topic but leave important gaps. Systematic reviews of barriers and facilitators to implementing chronic disease interventions have mostly drawn on qualitative studies or on single conditions, for example diabetes self-management or hypertension control, and have not examined how the underlying evaluations were designed (Gagliardi et al., 2011; Jeet et al., 2017). Reviews of PEs, in contrast, have concentrated on public health, school or community settings, where the organisational features of primary care, such as gatekeeping, multidisciplinary teams, continuity of care and payment systems, are less salient. To our knowledge, no review has systematically described the methods used in PEs conducted alongside RCTs of primary care interventions for NCDs, assessed the extent to which they follow recognised guidance, and synthesised their findings on implementation barriers and facilitators across conditions and health systems. This matters because primary care interventions are increasingly being adapted for and tested in diverse settings, including low-resource health systems where many of the assumptions underpinning interventions developed in high-income countries may not hold (Kruk et al., 2018; Legido-Quigley et al., 2013). We therefore conducted a systematic review of PEs alongside RCTs of primary care interventions aimed at improving outcomes for people with NCDs, using the MRC guidance for process evaluation as an organising framework. We had two aims. First, to describe and appraise the methods used, including the use of intervention theory and theoretical frameworks, the choice of data collection and analytic approaches, sampling, and the integration of qualitative and quantitative data. Second, to synthesise the principal findings of these evaluations regarding barriers and facilitators to implementation, with attention to the context in which interventions were delivered. This review makes three contributions. It provides the first comprehensive overview of how PEs in primary care chronic disease research are being designed and reported, identifying strengths and weaknesses that can inform methodological practice and the application of the MRC guidance. It offers a cross-condition synthesis of recurring implementation challenges, which may be more useful to intervention developers and health system decision-makers than condition-specific accounts. Finally, it draws out implications for how future interventions should be developed, with the aim of improving the fit between interventions, local needs and health system contexts, and thereby the chance that effective interventions can be implemented and sustained at scale. Design and reporting We conducted a systematic review of process evaluations (PEs) conducted alongside randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42016035572) before screening began. The review is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). We used the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions (Moore et al., 2015) as an organising framework for both data extraction and appraisal. This guidance specifies that a PE should describe the intervention and its causal assumptions, examine implementation (fidelity, dose, adaptations and reach), explore mechanisms of impact, and consider contextual influences on delivery and outcomes. Because we did not assess intervention effectiveness, we did not conduct a meta-analysis. Eligibility criteria Eligibility was defined using the Population, Intervention, Context and Study design elements. Studies were eligible if they reported a PE, defined as a study that assessed implementation, mechanisms of impact or context, alongside an RCT (individually or cluster randomised, including pilot and feasibility trials with a full-scale PE). The trial intervention had to be delivered in primary care or community-based primary health care settings and aim to improve outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, cancer, mental health conditions and musculoskeletal disorders. Interventions could be targeted at patients, providers, practices or the wider health system. We excluded studies of infectious diseases, those conducted solely in hospital or specialist settings, trials with no PE component, and PEs reported only as protocols without results. Studies that reported only a post hoc satisfaction survey, with no examination of implementation or context, were also excluded. The PE did not need to be published in the same paper as the trial, but it had to be clearly linked to an identified RCT. We included reports in any language for which translation was feasible, and the search was restricted to 1998 onward, reflecting the emergence of the contemporary complex intervention literature (Campbell et al., 2000). Search strategy We searched MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), EMBASE and Global Health from 1998 to June 2018. The strategy combined three concept blocks: (1) process evaluation terms (for example “process evaluation”, “implementation”, “fidelity”, “mixed methods”, “qualitative”); (2) primary care terms (for example “primary health care”, “general practice”, “community health worker”, “family practice”); and (3) non-communicable disease terms, together with a trial filter to identify randomised designs. Search terms were developed with an information specialist, piloted against a set of known PEs, and adapted to the syntax and controlled vocabulary of each database. We supplemented electronic searches by hand-searching the reference lists of included studies and of relevant methodological reviews, and by checking trial registries and linked publications to identify companion papers reporting PE findings. Study selection Records were exported to reference management software and de-duplicated. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text assessment. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating where consensus could not be reached. Agreement between reviewers at the full-text stage was calculated using Cohen’s kappa: κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the proportion expected by chance. Reasons for exclusion at full-text stage were recorded. Data extraction A standardised extraction form, structured around the MRC framework and piloted on five studies, was used. Two reviewers independently extracted data and a third reviewer checked a random sample (approximately 20%) of extractions for accuracy and consistency as quality assurance. Extracted information included: bibliographic details; country and income setting (World Bank classification); clinical condition; description of the intervention using the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) items (Hoffmann et al., 2014); level of intervention (patient, provider, practice or system); trial design; and the timing of the PE relative to the trial (concurrent, prospective or retrospective). For PE methods, we extracted whether the authors stated an explicit intervention theory or logic model; whether an existing theoretical or implementation framework was used (for example the Normalisation Process Theory, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, RE-AIM, or the Theoretical Domains Framework); the PE research questions; the components assessed (context, recruitment and reach, fidelity, dose, adaptation, mechanisms of impact, and unintended consequences); data collection methods (interviews, focus groups, observation, surveys, document review, routine data and audio-recorded consultations); sampling strategy and sample size; the respondents included; analytic approach; and whether qualitative and quantitative data were triangulated or integrated. We also recorded whether the PE findings were used to interpret trial outcomes. For findings, we extracted all reported barriers and facilitators to implementation, together with the authors’ interpretations and illustrative data, where available. These were extracted from the results and discussion sections, including participant quotations. Quality and reporting appraisal Rather than excluding studies on quality grounds, we appraised the methodological characteristics of PEs against the MRC guidance to describe the field and to identify strengths and weaknesses. Criteria included clarity of intervention theory, a priori specification of PE questions, appropriateness of sampling, use of multiple data sources, transparent analysis, and consideration of context. Qualitative components were additionally assessed with reference to the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative checklist, with the aim of contextualising the weight placed on individual findings rather than determining inclusion. Appraisal was carried out independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Data synthesis We conducted a two-part synthesis. First, the methodological data were summarised descriptively using frequencies and proportions, stratified by country income group, intervention level and whether a theoretical framework had been used. We cross-tabulated the presence of an explicit intervention theory against these characteristics, and used Fisher’s exact test to explore associations

Deep neural networks now inform decisions in settings where errors are costly, including autonomous driving (Bojarski et al., 2016), medical diagnosis (Esteva et al., 2017), and the prioritization of candidate compounds in drug development (Preuer et al., 2018). In these settings a point prediction is rarely sufficient. A practitioner also needs to know how much confidence to place in it, whether the input lies within the regime the model was trained on, and whether the model's uncertainty is large enough to justify deferring to an expert or running another experiment. Standard networks trained by maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimation provide no such information, and their softmax outputs are often poorly calibrated and overconfident, particularly under distribution shift (Guo et al., 2017; Ovadia et al., 2019). Uncertainty quantification (UQ) has therefore become a central requirement for the responsible deployment of deep learning. The Bayesian framework offers a principled route to UQ. Placing a prior over network weights and computing the posterior given the training data yields a predictive distribution, p(y | x, D) = ∫ p(y | x, w) p(w | D) dw, which captures epistemic uncertainty arising from limited data (Neal, 1996; MacKay, 1992). For modern networks with millions of parameters, however, the posterior is intractable, and exact methods such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo scale poorly. A range of approximations has been developed, including variational inference (Graves, 2011; Blundell et al., 2015), stochastic-gradient MCMC (Welling & Teh, 2011), Laplace approximations (Ritter et al., 2018), and deep ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). Among these, Monte Carlo dropout, or permanent dropout, has been especially popular because of its simplicity (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016). Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) is ordinarily used as a regularizer during training and switched off at test time. Gal and Ghahramani showed that if dropout is left active during inference, then T stochastic forward passes with independently sampled masks yield draws from an approximate posterior, corresponding to a variational distribution over weights. The predictive mean and variance can then be estimated as E[y] ≈ (1/T) Σₜ f(x; ŵₜ), Var[y] ≈ (1/T) Σₜ f(x; ŵₜ)ᵀ f(x; ŵₜ) − E[y]ᵀ E[y] + τ⁻¹I, where ŵₜ denotes the weights under the t-th dropout mask and τ is a precision term capturing observation noise. The method requires no change to the architecture or training procedure of an existing dropout network, which has made it attractive in applications ranging from medical image segmentation (Kendall & Gal, 2017) to molecular property prediction. This convenience comes at a cost that is easily overlooked. Permanent dropout moves the computational burden from training to inference: each prediction requires T forward passes, with T typically in the tens to hundreds for stable estimates of predictive variance and tail quantiles. The energy cost of inference is already a dominant share of the lifecycle footprint of deployed models (Patterson et al., 2021), and multiplying it by T can be prohibitive for high-throughput screening pipelines, for real-time systems, and especially for edge platforms with strict power budgets, such as wearable medical devices, vehicles, and embedded sensors. Practitioners are consequently forced to trade uncertainty fidelity against latency and energy, often by reducing T to the point where the uncertainty estimates become noisy. Neuromorphic computing offers a potential remedy. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse, event-driven binary spikes rather than dense real-valued activations, and when run on dedicated hardware such as Intel's Loihi (Davies et al., 2018), IBM's TrueNorth (Merolla et al., 2014), or SpiNNaker (Furber et al., 2014), they can perform inference at orders of magnitude lower energy than conventional processors, since computation occurs only when spikes arrive (Roy et al., 2019). Historically, the obstacle to adopting SNNs has been the difficulty of training them directly, owing to the non-differentiability of spike generation (Neftci et al., 2019). An alternative has emerged in the form of ANN-to-SNN conversion, in which a conventional network is trained with standard backpropagation and its parameters are then mapped onto spiking neurons whose firing rates approximate the original activation functions (Cao et al., 2015; Diehl et al., 2015; Rueckauer et al., 2017). Recent work has refined these techniques to the point of near-lossless conversion for deep architectures (Hunsberger & Eliasmith, 2016; Deng & Gu, 2021; Bu et al., 2022), and software frameworks such as Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014) make such conversions accessible and deployable across neuromorphic backends via NengoDL and related tools. Despite this progress, the neuromorphic literature has focused almost exclusively on point-prediction accuracy, typically on image classification benchmarks. Whether converted SNNs can faithfully reproduce the full predictive distribution of a stochastic network, and thus support Bayesian-style UQ, has received comparatively little attention. The few existing efforts on probabilistic spiking computation have either exploited the intrinsic stochasticity of spiking neurons for sampling (Buesing et al., 2011; Neftci et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2019) or trained Bayesian SNNs through bespoke procedures, requiring specialized training and sacrificing the convenience of conversion. No work, to our knowledge, has asked whether permanent dropout, with its unusually simple requirement of random masking at inference, can be carried over to a converted SNN so that the energy advantages of neuromorphic hardware offset the multiplicative cost of repeated sampling. The question is non-trivial: spiking approximations introduce their own quantization and temporal noise, which could inflate, distort, or mask the dropout-induced variability on which the UQ depends. In this paper we investigate the following research question: can a dropout network be converted to a spiking network such that, when dropout is kept active during inference, the resulting predictive distribution is statistically indistinguishable from that of the original classical network? Answering this would establish that approximate Bayesian inference via permanent dropout can be moved onto neuromorphic platforms without retraining or architectural redesign. We study this question in a domain where UQ is essential: predicting the response to combination drug therapies in cancer treatment. Combination therapy datasets are high-dimensional and expensive to generate, experimental coverage of the combinatorial space is sparse, and clinical or experimental follow-up based on overconfident predictions is costly (Preuer et al., 2018; Menden et al., 2019). Calibrated uncertainty is therefore directly actionable, guiding which combinations merit validation. Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose a pipeline that trains a standard dropout network, converts it to a spiking network in Nengo, and applies stochastic masking at inference to generate Monte Carlo predictive samples on spiking hardware-compatible models. Second, we compare the classical and spiking predictive distributions using measures of both pointwise agreement and distributional similarity, including means, variances, and calibration. Third, we show on a cancer combination therapy dataset that the spiking approximation yields a predictive distribution practically indistinguishable from the classical one. Finally, we discuss the implications for energy-efficient UQ at scale and on edge devices, and identify the conditions under which the approach is expected to hold. Data We used a publicly available combination-therapy screen of the kind commonly used for synergy prediction, drawn from the NCI-ALMANAC collection (Holbeck et al., 2017) and accessed through the DrugComb portal (Zagidullin et al., 2019). Each record is a pair of anticancer compounds, tested at fixed concentrations on one cell line from the NCI-60 panel, together with a continuous synergy score. We used the ComboScore as the regression target. Each drug was encoded by a 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprint of radius 2 (Rogers and Hahn, 2010). Fingerprints were combined symmetrically by summing the two drug vectors, so that the representation did not depend on drug order. Cell lines were represented by baseline expression of the 1,000 most variable genes, standardized and reduced to 100 principal components. The input vector was therefore the summed drug fingerprint, the cell-line components, and the log concentrations of both drugs. We split the data at the level of drug pairs, not individual measurements, to avoid leakage between replicates and dose levels: 70% for training, 10% for validation, and 20% for testing. Targets were standardized with training-set statistics. Because uncertainty quantification matters most under distribution shift, we also built a second test set, in which all combinations containing a randomly held-out 10% of compounds were removed from training. Results are reported for both the in-distribution and the shifted test sets. The entire partitioning procedure was repeated for five random seeds. Classical network and permanent dropout The reference model was a fully connected feed-forward network with three hidden layers of 256 units. It used ReLU activations and no biases on the hidden layers, which simplifies conversion to spiking form (Rueckauer et al., 2017). Dropout with probability p = 0.2 followed each hidden layer. Training minimized mean squared error with L2 weight decay, using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015). Learning rate and weight decay were tuned on the validation set, and early stopping was applied. At inference we kept dropout active, following the Monte Carlo dropout interpretation of Gal and Ghahramani (2016). For an input x, T stochastic forward passes with independent Bernoulli masks produce outputs ŷt = f(x; W, mt), where mt ~ Bernoulli(1−p). The predictive mean and variance are approximated as μ(x) ≈ (1/T) Σt ŷt, σ²(x) ≈ (1/T) Σt (ŷt − μ)² + τ⁻¹, where τ⁻¹ is the observation-noise term. We estimated τ⁻¹ on the validation set by maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood. Unless stated otherwise, T = 100. We assessed the convergence of the predictive moments by varying T from 5 to 500. Conversion to a spiking network The trained network was converted to a spiking network without retraining the weights, following the rate-based conversion framework of Diehl et al. (2015) and Rueckauer et al. (2017). Hidden ReLU units were replaced by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with membrane dynamics τm dv/dt = −v + J(t), with a spike emitted and the membrane reset when v reaches its threshold. Here J is the input current and τm the membrane time constant. For constant input J > 1, the steady-state firing rate is r(J) = [τref − τm ln(1 − 1/J)]⁻¹, where τref is the refractory period. We used τm = 20 ms and τref = 2 ms. The ReLU slope was matched to the LIF response curve through a gain scaling. Gains were normalized layer by layer using the 99.9th percentile of activations on the training data, to keep firing rates within the dynamic range of the neurons and to limit saturation (Rueckauer et al., 2017). For comparison, we also fine-tuned a variant of the network in which the LIF rate curve was smoothed (soft LIF) in the forward pass during training (Hunsberger and Eliasmith, 2015). Synaptic connections used exponential low-pass filters with τs = 5 ms to smooth spike trains. We implemented the network in Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014) and used NengoDL (Rasmussen, 2019) for weight transfer and for batched simulation. The simulation time step was 1 ms. Each test input was presented as a constant current for a window of Tpres = 100 ms, and the network state was reset between presentations.
