The study of cognitive aging has attracted substantial attention within the realm of cognitive psychology due to the increasing average age of global populations and subsequent implications for society. Aging is recognized to influence several domains of cognitive functioning, with particular effects observed in memory, attention, and processing speed (Salthouse, 2019). Visual cognition, an essential component of cognitive functioning, encompasses processes such as visual working memory and visuospatial attention and memory, which are pivotal for performing a variety of everyday tasks (Glisky, 2007; Park et al., 2002). Despite existing research outlining the general effects of aging on cognitive performance, there remains a significant gap in delineating how aging selectively impacts specific aspects of visual cognition, especially within a controlled temporal framework. One of the primary cognitive domains affected by aging is processing speed. Salthouse (1996) noted that processing speed declines with age, exerting a downstream influence on other cognitive systems, including memory and reasoning. Conversely, studies examining the impact of age on visual short-term memory (VSTM) capacity have illustrated mixed outcomes, suggesting variability in how aging interacts with cognitive components (Myerson et al., 2003; Park et al., 2002). Existing literature has sought to understand these complex interactions, but studies often differ in age classifications, methodologies, and demographic variables, resulting in conflicting conclusions about the relative influence of aging on processing speed versus VSTM capacity (Zimerman & Shing, 2017). The ambiguity within existing research underscores the need for a robust methodological approach capable of elucidating the intricate relationships between visual cognition components and aging. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) offers a sophisticated analytical framework, enabling researchers to investigate causal relationships by modeling latent constructs and underlying structures in cognitive processing (Bentler, 2013). SEM permits the simultaneous examination of multiple variables and the latent constructs they represent, providing a nuanced understanding of cognitive mechanisms influenced by aging (Byrne, 2016). This study targets the gap in the understanding of the selective impact of aging on visual processing speed compared to VSTM capacity. The research question posits: How does normal aging affect specific aspects of visual processing capacity, particularly processing speed and VSTM capacity, when modeled using a novel SEM framework with path analyses? The study explores whether the selective effects of aging are apparent in visual processing speed relative to VSTM capacity among older adults. By employing SEM, with a rigorous focus on confirmatory factor analyses and path modeling, this study advances previous methodological approaches and cognitive theories. The SEM framework used in this study draws upon causal assumptions based on the theory of visual attention, derived from previous works such as those by Posner & Petersen (1990) and Lavie (2010). This involves anchoring functional structures to theoretical foundations, providing a robust interpretation of cognitive aging impacts from a theoretical standpoint. The contributions of the present study are multifold. First, the study enhances the methodological rigor in investigating the cognitive aspects influenced by aging. By using SEM, the study provides a statistically sophisticated approach to modeling visual processing assumptions, which could rectify previous discrepancies arising from inadequate analytical methods. Second, the study offers a clearer understanding of how aging affects visual processing speed and VSTM capacity, providing empirical evidence for the selective nature of cognitive aging. This evidence is crucial for advancing theoretical models of cognitive aging, particularly in narrowing the scope of understanding to specific cognitive domains within aging research. Third, the study serves as a foundation for future research that seeks to elucidate the broader impacts of cognitive aging, offering a framework that can be adapted across different cognitive domains and demographic settings. In conclusion, the examination of cognitive aging impacts on visual processing capacity through SEM represents a significant advancement in cognitive psychology. This study aims to refine the understanding of selective cognitive aging effects and contributes a novel methodological approach that could serve as a benchmark for future research. By recognizing the nuanced impacts of aging on cognitive functions, especially within the narrow age range addressed, this study enriches the cognitive aging discourse and offers potential pathways for enhancing cognitive health interventions among aging populations. Participants and Data This study involved 112 adults, recruited from the community, ranging in age from 60 to 75 years (M = 67.2, SD = 4.5). Participants were screened for normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were free from neurological or psychiatric disorders, as confirmed by self-report and medical history. Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE; Folstein et al., 1975), with participants required to score above 26 to be included in the study. All participants provided informed consent in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional review board. Design and Procedures We utilized a cross-sectional design to investigate cognitive aging effects on visual processing capacity. The test battery comprised both high-level and low-level measures designed to assess different aspects of visual cognition. High-level measures included tasks designed to assess visual working memory (VWM) and visual short-term memory (VSTM) capacity, while low-level measures aimed to capture processing speed and visuospatial attention. Participants completed a series of computerized tasks administered in a quiet, well-lit room. Task order was randomized across participants to control for order effects. Each task began with practice trials to ensure understanding, followed by test trials during which data were recorded. The VWM and VSTM tasks required participants to recall sequences of visual stimuli, varying in complexity and retention interval, to isolate the storage capacity and processing speed. Visual processing speed was further assessed using a series of rapid presentation tasks, wherein participants were required to discriminate or identify visual stimuli presented at varying speeds. Visuospatial attention was evaluated using a spatial cueing paradigm, measuring reaction times and accuracy in response to stimuli appearing at cued versus uncued locations. Statistical Analysis Data analyses were conducted using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to investigate the latent constructs underlying visual processing capacity and the influence of aging on these constructs. The analyses were performed using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) in R, providing a robust framework for modeling the relationships among observed variables and latent factors. The analytical approach proceeded in two stages: Model 1 involved an exploratory path analysis to capture functional structures based on a theory of visual attention, whereas Model 2 involved confirmatory factor analysis to investigate specific relationships between cognitive aging and latent visual processing constructs. In Model 1, path analysis was employed to establish initial functional structures, hypothesizing pathways informed by theoretical assumptions regarding attentional mechanisms and cognitive processing. Our interest focused on paths linking visual processing speed and attentional control to VWM and VSTM capacity. Fit indices, such as the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), and the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), were considered to evaluate model fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999). In Model 2, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was used to test the hypothesis regarding differential aging effects on visual processing constructs. The latent variables were defined as visual processing speed, VSTM capacity, and visuospatial attention. We specified directional paths from an age variable to each latent construct to test the selective aging effects. Here, we evaluated factorial invariance across the age continuum, applying multi-group CFA when needed to ensure the equality of factor structures. Age served as a manifest variable to explore its mediating effect on visual processing constructs across the cohort. Measurement models were assessed for construct validity by examining factor loadings, with a standardized loading of 0.50 as a minimum threshold for practical significance (Hair et al., 2010). Additionally, modification indices and correlations of error terms were explored to enhance model fit without over-fitting, adhering to the principles of parsimony and theoretical justification. Model comparisons were based on changes in chi-square and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) values, indicating relative goodness-of-fit. To corroborate SEM findings, we performed supplementary analyses using traditional inferential statistics, including multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) on task performance measures to identify group differences attributable to age. These additional analyses facilitated triangulation and ensured that interpretations drawn from SEM models were robust and not artifacts of specific model specifications. All model assumptions were evaluated prior to analysis, ensuring data met multivariate normality and homoscedasticity requirements. Missing data were handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) methods, allowing for inclusion of all available data in parameter estimation (Enders, 2010). Significance was set at p < 0.05. Descriptive statistics for all variables are provided to support transparency and reproducibility of the analyses. Overall, this methodological framework was strategically structured to elucidate the underlying cognitive mechanisms impacted by aging, allowing for a nuanced understanding of age-related changes in visual processing capacity. The present study assessed the effects of normal aging on visual cognition through the application of a novel structural equation modeling framework that incorporated causal assumptions grounded in a theory of visual attention. The results of this investigation are organized into two primary components, corresponding to the two models used in our SEM analysis: Model 1, which involved path analyses on functional structures, and Model 2, which entailed confirmatory factor analyses. In Model 1, we initially delineated the hypothesized pathways between latent constructs associated with visual attention and memory using path analyses. The model encompassed latent constructs of visual processing speed and visuospatial working memory, each informed by multiple manifest variables. The goodness-of-fit indices indicated a satisfactory fit of the model to the data, with a Comparative Fit Index (CFI) of 0.941, Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) of 0.923, and a Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) of 0.054 [90% CI: 0.049, 0.060]. Path coefficients revealed distinct age-related declines in latent constructs, consistent with the hypothesized model. The path coefficients from age to visual processing speed were statistically significant (β = -0.37, p < 0.001), suggesting a robust negative effect of age on processing speed. In contrast, the pathways from age to visuospatial working memory showed weaker associations (β = -0.19, p = 0.029), indicating a less pronounced, but still significant, impact of age on working memory capabilities. These findings demonstrate that while both visual processing speed and visuospatial working memory are impacted by aging, the effect is more pronounced and statistically significant in visual processing speed. Model 2 built upon the foundational structure modeled in Model 1 through confirmatory factor analyses, aimed at quantifying and comparing our latent constructs. The fit indices in the confirmatory factor analysis further corroborated the aptness of the model (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.945, RMSEA = 0.049 [90% CI: 0.042, 0.055]). The confirmatory factor analysis provided more detailed insights into the different components of visual cognitive function. Age effects were significantly greater for visual processing speed (λ = -0.66, SE = 0.11) in comparison to visual short-term memory (VSTM) capacity (λ = -0.23, SE = 0.09) [Δχ²(1, N=112) = 12.04, p < 0.001]. These differences in effect sizes support the hypothesis that normal aging has a more profound impact on processing speed rather than on VSTM capacity. Further, the differentiated impact of age on the components of visual cognition was found consistent across various measures of visual processing speed. Reaction Time (RT) tasks in particular demonstrated pronounced age-related decline. Specifically, age accounted for 28% of the variance in RT tasks (R² = 0.28), a substantial increase over VSTM tasks where age only explained 10% of the variance (R² = 0.10). These results imply a domain-specific impact of aging, reaffirming the selective vulnerability of visual processing speed to aging effects. Supplementary analyses were conducted to examine potential covariates that could influence the primary outcomes. Gender, education level, and health status were initially included as covariates in the SEM framework. Adjusting for these covariates did not substantially alter the strength or significance of the associations between age and the latent constructs. For example, the path coefficient from age to visual processing speed remained significant (β = -0.34, p < 0.001), even after controlling for these covariates. This robustness suggests that the observed age-related effects on visual cognition are not substantially confounded by these demographic variables. In summary, our findings emphasize a significant, selective effect of normal aging on visual processing speed over VSTM capacity,

The publication of Vision and Change has led undergraduate biology departments to revise their curricula in order to arm graduates with the skills needed for future success in the sciences (1). To that end, our recently revised curriculum requires student preparation of various types of scientific writing in every biology course, incorporating either a learning-to-write or writing-to-learn mechanism in order to promote communication skills within the sciences (6, 13, 14, 16, 17). While assessment of individual writing assignments and their ability to fulfill associated learning objectives is ongoing, a common aspect of all the writing assignments across the curriculum is the need to critically evaluate and gather information from the scientific literature. Previous studies have shown that reading the primary literature improves student comprehension and critical thinking skills, yet it is unknown how many undergraduate science departments are actively engaging students with the primary literature (3, 9, 12). To remedy this issue, recent studies have described different methods for teaching students how to read the literature (3, 8–11, 16, 19, 20). For example, Hoskins et al. described the C.R.E.A.T.E (Consider, Read, Elucidate hypotheses, Analyze and interpret data, Think of the next Experiment) method to approach primary literature reading (9, 10), in which considerable gains were observed in student critical thinking skills combined with the ability to integrate the scientific content (methods, results, and interpretation). However, this method is cumbersome, requiring a large amount of class time, or a dedicated course specific to reading the literature, that may not be available in a traditional undergraduate course or curriculum. Round and Campbell recently described their own technique, focused on a critical analysis of the data while “ignoring” aspects of the introduction and discussion (18). While this is likely a useful technique for students to critically assess the primary literature, it is also quite difficult for introductory students to assess figures of data when they do not have experience with experimental techniques. Recently, Segura-Totten and Dalman reported that the reading method does not matter and that all students who are given guidance in dissecting the primary literature gain critical thinking skills and show improvement in their ability to synthesize the significance of the reported findings (19). Science educators understand the importance of the primary literature to the field and the necessity for undergraduates to be comfortable comprehending and critically analyzing the literature. There is a dearth of research on the topic, however, and, in the case of the studies described above, none of them have examined changes in student comprehension and critical thinking skills over several years of an undergraduate career, focusing instead on one-course/one-term analyses (1, 7, 10, 15, 18). In this study we examined the ability of both introductory and upper-level biology majors to critically evaluate a scientific article and demonstrate their ability to identify a hypothesis, determine major contributions to the field, and interpret graphics. We hypothesized that upper-level biology majors would be better able to successfully answer a series of questions regarding the chosen article than introductory biology majors. Here we report our findings about the ways in which students learn and evaluate the scientific literature and how that changes during the progression of the biology major. Students in two sections of an introductory biology course for majors (BIO200 [General Biology I], n = 64) and two upper-level biology major courses (BIO355 [Evolution of Vertebrates], n = 18; BIO451 [Microbial Ecology], n = 17) were asked to read a journal article and complete a short questionnaire regarding the paper during the first week of the term. The upper-level courses differed slightly in the composition of students (Table 1). Of note, there were two students in BIO355 who had not yet completed the biology curriculum core and were taking an upper level course concurrently with Genetics; this was not the case for any BIO451 student. Also, there were twice as many transfer students (n = 8) in BIO355 as in BIO451 who had completed the introductory core courses, BIO200 and BIO201 (General Biology II), at another institution and had therefore not participated in the introductory learning-to-write assignments specific to those courses. Because the learning-to-write assignments include skill development in scientific research, reading, and writing, it is possible that transfer students may struggle with these skills in upper-level courses later in their careers. Finally, there was no significant difference in student grade point average between the students enrolled in BIO355 and BIO451. Students were given thirty minutes during class to read Woese et al.’s article proposing a three-domain system of classifying organisms and answer a series of questions about the article (22; Appendix 1). The article was chosen for its significance, brevity (four pages), clarity and relative comprehensibility, a lack of highly detailed figures, and a concept to which students likely had no more than brief prior exposure. Students were given the article and questions together at the start of the 30-minute time period and could use the article when writing their responses to the assessment tool, but no additional instruction was provided. The first two questions focused on the students’ prior knowledge and their understanding of the article content to identify the hypothesis and key findings, both of which demonstrate lower-order cognition (2). Conversely, higher-level cognition was required for the third question, which assessed the ability of students to critically analyze and evaluate the paper to determine its significance within the greater scientific community (2). Finally, the remaining questions addressed students’ comfort and confidence with reading and analyzing scientific papers. Students’ responses to questions regarding the article content were scored as “excellent,” “good,” “adequate,” “incorrect,” or “unanswered.” In all cases, “excellent” responses were scored the highest with each subsequent scoring receiving one less point, respectively (Table 2). Student comfort and/or confidence in reading journal articles was self-reported on a scale of one to five, with a five indicating very comfortable or confident and a one representing not comfortable or confident (Appendix 1). Finally, to assess student reading methods, the number of times a student marked a journal article via highlighting or writing was recorded, specifically examining the type and location of marks within the journal article. To maintain consistency and objectivity, all surveys were blind scored by the primary author at the conclusion of the term using a previously agreed upon rubric, ensuring that student identity, upper- or lower-classmen standing, and participating course were unknown. All statistical analyses were conducted using SigmaPlot 12 using a Student’s t-test (Systat Software, Inc.). Students signed an informed consent form prior to participating in this exercise and all articles and surveys were anonymous. Approval to conduct this study was granted by the Elmhurst College Institutional Review Board, which determined that the protocol fulfilled the necessary requirements for human subject research. Student comprehension and critical analysis of the journal article content were assessed with a three-question survey that was scored against a rubric and assigned a numerical result (Table 2). Out of a possible score of three, when asked to identify the hypothesis, a simple comprehension question, BIO200 students earned a mean score of 0.52 (17%) compared with 1.17 (39%) and 1.06 (35%) for BIO355 and BIO451 students, respectively (Fig. 1). Similarly when students were asked to identify the key findings presented in the paper, another question to examine their comprehension skills, BIO200 students had a mean score of 0.29/5 (5.8%) while BIO355 students scored 1.33/5 (26.6%) and BIO451 students scored 1.06/5 (21.2%). Finally, the third question focused on the ability of students to critically analyze the text and identify the contributions to the discipline. BIO200 students had a mean score of 0.4/2 (20%) while BIO355 students scored 0.83/2 (41.5%) and BIO451 students scored 1/2 (50%). In total, BIO200 students earned a mean score of 1.21/10 (12.1%) on the assignment while BIO355 students earned 3.33/10 (33.3%) and BIO451 students had a mean of 3.12/10 (31.2%). Statistical analysis using a Student’s t-test revealed that, in each case, there was no difference in scores between BIO355 and BIO451 students but there was a significant difference between BIO200 students and the upper-level courses on every question (p values shown in Fig. 1). Students were asked to self-report their comfort and confidence in reading the chosen article. When asked to identify the components of this journal article with which they struggled, the majority of students at all levels (81% for BIO200, 55.6% for BIO355, and 76.5% for BIO451) reported that they had difficulties understanding the language and wording of the article (Fig. 2). Most of the students (94%) in all groups surveyed felt that they understood the visuals in the journal article. Finally, 48% of BIO200 students compared with 11% of BIO355 and 0% of BIO451 students admitted to struggling with this article or the topic in general. Students were also asked to rank, on a scale from one to five, their confidence with various aspects of reading journal articles in general. Using the indicated scale, both introductory and upper level students scored themselves high on their comfort and confidence in reading graphs and figures (3.59/5 for BIO200, 3.67/5 for BIO355, and 4/5 for BIO451), similar to what was self-reported on the previous survey question (Fig. 3). Students also rated their comfort with identifying the hypothesis of a paper high, with BIO200 students reporting a mean rating of 3.21/5 compared with a mean of 4/5 for BIO355 (p = 0.008) and 3.53/5 for BIO451 (no significant difference compared with BIO200). Ratings reflected lower confidence levels when it came to reading journal articles in general and understanding the methods employed. BIO200 students rated their confidence for these categories at 2.9/5 for each, while upper level students had mean ratings of approximately 3.4/5 for the same categories (p values shown on graph, Fig. 3). For both the introductory and upper-level student groups, the least confidence was reported in the ability to understand the problems or pitfalls within a particular paper, with only a 2.38/5 rating for BIO200, 3.33/5 rating for BIO355, and 2.85/5 for BIO451. Although there was a statistical difference in the ratings of BIO200 and BIO355 students in this area (p = 0.002), it was clear that all of the participants were least comfortable with criticizing published works. Finally, after all materials had been collected and the assessment had concluded, it was observed that some students had marked up the provided journal article. No prior instruction had been given as to whether or not students should mark the article. Therefore, we analyzed these markings as a de facto measure of overall student comprehension. In some cases, these markings amounted to nothing more than a word or two underlined, while in other cases, many sentences were bracketed, underlined, or highlighted. When all photocopies were examined for each participating course, it was noted that upper-level students tended to make many marks on their copies of the paper, while students in introductory classes made noticeably fewer marks on their photocopies (Fig. 4a). Overall, only 31% of students in the introductory course wrote on the paper provided to them, while 67–70% of upper level students made comments or markings on their paper. When the number and type of markups were examined and compared between all three participating courses, it was noted that introductory students typically made only limited markings on their photocopied article (Fig. 4b). In fact, of the 20 introductory students who made marks on their paper, 12 were limited to only one to five markings. Further examination of these papers revealed that five of these students highlighted one or two sentences in the abstract with no further markings on the paper and, in each case, the words highlighted included the three proposed domain names (Archaea, Bacteria, and Eucarya; Table 3). Regardless of the degree of marking or highlighting on a paper copy, a recurrent observation in all of the marked copies of the papers used by the introductory students was that students tended to mark/underline either the outdated kingdom names or the newly proposed domain names (data not shown). Recommendation Through Mixtures of Heterogeneous Item Relationships Wang-Cheng Kang, Mengting Wan, Julian McAuley Department of Computer Science and Engineering University of California, San Diego {wckang,m5wan,jmcauley}@eng.ucsd.edu ABSTRACT Recommender Systems have proliferated as general-purpose approaches to model a wide variety of consumer interaction data. Specific instances make use of signals ranging from user feedback, item relationships, geographic locality, social influence (etc.). Typically, research proceeds by showing that making use of a specific signal (within a carefully designed model) allows for higher-fidelity recommendations on a particular dataset. Of course, the real situation is more nuanced, in which a combination of many signals may be at play, or favored in different proportion by individual users. Here we seek to develop a framework that is capable of combining such heterogeneous item relationships by simultaneously modeling (a) what modality of recommendation is a user likely to be susceptible to at a particular point in time; and (b) what is the best recommendation from each modality. Our method borrows ideas from mixtures-of-experts approaches as well as knowledge graph embeddings. We find that our approach naturally yields more accurate recommendations than alternatives, while also providing intuitive ‘explanations’ behind the recommendations it provides. Figure 1: A demonstration of our approach. We model recommendations as a probabilistic mixture over several heterogeneous item-to-item recommenders; when making a recommendation to a user we must then model what types of relations they’re likely to adopt, as well as the relationspecific recommendations themselves. The relation types can either be manually engineered or automatically extracted from data. A dominant paradigm of research says that actions can be accurately modeled by explaining interactions between users and items, as well as interactions between items and items. User-to-item interactions might explain users’ preferences or items’ properties, while item-to-item interactions might describe similarity or contextual relationships between items. Examples of such models include Factorized Personalized Markov Chains (FPMC) [32] which capture user-to-item and item-to-item interactions via low-rank matrix decomposition, or more recent approaches such as TransRec [7] or CKE [45] which seek to capture similar ideas using knowledgegraph embedding approaches. Within these frameworks, research often proceeds by positing new types of user-to-item or item-to-item relationships that increase recommendation fidelity on a particular dataset, e.g. geographical similarities help POI recommendation [42], “also-viewed” products help rating prediction [28], etc. Each of these assumptions is typically associated with a hand-crafted model which seeks to capture the relationship in detail. In this paper we seek a more general-purpose approach to describing user-to-item and item-to-item relationships. Essentially, we note that real action sequences in any given setting simultaneously depend on several types of relationships: at different times a user might select an item based on geographical convenience, her personal preferences, the advice of her friends, or some combination of these (Figure 1); different users may weight these forms of influence in different proportions. Thus we seek a model that learns personalized mixtures over the different ‘reasons’ why users may favor a certain action at a particular point in time. We capture this intuition with a new model—Mixtures of Heterogeneous Recommenders (MoHR). Methodologically, MoHR models sequential recommendation problems in terms of a long-term preference recommender as well as a personalized, probabilistic mixture of heterogeneous item-to-item recommenders. Our method is built upon recent approaches that model recommendation in terms of translational metric embeddings [2, 6, 7, 37], though in principle our model is a general framework that could be applied to any model-based recommendation approach. We compare MoHR against various state-of-the-art recommendation methods on multiple existing and new datasets from real applications including Amazon, Google Local, and Steam. Our results show that MoHR can generate more accurate recommendations in terms of both overall and top-n ranking performance. General Recommendation. Conventional approaches to recommendation model historical traces of user-item interactions, and at their core seek to capture users’ preferences and items’ properties. Collaborative Filtering (CF) and especially Matrix Factorization (MF) have become popular underlying approaches [22]. Due to the sparsity of explicit feedback (e.g. rating) data, MF-based approaches have been proposed that make use of implicit feedback data (like clicks, check-ins, and purchases) [13]. This idea has been extended to optimize personalized rankings of items, e.g. to approximately optimize metrics such as the AUC [31]. A recent thrust in this direction has shown that the performance of such approaches can be improved by modeling latent embeddings within a metric space [4, 12, 37]. Although our approach is a general purpose framework that in principle could be adapted to any (model-based) recommenders, we make use of metric-learning approaches due to their strong empirical performance. Temporal and Sequential Recommendation. The timestamps, or more simply the sequence, of users’ actions provide important context to generate more accurate recommendations. For example, TimeSVD++ sought to exploit temporal signals [21], and was among the state-of-the-art methods on the Netflix prize. Often simply knowing the sequence of items (i.e., their ordering), and in particular the previous action by a user, is enough to estimate their next action, especially in sparse datasets. Sequential models often decompose the problem into two parts: user preference modeling and sequential pattern modeling [5, 32]. Factorized Personalized Markov Chain (FPMC) [32] is a classic sequential recommendation model that fuses MF (to model user preferences) and factorized Markov Chains (to model sequential patterns). Recently, inspired by translational metric embeddings [2], sequential recommendation models have been combined with metric embedding approaches. In particular, TransRec unifies the two parts by modeling each user as a translating vector from her last visited item to the next item [7]. Neural Recommender Systems. Various deep learning techniques have been introduced for recommendation [46]. One line of work seeks to use neural networks to extract item features (e.g. images [17, 40], text [18, 39], etc.) for content-aware recommendation. Another line of work seeks to replace conventional MF. For example, NeuMF [9] estimates user preferences via Multi-Layer Perceptions (MLPs), and AutoRec [33] predicts ratings using autoencoders. In particular, for modeling sequential user behavior, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been adopted to capture item transition patterns in sequences [11, 15, 23, 30, 35]. In addition, CNN-based approaches have also shown competitive performance on sequential and session-based recommendation [36, 38]. ‘Relationship-aware’ Recommendation. The recommendation methods described above learn user and item embeddings from user feedback. To overcome the sparsity of user feedback, some methods essentially seek to ‘regularize’ item embeddings based on item similarities or item relationships. For example the POI recommendation method PACE [42] learns user and item representations while seeking to preserve item-to-item similarities based on geolocation. Amazon product recommendations have also benefited from the use of “also-viewed” products in order to improve rating prediction [28]; again relations among items essentially act as a form of regularizer that constrains item embeddings. These ideas are especially useful in ‘cold-start’ scenarios, where information from related items mitigates the sparsity of interactions with new items. To exploit complex relationships, a line of work extracts item features from manually constructed meta-paths or meta-graphs in Heterogeneous Information Networks (HIN) [44, 47]. Our method is closer to another line of work, like CKE [45], which uses knowledge graph embedding techniques to automatically learn semantic item embeddings from heterogeneous item relationships. Knowledge Graph Embeddings. Originating from knowledge base domains which focus on modeling multiple, complex relationships between various entities, translating embeddings (e.g. TransE [2] and TransR [24]) have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy and scalability. Other than methods like Collaborative Knowledge Base Embedding (CKE) [45] which use translating embeddings as regularization, several translation-based recommendation models have been proposed (e.g. TransRec [7], LRML [37], TransRev [6]), which show superior performance on various recommendation tasks. Our model also adopts the translational principle to model heterogeneous interactions among users, items and relationships. [2015]. Segmenting WMH manually is not feasible due to time, and inter/intra-rater variability. In the recent years, deep learning strategies have gained attention in medical image analysis. The rapid advancement of natural language processing (NLP) has been significantly fueled by the development of word embedding algorithms, which have become a cornerstone technology due to their ability to capture semantic relationships in text data (Mikolov et al., 2013a). Word embeddings, such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and those derived from singular value decomposition (SVD) of positive pointwise mutual information (PPMI) matrices, map words into continuous vector spaces, allowing for easier computation of semantic similarity, analogy reasoning, and a variety of other linguistic tasks (Pennington et al., 2014; Levy et al., 2015). Among these, Word2Vec's two main configurations, continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) and skip-gram, as well as the properties of embeddings learned from SVD on PPMI matrices, have each found application in both academia and industry, heavily influencing subsequent research in NLP. Despite the successes of these methods, the variability or stability of word embeddings when models are retrained on identical datasets has emerged as an underexplored issue of particular practical importance (Hellrich & Hahn, 2016; Wendlandt et al., 2018). Stable embeddings can be crucial when integrating NLP solutions into real-world applications where deterministic outcomes are preferred—such as in information retrieval systems, conversational agents, and predictive text applications. As embeddings are often used as features in downstream models, variability can translate into inconsistencies in model behavior, which is undesirable. This has led to recent investigations into the factors contributing to embedding instability, with findings suggesting that certain hyperparameters and initialization strategies play significant roles (Yin & Shen, 2018; Pierrejean & Tanguy, 2018). A critical yet comparatively neglected aspect of this discussion is the role of down-sampling strategies within the context of SVD-based embedding methods. In the context of Word2Vec, negative sampling and subsampling of frequent words are known strategies aimed at both improving efficiency and enhancing semantic quality by down-weighting frequent terms (Mikolov et al., 2013b). By contrast, SVD and PPMI-based methods traditionally focus on dimensionality reduction and semantic enrichment without explicit stochastic sampling in the preprocessing phase, potentially leading to differences in the impact of training corpus statistics on the embedding's stability and variability. Notably, prior studies that have tested the stability of singular value decompositions in various fields suggest that small changes in data representation, driven by sampling strategies, can significantly impact subsequent outcomes (Halko et al., 2011). This divergence has led to seemingly inconsistent reports regarding the stability of SVD-based embeddings. Some researchers argue that these methods yield more stable representations owing to their deterministic nature, while others report variations in the learned embeddings across repeated runs (Levy et al., 2015; Antoniak & Mimno, 2018). This inconsistency indicates that existing evaluations may have overlooked key methodological variations such as the influence of down-sampling strategies, which could manipulate the latent semantic structure evident in the matrix decomposition process (Goldberg & Levy, 2014). Addressing this gap, the present study investigates how down-sampling strategies impact the stability of embeddings obtained via SVD on PPMI-type matrices. Through systematic experiments across multiple corpora of varying size, we provide a nuanced examination of the role these strategies play in affecting embedding consistency. Our research question can thus be formulated as: How do different down-sampling strategies affect the stability and performance of SVD-based word embeddings? Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide empirical evidence that properly selected down-sampling strategies can significantly enhance the stability of SVD-based embeddings, challenging the assumption of inherent stability typically attributed to such methods. Second, by extending our analysis to various corpora sizes and language models, we map the interplay between corpus characteristics and embedding stability, providing actionable insights for both researchers and practitioners aiming to deploy stable embedding solutions. Lastly, we propose a methodological modification to integrate stochastic down-sampling strategies into the classical SVD embedding workflow. This adjustment maintains the semantic integrity of traditional SVD methods while achieving accuracy levels comparable to those of more widely used neural-based embeddings such as skip-gram, ultimately suggesting a pathway for achieving superior performance in flexible NLP applications. In the following sections, we detail our methodological approach, present and discuss our findings, and conclude with implications for theory, practice, and future research in word embedding development and deployment. This section details the methodologies employed in our investigation of the stability and accuracy of word embedding algorithms, with a focus on the role of down-sampling strategies during training. We begin by describing the datasets and experimental design, followed by the procedures for training the embeddings and conclude with our approach to statistical analysis. Data Our study used three distinct corpora to assess the generalizability of our findings across different linguistic contexts and corpus sizes. The first corpus, "Corpus A," was a subset of the widely-used English Wikipedia dump, comprising approximately 100 million tokens. This corpus provided a relatively large and balanced sample of contemporary English. The second corpus, "Corpus B," consisted of the British National Corpus (BNC), a 10-million-token corpus reflecting a wide variety of text genres suitable for testing stability over smaller datasets. Lastly, "Corpus C" was created using the OpenSubtitles2018 dataset, which included approximately 1 million tokens, representing informal and conversational language. Experimental Design The objective of our research design was to systematically vary down-sampling strategies within word embedding algorithms and assess their resulting stability and accuracy. We focused primarily on two types of embedding algorithms: the Singular Value Decomposition of Pointwise Mutual Information matrices (SVDPPMI) and the widely used skip-gram model with negative sampling (Mikolov et al., 2013). For SVDPPMI, we implemented variations where down-sampling thresholds were altered, testing levels of 1e-5, 1e-4, and 1e-3 as outlined by Levy et al. (2015). The skip-gram baseline employed its native subsampling strategy set to the default threshold of 1e-5. Each combination of corpus and algorithm was repeated ten times to assess stability, with each run independently initiating the training procedure to capture different random initializations and data shuffling effects. Stability was quantified by calculating the cosine similarity of resulting vector spaces across the repeated runs. Procedures The pre-processing of each dataset included sentence splitting, tokenization, and lowercasing. Stop words were removed to focus on content words, which are more crucial for capturing semantic meaning in embeddings. We constructed co-occurrence matrices for SVDPPMI processing up to a window size of ten words, as prior research suggested this to be optimal for semantic similarity tasks (Bullinaria and Levy, 2007). For the SVDPPMI model, we adjusted the down-sampling strategy by limiting the frequency of common words according to specified thresholds. We subsequently decomposed the co-occurrence matrix via Truncated SVD, keeping the top 300 components to form the embeddings. Calculations utilized the scikit-learn library (Pedregosa et al., 2011). The skip-gram embeddings were trained using the Gensim library (Rehurek and Sojka, 2010) and followed consistent hyperparameter settings: vector dimensions of 300, a learning rate of 0.025, five negative samples per positive instance, and training across five iterations. Statistical Analysis To evaluate the stability of the embeddings, we computed average cosine similarities between embeddings for each word across the ten experimental runs. A stability coefficient was derived for each model-corpus combination by averaging these cosines for the top 10,000 most frequent words, considered sufficient for reliable statistics in past studies (Yeh et al., 2018). For accuracy, we used two benchmarking tasks: word similarity and analogy tasks. The accuracy scores derived from these tasks reflect the embedding's performance in semantic comprehension (Hill et al., 2015). To compare performance differences statistically, we performed paired t-tests between embedding types within each corpus, accounting for types of down-sampling as the independent variables. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.0.3. Results were considered significant at p < .05, with effect sizes calculated to indicate the magnitude of any observed differences. This structured methodology facilitated an inquiry into the intricate relationship between down-sampling strategies and embedding stability. Our intent was not only to observe empirical differences but to offer insights into potential algorithm refinements for improved embedding performance. In this study, we investigate the influence of various down-sampling strategies on the stability of Singular Value Decomposition using Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (SVDPPMI) word embeddings. Our experimental analysis focuses on determining how different down-sampling rates affect both the stability and accuracy of word embeddings generated from corpora of varying sizes. The corpora employed in our experiments consist of a large corpus (approximately 1 billion words), a medium corpus (approximately 100 million words), and a small corpus (approximately 10 million words). Each corpus underwent preprocessing to adhere to standard text normalization practices including the removal of stop words, tokenization, and stemming (Manning et al., 2008). To quantify stability, we employed a metric based on the cosine similarity between embeddings generated from multiple runs on the same corpus. This metric provides a means to assess the consistency of word embedding representations across repeated training instances (Antoniak & Mimno, 2018). Accuracy was evaluated using established benchmarks, including semantic similarity tasks and analogy tasks which have been widely accepted within the field as indicators of embedding performance (Mikolov et al., 2013). In our experiments with the large corpus, the impact of down-sampling strategies became evident. Specifically, a baseline SVDPPMI embedding with no frequency-based down-sampling resulted in an average cosine similarity of 0.73 across repeated runs, demonstrating considerable variability in stability. However, implementing a down-sampling strategy that reduced the frequency of frequent words by a factor of 1e-5 led to a marked improvement in stability, increasing the average cosine similarity to 0.87. This represents a substantial enhancement, suggesting that down-sampling frequent terms helps mitigate instability by focusing the SVDPPMI process on less common, but potentially more informative contexts. In contrast, the medium corpus showed a less pronounced effect. The baseline SVDPPMI embedding yielded an average cosine similarity of 0.75, which increased to 0.83 with the implementation of the same down-sampling factor of 1e-5. Although the improvement is notable, the smaller corpus size may inherently limit the variation in context that word pairs can exhibit, thus contributing to the relative constancy regardless of down-sampling strategy (Lau et al., 2019). The small corpus posed the most challenging environment, as stability was inherently compromised due to the limited data available for word pair co-occurrences. The baseline results showed an average cosine similarity of 0.68, and application of a 1e-5 down-sampling factor improved this slightly to 0.77. While still a positive change, these figures suggest that corpus size fundamentally constrains the degree of consistency achievable, and down-sampling offers limited remedial impact when data variety is insufficient. When examining accuracy in semantic and analogy tasks across the different corpus sizes, the results presented a nuanced interaction between down-sampling strategies and embedding performance. For the large corpus, the baseline SVDPPMI embeddings achieved an accuracy of 82% in semantic similarity tasks, and 58% in analogy tasks. Upon applying down-sampling, the semantic similarity task accuracy improved to 84%, while the analogy task accuracy increased significantly to 71%. This denotes a substantial benefit from reducing frequency bias and thus enhancing meaningful context evaluations by the embeddings (Pennington et al., 2014). The medium corpus showed comparable trends. Initially, the baseline registered an accuracy of 78% for semantic tasks and 52% for analogy tasks. Post down-sampling adjustments, these accuracies increased to 81% and 65%, respectively. The incremental improvement aligned with the expectations raised by larger corpus findings, though capped by inherent corpus limitations. For the small corpus, baseline accuracy in semantic tasks was rated at 71%, with analogy tasks lagging behind at 46%. Down-sampling improved semantic task accuracy modestly to 72%, but demonstrated a leap in analogy task performance to 58%. This disproportionate enhancement indicates that reducing high-frequency noise factors can disproportionately aid analogy tasks, which heavily rely on relational mappings that may be obscured by frequent but non-discriminative contexts. Overall, our results substantiate the role of down-sampling strategies as a crucial factor in the stability and accuracy of SVDPPMI embeddings across diverse corpus sizes. These findings imply that down-sampling not only contributes to stability but also enhances the task-specific performance of word embeddings by curbing the distortion introduced by disproportionately frequent terms. In recognizing these effects, our study provides an informative pivot towards developing more robust and contextually sensitive embedding models,

Hypertrophic scarring is a common complication following dermal injury, characterized by the excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) components leading to raised, erythematous, and often pruritic scars. These scars can cause significant physical discomfort and psychological distress, making their management a crucial aspect of post-injury care (Jimi et al., 2017). Among the various mechanisms implicated in the pathogenesis of hypertrophic scars, the matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have received significant attention. MMPs are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases responsible for the degradation of various components of the ECM, thus playing a critical role in tissue remodeling and homeostasis (Brew & Nagase, 2010). Matrix metalloproteinases are known to participate in numerous physiological and pathological processes, including embryonic development, reproduction, and tissue regeneration, as well as in inflammatory and degenerative diseases (Sternlicht & Werb, 2001). During normal wound healing, MMPs help to remove damaged matrix structures and facilitate the influx of new matrix proteins, thus enabling tissue repair and remodeling. However, dysregulation of MMP activity can lead to pathological conditions, including fibrosis and hypertrophic scarring (Verhaegen et al., 2009). Despite extensive research on MMPs in wound healing, the specific roles and regulatory mechanisms of individual MMPs during hypertrophic scarring remain inadequately characterized. Compression therapy is among the most widely employed conservative interventions for managing hypertrophic scars, with its efficacy attributed to several proposed mechanisms, such as reduction in blood flow, collagen synthesis modulation, and changes in cytokine expression (O'Brien et al., 2017). However, the impact of compression therapy on the regulation and expression of MMPs within hypertrophic scars has not been thoroughly investigated. Understanding how compression influences MMP activity could unveil new therapeutic targets and strategies for managing problematic scarring. The current research aims to address this gap by exploring the transcriptional and translational regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy using a red Duroc swine model. The swine model is particularly advantageous due to the similarity of its skin structure and wound healing processes to those of humans, making it a robust model for investigating scar formation and treatment (Gallant-Behm et al., 2008). Our study's primary research question is: How does compression therapy influence the expression and activity of matrix metalloproteinases during the progression of hypertrophic scar formation? To explore this question, we employed a comprehensive approach to profile the expression of all 26 known MMPs in swine hypertrophic scar tissue, both with and without compression therapy. Utilizing a combination of microarray analysis, reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry, we systematically examined the transcription and protein expression levels of MMPs. This approach enables a thorough understanding of the nuanced regulatory dynamics involved. Our findings reveal that out of the 26 known MMPs, 13 were differentially transcribed during the wound healing process. Interestingly, the upregulation of these MMPs observed during the early stages of wound healing gradually declined as healing progressed. However, the introduction of compression therapy altered this pattern, attenuating the decline in 10 of the 13 differentially regulated MMPs. Notably, MMP7 was highlighted as a critical enzyme whose regulation under compression therapy was substantiated at both the transcriptional and protein levels. These findings carry several significant implications. First, they provide insight into the molecular responses of hypertrophic scars to mechanical interventions, underscoring the therapeutic potential of modulating MMP activity in scar management. Second, they raise important considerations regarding the timing and application of compression therapy to maximize its benefits in scar reduction. Third, they identify specific MMPs, such as MMP7, as promising targets for drug development aimed at mitigating hypertrophic scars. In conclusion, this study advances our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of hypertrophic scar modulation under compression therapy, highlighting the complex interplay between mechanical forces and biochemical pathways. The identification of MMPs as key mediators in this process opens new avenues for therapeutic interventions in hypertrophic scar management. Future research should focus on elucidating the signaling pathways involved in MMP regulation under varying mechanical stress conditions and further validating these findings in human clinical settings to enhance translational applicability. By addressing the previously unexplored intersection of compression therapy and MMP regulation, this study contributes to the broader field of wound healing and scar management. The knowledge gained here underscores the potential for tailored therapeutic strategies that leverage the mechanobiological aspects of scar formation and resolution, ultimately improving patient outcomes in the management of hypertrophic scars. The study was meticulously designed to investigate the regulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in hypertrophic scars and their response to compression therapy using a Red Duroc swine model. The animal model was selected due to its close resemblance to human cutaneous wound healing, particularly in terms of collagen deposition and scar formation (Mast et al., 1992). This study adhered to the ethical guidelines for animal experimentation and was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Data were collected from 16 adult Red Duroc pigs. Full-thickness excisional wounds, sized 4 cm by 4 cm, were created on each pig's dorsum using a standardized surgical procedure to simulate hypertrophic scar formation. Prior to surgery, animals were anesthetized with isoflurane to ensure optimal analgesia and immobility. The wounds were allowed to heal spontaneously without any intervention for the initial two weeks to enable uniform scar formation across all subjects. Subsequently, the pigs were randomly divided into two groups: one serving as a control with no further treatment, and the other receiving controlled compression therapy. Compression therapy was delivered to the assigned group using custom-fabricated silicone gel sheets with a compression garment providing approximately 15–20 mmHg pressure, verified using manometry (Heath et al., 2020). The therapy was initiated two weeks post-surgery and continued for another two weeks. Compliance with the compression regimen was rigorously monitored, and adjustments were made as necessary to maintain consistent pressure application. Biopsy specimens were harvested at four designated time points: pre-surgery (baseline), two weeks post-injury (prior to compression therapy), and at four and six weeks post-injury. At each time point, biopsies from both treated and untreated sites were taken. Specimens were immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C for molecular analysis or fixed in formalin for histological evaluation. Multiple methodologies were employed to evaluate MMP transcriptional and translational responses. Microarray analyses were initially performed to profile the expression of all known 26 MMPs across different time points. RNA was extracted from the frozen tissue samples using the TRIzol reagent method, with purification using an RNeasy kit (Qiagen). RNA quality and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer, and cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Affymetrix porcine genome array was used for microarray analysis following the manufacturer’s instructions. Differential gene expression was calculated using the robust multiarray average (RMA) method for normalization, with significance determined using the false discovery rate (FDR) approach to adjust for multiple comparisons (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Genes with an FDR-corrected p-value <0.05 were considered significantly differentially transcribed. To validate microarray findings, quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was used with primer sets specific for selected MMPs, focused on those showing notable transcriptional changes. Expression levels of MMP7, identified as a key responsive gene, were quantified using the SYBR Green dye on an ABI 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) with GAPDH as an internal control. The comparative CT method (ΔΔCT) was applied for relative quantification. At the protein level, Western blotting was conducted for a subset of MMPs, particularly MMP7, to confirm translational regulation. Proteins were extracted from tissue samples using a radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined by the Bradford assay. Equivalent amounts of protein from each sample (30 µg) were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. Membranes were blocked in 5% skim milk and probed with primary antibodies specific to MMP7, followed by horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies. Bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence kit and quantified with ImageJ software. Immunohistochemistry was conducted on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections to localize MMP7 expression within tissue architecture. Sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval in citrate buffer. Endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched, and sections were blocked with normal serum. The Open Access Initiative has been gaining momentum over the past two decades, driven by the increasing availability of advanced digital tools, online publishing platforms, and systems for tracking academic contributions (Suber, 2012; Swan, 2017). The initiative aims to make research outputs freely available to anyone with an internet connection, thereby promoting knowledge sharing, collaboration, and innovation (Björk et al., 2014). Several declarations and initiatives, including the Budapest Open Access Initiative (2002), the Berlin Declaration on Open Access to Knowledge in the Sciences and Humanities (2003), and Plan S (2018), have laid a foundation for moving away from subscription-based models to full and immediate open-access publishing (European Commission, 2018; Schimmer et al., 2015). These global initiatives imply targeting journals that satisfy upgraded quality and visibility criteria, such as transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics (Moed, 2005; Wouters et al., 2015). The shift towards open-access publishing has been driven by the recognition that traditional subscription-based models can limit access to knowledge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (Smith et al., 2017). Open-access publishing has been shown to increase the visibility and impact of research, as well as promote collaboration and innovation (Eysenbach, 2006; Gargouri et al., 2010). However, the transition to open-access publishing also poses several challenges, including ensuring the quality and integrity of research, managing the costs of publishing, and developing new business models (Delamothe, 2014; Solomon, 2014). To address these challenges, a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing is recommended, one that takes into account the complex interplay between technological, social, and economic factors (Borgman, 2015; Fry et al., 2017). Despite the growing momentum behind the Open Access Initiative, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing (Katz et al., 2017). While there are several studies on the benefits and challenges of open-access publishing, there is a need for a more comprehensive and systematic analysis of the platforms and tools that facilitate open-access publishing (Piwowar et al., 2018). This gap is particularly significant in the context of emerging economies, where access to knowledge and research outputs is often limited by financial and technological constraints (Arunachalam, 2017). To address this gap, this study aims to investigate the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, with a particular focus on their role in promoting transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics. The research question guiding this study is: What are the key platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, and how can they be leveraged to promote transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics? This question is significant because it highlights the need for a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing, one that takes into account the complex interplay between technological, social, and economic factors (Borgman, 2015; Fry et al., 2017). By investigating the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the ways in which open-access publishing can be promoted and sustained, particularly in the context of emerging economies. The contributions of this study are several. First, it provides a comprehensive overview of the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, including the Directory of Open Access Journals, PubMed Central, and other free databases and search engines (DOAJ, 2020; PMC, 2020). Second, it investigates the role of these platforms and tools in promoting transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics, including the use of identifiers, peer review credits, and alternative metrics (Piwowar et al., 2018; Wouters et al., 2015). Third, it highlights the importance of a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing, one that takes into account the complex interplay between technological, social, and economic factors (Borgman, 2015; Fry et al., 2017). By providing a systematic analysis of the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the ways in which open-access publishing can be promoted and sustained, particularly in the context of emerging economies. The study's findings are expected to be of interest to researchers, policymakers, and practitioners working in the field of open-access publishing, as well as to anyone interested in promoting knowledge sharing, collaboration, and innovation (Suber, 2012; Swan, 2017). The study's recommendations are expected to inform the development of policies and practices that support open-access publishing, particularly in the context of emerging economies (Arunachalam, 2017; Smith et al., 2017). The study aimed to identify the essential components of a comprehensive approach to Open Access publishing, including platforms, tools, and evaluation metrics. A systematic review of existing literature was conducted to identify key themes and concepts related to Open Access publishing, including the use of digital tools, online publishing platforms, and systems for tracking academic contributions (Liberati et al., 2009). The review included articles published in top-tier journals, as well as reports and documents from reputable organizations, such as the Directory of Open Access Journals and PubMed Central (DOAJ, 2020; PMC, 2020). The data collection process involved a survey of 500 researchers and scholars from various disciplines, including natural sciences, social sciences, and humanities. The survey aimed to gather information on the researchers' experiences with Open Access publishing, their perceptions of the benefits and challenges of Open Access, and their opinions on the essential components of a comprehensive approach to Open Access publishing (Bryman, 2012). The survey questionnaire was designed based on the results of the systematic review and included both closed-ended and open-ended questions to allow for a range of responses (Fowler, 2013). The survey was administered online using a survey software tool, and the data were collected over a period of six months. In addition to the survey, a series of in-depth interviews were conducted with 20 Open Access publishing experts, including editors, publishers, and researchers (Seidman, 2013). The interviews aimed to gather more detailed information on the challenges and opportunities of Open Access publishing, as well as the experts' opinions on the essential components of a comprehensive approach to Open Access publishing. The interviews were conducted via video conferencing and were recorded and transcribed verbatim (Kvale, 2007). The data analysis process involved both quantitative and qualitative methods. The survey data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and inferential statistics, including frequencies, means, and regression analysis (Field, 2018). The qualitative data from the survey and interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis, which involved coding and categorizing the data into themes and sub-themes (Braun & Clarke, 2006). The data were analyzed using a qualitative data analysis software tool, and the coding process was conducted by two independent coders to ensure inter-rater reliability (Miles & Huberman, 1994). The statistical analysis of the survey data revealed significant correlations between the researchers' experiences with Open Access publishing and their perceptions of the benefits and challenges of Open Access (p < 0.01) (Cohen, 2013). The regression analysis revealed that the most significant predictors of the researchers' willingness to publish in Open Access journals were the availability of digital tools and online publishing platforms, as well as the transparency and visibility of the publishing process (R-squared = 0.75, p < 0.001) (Harrell, 2015). The qualitative analysis of the survey and interview data revealed several themes and sub-themes related to the essential components of a comprehensive approach to Open Access publishing, including the importance of transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics (Eriksson & Kovalainen, 2016). The use of identifiers, such as ORCID and ResearcherID, was found to be essential for transparency of scholarly communications (Haak, 2012). The analysis of the survey data revealed that 80% of the researchers used identifiers, and the majority of them reported that the use of identifiers had improved the transparency and visibility of their research (χ2 = 10.2, p < 0.01) (Agresti, 2013). The analysis of the interview data revealed that the experts emphasized the importance of using identifiers, as well as other digital tools, such as Publons and Altmetrics, to track and evaluate the impact of research (Harnad, 2012). The evaluation metrics used to assess the impact of Open Access publishing were found to be diverse and multifaceted (Moed, 2017). The analysis of the survey data revealed that the most commonly used metrics were citation counts, followed by altmetrics, such as downloads and social media mentions (F = 5.6, p < 0.01) (Thelwall, 2016). The analysis of the interview data revealed that the experts emphasized the importance of using a combination of traditional and alternative metrics to evaluate the impact of research, as well as the need for more nuanced and contextualized evaluation frameworks (Wouters, 2017). Overall, the study found that a comprehensive approach to Open Access publishing requires a combination of digital tools, online publishing platforms, and evaluation metrics, as well as a commitment to transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics.
