The transformative concept of the smart home has increasingly gained traction over the past decade, sparking innovation and integration in various domains of technology and everyday living. As a nexus of varied interconnected devices, smart homes depend heavily on efficient data management and network optimization to ensure a seamless user experience. With smart home devices expected to surpass a value of $53 billion by 2022 (Smith & Jones, 2020), the sophistication and volume of data traffic within and through these environments are poised to escalate. Key to realizing the potential of smart homes is the capacity for efficient and secure network management, specifically concerning the classification and handling of encrypted data packets. As smart devices proliferate, they necessitate differing levels of network resources and quality of service (QoS) provisions depending on their functions, which range from simple sensors to bandwidth-intensive high-definition streaming equipment (Chen et al., 2021). Traditional network management methodologies, which primarily focus on static resource allocation and heuristic-based traffic identification techniques, fall short in addressing dynamic and complex traffic patterns typically observed in smart home environments. This limitation primarily stems from an inability to accurately classify encrypted data packets, which are prevalent in ensuring the privacy and security of personal information (Kumar, Liu & Kortesniemi, 2019). Moreover, with the increasing reliance on software-defined networking (SDN), there is a growing capacity for improved network management from the core network. However, solely optimizing core networks has proven insufficient for end-to-end QoS enhancement. This inadequacy demonstrates the need for innovative approaches that extend into the user's domain, particularly at the level of the smart home gateway (Wang & Zanella, 2022). Despite these advances, existing approaches largely overlook the potential of leveraging machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques for encrypted packet classification directly in smart home gateways. Current solutions often involve binary-specific components and integrations that require significant computational resources, making them impractical for real-time applications within the limited capabilities of many smart home systems (Haddadi et al., 2020). Furthermore, many techniques suffer from invasiveness, compromising privacy or affecting the encryption levels of the data packets being transmitted (Brown, Anderson & Flynn, 2019). These gaps present an opportunity for developing a hierarchical classification framework that accommodates both the overarching service level and finer application-specific requirements, potentially enabling more effective resource allocation and QoS provision. This consideration raises a pertinent research question: How can a hierarchical encrypted packet classification scheme be devised and implemented effectively within smart home gateways to enhance end-to-end QoS while maintaining user privacy and security? Addressing this challenge requires a multidimensional approach that not only leverages advanced ML and DL models for real-time classification but also integrates seamlessly into existing network infrastructures without necessitating significant resource overheads. The contribution of this paper is twofold. Firstly, it proposes a novel hierarchical classification scheme that divides the classification process into two distinct levels: service-level and application-level. At the service level, we propose a rapid classification system based on state-of-the-art deep learning architectures that can categorize data packets according to their QoS requirements. This approach allows for real-time adaptation and management of network resources, ensuring that high-priority services receive the necessary bandwidth and latency requirements. Secondly, for application-level classification, we develop a non-real-time framework that focuses on providing high accuracy by deploying more computationally intensive but precise classification models. This dual-model approach not only facilitates more nuanced network management but also offers additional functionalities such as statistical data collection, billing, and the provisioning of context-aware services, all without infringing upon user privacy or compromising data security. Through an extensive evaluation, this paper demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed classification scheme in a practical smart home scenario. The results indicate significant improvements in the precision of encrypted packet classification and resource allocation efficiency, thereby enhancing the overall QoS and QoE for end-users. By bridging the existing gap between network management and user-centric service delivery within smart home ecosystems, this research sets a foundation for future developments in secure and efficient smart home data management methodologies. This section describes the methodologies deployed to investigate the efficacy and accuracy of a hierarchical encrypted packet classification system, specifically designed for smart home gateways. The methods encapsulated herein include the data collection process, the research design, the experimental procedures, and the statistical analysis employed. Data collection focused on two primary sources: publicly available encrypted datasets and proprietary data from a smart home environment simulated to reflect real-world conditions. The public dataset comprises network traffic traces encompassing a wide array of applications commonly used in smart home settings, such as real-time video streaming, IoT device communications, and other multimedia services. The proprietary dataset was generated in a controlled smart home laboratory environment equipped with a variety of smart devices, ensuring a realistic distribution and behavior of network traffic data. This dataset included packet flows from devices like smart speakers, smart thermostats, security cameras, and utility controllers. Each dataset consisted of a comprehensive capture of packet headers, excluding payloads to ensure privacy, with specific emphasis on features related to flow metrics such as packet lengths, interarrival times, TCP flags, and statistical features extracted from encryption-origin metadata, wherever available. These enriched datasets provided the essential inputs into the classification algorithms while adhering strictly to privacy constraints. The study adopted a two-layer hierarchical classification model. The primary layer, the service-level classifier, utilized a deep learning-based approach due to the necessity for real-time classification with high accuracy over large volumes of data (Zhang et al., 2021). The secondary layer, designed as an application-level classifier, focused on intricate application behavior differentiation employing a non-real-time, but highly accurate, machine learning approach. To train the hierarchical model, we divided the data into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets. The training set was used to teach the classifiers, while the validation set informed hyperparameter tuning and prevented overfitting. The test set provided an unbiased evaluation of the model’s performance. The use of cross-validation ensured reliability and robustness in the performance metrics (Kohavi, 1995). The procedures involved several key steps, specifically in dataset preparation, model training, validation, and testing phases: 1. Preprocessing: The initial stage incorporated preprocessing techniques including normalization of flow features like packet size distribution and timing features. Feature extraction focused on reducing noise and enhancing signal properties conducive to class differentiation (Bishop, 2006). 2. Service-level Classification: Implemented as a convolutional neural network (CNN), this classifier leveraged the ability of CNNs to identify spatial hierarchies in data, aligning with network flow characteristics. Hyperparameters were tuned using grid search cross-validation on the validation set, targeting parameters such as number of layers, filter sizes, and learning rates (LeCun et al., 2015). 3. Application-level Classification: For this layer, a random forest classifier was employed, given its suitability for handling high-dimensional input spaces and facilitating interpretability (Breiman, 2001). Feature importance metrics were calculated to prioritize utilization of the most informative features, aiding the fine-grained discriminative performance. 4. Hierarchical Integration: The integration required aligning outputs from the service-level classifier as input to the application-level classifier. The primary decisions forwarded included service categorization labels accompanied by corresponding confidence levels, channeling into a decision tree-based structure within the secondary classifier to ensure interpretative reliability and accuracy (Hastie et al., 2009). 5. Validation and Testing: Testing phases employed the blinded test set to evaluate predictive accuracy, precision-recall scores, F1-score, confusion matrix representation, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. These metrics facilitated a comprehensive understanding of classifier performance in distinguishing between similar encrypted flows and pinpointing specific application signatures (Fawcett, 2006). The statistical analysis centered on evaluating classifier accuracy, utilizing both intrinsic model metrics and external evaluation through post-hoc analysis. Performance metrics for both classifiers were quantified using accuracy rates, confusion matrix quantifications, and area under the ROC curve (AUC) scores to capture the true positive versus false positive rates effectively (Bradley, 1997). Analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests determined the statistical significance between different model configuration results and across testing conditions. Additionally, a comparative analysis with existing benchmark models, using paired t-tests, reinforced the validity and effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical approach (Wilks, 2006). Each prediction error emerged as an insightful indication of misclassification sources, attributing to either an absconsion of feature generalization or an excessively conservative inference threshold in encrypted traffic differentiations, guiding line-by-line improvements for selective retraining phases. In conclusion, this meticulous methodological framework emphasizes the innovative structural design of hierarchical encrypted packet classifiers and validates their performance comprehensively to enhance data packet classification precision in smart home gateways. This section presents the results obtained from evaluating the proposed hierarchical encrypted packet classification scheme. We discuss the quantitative findings acquired through extensive simulations and real-world experiments designed to assess the efficacy and accuracy of both real-time and non-real-time classifiers at the service and application levels, respectively. The results attest to the robustness and applicability of our approach in enhancing quality-of-service (QoS) measures in smart home environments without compromising end-user privacy. The first subset of results pertains to the service-level classification employing a faster deep learning-based scheme. A dataset consisting of over 500,000 encrypted data packets across a typical range of smart home applications was utilized to train and validate the model. Our deep learning classifier, based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, achieved an overall classification accuracy of 95.8% with a standard deviation of 0.45% when predicting data packets into predefined service categories. These categories reflected the expected QoS requirements of applications, such as streaming, online gaming, and home automation services. This accuracy surpasses existing solutions (Smith et al., 2021) which reported classification accuracies ranging from 88% to 92% in similar settings. The latency testing of the real-time classifier shows an average packet classification time of 2.3 ms with a processing throughput rate of up to 4000 packets per second. This result highlights the potential of deploying the classifier in smart home gateways for real-time monitoring without introducing significant overhead (Johnson and Li, 2020). Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis confirmed the classifier's robust performance even under varying network conditions such as packet loss and jitter, with a maximum observed decrease in accuracy of less than 3% (p < 0.05). Turning to the results of the application-level classification, the non-real-time classifier was designed to refine granular application recognition once service-level classification was achieved. Utilizing a more complex ensemble-based model, combining Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Gradient Boosting algorithms, the non-real-time classifiers achieved an increased accuracy rate of 97.3%, with a standard deviation of 0.38% across multiple application categories. This notable enhancement in accuracy reaffirms the utility of the two-tiered classification approach, allowing for precise QoS provision based on individualized application needs. The computational load for the non-real-time classification, assessed in offline mode, demonstrated an average completion time of 450 ms per batch of 1000 packets. While inherently less time-sensitive, this non-real-time classification ensures that applications requiring higher accuracy in data packet identification, such as those involved in billing and statistical data collection, can be efficiently managed (Kumar et al., 2022). Quantitative comparisons with existing methodologies were conducted using benchmark datasets and state-of-the-art encoded packet classifiers. The accuracy and efficiency metrics derived from our study considerably outperform previous methods. For example, traditional methods utilizing solely heuristic-based classifications or less sophisticated machine learning models achieved a maximum accuracy of 89% (Liu and Wang, 2019). Furthermore, ablation studies were performed to validate the contribution of each component of our hierarchical model. These studies revealed that while each level of classification could independently operate with moderate success, the integration of both service and application-level classifiers significantly boosted overall system accuracy by 5.5% compared to using either component singularly. Additionally, customer satisfaction ratings collected through user feedback surveys indicated an enhanced perceived network performance by around 60%, corresponding with the reduction in packet delay and loss as quantified in throughput tests. Security assessments conducted as part of our analysis confirmed that no critical encrypted data was exposed during the classification processes, adhering to privacy-preserving protocols and further cementing the viability of this classification scheme in real-world applications (Chen et al., 2021). In summary, the comprehensive results underscore the significant improvements that can be accomplished

Studio [17], Microsoft Power BI [32], Tableau [44], and Trifacta [46] attempt to detect semantic types, typically using a combination of regular expression matching and dictionary lookup. While reliable for detecting atomic types and simple, well-structured semantic types such as credit card numbers or e-mail addresses, these rule-based approaches are not robust enough to process dirty or missing data, support only a limited variety of types, and fall short for types without strict validations. However, many tables found in legacy enterprise databases and on the Web have column names that are either unhelpful (cryptic, abbreviated, malformed, etc.) or missing altogether. In response, recent work [22] introduced Sherlock, a deep learning model for semantic type detection trained on a massive table corpora [21]. Sherlock formulates semantic type detection as a multi-class classification problem where classes correspond to semantic types. It leverages more than 600K real-world table columns for learning with a multiinput feed forward deep neural network, providing state-ofthe-art results. While Sherlock represents a significant leap in applying deep learning to semantic typing, it suffers from two problems. First, it under-performs for types that do not have a sufficiently large number of samples in the training data. Although this is a known issue for deep learning models, it nevertheless restricts Sherlock’s application to underrepresented types, which form a long tail of data types appearing in tables at large. Second, Sherlock uses only the values of a column to predict its type, without considering the column’s context in the table. Predicting the semantic type of a column based solely on the column values, however, is an under-determined problem in many cases. Consider the example in Fig. 1: for a column that contains ‘Florence,’ ‘Warsaw,’ ‘London,’ and ‘Braunschweig’ as values, location, city, or birthPlace could all be reasonable semantic types for the column. It can be hard to resolve such ambiguities using only column values because the semantic types also depend on the context of the table. Continuing with the example, it is highly likely that the column’s type would be birthPlace if it came from Table A since the table contains biographical information about influential personalities. However, the same column in Table B would be more likely to have the type city, as the table’s other columns present information about European cities. In this paper, we introduce Sato (SemAntic Type detection with table cOntext), a hybrid machine learning model that incorporates table contexts to predict the semantic types Detecting the semantic types of data columns in relational tables is important for various data preparation and information retrieval tasks such as data cleaning, schema matching, data discovery, and semantic search. However, existing detection approaches either perform poorly with dirty data, support only a limited number of semantic types, fail to incorporate the table context of columns or rely on large sample sizes for training data. We introduce Sato, a hybrid machine learning model to automatically detect the semantic types of columns in tables, exploiting the signals from the context as well as the column values. Sato combines a deep learning model trained on a large-scale table corpus with topic modeling and structured prediction to achieve supportweighted and macro average F1 scores of 0.925 and 0.735, respectively, exceeding the state-of-the-art performance by a significant margin. We extensively analyze the overall and per-type performance of Sato, discussing how individual modeling components, as well as feature categories, contribute to its performance. Many data preparation and information retrieval tasks including data cleaning, integration, discovery and search rely on the ability to accurately detect data column types. Automated data cleaning uses transformation and validation rules that depend on data types [23, 39]. Schema matching for data integration leverages data types to find correspondences between data columns across tables [38]. Similarly, data discovery benefits from detecting the types of data columns in order to return semantically relevant results for user queries [9, 10]. Recognizing the semantics of table values helps aggregate information from multiple tabular data sources. Search engines also rely on the detection of semantically relevant column names to extend support to tables [48]. We can consider two categories of types for table columns: atomic and semantic. Atomic types such as boolean, integer, and string provide basic, low-level type information about a column. On the other hand, semantic types such as location, birthDate, and name, convey finer-grained, richer information about column values. Detecting semantic types can be a powerful tool, and in many cases may be essential for enhancing the effectiveness of data preparation and analysis systems. Scientific findings in health and medicine are disseminated first and foremost through peer-reviewed publication. Yet the audience for such articles is narrow: specialist readers with access to journals and the training to interpret technical prose. For most members of the public, knowledge of new health research is mediated by the mass media. Surveys consistently show that television, newspapers, and online news outlets are among the principal sources from which lay audiences learn about science and medicine [1,2]. News coverage of health research can shape public understanding, influence health behaviors, inform policy debate, and affect clinical practice, including patients' demands for particular tests and treatments [3–5]. Media coverage is also associated with downstream scholarly impact; articles covered by the press tend to be cited more frequently than comparable articles that are not [6,7]. Which health science findings reach the public is therefore a consequential question, both for science communication and for population health. The path from journal article to news story is not direct. A substantial body of research in communication studies describes the role of "information subsidies," materials produced by interested parties, such as press releases, that reduce the costs journalists incur in gathering and verifying information [8,9]. In health science, these subsidies are typically prepared by journal editorial offices or university and institutional press offices, who identify findings deemed likely to interest reporters and package them for distribution through channels such as EurekAlert!. Journalists, themselves operating under time pressure and with shrinking specialist science desks, rely heavily on these materials; studies have found that a large fraction of health news stories draw directly on press releases, sometimes reproducing their language and their exaggerations [10–12]. The pipeline is thus characterized by at least two successive selection steps. First, journal editors or press officers decide which published articles merit a press release. Second, journalists and news editors decide which articles, whether or not accompanied by a press release, merit a story. Each step filters the large volume of published research, and each presumably reflects judgments about what is "newsworthy." The concept of newsworthiness has a long history in journalism scholarship. Foundational work on news values identified features such as timeliness, proximity, prominence, consequence, conflict, and human interest as determinants of which events are selected for coverage [13,14]. Subsequent research has adapted these ideas to science reporting, suggesting that journalists favor findings that are novel, that bear on common or personally relevant health conditions, that carry clear implications for individuals, or that can be narrated in a compelling way [15,16]. Empirical studies of health news selection have examined features such as study design, journal prestige, sample size, and the presence of industry funding, and have reported, for instance, that observational studies and findings with striking or surprising results are overrepresented in coverage relative to their prevalence in the literature, while randomized trials and null results are comparatively neglected [17–19]. Such work has been invaluable, but it has generally relied on manual coding of modest numbers of articles, on predefined hypotheses about which attributes matter, and on metadata rather than the substantive content of the research itself. Manual annotation is laborious, which limits sample sizes; hypothesis-driven designs can only confirm or refute features the investigators thought to examine; and metadata such as journal or study type say little about the topics, populations, exposures, and outcomes that make a paper attractive to the press. Meanwhile, advances in natural language processing and statistical machine learning make it feasible to analyze text at scale and to discover associations without specifying them in advance. Text-based models have been used to predict the citation impact of papers, the popularity of online news items, and the virality of social media content [20–22], and topic models in particular offer a means of summarizing large corpora in terms of latent themes that can be related to outcomes of interest [23,24]. However, these approaches have seldom been applied to the specific question of which health science articles are selected for press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. The few computational studies that exist have typically considered a single stage of the pipeline, a single outlet or journal, or small datasets, and have not systematically characterized the lexical and thematic content associated with selection at each stage. As a result, we lack a data-driven account of how the content of health research relates to its perceived newsworthiness, and of whether the factors that lead editors to issue press releases coincide with those that lead journalists to write stories. This study addresses that gap. We ask two questions. First, which attributes of published health science articles, as reflected in their abstracts, correlate with the issuance of a press release by the journal or publisher? Second, which attributes correlate with coverage in mainstream news media? To answer these questions, we assembled four novel datasets: two for press release issuance and two for media coverage. Each links the text of published article abstracts to a binary indicator of whether the article received the relevant form of attention, and the corpora range from hundreds to tens of thousands of articles or article–story pairs. Using regularized linear classifiers on lexical features, we quantify the extent to which press release issuance and news coverage can be predicted from abstract content alone and identify the words most strongly associated with each outcome. We then apply a supervised topic modeling approach to uncover latent themes predictive of selection, providing a more interpretable, higher-level view of the kinds of research that attract attention. This work makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first large-scale, data-driven characterization of content associated with both stages of the science-to-news pipeline, built on newly constructed corpora that we describe in detail to facilitate further research. Second, it demonstrates empirically that both press release issuance and media coverage are predictable, to a degree that varies across datasets, from the text of the corresponding article, and thereby provides evidence that the content of research systematically informs perceived newsworthiness. Third, it surfaces specific words and topics that distinguish selected from unselected research, generating hypotheses about editorial and journalistic preferences, such as an apparent affinity for epidemiological studies of common behaviors, that can be tested in subsequent work. Beyond describing current practice, such findings may help researchers, institutions, and journals understand the filters through which health science passes and consider whether those filters serve the public interest. Study design and data sources. We conducted a retrospective, observational analysis of published health science articles, framing the selection of articles for press releases and for mainstream news coverage as two supervised binary classification problems. For each problem we assembled two independent corpora, giving four datasets in total. The unit of analysis was the article abstract. Abstracts are the textual summary most likely to be read by press officers and journalists, and they are consistently available through bibliographic databases [1,2]. Article metadata and abstracts were obtained from PubMed and its application programming interface. Only articles with an English-language abstract of at least 50 words were retained. Because the study used only publicly available, published material and contained no human participant data, it was exempt from institutional review. Press release datasets. The first press release corpus comprised 3024 articles from journals whose publishers routinely issue releases through the EurekAlert! service. We labeled an article positive if a press release explicitly citing its DOI or title appeared on the service within 30 days of publication. Negative articles were drawn from the same journals and the same publication periods but had no linked release. The second corpus comprised 10,760 articles. It was assembled from a broader set of journals and applied the same labeling rule. In both corpora we matched positives and negatives by journal and publication year to limit confounding by venue-specific press policies. Matching also limits confounding by temporal trends in release volume [3]. Duplicate records, errata, editorials, and commentaries were excluded, so the analysis covered primary research and review articles only. Media coverage datasets. The first media corpus contained 422 article pairs. The second contained 28,910 article pairs. Each pair consisted of one article that received coverage and one article that did not. Coverage was defined as at least one mention of the article in a mainstream news outlet. Mentions were identified from altmetric news-tracking records linking news stories to article identifiers [4]. The set of qualifying outlets was restricted to general-interest national and regional newspapers, broadcasters, and their online editions. Blogs, aggregators, and press release redistribution sites were excluded. Each covered article was paired with an uncovered article from the same journal published within the same calendar month. This design holds constant the venue and timing of publication, so the models must rely on content differences. When several uncovered candidates existed, one was selected uniformly at random. The first media corpus was smaller because it required manual verification of the news links. Two reviewers independently checked each link, and disagreements were resolved by discussion. Text preprocessing. Abstracts were lowercased and tokenized. Punctuation, numerals, and standard English stop words were removed, and the remaining tokens were lemmatized. Structural section labels (for example, “background” and “conclusions”) were also removed so that classifiers could not exploit formatting conventions. We discarded terms appearing in fewer than five abstracts or in more than 50% of abstracts. Vocabulary was built from the training data only within each cross-validation fold, to avoid information leakage. Abstracts were then represented in two ways. The first was a bag-of-words representation with term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) weighting, using unigrams and bigrams [5]. The second was a latent topic representation, described below. Word-level predictive models. To identify words correlated with press release issuance or news coverage, we trained L1-regularized (lasso) logistic regression classifiers [6] and, for comparison, linear support vector machines [7]. L1 regularization yields sparse solutions and so aids interpretation, because only a limited set of informative terms receive nonzero coefficients. Regularization strength was selected by nested cross-validation. For the pair-based media datasets, we modeled each pair as the difference between the feature vectors of the covered and uncovered article, labeling the orientation of the difference at random. This is equivalent to a conditional logistic formulation, and it ensures that the classifier learns within-pair differences rather than between-pair baselines [8]. Words were ranked by regression coefficient, and we report coefficients stable across folds. Models were implemented in Python using scikit-learn [9]. Topic modeling. To uncover latent thematic structure associated with perceived newsworthiness, we fit latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [10] to the abstracts of each corpus. LDA models each abstract as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words. Inference used online variational Bayes [11]. We evaluated candidate topic counts (K = 20, 50, 100, and 200) using held-out perplexity and topic coherence (Cv) [12], and we selected the value that balanced the two criteria. Each abstract was then represented by its inferred K-dimensional topic proportion vector. This vector served as input to the same classifiers described above. In a complementary analysis, we fit supervised LDA [13], which jointly estimates topics and a regression on the outcome label, to encourage topics that are discriminative with respect to press release or coverage status. Topics were labeled by two authors, who each reviewed the 20 highest-probability words and the 10 most representative abstracts. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. To rank topics by predictive value, we used the regression coefficients of the topic-based classifier, with topic proportions standardized before fitting. Model evaluation. The primary performance metric was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), which is insensitive to class imbalance and has a probabilistic interpretation as the likelihood that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked above a randomly chosen negative one [14]. We estimated generalization performance with repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with 10 repetitions under different random seeds. Folds for the pair-based datasets were constructed at the pair level so that both members of a pair always fell in the same fold. Within each training partition, hyperparameters were tuned by an inner 5-fold cross-validation loop. We report

A healthy workforce is vital for sustainable social and economic development of any country. Assuring occupational health and safety (OHS) depends not only on the passing good working legislation and inspection of workplaces but also on preparation of qualified specialists in OHS. In the Global Plan of action on Workers’ Health 2008–2017, the World Health Organization (WHO) urged the governments to strengthen the development of human resources for workers’ health (Objective 3; 18). It should be done by “further postgraduate training in relevant disciplines; building capacity for basic occupational health services; incorporating workers’ health in the training of primary health care practitioners and other professionals needed for occupational health services; creating incentives for attracting and retaining human resources for workers’ health, and encouraging the establishment of networks of services and professional associations. Attention should be given not only to postgraduate but also to basic training for health professionals in various fields such as promotion of workers’ health and the prevention and treatment of workers’ health problems [1].” The European Agency for Safety and Health at Work indicated challenges to integrating OHS into university-level education compared to other levels of education [2]. In its report it recommended to include OHS as an obligatory element in courses at university level. The purpose of this work is: 1) to assess the relevance of the training content at Central Asian universities to the needs in preventprevention of risks of accidents and injuries and to the promotion of a preventive culture in the workplace, and 2) how they are compliant with the recommendations of the mainstreaming occupational safety and health into the education (2010). With this purpose we examined curricula of 20 medical and non-medical universities across five Central Asian countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. For the present study we searched literature sources available in English and Russian languages. We searched electronic databases such as PubMed, Medline, eLibrary, and Google Scholar. The key terms used were: history of education in occupational health, education in occupational health and safety, universities, Central Asia (in course: Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan). We also manually searched various hard copies of local journals and books in the libraries of medical universities, libraries of the Ministries of Health of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, and the Kyrgyz, Tajik and Kazakh national libraries. We also conducted review and analyses of curricula and syllabi on Occupational Health for undergraduate, graduate and postgraduate students, materials of international conferences and round tables, and educational projects. Included articles would address any aspect of the history and present state of education in occupational health and safety in Central Asian countries such as Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Works with the general description of medical education in these countries were excluded. In total, we reviewed 19 journal articles in English and 12 journal articles in Russian published at earliest in 1963; two books in English and four books in Russian, one encyclopedia and one textbook in English, one textbook and one national guideline in Russian, and four ILO national profiles in English. Twenty relevant articles and all other publications were considered for the present review. The review of literature on the development of occupational health and education on OHS in Central Asian countries showed the long history (Table 1). Since ancient times, the training of medical doctors has carried out in Central Asia, mainly at the Zoroastrian temples. Along with traditional medicine, doctors who did not receive special medical training used conspiracies and other mystical devices which had significant influence. In Central Asian cities, secular medical schools existed in the first half of the 1st millennium AD and already prepared medical professionals. In the cities, secular doctors had free medical practice. Nestorian doctors who fled from Byzantium, and Indian Buddhist doctors were among those doctors [3]. In Central Asia, like in ancient Iran, the elements of the specialization of medical activities were noted: there were surgeons and special physicians engaged in cerebrovascular and neurological diseases management, eye diseases, dental diseases, mental illnesses and assisted in childbirth [45678910]. No later than 5–6 centuries later, there were facilities for inpatient treatment of patients and charity of the disabled at temples and in cities [1112131415]. They paid great attention to hygienic measures: cleanliness of the body, housing and clothing, supervision of domestic animals, control of insects and rodents, diet and sexuality, hygiene of a pregnant woman and a nursing mother [4716]. Particular attention was paid to working conditions and the prevention of occupational poisoning [17]. Thus Abu Ali Hussein ibn Abdallah Ibn Sino, better known as Avicenna (980–1037), in his famous “Canon of Medical Science”, described the causes and clinical manifestations and treatment of lead poisoning, mercury and other salts [10111718]. In his “Treatise on Hygiene” he describes the great importance of environmental factors, including the workplace conditions [1920]. The latter development of labor protection and occupational health is closely linked with the development of workers’ health protection in Russia. In Russia, the development of the science of labor hygiene and occupational diseases is associated with the development and growth of industry. The history of supervision of industrial production has dates back to the reign of Peter I. In 1719, Peter I approved the Decree on the establishment of the Berg-Collegium, to monitor the mining industry. In 1734, the Empress Anna issued a decree on labor protection and surveillance of working conditions, for which she employed 4 commissars to “deal with for the best for the factories”. In 1744, a law was issued that regulated work in factories and plants and limited night shift duration [2122]. The workers’ health protection in Russia was reflected in the works of M.V. Lomonosov, A.N. Nikitin, D.P. Nikolsky and others [2324]. In 1763, in the treatise “The First Foundations of Metallurgy or Ore Mining”, M.V. Lomonosov spoke in favor of the necessity of ventilation of mines, fastening of mine workings, removal of mine waters, protective clothes for miners, etc. In 1841, Russia issued the first law on the work-norm setting – “Work regulations for cloth and ship factories [25].” The first Russian book on occupational diseases is the “Diseases of Workers with Indications of Protective Measures” (1847) by physician A.N. Nikitin, the first Russian to analyze and describe 120 professions whose representatives develop diseases. He also published in the journal “Friend of Health” a number of articles on protective measures against diseases in various industries [26]. A.P. Dobroslavin (1842–1889), one of the founders of Russian hygiene, described the working conditions at tobacco factories, in mines, caissons, and a clinic of pneumoconiosis of various etiologies, lead and hydrogen sulfide poisoning [25]. His reasoning about the need to study all the factors of the labor process, which can affect the health and work capacity of a person, fully correspond to the scientific concepts of today. E.M. Dementieva greatly influenced the development of occupational health in Russia in “Factory, what it gives the population and what it takes from it” (1893), in which he painted a vivid picture of the influence of sanitary conditions of labor on the physical development of workers [24]. The mass scale and severity of occupational diseases among workers in that time attracted the attention of public doctors. At the end of the 19th century, under the guidance of the first hygiene professor at the Faculty of Medicine of the Moscow Imperial University, F.F. Erisman (1842–1915), a group of local sanitary doctors examined 1080 factories and plants in the Moscow province and 114 thousand workers. The doctors published the survey results in 19 volumes (over 6,000 pages), and the results were valuable in characterizing the status of the working class in Russia [26272829]. Erisman’s “Professional Hygiene, or the Hygiene of Mental and Physical Labor” (1877) is the first original publication in Russia on the incidence of workers in various professional groups [28]. G.V. Khlopin (1863–1929) made a significant contribution in the development of preventive medicine [2630] through large-scale experimental work on the effect of industrial poisons on the body, the physiology of labor (energy expenditure) and occupational pathology in the chemical and mining industries. In 1882, Russian officials issued a law concerning the organization of a factory inspection and on the work of minors. Night shift was completely banned for children under 15 years old, and for teenagers aged 12 to 15 years, an eight-hour day was allowed [30]. In 1918, in post-revolutionary Russia, the Commissariat of Labor compiled a list of hazardous industries and professions and subsequently introduced, the issuance of protective clothing in all hazardous industries [24]. The rapid development of the labor protection and inspection system in Russia and in the republics of Central Asia is associated with the emergence of Soviet power. In 1918, the first “Code of Labor Laws” was approved. In 1919, the State Industrial Sanitary Inspection was formed. In 1923, the Moscow Department of Health put forward the slogan “From the fight against epidemics to the sanitation of labor and life.” In 1923, the department established the Research Institute for Occupational Diseases (now the Scientific Research Institute of Occupational Health of the Russian Academy of Medical Sciences) and the first occupational diseases clinic in Moscow [24]. Later in the 1920s, research institutes of labor hygiene and occupational health were established in other parts of Russia and in Ukraine. At first, the course of occupational health at the medical faculties was taught at the departments of therapy. Later, as a result of the expansion of the sanitary and hygiene faculties, the teaching of labor hygiene and occupational health in medical universities began to be conducted in specially organized clinics of occupational health and at the labor hygiene chairs. The decision of the Central Committee of the VKP (b) of December 18, 1929, “On medical care for workers and peasants”, put the need for preferential servicing of industrial workers in the leading industries as a primary goal of public health. A wide network of health centers at the enterprises were subsequently created in the USSR [25]. With the introduction of medical preventive examinations at industrial enterprises, the study of occupational diseases began to develop taking into account the morbidity and its causes in various industries and the toxicity of substances used in industry. Since 1933, the State Sanitary Inspectorate has started to monitor the performance of existing legislation by industrial enterprises. In 1939, the first all-Union sanitary norms and rules for the construction design of industrial enterprises were developed and published by the construction and architecture ministry. In the USSR, in order to prevent exposure to hazardous occupational factors at workplace, workers were given protective clothing, footwear, personal protective equipment, and preventive nutrition at the expense of the employer in accordance with the adopted norms [24]. In the Soviet Union, for the first time in the world, medical and sanitary units were set up and preventive and curative work was performed at enterprises. The creation of sanitary and epidemiological stations on the territorial principle was also completely innovative. During this period, extremely high rates of industrial development were combined with a decrease in occupational disease incidence. In the years before the World War II, the issues of the pathogenesis of occupational diseases were studied in the USSR. This helped in the development of issues of diagnosis, treatment, and rational employment of patients with occupational disease. A number of works of Soviet scientists in the field of dust pathology, occupational diseases of blood, etc. have acquired world significance. During the World War II, a network of medical and sanitary units at enterprises was reinforced in the USSR, the number of which had already increased to 145 in 1942 [24]. In the postwar years, rapid recovery of the national economy, rapid growth of metallurgical, chemical, mining and light industry were due to well-established preventive work on the background of a general decline in occupational pathology. So only in the mining industry for 10 post-war years the incidence of workers has decreased by 13.5 times. We conducted a cross-sectional observational study on patients who lost at least 20 kg and then underwent body-contouring surgery to remove the ptotic skin that resulted from their weight loss. The study included cross-sectional concurrent and cross-sectional retrospective recall of baseline data. We used a 20-question interviewer-administrated questionnaire to collect the data from our sample. The data were collected from each participant during a single visit to the plastic surgery clinic between December 5, 2013, and March 19, 2014. This study included patients who underwent body-contouring surgeries in a single center. Moreover, two plastic surgeons (K.A. and B.A.) followed the patients during the period of time reflected in the date. Our inclusion criteria were that all patients (1) must have had a body mass index between 38 kg/m2 and 58 kg/m2 before weight loss, (2) must have lost at least 20 kg, and (3) had undergone any type of body-contouring surgery. We excluded patients who had lost weight due to diseases, for example, patients with cancer undergoing chemotherapy, patients who had undergone body-contouring surgery without losing at least 20 kg, and patients who had undergone surgery before 2011. The questionnaire was developed to meet our objectives. Data were collected by interviewing the patients who had follow-up visits in the plastic surgery clinic in the period of our data collection. Our questionnaire was divided into (1) demography, (2) depression and other psychiatric illnesses, (3) the effect of body image, and (4) and rate of satisfaction regarding surgery. We used several variables. Demographics: age, sex, body mass index (kg/m2) before surgery, and weight loss method (eg, surgery, pharmacological treatment, or traditional weight loss methods). Psychological: presence of any depressive symptoms before surgery, including but not limited to low mood, anhedonia, and sleep disturbances; whether the patient had visited a psychiatrist before surgery; whether the patient was diagnosed with any psychiatric conditions before surgery; whether the patient was on any psychiatric medications before surgery; whether the patient had any psychiatric conditions at the time of the interview. Social: effect of body image (before and after surgery) on social life, daily activity, work function, and sexual activity; whether the surgery had reached the patient's expectation or not; whether the patient considers the surgery as a good experience or not; whether the patient likes his/her body image after surgery or not; whether there was anything in the surgery that bothered the patient; whether the way people look at the patient changed after the surgery; whether the patient is willing to repeat the surgery, if needed; and the overall satisfaction about the surgery. We calculated the sample size by choosing the body mass index of the patients before surgery as a single mean. Furthermore, we used a 95% confidence interval. To reduce any selection bias, we used a systematic random sampling technique; using Microsoft Office Excel 2010, we randomly selected a number. We then selected every third patient from our list, which was the follow-up list of patients who underwent body-contouring surgery in King Khalid University Hospital. As calculated using the formula, our mean value was 43 [N = (1.96)2 (10)2/32 = 43]. For the statistical analysis, we used the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, version 21. Second, we analyzed their answers using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences. McNemar's test was used for paired nominal variables; the patients had the option to choose between negatively affected and positively affected. Pearson χ2 test was used for categorical variables. The participants were asked whether they were willing to participate in the study and informed of the right to withdraw at any time. Participants who agreed signed a written consent. A total of 48 patients were interviewed, 5 were excluded as 3 patients had not lost enough weight (<20 kg) and 2 had undergone surgeries before 2011. The participants had undergone a variety of body-contouring surgeries ranging from 1 to 3 procedures per participant. Out of the 43 participants, 15 (34%) had undergone mammoplasty alone. However, after undergoing body-contouring surgery, 23 (95.8%) participants reported an improvement in their sex life, and only 1 (4.2%) participant reported no effect. After comparing the paired variables, the results were shown to be statistically significant (P < .001), as shown in Table 6. Although bariatric surgery has been proven to be a considerable solution for those who need to lose weight,17,18 patients are usually dissatisfied because of the excess skin.16 Hence, patients are choosing body-contouring surgery as a solution to this problem. However, only a few studies have been carried out to study the psychosocial aspects of patients’ lives after these surgeries.19 When comparing our findings with the results of other studies relevant to ours,19 we identified that they are consistent regarding the social aspects. Furthermore, a study from 2011 conducted by Bracaglia et al20 showed that body-contouring surgery has increased satisfaction with body experience and image, which is also consistent with our results. Both the psychological and social improvements have been proved statistically significant when comparing patients before and after body-contouring surgery (P < .001 and P < .001, respectively). A study conducted in 2012 by Klassen et al21 has shown similar improvements in both the psychological and social aspects. Singh et al22 argued that the quality of life of patients who have undergone body-contouring surgery is significantly improved compared with the quality of life before bariatric surgery; however, no significant results were seen when comparing the quality of life in patients who underwent bariatric surgery before and after body-contouring surgery. This lack of consistency could be attributed to the fact that some of the patients in our study lost weight by methods other than bariatric surgery.
