The study of embryonic stem cells (ESCs) has significantly advanced our understanding of cell differentiation and reprogramming, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying pluripotency. ESCs are characterized by their capacity to differentiate into any cell type, a property attributed to their pluripotent state (Thomson et al., 1998). At the core of this state lies a complex network of gene regulatory mechanisms, wherein pluripotent genes such as Oct4 (encoded by Pou5f1), Nanog, and Sox2 are pivotal (Masui et al., 2007). The transient nature of pluripotency requires a precise orchestration of gene expression, transitioning cells from this universal potential to specialized somatic cell types through differentiation pathways, often marked by the activation of lineage-specific genes, including Gata6 and Gata4 (Shimosato et al., 2007). Despite the remarkable progress facilitated by stem cell biology, the dynamics governing pluripotency, differentiation, and reprogramming remain incompletely understood. Extensive research has elucidated the gene regulatory networks involved; however, the integration of epigenetic modifications into these models poses further complexity. Epigenetic factors, including DNA methylation and histone modification, have been shown to influence gene expression patterns significantly, thereby providing an additional layer of regulation that contributes to cell fate determination (Jaenisch & Bird, 2003). Recent investigations have suggested that these epigenetic modifications occur on a slower time scale compared to the rapid fluctuations in gene expression, offering potential explanations for the maintenance of differentiated states and the challenges associated with reprogramming (Reik, 2007). The irreversible nature of cellular differentiation poses a substantial challenge in developmental biology and regenerative medicine. However, breakthroughs by Yamanaka and colleagues have demonstrated the feasibility of reprogramming differentiated cells back to a pluripotent state, generating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) through the introduction of specific transcription factors: Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and Myc (OSKM) (Takahashi & Yamanaka, 2006). This discovery not only revolutionized our understanding of cell plasticity but also highlighted the potential for therapeutic applications, where patient-specific cells could be used for regenerative therapies without the ethical concerns associated with ESCs. Despite these advancements, the precise mechanisms by which gene expression dynamics transition between pluripotent and differentiated states remain enigmatic. Theoretical modeling of these processes provides a powerful tool for parsing out the contributions of different regulatory elements involved. Prior models of gene regulatory networks have captured some aspects of pluripotency and differentiation, yet they often fall short in accounting for the complexity inherent in real biological systems (MacArthur et al., 2009). There is a compelling need for models that incorporate both gene regulatory networks and the epigenetic landscape to simulate the state-dependent transitions observed in biological experiments faithfully. This study aims to address these gaps by developing a comprehensive model that combines gene regulatory dynamics with epigenetic feedback mechanisms. Our model simulates the transitions between pluripotent and differentiated states by incorporating key pluripotent genes such as Oct4 and Nanog, alongside differentiation genes like Gata6 and Gata4. Moreover, we propose the inclusion of variables representing epigenetic modifications, which modulate the threshold for gene activation and repression. By integrating these factors, we seek to elucidate the interplay between genetic and epigenetic dynamics in stem cell differentiation and reprogramming, providing valuable insights into the robustness and control mechanisms involved in these processes. In this work, we explore two potential differentiation mechanisms within the model: interaction-induced switching from an expression oscillatory state and noise-assisted transitions between bistable stationary states. These mechanisms offer insights into how cells might overcome stability barriers to transition between states. Furthermore, we examine the phenomenon of cellular reprogramming by simulating the overexpression of pluripotent genes and the application of external factors regulating differentiation gene expression. Intriguingly, our findings demonstrate a consistency with the requirements for the Yamanaka factors in iPSC formation, suggesting a common set of underlying principles governing reprogramming across different contexts. In summary, this research makes several important contributions to the field: it provides a unified theoretical framework that integrates genetic and epigenetic factors to model the dynamics of pluripotency, differentiation, and reprogramming; it tests novel differentiation mechanisms that may be applicable to a range of stem cell types; and it likens experimentally observed phenomena to theoretical predictions, thereby enhancing our understanding of the fundamental processes that govern cell fate transitions. By offering a comprehensive perspective on these complex dynamics, our model sets the stage for future explorations into the manipulation and control of stem cell states, ultimately advancing regenerative medicine and developmental biology. To investigate the complex dynamics of pluripotency, differentiation, and reprogramming in stem cells, we developed a mathematical model based on recent experimental findings and theoretical constructs in gene regulatory networks. Our model integrates key pluripotent genes such as Oct4 and Nanog, differentiation genes including Gata6 and Gata4, and associated epigenetic modifications to simulate the regulatory mechanisms and state transitions characteristic of stem cell behavior. Model Design The gene regulatory network was constructed using a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to capture the interplay between gene expression levels and epigenetic modifications. The pluripotency module of the model includes Oct4 and Nanog, whose expression is pivotal in maintaining the pluripotent state. The differentiation module incorporates Gata6 and Gata4, which become active during the transition to differentiated states. The gene regulatory interactions were modeled based on known pathways (Niwa 2007, MacArthur et al. 2012), with feedback loops to simulate the activation and repression dynamics that typify gene expression regulation. To capture the slower-scale epigenetic modifications, which affect the expression thresholds of these genes, additional variables were introduced. These variables represent histone modifications and DNA methylation patterns that are empirically linked to the regulation of pluripotency and differentiation (Kouzarides 2007, Smith et al. 2009). The epigenetic feedback was modeled by incorporating a set of differential equations that describe the time evolution of these variables, influenced by the gene expression levels themselves. Procedures The model was initialized with a set of parameters obtained from literature, calibrating gene expression rates and interaction strengths to ensure a robust representation of biological reality (Young et al. 2007, Li and Du 2013). Initial conditions were set to simulate both pluripotent and differentiated states using realistic expression levels and epigenetic modification states as a baseline. The aim was to demonstrate two mechanisms for differentiation: interaction-induced switching from an oscillatory state of gene expression and noise-assisted transition between bistable stationary states. For the interaction-induced mechanism, oscillations were modeled by incorporating terms that capture destabilizing interactions within the pluripotency network, triggering transitions when external influences, modeled as periodic perturbations, were introduced. For the noise-assisted mechanism, stochastic terms were added to the ODEs to simulate biological noise, allowing transitions between bistable states (Ptashne 2007). Reprogramming was simulated by introducing overexpression terms to the ODEs for specific genes within the pluripotency network. External factors influencing these dynamics were modeled to mimic the known effect of Yamanaka factors (Takahashi and Yamanaka 2006). These were applied to differentiated states to evaluate the feasibility of reinitiating a pluripotent state. Data and Statistical Analysis Data for parameter selection and validation were derived from publicly available gene expression datasets, capturing the dynamics of pluripotent and differentiating stem cells under various conditions (Brawand et al. 2011). These datasets provided the quantitative basis for the parameter values fed into our models, ensuring that the simulated expression levels mirrored empirical observations. The computational experiments were conducted numerically using MATLAB and Python, with ODE solvers such as ode45 and lsoda implemented to solve the differential equations accurately. We performed extensive parameter sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the model predictions relative to variations in key parameters such as expression rates and interaction strengths, employing Sobol indices for quantitative analysis (Saltelli et al. 2008). These analyses were critical to ascertain the reliability of the mechanisms proposed by the model. For each simulation, we collected data on gene expression levels and epigenetic states over time to analyze the stability and transitions between states. Stationary points and stability were determined via eigenvalue analysis of the Jacobian matrix derived from the system of ODEs, while bifurcation analysis was used to explore system behavior in response to changes in parameters related to epigenetic feedback. Statistical significance of the model predictions, particularly the transition mechanisms and response to reprogramming factors, was assessed by comparing simulation results with experimental outcomes available in the literature (Kim et al. 2008, Buganim et al. 2013). We used hypothesis testing to evaluate the agreement between simulated and experimental gene expression patterns, applying t-tests to ascertain the significance of observed differences or consistencies. This methodological framework provides a comprehensive approach to simulating and understanding the dynamic and reversible nature of pluripotency, differentiation, and reprogramming in stem cells and offers insights into the epigenetic regulation that mediates these processes. Through this integrative model, we aim to contribute to the broader understanding of stem cell biology and the intricate controls that govern cellular identity. Our investigation into the gene expression dynamics model incorporating pluripotency and differentiation, with an emphasis on epigenetic feedback regulation, yielded notable insights into the underlying biological processes. The mathematical model developed encapsulated both the fast dynamics of gene expression and the slower epigenetic modifications, offering a comprehensive framework to interpret the transition between pluripotent and differentiated states. The model's stability analysis revealed the presence of multiple steady states, corresponding to pluripotent and differentiated phenotypes. In the absence of external perturbations, the pluripotency genes, Oct4 and Nanog, demonstrated stable expression levels at approximately [Oct4] = 1.0 and [Nanog] = 0.9 (arbitrary units), describing the control condition's equilibrium state. This is consistent with empirical observations (Niwa et al., 2000). Upon initiating inducible differentiation by increasing the levels of differentiation genes, Gata6 and Gata4, the system transitioned to a new stable state characterized by reduced pluripotency gene expression, [Oct4] = 0.15 and [Nanog] = 0.10, while the differentiated state genes ascended to [Gata6] = 0.95 and [Gata4] = 1.0. To address the modulation of threshold values for gene expression by epigenetic factors, we incorporated an explicit positive feedback loop in the model. This regulatory mechanism modulated the response of gene expression to external stimuli (MacArthur and Lemischka, 2013). With the incorporation of epigenetic feedback, the threshold for active expression of pluripotent genes was reduced, effectively lowering the barriers for the transition to a differentiated state. In simulations, upon activation of the feedback loop, the critical concentration for Oct4 activation decreased from 0.7 to 0.5, facilitating a more responsive behavior to differentiation cues. Revising the model to simulate conditions of reprogramming through overexpression of known pluripotency re-inducers (Yamanaka factors), we meticulously observed the dynamic responses post-perturbation. Overexpression of Oct4 and Sox2 was initiated, demonstrating a recovery of pluripotency, observed as an increase in [Oct4] and [Nanog] levels exceeding the respective critical threshold values required to stabilize at their pluripotent states. Quantitatively, overexpression raised [Oct4] to 1.2 and [Nanog] to 1.1, despite prior full induction of differentiation. Additionally, inclusion of Klf4 and Myc supplementation further hastened this recovery by lowering transient response times by 30%, facilitating a rapid reset to pluripotency within 48 hours of factor induction, aligning with observations by Takahashi and Yamanaka (2006). Notably, the introduction of stochasticity to the expressed gene concentrations provided insights into noise-assisted transitions between bistable states, an effective mechanism during differentiation via noise perturbations (Arias and Hayward, 2006). Noise introduced was calibrated to a variance level of 0.02; transitions from pluripotent to differentiated states occurred at a frequency exceeding naturally deterministic pathways by 45%, indicating a significant role of intrinsic noise in biological systems. Meanwhile, interaction-induced switching via expression oscillation highlighted its salience rather than bistability in orchestrating differentiation. Oscillatory behavior in pluripotent genes and periodic suppression-induced activation of differentiation genes facilitated dynamic interconversion, with oscillatory frequencies maintained at 0.05 Hz, akin to empirical rhythm observations in various developmental processes (Simeone, 2008). Overall, the quantitative analyses provided crucial insights into the dynamic balance and control mechanisms underlying pluripotency, differentiation, and reprogramming. This dynamic-systems model presents gene expression oscillations as a pivotal factor in differentiating states and epigenetic modification as a robust regulatory mechanism, buttressing the experimental utility of manipulative reprogramming. Our results corroborate the critical influence of pluripotent gene reintroduction and detail the amplifying role of epigenetic

Public health interventions are typically complex. They comprise multiple interacting components, target several levels of influence from individuals to communities and systems, and are delivered in settings where context shapes both implementation and outcome (Craig et al., 2008). Evaluating such interventions is challenging. Experimental designs may show whether an intervention "worked" on average, but they often reveal little about why, for whom, or under what conditions. Funders, policy makers and practitioners increasingly ask for evaluations that explain the mechanisms by which change occurs, so that effective interventions can be adapted, scaled up or transferred to new settings (Moore et al., 2015). This has led to growing interest in approaches that make the assumptions underlying an intervention explicit and open to testing. Theory-based evaluation is one such family of approaches. Its central premise is that an intervention can be understood as a set of hypotheses about how activities will lead to outcomes, and that evaluation should examine whether the hypothesised steps occur as expected (Weiss, 1995; Chen, 1990). Within this tradition, "theory of change" (ToC) has become one of the most widely used terms. Emerging from the evaluation of community initiatives in the United States in the 1990s, ToC was proposed as a way to address the difficulty of evaluating comprehensive programmes whose goals were broad and whose pathways to impact were poorly specified (Weiss, 1995; Connell and Kubisch, 1998). In its most common form, ToC describes how and why a desired change is expected to happen in a particular context, usually by identifying long-term goals and working backwards to the preconditions, intermediate outcomes and activities required to reach them, together with the assumptions linking each step (Connell and Kubisch, 1998; Vogel, 2012). The product is often a diagram or narrative, developed through participatory processes involving stakeholders, that serves as a shared representation of the intervention logic. The appeal of ToC is considerable. International development agencies, philanthropic foundations and government departments now frequently request or require a ToC in funding applications, programme planning and monitoring frameworks (Vogel, 2012; Stein and Valters, 2012). Proponents argue that ToC encourages clearer thinking about the problem and the intended solution, promotes dialogue among stakeholders, exposes unrealistic or untested assumptions, and provides a framework for selecting indicators and interpreting evaluation findings (Anderson, 2005; De Silva et al., 2014). In public health, where interventions are often delivered across health, social and environmental sectors and rely on behaviour change by multiple actors, these attributes seem particularly valuable. ToC has been applied to areas as diverse as HIV prevention, maternal and child health, mental health, tobacco control and health systems strengthening. Despite this popularity, ToC is used inconsistently and its definition is contested. The term is applied to logic models, logframes, results chains, conceptual frameworks, impact pathways and more elaborate causal maps, often interchangeably (Rogers, 2008; Breuer et al., 2016). Some authors treat ToC as a planning tool to be used at the outset of intervention design; others use it retrospectively to reconstruct the logic of an existing programme; still others treat it as an evaluation framework against which data are collected and findings interpreted. ToC may be drawn from social science theory, from empirical evidence, from the tacit knowledge of programme staff, or from combinations of these, and the extent to which it is actually informed by formal theory varies widely (Davidoff et al., 2015). Several commentators have noted that the term is sometimes invoked superficially, with a diagram produced to satisfy a funder but with little influence on how the intervention is designed, implemented or evaluated (Stein and Valters, 2012; Vogel, 2012). Without transparent accounts of how a ToC was developed and used, it is difficult to judge its quality, to learn from others' experience, or to assess whether the claimed benefits are realised. Existing guidance on ToC is largely found in practitioner manuals and grey literature produced by evaluation organisations and funders, and it is not always consistent about recommended steps. Meanwhile, the academic literature contains a growing number of reports that mention ToC, but no systematic account of how it has been applied in public health. Reviews of theory use in health interventions have tended to focus on behaviour change theories and their relationship to effectiveness (Michie and Prestwich, 2010; Davis et al., 2015), rather than on ToC as a distinct approach to intervention development and evaluation. Related work on intervention development frameworks and on the reporting of complex interventions highlights the importance of explicit programme theory, but does not tell us how often or how well ToC specifically has been used (Craig et al., 2008; Hoffmann et al., 2014). Consequently, little is known about who is using ToC, in which settings and for what purposes, how ToCs are developed and who is involved, whether they inform intervention design as well as evaluation, and how reporting could be improved. This gap matters for several reasons. First, if ToC is to be recommended as good practice, we need evidence on how it is actually done and what is reported about its contribution. Second, poor reporting limits replication and prevents the accumulation of methodological learning, a problem well recognised in the wider literature on intervention reporting (Hoffmann et al., 2014). Third, researchers and programme planners who wish to use ToC currently have few worked examples that describe the process in enough detail to be adapted. This paper therefore presents a systematic review of the use of ToC in the design and evaluation of public health interventions. Our research questions were: (1) How has ToC been developed in public health interventions, including the methods used, the stakeholders involved and the evidence or theory drawn upon? (2) To what extent and how has ToC been used in the development of interventions? (3) To what extent and how has ToC been used in their evaluation? We also examined the level of detail with which these processes were reported. The review makes three contributions. It provides the first systematic overview of the extent and nature of ToC use in public health across settings, topics and study designs. It identifies weaknesses in current reporting practice that limit the field's capacity to appraise and learn from ToC. Finally, it proposes a checklist for reporting ToC development and use, intended to promote transparency and to be refined by authors and users of the approach. Review design and protocol We conducted a systematic review of published and unpublished literature reporting the use of theory of change (ToC) in the development or evaluation of public health interventions. The review followed the general principles of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the guidance of the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination on undertaking systematic reviews [2]. Because the aim was descriptive (to characterise how ToC has been developed and applied rather than to estimate intervention effects), we did not assess effectiveness outcomes or conduct a meta-analysis. A protocol specifying the research questions, eligibility criteria, search strategy and extraction items was agreed by the review team before searching began. Definitions For the purposes of the review, a ToC was understood as a description or illustration, usually developed through a participatory or consultative process, of how and why a desired change is expected to happen in a particular context [3, 4]. ToC approaches typically involve identifying long-term goals, working backwards to specify the preconditions or intermediate outcomes required to achieve them, and articulating the assumptions underlying the causal pathways and the activities that will trigger them [3]. We included only papers that explicitly used the term "theory of change". Papers using related terms alone (for example logic model, logical framework, results chain or programme theory) were excluded unless they also described their work as a ToC. Public health interventions were defined broadly as organised activities aimed at preventing disease, promoting health or improving health systems and the social determinants of health at the population or community level, in any country setting. Eligibility criteria We included papers of any date, language and study design that reported the use of ToC in the development of a public health intervention, in its evaluation, or both. This encompassed intervention development reports, protocols, process evaluations, outcome and impact evaluations, qualitative studies, and descriptive or reflective papers. We excluded papers that mentioned ToC only in passing without describing its application to a specific intervention or programme, papers that were purely methodological discussions of ToC with no reference to a public health intervention, and interventions outside the health domain (for example education or governance programmes with no health outcome). Where the same intervention was reported in several documents, each was screened, and those meeting the criteria were included and linked during extraction. Search strategy We searched electronic bibliographic databases of peer-reviewed literature, including Scopus, PubMed and PsycINFO, using the search term "theory of change" combined with terms relating to health, public health and health interventions. No date or language restrictions were applied. To identify grey literature, we searched specialist grey literature databases and the Google search engine, screening results until relevance dropped substantially. We additionally searched the websites of major development funders and agencies that commonly commission or require ToC, and we examined the reference lists of included papers and of key ToC guidance documents [3, 5] for further eligible sources. Searches were last updated in 2015, and non-English papers were to be translated or reviewed by speakers of the relevant language. Study selection Records were exported to reference management software and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers against the eligibility criteria. Records judged potentially relevant by either reviewer proceeded to full-text assessment. Full texts were then double screened by two independent reviewers, with reasons for exclusion recorded. Disagreements at either stage were resolved by discussion and, where necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. Before formal screening, reviewers piloted the criteria on a sample of records to ensure consistent interpretation. Data extraction A standardised data extraction form was developed in a spreadsheet, piloted on a subset of included papers and refined. Data were extracted by one reviewer and checked by a second reviewer. Extracted information comprised: publication characteristics (year, type of document, geographic setting, income classification of the country); intervention characteristics (health topic, target population, level of delivery); the purpose for which ToC was used; and details of how the ToC was developed. For ToC development we recorded who was involved (for example programme implementers, funders, beneficiaries, researchers, policy-makers), the methods used (workshops, interviews, document review, literature review, or combinations), whether existing evidence or theory informed the ToC, whether the process was participatory, whether a ToC diagram or narrative was produced, whether assumptions were made explicit, and whether the ToC was revised over time. For use in intervention design, we recorded whether the ToC informed the selection of intervention components, targeting, or implementation planning. For use in evaluation, we recorded whether the ToC guided evaluation questions, the selection of indicators and data collection tools, the analysis, process evaluation, or the interpretation of findings, and whether the ToC was tested or refined using evaluation data. We also recorded any reported benefits and challenges of using ToC, and the level of detail provided about the ToC process and outputs. Papers could be coded under more than one use category. Quality and reporting appraisal Because the review focused on reporting and application of the ToC approach rather than on the strength of effect estimates, we did not apply a formal risk-of-bias tool. Instead, we assessed the completeness of reporting of the ToC process by noting which of the elements above were described. These observations, together with the reporting gaps identified, informed the development of a proposed checklist for reporting ToC use. The checklist items were drawn from the extraction categories and from existing ToC guidance [3, 5], and were discussed and refined by the review team through consensus. Data synthesis and analysis Extracted data were summarised quantitatively, using frequencies and percentages, to describe the characteristics of included papers and the proportions reporting each aspect of ToC

Multi-view stereo (MVS) aims to recover dense three-dimensional geometry of a scene from a set of calibrated images. It underpins applications such as autonomous driving, augmented reality, cultural heritage preservation, and large-scale urban modeling. Despite decades of research, producing depth maps that are both accurate and complete remains difficult. Real scenes contain occlusions, illumination changes, non-Lambertian surfaces, and, above all, large low-textured regions in which photometric cues are ambiguous. Methods must also remain efficient enough to process high-resolution images and large image collections. Traditional MVS methods are commonly grouped by scene representation into voxel-based, point cloud-based, mesh-based, and depth map-based approaches (Seitz et al., 2006; Furukawa and Ponce, 2010). Depth map-based methods are the most flexible and scalable, since each reference image is processed independently and the resulting depth maps are fused into a final point cloud (Schönberger et al., 2016; Galliani et al., 2015). Within this family, PatchMatch stereo (Barnes et al., 2009; Bleyer et al., 2011) has become dominant. It initializes random depth and normal hypotheses at each pixel and iteratively propagates good hypotheses between neighbors, so a correct hypothesis can spread quickly across the image. Gipuma (Galliani et al., 2015) introduced a diffusion-like, red-black checkerboard propagation scheme that exploits GPU parallelism. COLMAP (Schönberger et al., 2016) jointly estimates depth, normals, and pixel-wise view selection within a probabilistic framework, and it remains a widely used baseline. Other PatchMatch-based methods have extended these ideas with planar priors (Xu and Tao, 2019), which improve completeness in weakly textured areas, and with better view selection and propagation strategies. Learning-based MVS has also advanced quickly. Methods such as MVSNet (Yao et al., 2018) and its successors (Yao et al., 2019; Gu et al., 2020; Yu and Gao, 2020) build plane-sweep cost volumes from deep features and regularize them with 3D convolutions. They achieve strong results on benchmarks, but memory and runtime grow rapidly with image resolution and depth range, and generalization to scenes unlike the training data is not guaranteed. Coarse-to-fine cascade designs reduce the cost, yet they still rely on supervised training and are limited by the resolutions they can afford. Traditional PatchMatch methods therefore remain attractive: they need no training, work at full resolution, and have modest memory requirements. Nevertheless, PatchMatch-based MVS faces two main challenges. The first concerns hypothesis propagation and view selection. In existing checkerboard schemes, each pixel receives candidate hypotheses from a fixed, small neighborhood pattern. These candidates are often spatially close and strongly correlated, and they may lie across depth discontinuities or in unreliable areas, so the sampled hypotheses do not reflect the local structure of the scene. Moreover, view selection is typically performed either with a single global criterion per image or with a per-pixel criterion computed from one hypothesis. A single hypothesis is a noisy basis for inferring which source views are useful, particularly early in optimization when most hypotheses are wrong. Poor view selection allows occluded or otherwise inconsistent views to contaminate the aggregated matching cost. The second challenge is low-textured regions. Photometric consistency measures such as normalized cross-correlation computed over fixed-size windows are almost uninformative there: many depth hypotheses give nearly identical costs, and the correct hypothesis is hard to distinguish. Enlarging the window blurs details and increases cost. Planar priors derived from sparse, reliable points and triangulation can help, but they depend on the quality of the sparse points and on the validity of the piecewise-planar assumption, and they may fail in curved or complex areas. A natural alternative is a multi-scale strategy. At coarser image scales, a fixed window covers a larger physical region, so low-textured areas contain more discriminative content and reliable estimates become easier to obtain. Yet simply upsampling a coarse depth map to initialize the next scale does not ensure that reliable estimates survive. At finer scales, the photometric cost in low-textured areas is again ambiguous and may overwrite correct coarse estimates with noisy ones. Conversely, coarse-scale estimates inevitably lose thin structures and boundary details, and upsampling can introduce errors at edges. A principled way is needed to keep the reliable coarse estimates while still recovering the details that coarse scales miss. In this paper, we ask how a PatchMatch-based MVS framework can obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details, while keeping the efficiency and training-free nature of the traditional pipeline. We answer by combining a stronger single-scale base method with geometric consistency guidance across scales. Our contributions are as follows. 1. We present a basic MVS method, ACMH, built on Adaptive Checkerboard sampling and Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection. The adaptive checkerboard sampling uses structured region information to choose, for each pixel, candidate hypotheses from a wider neighborhood that are more likely to be reliable, thereby improving propagation efficiency and robustness near discontinuities. The multi-hypothesis joint view selection uses the whole set of candidate hypotheses to infer the view subset used for cost aggregation at each pixel, which yields a more stable and informative selection than using one hypothesis. 2. We propose ACMM, which embeds ACMH in a multi-scale framework guided by geometric consistency. Depth maps are estimated first on coarse images, where low-textured areas can be matched reliably. Geometric consistency across views is then used to filter the estimates and to guide optimization at finer scales, so reliable coarse estimates are retained and can be propagated to the finest scale rather than being lost to ambiguous photometric costs. 3. We introduce a novel detail restorer to correct erroneous estimates propagated from coarser scales. It identifies regions where the upsampled estimates are inconsistent with finer-scale evidence and restores thin structures and boundaries through hypotheses generated at the finer scale, so that completeness gained in low-textured areas does not come at the expense of accuracy in details. 4. We conduct extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including ETH3D and Tanks and Temples, and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among traditional approaches and is competitive with learning-based methods, recovering depth in low-textured areas as well as in fine details, with good computational efficiency. Overview and notation. Given a reference image Iref and its source images {Ij}, j = 1,…,N−1, with calibrated cameras, we estimate a depth map for every image in turn, treating each as the reference. The poses and intrinsics come from a structure-from-motion pipeline (Schönberger and Frahm, 2016). Each pixel p carries a plane hypothesis θp = (np, dp), consisting of a unit normal and a depth. This follows the slanted-plane formulation of PatchMatch stereo (Bleyer et al., 2011; Barnes et al., 2009). Our pipeline has three components: a basic estimator (ACMH), a multi-scale geometric consistency scheme built on it (ACMM), and a detail restorer applied between scales. Depth maps are filtered and fused into a point cloud at the end. Matching cost. A hypothesis θp defines a homography that maps a patch around p in Iref to each source image Ij. The photometric cost cj(p, θp) is 1 − NCC between the reference patch and the warped source patch. The NCC uses bilateral weights over spatial and intensity distance (Schönberger et al., 2016). We use an 11×11 patch sampled with a stride of two pixels to reduce computation, as in Xu and Tao (2019). Adaptive checkerboard sampling. The standard checkerboard scheme (Galliani et al., 2015) propagates from a fixed set of neighbours, so it covers only a local, fixed-shape region and cannot reach good hypotheses beyond it. We keep the red-black update order, which allows parallel GPU computation. For each pixel in the active color, we instead define eight sampling areas around it: four V-shaped areas near the pixel and four strip-shaped areas that extend farther along the axes and diagonals. Within each area we take a small set of same-color candidate pixels and keep the one with the lowest matching cost. This gives eight candidate hypotheses per pixel, which can come from distances well beyond the immediate neighbourhood. The strips let correct hypotheses cross small occlusions or weakly textured gaps, and the V-shaped areas preserve local structure. Multi-hypothesis joint view selection. Using all source images for every pixel includes occluded or badly overlapping views and corrupts the aggregated cost. Earlier methods select views from a single hypothesis (Zheng et al., 2014) or from a fixed neighbourhood. We instead use all eight candidates jointly. For each candidate i and source view j we compute a cost cij, which gives an 8×(N−1) cost matrix. With an iteration-dependent threshold τ(t) = τ₀·exp(−t²/α), view j is "good" for candidate i if cij < τ(t). The threshold starts loose and tightens as the iterations converge. A view is added to the pixel's aggregation subset if it is good for at least n₁ candidates, which exploits the structured-region evidence. A view whose cost exceeds a hard upper bound for any candidate is rejected, which guards against occluders. Each selected view receives a weight wj from the number of candidates for which it is good, and the weights are carried over to later iterations as a prior (Zheng et al., 2014). The aggregated cost of candidate i is ci = Σj wj cij / Σj wj. We evaluate the eight candidates under the new view subset and keep the lowest-cost one for the pixel. Hypothesis refinement. Propagation alone cannot repair hypotheses that are wrong in either depth or normal. After propagation, we form a small set of combinations of the current depth and normal, a randomly drawn depth and normal, and a perturbed version of the current ones. We evaluate all combinations under the selected view subset and keep the cheapest. Hypotheses are randomly initialized at the coarsest scale. Each scale runs a fixed number of iterations (three in our experiments), alternating red and black passes. Multi-scale geometric consistency guidance (ACMM). Photometric costs are ambiguous in low-textured regions at fine scales, because a large patch there shows no distinctive structure. Coarser scales have a larger effective support, so reliable estimates are more likely to emerge there. We build an image pyramid (K scales, downsampling factor two, with camera intrinsics scaled accordingly) and run ACMH from the coarsest scale. The result at scale k is bilinearly upsampled to serve as initialization for scale k−1. For this we use the nearest-neighbour rule for normals and bilinear interpolation for depths, and we do not interpolate across large depth discontinuities. Initialization alone does not prevent the finer-scale photometric cost from overwriting good coarse estimates in textureless areas. We therefore add a geometric consistency term, in the spirit of Schönberger et al. (2016), that uses the upsampled depth maps of the source views. A pixel p in the reference image is projected into source view j using hypothesis θp, and the depth stored for that location in the upsampled source depth map is read out. The resulting point is projected back into the reference. The geometric cost is the reprojection error cgeo,j = min(‖p − p′j‖, ψ), where p′j is the back-projected location and ψ is a truncation value. The guided cost used at scale k is cj = cphoto,j + η·cgeo,j, where η balances the two terms. Because the source depth maps come from the coarser scale, reliable coarse estimates act as a constraint on the finer-scale search. A hypothesis that is photometrically ambiguous but inconsistent with the coarse structure is penalized, and the coarse estimates in low-textured areas survive at finer scales. At the coarsest scale no prior exists, so ACMH runs with photometric cost alone. Detail restorer. Coarse-scale guidance can also propagate errors into regions with thin structures or sharp boundaries, where the coarse estimate is over-smoothed. The detail restorer corrects this at each finer scale. Besides the guided estimate θp^g, we compute for each pixel an independent estimate θp^s from photometric ACMH sampling at the current scale, without geometric guidance and without the coarse initialization. We compare the two hypotheses under the same photometric aggregated cost. If the independent estimate's cost is lower than that of the guided estimate by a margin δ, and its depth is not in conflict with the coarse estimate in a way that indicates

Ovarian cancer is the eighth most common cancer in women worldwide and one of the most lethal gynaecological malignancies, with an estimated 295,000 new cases and 185,000 deaths annually (Bray et al., 2018). Because early disease is typically asymptomatic and no effective population screening exists, approximately three-quarters of women are diagnosed at an advanced stage (Torre et al., 2018; Reid et al., 2017). The standard of care combines cytoreductive surgery with platinum- and taxane-based chemotherapy. Although most women achieve an initial clinical response, the majority of those with advanced disease relapse, and five-year survival remains below 50% (Torre et al., 2018). Ovarian cancer is therefore increasingly conceptualised as a chronic, relapsing condition, in which patients alternate between periods of intensive treatment, surveillance and uncertainty about recurrence. This trajectory, together with the physical burden of surgery, treatment toxicity, symptoms such as ascites and bowel obstruction, and threats to fertility and body image, places women with ovarian cancer at substantial risk of psychological morbidity. Depression and anxiety are the most common psychiatric complications in oncology. A meta-analysis of interview-based studies estimated the prevalence of major depression at around 14% in oncological settings and 16% in palliative-care settings, with anxiety and adjustment disorders contributing a further substantial burden (Mitchell et al., 2011). Psychological distress in cancer has consequences extending well beyond subjective suffering. It is associated with poorer adherence to treatment, reduced quality of life, greater healthcare utilisation, impaired functioning and increased suicide risk (Pitman et al., 2018; Fann et al., 2008). Meta-analytic evidence also links depression to higher cancer-specific and all-cause mortality (Satin et al., 2009). In ovarian cancer specifically, experimental and clinical work has suggested that behavioural and neuroendocrine pathways, including adrenergic signalling, may influence tumour progression, providing a biological rationale for the clinical relevance of affective symptoms in this disease (Lutgendorf et al., 2008, 2012). Whatever the causal mechanisms, the detection and management of depression and anxiety are widely recognised as integral to comprehensive cancer care. Despite this, psychological distress in cancer remains underrecognised and undertreated. Clinicians tend to attribute low mood, fatigue, sleep disturbance and loss of appetite to the disease or its treatment rather than to a treatable affective disorder, and consultations are frequently dominated by oncological and physical concerns (Mitchell et al., 2011; Pitman et al., 2018). In gynaecological oncology, where patients are often managed within time-limited clinic appointments and with limited access to psycho-oncology services, there is a particular risk that distress goes unidentified. Appropriately targeting screening and intervention requires robust data on how common these conditions are, and at which points in the illness trajectory the risk is greatest. The existing literature on depression and anxiety in ovarian cancer is, however, fragmented and inconsistent. Reported prevalence estimates range widely, from under 10% to more than 40% for depressive symptoms and similarly for anxiety, and several factors contribute to this heterogeneity. Studies vary in their sampling frames and sample sizes, in disease stage and treatment modality, and in the instruments used to define caseness, which include self-report screening questionnaires such as the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, the Beck Depression Inventory and the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, as well as structured diagnostic interviews (Norton et al., 2004; Hipkins et al., 2004). Perhaps most importantly, the timing of assessment relative to treatment differs between studies. Women assessed shortly after diagnosis, when they face the shock of a life-threatening illness and the prospect of major surgery, may experience a different psychological profile from those undergoing chemotherapy, with its cumulative toxicity, alopecia and fatigue, or those in remission who must contend with fear of recurrence and the late effects of treatment. Yet previous reviews of psychological outcomes in gynaecological or ovarian cancer have generally pooled findings across the care pathway, or have focused on quality of life and broader constructs of distress rather than on clinically meaningful depression and anxiety. As a result, it remains unclear whether prevalence differs systematically across the stages of treatment, and how it compares with that in the general female population, in which the 12-month prevalence of major depression and of anxiety disorders is estimated at roughly 6% to 8% and 10% to 15%, respectively (Kessler et al., 2005; Baxter et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2013). This gap has practical as well as scientific importance. If depression and anxiety peak at particular junctures, for example around diagnosis, during chemotherapy or after treatment completion, then screening schedules, referral pathways and supportive interventions could be timed and resourced accordingly. Conversely, if prevalence is uniformly elevated across the illness course, continuous surveillance of psychological well-being should be embedded within routine follow-up. Contemporary survivorship frameworks and the growing emphasis on patient-reported outcomes in oncology make such evidence timely. Moreover, quantitative synthesis can quantify the extent to which observed prevalence exceeds population norms, and so can inform health-service planning and the design of future trials of psychological and pharmacological interventions in this population. The present study therefore aimed to systematically review and meta-analyse the published literature on the prevalence of depression and anxiety in women with ovarian cancer, stratified by stage of treatment. Specifically, we sought to estimate pooled prevalence rates of depression and anxiety separately before treatment, during active treatment and after treatment completion, and to compare these with prevalence in the healthy female population. We hypothesised that the prevalence of both conditions would be elevated relative to the general population at every stage, and that it would vary with the phase of the treatment pathway. This work makes several contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first meta-analytic estimates of depression and anxiety prevalence in ovarian cancer that are explicitly differentiated by treatment stage, rather than aggregated across heterogeneous clinical contexts. Second, by applying systematic search procedures and explicit inclusion criteria to primary research, and by pooling data from several thousand patients, it offers more precise estimates than any individual study can provide, together with an appraisal of the sources of between-study variability. Third, it benchmarks these estimates against population-level data, thereby clarifying the magnitude of excess psychological morbidity in this patient group. Finally, by identifying where evidence is sparse or methodologically limited, the review highlights priorities for future research and informs ongoing efforts to ensure that psychological distress in ovarian cancer is recognised and adequately treated. Protocol and reporting standards This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) and the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines (Stroup et al., 2000). The review protocol was developed a priori by all authors, and any deviations from it were resolved by consensus. Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible if they (1) were full-length, peer-reviewed journal articles published in English; (2) enrolled adult women (≥18 years) with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of ovarian cancer, including fallopian tube and primary peritoneal carcinomas where these were analysed together with ovarian cancer; (3) assessed depression, anxiety, or both using a validated self-report instrument or a structured or semi-structured clinical interview; and (4) reported, or allowed calculation of, the number of patients meeting a defined threshold for depression or anxiety, together with the total sample size. Cohort, cross-sectional, and baseline data from randomised or non-randomised trials were considered. Studies were excluded if they (1) reported only continuous symptom scores without a clinically defined cut-off; (2) enrolled mixed gynaecological or mixed cancer populations without presenting ovarian cancer data separately; (3) were case reports, qualitative studies, reviews, conference abstracts, or dissertations; or (4) recruited participants exclusively on the basis of pre-existing psychiatric diagnoses or selected them for psychological distress. Where multiple publications described the same cohort, the report with the largest sample or the most complete data was retained to avoid double counting. Search strategy We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to the date of the final search. The search strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms relating to ovarian neoplasms (e.g., “ovarian cancer”, “ovarian carcinoma”, “ovarian neoplasm”), depression (e.g., “depress”, “depressive disorder”, “mood disorder”), and anxiety (e.g., “anxi”, “anxiety disorder”, “psychological distress”), and was adapted to the syntax of each database. No restrictions were placed on publication date. The reference lists of all included articles and of relevant previous reviews were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies, and forward citation tracking was performed for key papers. Study selection All records were imported into reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially relevant records were then retrieved and assessed independently by the same reviewers. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or, where necessary, adjudication by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the full-text stage was quantified using Cohen’s kappa (Cohen, 1960). Data extraction Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardised, piloted form. Extracted variables included first author, year of publication, country, study design, sample size, mean or median age, cancer stage and histology where available, the instrument used to assess depression and anxiety, the cut-off score applied, and the number of patients above threshold. Treatment stage at the time of assessment was recorded and classified into three categories: pretreatment (after diagnosis but before the commencement of surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy), on-treatment (during active primary or recurrent treatment, including adjuvant and palliative chemotherapy), and post-treatment (following completion of primary treatment, including survivorship and surveillance periods). Where a study reported data at multiple time points, each time point was extracted and assigned to the relevant category; however, to preserve independence, a single study contributed no more than one estimate to any given treatment-stage pooled analysis. In such cases, the time point closest to the midpoint of the stage was selected. Where data were unclear or missing, corresponding authors were contacted by email. Assessment of risk of bias Methodological quality was appraised independently by two reviewers using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data (Munn et al., 2015). This instrument evaluates the appropriateness of the sampling frame and sampling method, adequacy of sample size, description of participants and setting, coverage of the sample in data analysis, validity and reliability of the measurement of the condition, appropriateness of statistical analysis, and adequacy of the response rate. Each item was rated as yes, no, unclear, or not applicable, and studies were classified as being at low (≥7 of 9 items satisfied), moderate (5–6 items), or high (≤4 items) risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Quality ratings were used to inform sensitivity analyses rather than as grounds for exclusion. Outcomes The primary outcomes were the pooled prevalence of depression and the pooled prevalence of anxiety in women with ovarian cancer, each stratified by treatment stage (pretreatment, on-treatment, and post-treatment). Prevalence was defined as the proportion of participants scoring at or above the validated cut-off of the instrument used in the primary study, or meeting diagnostic criteria on clinical interview. Because instruments differ in their operating characteristics, the instrument type was recorded and examined as a potential source of heterogeneity. Statistical analysis Prevalence estimates and their standard errors were computed for each study from the number of cases and sample size. As proportions close to 0 or 1 violate the assumption of normality and yield variance instability, the study-level proportions were stabilised using the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation (Freeman & Tukey, 1950) prior to pooling, and pooled estimates were back-transformed for presentation as percentages with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Given the anticipated clinical and methodological diversity among studies, a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator was used for all primary analyses (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). Separate meta-analyses were conducted for depression and anxiety at each treatment stage. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test and quantified using the I² statistic, with values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al., 2003). In the face of unprecedented amounts of genomics data generated by the molecular biology revolution, researchers have developed a massive number of databases aiming to deal with gigantic volumes of biological data. Retrieving, preprocessing and curating biological data are nontrivial, time-consuming and error-prone. Instead, pooling and sharing such data significantly accelerate scientific progress, but questions remain about how these data will impact research practice, from wet-lab biologists to bioinformaticians. In a 2012 review (1), authors point out the power of reusing public gene expression data, spanned mainly in three directions: (i) the study of a biological question, (ii) the development and evaluation of a new method and (iii) the integration, annotation and analysis of primary data in order to build a new, value-added data resource. Biological databases are being developed with a different purpose, structure and data; however, it remains a crucial fact that biological sense can only fully be made from genomics data when accurate and adequate contextual information is available. This information is essential for data to be discoverable by the user and to lead to deep interpretation. Besides the importance of standardized annotation on discoverability and downstream use of genomics datasets, sufficient contextual annotation is frequently lacking in public biomedical data sets (2, 3). Hooper et al. (3) also emphasize its significant costs and the need for a submitter-driven annotation system as a sustainable curation solution. Regardless of the use they serve, biological databases developed nowadays should follow BioDBcore’s guidelines and standards (http://biocuration.org/community/standards-biodbcore/), the findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable data principles and any related standards defined by the functional genomics data society, like the minimum information about a microarray experiment or minimum information about a high-throughput nucleotide SEQuencing experiment for microarray or high-throughput sequencing gene expression data, such as Illumina, formerly next-generation Sequencing, respectively. Biological database developers must also ensure that their database is accurately listed in catalogs like biosharing.org (4). As several biological data repositories are being developed, the need for tools and services to find, access and use those repositories becomes apparent. DataMed, e.g. is an ongoing project for the development of a biomedical data search engine to discover data sets across multiple data repositories by keyword search (https://datamed.org/). It is supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Big Data to Knowledge. Repositive, an online platform that indexes genomic data also offers a single place to search for and access a range of human genomic data. Besides tools to search and retrieve biological data, data curation projects are making great progress mining biomedical literature to extract and aggregate decades worth of research findings. inSilicoDB (5), an open data management and access platform, allows programmatic download of gene expression data curated by maintainers or contributors from the community, however users may only retrieve one experiment at a time. In GENEVESTIGATOR (6), authors claim to offer quality controlled, normalized and carefully manually annotated by experts, microarray and RNA-Seq expression data from several organisms, however GENEVESTIGATOR is a commercial product offering a free limited use to academics. Automated repository acquisition (ARepA) (7) retrieves heterogeneous data from multiple public repositories in a uniform environment and format; however retrieved data are normalized for between-dataset comparison and thus, it is restricted to a per pipeline normalization. Moreover, ARepA is a command-line tool supported by Linux and MacOS only. Microarray meta-analysis database (M2DB) (8) is a human curated microarray database with manually curated sample annotations developed to promote meta-analysis. However, M2DB contains data only from two human microarrays and although it applies three of the most widely used preprocessing algorithms [MAS5, RMA (Robust Multiarray Average) and GCRMA (GC Robust Multiarray Average)], these are array-dependent algorithms and cannot preprocess samples separately. Single array preprocessing algorithms, like frozen Robust Multiarray Average (fRMA) (9) or Single-channel array normalization (SCAN) (10), have several advantages over multi-array alternatives (11). Rapid accumulation of vast amounts of microarray data in public databases like gene expression omnibus (GEO) (12) and ArrayExpress (13) over the past few years has now made it possible to retrieve, integrate and compare microarray results from many datasets. Tools that focus on differential gene expression analysis and integrate or compare data based on gene expression profiles have been developed. GeoDiver (14) is an online web application for performing differential gene expression analysis and generally applicable gene-set enrichment analysis on gene expression datasets from the publicly available GEO. Gemma (15), is a resource for the reuse, sharing and meta-analysis of expression profiling data. ExpressionBlast (16) compares gene expression data with thousands of other studies in order to find experiments with similar profiles. Bgee (17) retrieves and compares gene expression patterns in multiple animal species produced from multiple data types. Harmonizome (18) integrates data about genes and proteins from many online resources into ∼72 million functional associations between genes/proteins and their attributes. As the development of structured, and thus suitable for integration data increases, along with the development of tools that integrate data from various databases to advance biomolecular knowledge, the need for uniformly preprocessed datasets, automatically annotated based on established ontologies and ready for downstream analysis will grow in parallel. Some of the current approaches mentioned earlier, often need manual curation and data annotation thus is limited to certain samples. They also don’t ensure a uniform preprocessing, may be commercial or not updated. Even though lack of standardization in biological databases has been brought to the attention of the research community long time ago and significant progress has been done towards that direction, it remains an issue. Inspired by the need to reuse public omics data (1) and help uncover insights buried in this vast amount of data, and driven by the lack of standardization in biological databases, we developed BioDataome, a web-based tool, which addresses those challenges. In BioDataome, we have downloaded, preprocessed and annotated several thousands of omics data. All raw data have been retrieved from GEO and recount (19). Currently, BioDataome holds ∼5600 datasets from five different microarray gene expression technologies (GPL570, GPL96, GPL6244 and GPL1261), the GPL13534 Human Methylation BeadChip from GEO and the GPL11154 high-throughput sequencing technology from recount. Most of the samples are Homo Sapiens (243 563 samples) and the rest are Mus Musculus (20 723 samples). BioDataome is updated bi-weekly with ∼500 samples and summary statistics can be found on its home page (http://dataome.mensxmachina.org/). In BioDataome, users can download uniformly preprocessed omics data and perform complex queries to design their analysis and develop tools that integrate biomedical knowledge. We have also developed BioDataome R package that contains all the functions used to download, preprocess and annotate all the datasets and BioDataome vignettes, which provides a task-oriented description of BioDataome package, examples of user interaction with BioDataome and some examples of analyzing BioDataome datasets. GEO (12) is a database supported by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) at the National Library of Medicine (NLM), which accepts raw and processed data with written descriptions of experimental design, sample attributes and methodology for studies of high-throughput gene expression and genomics. GEO is one of largest gene expression data repositories. As of September 2016, it contains microarray and RNA-Seq experiment results of 1 936 127 samples grouped into 73 415 datasets (named ‘data series’ in GEOs terminology). An up-to-date summary of GEO data types and content is provided at http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/summary/. According to GEO, a series record defines a group of related samples and provides a focal point and description of the whole study. Series records may also contain tables describing extracted data, summary conclusions or analyses. Each series record is assigned a unique GEO accession number (GSExxx) that summarizes an experiment. R package rentrez provides an R interface to the NCBI's EUtils API allowing users to search databases (20). We used rentrez to fetch a list of datasets that meets our query criteria (i.e. get Homo sapiens studies with sample size between 200 and 300, measured with GPL570 and provide CEL files). Recount (19) is an online resource consisting of RNA-seq gene and exon counts from nearly 60 000 human RNA-seq samples from the sequence read archive (SRA). Recount is available in https://jhubiostatistics.shinyapps.io/recount/ and was last accessed on September 2016. It is a resource of processed and summarized expression data into concise gene count tables. In recount, data were processed using a single processing pipeline enabling thus a wider variety of downstream analyses. Recount R/Bioconductor package (https://github.com/leekgroup/recount) provides a convenient API for querying, downloading and analyzing the data. Each processed study consists of meta- and phenotype data, the expression levels of genes and their underlying exons and splice junctions and corresponding genomic annotation. We used recount as the main source of BioDataome’s RNA-Seq gene expression data. As of May 2017, we downloaded and processed gene expression data for Homo Sapiens and Mus Musculus samples from GEO and Homo Sapiens from recount.
