Aphasia, a condition characterized by language-cognitive impairments resulting from stroke, has been a topic of extensive research in the fields of neurology, linguistics, and cognitive psychology (Benson, 1979; Goodglass, 1993). The complex and heterogeneous nature of aphasia has led to the development of various diagnostic frameworks and taxonomies, aiming to capture the diverse patterns of language deficits and paraphasias (i.e., naming errors) exhibited by individuals with aphasia (Kertesz, 1979; Luzzatti et al., 2001). Despite the fact that both language deficits and paraphasias feature prominently in diagnostic criteria, most research has focused primarily on the lesion correlates of language deficits, with minimal attention paid to the pattern of patients' paraphasias (Dronkers et al., 2004; Hillis et al., 2006). This disparity in research focus has resulted in a limited understanding of the complex interplay between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their underlying neural bases. The diagnostic criteria for aphasia typically include a combination of language deficits, such as anomia (difficulty naming objects), alexia (difficulty reading), and agrammatism (difficulty with grammatical structures), as well as paraphasias, including semantic, phonological, and neologistic errors (Goodglass, 1993; Kertesz, 1979). However, the majority of studies have investigated the neural correlates of language deficits in isolation, without considering the pattern of paraphasias exhibited by individuals with aphasia (Damasio, 1992; Demonet et al., 2005). This approach has led to a fragmented understanding of the relationship between language deficits, paraphasias, and their underlying neural mechanisms. Recent studies have begun to address this gap by exploring the neural correlates of specific types of paraphasias, such as semantic and phonological errors (Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006; Schwartz et al., 2009). However, these studies have typically employed experimenter-derived methods to combine across error types, which may not accurately capture the complex patterns of paraphasias exhibited by individuals with aphasia (Caramazza & Hillis, 1990). Furthermore, the use of a priori categories to classify paraphasias may not account for the inherent variability and individual differences in error patterns (Nickels, 2002). To overcome these limitations, a data-driven approach is necessary to fuse patient impairments and their pattern of errors into a unified model of chronic post-stroke aphasia. The primary research question guiding this study is: What is the triangulation of language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases in post-stroke aphasia? To address this question, we employed a data-driven approach, using principal component analysis (PCA) to identify the underlying patterns of paraphasias and language deficits in a cohort of individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia. By analyzing the co-occurrence of fifteen error types, we aimed to establish a comprehensive model of the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates. This approach allowed us to avoid focusing on a subset of errors or using experimenter-derived methods to combine across error types, instead capturing the complex and multifaceted nature of aphasia. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we provide a comprehensive model of the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates, which can inform the development of more effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for individuals with aphasia. Second, our data-driven approach offers a novel method for analyzing the complex patterns of paraphasias and language deficits in aphasia, which can be applied to future research in this field. Third, by identifying the unique lesion correlates of specific error types and language deficits, we contribute to the existing literature on the neural basis of language processing and its relationship to aphasia (Damasio, 1992; Demonet et al., 2005). Overall, this study aims to advance our understanding of the complex and multifaceted nature of aphasia, and to provide a foundation for the development of more effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for individuals with post-stroke aphasia. This study utilised a cross-sectional design, examining the language and cognitive abilities of 105 patients with chronic post-stroke aphasia (M = 62.4 years, SD = 10.1, range = 45-85 years). Patients were recruited from local stroke support groups and speech-language pathology clinics, and were included if they had a single left-hemisphere stroke, were at least six months post-stroke, and had no prior history of neurological or psychiatric disorder (Kertesz, 1982). All patients provided informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee. Language and cognitive assessment was conducted using a comprehensive battery of 25 tests, including measures of lexical-semantic processing (e.g., Boston Naming Test, Pyramid and Palm Trees Test; Howard & Patterson, 1992), phonological processing (e.g., Nonword Repetition Test, Phonological Awareness Test; Gathercole & Baddeley, 1996), speech production (e.g., Test of Speech Fluency, Sentence Repetition Test; Shewan, 1988), and executive-cognitive function (e.g., Trail Making Test, Stroop Test; Lezak, 1995). Each test was administered by a trained speech-language pathologist, and patient responses were audiotaped and transcribed for subsequent error analysis. Error analysis was conducted using a standardized protocol (Kelly & Armstrong, 2001), in which patient responses were categorized into 15 error types, including omission errors, semantically-related responses, phonologically-related responses, dysfluent responses, and circumlocutions, among others. This error categorization system has been previously validated (Nickels, 2002) and has been shown to be reliable across different examiners (Croot et al., 2003). Error types were counted and calculated as a proportion of the total number of responses for each patient. In order to reduce the dimensionality of the error data and identify underlying patterns of co-occurrence, principal component analysis (PCA) was used. PCA is a statistical technique that is well-suited to analyzing complex, high-dimensional data sets (Jolliffe, 2002), and has been previously used to examine language and cognitive impairments in aphasia (Mirman et al., 2010). The error data were first standardized using z-scores, and then submitted to PCA using a varianceimax rotation (Kaiser, 1958). The number of components to retain was determined using the scree plot method (Cattell, 1966), which indicated that five components should be retained. The resulting components were then examined for their relationship to the patients' language and cognitive abilities. To do this, the patients' performance on the comprehensive language and cognitive assessment battery was analyzed using an additional PCA. This PCA was conducted on the 25 language and cognitive tests, and used a similar procedure to that described above. The resulting components were then aligned with the error-related components using a procrustes rotation (Schönemann, 1966), which allowed for the identification of the relationships between the error types and the language and cognitive impairments. Lesion analysis was conducted using MRI scans, which were available for 80 of the 105 patients. Lesion location and extent were calculated using the Automated Lesion Identification algorithm (Damasio, 2005), and were then examined for their relationship to the identified components. Specifically, voxel-wise lesion-symptom mapping (VLSM) was used to examine the relationship between lesion location and the components (Bates et al., 2003). VLSM is a statistical technique that allows for the examination of the relationship between lesion location and behavioral deficits, and has been previously used to examine language and cognitive impairments in aphasia (Turkeltaub et al., 2011). Statistical analysis was conducted using R version 3.6.1 (R Core Team, 2020), and included descriptive statistics, PCA, and VLSM. The level of statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and Bonferroni correction was used to control for multiple comparisons. The results of the PCA and VLSM analyses were then used to inform the development of a model of the triangulation of language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates in post-stroke aphasia. The principal component analysis (PCA) of the patients' error patterns revealed five underlying components, which accounted for 75.6% of the total variance in the data (Bartlett's test of sphericity: χ² = 2345.6, p < 0.001) (Kaiser, 1960). The first component, which explained 23.1% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of omission errors (0.85), and to a lesser extent, semantically-related responses (0.41) and dysfluent responses (0.35). The second component, which accounted for 18.5% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of semantically-related responses (0.83) and phonologically-related responses (0.56). The third component, which explained 15.6% of the variance, was defined by high loadings of phonologically-related responses (0.81) and dysfluent responses (0.49). The fourth component, which accounted for 10.3% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of circumlocutions (0.89) and mixed errors (0.63). The fifth component, which explained 8.1% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of dysfluent responses (0.75) and omission errors (0.51). To further investigate the relationship between the patients' error patterns and their language and cognitive impairments, we conducted an additional PCA on the combined data (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2001). This analysis revealed seven unique fused impairment-paraphasia factors, which accounted for 82.1% of the total variance in the data (Bartlett's test of sphericity: χ² = 3512.9, p < 0.001). The first factor, which explained 21.5% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of phonological working memory tasks (0.85), phonologically-related responses (0.73), and expressive phonological abilities (0.69). The second factor, which accounted for 17.3% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of semantic tasks (0.88), semantically-related responses (0.63), and executive-cognitive skills (0.56). The third factor, which explained 13.5% of the variance, was defined by high loadings of speech fluency tasks (0.92), dysfluent responses (0.83), and speech quanta (0.61). The fourth factor, which accounted for 11.4% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of phonological (input) discrimination tasks (0.89), phonologically-related responses (0.65), and circumlocution-type errors (0.58). The fifth factor, which explained 9.5% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of executive-cognitive skills (0.85), semantically-related responses (0.63), and speech quanta (0.56). The sixth factor, which accounted for 8.2% of the variance, was defined by high loadings of circumlocution errors (0.93) and mixed errors (0.75). The seventh factor, which explained 6.1% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of output phonology tasks (0.87), phonologically-related responses (0.69), and expressive phonological abilities (0.61). The lesion analysis revealed that three components had unique lesion correlates. The phonological working memory component was associated with damage to the primary auditory region (Brodmann area 41), with a peak lesion overlap of 75.6% (n = 25 patients) (Rademacher et al., 2001). The semantic component was associated with damage to the anterior temporal region (Brodmann area 38), with a peak lesion overlap of 68.2% (n = 22 patients) (Damasio et al., 2000). The fluency component was associated with damage to the pre-central gyrus (Brodmann area 4), with a peak lesion overlap of 61.9% (n = 20 patients) (Mohr et al., 1978). These findings are consistent with existing literature on the neural basis of language processing (Geschwind, 1970). The pattern of co-occurrence between the fifteen error types was also examined. The results showed that omission errors co-occurred with semantically-related responses (r = 0.56, p < 0.01) and dysfluent responses (r = 0.49, p < 0.05). Semantically-related responses co-occurred with phonologically-related responses (r = 0.63, p < 0.001) and circumlocutions (r = 0.51, p < 0.05). Phonologically-related responses co-occurred with dysfluent responses (r = 0.59, p < 0.01) and mixed errors (r = 0.46, p < 0.05). These findings suggest that the patients' error patterns are complex and multifaceted, and that different error types are related to different underlying language and cognitive impairments. The correlations between the patients' error patterns and their language and cognitive impairments were also examined. The results showed that phonological working memory tasks were correlated with phonologically-related responses (r = 0.71, p < 0.001) and expressive phonological abilities (r = 0.65, p < 0.01). Semantic tasks were correlated with semantically-related responses (r = 0.68, p < 0.001) and executive-cognitive skills (r = 0.56, p < 0.05). Speech fluency tasks were correlated with dysfluent responses (r = 0.79, p < 0.001) and speech quanta (r = 0.63, p < 0.01). These findings suggest that the patients' error patterns are related to their underlying language and cognitive impairments, and that different error types are associated with different cognitive and linguistic processes. In conclusion, the results of this study provide new insights into the complex relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases in post-stroke aphasia. The findings suggest that the patients' error patterns are multifaceted and related to different underlying language and cognitive

Introduction The evolution of mental health care and its delivery has been a pivotal focus in contemporary health systems, particularly in the context of the United Kingdom. A significant milestone in this regard has been the introduction of the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme in England. Established in 2008 by the Department of Health in response to the increasing prevalence of common mental health disorders, IAPT aimed to transform the landscape of mental healthcare by expanding access to evidence-based psychological therapies, primarily cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), for individuals suffering from conditions such as depression and anxiety (Clark, 2011). This paper examines the IAPT initiative to understand its inception, evolution, impact, and the broader implications on psychological therapy and mental health care in the UK. Despite the growing prevalence of mental health issues globally, traditional approaches to mental health treatment have faced criticism for limited accessibility and effectiveness. Prior to the establishment of IAPT, access to psychological therapies in the UK was often restricted due to high costs and limited availability of services, resulting in significant treatment gaps. Many patients were either untreated or relied heavily on pharmacological interventions (Layard, 2006). Recognizing this gap, the IAPT programme was launched as part of a broader policy initiative to improve mental health services through early intervention, enhanced accessibility, and evidence-based practices (Department of Health, 2008). The programme represents a paradigm shift from the predominant biomedical model to include psychological approaches in addressing mental health concerns. IAPT's expansion and structuring of services pose a critical question: how effective has the programme been in addressing the service gaps in mental health care? Moreover, what impact has it had on the perceptions and practices surrounding psychological therapy? While extensive data have highlighted IAPT’s role in increasing accessibility — with over two million people accessing IAPT services by 2020 (NHS Digital, 2020) — there remains debate regarding its long-term efficacy, sustainability, and broader societal effects. Some critics have raised concerns about the potential over-standardization of therapy and reliance on CBT as the dominant modality, potentially overlooking the complexities of individual patient needs and diverse therapeutic approaches (Gyani et al., 2013). This study seeks to contribute to the discourse surrounding psychological therapy and mental healthcare by elucidating the processes through which the IAPT initiative was developed, operationalized, and sustained as a national strategy. We aim to analyze both qualitative and quantitative data to assess the programme's outcomes and its integral role in the transformation of mental healthcare. The research question guiding this examination is thus: In what ways has the introduction of the IAPT initiative reshaped access to psychological therapy, accountability within mental health services, and the overarching framework of mental healthcare in the UK? This enquiry seeks to fill existing gaps in the literature that often discuss the efficacy of psychological therapies in isolation, without considering their integration within health system frameworks. By situating IAPT within the broader context of health policy and service provision, we aim to uncover the multidimensional impacts of the programme. The paper provides an innovative contribution by framing IAPT as both a content and context within UK mental health services, exploring how it has influenced subsequent initiatives and the broader discourse on mental health treatment. In doing so, the study challenges and extends current understandings of health system reform, particularly in the realm of mental health, which has typically been dominated by discussions of biomedicalization and pharmacological treatment strategies. Furthermore, by documenting the economic rationales behind the establishment of IAPT and its subsequent operational strategies, we consider the implications of intertwining economic expertise with health service delivery. This approach reveals how psychotherapeutic interventions have been economically validated within the healthcare system, suggesting a potential shift in the value placed on psychological versus pharmacological treatments (Layard et al., 2007). Thus, this paper lends itself to re-evaluating the role of economic factors in shaping health policy decisions, highlighting an area often underexplored in health service research. In summary, this study offers a comprehensive exploration of the IAPT programme and its significance in the transformation of psychological therapy and mental health services in the UK. By contextualizing IAPT within existing health policy frameworks and examining its implications, the paper aims to enrich discussions on health system reforms and the dynamics of therapy access and accountability. Ultimately, this analysis seeks to foster a more nuanced understanding of the role psychological therapies play in contemporary healthcare, challenging assumptions of linear trajectories of biomedicalization while underscoring the complex interrelations of health policy, economic rationale, and mental healthcare delivery. The present study utilized a mixed-methods approach to evaluate the impact and proliferation of the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme in the United Kingdom's public mental healthcare system. Drawing evidence from quantitative data sources and qualitative interviews, our analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of how the programme has transformed mental health service delivery, access, and accountability (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2011). Data Collection To achieve a robust examination of the IAPT initiative, our data collection was twofold. Firstly, we gathered quantitative data from the National Health Service (NHS) databases, which provided information on therapy utilization rates, patient demographics, treatment outcomes, and programme coverage across different regions. Specifically, we analyzed data from April 2015 to March 2020, a period during which the programme underwent significant development and extension (NHS Digital, 2020). Secondly, qualitative data was collected through semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders, including therapists, programme administrators, policymakers, and service users. These interviews aimed to obtain detailed insights into the experiences and perceptions of those directly involved or affected by the IAPT services (Smith, 2007). Study Design This research employed a cross-sectional study design integrated with a longitudinal component, allowing for examination of changes over time while simultaneously capturing snapshots of specific periods. The quantitative analysis focused on evaluating trends in therapy uptake, treatment effectiveness, and geographical coverage across England. The qualitative analysis utilized thematic coding to extract meaningful insights concerning the stakeholders' experiences, understanding, and perspectives of the programme (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Participants Quantitative data were population-based, covering all regions in England where IAPT services were operational. The qualitative component included 50 stakeholders, purposively sampled to ensure diverse representation across roles, regions, and experiences with the programme. Ethical approval was obtained from the University Research Ethics Committee, and participants were assured confidentiality and anonymity throughout the study (Wiles, 2013). Procedures For the quantitative component, data on therapy utilization and outcomes were extracted from NHS Digital, which maintains comprehensive records of mental health service delivery within the public healthcare system. Variables considered included patient demographics, referral rates, treatment types, session numbers, Recovery Rates, and Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation (CORE) scores. The qualitative interviews were conducted either face-to-face or via video conferencing, depending on participant preference and availability. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and subjected to thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and themes (Miles, Huberman, & Saldana, 2014). An interview guide was developed to steer discussions, focusing on participants' perceptions of the programme's accessibility, accountability measures, challenges faced in service delivery, and the overall impact of IAPT on mental health care. The interview questions were pilot-tested for clarity and relevance among a small subset of participants before full deployment. Statistical Analysis The quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS Version 26 for descriptive and inferential statistics. Descriptive statistics provided an overview of therapy coverage, utilization trends, and patient demographics, highlighting variations by age, gender, and geographical location. Inferential statistics involved t-tests and ANOVA to examine differences in outcomes between demographic groups and regions, while regression analysis assessed predictive factors for successful treatment outcomes (Field, 2018). For the qualitative data, NVivo 12 software facilitated the coding and organizational analysis of interviews, following an inductive thematic analysis approach as proposed by Braun and Clarke (2006). Themes were developed iteratively, ensuring analytic rigor through peer debriefing and triangulation with quantitative findings. Regular team meetings were held to discuss and refine the emerging themes and ensure fidelity to the data (Guba & Lincoln, 1989). By integrating quantitative and qualitative data, this study provides a comprehensive evaluation of IAPT, exploring both its statistical effectiveness and stakeholder perspectives. The dual approach ensured a nuanced understanding of how IAPT has been operationalized and perceived across the mental healthcare landscape, reinforcing the programme's significance in the wider context of UK health service provision (Tashakkori & Teddlie, 2010). This methodological rigor not only enhances the reliability of the findings but also contributes to the ongoing discourse on the intersection of psychological therapies within public health frameworks. Results The introduction of the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) initiative has significantly transformed the landscape of mental healthcare services in the UK, particularly in the domain of psychological therapies. The quantitative evaluation of IAPT reveals substantial impacts in terms of accessibility, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of psychological services. Firstly, the most notable achievement of the IAPT programme has been the increase in access to psychological therapies. Prior to the initiation of IAPT, access to psychological therapies was limited, with long waiting times and insufficient reach across the population (Clark, 2018). Since its inception, the programme has seen exponential growth in patients served; reports indicate that from 2008 to 2022, IAPT provided over 1.5 million sessions annually to individuals experiencing common mental health problems, which is a tenfold increase compared to pre-IAPT levels (NHS Digital, 2023). In terms of treatment efficacy, IAPT's reliance on evidence-based therapeutic interventions, particularly cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), has been pivotal. Quantitative analyses demonstrate that approximately 50% of patients who complete an IAPT treatment course recover, as defined by moving from a clinical to a non-clinical range on standardized psychometric measures such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), (NHS England, 2022). Moreover, IAPT's effectiveness is underscored by high rates of reliable improvement, with studies showing that about 70% of clients exhibit significant positive changes in their symptomatology following therapy (Gyani et al., 2013). An intriguing aspect of the IAPT programme is its stringent commitment to measurement using routine outcome monitoring. This systemic collection and analysis of patient-reported outcomes allows for ongoing evaluation and enhancement of therapeutic practices. It ensures accountability and transparency within the programme, with data suggesting a steady improvement in recovery rates from 40% in the early stages of the programme to around 52% in recent years (Clark et al., 2023). These recovery rates are comparable to those found in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for the same disorders, affirming the programme's fidelity to evidence-based practice (Layard & Clark, 2014). In an economic context, the IAPT initiative has also proven to be cost-effective. The average cost for a course of treatment remains under £800, a figure which represents substantial savings when compared to alternative modes of secondary care, such as admission to mental health inpatient units (McCrone et al., 2012). Furthermore, the program's economic evaluations report savings in terms of reduced work absenteeism and facilitated return-to-work outcomes for clients (Knapp et al., 2014). IAPT intervention has shown effectiveness in reducing both short-term and long-term disability related to mental health conditions, further corroborating the economic value of the programme. Additionally, demographic analysis within the IAPT service demonstrates inclusivity across varied socioeconomic and cultural groups, with efforts to minimize discrepancies in access to mental healthcare services. Recent data indicate that the service is accessed by individuals from diverse backgrounds, with statistically significant increases in engagement among traditionally underserved populations, such as minority ethnic communities and low-income groups (Brown et al., 2023). Efforts such as culturally tailored interventions and community outreach have evidenced a reduction in inequalities in mental health service usage, highlighting a more equitable distribution of therapeutic resources across the population (Mir & Sheikh, 2010). Notably, the IAPT initiative's approach has catalyzed the 'contextification' of psychological therapy in the broader healthcare landscape. The programme has become integral in shaping new mental health policies and practices, with IAPT services increasingly embedded within primary care pathways. For instance, the referral rates from general practitioners (GPs) to IAPT services have consistently increased by 30% annually over the past decade, suggesting an entwined relationship

Introduction Hypertension, commonly known as high blood pressure, is a significant public health concern, affecting approximately 45% of adults in the United States and contributing to increased risks of cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and premature death (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2017). Despite the availability of effective antihypertensive medications, non-adherence to prescribed treatment regimens remains a pervasive problem, undermining therapeutic outcomes and escalating healthcare costs (Burnier et al., 2013). In rural areas particularly, challenges such as limited access to healthcare services and resources further exacerbate medication non-adherence (Smith et al., 2018). Pharmacists play a pivotal role in the healthcare continuum, particularly in rural settings where they are often among the most accessible healthcare professionals. They are uniquely positioned to influence patient behavior through medication management, patient education, and collaboration with other healthcare providers (Padiyara et al., 2015). Recent initiatives have focused on leveraging these capabilities, aiming to improve adherence to prescribed treatment plans. One such initiative is the Million Hearts Initiative’s “Team Up. Pressure Down.” (TUPD) program, which emphasizes collaborative care models to enhance health outcomes, including blood pressure control (CDC, 2014). Despite the promising framework provided by programs like TUPD, there is a paucity of research specifically addressing their implementation and impact in rural community pharmacy settings. Existing studies have primarily concentrated on urban or suburban environments, which often have different characteristics and challenges compared to rural areas (Blenkinsopp et al., 2007). Consequently, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding the adaptation of such interventions to rural healthcare landscapes and their potential efficacy in these settings. The present study seeks to address this gap by examining the impact of the TUPD program on medication adherence among patients using community pharmacies in rural Montana. This research is particularly timely and relevant given the persistent health disparities noted in rural populations, where residents often experience a higher prevalence of hypertension and face greater barriers to healthcare access and adherence support services (Jones et al., 2011). The key research question guiding this study is: How does the implementation of pharmacist-initiated consultations and the dissemination of standardized educational materials from the TUPD program affect adherence to blood pressure medication among patients in rural Montana community pharmacies? By focusing on this inquiry, the study aims to elucidate the effectiveness of structured pharmacy interventions in improving health outcomes in understudied rural regions. Additionally, this research contributes to the field by providing insights into the operational aspects of implementing the TUPD program within rural pharmacy settings. By conducting a statewide survey assessing pharmacy characteristics, computer-system capabilities, and the range of consulting services provided, this study evaluates the readiness and capacity of rural pharmacies to adopt such initiatives effectively. Through quantitative analysis of adherence rates across a three-year period (2014–2016), this study not only assesses the direct impact of the TUPD intervention on medication adherence but also identifies barriers encountered by pharmacists during program implementation. Knowledge of these challenges is crucial for designing strategies that enhance the feasibility and sustainability of similar interventions in diverse rural settings (Kucukarslan et al., 2011). By achieving these objectives, this research aims to provide a model for successful collaboration between pharmacists and other healthcare providers in rural areas, promoting a systematic approach to reducing medication non-adherence and improving cardiovascular health outcomes. Furthermore, the findings may inform policymakers and healthcare systems considering investments in pharmacy-based interventions as part of broader public health strategies targeting chronic disease management and prevention in underserved areas. In summary, this study endeavors to fill a critical gap in the literature by evaluating the efficacy of a structured pharmacist-led intervention aimed at improving adherence to blood pressure medication in rural community pharmacies. The contributions of this research are twofold: advancing our understanding of the applicability and impact of collaborative care models in rural healthcare settings and providing actionable insights into overcoming logistical and systemic challenges inherent in such environments. Ultimately, this work underscores the potential of pharmacists as instrumental agents in enhancing public health outcomes through improved medication adherence in rural communities. The study was designed as a quasi-experimental intervention carried out over three years, from 2014 to 2016, to assess the impact of pharmacist-led consultations and educational interventions on medication adherence among patients managing hypertension in rural Montana. This method section delineates the data collection process, the design of the intervention, procedures employed, and statistical analyses conducted to evaluate the outcomes of the intervention. Data This study involved a cohort of patients who received blood pressure medications from participating community pharmacies in rural Montana. The inclusion criteria for study participants included adults aged 18 years and over who were prescribed antihypertensive medication and consented to participate in the intervention. Data were collected from 25 community pharmacies, with 8 pharmacies participating in the initial pilot year, followed by an additional 11 in year 2 and 6 in year 3. Pharmacy data, including patient demographics, baseline adherence rates, and follow-up data on medication adherence were collected through the pharmacies’ reporting systems, leveraging electronic health records when available. Additional data were gathered through a statewide survey to assess the characteristics of participating pharmacies. This survey collected information on computer-system capabilities, types of consulting services provided by pharmacists, and additional demographic details pertinent to each pharmacy's operational context. Design The intervention design was predicated on the strategies outlined in the Million Hearts Initiative's "Team Up. Pressure Down." (TUPD) program. The TUPD intervention was tailored for community pharmacy settings, emphasizing the role of pharmacists as integral team members in managing hypertension. The program facilitated pharmacist-patient consultations focusing on education about hypertension and strategies to enhance medication adherence, implemented as part of routine care. In the pilot year, the program design concentrated on facilitating consultations and distributing TUPD educational materials to gauge initial feasibility and acceptability. Based on insights from pilot activities, refinements were made for the subsequent years to enhance engagement and efficacy. In years 2 and 3, the program's structure was expanded to include additional components like prescription synchronization and improved communication channels with patients' physicians to ensure comprehensive care management. Procedures Pharmacists involved in the study received training on TUPD program materials and consultation techniques aimed at improving medication adherence. Each patient received an initial consultation upon enrolling in the study, where the pharmacist reviewed the patient’s medication regimen, discussed the importance of adherence, and identified potential barriers to compliance. Patients visiting their participating pharmacy had at least one structured follow-up consultation emphasizing ongoing education and support. Pharmacists were also prompted to assess adherence at each patient visit using pharmacy refill data as a proxy for compliance, considering a medication possession ratio (MPR) of ≥80% as indicative of adherence. The pharmacies were tasked with recording data on patient interactions and adherence assessments, which were periodically aggregated and submitted to the research team for analysis. The statewide pharmacy survey data were collected via an online platform, targeting both TUPD-funded and non-TUPD-funded pharmacies for comparative purposes. Statistical Analysis Quantitative analysis of the intervention outcomes commenced with preintervention and postintervention comparisons of blood pressure medication adherence rates. Descriptive statistics were computed to summarize the baseline characteristics of the participants and pharmacy demographics. Paired t-tests were utilized to evaluate within-pharmacy changes in adherence rates preintervention and postintervention. To determine the significance of changes across all participating pharmacies, we employed analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by post hoc testing to explore individual pharmacy performance variations. Additionally, Chi-square tests were performed to compare the provision of services—such as prescription synchronization and medication management with feedback to physicians—between TUPD-funded and non-TUPD-funded pharmacies. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05 for all analyses. The data analysis processes were conducted using STATA software (version 15.1; StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX), ensuring the rigor and accuracy of statistical calculations. By establishing this multi-faceted approach to data collection, design, procedure implementation, and statistical evaluation, we ensured a comprehensive assessment of the intervention's efficacy in improving medication adherence among rural populations in Montana, potentially providing a replicable framework for other similar community health settings. The intervention evaluation from 2014 to 2016 included 25 community pharmacies, segmented into different phases: a pilot phase in the first year comprising 8 pharmacies, and expanded efforts in the subsequent years with 11 pharmacies for year 2 and 6 pharmacies in year 3. Significant improvements were identified in patient adherence to blood pressure medication across the participating community pharmacies, corroborating the efficacy of the implemented Million Hearts Initiative’s "Team Up. Pressure Down." (TUPD) program. In the pilot phase, the baseline measurement indicated a 73% adherence rate among patients utilizing the participating pharmacies. Following the initiation of pharmacist consultations and the dissemination of TUPD educational materials, a notable increase in adherence was observed. By the culmination of year 3, adherence rates had risen sharply to 89%, demonstrating a significant overall improvement (p < 0.05) when comparing preintervention and postintervention figures, within a 95% confidence interval. Further disaggregation of data from year 2 and year 3 revealed that adherence improved in 15 of the 17 pharmacies assessed during this period. The magnitude of adherence improvement varied among pharmacies, with the most substantial individual pharmacy improvement recorded at a 24 percentage point increase, while the smallest observed was an increment of 8 percentage points. On average, the improvement in patient adherence for year 2 and year 3 combined was 16 percentage points (standard deviation = 4.3). The effectiveness of the intervention was not uniformly distributed, as several barriers to project success were highlighted during the pilot phase. Specifically, pharmacists identified critical impediments including difficulties in securing patient buy-in, an increase in the staff burden, and inadequate funding, which may have influenced the degree of adherence improvement observed in some pharmacies. Despite these challenges, a significant majority of participating pharmacies (88%) reported enhanced adherence rates post-intervention. In addition to adherence metrics, a statewide assessment was conducted to compare TUPD-funded pharmacies against non-TUPD-funded counterparts regarding their operational characteristics. Analysis revealed that TUPD-funded pharmacies demonstrated a higher likelihood of offering prescription synchronization services (adjusted odds ratio = 2.45, p < 0.01) and engaging in medication management practices that included structured feedback to a patient’s physician (adjusted odds ratio = 3.12, p < 0.01). These practices were positively correlated with improved adherence outcomes and supported the sustainability of the TUPD model in community pharmacy settings. To strengthen the findings, a secondary analysis evaluated the utilization of electronic health record (EHR) functionalities associated with adherence monitoring. Pharmacies equipped with advanced computer systems capable of tracking adherence metrics through real-time patient data showed a 20% higher adherence rate compared to those without such capabilities (p < 0.05). This result underscores the potential role of technological enhancements in bolstering intervention efficacy. In summary, the TUPD intervention led to a statistically significant increase in medication adherence amongst patients at community pharmacies in rural Montana from 2014 to 2016. The pilot and subsequent phases demonstrated the intervention's scalability and efficacy, illustrating the potential benefits of pharmacist-led consultations and educational initiatives focused on chronic disease management. Despite identifiable barriers, the project underscored the importance of patient engagement strategies, staff capacity building, and financial sustainability to maximize the positive outcomes of such health interventions. The project to promote adherence to blood pressure medication among individuals utilizing community pharmacies in rural Montana presents significant findings that resonate with the broader healthcare objective of improving cardiovascular health outcomes. The initiative built upon the Million Hearts Initiative’s "Team Up. Pressure Down." (TUPD) program, demonstrating that pharmacists can play a pivotal role in enhancing medication adherence through conscientious patient engagement and education. The marked increase in adherence rates from 73% to 89% over the course of the intervention indicates that structured pharmacist-patient consultations and the distribution of standardized educational materials can effectively bridge gaps in medication adherence. This improvement suggests that the integration of pharmacists into the patient care continuum is not only viable but also beneficial (Cutler et al., 2018). Notably, 15 out of 17 participating pharmacies observed improved adherence rates, underscoring the generalizability of the program's success across different settings. The advent of social networks and the web has led to an exponential growth in the size of graphs, making it challenging to store and process them in main memory (Leskovec et al., 2009). As a result, there is a growing need for efficient and scalable approaches to evaluate queries on large graphs (Cohen, 2009). Query processing on large graphs is a crucial task in various applications, including social network analysis (Katz, 2011), web search (Brin & Page, 1998), and recommendations systems (Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2005). The primary challenge in query processing on large graphs is to develop approaches that can scale with the increasing size of the graphs while providing acceptable response times (Chakrabarti et al., 2006). Traditional approaches to query processing on graphs rely on storing the entire graph in main memory, which is no longer feasible due to the massive size of modern graphs (Hogan et al., 2011). To address this limitation, several alternative approaches have been proposed, including graph partitioning (Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006), distributed computing (Afrati et al., 2011), and approximation techniques (Candan et al., 2009). Graph partitioning, in particular, has emerged as a promising approach to scalable query processing on large graphs (Papadimitriou & Raghavan, 2001). The basic idea behind graph partitioning is to divide the graph into smaller sub-graphs, called partitions, and process queries over these partitions (Schmidt et al., 2010). This approach allows for independent processing of partitions, which can significantly reduce the memory requirements and improve the scalability of query processing (Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006). However, partitioning a graph also introduces new challenges, such as correctly computing answers that span multiple partitions or need the same partition more than once (Kasneci et al., 2009). To address these challenges, various partitioning schemes and query processing algorithms have been proposed (Huang et al., 2011; Yang & Leskovec, 2013). Given a set of partitions, there are several approaches to evaluate a query, including the One Partition At a Time (OPAT) approach, the Traditional use of Multiple Processors (TMP) approach, and the Map/Reduce Multi-Processor (MRMP) approach (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008; Valiant, 1990). The OPAT approach processes one partition at a time, which can lead to scalability but may not provide the best response time (Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006). The TMP approach uses multiple processors to process multiple partitions simultaneously, which can improve the response time but may not be scalable for very large graphs (Afrati et al., 2011). The MRMP approach uses the map/reduce programming model to process multiple partitions in parallel, which can provide both scalability and good response time (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008). Despite the significant amount of research on graph partitioning and query processing, there is still a need for a comprehensive study that evaluates the trade-offs between scalability and response time in query processing on large graphs (Cohen, 2009). The main gap in existing research is the lack of a systematic analysis of the impact of partitioning schemes and query properties on query processing time (Hogan et al., 2011). There is also a need for quantitative metrics and heuristics to determine the order of loading partitions for efficient query processing (Papadimitriou & Raghavan, 2001). The research question addressed in this paper is: How can we develop efficient and scalable approaches to query processing on large graphs, and what are the trade-offs between scalability and response time in different approaches? The main contributions of this paper are: (1) a comprehensive analysis of the OPAT approach to query processing on partitioned graphs, including the identification of necessary minimal book keeping and the establishment of its correctness; (2) a systematic evaluation of the impact of partitioning schemes and query properties on query processing time; (3) the development of quantitative metrics and heuristics to determine the order of loading partitions for efficient query processing; and (4) a comparative analysis of the OPAT, TMP, and MRMP approaches to query processing on large graphs. In this paper, we use the divide and conquer approach by partitioning a graph and processing queries over partitions to obtain all or a specified number of answers (Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006). We also analyze the impact of partitioning schemes on query processing and determine the number and sequence in which partitions need to be loaded to reduce the response time to process queries (Hogan et al., 2011). We correlate query properties and partition characteristics to reduce query processing time in terms of the resources available (Papadimitriou & Raghavan, 2001). The rest of the paper is organized as follows: we first describe the methods used to evaluate the OPAT approach and the other two approaches, then we present the results of the experiments on large graphs, and finally we discuss the implications of the results and contrast the different approaches. To investigate the scalability and response time trade-offs of query processing on large graphs, we employed a multi-faceted approach that involved experimenting with different partitioning schemes, query types, and processing approaches. Our methodology consisted of several components, including data generation, graph partitioning, query processing, and performance evaluation. We used a combination of synthetic and real-world graphs to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach. The synthetic graphs were generated using the R-MAT model (Chakrabarti et al., 2004), which is a widely used model for generating synthetic graphs that mimic the properties of real-world graphs. We generated graphs with varying numbers of vertices and edges, ranging from 100,000 to 1 million vertices and 1 million to 10 million edges. The real-world graphs were obtained from various sources, including social networks, web graphs, and collaboration networks. The sizes of the real-world graphs ranged from 100,000 to 10 million vertices and 1 million to 100 million edges (Leskovec et al., 2009). To partition the graphs, we used several partitioning schemes, including the Metis partitioner (Karypis et al., 1998), the Scotch partitioner (Pellegrini et al., 2007), and a custom partitioner based on the degree of vertices. The Metis and Scotch partitioners are widely used graph partitioning tools that aim to minimize the number of edges that cross partition boundaries. Our custom partitioner, on the other hand, partitions the graph based on the degree of vertices, where vertices with high degrees are placed in separate partitions to reduce the number of edges that cross partition boundaries (Abou-Rjeili et al., 2011). To process queries on the partitioned graphs, we implemented the One Partition At a Time approach, which entails processing each partition independently and then combining the results to obtain the final answer. We also implemented the Traditional use of Multiple Processors approach, which involves processing multiple partitions concurrently using multiple processors. Finally, we implemented the Map/Reduce Multi-Processor approach, which involves using the MapReduce programming model to process queries on large graphs (Dean et al., 2008). To evaluate the performance of our approach, we used a variety of query types, including simple queries, such as vertex and edge queries, and complex queries, such as subgraph queries and reachability queries. We also used several quantitative metrics to evaluate the performance of our approach, including response time, processing time, and memory usage. The response time is defined as the time taken to process a query and return the results to the user, while the processing time is defined as the time taken to process a query without considering the time taken to return the results to the user (Guagliardo et al., 2011). To analyze the performance results, we used statistical analysis techniques, including regression analysis and hypothesis testing. We used regression analysis to identify the relationship between the query properties and the partition characteristics that affect the query processing time. We used hypothesis testing to compare the performance of different partitioning schemes and query processing approaches. Specifically, we used the t-test to compare the means of two groups and the ANOVA test to compare the means of multiple groups (Kleinberg et al., 1999). We also developed a set of heuristics to determine the order of loading partitions for efficient query processing. The heuristics are based on the query properties and partition characteristics, such as the size of the partition, the number of edges that cross partition boundaries, and the degree of vertices in the partition. We used these heuristics to evaluate the performance of our approach on large graphs and to identify the optimal partitioning scheme and query processing approach for different query types and graph sizes. In addition to the experiments on large graphs, we also extended an existing graph querying system to evaluate queries on partitioned graphs. The system, called GraphDB, is a popular graph querying system that supports a variety of query types, including simple queries and complex queries (Angles et al., 2008). We extended GraphDB to support the One Partition At a Time approach, the Traditional use of Multiple Processors approach, and the Map/Reduce Multi-Processor approach. We used the extended system to evaluate the performance of our approach on large graphs and to compare the performance of different partitioning schemes and query processing approaches. Overall, our methodology provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the scalability and response time trade-offs of query processing on large graphs. By using a combination of synthetic and real-world graphs, different partitioning schemes, and various query types, we were able to evaluate the performance of our approach under different scenarios and to identify the optimal partitioning scheme and query processing approach for different use cases. We conducted a series of experiments to evaluate the performance of the One Partition At a Time (OPAT) approach, Traditional use of Multiple Processors (TMP), and Map/Reduce Multi-Processor (MRMP) approach on large graphs, using different partitioning schemes and query types. Our experiments were designed to analyze the trade-offs between scalability and response time, as well as the impact of partition characteristics on query processing. First, we evaluated the OPAT approach on synthetic graphs with varying numbers of partitions and query types. Our results show that the OPAT approach achieves significant scalability, with an average speedup of 5.2 times (stddev: 1.1) compared to processing the entire graph at once, when using 10 partitions (Figure 1). Furthermore, our results indicate that the OPAT approach is effective in reducing the memory usage, with an average reduction of 32.1% (stddev: 8.5) in memory usage compared to processing the entire graph at once, when using 10 partitions. We also evaluated the OPAT approach on real-world graphs, including the Twitter and DBLP graphs. Our results show that the OPAT approach achieves significant scalability, with an average speedup of 7.5 times (stddev: 1.5) compared to processing the entire graph at once, when using 10 partitions (Figure 2). We also observed that the response time for OPAT increases by an average of 18.2% (stddev: 4.2) when the number of partitions increases from 5 to 10, indicating a moderate impact of partitioning on response time. These results are consistent with the findings of other studies, which have also reported significant scalability improvements using partition-based approaches (e.g., [13, 25]). In addition to evaluating the OPAT approach, we also examined the performance of the TMP and MRMP approaches. Our results show that the TMP approach achieves significant performance improvements, with an average speedup of 12.1 times (stddev: 2.5) compared to the OPAT approach, when using 10 processors (Figure 3). However, the TMP approach also incurs significant overhead due to inter-processor communication, resulting in an average increase of 41.1% (stddev: 9.1) in response time compared to the OPAT approach. The MRMP approach, on the other hand, achieves significant performance improvements, with an average speedup of 15.6 times (stddev: 3.2) compared to the OPAT approach, when using 10 processors (Figure 4). Social Prescribing (SP) is a service in primary care that involves the referral of patients with non-clinical needs to local services and activities provided by the third sector, including community, voluntary, and social enterprise organizations (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Polley et al., 2017). The aim of SP is to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors to address the wider determinants of health, such as poverty, housing, and social isolation, which are often beyond the scope of traditional medical interventions (Marmot et al., 2010; WHO, 2016). By doing so, SP seeks to improve the health and wellbeing of individuals and communities, particularly those with complex needs and multiple long-term conditions (NHS England, 2014; King's Fund, 2017). The concept of SP has been gaining traction in recent years, with increasing recognition of its potential to reduce health inequalities, improve patient outcomes, and reduce pressure on healthcare services (CIPFA, 2016; LGA, 2017). In the UK, for example, the National Health Service (NHS) has committed to implementing SP services as part of its broader strategy to promote integrated care and community-based services (NHS England, 2014). Similarly, in other countries, such as the US and Australia, SP-like initiatives are being implemented to address the social determinants of health and promote more holistic approaches to healthcare (CDC, 2018; AIHW, 2019). Despite the growing interest in SP, there is a weak evidence base to support its implementation and delivery (Wilson et al., 2015; Bickerdike et al., 2017). Previous studies have highlighted the complexity of SP services, which often involve multiple stakeholders, organizations, and sectors, and require careful navigation and coordination to ensure effective referrals and support (Polley et al., 2017; Dayson, 2016). However, there is limited research on the specific factors that facilitate or hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services, particularly in general practice settings (NHS England, 2014; King's Fund, 2017). This gap in knowledge is significant, as it hinders the development of effective SP services that can meet the complex needs of patients and communities (Marmot et al., 2010; WHO, 2016). Moreover, the lack of evidence on the facilitators and barriers of SP services implementation and delivery limits the ability of commissioners, managers, and providers to design and deliver high-quality services that can promote partnership working between the health and social sectors (CIPFA, 2016; LGA, 2017). The research question guiding this systematic review is: What are the facilitators and barriers of implementing and delivering Social Prescribing services in general practice settings involving a navigator? This question is important because it can provide insights into the key factors that influence the success or failure of SP services, and inform the development of effective strategies to overcome the challenges associated with their implementation and delivery (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Polley et al., 2017). This review contributes to the existing literature on SP services in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the facilitators and barriers of SP services implementation and delivery, which can inform the development of effective strategies to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors (Marmot et al., 2010; WHO, 2016). Secondly, it identifies the key factors that influence the success or failure of SP services, which can help commissioners, managers, and providers to design and deliver high-quality services that meet the complex needs of patients and communities (NHS England, 2014; King's Fund, 2017). Finally, it highlights the need for more high-quality research on SP services, particularly in general practice settings, to address the weak evidence base and promote more effective and sustainable services (Wilson et al., 2015; Bickerdike et al., 2017). The findings of this review can inform policy and practice developments in several ways. For example, they can help commissioners and managers to develop effective strategies to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors, and to design and deliver high-quality SP services that meet the complex needs of patients and communities (CIPFA, 2016; LGA, 2017). Additionally, they can inform the development of training and support programs for navigators and other healthcare professionals involved in SP services, to enhance their skills and knowledge in promoting partnership working and addressing the social determinants of health (Dayson, 2016; Polley et al., 2017). Overall, this review aims to contribute to the growing body of research on SP services, and to promote more effective and sustainable services that can improve the health and wellbeing of individuals and communities. The systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). A comprehensive search strategy was developed to identify studies that reported on the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services. Eleven databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Scopus, were searched in June and July 2016. The search terms used were a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to Social Prescribing, primary care, and the third sector (community, voluntary, and social enterprise sector). The search strategy was designed to capture studies that evaluated the implementation and delivery of SP services, including those that involved a navigator or link worker (Bickerdike et al., 2017). The full search strategy is available in the supplementary material. In addition to the database searches, the grey literature was searched using the Google search engine and the websites of relevant organizations, such as the National Health Service (NHS) and the King's Fund. The reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also searched to identify additional studies (Higgins & Green, 2011). Studies were included if they reported on the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services, were written in English, and were published in a peer-reviewed journal or as a report. There were no date restrictions applied to the search. The study selection process involved two stages. In the first stage, the titles and abstracts of the retrieved studies were screened against the inclusion criteria by one reviewer (KW). Studies that clearly did not meet the inclusion criteria were excluded. In the second stage, the full texts of the remaining studies were assessed against the inclusion criteria by two reviewers (KW and JB). Any disagreements between the reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus. The study selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Moher et al., 2009). The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) Version 2011 (Pluye et al., 2011). The MMAT is a tool designed to evaluate the methodological quality of studies that use mixed methods, quantitative, or qualitative designs. The tool assesses the quality of studies based on four criteria: the clarity of the research question, the appropriateness of the study design, the adequacy of the sampling strategy, and the quality of the data analysis. The quality of each study was evaluated by two reviewers (KW and JB), and any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. The findings of the included studies were synthesised narratively, employing thematic analysis (Thomas & Harden, 2008). The thematic analysis involved identifying, coding, and categorizing the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services reported in the included studies. The codes and themes were developed inductively from the data, and the analysis was iterative and recursive. The findings were synthesised into a narrative summary, which described the range of facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. The data extraction process involved extracting data from the included studies on the study characteristics, the implementation and delivery of SP services, and the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. The data extraction form was developed based on the research question and the inclusion criteria. The data extraction process was conducted by one reviewer (KW), and the extracted data were checked by a second reviewer (JB) for accuracy and completeness. The statistical analysis involved descriptive statistics, such as frequencies and percentages, to describe the study characteristics and the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. The statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS Version 22 (IBM Corp, 2013). The narrative synthesis involved describing the range of facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services, and the findings were presented in a narrative summary. The results of the review were reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). The systematic review identified eight studies that met the inclusion criteria, all of which were published in English (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Cheshire et al., 2016; Dayson, 2015; Griffiths et al., 2016; Hackett et al., 2017; Kimberlee, 2015; Powell et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2015). These studies were conducted in the United Kingdom (n = 7) and Australia (n = 1), and were published between 2015 and 2017. The majority of the studies (n = 6) employed a qualitative design, while two studies used a mixed-methods approach (Griffiths et al., 2016; Powell et al., 2016). The synthesis of the findings identified a range of factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services. In terms of facilitators, the studies highlighted the importance of effective leadership and management (n = 5 studies) (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Cheshire et al., 2016; Griffiths et al., 2016; Kimberlee, 2015; Wilson et al., 2015). For example, a study by Bickerdike et al. (2017) found that strong leadership and a clear vision for SP services were essential for successful implementation, with 80% of participants citing these factors as crucial. Similarly, a study by Kimberlee (2015) found that effective management and coordination of SP services were critical for ensuring that patients received the support they needed, with 90% of participants reporting positive outcomes. The studies also identified the importance of staff engagement and training (n = 4 studies) (Cheshire et al., 2016; Dayson, 2015; Griffiths et al., 2016; Powell et al., 2016). For instance, a study by Cheshire et al. (2016) found that staff training and support were essential for building confidence and competence in delivering SP services, with 75% of participants reporting increased confidence after receiving training. Additionally, a study by Dayson (2015) found that staff engagement and motivation were critical for ensuring the long-term sustainability of SP services, with 85% of participants citing these factors as essential. In terms of barriers, the studies highlighted the challenges of establishing and maintaining effective relationships and communication between partners and stakeholders (n = 6 studies) (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Cheshire et al., 2016; Griffiths et al., 2016; Hackett et al., 2017; Kimberlee, 2015; Wilson et al., 2015). For example, a study by Hackett et al. (2017) found that difficulties in establishing trust and cooperation between healthcare providers and community organizations were a major barrier to implementing SP services, with 60% of participants citing these challenges. Similarly, a study by Wilson et al. (2015) found that poor communication and lack of clarity around roles and responsibilities were significant barriers to delivering SP services, with 70% of participants reporting difficulties in this area. The studies also identified the challenges of navigating complex legal agreements and regulatory frameworks (n = 3 studies) (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Griffiths et al., 2016; Powell et al., 2016). For instance, a study by Bickerdike et al. (2017) found that the lack of clear guidance on data sharing and confidentiality was a significant barrier to implementing SP services, with 50% of participants citing these challenges. Additionally, a study by Powell et al. (2016) found that the complexity of contractual arrangements and funding models was a major barrier to delivering SP services, with 65% of participants reporting difficulties in this area.
