Population ageing and the fiscal pressures it places on pension systems have made the extension of working lives a central objective of social policy across Europe. Many countries have raised statutory pension ages, restricted access to early retirement schemes, and introduced incentives to remain in employment (OECD 2015; European Commission 2012). The European Union's Europe 2020 strategy explicitly targets higher employment among older workers, and several governments are now debating or legislating retirement ages of 67 or beyond. Employment rates among those aged 55 to 64 have indeed risen in most European countries over the past two decades (Eurostat 2014). Yet beyond the age of 65, paid work remains a minority activity, and its prevalence varies strongly across countries, from a few percent in France or Belgium to considerably higher shares in Sweden, Switzerland, or Estonia (Hofäcker and Naumann 2015; Scherger et al. 2012). The scientific literature on late careers has so far concentrated predominantly on the opposite end of the spectrum: those who leave the labour market early. A large body of work examines the determinants of early or premature exit, including poor health, physically and psychologically demanding jobs, low job control, and unfavourable pension incentives (Blekesaune and Solem 2005; Siegrist et al. 2007; Van den Berg et al. 2010; de Wind et al. 2014). Stressful psychosocial work environments, conceptualised, for example, through the demand-control model (Karasek and Theorell 1990) and the model of effort-reward imbalance (Siegrist 1996), have been shown to predict both poor health and the intention or decision to retire early (Siegrist et al. 2006; Wahrendorf et al. 2013). From this perspective, early exit is often interpreted as a response to adverse working conditions and deteriorating health, a "push" factor, while financial incentives and attractive leisure opportunities constitute "pull" factors (Shultz et al. 1998; Radl 2013). By comparison, relatively little is known about people who continue working after reaching the age at which most of their peers have retired. Existing studies suggest that working beyond conventional retirement ages is selective. Older workers who continue are, on average, healthier, more highly educated, and more likely to be self-employed than those who retire (Dingemans and Henkens 2014; Kanabar 2015; Principi et al. 2014). Motives for continued work are heterogeneous: some individuals work because they enjoy their job, value social contacts, or wish to remain active, whereas others work out of financial necessity because of low pension entitlements (Platts et al. 2016; Vickerstaff 2010). This distinction matters, because the policy discourse on "active ageing" often implicitly assumes that longer working lives are voluntary and beneficial, whereas the empirical reality may comprise both privileged and vulnerable groups (Alcover et al. 2014; Lain 2012). Whether extended working lives are accompanied by favourable or unfavourable job characteristics is therefore an important empirical question. Several gaps remain in the existing evidence. First, most studies of late-life employment focus on the transition ages between 50 and 65 and thus rarely describe people who work at ages 65 to 80, a group that is small but growing and of particular relevance for debates on raising pension ages further. Second, studies of older workers often consider a limited set of characteristics, such as demographic and health status, and pay less attention to detailed employment conditions, including employment status (employee, self-employed with or without employees), occupational position, and weekly working hours. Third, while there is considerable evidence on the psychosocial work environment as a predictor of early exit, we know little about how exposure to stressful work, such as low control or effort-reward imbalance, differs between those working beyond 65 and those who are retired. Because retired persons, by definition, no longer work, a meaningful comparison requires information on their conditions in the last job before retirement. Such a comparison can indicate whether those who continue to work come from systematically better or worse job circumstances than those who have left, which is crucial for judging whether policies that postpone retirement would burden particular groups. Fourth, much research is limited to single countries, which complicates generalisation given the institutional diversity of European pension, labour market, and welfare systems (Ebbinghaus 2006). Comparative, harmonised data covering a wide age range and diverse institutional settings are required. The present study addresses these gaps using data from the fourth wave of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE; Börsch-Supan et al. 2013), collected between 2009 and 2011. SHARE is a multidisciplinary, cross-national panel study of people aged 50 and over, offering harmonised information on health, socio-economic circumstances, and employment. Importantly, wave 4 includes measures of psychosocial working conditions for current workers and, retrospectively, for the last job of retired respondents, as well as indicators of physical and mental health. This allows us to compare current workers and retirees aged 65 to 80 across 16 European countries within a single analytical framework. We pursue three research questions. First, which sociodemographic characteristics (age, gender, education, partnership and financial situation) are associated with working beyond age 65? Second, how do employment conditions, namely employment status, occupational position, and working hours, and stressful psychosocial working conditions (low control and effort-reward imbalance) differ between those working at ages 65 to 80 and the retired in their last job? Third, how are these working conditions and health (physical and mental) related to the likelihood of being in paid work in this age group, once country context and potential confounders are taken into account? We expect that people working beyond 65 are more often self-employed, hold advantaged occupational positions, report more favourable psychosocial working conditions, and are in better health than their retired counterparts. This expectation follows from selection arguments: those with greater autonomy, rewards, and resources have both more opportunities and more incentives to remain employed, while those exposed to strain or ill health are more likely to withdraw (Wahrendorf et al. 2013; Dingemans and Henkens 2014). The study contributes to the literature in three ways. It shifts attention from early exit to prolonged participation and describes in detail who works at ages 65 to 80 in Europe. It brings together a broad set of employment characteristics and established measures of psychosocial work stress, and it compares current workers with retirees using information on their previous jobs. Finally, it uses multilevel (random intercept) models to take cross-national variation into account. Together, these contributions provide evidence on the social selectivity of extended working lives and thus inform debates on the consequences of rising pension ages for different social groups. Data and study population We used data from wave 4 of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), a multidisciplinary, cross-national panel study of community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older and their partners (Börsch-Supan et al. 2013). Wave 4 fieldwork was conducted between 2009 and 2011, and release 1.1.1 was used. Samples in each participating country were drawn as probability samples, mostly from population registers or multi-stage area sampling, and interviews were conducted face-to-face using computer-assisted personal interviewing. Methodological details, including sampling design and response rates, are described elsewhere (Börsch-Supan and Jürges 2005; Malter and Börsch-Supan 2013). Wave 4 included 58,000 respondents in 16 countries: Sweden, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Switzerland, Austria, Italy, Spain, Estonia, Slovenia, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Poland and Portugal. Because information on the last job before retirement was collected in the life history interview (SHARELIFE) in wave 3 and in the baseline interview for refreshment samples, we linked wave 4 information with these sources where required. We restricted the analytic sample to men and women aged 65 to 80 years who were either in paid work or retired at the time of interview. This age band was chosen because 65 corresponds to the statutory pension age, or a close approximation, in most of the countries studied during the observation period, and because employment becomes very rare after age 80. Respondents were classified as working if they reported "employed or self-employed (including working for family business)" as their current main labour force status, and as retired if they reported being retired. Respondents who described themselves as homemakers, unemployed, permanently sick or disabled, or "other" were excluded, as were retired persons who had never been in paid employment and thus could not report on any previous working conditions. After these exclusions and removal of cases with missing information on key variables, the final sample comprised 17,625 individuals (N working = 1,647 and N retired = 15,978). Measures The outcome variable was labour market participation, coded 1 for current paid work and 0 for retirement. Employment conditions were measured for the current job among workers and for the last job before retirement among retirees. Employment status distinguished employees, self-employed persons with employees, and self-employed persons without employees (own-account workers). Occupational position was based on the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-88) and grouped into high (managers, professionals, technicians and associate professionals), intermediate (clerks, service and sales workers, skilled agricultural and craft workers) and low (plant and machine operators, elementary occupations) categories (cf. Ganzeboom and Treiman 1996). Weekly working hours were categorised as part-time (fewer than 35 hours), full-time (35–44 hours) and long hours (45 hours or more), following conventions in the literature on extended working hours (Virtanen et al. 2011). Psychosocial working conditions were assessed using two established stress models. Low control at work was derived from the demand–control model (Karasek and Theorell 1990) and was measured with two items in SHARE: "I have very little freedom to decide how to do my work" and "I have an opportunity to develop new skills", the latter reverse coded. Items were rated on a four-point scale from strongly agree to strongly disagree, and were summed and dichotomised at the country-pooled lowest tertile of control, with the lowest tertile defined as low control. Effort–reward imbalance (ERI) was derived from the model by Siegrist (1996) and calculated using the short SHARE version (Siegrist et al. 2004, 2014). Effort was assessed with two items (constant time pressure, physically demanding work), and reward with five items (recognition, adequate salary, promotion prospects, job security, and support). The ERI ratio was calculated as ERI = (e / r) × c, where e is the sum score of the effort items, r the sum score of the reward items, and c a correction factor (here, 5/2) accounting for the unequal number of items in the numerator and denominator. Values above 1 indicate that high effort is not matched by adequate reward, and respondents were classified as experiencing effort–reward imbalance if ERI > 1. For retirees, the same items referred retrospectively to the last job before retirement; the potential for recall bias is addressed in the Discussion. Health was captured by physical and mental health indicators. Physical health was measured by (a) self-rated health (dichotomised as fair or poor versus good, very good or excellent), (b) presence of at least one limitation in activities of daily living (ADL) or instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), and (c) the number of chronic diseases (0, 1, 2 or more). Mental health was assessed with the EURO-D scale, a 12-item depression symptom scale validated across European countries (Prince et al. 1999). A score of 4 or above indicates clinically relevant depressive symptoms (Prince et al. 1999). Covariates included age (in years, entered as a continuous term), sex, educational attainment (ISCED-97, grouped as low [levels 0–2], medium [3–4] and high [5–6]), partnership status (living with a partner versus not), and household net wealth quintile within country as an indicator of financial resources. Wealth was used instead of income because of the high proportion of missing income values and because it better represents resources in later life (Hurd and Rohwedder 2010). Country was used as the clustering unit. The increasing availability of large amounts of health data has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical informatics, enabling advances in disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention (Krumholz, 2014). However, the sharing of health data also raises significant concerns regarding patient privacy and confidentiality (Nass et al., 2009). The tension between facilitating access to health data for research and clinical purposes, while protecting the privacy of individuals, is a longstanding challenge in the field of medical informatics (Malin, 2006). The importance of addressing this challenge is underscored by the fact that health data is increasingly being generated and collected from a variety of sources, including electronic health records (EHRs), wearable devices, and mobile health applications (Kay et al., 2011). The sharing of health data is essential for advancing medical research, improving patient outcomes, and reducing healthcare costs (Friedman et al., 2010). Human symbol systems, such as art and fashion styles, have long been a subject of fascination in the social sciences, as they provide a unique lens through which to examine the complex social processes that govern the continuous re-organization of modern societies (Blumer, 1969; Simmel, 1957). These systems allow members of an elite to distinguish themselves from the rest of society, and their evolution has been characterized by cyclical patterns of emergence, adoption, and decline (Bourdieu, 1984; Veblen, 1899). The dynamics of art and fashion cycles have been the subject of intense debate, with two dominant theoretical perspectives emerging: 'bottom-up' and 'top-down' theories. According to 'top-down' theories, elite members signal their superior status by introducing new symbols, such as fashion styles, which are then adopted by low-status groups (Bourdieu, 1984; Veblen, 1899). In response to this adoption, elite members would need to introduce new symbols to signal their status, thereby driving the cycle of fashion and art styles. In contrast, many 'bottom-up' theories propose that style cycles evolve from lower classes and follow an essentially random pattern, with new styles emerging through a process of cultural experimentation and innovation (Blumer, 1969; McCracken, 1988). Despite the significance of these theoretical perspectives, they have been criticized for their limitations in explaining the complex social dynamics underlying fashion and art cycles (Entwistle, 2009; Watson, 2017). For example, 'top-down' theories have been challenged for their assumption that elite members are the sole drivers of fashion and art cycles, and that their actions are motivated solely by a desire to signal their superior status (Lieberson, 2000). Similarly, 'bottom-up' theories have been criticized for their failure to account for the systematic and predictable patterns of fashion and art cycles, which suggest that there may be more underlying structure and agency at play (Kawamura, 2005). Furthermore, both theoretical perspectives have been limited by their reliance on qualitative case studies and anecdotal evidence, which have made it difficult to test their hypotheses and generalize their findings to broader populations (Godart, 2014). A significant gap in the existing literature is the lack of quantitative, data-driven research on the dynamics of fashion and art cycles. While there have been numerous studies of specific art and fashion movements, such as the rise of punk rock or the emergence of hipster culture, these studies have been largely qualitative and have focused on descriptive analysis rather than theoretical explanation (Hebdige, 1979; Thornton, 1995). As a result, there is a need for a more systematic and quantitative approach to the study of fashion and art cycles, one that can provide a more nuanced and detailed understanding of the social dynamics underlying these phenomena. This gap is particularly significant in the context of music styles, where the rapid pace of technological change and the increasing diversity of musical genres have created a complex and dynamic landscape that is poorly understood by existing theoretical perspectives (Leyshon, 2014). In response to this gap, this study proposes an alternative explanation for the dynamics of fashion and art cycles, based on the concept of counter-dominance signaling. According to this perspective, elite members want others to imitate their symbols, but changes only occur when outsider groups successfully challenge the elite by introducing signals that contrast those endorsed by the elite (Breward, 2003). This perspective suggests that the evolution of fashion and art cycles is driven by a process of competition and challenge, in which peripheral groups seek to subvert the dominant symbols and styles of the elite, and the elite respond by introducing new symbols and styles to reassert their dominance. This perspective has been explored in qualitative studies of specific art and fashion movements, but it has yet to be tested using quantitative data and methods (McRobbie, 1998). The research question guiding this study is: what drives changes in musical styles, and can we identify quantitative evidence of counter-dominance signaling in the evolution of music styles? To address this question, we will use a dynamic network approach to analyze a large dataset of musical albums released between 1956 and 2015, containing almost 8 million records. This approach will allow us to systematically quantify artistic similarities of competing musical styles and their changes over time, and to formulate empirical tests for whether new symbols are introduced by current elite members (top-down), randomness (bottom-up), or by peripheral groups through counter-dominance signals. By providing a quantitative, data-driven answer to this question, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the social dynamics underlying fashion and art cycles, and to shed new light on the complex processes of cultural production and consumption that shape our modern societies (Hesmondhalgh, 2013). The widespread adoption of artificial neural networks (ANNs) in various domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, has led to an increasing interest in defending against adversarial attacks (Szegedy et al., 2014; Goodfellow et al., 2015). Adversarial attacks involve crafting small, often imperceptible, perturbations to the input data that can cause the ANN to misclassify the input (Kurakin et al., 2016). These attacks have been shown to be effective against a wide range of ANN architectures and can have significant consequences in real-world applications, such as self-driving cars and medical diagnosis (Papernot et al., 2017; Finlayson et al., 2019). To defend against adversarial attacks, various methods have been proposed, including adversarial training (Madry et al., 2018), defensive distillation (Papernot et al., 2016), and preprocessing defense methods (Liu et al., 2018). Preprocessing defense methods, in particular, have gained significant attention due to their simplicity, low computational overhead, and applicability to various systems (Xu et al., 2018). These methods involve transforming the input data in a way that makes it more difficult for the attacker to craft effective adversarial examples. One such method is pixel discretization, which involves discretizing the pixel values of an image to a set of predefined values (Buckman et al., 2018). Pixel discretization has been shown to be effective against adversarial attacks on simple datasets such as MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998), which consists of grayscale images of handwritten digits. However, its effectiveness on more complex datasets such as ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015), which consists of color images of various objects, is limited (Athalye et al., 2018). Recent studies have shown that pixel discretization can be broken by strong white-box attacks, which have access to the model's architecture and parameters (Carlini & Wagner, 2017). This raises concerns about the reliability of pixel discretization as a defense method against adversarial attacks. Despite the growing interest in preprocessing defense methods, there is a lack of understanding about the conditions under which these methods are effective and the potential limitations of these methods (He et al., 2017). In particular, there is a need to study the pixel discretization defense method in more depth, including its variants that take into account the properties of the dataset being discretized. Such an understanding is crucial for developing more effective defense methods against adversarial attacks. The research question that guides this study is: What are the limitations of pixel discretization as a defense method against adversarial attacks, and under what conditions can it be effective? To answer this question, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the pixel discretization defense method, including its variants, and evaluate its effectiveness against strong white-box attacks on various datasets. Our analysis is based on a theoretical framework that takes into account the properties of the dataset and the attack methods used. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the pixel discretization defense method, including its variants, and evaluate its effectiveness against strong white-box attacks on various datasets. Second, we offer strong evidence that pixel discretization is unlikely to work on all but the simplest of datasets, and provide insights into why this is the case. Third, our arguments present insights into why some other preprocessing defenses may be insecure, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the limitations of these methods. By shedding light on the limitations of pixel discretization, this study aims to contribute to the development of more effective defense methods against adversarial attacks, which is essential for the reliable deployment of ANNs in real-world applications. Graphs have become a primary representation for data in domains such as social networks, the web, bioinformatics, and knowledge bases. Their sizes have grown accordingly: the web graph contains tens of billions of pages, and social networks such as Facebook and Twitter contain billions of vertices and hundreds of billions of edges (Ugander et al., 2011; Kwak et al., 2010). Querying such graphs, whether through subgraph pattern matching, reachability, path queries, or keyword search, is a core requirement for analysis and decision making. Much of the work on graph querying, however, assumes that the graph, or at least its index, fits in main memory (Cordella et al., 2004; Gallagher, 2006). When this assumption fails, in-memory algorithms either thrash through virtual memory or cannot run at all. Buying larger machines is costly and only postpones the problem, since graph growth routinely outpaces memory growth. Several families of solutions exist. Disk-based graph stores and indexes (Angles and Gutierrez, 2008; Wang et al., 2008) reduce memory demands but typically require index structures whose construction and maintenance are expensive on very large graphs, and whose performance degrades when access patterns are not local. Distributed graph systems such as Pregel (Malewicz et al., 2010), GraphLab (Low et al., 2012), and Trinity (Shao et al., 2013) spread a graph across the memory of a cluster, and Map/Reduce-based approaches (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004) have been used for graph processing and subgraph matching (Lin and Schatz, 2010; Sun et al., 2012). These approaches generally presuppose a cluster large enough to hold the graph and are oriented toward whole-graph analytics (e.g., PageRank, connected components) rather than ad hoc queries that return a user-specified number of answers. Such resources are not always available, and many users need to query large graphs on a single commodity machine or a small, fixed set of machines. In this paper we pursue a divide-and-conquer strategy. The graph is partitioned into pieces, each small enough to fit in memory, and queries are evaluated over the partitions. Because scalability is then bounded by the size of a partition rather than the size of the graph, a graph of any size can be queried with a fixed amount of memory. The strategy is simple to state but raises nontrivial problems. First, a query answer may span several partitions, so a partition-local evaluation is incomplete: matches crossing partition boundaries must be found by combining partial results from different partitions. Second, an answer may require the same partition more than once, for example when a path leaves a partition and later re-enters it, or when different query components map into the same partition at different stages. Third, answers must be neither lost nor duplicated, which requires careful bookkeeping of intermediate results without retaining so much state that the benefit of partitioning is lost. Finally, because loading a partition from disk dominates the cost, the response time depends strongly on how many partitions are loaded and in what order, which in turn depends on how the graph was partitioned and on the characteristics of the query. We consider three ways to evaluate a query given a set of partitions: (i) One Partition At a Time (OPAT), in which a single partition is resident in memory at any time and partial results are carried between loads; (ii) a traditional multi-processor approach, in which several processors, each with its own memory, process different partitions concurrently and exchange intermediate results; and (iii) a Map/Reduce approach, in which partitions are processed in map tasks and partial answers are combined in reduce tasks. OPAT provides scalability through independent processing of partitions and is the main focus of this paper. The latter two address response time in addition to scalability, and we present and analyze them to place OPAT in context. The research questions addressed are the following. (1) What is the minimal information that must be maintained across partition loads so that a query over a partitioned graph yields exactly the same answers as over the unpartitioned graph, including answers that span several partitions or revisit a partition? (2) How do partitioning schemes, such as those based on balanced edge-cut minimization (Karypis and Kumar, 1998), hash or range assignment, and locality-preserving methods, influence the number of partition loads and the volume of intermediate results for different query types? (3) Given a query and a set of partitions, can quantitative partition and query metrics be used to select a loading order that reduces response time, particularly when only a specified number of answers is required rather than the complete answer set? (4) How do the three evaluation approaches compare in scalability and response time under varying resource constraints? Our work differs from earlier work on partitioned or distributed graph querying in several respects. Many systems partition a graph for load balancing and assume that all partitions are concurrently available (Malewicz et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011). Work on distributed subgraph matching often relies on replicating boundary neighborhoods or on precomputed indexes to avoid cross-partition joins (Fan et al., 2010), which increases storage and preprocessing and may not bound the memory used. Out-of-core graph systems such as GraphChi (Kyrola et al., 2012) and X-Stream (Roy et al., 2013) process a graph in sequentially loaded pieces but target iterative analytics in which every vertex or edge is visited in each pass; they do not address queries that can terminate early or that have selective structure. In contrast, we treat query answering as the central problem, establish correctness conditions for cross-partition and repeated-partition answers, and exploit query selectivity and partition characteristics to determine how many partitions need to be loaded and in which sequence. The contributions of this paper are as follows. 1. We present an OPAT query evaluation framework for partitioned graphs that identifies the necessary minimal bookkeeping, and we prove that it computes complete and duplicate-free answers, including those that span multiple partitions or require the same partition more than once. 2. We analyze the interaction between partitioning schemes and query processing, and we correlate query properties (e.g., structure, size, selectivity, and the number of answers requested) with partition characteristics to estimate the number of loads and the resources needed. 3. We define a set of quantitative metrics over partitions and intermediate results and use them to formulate heuristics for ordering partition loads, aimed at reducing response time both for all answers and for a specified number of answers. 4. We extend an existing graph querying system to evaluate queries on partitioned graphs and report experiments on large synthetic and real-world graphs, using several partitioning schemes and a variety of query types, to evaluate the heuristics. 5. We develop and analyze the multi-processor and Map/Reduce approaches, and we contrast all three approaches with respect to scalability, response time, and resource requirements, providing guidance on when each is appropriate. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the query model and the partitioned-graph evaluation framework, including the correctness argument. Section 3 presents partitioning analysis, metrics, and heuristics. Section 4 describes the multi-processor and Map/Reduce approaches. Section 5 reports the experimental evaluation, and Section 6 discusses the findings and concludes. Problem setting and overall design We model a graph as a directed, labeled multigraph G = (V, E, λ), where λ assigns labels to vertices and edges. A query Q is a connected pattern of k edges with optional label and value predicates. It is evaluated under subgraph-isomorphism semantics (Ullmann, 1976) with a result limit r, where r is either all answers or a user-specified number. G is divided into n partitions {P₁,…,Pₙ}. Each vertex belongs to exactly one partition, and edges whose endpoints lie in different partitions are cut edges. Each partition is stored as a self-contained unit that holds its internal edges, its outgoing cut edges, and a catalogue of its boundary vertices. A partition is sized so that it, together with the intermediate results it produces, fits in the memory budget M. Query evaluation therefore needs no more than M, regardless of |G|. We study three evaluation strategies: (i) One Partition At a Time (OPAT), (ii) a traditional multiprocessor approach with shared or message-passing workers, and (iii) a Map/Reduce formulation (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004). OPAT is the primary experimental subject. The other two are specified and analyzed with a cost model, and their behavior is compared to OPAT on the same workloads. OPAT evaluation and minimal bookkeeping OPAT loads one partition at a time into memory and evaluates Q against it with the in-memory engine. A partial match is a binding of a connected subset of Q's edges to graph edges. When a partial match reaches a boundary vertex v whose continuation edge lies in another partition Pj, it is suspended. Two answers can then be lost or duplicated. The first is an answer that spans partitions, which is lost if the suspension is not recorded. The second is an answer that needs the same partition more than once, which is lost if a partition is considered finished after one visit. To prevent both, we keep a minimal record for each suspended partial match m: B(m) = ⟨σ(m), e(m), π(m)⟩, where σ is the vertex-to-query-node binding, e is the next query edge to be matched together with the boundary vertex that must be expanded, and π is the set of (partition, query-edge) expansions that m has already consumed. Storing π, and not only a set of visited partitions, is what allows a partition to be reloaded for a different query edge without repeating work. Final answers, together with the suspended partial matches, are written to disk between loads. Each partition Pi also carries a "pending" queue of the suspended matches that need it. Processing proceeds as follows. (1) Choose the next partition by the ordering heuristic below. (2) Load it, together with its pending queue. (3) Extend the pending partial matches, and start new matches of Q from its internal edges. (4) Emit completed answers, and re-queue any match that again reaches a boundary into another partition. (5) Stop when r answers have been found or when all pending queues are empty. Only partitions with non-empty pending queues, or those not yet used to seed matches, are candidates at step 1. Correctness is argued as soundness and completeness. Soundness holds because every emitted answer is a binding that satisfies all Q edges and predicates against edges that physically exist in G. Completeness follows by induction on the number of query edges matched. Any answer is a sequence of edge matches; whenever the sequence crosses from Pa to Pb, the cut edge is held in Pa's boundary catalogue and a record B(m) is appended to Pb's queue. Hence the answer is eventually extended, however many times partitions are revisited. Duplicate suppression follows from π, because the pair (σ, e) uniquely identifies the expansion and is consumed once. We verified both properties empirically by comparing the OPAT result sets with those of the unpartitioned in-memory engine on all graphs that fit in memory (set equality, 100% agreement required). The imbalance tolerance is 1.05 for all schemes, and n ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32, 64}. The advent of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in the management of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection marked a pivotal shift, transforming a once fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition (Deeks et al., 2013). As a consequence, the life expectancy of individuals living with HIV has seen a dramatic increase, aligning more closely with that of the general population (Samji et al., 2013). However, this prolonged survival has introduced new clinical challenges, notably an increased burden of chronic non-communicable diseases, including chronic kidney disease (CKD) (Guaraldi et al., 2011). CKD, characterized by a persistent reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and/or markers of kidney damage, poses a significant health concern globally, with estimates indicating that it affects approximately 10% of the world's population (Coresh et al., 2007). In the context of HIV, CKD can arise as a direct consequence of HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN), particularly in populations of African ancestry, or as a complication of prolonged ART, which has been associated with nephrotoxicity (Mocroft et al., 2010). Furthermore, traditional risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes, which are increasingly prevalent in the aging HIV population, further exacerbate the risk of CKD (Sanyaolu et al., 2018). Previous studies have documented the prevalence of CKD in HIV-infected populations across various regions, yet findings have been inconsistent, likely due to differences in study design, population characteristics, and CKD definition criteria (Wyatt et al., 2001; Lucas et al., 2004). In particular, the lack of a consensus on the most appropriate equation for estimating GFR — whether the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD), Cockcroft-Gault, or Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) formula — has led to variability in CKD prevalence estimates (Stevens et al., 2009). This variability complicates efforts to formulate standardized care protocols and public health strategies at both regional and global levels. The gap in knowledge becomes more pronounced in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly within the African continent, where the prevalence of HIV remains disproportionately high (UNAIDS, 2016). Here, infrastructural challenges and limited healthcare resources often hinder comprehensive disease management and the integration of CKD screening into HIV care (Katz et al., 2013). Thus, understanding the regional prevalence of CKD among HIV-infected adults and the specific contributory factors within these settings is crucial for the development of targeted interventions. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to address these gaps by providing robust estimates of the prevalence of CKD in the global HIV-infected adult population, with a focussed analysis based on different GFR estimating equations. We further explore geographical variations, taking into consideration the distinct epidemiological and socio-economic contexts across World Health Organization (WHO) regions. By synthesizing data from diverse settings, this research seeks to highlight disparities in CKD prevalence and to offer insights into region-specific risk factors that may influence kidney health in individuals living with HIV. Our research is anchored in several key questions: What is the prevalence of CKD among adults living with HIV globally, and how does it vary by geographical region? How do different eGFR equations impact the estimated prevalence of CKD in this population? What are the underlying factors contributing to the observed regional disparities in CKD prevalence? Our analysis incorporates a comprehensive examination of demographic and clinical parameters, including comorbid hypertension, diabetes, hepatitis coinfections, and ART status, thus enabling a nuanced understanding of the multiplicity of factors influencing CKD prevalence. The contributions of this study are multifaceted. Firstly, it provides a global snapshot of CKD prevalence in the HIV-positive adult population, stratified by region and GFR estimation methods, thus offering a much-needed comparative perspective that could inform global health policy. Secondly, it identifies significant regional discrepancies that underscore the need for tailored public health strategies. Finally, our findings could serve as a platform for future research endeavors aimed at delineating the pathophysiological mechanisms underpinning CKD development in the context of HIV infection and ART. In conclusion, given the escalating burden of CKD in the aging HIV-infected population, proactive measures including the formulation of international guidelines for CKD screening and management in HIV patients must be prioritized. This study provides a critical evidence base that can inform such initiatives, thus facilitating improved health outcomes for individuals living with HIV worldwide. The present systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to establish the global and regional prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the adult HIV-infected population. This section delineates the methodological framework utilized, including data sources, study selection, inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction, quality assessment, and statistical analysis procedures. The study design is registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number CRD42016036246. Data Sources and Search Strategy An exhaustive literature search was executed across multiple databases, specifically PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO, and African Journals Online (AJOL), to identify pertinent articles published from January 1982 to May 2016. The search strategy employed a combination of subject headings and keywords, including "HIV," "AIDS," "chronic kidney disease," "CKD," "prevalence," "estimated glomerular filtration rate," "eGFR," "MDRD," "Cockcroft-Gault," and "CKD-EPI." Boolean operators and truncations ensured a comprehensive retrieval of relevant studies. The search was limited to studies involving adult populations and published in English. Additionally, references from identified articles were manually screened to capture any studies potentially missed by the electronic search. Study Selection and Eligibility Criteria The selection of studies adhered to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eligible studies were those that reported on the prevalence of CKD among adults diagnosed with HIV and included the assessment of kidney function using at least one of the following equations: Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD), Cockcroft-Gault, or CKD Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI). Studies were excluded if they did not present primary data, focused on pediatric populations, or assessed other comorbid conditions without stratifying CKD data for HIV-infected individuals. Two independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of identified records for relevance and eligibility. The full texts of potentially eligible studies were retrieved and assessed against the inclusion criteria. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer arbitrated unresolved conflicts to reach a consensus. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment Data extraction was meticulously performed using a standardized form to capture essential details from each selected study. Extracted data encompassed study characteristics such as author information, publication year, study period, geographical location, sample size, mean age of participants, gender distribution, diagnostic criteria for CKD, and prevalence estimates categorized by the utilized eGFR equation. Where available, data on potential covariates, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hepatitis B and C coinfection, CD4 count, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, were also collected. The methodological quality of the included studies was appraised using a modified version of the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, adapted specifically for prevalence studies. This assessment facilitated the evaluation of potential biases related to the selection of participants, assessment of CKD outcomes, and adequacy of follow-up, where applicable. Each study was independently graded by two reviewers, and any differences in quality ratings were reconciled through discussion. Statistical Analysis The principal measure of interest was the pooled prevalence of CKD among HIV-infected adults. Given the variability in CKD definitions and population characteristics, a random-effects meta-analysis model was deemed most suitable for combining prevalence estimates. The Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation was employed to stabilize variance and normalize the distribution of prevalence proportions prior to pooling, thereby minimizing the impact of studies with extreme prevalence figures (Nyaga et al., 2014). Heterogeneity among studies was quantified using the I^2 statistic, with values exceeding 50% suggestive of substantial heterogeneity (Higgins et al., 2003). Sources of heterogeneity were explored through subgroup analyses stratified by World Health Organization (WHO) region. Additional subgroup analyses were conducted to assess the influence of specific variables, including the presence of comorbidities such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus, although factors such as gender, hepatitis B or C coinfection, CD4 count, and ART status were not found to significantly impact prevalence estimates. The statistical significance of discrepancies across eGFR methods was evaluated using Cochran's Q test. Publication bias was assessed through visual inspection of funnel plots, complemented by Begg's and Egger's tests to quantitatively detect asymmetry. Sensitivity analyses were undertaken by excluding studies with low-quality scores or those contributing extreme prevalence values, to ascertain the robustness of the pooled estimates. All statistical analyses were performed using Stata software version 15.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all tests, barring adjustments for multiple comparisons where applicable. Results In the systematic review and meta-analysis devised to ascertain the prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the global adult HIV-infected population, we identified and included data from 61 eligible studies, collectively involving 209,078 individuals living with HIV across 60 countries. The investigation utilized three distinct methods for estimating glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), namely the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD), Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI), and Cockcroft-Gault equations, to quantify CKD prevalence within this cohort. Our analysis revealed considerable variability in CKD prevalence depending on the estimation formula employed. The MDRD method yielded an overall CKD prevalence of 6.4% (95% Confidence Interval [CI] 5.2–7.7%), while the CKD-EPI method produced a prevalence of 4.8% (95% CI 2.9–7.1%). The Cockcroft-Gault equation reported a significantly higher CKD prevalence of 12.3% (95% CI 8.4–16.7%). The statistical comparison across these estimators indicated significant differences (p = 0.003). Sub-group analyses by World Health Organization (WHO) regions revealed stark regional disparities in CKD prevalence among HIV-infected adults. Africa emerged as the region with the highest prevalence of CKD when determined using the MDRD equation, at 7.9% (95% CI 5.2–11.1%). Within this continent, further stratification showed pronounced variability: the West African sub-region reported the highest prevalence at 14.6% (95% CI 9.9–20.0%), while Southern Africa exhibited the lowest prevalence at 3.2% (95% CI 3.0–3.4%). Comparatively, other regions such as South-East Asia (5.1%, 95% CI 3.9–6.4%), the Americas (4.5%, 95% CI 2.8–6.6%), and Europe (3.8%, 95% CI 2.5–5.3%) showed lower prevalence rates, indicating significant geographical heterogeneity (I² = 92.7%). Chronological analysis displayed a gradual increase in the prevalence of CKD over time, particularly notable from studies published in the last decade of our search timeframe. Studies from the period 2006-2016 accounted for a higher pooled prevalence (7.1%, 95% CI 4.9–9.8%) compared to those published before 2006 (3.9%, 95% CI 2.4–5.5%). The study further explored potential sources of heterogeneity via subgroup analyses focusing on demographic and clinical co-variates. Comorbid hypertension and diabetes mellitus emerged as significant contributors to increased CKD prevalence among HIV-infected individuals. Patients with hypertension showed an aggregated CKD prevalence of 9.8% (95% CI 7.2–12.6%), while those with diabetes had a prevalence rate climbing to 15.3% (95% CI 10.7–20.7%). In contrast, variability analysis by CD4 count, ART status, gender, and coinfections with hepatitis B or C did not yield statistically significant distinctions contributing to CKD prevalence, suggesting these factors did not explicate the observed heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses affirming the robustness of our findings corroborated these results. Analysis excluding studies of lower methodological rigor or those employing non-standardized definitions of CKD produced similar prevalence estimates, thus supporting the stability of the outcomes. The prevalence variations discerned through our comprehensive analysis underscore the alarming frequency of CKD among the HIV-infected populace globally, with pronounced regional and clinical disparities. These results substantiate the exigency for improved CKD screening protocols and tailored treatment paradigms within HIV healthcare initiatives, particularly targeting high-risk regions such as Africa. Significantly, our findings advocate for the integration of standardized CKD screening and management guidelines within the ambit of global HIV treatment frameworks to alleviate long-term renal complications within this vulnerable population. The present systematic review and meta-analysis provides a comprehensive synthesis of the global prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the adult HIV-infected population, revealing significant epidemiological variations across different regions and highlighting a critical intersection of HIV management and non-communicable disease strategy. Our findings indicate that the prevalence of CKD in this population is substantial, fluctuating based on the method of eGFR calculation and geographical location, which has profound implications for clinical practice and policy-making. Cancer is one of the leading causes of adult deaths worldwide. Every year about 14 million new cancer cases are detected and 8 million people die of cancer.[1] However, there is a marked difference in the distribution of cancer sites across different regions of the world. In contrast to developed countries, cervical cancer is a public health problem in developing countries like India, so much so that India alone accounts for one-quarter of the worldwide burden of cervical cancers.[12] It is the one of the leading cause of cancer mortality, accounting for 17% of all cancer deaths among women aged between 30 and 69 years. It is estimated that cervical cancer will occur in approximately 1 in 53 Indian women during their lifetime compared with 1 in 100 women in more developed regions of the world.[2] Screening for cancer is known to reduce mortality by early detection and treatment. However, there are two prerequisites for screening to reduce the rate of death from cancer. First, screening must advance the time of diagnosis of cancers that are destined to cause death. Second, early treatment of these cancers must confer some advantage over treatment at clinical presentation.[34] Unlike other cancer sites, cervix can be subjected to screening for early diagnosis and treatment. However, despite availability of various cervical cancer screening methods, as well as large burden of disease in India, there is no countrywide government-sponsored public health policy on prevention of cervical cancer by either screening or vaccination or both. Therefore, this study was carried out to understand and present burden of cervical cancer in India, as well as to appraise the various cervical cancer screening methods and studies conducted for evaluating screening test for the detection of cervical carcinoma. However, since India is culturally, economically, and sociodemographically dissimilar from other Western countries, we limited the scope of our study to screening trials conducted in Indian population, so as to provide locally relevant evidence-based recommendations for cervical cancer screening in Indian population. This paper is based on information gathered from a review of peer-reviewed publications on cervical cancer screening and prevention in India. MEDLINE (http://www.pubmed.com) and Web of Science electronic database were searched from January 1990 to December 2015 using the keywords such as “cervical cancer”, “screening”, “early detection”, “human papillomavirus (HPV)”, “cervical cytology” and “visual inspection”, and their corresponding MeSH terms were also used in combination with Boolean operators “OR, AND.” We also examined bibliographies of included articles to identify additional references. The search strategy was limited to English language. Only journal article type was included. Figure 1 presents the search strategy and screening process. Study designs eligible for inclusion in our study were randomized controlled trials, nonrandomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and cross-sectional studies conducted to evaluate the performance of the screening tests for detection of cervical cancerStudies conducted in India only were included in the study. Studies not providing data on sensitivity and specificity of screening test were evaluated and excluded from the study. The title and abstract of each citation were screened first, and full report was screened second if necessary to select the relevant articles according to selection criteria. Full texts of these selected studies were retrieved, reviewed, and extracted for relevant data by authors independently. A total of 11 studies were included in the review, and their findings have been presented. The descriptive statistical data for cervical cancer (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition, C53) were mainly obtained from publications of the Indian Cancer Registry, Union for International Cancer Control, International Agency for Research on Cancer, and WHO (GLOBOCAN-2012). The National Cancer Registry Programme (NCRP) has been in existence since 1982, and permanent institute (National Centre for Disease Informatics and Research) of the Indian Council of Medical Research is the crucial repository of data from the collaborating cancer registries located in medical colleges/institutions and hospitals throughout India. As of March 2016, there are 29 hospital-based cancer registries (including all Regional Cancer Centres) and 29 population-based cancer registries (PBCRs) under NCRP.[56] The data obtained from these Indian Cancer Registries indicate that cervical cancer contributes to approximately 6–29% of all cancer in females. The age-adjusted incidence rate of cancer cervix was found to vary widely among registries, highest being 23.07/100,000 in Mizoram State, followed by 22.54/100,000 in Pasighat and the lowest being 4.91/100,000 in Dibrugarh district. The older PBCRs such as Bengaluru, Bhopal, Chennai, Delhi, and Barshi Rural reported an age-adjusted incidence rate between 13 and 16/100,000 [Table 1].[5] All the major registries from 1998 to 2014 reported a statistically significant decreasing trend (negative annual percentage change) of cervical cancer [Table 2].[5] More than 85% of patients in were from age group 40 years and above. The maximum numbers of cases were reported in 50–59 years of age group amounting to 27.37% of all cervical carcinoma cases [Table 3].[5] The 5-year relative survival rate for cancer cervix in India has been reported to be approximately 46% (34–60),[7] which much lesser than survival rates reported from other Asian countries such as China, South Korea, Singapore, and Thailand [Table 4]. In addition, cervical cancer survival rates in India also shows a wide variation ranging from 59.6% in Chennai to 34.5% in Bhopal. The 5-year age-standardized relative survival of cervical cancer for different Indian registries and its comparison with other Asian registries are shown in Table 4.[78] Cervix is amenable to screening by a number of methods which include visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), magnified VIA (VIAM) visual inspection with Lugol's iodine (VILI), the Papanicolaou test, and HPV DNA testing. The pooled sensitivity and specificity for VIA was found to be 67.65% and 84.32%, for VIAM, the pooled sensitivity and specificity were 65.36% and 85.76% and for VILI, the pooled sensitivity and specificity were 78.27% and 87.10%, respectively. The pooled sensitivity and specificity for cytology positivity at low-grade squamous intraepithelial neoplasia threshold were 62.11% and 93.51% and for HPV, the pooled sensitivity and specificity were 77.81% and 91.54%, respectively. In today's era, in spite of the availability of HPV vaccines and affordable and effective methods for early detection and treatment of cervical cancer precursor lesions, cervical cancer still continues to be a public health problem in India. The age-adjusted incidence rates of cancer cervix reported by majority of Indian cancer registries are much higher than the world age-adjusted incidence rate of 7.9/100,000 population but is lower or similar to cervical cancer incidence rates of 19.2/100,000 population seen in the South-East Asian region.[1] The high burden of cervical cancer in India and Southeast Asian countries is due to poor to moderate living standards, a high prevalence of HPV (more than 10% in women aged more than 30 years) and due to lack of screening.[27] There is a wide variation (range: 4.91–23.07/100,000) in the incidence rates reported by individual PBCRs [Table 1], more so these extreme rates have been reported by newer registries. This is because some PBCRs are reporting the data for the first time and hence, it needs to be viewed with some caution as in the initial years of registry operation there could be some degree of over/under reporting.[5] Most of the major registries have shown a decreasing trend of cervical cancer, however, the decrease was very small. The mean annual percentage decrease in the average age-adjusted rate ranged from 1.81% to 3.48% among various registries. It should be noted that in India most of the cervical cancer cases are detected with regional spread of the disease, and a very small proportion are diagnosed at a localized stage. In India, an organized mass-screening program for early detection of cervical cancer is not in practice; hence, this decrease cannot be attributed to screening.[28] Moreover, it is also highly probable that cervical cancer incidence rates are an underestimate for India possibly due to underdiagnosis of cervical cancer cases in rural areas and among most impoverished women, as well as due to noninclusion of subclinical cervical cancers in routine hysterectomy specimens not subjected to histopathology, which is a common practice in many regions of India.[29] On the other hand, it has also been suggested that probably an improvement in the living standard of women may have resulted in a reduction in the incidence of cervical cancer, but the same has not been substantiated.[30] The 5-year age-standardized (0–74 years) relative survival for cervical cancer in India is much lower as compared to certain South East Asian countries [Table 4]. This can be attributed to the absence of a nationwide screening program as survival is determined by age and the extent of disease, with younger women having longer survival.[31] A wide variation of survival rates is also observed between rural and urban India. This could be because Indian registries suffer with the problem of under-reporting of death, which is more pronounced in the rural area. In addition, the lack of health infrastructure in rural India results in lower survival rates as compared to urban areas. In India, despite such alarming statistics there has been no synchronized initiative from public health authorities for prevention and control cervical cancer. In developed countries, conventional cytology screening programs have shown a marked decline in the incidence of cervical cancer.[2732] However, its successful implementation requires a variety of requirements to be fulfilled, which are not feasible in many low-resource settings where a high risk of cervical cancer is experienced. For instance, cytology screening requires a laboratory infrastructure, microscopes, several resource personnel (smear collectors, cytotechnicians, and pathologists), consumables (slides, fixative, Pap stain containing five dyes, and three solutions), and several steps with inbuilt quality assurance procedures. Moreover, cytology must be repeated at frequent 3–5-year intervals to ensure satisfactory sensitivity and optimum detection of cervical cancer precursor lesions and repeat visits are necessary after a positive cytology for diagnosis and treatment, which may lead to drop outs. Several years of cytology screening in low- and middle-income countries have not led to significant reductions in cervical cancer in these countries, possibly due to the difficulties in offering high-quality cytology, programmatic deficiencies in follow-up and treatment of screen-positive women, and also due to the considerable financial, technical, and logistic inputs necessary for effective cytology programs.[2533] Hence, these challenges have prompted the search for programs based on alternative cervical screening tests, which are implementable in resource-poor settings. VIA is one of the alternative methods for cervical cancer screening that has been widely investigated. In our review of Indian studies, the sensitivity of VIA has been found to be better than cytology, but its specificity is lower [Table 4].[1617181920212223242526] However, the biggest advantage of visual tests is that it can be implemented through primary health-care workers, it does not require a laboratory infrastructure, and the results are obtained immediately following testing, allowing diagnosis and treatment to be instituted during the same visit. It has been well established that cervical neoplasia is caused by persistent infection with certain oncogenic types of HPV. Indian studies of testing for HPV DNA indicate higher sensitivity and comparable specificity as compared to visual inspection and cytology. However, the requirement of sophisticated laboratory infrastructure and high cost make it impracticable to be implementable in resource-poor, low-income countries.
