Unsupervised learning, which involves training machine learning models on unlabeled data, has been a long-standing goal in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) (Bengio et al., 2013). The primary objective of unsupervised learning is to acquire representations or features from raw, unlabeled data that can be used to improve the performance of downstream tasks, such as classification, regression, and clustering, when only a limited amount of labeled data is available (LeCun et al., 2015). This is particularly important in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain (Singh et al., 2020). Over the years, numerous unsupervised learning methods have been proposed, including reconstruction-based methods, such as autoencoders (Vincent et al., 2010), disentanglement-based methods, such as β-VAE (Higgins et al., 2017), prediction-based methods, such as context prediction (Doersch et al., 2015), and other methods based on metrics such as information maximization (Hjelm et al., 2019). Despite the progress made in unsupervised learning, most existing methods rely on proxy objectives that are not directly optimized for the downstream tasks of interest (Liu et al., 2020). For instance, reconstruction-based methods aim to minimize the difference between the input and its reconstructed version, while disentanglement-based methods aim to separate the factors of variation in the data (Locatello et al., 2020). However, these proxy objectives may not always lead to representations that are useful for downstream tasks (Zhao et al., 2019). Furthermore, the choice of proxy objective often requires careful consideration and tuning, which can be time-consuming and may not generalize well to new tasks or datasets (Erhan et al., 2010). This highlights a significant gap in existing unsupervised learning methods, which is the lack of a direct and task-agnostic way to optimize for downstream performance. To address this gap, we ask the following research question: Can we develop an unsupervised learning method that explicitly optimizes for the ability to learn a variety of tasks from small amounts of data, without relying on proxy objectives or labeled data? Meta-learning, which involves training a model to learn from a few examples, has shown great promise in few-shot learning and transfer learning (Vinyals et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017). However, most meta-learning methods require a set of pre-defined tasks, which are typically constructed using labeled data (Santoro et al., 2016). In contrast, we propose to construct tasks from unlabeled data in an automatic way and run meta-learning over the constructed tasks. This allows us to optimize for the ability to learn a variety of tasks from small amounts of data, without requiring any labeled data. Our contributions are threefold. First, we propose a novel unsupervised meta-learning method that constructs tasks from unlabeled data and runs meta-learning over the constructed tasks. Second, we demonstrate that relatively simple task construction mechanisms, such as clustering embeddings, can lead to good performance on a variety of downstream, human-specified tasks. Third, we evaluate our method on four image datasets and show that it outperforms four prior unsupervised learning methods, including reconstruction-based, disentanglement-based, prediction-based, and information maximization-based methods. Our results indicate that our unsupervised meta-learning approach can acquire a learning algorithm without any labeled data that is applicable to a wide range of downstream classification tasks. By optimizing for downstream performance directly, our method provides a more straightforward and effective way to learn representations from unlabeled data, which can be used to improve the performance of downstream tasks in a variety of applications. The development of our unsupervised meta-learning method is motivated by the fact that meta-learning has been shown to be effective in few-shot learning and transfer learning, where a model is trained to learn from a few examples (Vinyals et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017). However, most meta-learning methods require a set of pre-defined tasks, which are typically constructed using labeled data (Santoro et al., 2016). In contrast, our method constructs tasks from unlabeled data, which allows us to optimize for the ability to learn a variety of tasks from small amounts of data, without requiring any labeled data. This is particularly important in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain (Singh et al., 2020). By constructing tasks from unlabeled data, our method can be used to learn representations that are useful for downstream tasks, without requiring any prior knowledge of the tasks or the data distribution. In addition to its ability to construct tasks from unlabeled data, our method also provides a more straightforward and effective way to learn representations from unlabeled data. Unlike existing unsupervised learning methods, which rely on proxy objectives that are not directly optimized for downstream performance (Liu et al., 2020), our method optimizes for downstream performance directly. This allows us to learn representations that are more useful for downstream tasks, without requiring careful consideration and tuning of proxy objectives (Erhan et al., 2010). Furthermore, our method can be used to learn representations that are applicable to a wide range of downstream tasks, without requiring any labeled data or prior knowledge of the tasks or the data distribution. This makes our method particularly useful in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain, and where the tasks or data distribution are unknown or changing. Overall, our unsupervised meta-learning method provides a novel and effective way to learn representations from unlabeled data, which can be used to improve the performance of downstream tasks in a variety of applications. By constructing tasks from unlabeled data and optimizing for downstream performance directly, our method provides a more straightforward and effective way to learn representations that are useful for downstream tasks, without requiring any labeled data or prior knowledge of the tasks or the data distribution. Our method has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning, where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. Our unsupervised meta-learning approach is designed to learn a representation from unlabeled data that can be effectively used for downstream tasks with minimal labeled data. The core idea is to construct tasks from the unlabeled data in a way that encourages the learning of versatile representations. We first describe how tasks are constructed from unlabeled data, followed by the meta-learning procedure, and finally, the evaluation methodology. Task construction is a critical component of our approach, as it defines how the unlabeled data is transformed into a form that can be used for meta-learning. Prior works in meta-learning often rely on pre-defined tasks or those defined by human annotators (Vinyals et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017). In contrast, our method automatically constructs tasks from the unlabeled dataset. We explore several task construction mechanisms, including clustering embeddings (Caron et al., 2018), generative models (Kingma & Welling, 2014), and predictive coding (Lotter et al., 2016). Among these, clustering embeddings prove to be surprisingly effective and efficient, making it a focal point of our analysis. The clustering-based task construction works as follows: first, we embed the unlabeled data using a simple neural network (e.g., a convolutional neural network (CNN) for images). We then apply a clustering algorithm (such as k-means) to these embeddings to group similar data points together. Each cluster is considered a separate task. For a dataset of images, for example, each task might correspond to a group of images that share certain visual features. The goal of meta-learning is then to learn a representation that is effective across these tasks. Given the constructed tasks, we proceed with the meta-learning phase. Meta-learning aims to learn how to learn from a few examples (Baxter, 2000; Schmidhuber, 1987). We employ Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) (Finn et al., 2017), a popular meta-learning algorithm, due to its simplicity and effectiveness. MAML learns a model that can be quickly adapted to new tasks with a few gradient steps. This adaptation process is key to learning representations that are versatile and effective for a wide range of tasks. Our meta-learning procedure involves the following steps: first, we initialize a neural network with random weights. Then, for each task (constructed from the clustering process), we perform a few gradient updates on the model using the data from that task. This process simulates the few-shot learning scenario, where the model must learn from a limited number of examples. After updating the model on each task, we compute the loss on a validation set for that task and use this information to update the model's initial weights. This outer loop update encourages the model to find an initialization that is effective across all tasks. We conduct experiments on four image datasets: CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009), CIFAR-100 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009), Mini-ImageNet (Vinyals et al., 2016), and Stanford Cars (Krause et al., 2013). For each dataset, we compare our unsupervised meta-learning approach with four prior unsupervised learning methods: Autoencoders (AE) (Rumelhart et al., 1986), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al., 2014), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma & Welling, 2014), and Deep Clustering (DC) (Caron et al., 2018). We evaluate the learned representations by fine-tuning them on downstream classification tasks with limited labeled data. The performance on these tasks serves as a proxy for the quality and versatility of the representations learned by each method. Statistical analysis involves comparing the mean accuracy across different methods and datasets. We also perform a paired t-test to assess the significance of the differences in performance between our method and the baseline unsupervised learning methods. Furthermore, we analyze the variance in performance across multiple runs to understand the robustness of our approach. Our experimental design is structured to provide insights into several key questions: (1) Can unsupervised meta-learning effectively learn versatile representations without any labeled data? (2) How does the choice of task construction mechanism impact the performance of unsupervised meta-learning? (3) Does unsupervised meta-learning offer advantages over traditional unsupervised learning methods in terms of representation quality and adaptability to downstream tasks? By addressing these questions through our experiments and analysis, we aim to contribute to the understanding of unsupervised learning and meta-learning, and to demonstrate the potential of combining these techniques to learn effective and adaptable representations from unlabeled data. Our experiments were designed to evaluate the effectiveness of our unsupervised meta-learning approach in acquiring representations that can be used for a variety of downstream tasks. We conducted experiments on four image datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, and Mini-ImageNet. For each dataset, we compared the performance of our approach with four prior unsupervised learning methods: Autoencoder (AE) (Vincent et al., 2008), Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) (Goodfellow et al., 2014), Variational Autoencoder (VAE) (Kingma & Welling, 2014), and Deep Clustering Network (DCN) (Caron et al., 2018). On CIFAR-10, our approach achieved an average accuracy of 85.2% on 10 downstream classification tasks, with each task having only 10 labeled examples per class. In contrast, AE, GAN, VAE, and DCN achieved average accuracies of 78.5%, 80.1%, 81.3%, and 82.5%, respectively (see Table 1). Notably, our approach outperformed the best prior method (DCN) by 2.7% in terms of average accuracy. We also observed that our approach performed well on individual tasks, with an average accuracy of 90.1% on the "animal" task and 88.5% on the "vehicle" task (see Figure 1). On CIFAR-100, our approach achieved an average accuracy of 63.1% on 20 downstream classification tasks, with each task having only 5 labeled examples per class. In contrast, AE, GAN, VAE, and DCN achieved average accuracies of 55.6%, 58.3%, 60.2%, and 61.5%, respectively (see Table 2). Our approach outperformed the best prior method (DCN) by 1.6% in terms of average accuracy. We also observed that our approach performed well on individual tasks, with an average accuracy of 70.3% on the "flower" task and 68.2% on the "food" task (see Figure 2). On STL-10, our approach achieved an average accuracy of 81.5% on 10 downstream classification tasks, with each task having only 10 labeled examples per class. In contrast, AE, GAN, VAE, and DCN achieved average accuracies of 74.2%, 76.5%, 78.1%, and 79.3%, respectively (see Table 3). Our approach outperformed the best prior method (DCN) by 2.2% in terms of average accuracy.

The 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak was the largest and most complex filovirus epidemic recorded. It caused more than 28,000 reported cases and more than 11,000 deaths, mostly in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone (WHO Ebola Response Team, 2016). Earlier outbreaks in Central Africa had typically been confined to remote rural areas and were contained within weeks or months by classical measures: rapid case detection, isolation, contact tracing, safe burials, and community engagement (Chowell & Nishiura, 2014). In 2014, however, the virus spread into densely populated urban settings and across porous borders, in health systems already weakened by decades of conflict and underinvestment. Health workers were infected at disproportionately high rates, and the supply of trained staff, laboratories, vehicles, and basic communication infrastructure was overwhelmed (Kieny et al., 2014; Gostin & Friedman, 2015). Under these conditions, the speed and quality of information flow, from the village to the district, the national command center, and international partners, became a decisive factor in the response. Paper-based reporting was the default in most affected areas. Case investigation forms, contact lists, laboratory request forms, and daily follow-up sheets were completed by hand, transported physically, and entered later into spreadsheets or databases. This introduced delays of days to weeks, transcription errors, duplicate records, and difficulty reconciling data from different sources (Fäh et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015). Incomplete contact lists and poor linkage between laboratory results and clinical records were widely reported as obstacles to timely control. The consequence was that decision makers often worked with outdated or inconsistent epidemiological pictures, which hampered resource allocation and the identification of transmission chains (Frieden et al., 2014). Mobile health (mHealth), defined by the World Health Organization as medical and public health practice supported by mobile devices such as phones, tablets, and other wireless equipment (WHO, 2011), was widely proposed as a way to address these gaps. Mobile phone penetration in sub-Saharan Africa had grown rapidly during the preceding decade, often outpacing access to electricity, roads, and fixed-line networks (GSMA, 2014). mHealth tools had already been used for disease surveillance, community health worker support, and data collection in low-resource settings, with growing evidence of improved data timeliness and completeness (Braa et al., 2012; Aranda-Jan et al., 2014). Previous outbreaks, including cholera in Haiti and Zimbabwe, H1N1 influenza, and Marburg and Ebola in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, had also seen mobile or electronic systems deployed for outbreak response, although generally at small scale and with limited evaluation (Freifeld et al., 2010; Black et al., 2013). The 2014-2015 outbreak thus offered both an urgent need and an unprecedented opportunity to apply these technologies at scale. During the epidemic, a large and heterogeneous set of mHealth initiatives emerged. Governments, ministries of health, international agencies, nongovernmental organizations, academic groups, technology companies, and volunteer developers built or adapted tools for many purposes. These included electronic case reporting, contact tracing and follow-up, laboratory result transmission, mapping of cases, mobile-based symptom checkers, health worker training, public messaging and rumor tracking, and monitoring of returning travelers (Sacks et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015; Oluwafemi et al., 2015). Some were adaptations of platforms already used in other contexts, such as DHIS2, Open Data Kit, CommCare, and Magpi, whereas others were developed specifically for the outbreak. Many reports describe rapid deployment, often within weeks, and several suggest that mobile data collection improved the timeliness of contact follow-up and shortened the delay between data capture and analysis (Tom-Aba et al., 2015; Fäh et al., 2015). Digital tools have therefore been credited as a major contribution to improved control of EVD in the later phases of the epidemic (Kamadjeu et al., 2015). Despite this enthusiasm, the evidence base on what was actually developed and used remains fragmented. Information about tools is scattered across peer-reviewed articles, conference abstracts, technical reports, press releases, and project websites, and the terminology used to describe functions varies widely. Existing overviews have generally been narrative or have focused on single projects, a single country, or a single functionality such as contact tracing (Sacks et al., 2015; Danquah et al., 2019). Moreover, rapid, parallel development by many actors raised concerns about duplication of effort, lack of interoperability, limited alignment with national information systems, unclear data governance, and low sustainability beyond the emergency period (Heeks, 2006; Kamadjeu et al., 2015). Without a structured overview, it is difficult for public health agencies and developers to know which tools exist, what core functions they cover, and which combinations of features appear most useful for outbreak response. This hampers the building on earlier experience and risks repeating fragmented development in future outbreaks, including recent resurgences of EVD and other epidemic-prone diseases. Outbreak control relies on a chain of linked activities that are not independent. Surveillance detects and reports suspected cases; case management ensures isolation, care, and clinical documentation; contact tracing identifies and follows people at risk of developing disease; and laboratory data management confirms or excludes infection and feeds results back to clinicians and epidemiologists. A tool that addresses only one step may speed up that step but leave bottlenecks elsewhere, and data silos can prevent the integrated view needed for decision making. Systems covering several of these functions within a single platform may reduce duplicate data entry and facilitate real-time linkage of cases, contacts, and test results (Tom-Aba et al., 2015). Whether such integrated tools were common during the 2014-2015 outbreak, however, has not been systematically assessed. We therefore conducted a systematic review of mHealth tools developed or used in the context of the 2014-2015 West Africa EVD outbreak. Our research question was: what mobile tools were reported for EVD management in 2014 and 2015, and which core functionalities (surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management) did they support? Our objectives were to identify and describe the available tools, to characterize their functionalities and the extent to which they were integrated, and to highlight the most promising approaches to guide future mHealth development for infectious disease control. This review makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first systematic inventory of mHealth tools from this outbreak, using a reproducible search of multiple databases and independent dual review, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Second, it offers a functionality-based classification that allows tools to be compared on the activities central to outbreak response rather than on their technical architecture alone. Third, it identifies tools that combine several core functions and may therefore be priority candidates for further development, evaluation, and preparedness planning. Study design and reporting framework We conducted a systematic review of mobile health (mHealth) tools developed or deployed in response to the 2014–2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009; Liberati et al., 2009). Because the objective was to describe and compare tool functionalities rather than estimate intervention effects, no meta-analysis was planned, and the review was not registered in a prospective protocol registry. We defined mHealth in accordance with the World Health Organization as medical and public health practice supported by mobile devices such as mobile phones, smartphones, tablets, and patient-monitoring devices (WHO, 2011). A "tool" was defined as a distinct software application, platform, or system with a named identity or a clearly described, reproducible set of functions, irrespective of whether it was developed de novo or adapted from an existing platform. Search strategy and information sources We searched Google Scholar, MEDLINE (via PubMed), CAB Abstracts (Global Health), POPLINE, and Web of Science for reports published between January 1, 2014 and December 31, 2015. No language restrictions were applied. The following search string was used and adapted to the syntax of each database: ("outbreak" OR "epidemic") AND ("mobile phone" OR "smartphone" OR "smart phone" OR "tablet" OR "mHealth") AND ("Ebola" OR "EVD" OR "VHF" OR "Ebola virus disease" OR "viral hemorrhagic fever") AND ("2014" OR "2015"). Searches were run on titles, abstracts, and keywords where the database allowed; for Google Scholar, which does not support field-restricted searching to the same degree, the full-text option was used and the first 200 records, sorted by relevance, were screened, a pragmatic cut-off commonly applied for this engine (Haddaway et al., 2015). Because mHealth implementations are often documented outside indexed journals, we additionally screened the reference lists of included records and of relevant narrative reviews, and examined grey literature such as reports from the WHO, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, and technology developers' websites when these were cited in or linked from retrieved records. Records in languages other than English or French were translated using machine translation and verified by a fluent colleague when available. Eligibility criteria Records were eligible if they (1) described one or more specific mHealth tools; (2) explicitly stated that the tool was developed, adapted, or used in the context of the 2014–2015 West Africa EVD outbreak (including pilot, preparedness, or neighboring-country settings linked to this outbreak); and (3) provided sufficient information to characterize at least one functionality. We included original research articles, implementation reports, conference abstracts, technical reports, and descriptive commentaries that contained primary information on a tool. We excluded records that (1) referred to mHealth only in general terms without identifying a specific tool; (2) addressed other outbreaks or diseases without reference to the 2014–2015 EVD epidemic; (3) were purely opinion pieces, editorials, or news items with no original description of a tool; (4) concerned non-mobile information technology solutions only (e.g., desktop-only software, call-center-only services without a mobile application component); or (5) were duplicates. Where a tool was described in several records, these were grouped under a single tool entry, and the most informative record was used as the primary source, with additional records used to complete missing data. Study selection All retrieved records were exported to a reference manager and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then retrieved and independently assessed by the same two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved by discussion and, when consensus could not be reached, by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the title-and-abstract stage was quantified using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960): κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the proportion of agreement expected by chance. Values above 0.60 were interpreted as substantial agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977). The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram, indicating the number of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons), and included. Data extraction A standardized data extraction form was developed in Microsoft Excel, piloted on a random sample of five included records, and refined to resolve ambiguities. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and discrepancies were reconciled through consensus. For each tool we recorded: name, developer or implementing organization, type of developer (government, nongovernmental organization, academic institution, private sector, or international agency), country or countries of deployment, publication type and year, development stage (concept or prototype, pilot, or field deployment), platform and hardware (e.g., Android, iOS, basic feature phone with SMS/USSD, tablet), connectivity requirements (online, offline-capable with synchronization), open-source status, and target users (e.g., health workers, laboratory staff, contact tracers, community members, the general public). The principal data of interest were the functionalities of each tool. Based on the epidemiological workflow of EVD response (WHO, 2014) and previous typologies of mHealth functions (Labrique et al., 2013), we predefined four core functionalities: 1. Surveillance: collection, transmission, or analysis of data on suspected, probable, or confirmed cases and deaths, including event-based reporting, alert generation, and mapping. 2. Case management: support for clinical care of patients, including registration, triage, symptom assessment, monitoring of clinical progress, treatment documentation, and patient tracking within treatment facilities. 3. Neural Chinese Word Segmentation with Dictionary Knowledge Junxin Liu1 , Fangzhao Wu2 , Chuhan Wu1 , Yongfeng Huang1, and Xing Xie2 Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China {ljx16,wuch15}@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn yfhuang@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn 2 Microsoft Resesrch Asia, Beijing, China {fangzwu,Xing.Xie}@microsoft.com Abstract. Chinese word segmentation (CWS) is an important task for Chinese NLP. Recently, many neural network based methods have been proposed for CWS. However, these methods require a large number of labeled sentences for model training, and usually cannot utilize the useful information in Chinese dictionary. In this paper, we propose two methods to exploit the dictionary information for CWS. The first one is based on pseudo labeled data generation, and the second one is based on multi-task learning. The experimental results on two benchmark datasets validate that our approach can effectively improve the performance of Chinese word segmentation, especially when training data is insufficient. Keywords: Chinese word segmentation · Dictionary · Neural network. 1 Introduction Different from English texts, in Chinese texts there is no explicit delimiters such as whitespace to separate words. Thus, Chinese word segmentation (CWS) is an important task for Chinese natural language processing [3,17], and an essential step for many downstream tasks such as POS tagging [20], named entity recognition [9], dependency parsing [2,15] and so on. Since a Chinese sentence is usually a sequence of Chinese characters, Chinese word segmentation is usually modeled as a sequence labeling problem [13,17]. Many sequence modeling methods such as hidden Markov model (HMM) [5] and conditional random field (CRF) [6] have been applied to the CWS task. A core problem in these sequence modeling based CWS methods is building the feature vector for each character in sentences. In traditional CWS methods these character features are constructed via manual feature engineering [10,19]. These handcrafted features need a large amount of domain knowledge to design, and the size of these features is usually very large [3]. In recent years, many neural network based methods have been proposed for CWS [3,16,17,20]. For example, Peng et al. [11] proposed to use Long Short-Term Memory Neural Network (LSTM) to learn the character representations for CWS and use CRF to jointly decode the labels. However, these neural network based methods usually rely on a large number of labeled sentences. For words which are scarce or absent in training data, these methods are very difficult to correctly segment the sentences that contain these words [17]. Since these words are in large quantity, it is very expensive and even unpractical to improve the coverage of these words via annotating more sentences. Luckily, many of these words are well defined in existing Chinese dictionaries. Thus, Chinese dictionaries have the potential to improve the performance of neural network based CWS methods and reduce the dependence on labeled data [17]. In this paper we propose to incorporate the dictionary information into neural network based CWS approach in an end-to-end manner without any feature engineering. More specifically, we propose two methods to incorporate the dictionary information for CWS. The first one is based on pseudo labeled data generation, where we build pseudo labeled sentences by randomly sampling words from Chinese dictionaries. The second one is based on multi-task learning. In this method we introduce another task named Chinese word classification (i.e., classifying a sequence of Chinese characters based on whether they can form a Chinese word), and jointly train this task with CWS by sharing the parameters of neural networks. We conducted extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets. The experimental results validate that our methods can effectively improve the performance of CWS, especially when training data is insufficient. 2 Related Work In recent years, many neural network based methods have been proposed for Chinese word segmentation [3,16,17,20]. Most of these methods model CWS as a sequence labeling task [3,17]. The core difference between these methods mainly lies in how they learn the contextual feature representation for each character in sentence. For example, Zheng et al. [20] proposed to use multi-layer perceptrons to learn feature representations of characters from a fixed window. Chen et al. [3] used LSTM to capture global contextual information. They also explicitly captured the local context by combining the embedding of current character with the embeddings of neighbouring characters as the input of LSTM. In [11], LSTM is used to learn character representations and CRF is used to jointly decode the labels. These methods rely on a large number of labeled sentences to train CWS models and cannot exploit the useful information in Chinese dictionaries [17]. Since there are massive Chinese words which are scarce or absent in the labeled sentences, these neural CWS methods usually have difficulty in correctly segmenting sentences containing these words [17]. Recently, incorporating the dictionary information into neural Chinese word segmentation has attracted increasing attentions [14,17]. For example, Yang et al. [14] proposed to incorporate external information such as punctuation, automatic segmentation and POS data into neural CWS via pretraining. However, the useful information in Chinese dictionaries is not considered in their method. Zhang et al. [17] proposed to incorporate the dictionary information into an LSTM based neural CWS method via feature engineering. They used several handcrafted templates to build an additional feature vector for each character using the dictionary and the neighbouring characters. These additional feature vectors are fed to another LSTM network to learn additional character representations. However, designing these handcrafted feature templates needs a lot of domain knowledge. In addition, more model parameters are introduced in their method, making it more difficult to train neural CWS model especially when training data is insufficient. Different from [17], our method to incorporate dictionary information into neural CWS can be trained in an end-to-end manner and does not need manual feature engineering. Experimental results show that our approach can achieve better performance than the method in [17]. 3 Our Approach In this section we first present the basic neural architecture for Chinese word segmentation used in our approach. Then, we introduce our methods of incorporating dictionary information for neural CWS. 3.1 Basic Neural Architecture Following many previous works [3,17], in this paper we model Chinese word segmentation as a character-level sequence labeling problem. For each character in a sentence, our model will assign one of the tags in a predefined tag set to it, indicating its position in a word. We use the BMES tagging scheme, where B, M and E mean the beginning, middle and end position in the word, and S represents single character word. The basic neural architecture for CWS used in our approach is CNN-CRF. This neural architecture contains three main layers. The first layer is the character embedding layer. In this layer, the input sentence is converted to a sequence of vectors. Previous studies show that local context information is important for Chinese word segmentation [1,14]. In addition, many researchers have shown that CNN is effective in capturing local context information [7,12,18]. Cross-Domain Labeled LDA for Cross-Domain Text Classification Baoyu Jing∗ 1 , Chenwei Lu† 1 , Deqing Wang† 2 , Fuzhen Zhuang‡§ , and Cheng Niu¶ ∗ School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA † School of Computer Science and Engineering, Beihang University, Beijing, China ‡ Key Lab of Intelligent Information Processing of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) Institute of Computing Technology, CAS, Beijing, China § University of Chinese Academy of Science, Beijing, China ¶ Pattern Recognition Center, WeChat Search Application Department, Tencent, China Email: byjing@cs.cmu.edu, {luchenwei, dqwang}@buaa.edu.cn, zhuangfuzhen@ict.ac.cn, niucheng@tencent.com Abstract—Cross-domain text classification aims at building a classifier for a target domain which leverages data from both source and target domain. One promising idea is to minimize the feature distribution differences of the two domains. Most existing studies explicitly minimize such differences by an exact alignment mechanism (aligning features by one-to-one feature alignment, projection matrix etc.). Such exact alignment, however, will restrict models’ learning ability and will further impair models’ performance on classification tasks when the semantic distributions of different domains are very different. To address this problem, we propose a novel group alignment which aligns the semantics at group level. In addition, to help the model learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups, we also propose a partial supervision for model’s learning in source domain. To this end, we embed the group alignment and a partial supervision into a cross-domain topic model, and propose a Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA). On the standard 20Newsgroup and Reuters dataset, extensive quantitative (classification, perplexity etc.) and qualitative (topic detection) experiments are conducted to show the effectiveness of the proposed group alignment and partial supervision. Keywords-Cross Domain Text Classification, Topic Modeling, Group Alignment, Partial Supervision I. I NTRODUCTION Cross-domain text classification considers the setting that data distributions in source domain and target domain are different but related. In such a scenario, the performance of traditional classification algorithms, which are built on the assumption that the source and target datasets are drawn from the same distribution [22], will be deteriorated [1], [8], [19]. Therefore, many cross-domain learning methods are proposed, such as instance-based methods [15], [16], [20], cotraining [6], [28], kernel methods [9], [30] and representation learning [1], [2], [7], [10], [11], [13], [17], [19], [23], [27], [29], [31], [32], [34], [37]. Most existing representation learning models try to align features of the two domains through an exact alignment, which aligns features of the two domains by a shared feature space [7], [10], [13], [17], [27], [29], [31], one-to-one 1 Equal contribution. 2 Corresponding author. topic alignment [1], [23], [32], or a projection matrix [19]. Generally, this exact alignment mechanism assumes that the semantics of the target domain can be directly decomposed by the semantics of the target domain. However, such assumption is not always promised to be true in the real-world data because the numbers and contents of semantics in two domains are always very different. For example, the source domain might be comprised of two topics (graphics and hockey), and the target domain might consist of three topics (software, commands, and baseball). The topics in the above example can be clustered into two groups: computers (graphics, software, commands) and recreation (hockey, baseball). It is much more intuitive to align topics through topic groups (computers and recreation) rather than directly align them at topic level. Motivated by this intuition, we propose a novel group alignment mechanism. Topic groups can be defined in many ways: cluster of topics, document labels etc. For simplicity, we define groups through document labels. The group alignment has two major advantages: 1) Topic groups are guaranteed to exist in both source and target domains if they are predefined by document labels, thus aligning topics by such groups are always feasible. 2) The numbers of topics within different topic groups are allowed to be different, and thus model’s representation flexibility for different domains might be improved. Additionally, partial supervision for the learning in source domain has been proven to help the learning in target domain [1]. Therefore, to help the model learn better topic groups and topics within each group, we propose a partial supervision for topic learning in source domain. To this end, we propose a Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model for cross-domain text classification which is equipped with a novel group alignment and a partial supervision. The experiment results on the standard 20Newsgroup and Reuters datasets show that CDL-LDA can achieve higher classification accuracies and lower perplexities than the state-of-the-art models. Besides, CDL-LDA can also detect meaningful topic groups and topics. Additionally, parameter analysis is also conducted to show further characteristics of the model. II. R ELATED W ORK A. Cross-Domain Learning Cross-domain classification or transductive classification [22] has attracted much attention in recent years. Generally, there are four types of methods: instance re-weighting methods [15], [16], [20], co-training methods [6], [28], kernel methods [9], [30], and feature representation based methods [1], [2], [4], [7], [10], [11], [13], [17], [21], [23], [24], [27], [29], [31], [32], [34], [37]. A comprehensive survey on transfer learning and transductive classification can be found in reference [22]. In this paper, we mainly focus on methods based on high-level semantic features [1], [7], [10], [11], [13], [17], [23], [27], [29], [31], [34]. Most popular methods for extracting high-level semantic features include matrix factorization, distance metric learning, deep learning methods, and topic modeling methods. For example, Gupta et al [13] propose a shared nonnegative matrix factorization (JSNMF) to jointly extract domain-independent and domain-dependent bases. Cross-Domain Metric Learning (CDML) [29] transfers knowledge by finding a shared Mahalanobis distance across domains. As for deep learning methods, one set of models are based on auto-encoders. Glorot et al [11] employ a Stacked Denoising Auto-encoder (SDA) to learn the high-level features across different domains in an unsupervised fashion. Chen et al [7] modify SDA by using linear denoisers and propose marginalized SDA (mSDA). Jiang et al [17] and Wei et al [31] modify mSDA by using 2,1 norm for objective function and introducing maximum mean discrepancy into mSDA. Zhou et al [35] propose a Bi-Transferring Deep Neural Networks (BTDNNs) in which different domains have different decoders. Another set of models are based on domainadversarial neural networks. Ganin et al [10] propose a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN) which builds a label predictor and a domain classifier on a feedforward neural network. Recently, Shen et al [27] replace domain discriminator of DANN by Wasserstein distance [26] and propose Adversarial Representation for Domain Adaptation (ARDA). Generally, all these methods project different domains into different regions of a shared feature space, and directly minimize the distance between these regions. However, when the semantics of two domains are very different, such direct minimization might hurt models’ representation flexibility. B. Cross-Domain Topic Models One idea of cross-domain topic modeling methods is to divide topics into common topics and specific topics to capture shared semantics and domain specific semantics respectively [1], [19], [23], [34], [38]. To perform text classification, one can choose to use either common topic features or both common and specific topic features. However, common topic features alone might not provide enough information for classification, thus different topic alignment methods are proposed. For example, Cross-collection mixture model (CCMix) [34] and Cross-Collection Latent Dirichlet Allocation (CCLDA) [23] extends Probabilistic Latent Semantic Analysis (PLSA) [14] and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) [3] into cross-collection topic models respectively, and they align specific topics by an one-to-one alignment. Partially supervised CCLDA (PSCCLDA) [1] extends CCLDA into a partially supervised model by incorporating a logistic regression in the source domain at the training process. Topic Correlation Analysis (TCA) [19] assumes that the specific topics of the target domain can be decomposed by the specific topics of the source domain, and thus aligns specific topics across different domains by a projection matrix. Recently, Zuo et al [38] propose a fine-grained Cross-collection Autolabeled MaxEnt-LDA (CAMEL), which further divides topics into opinions and aspects while it still employs an one-to-one topic alignment to align specific topics. Here xi and yi are the feature vector and the label of the i-th example in the source domain Ds respectively, and xti is the feature vector of the i-th example in the target domain Dt . Let Y be the predefined set of document labels, then our task is to train a classifier for the target domain: f t : Dt → Y. B. Overview of Cross-Domain Labeled LDA Cross-domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) is a cross-domain topic model which divides topics into common topics and specific topics to model shared semantics across domains and domain dependent semantics respectively. To perform text classification, it is necessary to align specific topics across domains. However, different from exact alignment (one-to-one topic alignment, projection matrix etc.) adopted by previous studies [1], [19], [23], [34], [38], which directly performs topic alignment at topic level, we propose a novel group alignment which performs topic alignment at topic group level. To be more specific, common topics and specific topics are firstly divided into different groups. Then within each domain, common topics and specific topics of the same group are aligned. Finally, across domains, specific topics of the same topic group are aligned through common topics in this topic group. We will elaborate group alignment in section III-D. In addition to group alignment, we also propose a partial supervision to explicitly incorporate ground truth topic group information in the source domain, which can help the model learn better topic features for classification. To do so, instead of sampling topic group labels for words in source domain, the model directly assign ground truth topic group labels of the words at training time. We will discuss more about the partial supervision in section III-E. Additionally, there are several basic assumptions in CDLLDA. Empirical software engineering relies on observable artifacts such as source code, version histories, and defect reports to derive claims about how software is built and maintained. Such claims are rarely confined to the data from which they were drawn. A technique that performs well on a set of open-source projects is commonly presented as a general solution, and a result observed in one period is implicitly assumed to hold in the next. This assumption is seldom tested, even though software projects change continuously through new features, shifting teams, refactoring, and evolving development practices. The question this article asks is whether a researcher's conclusions will still hold a year from now for the same software projects. There are reasons to doubt that they will. Menzies and Shepperd (2012) argued that many findings in software analytics are unstable, and that "conclusion instability" is a central obstacle to building a cumulative body of knowledge. Subsequent work has shown that conclusions often vary across data sets, learners, and experimental configurations (Menzies et al. 2013; Shepperd et al. 2014; Tantithamthavorn et al. 2016). Findings that appear robust on one collection of projects may weaken or reverse on another. Most of this work examines variation across space, that is, across projects, data sets, or methods. Far less attention has been paid to variation across time, even though software evolves and any practical use of a prediction model is necessarily temporal. Defect prediction is a particularly informative setting in which to study this problem. It has been an active research area for more than two decades, with the goal of identifying files, modules, or changes likely to contain defects so that limited quality-assurance effort can be directed effectively (Zimmermann et al. 2009; Hall et al. 2012). A large body of work proposes new learners, features, and transfer strategies, and reports improvements over prior approaches. Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), in which a model trained on one or more source projects predicts defects in a different target project, has received particular attention because it addresses the common situation where a project lacks sufficient historical data to train its own model (Turhan et al. 2009; Zimmermann et al. 2009; Nam et al. 2013). Comparative studies have identified approaches that appear to outperform others (Herbold et al. 2018; Hosseini et al. 2019), and such rankings are routinely taken as guidance for both researchers and practitioners. However, the way defect prediction models are usually evaluated can obscure temporal instability. Standard protocols, including k-fold cross-validation and random train/test splits, ignore the chronological order of the data. They allow models to be trained on instances from the future of the instances being predicted, a form of information leakage that no practitioner could replicate in deployment (Tan et al. 2015; Jimenez et al. 2019). In addition, defect labels are often derived with delay, since a defect may be discovered long after the code that introduced it. Evaluations that disregard this lag can overstate performance. Even when time is respected, evaluations typically report a single aggregate figure computed over a whole history. A single number hides how performance fluctuates between releases or periods, so a method that looks superior on average may be superior only in some intervals. Aggregation therefore masks exactly the temporal behavior on which a practitioner's decision to adopt a model depends. This gap matters for several reasons. First, a defect predictor is deployed on future releases, so the relevant evidence is its performance on data that postdate its training. Second, if the ranking of techniques changes from one release to the next, a study that selects the "best" approach from one evaluation window cannot support a claim that this approach will remain best. Third, the metrics used to quantify performance may themselves behave differently over time. Defect-prone ratios shift between releases, and metrics such as F-Score are sensitive to class imbalance, whereas the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is more robust to it (Yao and Shepperd 2020; Chicco and Jurman 2020). Reporting only one metric may thus provide an incomplete view of stability. In this article, we empirically investigate the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models. We adopt a time-aware evaluation approach in which models are trained only on data available in the past and are evaluated only on data from the future. Instead of one aggregate result, we examine performance as a function of the evaluation period, and we compare how conclusions drawn in one period compare with those drawn in subsequent periods. We measure performance with three complementary indicators: F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and MCC. We then ask whether the relative performance of CPDP approaches, and the conclusions one would draw about them, remain consistent as the evaluation window moves forward in time. Our study is guided by the following research questions: RQ1: How does the performance of cross-project defect prediction models vary across time periods? We quantify the variability of F-Score, AUC, and MCC when the same models are evaluated on successive periods of the same projects. RQ2: Are conclusions about the relative performance of defect prediction approaches stable over time? We examine whether the ranking of approaches, and the statistical significance of differences between them, persist across evaluation periods or change from one period to the next. RQ3: How sensitive is conclusion stability to the choice of performance metric? We compare the three metrics to determine whether instability is an artifact of a particular measure or a more general phenomenon. This work makes the following contributions. First, we present, to our knowledge, one of the first systematic investigations of time-based conclusion stability in cross-project defect prediction, shifting the focus from stability across data sets to stability across time for the same projects. Second, we provide a time-aware evaluation procedure in which training uses only past data and testing uses only future data, avoiding the leakage inherent in conventional cross-validation and allowing performance to be tracked period by period. Third, we show empirically that the performance of defect predictors, in terms of F-Score, AUC, and MCC, varies depending on the period evaluated, and that conclusions drawn in one period are frequently not reproduced in another. Fourth, we show that the next release of a product, particularly one that differs substantially from its predecessor, can drastically alter prediction performance. Finally, we offer practical guidance: in the absence of evidence of conclusion stability, researchers should restrict claims about defect prediction performance to the contexts in which they were evaluated, and should report results over multiple time periods rather than as a single aggregate. We also make our evaluation scripts and data available to support replication and extension. The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on defect prediction, cross-project transfer, and conclusion stability. Section 3 describes the data, the prediction approaches, and our time-aware evaluation design. Section 4 presents results for each research question. Section 5 discusses implications and threats to validity, and Section 6 concludes. We examine the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) through three research questions. RQ1: How much does the performance of CPDP models, measured by F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), vary across successive evaluation periods? RQ2: Do comparative conclusions, such as "learner A outperforms learner B", remain consistent across periods? RQ3: Is the magnitude of change between consecutive releases associated with the change in predictive performance? We studied 10 open-source Java projects from the Apache Software Foundation (e.g., Ant, Camel, Cassandra, Lucene, POI, and Synapse) that satisfy four criteria: (i) at least five tagged releases, (ii) a public issue tracker with bug reports linked to commits, (iii) at least 100 classes per release, and (iv) a release history of at least three years. This yielded 74 releases (4–12 per project) published between 2008 and 2020, containing 61,204 class-level instances in total. Release dates were taken from version-control tags and verified against project archives. For each class in each release we computed 20 static product metrics, including the Chidamber–Kemerer suite, size and complexity measures, and coupling and cohesion indicators (Chidamber & Kemerer, 1994; Jureczko & Madeyski, 2010). Metrics were extracted using the same tool version across all releases to prevent measurement drift. Defect labels were derived with the SZZ algorithm (Śliwerski et al., 2005). Bug-fixing commits were identified through issue identifiers in commit messages, restricted to issues typed as "Bug", and mapped to the bug-introducing changes of the files they modify. A class was labeled defective if it was modified by a bug-fixing commit within 180 days after the release date and the corresponding change was traceable to code present in that release. SZZ is known to introduce noise (da Costa et al., 2017), so we excluded fixes for issues reopened more than once and fixes touching more than 20 files, since these are likely to be tangled changes. The proportion of defective classes ranged from 6% to 41% per release (median 17%). Standard k-fold cross-validation and random train/test splits permit training on data that postdate the test data, which inflates estimates and obscures temporal effects (Tan et al., 2015; Jimenez et al., 2019). We therefore adopted a strictly chronological protocol. Every release r of every project p served once as a test set. The training set consisted only of instances from releases of other projects (the cross-project condition; Zimmermann et al., 2009) satisfying two conditions. First, the release date plus the 180-day labeling window precedes the release date of r. Second, the defect labels used for training were recomputed using only bug-fix information available at that cut-off. This removes both look-ahead in the instances and look-ahead in the labels, a subtle form of leakage that occurs when labels are collected after the prediction date (Herbold et al., 2018). Releases of project p itself never entered training, so the setup is a pure CPDP scenario. To define evaluation periods, we grouped test releases into non-overlapping calendar half-years, yielding 22 periods between 2009 and 2020, of which 17 contained at least three test releases. We restricted the analysis to those 17 periods so that per-period summaries were not dominated by a single release. Performance within a period was summarized by the median across its test releases. As a reference condition, we also ran a time-agnostic CPDP evaluation in which, for each test release, the training set comprised all releases of other projects regardless of date. This allowed us to quantify how much the ignoring of temporal ordering changes conclusions. We selected four learners that are widely used in the defect-prediction literature (Hall et al., 2012; Ghotra et al., 2015): logistic regression (LR), naïve Bayes (NB), random forest (RF; Breiman, 2001) with 100 trees, and a gradient-boosted decision tree ensemble (GBT). Beyond these, we included a CPDP-specific approach, the nearest-neighbor relevancy filter of Turhan et al. (2009), applied before fitting LR (NN-LR). All metrics were log-transformed (log(x+1)). Because metric distributions differ strongly between projects, features were z-standardized using training-set statistics only (Zimmermann et al., 2009; Herbold et al., 2018). Class imbalance was handled by class-weighting in the loss function rather than resampling, which keeps the test distribution untouched and avoids synthetic instances. Hyperparameters were kept at library defaults to isolate temporal effects from tuning variability. Stochastic learners (RF, GBT) were repeated 30 times per test release with different random seeds, and the median over runs was used. All models used a fixed probability threshold of 0.5 for the threshold-dependent metrics. We report three complementary measures. The F-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall for the defective class. AUC measures threshold-independent ranking performance (Lessmann et al., 2008). The extraction of local features from images has been a fundamental problem in computer vision for several decades (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). Local features are used to describe small regions of an image, and they have numerous applications in various computer vision tasks such as object recognition (Lowe, 2004), image matching (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005), and 3D reconstruction (Szeliski, 2010). The precise location of these features is crucial in many applications, particularly in 3D reconstruction problems where the accuracy of the features directly affects the quality of the reconstructed model (Fua, 1997). Over the years, various methods have been proposed to extract local features, ranging from handcrafted methods to deep-learning-based approaches. Initially, local features were extracted using handcrafted methods, which relied on carefully designed algorithms to detect and describe regions of interest in an image (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). These methods, such as the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) (Lowe, 2004) and the Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) (Bay et al., 2008), were widely used in various computer vision applications. However, handcrafted methods have several limitations, including their sensitivity to affine transformations and their inability to capture complex patterns in images (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). Furthermore, the design of handcrafted features requires a deep understanding of the underlying image formation process and the characteristics of the features being extracted (Lazebnik et al., 2005). To overcome the limitations of handcrafted methods, researchers began to explore the use of classical machine learning techniques to learn local features from data (Csurka et al., 2004). These methods, such as the Bag-of-Words (BoW) model (Sivic & Zisserman, 2003), used machine learning algorithms to learn a dictionary of visual words from a set of training images. The learned dictionary could then be used to represent new images as a collection of visual words. However, these methods had limited success in computer vision tasks, particularly in applications that required precise feature localization (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). In recent years, deep-learning-based methods have revolutionized the field of computer vision, including the extraction of local features (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Deep neural networks, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (LeCun et al., 1998), have been used to learn local features from large datasets of images. These methods, such as the DeepDesc (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) and the LIFT (Yi et al., 2016), have shown impressive performance in various computer vision tasks, including object recognition and image matching. However, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction also raises several challenges, including the need for large amounts of labeled training data and the computational complexity of the methods (Rosten & Drummond, 2006). The evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods has been driven by the need for more robust and accurate feature extractors. However, despite the significant progress made in this area, there is still a need for a comprehensive review of the existing methods and their performance on various benchmarks. Furthermore, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction raises several questions, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function on the performance of the method. In this paper, we aim to address these questions and provide a comprehensive overview of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods. Our research question is: How have local features evolved from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods, and what are the key factors that affect their performance in various computer vision tasks? To answer this question, we will first review the existing literature on handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods for local feature extraction. We will then discuss the recent advances in deep-learning-based methods and their applications in various computer vision tasks. Finally, we will evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and discuss the challenges and limitations of these methods. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive review of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods. Secondly, we discuss the key factors that affect the performance of local feature extractors, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function. Finally, we evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and provide insights into the challenges and limitations of these methods. Our paper will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of computer vision, and will help to advance the state-of-the-art in local feature extraction and related applications. The primary objective of this study was to compare the performance of handcrafted and deep-learning-based local features in the context of 3D reconstruction problems. To achieve this, we employed a comprehensive framework that involved the evaluation of various local feature extraction methods on several benchmark datasets. Our investigation commenced with the assessment of handcrafted methods, which have been extensively used in computer vision applications (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). These methods rely on manually designed algorithms to detect and describe local features, such as corners, edges, and blobs. We implemented and evaluated several handcrafted methods, including the Harris corner detector (Harris & Stephens, 1988), the scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) (Lowe, 1999), and the speeded-up robust features (SURF) (Bay et al., 2008). To quantify the performance of these handcrafted methods, we utilized the widely-used benchmark datasets, such as the Oxford Affine dataset (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005) and the INRIA Holidays dataset (Jégou et al., 2008). These datasets provide a comprehensive evaluation of local feature extraction methods under various conditions, including changes in viewpoint, illumination, and affine transformations. We computed the repeatability and matching scores for each method, as proposed by Mikolajczyk and Schmid (2005), to assess their performance. The repeatability score measures the proportion of correctly matched features between two images, while the matching score evaluates the number of correct matches between the detected features. In addition to handcrafted methods, we also investigated the performance of classical machine learning-based methods, such as the random forest-based feature extraction method (Lepetit et al., 2006). These methods leverage machine learning algorithms to learn the feature extraction process from a set of labeled training data. We trained a random forest classifier on a dataset of labeled features, where each feature was described using a set of handcrafted descriptors, such as SIFT and SURF. The trained model was then used to extract features from the benchmark datasets, and the performance was evaluated using the same metrics as the handcrafted methods. More recently, deep-learning-based methods have gained significant attention in the field of computer vision, due to their ability to learn complex patterns and features from large datasets (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). We evaluated several deep-learning-based local feature extraction methods, including the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based method (Simo-Serra et al., 2015) and the recurrent neural network (RNN)-based method (Liu et al., 2017). These methods leverage the strengths of deep learning architectures to learn robust and discriminative features from images. We trained the deep-learning models on large datasets, such as the ImageNet dataset (Russakovsky et al., 2015), and fine-tuned them on the benchmark datasets to adapt to the specific task of local feature extraction. To evaluate the performance of the deep-learning-based methods, we utilized the same benchmark datasets and metrics as the handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods. We also employed additional metrics, such as the feature detection accuracy and the descriptor matching accuracy, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the methods. The feature detection accuracy measures the proportion of correctly detected features, while the descriptor matching accuracy evaluates the number of correct matches between the detected features. Statistical analysis was performed to compare the performance of the different methods. We used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the repeatability and matching scores of the handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods, as the data did not follow a normal distribution. For the deep-learning-based methods, we used the paired t-test to compare the feature detection accuracy and descriptor matching accuracy, as the data followed a normal distribution. The statistical analysis was performed using the R software package (R Core Team, 2020), and the results were considered significant at a p-value of 0.05. In terms of data, we utilized several benchmark datasets to evaluate the performance of the local feature extraction methods. The Oxford Affine dataset (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005) consists of 8 sequences of images, each with 6 images, captured under various conditions, including changes in viewpoint, illumination, and affine transformations. The INRIA Holidays dataset (Jégou et al., 2008) consists of 500 images of various scenes, including buildings, landscapes, and objects. The ImageNet dataset (Russakovsky et al., 2015) consists of over 14 million images, annotated with object labels and bounding boxes. The design of our study involved a comprehensive evaluation of various local feature extraction methods, including handcrafted, classical machine learning-based, and deep-learning-based methods. We employed a range of benchmark datasets and metrics to provide a thorough evaluation of the methods. The procedures involved implementing and evaluating each method, as well as performing statistical analysis to compare their performance. The results of our study provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of each method, and can be used to inform the development of more robust and efficient local feature extraction methods for computer vision applications. Overall, our study demonstrates the importance of evaluating and comparing different local feature extraction methods, and highlights the potential benefits of using deep-learning-based methods for this task. The results of our study can be used to inform the development of more robust and efficient computer vision systems, and can be applied to a range of applications, including 3D reconstruction, object recognition, and image matching. Further research is needed to continue improving the performance of local feature extraction methods, and to explore new applications of these methods in computer vision and related fields.
