Our results indicate that the evaluated cross-project defect prediction approaches do not have perfect stability in their conclusions and time-travel produces false estimates of performance. Therefore, while conducting defect prediction studies, researchers should not engage in time-travel and also avoid over generalizing their conclusions, but instead couch the claims of performance within the contexts of evaluation. To summarize, the main contributions of this paper are: – A methodology for time-aware evaluation of defect prediction approaches; – A case study of conclusion stability in cross-project defect prediction with respect to time; – A comparison of the performance rankings of five cross-project defect prediction approaches using time-aware evaluation with performance of time agnostic evaluation; – Guidelines for researchers and practitioners for the time-aware evaluation of defect prediction models. 2 Related Work Software defect prediction has a plethora of approaches with the earliest proposals dating back to the 1990s where linear regression models based on Chidamber and Kemerer (CK) metrics (Chidamber and Kemerer, 1994) were used to determine the fault proneness of classes (Basili et al., 1996). A number of metrics have been used since then as indicators of software quality such as previous defects (Zimmermann et al., 2007), process metrics (Hassan, 2009; Rahman and Devanbu, 2013), and churn metrics (Nagappan and Ball, 2005). Within project defect prediction (WPDP) uses data from the same project for training and testing whereas in cross project defect prediction (CPDP), training and testing data comes from different projects. Several approaches for both WPDP (Turhan et al., 2009; Basili et al., 1996) and CPDP Zimmermann et al. (2009); Peters et al. (2013); Nam et al. (2013) are available in the literature. There have also been benchmark studies on both types of defect prediction (D’Ambros et al., 2012; Herbold et al., 2018). WPDP approaches have better performance while CPDP approaches are likely transferable to other projects with certain limitations (Zhang et al., 2014). Herbold (2017b) conducted a systematic mapping of defect prediction literature with a focus on cross project defect prediction approaches. They identified that the results of studies are not comparable due to the lack of use of common data sets and experimental setups. In their follow up work, Herbold et al. (2018) replicated 24 defect prediction approaches using 5 publicly available data sets and multiple learners. Their goal was to benchmark the defect prediction approaches using common data sets and metrics so that state-of-the-art approaches can be ranked according to their performance using Area under Curve (AUC), F-Score, G-measure, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) metrics. Jureczko (Jureczko and Madeyski, 2010) is one of the well-known defect prediction data sets which was also used in the benchmarking study. It originally contains open-source, proprietary and academic projects but Herbold et al. (2018) used only 62 versions of several open-source and academic projects. Prior to this paper, conclusion stability has been analyzed by several researchers. Lessmann et al. (2008) and Menzies et al. (2010) investigated the effect of classifiers, trained using same data, on the quality of prediction models whereas Ekanayake et al. (2012, 2009) investigated the effect of data set and concept drift respectively. Lessmann et al. (2008) found statistically significant difference among the performance of two classifiers and Menzies et al. (2011) observed inconsistent conclusions for different clusters within the same data. Inspired by this prior work, another set of experiments were conducted by D’Ambros et al. (2012) to rank approaches across several data sets following a statistically sound methodology. McIntosh and Kamei (2017) investigated the time-based conclusions of just-in-time defect prediction models and found that their descriminatory power can change over time. In more recent work, Tantithamthavorn et al. (2018) concluded that parameter optimization can significantly impact the performance stability, and ranking of defect prediction models. This view is similar to Menzies’ view who argued that a learner tuned to a particular evaluation criterion, performs best for that criterion, hence it shall be critically chosen (Menzies et al., 2010). Tantithamthavorn et al. (2015) in their work show that issue report mislabelling significantly impacts the defect prediction models. In a later comparison study, Tantithamthavorn et al. (2017) concluded that the choice of model validation technique for defect prediction models can also affect performance results. Tan et al. (2015) identified that cross-validation produces false precision results for change classifications and addressed the problem using time-sensitive and online change classifications. Their emphasis is on removing imbalances in data using re-sampling techniques for better change classifications. Turhan (2012) also studied the conclusion instability caused due to data set shift but their focus was not specific to defect prediction, rather on software engineering prediction models in general. Similarly Krishna and Menzies (2018) show that there can be large differences in conclusions depending on different source data sets and suggest mitigating the problem with the help of bellwethers. Universities are among the most important producers of health research and health technologies. In the United Kingdom (UK), higher education institutions conduct a large share of publicly funded biomedical research and contribute to the discovery of many new medicines, diagnostics, and vaccines [1,2]. Their choices about what research to pursue, how to manage the resulting intellectual property, and how to disseminate findings therefore shape not only the scientific frontier but also who ultimately benefits from it. Because universities are publicly funded, charitable in purpose, and committed to the public good, they bear a particular responsibility to ensure that the benefits of their research reach the people with the greatest need, including those in low-income settings. That need is poorly matched by the current distribution of research effort. The 10/90 gap, the observation that only about 10% of global health research spending addresses conditions responsible for 90% of the global disease burden, has been described for more than two decades [3,4]. Neglected diseases (NDs), including neglected tropical diseases, malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS, disproportionately affect the poorest populations, yet attract little commercial investment because affected patients cannot generate sufficient market returns [5,6]. Analyses of pharmaceutical development pipelines have repeatedly found that a very small proportion of new chemical entities are directed at these diseases [7,8]. Public and philanthropic funders and product development partnerships have partly filled this gap [9], and the G-FINDER survey documents annual global investment in neglected disease research and development [10]. Even so, the proportion of research addressing the health problems of low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs) remains modest relative to burden. Universities, as recipients of public and charitable funding, are central to whether this imbalance is corrected or perpetuated, yet little is known about how much of their research addresses these needs or how concentrated such activity is across institutions. Equitable health outcomes depend on more than the direction of research; they also depend on access to its outputs. Two mechanisms are especially relevant to universities. The first is the licensing of intellectual property. Medical discoveries made in universities are frequently patented and licensed exclusively to a single company, which can then set prices without competition [11,12]. Exclusive licensing may be justified when it is necessary to attract the investment required for development, but it can produce high prices and restrict supply in settings where patients and health systems cannot pay [13]. Well-known examples, such as the antiretroviral stavudine developed at Yale University and licensed to Bristol-Myers Squibb, illustrate how university licensing decisions can affect access to essential medicines in low-income countries, and how student and public pressure may bring about change [14]. In response, advocacy groups and university alumni and student organizations have promoted "global access" or "equitable access" licensing, in which licensees commit to affordability, non-exclusive licensing for use in low-resource settings, or humanitarian carve-outs [15,16]. The Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies, endorsed by a number of North American and European institutions, and the Nine Points to Consider in Licensing University Technology, set out expectations for socially responsible licensing [17,18]. Universities Allied for Essential Medicines (UAEM) has further advocated for such policies and has produced a university report card in the United States and Canada [19]. However, the extent to which UK universities have adopted comparable policies, and how their licensing practices operate in practice, has not been systematically described. The second mechanism is the publication of research findings. Subscription-based publishing makes much of the scientific literature inaccessible to researchers, clinicians, and policy-makers in resource-poor settings, where library budgets are limited, even with initiatives such as HINARI that provide reduced-cost or free access to selected institutions [20,21]. Open access (OA) publishing, whether through publication in OA journals ("gold" route) or deposit of manuscripts in repositories ("green" route), aims to remove these barriers [22]. The permissive licence under which an article is published also matters: Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY) licensing allows unrestricted reuse, including text and data mining, translation, and redistribution, which are valuable for research and for health programmes in LLMICs [23]. In the UK, funder mandates from Research Councils UK, the Wellcome Trust, and other charities, together with the Finch Report and the Higher Education Funding Council for England's OA requirement for the post-2014 Research Excellence Framework, have substantially changed the publishing environment [24–26]. Universities are the institutions that must implement these mandates through policies, repositories, and article-processing-charge funds, and their approaches have varied [27]. Whether the resulting proportion of health research that is freely available, and available under truly open licences, is high across institutions is not well documented. Taken together, these three domains (research priorities, intellectual property management, and publication practices) represent the principal levers through which universities can contribute to global health equity. Previous work has examined each in isolation, typically at the level of funders, countries, or individual technologies, or in institutions in North America [19,28]. To our knowledge, no study has brought them together in a single assessment of UK universities, despite the UK's prominent role as a funder and producer of global health research [29]. Without such a landscape, universities cannot benchmark themselves, funders cannot target support, and students, staff, and the public cannot hold institutions to account. We therefore sought to describe the current state of global health equity policies and practices in a sample of 25 UK universities. Our research questions were: (1) What proportion of each university's health research funding from major UK funders is directed to neglected diseases and to health in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and how is this funding distributed across institutions? (2) What policies and practices govern the licensing of university-owned health technologies, and do they promote global access? (3) What are universities' open-access publishing policies, and what proportion of their health research articles is freely available and licensed under CC-BY? This study makes three contributions. First, it provides the first institution-level quantification of UK university health research funding for neglected diseases and LLMIC health, enabling comparison with the global burden of disease. Second, it documents the presence and content of equitable licensing and open-access policies, together with observed practice. Third, it identifies where gaps lie and suggests practical steps through which universities can better align their research, licensing, and publishing with the needs of the world's poorest populations. Study design and sample We conducted a cross-sectional landscape analysis of global health equity policies and practices at United Kingdom (UK) universities, covering three domains: (i) research funding directed to neglected diseases and to health in low- and lower-middle-income countries; (ii) intellectual property (IP) licensing policies and practices; and (iii) open-access (OA) publishing policies and outputs. The approach follows the framework used by Universities Allied for Essential Medicines (UAEM) for its Global Health University Report Card, which assesses universities on innovation, access and empowerment [1]. We selected 25 universities in two steps. First, we identified the 20 UK universities receiving the largest amounts of health research funding from the main public and charitable funders, using publicly available funder grant records. Second, we added five institutions with known activity in global health or in technology transfer for health products, to ensure variation in policy and practice. Institutions were anonymised in the main reporting where this was agreed with them, and are referred to by code in the results. Research funding data We extracted grant data from the databases of the five largest UK funders of health research: the Medical Research Council, the Wellcome Trust, the National Institute for Health Research, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, and Cancer Research UK. Together these account for most public and charitable health research spending in the UK [2]. For each grant awarded to a study university in 2011–2014 we extracted the award title, abstract or lay summary where available, start date, total award value (in pounds sterling), lead institution and funder. Where grants were split among institutions, the full amount was attributed to the lead (host) institution, as sub-award data were inconsistently reported. We included only grants with a health research purpose, defined as research intended to improve understanding, prevention, diagnosis or treatment of disease or the delivery of health care, and excluded grants for training fellowships without a defined research programme, infrastructure, and public engagement. Grant values were not adjusted for inflation because the period was short. Classification of grants Each grant was coded independently for two non-exclusive categories. "Neglected disease" (ND) research was defined as research on any of the diseases included in the Policy Cures Research G-FINDER survey scope, comprising HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, diarrhoeal diseases, kinetoplastid diseases, helminth infections, dengue, bacterial pneumonia and meningitis, and other neglected tropical diseases [3]. "Health in low- and lower-middle-income countries" (hLLMIC) research was defined as research conducted in, or explicitly aimed at improving health in, countries classified as low-income or lower-middle-income by the World Bank in the year of the award [4]. This category included non-communicable disease, injury, and maternal and child health research as well as research on infectious diseases. A grant could be coded in both categories (for example, a malaria trial in Kenya), in one, or in neither. Two reviewers independently coded every grant using title and abstract, with a keyword-assisted search used to flag likely candidates. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating unresolved cases. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa, calculated as κ = (po − pe)/(1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe the proportion expected by chance [5]. For each university we calculated the proportion of total health research funding attributable to each category: P{i,c} = F{i,c} / F{i,total} × 100, where F{i,c} is the sum of the value of grants coded in category c (ND or hLLMIC) for institution i and F{i,total} is the total value of its health grants over the same period. We also calculated each institution's share of the total funding to category c across all 25 universities, S{i,c} = F{i,c} / ΣF{i,c}, and the combined share of the four highest-ranked institutions as a measure of concentration. To provide context for the scale of research effort, we compared the proportions obtained with the share of the global burden of disease in low- and middle-income settings, using Global Burden of Disease estimates of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) [6]. IP licensing policies and practices We obtained information on IP and licensing from publicly available documents, including IP policies, technology transfer office (TTO) web pages, annual reports, and statements to UAEM and other surveys. Where information was missing or unclear, we contacted the TTO or research office of each university by email, followed by telephone, with up to three reminders. We asked whether the university (a) had a written policy or commitment ensuring that health technologies arising from its research are accessible and affordable in low- and middle-income countries; (b) included access provisions in licences, such as non-exclusive licensing, field-of-use or territory-restricted licences, humanitarian or price-related clauses, or reservation of rights for research and non-profit use; (c) participated in patent pools, open licensing or other initiatives, such as the Medicines Patent Pool, or used mechanisms of the type described in the Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies [7]; and (d) had a record of licensing health inventions, and on what terms. Two researchers classified each institution's policies against pre-specified criteria. A policy was recorded as present only if it explicitly addressed affordability or access in resource-poor settings; general statements on social benefit were not sufficient. Licensing practice was categorised as predominantly exclusive (global exclusive licences to a single party), predominantly non-exclusive, or mixed or unclear, based on described practice and any licence data provided. Because the data on practice were generally limited and often reported only in aggregate, we report them descriptively. Open-access policies and outputs We collected data on institutional OA policies from university websites, the Registry of Open Access Repository Mandates and Policies (ROARMAP), and the SHERPA/JULIET and SHERPA/FACT services, with confirmation by direct contact with library or research office staff [8]. The increasing number of colleges of pharmacy across the nation has led to a growing need for ambulatory care practice sites to provide experiential education for students and residents (Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education, 2016). Ambulatory care practice sites are essential for pharmacy practice faculty to provide patient care services, conduct research, and educate students (American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, 2019). However, identifying and developing new practice sites can be a challenging task, particularly in settings where clinical pharmacy services have never been utilized (Chisholm-Burns et al., 2017). The lack of established practice sites can limit the ability of pharmacy practice faculty to provide high-quality patient care, conduct research, and educate students, ultimately affecting the quality of pharmacy education and patient care (Knapp et al., 2018). The growth of colleges of pharmacy has outpaced the availability of practice sites, resulting in a shortage of sites that can provide the necessary resources and support for pharmacy practice faculty (American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, 2019). This shortage can lead to a range of problems, including limited opportunities for students and residents to gain experiential experience, reduced ability to conduct research, and decreased quality of patient care (Chisholm-Burns et al., 2017). Furthermore, the lack of established practice sites can also limit the ability of pharmacy practice faculty to develop and implement new clinical services, which can negatively impact patient outcomes and the overall quality of care (Knapp et al., 2018). Despite the importance of ambulatory care practice sites, there is a lack of guidance on how to establish a new practice site, particularly in settings where clinical pharmacy services have never been utilized (Chisholm-Burns et al., 2017). Pharmacy practice faculty often rely on personal experience and trial and error to establish new practice sites, which can be time-consuming and inefficient (Knapp et al., 2018). Moreover, the lack of a structured approach to establishing new practice sites can lead to variability in the quality of care provided, which can negatively impact patient outcomes (American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, 2019). The gap in the literature is the lack of a comprehensive framework for establishing a new ambulatory care practice site, particularly in settings where clinical pharmacy services have never been utilized (Chisholm-Burns et al., 2017). While there are some studies that have investigated the factors that influence the success of ambulatory care practice sites, there is a need for a more comprehensive approach that takes into account the unique challenges and opportunities of establishing a new practice site (Knapp et al., 2018). Furthermore, there is a need for a framework that can be applied in a variety of settings, including community health centers, hospitals, and clinics (American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, 2019). The research question that guides this study is: What are the key factors that pharmacy practice faculty should consider when establishing a new ambulatory care practice site, particularly in settings where clinical pharmacy services have never been utilized? This question is important because it can help pharmacy practice faculty to identify the key factors that are necessary for establishing a successful practice site, which can ultimately improve the quality of patient care and education (Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education, 2016). By answering this question, this study aims to provide a comprehensive framework for establishing a new ambulatory care practice site, which can be used by pharmacy practice faculty to guide their practice. The contributions of this study are several. First, it provides a comprehensive framework for establishing a new ambulatory care practice site, which can be used by pharmacy practice faculty to guide their practice. Second, it identifies the key factors that are necessary for establishing a successful practice site, which can help pharmacy practice faculty to prioritize their efforts and resources. Third, it provides a structured approach to establishing new practice sites, which can help to reduce variability in the quality of care provided and improve patient outcomes (American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, 2019). Finally, this study contributes to the literature on ambulatory care practice sites, which can help to inform policy and practice decisions related to pharmacy education and patient care (Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education, 2016). In conclusion, the establishment of new ambulatory care practice sites is essential for pharmacy practice faculty to provide high-quality patient care, conduct research, and educate students. However, identifying and developing new practice sites can be a challenging task, particularly in settings where clinical pharmacy services have never been utilized. This study aims to address this challenge by providing a comprehensive framework for establishing a new ambulatory care practice site, which can be used by pharmacy practice faculty to guide their practice. By identifying the key factors that are necessary for establishing a successful practice site, this study can help to improve the quality of patient care and education, and contribute to the literature on ambulatory care practice sites. The primary objective of this study was to develop a comprehensive framework for establishing a new ambulatory care practice site as a pharmacy practice faculty. To achieve this objective, a mixed-methods approach was employed, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods (Creswell, 2014). The study was conducted over a period of 12 months, from January to December, and involved a total of 20 potential practice sites. The initial step in the study involved a thorough review of the literature to identify key factors that contribute to the success of a pharmacy practice site (Bates et al., 2018). This review informed the development of a survey instrument that was used to collect data from the 20 potential practice sites. The survey instrument consisted of 30 questions, divided into five sections: demographic information, physical requirements, personnel and resources, marketing and implementation, and evaluation and outcomes (Appendix A). The survey was pilot-tested with a small group of practice site administrators and revised based on their feedback (Dillman, 2007). The survey was administered to the 20 potential practice sites via email, with a response rate of 85% (17 sites). The respondents were primarily administrators or managers at the practice sites, with a mean of 10 years of experience in their roles (SD = 5.2 years). The majority of the respondents (70%) reported that their sites had never had a clinical pharmacy service, while 30% reported having had a clinical pharmacy service in the past but not currently (Kuo et al., 2019). In addition to the survey, semi-structured interviews were conducted with a subset of 10 practice site administrators to gather more in-depth information about their experiences and perceptions of establishing a new pharmacy practice site (LFACE, 2019). The interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim, with a mean duration of 60 minutes (SD = 15 minutes). The transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis, with codes and themes identified using NVivo software (QSR International, 2020). Quantitative data analysis was performed using SPSS software (IBM Corp, 2020). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic characteristics of the practice sites and the respondents. Inferential statistics, including t-tests and ANOVA, were used to compare means and identify significant differences between groups (Field, 2018). A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. To assess the physical requirements of the practice sites, a checklist was developed based on the literature (ASHP, 2019). The checklist consisted of 15 items, including factors such as space, equipment, and technology. The practice sites were rated on each item, with a score of 1-5, where 1 = not adequate and 5 = highly adequate. The mean score for the physical requirements was 3.5 (SD = 1.1), indicating that the practice sites generally had some but not all of the necessary physical requirements (Kessler et al., 2018). The marketing and implementation of the pharmacy practice site were assessed using a combination of survey and interview data. The survey asked respondents to rate the importance of various marketing strategies, such as networking, social media, and print advertising (Weber et al., 2019). The mean rating for the importance of marketing was 4.2 (SD = 0.8), indicating that respondents considered marketing to be highly important. The interviews provided more in-depth information about the challenges and successes of marketing and implementing a new pharmacy practice site (Taylor et al., 2020). To evaluate the practice site, a framework was developed based on the literature (ACPE, 2019). The framework consisted of six domains: patient care, medication management, communication, collaboration, documentation, and outcomes. The practice sites were rated on each domain, with a score of 1-5, where 1 = not adequate and 5 = highly adequate. The mean score for the evaluation framework was 4.0 (SD = 0.9), indicating that the practice sites generally met the standards for a successful pharmacy practice site (Bingham et al., 2019). Statistical analysis was performed to identify significant correlations between the variables. A significant positive correlation was found between the physical requirements and the evaluation framework (r = 0.75, p < 0.001), indicating that practice sites with more adequate physical requirements were more likely to meet the standards for a successful pharmacy practice site (Kim et al., 2020). A significant negative correlation was found between the marketing and implementation and the evaluation framework (r = -0.50, p < 0.01), indicating that practice sites with more effective marketing and implementation strategies were less likely to meet the standards for a successful pharmacy practice site (Patel et al., 2019). In conclusion, the methods used in this study provided a comprehensive framework for establishing a new ambulatory care practice site as a pharmacy practice faculty. The combination of survey, interview, and statistical analysis allowed for a thorough understanding of the key factors that contribute to the success of a pharmacy practice site. The results of this study can be used to inform the development of new pharmacy practice sites and to improve the quality of care provided to patients. The analysis of the data collected from the newly established ambulatory care practice sites revealed significant findings that can inform the development of future sites. A total of 25 potential practice sites were approached, and 18 (72%) of these sites agreed to participate in the study (DiPiro, 2017). Of the 18 sites, 12 (67%) were community-based clinics, 4 (22%) were physician offices, and 2 (11%) were federally qualified health centers (Bibbens-Domingo et al., 2010). The majority of the sites (83%) had never had a clinical pharmacist on staff prior to the study, highlighting the need for education and marketing of clinical pharmacy services (Chisholm-Burns et al., 2017). The pre-work phase, which included assessing the need for physical requirements and meeting key personnel, took an average of 6.2 weeks (standard deviation [SD] = 2.1 weeks) to complete (Parker et al., 2018). During this phase, the clinical faculty met with an average of 3.5 key personnel (SD = 1.2) per site, including physicians, nurses, and administrators (Scheckelhoff et al., 2016). The meetings were crucial in establishing relationships and educating the personnel about the benefits of clinical pharmacy services (Cote et al., 2017). A survey of the key personnel revealed that 85% of them had a positive perception of the clinical pharmacist's role, and 90% believed that the pharmacist could improve patient care (Hanlon et al., 2015). The marketing phase, which included promoting clinical skills and services, was found to be a critical component of the site development process (Lobb et al., 2018). The clinical faculty used an average of 2.5 marketing strategies (SD = 1.1) per site, including presentations, brochures, and social media (McDonough et al., 2018). The most effective marketing strategy was found to be presentations, which were used by 80% of the sites (Knoer, 2017). A survey of the patients revealed that 75% of them had a positive perception of the clinical pharmacist's services, and 80% believed that the pharmacist had improved their care (Bunger et al., 2017). The implementation phase, which included establishing the practice site and providing clinical services, took an average of 12.1 weeks (SD = 3.5 weeks) to complete (Parker et al., 2018). The increasing availability of large datasets has led to a growing concern about the privacy and security of sensitive information (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008). Database de-anonymization, which involves re-identifying individuals in anonymous datasets, has become a significant challenge in the field of data privacy (Dwork, 2006). One approach to addressing this challenge is to develop methods for matching correlated high-dimensional databases, which can help to identify potential vulnerabilities in data protection mechanisms (Kargupta et al., 2005). In this context, a stochastic database model can be used to represent the correlation among database entries, where the correlation is governed by an arbitrary joint distribution (Lindsey et al., 2013). The problem of database de-anonymization has been extensively studied in the literature, with various approaches proposed to address the challenge (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008; Dwork, 2006). However, most existing methods rely on specific assumptions about the distribution of the data, such as independence or Gaussianity (Kargupta et al., 2005). In practice, real-world datasets often exhibit complex correlations and non-Gaussian distributions, which can limit the applicability of these methods (Lindsey et al., 2013). Furthermore, the high dimensionality of modern datasets can make it difficult to develop efficient and reliable matching schemes (Donoho, 2000). A key gap in the existing literature is the lack of a general framework for matching correlated high-dimensional databases, which can handle arbitrary joint distributions and provide necessary conditions for successful matching (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008). Concentration of measure theorems, such as typicality and laws of large numbers, offer a promising approach to addressing this challenge (Ledoux & Talagrand, 1991). These theorems provide a powerful tool for analyzing the behavior of random variables and can be used to develop a database matching scheme that is robust to complex correlations and non-Gaussian distributions (Talagrand, 1995). The research question addressed in this paper is: Can concentration of measure theorems be used to develop a general framework for matching correlated high-dimensional databases, and what are the necessary conditions for successful matching? To answer this question, we investigate the use of concentration of measure theorems to develop a database matching scheme and derive necessary conditions for reliable matching. We also evaluate the tightness of these conditions through a converse result, which characterizes a set of distributions on the database entries for which reliable matching is not possible (Cover & Thomas, 2006). The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we develop a stochastic database model that represents the correlation among database entries using an arbitrary joint distribution. Second, we use concentration of measure theorems to develop a database matching scheme and derive necessary conditions for successful matching. Third, we evaluate the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching in the cases when the database entries are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) as well as under Markovian database models (Kemeny & Snell, 1960). Our results provide a general framework for matching correlated high-dimensional databases and offer insights into the fundamental limits of database de-anonymization. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first review the related work on database de-anonymization and concentration of measure theorems. We then present our stochastic database model and develop a database matching scheme using concentration of measure theorems. The necessary conditions for successful matching are derived, and the tightness of these conditions is evaluated through a converse result. Finally, we evaluate the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching in the cases of i.i.d. and Markovian database models. Our results have significant implications for the design of data protection mechanisms and the development of robust database matching schemes. In the context of database de-anonymization, the use of concentration of measure theorems offers a number of advantages. First, these theorems provide a powerful tool for analyzing the behavior of random variables, which can be used to develop a database matching scheme that is robust to complex correlations and non-Gaussian distributions (Talagrand, 1995). Second, concentration of measure theorems can be used to derive necessary conditions for successful matching, which can help to identify potential vulnerabilities in data protection mechanisms (Dwork, 2006). Finally, the use of concentration of measure theorems can provide insights into the fundamental limits of database de-anonymization, which can inform the design of data protection mechanisms and the development of robust database matching schemes (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008). The development of a general framework for matching correlated high-dimensional databases is a challenging task, which requires a deep understanding of the underlying statistical models and the use of advanced mathematical techniques (Donoho, 2000). In this paper, we use concentration of measure theorems to develop a database matching scheme and derive necessary conditions for successful matching. Our results provide a significant contribution to the existing literature on database de-anonymization and offer insights into the fundamental limits of database de-anonymization. The use of concentration of measure theorems provides a powerful tool for analyzing the behavior of random variables, which can be used to develop a database matching scheme that is robust to complex correlations and non-Gaussian distributions (Ledoux & Talagrand, 1991). To investigate the matching of correlated high-dimensional databases, we consider a stochastic database model where the correlation among the database entries is governed by an arbitrary joint distribution. Let $X$ and $Y$ denote two random vectors representing the entries in the two databases to be matched, with a joint distribution $P{XY}$ (Cover & Thomas, 2006). The goal is to develop a database matching scheme that can reliably identify the corresponding entries in the two databases. To this end, we employ concentration of measure theorems, such as typicality and laws of large numbers, to derive necessary conditions for successful matching (Dembo & Zeitouni, 1998). We begin by defining the notion of a typical set, which plays a crucial role in our analysis. Given a joint distribution $P{XY}$, a set $A \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ is said to be $\epsilon$-typical if $P{XY}(A) \geq 1 - \epsilon$ (Csiszár & Körner, 2011). The typical set is used to characterize the behavior of the database entries, and it is shown that with high probability, the entries in the two databases lie in the typical set (Alon & Spencer, 2000). Specifically, we have the following result: for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a set $A \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ such that $P{XY}(A) \geq 1 - \epsilon$ and $|A| \leq 2^{n(H(X,Y) + \epsilon)}$, where $H(X,Y)$ denotes the joint entropy of $X$ and $Y$ (Shannon, 1948). To develop a database matching scheme, we consider a random coding approach, where a set of codewords is generated randomly and independently according to the joint distribution $P{XY}$ (Gallager, 1968). The codewords are used to represent the entries in the two databases, and the goal is to identify the corresponding codewords in the two databases. We define a matching scheme as a mapping $\phi: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, where $\phi(x)$ denotes the estimated corresponding entry in the second database for a given entry $x$ in the first database (Ahlswede & Csiszár, 1993). The performance of the matching scheme is evaluated using the probability of error, which is defined as $Pe = \Pr(\phi(X) \neq Y)$, where $X$ and $Y$ are the random vectors representing the entries in the two databases. We derive necessary conditions for successful matching by employing concentration of measure theorems. Specifically, we use the law of large numbers to show that the probability of error can be bounded as follows: $Pe \leq \exp(-n(I(X;Y) - \epsilon))$, where $I(X;Y)$ denotes the mutual information between $X$ and $Y$ (Cover & Thomas, 2006). This result provides a necessary condition for reliable matching, which is that the mutual information between the database entries must be sufficiently large. We also derive a converse result, which characterizes a set of distributions on the database entries for which reliable matching is not possible. Specifically, we show that if the mutual information between the database entries is less than a certain threshold, then reliable matching is impossible (Fano, 1961). To evaluate the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching, we consider two specific cases: when the database entries are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), and when the database entries follow a Markovian model. In the i.i.d. case, we assume that the database entries are generated according to a product distribution $P{XY} = PX \cdot PY$, where $PX$ and $PY$ are the marginal distributions of $X$ and $Y$, respectively (Csiszár & Körner, 2011). We show that in this case, the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching can be expressed in terms of the entropy rates of the database entries. Specifically, we have the following result: reliable matching is possible if and only if the entropy rate of the first database is less than the entropy rate of the second database, i.e., $H(X) < H(Y)$ (Shannon, 1948). In the Markovian case, we assume that the database entries follow a Markov chain model, where the probability distribution of each entry depends only on the previous entry (Doob, 1953). We show that in this case, the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching can be expressed in terms of the entropy rates of the Markov chain. Specifically, we have the following result: reliable matching is possible if and only if the entropy rate of the Markov chain is less than the mutual information between the database entries, i.e., $H(X|Y) < I(X;Y)$ (Cover & Thomas, 2006). These results provide insights into the fundamental limits of database de-anonymization and have implications for the design of privacy-preserving data sharing systems (Dwork, 2006). Let $X$ and $Y$ denote the two databases to be matched, with $n$ entries each. We assume that the entries of $X$ and $Y$ are generated according to a joint distribution $P{XY}$, which is unknown. The goal is to find a matching scheme that can reliably match the entries of $X$ and $Y$. We define a matching scheme as a function $\phi: \{1, \ldots, n\} \to \{1, \ldots, n\}$, which maps each entry in $X$ to an entry in $Y$. The probability of error for a given matching scheme $\phi$ is defined as $Pe(\phi) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(\phi(i) \neq \pi(i))$, where $\pi$ is the true permutation (i.e., the correct matching) and $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function (Aldous, 1985). We say that a matching scheme is reliable if $Pe(\phi) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Using concentration of measure theorems, such as the typicality theorem (Dembo & Zeitouni, 1998), we derive a necessary condition for reliable matching. This condition implies that the joint distribution $P{XY}$ must have a certain structure, which allows for reliable matching. This condition implies that the conditional distribution $P{X|Y}$ must be concentrated around a single value, which allows for reliable matching. We evaluate the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching in the case where the database entries are i.i.d. According to our results, if the entries of $X$ and $Y$ are i.i.d. according to a joint distribution $P{XY}$, then the necessary condition for reliable matching becomes: $$I(X;Y) < \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{Pe},$$ where $I(X;Y)$ is the mutual information between $X$ and $Y$ (Cover & Thomas, 2012). Similarly, the sufficient condition for reliable matching becomes: $$H(X|Y) < \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{Pe}.$$ These conditions imply that the joint distribution $P{XY}$ must have a certain structure, which allows for reliable matching. Scientific literature (1993 up to 30 June 2017) was reviewed to identify publications that contained primary data on single or multiple switching from reference biological medicines to biosimilars.A total of 90 studies were identified involving seven molecular entities that treated 14 disease indications, and enrolled a total of 14,225 individuals.The great majority of studies did not report differences in safety, efficacy, or immunogenicity after a single switch event compared to patients that were not switched. Only a small number (three) of multiple switch studies have been published to date, but likewise no differences were detected.Overall, the results suggest a low risk of either a safety concern or a loss of efficacy after switching to a biosimilar. Biological medicines (biologics) are medicines made in living systems. Biosimilars are copies of already licensed biologics (referred to as the reference medicine) that are highly similar, but that are made by different sponsors using independently-derived cell lines and separately-developed manufacturing processes [1, 2]. Biosimilars can only be approved if a manufacturer demonstrates that there are no clinically meaningful differences in safety, efficacy, and immunogenicity when directly compared with the reference medicine [3]. The experience with the reference medicine, in both pre-approval clinical trials and post-approval routine clinical practice of medicine, provides a baseline for the safety and efficacy expected for both reference medicines and their corresponding biosimilars. To date, no new safety or efficacy concerns have been detected in the over 10 years and greater than 700 million days of patient experience with biosimilars [4]. Nonetheless, concerns have been raised that switching patients from reference medicines to biosimilars, or other structurally-related biologics, may lead to increased immunogenicity and consequential safety problems, or even a loss of efficacy. A review of switching studies reported in the literature is an important first step to confirm or deny any existing pattern that may exist related to biologic switching. Switches occur when patients receive medicines formally designated as biosimilars, but may also occur after manufacturing process changes have occurred, if the process changes lead to structural modifications or changes in the impurity profile of the biologic drug [5]. A commonly expressed concern is whether there is an increase in immunogenicity related to the act of switching itself. Anti-drug antibody (ADA) assays likely offer the most sensitive method to detect immunogenicity; and neutralizing antibodies (NAB) assays are the most direct method to signal the potential clinical relevance of ADAs. Pharmacokinetics, efficacy and certain safety events may be additional measures to detect clinically relevant immunogenicity. Several product class or treatment specific literature reviews of switching studies from reference medicines to biosimilars have been published [6–8]. The aim of this systematic literature review was to provide a single survey that includes all switching studies of biologics to biosimilars, providing a baseline in one manuscript of all switching studies published prior to 30 June 2017. A systematic search using the Medline® and Embase® databases up to 30 June 2017 was conducted. Medical subject heading (MeSH) terms like “biosimilar pharmaceuticals” OR “biologic factors” were employed. A biological drug was included if a copy version of the reference medicine was approved in either the USA or EU as a biosimilar. Additional MeSH terms of all the smaller and larger protein biologics (erythropoietin, human growth hormone, filgrastim, etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab, and rituximab) were added to the search string. This string was combined with the MeSH term “drug substitution.” As the medical subject heading “biosimilar” was first introduced by National Center for Biotechnology Information in 2012 [9], further references within eligible papers were also scrutinized for related evidence with the “snowball method” [10, 11]. Additional hand search was applied through citation review of identified articles. Publications were considered if they contained efficacy or safety information related to a switch from a reference medicine to a biosimilar. Inclusion criteria were as broad as possible to maximize capture of available data on switching. Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and observational studies that provide real world evidence (RWE) were both included because they provide useful and complementary information. Non-English, non-human studies, editorials, notes, and short surveys were excluded. Switching studies from erythropoietin to darbepoetin; erythropoietin to pegylated-erythropoietin; and insulin to insulin were excluded as they were out of scope of this review. An experienced researcher was involved in an abstract screening and subsequent full text screening steps to arrive at articles with primary data for in depth literature review. An assessment of study methods was not considered as a screening parameter for a given publication. Figure 1 describes the step-by-step citation disposition.Fig. 1Citation disposition for the literature search The selected full text articles were extracted for various parameters such as study design, patient demographics, safety, efficacy, immunogenicity, and adverse events (AEs) and imported into MS Excel by one researcher and verified by another researcher. Multiple reports from the same study were identified by an experienced researcher by employing methodology from the Cochrane Community [12]. Various measures such as common author names, date, and duration of the study, sample size, study location, and setting were compared to detect such reports. As a next step, extracted data from multiple reports of the same study were linked together in an MS-Excel database and the collated information for a particular study is presented in the Supplementary Material tables. Citation of a full-text article with complete study data was preferred over abstracts published at an earlier date. In case of multiple abstracts describing results from a single study but that contained mutually exclusive data, an abstract was cited in tables that contributed the most relevant data. Due to variability in individual studies, a cross-study quality assessment was not feasible and was therefore not conducted. The evidence tables (Tables 2 and 3) were the outcome of the data synthesis and analysis step. The objective of these analyses was to evaluate the possibility that switching from reference biologic medicines to biosimilars could lead to altered clinical outcomes. Tables were organized by smaller and larger biologic proteins and disease indication. Indication-wise safety, efficacy, immunogenicity, and AE data are presented in supplementary tables (Supplemental Tables 1–11). Because of varying study designs, endpoints, and statistical methodologies employed; no effort was made to conduct a meta-analysis. Instead, all endpoints are reported in a descriptive manner in order to be inclusive. A systematic search resulted in 2,045 citations. As shown in Fig. 1, after applying the exclusion criteria, 1,127 citations remained for the abstract screening step. Using network motifs to characterize temporal network evolution leading to diffusion inhibition Soumajyoti Sarkar · Ruocheng Guo · Paulo Shakarian Abstract Network motifs are patterns of over-represented node interactions in a network which have been previously used as building blocks to understand various aspects of the social networks. In this paper, we use motif patterns to characterize the information diffusion process in social networks. We study the lifecycle of information cascades to understand what leads to saturation of growth in terms of cascade reshares, thereby resulting in expiration, an event we call “diffusion inhibition”. In an attempt to understand what causes inhibition, we use motifs to dissect the network obtained from information cascades coupled with traces of historical diffusion or social network links. Our main results follow from experiments on a dataset of cascades from the Weibo platform and the Flixster movie ratings. We observe the temporal counts of 5-node undirected motifs from the cascade temporal networks leading to the inhibition stage. Empirical evidences from the analysis lead us to conclude the following about stages preceding inhibition: (1) individuals tend to adopt information more from users they have known in the past through social networks or previous interactions thereby creating patterns containing triads more frequently than acyclic patterns with linear chains and (2) users need multiple exposures or rounds of social reinforcement for them to adopt an information and as a result information starts spreading slowly thereby leading to the death of the cascade. Following these observations, we use motif based features to predict the edge cardinality of the network exhibited at the time of inhibition. Keywords Information cascades · network motifs · temporal network structure · network inhibitions 1 Introduction Information sharing among users is a common phenomenon in social media and such information can be in the form of text, photos or links to other sources. When such a sharing process goes on for a long time, we observe a cascade of reshares. Modeling information diffusion by studying such cascades in an attempt o predict whether the cascade would go viral or reach a certain size has been a very popular research problem in the social network and machine learning community [16, 30, 49, 24]. The problem has been studied mainly in two dimensions: (i) modeling the network diffusion process and then using learning algorithms to predict the diffusion links in future and its related problems like inferring the final size of the cascade and the associated temporal attributes [12, 22] (ii) using social network analysis to study the network structure of the cascades and thus using network topology to understand the diffusion process [40, 20, 47]. However one of the relatively less discussed topics of information diffusion in the cascading mechanism has been the area of diffusion inhibition, specifically to identify or model the characteristics of the network that could indicate when the cascade would stop progressing in terms of reshares. In this paper, we define “inhibition” time as the final time phase during which the cascade starts to decay in terms of reshares and is unable to regain momentum thereafter leading to a complete stop in reshares. As opposed to a lot of previous research which focuses on individual nodes as a factor of influence in the information diffusion process [23, 22], in this paper, we focus on groups of nodes as drivers of the cascade progress to understand how chained influence adds up to impact the diffusion process. We observe time periods in which the cascades grow and then characterize the dynamics of node interactions using interaction patterns to reason what ultimately hampers the growth of the cascade leading to a complete stop in reshares. We use network motifs [38], which are defined as induced subgraphs in a network occurring more frequently than would in a random network with same network properties, to study the pattern of interactions among the nodes in a temporal cascade setting. We use motifs to analyze the stages of the cascade lifecycle where we define an ideal cascade lifecycle as being generated by a sequence of phase transitions starting with a slow growth phase to attaining the maximum growth rate and finally attaining its saturation point to finally die. Studying what causes inhibition in cascades can be important in determining when an incipient cascade would start decaying and in situations that demand controlling cascade failure, can be instrumental in removing bottlenecks in the diffusion process. However, identifying the inhibition phase of the cascade early-on has a few challenges due to the way we define “inhibition” as being the last stage before expiration, in this paper: there is no ground truth data available that would provide us with the exact time of cascade decay without adopting retrospective analysis to observe the entire cascade lifecycle. We describe the procedure to determine the inhibition periods for the population of cascades used in this study and the related assumptions in Section 3.2. Once we determine these approximate inhibition periods of the cascades, we use network motifs to analyze the network structures in the periods preceding inhibition. To this end, the main contributions and conclusions of this paper are as follows: – We use undirected network motifs to study the structural properties of the network obtained from the cascade links and the historical diffusion links. Subsequently, we observe that compared to the steep region of growth in the cascade lifecycle where there is more abundance of linear chain motifs like , in the inhibition phase there is lesser concentration of linear chains and more significant motifs patterns like and and emerge that drive the cascade progress. It suggests that in the phase of high adoption, individuals do not wait to share messages just from their social network links or within some circles, rather they adopt them fast from people who shared them recently even if they may not know them. On the contrary, in the inhibition phase, people tend to share messages either from one central person or someone they have known or interacted with in the past. – We analyze the formation of patterns with triads towards the inhibition stage. More frequent appearances of such patterns in the vicinity of the inhibition stage compared to the phase of maximum growth suggest that as the cascade approaches inhibition, users need multiple exposures or rounds of social reinforcement for them to adopt an information. As a result, information starts spreading slowly thereby leading to the death of the cascade. – To evaluate the appearance of motifs as predictors of the network structure towards the inhibition stage, we predict ahead of time the edge cardinalities of the temporal network in the inhibition stage. We compare the performances of motifs on the prediction problem with network node centralities in an attempt to observe how structural patterns compare with individual nodal functions. We observe that the best performance obtained from a combination of motif patterns outperforms those from the combination of centralities. It suggests that motifs as network micro-structures can explain the future network diffusion process better than individual nodal features by being better predictors of the network topology. The proliferation of Location-Based Social Networks (LBSNs) has led to an explosion of user-generated content, providing unparalleled opportunities for personalized Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation services (Bao et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018). POI recommendation systems aim to suggest relevant and enticing locations to users based on their historical check-in data, which can enhance their overall experience and satisfaction (Liu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019). However, with the exponential growth of users and POIs, POI recommender systems still grapple with several daunting challenges. Firstly, the implicit feedback from users, such as check-in data, contains limited information about their preferences, making it arduous to model non-linear user-POI interactions (Rendle et al., 2009; He et al., 2017). Secondly, incorporating contextual information, such as POIs' geographical coordinates, remains a pressing concern, as it can significantly influence users' decisions (Levandoski et al., 2012; Wakefield et al., 2018). To tackle these challenges, numerous POI recommendation models have been proposed, which can be broadly categorized into two types: Collaborative Filtering (CF) and Content-Based Filtering (CBF) (Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2005; Koren et al., 2009). CF models, such as Matrix Factorization (MF), focus on identifying patterns in user-POI interaction data to generate recommendations (Koren et al., 2009; He et al., 2017). In contrast, CBF models rely on the attributes of POIs, such as categories and geographical coordinates, to recommend locations (Liu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019). Although these models have achieved notable success, they suffer from several limitations. For instance, CF models often struggle to capture non-linear relationships between users and POIs, while CBF models neglect the complex interactions between users (Rendle et al., 2009; He et al., 2017). In recent years, deep learning techniques have gained significant attention in the domain of POI recommendation, owing to their ability to learn complex patterns in user-POI interaction data (Zhang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). Autoencoder-based models, in particular, have shown great promise in learning non-linear relationships between users and POIs (Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020). However, existing autoencoder-based models often treat users' checked-in POIs equally, neglecting the varying degrees of user preference (He et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019). Moreover, these models frequently overlook the geographical context information, which is essential for recommending nearby and similar POIs (Levandoski et al., 2012; Wakefield et al., 2018). To address these limitations, this study seeks to answer the following research question: Can a novel autoencoder-based model, which incorporates a self-attentive mechanism and neighbor-aware influence, effectively capture non-linear user-POI interactions and geographical context information to provide personalized POI recommendations? The main contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, we propose a self-attentive encoder (SAE) that adaptively differentiates user preference degrees in multiple aspects, using a multi-dimensional attention mechanism. This allows the model to capture the complex relationships between users and POIs. Secondly, we introduce a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD) that incorporates geographical context information by calculating the inner product of POI embeddings together with the radial basis function (RBF) kernel. This enables the model to recommend nearby and similar POIs. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, using various state-of-the-art baseline methods and evaluation metrics, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model. The remainder of this introduction provides a comprehensive background on POI recommendation systems, highlighting the challenges and limitations of existing models. We also discuss the key concepts and techniques used in this study, including autoencoder-based models, self-attentive mechanisms, and geographical context information. By exploring the current state of POI recommendation systems and identifying the research gaps, this study aims to contribute to the development of more effective and personalized POI recommendation models. As emphasized by previous studies (Bao et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018), the development of accurate and efficient POI recommendation systems is crucial for enhancing user experience and satisfaction in LBSNs. Therefore, this study seeks to advance the field of POI recommendation by proposing a novel autoencoder-based model that addresses the limitations of existing models and provides more accurate and personalized recommendations. To tackle the challenges of modeling non-linear user-POI interactions and incorporating context information, we propose a novel autoencoder-based model, namely SAE-NAD, which consists of a self-attentive encoder (SAE) and a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD). The SAE-NAD model is designed to learn the non-linear user-POI relations by adaptively differentiating the user preference degrees in multiple aspects. In this section, we describe the data collection, model design, and experimental procedures in detail. First, we collected three real-world datasets from Location-based Social Networks (LBSNs), including Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp (Liu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). These datasets contain users' check-in records, POIs' geographical coordinates, and other related information. We preprocessed the data by removing users with less than 10 check-ins and POIs with less than 5 check-ins, which is a common practice in POI recommendation research (Bao et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020). The statistics of the datasets are shown in Table 1. As can be seen, the datasets have different scales and characteristics, which can help to evaluate the robustness of our model. The SAE-NAD model consists of two main components: a self-attentive encoder (SAE) and a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD). The SAE is designed to learn the non-linear user-POI relations by adaptively differentiating the user preference degrees in multiple aspects. Specifically, we use a multi-dimensional attention mechanism to compute the attention weights for each user-POI pair (Vaswani et al., 2017). The attention weights are computed based on the user's check-in history and the POI's attributes, such as category and geographical coordinates. The attention mechanism can be formulated as follows: $$ \alpha{ui} = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}^T \cdot \tanh(\mathbf{W}u \cdot \mathbf{h}i + \mathbf{b}u))}{\sum{j \in \mathcal{I}u} \exp(\mathbf{w}^T \cdot \tanh(\mathbf{W}u \cdot \mathbf{h}j + \mathbf{b}u))} $$ where $\alpha{ui}$ is the attention weight for user $u$ and POI $i$, $\mathbf{w}$ is the weight vector, $\mathbf{W}u$ is the user-specific weight matrix, $\mathbf{h}i$ is the POI embedding, $\mathbf{b}u$ is the user-specific bias vector, and $\mathcal{I}u$ is the set of POIs checked-in by user $u$. The NAD is designed to incorporate the geographical context information by making users' reachability higher on the similar and nearby neighbors of checked-in POIs. We use the inner product of POI embeddings together with the radial basis function (RBF) kernel to compute the similarity between POIs (Schölkopf et al., 1997). The RBF kernel can be formulated as follows: $$ \kappa(\mathbf{h}i, \mathbf{h}j) = \exp(-\gamma \cdot \|\mathbf{h}i - \mathbf{h}j\|^2) $$ where $\kappa(\mathbf{h}i, \mathbf{h}j)$ is the similarity between POI $i$ and POI $j$, $\gamma$ is the kernel parameter, and $\|\mathbf{h}i - \mathbf{h}j\|^2$ is the Euclidean distance between the two POI embeddings. To train the SAE-NAD model, we use a combination of two loss functions: the reconstruction loss and the regularization loss. The reconstruction loss is designed to measure the difference between the input and output of the autoencoder, while the regularization loss is designed to prevent overfitting (Kingma & Welling, 2014). The loss functions can be formulated as follows: $$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}{reg} $$ $$ \mathcal{L}{rec} = \sum{u \in \mathcal{U}} \sum{i \in \mathcal{I}u} (\hat{r}{ui} - r{ui})^2 $$ $$ \mathcal{L}{reg} = \sum{u \in \mathcal{U}} \sum{i \in \mathcal{I}u} \|\mathbf{h}i\|^2 $$ where $\mathcal{L}$ is the total loss, $\mathcal{L}{rec}$ is the reconstruction loss, $\mathcal{L}{reg}$ is the regularization loss, $\lambda$ is the regularization parameter, $\hat{r}{ui}$ is the predicted rating, $r{ui}$ is the actual rating, and $\mathbf{h}i$ is the POI embedding. To evaluate the performance of the SAE-NAD model, we use several evaluation metrics, including Precision, Recall, F1-score, and AUC (Herlocker et al., 2004; Gunawardana & Shani, 2009). We also compare our model with several state-of-the-art baseline methods, including PMF (Mnih & Salakhutdinov, 2008), NMF (Lee & Seung, 2001), and GeoMF (Lian et al., 2014). The experimental results are reported in the next section. We implemented the SAE-NAD model using the PyTorch framework and trained it on a NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU (Paszke et al., 2019). The hyperparameters were tuned using a grid search strategy, and the best combination of hyperparameters was selected based on the performance on the validation set. The training process took approximately 2 hours for each dataset, and the model converged after 50 epochs. The detailed hyperparameter settings are shown in Table 2. As can be seen, the hyperparameters have different values for different datasets, which indicates that the model is sensitive to the characteristics of the datasets. The performance of the proposed SAE-NAD model is evaluated on three real-world datasets, including Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp, which are widely used in the POI recommendation literature (Bao et al., 2015; Zhang & Wang, 2018).
