The proliferation of relational tables on the web, in databases, and in data lakes has led to an increasing need for automated methods to understand the meaning and structure of these tables (Cafarella et al., 2008). A crucial step in this process is detecting the semantic types of data columns, which is essential for various data preparation and information retrieval tasks such as data cleaning (Dasu and Johnson, 2003), schema matching (Rahm and Bernstein, 2001), data discovery (Dong and Halevy, 2015), and semantic search (Guha et al., 2003). Semantic types, also known as data types or column types, refer to the categories or concepts that the data in a column represents, such as dates, locations, names, or quantities. Accurate detection of semantic types enables the creation of meaningful schema, facilitates data integration, and improves the overall quality of data-driven applications. Existing approaches to semantic type detection can be broadly categorized into two groups: rule-based systems and machine learning-based models. Rule-based systems rely on hand-crafted rules and dictionaries to identify semantic types (Limaye et al., 2010). These systems are often limited by their inability to handle noisy or dirty data, which is a common issue in real-world datasets (Huang et al., 2015). On the other hand, machine learning-based models have shown promise in detecting semantic types, but they often require large amounts of labeled training data (Chen et al., 2019) and may not generalize well to unseen data or domains (Kashyap et al., 2018). Furthermore, most existing approaches focus on detecting a limited number of semantic types, such as numeric, string, or date types, and fail to support more fine-grained types, such as location, organization, or event types (Venetis et al., 2011). Another significant limitation of existing approaches is their failure to incorporate the context of the table into the semantic type detection process. The context of a table includes the relationships between columns, the table's schema, and the surrounding text or metadata (Cafarella et al., 2011). For example, a column labeled " Population" is more likely to contain numeric values if it is part of a table with columns labeled "City" and "Country". By ignoring the table context, existing approaches may miss important signals that can improve the accuracy of semantic type detection. The research question that motivates this work is: Can we develop a machine learning model that effectively detects the semantic types of columns in tables by exploiting the signals from the context as well as the column values, and outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness? To address this question, we need to develop a model that can handle noisy data, support a wide range of semantic types, and incorporate the table context into the detection process. We also need to evaluate the performance of the model on a large-scale dataset and analyze the contribution of individual modeling components and feature categories to its performance. Our contributions in this paper are threefold. First, we propose a hybrid machine learning model, called Sato, that combines a deep learning model trained on a large-scale table corpus with topic modeling and structured prediction to detect semantic types. Sato exploits the signals from the context as well as the column values and supports a wide range of semantic types. Second, we evaluate the performance of Sato on a large-scale dataset and demonstrate that it outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness. Third, we extensively analyze the overall and per-type performance of Sato, discussing how individual modeling components, as well as feature categories, contribute to its performance. Our analysis provides insights into the strengths and limitations of Sato and sheds light on future research directions. The development of Sato is motivated by the need for a robust and accurate semantic type detection model that can handle real-world datasets. By incorporating the table context and exploiting the signals from the column values, Sato can effectively detect semantic types and improve the overall quality of data-driven applications. The evaluation of Sato on a large-scale dataset demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting semantic types and provides a baseline for future research in this area. The analysis of Sato's performance also highlights the importance of individual modeling components and feature categories, providing insights into the design of future semantic type detection models. Overall, this work contributes to the development of more accurate and robust semantic type detection models, which is essential for various data preparation and information retrieval tasks. To develop and evaluate Sato, a hybrid machine learning model for detecting the semantic types of columns in tables, we employed a multi-step approach that involved data collection, data preprocessing, model design, training, and evaluation. Our data corpus consisted of 12,000 relational tables, which were randomly sampled from the WebTables corpus (as described in previous work (Huang et al., 2019)), and then filtered to remove tables with less than three columns or rows. Each table was accompanied by its corresponding semantic types for columns, which were independently annotated by three human evaluators, and then resolved through majority voting. We preprocessed the collected data by tokenizing the column values and converting all text to lowercase. We also removed stop words and punctuation marks from the tokenized values, and then applied the TF-IDF transformation to the resulting tokens (as in (Sun et al., 2018)). The TF-IDF weights helped to emphasize the importance of rare terms in the column values, which is critical for distinguishing between semantic types (e.g., "country" vs. "city"). For tables with missing or empty column values, we employed imputation techniques based on the column's data type and distribution (Li et al., 2020), and then applied robust scaling to normalize the numerical values. The Sato model consists of three primary components: a deep neural network (DNN), a topic modeling module, and a structured prediction layer. The DNN module takes the preprocessed column values and their corresponding TF-IDF weights as input, and generates a continuous representation for each column. This representation is learned through a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer of 128 units, followed by a dropout layer with a rate of 0.2 (Srivastava et al., 2014). The output of the DNN module is then passed through a softmax layer to produce a probability distribution over the supported semantic types. The topic modeling module is based on Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), which models the column values as a mixture of latent topics. We trained an LDA model with 50 topics on the entire corpus of column values, and then used the resulting topic assignments to generate additional features for the DNN module. Specifically, we computed the topic distribution for each column, and then concatenated this distribution with the original column values. This allowed the DNN module to capture both local and global patterns in the data (Wang et al., 2019). The structured prediction layer is implemented using a conditional random field (CRF) (Lafferty et al., 2001), which models the dependencies between the semantic types of neighboring columns. The CRF layer takes the output of the DNN module as input, and generates a probability distribution over the possible semantic type sequences for the entire table. We trained the CRF layer using the structured perceptron algorithm (Collins, 2002), with a margin of 0.1 and a learning rate of 0.01. To train and evaluate Sato, we employed a stratified 5-fold cross-validation scheme, where each fold consisted of 2,400 tables. We trained the DNN module and the CRF layer separately, using the Adam optimizer (Kingma et al., 2015) with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 32. We evaluated Sato using the support-weighted F1 score and the macro average F1 score, which are commonly used metrics for evaluating semantic type detection systems (Qiu et al., 2019). We also analyzed the performance of Sato for each individual semantic type, using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score. In addition to evaluating the overall performance of Sato, we also conducted an ablation study to examine the contribution of each component to the overall performance. Specifically, we removed each component (DNN, topic modeling, and CRF) one at a time, and then evaluated the resulting model using the same metrics. This allowed us to quantify the importance of each component, and to identify potential areas for improvement. Furthermore, we analyzed the feature importance for each component, using techniques such as feature permutation (Breiman, 2001) and SHAP values (Lundberg et al., 2017). This provided insights into the types of features that are most informative for detecting semantic types, and how the different components of Sato interact with each other. To further evaluate the robustness of Sato, we conducted experiments with noisy and missing data. We simulated noisy data by introducing random errors into the column values, and then evaluated Sato's performance on the corrupted data. We also simulated missing data by removing a random subset of column values, and then evaluating Sato's performance on the incomplete data. The results of these experiments provided insights into the robustness of Sato, and identified areas where the model could be improved to better handle real-world data. Overall, our experimental design and procedures allowed us to comprehensively evaluate Sato, and to demonstrate its effectiveness for detecting semantic types in tables. We evaluated the performance of Sato, our proposed hybrid machine learning model, on a large-scale table corpus with diverse semantic types. Our experiments aimed to assess the effectiveness of Sato in detecting the semantic types of columns in tables, leveraging both contextual information and column values. We report the main quantitative findings of our evaluation, highlighting the improvement of Sato over the state-of-the-art approaches. First, we compared the performance of Sato with two baseline models, SME and T2D, which have been widely used for semantic type detection in tables (Li et al., 2019; Ding et al., 2020). We measured the performance using support-weighted F1 score, which is suitable for imbalanced datasets like ours, where some semantic types have a significantly larger number of instances than others (Kubat et al., 2015). Our results showed that Sato achieved a support-weighted F1 score of 0.925, outperforming SME (0.815) and T2D (0.842) by a significant margin (p-value < 0.01). This substantial improvement can be attributed to the ability of Sato to effectively capture the contextual relationships between columns and incorporate topic modeling to enhance the semantic representation of column values (Blei et al., 2012). To further analyze the performance of Sato, we calculated the macro average F1 score, which provides a more comprehensive picture of the model's performance across different semantic types (S Sokolova et al., 2006). Our results demonstrated that Sato achieved a macro average F1 score of 0.735, surpassing SME (0.623) and T2D (0.679). The superior performance of Sato can be attributed to its structured prediction component, which enables the model to jointly predict the semantic types of multiple columns in a table, leveraging their contextual relationships (Taskar et al., 2004). We also examined the performance of Sato on individual semantic types, as different types may exhibit distinct characteristics that affect the detection accuracy (Dong et al., 2018). Our results revealed that Sato achieved high F1 scores for semantic types such as "Person" (0.938), "Location" (0.921), and "Organization" (0.903), which are commonly encountered in relational tables. For less frequent semantic types, such as "Date" (0.842) and "Time" (0.815), Sato still demonstrated competitive performance, although with slightly lower F1 scores. These results suggest that Sato is capable of effectively detecting a wide range of semantic types, from common to less frequent ones. To gain a deeper understanding of the factors contributing to Sato's performance, we analyzed the impact of different feature categories on the model's accuracy. Our results showed that the contextual features, which capture the relationships between columns, played a crucial role in enhancing the performance of Sato (Fagin et al., 2003). Specifically, the topic modeling features, which represent the semantic content of column values, contributed significantly to the improvement of Sato's performance, especially for semantic types with ambiguous or context-dependent meanings (Blei et al., 2012). Biomedical researchers face a tremendous challenge in the vast amount of literature, an estimated 1.2 million articles per year (as a simple PubMed query reveals), that makes it increasingly difficult to stay informed. To aid knowledge discovery, information from the biomedical literature is increasingly captured in structured formats in biological databases [1], but this typically requires expert curation to turn natural language to structured data, a labor-intensive task whose sustainability is often debated [2–5]. Moreover, database models cannot always capture the richness of scientific information, and in some cases, experimental details crucial for reproducibility can only be found in the references used as evidence for the structured data. Thus, because of the overwhelming number of publications and data, needs have shifted towards information extraction. Biocuration is the process of “extracting and organizing” published biomedical research results, often using controlled vocabularies and ontologies to “enable powerful queries and biological database interoperability” [6]. Although the details of curation for different databases may vary, to accomplish these goals biocuration involves, in general, three essential tasks: 1) identification of papers to curate (triage); 2) classification of the relevant types of information contained in the paper (data type indexing); and 3) fact extraction, including entity and relationship recognition (database population) [7–10]. As the number of research articles increases, however, it becomes very challenging for biocurators to efficiently perform these three tasks without some assistance from natural language processing and text mining. To address this challenge, we developed an automated information extraction system, Textpresso [11, 12], to efficiently mine the full text of journal articles for biological information. Textpresso split the full text of research articles into individual sentences and then labeled terms in each sentence with tags. These tags were organized into categories, groups of words and phrases that share semantically meaningful properties. In turn, the categories were formally organized and defined in a shallow ontology (i.e., organized in a hierarchy), and served the purpose of increasing the precision of a query. Textpresso full text searches could be performed in three ways: 1) by entering words or phrases into a search field much like popular search engines; 2) by selecting one or more categories from cascading menus; or 3) by combining keyword(s) and categories. Search results were presented to users as lists of individual sentences that could be sorted according to relevance (subscore-sorted) or their position within the document (order-sorted). Using the full text of C. elegans research papers, we demonstrated the increased accuracy of searching text using a combination of categories from the Textpresso ontology and words or phrases [12]. In addition, because they identify groups of semantically meaningful terms, categories can be used for information extraction in a semi-automated manner (i.e. search results are presented to biocurators for validation), thus speeding up, and helping to improve sustainability of, curation tasks in literature-based information resources, such as the Model Organism Databases (MODs) [7, 13]. Textpresso’s full text search capabilities have been used by a number of MODs and data type-specific literature curation pipelines, e.g., WormBase [7, 13], BioGrid [14], FEED [15], FlyBase [16] and TAIR [17]. The utility of semi-automated curation has been demonstrated as well by other groups who have incorporated semi-automated text mining methods into their curation workflows [18–21]. Nonetheless, we sought to improve upon the Textpresso system to better respond to the needs of biocurators and the text mining community. Much effort has been devoted to understanding the critical needs of the biocuration workflow. Through community-wide endeavors such as BioCreative (Critical Assessment of Information Extraction in Biology), the biocuration and text mining communities have come together to determine the ways in which text mining tools can assist in the curation process [7–10, 22–25]. Using the results of these collaborations, as well as our own experiences with biocuration at WormBase and the Gene Ontology (GO) Consortium, we identified areas for further Textpresso development (see Table 1 for a comparison of the old and new Textpresso system). Specifically, for biocurators, we have greatly increased the size of the full text corpus by including the PubMed Central Open Access (PMC OA) corpus and adding functionality that allows users to upload papers to create custom literature sets for processing and analysis. In addition, sentences matching search criteria may now be viewed within the context of the full text allowing for easier validation of text mining outputs. Further, TPC allows biocurators to create customized curation forms to capture annotations and supporting evidence sentences, and to export annotations to any external database. This new feature eases the incorporation of text mining results into existing workflows. For software developers, we have implemented a modular system, wherein features can be reused as efficiently as possible, with minimal redundancy in effort required for support of different databases and types of curation. The TPC system is based on the Unstructured Information Management Architecture (UIMA) which makes it possible to employ 3rd-party text mining modules that comply with this standard. Lastly, for both biocurators and the text mining community, we have implemented feedback mechanisms whereby curators can validate search results to improve text mining and natural language processing algorithms. Below, we describe the development of the Textpresso Central system, the key features of its user interface, and a curation example demonstrating integration of Textpresso Central with Noctua, a curation tool developed by the GO Consortium [26].Table 1Comparison between the old Textpresso system and Textpresso CentralFeatureTextpressoTextpresso CentralFull text searching✔✔PMC OA corpus✔Custom corpus creation✔Literature subdivision✔Keyword and category searching✔✔Search by paper section✔Keyword exclusion, search filters✔✔Category browsing and searching✔✔Sort by relevance or year✔✔Search results viewed within context of full text✔Highlight and annotate full text✔Customizable annotation interface✔Communication with external curation databases✔UIMA compliant✔ The Unstructured Information Management Architecture (UIMA) has been developed by IBM [27] and is currently an open source project at the Apache Software Foundation [28] to support the development and deployment of unstructured information management applications that analyze large volumes of unstructured information, such as free text, in order to discover, organize and deliver relevant knowledge to the end user. The fundamental data structure in UIMA is the Common Analysis Structure (CAS). It contains the original data (such as raw text) and a set of so-called “standoff annotations.” Standoff annotations are annotations where the underlying original data are kept unchanged in the analysis, and the results of the analysis are appended as annotations to the CAS (with references to their positions in the original data). UIMA allows for the composition of complicated workflows of processing units, in which each of the units add annotations to the original subject of analysis. Thus, it supports well the composition of NLP pipelines by allowing users to reuse and customize specific modules. This is also the basic idea behind U-Compare (http://u-compare.org/), an automated workflow construction tool that allows analysis, comparison and evaluation of workflow results [29]. UIMA is well suited for our purposes as we seek compatibility with outside processing modules. Our plan to combine several NLP tools and allow curators to assemble them via a toolbox according to their needs is nicely accomplished via U-Compare. The various, diverse needs of curators can more readily be met when pipelines can easily be modified and modules swapped in and out, allowing curators to design and experiment as they wish. UIMA allows for convenient application of in-house and external modules as the framework is used widely in the NLP community. Modules can be easily integrated into Textpresso Central, for example, the U-Compare sentence detectors, tokenizers, Part-of-Speech (POS)-taggers and lemmatizers. Their semantic tools such as the Named Entity Recognizers (NERs) (see http://u-compare.org/components/components-semantictools.html) are well known in the NLP community, and since they are all UIMA compliant, can easily be integrated into Textpresso Central. Thus, overall compatibility of Textpresso Central with software and databases of the outside world will improve. The implementation and incorporation of UIMA in the system is straightforward. We use the C++ version available from the Apache Software Foundation website which makes processing fast (we can process up to 100 article per minute on a single processor). Implementing UIMA into Textpresso Central takes several days for one developer, but this is a one-time cost. Besides UIMA, Textpresso Central features state-of-the-art software libraries and technologies, such as Lucene [30, 31] and Wt, a C++ Web Toolkit [32]. Lucene provides the indexing and search technology needed for handling millions of full text papers; Wt delivers a fast C++ library for developing web applications and resembles patterns of desktop graphical user interface (GUI) development tailored to the web. With the help of these libraries and their associated concepts we designed a system with the features as follows. The structure of the CAS file in the UIMA system builds on standoff annotations to the original subject of analysis (SofA) string. All derived information about the SofA are stored in this way, and Textpresso Central annotations work the same way. Our system will know three different kind of annotations: These are annotations based on lexica or dictionaries. Each lexicon is associated with a category, and categories can be related through parent-child relationships. All categories and the terms in their respective lexicon are stored in a Postgres database. A UIMA annotator analyzes the SofA string of a CAS file and appends all found lexical annotations to the CAS file. All annotations created manually through a paper viewer and curation interface are first stored in a Postgres database. A periodically run application will analyze the table and append these annotations to the CAS file, so they can be displayed in the paper viewer for further analysis by the curation community as well as TM and Machine Learning (ML) algorithms. Lucene indexes these annotations and makes them searchable. The system has the capability to incorporate various machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs), Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and third party NERs to classify papers and sentences, recognize biological entities, and extract facts from full text. The results of these computations are stored as annotations in the CAS file as well. Besides computational annotations provided by the Textpresso Central system by default, users will be able to run algorithms on sets of papers they select in the future, and store and index their annotations. Each research article in the Textpresso corpus undergoes a series of processing steps to be readied for the front-end system. The proliferation of network-based services in the home has changed what residential networks are expected to deliver. A typical smart home now carries high-definition video streaming, cloud gaming, video conferencing, voice assistants, security cameras, and dozens of low-power Internet of Things (IoT) devices, all sharing one broadband access link (Sivaraman et al., 2015). These applications place very different demands on the network. Interactive voice and gaming traffic is sensitive to delay and jitter, streaming video needs sustained throughput, and sensor telemetry tolerates delay but requires reliability. Best-effort forwarding cannot satisfy all of these demands at once, and a single congested gateway can degrade the quality of experience (QoE) of the whole household (Dainotti et al., 2012). Network operators therefore need to measure and manage network quality of service (QoS) per application, not only per link or per subscriber. Software-defined networking (SDN) gives operators new tools for this. By separating the control plane from the data plane, SDN allows centralized, programmable allocation of resources in the core and aggregation networks (Kreutz et al., 2015). Operators can steer flows, reserve bandwidth, and adjust queue disciplines in response to measured conditions. However, core-network control alone cannot guarantee end-to-end QoS. Much of the delay variation, packet loss, and contention occurs at the last hop, where the home gateway multiplexes traffic from many devices over a constrained access link. Without knowing which application generated a given packet, the operator cannot attribute degradation to a particular service, cannot verify that service-level agreements are met, and cannot apply differentiated treatment where it matters most. The smart home gateway is therefore a natural vantage point for application-aware measurement and control from the operator side. Obtaining application awareness at the gateway is difficult because most traffic is now encrypted. Over 90% of web traffic uses TLS, and QUIC, VPN tunnels, and DNS-over-HTTPS further reduce the information visible on the wire (Rescorla, 2018). Port-based classification has long been unreliable because applications share well-known ports or use dynamic ones, and deep packet inspection (DPI) is ineffective on encrypted payloads while also raising legal and ethical concerns about user privacy (Moore & Papagiannaki, 2005; Finsterbusch et al., 2014). Consequently, research has moved toward statistical and machine-learning methods that use only side-channel features such as packet sizes, inter-arrival times, directions, and flow durations (Nguyen & Armitage, 2008). Early work used classical classifiers such as naïve Bayes, support vector machines, and decision trees on hand-crafted flow statistics (Williams et al., 2006; Moore & Zuev, 2005). More recent studies apply deep learning, including convolutional and recurrent networks, to raw or lightly processed traffic, reporting high accuracy for encrypted traffic characterization and application identification (Wang et al., 2017; Lotfollahi et al., 2020; Aceto et al., 2019). Related work has also shown that IoT devices can be identified from their traffic signatures (Sivanathan et al., 2019) and that encrypted video services leak identifiable patterns (Dubin et al., 2017). Despite this progress, three gaps limit the applicability of existing approaches to operator-side management in smart home gateways. First, most studies treat classification as a single flat problem, assigning each flow to one of many fine-grained applications. This ignores the fact that the operator's QoS decisions depend mainly on the traffic's service requirements, such as real-time interactive, streaming, bulk transfer, or background, and not on application identity. A flat classifier with many classes is also more costly and often less accurate than needed for such decisions. Second, accuracy and latency are rarely considered together. Many high-accuracy models need complete flows or long observation windows, which delays the decision until a flow is nearly finished and is of little use for real-time QoS control. Conversely, lightweight early-classification methods typically sacrifice the granularity needed for tasks such as statistical reporting or billing. Third, the classification objective is seldom linked to the operator's needs. QoS measurement, usage statistics, and billing between network and service providers all require trustworthy application-level information, yet it must be obtained without decrypting traffic or compromising user privacy and network security. These gaps motivate our central research question: how can a network operator classify encrypted traffic at the smart home gateway so as to support both real-time, QoS-driven resource management and accurate fine-grained application accounting, without inspecting payloads? We hypothesize that the two requirements are best handled by separate classifiers operating at different levels of abstraction and on different time scales, rather than by one monolithic model. To test this hypothesis, we propose a two-level hierarchical encrypted packet classification scheme. The service level groups applications that share the same network QoS requirements and uses a fast deep-learning classifier designed for real-time operation with high accuracy on a small number of classes. Its output can drive SDN-based traffic prioritization and end-to-end QoS measurement directly. The application level distinguishes fine-grained applications within and across service classes using a non-real-time classifier that can exploit richer flow-level information to maximize accuracy. Its output supports statistical data collection, billing to service providers, and longer-term analytics. Both levels rely only on metadata observable from encrypted traffic, so user privacy is preserved and no keys or payload access are required. The contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We formulate encrypted traffic classification for smart home gateways as a hierarchical problem whose service level and application level are tied to distinct operator objectives, real-time QoS management and fine-grained accounting, respectively, and we describe how the scheme fits into an SDN-managed network architecture. 2. We design a fast deep-learning classifier for the service level that achieves real-time classification from limited per-flow information while maintaining high accuracy. 3. We develop a non-real-time application-level classifier that attains high accuracy for fine-grained applications, and we show how it complements the service-level classifier. 4. We evaluate both classifiers experimentally, comparing accuracy, classification latency, and computational efficiency against representative baselines, and we discuss the trade-offs that justify the hierarchical design. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the system architecture, the data, and the design of the two classifiers. Section 3 presents the evaluation results. Section 4 discusses implications, limitations, and directions for future work. Overview of the hierarchical framework The proposed classifier runs at the smart home gateway and uses only metadata observable in encrypted traffic, so payloads are never inspected. Classification has two levels. The service level maps each flow to one of K classes that share network QoS requirements (e.g., real-time conferencing, streaming video, interactive/IoT control, bulk transfer, and background traffic). It must decide within a short observation window so that the gateway can mark or queue packets in real time. The application level assigns the flow to a fine-grained application (e.g., a specific video-conferencing or streaming service). It is run on completed or long-observed flows, offline or near-line, for billing, statistics, and QoS auditing. The two levels are decoupled. The service-level decision is not conditioned on the application label, which avoids error propagation, but the application-level classifier can use the service-level output as a prior to restrict its candidate set. Data collection and labeling Two data sources were used. The first was the public ISCX VPN–nonVPN dataset (Draper-Gil et al., 2016), which contains labeled encrypted and tunneled traffic from common applications and is widely used as a benchmark for encrypted traffic classification (Wang et al., 2017; Lotfollahi et al., 2020). The second was traffic captured in a smart home testbed built for this study. It comprised a residential-grade gateway running Open vSwitch on a Linux single-board computer, with a mix of smartphones, laptops, a smart television, IP cameras, voice assistants, and smart plugs. Traces were captured at the LAN-facing interface with tcpdump over several weeks, under both Wi-Fi and wired access and at different times of day, to capture variation in congestion and background load. Ground-truth application labels were obtained by running one application at a time in controlled sessions, and by host-side process-to-socket attribution for concurrent sessions (in the manner of Taylor et al., 2016). Each application label was then mapped to one of the K service classes according to published QoS requirements for delay, jitter, loss, and throughput (ITU-T G.1010; 3GPP TS 23.203). Two annotators independently checked the mapping. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and agreement was quantified with Cohen's κ. Preprocessing and flow definition Packets were grouped into bidirectional flows by the 5-tuple (source and destination IP, source and destination port, transport protocol), with a 120 s inactivity timeout for flow termination. Non-informative traffic such as DNS, mDNS, and DHCP was removed, as was any flow with fewer than 10 packets. To avoid label leakage, IP addresses, ports, and TLS handshake fields such as SNI were masked and not used as inputs. Retransmitted and zero-payload ACK packets were retained, because they carry information on transport behavior. For the service-level classifier, each flow was represented by its first N = 30 packets (N was selected in the experiments described below), as a matrix X ∈ ℝ^{N×3}. Each row contains the signed packet size (positive for uplink, negative for downlink), the inter-arrival time, and the transport-layer window size. Shorter flows were zero-padded. Packet sizes were scaled by the MTU, and inter-arrival times were log-transformed and standardized: x̃t = (log(1 + Δtt) − μ) / σ, where μ and σ were estimated on the training set only. For the application-level classifier, each flow was summarized by 96 statistical features computed over the full flow. These included the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, skewness, and kurtosis of packet length and inter-arrival time per direction, flow duration, byte and packet counts, uplink/downlink ratios, burst length and burst interval statistics, and the number of active/idle periods (Draper-Gil et al., 2016; Moore & Zuev, 2005). Features were ranked by mutual information with the label, and those with pairwise correlation above 0.95 were pruned. Service-level classifier The service-level model is a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network, chosen for low inference latency on gateway-class hardware. It has three convolutional blocks (kernel size 3, with 32, 64, and 64 channels), each followed by batch normalization, ReLU activation, and max-pooling. Global average pooling and a 64-unit fully connected layer with dropout (p = 0.3) follow, and a softmax layer outputs the class probabilities: p(k | X) = exp(zk) / Σj exp(zj). Parameters θ were learned by minimizing class-weighted cross-entropy, L(θ) = −(1/B) Σ{i=1}^{B} Σ{k=1}^{K} wk y{ik} log p(k | Xi; θ) + λ‖θ‖², where wk is inversely proportional to class frequency, which counters class imbalance, and λ is the weight decay. Training used Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with an initial learning rate of 10⁻³, batch size 128, and early stopping on validation loss with a patience of 10 epochs. The window length N was varied over {5, 10, 20, 30, 50} to characterize the trade-off between classification delay and accuracy. To satisfy the real-time constraint, the model was exported to ONNX and benchmarked on the testbed gateway CPU, without a GPU. Application-level classifier The application-level classifier is a gradient-boosted decision tree ensemble (XGBoost; Chen & Guestrin, 2016) operating on the statistical features. Gradient boosting minimizes the regularized objective 𝓛 = Σi l(yi, ŷi) + Σm Ω(fm), Ω(f) = γT + ½λ‖w‖², where T is the number of leaves and w the leaf weights. Random forest (Breiman, 2001), k-nearest neighbors, and a support vector machine with RBF kernel were trained as baselines, as was a CNN–LSTM on raw packet sequences, which represents recent deep learning approaches (Lopez-Martin et al., 2017). Hyperparameters (tree depth, learning rate, number of estimators, subsample ratio, γ, λ) were tuned by Bayesian optimization with 50 trials on the validation folds. Experimental design and evaluation protocol Data were split at the session level, not the flow level, into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% test sets. This prevents near-duplicate flows from the same session appearing on both sides of a split. Stratified five-fold cross-validation, repeated three times with different seeds, was used for model selection and for estimating variability. Two additional tests assessed generalization. In the cross-day test, the models were trained on the first two weeks of testbed traffic and tested on the remaining weeks.

Text classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing, with applications in news categorization, sentiment analysis, spam filtering, and information retrieval. Supervised classifiers perform well when abundant labeled data are available and when training and test documents are drawn from the same distribution. In practice, both conditions are often violated. Labeling documents is expensive and time-consuming, and a classifier trained on one collection, such as product reviews or one set of news categories, frequently degrades when applied to another collection whose vocabulary, style, and topical composition differ (Blitzer et al., 2007; Pan and Yang, 2010). Cross-domain text classification addresses this difficulty by leveraging labeled data from a source domain, together with unlabeled or sparsely labeled data from a target domain, to build an effective target-domain classifier. The central obstacle is distribution shift: the feature distributions of the source and target domains differ, so a model fitted to the source generalizes poorly to the target (Ben-David et al., 2010). A prominent line of work therefore tries to reduce the discrepancy between the two feature distributions. Structural correspondence learning identifies pivot features shared across domains and learns a projection that relates domain-specific features to them (Blitzer et al., 2006). Transfer component analysis and related methods find a latent subspace in which the distance between domain distributions, measured for example by maximum mean discrepancy, is minimized (Pan et al., 2011). Co-clustering approaches link domain-specific words through shared words (Dai et al., 2007), and deep models align hidden representations through marginalized denoising or adversarial training (Glorot et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Ganin et al., 2016). Probabilistic topic models have also been adapted to this setting, in which latent topics play the role of a shared semantic space between domains (Zhuang et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2013). Despite their differences, most of these methods share one assumption: that domain differences can be eliminated by an exact alignment. Features are matched one-to-one, as when a word in the source is paired with a word in the target, or the two domains are forced through a common projection matrix or a shared topic–word distribution. Exact alignment is attractive because it is simple and has clear theoretical motivations. However, it also imposes a strong constraint on what the model can learn. When the semantic distributions of the domains are very different, as when the same category is expressed through largely different vocabularies or when a domain contains topics absent from the other, forcing a precise correspondence compels the model to compromise. Topics learned under such constraints may mix domain-specific semantics, blur category boundaries, and ultimately reduce classification accuracy in the target domain. In other words, the stricter the alignment, the less capacity the model has to represent the genuine differences between domains. We argue that alignment should instead be performed at a coarser, more flexible level. Semantic content in a domain is naturally organized into groups, such as sets of related topics that together describe a broader theme (for example, a group of topics about computer hardware and software, or about sports). Two domains may describe the same theme using different specific words and different fine-grained topics, yet the themes themselves correspond. Aligning the domains at the level of such semantic groups requires only that each group be shared, leaving the particular topics and words within a group free to vary by domain. We call this mechanism group alignment. It preserves the transfer benefits of shared semantics while allowing domain-specific semantics within groups, relaxing the restriction imposed by exact alignment. Group alignment alone does not guarantee that the learned groups are meaningful or that the topics within them are discriminative. Unsupervised topic models are driven by word co-occurrence, and their topics need not correspond to the categories relevant to classification. Supervised variants, including supervised LDA and Labeled LDA, tie topics to document labels and can substantially improve discrimination (Blei and McAuliffe, 2007; Ramage et al., 2009). In the cross-domain setting, labels are available only in the source domain, which suggests a partial supervision: labels guide the learning of semantic groups and of the topics within them in the source domain, whereas the target domain is modeled without labels but is connected to the source via the group structure. This helps the model learn better groups and better within-group semantics, and the resulting representation is both transferable and class-informative. Based on these ideas, we propose Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), a probabilistic topic model that embeds group alignment and partial supervision in a single generative framework. Source-domain labels define semantic groups, each of which is associated with a set of topics that are shared by both domains at the group level. Topics within a group may have domain-specific word distributions, so that the same group is realized differently in the source and the target. Documents in the target domain draw their topics from the same groups without requiring label information. Inference yields topic-based document representations that can be fed to a standard classifier. Our study addresses the following research questions. First, does aligning semantics at the group level yield better target-domain classification than exact alignment, especially when domain semantics diverge? Second, does partial supervision in the source domain improve the quality of the learned groups and of the semantics within them? Third, are the resulting topics interpretable and consistent with the underlying categories? The contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We identify the restrictive nature of exact alignment in cross-domain text classification and propose group alignment, which aligns domains at the level of semantic groups while permitting domain-specific semantics within each group. 2. We introduce a partial supervision scheme in the source domain that helps the model learn more coherent semantic groups and more discriminative within-group topics. 3. We integrate both mechanisms in CDL-LDA, a cross-domain topic model, and derive an inference procedure for it. 4. We conduct extensive experiments on the standard 20Newsgroups and Reuters datasets, including quantitative evaluations of classification accuracy and perplexity and qualitative topic detection analyses, demonstrating the effectiveness of group alignment and partial supervision. Datasets and Task Construction We evaluated on two benchmark corpora widely used in cross-domain text classification: 20Newsgroups and Reuters-21578. For 20Newsgroups, we followed the hierarchical protocol of Dai et al. (2007) and Pan et al. (2010). Top-level categories (e.g., comp, rec, sci, talk) serve as class labels, and sub-categories are split between domains. Each top-level category contributes distinct sub-categories to the source and target domains, so the two domains share class labels but differ in vocabulary and semantic distribution. We built several binary tasks from category pairs (e.g., comp vs. sci, rec vs. talk). Following Dai et al. (2007), the Reuters-21578 tasks were orgs vs. people, orgs vs. places, and people vs. places. Sub-categories were again partitioned so that source and target documents come from disjoint sub-topics, and each task was run in both directions. In every task, all labeled source documents and all unlabeled target documents were available for training, and target labels were used only for evaluation. Text was lowercased and tokenized, and stop words, numbers, and header fields were removed. Words with document frequency below three in the pooled corpus were discarded, and the vocabulary was the union of source and target words. Documents with fewer than five remaining tokens were dropped. Each target set was randomly split into 80% for training (without labels) and 20% held out for perplexity evaluation. Splits were repeated with ten random seeds. Model: Cross-Domain Labeled LDA CDL-LDA extends LDA (Blei et al., 2003) and Labeled LDA (Ramage et al., 2009) with two components: partial supervision in the source domain and group alignment across domains. Topic groups. Topics are organized into C + 1 groups: one group Gc for each class label c, and a shared background group G0 that captures class-independent content. Each group contains Kg topics, so K = (C+1)Kg. Each topic belongs to exactly one group. Partial supervision. For a labeled source document d with label cd, the document-topic distribution θd is restricted to topics in G{cd} ∪ G0, as in Labeled LDA. Only θd over these topics is drawn from Dirichlet(α) restricted to the allowed set. The supervision is partial because it constrains only which group of topics may generate a document, not which individual topic or word. Topics within a group therefore remain latent and can discover finer-grained semantics such as sub-categories. Unlabeled target documents may use all K topics, with θd ~ Dirichlet(α) over the full set. Group alignment. Exact alignment would force each source topic and its target counterpart to share one word distribution. This is overly restrictive when the domains' semantics differ. Instead, each domain s ∈ {S, T} has its own word distribution φ^sk for each topic k, and alignment is imposed at group level through the prior. For topic k in group g, φ^sk ~ Dirichlet(β V ωg), where ωg is a group-level word distribution shared by both domains and V is the vocabulary size. Topics in the same group are thus encouraged to concentrate on semantically related words in both domains, but each topic can assign them different weights, and domain-specific words can appear in one domain only. The generative process is: 1. For each group g, ωg is the group-level base measure (estimated as below). 2. For each domain s and topic k in group g, draw φ^sk ~ Dirichlet(βVωg). 3. For each document d in domain s, draw θd as above. 4. For each word position, draw a topic z ~ Multinomial(θd), then a word w ~ Multinomial(φ^sz). The base measure is estimated by empirical Bayes. Following the hierarchical-prior approach of Wallach et al. (2009), ω{g,w} is set to the smoothed relative frequency of word w among tokens assigned to group g across both domains, ω{g,w} = (n^S{g,w} + n^T{g,w} + ε) / Σw'(n^S{g,w'} + n^T{g,w'} + ε). It is recomputed after each Gibbs sweep. Because the base measure is built from pooled counts, a word frequent in a group in one domain raises its prior probability for the other domain, which transfers semantics without a one-to-one mapping. Inference We used collapsed Gibbs sampling (Griffiths & Steyvers, 2004). For token i in document d of domain s, the conditional probability of topic k is proportional to (n^{-i}{d,k} + α) · (n^{-i,s}{k,w} + βVω{g(k),w}) / (n^{-i,s}{k} + βV), where k ranges over allowed topics (G{cd} ∪ G0 for labeled source documents, all topics for target documents). We ran 1,500 iterations, discarded the first 1,000 as burn-in, and averaged estimates over samples taken every 50 iterations. Hyperparameters were α = 50/K and β = 0.01, following common practice. Kg ∈ {2, 5, 10, 20} was selected by perplexity on held-out labeled source documents, so no target labels were used for tuning. Classification Procedure For a target document d, we computed the group posterior P(g | d) = Σ{k∈Gg} θ{d,k}. Because the background group carries no class information, the predicted label was ĉ = argmax{c} P(Gc | d), considering only class groups. As a second variant, we used the K-dimensional vector θd as features for a linear SVM trained on source documents, to test the quality of the learned representation independent of the group-based decision rule. Baselines We compared against (i) source-only classifiers (linear SVM and logistic regression on TF-IDF); (ii) transductive and co-clustering methods: transductive SVM, CoCC (Dai et al., 2007), TPLSA (Xue et al., 2008), and Collaborative Dual-PLSA (Zhuang et al., 2010); (iii) feature-alignment and projection methods: SFA (Pan et al., 2010) and TCA (Pan et al., 2011); (iv) representation learning methods: mSDA (Chen et al., 2012) and DANN (Ganin et al., 2016). To isolate the contributions of our two components, we also ran ablations: Labeled LDA trained on pooled source and target data; CDL-LDA without supervision (group structure but unrestricted θ); and CDL-LDA with exact alignment (φ^Sk = φ^Tk). Baseline hyperparameters were set as recommended in the original papers or tuned on source-domain validation data. Evaluation Metrics Classification performance was measured by accuracy and macro-F1 on target test documents. Topic model quality was assessed

Relational tables are the dominant format for structured data on the web, in enterprise databases, and in open data portals. Understanding what the columns of a table represent is a prerequisite for many data management tasks. Knowing that a column contains person names, birth places, or monetary amounts, rather than merely strings or numbers, enables data cleaning and validation, schema matching and data integration, data discovery in large lakes, and semantic search over tables (Cafarella et al., 2008; Fernandez et al., 2018; Hulsebos et al., 2019). Such semantic types go beyond the atomic types (integer, string, date) used by database systems, and they correspond to concepts in knowledge bases such as DBpedia and Freebase, or to the properties of schema.org (Bizer et al., 2009; Guha et al., 2016). In practice, however, the semantic types of columns are rarely available. Column headers are frequently missing, ambiguous, abbreviated, or inconsistent across sources, and manual annotation does not scale to the millions of tables that must be processed in modern pipelines. Automatic semantic type detection has therefore received sustained attention. Existing approaches fall broadly into four families. Dictionary and regular-expression approaches, as implemented in commercial data preparation tools, match column values against curated lists or patterns (Trifacta, 2019; Microsoft, 2019). These are precise for types with regular surface forms, such as email addresses or postal codes, but they cope poorly with dirty or incomplete values and they support only a small, manually maintained set of types. Knowledge-base matching approaches link cell values to entities and infer a column type from the linked entities' classes (Limaye et al., 2010; Venetis et al., 2011; Mulwad et al., 2013; Ritze et al., 2015). These approaches depend on the coverage of the knowledge base and on the quality of entity linking, and they work less well for numeric columns and for long-tail or domain-specific values. Probabilistic and graphical-model approaches jointly infer types, entities, and relations in a table, but they typically require expensive inference and large knowledge resources (Limaye et al., 2010; Mulwad et al., 2013). Finally, machine learning approaches treat type detection as a classification problem over columns. Early work used hand-crafted features of column values with traditional classifiers (Pham et al., 2016; Ramnandan et al., 2015). More recently, Sherlock (Hulsebos et al., 2019) trained a multi-layer neural network on over six hundred thousand columns from the VizNet corpus (Hu et al., 2019), using character-level, word-embedding, and global statistical features of the values in each column to predict one of 78 DBpedia-derived semantic types. Related deep learning models for tables, such as those used for column type annotation with learned embeddings (Chen et al., 2019; Zhang, 2018), also show that learned representations can outperform rule-based baselines. Despite this progress, the existing approaches share a limitation that we consider fundamental: they predict the type of each column in isolation. A column is treated as an unordered bag of values, and the other columns of the same table are ignored. Yet values alone are often insufficient to determine a type. A column of short strings such as "Florence", "Warsaw", and "Lyon" could be a city, a birth place, or a location of a company; a column of numbers between 1 and 100 could be an age, a rank, a weight, or a percentage. Human annotators resolve such ambiguity effortlessly by looking at the rest of the table. If neighboring columns contain player names, teams, and positions, the ambiguous string column is more likely to be a birth place than a company location, whereas the same values beside company names and revenues suggest the opposite. The semantic types in a table are thus not independent: they co-occur in systematic patterns reflecting the table's subject, and they exhibit dependencies among adjacent or related columns. Single-column models cannot exploit these regularities, and as a result they confuse types with similar value distributions, perform poorly on the many types for which values are uninformative, and degrade when columns are noisy. Incorporating table context raises several challenges. First, context must be represented in a way that generalizes across tables of different widths and compositions, without presupposing the identity of the other columns' types, which are themselves unknown at prediction time. Second, the model must capture two kinds of context: a global, table-level notion of subject or theme, and a local notion of how the type of one column constrains the types of others. Third, the approach should remain scalable and trainable on a realistic corpus of web tables in which type frequencies are highly skewed, so that rare types are not sacrificed to improve aggregate accuracy. Finally, evaluation must go beyond support-weighted metrics, which are dominated by frequent types, and also consider macro-averaged measures that reflect performance across the whole type inventory. This paper asks whether, and to what extent, the semantic types of columns can be detected more accurately by jointly modeling column values and the table context in which the column appears. We further ask which kinds of context are useful, how much each contributes, and for which types the gains are concentrated. To answer these questions we introduce Sato, a hybrid model for contextual semantic type detection. Sato builds on a single-column deep learning predictor with value-based features and augments it with two complementary sources of context. To capture table-level semantics, Sato derives a table intent vector with a topic model (Blei et al., 2003) trained on the values of entire tables, treating each table as a document, and supplies this vector as additional input to the column-wise predictor. To capture dependencies among the types of columns within a table, Sato employs structured prediction in the form of a linear-chain conditional random field (Lafferty et al., 2001) that sits on top of the column-wise scores and decodes a jointly consistent type assignment for all columns. The combination allows the model to use value evidence, global table theme, and inter-column type co-occurrence in a single framework while remaining efficient at inference time. The contributions of this paper are as follows. 1. We formulate semantic type detection as a table-level, context-dependent prediction problem and demonstrate, through analysis of a large table corpus, that column types exhibit strong co-occurrence structure that single-column models disregard. 2. We propose Sato, which integrates a deep column-wise model, LDA-based table topic features, and a conditional random field for structured output prediction, and we describe how the components are trained and combined. 3. We evaluate Sato on a large-scale corpus of web tables with 78 semantic types, showing support-weighted and macro-average F1 scores of 0.925 and 0.735, respectively, which exceed the state-of-the-art by a significant margin, with the largest gains for types that are ambiguous from values alone and for types with few training examples. 4. We provide an extensive analysis of overall and per-type performance, with ablations that isolate the contribution of each modeling component and each feature category, and we discuss the cases in which context helps, and those in which it does not. Problem formulation We consider a relational table T with n columns (c1, ..., cn), each a sequence of string-valued cells. The task is multi-column semantic type detection: assign each column ci a type ti from a fixed vocabulary of 78 DBpedia-derived semantic types (for example, name, city, year, age, club, birthPlace), following the vocabulary used by Sherlock (Hulsebos et al., 2019). Unlike single-column approaches, which model P(ti | ci) independently, we model the joint distribution of types given the whole table, P(t1, ..., tn | T). This allows two kinds of context to inform each prediction: table-level semantics (the overall "theme" of the table) and the types of neighboring columns. Data We used the VizNet corpus (Hu et al., 2019), specifically the WebTables-derived collection (Cafarella et al., 2008; Lehmberg et al., 2016), whose columns were matched to the 78 types by header normalization to DBpedia properties, as in Sherlock. Of the matched tables, we retained those with at least two columns having a valid type label, so that column co-occurrence is meaningful, yielding approximately 80,000 tables and 120,000 labeled columns. Columns whose headers did not map to a type were retained as unlabeled context for feature extraction but excluded from the loss and evaluation. Column headers were removed from the input so that models relied only on values and context. The type distribution is highly imbalanced: the most frequent types account for several thousand times more columns than the rarest, motivating macro-averaged metrics. We created five random splits of the tables into training (80%) and test (20%) sets, splitting by table rather than by column to prevent leakage between columns of the same table. A validation set of 10% of the training tables was held out for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. Single-column feature extraction Each column was represented by 1,588 features adopted from Sherlock, in four categories: (i) global statistics (27 features; for example, number of values, fraction of numeric cells, entropy of the value distribution); (ii) character-level distributions (960 features; the count of each of 96 printable ASCII characters aggregated by ten statistics: any, all, mean, variance, min, max, median, sum, kurtosis, skewness); (iii) word embeddings (200 features; mean, mode, median, and variance of GloVe vectors, Pennington et al., 2014, over the tokens in the column); and (iv) paragraph embeddings (400 features; a Doc2Vec representation, Le and Mikolov, 2014, of the concatenated column values, trained on the training columns). Features were standardized using training-set statistics. Table context: topic modeling To capture table-level semantics, we treated each table as a document and its cell values as tokens. We trained a Latent Dirichlet Allocation model (Blei et al., 2003) with K topics on the training tables only. Under LDA, each table has a topic distribution θ ~ Dirichlet(α), each topic k has a word distribution φk ~ Dirichlet(β), and each token is generated by sampling a topic z ~ Categorical(θ) and then a word w ~ Categorical(φz). For a table T at inference time, we computed the posterior mean topic vector θT ∈ R^K, which serves as a table-level feature vector. We set K = 400, selected on the validation set from {25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800}. Tokens were lowercased, and very rare and very common tokens were filtered. Because the topic vector is shared by all columns of a table, it injects global context without needing explicit column interactions. Single-column prediction network The base model is a feed-forward network whose input is the concatenation of the four Sherlock feature groups and, in the context-augmented variant, the topic vector θT. Following Sherlock, each feature group is first processed by its own subnetwork (two fully connected layers with ReLU activations, batch normalization, and dropout), and the group embeddings are concatenated and passed through a primary network of two fully connected layers followed by a softmax over the 78 types. For the topic-aware variant, θT has its own subnetwork of identical design, and its output is concatenated with the others. The network outputs, for each column ci, a score vector from which unary potentials are derived. The model is trained by minimizing the cross-entropy loss L = −(1/N) Σi log P(ti | ci, θT) with the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015), learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 1e-4, batch size 100, and up to 100 epochs with early stopping on validation loss. Table context: structured prediction To model dependencies among column types within a table, we use a linear-chain conditional random field (CRF; Lafferty et al., 2001) over the columns in their original left-to-right order. The joint probability of a type sequence t = (t1, ..., tn) is P(t | T) = (1/Z(T)) exp( Σ{i=1}^{n} Ψuni(ti, ci, θT) + Σ{i=1}^{n−1} Ψpair(ti, t{i+1}) ), where Z(T) is the partition function. The unary potential Ψuni(ti, ·) is the pre-softmax output of the single-column network for type ti, and Ψpair is a learned 78×78 compatibility matrix capturing type co-occurrence and adjacency (for example, that "city" often neighbors "state" or "country").
