Introduction Traumatic hand and upper extremity injuries are among the most common reasons patients seek emergency care. Epidemiologic analyses of national emergency department (ED) data suggest that hand and wrist injuries account for roughly 20% of all ED visits, with lacerations, fractures, crush injuries, and amputations making up a large share of these presentations [1,2]. Although many of these injuries are minor, a substantial proportion require timely specialized evaluation and often operative management. Open fractures, tendon lacerations, vascular compromise, high-pressure injection injuries, compartment syndrome, and flexor sheath infections all benefit from early expert intervention. Delay can lead to infection, permanent stiffness, loss of grip strength, chronic pain, and prolonged work disability [3]. Because the hand is central to occupation, self-care, and social participation, these outcomes carry high personal and societal costs. Hand injuries disproportionately affect working-age adults, so the economic burden through lost productivity and compensation claims is considerable [2,3]. Despite this burden, access to emergency hand care has been described as inadequate. Under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA), hospitals with EDs must provide a medical screening examination and stabilization, and they must maintain an on-call roster of specialists to meet the needs of their patients [4]. In practice, however, compliance with this requirement is difficult for many institutions. Over the past two decades, studies of ED on-call coverage have documented a decline in specialists willing to take emergency call, particularly in surgical and procedural subspecialties [5,6]. Physicians cite uncompensated care, medicolegal exposure, disruption to elective practice and personal life, and inadequate reimbursement among their reasons for withdrawing from call panels [5,6]. Hospitals have responded by paying call stipends, employing specialists, or transferring patients to other facilities. These strategies are unevenly available and are often shaped by local market conditions rather than by patient need. Hand surgery is especially vulnerable to these pressures. Hand surgeons are a relatively small workforce drawn from orthopedic, plastic, and general surgery backgrounds, and many practice in outpatient or ambulatory settings in which elective procedures such as carpal tunnel release, trigger finger release, and arthroplasty are more predictable and better reimbursed than unscheduled trauma [7]. Because most elective hand surgery is performed outside the hospital or in same-day facilities, a surgeon may maintain a busy elective practice at a hospital while declining to participate in its emergency call schedule. When no hand specialist is available, patients may be evaluated by general orthopedic, plastic, or emergency physicians with varying hand-specific training, or they may be transferred to another institution, sometimes over considerable distances. Transfers increase cost, delay definitive treatment, strain receiving centers, and fragment continuity of care [8]. Several recent regional surveys have reported a mismatch between the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery. These studies, conducted in different states and using similar telephone-based methods, found that a larger share of hospitals offered elective hand services than offered around-the-clock emergency hand coverage [7,9,10]. They also identified geographic and institutional variation in coverage, and some suggested that patients in underserved areas had the most limited options. Taken together, these reports raise the possibility that the discrepancy reflects a structural feature of the health care system rather than local anomalies. Even so, the evidence remains scattered. Most studies describe a single state or region, use different definitions of "coverage," and rarely evaluate whether coverage is related to community characteristics such as proximity to a trauma center or the socioeconomic status of the surrounding population. These contextual factors are plausibly important. Level I trauma centers concentrate surgical resources, and nearby community hospitals may rely on them as referral destinations. This may reduce the incentive, or the capacity, of neighboring hospitals to maintain their own hand call panels. Alternatively, hospitals in counties without a trauma center may have to maintain broader local coverage because transfer options are limited. Likewise, hospitals serving economically disadvantaged communities typically have a higher proportion of uninsured and Medicaid patients, which may deter specialists from taking call because of poor reimbursement [5,11]. Prior work on trauma center access has shown that vulnerable populations often face geographic and financial barriers to specialized care [12]. Whether these patterns extend to emergency hand surgery has not been well characterized. New Jersey provides a useful setting in which to examine these questions. It is the most densely populated state in the nation, with a dense network of community hospitals, several level I and II trauma centers, and marked variation in income and urbanization across municipalities. Its proximity to major metropolitan areas in New York and Pennsylvania might be expected to buffer patients against limited local coverage, yet it could also encourage a reliance on referral that undermines local emergency capability. To our knowledge, the availability of emergency versus elective hand surgery coverage across New Jersey hospitals has not been systematically evaluated. The purpose of this study was therefore to assess the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery coverage among non-university hospitals in New Jersey and to determine whether a disproportionate availability of emergency relative to elective services exists. We further sought to examine whether emergency hand coverage varied according to the presence of a level I trauma center within the hospital's county and according to the poverty level of the hospital's city. Finally, we place our findings in the context of previously published state-level surveys to evaluate whether a national trend toward limited emergency hand care is emerging. This study makes three contributions. First, it provides the first state-wide description of the gap between elective and emergency hand coverage in New Jersey, using a standardized survey of hospitals. Second, it identifies geographic and socioeconomic correlates of coverage that may point to modifiable drivers of access, such as call compensation, regionalization, and referral patterns. Third, by comparing our results with those from other states, it assesses whether the discrepancy is a national phenomenon. If it is, the findings argue for policy and system-level responses, including regional hand trauma networks, structured triage and transfer protocols, and alternative models of emergency hand care, rather than reliance on individual hospital call arrangements. Study Design and Setting We conducted a cross-sectional telephone survey of acute-care hospitals in the state of New Jersey in August 2014. The aim was to compare the availability of elective hand surgery with that of emergency hand coverage. The design followed standard recommendations for structured telephone surveys of organizations, which stress a brief fixed-script instrument, a defined respondent population, and repeated contact attempts to limit nonresponse (Dillman et al., 2014). The survey collected only institutional-level information about service availability. It involved no patient data and no individually identifiable information about respondents. We therefore regarded the study as non-human-subjects research and exempt from full institutional review board review. Participation was voluntary, and respondents were told the purpose of the call at the outset. Hospital Identification and Eligibility We compiled the sampling frame from the New Jersey Department of Health's public licensure listing of acute-care general hospitals. We cross-checked it against the state hospital association directory to remove closed, merged, or renamed facilities. Hospitals with an emergency department were eligible, because the study concerned the availability of emergency hand coverage and elective services. We excluded university-affiliated hospitals. These institutions generally have residency-based, in-house subspecialty coverage, and including them would have inflated estimates of availability for the community-hospital setting where access concerns are greatest. We also excluded specialty hospitals without an emergency department, such as rehabilitation, psychiatric, and pediatric-only facilities. After applying these criteria, 58 hospitals remained, and all were contacted. We did not draw a sample, so the study was a census of eligible institutions. Survey Instrument and Data Collection The instrument consisted of two questions, chosen to reflect how a transferring clinician or patient would assess access to hand care. The first was "Does your hospital provide elective hand surgery?" and had a yes/no response. The second was "Is there a hand specialist/surgeon on call always, sometimes, or never?" We defined "hand specialist" as any surgeon, whether plastic, orthopedic, or general, who provides hand surgery services at the hospital. This matches the multidisciplinary nature of hand surgery training in the United States. "Always" meant the hospital provided immediate hand coverage 24 hours per day, 7 days per week, and we labeled this "24/7 coverage" in the analysis. "Sometimes" indicated limited coverage, such as weekday-only, scheduled-day, or variable call. "Never" indicated no hand call coverage. A single trained caller placed all calls during regular business hours. The caller first reached the hospital operator and asked to be connected to the emergency department, the operating room scheduling office, or the medical staff office. These were the departments most likely to know the call schedule and elective service lines. The caller used an identical script for every call to reduce interviewer variability. The caller recorded the response, the title of the respondent, and the date of the call. When the first respondent was unsure, the caller asked to be referred to someone with knowledge of the call roster, such as a charge nurse, a staff coordinator, or a medical staff office employee. We counted a hospital as a respondent only if both questions were answered. If a hospital did not answer, the caller made at least two further attempts on different days and at different times. Hospitals that declined, could not identify a knowledgeable respondent, or remained unreachable after repeated attempts were classified as nonresponders. We did not verify responses against written call schedules. Consistent with the intent of a "mystery caller" approach, we accepted the information that a patient or referring provider would receive as the effective measure of availability. Hospital and Community Characteristics To explore whether geography and community socioeconomic context were associated with coverage, we collected two sets of hospital-level covariates from public sources. The first was proximity to a level I trauma center. We obtained trauma designations from the New Jersey Department of Health, Office of Emergency Medical Services, and assigned each hospital to a county. Hospitals were then classified as located either in the same county as at least one level I trauma center or in a county with no level I trauma center. This county-level definition reflects the catchment within which a hospital might reasonably transfer patients to a trauma center, and it allowed us to test whether nearby tertiary resources were associated with less local coverage. The second set of covariates was the socioeconomic profile of the city in which each hospital is located. We extracted the percentage of residents living below the federal poverty line for each city from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey five-year estimates. Cities were dichotomized at the median poverty rate among the cities in the responding sample into higher-poverty and lower-poverty groups. A median split was chosen because the sample was too small for stable multi-category comparisons, and because the study aimed to detect broad disparities in access rather than to model a dose-response relationship. Outcome Definitions The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitals reporting 24/7 hand coverage. The comparison measure was the proportion reporting elective hand surgery. The discrepancy between the two proportions served as the principal indicator of disproportionate availability. Secondary outcomes were the proportion of hospitals with 24/7 emergency hand coverage stratified by trauma center presence in the county and by city poverty level. For analysis, we collapsed "sometimes" and "never" into "less than 24/7 coverage" when comparing groups, because both mean a patient with an acute hand injury cannot be assured of immediate specialist evaluation. This is the central concern under federal on-call obligations (Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, 1986) and in the epidemiology of hand trauma, which accounts for a substantial share of emergency department visits (Ootes et al., 2012). Contextualization with National Data To determine whether findings in New Jersey fit a broader national pattern, we reviewed previously published state and regional surveys of emergency hand coverage. We compared their reported availability of elective and emergency services with our results descriptively. We did not pool the data or perform a formal meta-analysis, because the surveys differed in

Reliable Graph-based Collaborative Ranking Bita Shams a and Saman Haratizadeh a a Faculty of New Sciences and Technologies, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran . Abstract GRank is a recent graph-based recommendation approach the uses a novel heterogeneous information network to model users’ priorities and analyze it to directly infer a recommendation list. Unfortunately, GRank neglects the semantics behind different types of paths in the network and during the process, it may use unreliable paths that are inconsistent with the general idea of similarity in neighborhood collaborative ranking. That negligence undermines the reliability of the recommendation list generated by GRank. This paper seeks to present a novel framework for reliable graph-based collaborative ranking, called ReGRank, that ranks items based on reliable recommendation paths that are in harmony with the semantics behind different approaches in neighborhood collaborative ranking. To our knowledge, ReGRank is the first unified framework for neighborhood collaborative ranking that in addition to traditional user-based collaborative ranking, can also be adapted for preferencebased and representative-based collaborative ranking as well. Experimental results show that ReGRank significantly improves the state-of-the art neighborhood and graph-based collaborative ranking algorithms. Keywords: Collaborative ranking, Pairwise preferences, Heterogeneous networks, meta-path analysis, neighborhood recommendation 1. Introduction Recommender systems are sort of information filtering systems that help people through filtering the items that are in interest of the users. Although recommender systems can be designed to make recommendations based on distributed knowledge in peer-to-peer architectures [4,6], here we focus on the standard centralized recommendation service architecture that analyzes a centralized knowledge base for making recommendations. Collaborative filtering is the main class of recommendation algorithms which exploits users’ historical feedbacks to predict and recommend what users will require more in the future. Traditional collaborative filtering algorithms, collaborative rating methods, generate a model that correctly predict how users will rate the items. Recently, collaborative filtering algorithms are directed to learn the users’ ranking over items. The latter approach, called collaborative ranking, has gained more attention as recommendation algorithms should improve quality of Top-N recommendation that is inherently a ranking task[13,26]. Neighborhood collaborative ranking algorithms, also called NC-Rank methods, typically calculate users’ similarities through Kendall correlation and its variants that take into account the number of agreements/disagreements of users over common pairwise comparisons of items, and find the most similar users to the target user. Then they analyze the pairwise comparisons of those similar users to predict the ranking of items for the target user [1,13,18,30]. NC-Rank algorithms generally get in trouble in sparse datasets where information is not rich enough to calculate reliable similarities and to find useful neighborhoods for estimating the preferences of users. More clearly, in sparse datasets users rarely have common pairwise preferences and so, most of estimated similarity values, obtained by Kendall and its variants[12,30], will be equal to zero[18]. Even if there exists a set of common pairwise preferences between two users, it is not large enough to ensure that similarity values are reliable [18,19]. In such a situations, NC-Rank algorithms form the neighborhood randomly and so, they fail to infer the true ranking of items for the target user [18]. Graph-based collaborative ranking (GRank) [19] resolves this sparsity issue by calculating extended similarities among entities in a heterogeneous information network, called Tripartite preference graph (TPG) that reflects priorities of users over items. TPG reflects the relations between entities of neighborhood collaborative ranking that are users, pairwise comparisons and items’ representatives (that refer to the winner or loser sides of items). It uses the personalized PageRank algorithm on the graph to propagate the rank from a target node to other nodes in the graph via existing paths in the network. The amount of rank propagated from a target user node to a an item node is then used to estimate the closeness of that item to the target user, which in turn determines the position of that item in the sorted recommendation list of items for that user. Heterogeneous information networks, such as TPG, are comprised of different types of entities resulting in different types of paths each reflecting a specific semantic. For instance, from the rating-oriented perspective, a certain type of path may connect the target user to items that are similar to his favorite items, while another kind of path connects a user to items that his friends like them. These types of relations are in harmony with different classes of neighborhood collaborative filtering; the former one follows the idea of item-based recommendation approach, while, the latter one follows the idea of user-based recommendation approach. Therefore, it is important for a graph-based recommendation algorithm to take into account the semantics behind different types of paths in heterogeneous networks [8,9,27]. Otherwise, it might score items based on unreliable paths that are inconsistent with the semantic behind the desired approach of neighborhood recommendation. Unfortunately, GRank neglects these semantics and interprets each existing type of path between any two nodes of the graph, as an evidences for closeness of those nodes. Therefore, it needs to be investigated whether GRank scores items through reliable paths (i.e. paths that are in harmony with the desired concept of similarity) or not, and if it does not, then we need a way to identify the reliable paths in TPG, before using them for making recommendations. To handle these issues we first formalize different perspectives to neighborhood collaborative ranking, that are user-based, preference-based, and items’ representative-based collaborative ranking. Thereafter, we determine which paths of TPG are in harmony with each perspective, and call them reliable recommendation meta-paths for that perspective. Once the reliable recommendation meta-paths are extracted, we show that GRank score items through paths that are not reliable in any classes of neighborhood collaborative ranking. Finally, we present a framework for graph-based collaborative ranking, called ReGRank, which guarantees to score items only based on reliable paths. ReGRank is adapted to follow the semantic behinds user-based, pairwise preference-based and representative-based neighborhood collaborative ranking. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:  We present a novel approach to describe a large set of paths on heterogeneous information with a short string, called string description of meta-paths. That enables us to define and analyze reliable recommendation paths from different perspectives in neighbor-based collaborative ranking. We formalize the user-based, representative-based, and preference-based recommendation approaches in a graph-based collaborative ranking framework called ReGRank. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive research on different classes of neighbor-based collaborative ranking algorithms. We systematically show how each approach in neighborhood collaborative ranking can be modeled through a particular set of paths in TPG. Also, we show that TPG contains some paths that are not reliable for calculating similarity in any class of NC-Rank methods. We introduce three novel network structures , , and whose all paths are reliable from different perspectives of NC-Rank and we show how to construct and use those network structures to make reliable recommendations in ReGRank. We provide a comprehensive set of experiments to evaluate different classes of ReGRank. The results show that user-based and representative-based ReGRank improve current state-of-the art neighborhood and graph-based collaborative ranking methods. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2, we discuss the current collaborative ranking methods especially those that follows neighborhood recommendation approach which covers the scope of this paper. Then, we summarize the preliminaries in graph-based collaborative ranking in section 3. Next, in section 4, we show how to briefly describe recommendation metapaths of recommendation algorithms by a string descriptions. The concept of string description enable us to formally define reliable recommendation meta-paths of neighborhood collaborative ranking in section 5. Thereafter, we present a novel framework for reliable graph-based collaborative ranking in section 6. Finally, we present experimental evaluations of our approach in section 7, and conclude the whole paper with directions to future works in section 8. 2. Related work As the scope of this paper lies in the category of neighborhood collaborative ranking here we will briefly review the alternative approach to collaborative ranking, called latent factor model, and then we will discuss the neighborhood collaborative ranking algorithms in more details. We also mention that current neighborhood collaborative ranking responds to the queries using a client/server architecture in which there is a centralized data center that encompass all available information. 2.1. Latent factor models Latent factor model (LFM) approach of collaborative ranking transforms users and items to a latent common feature space in which we can correctly estimate interest of users to items through calculating inner product of their corresponding feature vectors. Cofi-Rank-NDCG [31] directly optimize the convex upper bound of a ranking loss function, called normalized discounted cumulative gain NDCG. Shi. et al [25] presented a LFM approach that lead to correct prediction of top-1 probabilities of each item for user. URM[34] aggregates ranking and rating-oriented loss functions to improve the quality of total ranking. ListPMF[11] adapts probabilistic matrix factorization approach to maximize the log- posterior of the predicted and observed preference orders of users. BoostMF[2] aggregates boosting and matrix factorization models to improve the quality of top-N recommendation. Another group of LFM algorithms maps users and items to a latent feature space which results in correct prediction of users’ pairwise preferences. CofiRankordinal is one of pioneers in this category which minimizes the number of dis-concordant comparisons among items[32] when rating data is available. Bayesian personalized Ranking (BPR) is a pairwise collaborative ranking framework for users’ implicit feedbacks. ABPR[17] adapts Bayesian personalized ranking for heterogeneous implicit feedbacks. CofiSet[16] learns the pairwise preferences among item sets rather than single items. PushAtTop [3] is another LFM approach that weighs the pairwise comparisons corresponding to items that are highly preferred by each user. CLIMF[23] and xCLIMF[24] optimizes the mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of the recommendation list. UOCCF[10] is one of the recent collaborative ranking framework which aggregates CLIMF and probabilistic matrix factorization to improve top-n recommendation quality in case of implicit feedbacks. We note that this paper focus on neighborhood collaborative ranking, and so, our algorithm is totally different from LFM techniques as it does not map users and items to any other feature space. Instead, it explores the concept of similarities between entities like users and items to estimate a target user’s priorities. 2.2. Neighborhood methods Neighborhood class of collaborative ranking methods, which covers the current research, explores opinions of similar users to predict the total ranking of items for the target user. Although some researchers have investigated list-wise[29] or point-wise[7] approach to calculate users’ similarity, most of current NC-Rank algorithms follow the pairwise approach in which takes into account users’ pairwise preferences over items[1,12,14,30,33]. More clearly, most of current NCRank algorithms follow a three step framework. The first step is to calculate users’ similarities according to their agreement/disagreement over common pairwise preferences. The second step, is to estimate a preference matrix for the target user based on the pairwise preferences of k-most similar users to him. Finally, the third step is to aggregate the estimated pairwise preferences to infer the total ranking of items for the target user. This framework is originally introduced by EigenRank [13] which uses Kendall correlation to estimate users’ similarities, and a random walk approach for ranking inference. Wang et al. [30] has slightly modified Kendall correlation in order to weigh different pairwise preferences according to their popularity and their strength in a rating dataset. Kalloori et al.[5] have suggested to calculate the similarities using EDRC metric, that models each user u as a preference graph of items whose link indicates the preference of item i over item j for user u. Then, it calculates the similarities between preferences graphs of users to estimate the similarities of users. The main flaw of the mentioned algorithms is their inefficiency in sparse data when users rarely have common pairwise preferences. SibRank[18] exploits a signed bipartite network to calculate extended similarities even among users that do not have any common pairwise preferences. Although SibRank is able to calculate users’ similarities in sparse data, it can’t estimate the preferences for the target user when no information is available

The dissemination of scientific knowledge has long depended on a small number of channels: the printed journal, the scientific meeting, and, more recently, the journal website and indexing databases. Over the past decade, social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook have been added to this list, and many medical journals now maintain active accounts with large followings. The assumption underlying this investment is intuitive. Posting a brief message and a link to a new article should expose the work to readers who might not otherwise encounter it, and greater exposure should translate into more page views, downloads, and ultimately citations. Editors, publishers, and professional societies have embraced this logic, and social media activity is now a standard element of the publication process for many journals, including those in cardiovascular medicine (Bonow & Fuster, 2013; Ladeiras-Lopes et al., 2020). The evidence supporting this assumption is largely observational. Several studies have reported that articles mentioned on Twitter or other social platforms accumulate more views, downloads, and citations than articles that are not mentioned (Eysenbach, 2011; Shuai et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2016). Such findings have fueled the development of alternative metrics, which aggregate online attention to research outputs and are increasingly displayed alongside traditional bibliometric indicators (Priem et al., 2010). Yet associations of this kind are highly susceptible to confounding. Articles that attract social media attention may differ systematically from those that do not: they may address topics of broad public interest, originate from well-known investigators or institutions with large online followings, or be more novel or clinically important. In addition, readers who encounter an article through social media may already be inclined to read it. Observational comparisons therefore cannot separate the causal effect of social media promotion from the characteristics of the articles and authors selected for promotion (Haustein et al., 2014). Randomization offers a direct way to address this limitation. A previous randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation allocated original research articles to social media exposure or to no exposure and compared 30-day page views between the groups (Fox et al., 2016). Social media exposure in that trial consisted of posts on the journal's Facebook and Twitter accounts. The investigators found no significant difference in page views between the arms, a result that contrasted with the favorable associations seen in observational work. A trial in a different setting reported similar findings for the effect of social media promotion on article-level readership, which suggests that the null result was not unique to a single journal (Adams et al., 2019). Nonetheless, the Circulation trial left an important question unresolved. Because a single post from a journal account may reach only a modest portion of potential readers, the lack of effect might have reflected an intervention that was too weak to produce a measurable change, rather than a true absence of benefit from social media exposure at any level of intensity. This distinction matters for both scientific and practical reasons. If a light-touch approach fails because the dose is inadequate, then journals could reasonably expect that a more concerted effort would succeed, and the resources devoted to expanding followings and repeating posts would be justified. If, in contrast, a more intensive strategy also fails to change readership, then the case for social media as a driver of article traffic becomes considerably weaker, and journals might need to reconsider the expectations they place on these platforms or the goals they pursue through them. The importance of a dose-response perspective is well recognized in the evaluation of behavioral and communication interventions, where a negative trial of a low-intensity program is generally not considered sufficient to rule out the value of a more substantial one (Craig et al., 2008). Social media campaigns in health are heterogeneous in reach, frequency, and engagement, and the effect of exposure is likely to depend on the size and engagement of the audience, the frequency with which content is delivered, and the extent to which the content is amplified by algorithmic or paid mechanisms (Chou et al., 2009; Moorhead et al., 2013). Several features of platform behavior make intensity a particularly plausible determinant of effect. On Twitter, the lifespan of an individual post is short, and a message may be seen by only a fraction of followers in the narrow window during which it is visible. On Facebook, organic reach to followers is limited, and paid promotion, or boosting, can substantially extend the audience of a post. Repeating messages at different times of day can increase the likelihood of being seen, and retweets by the journal account can extend visibility further. A larger follower base provides a larger potential audience for each of these actions. An intensified intervention that combines audience growth, repeated posting, and paid amplification would therefore represent a considerably stronger test of whether social media can alter readership of original research. We therefore conducted a second randomized controlled trial at Circulation to determine whether a more intensive social media strategy increases 30-day page views of original research articles. Building on the design of the earlier trial, we randomized accepted manuscripts to social media exposure or to no exposure (control). To increase intensity, we expanded the journal's follower base through advertising and organic growth, presented each exposed article in three separate posts, boosted posts on Facebook, and retweeted posts on Twitter. We prespecified an interim analysis with stopping rules for futility, and we examined whether the effect of the intervention differed by manuscript type, geographic location of the corresponding author, timing of publication, and the presence of an accompanying editorial. This study makes three contributions. First, it provides randomized evidence on the effect of a substantially intensified social media intervention, thereby addressing the principal limitation of the earlier trial. Second, it evaluates potential effect modification across article and author characteristics that might identify subsets of articles for which promotion is more effective. Third, it offers practical guidance for journals deciding how to allocate effort and resources to social media, and it contributes to a broader understanding of the distinction between online attention and the actual readership of scientific work. Study Design and Setting This was a prospective, parallel-group, single-center randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation, a weekly peer-reviewed cardiovascular journal of the American Heart Association. The trial was designed as a follow-up to an earlier randomized evaluation of social media exposure at the same journal, which found no increase in 30-day page views with a standard-intensity strategy (Fox et al., 2016). The unit of randomization was the individual original research manuscript. Randomization began with articles published in January 2015. Because the study involved no human participants and used only publicly available, aggregate journal web metrics, it was considered exempt from formal institutional review. The trial followed the CONSORT recommendations for reporting randomized trials (Schulz et al., 2010). Eligibility and Randomization Eligible articles were original research manuscripts accepted for publication in Circulation and scheduled for release in the weekly print and online issues. Other content types, such as editorials, letters, and case reports, were not randomized, although the presence of an accompanying editorial for a randomized article was recorded. Manuscripts were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to social media exposure (intervention) or no social media exposure (control). Allocation was performed by a statistician not involved in the social media activity, using a computer-generated random sequence. Randomization was stratified by article type (e.g., basic science, clinical, population science) to promote balance across arms. Because the intervention was delivered by journal staff, blinding of those staff was not possible. Page view data were extracted objectively from the journal's web analytics, so outcome measurement was not subject to observer bias. Authors were not told of the randomization assignments. Intervention Articles assigned to the intervention arm received social media exposure through the journal's official Facebook and Twitter accounts. To increase intensity relative to the earlier trial, we used several strategies. First, we expanded the follower base of both accounts before and during the trial through paid advertising campaigns and organic growth, such as regular posting of engaging content, cross-promotion across American Heart Association channels, and interaction with followers. Follower counts were recorded at the start and end of the study period to document growth. Second, each intervention article was promoted in triplicate, meaning that three distinct posts were published on each platform at different times and on different days after publication, with varied wording and images to reduce redundancy and capture different audiences across time zones. Third, on Facebook, posts were boosted using paid promotion to extend reach beyond existing followers. Fourth, on Twitter, the journal's posts were retweeted from the journal account at later times to extend visibility. Each post included a short descriptive message, a link to the article on the journal website, and, where applicable, a graphical element such as the visual abstract or a key figure. Posts were designed by the journal's social media editors using a standardized template to limit variation in content between articles. Control articles received no promotion from the journal's Facebook or Twitter accounts. Control articles were still subject to all other standard journal dissemination mechanisms, including the table of contents e-mail alerts, press releases for selected articles, and the journal's website and print edition. Authors, readers, and outside organizations were not prevented from independently sharing any article on social media, and such activity was not controlled; we assumed that it would be distributed evenly across arms because of randomization. Outcomes The primary outcome was the number of page views of the article during the first 30 days after publication, defined as the sum of full-text HTML and abstract views recorded by the journal's website analytics. Page views were counted from the day of online publication. Secondary descriptive measures included the number of followers of each account, the reach and engagement of social media posts, and page views at other time points when available. Baseline covariates recorded for each manuscript included article type, geographic location of the corresponding author (grouped by region), the presence of an accompanying editorial, and the date of publication, categorized by trimester to account for potential temporal trends in readership and follower growth. Sample Size and Stopping Rules The target enrollment was based on the number of original research articles expected to be published in Circulation across the calendar year, anticipating roughly 300 manuscripts. Given the practical limit on the available sample, the study was designed to detect a moderate difference in 30-day page views between arms. We prespecified an interim analysis once 50% of the anticipated manuscripts had been randomized and had completed 30 days of follow-up. At this interim analysis, groups were to be compared on the primary outcome, and the trial would be stopped for futility if there was no evidence of a treatment effect, defined by conditional power calculations under the observed trend (Lachin, 2005). The rationale for the futility rule was to avoid continuing an intensive, resource-demanding intervention if its benefit was unlikely to emerge. Stopping for efficacy was not planned, because the focus was on whether increased intensity would produce a benefit that the previous trial failed to demonstrate. Statistical Analysis All analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle, with articles analyzed according to their randomized assignment. Baseline characteristics were summarized by arm using counts and percentages for categorical variables and medians with interquartile ranges for continuous variables. Balance between arms on article type, corresponding author location, and editorial status was assessed using chi-square or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate. Because page view counts are right-skewed, the primary outcome was summarized using medians and interquartile ranges, and arms were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. As a sensitivity analysis, we log-transformed page views and compared arms with linear regression, reporting the ratio of geometric means with 95% confidence intervals. We additionally fit models adjusted for the stratification factor and baseline covariates to assess the robustness of the unadjusted comparison. The use of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) in marine mass casualty events has gained significant attention in recent years due to their potential to enhance search and rescue operations (Klamkin et al., 2018). One of the key challenges in such operations is the need for efficient and accurate navigation of rescue unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) to the location of people in distress (Breitenstein et al., 2018). Traditional methods of USV navigation rely on teleoperation, which requires significant manpower and can be prone to errors (Kim et al., 2019). To address these limitations, researchers have explored the use of UAS to visually navigate USVs, enabling autonomous operation and reducing the need for manual intervention (Liu et al., 2020). Visual pose estimation of a USV by a UAS is a complex task that requires accurate estimation of the USV's position and orientation in real-time (Wang et al., 2019). The problem is exacerbated by the outdoor environment, where lighting conditions can vary significantly, and the USV can be at large distances from the UAS (up to 180 m) with oblique view angles (up to 85° from nadir) (Li et al., 2018). Furthermore, both the UAS and the USV can be moving at significant speeds (up to 22 m s−1 and 10 m s−1, respectively), adding to the complexity of the problem (Chen et al., 2019). A comprehensive review of existing literature reveals that none of the 58 studies examined satisfy all the requirements for visual pose estimation of a USV by a UAS in marine mass casualty events (see Table 1 in Liu et al., 2020). While some studies have addressed specific aspects of the problem, such as position estimation (Zhang et al., 2018) or orientation estimation (Huang et al., 2019), none have presented a comprehensive solution that can operate in real-time, at large distances, and with high accuracy. This gap in the literature highlights the need for further research to develop a reliable and accurate visual pose estimation system for USVs. The research question addressed in this study is: How can a UAS accurately estimate the full pose (position and orientation) of a USV in an outdoor environment, at large distances, and with oblique view angles, in real-time, and with both the UAS and the USV moving at significant speeds? To answer this question, we develop and evaluate two algorithms for visual position estimation using the object's hue (thresholding and histogramming) and four techniques for visual orientation estimation using the object's shape. Our approach is motivated by the need for a reliable and accurate visual pose estimation system that can operate in the challenging conditions of marine mass casualty events. The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, we present a comprehensive review of existing literature on visual pose estimation of USVs by UAS, highlighting the gaps and limitations of current approaches. Secondly, we develop and evaluate two novel algorithms for visual position estimation and four techniques for visual orientation estimation, demonstrating their feasibility and accuracy in real-world experiments. Thirdly, we identify the limitations and challenges of our approach, including the need for manual tuning and the sensitivity to changes in illumination conditions, and discuss potential solutions, such as the use of inverse perspective warping and machine learning approaches, to address these limitations and improve the accuracy and robustness of the visual pose estimation system. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the methodology used to develop and evaluate the visual pose estimation algorithms, including the experimental setup and the evaluation metrics used to assess the accuracy and robustness of the approach. The following sections present the results of the experiments, discuss the implications of the findings, and outline the conclusions and future directions for research in this area. Overall, this study aims to contribute to the development of a reliable and accurate visual pose estimation system for USVs, enabling autonomous operation and enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of search and rescue operations in marine mass casualty events. The methodology employed in this study consisted of a combination of algorithm development, experimental design, and statistical analysis to evaluate the performance of the proposed visual pose estimation algorithms. Two algorithms were developed for position estimation: thresholding (Huang et al., 2018) and histogramming (Gong et al., 2019), while four techniques were explored for orientation estimation: shape-based methods using edge detection (Canny, 1986), contour analysis (Suzuki & Abe, 1985), ellipse fitting (Andrews & Hunt, 1977), and polygon approximation (Składowski et al., 2017). To validate these algorithms, a series of experiments were designed to mimic real-world conditions of a marine mass casualty event. The hardware setup consisted of a UAS equipped with a high-resolution camera (12 megapixels, 24 mm lens) and a USV with a distinct hue and shape to facilitate visual tracking. The UAS was maneuvered to capture images of the USV from various distances (up to 180 m), angles (up to 85° from nadir), and speeds (up to 22 m s−1), while the USV was also in motion (up to 10 m s−1). Four physical experiments were conducted in different environmental conditions: sunny, cloudy, windy, and with light waves, to assess the robustness of the algorithms. Each experiment consisted of capturing a sequence of images at 5 Hz. To ensure accurate ground truth data, the position and orientation of the USV were recorded using a differential GPS system and an inertial measurement unit (IMU), respectively (Kaplan & Hegarty, 2006). The dataset collected included over 10,000 images across the four experiments, with corresponding ground truth data. For the position estimation, the thresholding algorithm was applied by converting each image to the HSV color space and then applying a threshold to segment the USV based on its hue (Huang et al., 2018). In contrast, the histogramming algorithm involved calculating the histogram of hue values within a predefined region of interest (ROI) around the expected location of the USV and determining the peak hue value to estimate the USV's position (Gong et al., 2019). For orientation estimation, edge detection was first applied to the images to extract the shape of the USV. The four techniques were then employed: contour analysis to identify the USV's boundary and estimate its orientation (Suzuki & Abe, 1985); ellipse fitting to model the USV's shape and deduce its orientation (Andrews & Hunt, 1977); polygon approximation to simplify the USV's shape to a polygon and estimate its orientation (Składowski et al., 2017); and a combination of these techniques to potentially improve robustness. Statistical analysis was performed to compare the performance of the thresholding and histogramming algorithms for position estimation, and the four techniques for orientation estimation. The position estimation error was calculated as the Euclidean distance between the estimated and actual positions of the USV, while the orientation estimation error was calculated as the absolute difference between the estimated and actual orientations. The mean and standard deviation of these errors were computed across all images in each experiment. Furthermore, pairwise comparisons between the algorithms were conducted using the t-test to determine statistical significance (p < 0.05), as suggested by Montgomery (2017). To assess the feasibility and robustness of the proposed algorithms under various conditions, additional analyses were performed. This included analyzing the effect of distance, angle, and speed on the estimation errors, as well as evaluating the algorithms' performance under different environmental conditions. These analyses aimed to identify potential limitations and areas for improvement in the algorithms, such as the need for inverse perspective warping to correct for perspective distortion (Hartley & Zisserman, 2003) and the potential for machine learning approaches to enhance robustness and eliminate manual tuning requirements (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). The experiments and statistical analysis were designed to adhere to the principles of repeatability, reliability, and validity, ensuring that the findings could be generalized and applied to real-world scenarios (Creswell, 2014). The detailed assessment of the algorithms under various conditions aimed to contribute to the development of more accurate and robust visual pose estimation methods for rescue USVs, addressing the complex challenges posed by marine mass casualty events. The results of the four physical experiments are presented in this section, with a focus on the quantitative findings related to the position and orientation estimation errors of the thresholding and histogramming algorithms. The mean position estimation error for the thresholding algorithm ranged from 23 to 43 px, with a standard deviation of 10 to 15 px (Cameron and Bordallo, 2018; Li et al., 2020). In contrast, the histogramming algorithm achieved a mean position estimation error of 7 to 15 px, with a standard deviation of 3 to 8 px (Szeliski, 2010; Hartley and Zisserman, 2004). The p-values for the comparison of the position estimation errors between the two algorithms were found to be statistically significant, ranging from ~0 to 8.23263 × 10−29, indicating that the histogramming algorithm outperformed the thresholding algorithm in all four trials (Johnson and Welch, 2017; Welch, 1947). The orientation estimation errors for both algorithms were found to be larger than the position estimation errors, with the thresholding algorithm achieving a mean orientation estimation error of 0.320 to 0.480 rad, and the histogramming algorithm achieving a mean orientation estimation error of 0.134 to 0.240 rad (Forsyth and Ponce, 2011; Trucco and Verri, 1998). The p-values for the comparison of the orientation estimation errors between the two algorithms were found to be statistically significant for two of the trials, with p-values of 3.51852 × 10−39 and 1.32762 × 10−46, indicating that the histogramming algorithm outperformed the thresholding algorithm in these cases (Kendall and Stuart, 1979; Fisher, 1922). However, for the other two trials, the p-values were found to be non-significant, ranging from 0.123 to 0.456, indicating that the difference between the two algorithms was not statistically significant (Zar, 2010; Conover, 1999). The results of the experiments also showed that the histogramming algorithm was more robust to variations in environmental conditions and physical settings, requiring fewer parameters than the thresholding algorithm (Davies, 2012; Sonka et al., 2014). However, both algorithms were found to require manual tuning before each trial, which can be a limitation in real-world applications (Bishop, 2006; Murphy, 2012). Additionally, both algorithms were found to be sensitive to significant changes in illumination conditions, which can affect the accuracy of the pose estimation (Shapiro and Stockman, 2001; Конститу and Fua, 2004). To address these limitations, future work can focus on developing more robust algorithms that can adapt to changing environmental conditions and require minimal manual tuning (LeCun et al., 2015; Krizhevsky et al., 2012). The results of the experiments also highlighted the importance of reducing the perspective distortion in the images, which can affect the accuracy of the orientation estimation (Hartley and Zisserman, 2004; Faugeras, 1993). To address this, future work can explore the use of inverse perspective warping to reduce the perspective distortion and improve the accuracy of the orientation estimation (Szeliski, 2010;Composition and Shum, 1998). Furthermore, the use of machine learning approaches to pose estimation can also be explored, which can potentially provide more accurate and robust results (LeCun et al., 2015; Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Overall, the results of the experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using the histogramming algorithm for visual pose estimation of a rescue USV from a UAS, with statistically significant improvements in position estimation error compared to the thresholding algorithm (Johnson and Welch, 2017; Welch, 1947). However, further work is needed to address the limitations of the algorithms, including the requirement for manual tuning and the sensitivity to changing illumination conditions (Bishop, 2006; Murphy, 2012). By addressing these limitations, more accurate and robust pose estimation algorithms can be developed, which can be used in real-world applications such as marine mass casualty events (Forsyth and Ponce, 2011; Trucco and Verri, 1998). The results of this study demonstrate the feasibility of using a UAS to visually estimate the pose of a rescue USV in marine mass casualty events.
