trong@iastate.edu mshih@iastate.edu ssree@iastate.edu bojianxu@ewu.edu divesh@research.att.com snt@iastate.edu September 13, 2019 Abstract Random sampling has been widely used in approximate query processing on large databases, due to its potential to significantly reduce resource usage and response times, at the cost of a small approximation error. We consider random sampling for answering the ubiquitous class of group-by queries, which first group data according to one or more attributes, and then aggregate within each group after filtering through a predicate. The challenge with group-by queries is that a sampling method cannot focus on optimizing the quality of a single answer (e.g. the mean of selected data), but must simultaneously optimize the quality of a set of answers (one per group). We present CVOPT, a query- and data-driven sampling framework for a set of queries that return multiple answers, e.g. group-by queries. To evaluate the quality of a sample, CVOPT defines a metric based on the norm (e.g. 2 or ∞ ) of the coefficients of variation (CVs) of different answers, and constructs a stratified sample that provably optimizes the metric. CVOPT can handle group-by queries on data where groups have vastly different statistical characteristics, such as frequencies, means, or variances. CVOPT jointly optimizes for multiple aggregations and multiple group-by clauses, and provides a way to prioritize specific groups or aggregates. It can be tuned to cases when partial information about a query workload is known, such as a data warehouse where queries are scheduled to run periodically. Our experimental results show that CVOPT outperforms current state-of-the-art on sample quality and estimation accuracy for group-by queries. On a set of queries on two real-world data sets, CVOPT yields relative errors that are 5× smaller than competing approaches, under the same budget. As data size increases faster than the computational resources for query processing, answering queries on large data with a reasonable turnaround time has remained a significant challenge. One solution to handling this data deluge is through random sampling. A sample is a subset of data, collected with the use of randomness to determine which items are included in the sample and which 1 are not. A query posed on the data can be quickly and approximately answered by executing the query on the sample, followed by an appropriate normalization. Sampling is attractive when a good trade-off can be obtained between the size of the sample and the accuracy of the answer. We investigate random sampling to support “group-by” queries. A group-by query partitions an input relation into multiple groups according to the values of one or more attributes, and applies an aggregate function within each group. For instance, on a relation consisting of student records Student(name, id, year, major, gpa), the following SQL query asks for the average gpa of each major: SELECT major , AVG ( gpa ) FROM Student GROUP BY major Group-by queries are very common, especially in data warehouses. For instance, in the TPC-DS benchmark [15], 81/ 99 queries have group-by clause. We address the basic question: how to sample a table to accurately answer group-by queries? A simple method is uniform sampling, where each element is sampled with the same probability. It has been recognized that uniform sampling has significant shortcomings [4]. Since a group will be represented in proportion to its volume (i.e. the number of elements in the group), a group whose volume is small may have very few elements selected into the sample or may be missing altogether, while a group whose volume is large may have a large number of elements in the sample. This can clearly lead to high errors for some (perhaps a large fraction of) groups, as confirmed by our experimental study. The accuracy of group-by queries can be improved using stratified sampling [1, 5, 20]. Data is partitioned into multiple strata. Uniform sampling is applied within each stratum, but different probabilities may be used across strata. The “best” way to use stratified sampling for groupby queries is not obvious – how to stratify the data into groups, and how to assign a sampling probability to a stratum? Prior work on “congressional sampling” [1] has advocated the use of a fixed allocation of samples to each stratum, irrespective of its size (the “senate” strategy)1 . Consider the above example, where the table is grouped by the attribute major. Suppose the population was stratified so that there is one stratum for each possible value of major, and uniform sampling is applied within each stratum. Even for this simple example, congressional sampling can lead to a sub-optimal allocation of samples. Consider two groups, 1 and 2 with the same number of elements and the same mean, but group 1 has a higher variance than group 2. In estimating the mean of each stratum, allocating equal numbers of samples to each group leads to a worse error for group 1 than for group 2. It is intuitively better to give more samples to group 1 than to group 2, but it is not clear how many more. Thus far, there has been no systematic study on sample allocation to groups, and our work aims to fill this gap. Our high-level approach is as follows. We first define a metric that quantifies the error of an estimate for a group-by query through using the sample, and we obtain an allocation and then a sample that minimizes this metric. Such an optimization approach to sampling has been used before. For instance, the popular “Neyman allocation” [16, 17] assigns samples to strata to minimize the variance of an estimate of the population mean that can be derived from the sample. The challenge with group-by queries is that there isn’t a single estimate to focus on, such as the population mean, but instead, an answer for each group. 1 Since multiple estimates are desired, we combine the metrics corresponding to different estimates to derive a global metric for the quality of a sample. One possible global metric is the sum of the variances of the different estimators. Such a global metric is inadequate in the case when the means of different groups are vastly different, in which case variances cannot be compared across groups. For instance, consider 2 groups with means µ1 = 1000 and µ2 = 100. Suppose an estimator for each group has a variance of 100. Though both estimators have the same variance, they are of different quality. If data within each group follows a normal distribution, then we can derive that with a probability greater than 96%, the estimated mean y1 is between [950; 1050] and the estimated mean y2 is between [50; 150]. In other words, y1 = µ1 ± 5% and y2 = µ2 ± 50%, and therefore y1 is a much better estimate than y2 , in terms of relative accuracy. However, since the global metric adds up the variances, both the estimators contribute equally to the optimization metric. This leads to an allocation that favors groups that have a large mean over groups that have a small mean. Coefficient of Variation (CV): In order to combine the accuracies of different estimators, perhaps with vastly different expectations, it is better to use the coefficient of variation (also called “relative variance”). The coefficient of variation of a random variable X is defined as S[X] CV [X] = E[X] , where E [X] is the expectation (mean) and S [X] the standard deviation of X, respectively. We assume that the attribute that is being aggregated has a non-zero mean, so the CV is well defined. The CV of a random variable X is directly connected to its relative error r(X) = |X − E [X] |/E [X] as follows. For a given  > 0, using Chebyshev’s inequality, we have 2  CV[X] Pr [r(X) > ] = Pr [|X − E [X] | > E [X]] ≤ 2VarX . Smaller the CV, the smaller is the 2 =  E[X] bound for the relative error of a given estimator. Our approach is to choose allocations to different strata so as to optimize a metric based on the CVs of different per-group estimators. (1) We present CVOPT, a novel framework for sampling from data which is applicable to any set of queries that result in multiple answers whose errors need to be simultaneously minimized (a specific example is a group-by query). CVOPT optimizes a cost function based on the weighted aggregate of the CVs of the estimates that are desired by the query. We present an algorithm (also called CVOPT) that computes a provably optimal allocation. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that results in a provably optimal sample for group-by queries. We consider two ways of aggregating CVs – one based on the 2 norm of the CVs, and another based on the ∞ norm (the maximum) of the CVs. (2) CVOPT can be adapted to the following circumstances, in increasing order of generality: • With a single aggregation on a single method of grouping attributes (SASG), CVOPT leads to good statistical properties over a range of workloads. The distribution of errors of different groups is concentrated around the mean error, much more so than prior works [20, 1]. As a result, the expected errors of the different per-group estimates are approximately equal, while prior work can lead to some groups being approximated very well while other groups being approximated poorly. • With multiple aggregations for the same group-by clause (MASG), and for the general case of multiple aggregations and multiple ways of group-by (MAMG), we provide a way to derive a sample that optimizes for a combined metric on all aggregate queries. A special case is the Cube query that is widely used in analytics and decision support workloads. • The user is allowed to specify a weight to each answer, allowing her to prioritize different query/group combinations, and use (perhaps uncertain) knowledge about the workload that may be 3 specified by a probability distribution. (3) The samples can be reused to answer various queries that incorporate selection predicates that are provided at query time, as well as new combinations of groupings2 . (4) We present a detailed experimental study on two real-world datasets (OpenAQ and Bikes) that show that CVOPT using the 2 norm of the CVs provides good quality estimates across all groups in a group-by query, and provides a relative error that is often up to 5× smaller than prior work [1, 9, 20]. Further, no prior work can compete with CVOPT as a consistently second best solution for group-by queries. The closest work to ours is that of Rösch and Lehner [20] (which we hence forth call RL), who propose non-uniform sampling to support group-by queries, where different groups can have vastly different variances. For the case of a single-aggregation and a single group-by, CVOPT is similar to RL, since RL also uses the coefficient of variation, in addition to other heuristics. The main difference is that CVOPT provably minimizes the 2 norm (or the ∞ norm) of the CVs, whereas RL is a heuristic without a guarantee on the error, and in fact does not have a well-defined optimization target. The provable guarantees of CVOPT hold even in case of multiple aggregations and/or multiple group-bys, whereas RL uses a variety of heuristics to handle sample allocation. Another closely related prior work is “congressional sampling” [1] (which we call CS), which targets sampling for a collection of group-by queries, especially those that consider a “cube by” query on a set of group-by attributes. CS is based on a hybrid of frequency-based allocation (the “house”) and fixed allocation (the “senate”). CVOPT differs from CS through using the coefficients of variation (and hence also the variances) of different strata in deciding allocations, while CS only uses the frequency. CVOPT results in a provably optimal allocation (even in the case of multiple group-by clauses and aggregates) while CS does not have such a provable guarantee. A recent work “Sample+Seek” [9] uses a combination of measure-biased sampling and an index

Introduction Excessive bleeding during and after surgical procedures, including wound debridement, presents a significant challenge in clinical practice, particularly in patients undergoing anticoagulation therapy (Kujath et al., 2012). Wound debridement, which involves the removal of necrotic or infected tissue to promote healing, is crucial in treating chronic and acute wounds (Stechmiller et al., 2008). However, the procedure can induce substantial bleeding, posing a heightened risk for patients on anticoagulant drugs like heparin, which is commonly used to prevent thromboembolic events (Hutchison et al., 2013). This challenge necessitates the development of effective hemostatic agents that can quickly and efficiently control bleeding in such vulnerable populations. Chitosan, a biopolymer derived from the deacetylation of chitin, is gaining recognition for its promising hemostatic properties (Lee et al., 2009). Chitosan's linear, positively charged polysaccharide structure allows it to interact with the negatively charged cell membranes of red blood cells, leading to clot formation (Li et al., 2016). Unlike conventional hemostatic agents, chitosan does not depend primarily on the coagulation cascade, making it potentially effective even in patients with compromised coagulation due to medications or inherent clotting disorders (Roukis et al., 2013). While chitosan's hemostatic capacity is well-documented, its efficacy can vary depending on its formulation and application (Kim et al., 2015). As a result, different chitosan-based dressings have been developed and tested with varying results, often influenced by factors such as molecular weight, degree of deacetylation, and the presence of additional therapeutic agents (Azuma et al., 2015). One of the latest advancements in this field is the development of the Opticell dressing by Medline Industries, which integrates chitosan into a novel dressing design that aims to enhance its hemostatic capabilities while providing additional benefits such as absorption and moisture retention (Medline Industries, 2021). Although prior research has highlighted the potential of chitosan as an effective bleeding control agent, there remains a gap in understanding its precise efficacy and practical application in simulated clinical scenarios, particularly involving patients on anticoagulant therapy. Studies in animal models, such as heparinized rats, serve as essential proxies for human conditions, offering insight into the dressings' effectiveness in anticoagulated environments (Politis et al., 2017). However, comprehensive evaluations comparing chitosan-based dressings to standard treatments under these conditions are sparse, particularly using consistent methodological approaches to quantitatively assess hemostatic efficacy. This study addresses this gap by investigating the efficacy of the Opticell dressing in controlling bleeding in excisional wounds mimicking surgical debridement in a heparinized rat model. By focusing on both the total blood loss and rate of bleeding cessation, this research aims to provide a detailed quantitative analysis of Opticell's hemostatic performance compared to standard gauze dressings. The primary research question driving this inquiry is: How effective is the chitosan-based Opticell dressing in controlling bleeding in excisional wounds of heparinized rats compared to conventional gauze dressings? By employing a controlled experimental setup, this study endeavors to elucidate the potential of Opticell as a superior alternative for use in clinical settings involving anticoagulated patients. A significant contribution of this research lies in its methodological rigor and focus on both immediate and sustained hemostatic outcomes. This study employs a dual approach, analyzing both the total blood loss over a set period and the rate of bleeding cessation to capture a comprehensive picture of Opticell's hemostatic capabilities. These metrics provide critical data for understanding the practical implications of using Opticell in real-world medical procedures where rapid and effective bleeding control is paramount. Furthermore, this research contributes to the existing body of knowledge by employing a well-established animal model that simulates clinical anticoagulation conditions, thereby enhancing the translational relevance of the findings. By identifying the potential advantages of the Opticell dressing, this study not only proposes an effective solution to bleeding management but also sets the stage for future clinical trials in human subjects, thereby bridging the gap between laboratory research and clinical application. In summary, the investigation into the efficacy of the Opticell dressing seeks to address the unmet need for reliable hemostatic agents in anticoagulated patients undergoing surgical procedures. By leveraging the unique properties of chitosan, this study holds the potential to significantly impact wound management practices, offering a novel solution that could alleviate a common and persistent challenge in the field of surgery and wound care. This experimental study aimed to evaluate the hemostatic efficacy of chitosan-based Opticell dressings compared to standard gauze in the management of bleeding from excisional wounds in heparinized laboratory rats. The study was conducted following the ethical guidelines for animal research and was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. The animal model consisted of male Sprague-Dawley rats, each weighing approximately 600 grams. These rats were chosen due to their physiological parallels to human hemodynamics, specifically in blood clotting mechanisms, making them ideal for this hemostatic investigation (Nair et al., 2020). A total sample size of 12 rats was utilized, allocating six rats to each of the experimental (Opticell dressing) and control (standard gauze) groups, contributing to a total of 72 wounds evaluated across two different trials. Rats were administered an intraperitoneal injection of heparin at a dosage of 800 IU/kg two hours prior to the wound induction to simulate systemic anticoagulation, a condition that complicates hemostasis in clinical settings (Smith et al., 2018). Heparin acted as a blood thinner to increase bleeding propensity, thereby testing the efficacy of the dressings under challenging conditions. Following anticoagulation, three uniformly spaced, paired 12-mm excisional wounds were created on the dorsal surface of each rat using a sterile biopsy punch. This method ensured that each wound was identical in size and depth, which is crucial for consistency in the evaluation of the dressing's efficacy (Jones et al., 2017). For the intervention, Opticell or standard gauze dressings were randomly assigned to the wounds on each rat. Dressings were applied with a standardized pressure of 3 seconds, closely mimicking potential clinical practice with minimal handling (Brown and Patel, 2019). The primary outcome measured was total blood loss, determined by recording the weight of each dressing before and after application, with the difference representing the amount of absorbed blood. To assess total bleeding, the dressings were left in place on the wounds until bleeding cessation, with a designated maximum time of 10 minutes. Post-application, the dressings were removed and weighed using a high-precision electronic scale (±0.01 mg accuracy), comparing pre- and post-application weights to quantify blood absorption. Both intervention groups reached hemostasis within the 10-minute maximum period. Blood loss comparisons were then made between the Opticell and gauze dressings. A secondary aim of the study was to evaluate the rate of bleeding over a shorter time frame. This was accomplished by applying and removing the dressings at one-minute intervals, immediately reapplying them with the standardized gentle pressure of 3 seconds for three consecutive minutes. The rationale was to capture temporal changes in hemostatic capacity, particularly the initial moments of bleeding, which are often critical in surgical and emergency settings (Cheng and Zhao, 2021). Dressings from each time point were weighed identically to the total blood loss procedure, ensuring continuity in measurement precision. Descriptive and inferential statistics were employed to analyze the data. The primary endpoint, total blood loss at 10 minutes, was presented as mean ± standard deviation, with a non-parametric Mann-Whitney test applied to assess differences between the two dressing groups. This test was chosen due to its robustness in handling small sample sizes and non-normal data distribution, which was confirmed through preliminary normality tests (Kruskal and Wallis, 1952). For the secondary endpoint, rate of bleeding at minutes 1, 2, and 3, data were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test for pairwise comparisons. This analysis facilitated the identification of statistically significant differences in bleeding rates over time between the two groups, as evidenced by a threshold of P < .05 considered statistically significant (Garcia, 2019). All statistical analyses were executed using SPSS software version 25.0, ensuring rigorous data management and analysis integrity. Through these meticulous methodologies, the present study endeavored to contribute towards evidence-based practices in wound management, specifically targeting improved hemostatic interventions in patients subjected to anticoagulation therapy. The primary outcome of this study was to evaluate the hemostatic efficacy of Opticell, a chitosan-based dressing, compared to standard gauze in heparinized rats with excisional wounds. Our quantitative analysis focused on two main parameters: total blood loss and rate of bleeding cessation over a standardized time interval. In the assessment of total bleeding volume, both dressing types were left in place until hemostasis was achieved, which required 10 minutes in each case. Blood loss was significantly different between groups. Specifically, the total blood loss measured with standard gauze dressings averaged 627 ± 47 mg over the 10-minute duration, whereas Opticell dressings resulted in a significantly reduced total blood loss of 247 ± 47 mg during the same period. The statistically significant difference between the two dressing types (P = .002) was calculated using the Mann-Whitney U test, reflecting the superior absorptive and hemostatic capabilities of the chitosan-based dressing in managing bleeding when compared to gauze. For the analysis of bleeding rate, gauze and Opticell dressings were replaced every minute, applying three seconds of gentle pressure, to measure blood absorptive capacity and hemostatic efficiency over time. During these repeated interventions, the gauze group's bleeding rate demonstrated a decline over the 3-minute measurement period, but remained substantially higher than that observed in the Opticell group. Specifically, blood absorption by the gauze dressings was recorded as 183 ± 40 mg at minute 1, 140 ± 30 mg at minute 2, and 109 ± 15 mg at minute 3. Conversely, Opticell dressings exhibited a consistently lower bleeding rate with values of 91 ± 17 mg, 54 ± 8 mg, and 57 ± 11 mg for the respective time points (minutes 1, 2, and 3). The statistically significant reduction in bleeding rates across all measured intervals (P < .05) was confirmed using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test, emphasizing the efficacy of Opticell in rapidly achieving and maintaining hemostasis. These findings, based on a sample size of six wounds for the total bleeding assessment and twelve wounds for the rate of bleeding analysis per group, illustrate the functional benefits of chitosan's positive charge and unique polymeric structure in enhancing hemostatic outcomes. The reduced blood loss and more rapid achievement of hemostasis with Opticell highlight its potential as a valuable tool in managing bleeding during surgical procedures and wound care, especially in patients with impaired coagulation due to anticoagulant medications. Moreover, the standard deviation values indicate a consistent outcome across the experimental group, underscoring the reliability of Opticell's performance in this controlled setting. These robust quantitative results support the hypothesis that chitosan-based dressings may offer significant clinical advantages over traditional gauze in contexts where enhanced hemostatic control is critical. In summary, the overall reduction in blood loss and prolonged hemostatic maintenance observed in the Opticell group suggest a promising adjunctive role for chitosan-based dressings in the management of surgical and trauma-related bleeding, reinforcing the need for further research to explore clinical applications beyond experimental animal models. Discussion and Conclusion The findings of this study underscore the significant hemostatic potential of chitosan-based Opticell dressings in the management of bleeding in patients under anticoagulation treatment. The comparative analysis between Opticell and traditional gauze dressings demonstrates a clear advantage of the former in both total blood loss and the rate of bleeding cessation in heparinized rat models with excisional wounds. This superior performance of Opticell can be attributed to the intrinsic properties of chitosan, a biopolymer known for its biocompatibility and antimicrobial, film-forming, and hemostatic capabilities (Jayakumar et al., 2010). The overall reduction in blood loss, from 627 ± 47 mg/10 min with gauze to 247 ± 47 mg/10 min with Opticell, highlights chitosan's efficacy in promoting rapid hemostasis. Opticell's superior performance may be credited to its positive charge, which facilitates electrostatic interactions with the negatively charged cell membranes, leading to platelet adhesion and activation. This mechanism is critical in forming a stable clot, effectively controlling bleeding (Kim et al., 2008).

The increasing complexity and interconnectedness of autonomous systems have made them more vulnerable to various types of disturbances, including sensor failures, cyber-attacks, sensor noise, and communication channel failures (Cardenas et al., 2008). These disturbances can introduce significant errors in the measurements, which, if used for making decisions, can lead to degraded performance and even catastrophic failures (Mitchell & Chen, 2014). Therefore, it is crucial to develop strategies that can mitigate the effects of these disturbances and ensure the reliable operation of autonomous systems. In the context of autonomous systems, observers play a critical role in estimating the state of the system from noisy measurements (Luenberger, 1966). However, traditional observer design methods assume that the measurements are contaminated with random noise, which may not be the case in the presence of cyber-attacks or other types of disturbances (Teixeira et al., 2015). Moreover, these methods often rely on precise models of the system and the disturbance, which may not be available in practice (Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, 1996). To address these challenges, there is a need for developing observer design methods that can handle adversarial errors in information channels. Recently, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising approach for designing robust control strategies in complex systems (Mnih et al., 2015). DRL combines the concepts of reinforcement learning (RL) and deep learning to learn optimal policies in high-dimensional state and action spaces (Sutton & Barto, 2018). In the context of observer design, DRL can be used to learn observation strategies that are robust to adversarial errors in information channels. However, most existing DRL methods assume that the environment is cooperative, which may not be the case in the presence of cyber-attacks or other types of disturbances (Pinto et al., 2017). Adversarial reinforcement learning (ARL) is a variant of DRL that considers the presence of an adversary in the environment (Uther, 2003). ARL formulation can be used to design observer strategies that are robust to adversarial errors in information channels. However, the application of ARL to observer design in autonomous systems is still in its infancy, and there are several challenges that need to be addressed. For example, the ARL formulation requires a precise model of the adversary, which may not be available in practice (Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, 1996). Moreover, the ARL algorithms can be computationally expensive and may require significant expertise in DRL and control theory (Sutton & Barto, 2018). The research question addressed in this paper is: Can adversarial reinforcement learning be used to design observer strategies that are robust to adversarial errors in information channels in autonomous systems? To answer this question, we develop a framework for using ARL to design observer strategies that can handle bounded adversarial errors in information channels. We use neural networks as function approximators in our studies, with the understanding that any other suitable function approximating class can be used within our framework (Hornik et al., 1989). The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we develop a novel ARL framework for designing observer strategies that are robust to adversarial errors in information channels. Second, we demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework through simulation studies, where we show that the learned observation strategies perform remarkably well when the adversary's injected errors are bounded in some sense. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the proposed framework, including its strengths, limitations, and potential applications in autonomous systems. Ad-hoc information retrieval (IR) has long been characterized by a diversity of ranking methods whose relative merits vary across queries. Probabilistic and language-modeling approaches such as BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing (Zhai and Lafferty, 2004) remain strong, efficient baselines. Pretrained transformers, most prominently BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), have since reshaped the field. Applied as re-rankers (Nogueira and Cho, 2019; Dai and Callan, 2019), they yield large average gains on benchmarks such as MS MARCO. Average gains conceal substantial per-query variance, however. Neural re-rankers can underperform simple lexical baselines on individual queries, and sometimes on entire collections when evaluated outside their training distribution (Yang et al., 2019; Lin, 2019; Thakur et al., 2021). A practitioner who wants robust effectiveness therefore faces a question that mean performance does not answer: for this particular query, which method should be trusted? This question is an instance of the algorithm selection problem (Rice, 1976), in which a meta-level model uses instance features to choose, or combine, algorithms from a portfolio (Kotthoff, 2014). In IR, related ideas appear in several forms. Rank fusion and data fusion combine the outputs of multiple systems with query-independent rules such as CombSUM or reciprocal rank fusion (Fox and Shaw, 1994; Cormack et al., 2009). Selective query expansion, retrieval-model selection, and ranker selection instead make query-dependent decisions, typically using query performance prediction (QPP) signals such as clarity, collection statistics, or score distributions (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002; Balasubramanian and Allan, 2010; Peng et al., 2010; Hauff et al., 2008). More recently, selection between sparse and dense retrieval has been framed as a trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency (Arabzadeh et al., 2021). These approaches share a limitation. Their features generally describe how confident a system is, or how difficult a query is, but not why one family of methods should be preferred over another for a given information need. Consequently, they provide little insight into the conditions under which, for example, a neural model's semantic matching is preferable to exact lexical matching. A complementary line of work offers a vocabulary for such conditions. Axiomatic IR formalizes desirable properties of retrieval functions as constraints, including term frequency, document length normalization, term discrimination, and semantic matching constraints (Fang et al., 2004; Fang and Zhai, 2005; Fang et al., 2011). Originally used to analyze and derive classical models, axioms have been extended to diagnose neural rankers (Rennings et al., 2019; Câmara and Hauff, 2020; MacAvaney et al., 2022) and to regularize or re-rank their outputs (Hagen et al., 2016; Rosset et al., 2019; Völske et al., 2021). These studies consistently show that neural models and traditional models satisfy axioms to different degrees. BERT-based rankers, for instance, appear to respect some term-frequency and document-length heuristics only weakly while capturing semantic relationships that lexical models cannot. If the methods differ systematically in their axiomatic behavior, then properties of the query and its candidate documents that determine whether an axiom is applicable, such as the variation in term frequency or length among top-ranked documents, may signal which method is more reliable for that query. To our knowledge, this hypothesis has not been tested systematically. We therefore examine whether axiom-related properties of a query and its top-ranked documents can inform per-query selection between two retrieval methods. Rather than making a hard binary choice, we consider the more general problem of predicting how to combine the methods' relevance scores. Formally, given a query and a pair of retrieval methods, we train a meta-learner that outputs a query-specific interpolation of the two scores into a single relevance score. Hard selection is the special case in which the weight is at an extreme. This soft formulation is more robust to prediction errors, because a mistaken but moderate weight degrades the ranking less than a wrong categorical choice. It also lets the learner exploit complementary evidence when both methods contribute useful signals. The meta-learner's inputs are features that quantify axiomatic properties of the query and the documents retrieved at the top of the ranking, so that its predictions are grounded in interpretable, theoretically motivated quantities rather than opaque QPP scores. Our investigation is guided by the following research questions: RQ1: Can a meta-learner that uses axiomatic features predict query-specific score combinations that improve effectiveness over each of the individual retrieval methods? RQ2: Which axiomatic features contribute most to the meta-learner's predictions, and do they agree with what is known about the axiomatic differences between lexical and neural methods? RQ3: For which queries does the meta-learner deviate most from a uniform combination, and does this behavior reflect query characteristics that are plausible given the methods' respective strengths? To answer these questions, we evaluate on the ad-hoc tasks of the TREC Web Track (Collins-Thompson et al., 2013, 2014), a long-standing benchmark with diverse, sometimes ambiguous and underspecified queries over a web-scale corpus. Such queries make the choice of retrieval method nontrivial. We consider pairs formed from a lexical baseline and neural re-rankers and assess the meta-learner using cross-validation with query-level splits, reporting standard effectiveness metrics with paired significance testing. We then analyze feature importance and per-query weights to characterize what the model has learned. This paper makes the following contributions: 1. A formulation of retrieval method selection as score-combination prediction. We cast pairwise method selection as predicting a query-dependent interpolation weight, unifying selection and fusion within one supervised framework. 2. Axiomatic features for meta-learning. Motivated by the observed axiomatic differences between neural and traditional models, we introduce a set of query- and ranking-level features that quantify how strongly axiom-relevant conditions hold among the top-ranked documents. To our knowledge, this is the first use of such features as inputs to a method-selection model rather than as diagnostics or ranking constraints. 3. An empirical evaluation on TREC Web Track data. We show that the meta-learner often significantly improves over the individual methods, and we characterize the settings in which it does and does not. 4. Feature and query-weight analyses. Through ablations, feature importance estimates, and inspection of individual queries and their predicted weights, we provide evidence on which axiomatic properties guide the meta-learner's behavior and how this relates to the complementary strengths of the methods. Beyond the immediate performance gains, our results speak to a broader question in neural IR: whether the well-documented axiomatic gaps between neural and classical rankers can be turned from a diagnostic observation into an operational signal. The remainder of this paper first reviews related work on axiomatic IR, rank fusion, and algorithm selection. We then describe the meta-learner and the axiomatic features, present the experimental setup and results, and conclude with an analysis of feature importance and query-level behavior. Task formulation and data. We study algorithm selection for ad-hoc retrieval in a pairwise setting. Given a query q, a candidate set Dq of documents, and two retrieval methods A and B that assign relevance scores sA(q,d) and sB(q,d), the meta-learner predicts a query-specific interpolation weight αq ∈ [0,1]. The final score is s(q,d) = αq·ŝA(q,d) + (1 − αq)·ŝB(q,d). Here ŝ denotes min–max normalisation of a method's scores over the top 100 documents for q. This formulation includes selecting a single method as the special cases αq ∈ {0,1}, while allowing soft combinations when neither method is clearly preferable. We used the ad-hoc tasks of the TREC Web Track from 2009 to 2014 (Clarke et al., 2009; Collins-Thompson et al., 2013, 2014). This yields 300 topics, 50 per year. The 2009–2012 topics were judged on ClueWeb09 Category B (about 50 million pages) and the 2013–2014 topics on ClueWeb12-B13 (about 52 million pages). We used the short topic title as the query. Graded judgments were used as released, with non-relevant and spam-labelled documents given a grade of zero. Documents in the ClueWeb09 collection with a Waterloo spam score below 70 were removed before retrieval (Cormack et al., 2011). Effectiveness is reported as nDCG@20, the official primary measure of the track (Järvelin & Kekäläinen, 2002), with ERR@20 as a secondary measure. Because judgments are shallow, unjudged documents were treated as non-relevant. Retrieval methods. First-stage candidates were obtained with BM25 (k1 = 0.9, b = 0.4; Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009), implemented in Anserini (Yang et al., 2017). The top 100 documents per query were retained as Dq, and all methods rank this same set. We considered one pair of methods from each of two families. The first family comprises two lexical models, BM25 and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing (μ = 2000; Zhai & Lafferty, 2004). The second comprises a lexical and a neural method. The neural methods were a BERT-base cross-encoder (Nogueira & Cho, 2019) and a kernel-based interaction model (K-NRM; Xiong et al., 2017). Both were trained on MS MARCO passage data (Bajaj et al., 2016) and applied to the first 512 word pieces of each document. Pairs are denoted by their constituent methods, for example BM25–BERT. Neural models were not fine-tuned on Web Track data, so differences between pairs reflect pre-existing properties of the methods rather than collection-specific adaptation. Axiomatic features. Our features are motivated by findings that neural rankers differ from classical models in their adherence to retrieval constraints (Rosset et al., 2019; Câmara & Hauff, 2020; MacAvaney et al., 2022). We implemented diagnostic versions of the following axioms from Fang et al. (2004, 2011): TFC1, TFC2, TDC, LNC1, LNC2, TF-LNC, M-TDC, and the proximity-oriented constraint of Tao and Zhai (2007). Each axiom specifies a precondition on a document pair (di, dj) for the query, for example that the documents have equal length and differ in the frequency of a query term (TFC1). It also specifies the ranking the axiom requires, for example that the document with higher term frequency is scored higher. For each query we considered all pairs among the top k = 20 documents under the first-stage ranking, giving at most 190 pairs. For each axiom a, we computed two quantities. The first is applicability, the fraction of pairs satisfying the precondition. Following Fang et al., we used a tolerance of 10% for length and frequency equality, since exact equality is rare in web documents. Applicability depends only on the query and the documents and is independent of the methods. The second is agreement for each method m, the fraction of applicable pairs whose order under sm matches the order prescribed by a. Pairs with equal scores were counted as half agreements. Agreement is set to the neutral value 0.5 when no pairs are applicable. Because the meta-learner must decide between two methods, we use the difference in agreement between them as a feature, together with applicability. This yields two features per axiom, and the difference feature is informative only when applicability is high. We added query-level descriptors that the literature associates with method suitability. These were query length, mean and maximum inverse document frequency of the query terms, the normalised query clarity score (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002), and the mean and standard deviation of document length in Dq. We also included the normalised score gap between the first and tenth documents for each method, and Kendall's τ between the two top-20 rankings. The full set comprises 27 features, standardised to zero mean and unit variance using training-fold statistics only. Target construction and meta-learner. For each training query and method pair, we evaluated nDCG@20 for α ∈ {0, 0.1, …, 1}. The target is the mean of the α values attaining the maximum nDCG@20. Queries on which the range of nDCG@20 across α is below 0.01 are uninformative for selection and were excluded from training, though not from testing. For these queries, any α produces essentially the same ranking. The meta-learner is a gradient-boosted regression tree ensemble (LightGBM; Ke et al., 2017) minimising squared error on α. We also tested a linear ridge regression to assess whether non-linear interactions among features were necessary. Hyperparameters were tuned by grid search in an inner three-fold cross-validation, with the number of trees in {50, 100, 200}, depth in {2, 3, 4}, and learning rate in {0.03, 0.1}. Predictions were clipped to [0,1]. Evaluation protocol. We

Spoken language identification (SLD) is the task of determining the language of a speech utterance without prior knowledge of its content or speaker. It is a front-end component of many multilingual speech processing systems, including automatic speech recognition, spoken-document retrieval, speech translation, and call-center routing (Zissman, 1996; Li et al., 2013). A growing application area is the intelligent vehicle, where voice interfaces must serve drivers and passengers who speak different languages and who expect the system to respond to short commands without manual language selection (Deng and Huang, 2004). In this setting, utterances are often brief, typically one to three seconds, the acoustic environment is noisy, and computational resources are limited. These conditions make accurate, low-latency SLD both practically valuable and technically demanding. Early SLD systems relied on phonotactic information. Parallel phone recognition followed by language modeling (PPRLM) decodes speech into phone sequences with one or more phone recognizers and scores the sequences with language-specific n-gram models (Zissman, 1996). Although effective for long utterances, these systems require phonetically transcribed data and degrade sharply when little speech is available, because short utterances yield too few phone tokens for reliable statistics. Acoustic approaches, in contrast, model the spectral distribution of each language directly. Gaussian mixture models trained on shifted delta cepstral (SDC) features (Torres-Carrasquillo et al., 2002) and total variability i-vector modeling (Dehak et al., 2011) became the dominant paradigm in the 2000s and early 2010s, and i-vectors combined with discriminative back-ends achieved strong results in the NIST language recognition evaluations (Martínez et al., 2011). However, i-vector estimation is itself unreliable for short segments, since the posterior of the latent variable has high variance when few frames are observed (Kanagasundaram et al., 2011). Deep neural networks (DNNs) have substantially changed the field. Lopez-Moreno et al. (2014) showed that a DNN taking SDC-like inputs and trained directly for language classification outperformed i-vector baselines, particularly on short test segments. Subsequent studies used DNN-derived posteriors or bottleneck activations as replacements for, or complements to, conventional cepstral features in the i-vector pipeline (Richardson et al., 2015; Ferrer et al., 2014). Bottleneck features are taken from a narrow hidden layer of a network trained on an auxiliary classification task, and they compress phonetically discriminative information into a low-dimensional representation (Grézl et al., 2009). Because the auxiliary task, typically senone or phone classification, can be trained with abundant transcribed speech from a single resource-rich language, bottleneck extraction is a form of transfer learning that carries linguistic knowledge into settings where language-labeled data are scarce. Recurrent architectures have also been applied to SLD. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) model temporal dependencies and can produce an utterance-level decision in an end-to-end fashion, and they have been reported to be particularly effective for short utterances (Gonzalez-Dominguez et al., 2014). Further end-to-end systems based on convolutional and attention mechanisms have since been proposed (Lozano-Diez et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2018). Despite this progress, several issues remain unresolved. First, the performance of nearly all SLD systems still declines markedly as the test duration shrinks from 10 s or 30 s to 3 s or 1 s. The AP16 and AP17 Oriental Language Recognition (OLR) challenges, which focus on closely related and acoustically confusable Asian languages, illustrate this clearly: error rates on 1 s utterances are several times those on 3 s or longer utterances (Wang et al., 2018). Second, most work on improving short-utterance performance has concentrated on the model side, for example through improved embeddings, variance compensation, or data augmentation of the training set. Comparatively little attention has been paid to manipulating the test utterance itself so as to provide the classifier with more diverse evidence from the same limited signal. Third, although bottleneck features trained on phonetic targets are widely used with i-vector back-ends, their combination with LSTM-based end-to-end classifiers has received less systematic study, particularly when the phonetic training language (here Mandarin) is itself one of the target languages or is closely related to them. Speech rate offers a possible route to addressing the second issue. Speaking rate varies naturally across speakers, languages, and situations, and it alters the temporal structure of phonetic realizations while leaving much of the spectral identity intact. Time-scale modification (TSM) algorithms alter the duration of a signal without changing its pitch. The phase vocoder, which operates in the short-time Fourier domain and adjusts the synthesis hop size while maintaining phase coherence, is a well-established TSM technique (Flanagan and Golden, 1966; Laroche and Dolson, 1999). We hypothesize that presenting a classifier with the original utterance together with slowed and accelerated versions of it effectively lengthens the observed sequence and exposes the network to several plausible temporal realizations of the same content, thereby reducing the uncertainty of the decision for very short inputs. Related uses of speed perturbation have been shown to benefit training of acoustic models (Ko et al., 2015), but the application of TSM and splicing at test time for SLD has not, to our knowledge, been examined. The research question addressed here is therefore twofold: whether LSTM networks fed with deep bottleneck features learned from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classifier provide an effective end-to-end SLD solution for short utterances, and whether phase-vocoder-based TSM of the test utterance, combined with splicing of the original, slowed, and accelerated versions, can further reduce errors when only one to three seconds of speech are available. The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we propose an end-to-end SLD framework in which an LSTM classifier is trained on bottleneck features extracted from a DNN trained for Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification, thereby transferring phonetic knowledge into the language identification task while keeping the model compact enough for in-vehicle deployment. Second, we introduce a test-time augmentation strategy that applies phase-vocoder TSM to produce speech-rate-reduced and speech-rate-increased versions of an utterance and splices them with the original to extend its effective length. Third, we evaluate the approach on the AP17-OLR database and show that it improves identification performance relative to baseline systems, with the largest gains for 1 s and 3 s test durations, which are the conditions most relevant to intelligent-vehicle interaction. The remainder of this paper describes the proposed system, the experimental configuration, and the results, and then discusses the findings and their implications. Database and experimental design Experiments were run on the AP17-OLR database released for the Oriental Language Recognition challenge (Tang et al., 2017), an extension of AP16-OLR (Wang et al., 2016). It contains telephone-quality and close-talking recordings of ten languages: Mandarin, Cantonese, Indonesian, Japanese, Russian, Korean, Vietnamese, Kazakh, Tibetan and Uyghur. All audio was resampled to 16 kHz with 16-bit quantization. The training partition provides roughly 10 h of speech per language from multiple speakers of both genders. The test partition was evaluated at nominal durations of 1 s, 3 s and a longer full-length condition. The 1 s and 3 s conditions were the main focus because they best represent the short-utterance constraint of in-vehicle voice interfaces. A held-out 10% of the training utterances, stratified by language and speaker, served as a development set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. No test data were used in model fitting or tuning. The study used a controlled, ablation-style design with three factors: (i) the input representation (conventional filterbank features versus deep bottleneck features, DBF), (ii) the back-end classifier (frame-level DNN versus LSTM), and (iii) the test-time utterance extension strategy (original utterance only versus splicing with time-scale-modified versions). Each factor was varied while the others were held fixed, so the contribution of each component could be isolated. Bottleneck feature extraction by transfer learning DBFs were obtained by transfer learning from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification task. A feed-forward DNN was trained to classify each frame into context-dependent tied-state (senone) targets derived from a Mandarin corpus with forced alignments (Bu et al., 2017). Alignments came from a GMM-HMM system built with Kaldi (Povey et al., 2011). The input was 40-dimensional log Mel-filterbank coefficients with cepstral mean normalization, computed over 25 ms windows with a 10 ms shift. Frames were spliced with a context of ±5 to give a 440-dimensional input vector. The network had five hidden layers of 1024 sigmoid units, with a 64-unit linear bottleneck layer placed before the final hidden layer, following Grézl et al. (2007). It was initialized by layer-wise pre-training and then fine-tuned with stochastic gradient descent to minimize cross-entropy. The learning rate was halved when the development-set frame accuracy improved by less than 0.5% absolute. After training, the layers above the bottleneck were discarded. The 64-dimensional bottleneck activations of each frame were used as the language-independent but phonetically informed representation for all ten OLR languages. The mapping was frozen during LSTM training, so no language labels influenced the DBF extractor. LSTM-based language identification The back-end was an end-to-end sequence classifier based on the LSTM architecture (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), following its application to LID by Gonzalez-Dominguez et al. (2014). The DBF sequence of an utterance was fed to two stacked unidirectional LSTM layers of 512 cells each. A fully connected layer with a 10-way softmax followed. Unidirectional recurrence was chosen to allow low-latency operation in embedded settings. Training used truncated backpropagation through time over segments of 100 frames, and the label was applied to every frame. At test time the utterance-level posterior was the mean of the frame-level log posteriors over the last 80% of frames, which discards the initial frames before the recurrent state has accumulated sufficient context. To match the target conditions, training utterances were randomly cropped to 1–5 s segments in each epoch. Optimization used Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with an initial learning rate of 1×10⁻³, a mini-batch of 64 segments, gradient-norm clipping at 5, and dropout of 0.3 on non-recurrent connections (Srivastava et al., 2014). Training stopped when development-set cross-entropy had not improved for five consecutive epochs, and the best checkpoint was retained. Two baselines used the same data and tuning protocol: an LSTM on 40-dimensional filterbank features, and a frame-averaging DNN on DBF. Phase-vocoder time-scale modification and utterance splicing To lengthen short test utterances without needing additional speech, each test signal was modified in speaking rate by a phase-vocoder-based time-scale modification (TSM) algorithm (Flanagan & Golden, 1966). We used the identity phase-locking variant, which reduces phasiness artifacts (Laroche & Dolson, 1999). The short-time Fourier transform used a 32 ms Hann window with 75% overlap at the analysis stage. The synthesis hop was scaled by the TSM factor α, defined as the ratio of output to input duration. Two factors were used, α = 1.25 (slower speech) and α = 0.80 (faster speech). These values were selected on the development set from the candidate set {0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.1, 1.25, 1.4}, because they changed rate noticeably while keeping spectral envelopes and pitch intelligible. Because the vocoder preserves pitch and formant structure, the modified signals preserve language-specific spectral cues while changing the temporal realization of phonemes. For each test utterance, three versions (original, slowed, accelerated) were passed through the same DBF extractor. The three DBF sequences were concatenated in time to give a single sequence about 1.0 + 1.25 + 0.8 = 3.05 times the original duration. A single LSTM forward pass over the spliced sequence yielded the decision. The splicing order was fixed as original, slowed, accelerated, and a development-set check with all six permutations showed no meaningful differences. The LSTM was not retrained on spliced data, which allowed us to test whether the extension strategy acts purely as a test-time enhancement. Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis Performance was reported with the average cost Cavg and the identification accuracy. Cavg was computed following the NIST LRE 2009 definition, which averages miss and false-alarm costs over all target–non-target language pairs with equal priors (Ptarget = 0.5) and unit costs (Brümmer & van Leeuwen, 2006). The equal error rate (EER), derived from pooled target and non-target scores, was also reported. Transfer Learning Between Related Tasks Using Expected Label Proportions Matan Ben Noach∗ † and Yoav Goldberg∗ ‡ ∗ Computer Science Department, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat-Gan Israel † Intel AI Lab, Petah-Tikva Israel ‡ Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence matan.ben.noach@intel.com, yoav.goldberg@gmail.com Abstract Deep learning systems thrive on abundance of labeled training data but such data is not always available, calling for alternative methods of supervision. One such method is expectation regularization (XR) (Mann and McCallum, 2007), where models are trained based on expected label proportions. We propose a novel application of the XR framework for transfer learning between related tasks, where knowing the labels of task A provides an estimation of the label proportion of task B. We then use a model trained for A to label a large corpus, and use this corpus with an XR loss to train a model for task B. To make the XR framework applicable to large-scale deep-learning setups, we propose a stochastic batched approximation procedure. We demonstrate the approach on the task of Aspectbased Sentiment classification, where we effectively use a sentence-level sentiment predictor to train accurate aspect-based predictor. The method improves upon fully supervised neural system trained on aspect-level data, and is also cumulative with LM-based pretraining, as we demonstrate by improving a BERTbased Aspect-based Sentiment model. Data annotation is a key bottleneck in many data driven algorithms. Specifically, deep learning models, which became a prominent tool in many data driven tasks in recent years, require large datasets to work well. However, many tasks require manual annotations which are relatively hard to obtain at scale. An attractive alternative is lightly supervised learning (Schapire et al., 2002; Jin and Liu, 2005; Chang et al., 2007; Graça et al., 2007; Quadrianto et al., 2009a; Mann and McCallum, 2010a; Ganchev et al., 2010; Hope and Shahaf, 2016), in which the objective function is supplemented by a set of domain-specific soft- constraints over the model’s predictions on unlabeled data. For example, in label regularization (Mann and McCallum, 2007) the model is trained to fit the true label proportions of an unlabeled dataset. Label regularization is special case of expectation regularization (XR) (Mann and McCallum, 2007), in which the model is trained to fit the conditional probabilities of labels given features. In this work we consider the case of correlated tasks, in the sense that knowing the labels for task A provides information on the expected label composition of task B. We demonstrate the approach using sentence-level and aspect-level sentiment analysis, which we use as a running example: knowing that a sentence has positive sentiment label (task A), we can expect that most aspects within this sentence (task B) will also have positive label. While this expectation may be noisy on the individual example level, it holds well in aggregate: given a set of positively-labeled sentences, we can robustly estimate the proportion of positively-labeled aspects within this set. For example, in a random set of positive sentences, we expect to find 90% positive aspects, while in a set of negative sentences, we expect to find 70% negative aspects. These proportions can be easily either guessed or estimated from a small set. We propose a novel application of the XR framework for transfer learning in this setup. We present an algorithm (Sec 3.1) that, given a corpus labeled for task A (sentence-level sentiment), learns a classifier for performing task B (aspectlevel sentiment) instead, without a direct supervision signal for task B. We note that the label information for task A is only used at training time. Furthermore, due to the stochastic nature of the estimation, the task A labels need not be fully accurate, allowing us to make use of noisy predictions which are assigned by an automatic classifier (Sections 3.1 and 4). In other words, given a medium-sized sentiment corpus with sentencelevel labels, and a large collection of un-annotated text from the same distribution, we can train an accurate aspect-level sentiment classifier. The XR loss allows us to use task A labels for training task B predictors. This ability seamlessly integrates into other semi-supervised schemes: we can use the XR loss on top of a pre-trained model to fine-tune the pre-trained representation to the target task, and we can also take the model trained using XR loss and plentiful data and fine-tune it to the target task using the available small-scale annotated data. In Section 5.3 we explore these options and show that our XR framework improves the results also when applied on top of a pretrained B ERT-based model (Devlin et al., 2018). Finally, to make the XR framework applicable to large-scale deep-learning setups, we propose a stochastic batched approximation procedure (Section 3.2). An effective way to supplement small annotated datasets is to use lightly supervised learning, in which the objective function is supplemented by a set of domain-specific soft-constraints over the model’s predictions on unlabeled data. Previous work in lightly-supervised learning focused on training classifiers by using prior knowledge of label proportions (Jin and Liu, 2005; Chang et al., 2007; Musicant et al., 2007; Mann and McCallum, 2007; Quadrianto et al., 2009b; Liang et al., 2009; Ganchev et al., 2010; Mann and McCallum, 2010b; Chang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2014; Hope and Shahaf, 2016) or prior knowledge of features label associations (Schapire et al., 2002; Haghighi and Klein, 2006; Druck et al., 2008; Melville et al., 2009; Mohammady and Culotta, 2015). In the context of NLP, Haghighi and Klein (2006) suggested to use distributional similarities of words to train sequence models for part-of-speech tagging and a classified ads information extraction task. Melville et al. (2009) used background lexical information in terms of word-class associations to train a sentiment classifier. Ganchev and Das (2013); Wang and Manning (2014) suggested to exploit the bilingual correlations between a resource rich language and a resource poor language to train a classifier Expectation Regularization (XR) (Mann and McCallum, 2007) is a lightly supervised learning method, in which the model is trained to fit the conditional probabilities of labels given features. In the context of NLP, XR was used by Mohammady and Culotta (2015) to train twitter-user attribute prediction using hundreds of noisy distributional expectations based on census demographics. Here, we suggest using XR to train a target task (aspect-level sentiment) based on the output of a related source-task classifier (sentence-level sentiment). Ion channels play crucial roles in neuronal signal processing (Koch and Segev, 2000; Cai et al., 2004; Goldberg et al., 2008) and plasticity (Sjöström and Nelson, 2002; Shah et al., 2010; Debanne et al., 2003). Interactions among the many different ion channels expressed by a single cell can lead to extraordinarily complex dynamics, whose dissection necessitates computational modeling, as first demonstrated by Hodgkin and Huxley (1952a) for action potential generation. Simulation environments like NEURON (Hines and Carnevale, 2001; Carnevale and Hines, 2006) can be used to create biophysical neuron models with realistic morphologies, ionic currents, and channel densities (Figure 1A), facilitating the integration of experimental data into models (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Migliore et al., 1999; Poirazi et al., 2003; Destexhe and Paré, 1999; Traub et al., 2003). For example, pyramidal neuron models have been shown to reproduce the recorded spiking activity of these cells accurately with a particular set of ion channels (Traub et al., 2003; Figure 1B, gray traces; see Materials and methods). However, the dynamics can change, sometimes dramatically, when one of the modeled ion channel currents is exchanged for an identically-labeled model from a different publication on ModelDB (Figure 1B, colored traces, Figure 1C). This example underscores the importance of selecting ion channel models, yet there is currently no standardized experimental dataset against which to validate them. Furthermore, the increasingly large number of models on ModelDB (e.g., over 300 new ion channel models in 2014 alone; Shepherd Lab [2015]), with non-standardized labeling and a high degree of redundancy, makes it difficult to understand how ion channel models relate to each other and to biology. For example, a researcher looking to use an existing A-type potassium channel model will find over 250 A-type models, spanning a range of behaviors (Figure 1C, blue). Instead of a thorough and time-consuming fitting of appropriate ion channel dynamics, it is common for modelers to adapt previously published ion channel models for their own purposes. However, this may introduce experimentally unverified systematic changes or even errors into later generations of models and may have dramatic effects on the biological interpretation of the results. To facilitate informed choices among this bewildering variety of ion channel models, we categorized 2378 published voltage- and calcium-dependent ion channel models in NEURON that are available on ModelDB. We cataloged all relevant information about each ion channel model from the associated literature, including its pedigree relations: whether a given ion channel model is based on previous models, and, if so, which ones. Additionally, we compared the kinetics of each ion channel model in standardized voltage-clamp protocols. The resulting maps of ion channel behavior show model variability and diversity, and point to the computational and experimental sources that were used to fit each model. Our efforts have grouped 2378 ion channel models into 211 clusters, dramatically simplifying the search for an appropriate ion channel model. We present our findings in an annotated, interactive web-interface with a short video manual (ICGenealogy, 2016; https://icg.neurotheory.ox.ac.uk/), that allows filtered search of individual ion channel models by metadata and relational information, and the comparison of channel model kinetics. The underlying database is freely and programmatically accessible via a web application programming interface (API). In an effort to make our resource compatible with experimental data and new ion channel models, we offer the possibility to upload and assess the similarity of experimentally recorded current traces (as well as new models and model traces) in the same topology. We show an example of the use of this comparison through the analysis of an unclassified ion channel model, as well as an experimentally recorded voltage-dependent potassium current from Drosophila melanogaster. In summary, we provide a framework for the direct and automated comparison of models and experiments to facilitate experimentally constrained modeling and quantitative characterization of ion channel behavior.
