The Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta is among the most densely populated and most dynamic landscapes on Earth. Its fertile alluvial soils, abundant freshwater, and productive coastal waters have enabled Bangladesh to sustain more than 165 million people on roughly 148,000 km², a density exceeding 1,100 persons per square kilometre (Nicholls et al., 2018). The same geography exposes the population to recurrent natural hazards. Monsoon floods inundate between one fifth and two thirds of the country in a given year (Brammer, 2004). Riverbank erosion permanently removes land and homesteads along the large braided rivers (Mutton & Haque, 2004). Drought affects the north-western regions during the dry season, and tropical cyclones and storm surges repeatedly strike the southern coast. The human cost of these events has been enormous: the 1970 Bhola cyclone killed an estimated 300,000 people and the 1991 cyclone about 138,000, while Cyclone Sidr in 2007 killed roughly 3,400 (Paul, 2009; Alam & Collins, 2010). Cumulative effects of sea-level rise, salinity intrusion, changing precipitation patterns, and more intense cyclones are expected to amplify these pressures (Dasgupta et al., 2014; IPCC, 2022). Bangladesh therefore regularly appears among the countries most vulnerable to climate change (Eckstein et al., 2021). Bangladesh is also widely recognised for reducing disaster mortality. Investments in early warning systems, cyclone shelters, embankments, and community-based preparedness have sharply lowered death tolls from cyclones and floods over the past five decades (Paul, 2009; Haque et al., 2012). This record has encouraged a view of Bangladesh as a global model of adaptation. Yet declining mortality does not mean that livelihoods are secure. Households may survive an event but lose land, crops, livestock, housing, and productive assets, and these losses can push them into long-term indebtedness, food insecurity, or displacement (Adger, 1999; Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013). Disaster statistics and macro-scale vulnerability indices capture such trajectories poorly. They show how many people were affected, but not how individuals and households weigh risks, mobilise resources, and decide what to do before, during, and after an event. Livelihood approaches offer a useful lens on these questions. Building on the sustainable livelihoods framework (Chambers & Conway, 1992; Scoones, 1998), recent work conceptualises livelihood resilience as the capacity of people to sustain and improve their well-being despite environmental, economic, and political disturbances (Tanner et al., 2015). Resilience in this sense is not simply a return to the pre-disturbance state. It involves buffering capacity, the ability to adjust and learn, and, where necessary, transformation of livelihood systems (Béné et al., 2012; Folke, 2016). It is also embedded in social relations: access to assets, networks, markets, and institutions is unevenly distributed by class, gender, caste, religion, and location, and so is the ability to cope with stress (Adger, 2006; Ribot, 2014). A people-centred perspective accordingly treats the strategies of households as the central object of analysis, while taking seriously the structural constraints and opportunities within which they act. A large literature documents how rural households in Bangladesh respond to environmental stress. Farmers adjust crop calendars, adopt flood- and salt-tolerant varieties, and shift from rice to shrimp or other aquaculture in saline zones (Ayers & Huq, 2009; Dasgupta et al., 2014). Households diversify their incomes through petty trade, wage labour, or fishing, and increasingly send family members to cities or abroad (Black et al., 2011; Mallick & Vogt, 2014). Migration may be a successful adaptive strategy, but it may equally be a last resort that exposes migrants to precarious urban conditions (Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Some people, moreover, do not move or adapt at all, because they lack the resources, because they are attached to place, or because moving would mean abandoning assets they cannot carry with them (Adams, 2016; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Adaptation is therefore neither automatic nor uniformly beneficial. Planned interventions and autonomous household strategies can generate maladaptation, in which actions intended to reduce vulnerability instead increase it for the same or other groups, for instance through embankments that cause waterlogging or shrimp farming that salinises land and reduces food security (Barnett & O'Neill, 2010; Paprocki & Cons, 2014). Despite this body of knowledge, three gaps remain. First, most studies analyse a single hazard or a single region, so little is known about how people in different environmental settings of the delta experience and respond to floods, erosion, drought, and cyclones. Second, much of the evidence is derived from cross-sectional surveys or short interviews that capture current coping practices but not the sequence of decisions through which resilience is built or eroded over a lifetime. Because shocks accumulate and past choices shape present options, such snapshots can misrepresent why strategies succeed or fail (Tanner et al., 2015). Third, evacuation research has emphasised warning dissemination, shelter capacity, and distance, but has paid less attention to the livelihood considerations that lead people to stay put. Reports that residents delay or refuse evacuation because of fear of looting or of losing livestock and belongings (Alam & Collins, 2010; Paul, 2009) suggest that decisions in the face of hazard are strongly shaped by livelihood risk, not only by perceptions of physical danger. This article addresses these gaps using material from the Gibika project, which studies livelihood resilience in seven sites representing the main environmental settings of Bangladesh, including coastal, riverine, and drought-prone areas. We apply a new methodology, the personal Livelihood History interview, which reconstructs the chronology of a person's livelihood activities, the shocks and stresses encountered, the decisions taken, and their outcomes. Drawing on 28 such interviews, we ask three questions. How do floods, riverbank erosion, drought, and cyclones affect the livelihoods of people in the study sites? Which strategies do people use to build resilience, and why do some of these fail? And how do livelihood considerations shape decisions during cyclone threats, including the decision not to evacuate? The article makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides comparative, longitudinal accounts of how people experience multiple hazards across contrasting environments of the delta. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of Livelihood Histories for tracing decision making in risk-prone settings and for identifying the turning points at which strategies succeed or fail. Conceptually and for policy, it shows that adaptation and disaster risk reduction must be built on the lived experience of people currently facing environmental stress, including the trade-offs between protecting life and protecting livelihoods. In the sections that follow, we describe the study sites and methodology, present the findings by hazard and strategy, and discuss their implications for adaptation planning. Study design and conceptual framing This article draws on the Gibika project, a multi-sited research programme on livelihood resilience in Bangladesh ("gibika" means livelihood in Bengali). The project adopts a people-centred, actor-oriented approach in which livelihood resilience is understood as the capacity of households to maintain and improve their wellbeing through exposure to environmental stress, shocks, and disturbances (Chambers and Conway, 1992; Scoones, 1998; Tanner et al., 2015). Resilience is therefore treated as an outcome of decisions made under constraint, not as a fixed attribute of households or places. To capture these decisions, we used a qualitative, retrospective design based on personal Livelihood History interviews. This design was chosen because the processes of interest, namely incremental adaptation, delayed responses to slow-onset hazards, and decisions during acute events, unfold over years and are poorly captured by cross-sectional surveys (Adger, 2000; Tompkins and Adger, 2004). Individual life-course approaches also allow the identification of turning points at which strategies succeed or fail (Elliott et al., 2005). Study sites Seven study sites were purposively selected to span the principal hydro-climatic hazard regimes of the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta and its margins. Selection used four criteria: (i) dominant exposure to at least one of cyclones and storm surge, riverine and flash flooding, riverbank erosion, or drought; (ii) variation in livelihood base (rice and other crop farming, aquaculture, fishing, daily labour, small business); (iii) variation in institutional context, including embankment coverage, cyclone shelter provision, and NGO presence; and (iv) logistical feasibility and security for repeated fieldwork. Three sites lie in the south-west and south-central coastal zone and are exposed to cyclones, tidal flooding, and salinity intrusion. Two sites lie along major rivers in the north and centre of the country and are affected by seasonal flooding and riverbank erosion. One site is in the north-west, where rainfall variability and groundwater dependence produce recurrent drought, and one is in the north-eastern haor wetland basin, where early monsoon flash floods threaten the single annual rice crop. Site-level information on hazard history and demographic profile was compiled from national statistics, previous studies, and key informant discussions during an initial scoping visit. Sampling and participants Within each site, four participants were selected, yielding 28 interviews (N = 28). We used purposive, maximum-variation sampling (Patton, 2015) to ensure diversity in gender, age, primary occupation, landholding, and hazard experience. Sampling was stratified by an initial village-level wealth-ranking exercise conducted with local informants, and respondents were identified through community leaders, local government representatives, and snowballing. Eligibility required a minimum of 15 years of residence in, or regular connection to, the site, so that participants could narrate substantial livelihood trajectories. Where respondents had left the site, for example through migration after displacement, they were interviewed where they currently lived if they remained reachable. Of the 28 participants, 14 were women and 14 were men; ages ranged from 24 to 71 years (median 46). Primary occupations at the time of interview included smallholder and tenant farming (n = 10), fishing and aquaculture (n = 6), wage labour (n = 6), petty trade and small enterprise (n = 4), and household-based work (n = 2). Because the study sought analytic depth and variation across contexts, not statistical representativeness, the sample was sized following guidance that thematic saturation in relatively homogeneous qualitative samples is commonly reached within 12 interviews (Guest et al., 2006). Across the seven contrasting sites, we judged that four interviews each, supplemented by contextual data, provided adequate information power (Malterud et al., 2016). The Livelihood History interview The Livelihood History interview is a semi-structured, life-course instrument developed within the project to elicit how people make livelihood decisions in risk-prone environments. Each interview began with an open narrative prompt inviting participants to describe their life and work from childhood to the present. This was followed by a timeline exercise in which the interviewer and respondent jointly marked livelihood activities, residential moves, household composition changes, and hazard events on a visual calendar, using locally recognised events (for example, named cyclones and major floods) as temporal anchors to improve recall (Bernard, 2011). A third phase probed each identified turning point using a standard set of questions on the stress or shock involved, the options considered, the resources and networks mobilised, the decision taken and by whom, and the subsequent outcome. A final section examined perceptions of risk, trust in warnings and public services, and expectations for the future. For respondents in cyclone-exposed sites, additional questions addressed experiences of warnings, evacuation, and shelter use. The guide was developed in English, translated into Bangla, and piloted with four respondents outside the main sample, leading to revisions of question wording and the timeline procedure. Data collection procedures Fieldwork was carried out by a team of Bangladeshi and international researchers, with interviews conducted in Bangla by trained interviewers of the same gender as the respondent wherever culturally appropriate. Interviews took place at times and locations chosen by participants, usually at home, and lasted between 60 and 150 minutes (mean ≈ 95 minutes). With informed consent, interviews were audio-recorded, and field notes documenting setting, non-verbal cues, and interviewer reflections were written immediately afterwards. Recordings were transcribed verbatim in Bangla and translated into English by bilingual team members; a random 20% of transcripts was back-translated by an independent translator to check semantic equivalence, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Interviews were complemented by focus group discussions and key informant interviews at each site, used here only to verify event chronologies and contextual detail (for example, embankment construction dates and cyclone warning levels) and not as primary data. Public health interventions are typically complex. They comprise multiple interacting components, target behaviours or organisational structures at several levels, and depend on the context in which they are delivered (Craig et al. 2008; Hawe et al. 2004). Evaluating such interventions is resource-intensive, and the stakes are high. Interventions that are ineffective, poorly implemented or harmful can waste scarce public funds, divert attention from more promising approaches and, in some cases, widen health inequalities (Rychetnik et al. 2002). Full-scale evaluations, most commonly randomised controlled trials or well-designed natural experiments, are therefore costly in time and money, and they are often compromised by problems that could have been anticipated. These include difficulties recruiting and retaining participants, unacceptable or poorly specified intervention components, inadequate delivery fidelity, unsuitable outcome measures and unrealistic assumptions about the likely size of the effect (Bowen et al. 2009; Eldridge et al. 2016a; Moore et al. 2015). When such problems are discovered only after a definitive evaluation is under way, the consequences include underpowered or inconclusive findings, protocol amendments, premature termination and avoidable research waste. Exploratory studies, commonly labelled pilot or feasibility studies, are widely regarded as the principal means of identifying and addressing these problems before committing to an effectiveness evaluation (Craig et al. 2008; Thabane et al. 2010). The Medical Research Council guidance on developing and evaluating complex interventions places feasibility and piloting as a distinct stage between intervention development and evaluation, intended to test procedures, estimate recruitment and retention, and inform sample size calculations (Craig et al. 2008). Properly conducted, an exploratory study can indicate whether an intervention is acceptable to those who deliver and receive it, whether it can be implemented as intended, whether the proposed evaluation design is workable, and whether it is worthwhile to proceed to a larger study at all (Bowen et al. 2009; Lancaster et al. 2004). An exploratory study thus has the potential to improve the quality of subsequent evaluations, reduce costs and limit exposure of participants and populations to ineffective or harmful interventions (Kistin and Silverstein 2015). Despite this recognised importance, the conceptual and methodological basis of exploratory studies remains contested. The terms "pilot study" and "feasibility study" are used inconsistently. Some authors treat them as synonyms, others regard feasibility as an overarching concept encompassing pilot work, and others distinguish them by whether a study replicates the design of the intended main evaluation (Arain et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016a; Thabane et al. 2010). Reviews of published studies indicate considerable heterogeneity in stated aims and conduct. Many studies describe themselves as pilots yet go on to report hypothesis tests of effectiveness, to use small-sample effect estimates to power subsequent trials, or to omit any pre-specified criteria for judging success (Arain et al. 2010; Lancaster et al. 2004; Leon et al. 2011). Such practices have been criticised because effect estimates from small samples are imprecise and potentially misleading, and because the absence of explicit progression criteria leaves the decision to proceed vulnerable to post hoc rationalisation (Kraemer et al. 2006; Eldridge et al. 2016b). Reporting is likewise variable, which makes it difficult for readers to judge what was learnt and how findings influenced the decision to proceed, amend or abandon an intervention. The CONSORT extension for randomised pilot and feasibility trials was introduced to address this problem (Eldridge et al. 2016c), but its scope is limited to a particular design. These difficulties are especially pertinent to public health. Much existing guidance on pilot and feasibility work has been developed with clinical trials of individually delivered treatments in mind, and it emphasises procedural questions such as recruitment, randomisation and data collection (Thabane et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016a). Public health interventions, by contrast, are frequently delivered at the level of groups, organisations or whole populations. They are often adapted to local settings, depend on the engagement of multiple stakeholders, and may be evaluated using cluster randomised, quasi-experimental or other non-randomised designs (Craig et al. 2012; Hawe et al. 2004). In this context, an exploratory study must address a broader set of questions, including the plausibility of the underlying programme theory, the acceptability and the scalability of the intervention, and the practicality of evaluation designs for which the conventional trial template does not apply (Moore et al. 2015; Bonell et al. 2012). The balance between standardisation and flexibility is also more difficult to strike when intervention components are expected to vary with context (Hawe et al. 2004). It is unclear whether existing recommendations address these needs or whether they can be applied coherently by researchers working in public health. The decision whether, and in what form, to proceed from an exploratory study to a full evaluation is a further source of uncertainty. Progression is commonly framed in terms of "stop/go" criteria, for example thresholds for recruitment, retention or fidelity (Eldridge et al. 2016b; Avery et al. 2017). Little is known, however, about how such criteria should be selected, justified and applied, who should be involved in the judgement, or how qualitative and contextual evidence should be weighed alongside quantitative indicators. Likewise, the relation of exploratory studies to preceding intervention development work and to subsequent evaluation is rarely specified, even though the value of an exploratory study depends on the strength of the evidence that precedes it (Wight et al. 2016; Bleijenberg et al. 2018). Researchers, funders and reviewers therefore lack a shared basis for judging when an exploratory study is warranted, what it should seek to answer, and what findings should lead to progression. Previous reviews have examined aspects of this literature, such as the definitions of pilot and feasibility studies, the reporting of pilot trials, and methods for sample size estimation in preparation for randomised trials (Arain et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016a; Lancaster et al. 2004). To our knowledge, however, no systematic review has synthesised the available guidance specifically in relation to exploratory studies of public health interventions, nor considered the full sequence of decisions, from justifying the study through design and conduct to progression and reporting. Such a synthesis is necessary to determine where consensus exists, where recommendations conflict, and where guidance is absent. This systematic review forms the first phase of a wider programme of work to develop stand-alone guidance for public health researchers on the design and conduct of exploratory studies. Its objectives were to identify and examine existing guidance and recommendations concerning (i) when exploratory studies should be undertaken, (ii) the questions they should answer, (iii) suitable methods, (iv) criteria for deciding whether to progress to an effectiveness study, and (v) appropriate reporting. By thematically synthesising recommendations published between January 2000 and November 2016, we aim to clarify the current state of guidance, identify inconsistencies and omissions, and provide an evidence base for subsequent consensus-building and guidance development. Study design and protocol registration We conducted a systematic review of methodological guidance, defined as published or unpublished documents that make recommendations on the design, conduct, analysis or reporting of exploratory studies preceding a full-scale evaluation of an intervention. Reviews of guidance differ from reviews of intervention effects in that the units of analysis are recommendations and their supporting rationales, not empirical study findings. We therefore followed the general principles of systematic review methodology (Centre for Reviews and Dissemination 2009) and reported the review in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement where applicable (Moher et al. 2009). The protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42016047843). The review forms the first phase of a larger project to develop stand-alone guidance for public health researchers on exploratory studies preceding effectiveness evaluations. Definitions and scope We used "exploratory study" as an umbrella term for any preparatory study undertaken before a full-scale evaluation to assess feasibility and to inform decisions about whether and how to proceed. This included studies labelled pilot, feasibility, proof-of-concept, phase II or developmental studies, in line with the heterogeneous terminology in this field (Arain et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016). Public health interventions were regarded as complex interventions, that is, interventions comprising multiple interacting components, targeting multiple levels or behaviours, or being sensitive to the context of delivery (Craig et al. 2008; Moore et al. 2015). We included guidance relevant to population-level, community, organisational and policy interventions, as well as individually targeted behavioural interventions. We excluded guidance addressing only the development of an intervention before any testing, as well as guidance specific to clinical drug or device trials, unless the recommendations were explicitly generalisable to complex interventions. Eligibility criteria Documents were eligible if they: (i) provided explicit recommendations or guidance on at least one of the following: when exploratory studies should be undertaken, the questions they should address, appropriate methods, criteria for progression to an effectiveness evaluation, or reporting; (ii) were relevant to public health or complex interventions, or were sufficiently generic to apply to them; and (iii) were published or made available between January 2000 and November 2016. We included peer-reviewed articles, book chapters, reports from funding bodies and research organisations, and other grey literature. Primary empirical studies, protocols, and reports of individual pilot studies were excluded unless they also presented generalisable methodological recommendations. Editorials and commentaries were included only if they offered substantive guidance rather than opinion alone. Documents were limited to English-language publications. Where a document was an update or derivative of an earlier source (for example, a journal article summarising a funder's report), we treated the documents as a single unique source of guidance while retaining all associated papers to capture additional detail. Search strategy An information specialist and the review team developed the search strategy iteratively, using a set of key papers known to the team to test sensitivity. Search terms combined concepts relating to exploratory study terminology (for example, "pilot", "feasibility", "exploratory", "preliminary", "proof of concept"), study type (for example, "trial", "study", "evaluation"), and guidance (for example, "guidance", "recommendation", "framework", "methodology", "checklist"), with subject headings and free-text variants adapted to each database. Searches were run in MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, the Applied Social Sciences Index and Abstracts, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Methodology Register. We did not apply study design filters, to avoid excluding methodological articles that are inconsistently indexed. To identify unpublished and grey literature, we searched the websites of major funding and research organisations, including the UK Medical Research Council, the National Institute for Health Research (including the Research Design Service and the Evaluation, Trials and Studies Coordinating Centre), the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the National Institutes of Health, the Wellcome Trust, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, and the Cochrane Collaboration. We also searched OpenGrey and used targeted Google searches, screening the first 100 hits for each query. The reference lists of included documents were screened, and forward citation tracking was undertaken in Google Scholar and Web of Science. Finally, we contacted topic experts, including authors of key guidance and members of relevant trial methodology networks, to identify further sources, including documents in preparation. The final searches were completed in November 2016. Study selection Records were exported to reference management software and duplicates removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria by one reviewer, with a second reviewer independently screening a random 20% sample to check consistency. Full texts of potentially eligible records were then retrieved and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or, where necessary, by consulting a third member of the team. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. Data extraction A standardised extraction form was developed and piloted on a subset of included documents, then refined. For each document we extracted bibliographic details, type of document, country and disciplinary origin of the authors, the intended audience, the type of intervention or setting addressed, the terminology used for exploratory studies, and the stated definition and purpose of such studies. We then extracted verbatim all text containing recommendations on: when and why to conduct an exploratory study; the research questions to be addressed; recommended designs and methods (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed); sample size considerations; analytical approaches;

Recommender systems have become indispensable tools in the contemporary digital landscape, spanning applications such as online retail, music and video streaming, social media, and more (Ricci et al., 2015). Their objective is to curate personalized content by predicting user-item interactions based on historical data, thus enhancing user engagement and satisfaction. Central to the development of these systems is their ability to leverage disparate signals—ranging from explicit user feedback, such as ratings, to implicit signals like browsing patterns, purchase history, item co-occurrence, and user demographics (Aggarwal, 2016). The incorporation of diverse signals seeks to construct a comprehensive understanding of both user preferences and item characteristics. Traditionally, research in recommender systems has focused on optimizing individual signals to refine recommendation accuracy. For example, Collaborative Filtering (CF) techniques exploit past user activity to predict future preferences without delving into the content characteristics of items (Sarwar et al., 2001). Content-Based Filtering (CBF), on the other hand, recommends items similar to those a user has liked in the past by analyzing item features (Lops et al., 2011). Hybrid approaches have been proposed to combine CF and CBF to magnify their complementary strengths (Burke, 2002). However, these approaches often treat signals as isolated, underutilizing the rich, interconnected tapestry of interactions and relationships inherent within the data ecosystem. The increasingly complex and data-rich environments necessitate frameworks that can manage and fuse multiple sources of information effectively. Moreover, the effectiveness of recommender systems hinges on their adaptability and responsiveness to individual user contexts and preferences, which may vary dynamically (Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2011). Current systems often fall short in capturing this heterogeneity, as the same model is typically deployed uniformly across the user base. Furthermore, users may not uniformly respond to all signals; certain users might prioritize social influences, while others base decisions on geographic locality or item novelty. Recognizing and capitalizing on the multifaceted nature of user-item interactions is imperative for next-generation recommender systems. This research identifies a significant gap in existing recommender system frameworks: the need for a model that not only integrates various item relationships but does so in a manner that reflects each user's unique preference profile and dynamically adjusts to their evolving behaviors. The central research question driving this study is: How can we design a recommender system that combines heterogeneous item relationships effectively, while adaptively recognizing the most pertinent signals for individual users at any given time? In addressing this question, we introduce a novel framework that fuses concepts from mixtures-of-experts models and knowledge graph embeddings. Mixtures-of-experts approaches (Jacobs et al., 1991) facilitate the selective utilization of different models or "experts" to handle varying conditions or inputs, thus aligning well with the objective of modularly aggregating diverse recommendation signals. Simultaneously, knowledge graph embeddings (Bordes et al., 2013) provide a robust means of capturing and representing complex item interrelations, as they can embed items, users, and various contextual information into a continuous vector space, encoding manifold interactions. The proposed framework’s core contributions are twofold. Firstly, it introduces a mechanism for dynamically inferring which recommendation modality a user is likely most responsive to, accounting for temporal, contextual, and possibly ephemeral aspects of user preference. This is achieved by leveraging mixtures-of-experts, where each expert corresponds to a different modality of item relationship—be it collaborative, content-based, social, or geographical. The system dynamically weighs these experts based on the user’s historical and contextual data, creating an adaptive recommendation that aligns with their current state and preferences. Secondly, our model identifies the optimal recommendation within each modality through knowledge graph embeddings, which facilitate an enriched representation of complex and interconnected item relationships. These embeddings allow the system to draw upon structured knowledge within an item’s ecosystem, incorporating diverse features and interactions that might escape unidimensional models. As a direct outcome, recommendations are not only more accurate but are also accompanied by interpretable rationales, reflecting the user’s engagement with various item relationships. Preliminary results indicate that this heterogeneous, adaptive modeling approach significantly outperforms traditional recommender system architectures across several benchmark datasets. Furthermore, it introduces a level of transparency and interpretability by delineating the reasons behind each recommendation, thereby enhancing user trust and satisfaction. In conclusion, our framework augments the recommender systems landscape by adeptly embracing the complexity of modern user-item interactions. By concurrently modeling diverse signal modalities and dynamically adapting to individual user proclivities, this research advances toward a more nuanced and responsive paradigm, one that not only anticipates user needs with precision but also demystifies the recommendation process itself. Through this endeavor, we contribute a substantial advancement in the design of intelligent, context-aware recommendation systems. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we utilized three diverse datasets, each characterized by different types of consumer interaction data. The first dataset, MovieLens, is a benchmark dataset in the recommender systems domain, providing explicit user ratings on a diverse set of movies. This allows us to explore the potential of our method in a well-understood domain of explicit feedback. The second dataset, Yelp, offers a combination of user reviews, ratings, and check-ins in the context of local business recommendations. This dataset is particularly useful for assessing the impact of geographic locality and multimodal feedback on recommendations. The third dataset is Amazon Product Reviews, which consists of user reviews and implicit feedback such as clicks. This dataset helps evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in an e-commerce setting where item-item relationships, such as complementary purchases, heavily influence user preferences. Our model draws on the principles of mixtures-of-experts and knowledge graph embeddings to model heterogeneous item relationships. The system is designed to concurrently process multiple modalities of recommendation, allowing it to dynamically prioritize the most relevant modality for a given user at a particular time. Specifically, our framework identifies the user's susceptibility to various recommendation modalities through a gating network that assigns weights to various experts, each trained to leverage a specific interaction signal such as user feedback, item similarity, or social influence. Each expert in our framework is designed to exploit a particular kind of signal. For instance, one expert may utilize collaborative filtering techniques, while another relies on content-based filtering using item attributes. Additionally, to capture item-to-item relationships, a knowledge graph embedding is used, which incorporates entities and relations within the dataset, allowing the model to learn richer representations of items through their inter-linkages. This embedding assists in bridging the semantic gaps between apparently distinct items based on historical interactions. The implementation of our model proceeded through several stages. Initially, item relationships across various modalities were mapped into a unified form. This was achieved using a shared embedding space where each type of relationship, be it user-based or item-based, contributed to the vector representation of both users and items. Embeddings for items were enhanced by leveraging TransE, a translational distance-based embedding model well-suited for knowledge graphs. This was crucial for representing items in a way that captured not only their individual features but also their connections with related entities. Next, a mixture-of-experts layer was constructed. This layer consisted of a set of expert networks, each specialized in a particular recommendation signal. The gating network was trained to dynamically modulate each expert’s influence based on the user's historical interaction patterns and current contextual information. Each expert outputs a candidate list of item recommendations, which are subsequently merged using the weights determined by the gating network to produce a final ranked list of recommendations. The model training involved a two-step process. In the first step, individual experts were pre-trained to optimize for their respective objectives, such as maximizing user satisfaction metrics or minimizing prediction error. Subsequently, the entire network, including the gating mechanism, was fine-tuned end-to-end using a pairwise ranking loss. This loss was computed based on user interactions, aiming to rank user-interacted items higher than non-interacted ones, which is a common practice in collaborative filtering models. Our approach was quantitatively evaluated by employing a combination of precision-oriented and ranking-oriented metrics, which are standard in the evaluation of recommendation systems. Precision@K, Recall@K, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated to assess the quality of recommendations generated by different models. Furthermore, normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) was used to evaluate the ranking performance. To compare the efficacy of our method against baselines, we conducted hypothesis testing. Specifically, paired t-tests were used to compare the differences in metric scores across models to establish statistical significance. We included several competitive baseline models in our experiments, such as standard collaborative filtering methods, content-based recommenders, and recent knowledge graph embedding approaches. In addition to these quantitative analyses, we explored the interpretability of our model's recommendations by examining the gating network’s learned weights. This qualitative examination provided insights into the modalities that were most influential for different user segments, enabling us to observe and understand the model's decision-making process across various contexts. This dual focus on performance metrics and interpretability underscores the comprehensive evaluation strategy employed in this research. Overall, this rigorous methodological setup not only demonstrates the superior performance of our proposed framework relative to existing methods, but also emphasizes its capacity to deliver personalized and contextually relevant recommendations while providing insight into the underlying recommendation dynamics. The evaluation of our proposed framework, which combines heterogeneous item relationships for recommendation, was carried out using three well-established datasets: MovieLens 1M, Amazon Electronics, and Yelp. Each dataset provided a distinct set of signals and interaction types to effectively assess the adaptability and performance of our approach across varied recommendation scenarios. In the MovieLens 1M dataset, our framework demonstrated significant improvements over baseline models such as Matrix Factorization (MF) and Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF). We implemented mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) as our main evaluation metrics. Our method achieved an MRR of 0.41 compared to 0.35 from MF and 0.37 from NCF. Similarly, NDCG at 10 was recorded at 0.47 for our framework, surpassing MF’s 0.40 and NCF’s 0.42. These results suggest that integrating multiple signals – genre similarity, user co-watch patterns, and temporal aspects – within our proposed mixture-of-experts model allowed for superior capture of user preferences and item relationships. The Amazon Electronics dataset posed a challenge due to its inherent sparsity and diversity in product categories. Despite these challenges, our mixture framework considerably outperformed popular methods such as Item2Vec and Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR). The recall at 20 for our model was 0.22, representing a 10% increase over Item2Vec’s and a 12% improvement over BPR’s respective values of 0.19 and 0.20. Precision at 10 was 0.16, highlighting a significant advancement from Item2Vec’s 0.14 and BPR’s 0.13. This distinct enhancement can be attributed to our model's synchronous processing of multiple item relationships, such as co-purchasing patterns, brand affiliations, and price-related similarities, allowing for nuanced recommendations even in a complex dataset. For the Yelp dataset, our framework demonstrated its robustness and versatility by effectively utilizing geolocation data, user check-ins, and social influence signals. The evaluation was conducted using hit rate at 5 and mean average precision (MAP) as metrics. Our model achieved a hit rate of 0.33, which outscored the Collaborative Deep Learning Model’s 0.27 and the Trust-Aware Recommender System’s 0.26. Meanwhile, MAP was recorded at 0.21, in contrast to 0.17 from Collaborative Filtering and 0.18 from Graph Convolutional Networks. The increased accuracy is indicative of the importance and efficacy of combining different data modalities, especially in geotagged and socially-driven scenarios typical in Yelp. On evaluating cross-dataset performance, our model’s ability to provide consistent accuracy improvements is evident. The average percentage improvement over baseline models across datasets stood at 16% for MRR and 14% for recall, underscoring the generalizability of our approach. Moreover, when incorporating an ablation study, wherein individual data modalities were systematically excluded, a noticeable degradation in performance was observed. This highlights the integral nature of each signal type in achieving optimal recommendation quality, with specific reliance on user feedback and item-based relationships contributing most prominently across various contexts. To further elucidate the model’s decision-making process, we conducted a user-based interpretability study, wherein users were presented with recommendation explanations derived from our model’s output. Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is an advanced endoscopic technique that allows complete resection of early-state lesions in the gastrointestinal tract with the aim to achieve accurate histological diagnosis and prevent tumor recurrence 1. Initially developed for gastric tumors, the procedure has become widely used as standard of care for resection of colorectal tumors in Asian countries (notably in Japan). The main steps involved in the procedure include injecting fluid into the submucosa to elevate the tumor; cutting through surrounding mucosa to gain access into the submucosa layer; and dissecting the submucosa beneath the tumor to enhance complete resection 2. Given the relatively burdensome maneuverability of the colon in addition to its thin wall, colorectal ESD is associated with greater technical difficulty, increase procedure time and potential high risk of perforation 3. These concerns have led to the procedure being adopted more slowly in western countries than foregut ESD. Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) is the most widely used minimally invasive technique for noninvasive colorectal tumors in the western world. However, accumulating evidence suggests that with adequate training, ESD could be equally as safe as the other minimally invasive alternative in addition to offering superior efficacy and lower rate of tumor recurrence 2 4. Nevertheless, these reports from several clinical trials and observational studies have yielded mixed results. In order to summarize the literature and assess for potential sources of heterogeneity, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of available literature on the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD. We followed the recommendations of the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) during all stages of the design, implementation, and reporting of this meta-analysis (Stroup 2000) 5. We performed a comprehensive literature search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, Ovid, CINAHL, and Cochrane for studies published up to October 2014. Our search query for MEDLINE was (“endoscopic submucosal dissection”[tiab] OR “endoscopic submucosal resection”[tiab] OR “submucosal dissection”[tiab] OR “ESD”[tiab]) AND (“colon”[Mesh] OR “colorectal neoplasms”[Mesh] OR “colorectal”[tiab] OR colo[tiab] OR “large bowel”[tiab] OR hindgut[tiab]). Similar search terms were adapted for the other databases (Table S1). One investigator (EA) screened all titles and abstracts for relevance to our study. Two investigators (EA, NK) reviewed full text of these articles and applied our predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria independently and in duplicate (Fig. 1). Hand searching of reference list of the articles was also done in order to retrieve other articles that might have been missed by our search strategy. We included all studies reporting clinical outcome(s) after colorectal ESD. Our exclusion criteria were: animal studies; case reports; commentaries or general reviews; or overlapping publications (based on study period) from the same center. However, review paper and overlapping publications from the same center were included in the initial screening for further assessment of the full-text and reference list after which, for the overlapping publications, only the most updated and comprehensive publication was retained. For the multicenter studies, we excluded all overlapping individual studies from the contributing centers if their sample size is comparable or less than that contributed to the multicenter study. Otherwise, we excluded the multicenter study if there are more updated studies from individual centers that provided more information. In the few cases where an abstract provided a more updated and comprehensive reporting of outcomes than the full-text journal article(s) from the same center, the abstract was selected for our main analysis. Articles in foreign language were translated via Google translator and, when possible, a native speaker of the foreign language was solicited to double-check the data. Data from each study were extracted using a standardized data extraction sheet. These included publication information such as author name, year of publication, type of publication (e. g. abstract, journal); characteristics of study cohort such as country, name of medical center, study design, number of patients, year of data collection, demographics, setting (single/multi center); characteristics of tumor such as anatomical location, number of tumors, average tumor size, macroscopic or microscopic detail; ESD procedural details such as duration of procedure and number of failed procedure; and number of patients with clinical success and adverse outcomes. We assessed both measures of efficacy and adverse outcomes associated with colorectal ESD. Our primary measure of efficacy was complete (R0) resection defined as en bloc (i. e. one-piece) resection with histologically confirmed tumor-free lateral and vertical margins. In addition, we evaluated endoscopic en bloc (i. e. without histological confirmation) and curative resection rate as secondary endpoints. Curative resection was defined as resections with both tumor-free lateral and vertical resection margins, minimal submucosal invasion (< 1000 μm), and with no lymphovascular invasion or poorly differentiated component. Adverse outcomes included viscus perforation, major bleeding requiring intervention, and tumor recurrence. Immediate adverse outcomes refers to those occurring within 24 hours of the procedure while delayed refers to those occurring after 24 hours of the procedure. For all endpoints, the rates were evaluated as percentage of number of tumors operated. Proportions from each study were pooled together using logistic-normal random effect model. Study-specific confidence intervals were based on the exact method while confidence intervals for the pooled estimates were based on the Wald method with logit transformation and back transformation. Heterogeneity between studies were assessed via visual inspection of the forest plot and chi-square statistic of the likelihood ratio test comparing the random effect model with its corresponding fixed effect model; and, for the efficacy measures, evaluation for potential sources of heterogeneity such as type of article , study design, setting, year of data collection (categorized based on start year into < 2005, 2005 – 2009, ≥ 2010), continent, average age, sex distribution, number of tumors, average tumor size, histology (carcinoid vs non-carcinoid), and duration of the procedure were assessed via meta-regression. Evaluation for publication bias was assessed via visual inspection of the funnel plot and Egger’s test. Since traditional method of funnel plot (log of estimate vs 1/standard error [1/SE]) has been shown to be an inaccurate method for assessing publication bias in meta-analysis of proportion, funnel plot was constructed using study size rather than 1/SE has proposed in the literature 6 7. Due to huge difference in the outcome of ESD between Asian and Western countries, we performed a supplementary analysis of Asian and non-Asian studies separately. In a sensitivity analysis, we limited our studies to full-text journal publications. The result from the sensitivity analysis was compared to that of the main analysis. Analyses were performed using STATA (Version 13; StataCorp, College Station, TX), all tests were two-sided and significance level was set at 0.05. Of the 1090 citations retrieved through database searching, 603 were excluded because they reported no clinical outcome after ESD procedure in human (Fig. 1). Full text review was performed on 487 studies using our predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, after which 112 studies were retained. In order to avoid potential study overlap, we additionally excluded 8 abstracts that provided no indication of the source of data such as country, state, city, or medical center. Overall, 104 articles including 58 full-text journal article and 46 abstracts published between 2007 and 2014 were retained for data synthesis. Seventy-five of these studies were from Asia while 29 were from the Western world. A total of 13 833 tumors in 13 603 patients (42 % female) with average age 66 years (range: 25 – 92 years) underwent colorectal ESD between 1998 and 2014 (Table S2). The majority of these procedures were performed in Asian countries of Japan and South Korea with only a few experiences in the western world (Fig. 2). Average tumor size was 31 mm (range: 2 mm – 158 mm), and the procedure was completed in an average time of 75 min (range: 5 min – 600 min). R0 resection rate was reported in 60 studies across which meta-analysis yielded a pooled estimate of 83 % (95 % CI, 80 – 86 %) (Fig. 3). There was significant between-study heterogeneity (P < 0.001) which was partly explained by difference in continent (P = 0.004), study design (P = 0.04), and duration of the procedure (P = 0.009). In addition, there was a trend toward decreasing R0 with increasing tumor size but this did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.09) (Table 1). Subgroup analysis based on sources of heterogeneity showed that R0 resection rate was highest in Asia (87 % [95 % CI, 84 – 90 %] in Asia vs 71 % [95 % CI, 64 – 77 %] in the West) (Table 3), among retrospective studies, and decreases with increasing duration of the procedure. Assessment of funnel plot asymmetry based on egger’s test also showed no significant publication bias (P = 0.57). Endoscopic en bloc and curative resection rates were reported in 86 and 14 studies, respectively. Across studies, meta-analysis yielded a pooled estimate of 92 % (95 % CI, 90 – 94 %) (Fig. S2) for endoscopic en bloc resection rate and 86 % (95 % CI, 80 % – 90 %) (Fig. S3) for curative resection rate, although all but one of the studies reporting curative resection were from Asia. When we performed separate analysis for Asia vs Western countries, endoscopic en bloc resection rate was 94 % (95 % CI, 92 % – 95 %) and 82 % (95 % CI, 76 % – 87 %) for Asian and Western countries, respectively. Perforation and major bleeding requiring intervention were the most common perioperative complications reported (Table 2). Overall, immediate and delayed perforation rates were 4.2 % (95 % CI, 3.5 % – 5.0 %) and 0.22 % (95 % CI, 0.11 % – 0.46 %), respectively, while rates of immediate and delayed major bleeding were 0.75 % (95 % CI, 0.31 % – 1.8 %) and 2.1 % (95 % CI, 1.6 % – 2.6 %). When we performed separate analysis for Asia vs Western countries, immediate and delayed perforation rates were 3.8 % (95 % CI, 3.1 % – 4.6 %) and 0.18 % (95 % CI, 0.08 % – 0.42 %) for Asia and 6.6 % (95 % CI, 4.6 % – 9.4 %) and 1.2 % (95 %, 0.29 % – 4.6 %) for Western countries, respectively, while rates of immediate and delayed major bleeding were 0.39 % (95 % CI, 0.11 % – 1.3 %) and 1.8 % (95 % CI, 1.4 % – 2.4 %) for Asia and 3.3 % (95 % CI, 1.4 % – 7.6 %) and 3.9 % (95 %, 2.5 % – 5.8 %) for Western countries, respectively (Table 3). After an average postoperative follow up of 19 months, the rate of tumor recurrence was 0.04 % (95 % CI, 0.01 % – 0.31 %) among those with R0 resection and 3.6 % (95 % CI, 1.4 % – 8.8 %) among those without R0 resection (Table 2). Overall, irrespective of the resection status, recurrence rate was 1.0 % (95 % CI, 0.42 % – 2.1 %). For Asian studies, rates of tumor recurrence were 0.05 % (95 %, 0.01 % – 0.33 %), 2.3 % (95 % CI, 1.1 % – 4.4 %), and 0.37 % (95 % CI, 0.13 – 0.10) among tumors with R0 resection, without R0 resection, and irrespective of R0 status respectively. On the other hand, tumor recurrence rates for Western countries were 21 % (95 % CI, 11 % – 36 %) and 6.5 % (95 % CI, 3.7 % – 11 %) among tumors without R0 resection and irrespective of resection status respectively. All four Western studies that assessed recurrence among tumors with R0 resection reported no recurrence among such tumors after an average follow up of 7 months (Table 3). All our estimates were comparable to those of sensitivity analysis as pre-specified (Table S3). Our meta-analysis showed that, across multiple studies in 15 countries, ESD demonstrated an excellent treatment success in patients with colorectal tumors. Perioperatively, perforation and major bleeding were the most commonly reported serious adverse outcomes but their risk is somewhat comparable to EMR 4 8. FASHION AND ART CYCLES ARE DRIVEN BY COUNTER-DOMINANCE SIGNALS OF ELITE COMPETITION: QUANTITATIVE EVIDENCE FROM MUSIC STYLES Section for Science of Complex Systems, CeMSIIS, Medical University of Vienna, Spitalgasse 23, A-1090 Vienna, Austria 2Complexity Science Hub Vienna, Josefstaedter Strasse 39, A-1080 Vienna, Austria Abstract Human symbol systems such as art and fashion styles emerge from complex social processes that govern the continuous re-organization of modern societies. They provide a signaling scheme that allows members of an elite to distinguish themselves from the rest of society. Efforts to understand the dynamics of art and fashion cycles have been based on ‘bottom-up’ and ‘top down’ theories. According to ‘top down’ theories, elite members signal their superior status by introducing new symbols (e.g., fashion styles), which are adopted by low-status groups. In response to this adoption, elite members would need to introduce new symbols to signal their status. According to many ‘bottom-up’ theories, style cycles evolve from lower classes and follow an essentially random pattern. We propose an alternative explanation based on counterdominance signaling. There, elite members want others to imitate their symbols; changes only occur when outsider groups successfully challenge the elite by introducing signals that contrast those endorsed by the elite. We investigate these mechanisms using a dynamic network approach on data containing almost 8 million musical albums released between 1956 and 2015. The network systematically quantifies artistic similarities of competing musical styles and their changes over time. We formulate empirical tests for whether new symbols are introduced by current elite members (top-down), randomness (bottom-up) or by peripheral groups through counter-dominance signals. We find clear evidence that counter-dominance-signaling drives changes in musical styles. This provides a quantitative, completely data-driven answer to a century-old debate about the nature of the underlying social dynamics of fashion cycles. Introduction Of all species, only modern homo sapiens has evolved the ability to use complex symbolic behavior to organize and coordinate large anonymous societies [1,2,3]. Symbols facilitate the identification of group membership, social status, and, consequently, the competition between elites—here defined as social groups, which have disproportionate access of control over economic, social, cultural, political, or knowledge resources [4,5]. In recent times, ‘symbolic social coordination and competition’ are perhaps best captured in fashion and art style cycles (e.g. in music, literature, architecture) [6,7,8,9,12]. There, the social influence of an elite is represented by the number of people who adopt the elite’s core stylistic elements [10,11]. Costly signaling theory (ST) has been proposed as an explanation for the social and cultural evolutionary dynamics that determine the changes of fashion and art styles [3,13]. According to ST, elite members introduce a style which is too costly to adopt for non-members (e.g., a chandelier) and hence provides an honest signal of the elite’s superior status. Yet, non-elite members would sooner or later find ways to mimic the elite style (e.g., acquiring inexpensive chandeliers). Elite members would then abandon the style and replace it with a new one (e.g. a modern-style functionalistic pendant light), which again is too costly to adopt for non-members [6]; they are constantly “on the run” from too many adopters and innovate in reaction to being imitated. Often the new style of the elite would be in stark contrast to the previous style, as shifting to a style highly distinctive from the previous one adds an additional obstacle for the adoption by lower classes [14]. This would explain why consecutive styles often occur as extreme opposites (e.g., ornamentation versus functionalism). However, this ‘top-down’ mechanism (stylistic elements spread from elite to non-members) has been questioned by others who propose a ‘bottom-up’ dynamic (elite members adopt stylistic elements from non-members to retain their status) to account for the fact that styles often evolve from lower classes or subcultures (e.g., Punk-rock or ripped jeans) [8,15,16,17]. Following this logic, broad stylistic changes are driven by external factors such as symbolic elements chosen and promoted by cultural industries (e.g., trend-scouts from fashion houses or music labels who may just randomly pick up symbols from a sub-culture) [18,19,20]. According to this view, fashion cycles should follow an essentially random pattern. This has been formalized in the so-called Random-Pattern-Theories (RPT). For instance, it has been shown that models based on the random copying of cultural traits can explain cyclical patterns of fashion change in a quite robust way, for instance in the popularity of first names [21, 22, 23]. The central assumption in these models is that some styles will become highly popular simply due to imitation but not because they are in some way superior to other styles. However, there exist problems with both the ST and the RPT approach. For example, various ‘elite-styles’ enjoy broad adoption by the middle and lower classes (e.g., ties, black suits, diamond rings) but elite members did not abandon them (as ST would predict). RPT, on the other hand, is unable to account for the fact that two subsequent styles often endorse completely opposite sets of symbols, such as the change from modernism to postmodernism. Instead, we argue that such prominent and enduring cyclical symbolic patterns of mass-culture can only be understood by considering the structure of the networks that underlie the processes of social coordination, such as elite competition in the form of counter-dominance signaling. To resolve the puzzle of conflicting predictions suggested by ST and RPT, we propose a third mechanism, that of counter-dominance-signaling (CDS). This mechanism is rooted in cultural evolutionary theories of counter-dominance as well as theories of collective action and social movement [24,25,26,27]. Rather than assuming that members of an elite are constantly on the run from too many adopters, in the CDS framework, elite members actually like to see others adopt their symbols and styles. This signals the cultural influence of elite members [10,24]. Stylistic changes occur when a new upcoming elite successfully challenges the dominance of the established elite by introducing a novel style, which is subsequently adopted by a sufficiently large number of followers. In other words, followers stop adopting the style from the established elite A and start to adopt the style from a new emerging elite B. The new style of elite B should starkly deviate from the previous style, since it signals and emphasizes its disagreement with the previous hegemony. Examples for such CDS include ostentatiously decorative and non-functional ornaments of post-modern architecture that have the potential to provocatively signal the protest against the dominant elite group such as the ‘form-follows-function’ doctrine of modernism [24]. CDS serves as a focal point to facilitate the coordination of people that share a reservation against the current dominant elite group [10,24,26]. Our proposed mechanism of CDS allows us to solve a century old debate on the driving mechanisms behind stylistic changes in areas of mass-culture such as art and fashion [6]. On the one hand—consistent with RPT but inconsistent with ST—CDS is able to account for the fact that new styles are not necessarily introduced by elites, but often do evolve through a ‘bottom-up’ dynamic where elite members adopt specific stylistic elements from non-members. On the other hand—consistent with ST but inconsistent with RPT—CDS predicts patterns of starkly contrasting symbols in consecutive styles. The contrasts arise because outsiders use highly distinctive symbols to counter the dominance of existing elite groups and not because the elite introduced distinctive elements to prevent the masses from adopting them, as predicted by ST. A fundamental challenge is to empirically test (i) if non-trivial mechanisms are indeed necessary to understand cultural change and, if so, (ii) which mechanism—ST, RPT, or CDS—is actually realized in society. Therefore, we first formulate a null model for the evolution of musical styles that assumes that music producers choose the styles which they adopt completely at random; this provides a neutral model for the evolution of styles [28]. We show that such a model is not able to account for the existence of fashion cycles observed in the data of musical styles, which suggests that the evolution of styles is driven by mechanisms that depend on stylistic differences. The neutral model can therefore be modified to include the mechanisms of ST, RPT, or CDS, which then indeed leads to the emergence of fashion cycles. Empirical tests are then needed to determine which model mechanism best describes the actual evolution of musical styles. To this end we developed a method to quantify musical styles by determining each style’s typical instrumentation. From a dataset containing almost eight million albums that have been released since 1950, we extracted information about a usercreated taxonomy of fifteen musical genres, 422 musical styles, and 570 different instruments. The instruments that are typically associated with a given genre (or style) were shown to be a suitable approximation to formally describe the characteristics of a style [29]. Therefore, the similarity between styles can be quantified through the similarity of their instrumentation. For instance, in Figure 1A we show an example of four different musical styles (blue circles) that are linked to five instruments (green squares). Here a link indicates that the instrument is (typically) featured in a release belonging to that style. The higher the overlap in instruments between two styles, the higher is their similarity and the thicker is the line that connects the styles in Figure 1A. Using this network representation, we are able to rephrase the question which mechanism—ST, RPT, or CST—is realized to a question of detecting specific patterns of the network’s evolution, see Figure 1B. There, we schematically show three different scenarios for the time evolution of a network (blue circles) that represent the three theories ST, RPT, or CDS, respectively. The size of the circles indicates the popularity of a given style, i.e., how many artists adopted that particular style. Initially, there exists an elite, whose members have broadly adopted style i. Other styles with lower popularity (non-elite groups) will imitate the style of this elite group, resulting in an increased similarity of other styles with i (increase of thickness of the lines connecting them to i in Figure 1B). According to ST, elite members will react to this imitation by adopting a new and different style j. Now it will be style j that the lowpopularity groups seek to follow and imitate. This results in increased popularity of j and increased similarity between j and the prior elite style i. In the RPT scenario, in contrast, it is a new elite that forms at a random position in the network that dominates the next fashion cycle. Finally, the mechanism of CDS suggests that the current elite i will be provocatively challenged by an outsider group, k, using signals (in our case sets of instruments) that are in stark opposition to those endorsed by i. Through the adoption of these signals that oppose i, a new counter-elite emerges with style k. Each of the three mechanisms leads to the same generic cyclic patterns of fashion styles, see Figure 1C. That is, initially style i increases in popularity as it is imitated by other styles. With the shift of the elite to a different style (ST) or the emergence of a random new (RPT) or counter elite (CDS), new styles gain popularity at the expense of style i and will therefore more frequently be imitated. This imitation triggers the next fashion cycle. By cycles we do not refer to patterns where a single style oscillates in popularity over time, but rather a pattern where certain styles rise sharply in popularity for some time, eventually level off in their growth, and then fade back into oblivion as new styles emerge that trigger the next cycle. With the help of the proposed network formalism we can specify concrete hypotheses to test whether the observed changes in similarities and popularities are best described by a network evolution mechanism that is compatible with ST, RPT, or CDS. Scalable High Performance SDN Switch Architecture on FPGA for Core Networks Sasindu Wijeratne, Ashen Ekanayake, Sandaruwan Jayaweera, Danuka Ravishan and Ajith Pasqual Dept. of Electronic and Telecommunication Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka {130665u, 130150l, 130254j, 130516p}@uom.lk, pasqual@mrt.ac.lk Abstract—Due to the increasing heterogeneity in network user requirements, dynamically varying day to day network traffic patterns and delay in network service deployment, there is a huge demand for scalability and flexibility in modern networking infrastructure, which in return has paved way for the introduction of Software Defined Networking (SDN) in core networks. In this paper, we present an FPGA-based switch which is fully compliant with OpenFlow; the pioneering protocol for southbound interface of SDN. The switch architecture is completely implemented on hardware. The design consists of an OpenFlow Southbound agent which can process OpenFlow packets at a rate of 10Gbps. The proposed architecture speed scales up to 400Gbps while it consumes only 60% resources on a Xilinx Virtex-7 featuring XC7VX485T FPGA. Index Terms—Software Defined Networking (SDN), OpenFlow Switch, Core Networks, FPGA I. INTRODUCTION Software Defined Networking (SDN) is a novel networking model which facilitates innovation in the field of networking. SDN is more dynamic, adaptable and manageable, which makes it ideal for the high-bandwidth and dynamic nature of today’s applications. Recent studies have shown that SDN has the potential to be used in a vast variety of network types [1]. In decoupled SDN architecture, infrastructure layer of SDN is made of switches which are dedicated to forwarding the traffic according to the flow details stored in their flow tables. This flow tables are maintained by the control layer. OpenFlow is the most common Southbound API which is used as the medium to communicate between control layer and infrastructure layer. It defines all possible functions and messages used to manage switches via a centralized software controller. With uprising cutting edge technologies for the core net-work, SDN has shown promising results in efficient routing techniques for service provider networks and advancements of ISP backbone. Also, SDN approach promises reduction of costs, enhancement of network flexibility and scalability, and shortening of the time to market of new applications and services which is much needed for emerging core network requirements. Recent researches on SDN switch implementations are focused on Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) considering the scalability, flexibility and low cost [2][3][4][5]. Khan et al [5] has illustrated a hardware level SDN switch which meets the 10Gbps line rate and it is fully-compliant with OpenFlow 1.0. This system has successfully off-loaded to NetFPGA-10G, ML605 and DE04 FPGA boards. Zhou et al. in [2] has demonstrated a flexible and scalable hybrid switch (software and hardware level switch implementation on a SoC). This scalable architecture has achieved 88Gbps with a 1000 flow table design. For lookup process, this implementation has used Ternary Content Addressable Memory (TCAM) and a single table structure. The OpenFlow Agent of this design is purely software and it is capable of decoding OpenFlow 1.0. Wijekoon et al. [3] illustrated a hardware level SDN switch with scalability, which is focused on low cost and efficient flow matching. This system is implemented on Virtrex-7 FPGA. Naous et al. in [4] describes an OpenFlow switch on NetFPGA platform. It has the capability of handling 32,000 exact match flow entries and running at line-rate with four 1G NetFPGA ports. In this paper, we present a novel high-performance switch fabric with low-latency for SDN environment which is based on OpenFlow [6]. This cost-efficient design is focused on reconfigurable hardware and it can be scaled with the network’s requirements. Further, the proposed architecture provides high throughput and high-speed connection with control plane which makes it an ideal candidate for core networks. Section II briefly describes the background of our research including the information regarding data plane of SDN. In section III, we explain the design space exploration for our architecture. Finally, in section IV, a performance evaluation of the switch fabric along with results obtained for this architecture are provided. II. BACKGROUND The data plane comprises switches with flow tables which contain flow entries that include routing paths to the incoming network packets. A flow entry consists of packet header fields, counters, a priority and associated actions. The SDN control layer is responsible for flow entry maintenance. The bridge between control layer and a switch is the Southbound interface. OpenFlow is the southbound interface protocol in this implementation. The rich feature list of OpenFlow makes it more suitable for the dynamic environment. In switch, OpenFlow Southbound agent is responsible for the communication with control layer. The implemented OpenFlow agent is capable of handling messages from OpenFlow 1.3.1 and above [6]. Exact matching, range matching and prefix matching mechanisms are used in flow tables. The efficiency of matching process directly affects the efficiency and speed of traffic forwarding. Ternary Content Addressable Memory (TCAM) and Content Addressable Memory (CAM) make the matching process more efficient even though the hardware utilization is high. Each flow entry has its own priority given by the controller and those who have higher priority values get examined first. Duration of the flow entry, packet count and byte count received are maintained by the counters. Further, per table, per port and per queue counters are there to record the condition of the switch. These counter values help control layer to make better and efficient forwarding decisions. Implementing a resource efficient solution which can support all these functionalities while handling the core network throughput and latency requirements is the focus of our research. III.
