Abstract. Intrinsic image decomposition is a challenging, long-standing computer vision problem for which ground truth data is very difficult to acquire. We explore the use of synthetic data for training CNN-based intrinsic image decomposition models, then applying these learned models to real-world images. To that end, we present CGI NTRINSICS, a new, large-scale dataset of physically-based rendered images of scenes with full ground truth decompositions. The rendering process we use is carefully designed to yield high-quality, realistic images, which we find to be crucial for this problem domain. We also propose a new end-to-end training method that learns better decompositions by leveraging CGI NTRINSICS, and optionally IIW and SAW, two recent datasets of sparse annotations on realworld images. Surprisingly, we find that a decomposition network trained solely on our synthetic data outperforms the state-of-the-art on both IIW and SAW, and performance improves even further when IIW and SAW data is added during training. Our work demonstrates the suprising effectiveness of carefully-rendered synthetic data for the intrinsic images task. Intrinsic images is a classic vision problem involving decomposing an input image I into a product of reflectance (albedo) and shading images R · S. Recent years have seen remarkable progress on this problem, but it remains challenging due to its ill-posedness. An attractive proposition has been to replace traditional hand-crafted priors with learned, CNN-based models. For such learning methods data is key, but collecting ground truth data for intrinsic images is extremely difficult, especially for images of real-world scenes. One way to generate large amounts of training data for intrinsic images is to render synthetic scenes. However, existing synthetic datasets are limited to images of single objects [1,2] (e.g., via ShapeNet [3]) or images of CG animation that utilize simplified, unrealistic illumination (e.g., via Sintel [4]). An alternative is to collect ground truth for real images using crowdsourcing, as in the Intrinsic Images in the Wild (IIW) and Shading Annotations in the Wild (SAW) datasets [5,6]. However, the annotations in such datasets are sparse and difficult to collect accurately at scale. Inspired by recent efforts to use synthetic images of scenes as training data for indoor and outdoor scene understanding [7,8,9,10], we present the first large-scale scene-level intrinsic images dataset based on high-quality physically-based rendering, which we call CGI NTRINSICS (CGI). CGI consists of over 20,000 images of indoor scenes, based on the SUNCG dataset [11]. Our aim with CGI is to help drive significant progress towards solving the intrinsic images problem for Internet photos of real-world scenes. We find Fig. 1. Overview and network architecture. Our work integrates physically-based rendered images from our CGI NTRINSICS dataset and reflectance/shading annotations from IIW and SAW in order to train a better intrinsic decomposition network. that high-quality physically-based rendering is essential for our task. While SUNCG provides physically-based scene renderings [12], our experiments show that the details of how images are rendered are of critical importance, and certain choices can lead to massive improvements in how well CNNs trained for intrinsic images on synthetic data generalize to real data. We also propose a new partially supervised learning method for training a CNN to directly predict reflectance and shading, by combining ground truth from CGI and sparse annotations from IIW/SAW. Through evaluations on IIW and SAW, we find that, surprisingly, decomposition networks trained solely on CGI can achieve state-of-the-art performance on both datasets. Combined training using both CGI and IIW/SAW leads to even better performance. Finally, we find that CGI generalizes better than existing datasets by evaluating on MIT Intrinsic Images, a very different, object-centric, dataset. Optimization-based methods. The classical approach to intrinsic images is to integrate various priors (smoothness, reflectance sparseness, etc.) into an optimization framework [13,14,15,16,17,5]. However, for images of real-world scenes, such hand-crafted prior assumptions are difficult to craft and are often violated. Several recent methods seek to improve decomposition quality by integrating surface normals or depths from RGB-D cameras [18,19,20] into the optimization process. However, these methods assume depth maps are available during optimization, preventing them from being used for a wide range of consumer photos. Learning-based methods. Learning methods for intrinsic images have recently been explored as an alternative to models with hand-crafted priors, or a way to set the parameters of such models automatically. Barron and Malik [21] learn parameters of a model that utilizes sophisticated priors on reflectance, shape and illumination. This approach works on images of objects (such as in the MIT dataset), but does not generalize to real world scenes. More recently, CNN-based methods have been deployed, including work that regresses directly to the output decomposition based on various training datasets, such as Sintel [22,23], MIT intrinsics and ShapeNet [2,1]. Shu et al. [24] also propose a CNN-based method specifically for the domain of facial images, where ground truth geometry can be obtained through model fitting. However, as we show in the evaluation section, the networks trained on such prior datasets perform poorly on images of real-world scenes. Two recent datasets are based on images of real-world scenes. Intrinsic Images in the Wild (IIW) [5] and Shading Annotations in the Wild (SAW) [6] consist of sparse, crowd-sourced reflectance and shading annotations on real indoor images. Subsequently, several papers train CNN-based classifiers on these sparse annotations and use the classifier outputs as priors to guide decomposition [6,25,26,27]. However, we find these annotations alone are insufficient to train a direct regression approach, likely because they are sparse and are derived from just a few thousand images. Finally, very recent work has explored the use of time-lapse imagery as training data for intrinsic images [28], although this provides a very indirect source of supervision. Synthetic datasets for real scenes. Synthetic data has recently been utilized to improve predictions on real-world images across a range of problems. For instance, [7,10] created a large-scale dataset and benchmark based on video games for the purpose of autonomous driving, and [29,30] use synthetic imagery to form small benchmarks for intrinsic images. SUNCG [12] is a recent, large-scale synthetic dataset for indoor scene understanding. However, many of the images in the PBRS database of physically-based renderings derived from SUNCG have low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and non-realistic sensor properties. We show that higher quality renderings yield much better training data for intrinsic images. To create our CGI NTRINSICS (CGI) dataset, we started from the SUNCG dataset [11], which contains over 45,000 3D models of indoor scenes. We first considered the PBRS dataset of physically-based renderings of scenes from SUNCG [12]. For each scene, PBRS samples cameras from good viewpoints, and uses the physically-based Mitsuba renderer [31] to generate realistic images under reasonably realistic lighting (including a mix of indoor and outdoor illumination sources), with global illumination. Using such an approach, we can also generate ground truth data for intrinsic images by rendering a standard RGB image I, then asking the renderer to produce a reflectance map R from the same viewpoint, and finally dividing to get the shading image S = I/R. Examples of such ground truth decompositions are shown in Figure 2. Note that we automatically mask out light sources (including illumination from windows looking outside) when creating the decomposition, and do not consider those pixels when training the network. However, we found that the PBRS renderings are not ideal for use in training realworld intrinsic image decomposition networks. In fact, certain details in how images are rendered have a dramatic impact on learning performance: Fig. 2. Visualization of ground truth from our CGI NTRINSICS dataset. Top row: rendered RGB images. Middle: ground truth reflectance. Bottom: ground truth shading. Note that light sources are masked out when creating the ground truth decomposition. Rendering quality. Mitsuba and other high-quality renderers support a range of rendering algorithms, including various flavors of path tracing methods that sample many light paths for each output pixel. In PBRS, the authors note that bidirectional path tracing works well but is very slow, and opt for Metropolis Light Transport (MLT) with a sample rate of 512 samples per pixel [12]. In contrast, for our purposes we found that bidirectional path tracing (BDPT) with very large numbers of samples per pixel was the only algorithm that gave consistently good results for rendering SUNCG images. Comparisons between selected renderings from PBRS and our new CGI images are shown in Figure 3. Note the significantly decreased noise in our renderings. This extra quality comes at a cost. We find that using BDPT with 8,192 samples per pixel yields acceptable quality for most images. This increases the render time per image significantly, from a reported 31s [12], to approximately 30 minutes.1 One reason for the need for large numbers of samples is that SUNCG scenes are often challenging from a rendering perspective—the illumination is often indirect, coming from open doorways or constrained in other ways by geometry. However, rendering is highly parallelizable, and over the course of about six months we rendered over ten thousand images on a cluster of about 10 machines. Tone mapping from HDR to LDR. We found that another critical factor in image generation is how rendered images are tone mapped. Renderers like Mitsuba generally produce high dynamic range (HDR) outputs that encode raw, linear radiance estimates for each pixel. In contrast, real photos are usually low dynamic range. We find that a simpler tone mapping method produces more natural-looking results. Again, Figure 3 shows comparisons between PBRS renderings and our own. Note how the color and illumination features, such as shadows, are better captured in our renderings (we noticed that shadows often disappear with the Reinhard tone mapper). In particular, to tone map a linear HDR radiance image IHDR , we find the 90th γ 1 percentile intensity value r90 , then compute the image ILDR = αIHDR , where γ = 2.2 is a standard gamma correction factor, and α is computed such that r90 maps to the value 0.8. The final image is then clipped to the range [0, 1]. This mapping ensures that at most 10% of the image pixels (and usually many fewer) are saturated after tone mapping, and tends to result in natural-looking LDR images. Using the above rendering approach, we re-rendered ∼ 20,000 images from PBRS. We also integrated 152 realistic renderings from [30] into our dataset. Breast cancer is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with approximately 2.3 million new cases diagnosed annually (Bray et al., 2018). A subset of women with locally advanced breast cancer presents with fungating tumor masses that erode and infiltrate the surrounding breast skin, classified as T4b breast cancers (Edge & Compton, 2010). These patients often experience chronic pain, large open wounds, frequent infections, malodorous drainage, social isolation, and general debilitation, which pose enormous therapeutic challenges (Grocott et al., 2016). The advanced nature of the disease necessitates palliation, while minimizing recovery time and maximizing quality of life, as the primary treatment objective (Temple et al., 2017). The management of T4b breast cancers is complex and requires a multidisciplinary approach, involving surgical oncologists, medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, and plastic surgeons (Brennan et al., 2018). Surgical resection of the tumor, followed by chest wall reconstruction, is often considered the most effective treatment option for these patients (Katz et al., 2017). However, the decision to operate is frequently delayed due to the presence of distant metastases, which are found in up to 50% of patients at the time of diagnosis (Rastogi et al., 2018). Additionally, the emergency department presentation of these patients in a hemodynamically unstable condition, such as hemorrhagic or septic shock, necessitates immediate medical attention and may further delay reconstruction (Larkin et al., 2019). Despite the importance of palliation in the management of T4b breast cancers, there is a paucity of research on the reconstructive techniques used in this patient population. Previous studies have focused primarily on the surgical management of the tumor, with limited attention to the reconstruction of the chest wall and the subsequent impact on patient outcomes (Grobmyer et al., 2017). Furthermore, the existing literature on chest wall reconstruction in breast cancer patients is largely limited to smaller, non-fungating tumors, and the applicability of these findings to T4b breast cancers is unclear (Recht et al., 2018). The research question guiding this study is: What are the outcomes of surgical resection and chest wall reconstruction in patients with fungating T4b breast cancers, and how do these interventions impact pain, wound care needs, and quality of life? This study aims to address the gap in the current literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the reconstructive techniques used in this patient population and their effects on patient outcomes. The contributions of this research are threefold. Firstly, it provides a detailed description of the demographic, socioeconomic, and clinical characteristics of patients with fungating T4b breast cancers, which can inform the development of targeted treatment strategies. Secondly, it evaluates the efficacy of various reconstructive techniques, including split-thickness skin grafting and thoracoepigastric advancement, latissimus dorsi, trapezius, and extended transverse and vertical rectus abdominis flaps, in palliating pain and reducing wound care needs. Finally, it examines the postoperative complications and survival outcomes of patients undergoing chest wall reconstruction, which can help to identify areas for improvement in the management of these complex patients. The management of T4b breast cancers requires a comprehensive approach that addresses the patient's physical, emotional, and social needs (Harrison et al., 2019). The use of reconstructive surgery in this patient population is not only aimed at improving functional outcomes but also at enhancing quality of life and reducing the burden of disease (Lee et al., 2018). By exploring the outcomes of surgical resection and chest wall reconstruction in patients with fungating T4b breast cancers, this study seeks to contribute to the development of evidence-based guidelines for the management of these complex patients. The findings of this research can inform the decision-making process of healthcare providers and ultimately improve the care and outcomes of women with T4b breast cancers. The role of reconstructive surgery in the management of these patients is critical, as it can significantly impact pain, wound care needs, and quality of life (Grocott et al., 2016). However, the reconstructive techniques used in this patient population are often complex and require careful planning and execution (Katz et al., 2017). The use of advanced reconstructive techniques, such as microvascular free flaps, may be necessary to achieve optimal outcomes in patients with large or complex defects (Rastogi et al., 2018). In conclusion, the management of T4b breast cancers is a complex and challenging task that requires a comprehensive approach to care. This retrospective study was conducted at a single institution, with approval from the Institutional Review Board (IRB), to evaluate the management and reconstruction of breast cancer patients with fungating T4b tumors. The study population consisted of 12 consecutive patients who underwent resection of fungating T4b breast tumors and subsequent chest wall reconstruction between 2009 and 2014. Data were collected retrospectively from patient medical records, operative reports, and clinic follow-up notes (Higgins et al., 2011). Demographic, socioeconomic, and clinical data, including age, tumor size, stage, and presence of metastatic disease, were collected and analyzed (Feeney et al., 2013). Patient selection criteria included a diagnosis of breast cancer with a fungating T4b tumor, defined as a tumor with direct extension to the chest wall and/or skin, with or without ulceration, and/or skin nodules confined to the same breast (Edge et al., 2010). Patients with recurrences or secondary malignancies were excluded from the study. Data regarding patient comorbidities, such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease, were also collected to assess potential risk factors for postoperative complications (Katz et al., 2013). The surgical management of these patients was complex, requiring a multidisciplinary approach. Preoperative evaluation included computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET) scans to assess the extent of disease and potential for resection (Maki et al., 2013). Patients with significant comorbidities or poor performance status were considered for neoadjuvant chemotherapy or palliative care (Tahir et al., 2015). Surgical resection of the tumor was performed by a team of breast surgeons, with subsequent reconstruction by a team of plastic surgeons (Disa et al., 2013). Reconstructive procedures were tailored to the individual patient, taking into account the size and location of the defect, as well as the patient's overall health status (Losee et al., 2012). The reconstructive techniques used included split-thickness skin grafting, thoracoepigastric advancement, latissimus dorsi, trapezius, and extended transverse and vertical rectus abdominis flaps. These techniques have been previously described in the literature and are well-established methods for chest wall reconstruction (Zivec et al., 2014). Postoperative care was standardized, with all patients receiving intravenous antibiotics and pain management in the intensive care unit (ICU) (Carroll et al., 2015). Patients were discharged to a rehabilitation facility or home with wound care instructions and follow-up appointments with their surgeons (Park et al., 2012). Complications were defined as any adverse event occurring within 30 days of surgery, including wound infections, dehiscence, or need for reoperation (Fischer et al., 2013). Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software (version 22.0, IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics, including means, medians, and ranges, were used to summarize patient demographics, tumor characteristics, and postoperative outcomes (Pallant, 2013). Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, with postoperative survival time calculated from the date of surgery to the date of last follow-up or death (Kaplan et al., 1958). A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. In addition to descriptive statistics, we also performed univariate and multivariate analysis to identify potential risk factors for postoperative complications and survival. Variables analyzed included age, tumor size, stage, presence of metastatic disease, and comorbidities (Altman, 2012). Logistic regression analysis was used to identify independent predictors of postoperative complications, while Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify predictors of survival (Hosmer et al., 2013). The results of these analyses will be presented in the results section. The mean wound size for reconstruction was calculated using digital imaging software (ImageJ, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD), with measurements taken from preoperative and postoperative photographs (Bonfitness et al., 2015). Wound care needs were assessed using a standardized wound assessment tool, with scores ranging from 0 to 10 (WOCN, 2010). Pain was assessed using the visual analog scale (VAS), with scores ranging from 0 to 10 (Hjermstad et al., 2011). improvements in pain and wound care needs were defined as a reduction in VAS score or wound assessment score of ≥50% from preoperative to postoperative values. In conclusion, our study aimed to evaluate the management and reconstruction of breast cancer patients with fungating T4b tumors, using a retrospective cohort design and statistical analysis. The results of our study will provide valuable insights into the surgical management and reconstruction of these complex patients, highlighting the importance of a multidisciplinary approach and individualized care. Introduction Olfactory perception is a multifaceted sense that involves the detection and interpretation of chemical stimuli in the environment. It plays a crucial role in various aspects of daily life, from flavor perception to environmental awareness and memory formation. In individuals with visual impairments, the sense of smell is often presumed to be enhanced, potentially compensating for the lack of visual information. This notion has permeated popular culture, often depicted in narratives where blind individuals exhibit heightened olfactory abilities. However, the scientific exploration of this phenomenon reveals a more nuanced picture. While some studies suggest that blind individuals possess superior olfactory capabilities, others report no significant differences compared to sighted individuals. The perception that sensory compensation occurs in blind individuals spearheaded early research into cross-modal plasticity, a concept that refers to the brain's ability to reorganize and adapt following sensory loss. The visual cortex in blind individuals has been shown to engage in non-visual tasks, supporting the idea that the absence of one sense can enhance others (Theoret et al., 2004). However, while cross-modal plasticity is a well-documented phenomenon, the specific enhancement of olfactory perception in blind individuals remains contentious. Empirical investigations into olfactory function among blind individuals have yielded inconsistent findings, categorizing the existing literature into four primary domains: odor threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. The odor threshold refers to the minimum concentration of an odorant that an individual can detect, while odor discrimination concerns the ability to distinguish between different odors. Cued odor identification involves recognizing an odor when given an associative cue, whereas free odor identification requires identifying an odor without any cues. Studies within each of these domains have alternated between reporting enhanced olfactory performance among blind individuals and failing to observe any significant differences compared to sighted controls (Sorokowska et al., 2018). These conflicting results highlight a gap in understanding, which may stem from methodological differences across studies, such as variations in participant demographics, the testing paradigms employed, or even the specific odorants used. Additionally, the onset of blindness—whether congenital or acquired—could influence olfactory abilities differently. The distinction between early blind and late-blind individuals implicates the role of neural development and lifelong sensory experience in shaping sensory perception (Röder et al., 2004). Understanding the potential moderators influencing olfactory performance in blind individuals is crucial for elucidating the underlying mechanisms of sensory adaptation. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to address the inconsistencies in the existing literature on olfactory perception in blind individuals by quantitatively synthesizing findings across studies. Our research question asks whether baseline olfactory abilities—across the four domains identified—differ between blind and sighted individuals. By aggregating data from numerous investigations, this analysis endeavors to achieve greater statistical power and a more comprehensive understanding of olfactory function in the blind. Furthermore, this study contributes to the existing body of research by examining potential moderators, such as age, gender, and the onset of blindness, to ascertain their role in olfactory perception. While previous studies have hinted at factors that might modulate sensory abilities among the blind, a systematic exploration of these variables is lacking. By investigating these moderators, this review seeks to provide a nuanced perspective that accounts for individual differences, potentially illuminating why previous findings have been inconsistent. The outcomes of this research extend beyond academic interest, offering potential applications in developing rehabilitative strategies and technologies for visually impaired individuals. If blind individuals exhibit specific strengths or weaknesses in olfactory perception, customized therapeutic interventions or assistive technologies could be designed to capitalize on these abilities, further enhancing the quality of life for blind individuals. In summary, this paper endeavors to fill a critical gap in the understanding of olfactory perception in visually impaired individuals. By rigorously analyzing and synthesizing existing literature, we provide a clearer picture of whether and how blindness influences olfactory abilities. This research not only enhances theoretical knowledge but also has practical implications for improving sensory adaptation strategies in the visually impaired population. This systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to the guidelines outlined by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) to ensure the transparency and comprehensive reporting of findings. The methodological strategy was devised to identify studies exploring the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness, focusing specifically on olfactory threshold, odor discrimination, free odor identification, and cued odor identification in blind versus sighted individuals. Data Sources and Search Strategy The literature search was conducted using several electronic databases, including PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science, until October 2023. Keywords used in the search included "blindness," "visual impairment," "olfactory threshold," "odor discrimination," "odor identification," "olfactory perception," and "sensory compensation." Boolean operators (AND, OR) facilitated the combination of search terms to refine and expand the search scope. Additionally, references from pertinent reviews and primary articles were manually screened to ensure comprehensive coverage of the literature. Eligibility Criteria To be included in the meta-analysis, studies had to meet the following criteria: (1) involve human participants with documented blindness (either early or late onset), (2) comprise a comparative sighted control group, (3) assess olfactory functions through standardized and validated measures, (4) provide sufficient statistical data to calculate effect sizes (e.g., means, standard deviations, or t-statistics), and (5) be published in peer-reviewed journals in English. Studies focusing solely on diseases affecting olfactory functionality (e.g., anosmia due to neurological disorders unrelated to blindness) or using non-standardized olfactory assessments were excluded. Data Extraction and Coding Two independent reviewers (Author 1 and Author 2) systematically extracted relevant data from each included study. In cases of discrepancies, discussions were held with a third author until consensus was reached. Extracted data included study characteristics (first author, year of publication, country), participant demographics (sample size, age, gender distribution, onset of blindness), and outcome measures (reported test statistics, effect sizes). Where necessary, authors were contacted to obtain missing data. Study Design and Outcome Measures The primary outcome of interest was the difference in performance on specified olfactory tasks between blind and sighted individuals. The tasks were categorized into four domains: (1) odor threshold, (2) odor discrimination, (3) free odor identification, and (4) cued odor identification. Odor threshold procedures typically assessed the concentration at which individuals could reliably detect an odor. Odor discrimination tasks required participants to distinguish between different odors, while identification tasks involved naming or recognizing odors, either with or without cues. Statistical Analysis All statistical analyses were conducted using the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) software, version 3.0. Hedges' g was selected as the measure of effect size due to its applicability in accommodating different sample sizes. This approach allowed for the computation of a standardized mean difference between blind and sighted groups across various outcomes. Given the expected heterogeneity among studies, a random-effects model was used to summarize effect sizes, accounting for both within-study and between-study variability. Heterogeneity across studies was quantified using the I² statistic, which describes the proportion of variation due to heterogeneity rather than chance. I² values of 25%, 50%, and 75% were indicative of low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. Furthermore, publication bias was examined using Egger's test of the intercept and visual inspection of funnel plots. Asymmetry in these plots would suggest potential bias, which was further assessed through Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill method to adjust for unidentified studies' potential influence. Moderator Analysis To explore potential sources of heterogeneity and refine the analysis, we conducted moderator analyses examining the impact of age, gender distribution, and onset of blindness (early vs. late) on the observed effect sizes. Age and gender information were coded according to the reported demographics in each study. For onset, studies were categorized into early blind (onset before five years of age) and late blind (onset after five years of age). The moderator analyses were carried out using meta-regression techniques, exploring the extent to which these factors explained variability in effect size outcomes. Ethical Considerations This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Since this was a review and meta-analysis of published studies, no additional ethical approval was required. Data Synthesis and Reporting Synthesized results, including pooled effect sizes and moderator analysis outcomes, were displayed using forest plots. The results were interpreted in light of their clinical relevance and the statistical significance of findings at a threshold of p < 0.05. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of findings in the context of study quality and sample size variations. The full dataset and analytical code are available upon request to facilitate transparency and reproducibility. The primary aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to quantify differences in olfactory perception between blind and sighted individuals across various olfactory tasks, including odor threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. Each sub-section below reports the findings for these specific domains. Olfactory Threshold A total of 18 studies were included in the meta-analysis focusing on olfactory thresholds, encompassing a sample size of 1,227 participants, with 590 blind and 637 sighted individuals. The calculated overall effect size (Hedges' g) for olfactory threshold was -0.04 (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.07, p = 0.47), indicating no significant difference in olfactory threshold abilities between blind and sighted groups. The heterogeneity index (I²) was found to be 23%, suggesting low heterogeneity amongst the included studies (Tau² = 0.003, p = 0.18). These results suggest that the variance in the observed thresholds is largely homogenous, with minimal variability across studies. Olfactory Discrimination In terms of olfactory discrimination, data were pooled from 14 studies, which included 940 participants (455 blind and 485 sighted). The meta-analysis revealed a negligible effect size of 0.09 (95% CI: -0.05 to 0.24, p = 0.20), which was not statistically significant, emphasizing the similarity in discrimination abilities across both groups. The heterogeneity analysis reported an I² of 35% (Tau² = 0.007, p = 0.07), indicating a moderate level of heterogeneity. Although there was more variability among studies in this domain compared to olfactory threshold studies, the differences between studies were not significant enough to demonstrate a consistent advantage in discrimination for either group. Cued Odor Identification The analysis of cued odor identification involved 14 studies with a total sample of 968 individuals, consisting of 468 blind and 500 sighted participants. The effect size for cued odor identification was calculated as 0.03 (95% CI: -0.12 to 0.17, p = 0.69), demonstrating no significant difference between the groups. Heterogeneity was relatively low with an I² of 28% (Tau² = 0.004, p = 0.14), indicating that studies were fairly consistent in their results. As with the previous tasks, these findings suggest a parity in performance between blind and sighted participants on cued odor identification tasks. Free Odor Identification The capacity for free odor identification was assessed in 7 studies including 443 participants, with 224 blind individuals and 219 sighted individuals. The effect size observed for free odor identification was 0.05 (95% CI: -0.10 to 0.20, p = 0.54), again reflecting no significant difference between the groups. The heterogeneity index reported here was I² = 40%, indicating moderate heterogeneity (Tau² = 0.006, p = 0.10). This domain demonstrated the highest level of heterogeneity among the studies, although the variance was not statistically sufficient to indicate a clear pattern. Publication Bias Assessment of publication bias was undertaken using funnel plots and Egger's regression test for each olfactory domain. The funnel plots did not indicate substantial asymmetry for any of the modalities studied, and the Egger’s test results also showed non-significant small-study effects across tasks: olfactory threshold (p = 0.32), discrimination (p = 0.27), cued identification (p = 0.30), and free identification (p = 0.35). This suggests that the overall findings were not significantly skewed due to publication bias, strengthening the reliability of the meta-analytic results. Microsurgical free tissue transfer has become a cornerstone of reconstructive surgery. It is used to restore form and function after tumor resection, trauma, burns, and chronic wounds, and in the head and neck, breast, and extremities. With experienced teams and refined techniques, reported success rates now exceed 95% in many high-volume centers (Khouri et al., 1998; Pohlenz et al., 2012). Even so, vascular compromise at the anastomosis remains the leading cause of flap loss. Arterial inflow obstruction or venous outflow obstruction, usually due to thrombosis, kinking, compression, or vasospasm, occurs in roughly 5% to 25% of cases, depending on the series and the type of flap (Chen et al., 2007; Kroll et al., 1996). Most of these events occur within the first 48 to 72 hours after surgery (Kroll et al., 1996). The prognosis of a compromised flap depends strongly on how quickly the problem is recognized. Muscle and other metabolically active tissues tolerate warm ischemia poorly, and the no-reflow phenomenon limits reperfusion after prolonged ischemia (Wang et al., 2015). Salvage rates are high when re-exploration takes place within a few hours of vascular compromise. They fall sharply when the diagnosis is delayed, reaching about 30% or lower for flaps explored late (Yii et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2007). Reliable early detection is therefore as important to flap survival as the original operation. Many monitoring methods have been proposed. Clinical observation of skin color, capillary refill, temperature, turgor, and bleeding on pinprick is still the most widely used approach and the standard against which other techniques are compared (Smit et al., 2010). It costs little and needs no equipment. However, it is subjective and depends on the experience of the examiner. Intermittent assessment can miss events that develop between rounds, and nighttime examination under poor lighting is unreliable. Clinical signs also tend to appear late, when ischemia is already established. Buried flaps and those without a skin paddle, such as free jejunum or muscle flaps used in pharyngeal and intraoral reconstruction, cannot be assessed by skin appearance at all. Several adjunctive technologies have been developed to address these limitations. Handheld Doppler ultrasonography detects flow in the pedicle or in perforators, but it is operator dependent and intermittent, and it can give false reassurance when the signal comes from adjacent vessels (Smit et al., 2010). Implantable Doppler probes allow continuous monitoring of anastomotic flow but need a second invasive procedure to place and remove, may dislodge, and have been reported to produce false-positive results (Rozen et al., 2008). Laser Doppler flowmetry and photoplethysmography give continuous measures of microcirculatory perfusion. They are sensitive to motion, probe position, and ambient light, and they provide relative rather than absolute values (Hölzle et al., 2006). Tissue oxygen tension, pH, and temperature probes, microdialysis, and fluorescence angiography with indocyanine green offer physiological information. Their drawbacks include invasiveness, cost, the need for specialized personnel, and the lack of true continuous bedside measurement (Udesen et al., 2000; Smit et al., 2010). No single technique has become a universal standard, and the search for a monitor that is noninvasive, continuous, objective, and simple to use is still active. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) is an optical technique that may meet these requirements. Biological tissue is relatively transparent to light in the near-infrared range of about 700 to 900 nm. In this range oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin have distinct absorption spectra, so measuring light attenuation at several wavelengths allows the relative concentrations of each chromophore to be estimated. From these, a regional tissue oxygen saturation can be calculated (Jöbsis, 1977). Because the signal comes mainly from small vessels (arterioles, capillaries, and venules), NIRS reflects the balance between oxygen delivery and consumption in the microvascular bed. It does not require pulsatile flow. NIRS has been used for years to monitor cerebral oxygenation during cardiac and carotid surgery and in neonatal intensive care, and in muscle physiology and the evaluation of peripheral vascular disease (Murkin and Arango, 2009). Its use in reconstructive surgery has been explored more recently. Early clinical studies in breast reconstruction and in head and neck and extremity flaps suggested that falling tissue oxygen saturation accompanies both arterial and venous compromise and may precede visible clinical changes (Keller, 2009; Repez et al., 2008; Steele et al., 2011). Different devices, probe designs, and algorithms have been used, however, and published experience is still heterogeneous. Many reports concentrate on breast flaps or on small series. Descriptions of the temporal relationship between the fall in regional oxygen saturation and the onset of visible color change are limited. This relationship determines whether the technique has practical value for earlier intervention and salvage. Information on how NIRS performs across the varied flap types and recipient sites seen in routine practice is also limited, particularly for the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy (INVOS) system, which uses a disposable adhesive sensor with a continuous bedside display. The gap this study addresses can be stated briefly. Flap surveillance still relies largely on subjective clinical examination, and the available adjuncts are invasive, intermittent, or technically demanding. NIRS is promising, but evidence is needed on whether continuous, noninvasive measurement of regional oxygen saturation can reliably detect arterial and venous insufficiency in a mixed series of free flaps, and whether it does so before clinical signs appear. We therefore asked whether postoperative monitoring of regional oxygen saturation with the INVOS system can detect vascular compromise in free flaps early enough to allow successful salvage. We prospectively monitored 57 patients undergoing free tissue transfer. We recorded regional oxygen saturation continuously after surgery and compared the trends with clinical findings and with the outcomes of re-exploration. This study makes three contributions. First, it describes the use of the INVOS system as a continuous, noninvasive flap monitor in a consecutive clinical series. Second, it documents the temporal behavior of regional oxygen saturation in cases of arterial and venous insufficiency, particularly its decline before pallor or congestion became visible. Third, it reports that all patients in whom insufficiency was detected were salvaged by re-exploration, which supports NIRS as a practical addition to postoperative flap monitoring. Study Design and Patients We conducted a prospective, single-center observational study of consecutive patients who underwent microsurgical free tissue transfer in our department of plastic and reconstructive surgery. A total of 57 patients were enrolled. Eligible patients were adults who had free flap reconstruction with a cutaneous or musculocutaneous component large enough to accommodate the optical sensor. Reconstructive indications included head and neck cancer defects, breast reconstruction, and traumatic or oncologic defects of the extremities. We excluded patients with flaps that had no skin paddle (e.g., buried flaps), patients with severe skin pigmentation disorders or extensive scarring at the planned sensor site, and patients who could not be monitored for at least 72 hours. The institutional review board approved the protocol. All patients gave written informed consent, and the study followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Recorded demographic and clinical variables were age, sex, comorbidities (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking history), flap type, recipient site, ischemia time, and anastomotic details. Surgical Procedure and Standard Postoperative Care Experienced microsurgeons performed all operations under general anesthesia. Anastomoses were done under an operating microscope with 9-0 or 10-0 monofilament nylon. Arterial anastomoses were end-to-end or end-to-side according to recipient vessel conditions. Venous anastomoses were done by hand-sewn technique or with a coupling device. Venous outflow was reconstructed with one or two veins depending on flap type. Intraoperative vessel patency was confirmed by the milking test and by inspecting flap bleeding after reperfusion. We did not use routine postoperative anticoagulation beyond a standard protocol of low-dose aspirin and adequate hydration, with unfractionated heparin given only at the surgeon's discretion in high-risk cases. After surgery, patients were nursed in a warm room (about 25–28 °C) with the flap kept free of external pressure and with controlled head and limb positioning. Standard clinical monitoring was performed in parallel with the investigational device. It consisted of hourly assessment of flap color, temperature, turgor, capillary refill, and bleeding on pinprick for the first 24 hours, then every 2–4 hours until postoperative day 3, and every 8 hours thereafter. These clinical criteria have long been the reference standard for detecting vascular compromise (Disa et al., 2001; Smit et al., 2010). The nursing staff and clinicians who made clinical decisions applied the same criteria as for any patient. The clinical team also knew the oximetry readings, so decisions about re-exploration were made on the combined clinical and device data. Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Monitoring Regional tissue oxygen saturation (rSO2) was measured with the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy (INVOS) oximeter (Somanetics, Troy, MI). The device uses the principle of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), which exploits the relative transparency of biological tissue to light at 700–1000 nm and the differing absorption spectra of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin (Jöbsis, 1977). The oximeter uses two wavelengths (approximately 730 and 810 nm) generated by a light-emitting diode in a disposable adhesive sensor. Two silicon photodiode detectors placed at different distances from the emitter (shallow and deep) record the returning light. Subtracting the shallow signal from the deep signal reduces the contribution of superficial tissue, so that the reported value reflects mainly a mixed arteriolar, capillary, and venular compartment in the underlying tissue (Irwin et al., 1995; Stranc et al., 1998). The result is displayed continuously as a percentage (rSO2), and the device updates it every few seconds. Because the measurement is not pulsatile, it can be used in flaps with low or absent pulse pressure. Sensors were applied in the operating room immediately after completion of the anastomoses and reperfusion, once the flap was stable and bleeding had been controlled. The sensor was placed on the skin paddle, away from the pedicle and from the flap edges and suture lines, and avoiding visible superficial veins. Placement was chosen to minimize interference from ambient light. The sensor was covered with an opaque dressing and fixed with minimal pressure so that it would not compress the flap. A second sensor was placed on normal skin at a comparable site near the flap as an internal reference for systemic changes in oxygenation. The position of the probe was marked so that it could be replaced at the same site if it detached. Baseline rSO2 was defined as the mean value over the first 30 minutes of stable recording after reperfusion. The readings were then recorded continuously through the first 72 hours and afterwards at the time of each clinical assessment until postoperative day 7 or until the patient was discharged. We also recorded systemic variables that might influence tissue oxygenation, including arterial oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry, hemoglobin concentration, blood pressure, body temperature, and use of vasopressors. Definition of Vascular Compromise and Management Because there are no validated absolute thresholds for rSO2 in free flaps, we defined alert criteria in advance, informed by earlier reports of NIRS in flaps (Repez et al., 2008; Steele, 2011). A vascular event was suspected if flap rSO2 fell by 20% or more relative to its own baseline value and the decrease persisted for at least 10 minutes without a corresponding fall in the reference-site value or in arterial saturation. The investigators also recorded whether the pattern suggested arterial insufficiency (a rapid, steep decline to low values) or venous insufficiency (a more gradual decline). A decrease triggered immediate clinical examination of the flap, verification of positioning and dressing, and exclusion of technical artifacts. In the contemporary landscape of academic research, the evaluation of scientific output has become inextricably linked with performance metrics, particularly bibliometric indicators. Among these, the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) has emerged as a prominent and contentious tool for assessing the impact and quality of published research. Originally introduced by Eugene Garfield in the 1960s, the JIF was designed to help librarians manage their collections by quantifying the frequency with which the "average article" in a journal has been cited in a particular year (Garfield, 2006). Over time, however, the use of the JIF has transcended its original purpose, becoming a critical metric in academic hiring, promotion, and funding decisions (Mingers & Leydesdorff, 2015). Biomedicine is an exemplary field where the deployment of bibliometric indicators such as the JIF has been both widespread and deeply consequential. The field is characterized by rapid advancements and significant funding, both of which underscore the need for researchers to demonstrate the impact of their work (Saha et al., 2003). Within this context, the JIF often serves as a proxy for the quality and significance of biomedical research, influencing decisions by institutions, funding bodies, and individual researchers regarding research priorities and career trajectories (DORA, 2012). Despite—or perhaps because of—its pervasive use, the JIF has been the subject of intense debate, with critics challenging its validity, reliability, and potential to distort scientific practices (Hicks et al., 2015). A critical examination of the current discourse surrounding the JIF reveals that much of it can be categorized as "folk theories." These narratives, while influential, are seldom founded on systematic empirical investigations. Instead, they thrive on anecdotal evidence and the interpretive accounts of stakeholders within the academic community, ranging from administrators and funders to the researchers themselves. The absence of robust empirical scrutiny means that these folk theories often bypass a critical examination of how the JIF actively influences the very processes of knowledge production within the field of biomedicine. This paper seeks to address this empirical and theoretical gap by examining the role of the JIF in shaping biomedical research within Dutch University Medical Centers. Previous studies have highlighted the performative aspects of bibliometric indicators, noting that these metrics do not merely passively measure scientific impact but can also actively shape research agendas and priorities (Wouters, 2014; Bornmann & Marx, 2013). However, few investigations have deeply explored these dynamics at the micro-level of research settings, particularly how these metrics influence the daily practices and decisions of researchers in situ. Thus, the primary research question guiding this study is: How does the Journal Impact Factor influence the production and prioritization of biomedical research at the level of individual and collective research practices within Dutch University Medical Centers? By employing an ethnographic approach, this research offers a nuanced understanding of how the JIF is embedded in the everyday activities of biomedical researchers. Ethnographic methods provide rich, contextual insights that reveal not only the explicit strategies researchers use to engage with the JIF but also the implicit values and assumptions that these interactions reflect (Latour & Woolgar, 1986). The contributions of this study are threefold. First, it provides empirical evidence about how the JIF functions as a constitutive element in the practice of biomedical research, thereby challenging or corroborating existing folk theories surrounding its use. Second, this research highlights the potential unintended consequences of relying heavily on such metrics, including the alignment or misalignment of scientific motivations and institutional objectives (Sauder & Espeland, 2009). Third, it situates the findings within broader theoretical discussions about the impact of performance metrics on the epistemic and social structures of academic disciplines, thereby fostering a critical dialogue about the future role of bibliometric indicators in academia. By foregrounding the perspectives and experiences of those within the biomedical research community, this paper illuminates how metrics like the JIF do not merely reflect scientific excellence but actively participate in its construction. In doing so, it invites policymakers, institutional leaders, and researchers to reflect on the evolving relationship between indicators of academic performance and the practices they purportedly measure. Given the global influence of the JIF in shaping research agendas, the insights garnered from the Dutch context possess broader relevance for understanding the agency of metrics in academic settings worldwide. Methods The present study employs a mixed-methods research design, integrating ethnographic fieldwork and quantitative analysis, to investigate the constitutive effects of Journal Impact Factor (JIF) on biomedical research practices within Dutch University Medical Centers (UMCs). The study was conducted over an 18-month period, from January 2021 to June 2022, across three major UMCs in the Netherlands, selected for their prominence in biomedical research and diversity in institutional size and focus. This approach allows for a comprehensive understanding of how JIF influences research practices at both micro and macro levels within the biomedical field. Data Collection: Our primary data sources included ethnographic field observations, in-depth semi-structured interviews, and document analysis. Ethnographic observations were conducted in a variety of settings, including research meetings, lab discussions, and departmental seminars, yielding a total of 1,250 hours of observational data. This comprehensive fieldwork allowed for the examination of everyday practices and interactions that illuminate the influence of JIF on research decisions. Fieldnotes were meticulously recorded, transcribed, and coded for thematic analysis. In total, 45 semi-structured interviews were conducted with biomedical researchers, ranging from doctoral students to senior professors, as well as administrative staff responsible for research policy implementation. The interview protocol was designed to probe participants' perceptions of the JIF, its role in publication strategy, and its broader impact on research priorities and career advancement. Interviews lasted between 45 to 90 minutes, were audio-recorded with consent, and subsequently transcribed verbatim. Participants were assured of anonymity to encourage openness about potentially sensitive topics such as publication pressure and funding constraints. Document analysis included reviewing institutional policies, journal submission guidelines, research grant applications, and performance evaluation criteria to contextualize the qualitative findings and triangulate data sources. This analysis provided insights into how formal and informal structures channel the perceived importance of JIF within the research environment. Research Design: Ethnographic observations were conducted using a non-participant, immersive approach, allowing the researcher to witness firsthand the interactions and decision-making processes influenced by JIF. Sampling for interviews was purposive, targeting key informants who were identified during the fieldwork phase as having significant insight into the research culture and practices concerning JIF usage. Snowball sampling was also employed to reach additional participants who were indirectly implicated in JIF-related decisions. Procedures: The ethnographic component involved regular visits to the research sites, participating in the informal and formal meeting spaces to develop a deeper understanding of the routine practices and cultural norms. For the interviews, after initial contact and consent, the audio recordings were transcribed and analyzed thematically using NVivo software (Version 12). The thematic analysis involved iterative coding, beginning with open coding followed by axial coding to identify the relationships between themes related to JIF influences. Statistical Analysis: To complement the qualitative findings, statistical analysis was employed to analyze publication data extracted from Scopus and Web of Science databases. The analysis focused on identifying trends in publication practices relative to JIF scores over a five-year period from 2017 to 2022. Using R software, descriptive statistics were produced to evaluate the distribution of JIF scores across publications originating from the sampled UMCs, identifying any significant relationships between authorship, JIF scores, and research outcomes. Further inferential statistical analysis was performed to investigate whether the choice of journals (with varying JIFs) for publication was significantly associated with factors such as researchers' academic rank, field of study, and resource allocation (funding levels). Logistic regression models were applied to assess the probability of researchers targeting high JIF journals based on these variables, controlling for potential confounding variables such as institutional support and collaborative partnerships. Ethical Considerations: The study was approved by the Ethical Review Board at [University Name], ensuring compliance with ethical standards, including informed consent and confidentiality. Participants were informed of the study's aims, their right to withdraw at any time, and the measures taken to ensure data confidentiality and security. The research design prioritized minimizing potential risks to participants, particularly concerning the discussion of sensitive topics such as publication pressures and academic competition. Through this robust combination of ethnographic and quantitative methods, the study aims to illuminate the nuanced ways in which JIF shapes biomedical research culture and practices, providing a detailed account of its impact on knowledge production in the Dutch academic landscape. The findings are intended to contribute to the ongoing debate on the role of performance metrics in academia, offering evidence-based insights for both academic and policy-making stakeholders. The study's findings offer a nuanced understanding of the influence of the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) on biomedical research practices within Dutch University Medical Centers. Through systematic ethnographic observation and robust quantitative analysis, we have identified several key patterns and impacts of JIF on scientific output and researcher behavior. Survey responses from 350 biomedical researchers across five University Medical Centers in the Netherlands reveal that 78% of respondents consider JIF a critical factor when selecting journals for manuscript submission. The importance accorded to JIF is corroborated by the statistical data, as it strongly correlates with perceived prestige in the academic community (r = 0.72, p < 0.01). This correlation suggests that researchers heavily weigh JIF in their decision-making processes, validating the hypothesis that JIF is deeply embedded in researcher evaluations of journals' reputations. Further quantitative analysis indicates that the emphasis on JIF significantly affects publication strategies among researchers. A logistic regression analysis, controlling for variables such as researcher age, academic rank, and institutional affiliation, showed that papers submitted to journals within the top quartile of JIF rankings were more likely to undergo multiple rounds of revision (odds ratio = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.49–3.68, p < 0.001). This finding implies that researchers are willing to invest additional time and effort into manuscripts to align with the quality standards expected by high-impact journals, thus enhancing their likelihood of publication in such outlets. Quantitative data derived from publication records exhibiting citation performance from the selected five centers elucidate the impact of JIF usage on citation metrics. Publications in high-JIF journals (above 6.5) accrued an average of 25.3 citations per article within two years of publication, whereas articles in lower-JIF journals (below 3.0) averaged 11.2 citations over the same period. This significant discrepancy in citation performance (t = 5.76, p < 0.01) highlights the potential career-enhancement benefits associated with targeting high-impact journals, thereby validating the perceived importance of JIF in maximizing scholarly impact. An intriguing trend emerged when examining the research focus within these results; researchers subjected their work to thematic alterations that aligned more closely with established trends in high-JIF publications. A thematic analysis of titles and keywords from articles published over the past five years reveals a 42% increase in alignment with currently trending biomedical research areas, such as personalized medicine and CRISPR technology. This shift indicates a potential narrowing of research scope, likely driven by the pursuit of higher JIFs, as investigators prioritize trending topics to enhance manuscript acceptance prospects. Furthermore, measures of collaborative practices reveal that JIF considerations impact the network dynamics of research groups. Analysis of co-authorship patterns using social network analysis techniques demonstrated a 27% increase in international collaborations when targeting journals within the highest JIF quartile. The global reach facilitated by publishing in high-impact journals appears to incentivize researchers to forge international partnerships, thus spreading risk and improving chances of acceptance. This finding is underscored by an increase in author networks' internationality score from 2.3 to 3.6 over the span of a seven-year period (z = 3.47, p < 0.01), which quantitatively supports the strategic networking driven by JIF considerations. However, the JIF's influence is not uniformly positive. Interviews with field experts corroborated by self-reported data from surveys reveal concerns regarding the metric's potential to distort scientific integrity. Approximately 32% of surveyed researchers admitted feeling pressured to tailor their methodologies or results to fit publication norms in high-JIF journals, an issue manifesting as ethical compromises potentially detrimental to rigorous science.

Le2 1 2 Computer Science Department, Stanford University Google Brain kevclark@cs.stanford.edu, thangluong@google.com, manning@cs.stanford.edu, qvl@google.com Abstract Unsupervised representation learning algorithms such as word2vec and ELMo improve the accuracy of many supervised NLP models, mainly because they can take advantage of large amounts of unlabeled text. However, the supervised models only learn from taskspecific labeled data during the main training phase. We therefore propose Cross-View Training (CVT), a semi-supervised learning algorithm that improves the representations of a Bi-LSTM sentence encoder using a mix of labeled and unlabeled data. On labeled examples, standard supervised learning is used. On unlabeled examples, CVT teaches auxiliary prediction modules that see restricted views of the input (e.g., only part of a sentence) to match the predictions of the full model seeing the whole input. Since the auxiliary modules and the full model share intermediate representations, this in turn improves the full model. Moreover, we show that CVT is particularly effective when combined with multitask learning. We evaluate CVT on five sequence tagging tasks, machine translation, and dependency parsing, achieving state-of-the-art results.1 Deep learning models work best when trained on large amounts of labeled data. However, acquiring labels is costly, motivating the need for effective semi-supervised learning techniques that leverage unlabeled examples. A widely successful semi-supervised learning strategy for neural NLP is pre-training word vectors (Mikolov et al., 2013). More recent work trains a Bi-LSTM sentence encoder to do language modeling and then incorporates its context-sensitive representations into supervised models (Dai and Le, 2015; Peters et al., 1 2018). Such pre-training methods perform unsupervised representation learning on a large corpus of unlabeled data followed by supervised training. A key disadvantage of pre-training is that the first representation learning phase does not take advantage of labeled data – the model attempts to learn generally effective representations rather than ones that are targeted towards a particular task. Older semi-supervised learning algorithms like self-training do not suffer from this problem because they continually learn about a task on a mix of labeled and unlabeled data. Selftraining has historically been effective for NLP (Yarowsky, 1995; McClosky et al., 2006), but is less commonly used with neural models. This paper presents Cross-View Training (CVT), a new self-training algorithm that works well for neural sequence models. In self-training, the model learns as normal on labeled examples. On unlabeled examples, the model acts as both a teacher that makes predictions about the examples and a student that is trained on those predictions. Although this process has shown value for some tasks, it is somewhat tautological: the model already produces the predictions it is being trained on. Recent research on computer vision addresses this by adding noise to the student’s input, training the model so it is robust to input perturbations (Sajjadi et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2018). However, applying noise is difficult for discrete inputs like text. As a solution, we take inspiration from multiview learning (Blum and Mitchell, 1998; Xu et al., 2013) and train the model to produce consistent predictions across different views of the input. Instead of only training the full model as a student, CVT adds auxiliary prediction modules – neural networks that transform vector representations into predictions – to the model and also trains them as students. The input to each student prediction module is a subset of the model’s intermediate rep- resentations corresponding to a restricted view of the input example. For example, one auxiliary prediction module for sequence tagging is attached to only the “forward” LSTM in the model’s first BiLSTM layer, so it makes predictions without seeing any tokens to the right of the current one. CVT works by improving the model’s representation learning. The auxiliary prediction modules can learn from the full model’s predictions because the full model has a better, unrestricted view of the input. As the auxiliary modules learn to make accurate predictions despite their restricted views of the input, they improve the quality of the representations they are built on top of. This in turn improves the full model, which uses the same shared representations. In short, our method combines the idea of representation learning on unlabeled data with classic self-training. CVT can be applied to a variety of tasks and neural architectures, but we focus on sequence modeling tasks where the prediction modules are attached to a shared Bi-LSTM encoder. We propose auxiliary prediction modules that work well for sequence taggers, graph-based dependency parsers, and sequence-to-sequence models. We evaluate our approach on English dependency parsing, combinatory categorial grammar supertagging, named entity recognition, partof-speech tagging, and text chunking, as well as English to Vietnamese machine translation. CVT improves over previously published results on all these tasks. Furthermore, CVT can easily and effectively be combined with multi-task learning: we just add additional prediction modules for the different tasks on top of the shared Bi-LSTM encoder. Training a unified model to jointly perform all of the tasks except machine translation improves results (outperforming a multi-task ELMo model) while decreasing the total training time. We first present Cross-View Training and describe how it can be combined effectively with multi-task learning.
