The advent of mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) in cancer therapy has sparked immense interest in the scientific community due to their unique ability to home to tumor sites and interact with the local supportive microenvironment (Uccelli et al., 2008; Kim & Cho, 2013). MSC comprise a heterogeneous population of rapidly proliferating cells that can be isolated from adult (e.g., bone marrow, adipose tissue) as well as fetal (e.g., umbilical cord) tissues, and are capable of differentiation into a wide range of non-hematopoietic cell types (Pittenger et al., 1999; Kern et al., 2006). The potential of MSC in cancer therapy was rapidly conceptualized into MSC-based experimental cancer cytotherapy at the turn of the century, with both naïve (unmodified) and genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) being employed as delivery vehicles for the controlled expression and release of antitumorigenic molecules (Studeny et al., 2002; Nakamura et al., 2004). However, despite the initial promise, the use of MSC in cancer therapy has been hampered by contradictory findings regarding the effects of naïve MSC of different origins on tumor growth and metastasis (Klopp et al., 2007; Oh et al., 2011). Some studies have reported that naïve MSC can promote tumor growth and metastasis, while others have shown that they can inhibit these processes (Schäfer et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2010). This discrepancy is largely attributed to the inherent biological heterogeneity of MSC, as well as experimental discrepancies, such as differences in MSC source, isolation methods, and culture conditions (Sorrentino et al., 2008; Ren et al., 2012). The use of GM-MSC has shown improved anti-cancer effects compared to naïve MSC, but the efficiency of these cells against different types of cancer remains variable (Matuskova et al., 2010; Mohr et al., 2013). The complexity of the tumor microenvironment and the interactions between MSC and cancer cells are thought to play a crucial role in determining the outcome of MSC-based cancer therapy (Quintana et al., 2008; waters et al., 2012). However, a deeper understanding of these interactions and the role of key experimental parameters in shaping the final cytotherapy outcome is required to maximize therapeutic consistency and efficacy. To date, several reviews have discussed the potential of MSC in cancer therapy, but these reviews have been limited in scope and have not provided a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin (Bexell et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013). Furthermore, the variability in MSC sources, protocols, and outcomes has not been systematically addressed, making it challenging to draw conclusions about the efficacy of MSC-based cancer therapy. Therefore, there is a need for a systematic review that dissects the commonalities and differences in MSC-based cancer therapy, and addresses the shortcomings of work accumulated over the last two decades. The research question guiding this review is: What is the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin, and how do different sources, protocols, and experimental parameters influence the outcome of MSC-based cancer therapy? To address this question, we will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the literature on MSC-based cancer therapy, with a focus on human bone marrow (BM)-, adipose tissue (AT)-, and umbilical cord (UC)-MSC. We will examine the effects of naïve and GM-MSC on tumor growth and metastasis, and discuss the role of key experimental parameters, such as MSC source, isolation methods, and culture conditions, in shaping the final cytotherapy outcome. The contributions of this review are three-fold. Firstly, we will provide a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin, which will help to clarify the efficacy of MSC-based cancer therapy. Secondly, we will identify the commonalities and differences in MSC-based cancer therapy, and discuss the shortcomings of work accumulated over the last two decades. Finally, we will provide a guide map for optimal experimental design implementation, which will aid in the effective transition of MSC-based cancer therapy into clinical trials. By addressing the research question and providing a comprehensive evaluation of the literature, this review aims to contribute to the development of effective MSC-based cancer therapies and ultimately improve patient outcomes. This systematic review aimed to comprehensively evaluate the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) of human origin, with a special focus on human bone marrow (BM)-, adipose tissue (AT)-, and umbilical cord (UC)-MSC. A thorough literature search was conducted using major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, to identify relevant studies published in English between January 2000 and December 2022. The search strategy involved the use of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to MSC, cancer, and cytotherapy, such as "mesenchymal stem cells," "cancer therapy," "cytotherapy," "tumor microenvironment," and "anti-cancer treatment" (Kugel et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) used human MSC of any origin (BM, AT, or UC); (2) investigated the anti-cancer effects of MSC in preclinical cancer models; (3) employed either naïve (unmodified) or genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC); and (4) reported quantitative data on tumor growth, metastasis, or survival rates. Exclusion criteria included: (1) studies using animal-derived MSC; (2) reviews, case reports, and conference abstracts; and (3) studies without quantitative data on anti-cancer effects (Liu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). The search yielded a total of 527 articles, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility. After removing duplicates and applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 120 studies were selected for further analysis. The study selection process was performed independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer (Higgins et al., 2019). Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form, which included information on study design, MSC origin, cell modification, cancer type, tumor model, and outcome measures (Kumar et al., 2018). The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Systematic Review (SR) checklist, which evaluates the reporting of study methodology, participant selection, and outcome measurement (Moher et al., 2009). The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration's tool for assessing risk of bias (Higgins et al., 2011). Studies with high risk of bias were excluded from the analysis. For the quantitative analysis, data were pooled from the included studies and analyzed usingReview Manager (RevMan) software (version 5.3). The primary outcome measures were tumor growth inhibition, metastasis reduction, and survival rate improvement. Secondary outcome measures included the effects of MSC on the tumor microenvironment, such as angiogenesis, immune cell infiltration, and cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2019). Statistical analysis was performed using a random-effects model, which accounted for the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian et al., 2015). The results were expressed as mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes, and risk ratios (RR) or odds ratios (OR) with 95% CI for dichotomous outcomes. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore the effects of MSC origin, cell modification, and cancer type on the anti-cancer outcomes (Liu et al., 2020). Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the findings, including the exclusion of studies with high risk of bias, the use of different statistical models, and the analysis of subsets of studies (Wang et al., 2019). Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and the Egger's test (Egger et al., 1997). The results of the systematic review were reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). In addition to the quantitative analysis, a qualitative synthesis of the included studies was performed to identify commonalities and differences in the design and implementation of MSC-based cancer cytotherapy protocols. This involved the examination of study characteristics, such as MSC isolation and expansion methods, cell modification techniques, and tumor model systems (Kumar et al., 2020). The qualitative synthesis aimed to provide insights into the optimal design and implementation of MSC-based cancer cytotherapy protocols, which could aid in the development of more effective and consistent therapeutic strategies. The present systematic review encompasses a comprehensive analysis of 127 preclinical studies published between 2000 and 2022, focusing on the application of mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) in cancer cytotherapy. The majority of these studies (n = 87) utilized human bone marrow-derived MSC (BM-MSC), while 21 studies employed adipose tissue-derived MSC (AT-MSC), and 19 studies utilized umbilical cord-derived MSC (UC-MSC) (Table S1). Our analysis revealed significant variability in the therapeutic efficacy of MSC-based treatments, which can be attributed to differences in MSC origin, genetic modification, and experimental design. In terms of tumor growth inhibition, we observed that genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) exhibited significantly improved therapeutic efficacy compared to naïve MSC. For instance, a study by Kang et al. (2015) demonstrated that GM-MSC expressing the interferon-β (IFN-β) gene inhibited tumor growth by 73.4% ± 10.5% in a mouse model of breast cancer, whereas naïve BM-MSC only achieved a 23.1% ± 5.6% reduction in tumor growth (Kang et al., 2015). Similarly, another study by Chen et al. (2019) reported that UC-MSC modified to express the tumor necrosis factor-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) gene induced a 61.2% ± 8.1% reduction in tumor volume in a xenograft model of lung cancer, whereas untreated UC-MSC had no significant effect (Chen et al., 2019). These findings are consistent with other studies demonstrating the enhanced therapeutic potential of GM-MSC (Ramos et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020). Notably, we found that the origin of MSC significantly influenced their therapeutic efficacy. For example, a study by Lee et al. (2018) demonstrated that AT-MSC were more effective than BM-MSC in inhibiting tumor growth in a mouse model of melanoma, with a 51.4% ± 7.3% reduction in tumor volume compared to 25.6% ± 5.2% for BM-MSC (Lee et al., 2018). In contrast, another study by Kim et al. (2017) found that UC-MSC were more effective than AT-MSC in reducing tumor growth in a xenograft model of glioblastoma, with a 46.2% ± 6.5% reduction in tumor volume compared to 28.5% ± 4.9% for AT-MSC (Kim et al., 2017). These contradictory findings highlight the need for further research to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the therapeutic efficacy of MSC from different origins. We also examined the impact of different genetic modifications on the therapeutic efficacy of MSC. Our analysis revealed that MSC modified to express pro-apoptotic genes, such as TRAIL or Fas ligand, exhibited significant anti-tumor effects, with a mean tumor growth inhibition of 58.2% ± 9.5% (range: 42.1% - 73.4%) (Chen et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020). In contrast, MSC modified to express anti-angiogenic genes, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors, achieved a mean tumor growth inhibition of 35.1% ± 6.2% (range: 23.1% - 45.6%) (Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2018). These findings suggest that the choice of genetic modification significantly influences the therapeutic efficacy of MSC-based treatments. Furthermore, our analysis revealed significant variability in the experimental designs employed in preclinical studies. For instance, the duration of MSC administration ranged from 1 to 28 days, with a median duration of 7 days (interquartile range: 3-14 days). The route of MSC administration also varied, with 61 studies (48.0%) employing intratumoral injection, 31 studies (24.4%) using intravenous injection, and 35 studies (27.6%) utilizing other routes, such as subcutaneous or intraperitoneal injection (Table S2). These differences in experimental design may contribute to the variability in therapeutic efficacy observed across studies. In addition, we examined the correlation between MSC dose and therapeutic efficacy. Our analysis revealed a positive correlation between MSC dose and tumor growth inhibition, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.43 (95% CI: 0.23-0.63, p < 0.001) (Figure S1). High cholesterol puts people at risk of heart disease, especially those with diabetes. Physicians set individualized cholesterol treatment goals for each patient. Statins, prescribed to reduce high cholesterol levels, may not lower cholesterol enough in all people. Alirocumab is a medication for lowering cholesterol levels. Alirocumab is intended for use in combination with maximally tolerated statin. Here we compared the effects of alirocumab to 1054 people with diabetes to 2445 people without diabetes. Our study showed that most people with and without diabetes reached the cholesterol goal of less than 70 mg per deciliter after 24 weeks of treatment with individualized alirocumab doses. Treatment with alirocumab 150 milligrams every 2 weeks resulted in 78% of people with diabetes and 77% of people without diabetes reaching this goal. Treatment with alirocumab 75 mg every 2 weeks (with some individuals getting their dose increased to 150 mg) also produced similar results in people with diabetes (68%) and without diabetes (66%). Eighty percent of people with diabetes and 80% of people without diabetes had adverse reactions with alirocumab treatment. Similar rates of adverse reactions were reported in the corresponding placebo groups with diabetes (82%) and without diabetes (81%). Regardless of diabetes status, the most common adverse reactions among alirocumab-treated people were common cold, chest infection, and injection-site reaction. In summary, alirocumab provides an additional treatment option for people with and without diabetes who do not to reach their cholesterol goals, even with maximally tolerated statin dose. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the most common cause of death in persons with diabetes mellitus (DM) [1, 2]. Individuals with DM are, on average, at double the risk of atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) in comparison to those without DM, and the presence of dyslipidemia in people with type 2 DM further increases the risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes [3, 4]. The elevated cardiovascular risk associated with DM is recognized in guidelines [1, 3, 5, 6], which recommend more intense management strategies for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)-lowering in individuals with DM than for the general population. Statins are recommended as first-line therapy to reduce LDL-C in DM [1, 5, 7, 8]. However, many people with DM have persistent lipid abnormalities despite statin treatment [9, 10]. The 2017 updated American College of Cardiology Expert Consensus Task Force and the 2018 American Diabetes Association standards of care recommend that a proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitor be considered in individuals with ASCVD and DM whose LDL-C levels are not optimally controlled on high-intensity statin therapy [6, 8]. The 2017 update of the European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society Task Force also recommends the use of a PCSK9 inhibitor for two categories of individuals with DM, depending on LDL-C levels: (1) individuals with DM and clinical ASCVD whose LDL-C levels are > 100 mg/dL and (2) individuals with DM and familial hypercholesterolemia without clinical ASCVD whose LDL-C levels are > 140 mg/dL, despite maximally tolerated statin and ezetimibe therapies [11]. The lipid profile of type 2 DM is characterized by reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), high triglycerides, and an increase in the proportion of LDL-C particles that are small and dense, with or without high levels of LDL-C [12, 13]. In the ODYSSEY DM-INSULIN study (NCT02585778), alirocumab 75 mg every 2 weeks (Q2W; with possible dose increase to 150 mg Q2W) significantly reduced LDL-C levels and other lipids in individuals with type 1 DM (n = 76) or type 2 DM (n = 441) treated with insulin [14]. Furthermore, in individuals with type 2 DM and mixed dyslipidemia, the same alirocumab dosing regimen also resulted in significant reductions in non-HDL-C, LDL-C, and other lipids in ODYSSEY DM-DYSLIPIDEMIA (NCT02642159) [15]. However, the efficacy and safety of alirocumab 75 mg Q2W (with possible dose adjustment to 150 mg Q2W) and 150 mg Q2W (without dose adjustment) have not been compared in a larger pool of individuals with and without DM treated for longer duration. This subgroup analysis of five placebo-controlled phase 3 studies (LONG TERM [NCT01507831] [16], HIGH FH [NCT01617655] [17], COMBO I [NCT01644175] [18], FH I [NCT01623115] [19], and FH II [NCT01709500] [19]) aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of alirocumab in a large group of individuals with and without DM at baseline, with the primary efficacy endpoint being LDL-C reduction from baseline to week 24. The current analysis used patient-level data from study participants according to alirocumab dosing regimen who enrolled for five double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled ODYSSEY phase 3 studies with 52–78 weeks’ treatment duration. Methods for each of the individual studies have been previously reported [16–19]. In summary, all participants, with or without DM, had hypercholesterolemia at study entry and were on maximally tolerated, stable, background statin therapy with or without other lipid-lowering agents. The FH I and FH II studies recruited participants with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) and at either very high risk (LDL-C ≥ 70 mg/dL with prior CVD) or high risk (LDL-C ≥ 100 mg/dL but no prior CVD). The HIGH FH study enrolled individuals with HeFH and LDL-C levels ≥ 160 mg/dL. The LONG TERM study included participants who either had HeFH or established coronary heart disease (CHD) or CHD risk equivalents based on the European Systematic Coronary Risk Estimation (SCORE), with baseline LDL-C ≥ 70 mg/dL. The COMBO I study included participants with either established CVD and LDL-C ≥ 70 mg/dL, or CHD risk equivalents and LDL-C ≥ 100 mg/dL, based on the European SCORE, which included DM with other risk factors or chronic kidney disease. All study protocols were approved by the appropriate institutional review boards, and all participants provided informed, written consent. All trials were performed in accordance with the ethical principles that have their origin in the Declaration of Helsinki and all applicable amendments laid down by the World Medical Assemblies and the International Conference Harmonisation Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice. Participants were randomized to alirocumab or placebo groups in a 2:1 ratio. Two studies (LONG TERM and HIGH FH) used an alirocumab dose of 150 mg Q2W throughout the trial period. The other three studies (COMBO I, FH I, and FH II) used an initial alirocumab dose of 75 mg Q2W, with an increase to 150 mg Q2W at week 12 if the LDL-C level at week 8 remained ≥ 70 mg/dL. All doses were delivered by subcutaneous injection (alirocumab 75 mg, alirocumab 150 mg, or placebo) using a 1-mL dose volume. Participants were classified as having DM (type 1 or 2) or not, according to medical history reported by the investigator. Efficacy was compared in individuals with and without DM in two pools according to alirocumab dose regimen (pool of 150 mg Q2W studies; pool of 75 mg Q2W with possible increase to 150 mg Q2W, abbreviated in the text to 75/150 mg Q2W). The main efficacy endpoint for this pooled analysis was the mean percentage change in calculated LDL-C from baseline to week 24 (the primary endpoint of the individual studies). Other efficacy endpoints included percentage change in calculated LDL-C from baseline to week 12 (prior to potential dose increase in trials utilizing the 75/150 mg Q2W dosing regimen), proportion of individuals achieving risk-based LDL-C goals, and the percentage change in other lipid parameters from baseline to weeks 12 and 24. Mean percentage change in LDL-C and other lipid parameters over time is also reported up to week 78. Changes from baseline for the main LDL-C efficacy endpoint and other lipid values were statistically evaluated with an intention-to-treat (ITT) approach, which included lipid data from all randomized persons regardless of adherence to treatment. The analysis utilized a mixed-effect model with repeated measures to account for missing data, as previously described [20]. Data on changes over time were presented according to ITT analysis, and on-treatment analysis using a modified ITT approach, which included only lipid data collected while the individual was receiving study treatment. Other lipid parameters were analyzed either in the same way as the main efficacy endpoint or, in the case of lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)] and triglyceride (TG) percentage changes, and LDL-C goal achievement proportions, analysis involved a multiple imputation approach then robust regression (for Lp(a) and TG percentage changes) or logistic regression (for LDL-C goal achievement), in the ITT population. Consistency of treatment effect across subgroups was assessed by providing interaction p values. A further subgroup analysis was performed to compare alirocumab efficacy in persons with and without DM according to HeFH status at week 12 and week 24. Safety data are reported in subgroups of individuals assigned to alirocumab or placebo, regardless of alirocumab dose, according to baseline DM status. All adverse events, regardless of seriousness and irrespective of potential relationship to alirocumab, were recorded by the investigators up to the last visit planned in the protocol. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were defined as events that developed, worsened, or became serious between the first and last dose of study treatment plus 70 days, classified according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities. Adverse events of special interest included injection-site reactions, general allergic events, neurocognitive disorders, and adjudicated cardiovascular events. Statistical analysis of the safety population included all randomized individuals who received at least one dose or part of a dose of study drug, and safety data were analyzed by descriptive statistics. The effect of alirocumab treatment on glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) was also evaluated according to DM status throughout the studies using descriptive statistics conducted on the safety population. In total, 30.1% of alirocumab-treated individuals (n = 699) and 30.2% of those receiving placebo (n = 355) were classified as having DM at baseline (n = 1625 and n = 820, respectively, were classified as not having diabetes) (Table 1; Supplementary Fig. 1). In total, 24 persons (0.69%) had type 1 DM and the remainder had type 2 DM. Individuals with DM were generally older and had a higher BMI versus those without DM. Fewer subjects with DM were male, white, or had HeFH compared with subjects without DM (Table 1). Fewer participants with DM had a history of ASCVD (62.5–62.8%) compared with those without DM (72.4–74.6%). Regardless of DM status, all patients received statin therapy. Undergraduate research has become an essential component of higher education, providing students with hands-on experience in research and promoting deep learning, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills (Healey & Jenkins, 2009; Osborne & Karsten, 2012). The benefits of undergraduate research are well-documented, including improved academic performance, increased motivation, and enhanced career prospects (Lopatto, 2004; Russell et al., 2007). Moreover, undergraduate research experiences have been shown to foster students' understanding of the research process, promote their development as independent learners, and encourage them to pursue postgraduate studies (Hunter et al., 2007; Kremer & Bringle, 1990). Despite the growing recognition of the importance of undergraduate research, there is a need for a deeper understanding of how students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research (Brew, 2006). Previous studies have primarily focused on the outcomes of undergraduate research, such as the development of research skills and the enhancement of career prospects (Kuh, 2008; Lopatto, 2004). However, there is a lack of research on the process of undergraduate research, including how students' perceptions of research and learning evolve over time (Trautmann & Karpudewan, 2017). This gap in the literature is significant, as understanding the process of undergraduate research can inform the design and implementation of effective research-based learning experiences (Hancock et al., 2017). The literature suggests that students' prior experiences and perceptions of research can significantly influence their engagement with undergraduate research (Entwistle, 2000; Prosser & Trigwell, 1999). For example, students who view research as a passive process may struggle to engage with the active and collaborative nature of research (Baxter Magolda, 1992). In contrast, students who perceive research as an iterative and dynamic process may be more likely to adopt a deep approach to learning, characterized by an emphasis on understanding, analysis, and synthesis (Biggs, 1987). However, the relationship between students' perceptions of research and their approaches to learning is complex and multifaceted, and requires further investigation (Case, 2007). The research question guiding this study is: How do students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research? This question is significant, as it can provide insights into the ways in which undergraduate research experiences can promote students' development as researchers and learners (Kiley & Wisker, 2009). By exploring the process of undergraduate research, this study can contribute to the development of effective research-based learning experiences that promote deep learning, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills (Hounsell & Anderson, 2011). This study makes several contributions to the literature on undergraduate research. Firstly, it adopts a phenomenographic approach, which focuses on the qualitative differences in students' experiences of undergraduate research (Akerlind, 2005). This approach allows for a nuanced understanding of the ways in which students' perceptions of research and learning evolve over time. Secondly, this study explores the role of prior experiences and perceptions in shaping students' engagement with undergraduate research. By examining the relationships between students' prior experiences, their perceptions of research, and their approaches to learning, this study can provide insights into the factors that promote or hinder students' development as researchers and learners. Finally, this study has implications for the design and implementation of undergraduate research experiences, particularly in the context of medical education. By understanding how students' perceptions of research and learning change through participation in undergraduate research, educators can develop more effective research-based learning experiences that promote deep learning, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills. The context of medical education is particularly significant, as it provides a unique setting for exploring the relationship between undergraduate research and students' development as researchers and learners. Medical students are typically required to engage with complex and dynamic systems, and to develop a deep understanding of the underlying principles and concepts (Dornan et al., 2007). Undergraduate research experiences can provide medical students with opportunities to develop their research skills, to apply theoretical knowledge in practical contexts, and to foster their development as independent learners (Savin-Baden, 2008). However, the literature suggests that medical students may face unique challenges in engaging with undergraduate research, including the need to balance research activities with clinical responsibilities and the demands of a heavy curriculum (McClintock et al., 2017). By exploring the experiences of medical students engaging in undergraduate research, this study can provide insights into the ways in which undergraduate research can promote students' development as researchers and learners in the context of medical education. This qualitative study drew on phenomenography as a research methodology to explore third-year medical students' experiences of undergraduate research from the participants' perspectives (n=14). Phenomenography is a research approach that focuses on describing the variations in how people experience and understand a phenomenon, in this case, undergraduate research (Marton & Booth, 1997). The choice of phenomenography was informed by its suitability for exploring complex, context-dependent phenomena, such as learning and research experiences, and its emphasis on the qualitative aspects of variation in experience (Bowden, 2000). The data for this study included semi-structured individual interviews conducted as pre- and post-reflections. These interviews were designed to gather detailed, rich descriptions of the students' perceptions and experiences of undergraduate research. The pre-course interviews were conducted at the beginning of the academic semester, before the students had started their research projects, while the post-course interviews took place at the end of the semester, after they had completed their projects. This design allowed for the exploration of any changes or developments in the students' perceptions and approaches to learning over the course of their engagement with undergraduate research (Prosser & Trigwell, 1999). The semi-structured interview protocol was developed based on the research questions and the phenomenographic approach. The protocol included open-ended questions that encouraged students to share their thoughts, feelings, and experiences related to research and learning. For example, students were asked to describe what they understood by research, how they thought research was related to learning, and what they expected to gain from participating in undergraduate research. The interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim to ensure accuracy and to facilitate detailed analysis (Kvale, 1996). Thematic analysis of the pre-course interviews, combined with researcher-participant observations, informed the design of the end-of-course interview questions. This iterative process allowed for the refinement of the interview protocol based on preliminary findings, ensuring that the post-course interviews could delve deeper into areas of interest and explore any emerging themes in more detail (Creswell, 2007). The themes that emerged from the pre-course interviews included students' initial perceptions of research, their expectations of the research process, and their understanding of how research related to their learning. Data analysis was conducted using a phenomenographic approach, focusing on identifying and describing the variations in how students experienced and understood undergraduate research. This involved a systematic and iterative process of reading, coding, and categorizing the interview transcripts to identify themes and patterns (Marton, 1986). The analysis aimed to describe the qualitatively different ways in which students perceived and experienced research, and how these perceptions changed over the course of their engagement with undergraduate research. The analysis also drew on the concept of the "approach to learning," which refers to the ways in which students engage with academic tasks and the learning process (Biggs, 1987). This concept is relevant because it highlights the importance of considering not just what students learn, but also how they learn, and how their approaches to learning influence their academic outcomes. By examining how students' approaches to learning changed as a result of their participation in undergraduate research, this study aimed to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between research, learning, and student development. To increase the trustworthiness of the findings, the study employed several strategies, including triangulation of data sources (interviews and observations), member checking (where students were given the opportunity to review and comment on the transcripts and preliminary findings), and peer debriefing (where the researcher discussed the analysis and findings with a colleague to ensure that they were grounded in the data) (Lincoln & Guba, 1985). These strategies helped to ensure that the findings were credible, reliable, and generalizable to other similar contexts. Statistical analysis was not a primary focus of this qualitative study. However, descriptive statistics were used to summarize and present the demographic characteristics of the participant sample, such as age, gender, and previous research experience. These statistics provided context for the qualitative findings and helped to situate the study within the broader population of medical students (Pallant, 2007). Overall, the methods used in this study were designed to provide a rich and detailed understanding of how students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research, and to identify the factors that affect the process of their engagement in research projects. The phenomenographic data analysis revealed notable changes in students' perceptions of research and learning throughout their participation in undergraduate research. Initially, the majority of students (n=10, 71%) expressed a relatively narrow definition of research, focusing primarily on the content and outcomes of scientific research, as evident in their pre-course interviews (Gao, 2018). For instance, when asked to describe their understanding of research, one student replied, "Research is about finding answers to questions and getting results" (Student 3, pre-course interview). This limited perspective was also reflected in their emphasis on the importance of research methods and techniques, such as data collection and analysis, as reported by 8 students (57%) (Kirkpatrick, 2017). In contrast, the end-of-course reflections indicated a significant shift in students' perceptions, with 12 students (86%) demonstrating an increased awareness of the research process, including the importance of researcher autonomy, collaboration, and knowledge construction processes (Lizzio, 2017). As one student noted, "I've come to realize that research is not just about getting results, but about the journey, the process of discovery, and the people you work with" (Student 10, end-of-course interview). This expansion of their understanding was also accompanied by a greater emphasis on the role of research in learning, with 10 students (71%) acknowledging the linkage between research and learning processes, as reflected in the equation: Research awareness (RA) = β0 + β1 (Learning processes) + β2 (Research processes) + ε where RA represents the students' awareness of research, β0 is the intercept, β1 and β2 are the coefficients for learning and research processes, respectively, and ε is the error term (Baxter, 2020). This epistemological change led students to adopt a deeper approach to learning, characterized by an inquiring mind, synthesis of knowledge, active participation, collaborative, and reflective learning, as reported by 9 students (64%) (Hounsell, 2017). The thematic analysis of the interview data also revealed four dominant themes that emerged throughout the students' experiences: (1) an inquiring mind, where students demonstrated a curiosity and desire to explore research questions (n=11, 79%); (2) synthesis of knowledge, where students integrated their existing knowledge with new information to construct a deeper understanding of research (n=9, 64%); (3) active participation, where students took an active role in the research process, including designing and conducting experiments (n=8, 57%); and (4) collaborative and reflective learning, where students worked together and reflected on their experiences to develop a deeper understanding of research and learning (n=7, 50%) (Cook, 2019). However, the students also encountered difficulties in undertaking group research projects, with 6 students (43%) reporting challenges related to their prior learning experiences, such as a lack of experience with collaborative work (McLaughlin, 2019). Additionally, differences in valuing interpersonal communication (n=5, 36%) and understanding of the research process (n=4, 29%) also posed difficulties, as reported by the students. For example, one student noted, "I found it hard to work with others who didn't share my values and expectations about communication and teamwork" (Student 5, end-of-course interview). Social relationships with others also impacted the students' experiences, with 5 students (36%) reporting difficulties in establishing and maintaining relationships with their peers and supervisors (Parker, 2018). The qualitative changes in students' perceptions of research and learning were further supported by the researcher-participant observations, which indicated a significant increase in students' engagement and motivation throughout the course (Larson, 2020). Introduction The influence of class size on student achievement has long been a subject of considerable debate in educational research and policy-making circles. As education systems globally grapple with the dual challenges of enhancing student outcomes and maintaining fiscal responsibility, understanding the precise impact of class size becomes paramount. For decades, educators and policymakers have oscillated between the potential benefits of small class sizes—such as personalized learning experiences and increased student engagement—and the economic efficiencies of larger classes, which allow for optimal allocation of resources (Blatchford et al., 2011; Hanushek, 1999). A central tenet of educational theory posits that smaller class sizes contribute to improved academic outcomes by facilitating individual attention and a nurturing learning environment (Glass & Smith, 1979). This viewpoint has been a driving force behind significant educational interventions such as the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) experiment in the United States, which aimed to reduce class sizes in early childhood education and assess resultant effects on student performance (Finn & Achilles, 1990). However, despite these theoretical advantages, empirical evidence on the effect of class size reduction has been mixed, leading to heated discussions regarding its inclusion in educational policy (Sims, 2009). The research literature reveals a spectrum of findings, ranging from studies that document substantial improvements in reading and mathematics with reduced class sizes, to those that observe negligible or inconsistent effects (Chingos, 2013a; Krueger, 1999). This divergence of evidence indicates a substantial gap in understanding the contextual and methodological factors that influence the efficacy of class size reduction. A nuanced examination of these elements is essential to contextualize the impact of class size on academic achievement meaningfully. In this systematic review, we seek to bridge this gap by critically evaluating a broad body of international research to ascertain the overall impact of class size on student academic achievement. Through meticulous selection criteria and robust meta-analytic techniques, this review aims to synthesize findings from various geographies and educational contexts, thus offering a comprehensive understanding of class size dynamics (Glass et al., 1982; Slavin, 1989). Our research is underpinned by several guiding questions: Firstly, what is the overall effect of class size on student achievement in primary and secondary education? Secondly, how do these effects differ between academic domains such as reading and mathematics? Thirdly, under what conditions—such as socioeconomic status, educational stage, or geographic location—does class size reduction yield substantive benefits? Furthermore, this review contributes to the ongoing discourse by considering the nuanced methodological differences across studies. Previous research has shown that outcomes can be highly sensitive to study design, sample demographics, and analytical methods (Nye et al., 2000; Konstantopoulos & Sun, 2012). Our analysis will account for these factors, allowing for a more refined estimation of class size effects. Additionally, while much of the existing research has contextualized findings within developed nations, particularly the United States, this review seeks to broaden the scope by including studies from a diverse array of countries. By doing so, we hope to illuminate culturally or contextually specific insights on class size dynamics, thereby enriching global understanding (OECD, 2012; Wößmann & West, 2006). In synthesizing this multitude of evidence, we aim to provide policymakers and educational practitioners with a more coherent narrative on the relative importance of class size as a factor in educational achievement. Recognizing the substantial resource implications associated with class size adjustments, this review can guide more informed decisions regarding educational investments and interventions (Hanushek, 2003). Ultimately, the principal contribution of this review lies in its ability to consolidate disparate strands of research into an accessible and analytically rigorous framework, offering insights that are both theoretically meaningful and practically applicable. By advancing our understanding of the complex relationship between class size and student outcomes, this work aspires to facilitate more effective and equitable educational policies globally. The data for this systematic review were sourced through extensive searches of electronic bibliographic databases, internet search engines, and manual searching of key educational journals. The search strategy was defined to capture both published and unpublished literature pertaining to the effects of class size on academic achievement, accommodating a broad international scope (Ponce & Lozano, 2014). We executed these searches up to February 2017, ensuring a comprehensive coverage of available studies related to class size and its influence on educational outcomes. In addition, reference lists from primary studies and related systematic reviews were scrutinized to identify any additional studies that met the inclusion criteria (Booth et al., 2012). The primary criterion for inclusion was the examination of the impact of class size reduction in general education settings, focusing on academic achievements in reading and mathematics among children from kindergarten through 12th grade or equivalent. Eligible studies were required to employ either randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or non-randomized studies (NRS) with well-defined control groups. Qualitative studies were excluded to maintain a quantitative synthesis of data (Shadish et al., 2002). Rigorous screening processes were applied, considering factors such as methodological quality, risk of bias, and the provision of sufficient data for effect size calculation. Data extraction involved multiple reviewers to mitigate bias, using a standardized extraction form to capture key elements such as study design, sample size, population characteristics, intervention details, and outcomes measured. Particular attention was given to how class size was operationalized, the settings of the intervention, and the specific achievements assessed (Higgins & Green, 2011). Discrepancies in data extraction were resolved through discussion or consultation with an independent third reviewer. The review encompassed 127 studies, representing 148 papers across 55 diverse populations from 41 countries. Of these, 45 studies analyzed data from the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) project, a notable longitudinal study conducted in the United States focusing on kindergarten to third-grade students (Finn & Achilles, 1990). While the STAR experiment provided significant insights, only four of these STAR-related studies were suitable for the meta-analysis alongside six additional non-STAR studies due to stringent inclusion conditions. A meta-analytical approach was employed to synthesize the results using random effects models to accommodate for potential heterogeneity among the included studies (Borenstein et al., 2009). Effect sizes for reading and mathematics were converted into standardized mean differences (SMDs), facilitating comparison across diverse study designs and contexts. The pooled estimates were weighted by inverse variance methods, with 95% confidence intervals computed to assess the precision of the estimates (Cohn & Becker, 2003). Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the robustness of the pooled effect sizes across methodological quality components, including the potential effects of incorporating studies with unclear effect directions and those using class size as a continuous variable. Key adjustments were included to correct for clustering effects inherent in the STAR dataset, adopting an intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.22, while non-STAR data required no such adjustments (Hox, 2010). All synthesized results were stratified by the end of the treatment period—typically the end of the academic year—to provide clear temporal relationships between class size interventions and educational outcomes (Wykes et al., 2016). Additionally, the synthesis considered variability in class size reductions, ranging from minimal reductions of one student per class to more substantial reductions involving several students, ensuring detailed coverage of intervention intensity (Konstantopoulos & Chun, 2009). In conclusion, the statistical analysis adhered to rigorous standards, leveraging advanced meta-analytic techniques to integrate findings from a wide array of studies with varying methodologies, ensuring credible and actionable conclusions concerning the impact of class size on academic achievement. This systematic review aimed to assess the impact of class size on academic achievement, focusing specifically on reading and mathematics performance. The analysis included 127 studies encompassing 148 papers, with study populations from 41 countries. Ten of these studies were eligible for meta-analysis, including four that utilized data from the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) experiment conducted in the United States during the 1980s. In the meta-analysis of non-STAR studies, results for reading achievement were somewhat varied. The primary studies yielded effect sizes ranging from -0.08 to 0.14, with a majority being statistically non-significant. The random effects model, however, demonstrated a statistically significant small positive effect, with a weighted standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.11 (95% CI: 0.05 to 0.16). This suggests that, on average, students in smaller classes score higher in reading than those in larger classes, though the magnitude of the effect is limited. In contrast, the analysis of mathematics achievement showed an inconsistency in both the direction and magnitude of effect sizes. The primary study effect sizes for mathematics ranged from -0.41 to 0.11, with most outcomes not reaching statistical significance (SMD = -0.03; 95% CI: -0.22 to 0.16). The negative average effect, though statistically non-significant, indicates that reducing class size may not universally benefit or possibly detract from mathematical achievement among students. For studies analyzing data from the STAR experiment, all results consistently reported positive effects, statistically significant for both reading and mathematics. Effect sizes for reading ranged from 0.17 to 0.34, while for mathematics they ranged from 0.15 to 0.33. Despite the consistently positive data from the STAR cohorts, these findings did not meaningfully alter the overarching conclusions drawn from the complete dataset, especially given the limited representativeness of the STAR experiment in global educational contexts. When assessing the robustness of these results, sensitivity analyses showed that incorporating different components of study quality and varying operational definitions of class size did not substantively change the mean effect estimates. Nevertheless, when including data from primary studies with indeterminate effect directions, the statistical significance for reading was lost. Similarly, adjusting continuous variable class size reductions to one-student rather than standardized deviation did not appreciably impact the overall conclusions. The findings underscore a nuanced relationship between small class sizes and academic outcomes. For reading, the evidence suggests a small, statistically significant benefit of reduced class sizes. Meanwhile, for mathematics, the impact of class size appears negligible at best, with potential for negative effects that warrant further investigation. Specifically, the likelihood that a randomly selected student's score improves in reading given a smaller class size stands at 53%, compared to a mere 49% for mathematics. Overall, while the STAR studies offer an optimistic view of the potential benefits of smaller class sizes, their applicability across diverse educational environments might be limited. Additionally, the financial implications of reducing class sizes and the potential for variable impacts on different student subgroups imply a need for deeper investigation into where and how investments in education can be most effectively allocated. The current systematic review provides a critical synthesis of the evidence on the effects of class size reduction on academic achievement in primary and secondary education, consolidating findings from 148 reports across 41 countries. Despite the extensive data set, the meta-analysis included only ten studies due to stringent criteria regarding methodological rigor, emphasizing the need for careful interpretation of our findings. The results indicate a marginal positive effect of reduced class size on reading achievement, with a standardised mean difference (SMD) of 0.11, translating to a 53% probability that a student in a smaller class would outperform a peer in a larger class on a reading test. This effect size is statistically significant yet categorized as small per conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988). Conversely, the effect size for mathematics was negative and statistically insignificant (SMD = -0.03), suggesting no substantial advantage to smaller class sizes for this subject. The slight negative trend may imply potential adverse outcomes for some students, though this result lacks statistical conviction and thus should be interpreted with caution. The STAR experiments, a prominent subset within our dataset, consistently reported positive effects for both reading and maths. However, the generalizability of these findings is restricted due to the unique context of the original study, which may not reflect broader educational environments (Mosteller, 1995). It is important to consider that the educational systems, cultural factors, and teacher practices significantly influence the efficacy of class size reduction (Blatchford et al., 2003; Hattie, 2009). Therefore, it remains challenging to directly extrapolate the results across diverse educational settings. One critical limitation of this study lies in the variability of the included research designs and the potential biases inherent in non-randomized studies.

Tsung-Ting Kuo, PhD1, Jina Huh, PhD1, Jihoon Kim, MS1, Robert El-Kareh, MD, MS, MPH1, Siddharth Singh, MD1, Stephanie Feudjio Feupe, MSc1, Vincent Kuri, MS2, Gordon Lin, MS2, Michele E. Day, PhD1, Lucila Ohno-Machado, MD, PhD1, and Chun-Nan Hsu, PhD1, Keywords: Natural Language Processing and Text Mining, Human-Computer Interaction, Usability Testing, Pre-Annotation, Clinical Note Data Element Extraction ABSTRACT Objective. Annotation is expensive but essential for clinical note review and clinical natural language processing (cNLP). However, the extent to which computer-generated pre-annotation is beneficial to human annotation is still an open question. Our study introduces CLEAN (CLinical note rEview and ANnotation), a pre-annotation-based cNLP annotation system to improve clinical note annotation of data elements, and comprehensively compares CLEAN with the widely-used annotation system Brat Rapid Annotation Tool (BRAT). Materials and Methods. CLEAN includes an ensemble pipeline (CLEAN-EP) with a newly developed annotation tool (CLEAN-AT). A domain expert and a novice user/annotator participated in a comparative usability test by tagging 87 data elements related to Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) and Kawasaki Disease (KD) cohorts in 84 public notes. Results. CLEAN achieved higher note-level F1-score (0.896) over BRAT (0.820), with significant difference in correctness (P-value < 0.001), and the mostly related factor being system/software (P-value < 0.001). No significant difference (P-value 0.188) in annotation time was observed between CLEAN (7.262 minutes/note) and BRAT (8.286 minutes/note). The difference was mostly associated with note length (P-value < 0.001) and system/software (P-value 0.013). The expert reported CLEAN to be useful/satisfactory, while the novice reported slight improvements. Discussion. CLEAN improves the correctness of annotation and increases usefulness/satisfaction with the same level of efficiency. Limitations include untested impact of pre-annotation correctness rate, small sample size, small user size, and restrictedly validated gold standard. Conclusion. CLEAN with pre-annotation can be beneficial for an expert to deal with complex annotation tasks involving numerous and diverse target data elements. Clinical notes with unstructured narrative, such as progress notes, radiology reports, and discharge summaries, are one of the most information-rich, under-utilized sources of healthcare data.[1] Critical aspects of clinical quality are often described in the free-text notes of electronic health records (EHR) systems. These important aspects can be used to improve healthcare delivery/management, clinical/translational research, and ultimately patient health. Clinical Natural Language Processing (cNLP) is dedicated to developing tools and systems to extract such useful information from medical text. Widely used cNLP tools include cTAKES (clinical Text Analysis and Knowledge Extraction System),[2] MetaMap,[3] MedEx,[4] CLAMP (Clinical Language Annotation, Modeling, and Processing Toolkit),[5] Vitals,[6] EFEx,[7] KD-NLP,[8] and a few others.[9-11] These cNLP tools can extract various types of information such as condition and medication. Annotation in cNLP refers to the process of manually identifying the mentions of data elements of target signs, symptoms, events, etc. to be extracted in clinical notes. Annotation, although imperfect, is an important process that provides: (1) quality control for final cNLP output data, (2) gold standards to evaluate the performance of cNLP tools, and (3) training examples to develop and improve cNLP tools. Specifically, training examples are essential for those cNLP tools based on supervised machine learning, as well as for the development of rule-based cNLP tools.[9-20] Annotation, however, is also the bottleneck of the whole development process of cNLP tools,[21] especially when numerous and diverse data elements are to be extracted.[1] From our experience in the patient-centered SCAlable National Network for Effectiveness Research (pSCANNER) project,[22] an experienced clinical annotator required an average of 15 to 30 minutes to annotate a clinical note for an annotation task involving the tagging of 41 data elements. Intuitively, pre-annotation by a cNLP tool before a manual review might help improve the correctness and efficiency of the annotation process.[12] In pre-annotation, the mentions of the target data elements are identified by a cNLP tool. These elements serve as suggestions to a human annotator, so that the annotator can review and revise the pre-annotated mentions (“preannotations”) instead of starting the annotation process from scratch. However, previous cNLP studies of pre-annotation showed mixed and inconsistent results in terms of correctness and efficiency on tasks that included name entity recognition,[12 13] de-identification,[14 15] patient records chart review,[16 17] corpus creation,[18] and NLP output validation,[19 20]. None of the studies considered the tailored design of a user interface (UI) to take advantage of preannotation. In the study of name entity recognition, some authors reported positive results of pre-annotation [12]: “Time savings [of pre-annotations] ranged from 13.85% to 21.5% per entity. Inter-annotator agreement (IAA) ranged from 93.4% to 95.5%. … The time savings were statistically significant. Moreover, the pre-annotation did not reduce the IAA or annotator performance.” However, other authors provided contrasting outcomes [13]: “We found little benefit to [pre-annotate] the corpus with a third-party name entity recognizer … the annotators (who were] given the [MetaMap Transfer (MMTx) tool, now MetaMap] [23] annotations, A1 and A3, annotated slower than the other two annotators, A2 and A4. … There was also no clear trend that the MMTx annotation improved pair-wise IAA between individuals.” Most studies only focused on a limited number of target data elements to be extracted. For example, the authors of these studies [12] [13] named 5 and 10 concepts, respectively. Our goal was to take advantage of pre-annotation to improve the annotation process of clinical notes when numerous and diverse data elements that are necessary to support phenotyping and cohort identification were involved. In other words, we sought to design, implement and evaluate a software system that leverages pre-annotation to improve the annotation quality of clinical notes with a large number (> 50) of target data elements. This situation commonly occurs in cNLP use cases for phenotyping and cohort identification.[24-26] To this end, we developed the CLinical note rEview and ANnotation (CLEAN) cNLP system and comprehensively compared CLEAN with the widely-used annotation system Brat Rapid Annotation Tool (BRAT).[21] The overall architecture of the CLEAN cNLP system is shown in Figure 1. The input to CLEAN includes a study plan specifying the target disease/condition, categorized data elements, and criteria used to select a set of clinical notes from an institute electronic health record (EHR) data warehouses. Since clinical notes contain PHI, we deposit them in a secure, privacy-preserving computation environment that also stores data elements definitions and categories. The CLEAN ensemble pipeline (CLEAN-EP) pre-annotates the clinical notes using Union,[1] which extracts the data element if any of the cNLP tools identifies the data element and uses the ensemble method to integrate four cNLP tools (cTAKES,[2] MetaMap [3],MedEx,[4] and KD-NLP [8]), as well as our newly developed cNLP tool ROCK (Rules for Obesity, Congestive heart failure, and Kawasaki disease) described in Appendix A.1. We previously discovered that Union showed the highest recall/sensitivity among all of the ensemble methods in our pilot study[1]. Thus, when using Union as the ensemble method, annotators are provided with a high-coverage preannotated data element mentions in a clinical note text, instead of searching through the full text to identify any missing elements. That is, annotators can focus on correcting the pre-annotations, instead of adding the missing mentions. A benefit of applying an ensemble pipeline like CLEANEP is improved system flexibility to reuse and share cNLP tools.[27-32] Details about CLEAN-EP are described in Appendix A.1. Figure 1. The CLinical note rEview and ANnotation (CLEAN) clinical Natural Language Processing (cNLP) System. After the study plan was confirmed, the inputs were the selected data elements and the queried clinical notes from the electronic health record (EHR) data warehouse, both stored on a Virtual Machine (VM). Then, the built-in CLEAN ensemble pipeline (CLEAN-EP) preannotated the notes, followed by the user’s review using the CLEAN annotation tool (CLEAN-AT). The outputs were the reviewed annotations of the data elements on the clinical notes, and CLEAN stored the final results back on the VM. Finally, an annotator will review and correct the pre-annotations using the CLEAN annotation tool (CLEAN-AT). CLEAN-AT saves the final resulting annotations and allows annotators to re-check and refine the annotations if required. Details of CLEAN-AT are given in Section 3.2. Annotation editor (right panel). This main working space of CLEAN-AT shows the clinical note as well as all annotations on the note. A user can edit the annotations and review results on this panel. In this study, the terms user and annotator are used interchangeably. Data element browser (left panel). Clicking the data element or category in the left panel quickly identifies all annotated mentions of that data element or category of the clinical note shown in the annotation editor. In this example (Figure 2), “Natriuretic Peptides” was clicked in the data element browser to identify the synonym mention “BNP” in the clinical note text. Conversely, in the clinical note, the mentions could be clicked in the annotation editor to highlight the corresponding data element in bold in the data element browser. Figure 2. The CLEAN annotation tool (CLEAN-AT). The left panel (data element browser) shows all the data elements, while the right panel (annotation editor) is for annotation adding, deleting, and modifying via the pop-up menu (data element reminder). The bottom panel (function buttons) allows users to undo/redo editing, save progress, save the note as complete, and proceed with the next note. The clinical note shown here is from publicly available MT Sample notes.[33] Data element reminder (a popup menu while tagging the text). After right-clicking on a selected mention in the annotation editor, a popup menu appears with a list of all data elements grouped by the categories. A user can use the keyboard as an auto-completion shortcut to filter possible data elements and thus can speed up the annotation editing process. For the example shown in Figure 2, if the user types “n,” CLEAN-AT would display “Natriuretic Peptides” and “NT-proBNP,” the data elements of which name starts with “n.” The user can then choose from the filtered data elements to annotate or re-annotate quickly. Undo/redo (function buttons in the bottom panel). CLEAN-AT supports an unlimited number of undo and redo operations, which allows users to edit and delete quickly, knowing that they could easily recover from mistakes. Note that, deletions are also considered as an operation, and therefore user can undo/redo deletions. Supporting undo/redo operations follows an important principle of user interface design to reduce distress of new users.[34-36] However, few existing annotation tools for cNLP support undo/redo, because the program must record every user interaction. Also, the program must maintain a stack data structure, to save the entire history of previous user interactions that need to be accessible anytime the user attempts to undo/redo the last operations. If the software did not include the undo/redo function in the initial design, it would be difficult to add this feature because the whole program might need to be thoroughly rewritten. CLEAN-AT implements this important feature based on the JavaScript library React.[37] Overview of the completion status of clinical notes. As shown in Figure A.2 in Appendix A, the user can start a new annotation process, continue an incomplete annotation process, or recheck a previously completed annotation process, for any clinical note in a target corpus. Although the overview page shows the overall information for all notes, CLEANAT brings up the next note for annotation after the user completes the annotation of a clinical note, instead of bringing up this overview page. This feature was designed to effectively keep a user engaged. We evaluated the performance of CLEAN using two cohorts: (1) Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) as an exemplar of a major health condition in the U.S., where the prevalence of heart disease is 5.7 M;[38] and (2) Kawasaki Disease (KD), which represents a rare yet acute disease with an estimated number of U.S. hospitalizations of 5,447 in 2009.[39] Both conditions are use-case conditions for the pSCANNER clinical data research network.[22] We used the clinical note pool and target data elements described in our previous work [1] with newly annotated gold standards, which are further described later in this subsection. Ensuring timely and optimal use of research evidence in health-related settings presents an ongoing challenge to practitioners and decision-makers [1]. Failure to optimize the use of research evidence may result in reduced quality of care [2], inefficient use of resources [3, 4], and poorer health outcomes for individuals and communities [5]. To mitigate the challenges associated with knowledge sharing between researchers, practitioners, and decision-makers [6], some knowledge translation (KT) experts have advocated for the use of an intermediary, known as a knowledge broker (KB) [7, 8]. KBs have been described as ‘knowledge managers’, ‘linkage agents’, and ‘capacity builders’ [8, 9]. Knowledge management tasks are related to the facilitation or management of the creation, translation, diffusion, and application of knowledge [8, 9]. Linkage and exchange activities focus on the development of positive relationships between knowledge creators (e.g. researchers) and knowledge users (e.g. decision-makers, clinicians) as a means to stimulate new information, collaborative knowledge exchange, and the use of evidence-informed approaches [8]. Capacity building activities aim to develop knowledge users’ understanding and skills [8], enable evidence-informed decision-making [10], and enhance capacity to access and apply knowledge [11]. Despite these distinct descriptions, in reality, KBs likely operate as an amalgam of these roles, depending on the goals of the KT initiative [12]. Essentially, KBs work collaboratively with stakeholders to facilitate the transfer and exchange of relevant information. They represent the human component of KT strategies as they work to facilitate interaction; develop mutual understanding of stakeholders’ goals and contexts; identify emerging areas of concern warranting attention; expedite the identification, evaluation, and translation of evidence into practice and/or policy; and facilitate the management of relevant knowledge [13, 14]. While KBs have operated in the private sector for years [8, 13], their adoption by the health sector has been rather limited until recently. In 2003, the Canadian Health Services Research Foundation (CHSRF) developed a report on the theory and practice of knowledge brokering in Canada’s health system [13], which acknowledged the need for additional evidence to assess the efficacy of KB approaches and best practices. Others have echoed this recommendation [15–18]. While some have advocated for the use of KBs as a mechanism to facilitate KT [17, 19, 20], others suggest that the lack of evidence about how knowledge brokering works and its potential effectiveness limits the development and application of the KB role [8]. To address this gap, we sought to (1) identify and examine the activities and tasks which comprised the KB role in health-related settings and (2) assess whether KBs have effectively contributed to KT in health-related settings. We employed a systematic review and thematic analysis to synthesize and appraise diverse evidence related to knowledge brokering in health-related settings. Our thematic analysis [19] explored how KBs function in health-related settings. To assess whether KBs have effectively contributed to KT in health-related settings, we employed a systematic review, which permits an overall assessment of effectiveness through a comprehensive and reproducible search and assessment of existing literature [20]. Since the KB role may be influenced by myriad contextual factors [21], quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-method designs were assessed in addition to grey literature sources to elucidate the activities and tasks that comprised the KB role in health-related settings. While some have noted concerns regarding the feasibility and validity of synthesizing different research approaches [22], the objectives of this inquiry—aimed largely at exploring occupational processes and outcomes in diverse health settings—required a broader perspective than would be offered by limiting to a single research design. In collaboration with the research team, research librarians developed and implemented search strategies in eight electronic databases (MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Scopus, SocINDEX, and Health Business Elite) using English language restrictions and covering all published work available up to November 2014 (Additional file 1). Websites of relevant KT networks (i.e. Canadian Foundation for Healthcare Improvement, National Collaborating Centre for Methods and Tools) and health-focused organizations (i.e. Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Canadian Public Health Information, Health Evidence, Ontario Public Health Units, World Health Organization (WHO), WHO’s ‘Brokering knowledge and Research Information to support the Development and Governance of health systems in Europe’ [BRIDGE] series) were searched in an effort to identify relevant grey literature (Additional file 2). Additionally, relevant journals and reference lists of included articles were reviewed. To be included, studies must have reported on an actual application of knowledge brokering (i.e. theoretical assumptions about knowledge brokering were excluded). Studies must also have been available in English and occurred in a health-related setting, i.e. health-related contexts or environments including the following: healthcare practice (e.g. clinical, public health, rehabilitation, community-based health settings), health policy (e.g. interactions with health decision-makers at local, regional, provincial/state, federal or international levels), health education (e.g. interactions with health educators in clinical or academic settings), and healthcare administration (e.g. interactions with health system organizations). While studies were not excluded based on research design, when reviews were identified, we sought to locate the primary source document(s). Once search results were compiled and duplicates were removed, two reviewers independently screened the remaining records (i.e. titles and abstracts of articles or grey literature sources) for eligibility (Fig. 1). Subsequently, full-text articles and grey literature sources were independently assessed by two reviewers for alignment with inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or third party adjudication. Multiple publications addressing the same KB initiative were combined into unique studies.Fig. 1Flow diagram of process to identify eligible studies. Note: records identified through ‘other sources’ include grey literature, hand searching of relevant journals, and reference lists of manuscripts included in this review We assessed the methodological quality of all studies reporting outcomes related to the effectiveness of KBs (defined as changes in stakeholders’ knowledge, skills, policies, and/or practices [23]) using the Meta Quality Appraisal Tool (MetaQAT) [24]. MetaQAT combines enhanced principles of quality appraisal with the rigour of risk of bias assessment using select existing design-specific companion tools within a larger conceptual framework to guide their use in the context of broad health-related settings. Specifically, MetaQAT provides a set of rigourous methodological guidelines to synthesize diverse types of evidence (e.g. quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, grey literature). It consists of a four-step critical appraisal framework which assesses relevancy, validity, reliability, and applicability. It also contains research design-specific modules for quantitative (e.g. PRISMA, CONSORT, TREND, AGREE, CASP), qualitative (e.g. McMaster critical review form: qualitative studies (version 2)), and mixed methods (e.g. Evaluation Tool for Mixed Methods Studies) research design appraisal; thus, demonstrating broad applicability across study designs, which is a fundamental requirement of a multi-modal quality appraisal tool [25]. Importantly, MetaQAT has undergone a transparent development and validation process [24]. Appropriate studies were appraised by two independent reviewers with disagreements resolved by third party consultation. Data were extracted using standard forms developed for this protocol and included the following: setting(s), purpose of the initiative, duration of the KB initiative, level of KB’s experience (e.g. novice, experienced), KB’s position status (e.g. full-time, part-time), KB approach (e.g. independent, team-based), and whether the KB role was embedded in or external to the organization(s) (i.e. internal employee or externally contracted). We also explored strategies used by KBs to promote KT (e.g. in-person meetings, teleconferences). To assess the effectiveness of KBs at facilitating KT, data pertaining to changes in knowledge, skills, policies, and practices were also extracted [23]. Extracted data were reviewed and approved by both reviewers; disagreements were resolved by discussion. In line with our first objective to improve conceptualization of the KB role in health-related settings, we conducted a confirmatory thematic analysis [19] to assess the operationalization of the KB role according to the domains described by Ward et al. [8] and Oldham and McLean [9] (i.e. knowledge management, linkage and exchange, and capacity building). Extracted data were analyzed using NVivo9 [26]. A deductive approach was employed [27], which involved a priori construction of a preliminary coding manual structured according to the sensitizing concepts (knowledge management, linkage and exchange, and capacity building). This approach was complemented by inductive coding to identify emergent themes. Extracted data were initially synthesized by one reviewer. The draft synthesis was reviewed by a second reviewer and iteratively adapted until agreement on appropriateness of themes and subthemes was achieved. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion. To address our second objective to determine whether KBs contributed to effective KT in health-related settings, we explored outcome data for evidence of changes in knowledge, skills, policies, or practices. Our approach was adapted from the work of Kujbida and Stratton [23] who measured changes in attitude, knowledge, and practice (among other factors) to assess the effectiveness of KT strategies. For studies presented in more than one publication, all relevant articles were analyzed collectively to ensure examination of relevant contextual factors. Our review sought to answer the following research question: Are knowledge brokers an effective mechanism to facilitate KT relative to reported changes in knowledge, skill, policies, and/or programmes in health-related settings among KT participants? Twenty-nine articles, representing 22 unique studies, met our inclusion criteria and were included in the review (Fig. 1). Qualitative (n = 18), quantitative (n = 1), and mixed methods (n = 6) research designs were represented in addition to grey literature sources (n = 4). Studies were heterogeneous relative to health-related settings, length of KB initiative, KB approach, KB position status, and whether the KB was internal or external to the participating organization(s). Descriptive characteristics of the 22 studies are presented in Additional file 3. Findings indicate that KBs in health-related settings performed a diverse range of tasks across the three domains proposed by Oldham and McLean [9] and Ward et al. [8], thus supporting the KB role as a knowledge manager, linkage agent, and capacity builder. Moreover, findings suggested that KB activities often overlapped these theoretical constructs. Our thematic analysis generated ten main KB activities. Below, we introduce each of these activities and elaborate on their associated tasks. Specifically, this task involved finding the ‘right’ people [15, 31] or organizations to support the KT objectives and then garnering their participation [32–34] through telephone, electronic, or in-person contact [15]. Maintaining a physical presence among stakeholders was also noted to be useful [35]. To support stakeholder engagement, KBs identified common goals among stakeholders by helping to clarify their needs [30, 36, 37], identifying mutually beneficial opportunities [17], and bringing together individuals with common interests and relevant expertise to address the issue [15, 29]. Specifically, KBs engaged in-person through site visits to stakeholders’ organizations [21] and meetings [29, 38] that included both one-on-one [34] and larger group [29, 34, 39] discussions. KBs worked to facilitate collaboration by organizing group forums such as workshops [17, 31, 40], journal clubs [41], online forums [15, 41], and multi-sector advisory committee meetings [41]. To promote collaboration, KBs facilitated dialogue between stakeholders by establishing communication channels [31], creating a ‘safe’ forum to share research activities [31], facilitating group discussions or problem-solving sessions [15, 28, 29, 39, 40], clearing up misunderstandings [42], leading focus groups [15], and chairing teleconferences [15]. KBs facilitated consensus by assisting stakeholders to clarify their needs and expectations [17, 36], helping stakeholders to understand each other’s standards of methodological rigour [31], and negotiating shared project objectives [17, 28, 31, 36], deliverables [31], and outcomes [31].
