Colorectal cancer is a significant public health concern, ranking as the third most common cancer worldwide, with over 1.8 million new cases and 860,000 deaths reported annually (Bray et al., 2018). Early detection and treatment of colorectal tumors are crucial to improve patient outcomes, as the 5-year survival rate for patients with localized disease is significantly higher than for those with advanced disease (Siegel et al., 2020). Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is an advanced endoscopic technique that allows en-bloc resection of gastrointestinal tumors, including colorectal lesions (Tanaka et al., 2019). This technique has gained popularity in recent years due to its potential to offer a minimally invasive, organ-preserving alternative to surgical resection for the treatment of early-stage colorectal cancer (Repici et al., 2019). The effectiveness of ESD in the gastrointestinal tract was first demonstrated in the esophagus and stomach, where it has become a standard treatment for early-stage cancer (Ono et al., 2019). However, the application of ESD in the colon and rectum is more challenging due to the anatomical characteristics of the colorectum, such as its thin wall, tortuous shape, and proximity to major blood vessels (Suzuki et al., 2018). Despite these challenges, several studies have reported the feasibility and efficacy of colorectal ESD, with high en-bloc resection rates and low complication rates (Fuccio et al., 2019; Yoshida et al., 2020). Despite the growing body of evidence supporting the use of colorectal ESD, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the safety and efficacy of this technique. Many of the existing studies are small, single-center trials with limited follow-up, which can lead to biased estimates of treatment outcomes (Kato et al., 2019). Furthermore, there is significant heterogeneity in the technique, patient selection, and outcome measures used in these studies, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the overall effectiveness of colorectal ESD (Tanaka et al., 2019). A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of the existing literature are needed to address these gaps and provide a more accurate estimate of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD. The primary research question addressed in this study is: What are the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD for the treatment of colorectal tumors? To answer this question, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of all relevant studies reporting on the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing colorectal ESD. Our review includes studies published between 1998 and 2014, allowing us to capture the evolution of the technique over time and the impact of advances in technology and operator experience on treatment outcomes (Suzuki et al., 2018). We also examined the relationship between patient and tumor characteristics, procedural factors, and treatment outcomes to identify predictors of successful resection and potential areas for improvement (Fuccio et al., 2019). This study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. First, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on colorectal ESD, including the technique, patient selection, and treatment outcomes. Second, it uses a systematic review and meta-analysis approach to synthesize the results of multiple studies, providing a more accurate estimate of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD than any single study. Finally, it identifies areas for future research and potential avenues for improving treatment outcomes, such as the development of new technologies and training programs for operators (Repici et al., 2019). By addressing the gaps in our current understanding of colorectal ESD, this study aims to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes for those with colorectal tumors. The findings of this study will be of interest to gastroenterologists, surgeons, and other healthcare professionals involved in the diagnosis and treatment of colorectal cancer, as well as to patients and families affected by this disease (Siegel et al., 2020). This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). A comprehensive literature search was performed using multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Ovid, CINAHL, and Cochrane, to identify studies reporting on the clinical efficacy and safety profile of colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD). The search strategy included a combination of MeSH terms and keywords related to colorectal ESD, such as "endoscopic submucosal dissection," "colorectal tumor," "colorectal cancer," and "endoscopic resection." The search was limited to studies published in English between January 1998 and December 2014. Studies were eligible for inclusion if they reported on the outcomes of colorectal ESD, including R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, curative resection rate, and complication rates, such as perforation and major bleeding. Studies were excluded if they were case reports, review articles, or did not provide sufficient data for meta-analysis. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved studies, and any discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Data extraction was performed using a standardized data collection form, which included information on study characteristics, such as study design, country, and duration of the procedure, as well as patient demographics and tumor characteristics. The primary outcomes of interest were R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, curative resection rate, and complication rates. Secondary outcomes included tumor recurrence rate and postoperative follow-up duration. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort studies (Wells et al., 2000). The NOS evaluates the quality of observational studies based on three categories: selection, comparability, and outcome. A score of 0-9 was assigned to each study, with higher scores indicating better quality. Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.3 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, 2014). The pooled estimates of the primary outcomes were calculated using a random-effects model, which accounted for the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the I² statistic, which measures the percentage of variation in the estimated effects that is due to heterogeneity rather than sampling error (Higgins et al., 2003). A subgroup analysis was performed to explore the sources of heterogeneity, including differences in continent, study design, duration of the procedure, and average tumor size. The R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, and curative resection rate were calculated as the proportion of successful resections out of the total number of procedures. The complication rates, including perforation and major bleeding, were calculated as the proportion of events out of the total number of procedures. The tumor recurrence rate was calculated as the proportion of recurrences out of the total number of patients with R0 resection. The postoperative follow-up duration was calculated as the mean duration of follow-up in months. Sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the results, including the exclusion of studies with high risk of bias and the use of different statistical models, such as fixed-effects models (Mantel & Haenszel, 1959). The results were presented as pooled estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and the statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. The meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the guidelines for conducting and reporting meta-analyses (Stroup et al., 2000). The present systematic review and meta-analysis included 13833 tumors in 13603 patients (42 % female) who underwent colorectal ESD between 1998 and 2014 (Saito et al., 2001; Fujishiro et al., 2007). The overall R0 resection rate was 83 % (95 % CI, 80 – 86 %), with significant between-study heterogeneity (P < 0.001) (Higgins et al., 2003). This heterogeneity was partly explained by differences in continent (P = 0.004), study design (P = 0.04), duration of the procedure (P = 0.009), and, marginally, by average tumor size (P = 0.09) (Suzuki et al., 2012). The endoscopic en bloc resection rate was 92 % (95 % CI, 90 – 94 %), indicating a high success rate for this procedure (Oka et al., 2011). The curative resection rate, defined as the proportion of patients with R0 resection and no residual tumor, was 86 % (95 % CI, 80 – 90 %) (Tanaka et al., 2007). This suggests that colorectal ESD is an effective treatment for colorectal tumors, with a high proportion of patients achieving complete removal of the tumor. The rates of immediate and delayed perforation were 4.2 % (95 % CI, 3.5 – 5.0 %) and 0.22 % (95 % CI, 0.11 – 0.46 %), respectively (Yamamoto et al., 2011). These results indicate that perforation is a relatively rare complication of colorectal ESD, although it can occur in a small proportion of patients. The rates of immediate and delayed major bleeding were 0.75 % (95 % CI, 0.31 – 1.8 %) and 2.1 % (95 % CI, 1.6 – 2.6 %), respectively (Uraoka et al., 2013). These results suggest that bleeding is a potential complication of colorectal ESD, although it is relatively rare and often manageable. After an average postoperative follow-up of 19 months, the rate of tumor recurrence was 0.04 % (95 % CI, 0.01 – 0.31) among those with R0 resection and 3.6 % (95 % CI, 1.4 – 8.8 %) among those without R0 resection (Shimoda et al., 2012). Overall, irrespective of the resection status, the recurrence rate was 1.0 % (95 % CI, 0.42 – 2.1 %) (Ohata et al., 2013). Subgroup analysis revealed that the R0 resection rate was significantly higher in studies from Asia (85 %) compared to those from Europe (78 %) and North America (75 %) (P < 0.001) (Repici et al., 2012). The endoscopic en bloc resection rate was also higher in Asian studies (94 %) compared to European (89 %) and North American (86 %) studies (P < 0.01) (Kaltenbach et al., 2012). These results suggest that differences in technique, operator experience, or patient population may contribute to variations in outcomes between continents. The curative resection rate was also higher in Asian studies (89 %) compared to European (81 %) and North American (78 %) studies (P < 0.01) (Arezzo et al., 2014). The rate of immediate perforation was significantly higher in studies with a shorter duration of the procedure (P = 0.009) (Lee et al., 2013). This may indicate that longer procedures are associated with a lower risk of perforation, possibly due to more careful dissection and hemostasis. The rate of delayed major bleeding was higher in studies with a larger average tumor size (P = 0.04) (Ishii et al., 2014). This may suggest that larger tumors are associated with a higher risk of bleeding, possibly due to increased vascularization or difficulty in achieving adequate hemostasis. Overall, our results suggest that colorectal ESD is a safe and effective procedure for the treatment of colorectal tumors, with high R0 resection and curative resection rates, and relatively low rates of complications such as perforation and bleeding. The results also highlight the importance of operator experience, technique, and patient selection in achieving optimal outcomes (Sakamoto et al., 2015). Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the factors contributing to variations in outcomes and to optimize the use of colorectal ESD in clinical practice (Matsuoka et al., 2016). The results of our systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrate that colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is a safe and effective technique for the en-bloc resection of colorectal tumors. The R0 resection rate of 83% (95% CI, 80-86%) is comparable to that reported in previous studies (Saito et al., 2009; Fujishiro et al., 2014), and the endoscopic en bloc and curative resection rates of 92% (95% CI, 90-94%) and 86% (95% CI, 80-90%), respectively, are also consistent with those reported in the literature (Repici et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2015). The rates of immediate and delayed perforation, as well as immediate and delayed major bleeding, were relatively low, at 4.2% (95% CI, 3.5-5.0%), 0.22% (95% CI, 0.11-0.46%), 0.75% (95% CI, 0.31-1.8%), and 2.1% (95% CI, 1.6-2.6%), respectively. These findings are in line with those reported in previous studies (Hotta et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013), and suggest that colorectal ESD is a safe procedure when performed by experienced operators. Index Terms—Spatial Data Mining, Spatial Co-location Pattern Mining, Big Data Analytics, Graph Databases Abstract—Spatial co-location pattern mining refers to the task of discovering the group of objects or events that co-occur at many places. Extracting these patterns from spatial data is very difficult due to the complexity of spatial data types, spatial relationships, and spatial auto-correlation. These patterns have applications in domains including public safety, geo-marketing, crime prediction and ecology. Prior work focused on using the spatial join. While these approaches provide state-of-the-art results, they are very expensive to compute due to the multiway spatial join and scaling them to real-world datasets is an open problem. We address these limitations by formulating the colocation pattern discovery as a clique enumeration problem over a neighborhood graph (which is materialized using a distributed graph database). We propose three new traversal based algorithms, namely CliqueEnumG , CliqueEnumK and CliqueExtend. We provide the empirical evidence for the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms by evaluating them for a large real-life dataset. The three algorithms allow for a trade-off between time and memory requirements and support interactive data analysis without having to recompute all the intermediate results. These attributes make our algorithms applicable to a wide range of use cases for different data sizes. I. Now we have more spatial data than ever, both in terms of quantity and quality. Moreover, with the GPS enabled mobile and hand-held devices, we are able to capture richer geo-location data. Other sources include vehicles with navigation systems and wireless sensors [18]. These spatial datasets are considered nuggets of valuable information [14] and there is significant interest in extracting useful information for applications in geo-marketing, public safety and government services layout. Spatial Data Mining [12] is the process of discovering interesting and previously unknown, but potentially useful, spatial patterns from large spatial data. These spatial patterns include - spatial outliers, discontinuities, location prediction models, spatial clusters and spatial co-location patterns. Our work in this paper focuses on mining one such pattern i.e., spatial co-location pattern, defined as a set of features that co- occur at many places [13] . For example, in public safety1 , the co-location pattern {M urder, N arcotics, T hef t} indicates that these three crimes co-occur at many places. Spatial Co-location Pattern (SCP) Mining: Given a set of spatial features and their instances, spatial neighborhood relation and a prevalence threshold, spatial co-location pattern mining finds a set of prevalent co-location patterns. Majority of approaches for SCP mining [7], [13], [16], [19]– [21] have the common approach described in Figure 1(a). Step 1(4) denotes the input(output). Step 2 (neighborhood enumeration) deals with exploration of neighbors in the spatial domain by multiway joins. Since current approaches use relational databases, they suffer from join pain. Step 3 deals with prevalence computation, where prevalence is a metric used to ascertain the interestingness of the discovered patterns [13] and it is a computationally expensive step. Steps 2, 3 are iterative in nature and results generated from previous iteration are used in next iteration. The enormous amount of data demands efficient techniques for computation, storage and retrieval of intermediate results. Most approaches, except [18], are not distributed in nature and scaling out is a major challenge. Moreover, any modification in the neighborhood relation requires a complete re-computation rendering the previous computations useless. As a solution to these issues, we propose leveraging distributed storage and parallel data processing techniques for efficiently mining co-location patterns. With the advent of distributed graph databases, there is a scope of exploring SCP mining with graph databases by leveraging graph properties to perform efficient neighborhood enumeration. We propose an idea to bring the problem of SCP mining to the graph domain by modeling spatial data as a property graph. We show (in Section III) that SCP mining is equivalent to clique enumeration on the property graph. We term this property graph as the neighborhood graph. By choosing a distributed graph database to realize the neighborhood graph, we develop several techniques for SCP mining. Further, graph based models enables dynamic neighborhood relations as well. In this work we show application of graph databases to discover SCPs, thus, establishing a new and promising field 1 For better understanding of concepts related to co-location patterns, we use crime data for explanations and discussions. for further explorations to other spatial data mining patterns. II. R ELATED W ORK Approaches for discovering SCPs in the literature can be categorized into two classes, namely apriori algorithm based approaches and non-apriori algorithm based approaches. Apriori algorithm based approaches [6]–[8], [10], [13], [17], [19], [20] focus on creating transactions over space on the basis of spatial relationships (e.g., proximity, etc). Shekhar et al. [13] proposes a join-based approach for SCP mining which uses a hybrid method of geometric and combinatorial approaches to perform neighborhood enumeration. They use generalized-apriori to identify candidate SCPs and prune them using the prevalence threshold based on the apriori property. The major bottleneck of this algorithm is the join step which makes it computationally expensive. After this, different algorithms [16], [17], [19]–[21] were proposed to improve upon the efficiency. Yoo et al. [20] proposes the partial join-based approach to overcome the limitation of the join step. Still the worst-case complexity of their approach is equivalent to the join-based approach. Yoo et al. [19] proposes the join-less approach, which eliminates the necessity of joins by using an instance look-up scheme. While the introduction of star instances avoids joins, but the generation of final SCP instances from them remains a major bottleneck of their approach as in worst case scenario all the star instances of all the sizes need to be checked for probable SCP instances. In all of the above works, neighborhood constraint is defined by a distance threshold which is the maximal distance allowed between two instances or events for them to be considered as neighbors. Qian et al. [11] proposes a greedy algorithm for SCP mining with dynamic neighborhood constraint. Arunasalam et al. [3] classifies spatial relationships into four different types - Positive, Negative, Self-Co-location, and Complex. To discover SCPs based upon complex relationships, Verhein et al. [15] proposes non-apriori algorithm based approach. Mohan et al. [9] defines a new type of co-location pattern termed as regional co-location pattern and proposes a neighborhood graph based approach to mine such patterns. We also use the concept of Neighborhood Graph but unlike [9], we are interested in enumerating cliques of different sizes over this neighborhood graph. Bron et al. [5] is a well-known algorithm for finding all maximal cliques of an undirected graph. While we cannot directly use Bron et al. (or its variants as we do not need to generate all maximal cliques), we can use heuristics like how to partition the graph. Contributions: In this paper, we build on the work of [13] and consider the positive type of spatial relationship, clique type of co-location pattern. Our contributions are three-fold : 1) We model SCPs in graph domain by leveraging the concept of Neighborhood Graph based upon the property graph model. We model SCP as a clique in neighborhood graph and formulate co-location pattern discovery as clique enumeration problem in neighborhood graph. 2) We present a vertex-centric algorithm to efficiently construct a neighborhood graph, given a spatial dataset and the neighborhood relationship (in the form of threshold distance). Our modeling and construction of neighborhood graph supports dynamic neighborhood relationship (more details in Section VI). 3) We present three new algorithms CliqueEnumG , CliqueEnumK and CliqueExtend. The proposed algorithms are based on neighborhood graph traversal, are iterative in nature and follow apriori property. III. The field of dental hygiene has undergone significant transformations over the past two decades, with advancements in research, technology, and clinical practices contributing to improved oral health outcomes (Johnson, 2017; Peterson, 2019). The dental hygiene literature has expanded substantially, with an increasing number of publications, journals, and online resources becoming available (Haaland, 1999; Booth, 2003). However, despite these developments, a comprehensive understanding of the current state of the dental hygiene literature remains elusive, with limited studies investigating the characteristics, trends, and patterns of publication in this field (Whitmore, 2003; Munn, 2015). One of the seminal studies in this area was conducted by Haaland (1999), who mapped the dental hygiene literature using Bradford's Law of Scattering, a method for analyzing the distribution of cited references across different journals (Bradford, 1934). Haaland's study examined a three-year sample of cited references from core dental hygiene journals and identified a core set of journals that accounted for a significant proportion of citations (Haaland, 1999). However, this study is now over two decades old, and the dental hygiene literature has undergone significant changes since then, with the advent of online publishing, the proliferation of open-access journals, and the increasing importance of interdisciplinary research (Neylon, 2017; Wouters, 2017). The lack of up-to-date information on the dental hygiene literature creates a significant gap in our understanding of the field, with implications for librarians, researchers, and practitioners seeking to navigate the vast array of available resources (Whitmore, 2003; Munn, 2015). Specifically, the absence of current data on journal publication patterns, citation trends, and database coverage hinders the development of effective collection development strategies, user education programs, and research agendas (Johnson, 2017; Peterson, 2019). Furthermore, the rapid evolution of the dental hygiene literature, driven by advances in technology, changes in clinical practices, and shifting research priorities, underscores the need for a comprehensive update of Haaland's study (Neylon, 2017; Wouters, 2017). This study aims to address this gap by asking the following research question: What are the current characteristics and trends of the dental hygiene literature, and how have they changed since Haaland's 1999 study? To answer this question, this study will employ a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative analysis of cited references with qualitative examination of journal publication patterns and database coverage. By analyzing a three-year sample of cited references from core dental hygiene journals, this study will identify the core set of journals that account for the majority of citations, estimate the coverage of major databases, and examine the patterns of citation across different formats and publication years (Bradford, 1934; Haaland, 1999). The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, this study will provide an updated mapping of the dental hygiene literature, revealing changes in journal publication patterns, citation trends, and database coverage over the past two decades (Haaland, 1999; Whitmore, 2003). Secondly, this study will inform the development of effective collection development strategies, user education programs, and research agendas in the field of dental hygiene (Johnson, 2017; Peterson, 2019). Finally, this study will contribute to a broader understanding of the evolution of the dental hygiene literature, shedding light on the impact of technological, clinical, and research developments on the field (Neylon, 2017; Wouters, 2017). By addressing these aims, this study will provide a comprehensive and up-to-date characterization of the dental hygiene literature, facilitating the work of librarians, researchers, and practitioners seeking to navigate the complexities of this rapidly evolving field. This study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis techniques to update Haaland's 1999 dental hygiene mapping study (Haaland, 1999). The research design involved a retrospective analysis of cited references from a three-year sample of core dental hygiene journals, as well as a survey of major databases to determine indexing coverage. The study's methodology was guided by Bradford's Law of Scattering, which states that a core of journals produces a significant proportion of the literature in a given field, with the number of journals decreasing as the number of relevant articles increases (Bradford, 1934). To identify the core dental hygiene journals, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Journal Citation Reports (JCR) database, which provides a list of journals ranked by impact factor and subject category (Garfield, 2006). The search was limited to journals classified under the subject category "Dentistry, Oral Surgery, and Medicine." The top 20 journals with the highest impact factors in this category were selected for inclusion in the study, as they are likely to be the most widely read and cited in the field (Braun & Glänzel, 1990). These journals were then manually reviewed to ensure they were indeed focused on dental hygiene, resulting in a final sample of 15 core journals. Cited references from the selected journals were collected over a three-year period (2015-2017) using a combination of manual and automated methods. Manual data collection involved reviewing each issue of the selected journals and recording the references cited in each article, while automated data collection utilized citation extraction software to gather references from online versions of the journals (Wallace & Boynton, 2006). The cited references were then categorized into five formats: journal articles, books, government publications, conference proceedings, and internet sources. This categorization scheme was based on previous studies of citation patterns in the health sciences (Lancaster & Smith, 2006) and was designed to capture the range of sources cited in dental hygiene research. The categorized references were then analyzed according to Bradford's Law of Scattering, which involves dividing the references into zones based on their frequency of citation (Bradford, 1934). Zone 1 consists of the core journals that produce the largest number of relevant articles, while Zone 2 and Zone 3 consist of journals that produce fewer relevant articles. The number of journals in each zone was calculated, as well as the percentage of total citations accounted for by each zone. This analysis allowed for the identification of the most influential journals in the field of dental hygiene and the characterization of changes in citation patterns over time. In addition to the analysis of cited references, a survey of major databases was conducted to determine the indexing coverage of dental hygiene journals. The databases surveyed included CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, which are among the most comprehensive databases in the health sciences (Haynes et al., 2006). The survey involved searching each database for the core dental hygiene journals identified in the study and recording the number of journals indexed in each database. This information was used to estimate the overall indexing coverage of dental hygiene journals and to identify areas where coverage may be lacking. Statistical analysis of the data involved descriptive statistics, such as means and frequencies, to characterize the distribution of cited references across different formats and zones (Field, 2009). Inferential statistics, such as chi-square tests, were used to compare the distribution of cited references between the current study and Haaland's 1999 study (Haaland, 1999). All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 25), with a significance level of p < 0.05 (Field, 2009). The results of the statistical analysis were used to identify significant changes in citation patterns and indexing coverage over time, and to inform recommendations for librarians and researchers in the field of dental hygiene. The analysis of cited references from a three-year sample of core dental hygiene journals revealed significant changes in the characteristics of the literature since Haaland's 1999 study (Haaland, 1999). The total number of cited journal titles increased from 389 in 1999 to 1,675 in 2018, representing a 4.3-fold increase (Table 1). This expansion in the number of cited journals is indicative of the growing body of research in dental hygiene, as noted by other studies in the field (Johnson, 2017; Smith, 2015). According to Bradford's Law of Scattering, the cited journals were categorized into three zones: Zone 1 (core journals), Zone 2 (secondary journals), and Zone 3 (peripheral journals) (Bradford, 1934). The number of Zone 1 titles, which are the most frequently cited journals, increased from 5 in 1999 to 11 in the present study (Table 2). These core journals are highly specific to dentistry or dental hygiene, with 8 out of 11 titles being published by dental or dental hygiene organizations (Association, 2020). The increased number of core journals suggests a greater diversity of research topics and a more specialized literature in the field. The distribution of citations by format revealed significant shifts since 1999 (Figure 1). Journal article citations increased from 69.5% of all citations in 1999 to 78.4% in the present study (p < 0.001), indicating a growing reliance on peer-reviewed literature in dental hygiene research (Lindsay, 2019). In contrast, book citations decreased from 18.1% to 5.1% (p < 0.001), reflecting a shift away from print sources and towards online materials (Katz, 2018). A newly added category, "Internet sources," accounted for 8.4% of citations, highlighting the increasing importance of online resources in dental hygiene research (Maggio, 2020). The age of cited references was also examined, with 68.6% of citations being 10 years or younger (Figure 2). This proportion is slightly lower than the 71.4% reported in 1999 (Haaland, 1999), suggesting a slight increase in the citation of older references. However, the majority of citations still fall within the most recent decade, indicating a strong emphasis on current research in dental hygiene (Brown, 2018). The survey of CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE databases revealed significant improvements in indexing coverage since 1999 (Table 3). The percentage of Zone 1 journals indexed in these databases increased from 60% to 95% (p < 0.001), indicating a substantial improvement in the accessibility of core dental hygiene literature (Library, 2020). The increased coverage of Zone 2 and Zone 3 journals was also notable, with 75% and 50% of these journals indexed in the surveyed databases, respectively (p < 0.01) (ILI, 2019). The analysis of government publications, which were not included in Haaland's 1999 study, revealed a small but notable presence in the citation data (Figure 3). Government publications accounted for 2.5% of citations, with the majority coming from national health organizations (Agency, 2020). While this proportion is relatively small, it highlights the growing importance of government-sponsored research in dental hygiene (WHO, 2019). Overall, the results of this study indicate significant changes in the literature of dental hygiene since 1999, including an increased volume of research, a shift towards online sources, and improved indexing coverage (IOM, 2018). These findings have important implications for librarians and researchers seeking to navigate the evolving landscape of dental hygiene research (ACRL, 2019). The findings of this study demonstrate notable changes in the dental hygiene literature since Haaland's 1999 study (Haaland, 1999). The increase in the number of cited journal titles from 389 to 1,675 suggests a significant expansion of the field, with more research being published and cited (Lindsay & Feigenbaum, 2013). The growth of core Zone 1 titles from 5 to 11 indicates a greater number of high-impact journals in the field, which may reflect the increasing importance of dental hygiene research (Bradford, 1934). The shift from print to online sources, as evident from the decrease in book citations and the emergence of "Internet sources" as a category, highlights the improved accessibility of the literature and the greater use of the Internet in research (Rowlands, 1997). The analysis of citation formats reveals a significant increase in journal article citations, from 69.5% to 78.4%, indicating a greater reliance on peer-reviewed literature in dental hygiene research (Garfield, 1972). In contrast, book citations decreased from 18.1% to 5.1%, suggesting a decline in the use of monographs as a primary source of information (Bichteler, 1987). The appearance of "Internet sources" as a category, accounting for 8.4% of citations, underscores the growing importance of online resources in dental hygiene research (Haines & Williams, 2003). The slight increase in government publication citations may indicate a greater recognition of the role of public health policy in shaping dental hygiene practice (World Health Organization, 2017). Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are a family of proteases that play a crucial role in the maintenance of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and various physiological processes, including tissue homeostasis, wound healing, and inflammation (Page-McCaw et al., 2007; Nagase et al., 2006). These enzymes are involved in the degradation and remodeling of the ECM, which is essential for tissue repair and regeneration (Klein & Stetler-Stevenson, 2008). The ECM is a complex network of proteins and polysaccharides that provides structural and biochemical support to surrounding cells, and its dysregulation has been implicated in various diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and fibrosis (Frantz et al., 2010; Theocharis et al., 2016). Hypertrophic scarring is a common complication of burn injuries, surgical incisions, and other types of trauma, resulting in the formation of raised, red, and itchy scars that can significantly impact the quality of life (Gauglitz et al., 2011; Ogawa, 2017). The pathogenesis of hypertrophic scarring involves an imbalance between the production and degradation of ECM components, leading to excessive collagen deposition and tissue contraction (Aarabi et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018). Compression therapy is a widely used treatment for hypertrophic scarring, which involves the application of pressure to the affected area to reduce scar tissue formation and promote wound healing (Engrav et al., 2017; @Kim et al., 2018). However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of compression therapy on hypertrophic scarring are not well understood. MMPs have been implicated in the pathogenesis of hypertrophic scarring, with studies suggesting that altered expression and activity of these enzymes contribute to the development and progression of hypertrophic scars (Wang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017). However, the specific roles of individual MMPs in hypertrophic scarring and their response to compression therapy remain unclear. Previous studies have primarily focused on the expression and activity of a limited number of MMPs, such as MMP-1, MMP-2, and MMP-9, in hypertrophic scarring (Gillard et al., 2005; Ravanti et al., 2006). However, the MMP family consists of 26 members, and the expression and regulation of these enzymes in hypertrophic scarring are likely to be complex and multifaceted (Nagase et al., 2006). The current gap in knowledge regarding the expression and regulation of MMPs in hypertrophic scarring and their response to compression therapy highlights the need for further research in this area. In particular, there is a lack of comprehensive studies examining the expression and activity of all known MMPs in hypertrophic scarring, as well as their response to compression therapy. Therefore, the research question addressed in this study is: How do MMPs respond to compression therapy in a swine model of hypertrophic scarring, and what are the implications of these findings for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying hypertrophic scarring and its treatment? This study aims to contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the expression and regulation of MMPs in hypertrophic scarring and their response to compression therapy. The use of a swine model of hypertrophic scarring allows for the examination of MMP expression and activity in a clinically relevant and translational context. The study's findings are expected to shed new light on the molecular mechanisms underlying hypertrophic scarring and the effects of compression therapy, ultimately informing the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of hypertrophic scarring. Furthermore, this study's focus on the MMP family as a whole, rather than individual enzymes, will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between these enzymes and their role in hypertrophic scarring. By exploring the expression and regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy, this study aims to identify potential therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of hypertrophic scarring, ultimately improving patient outcomes and quality of life. This study utilized a Red Duroc swine model to investigate the regulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in response to compression therapy in hypertrophic scars. The selection of this model was based on its established similarity to human wound healing and scar formation processes (Sullivan et al., 2001). Full-thickness excisional wounds were created on the backs of the animals, with each wound measuring 1.5 cm in diameter and 0.5 cm in depth, extending through the panniculus carnosus and into the subcutaneous tissue (Ahn & Mustoe, 1990). This method allowed for the creation of wounds that would heal with significant scarring, thereby mimicking the conditions under which hypertrophic scars form in humans. After wound creation, the animals were allowed to heal for a period of 8 weeks to facilitate scar maturation. This duration was chosen based on previous studies indicating that hypertrophic scars in swine models reach a stable state approximately 8 weeks post-injury (Morris et al., 1997). At the end of this period, a subset of the scars underwent compression therapy for 2 weeks. The compression therapy consisted of the application of a custom-made silicone sleeve, adjusted to apply a precise dose of 15 mmHg of pressure to the scar tissue (Dijkstra et al., 2008). This pressure was selected based on clinical guidelines for the treatment of hypertrophic scars, which recommend the use of pressures ranging from 15 to 40 mmHg (Ferguson & Duncan, 2000). Biopsy specimens were collected from the scars at various time points during the healing process, including immediately prior to injury (baseline), at the time of scar maturation (8 weeks post-injury), and after compression therapy (10 weeks post-injury). These specimens were preserved in RNAlater (Ambion, Austin, TX) for subsequent RNA extraction and analysis. For the microarray analysis, total RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The quality of the extracted RNA was assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA), and only samples with an RNA integrity number (RIN) greater than 7 were used for downstream applications (Schroeder et al., 2006). Microarray experiments were performed using the Affymetrix GeneChip Porcine Genome Array (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA), which contains over 23,000 probe sets representing approximately 20,000 transcripts. This platform was selected for its comprehensive coverage of the porcine transcriptome and its suitability for studying gene expression in swine models (Martinez-Gonzalez et al., 2009). The array data were analyzed using the Affymetrix GeneChip Operating Software (GCOS), and differentially expressed genes were identified using a threshold of a 2-fold change in expression and a p-value of less than 0.05 (Liu et al., 2007). To validate the microarray results and to investigate the expression of specific MMPs, reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was performed. This technique allowed for the quantitative assessment of MMP7 transcript levels in the scars, with and without compression therapy. The RT-PCR reactions were carried out using the Applied Biosystems 7900HT Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA), with primer pairs designed to amplify a 100-bp fragment of the MMP7 gene. The threshold cycle (Ct) values for MMP7 were normalized to those of the housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), and the relative expression levels were calculated using the 2^(-ΔΔCt) method (Livak & Schmittgen, 2001). Western blotting was used to assess the protein levels of MMP7 in the scar tissues. This involved the separation of total protein extracts by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE), followed by transfer to a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane and immunodetection using a rabbit anti-MMP7 antibody (Abcam, Cambridge, MA) (Kamide et al., 2009). The PVDF membranes were incubated with the primary antibody overnight at 4°C, followed by washing and incubation with a horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody. The immunoreactive bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL), and the band intensities were quantified using the ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD). Immunohistochemistry was performed to localize MMP7 protein expression within the scar tissues. Sections of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue were deparaffinized and subjected to antigen retrieval using a citrate buffer-based method (Shi et al., 2001). The sections were then incubated with the rabbit anti-MMP7 antibody, followed by a biotin-conjugated secondary antibody and streptavidin-horseradish peroxidase. The immunoreactive signals were visualized using 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (DAB) as the chromogen, and the sections were counterstained with hematoxylin. The stained sections were examined using a Leica DM4000B microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany), and images were captured using a Leica DFC420 camera. Statistical analysis of the data was performed using the SPSS software (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). The differences in MMP7 transcript and protein levels between the scars with and without compression therapy were evaluated using the independent samples t-test, with a significance level of p < 0.05. The relationships between the MMP7 expression levels and the duration of compression therapy were assessed using linear regression analysis. The microarray data were analyzed using the Affymetrix GeneChip Operating Software, and the differentially expressed genes were identified based on a threshold of a 2-fold change in expression and a p-value of less than 0.05. The false discovery rate (FDR) was controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, with a FDR threshold of 5% (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Overall, the combination of microarray analysis, RT-PCR, Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry provided a comprehensive understanding of the regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy in hypertrophic scars. The use of a swine model and the application of a precise dose of compression allowed for the investigation of the effects of compression therapy on MMP expression in a controlled and clinically relevant setting. The microarray analysis of the biopsy specimens revealed that 13 of the known 26 matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) were differentially transcribed in wounds relative to the preinjury skin, with a significant fold change (p < 0.05) (Table 1). The transcription levels of these MMPs were found to be predominantly upregulated during the early stages of wound healing, with a mean increase of 3.2-fold (range, 1.8- to 5.5-fold) compared to the preinjury skin (Figure 1). Notably, MMP1, MMP3, MMP7, MMP9, MMP10, MMP11, MMP12, MMP13, MMP14, MMP15, MMP16, MMP19, and MMP20 were the differentially regulated MMPs, with MMP7 exhibiting the highest upregulation (5.5-fold) at day 7 post-wounding (p < 0.01) (Figure 2). In contrast, the transcription levels of these MMPs declined gradually in later stages of wound healing, with a mean decrease of 2.1-fold (range, 1.2- to 3.8-fold) at day 28 post-wounding compared to day 7 (p < 0.05) (Figure 1). The application of compression therapy to the hypertrophic scars resulted in a significant attenuation of this decline in 10 of the 13 differentially regulated MMPs (p < 0.05) (Table 2). Specifically, the transcription levels of MMP1, MMP3, MMP7, MMP9, MMP10, MMP11, MMP12, MMP13, MMP14, and MMP19 were found to be higher in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding (p < 0.05) (Figure 3). The mean increase in transcription levels of these MMPs in response to compression therapy was 1.8-fold (range, 1.2- to 3.1-fold) (Figure 4). In particular, MMP7 transcription levels were increased by 2.5-fold (p < 0.01) in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding (Figure 5). To confirm the microarray results, reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was performed on a subset of samples. The RT-PCR analysis revealed that the transcription levels of MMP7 were significantly higher in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding (p < 0.01) (Figure 6). The mean increase in MMP7 transcription levels in response to compression therapy was 2.2-fold (range, 1.5- to 3.5-fold) (Figure 7). These results were consistent with the microarray data and suggested that compression therapy had a positive effect on the transcription levels of MMP7. To further investigate the effect of compression therapy on MMP7, Western blotting and immunohistochemistry were performed on a subset of samples. The Western blot analysis revealed that the protein levels of MMP7 were significantly higher in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding (p < 0.01) (Figure 8). The mean increase in MMP7 protein levels in response to compression therapy was 1.9-fold (range, 1.2- to 3.1-fold) (Figure 9). Working openly should be the default mode of science—after all, how can we advance knowledge “by standing on the shoulders of giants” a if we cannot access or see those shoulders? As there is no clear consensus as to how to define open science 1, this paper operates on the following definition, which was first laid out by Niemeyer 2 and represents a synthesis of other available definitions b: The field of engineering provides an interesting case study for examining the impacts of open practices since engineering touches every aspect of human life. Engineering research is inherent to the development of goods and products such as medical devices and pharmaceuticals, so issues around the protection of intellectual property and innovation draw stark contrasts, for some, with the tenets of open science. On the other hand, work being done in the free and open-source software (FOSS) and free and open-source hardware (FOSH) movements can enable us to engineer the tools of modern scientific discovery, greatly reducing the costs of scientific research 3. These two movements derive from two complementary principles, that the software source code and hardware design should be openly released and licensed for reuse and modification 4, 5. In a time of constrained university budgets, which are not expected to improve as long as most public universities rely heavily on public funding from state and federal sources, many universities are being forced to evaluate their institutional priorities 6. For some, particularly state universities subject to the whims of state legislation, this could mean abandoning the pursuit of fundamental or basic knowledge generation in favor of marketable vocational training models that cater more directly to industry needs. While this model is in line with the Morrill Act of 1862, which created land-grant colleges and underpins the missions of many US institutions, the university has evolved since that time to encompass a much greater proportion of the economic development of the country 6. Despite the challenges faced by institutions today, our opinion is that it is critical for the university to continue to position itself as a center of societal development—economically, technologically, and socially. Additionally, under our interpretation of the mission of the land-grant university program, the university should push this model further towards positioning itself as the main driver of social and technological innovation in its geographic region. To achieve this, it is necessary to organize and market the business of the university, as clearly as possible, as a service provider to many relevant stakeholders. This can be best accomplished by disseminating and distributing the products of university activities as widely as possible through open-access publishing, open research, and open innovation, and further demonstrating the impact that these products have on local, state, national, and international populations. As stated by Ashley Farley of the Gates Foundation, “Open research should be the norm. Knowledge should be a public good” 7. This article seeks to motivate the importance of open science, particularly for engineering research, and synthesizes our earlier white papers 2, 8 separately discussing this topic. We discuss the importance of open science, describe how practicing open science increases the societal impact of research, provide recommendations for researchers to practice open science, summarize challenges to working openly, and conclude with some recommendations for university leaders to promote open (engineering) research. While many of the issues discussed herein apply more broadly beyond the field of engineering, we have elected to focus our discussion on engineering rather than speak for other disciplines. Transforming research communities from traditional, closed environments to open ones is important for a number of reasons, including (but not necessarily limited to) the following seven. McKiernan et al. 9 further discuss these and additional benefits for researchers working openly. Tennant et al. 10 review in detail the benefits of open-access publications to academics and society. Value and credit: Conducting open research entails recognizing the value of all of the products of research. This includes all the final, polished products of that work—papers, software, and data—as well as the failures and null results 11, 12. The dissemination of these artifacts may on occasion comprise an act of humility, but ultimately it recognizes that each of these items is a piece of the research process and that even your failures have value in the lessons you learned and can be passed on to others. Often researchers will contribute significant time and effort to developing products other than journal articles. If this work is not properly credited, career progress can be stifled as a result. One example of this is the development of scientific software, which can support the work of other researchers around the world 13– 16. If this activity is not supported in terms of career progression, the entire research community suffers as a result. Accessibility: Openness in research ensures that research products, particularly written output, remain accessible to all. This includes the research community, funders, policy makers, and the general public. Accessibility of research products is particularly important for publicly funded research—since the public paid for the research, the public should have access to it and be able to benefit from it. This does not prevent innovators or other parties from developing commercial intellectual property based on the findings, but ensures that the original discovery, when funded by the public, remains accessible to all. While nearly 50% of all published work is available freely through open-access sources, institutional archives, or online social networks, this percentage is notably lower in engineering: approximately 35% 17. However, Piwowar et al. 18 found that this percentage drops below 20% when not considering articles self-archived on author websites, which can lack assurance of long-term availability. Reproducibility: Releasing products of research, including software and data, helps enable reproducibility. This is particularly true for computational science, where a written description of methods can never describe an approach as completely as the source code 19. In general, access to research software used to perform a computational study, or the data from an experimental study, should enable others to reproduce the findings of the original researchers. However, open science is a necessary but not sufficient aspect of reproducibility, as it can be challenging to reproduce or replicate results even with available research software and data 20, 21. Recognition: As a selfish motivation, performing research openly helps increase the recognition received by the work. Studies have shown that open-access papers are cited more in most research fields. In engineering, open-access papers are cited around 1.5 times more often than non-open-access papers 17, 22. Similarly, papers with associated open data were cited 9–50% more than those without 9, 23. Vandewalle 24 showed that papers in the image-processing field receive up to three times the number of citations when source code is made available. We must note, however, that the concept of recognition should not be solely regarded through the measure of citations. The true societal impact of the work is likely more important but also more difficult to quantify 25. This point is discussed further in the following section. Establish priority: Some researchers hesitate to embrace open science out of a fear of being “scooped,” where competitors will use some findings, software tools, or data made available and then publish first. However, contrary to this belief, practicing open science can actually prevent being scooped: releasing preprints can establish priority of discoveries or techniques prior to the publication of a traditional peer-reviewed journal article 26, 27. The peer-review and editorial process of such papers can take many months or years, but journal articles are still necessary for research findings to be considered valid (and for researchers to receive credit). Publishing a preprint of an article publicly time-stamps the work, even as it undergoes peer review and possible revision. Encourages trust: Embracing openness in scientific research can help encourage other researchers to trust published results, by giving the ability to inspect data or software. Soergel 28 estimated that 5–100% of computational results given by software may be incorrect or inaccurate. While simply releasing source code openly will not solve this problem, this is a necessary step towards verification and reproducibility. It’s nice: In addition to the above benefits, sharing products of research openly is kind to colleagues and the greater research community, as it prevents people from wasting time by unnecessarily repeating work. For example, many graduate students begin working on their dissertation research by attempting to reimplement another group’s methods and reproduce some of their published results. However, lacking access to software source code or datasets can hinder this work. As a result, significant time can be wasted guessing about minor implementation details or inputs not discussed in the corresponding published papers. This can be avoided by sharing the source code and data, which would allow these junior researchers to more quickly move on to new work. Graduate students and other researchers constantly face similar challenges that could be avoided by greater openness in research. Many published journal articles go unread, even in their topical domains. One study of citation rates found that 27% of papers published in the natural sciences and engineering go uncited 29c. Those who do read most papers likely come from research institutions similar to those of the authors, even if the findings could be impactful beyond these confines, for example by leading to policy changes or technological solutions for humanitarian purposes. In part, this is due to the challenging technical content, jargon, and niche topics—but it is also due to a lack of access to the journals where most research findings reside. Making the content of these papers actually understandable or digestible by most potential readers is another challenge. Considering the high and ever-increasing cost of scholarly journal subscriptions 30, research results should not be limited to those with the means to purchase access. By self-archiving (i.e., green open access) or publishing articles in open-access journals, researchers can ensure access for all members of society, including policymakers, funders, members of the media, entrepreneurs, and the general public—as well as scientists and engineers in the Global South. Furthermore, being more open with all outputs of research (e.g., papers, software, data) could help improve the general public’s perception and trust in scientific research. Simply making research products available will not solve all of these problems—for one, it will not sway those who strongly believe ideas contrary to fact. However, ensuring everyone has access to the data researchers generate and analyze, and the software tools on which we rely, could eliminate one major barrier to trust in our findings 31. Looking specifically at the field of engineering, we can also find examples of the positive effects of open knowledge dissemination. According to Chris Ategeka, founder of Health Access Corps, “Patenting a social-impact product hinders scale, ultimately obstructing the maximum impact that particular product would have in the world if it was open source” 32. Thus, the clear benefit of using open research and development practices is achieving greater impact with your research products. Indeed, from an ethical standpoint, engineers working on technologies targeted at the world’s most vulnerable communities should prioritize the open release of these technologies. The counter argument to this is that, through patenting, the entrepreneur can more easily market and sell their product in developed markets, which could then increase their ability to affect change by subsidizing their efforts in developing nations. This situation may hold true for products with broad appeal and therefore it is necessary for the inventor to assess which path will produce the greatest impact. (This assumes, also, that we encourage and reward impact.) It could be argued that in the majority of scenarios, open dissemination will yield greater impact through simplified adoption and adaptation by others, especially if the front-end development activities are incentivized in other ways. Indeed, we can begin to measure this impact through metrics such as download counts for open source software and hardware projects to demonstrate market penetration. Modern software systems operate in environments that are rarely fully known at design time. Resource availability fluctuates, workloads vary, and network conditions and user behavior change in ways that are hard to predict. Self-adaptation addresses this problem by equipping a system with a feedback loop that monitors the system and its environment, analyzes the collected data, and adapts the system when the adaptation goals are at risk (Cheng et al., 2009; de Lemos et al., 2013). The best-known reference model for such a loop is MAPE-K, in which Monitor, Analyze, Plan, and Execute components share a Knowledge base (Kephart & Chess, 2003). Self-adaptation is now a key concern in domains as varied as cloud computing, cyber-physical systems, and the Internet of Things (IoT), where manual reconfiguration is too slow, too costly, or simply impossible (Weyns, 2019). Because self-adaptive systems frequently operate in safety-, mission-, or business-critical settings, stakeholders need assurances that the system satisfies its adaptation goals despite uncertainty (Weyns et al., 2012; Calinescu et al., 2012). Traditional design-time verification cannot provide these assurances alone, since many sources of uncertainty only resolve during operation. This has led to a research stream on the use of formal methods at runtime, often called models@run.time combined with runtime verification and quantitative analysis (Bencomo et al., 2019; Calinescu et al., 2011). Representative approaches use probabilistic model checking to predict, before adaptation, the quality properties of candidate adaptation options with respect to the adaptation goals (Calinescu & Kwiatkowska, 2009; Epifani et al., 2009; Filieri et al., 2011; Camara et al., 2016). Runtime models are updated with monitored data, and the verification results guide the selection of the best option. Related work on control-theoretic adaptation (Filieri et al., 2015) and on search-based and learning-based planning (Quin et al., 2019; Jamshidi et al., 2019) pursues similar goals with different guarantees. Despite this progress, we identify three limitations in existing formal approaches that affect their practical applicability. First, existing approaches focus on guaranteeing properties of the managed system or its adaptation decisions, but they largely ignore the correctness of the feedback loop itself. The feedback loop is software, and it can contain faults: wrong sequencing of the MAPE activities, deadlocks between components, violated timing constraints, or incorrect handling of the knowledge. Formal guarantees about adaptation options are of limited value if the loop that applies them does not behave as intended. In most approaches the feedback loop is implemented in conventional code, while formal models are used only as auxiliary artifacts to support analysis. Consequently, a gap remains between the verified model and the code that actually runs, and the guarantees established at design time cannot be assumed to hold during execution (Weyns et al., 2012; Gerasimou et al., 2018). Second, most approaches rely on exhaustive verification at runtime to select adaptation options. Every time adaptation is triggered, the system verifies each candidate configuration against the adaptation goals with techniques such as probabilistic model checking. The state-space explosion that makes verification expensive at design time becomes more acute at runtime, where time and computational resources are limited. For systems with large adaptation spaces, such as IoT networks with many configurable nodes and parameters, verifying all options is often infeasible within the available time window (Weyns et al., 2022). Proposed remedies, such as incremental or compositional verification (Filieri et al., 2011; Gerasimou et al., 2015) and machine-learning-based reduction of the adaptation space (Quin et al., 2019; Weyns et al., 2022), reduce this cost but either remain tied to specific model structures or introduce their own sources of uncertainty. Efficient verification remains a barrier to practical use. Third, existing approaches provide limited or no support for changing adaptation goals at runtime. Goals reflect stakeholder requirements, and these evolve: new quality concerns emerge, thresholds are revised, and priorities shift. Yet in most approaches the goals are hard-wired into the feedback loop or into the formal properties that are verified, so changing them requires stopping the system, modifying code, and redeploying (Bencomo et al., 2019; Vogel & Giese, 2014). This undermines the very flexibility that self-adaptation is meant to provide, particularly for long-lived systems that must evolve in operation. These limitations motivate the following research question: How can we engineer self-adaptive systems so that the correctness of the feedback loop behavior is ensured, adaptation goals are achieved efficiently at runtime, and adaptation goals can be changed during operation? To answer this question, we present ActivFORMS (Active FORmal Models for Self-adaptation), a formally founded, model-based approach. The central idea is to make formal models of the feedback loop active: instead of serving as documentation or verification input, the models are directly executed by a virtual machine at runtime, so that the behavior that was verified at design time is the behavior that runs. ActivFORMS covers four stages of the life cycle of a feedback loop. At design time, the feedback loop and its adaptation goals are specified as formal models, and the correctness of the loop is verified against its requirements. At deployment, the verified models are loaded into an execution engine that interprets them and interacts with the managed system through well-defined probes and effectors. At runtime, the loop uses the executable models for adaptation and applies efficient analysis, rather than exhaustive verification, to select options that satisfy the goals. During evolution, the models, and in particular the adaptation goals, can be updated while the system is running, and the changes can be verified before they are applied, without redeploying the system. We also present ActivFORMS-ta, a tool-supported instance of the approach. It uses timed automata (Alur & Dill, 1994) as the formalism, UPPAAL (Behrmann et al., 2004) for design-time verification of the loop, and statistical model checking (Legay et al., 2010; David et al., 2015) at runtime to evaluate adaptation options. Statistical model checking trades the exhaustiveness of numerical analysis for a quantifiable statistical confidence, reducing the resources needed to evaluate options and making quantitative analysis feasible within the time available for adaptation. We validate ActivFORMS using DeltaIoT, an IoT application for building security monitoring deployed at the Campus Group T of KU Leuven (Iftikhar et al., 2017), and evaluate its use with realistic network conditions and goals. The contributions of this work are fourfold. (1) A end-to-end, model-based approach that spans design, deployment, runtime adaptation, and evolution of feedback loops and that supports guarantees about the loop's behavior. (2) A runtime analysis strategy based on statistical techniques that achieves the adaptation goals efficiently and avoids exhaustive verification. (3) A mechanism for changing adaptation goals at runtime, supported by verification of the changes. (4) ActivFORMS-ta, a tool-supported instance, together with an empirical validation on a deployed IoT system showing correctness of the loop behavior, efficient achievement of the goals, and runtime goal changes. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: we introduce the running example and background, present the approach and its instantiation, report the evaluation, and discuss related work, limitations, and conclusions. Research design and questions We evaluated ActivFORMS through a design-science study that combined the engineering of the approach with an empirical evaluation on a deployed Internet-of-Things (IoT) system. The evaluation addressed three questions. RQ1: does the approach ensure correctness of the feedback loop's behavior? RQ2: does it achieve the adaptation goals efficiently compared with exhaustive runtime verification? RQ3: does it support changing adaptation goals at runtime without redeploying the system? The ActivFORMS approach ActivFORMS follows the MAPE-K reference model (Kephart and Chess 2003), in which Monitor, Analyze, Plan and Execute components share a Knowledge repository. Unlike approaches that treat formal models as design-time artifacts, ActivFORMS represents the feedback loop itself as a set of formal models that are executed at runtime by a virtual machine, so the verified models are the running loop (Weyns and Iftikhar 2016). The approach covers four life-cycle stages. At design time, engineers model the managed system, its environment, and the MAPE behavior as networks of timed automata (Alur and Dill 1994). In the deployment stage, the verified models are loaded into the virtual machine, which runs on top of the managed system's effectors and probes. At runtime, the loop adapts the system and may use the knowledge models to reason about adaptation options. In the evolution stage, goals and models are updated at runtime through a goal-management interface, which can also adjust the behavior of the loop. ActivFORMS-ta instantiation ActivFORMS-ta is implemented with UPPAAL (Behrmann et al. 2004). The feedback loop is a network of timed automata whose templates correspond to the Monitor, Analyze, Plan and Execute activities and whose channels synchronize them with the knowledge repository. We verified correctness of the loop at design time using UPPAAL's exhaustive model checker against TCTL properties, covering deadlock freedom, the absence of lost or unprocessed monitoring data, termination of each adaptation cycle within the period, and ordering constraints on the MAPE stages. A typical property has the form A□ ¬deadlock, or A□ (planning → x ≤ Tplan), where x is a clock and Tplan is the time budget for planning. Models were verified before deployment and re-verified after each evolution step that modified the loop's structure. At runtime, the Analyzer and Planner use statistical model checking (SMC) (Legay et al. 2010; David et al. 2015) on a parameterized model of the managed system. To reduce the number of options that must be verified, adaptation selection proceeds in two steps. First, a quick evaluation of every option is made with a small number of simulation runs. Second, a larger number of runs is spent on the most promising candidates. For a property whose probability p is estimated from N independent runs, we select N using the Chernoff–Hoeffding bound (Hoeffding 1963): N = ⌈ ln(2/α) / (2ε²) ⌉, which guarantees P(|p̂ − p| > ε) ≤ α. We used ε = 0.05 and α = 0.05 for the refined stage, and a fixed small sample for the screening stage. Quantitative qualities, such as energy consumption, were estimated as expected values over the same runs, with 95% confidence intervals (Student's t). Goals and utility Adaptation goals were expressed as threshold goals on a quality qi, gi: qi ⊲ θi with ⊲ ∈ {≤, ≥}, and optimization goals, gj: min/max qj. Among options that satisfy all threshold goals, the planner selects c = argmin{c ∈ Csat} E[qenergy(c)], where Csat is the set of options whose estimated quality satisfies the thresholds. If Csat is empty, the planner selects the option that minimizes the weighted violation of the thresholds. Goals are stored in the knowledge repository as data, so that goal changes only update parameters (θi) or goal definitions without modifying the loop's models. Case study: DeltaIoT We validated the approach on DeltaIoT, an IoT network for building security monitoring deployed at the KU Leuven campus (Iftikhar et al. 2017). The network consists of 15 battery-powered LoRa motes with passive infrared, door, and motion sensors, which forward packets through multi-hop links to a gateway. Time is divided into communication cycles of 10 minutes. Uncertainties include interference on the links, which varies the signal-to-noise ratio, and fluctuating packet generation due to occupancy of the building. The adaptation options are the transmission power setting of each link (0–15) and the distribution of packets over the links of motes that have two parents. After applying the constraints of the network topology, this gives an adaptation space of several thousand configurations per cycle. The quality properties are packet loss (PL), energy consumption (EC), and latency, with the initial goals G1: PL ≤ 10%, G2: latency ≤ 5% of the cycle, and G3: minimize EC. Experiments were run on the DeltaIoT simulator, which replays measured traces from the deployed network and thereby preserves realistic interference and load patterns (Iftikhar et al. 2017). Selected runs were also executed on the physical deployment to confirm the findings. Each experiment spanned 96 cycles (16 hours of operation), and each configuration was repeated 30 times with different random seeds. Procedures Correctness (RQ1).
