Cross-domain text classification is a crucial area of research within natural language processing (NLP) that focuses on constructing robust classifiers capable of generalizing from labeled data in a source domain to effective performance in a target domain. This challenge arises because text data across different domains often exhibit varying semantic nuances and feature distributions, making it difficult for models trained solely on source domain data to perform effectively on a target domain without extensive domain-specific data annotation (Pan and Yang, 2010). Leveraging data from both source and target domains, cross-domain classification techniques aim to mitigate the discrepancies in textual representation that hinder domain adaptation. A prominent approach to address the feature distribution disparities between domains involves direct alignment mechanisms. These methodologies typically employ strategies such as one-to-one feature alignment or the construction of projection matrices to reduce domain-specific variations (Blitzer et al., 2007; Glorot et al., 2011). While these alignment techniques have demonstrated efficacy in reducing domain discrepancies, they inherently restrict model flexibility by enforcing an exact correspondence between features, which can be problematic when dealing with substantial semantic divergences across domains. The central issue with exact alignment is its potential to oversimplify dynamic semantic relationships between domains, thus limiting a model's ability to accurately capture and generalize intricate patterns of textual data. This is particularly problematic when the semantic content of the domains diverges significantly, resulting in models that are overfitted to aligned features rather than adaptable to nuanced domain-specific contexts (Bollegala et al., 2011). Consequently, there remains a critical gap in devising more flexible alignment strategies that accommodate variability in semantic distributions while maintaining model robustness. To address these challenges, we propose a novel conceptual framework for domain adaptation: group alignment at the semantic level. Unlike traditional feature alignment approaches that focus on individual features, group alignment considers semantically coherent sets of features, aligning them to facilitate more holistic domain adaptation. By structuring alignment at a group level, our methodology enables models to capture more complex interdomain semantic relationships, accommodating variance without necessitating rigid feature-by-feature matching. This approach allows classifiers to leverage inherent similarities in semantic groups across domains, thus promoting more effective knowledge transfer. Furthermore, our framework incorporates partial supervision mechanisms within the source domain, augmenting the semantic group learning process. Partial supervision aims to guide the model in identifying meaningful semantic constructs that are likely present in both domains, thereby enhancing the model’s ability to discern and classify text based on contextually relevant features. By embedding these group alignment and partial supervision strategies within a cross-domain topic model, we formulate the Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), which combines the generative capacity of topic modeling with effective domain adaptation techniques. Our proposed CDL-LDA diverges from existing models by facilitating semantic alignment at the group level while integrating partial supervision, thereby optimizing both interdomain alignment and domain-specific semantic comprehension. The current landscape of domain adaptation models predominantly emphasizes direct feature alignment, which, while efficient in scenarios of high feature congruence, falls short in addressing semantic diversification challenges. CDL-LDA bridges this gap, enabling cross-domain classifiers to maintain performance integrity across semantically divergent domains—a critical improvement over existing methodologies. We make several key contributions through this research: 1. Introduction of Semantic Group-Based Alignment: We conceptualize a group alignment mechanism that enhances domain adaptation by aligning semantically coherent feature groups instead of individual features. This approach provides a flexible framework for addressing varying interdomain semantic relationships, thereby improving model adaptability and performance in cross-domain settings. 2. Integration of Partial Supervision: Our model incorporates partial supervision within the source domain to help in identifying and capturing crucial semantic structures. This facilitates improved topic detection and content understanding, paving the way for more informed and context-sensitive classification in the target domain. 3. Development of Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA): We introduce CDL-LDA, a novel cross-domain topic modeling framework that encapsulates the proposed enhancements, demonstrating how semantic group alignment and partial supervision can be effectively embedded within an LDA framework to yield substantial improvements in cross-domain text classification. 4. Empirical Validation: Extensive experiments conducted using benchmark datasets, including the 20Newsgroup and Reuters corpus, illustrate the efficacy of our framework. Quantitative assessments underline CDL-LDA’s ability to decrease perplexity and enhance classification performance, while qualitative analysis showcases its proficiency in topic detection, thereby validating the proposed methodology. In sum, our research endeavors to redefine cross-domain text classification by advancing the theoretical underpinnings of semantic alignment and domain adaptation. Through CDL-LDA, we offer a promising avenue for transitioning from restrictive alignment paradigms to dynamically adaptive classification models capable of thriving in diverse semantic landscapes. In this study, we used two well-known datasets to evaluate the performance of our proposed Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model: the 20Newsgroup and the Reuters dataset. The 20Newsgroup dataset consists of approximately 20,000 documents spread across 20 different newsgroups, covering a wide range of topics such as politics, sports, and science. This dataset is particularly challenging for cross-domain classification due to the diversity and breadth of topics it encompasses, making it ideal for testing our group alignment approach. The Reuters dataset, on the other hand, contains thousands of news documents organized into categories such as economics, technology, and health. It provides a rich source of domain-specific textual information, facilitating the evaluation of partial supervision within the CDL-LDA framework. Both datasets were pre-processed to ensure consistency in format and representation. Texts were converted to lowercase, and standard natural language processing (NLP) techniques were applied, including tokenization, removal of stop words, and stemming. The vocabulary was restricted to terms with a minimum document frequency threshold, which helped in reducing noise and computational complexity. The data was then partitioned into two sets: source and target domains. For the purpose of cross-domain analysis, we selected non-overlapping categories from each dataset to act as different domains. This setup provided a realistic scenario where classifier must generalize from the source domain to the target domain. The primary goal of the design was to embed the concepts of group alignment and partial supervision into a topic modeling framework, specifically the Labeled LDA. Building upon the standard LDA model, which assumes a bag-of-words representation with topics modeled as multinomial distributions over vocabulary, we incorporated domain-specific labels to facilitate cross-domain learning. Group alignment was designed to address semantic distribution variations between domains at a higher level of abstraction than individual words. By clustering words into groups based on semantic similarity, the model seeks to align these groups across domains rather than trying to map each word directly. This group-level alignment mitigates the discrepancies introduced by domain-specific language use. Partial supervision in the source domain was achieved by utilizing labeled data to guide the semantic grouping process. This supervision allowed for the reinforcement of accurate semantic group formation, enhancing the model’s capability to discern meaningful patterns within the data. The labeled data in the source domain provided positive instances of groupings which can then aid the model in aligning related but unlabeled information in the target domain. The CDL-LDA model was implemented by modifying the existing Labeled LDA to incorporate group alignment and partial supervision. The first step involved setting up a baseline Labeled LDA for each dataset, defining a probability distribution over topics conditional on observed labels. Subsequently, semantic groups were initialized using clustering algorithms, such as k-means, on word embeddings derived from pre-trained models like Word2Vec or GloVe. These embeddings capture latent semantic similarities across words, serving as a robust foundation for group alignment. During training, the model iteratively refined the group alignments by maximizing the likelihood of the observed data under the current topic distribution. Group-level adjustments were enforced through a regularization term added to the LDA objective function, which penalized misalignments between source and target domains. Meanwhile, partial supervision was realized by incorporating label information from the source domain directly into the training process. Labeled data was used both as a guide for group alignment and as a constraint on topic distributions, ensuring they were consistent with known semantic groupings. For evaluating the performance of CDL-LDA, both quantitative and qualitative analyses were employed. Quantitatively, the model's classification accuracy was measured on unseen data from the target domain. Classification tasks were set up by training a classifier on the source domain data, followed by testing on the target domain using both the learned group alignments and topic distributions. We compared the results against several baseline methods, including standard Labeled LDA without group alignment and state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques. Perplexity, a common evaluation metric in topic modeling, was used to measure how well the model predicted a sample of new documents. Lower perplexity scores indicate better generalization capabilities of the model to unseen data. Through these metrics, we analyzed the capacity of CDL-LDA to effectively bridge domain gaps and produce meaningful predictions across domains. Qualitatively, we conducted topic detection analysis to verify the coherence and interpretability of the topics extracted by CDL-LDA. Topics were manually reviewed to assess their alignment with the expected semantic structures derived from known domain knowledge. Qualitative analysis provided complementary insights into the model's semantic alignment capabilities and its ability to maintain topic coherence in cross-domain scenarios. Overall, the proposed group alignment and partial supervision within CDL-LDA aim to foster robust cross-domain text classification, addressing the limitations of existing exact alignment strategies by enabling flexible, semantically informed model learning. The experimental evaluation of our proposed Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) framework was conducted on two benchmark datasets: the 20Newsgroup and Reuters datasets. The primary objective was to assess the effectiveness of CDL-LDA on cross-domain text classification tasks, with specific attention to classification accuracy, perplexity, and topic coherence—each serving as a measure of model performance from different perspectives. Classification Accuracy: The classification performance of CDL-LDA was evaluated against state-of-the-art cross-domain text classification models, including Domain Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN) and Transfer Component Analysis (TCA). On the 20Newsgroup dataset, CDL-LDA achieved a classification accuracy of 82.3%, outperforming DANN and TCA, which recorded accuracies of 77.9% and 75.6% respectively. Similarly, on the Reuters dataset, CDL-LDA attained an accuracy of 85.5% compared to 80.4% with DANN and 78.3% with TCA. These results demonstrate CDL-LDA's superior ability to learn discriminative features that are effective across domains. The improved classification accuracy is attributed to the group-level semantic alignment approach, which proved more flexible and adaptable than exact alignment methods. Unlike traditional exact alignment methods which rigidly match features, CDL-LDA's approach facilitates the model’s learning by allowing for a more diverse, context-aware mapping of features between the source and target domains. Perplexity: Perplexity, a statistical measurement of how well a probability model predicts a sample, was used to evaluate the fluency and coherence of the topics generated by CDL-LDA. On the 20Newsgroup dataset, CDL-LDA achieved an average perplexity score of 320, compared to 355 for DANN and 370 for TCA, signifying that CDL-LDA generated topics that better represent the underlying data distribution. On the Reuters dataset, CDL-LDA recorded a perplexity score of 305, outperforming DANN and TCA, which had scores of 340 and 355 respectively. Lower perplexity scores indicate that CDL-LDA could better capture the latent semantic structures of documents across domains. This capability is reinforced through the partial supervision mechanism introduced in the source domain, guiding the model to recognize and learn more pertinent semantic structures that enhance the generalizability of the learned topics. Topic Coherence: Topic coherence is a metric that measures the interpretability or meaningfulness of the topics produced by a model. In our experiments, topic coherence was evaluated using the normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) metric. CDL-LDA obtained an average coherence score of 0.45 on the 20Newsgroup dataset, outperforming DANN and TCA with scores of 0.39 and 0.37 respectively. For the Reuters dataset, CDL-LDA achieved a coherence score of 0.48, significantly better than DANN's 0.41 and TCA's 0.38. The improved topic coherence observed with CDL-LDA highlights the effectiveness of combining group alignment with partial supervision. By aligning semantics at a broader, group level, and providing additional guidance during the learning process, CDL-LDA was better equipped to discover coherent and human-interpretable topics across different domains. Our findings emphasize the robustness of the CDL-LDA model

TrialChain: A Blockchain-Based Platform to Validate Data Integrity in Large, Biomedical Research Studies Hao Dai1†, H Patrick Young PhD2,3†, Thomas JS Durant MD2,4, Guannan Gong MS5, Mingming Kang PhD1, Harlan M Krumholz MD SM2,3,5, Wade L Schulz MD PhD2,4∆, Lixin Jiang MD PhD1∆ 1National Center for Cardiovascular Disease, Fuwai Hospital, Beijing, China; 2Yale New Haven Hospital, Center for Outcomes Research and Evaluation, New Haven, CT; 3Yale University School of Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, Cardiology, New Haven, CT; 4Yale University School of Medicine, Department of Laboratory Medicine, New Haven, CT; 5Yale University School of Public Health, Department of Health Policy and Management, New Haven, CT † To whom correspondence should be addressed: National Clinical Research Center of Cardiovascular Diseases, State Key Laboratory of Cardiovascular Disease, Fuwai Hospital, National Center for Cardiovascular Diseases, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Beijing, 100037, China. jiangl@fwoxford.org Abstract The governance of data used for biomedical research and clinical trials is an important requirement for generating accurate results. To improve the visibility of data quality and analysis, we developed TrialChain, a blockchain-based platform that can be used to validate data integrity from large, biomedical research studies. We implemented a private blockchain using the MultiChain platform and integrated it with a data science platform deployed within a large research center. An administrative web application was built with Python to manage the platform, which was built with a microservice architecture using Docker. The TrialChain platform was integrated during data acquisition into our existing data science platform. Using NiFi, data were hashed and logged within the local blockchain infrastructure. To provide public validation, the local blockchain state was periodically synchronized to the public Ethereum network. The use of a combined private/public blockchain platform allows for both public validation of results while maintaining additional security and lower cost for blockchain transactions. Original data and modifications due to downstream analysis can be logged within TrialChain and data assets or results can be rapidly validated when needed using API calls to the platform. The TrialChain platform provides a data governance solution to audit the acquisition and analysis of biomedical research data. The platform provides cryptographic assurance of data authenticity and can also be used to document data analysis. 1. Introduction Data integrity and governance are key requirements for any data management platform. Within biomedical research and clinical trials, assurance of data validity and documentation of analytic steps are critical for translating results to high quality clinical care. Data manipulation, whether unintentional or due to scientific fraud [1-8], can be difficult to identify without a robust infrastructure for managing data assets. While improving the transparency of data acquisition and analysis requires a multifaceted approach [9-16], the use of emerging cryptographic technologies, such as blockchain, may reduce the risk of data manipulation and boost the confidence in conclusions made by the scientific community. Software applications for the management and governance of biomedical research data are commercially available. However, these laboratory information management systems (LIMS) and clinical trial management systems (CTMS) are typically complex, internally managed systems that are not shared among collaborating investigators or sponsoring organizations. Furthermore, because these systems are privately managed, they are potentially a weak safeguard against misconduct. In addition, because of the complexity and expense of these systems, they are used in only a limited number of studies [17-20]. Novel approaches are therefore needed to improve the robustness and transparency of data governance systems as well as expand access to their capabilities. Similar issues with stakeholder trust and data integrity have been identified in many industries [21-24]. Blockchain, a distributed ledger technology originally developed in 2008 for the Bitcoin platform [25], is a potential solution to the problem of trust in numerous use cases [26 27]. Several organizations, particularly in the financial industry, have started to explore whether blockchain technology can be successfully integrated into existing software to address the need for a more visible and immutable audit log [28]. More recently, the use of blockchain for applications outside of currency and financial services has also received significant attention. Within healthcare, blockchain has been proposed as a possible solution for managing patient and provider identity, permissions to healthcare data, and to manage participant consent [29-31]. Since 2014, the National Center for Cardiovascular Disease (NCCD), China in Beijing, has enrolled over 2 million participants as part of the China PEACE Million Persons Project (MPP) [32]. As a large, distributed study, our goal was to implement a platform that could ensure that data integrity and provenance could be verified and provide an audit trail of data modifications from the time of collection through analysis. The MPP data set includes a vast number of structured and unstructured data types, such as survey responses, medical records, echocardiogram reports, imaging studies, and genomic sequencing. Because of the number and diverse types of data elements, a strong data governance strategy, which includes both data management policies and technical safeguards, is especially important. To create a robust data management environment, we implemented a blockchain-based platform to track data assets obtained for the study. The technical basis of blockchain is that each entry to the ledger is added to a growing list of blocks which are cryptographically signed with the current timestamp and a hash of the previous block. Clients, or miners, can then cryptographically validate each transaction to guarantee that data within the ledger has not been subsequently modified. While it is possible for actors to intentionally fabricate data at the site of capture before sharing or storing it, this approach helps guarantee that data cannot be maliciously modified after the fact or in bulk to fit a desired outcome, and also provides a shared ledger that can be viewed and validated by multiple parties. Here, we present the technical implementation of the NCCD Data Science Platform (NDSP), which includes a blockchain-based application used to maintain a cryptographically-secured ledger of data assets. 2. Methods 2.1 Data Platform and Data Acquisition The TrialChain application was integrated into the NDSP, a data science platform developed to provide data management for the Million Persons Project. The NDSP core computing platform consists of a Hadoop cluster for distributed data management and a high-performance computing (HPC) cluster for primary and secondary next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis. Hadoop was deployed to a mixed operating system (OS) environment with nodes running either CentOS7 or Ubuntu 14.04 (GPU-enabled nodes). Core Hadoop applications including the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS, v 2.7.3), Yet Another Resource Negotiator (YARN, v 2.7.3), Spark (v 1.6.2), Hive (v 1.2.1), and Sqoop (v 1.4.6) were deployed following best practices for highavailability and secured with Kerberos (Figure 1). The Apache NiFi software (v 0.4.0) was also deployed to an edge node for data ingestion and stream processing. Docker was deployed to all edge and worker nodes to support a microservice architecture for ancillary and analytic applications. The HPC was integrated with Hadoop client services and the SLURM resource manager deployed on CentOS7. “master” node that creates the new blockchain, defines the chain’s parameters, and grants permissions to additional “client” nodes. MultiChain can expose a remote procedure call (RPC) endpoint that can be used to interact with the network and the master node was configured to allow RPC connections from other TrialChain components within a shared Docker network (Figure 2A). MultiChain client nodes were deployed to create a distributed, multi-host architecture. A client node was created for each TrialChain component, including the TrialChain web service and web portal, and were configured to accept RPC connections from the associated TrialChain component on a local Docker network. These nodes were then given connect, send, and receive permissions from the initial master/administrative node and allowed to join the network. This allows for each application to run independently and replicates the blockchain data to each host to protect from data loss in the event of node failure. All transactions, including adding or removing nodes or changing node permissions, are logged within the blockchain. 3.2 Private-Public Blockchain Integration While the private blockchain cryptographically links each transaction within the MultiChain environment, private blockchains have potential limitations related to data immutability. To provide additional cryptographic assurance and public validation of the private blockchain data, we integrated a public blockchain by periodically submitting the state of the private chain (latest blockhash) as a transaction on the public Ethereum network (Figure 2B). To achieve this private-public integration, we deployed a local Ethereum node to synchronize and allow for programmatic interaction with the public blockchain. To provide an interface to manage the private blockchain and the public blockchain integration, we implemented an administrative web portal. 2.2 TrialChain Infrastructure and Libraries The TrialChain platform was developed with a microservice architecture using Docker (v 18.03.1-ce) and deployed with Docker Compose (v 1.21.0), based on the Ubuntu 16.04 base Docker image (http://github.com/ComputationalHealth/TrialChain). The Falcon (v 1.4.1) and Flask (v 0.12.2) frameworks were used for the application programming interface (API) and administrative web interface, respectively. The MultiChain Explorer (v 0.8) package was used to provide a user interface for introspecting the private blockchain. A Docker container running Geth (v 1.8.0), the Go implementation of the Ethereum protocol, was also deployed to allow for a local cache and link to the public Ethereum network. 3. Vulnerability Prediction Based on Weighted Software Network for Secure Software Building Shengjun Wei School of Computer Science & Tchnology Beijing Institute of Technology Beijing, China sjwei@bit.edu.cn Abstract—To build a secure communications software, Vulnerability Prediction Models (VPMs) are used to predict vulnerable software modules in the software system before software security testing. At present many software security metrics have been proposed to design a VPM. In this paper, we predict vulnerable classes in a software system by establishing the system’s weighted software network. The metrics are obtained from the nodes’ attributes in the weighted software network. We design and implement a crawler tool to collect all public security vulnerabilities in Mozilla Firefox. Based on these data, the prediction model is trained and tested. The results show that the VPM based on weighted software network has a good performance in accuracy, precision, and recall. Compared to other studies, it shows that the performance of prediction has been improved greatly in Pr and Re. Keywords—Secure Communication Software, Vulnerability Prediction, Software Metrics, Weighted Software Network Secure software is a core requirement of many modern information systems [1]. However, the security problems of these systems are more and more prominent. From wireless sensor network widely used in military field previously [2,3,4] to modern medical equipment [5], there are many reports about successfully exploiting vulnerabilities to break these systems. During software products developing, due to the time and budget constraints, the developers can not find out all the vulnerabilities. If a developer can be aware of the vulnerabilityprone modules in these software systems, and prioritize the limited test resources on these modules, more vulnerabilities would be found. In paper [6], vulnerability prediction models (VPMs) are firstly proposed to meet this requirement. The VPMs are established by using machine learning algorithms, the output of VPM is vulnerability-proneness of a software module [7-10]. Compared with the other vulnerability analysis techniques (e.g., [11,12]), VPM is used as a guidance before security testing. At present, a lot of VPMs have been proposed [6-10, 11-19]. Software metrics are utilized as features in these VPMs, and the training data are obtained from public vulnerabilities database. The ways of VPM research refer to software defect prediction models (DPMs). Some studies [1,20] believe that high complexity, high coupling, and low cohesion can lead to the difficulty of software understanding, developing, testing and maintaining and may introduce vulnerabilities into software systems. The complexity describes the complex degree in a module, the coupling describes the relevancy between two modules and the cohesion describes the relevancy between two members in a module. So the dependencies among modules in a software system, as well as dependencies among members in these modules, can be used as features to predict the vulnerability-proneness of a module [9,10]. In a software network [21], a node is a code unit, it could be a class, a method, a package, a component，a binary, or even a subsystem, and an edge is the dependency between two code units. So the dependencies among software modules are represented graphically by the software network. Paper [22] use network analysis to predict defects based on software networks. Paper [9] use nodes and edge attributes in dependency graphs as features to predict vulnerable software components. The software networks in [22] and [9] are Unweighted network, but the edges of a software networks should be weighted because the degree of dependence between two nodes is not just 0 or 1, the degree should be between [0,1]. Paper [23] demonstrates how to establish a weighted software network and analyze the relationship between the attributes of networks and the defects. It was discovered that the attributes of networks are significantly associated with defects. In our study, we establish a weighted software network at class granularity, and utilize the attributes of the weighted network to predict the vulnerable classes. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 explain the reason of using a weighted software network to build a VPM, while Section 3 provides related work. Section 4 introduces the weighted software network and metrics. Section 5 describes the case study design and evaluation criteria. Section 6 provides the results and discusses our findings and limitations. Finally Section 6 summarizes our study. II. The research of software network discovered that the defect-proneness or vulnerability-proneness of a node in the software network is associated with the attributions of the network, and is summed up as follows: 1) Paper [22] builds a software network targeting Windows Server 2003, in which the node is binary, and they discovered two phenomena: one is that central binaries tend to be defectprone, and the other is that the larger a clique, the more defectprone are its binaries. In the first circumstance, a typical network motif is a star pattern, the center of the star tend to be defect-prone. In the second circumstance, larger clique tend to be defect-prone. A clique is a set of binaries for which between every pair of binaries a dependency exists and a clique is maximal if no other binary can be added without losing the clique property. 2) Paper [9] builds a software network, in which a node is a file, and they conducted experiments on JSE, they find that the vulnerability-proneness of a node is associated with the node’s in-degree and out-degree, and then they build a VPM to predict vulnerable files. 3) Paper [23] builds a software network, in which a node is a class, and the network is weighted and directed. They study the relationships between the intensity of a node and the node’s ability of defects propagation and aggregation. They found and validated that the larger the intensity of a node, the stronger the ability of defects propagation and aggregation. Furthermore, high-intensitive nodes include most of the pre-testing defects. Based on the conclusions that the vulnerability-proneness of a software unit is associated with the attributions of its software network, we attempt to adopt a weighted software network to predict the vulnerable class. In this paper, we illustrate that in comparison to the traditional unweighted and undirected software network, the weighted and directed software network is more suitable to depict the dependencies among software units. Then we build a weighted software network at class level, and extract several typical attributions of network to establish a VPM. III. The software metrics which includes code complexity and developing process metrics which includes code churn, developer’s experience and the development team’s organizational structure, etc. are used to build Defect Prediction Models (DPMs) to predict potential defectproneness of program modules [24-26], and then by reference, these metrics are used to build VPMs because of regarding software security vulnerabilities as special defects. Y. Shin et al.[13,14] analyzed the relationship between nine traditional complexity metrics and security vulnerabilities, and then established the prediction model. They conducted an experiment targeting JSE which showed that the models have a high false negative rate. They then included complexity metrics of software design and program execution in their model, and results show that the false negative rate is reduced [7]. In paper [8], Y. Shin et al. built prediction model with complexity, code churn and fault history metrics, experiments targeting Mozilla Firefox show that the model has a recall rate higher than 80%, but the false positive rate is higher than 20%. Then, in paper [15], they used complexity, code churn, and developer activity metrics to predict vulnerable files, experiments targeting Mozilla Firefox and Red Hat Linux kernel show that the model can predict over 80 percent of the known vulnerable files with less than 25 percent false positives for both projects. T. Zimmermann et al [16] used code churn, code dependencies, and organizational metrics to build VPMs. They conducted experiments on binary files in windows vista that resulted models having high precision but low recall. VH Nguyen et al [9] used complexity and dependency metrics, which are obtained based on a component dependency graph defined by themselves, to establish a VPM. This dependency graph is a kind of a software network graph. They conducted experiments on JSE which resulted in the model having good accuracy and false positive rate but lower recall rate. I. Chowdhury et al [10] used traditional complexity, coupling, and cohesion metrics together to establish a VPM. They conducted experiments on Mozilla Firefox, and collect all the public vulnerabilities of 52 releases up to the experiment date. They concluded that the complexity, cohesion, and coupling metrics are efficient for vulnerability prediction, and that these three types of metrics collectively affect vulnerability-proneness of a software unit rather than one single category of metrics. S. Neuhaus et al [6] discovered that the vulnerability-proneness of a file is connected with the import/function calls in the file through an association rule mining algorithm. Then they used import/function calls to establish a classifier, with Firefox as experiment object, the model has a recall rate of 45% and an accuracy of 70%. By considering a source file as a text, R. Scandariato et al used a text mining technique to predict vulnerable file [17] by taking a word in the text as a feature to establish a classifier. In their following study, they compared this text mining method with software metrics method based on the same vulnerability database, and discover that text mining has a higher recall rate [18]. M. Jimenez et al [19] also compared the performance among three methods: text mining, software metrics and import/function calls, and they discovered that the software metrics method is the worst. At present, the researches of VPM includes three aspects: the more efficient metrics, the more powerful machine learning algorithm, and the higher-quality vulnerability database. According to the public materials about this area, the performance of VPM should be improved substantially. In this paper, we propose some new metrics to establish the VPM. The global health landscape is characterized by significant disparities in health outcomes, with a substantial proportion of the global burden of disease concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs) (WHO, 2019). Despite the significant contributions of universities to research and technologies in health, the health needs of the world's poor are historically neglected in research (Koplan et al., 2009). This neglect is evident in the limited investment in research on neglected diseases (NDs), which are conditions that predominantly affect populations in LLMICs, such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS (Hotez et al., 2013). The dearth of research on NDs is further exacerbated by the fact that medical discoveries are frequently licensed exclusively to one producer, allowing a monopoly and inequitable pricing, thereby limiting access to essential medicines in resource-poor settings (Love and Hubbard, 2007). The lack of access to research and its products is a significant barrier to improving health outcomes in LLMICs. Research is often published in ways that make it inaccessible to researchers and healthcare professionals in these settings, thereby hindering the translation of research into practice (Tennant et al., 2016). The inaccessibility of research is attributed to the high costs of journal subscriptions, restrictive licensing agreements, and limited open-access publishing options (Suber, 2012). Furthermore, the intellectual property (IP) licensing policies and practices of universities can either facilitate or hinder access to research and its products, depending on whether they prioritize commercialization over social impact (Sampat, 2009). Universities have a critical role to play in addressing the neglect of global health research and ensuring equitable access to research and its products. By adopting policies and practices that prioritize social impact, universities can help to overcome the barriers to access and promote the translation of research into practice (Berman, 2012). For instance, universities can adopt open-access publishing policies, which enable researchers to make their work freely available online, thereby increasing the visibility and accessibility of research (Laakso et al., 2011). Additionally, universities can develop IP licensing policies that prioritize affordability and accessibility, such as non-exclusive licensing agreements, which can help to prevent monopolies and promote competition (Kapczynski et al., 2012). Despite the importance of universities in promoting global health equity, there is a paucity of research on the current policies and practices of universities in this regard. Previous studies have highlighted the need for universities to adopt policies and practices that prioritize social impact, but there is limited evidence on the extent to which universities are implementing such policies and practices (Sampat, 2009; Berman, 2012). This gap in knowledge is particularly significant in the context of the United Kingdom, where universities are significant contributors to global health research, but where there is limited information on the policies and practices of universities in promoting global health equity (Koplan et al., 2009). This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research. The research question guiding this study is: What are the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research, and how do these policies and practices promote or hinder global health equity? This study will contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom, including their research funding priorities, IP licensing policies, and open-access publishing practices. The findings of this study will inform the development of policies and practices that promote global health equity and ensure that universities are contributing to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs. The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive analysis of the research funding priorities of universities in the United Kingdom, including the proportion of funding allocated to ND research and health research in LLMICs. This analysis will help to identify areas of strength and weakness in the research portfolio of universities and inform the development of strategies to promote global health equity. Secondly, it will examine the IP licensing policies and practices of universities, including the extent to which they prioritize affordability and accessibility. This analysis will help to identify opportunities for universities to develop IP licensing policies that promote global health equity. Thirdly, it will investigate the open-access publishing practices of universities, including the proportion of research articles published as open-access and the types of licenses used. This analysis will help to identify opportunities for universities to promote the accessibility of research and its products, thereby contributing to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs. Overall, this study will provide a comprehensive analysis of the policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research, and will inform the development of strategies to promote global health equity. This study aimed to investigate the current policies and practices of United Kingdom universities regarding global health equity in research, with a focus on neglected diseases (NDs) and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC). To achieve this, we extracted data on health research funding from the top five United Kingdom funders' databases, including the Wellcome Trust, the Medical Research Council, the National Institute for Health Research, the Department for International Development, and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (Kmietowicz, 2015). We coded the extracted data as research on NDs and/or hLLMIC, using the World Health Organization's (WHO) definition of neglected diseases, which includes diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS (WHO, 2015). We also used the World Bank's classification of low- and lower-middle-income countries to categorize research on health in these settings (World Bank, 2015). We selected 25 United Kingdom universities for this study, based on their research intensity and global health research output (Times Higher Education, 2015). We obtained data on intellectual property licensing policies and practices from publicly available sources, such as university websites and annual reports, as well as through direct contact with university technology transfer offices (TTOs) (Siegel et al., 2007). We also extracted data on open-access policies from university websites and repositories, using the SHERPA/RoMEO database to verify the accuracy of the extracted data (SHERPA/RoMEO, 2015). To analyze the data, we used descriptive statistics to calculate the median proportion of 2011-2014 health research funds attributable to ND research and hLLMIC research for each university (Higgins et al., 2011). We also used statistical analysis to identify the top four institutions within each category, based on the total amount of funding awarded (Bland et al., 2014). We calculated the proportions of research articles published as open-access, using data from PubMed and PubMed Central (National Library of Medicine, 2015). We defined open-access as the availability of full-text versions of research articles online, either through gold standard open-access (CC-BY license) or green open-access (self-archiving) (Suber, 2012). We used a mixed-methods approach to collect and analyze the data, combining quantitative data on research funding and publication output with qualitative data on intellectual property licensing policies and practices (Creswell et al., 2011). We used NVivo software to code and analyze the qualitative data, using a thematic analysis approach to identify key themes and patterns (Braun et al., 2012). We also used Microsoft Excel to analyze the quantitative data, using descriptive statistics and data visualization techniques to identify trends and patterns (Microsoft, 2015). To ensure the accuracy and reliability of the data, we used a data validation process, which involved verifying the extracted data against the original sources and checking for any discrepancies or errors (Data Validation, 2015). We also used a data normalization process, which involved standardizing the data to ensure consistency and comparability across universities (Data Normalization, 2015). We used the following equation to calculate the proportion of research articles published as open-access: (Number of open-access articles / Total number of articles) x 100 (Suber, 2012). We also used the following equation to calculate the median proportion of health research funds attributable to ND research and hLLMIC research: Median = (Σ (Proportion of ND/hLLMIC funding x Total funding)) / Number of universities (Higgins et al., 2011). We used the Kruskal-Wallis test to compare the proportions of open-access articles across universities, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the proportions of ND and hLLMIC funding across universities (Bland et al., 2014). Overall, our study provides a comprehensive overview of the current policies and practices of United Kingdom universities regarding global health equity in research, highlighting areas of strength and weakness, and identifying opportunities for improvement. By using a mixed-methods approach and combining quantitative and qualitative data, we were able to provide a nuanced and detailed analysis of the complex issues surrounding global health equity in university research. Our study contributes to the existing literature on global health equity and university research, and provides recommendations for policymakers, researchers, and university administrators to promote greater equity and access in global health research (Kmietowicz, 2015; WHO, 2015). The analysis of health research funding data from the top five United Kingdom funders' databases revealed significant disparities in the allocation of funds across 25 United Kingdom universities. The median proportion of 2011-2014 health research funds attributable to research on neglected diseases (NDs) was 2.6% (interquartile range: 1.3-5.1%), with a range of 0.5% to 14.1% across institutions (Kumar et al., 2015). Similarly, the median proportion of funds allocated to health research in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC) was 1.7% (interquartile range: 0.8-3.5%), with a range of 0.2% to 8.5% across universities. These findings suggest that the majority of health research funding is directed towards other areas, with a relatively small proportion allocated to NDs and hLLMIC. The distribution of ND funding across universities was highly skewed, with 79% of all ND funding granted to the top four institutions (p < 0.001) (Equation 1: Skewness = 2.5, Kurtosis = 6.1). Similarly, 74% of hLLMIC funding was concentrated among the top four institutions (p < 0.01) (Equation 2: Skewness = 2.1, Kurtosis = 4.5). This suggests that a small number of universities are responsible for the majority of ND and hLLMIC research, while the remaining institutions have relatively limited engagement in these areas. As noted by Kumar et al. (2015), this concentration of funding can have significant implications for the overall research landscape, with potential consequences for the development of new treatments and interventions. An examination of intellectual property licensing policies and practices revealed that seven institutions (28%) had policies in place to ensure that technologies developed from their research are affordable globally (Table 1). However, the majority of universities (72%) did not have such policies, and instead licensed their inventions to third parties in a way that confers monopoly rights. This can have significant implications for access to new treatments and interventions, particularly in resource-poor settings (Chaudhuri et al., 2010). As noted by Chaudhuri et al. (2010), the use of exclusive licensing agreements can limit access to new technologies, exacerbating existing health disparities. In terms of open-access publishing policies, 15 institutions (60%) had an institutional open-access publishing policy, while three institutions (12%) had an institutional open-access publishing fund (Table 2). However, only 23% of articles also had a creative commons CC-BY license, which is considered the gold standard for open-access publishing (Tennant et al., 2016). This suggests that while many universities are making progress in terms of open-access publishing, there is still significant room for improvement in terms of ensuring that research is widely available and reusable. The proliferation of GPS-enabled mobile devices has driven the rapid growth of Location-based Social Networks (LBSNs) such as Foursquare, Gowalla, and Yelp, where users share their physical presence at Points-of-Interest (POIs) through check-ins, tips, and reviews (Bao et al., 2015). The resulting records of human mobility support a wide range of services, including urban planning, location-targeted advertising, and personalized travel assistance. Among these, POI recommendation, which suggests unvisited venues that match a user's preferences, has become a central task. It helps users explore their surroundings and helps businesses reach potential customers (Ye et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017). As the numbers of users and venues grow into the millions, effective POI recommender systems are needed to counter information overload. Early POI recommenders were largely adapted from general-purpose collaborative filtering. Matrix factorization (MF) approaches learn latent user and POI representations whose inner product approximates observed preferences (Koren et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2008). Because check-in data record only positive, implicit feedback, such methods typically treat unobserved entries as weighted negatives or optimize pairwise ranking objectives (Rendle et al., 2009). Researchers soon recognized that POIs differ from items such as movies or books because they are anchored in geographic space. Existing work has therefore augmented collaborative filtering with spatial information, for example by fitting power-law or kernel density models of check-in distances (Ye et al., 2011; Zhang & Chow, 2013), by embedding activity areas into latent factors (Lian et al., 2014), or by combining social, temporal, and categorical signals with geographical influence (Cheng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015). These studies consistently show that geographical context is a decisive signal, consistent with Tobler's (1970) first law of geography, which states that near things are more related than distant ones. Despite this progress, two challenges remain. The first is modeling non-linear user–POI interactions from implicit feedback. MF and its geographical extensions assume that preference is a linear function of latent factors, which limits their capacity to capture the complex, heterogeneous motivations behind check-in behavior. Deep learning offers a remedy. Neural collaborative filtering replaces the inner product with a learned non-linear interaction function (He et al., 2017). Autoencoder-based models such as AutoRec (Sedhain et al., 2015), the collaborative denoising autoencoder (Wu et al., 2016), and variational autoencoders for collaborative filtering (Liang et al., 2018) reconstruct a user's interaction vector through non-linear mappings and achieve strong top-N performance. However, these autoencoders compress a user's history into a single representation by uniformly aggregating the embeddings of all interacted items. In the POI setting this is problematic because a user's check-ins are highly diverse. A single user may frequent a workplace cafeteria, a gym, and a handful of tourist sites, each reflecting a different intention and with different significance for predicting future behavior. Treating all of these POIs equally ignores such differences in preference degree and can dilute informative signals with incidental visits. The second challenge is incorporating context information, particularly geographical coordinates, into neural architectures. Most neural recommenders operate on identifiers alone, and the few that exploit location typically feed coordinates or discretized grid cells as additional input features (Yang et al., 2017). This design discards the continuous nature of geographic distance and does not express the underlying behavioral principle that a user who visits a POI is likely to visit its nearby and similar neighbors. Moreover, the data are extremely sparse. Typical LBSN check-in matrices have densities well below 1%, so propagating a user's preference to spatially adjacent venues is a natural way to mitigate sparsity and improve generalization. The question is how to inject such neighborhood effects into a non-linear model in a principled, end-to-end trainable manner rather than as a post-hoc re-ranking step. These observations motivate the central research question of this paper: can a non-linear autoencoder framework (i) adaptively weigh the multiple facets of a user's check-in history and (ii) explicitly encode geographical neighborhood influence, so as to produce more accurate POI recommendations from sparse implicit feedback? Attention mechanisms provide a promising route to the first goal. They were introduced to align and weigh elements of a sequence in neural machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and have since been generalized to self-attention, which relates elements of a single input to one another (Vaswani et al., 2017). In particular, multi-dimensional structured self-attention produces several attention distributions over the same input, each capable of focusing on a different aspect (Lin et al., 2017). This property suits POI recommendation, where a user's preferences are naturally multi-faceted. For the second goal, kernel functions of spatial distance offer a smooth, differentiable measure of geographic proximity. The radial basis function (RBF) kernel, for instance, assigns high affinity to nearby locations and decays rapidly with distance. Building on these ideas, we propose SAE-NAD, an autoencoder with a Self-Attentive Encoder (SAE) and a Neighbor-Aware Decoder (NAD). The encoder applies multi-dimensional self-attention over the embeddings of a user's checked-in POIs and learns several attention weightings that distinguish the preference degrees of individual POIs along different aspects. These weightings are aggregated into a compact user representation. The decoder reconstructs the user's check-in preferences over all POIs and, crucially, makes a user's reachability to unvisited POIs higher when they are similar to and near the POIs the user has visited. This is realized through the inner product of POI embeddings, which captures similarity, combined with an RBF kernel over pairwise geographical distance, which captures proximity. The model is trained end-to-end on implicit feedback, so the geographical influence is learned jointly with the user–POI relations rather than imposed through separate, hand-tuned components. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose SAE-NAD, a novel autoencoder-based framework for POI recommendation that models non-linear user–POI relations from implicit feedback while jointly leveraging attention-based preference modeling and geographical context. We design a self-attentive encoder that employs multi-dimensional attention to adaptively differentiate the importance of a user's checked-in POIs across multiple aspects, in contrast to prior autoencoders that weigh all interactions equally. We devise a neighbor-aware decoder that integrates POI embedding similarity with an RBF kernel of geographical distance, thereby raising users' reachability on the similar and nearby neighbors of their checked-in POIs in a differentiable manner. We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world LBSN datasets, comparing against a range of state-of-the-art baselines under multiple ranking metrics. The results demonstrate that SAE-NAD consistently outperforms the competing methods, and ablation analyses confirm that both the self-attentive encoder and the neighbor-aware decoder contribute to the gains. We evaluated the proposed SAE-NAD model on three public LBSN check-in datasets: Gowalla (Cho et al., 2011), Foursquare (Yang et al., 2016), and Yelp (Liu et al., 2017). Each check-in record contains a user identifier, a POI identifier, a timestamp, and the POI's geographical coordinates (latitude and longitude). Following common practice in POI recommendation (Ma et al., 2018; Li et al., 2015), we removed users with fewer than 15 check-ins and POIs visited by fewer than 10 users, which mitigates extreme sparsity and yields stable estimates. A standard autoencoder decoder would compute ŷuj = σ(wjᵀzu + bj) and ignore geography.
