Tobacco use remains the leading cause of preventable death worldwide, responsible for more than eight million deaths each year, of which roughly 1.2 million occur among non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke (World Health Organization [WHO], 2021). Although the burden of tobacco-related disease falls mainly on adults, the epidemic is sustained by initiation in adolescence and early adulthood. Most adult users begin before the age of 25, and nicotine dependence can develop within weeks of first use, well before young people have the capacity to assess long-term risks (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2012; DiFranza et al., 2007). The adolescent brain is particularly vulnerable to nicotine, with exposure linked to altered development of prefrontal circuits, impaired attention and cognition, and greater susceptibility to other substance use (Yuan et al., 2015; Counotte et al., 2011). Tobacco use among youth is therefore best understood not only as a risk behavior but as the primary pipeline through which the tobacco industry replaces the customers lost to disease and cessation. The Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS), coordinated by WHO and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, has provided school-based, nationally comparable estimates of tobacco use among students aged 13–15 years in more than 140 countries since 1999. These data show substantial heterogeneity. Current use of any tobacco product among adolescents exceeds 20% in several countries in Europe, the Western Pacific, and parts of the Americas, while in South-East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa smokeless tobacco accounts for a large share of use, often exceeding cigarette smoking (Veeranki et al., 2015; Xi et al., 2016). Gender gaps are narrowing in many settings, and the rapid spread of electronic nicotine delivery systems has reversed declines in nicotine use in high-income countries, with e-cigarette use among adolescents now exceeding cigarette use in several of them (Cullen et al., 2019; Gentzke et al., 2022). Youth tobacco use is thus changing in form, geography, and social distribution, and policies designed for conventional adult cigarette smoking may not be adequate. The international policy response has been organized largely around the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), adopted in 2003 and now ratified by more than 180 Parties, and the MPOWER package of measures derived from it: monitoring tobacco use and prevention policies, protecting people from tobacco smoke, offering help to quit, warning about the dangers of tobacco, enforcing bans on advertising, promotion and sponsorship, and raising taxes (WHO, 2008). Evidence from adult populations supports the effectiveness of these measures, and price increases in particular are considered the single most effective instrument, with youth typically more price-sensitive than adults (Chaloupka et al., 2012; International Agency for Research on Cancer, 2011). Other measures with youth-relevant evidence include comprehensive advertising bans, graphic health warnings and plain packaging, smoke-free legislation, minimum-age-of-sale laws with retailer enforcement, school-based and mass-media prevention programs, and, more recently, "Tobacco 21" laws and flavor restrictions (Hammond, 2011; Brown et al., 2014; Friedman et al., 2021; Kowitt et al., 2017). However, FCTC articles refer to minors mainly in the contexts of sales and access (Article 16), and most provisions are framed for the whole population. Evidence on whether, and through what mechanisms, population-level measures reach adolescents and young adults is uneven, and the evidence for youth-specific interventions is mixed. Systematic reviews of school-based programs, for example, show modest and often short-lived effects, with the strongest results for those using social-influence and life-skills approaches (Thomas et al., 2015), while the evidence on youth access laws is limited by weak enforcement and by the availability of social sources of tobacco (DiFranza, 2012). Several gaps in the literature motivate the present review. First, existing policy assessments, including the WHO Report on the Global Tobacco Epidemic and the Tobacco Control Scale in Europe, classify countries by the presence and strength of policies but rarely disaggregate by age or examine whether a policy is designed for, or reaches, young people (Joossens & Raw, 2012; WHO, 2023). Second, the term "youth" is used inconsistently, ranging from 10 to 24 years in different United Nations and national definitions, which complicates synthesis and cross-country comparison. Third, the literature is dominated by studies from high-income countries and by cigarette smoking, whereas the greatest growth in tobacco industry activity is in low- and middle-income countries, and smokeless tobacco, waterpipe, and novel products are often neglected in policy design and evaluation (Siddiqi et al., 2020; Sinha et al., 2015). Fourth, little attention has been paid to how young people engage with policies physically, physiologically, and psychologically: how they perceive warnings, respond to price signals, circumvent age restrictions through illicit or cross-border trade and social sourcing, and use peers as both risk factors and resources for cessation. Finally, existing reviews generally examine a single instrument, such as taxation, packaging, or school programs, rather than describing the overall landscape of policies, their documented impacts, and the national and international obstacles to implementation, including industry interference under Article 5.3 and the tension between public health goals and trade and economic interests (Smith et al., 2013; Gilmore et al., 2015). Given these gaps, a broad, structured synthesis is warranted. Because the field is heterogeneous in policy type, study design, outcomes, and population definitions, a conventional meta-analysis of effects is neither feasible nor the most useful first step. We therefore conducted an explorative systematic policy review, a design suited to mapping what policies exist, how they have been studied, what impacts have been reported, and where the evidence is thin (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005; Munn et al., 2018). Such a review can integrate peer-reviewed studies with surveillance data such as GYTS and with policy documents and grey literature, which are essential for capturing policies that have been adopted but not formally evaluated. The study addresses three research questions. First, what is the current situation of youth tobacco use, as documented in GYTS and related sources, and what tobacco control policies have been adopted that affect young people across countries and continents? Second, what impacts, intended and unintended, have been reported for these policies, both at the national level and in terms of youth engagement? Third, what national and international challenges, such as illicit trade and smuggling, smokeless tobacco, novel products, industry influence, and weak enforcement, constrain the control of tobacco use among youth, and what creative, youth-focused strategies might address them? This review makes four contributions. It provides an age-sensitive classification of tobacco control policies, distinguishing population-wide measures from those that explicitly target young people. It brings together situational, national, and global evidence in a single framework, anchored in the MPOWER strategies. It identifies neglected areas, notably smokeless tobacco and youth participation, that require research and policy attention. Finally, it argues that tobacco control for youth should be positioned as a social, public health, and quality-of-life priority rather than primarily as a matter of business and trade, and it outlines directions for more youth-centered policy and research. Study design and reporting framework We conducted an explorative systematic policy review that combined a structured literature search with a descriptive analysis of survey surveillance data. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 statement for the identification, screening, and reporting of records (Page et al., 2021). Because the topic spans peer-reviewed evaluations, government documents, and international instruments, we also used the scoping-review principles of Arksey and O'Malley (2005) and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (Tricco et al., 2018). These principles allowed us to map the breadth of evidence rather than to answer a single narrowly defined effectiveness question. The protocol was not registered, which is consistent with the explorative aim. The review questions were: (i) what is the current situation of tobacco use among youth; (ii) which tobacco control policies target or reach youth at the national level; (iii) what impacts have been reported; and (iv) what national and international challenges remain. Definition of youth and policy classification No single age definition is used across the tobacco control literature. The United Nations defines youth as 15–24 years, WHO defines adolescence as 10–19 years, and the Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS) samples students aged 13–15 years (Warren et al., 2008). We therefore applied a flexible operational definition of 10–24 years and recorded the exact age range reported in each source. This flexibility was a deliberate trade-off, and we return to it as a limitation. Policies were classified using the WHO MPOWER framework: Monitor tobacco use and prevention policies; Protect people from tobacco smoke; Offer help to quit; Warn about the dangers of tobacco; Enforce bans on advertising, promotion, and sponsorship; and Raise taxes (WHO, 2008). MPOWER operationalizes the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (WHO FCTC; WHO, 2003). Policies that did not map onto a single MPOWER domain were coded under two additional categories created inductively. These were youth-specific measures (minimum legal sales age, restrictions on youth access, school-based and peer-based programmes) and measures addressing illicit trade, including youth involvement in smuggling. Data sources and search strategy We searched PubMed, the Health Inter-Network Access to Research Initiative (HINARI), Scopus, and the Cochrane Library. We also searched Google and Google Scholar to capture grey literature, including government reports, WHO and CDC technical documents, and non-governmental organization evaluations. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH where available) with free text and Boolean operators. A representative PubMed string was: ("tobacco control" OR "smoking reduction" OR "tobacco policy" OR "FCTC" OR "MPOWER") AND (youth OR adolescent OR "young people" OR student) AND (prevalence OR tax OR "plain packaging" OR "warning label" OR advertis OR "smoke-free" OR "minimum age" OR incentive OR "peer-based" OR smuggling OR "smokeless tobacco"). Strings were adapted to the syntax of each database. For Google and Google Scholar, we screened the first 200 results per query, ranked by relevance (Haddaway et al., 2015). Additional records were identified by backward citation tracking of key reviews and by hand-searching the WHO FCTC, WHO Report on the Global Tobacco Epidemic, and CDC GYTS repositories. The search covered publications from January 2003, the year the WHO FCTC was adopted, to the date of the final search. Only English-language records were considered. The search strategy was shaped by five considerations: timeline (post-FCTC), specificity and popularity of the policies (those most often implemented or cited), reliability of the source, significance (relevance to youth and to national or global policy), and applicability (potential transferability across settings). To achieve geographic breadth, we purposively sought records from each WHO region and continent and from countries at different income levels, using World Bank income classifications. Exhaustive coverage of all countries was not feasible. Eligibility criteria We included records that (a) described, evaluated, or critiqued a tobacco control policy, programme, or legislation that targeted youth or whose effects on youth were reported; (b) reported youth tobacco prevalence or determinants of use; or (c) discussed national or international challenges to controlling youth tobacco use. Eligible designs included observational studies, quasi-experimental and experimental evaluations, systematic and narrative reviews, economic analyses, qualitative studies, and official policy documents. We excluded records that (a) addressed only adult populations; (b) were opinion pieces without policy content; (c) focused solely on clinical cessation pharmacotherapy; or (d) were duplicate publications. Studies of smokeless tobacco and emerging products were eligible, although we anticipated they would be underrepresented. Screening and selection All records were imported into reference-management software and de-duplicated. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then full texts, against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when necessary, by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the full-text stage was quantified with Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960): κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the agreement expected by chance. We interpreted κ using the benchmarks of Landis and Koch (1977), with values above 0.60 indicating substantial agreement. A total of 122 studies and documents met the inclusion criteria and entered the synthesis. Data extraction A standardized extraction form was piloted on ten records and then refined. For each record, one reviewer extracted, and a second verified, the following: author and year; country and WHO region; income

Characterizing IOMT/Personal Area Networks Landscape Adil Rajput (aiilahi@effatuniversity.edu.sa) Assistant Professor, Information System Department, Effat University An Nazlah Al Yamaniyyah, Jeddah 22332, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia Tayeb Brahimi (tbrahimi@effatuniversity.edu.sa) Assistant Professor, Natural Sciences, Mathematics, and Technology Unit, Effat University An Nazlah Al Yamaniyyah, Jeddah 22332, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia Abstract The attention garnered by the Internet of Things (IoT) term has taken the world by a storm. IOT concepts have been applied to various domains revolutionizing the way business processes are conducted. Health Informatics is a nascent multidisciplinary field that aims at applying information engineering concepts to healthcare. The information traditionally came from a variety of sources such as healthcare IT systems but recently is being stored in variety of IOT devices. Application of IOT concepts is becoming the norm giving rise to the Internet of Medical Things (IOMT). However, IOMT introduces many challenges such as the real-time nature, security, and privacy of data along with others. Thus, understanding the underlying structure of IOMT is of paramount importance. Given the importance of the underlying networks, we explore various solutions currently employed in developing the Personal Area Networks (PANs) that are the underlying cornerstone of IOMT). PANs allow the sensors to measure the change in various stimuli and transmit the information via LANs and WANs to various stakeholders. This chapter will look at three standards that are currently used by both academia and industry along with Body Area Networks (BANs). The chapter also provides a survey of prevalent IOMT applications along with various vendors that provide such services. Keywords: IOMT, IOT, Personal Area Networks (PANs), Smart Healthcare, Bluetooth, Body Area Networks (BANs), Cybersecurity, Data Security 1 Introduction Advances in the communication and technology realm have given rise to an interconnected world which has eliminated the need for human intervention. While the fields of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Decision Support System (DSS), and Machine Learning (ML) have been advocating various techniques to enhance the decision making and more importantly reduce the human-related errors, it is the inexpensive price of hardware that has made the IoT (Internet of Things) a reality. The term “Internet of Things” was first coined by Ashton (Ashton, 2009). Although many definitions exist for IoT, the IoT environment is characterized by a collection of “devices” connected together via a “network”. Such devices need both a hardware and software component - a system known as CyberPhysical System (CPS). The term CPS refers to the intertwined system of hardware and software components that allows the software to control the hardware components minimizing or eliminating the use of the human intervention. The prerequisite for such systems to operate is the underlying ubiquitous network be it on a Local Area Network (LAN) or Wide Area Network (WAN). Such a network allows the various hardware components to communicate with the software component in real time (or near real time). Almost in all cases, the CPS systems strive to minimize or eliminate the human intervention thus increasing the demand on both CPU, memory and the network. Given that the size of the hardware components is usually small (e.g., a wearable device), the power and memory capacity cause serious challenges as the size of the components connected and the demands placed on such devices. 1.1 The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) - known as the healthcare IoT (Ashton, 2009) technology ensures the availability and the analysis of healthcare data through smart medical devices and the web (Joyia et al., 2016; Dastjerdi et al., 2016; Islam et al., 2015, Singh et a;., 2014). Internet of Medical Things builds upon the underlying architecture of the IoT as it has a multitude of interconnected devices sending data over a network (mostly the Internet) to the cloud that can be accessed by the medical practitioners (Deliotte, 2018; Gatouillat et al., 2018, Díaz et al., 2016). Applications range from gathering data with remote monitoring systems to be analyzed in non-real time (e.g., sleep monitoring) to emergency notification services (e.g., pacemaker monitoring). Devices such as Fitbit, Garmin, Xiaomi, or Misfit wireless fitness tracker are used to monitor patients’ vital signs. Given the battery and computation limitations, the majority of the data is transmitted via the network (LAN and possibly WAN) placing high requirements on the network. Furthermore, the real-time nature of IoMT coupled with the nascent stage of development has brought forth various challenges to the helm. Such challenges include (but not limited to) security/privacy of data, efficient data handling, and transmission, and massive data volume (Joyia et al., 2016). Recent research and developments in advanced sensors, mobile applications, artificial intelligence, big data, 3D printing, and mobility have created new opportunities for medical technology companies to design and manufacture a wide range of affordable smart medical devices (Dey et al., 2018; Deliotte, 2018, McDonald et al., 2018; Raghupathi et al., 2014). 1.2 The idea behind IOMT centers around the concept of Personal Area Networks (PANs). A PAN is a small network that centers around a sensor device (could be attached to a machine or a human). The basic premise behind PAN network is the following: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Various devices and/or human body will have sensors connected to them Such devices communicate the status of each device using a network The network formed is ad-hoc and limited in range The devices have limited battery power and hence can be limited in terms of functionality Given the low power limitations, the network throughput can be low. Depending on the nature of the information, the information needs to be secured The goal of this chapter is to describe the various components that form the underlying basis of Personal Area Networks. The crux of this chapter is presented in the next section. First, we describe the two main components of IoT/IoMT namely the physical and network components. Then we delve deeper into the network component and explain the three standards that underly the network component of the PANs along with an overview of Body Area Networks (BANs). Section 3 discusses some of the prevalent applications in the IoMT world. Section 4 offers the concluding remarks along with future research directions. 2 Architectural Landscape Revisiting the Cyber-Physical system definition highlights the intertwined nature of the hardware and the software. Furthermore, the physical world we live in deals with information that is represented in an analog fashion. Such information is encoded as part of waves that can take on values over a continuum. On the other hand, computers and software only deal with a discrete set of values that can be mapped onto 0s and 1s. Both the health-care professionals along with the technology architects need to fully comprehend the underlying makeup of such systems to better address the implementation details along with the associated risks. Therefore, to delve into such details, we need to address the following: 1. Physical Components 2. Network Components The Physical components allow the analog signals to be transferred from a device/body to a node that can process such information and receive instructions on steps to be performed. The Network components actually allow the messages to be transferred between devices – both in asynchronous and synchronous mode. The IoT paradigm is made possible by both a physical and network component. The physical components make it possible for the devices to both follow changes on the physical level and take an action. The physical level is composed of various Micro-Electronic-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) devices (Hesu, 2002). In simple terms, MEMS systems are an amalgamation of both micro-electronic and micro-mechanical components along with a micro-sensor and a micro-actuator referred to as sensors and actuators going forward. The success of MEMS along with low cost of hardware has also given rise to Nano-Electronic-Mechanical Systems (NEMS) which follows the same idea but the size of hardware is even smaller than MEMS. While the electronic and mechanical components are worked on by a small number of experts, it is the sensors and actuators components that practitioners in the IoT realm deal with. 2.1.1 The sensors provide the ability to monitor physical stimuli such as temperature or humidity. This part is the job of the microelectronics components. Based on the certain changes in the stimuli, the actuators take certain actions underpinned by the micromechanical system. As an example, consider the timetemperature monitoring system which after detecting the temperature dropping past a certain temperature threshold would cause the heat to turn on. While such abilities used to be hardcoded into the hardware, the MEMS systems are characterized by a Central Processing Unit that would make programming such devices a reality. The sensors can be both digital and analog. A digital signal has a finite set of values while an analog signal is a continuous change of a given parameter over a period of time - mostly voltage. The voltage can oscillate between a minimum and maximum range on a continuous basis. As an example, some digital sensors represent the ‘on’/ ‘off’ state by using the value of 3.3 Volts. In other words, the sensor can take on only two values (0 for off or 3.3 V). On the other hand, an analog sensor can take any value on the continuum between 0 and 3.3V. The analog sensors need to provide a way to convert the analog signal to a digital one so that it can be processed by a software. An actuator is a mechanical component that is responsible for performing a certain action based on the input from the sensor. The actuator needs a source of energy that can be provided via various means such as an electric signal, liquid compression, change in pressure etc. In all cases the energy is received as a control signal which will then be converted into mechanical form causing the action to be performed. 2.2 The backbone of an IoT infrastructure is the network component. While a wired network can be used, wireless networks are now considered the norm. The hardware components describe in section 2.1 are connected via a network - hence the term Cyber-Physical systems. The term Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN) has become synonymous with the network component of the IoT systems. However, Personal Area Networks (PAN) more accurately describe the concept at hand. While a LAN allows connectivity with a high rate of transmission, PANs specifically cater to devices that have limited power and bandwidth. While the narrow definition assumes that the components belong to a particular individual, in reality, PANs take on a bigger meaning e.g., when applied to industrial IoT. Recall that IoT is characterized by devices that are low on power and resources. The challenge, therefore, becomes as to how information can be transmitted with such constraints. Many real-world recognition problems cannot be posed as standard multi-class classification, because only one class is well characterized during training. Examples include fault detection in industrial systems, intrusion detection, medical screening, and the verification of a person's identity. In these settings the class of interest is abundant or well defined, while the remaining data are rare, heterogeneous, or impossible to enumerate in advance (Chandola et al., 2009; Pimentel et al., 2014). One-class classification (OCC) addresses this scenario by learning a decision rule from examples of a single class and then deciding whether a new sample belongs to it (Khan & Madden, 2014; Perera et al., 2021). The best-known OCC methods are the One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM), which separates the data from the origin in a kernel-induced feature space (Schölkopf et al., 2001), and Support Vector Data Description (SVDD), which finds the minimum-volume hypersphere enclosing the target data (Tax & Duin, 2004). Both can be extended to non-linear boundaries through kernels and are widely used baselines. More recently, deep variants such as Deep SVDD have coupled representation learning with a compact description of the target class (Ruff et al., 2018). The performance of any one-class method depends heavily on the feature space in which the data are described. Because no negative samples are available to guide the choice of features, the data representation is often high-dimensional, redundant, or noisy, and the compactness assumption underlying SVDD may then be poorly satisfied. Dimensionality reduction is therefore commonly applied as a separate pre-processing step. Classical techniques such as Principal Component Analysis are unsupervised and optimize criteria like reconstruction error or variance. These criteria are not tied to the objective of the subsequent one-class classifier. Subspace Support Vector Data Description (S-SVDD) addressed this mismatch by jointly learning a linear or non-linear projection and the SVDD description, so that the target data become compact in a subspace optimized for the one-class objective (Sohrab et al., 2018). Related graph-embedded formulations similarly use the geometry of the target class to regularize the learned representation (Iosifidis et al., 2015). However, these approaches assume that every sample is represented by a single feature vector from a single source. This assumption is increasingly at odds with how data are acquired. Objects, events, and subjects are now routinely observed through multiple modalities: different sensors, imaging devices, or feature extractors that capture complementary aspects of the same underlying phenomenon (Baltrušaitis et al., 2019). Examples include visual and thermal imagery, audio and video streams, and multi-sensor measurements in industrial monitoring. Multimodal and multi-view learning exploits the consensus and complementarity among such sources and has been shown to improve robustness and accuracy compared with learning from a single source (Xu et al., 2013; Ramachandram & Taylor, 2017). Classical subspace methods such as Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) (Hotelling, 1936; Hardoon et al., 2004) and its kernel and deep extensions (Andrew et al., 2013) learn projections that maximize cross-modal correlation, and deep multimodal architectures learn shared representations (Ngiam et al., 2011). These techniques, however, are designed to model statistical dependence between modalities and do not take into account the objective of a downstream one-class classifier. Their projections are not optimized to make the class of interest compact, nor do they exploit the fact that training information is available only for that class. In the OCC literature, the multimodal setting is typically handled in one of two ways, both of which are limiting. The first is to train a separate one-class model on each modality and combine the resulting decision scores (late fusion). This ignores relations among modalities during representation learning and can be adversely affected by weak or noisy modalities. The second is to concatenate the features of all modalities into a single vector (early fusion) and apply a standard one-class method. This increases dimensionality, typically leaves modality-specific scale and noise characteristics unaddressed, and makes the description susceptible to the curse of dimensionality when training samples are limited. Neither strategy learns modality-specific mappings into a common space that is designed from the outset for describing the target class. Consequently, there is a clear gap: no existing approach jointly learns, for each modality, a transformation into a shared low-dimensional space and a single compact description of the target class using data from all modalities, while relying exclusively on target-class samples. The question motivating this work is therefore the following: can multimodal one-class learning be improved by learning modality-specific projections to a common subspace in which a single hypersphere, trained only on target data from all modalities, provides a tighter and more discriminative description than that obtainable from any single modality or from naive fusion? Answering this requires dealing with several challenges. The projections must be learned in conjunction with the data description, since otherwise the subspace is not adapted to the one-class criterion. The formulation must also admit regularization strategies that prevent degenerate solutions, such as collapsing all data onto a point, and that encourage consistency across modalities. Finally, it should handle both linear relations and the non-linear structure commonly encountered in real data. In this paper we introduce Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD), a method that extends the S-SVDD framework to data from multiple modalities. MS-SVDD iteratively optimizes two components: a set of modality-specific transformations that map each original feature space into a common subspace, and a joint SVDD description of the projected data from all modalities. The transformations are learned using information from the class of interest only, so the method remains a genuine one-class approach and requires no negative or outlier examples at training time. The contributions of this work are as follows: 1. We formulate the problem of learning a shared one-class-optimized subspace from multiple modalities and propose MS-SVDD, which jointly learns modality-specific projections and a single compact description of the target class. 2. We propose several regularization strategies for the method. These control the geometry of the learned subspace and the relationships among the projected modalities, which allows the formulation to be adapted to different degrees of cross-modal agreement. 3. We provide both linear and non-linear (kernel-based) formulations, together with an iterative optimization procedure, so that the method can be applied to data with simple as well as complex structure. 4. We conduct an extensive experimental evaluation on five multimodal datasets, comparing MS-SVDD with one-class methods trained on a single modality and on fused data from all modalities. The proposed method outperforms all competing approaches on four of the five datasets, which indicates that learning a task-specific common subspace is more effective than either individual-modality models or direct fusion. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background on SVDD and S-SVDD. Section 3 presents the proposed MS-SVDD method, its regularization strategies, and its linear and non-linear formulations. Section 4 describes the datasets and experimental protocol and reports the results, and Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. Problem formulation and notation Let 𝒳 = {X¹,…,X^M} denote data from M modalities, where X^m ∈ ℝ^{Dm×N} contains the N training samples of the target class represented in the m-th modality, with Dm the modality-specific dimensionality. Only target-class samples are used during training, in line with the one-class classification (OCC) setting (Tax & Duin, 2004). Samples are assumed to be paired across modalities. Each modality is z-score normalized using training statistics before projection. Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) seeks the smallest hypersphere, with centre a and radius R, enclosing most training data (Tax & Duin, 2004). Subspace SVDD (Sohrab et al., 2018) jointly learns a projection Q ∈ ℝ^{d×D} and the hypersphere in the projected space. We extend this idea to the multimodal case by defining a modality-specific projection Qm ∈ ℝ^{d×Dm} that maps every modality into a common d-dimensional subspace, where one shared hypersphere (a, R) describes data from all modalities. The multimodal objective is min{R,a,ξ,{Qm}} R² + C Σm Σi ξi^m + (λ/2) Ω({Qm}), subject to ‖Qm xi^m − a‖² ≤ R² + ξi^m and ξi^m ≥ 0 for i = 1,…,N and m = 1,…,M. Here C > 0 controls the trade-off between the volume of the hypersphere and the training errors, and Ω is a regularization term weighted by λ ≥ 0. Optimization procedure The problem is non-convex jointly in {Qm} and the hypersphere parameters, so we use an alternating scheme. With the projections fixed, the problem reduces to a standard SVDD on the pooled projected samples {Qm xi^m}, and its Lagrangian dual is a quadratic program, which we solve with a sequential minimal optimization solver (Chang & Lin, 2011). The dual variables αi^m satisfy 0 ≤ αi^m ≤ C and Σ{m,i} αi^m = 1, and the centre is a = Σ{m,i} αi^m Qm xi^m. With the dual variables fixed, each Qm is updated by gradient descent on the Lagrangian, ∂ℒ/∂Qm = 2 Σi αi^m (Qm xi^m − a)(xi^m)ᵀ + λ ∂Ω/∂Qm, with Qm ← Qm − η ∂ℒ/∂Qm. The step size η was set to 10⁻³ and the Adam update rule (Kingma & Ba, 2015) was used for stability. The two steps alternate until the relative change of the objective falls below 10⁻⁵ or 100 iterations are reached. Each Qm was initialized by one of three schemes: PCA of the corresponding modality (Jolliffe, 2002), a random Gaussian matrix with entries drawn from 𝒩(0, 1/Dm), or the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) directions between pairs of modalities (Hotelling, 1936). The default was PCA initialization; the other two were examined in an ablation. Because shared radius and centre are used, a test sample is scored in modality m by its distance ‖Qm x^m − a‖², and is accepted as a target if this distance does not exceed R². Regularization strategies We investigated three choices of Ω. (i) Norm regularization: Ω₁ = Σm ‖Qm‖²F, which limits the scale of the projections and prevents the trivial solution in which all data collapse to a point. (ii) Variance regularization: Ω₂ = Σm tr(Qm Sm Qmᵀ), where Sm is the scatter matrix of modality m. This penalizes the dispersion of the projected data and promotes compact descriptions. (iii) Cross-modal alignment: Ω₃ = Σ{m<l} Σi ‖Qm xi^m − Ql xi^l‖², which encourages paired samples from different modalities to coincide in the shared subspace, similarly to the correlation-maximization principle of CCA but without requiring non-target data. In all cases the rows of each Qm were rescaled to unit norm after each update when Ω₁ was not used, to avoid degenerate scaling. Non-linear formulation For the non-linear variant, each modality is implicitly mapped by a feature map φm to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel Km(x, y) = exp(−‖x − y‖²/2σm²) (Schölkopf & Smola, 2002). Following the representer theorem, the projection is parameterized as Qm = Λm Φmᵀ, where Φm = [φm(x1^m),…,φm(xN^m)] and Λm ∈ ℝ^{d×N}, so that Qm φm(x) = Λm km(x) with km(x) = [Km(x1^m, x),…,Km(xN^m, x)]ᵀ. The updates described above are then performed with respect to Λm, initialized by kernel PCA (Schölkopf et al., 1998). The width σm was set to the mean pairwise Euclidean distance in modality m multiplied by a factor chosen from the grid described below. Datasets Five publicly available multimodal datasets were used. Physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior (SB) have emerged as critical components in the understanding of lifestyle health determinants over the past few decades. Their bidirectional influence on health outcomes, particularly in relation to non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers, is well-established globally (Lee et al., 2012). The World Health Organization (WHO) has persistently highlighted the need for increased levels of PA and reduced sedentary time as a means to curb the rising burden of NCDs worldwide (World Health Organization, 2020). In low- and middle-income countries, including Thailand, the escalating prevalence of these health issues necessitates an in-depth examination of PA and SB patterns, associated determinants, and their health impacts (Ng et al., 2014; Knuth & Hallal, 2009). Thailand, a rapidly developing nation, faces significant public health challenges as it navigates the epidemiological transition from communicable to non-communicable diseases. According to the Thailand Ministry of Public Health (2015), NCDs account for nearly 75% of total deaths annually, with physical inactivity as a major contributing factor. Despite this alarming statistic, comprehensive data on PA and SB within Thai populations remain limited. There exists an emerging but fragmented body of research, mainly from isolated cross-sectional studies, which hinders the ability to implement robust evidence-based interventions and policies (Suwannaphant et al., 2014). The increasing need to address PA and SB within Thailand's public health agenda is underscored by several emergent health trends. Firstly, rapid urbanization and industrialization have prompted lifestyle changes that skew towards decreased physical activity and increased sedentary behaviours, such as prolonged sitting at workplaces and recreational screen time among both adults and youth (Pongsiri et al., 2016). Secondly, cultural attitudes and environmental factors may play unique roles in shaping PA and SB, necessitating localized research to distinguish these influences from generic global patterns (Sriramatr & Berry, 2017). While the global evidence highlights the health benefits of regular physical activity and the hazards of sustained sedentary behaviour, there is a notable gap in the systematic synthesis of these aspects specifically for the Thai context. This gap extends beyond basic epidemiological mapping to include weaknesses in understanding the sociocultural determinants and barriers that govern these behaviours within various Thai demographic cohorts (Wattanapisit et al., 2018). The primary objective of this systematic scoping review is to bridge this gap by mapping existing literature on PA and SB in Thailand, thereby providing a comprehensive overview that can guide future research directions and inform public health initiatives. Specifically, this review seeks to (i) chart the breadth of available evidence on PA and SB in Thailand, (ii) identify existing research gaps, and (iii) propose new research directions that are attuned to the local context and emergent public health needs. The focus on mapping evidence through a scoping review rather than a conventional systematic review is justified by the need to contextualize a diverse and broad range of PA and SB studies that utilize heterogeneous methodologies and theoretical frameworks. By adopting this methodological approach, we aim to provide a holistic understanding of the current research landscape, highlighting areas of prolific study and those requiring further exploration (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005). In addressing these gaps, our review underscores the necessity for research designs that extend beyond cross-sectional analyses to include longitudinal studies that can capture causative relationships and trends over time. Furthermore, we identify a marked deficit in the use of device-based measures of PA and SB in Thai research, which limits the accuracy of prevalence estimates and behavioural assessments. Utilising standardized and objective measurement tools will be crucial in future studies to yield reliable data that can underpin rigorous public health strategies (Tudor-Locke & Bassett, 2004). Additionally, while adults are overwhelmingly the focus of current Thai PA and SB research, there remains a critical need to expand this focus to vulnerable groups such as children and adolescents. Early intervention is key in establishing lifelong healthy habits and combating escalating obesity rates among Thai youth (Mo-Suwan et al., 2014). This demographic expansion should be paralleled by efforts to better understand sedentary behaviour as an independent health risk factor, an area relatively understudied within the Thai context (Saunders et al., 2012). In conclusion, the contributions of this scoping review lie in its capacity to systematically delineate the existing research on PA and SB in Thailand, highlighting strengths, revealing critical gaps, and providing a strategic framework to guide future research agendas. By doing so, it aims to facilitate a robust scientific foundation supportive of efficacious public health interventions that address the unique determinants and challenges of PA and SB within the Thai population. This systematic scoping review was conducted to comprehensively assess and synthesize the available literature on physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior (SB) in Thailand. The methodology employed for this review was guided by established frameworks for conducting systematic scoping reviews (Arksey & O’Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010), aiming to map existing research, identify gaps, and suggest directions for future investigations. A systematic search was performed across ten bibliographic databases to ensure a comprehensive capture of relevant studies. The databases included PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, ThaiLIS, ThaiJO, Health Systems Research Institute Database, and the Thai National Research Repository. This selection was made to encompass both international and local research outputs, acknowledging the value of grey literature in scoping reviews (Pham et al., 2014). To further enhance the breadth of the literature search, secondary searches were conducted. These included manual searches of reference lists from identified studies, examination of relevant Thai health organization websites (e.g., Ministry of Public Health, Thai Health Promotion Foundation), and exploration of Google and Google Scholar platforms for additional studies that might not be indexed in traditional bibliographic databases. The inclusion of multiple search strategies aimed to minimize publication bias and ensure a comprehensive overview of pertinent research (Briscoe, 2015). The inclusion criteria were designed to focus on studies that provided either quantitative or qualitative data pertinent to public health research on PA and/or SB in Thailand. Specifically, the review included studies published in Thai or English, dating from the inception of each database to the present search date, ensuring a historical to contemporary perspective. Two authors independently screened studies in two stages - title/abstract screening followed by full-text review. Any discrepancies in inclusion decisions were resolved through discussion and consensus, with a third author consulted when needed to ensure rigor and objectivity in the selection process (Colquhoun et al., 2014). Data from the included studies were extracted systematically using a pre-designed extraction form. Key information collected included study characteristics (e.g., authors, year of publication, journal), research focus (e.g., correlates, outcomes, prevalence, instrument validation), methodological aspects (e.g., study design, sample size, population group), and measurement of PA/SB (e.g., self-report, device-based measures). The extraction template was pilot-tested on a random selection of studies to ensure clarity and comprehensiveness. Data synthesis was conducted qualitatively through thematic analysis, consistent with the objectives of a scoping review. Studies were categorized based on the thematic focus as identified during data extraction, including correlates of PA/SB, outcomes associated with PA/SB, prevalence rates, and validation of instruments used to measure PA/SB. This thematic framework facilitated a structured synthesis of findings across various dimensions of the research (Thomas & Harden, 2008). Quantitative synthesis was not the primary aim of this scoping review due to the heterogeneity of study designs and outcomes. However, basic descriptive statistics were computed to summarize study characteristics, such as frequencies and percentages. The data were tabulated to enhance clarity and accessibility, serving to highlight the distribution of research topics, populations, and methodologies within the existing body of literature (Peters et al., 2015). Given the nature of the scoping review, statistical analysis focused on descriptive statistics rather than inferential statistics. Frequencies and proportions were calculated to determine the representation of various research topics and methodological approaches within the included studies. Additionally, trends over time were explored by examining the number of publications per year, stratified by specific research themes. Subgroup analyses were performed to examine research focus differences across demographic segments, such as age groups and health conditions. These analyses aimed to illuminate potential areas of underrepresentation or overlooking in the existing literature (Tricco et al., 2016). The overarching goal of the statistical analysis was to provide a comprehensive overview of the research landscape, facilitating the identification of gaps and underexplored areas that warrant future research attention. This structured approach was integral to guiding the subsequent discussion and formulation of recommendations for future research endeavors in the context of PA and SB in Thailand. The systematic scoping review identified a total of 564 studies focusing on physical activity (PA) and sedentary behaviour (SB) in Thailand. From the 25,007 articles initially screened, these studies were selected based on their relevance to public health research, utilizing both quantitative and qualitative data, and were published in English or Thai. The breakdown of these studies revealed that a substantial majority, specifically 80%, investigated PA exclusively, while a smaller proportion of studies addressed SB alone (6.7%). A notable 13.3% of studies examined both PA and SB concurrently. This distribution highlights a predominant research focus on physical activity, with less emphasis on understanding sedentary behaviour as an independent factor. Diving deeper into the thematic focus of the included studies, the most common area of research was the examination of correlates of PA and SB, which constituted 58.9% of the studies. This category encompasses investigations into various societal, environmental, and individual factors influencing PA and SB, suggesting a strong research interest in understanding potential determinants and influencing factors. Studies examining the outcomes of PA and SB were the second most prevalent, making up 22.2% of the total. These studies primarily centered on the impact of PA and SB on health outcomes and overall wellbeing. Prevalence studies, which accounted for 12.4% of the reviewed literature, provided crucial insights into the levels of PA and SB within different demographic groups. Instrument validation studies comprised a minor proportion, at 3.2%, indicating less focus on evaluating the tools used for PA and SB measurement. The methodological design of the studies showcased a clear preference for cross-sectional approaches, which were employed in 69.3% of the research. This preference highlights the predominance of studies focused on snapshot assessments of PA and SB at specific points in time. Interventional studies, which constituted 19.7% of the included research, explored the efficacy of various PA and SB behavior change strategies, encompassing a wide range of interventions from community-based programs to individual-focused strategies. Longitudinal studies were the least represented, at a mere 2.8%, illustrating a gap in research that explores the causative relationships and temporal dynamics of PA and SB. Measurement techniques used across the studies were predominantly self-reporting methods, utilized in 94% of the research. These might have included surveys and questionnaires assessing participants' PA and SB levels, showcasing a reliance on subjective reporting. Objective measures, such as pedometers or accelerometers, were far less frequently employed, featuring in just 2.5% of studies. The research designs predominantly targeting subjective self-reports suggest potential limitations in data accuracy, emphasizing the need for increased usage of objective measures in future studies. In terms of population demographics, both sexes were represented in the majority of studies (82.5%), signaling an inclusive approach in terms of gender analysis. Adults constituted the principal focus group, represented in 51.1% of the total studies. This predominance suggests a significant emphasis on adult PA/SB patterns and determinants within the Thai context. Following adults, older adults (26.9%) and adolescents (15.7%) were commonly studied populations. Research targeting children was minimal, occurring in only 6.3% of the studies—a finding that underscores a crucial gap in understanding the PA and SB patterns and influences among younger populations in Thailand. Clinical populations were another focal point of interest, investigated in the context of PA and SB in 15.3% of the total studies. Among these, the studies most frequently targeted individuals with cardiovascular disease (22%), diabetes (21%), and hypertension (21%). This concentration on clinical populations aligns with the need to address PA and SB as modifiable risk factors

Graphene-encapsulated copper nanoparticles (GECNs) have been extensively studied in the last decades because of their noble physical and chemical properties [1]. The core-shell structure GECNs enables its application in harsh environments because the graphene shell structure prevents oxidation of copper nanoparticles. Potential applications for GECNs are in wood and wood-based composite for their fungus and insect protection [2], electrical engineering [3], biomedical industry [4], etc. GECNs have been synthesized via many processes, including chemical vapor deposition (CVD) [5]. However, the formed graphene layers still have defects, and efforts have been made to improve the quality of the graphene structure. Epitaxial growth of graphene under a hydrogen gas environment showed an impressive improvement in graphene structure quality [6]. Hydrogen firstly helps to build an active surface of carbon, which is crucial for the subsequent graphene growth. Hydrogen also acts as an etching agent to eliminate defective sites and facilitates the growth of large-scale graphene [7]. Surface pretreatment can eliminate high protrusions and produce a smooth surface of the substrate and restore the defects of the substrate [8,9]. Surface pretreatment can also help dissolve the native oxide and passivate the substrate surface during graphitization [10]. Introducing a physical barrier is another effective way to improve the graphene layer structure quality. The idea situation is that carbon atoms start to grow into graphene right after the maximum process temperature is reached. Introducing an Al2O3 barrier between carbon source and metal catalyst retards the carbon diffusion process and reduces the pre-growth of graphene before reaching the maximum process temperature. The onset of growth is at a higher temperature when the thickness of the Al2O3 barrier is larger [11]. The configuration of heating chamber and the placement of metal catalysts also affect graphene growth. The one-end-close configuration restricts the carbon gas flow and consequently generates homogeneous graphene. The placement of metal catalyst affects the concentration of trapped carbon gas and subsequently determines the number of graphene layers formed [12]. The quality of the graphene structure can also be improved by controlling the concentration of carbon sources and reducing the cooling rate during CVD synthesis [13]. The concentration of carbon sources is proportionally related to the number of graphene layers formed. Reducing the cooling rate largely decreases the nucleation sites of graphene and makes it possible to grow large domains of graphene. The synthesis of GECNs has been explained by different mechanisms. Recently, scientists have been inclined toward the dissolution–precipitation theory for metals with a large dissolution capacity for carbon, and toward the self-limiting theory for metals with a poor dissolution capacity for carbon, such as copper [14]. Polymers such as poly (methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), fluorine (C13H10), and sucrose (C12H22O11) can be solid carbon sources [15] for synthesizing GECNs. Limited literature was found related to the study of various factors on the formation of GECNs using lignin as a carbon source. Lignin is a byproduct from the pulp and paper industries and contains more than 60% carbon. Approximately 70 million tons of lignin are produced every year [16], mainly used as fuel. Lignin has many potential value-added applications, including the manufacture of carbon fibers and graphene [17]. It is known that the GECN properties such as surface morphology, structure, and crystallinity can be affected by many factors including the concentration of the copper catalyst [18] and the temperature [19]. However, the effect of the concentration of a copper catalyst on the GECN size distribution is unclear. Our previous study results [20] indicated that the formation of graphene layers surrounding copper nanoparticles can start at 400 °C. Copper nanoparticles were incompletely to near-completely shelled by graphene layers as temperature increased from 300 °C to 500 °C, and the graphene layers were formed by the self-limiting mechanism. This paper reports our continuing study on the effects of higher temperature levels (600–1000 °C) and the weight ratio of copper-to-lignin on GECN properties. In this study, the role that copper atoms play in the growth of graphene layers and the size distribution of GECNs was investigated. The relationships between temperature, the lignin degradation process, and the reconstruction of the graphene layers are also discussed here. Deionized water purified BioChoice Lignin (BCL-DI) (Domtar Corp., Plymouth, NC, USA) was used as the carbon source. The metal catalyst, copper sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO4·5H2O), and nitric acid (HNO3) for purification were procured from Sigma-Aldrich. Experiment #1 was a 3 × 2 factorial experiment with three replicates per combination to evaluate temperature effects on the crystallinity of formed GECNs. The two factors were temperature (600, 800, and 1000 °C) and copper-to-lignin weight (oven-dried) ratio (0:1 and 1:4). The second experiment evaluated the copper lignin weight ratio effect (1:1, 1:2, and 1:4) at 1000 °C on the crystallinity of GECNs. All Cu-lignin samples were mixed using the following procedure: 3.9 g of CuSO4·5H2O (1 part of Cu by weight) and 12 g of BCL-DI (4 parts of lignin by weight) were first dispersed in distilled water, then heated at 80 °C, and stirred for 12 h followed by 24 h oven drying at 103 °C. Finally, the dried Cu-lignin mixture was ground well in an agate mortar before thermal treatment. Two porcelain boats, each holding 1.5 g of Cu-lignin mixture, were placed into the heating area of a 50 mm diameter, an 810 mm long quartz tube electric furnace (Lindberg/Blue M 1200) (Thermo Scientific™, Pittsburgh, PA, USA) equipped with a temperature controller (Lindberg/Blue UTC 150). Before heating, the air in the system was excluded by flowing argon gas for 15 min at a flow rate of 1800 standard cubic centimeter per minute (sccm). Then, temperature was raised to the target temperature level at a ramping rate of 20 °C/min and held at that temperature for 30 min. The heated Cu-lignin sample was cooled down naturally to ambient temperature under an argon atmosphere, and then transferred to a desiccator over CaCl2. The final weight of each sample was recorded, and its yield was calculated. All thermally treated Cu-lignin samples were purified with 20% HNO3 before characterization. For each trial, 0.5 g of GECNs was dispersed into 30 mL 20% HNO3 solution in a 125 mL of conical flask. The suspension was then heated up to the boiling point and kept boiling and stirring for 30 min. The suspension was filtered by a membrane (pore size: 0.45 µm) (VWR, Radnor, PA, USA) and rinsed with 550 mL of deionized water. The residue was dried in the oven at 60 °C for 6 h and then 103 °C overnight, weighed again, and stored in a glass vial for characterization. X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra was obtained from the X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku SmartLab, The Woodlands, TX, USA) utilizing Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). The scanning range was from 10° to 90°, with a scan speed of 1°/min. Fourier Transform Infra-red Spectroscopy (FTIR) spectra of the powder samples were obtained using Thermo Scientific™ Nicolet™ iS™50 FT-IR Spectrometer (attenuated total reflection (ATR) probe). The spectra were recorded with 64 scans in the range of 4000–400 cm−1 and a resolution of 4 cm−1. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) characterization was completed on a JOEL JEM-2100F. First, the sample was dispersed into acetone and sonicated for 15 min. One drop of the suspension was then dripped onto a 300 mesh copper grid with lacey carbon film (Agar Scientific) and air-dried overnight before characterization. The size distribution of nanoparticles was analyzed with the ImageJ software [21]. A two-factor analysis of variance (ANOVA) general linear model (GLM) procedure was performed for Experiment #1 data to analyze the significances of two main effects and their interactions on carbonization yield. The protected least significant difference (LSD) multiple comparison procedure was performed to Experiment #2 data to analyze Cu-to-lignin weight ratio effects on carbonization yield and GECNs’ sizes. All statistical analyses were performed at the 5% significance level using SAS version 9.2 software (SAS, Cary, NC, USA). Y% = [(mma − mb) − (mmb − mb) × 64/416]/[(mmb − mb) × 256/416] × 100(1) where mma represents boat and sample mass after thermal treatment, mb represents boat mass, mmb represents boat and sample mass before thermal treatment, and 64/416 and 256/416 represent fractions of copper and carbon source in the mixture, respectively. The ANOVA results of Experiment #1 indicated that the two-factor interaction was not significant. Therefore, the main effect mean comparisons indicated that Cu-lignin mixtures had significantly higher carbonization yields than samples of lignin alone, which might imply that copper was not only decomposed the lignin, but also kept carbon in the mixture by forming graphene layers. This observation was supported by FTIR spectra (Figure 1), which indicated that when the Cu-lignin mixture was heated at 600 °C (Figure 1a), there were traceable oxygen-containing groups in the fingerprint region indicated by the aromatic C=O bond at 1700 cm−1 and the C–O–C bond at 1050 cm−1 [20]; however, weaker peak intensities of oxygen-containing groups were detected for pure BCL-DI lignin. These indicated that a faster degradation of BCL-DI lignin occurred and resulted in lower carbonization yields, while the addition of copper retarded the degradation process, i.e., a lower amount of lignin was decomposed into gases, thus resulting in higher carbonization yields. This is the same trend as reported previously [23]. The reason was that more copper enabled a higher amount of lignin to be oxidized into carbonaceous gases vaporizing during the redox process of reducing copper ions to atoms and rendering the loss of carbon material. Figure 2 shows the XRD spectra of samples with two different Cu-to-lignin weight ratios treated at 1000 °C. The thermally treated sample with a higher Cu-to-lignin weight ratio of 1:1 had much higher intensity peaks at Cu (111), Cu (200), and Cu (220), respectively, than those with a lower Cu-to-lignin ratio of 1:4. These indicated that a higher Cu-to-lignin weight ratio of 1:1 resulted in extra copper atoms uncovered by graphene layers and oxidized during HNO3 purification [12]. This implies that there is an optimum Cu-to-lignin weight ratio that will cause all copper nanoparticles to be shelled by graphene layers.
