The large-scale collection of personal data by online services, healthcare providers, retailers, and social platforms has made it possible to release or share databases that describe individual behavior in fine detail. Such releases are routinely justified by the claim that identifiers have been removed or replaced by pseudonyms. A growing body of evidence shows that this form of anonymization offers weak protection. Sweeney (2002) showed that a small number of quasi-identifiers, such as ZIP code, birth date, and sex, can single out most individuals in a population, which motivated formal notions such as k-anonymity. Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) later demonstrated that an anonymized release of movie ratings could be linked to public profiles on a separate platform using only a handful of approximate observations per user. They subsequently applied the same principle to social-network graphs (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2009). These studies show that privacy leakage is often not a property of a single dataset. It arises from the statistical dependence between the released data and auxiliary information available to an adversary. Differential privacy (Dwork, 2006; Dwork & Roth, 2014) provides guarantees that are robust to such side information, but it is not what is deployed in many practical data-sharing settings. A principled understanding of when de-anonymization is feasible therefore remains essential for assessing the risk of sharing data. Two broad lines of work address this question. The first is algorithmic and empirical: it designs heuristics that exploit similarity between records or neighborhoods in graphs and evaluates them on real data (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008, 2009; Ji et al., 2016). The second is information-theoretic: it asks, under a probabilistic model for the data, how much correlation is necessary and sufficient to align two databases. In graph settings, this approach has produced sharp thresholds for matching correlated Erdős–Rényi graphs (Pedarsani & Grossglauser, 2011; Cullina & Kiyavash, 2016; Korula & Lattanzi, 2014). For databases with feature vectors, Cullina, Mittal, and Kiyavash (2018) characterized the fundamental limits of alignment under a permutation model, and Dai et al. (2019) obtained analogous results for jointly Gaussian features. These results suggest that the mutual information between corresponding records is the natural quantity that governs matching, and that matching becomes possible once the number of attributes per record is large enough relative to the logarithm of the number of records. Existing analyses, however, typically rely on specific distributional assumptions, such as Gaussian features, Bernoulli or Erdős–Rényi structure, or independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) entries. These assumptions are convenient but often unrealistic. Real attributes such as time-stamped ratings, location traces, or sequential medical measurements are heterogeneous and temporally correlated, so models must permit richer dependence. This paper addresses that gap. We study the matching of two high-dimensional databases in which each row corresponds to a user and each column corresponds to an attribute. One database is released with its rows permuted by an unknown permutation, and the other serves as the adversary's auxiliary information. The relation between corresponding entries is described by an arbitrary joint distribution, and the dependence across the attributes of a given user is allowed to be non-i.i.d. Our central question is: under what conditions on the joint distribution and on the relative sizes of the database dimensions can an adversary recover the unknown permutation with vanishing probability of error, and when is this provably impossible? Answering this question for general distributions, rather than for isolated families, would yield a unified criterion for the privacy risk of correlated releases. Our approach rests on concentration of measure (Ledoux, 2001; Boucheron et al., 2013). When the number of attributes grows, empirical statistics of a pair of rows concentrate sharply around their expectations. This is the mechanism behind the asymptotic equipartition property and the notion of typicality used in the proofs of channel coding theorems (Cover & Thomas, 2006). We exploit it as follows. A pair of rows drawn from the same user is, with high probability, jointly typical with respect to the underlying distribution, whereas a pair of rows from different users is jointly typical only with exponentially small probability. This asymmetry suggests a matching scheme that declares a pair of rows to be a match when they are jointly typical, and then selects the permutation consistent with these declarations. A union bound over the competing permutations, combined with laws of large numbers for the relevant empirical averages, yields explicit conditions under which the scheme succeeds. This typicality-based strategy was introduced for pairs of correlated graphs by Shirani et al. (2019). Here we develop it for databases with general entry distributions. The contributions of this work are as follows. 1. A general matching scheme and achievability result. We propose a typicality-based matching scheme for databases whose entries follow an arbitrary joint distribution. We show that if the number of users grows at most exponentially in the number of attributes, with a growth rate strictly below a limiting information quantity of the source, then the scheme recovers the permutation with probability tending to one. For i.i.d. entries, this quantity is the mutual information between a pair of corresponding entries. 2. A matching converse. We prove that the achievability condition is tight. We identify a class of joint distributions for which, when the database growth rate exceeds the same information quantity, the probability of correct matching vanishes for any matching scheme. Together with the achievability result, this yields a sharp phase transition between the regimes where de-anonymization is feasible and infeasible. 3. Evaluation under specific models. We evaluate the conditions for i.i.d. databases, recovering known thresholds as special cases and thereby validating the general framework. We then treat Markovian database models, in which entries within a row are temporally correlated. The relevant threshold is an information rate expressed through the stationary distribution and transition kernel of the underlying chain. The analysis shows how memory in the data changes the number of attributes needed for reliable matching relative to an i.i.d. model with the same marginals. 4. A proof technique that extends beyond the cases treated. The analysis uses only typicality and laws of large numbers. It does not depend on closed-form likelihood computations or on specific parametric families, so it applies whenever the relevant empirical averages concentrate. We indicate how this opens the way to other dependence structures. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the database model and the notion of matching reliability. Section 3 presents the matching scheme and the achievability theorem. Section 4 proves the converse. Section 5 specializes the results to i.i.d. and Markov models, and Section 6 discusses implications and open problems. Database model. We consider two databases, D⁽¹⁾ and D⁽²⁾, each with m rows (users) and n columns (attributes). Row i of D⁽¹⁾ is Xi = (X{i1}, …, X{in}) ∈ 𝒳ⁿ. The corresponding row of the second database is Yi = (Y{i1}, …, Y{in}) ∈ 𝒴ⁿ. Alphabets 𝒳 and 𝒴 are finite. Rows of the pair (Xi, Yi) are independent across users. Within a row, the joint law is specified by a distribution p{X^nY^n}. This is the i.i.d. model, p{XY}ⁿ, when entries are independent across columns. It is a stationary Markov model when the column index is interpreted as time. This construction follows the stochastic database models used to study de-anonymization of correlated data (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008; Cullina, Mittal, & Kiyavash, 2018; Dai, Cullina, Kiyavash, & Grossglauser, 2019). The released database D⁽²⁾ is anonymized: its rows are permuted by an unknown permutation Θ drawn uniformly from the symmetric group Sm and independent of all data. The released rows are therefore Ỹ{Θ(i)} = Yi. The adversary observes D⁽¹⁾ (identified, for example, a public auxiliary dataset) and D⁽²⁾. The adversary knows the joint distribution of the entries and wants to recover Θ. A matching scheme is a map Θ̂(D⁽¹⁾, D⁽²⁾) ∈ Sm. We call the matching reliable if the per-user error probability Pe = maxi P(Θ̂(i) ≠ Θ(i)) tends to zero as n → ∞. The number of users grows exponentially with the number of attributes, m = mn = 2^{nR+o(n)}, where R > 0 is the database growth rate. The main object of study is the set of pairs (R, p{XY}) for which reliable matching is possible. Matching scheme. The scheme is a typicality-based decoder in the spirit of joint-typicality decoding in channel coding (Cover & Thomas, 2006; Csiszár & Körner, 2011). For a pair of sequences (xⁿ, yⁿ), let π{xⁿ,yⁿ}(a,b) = n⁻¹ Σk 1{xk = a, yk = b} denote the joint empirical distribution. Fix εn > 0. The pair is εn-typical with respect to p{XY} if |π{xⁿ,yⁿ}(a,b) − p{XY}(a,b)| ≤ εn p{XY}(a,b) for all (a,b) ∈ 𝒳×𝒴. We choose εn → 0 slowly enough that n εn² / log m → ∞, which makes the typicality threshold compatible with the exponential scaling of m. For the Markov models, typicality is defined on the empirical distribution of consecutive pairs ((xk, yk), (x{k+1}, y{k+1})), as in the method of types for Markov sources (Csiszár & Körner, 2011). The decoder proceeds in three steps. (i) For every row i of D⁽¹⁾ and every row j of D⁽²⁾, it computes the joint empirical distribution of (Xi, Ỹj) and tests typicality. (ii) If exactly one row j of D⁽²⁾ is jointly typical with row i, it sets Θ̂(i) = j. (iii) If there is no such row, or more than one, it declares an error for row i, which in practice is resolved by an arbitrary guess. The computational cost is O(m² n), dominated by the m² pairwise comparisons. Analysis of error events. For a given row i, an error requires one of two events. The first, E₁, is that the true pair (Xi, Yi) is not εn-typical. The second, E₂, is that some incorrect row j ≠ Θ(i) is jointly typical with Xi. We bound P(E₁) with concentration inequalities for the empirical distribution. For the i.i.d. model, each count π(a,b) is an average of n independent bounded variables. Hoeffding's inequality (Hoeffding, 1963) together with a union bound over |𝒳||𝒴| symbols gives P(E₁) ≤ 2|𝒳||𝒴| exp(−2nεn² pmin²), where pmin is the smallest positive entry of p{XY}. This is the weak law of large numbers in quantitative form. For Markov models, we use the corresponding concentration bounds for functions of ergodic finite-state chains and their mixing properties (Boucheron, Lugosi, & Massart, 2013), whose rate constants depend on the spectral gap of the chain. For E₂, the incorrect row Ỹj is independent of Xi and has the marginal law of Y. By standard properties of typical sets (Cover & Thomas, 2006), the probability that independent sequences are jointly εn-typical is at most 2^{−n(I(X;Y) − δ(εn))}, where δ(εn) → 0 as εn → 0. A union bound over the m − 1 incorrect rows gives P(E₂) ≤ m · 2^{−n(I(X;Y) − δ(εn))}. Substituting m = 2^{nR+o(n)} shows that P(E₂) → 0 whenever R < I(X;Y). The achievability condition is therefore expressed through the mutual information I(X;Y) in the i.i.d. case. In the Markov case, the single-letter mutual information is replaced by the mutual information rate, lim{n→∞} n⁻¹ I(Xⁿ;Yⁿ), which exists for the jointly stationary ergodic processes considered. Converse procedure. To establish tightness, we characterize a set of distributions for which no scheme can be reliable. We apply Fano's inequality (Fano, 1961; Cover & Thomas, 2006) to the unknown permutation. Because Θ is uniform on Sm, H(Θ) = log m! = m log m − O(m). Define the average error probability P̄e = m⁻¹ Σi P(Θ̂(i) ≠ Θ(i)), which is bounded above by Pe. By Fano's inequality applied to the individual labels, together with the data-processing inequality, I(Θ; D⁽¹⁾, D⁽²⁾) ≥ H(Θ) − m hb(P̄e) − m P̄e log m. Loss of an upper limb is a life-altering event that affects a person's ability to work, care for themselves, maintain relationships, and participate in leisure activities. The hand and arm are central to manipulation, tactile exploration, and non-verbal communication, so their absence produces disability well beyond the physical deficit. Population estimates suggest that more than a million people in the United States live with limb loss, and the figure is projected to more than double by mid-century as vascular disease and diabetes become more prevalent (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2008). Lower-limb amputation is mostly dysvascular in origin. Upper-limb loss, by contrast, is mainly traumatic and tends to occur in younger, working-age people, including those injured in industrial accidents, road traffic collisions, and armed conflict (Dillingham et al., 2002; Atkins et al., 1996). Because these individuals face decades of life with limb loss, the quality of their care has large functional, psychological, and socioeconomic consequences. Prosthetic fitting is the best-known intervention for upper-limb amputation. Available devices range from passive cosmetic restorations and body-powered hooks to myoelectric hands and, more recently, multi-articulating and pattern-recognition-controlled systems. Techniques such as targeted muscle reinnervation have increased the number of intuitive control signals available to people with high-level amputations (Kuiken et al., 2009). Even so, technological sophistication has not translated reliably into sustained use. Surveys and reviews across 25 years of literature report substantial rates of prosthesis rejection and abandonment, which are often attributed to discomfort, weight, poor functional return, and insufficient training (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Davidson, 2002). Satisfaction depends on factors beyond the device, including the timing of fitting, the quality of follow-up services, and how well the user is prepared to operate the prosthesis in daily life (Pezzin et al., 2004; McFarland et al., 2010). Comparative evidence on myoelectric and body-powered devices also shows that neither is uniformly superior, which suggests that the user's training and context matter at least as much as the component technology (Carey et al., 2015). This situation points to rehabilitation as a critical but under-examined part of the care pathway. Prosthetic rehabilitation is the structured, multidisciplinary process that begins at or before amputation and continues after definitive fitting. It typically includes pre-prosthetic care such as wound healing, edema control, desensitization, and maintenance of range of motion and strength. It then moves to training in muscle control and signal acquisition, followed by donning and doffing, controlled operation of the terminal device, and bimanual functional activities. Throughout, it addresses phantom sensation and pain, and the psychosocial adjustment needed to reintegrate into work and community roles (Smurr et al., 2008; Resnik et al., 2012). As prosthetic technology grows more complex, these needs become greater. Advanced devices place heavier cognitive and motor demands on users, and clinicians have noted that the evidence base for training approaches has not kept pace with engineering developments (Resnik et al., 2012). Several rehabilitation strategies have been proposed or tested. They include general conditioning programs, graded motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, mirror therapy, myoelectric training with biofeedback, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual reality or augmented reality environments in which users practice control before or alongside physical device use. Mirror therapy and related visual-feedback methods have been investigated mainly for phantom limb pain (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996; Chan et al., 2007), and recent work suggests that virtual and augmented reality combined with myoelectric pattern recognition can both improve control and relieve pain (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2016; Powell & Thakor, 2013). These approaches draw on different theoretical bases, including motor learning, cortical reorganization, and task-specific practice, and they are applied in many settings and at different times after amputation. The resulting literature is varied. Most studies are small case series or single-center studies with heterogeneous outcome measures, and descriptions of the content, intensity, and sequencing of training are often incomplete. This fragmentation limits both clinical practice and research. Clinicians who plan rehabilitation for a new upper-limb amputee lack a consolidated summary of which components have been tried, how they are delivered, and what outcomes they are associated with. Health systems that must decide how much to invest in therapy services, as opposed to devices alone, have little synthesized evidence on the added value of rehabilitation. Previous reviews have mostly examined prosthesis design, control strategies, or user acceptance and abandonment (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Carey et al., 2015). Others have focused on phantom limb pain interventions or on lower-limb amputation. To our knowledge, few have systematically examined the content of rehabilitation programs specifically for people with upper-extremity amputations or considered what this body of work implies about the importance of rehabilitation to successful prosthetic use. The present review addresses this gap. Its central question is: what rehabilitation protocols have been described for people with upper-extremity amputation who receive or are being prepared for a prosthesis, and what do they indicate about the value of structured rehabilitation for functional outcomes? Following the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009), we searched the literature systematically, applied explicit inclusion criteria, extracted data on intervention components, and assessed methodological quality. The review makes three contributions. First, it identifies and catalogs the components of upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation reported in the literature, including general exercise, motor tasks, phantom exercises, muscle training, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image and virtual reality exercises. This gives clinicians a consolidated reference. Second, it appraises the methodological quality of the available studies, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of the evidence and indicating where more rigorous trials are needed. Third, it argues that rehabilitation should be regarded as an integral part of prosthetic provision rather than an optional adjunct, with implications for service planning, clinical guidelines, and future research on upper-limb loss. Design and Reporting Framework This systematic review was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Statement 2009 (Moher et al., 2009). The review question was framed using the PICO structure: the population comprised individuals of any age with an acquired or congenital upper extremity amputation or limb deficiency; the intervention was any prosthetic rehabilitation program, including pre-prosthetic and prosthetic training; the comparator was an alternative rehabilitation approach, standard care, or no comparator in the case of single-group designs; and the outcomes were functional performance, prosthesis use, muscle control, pain, and related patient-reported measures. Because the aim was to describe and appraise the content and importance of rehabilitation protocols rather than to estimate a pooled treatment effect, a narrative synthesis was planned in advance. A formal protocol was not registered. Data Sources and Search Strategy A systematic literature search was performed to identify studies concerning prosthetic rehabilitation of the upper extremity. The electronic databases searched were PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, PEDro, and Google Scholar. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords linked with Boolean operators. Terms for the population included "upper extremity," "upper limb," "arm," "hand," "amputee," and "amputation"; terms for the intervention included "rehabilitation," "prosthesis," "prosthetic training," "myoelectric," "occupational therapy," "physical therapy," and "virtual reality." An example of the PubMed strategy was: ("upper extremity" OR "upper limb") AND (amputation OR amputee) AND (rehabilitation OR "prosthetic training" OR prosthesis). Search syntax was adapted to the indexing rules of each database. The reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant reviews were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies. No restriction was placed on year of publication up to the date of the final search, and only articles published in English were considered. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they (a) involved participants with upper extremity amputation or limb loss at any level, from partial hand to shoulder disarticulation; (b) examined a rehabilitation intervention directly connected with prosthetic fitting or use, whether delivered before, during, or after prosthesis provision; (c) reported at least one functional, physical, or patient-reported outcome; and (d) were original research published in a peer-reviewed journal. Randomized controlled trials, non-randomized trials, cohort studies, case series, and case reports were eligible. Studies were excluded if they concerned lower extremity amputation exclusively, addressed only surgical or purely technological aspects of prosthesis design without a rehabilitation component, were narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, or animal and laboratory studies, or if the full text was unavailable. Study Selection All records retrieved were exported to reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then obtained and assessed independently by the same reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted when consensus could not be reached. The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram that recorded the number of records identified, screened, excluded with reasons, and included. The initial search identified 620 records, of which nine studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were retained for data extraction. Data Extraction A standardized extraction form was developed and piloted on two studies before full use. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and discrepancies were reconciled by consensus. Extracted information included first author and year of publication, country, study design, sample size, participant characteristics (age, sex, amputation level, etiology, time since amputation), type of prosthesis (body-powered, myoelectric, or cosmetic), details of the rehabilitation protocol (components, content, frequency, duration, and setting), outcome measures, and principal findings. Particular attention was given to the specific components of each protocol, which were categorized inductively into general exercise programs, motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, Muscle Training System use, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education exercises, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image or virtual reality exercises. Where information was missing or unclear, it was recorded as not reported, and corresponding authors were not contacted. Assessment of Methodological Quality The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers. Because the included studies were expected to vary in design, the instrument was selected according to study type. Randomized and controlled trials were appraised with the PEDro scale, which scores eleven items related to eligibility, randomization, allocation concealment, baseline comparability, blinding, follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis, between-group comparisons, and point and variability measures (Maher et al., 2003). Case series and case reports were appraised with the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Studies were then classified as being of high, moderate, or low quality according to the proportion of criteria satisfied. Risk of bias judgments were considered when interpreting results, but quality scores were not used as a basis for excluding studies, since the number of eligible studies was small. Inter-rater agreement was examined during the process, and disagreements were resolved by discussion. Data Synthesis and Statistical Analysis Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity was anticipated and subsequently confirmed with respect to participant characteristics, amputation levels, prosthesis types, rehabilitation content, intervention length, and outcome measures. For this reason, a quantitative meta-analysis was judged inappropriate, and no pooled effect estimates, forest plots, or formal statistical tests of heterogeneity or publication bias were calculated. Instead, a structured narrative synthesis was undertaken. Study characteristics and results were tabulated, and findings were grouped according to the type of rehabilitation component and the outcome domain addressed. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages, were used to summarize the number of studies by design, quality category, and protocol component. Where original studies reported effect sizes, means, standard deviations, or p values, these were reported as published without reanalysis. The consistency of direction of findings across studies was considered in drawing conclusions regarding the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation, and the limitations in the strength of evidence arising from small samples and variable study quality were taken into account in the interpretation. Study selection The electronic search identified 620 records. After screening of titles and abstracts and assessment of full texts against the eligibility criteria, 9 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were retained for data extraction (9/620; 1.5%) [S1–S9]. The selection process followed the PRISMA 2009 flow diagram. The remaining 611 records (98.5%) were excluded because they were duplicates, were unrelated to the upper extremity, or did not describe a prosthetic rehabilitation programme. In response to demographic ageing and its consequences, European governments aim to increase labour market participation of older workers and have started to expand the state pension age beyond age 65. In this context, research has established solid evidence on determinants of employment participation in older ages, including contextual factors (e.g. tax incentives) (Börsch-Supan et al. 2009; Gruber and Wise 1999; Wise 2010) and a number of individual characteristics, such as work and employment conditions. Results of this research are instrumental, as they help to identify aspects that predict retirement behaviour, and thus, help to develop measures to promote extended working lives. However, most studies are based on occupational cohorts, often recruited from specific occupational groups during midlife. In these studies, baseline factors of working populations are usually linked to the likelihood of retirement during a follow-up period. This has an important drawback for existing knowledge, and in particular, about the work and employment conditions of people working beyond the state pension age. Specifically, because information on employment and working conditions refers to midlife, less is known about the working conditions people actually have at work beyond the state pension age. A person’s decision to work beyond the state pension age may, however, also be related to his or her conditions at work beyond state pension age. In other words, much research exists on those aspects in midlife that are prospectively linked with premature exits from the labour market, but comparatively little is known about people working longer, and about their working and employment conditions. Using wave 4 data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), the present paper, describes employment and working conditions of employed men and women aged 65 or older. In addition, we compare conditions of older workers with those which retired people in the same age group had in their last job. Besides socio-demographic factors (e.g. partnership situation, material circumstances) and health (both physical and mental), the focus is on employment conditions (e.g. self-employment, occupational position) as well as psychosocial stress at work. The latter will be measured in terms of two theoretical models of work stress, the demand-control model (Karasek and Theorell 1990) and the effort-reward imbalance model (Siegrist et al. 2004) (see Methods for details). But before presenting our analyses, the next section will briefly summarise how the above mentioned factors (sociodemographic factors, health and working conditions) have previously been related to labour market participation in older age (for a detailled review see: Hasselhorn and Wenke 2015). Sociodemographic characteristics include sex, partnership situation, parenthood, educational qualifications and economic circumstances. For example, women or people in a partnership seem more likely to have shorter employment histories than men or people not in a partnership (Kubicek et al. 2010; Lund and Villadsen 2005; Majeed et al. 2015; Wahrendorf 2015). In addition, high educational qualifications and advantaged economic circumstances were linked to later retirement (Komp et al. 2010). Secondly, health was linked to labour market participation, mostly because people in poor health claim disability pension (Harkonmäki et al. 2006; Leijten et al. 2015; Van Den Berg et al. 2010; van Rijn et al. 2014; Virtanen et al. 2014). This concerns a variety of chronic diseases, as well as mental and physical health functioning. A third important factor related to extended working lives refers t0 the workplace itself including work and employment conditions (van Solinge and Henkens 2014). For example, working in disadvantaged occupations (in particular elementary manual occupations with high physical demands) was linked to earlier retirement (Lain and Vickerstaff 2014), and bridge employment (Dingemans et al. 2016). Studies have also shown that self-employed people tend to have an extended working life (McNair et al. 2004), and that people reduce working time when they age (Nikolova and Graham 2014). Additionally, there is growing evidence that psychosocial working conditions are linked to early retirement. Specifically, evidence exists for high psychosocial demands, low control at work and low reward (Blekesaune and Solem 2005; Canivet et al. 2012; Carr et al. 2015; de Wind et al. 2014; Elovainio et al. 2005; Hintsa et al. 2015; Juvani et al. 2014; Laine et al. 2009; Robroek et al. 2013; Schnalzenberger et al. 2014; Siegrist and Wahrendorf 2011; Van Den Berg et al. 2010). Yet, in each of these studies psychosocial working conditions refer to midlife, and thus, conditions of older workers remain less explored. In summary, the current study has two objectives: (a) a description of men and women working beyond state pension age, including their health, employment and working conditions, and (b) the comparison of health, employment and working conditions with retired in the same age group. We use data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE, Release 5.0) collected between 2004 and 2012 across 16 European countries (Börsch-Supan et al. 2013b). SHARE is the first cross-national, longitudinal research project collecting data on a variety of social, economic and health-related topics among nationally representative samples of older adults. The survey started 2004–2005 in eleven countries (Sweden, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Switzerland, Austria, Italy, Spain and Greece), with on-going waves of data collection in two-year intervals. Two new countries joined SHARE in wave 2 (the Czech Republic and Poland) and four in wave 4 (Estonia, Hungary, Portugal and Slovenia), while Greece left SHARE at this point. In contrast to remaining waves, wave 3 of SHARE consists of a separate retrospective assessment of respondents’ previous life, with limited information on current information only (also called SHARELIFE). Although more recent data (wave 5, 2012–2013) of SHARE exists, we use wave 4 data (collected 2010–2012) and earlier, because information on current working conditions was not collected in wave 5 (only among new cohort members and newly employed people). In each country, the initial sample is based on probability household samples where people above 50 years were interviewed plus their (possibly younger) partners in the household using Computer Assisted Personal Interviews (CAPI). At wave 1 the average household response rate was 62 % (with rates above 50 % in 8 out of 11 countries), 61 % in countries that joined SHARE in wave 2 and 56 % in wave 4. This is above average compared with other European surveys, and it corresponds to the observed general decline in survey participation over the past years both in Europe and worldwide. Notably, the sample size of SHARE increased substantially in wave 4, both because four new countries entered SHARE for the first time and because a large refreshment sample was drawn in countries that were already part of the survey. This not only includes respondents from younger cohorts (so called “refreshers” to maintain population representation), but also a new sample across the full age range, in order to increase the sample size (Malter and Börsch-Supan 2013). In terms of panel attrition, the average percentage of respondents lost between the waves was below 20. More details about SHARE and its methods are available online (www.share-project.org) or described elsewhere (Börsch-Supan et al. 2013a; Malter and Börsch-Supan 2013). We restrict the sample to older men and women aged 65 years or older. This includes working people who answered that “employed or self-employed” best describes their current job situation and those who declared themselves “retired”. Then, we exclude people above the age of 80 because they may have particular work situations (e.g. working in a family run business). This results in a total sample of 8751 women and 8874 men (n = 17,625). Sociodemographic variables: In addition to sex and age, we include wealth, education and partnership situation. Wealth is based on household total net worth, both including financial wealth (savings, net stock value, mutual funds and bonds) and housing wealth (value of primary residence, other real estates, own business share and cars). For the analyses, we adjusted for household size in accordance with the OECD equivalent-scale, and thereafter calculated country-specific quartiles for the final sample (very low, low, high, very high). Because our wealth measure is based on accumulated savings and not on direct income, it may be more appropriate for older populations as an indicator of financial circumstances. Education is measured according to the International Standard Classification of Educational Degrees (ISCED-97) that we regroup into “low education” (pre-primary, primary or lower secondary education), “medium education” (secondary or post-secondary education), and “high education” (first and second stage of tertiary education). In the case of partnership, we use a binary indicator of whether the respondents lives with a partner or not (regardless the marital status). Work and employment conditions: In sum, we use five measures to investigate work and employment conditions. In addition to employment status, occupational position and years in job, these are working hours and psychosocial work stress. For those who are employed, conditions refer to the current job. For those who are retired, we use information on the last job before entering retirement. In case persons participated for the first time in wave 4, this information was collected retrospectively. In the cases where people participated and worked in previous waves, this information is recovered from previous waves. Employment status: We distinguish between “employers” (self-employed with employees), “self-employed” who work on their own account (self-employed without employees), and salaried “employees” who are employed by an individual or an organisation. This corresponds to the primary classification scheme of the European Socio-economic Classification (ESeC) (Rose and Harrison 2007). Occupational position: As an indicator of occupational position, we regroup jobs into three categories based on the 10 major groups of International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-88), developed by the International Labour Office (ILO 1990): “Managers and professionals” (groups 1 & 2, e.g. Director, chief executive, or health professional) “Other skilled workers” (major groups 3–8 & 10, e.g. medical assistant, cook or crane operator) and “Elementary occupations” (major group 9, e.g. cleaner, watchman or street vendor). Years in job: To assess years in job, we calculate how long the respondent has already worked in his or her job (for those employed), or the number of years spent in the last job (for those retired). Working hours: We use the self-reported total hours worked per week. For retired people, however, a retrospective assessment of working hours in the last job was not conducted in the survey (possibly due to recall bias). Information, therefore, could only be recovered for those retired people who participated and worked during previous waves, which results in a smaller subsample of retired people with information on working hours. Psychosocial work stress: We use two measures of psychosocial work stress, that rely on the original questionnaires of two prominent theoretical models of work stress: the demand-control (Karasek and Theorell 1990), and the effort-reward imbalance model (Siegrist et al. 2004). The former model identifies stressful work in terms of high demands in combination with low control, whereas the latter model measures stressful environment in terms of an imbalance between high efforts spent at work and low rewards received in turn. Both work stress models cover different, but equally relevant, aspects of the workplace, where lack of control and reward frustration matter most. The restrictions of a multi-disciplinary approach, though, meant it was not possible to include the full questionnaires of the two models. Therefore, SHARE includes abbreviated versions of original scales, where items that cover the core dimensions of the two models were selected on the basis of psychometric properties. For the demand-control model, the measurement was restricted to the control dimension as a core dimension that showed the highest predictive power (e.g. Marmot et al. 1997). This was measured by the sum score of two Likert-scale items, ranging from 2 to 8, with higher scores indicating lower control at work. To measure effort-reward imbalance, we use 2 out of 6 items to measure ‘effort’ and 5 out of 11 items to assess ‘reward’ at work. ‘Effort-reward imbalance’ was then calculated by dividing the sum score of the ‘effort’ items (nominator) though the sum score of the ‘reward’ items (adjusted for number of items; denominator). 1 Introduction Graphs are a natural abstraction for social, biological, and information systems, and many of them are now very large. Facebook reports billions of users, and bibliographic databases such as DBLP index millions of authors and publications. A recurring task on such graphs is to find communities, which are groups of vertices that are densely connected internally and share common characteristics (Girvan and Newman 2002; Fortunato 2010). Traditional community detection (CD) partitions an entire graph and is therefore costly on large networks. It also produces communities that are not tailored to any particular user. Community search (CS) addresses both limitations. Given a query vertex q, CS finds a cohesive subgraph containing q, usually online and without examining the whole graph (Sozio and Gionis 2010; Cui et al. 2014; Fang et al. 2020). Personalized communities of this kind support product advertisement, social event recommendation, and the discovery of functional modules in protein interaction networks (Huang et al. 2014; Fang et al. 2016). Structural cohesiveness is typically expressed through minimum-degree constraints. Under the k-core model (Seidman 1983; Batagelj and Zaversnik 2003), every vertex in the community has at least k neighbors inside it. Stronger models include the k-truss (Huang et al. 2014; Huang and Lakshmanan 2017), the k-clique, and the k-edge-connected component. These approaches use only topology, so the communities they return can be internally dense yet semantically incoherent. A hub vertex with many weak ties may be placed in a community that shares no theme with its members. Recent work has therefore used vertex attributes. Attributed community queries return subgraphs whose members share a set of keywords (Fang et al. 2016; Fang et al. 2017), and related models consider numerical attributes or geographical locations. These models treat attributes as a flat set of independent labels. In many real networks, however, the labels attached to a vertex are organized hierarchically. In bibliographic networks, an author's research interests can be mapped onto the ACM Computing Classification System, where "Machine learning" is a specialization of "Computing methodologies." In biomedical networks, genes and proteins are annotated with Gene Ontology terms (Ashburner et al. 2000), and publications are indexed with Medical Subject Headings. Online retailers and social platforms organize items and user interests into category trees. We call a graph whose vertices carry such hierarchical labels a profiled graph, and the label hierarchy attached to a vertex its P-tree. This is a rooted subtree of a global taxonomy. Because a P-tree contains a label together with the ancestors that generalize it, two vertices can share a meaningful theme even if they have no identical leaf-level labels. For example, one author may work on "deep learning" and another on "support vector machines". Both are connected through the shared ancestor "machine learning," which a flat keyword model cannot capture. This observation exposes a gap in existing work. Structure-only CS ignores semantics entirely. Keyword-based CS can only match identical labels and therefore misses communities whose members are related at different granularities. It also cannot report how specific the shared theme is. Existing methods return a community with a flat set of shared labels, whereas a user exploring a profiled graph often needs to know the maximal common subtree of the members' P-trees. That subtree describes the community's theme at the most informative level of detail. In a preliminary study on a DBLP-derived graph with ACM-CCS profiles, k-core communities containing a given author had on average only 1.3 common labels at depth two or deeper in the taxonomy. This suggests that structurally cohesive communities are often thematically loose. In this paper, we study the profiled community search (PCS) problem. Given a profiled graph G, a query vertex q, and an integer k, PCS returns subgraphs that satisfy two conditions. They are structurally cohesive, meaning each vertex has degree at least k within a connected subgraph containing q. They are also semantically cohesive, meaning their vertices share a common subtree of P-trees that is maximal and contains the P-tree structure rooted at the taxonomy's root. Each answer is thus a profiled community (PC) paired with its shared theme, represented as a maximal common subtree. We ask three questions. Can hierarchical profiles yield communities that are more cohesive and more interpretable than those from structure-only and keyword-based CS? Can PCS be solved exactly at the scale of real networks? Can it be answered online, at interactive latencies? PCS poses several challenges. The number of candidate subtrees of a P-tree grows exponentially with its size, so enumerating every subtree and testing it for a qualifying k-core is infeasible. A naive algorithm that does this required hours on graphs with only tens of thousands of vertices in our experiments. Moreover, the subtree space has a structure that flat-set approaches cannot exploit directly. A candidate subtree must be rooted, so that a label can only be included if all its ancestors are included. Pruning rules designed for itemset lattices must therefore be adapted to tree-shaped candidates. Finally, because different query vertices induce different search spaces, a practical solution should rely on a reusable index instead of recomputation for every query. We make the following contributions. 1. Problem formulation. We introduce the PCS problem and formalize profiled graphs, P-trees, and profiled communities. We show that the maximal common subtree semantics yield themed communities at a granularity that adapts to the data, and we analyze their basic properties, including anti-monotonicity of the k-core with respect to subtree inclusion. This property underlies our pruning strategies. 2. Index and algorithms. We design the CP-tree, a compact index that organizes the vertices of G by their labels over the taxonomy and stores, for each node, the core numbers needed to retrieve candidate vertex sets. On top of it we develop a basic query algorithm that traverses candidate subtrees level by level, together with advanced algorithms that use anti-monotonicity and vertex-set intersection to avoid verifying most candidates. We also give an efficient index construction method, and we analyze the time and space complexity of all procedures. 3. Effectiveness evaluation. We evaluate PCS on five real graphs, including DBLP and a PubMed-based biomedical network. We measure community quality using structural measures such as density and clustering coefficient, and semantic measures such as label-based similarity and the depth of the shared theme. PCS communities consistently outperform those from k-core, k-truss, and keyword-based CS. For instance, on DBLP they have on average 2.1 times the number of shared labels of structure-only communities, and their shared themes lie 1.8 levels deeper in the taxonomy. A case study of well-known researchers shows that PCS separates an author's distinct research areas into different, interpretable communities that other approaches merge. 4. Efficiency evaluation. Our index-based algorithms are two to three orders of magnitude faster than the naive approach. They answer queries on graphs with over one million vertices in under a second on average, which supports online use. The CP-tree can be built in minutes and has a space overhead proportional to the total size of the vertex P-trees, which makes it practical for large profiled graphs. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 formally defines the PCS problem. Section 4 presents the CP-tree index and the query algorithms. Section 5 reports experimental results, and Section 6 concludes the paper. Problem formulation. We model a profiled graph as an undirected graph G(V, E) in which each vertex v ∈ V is associated with a profile P(v), a rooted subtree of a global concept hierarchy T (for example, the ACM Computing Classification System or the Medical Subject Headings, MeSH). A profile is closed under ancestors: if a label belongs to P(v), so do all of its ancestors up to the root. This property allows the set of labels of a vertex to be treated as a rooted subtree, which we call a P-tree. The common P-tree of a vertex set S is the intersection of the P-trees of its members. It is itself a rooted subtree and is therefore well defined. Cohesiveness is measured by the minimum-degree criterion, which underlies the k-core (Seidman, 1983) and has been widely adopted in community search (Sozio & Gionis, 2010; Fang et al., 2016; Fang et al., 2017). Given a query vertex q and an integer k, a profiled community is a connected subgraph Gq ⊆ G that (i) contains q, (ii) has minimum degree at least k, and (iii) has a maximal common P-tree. Maximality means that no connected k-core containing q shares a strictly larger common P-tree. The profiled community search (PCS) problem returns all such pairs (Gq, M), where M is the maximal common P-tree of Gq. Several incomparable maximal subtrees may exist, so a query can return several communities, each characterized by a different theme. Datasets. We evaluated PCS on four real profiled graphs (Table 1). Flickr contains users linked by friendship, with profiles built from image tags mapped to a taxonomy of visual concepts. DBLP is a co-authorship network in which author profiles are derived from the ACM Computing Classification System tags of their publications. PubMed is a co-authorship network whose profiles are based on MeSH headings. DBpedia is an entity-relationship network whose entities are labeled with ontology classes. The graphs ranged from 0.9 million to 8.2 million vertices and from 5.4 million to 51 million edges. Average profile sizes ranged from 7.3 to 18.6 labels, and the hierarchies had depths of 4 to 11 levels. We removed self-loops and duplicate edges, retained only the largest connected component, and discarded vertices with empty profiles. Each profile was then completed with all ancestor labels to ensure the subtree property. We also generated synthetic profiled graphs by attaching random subtrees of a fixed hierarchy to the vertices of Barabási–Albert graphs, which let us vary graph size and profile size independently in the scalability experiments. Query workload. For each dataset we sampled 200 query vertices uniformly at random from those with core number at least 6 (Batagelj & Zaversnik, 2003), so that nontrivial communities exist for the default parameter k = 6. We also varied k from 4 to 8 in the sensitivity analysis. All reported figures are means over the workload unless stated otherwise. Baseline algorithm. The anti-monotone structure of the problem motivates a level-wise search in the spirit of Apriori (Agrawal & Srikant, 1994). If a P-tree T′ is shared by a k-core containing q, every subtree of T′ rooted at the root is also shared by that k-core. The basic algorithm therefore starts from the single-node tree consisting of the root. At each iteration it expands every feasible tree by one leaf label, taken from a child of an existing node that also appears in P(q), and generates candidate trees whose sub-trees were all feasible. Feasibility of a candidate T′ is verified by restricting G to the vertices whose profiles contain T′, computing the k-core, and checking whether q lies in its connected component. The process terminates when no candidate survives, and the feasible trees from the last non-empty level are the maximal common P-trees. Although correct, this approach repeatedly traverses the graph and repeats subtree-containment tests, and its cost grows quickly with profile size and hierarchy depth. CP-tree index. To support online queries, we developed the compressed profile tree (CP-tree) index. It is constructed by merging the label hierarchy with the k-core decomposition of G. For each label x in T, let Vx be the set of vertices whose profiles contain x, and let G[Vx] be the induced subgraph. Because G[Vx] ⊆ G[Vy] whenever y is an ancestor of x, the induced subgraphs are nested along every root-to-leaf path. This allows the core decomposition of G[Vx] to be stored incrementally. Each CP-tree node stores the label x and a compressed list of vertices with their core numbers in G[Vx], and a vertex is stored only at the deepest node on each path where its core number changes. A query for (q, k, T′) then retrieves the connected k-core of q in G[V{T′}] from the index without scanning

Panic disorder is a common and burdensome anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, persistent concern about further attacks or their consequences, and often maladaptive behavioral changes such as avoidance of situations associated with feared bodily sensations (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Population-based surveys estimate lifetime prevalence at roughly 2% to 5% and 12-month prevalence at around 2% to 3%, depending on the diagnostic criteria and region (Kessler et al., 2005; Wittchen et al., 2011). Panic disorder typically begins in early adulthood and, if untreated, tends to follow a chronic or relapsing course. It is associated with marked functional impairment, reduced quality of life, high rates of comorbid depression and agoraphobia, and substantial healthcare utilization, particularly in primary and emergency care settings (Roy-Byrne et al., 2006; Wittchen et al., 2011). Effective and widely accessible treatment is therefore a public health priority. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the best-established psychological treatment for panic disorder. Its core components include psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic misinterpretations of bodily sensations, interoceptive exposure, and in vivo exposure to avoided situations. Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) consistently report large effects of CBT relative to waitlist and other inactive controls, as well as durable gains at follow-up (Mitte, 2005; Otte, 2011). A network meta-analysis of psychological therapies for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia likewise found CBT-based approaches, especially those including exposure, to be superior to many comparators (Pompoli et al., 2016). Clinical guidelines in several countries accordingly recommend CBT as a first-line treatment, alongside pharmacotherapy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Despite this evidence, most people with panic disorder never receive adequate care. Epidemiological data from the World Mental Health Surveys show that only a minority of individuals with anxiety disorders receive minimally adequate treatment, with the shortfall most pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (Kohn et al., 2004; Alonso et al., 2018). Even in high-income health systems, access to therapists trained in evidence-based CBT is constrained by workforce shortages, long waiting times, and geographic disparities. At the individual level, stigma, cost, time constraints, limited mental health literacy, and reluctance to engage in face-to-face exposure exercises further hinder help-seeking (Andrade et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2004). Closing this treatment gap requires delivery models that are scalable and flexible while retaining the active ingredients of CBT. Internet-delivered psychological treatments have been proposed as one such model. These interventions deliver structured therapeutic content, typically in modular form, via web-based platforms or, more recently, mobile applications, and often combine text, audio, video, and interactive exercises with homework assignments and self-monitoring. They can be accessed at any time and place, may reduce therapist time per patient, and may lower the threshold for seeking help because of their anonymity and convenience (Andersson & Titov, 2014). Meta-analytic evidence indicates that Internet-delivered CBT can produce clinically meaningful improvements across anxiety disorders and, in some trials, outcomes comparable to those of face-to-face treatment (Andrews et al., 2010; Olthuis et al., 2016). For panic disorder specifically, early trials showed that therapist-supported Internet-based CBT could achieve effects similar to those of live therapy (Carlbring et al., 2005), and subsequent studies have examined a growing range of formats. Several features distinguish current internet-delivered treatments and may influence both their effectiveness and their feasibility in routine care. First, the degree and type of human support vary substantially, from regular individualized therapist feedback, to minimal or on-demand contact, to fully self-guided programs with no personal contact. Reviews across mental disorders suggest that guided interventions generally yield larger effects and better adherence than unguided formats, although the differences are smaller when support is brief or administrative in nature (Baumeister et al., 2014; Johansson & Andersson, 2012). Because therapist time is the main cost driver of guided programs, the question of how much guidance is necessary is central to implementation. Second, treatment approaches differ in scope. Disorder-specific programs target the maintaining mechanisms of panic disorder directly, whereas transdiagnostic programs address common processes across anxiety and mood disorders and may therefore suit patients with comorbidity or diagnostic uncertainty, as well as services seeking to offer a single flexible program (Newby et al., 2015). Third, theoretical orientation is no longer confined to CBT, as alternative frameworks such as psychodynamic or acceptance-based approaches are being adapted for online delivery. Efficacy under trial conditions does not guarantee real-world benefit. The potential of internet-delivered treatments depends equally on their acceptability to users and providers, commonly operationalized through attrition, adherence to treatment modules, and treatment satisfaction. Dropout and nonusage are persistent problems in digital health, a phenomenon described as the "law of attrition" (Eysenbach, 2005). Attrition and adherence rates vary widely across trials and are influenced by program design, support, and participant characteristics (Christensen et al., 2009; Kelders et al., 2012). Moreover, uptake outside research settings is limited by skepticism among both the public and health professionals, concerns about the therapeutic relationship, data security, and suitability for severe or complex presentations (Apolinário-Hagen et al., 2018; Andersson & Titov, 2014). Because clinicians often act as gatekeepers who recommend, prescribe, or integrate digital programs into stepped-care pathways, they need a clear and current overview of which formats work, for whom, and with what level of user engagement. The existing evidence syntheses only partly meet this need. Many reviews pool findings across anxiety disorders or across mental disorders in general, which can obscure differences between diagnostic groups (Andrews et al., 2010; Olthuis et al., 2016). Panic disorder has distinctive treatment components, particularly interoceptive exposure, whose translation into unsupervised digital formats may pose particular challenges. In addition, the field has developed rapidly: newer trials have tested self-guided and transdiagnostic programs, compared different support intensities, and examined alternatives to CBT. These developments have not been summarized with a dual focus on clinical effectiveness and acceptability indicators specific to panic disorder. Consequently, little is known about the relative usefulness of different support formats and treatment approaches in this population. To address this gap, the present narrative review synthesizes recent RCT evidence on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder. We pursued two overarching questions. First, how efficacious are internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder compared with control conditions, and do outcomes differ according to the format of support (e.g., guided versus self-guided) or the treatment approach (e.g., disorder-specific versus transdiagnostic)? Second, how acceptable are these interventions, as reflected in attrition, adherence, and participant satisfaction? We restricted the review to trials published within the past five years to capture the current generation of programs and to reflect technological and methodological developments in the field. This review contributes in three ways. It provides a panic disorder-specific update on the efficacy of internet-delivered treatments, complementing broader anxiety-focused syntheses. It systematically contrasts support formats and treatment approaches that are directly relevant to decisions about implementation in routine and stepped care. Finally, it integrates efficacy data with indicators of acceptability, thereby identifying where the evidence is strong, where it is limited, and which research priorities, such as improving uptake and identifying moderators of outcome, should guide future trials. Design We conducted a narrative review of recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder. A narrative synthesis was chosen over a quantitative meta-analysis because the interventions, support formats, comparison conditions, and outcome measures were expected to be too heterogeneous to pool meaningfully (Popay et al., 2006). The literature search and reporting followed the structure of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) where applicable to a narrative format. The review was not prospectively registered. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they (a) were RCTs published in English-language peer-reviewed journals between 10 December 2012 and 12 December 2017; (b) included adult participants (≥18 years) with a primary diagnosis of panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia, established according to DSM-IV, DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), or ICD-10 criteria, ideally by a structured or semi-structured clinical interview; (c) evaluated a psychological treatment delivered predominantly via the internet (e.g., web-based or browser-based programs, including those accessed on mobile devices), irrespective of whether therapist guidance was provided; and (d) reported at least one symptom-related outcome for panic disorder, such as panic frequency or severity, agoraphobic avoidance, or general anxiety symptoms. No restrictions were placed on the theoretical orientation of the intervention, the type of support (self-guided, minimally guided, or therapist-guided), or the comparison condition. Eligible comparators included waitlist, attention or placebo controls, treatment as usual, face-to-face therapy, and alternative internet-delivered programs. Transdiagnostic or disorder-specific programs were both considered, provided that outcome data were reported for participants with panic disorder or the trial sample was defined by this diagnosis. We excluded study protocols, uncontrolled or non-randomized trials, secondary or follow-up analyses that did not report new data on efficacy or acceptability, conference abstracts, dissertations, and studies conducted exclusively with children or adolescents. Interventions that used the internet only as an adjunct to face-to-face treatment (e.g., therapist-delivered sessions supplemented by online homework) or delivered only by telephone or videoconference without a structured online program were also excluded. Trials of pharmacological or purely psychoeducational information websites without a therapeutic component were not considered. Information Sources and Search Strategy A systematic search was performed in PubMed/Medline and PSYNDEX, which together cover biomedical and German- and English-language psychological literature. The search covered the period from 10 December 2012 to 12 December 2017, thereby reflecting the most recent five years of research in this rapidly developing field. The search string combined terms for the condition (“panic disorder” OR “panic attack” OR “agoraphobia”), the mode of delivery (“internet” OR “online” OR “web-based” OR “computer” OR “digital” OR “e-health” OR “mobile”), and the study design (“randomized controlled trial” OR “randomised” OR “RCT” OR “controlled trial”). Controlled vocabulary (Medical Subject Headings in PubMed/Medline) was combined with free-text terms in titles and abstracts, and the strategy was adapted to the syntax of each database. In addition, we conducted a hand search by screening the reference lists of included articles and of recent reviews and meta-analyses on internet-delivered treatments for anxiety disorders (e.g., Andersson et al., 2014; Olthuis et al., 2016) to identify trials not captured by the database search. Study Selection Records were exported to a reference management program, and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria, and the full texts of potentially relevant articles were subsequently retrieved and assessed in detail. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented. Disagreements or uncertainties regarding eligibility were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached. Where multiple publications reported on the same trial, the primary outcome paper was used as the main source and complemented with information from related publications. Data Extraction Data were extracted using a standardized form. For each study, we recorded the authors, year of publication, country, sample size, and participant characteristics (mean age, proportion of women, diagnostic procedure, and comorbidity criteria). Intervention characteristics included the theoretical approach (e.g., Cognitive Behavioral Therapy [CBT] versus other approaches), the specificity of the content (disorder-specific versus transdiagnostic), program duration in weeks, number of modules, and the type and amount of human support (self-guided, minimal guidance, or therapist guidance, and whether support was provided via email, telephone, or a messaging platform). We also extracted information on the comparison condition, the primary and secondary outcome measures, the timing of assessments (post-treatment and follow-up), and the analytic approach (intention-to-treat versus completer analyses). Outcomes Efficacy was defined as the superiority of an internet-delivered intervention over a control condition, or differences between active treatment formats, on measures of panic symptoms. These included, for example, the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Shear et al., 1997), the Body Sensations Questionnaire, the Agoraphobic Cognitions Questionnaire, and the Mobility Inventory (Chambless et al., 1984, 1985), as well as broader anxiety and depression measures when reported. Where available, between-group effect sizes (Cohen’s d or Hedges’ g) were extracted as reported by the authors, with values of approximately 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 interpreted as small, moderate, and large, respectively (Cohen, 1988).
