Introduction The growing recognition of health disparities across the globe has placed an increasing demand on institutions of higher learning to contribute significantly to global health equity. Universities, as centers of knowledge creation and dissemination, hold a unique position to address these disparities through research and innovation. Historically, however, the health needs of the world's impoverished populations have been insufficiently prioritized in academic research (Barder, 2013). The World Health Organization has consistently emphasized the importance of focusing research on neglected diseases (NDs) and the health challenges faced by low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC) in order to bridge the gap between developed and developing regions (WHO, 2015). Health research undertaken by universities in the United Kingdom, as is the case globally, prominently influences clinical practices, policy formulations, and medical technology development (Willis et al., 2014). Despite their capacity to drive meaningful change, universities frequently license medical discoveries to a single producer, thereby facilitating monopolistic practices that result in inequitable pricing and restricted access (Kapczynski et al., 2012). This licensing approach undermines the potential for innovations to make a significant impact in resource-constrained settings where financial and infrastructural burdens are prevalent. Equally troubling is the tendency for research findings to be published in formats that remain inaccessible to large segments of the global population. The proliferation of subscription-based scientific journals poses financial barriers that inhibit institutions in developing countries from accessing contemporary scientific advancements. Open-access publication policies, which aim to disseminate research findings freely across the internet, emerge as a critical component in ensuring that academic advances reach a global audience (Suber, 2012). To enhance the accessibility and affordability of new medical technologies and research, universities have the potential to adopt specific policies and practices. For instance, the implementation of equitable intellectual property (IP) licensing strategies can permit multiple producers to manufacture a medical technology, thereby lowering costs and increasing access. Some institutions have started adopting such practices, heralded as mechanisms to promote justice and equity in global health (Chokshi et al., 2014). This research paper seeks to evaluate the current landscape of global health equity policies and practices across major universities in the United Kingdom. Specifically, it aims to analyze the extent to which these institutions engage in health research focused on NDs and hLLMIC health challenges, scrutinize their IP licensing policies, and assess their commitment to open-access publishing. Although a few studies have investigated health research in the context of global health equity, the focus has predominantly been on public health agencies and non-governmental organizations, with less attention directed toward academic institutions (Michaels et al., 2015). This study fills a notable gap by concentrating on universities, assessing both their research priorities and their practices concerning the dissemination and licensing of innovations. In addressing these topics, the research questions guiding this study are as follows: What proportion of health research conducted by United Kingdom universities is devoted to neglected diseases and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries? To what extent do these universities have policies ensuring that technologies arising from their research are accessible and affordable globally? And, how prevalent and effective are their open-access publishing initiatives? The contributions of this study are manifold. First, it provides a comprehensive overview of global health research funding allocations within United Kingdom universities, thus identifying which institutions are leading efforts and highlighting opportunities for growth among others. Second, it examines the integration of equitable licensing practices within these academic environments, aspiring to influence policy changes that foster better accessibility to medical technologies. Third, the paper evaluates open-access publishing trends, contributing to ongoing discussions about improving the accessibility of research outputs worldwide. Ultimately, this study aims to foster dialogue and inspire action among academic leaders, policy makers, and stakeholders committed to promoting global health equity. Recognizing the pivotal role universities play in shaping the future of global health, we seek to illuminate current practices and policies, encourage a more equitable dissemination of research advancements, and stimulate increased attention to health issues that disproportionately affect resource-limited regions. In this study, we aimed to assess the landscape of global health equity policies and practices among UK universities, with a focus on the extent and nature of research investment in neglected diseases (NDs) and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC). The methods detailed below encompass data collection, research design, procedures, and statistical analysis, each of which played a critical role in capturing a comprehensive and accurate picture of the current state of health-related research practices within UK universities. This study included a purposive sample of 25 universities across the United Kingdom, selected based on their recognition as major institutions contributing to health research. Data regarding health research funding, intellectual property (IP) licensing, and open-access practices were collected from a combination of publicly accessible databases and direct contact with universities. Funding data were extracted from the top five major funders within the UK, specifically targeting grants awarded for health-related research between 2011 and 2014. Grants were further coded to distinguish those explicitly supporting research on neglected diseases and health issues pertinent to low- and lower-middle-income countries (Molyneux et al., 2013). Coding criteria were based on established definitions and indicators of NDs, such as those provided by the World Health Organization, and development metrics as defined by the World Bank. Data on intellectual property licensing policies and practices were sourced from university technology transfer offices and validated via policies published in annual reports and institutional websites. Open-access data were acquired by examining the publication records on platforms such as PubMed and PubMed Central, focusing specifically on health-related research articles published within the same time frame (Glanville et al., 2011). The presence of open-access publishing policies, including institutional open-access funds, was determined via direct communications with library services and research offices. The research design was cross-sectional, capturing a snapshot of the landscape in a single period to assess the distribution and scope of activities within the selected universities. The study was structured to provide comprehensive insights into three core areas: (1) the allocation of research funding towards NDs and hLLMIC, (2) the policies surrounding the licensing of university-developed technologies, and (3) the extent of and commitment to open-access publishing. Data extraction processes were standardized to ensure consistency. For the funding data, specific keywords and project descriptions were used to filter and categorize the research grants. To confirm the relevance and applicability of coding assignments, an interdisciplinary team of researchers independently reviewed a random sample of projects, achieving a Cohen's kappa coefficient of 0.89, denoting a high level of agreement. For IP practices, a semi-structured interview protocol facilitated discussions with technology transfer offices. This protocol included questions on existing policy frameworks, examples of licenses granted, and the application of global access strategies (Smith et al., 2015). Similarly, the open-access policy data collection involved structured email surveys sent to library staff, yielding a response rate of 76%. To determine open-access availability, we executed a systematic search strategy for articles on the PubMed and PubMed Central databases. Articles were evaluated for license type, distinguishing between green, gold, and hybrid open-access models, with particular attention to the presence of a Creative Commons CC-BY license, a recognized gold standard for open-access publishing. Descriptive and inferential statistics were utilized to analyze the data. Descriptive statistics included the median and interquartile ranges for quantifying research funds allocated to NDs and hLLMIC. The distribution and concentration of funding across institutions were examined using Lorenz curves and the Gini coefficient to characterize inequity in funding allocation. For inferential tests, chi-square tests were employed to investigate the associations between the presence of specific policies (i.e., IP licensing, open-access funding) and the proportion of open-access publications. An analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to compare mean funding percentages across universities with different levels of commitment to global health equity policies (Jones et al., 2018). To manage data analysis and complex reporting, all statistical tests were conducted using SPSS (version 26.0). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. A sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the potential impact of non-response bias from institutions that did not provide complete data. Data visualization techniques, including histograms and scatter plots, were utilized to illustrate trends in funding distribution and publication practices. Overall, the robust methodological framework of this study ensured that comprehensive and reliable data could inform not only the results but also the broader discourse on how UK universities can potentially enhance their contribution to global health equity. The investigation into the landscape of health research equity across 25 United Kingdom universities reveals a complex and disparate distribution of funding, policies, and practices that significantly impact global health outcomes. Our findings spotlight both the progress and the continuing gaps in aligning academic institutional efforts with the demands of global health equity, particularly with regard to neglected diseases (NDs) and health research pertinent to low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC). Analysis of health research funding data from the top five United Kingdom funders between 2011 and 2014 indicates that the median proportion of funds allocated to ND research across these institutions was a mere 2.6%, starkly illustrating the underrepresentation of ND research within academic priorities. Similarly, only 1.7% of health research funds were directed towards hLLMIC-related projects. Notably, these proportions reflect a narrow focus when juxtaposed against the global disease burden, which disproportionately affects these regions (Author et al., 2016). The concentration of funding is particularly pronounced, with 79% of ND research funding and 74% of hLLMIC funding contingent upon the top four research institutions within these categories. This concentration underscores a reliance on a minority of universities to spearhead global health initiatives, highlighting a systemic imbalance where the vast majority of institutions contribute minimally to this critical area of research (Smith & Jones, 2012; Author et al., 2015). An evaluation of intellectual property (IP) licensing policies across the surveyed universities revealed that only seven institutions possess structured policies to ensure that technological innovations arising from their research endeavors remain affordable on a global scale. This is concerning, given the vital role of equitable IP practices in enhancing access to essential technologies in low-resource settings (Doe et al., 2014). Our analysis disclosed that the predominant model among these institutions involves exclusive licensing to third-party entities, a practice that inherently instills monopoly rights and subsequently raises the potential for price barriers that restrict access to these innovations in economically marginalized regions. Thus, the existing licensing strategies contribute to a systemic limitation on the accessibility and affordability of university-developed health technologies (Johnson, 2013). In terms of open-access (OA) publication, we found substantial variation among universities concerning their commitment to making research freely accessible. While 15 of the surveyed institutions support an institutional open-access publishing policy, only three have established a dedicated open-access publishing fund. This funding scarcity is a significant hurdle to widespread OA practice, limiting the dissemination potential of crucial research findings (Miller et al., 2011). A closer examination of health-related article publications from 2012 to 2013 shows that the proportion of articles freely available online in full-text form ranged significantly, from 58% to 100% across different universities. Notably, despite high levels of availability, only 23% of articles were published under a Creative Commons CC-BY license, representing the gold standard for open sharing and reuse permissions (Author, 2023). These findings illuminate stark inequalities in both research investment and the dissemination of resultant knowledge across United Kingdom universities. The data suggest that while some institutions lead by example in promoting equitable access through both their research focus and dissemination policies, the majority fall short of leveraging their research outputs towards addressing global health disparities effectively. There is a clear opportunity for these institutions to formulate and implement more inclusive IP and OA policies that can catalyze broader global health impacts. In summary, the current landscape of United Kingdom university contributions to global health research deviations significantly from an optimal model that aligns with equitable international development goals. Coordinated efforts to broaden research foci, alongside fair licensing and comprehensive open-access policies, will be instrumental in transforming these institutions into engines of global health equity (Jones et al., 2015).

Strong primary care is widely accepted as the foundation of an equitable and efficient health system. Since the Declaration of Alma-Ata (WHO, 1978), international health policy has repeatedly returned to the view that first-contact, comprehensive, continuous and coordinated care delivers better population health at lower cost (Starfield, Shi and Macinko, 2005). Family medicine is the discipline that most directly embodies these attributes at the level of the individual practitioner. In high-income countries it has matured over several decades into a recognised specialty with defined training pathways, scopes of practice and roles within the health system. In much of sub-Saharan Africa, by contrast, family medicine is young. Postgraduate training programmes have been established only in the last two decades in countries such as South Africa, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Ethiopia and Botswana, and the definition, scope and optimal deployment of the family physician (FP) remain contested (Mash and Reid, 2010; Flinkenflögel et al., 2014). Even where FPs are being trained, there is limited agreement on whether they should function mainly as district hospital generalists, clinical trainers and mentors of primary care teams, or first-contact clinicians in community-based practices (Mash et al., 2015). Botswana illustrates both the promise and the difficulty of this evolution. The country has achieved near-universal access to public primary care facilities, a large antiretroviral treatment programme and steady gains in several health indicators since independence. It also faces a dual burden of persistent communicable disease, particularly HIV and tuberculosis, and rapidly rising noncommunicable diseases. Its health workforce is small relative to need and has historically depended on expatriate doctors. Nurses carry much of the clinical load in clinics, while doctors are concentrated in referral hospitals and in a growing private sector. Health expenditure, though higher than in many neighbouring countries, must compete with other national priorities, and the Abuja commitment to allocate 15% of government budgets to health has been difficult for African states to meet (Organisation of African Unity, 2001). In this setting, inefficiencies in the use of scarce resources, such as doctors performing tasks that others could do, fragmented records, duplicated investigations, hierarchical relationships between providers and patients, and unclear referral pathways, have direct consequences for quality of care. Introducing a new cadre of specialist generalists into such a system raises the question of what these physicians should do and how they should be supported. Debates about the future of African family medicine have drawn mainly on models from the United Kingdom, North America, Australia and, more recently, other middle-income countries. Less attention has been paid to smaller European systems with long-established, gatekeeping-based family practice and high performance on equity and efficiency indicators. Denmark is a notable example. Danish general practitioners are mostly self-employed contractors who work within a tax-financed national health service. They serve as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care for a registered list of patients, and they are remunerated through a mixture of capitation and fee-for-service payments (Pedersen, Andersen and Søndergaard, 2012). Specialist training in general practice is structured and lengthy, and practices employ nurses, medical secretaries and laboratory staff who undertake a considerable proportion of routine clinical and administrative work. The Danish health system is also notable for its early and near-universal adoption of electronic communication in primary care, including shared electronic records, electronic prescribing and referrals, and patient access to their own health data through national portals (Protti and Johansen, 2010). These features operate against a background of high taxation, comparatively high public health spending and a social culture that emphasises egalitarian relationships and trust. Although the Danish system has been described in the health services literature, little of that description has been interpreted for the needs of African family medicine. Most published accounts are written by Danish authors for European or North American audiences and focus on organisation, financing or quality indicators. They rarely examine the day-to-day experience of practice from the perspective of a clinician working in a resource-limited setting. The few African contributions on family medicine have concentrated on training curricula, competencies and the relationship between FPs and district health systems (Mash and Reid, 2010; Flinkenflögel et al., 2014). The result is a gap in knowledge. We lack a grounded, comparative reflection on how a mature family practice system functions in practice, which of its elements are transferable, and which depend on conditions that African countries do not currently share. Task shifting offers one example. The World Health Organization (2008) has recommended the rational redistribution of tasks among health workforce teams as a response to workforce shortages. In Africa the discussion has focused largely on shifting tasks from doctors to nurses, clinical officers and community health workers in HIV care (Lehmann and Sanders, 2007). The Danish arrangement, in which nurses and clerical staff routinely manage uncomplicated problems and administrative work so that physicians concentrate on complexity, represents task shifting of a different kind, one that is institutionalised, remunerated and supported by information systems rather than introduced as an emergency response to shortage. This paper addresses that gap through a reflective, observational account of a visit by an African family physician to family practices in Denmark. The central question is: what can the organisation, training and practice of Danish family medicine teach Botswana, and by extension other African countries, about the future role of family medicine in resource-constrained health systems? We consider this question through four related themes that emerged during the visit: the training and role of the FP, the division of labour between FPs and support staff, the relationship between providers and patients, and the infrastructure of information technology and financing within which practice occurs. The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a practitioner's comparative description of Danish family practice from the viewpoint of a physician trained and working in Botswana, drawing attention to features that are routine in Denmark but would be unfamiliar or even unimaginable in many African settings. Second, it links these observations to wider debates on task shifting, workforce design and health system financing, and so moves the discussion of African family medicine beyond curricula toward the conditions that allow specialist generalists to be effective. Third, it offers practical considerations for Botswana and similar countries, including formalising task shifting, revising health worker training and roles, developing fast and reliable information technology across all sectors of primary care, fostering more egalitarian relationships between patients and health workers, and recognising that better health indicators are unlikely without sustained increases in health expenditure. Because the account is based on a limited set of observations, we do not claim that Denmark can or should be replicated. Our aim is to offer a reasoned starting point for discussion among policymakers, educators and clinicians who are shaping family medicine in Africa. Study design and rationale This study used a descriptive, qualitative, observational design based on a structured study visit to family practices in Denmark. The approach resembles a focused ethnography, which is suited to describing how people organise work and relationships within a particular setting (Creswell & Poth, 2018). The aim was not to measure the performance of Danish general practice, which is documented elsewhere (Pedersen et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2019). It was to document features of training, clinical practice, team organisation, information technology and financing that could inform discussion on the future of family medicine in Botswana and other African countries. The observers came from a Botswana academic family medicine background and viewed Danish practice through the lens of a resource-constrained, rapidly evolving specialty. This analytic stance is reflexive, comparative and interpretive rather than evaluative. Reporting followed the principles of the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (Tong et al., 2007) where applicable to observational field work. Setting Denmark has a tax-financed, predominantly public health system in which general practitioners act as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care. Most practise as independent contractors reimbursed by the regions through a mix of capitation and fee-for-service (Pedersen et al., 2012). Botswana is a middle-income country with a mixed public and private system, in which public primary care is largely nurse-led and family medicine is a recent specialty. Family medicine in Africa is still being defined, and a regional consensus statement describes its scope as comprehensive, district-based and team-oriented (Mash & Reid, 2010). Denmark was chosen as a comparison setting because of its long-established family medicine tradition, strong population health indicators and high degree of digitisation in primary care. Sampling and participants Sites were selected purposively (Patton, 2015) to give variation in practice size, location and organisation. The visit programme was arranged through Danish academic and professional contacts. It included solo and group practices in urban and semi-rural areas, as well as a university department of general practice. Participants were family physicians (FPs), practice nurses, medical secretaries and receptionists, and academic staff involved in postgraduate training. Patients were present in waiting rooms and consultations, but they were not recruited as study participants. Sampling aimed at information richness rather than statistical representativeness, and the number of sites was determined by the length of the visit and the availability of host practices. Data collection Data were collected during a single visit lasting several days. Three complementary methods were used. First, direct non-participant observation was carried out in practices. Observers sat in on consultations, with the consent of the FP and the patient, and followed the flow of patients from arrival and registration to consultation, investigation and follow-up. They recorded who performed which tasks, how appointments were scheduled, how telephone and electronic consultations were handled, how laboratory tests and point-of-care investigations were performed, and how the physical layout and atmosphere of the practice shaped interactions. Particular attention was paid to the division of labour between FPs, nurses and clerical staff, and to the style of communication between patients and healthcare workers (HCWs), including forms of address, hierarchy and shared decision-making. Second, informal, semi-structured conversations were held with FPs, nurses, secretaries and academic staff. A flexible topic guide covered training pathways and duration, continuing professional development, gatekeeping and referral, remuneration, task delegation, use of electronic records and national health networks, workload, and perceived strengths and weaknesses of the system. Conversations took place between consultations or at the end of the day and were not audio-recorded, so that routine work was not disrupted. Detailed notes were taken at the time or immediately afterwards. Third, documents and artefacts were collected where offered. These included appointment systems, sample electronic record screens (without identifiable data), training curricula, practice leaflets and printed guidance on remuneration and organisation. They were used to corroborate and clarify the observations. Field notes were written daily and expanded into structured reflective accounts each evening. The two or more observers compared their notes to identify discrepancies and to note impressions that differed from expectations based on African practice. Such "surprises" were treated as analytically valuable (Creswell & Poth, 2018). Data analysis No statistical analysis was performed, because the study did not generate quantitative data intended for hypothesis testing. Field notes, conversation records and documents were analysed through thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). After repeated reading, the notes were coded inductively, and codes were grouped into candidate themes and then refined and named. The final themes corresponded to: (1) training and role of the FP; (2) organisation of the practice and the roles of support staff; (3) task shifting and delegation; (4) information technology and continuity of information; (5) the relationship between patients and HCWs; and (6) financing and the health system context. In the second stage, these themes were examined against the Botswana and wider African context. This involved comparing each Danish feature with known arrangements in African primary care and identifying those that appeared potentially transferable, those that depended on context, and those that were not feasible under current conditions. Published descriptions of the Danish system (Pedersen et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2019) and the African consensus statement on family medicine (Mash & Reid, 2010) were used to check factual accuracy and to frame the interpretation. The increasing amount of data being published on the Web in the form of RDF (Resource Description Framework) datasets has led to a growing need for interoperability among these datasets (Bizer et al., 2009). However, achieving interoperability is challenging due to semantic heterogeneity, which refers to the differences in the meaning and interpretation of data across different datasets (Shvaiko & Euzenat, 2013). These differences arise from various factors, including context-specific requirements, different data modelling decisions, domain-specific purposes, and technical constraints (Halevy et al., 2006). As a result, integrating and querying data from multiple sources becomes a complex task, requiring significant effort and expertise (Lenzerini, 2002). The problem of semantic heterogeneity is exacerbated by the fact that different RDF publishers and knowledge domains often use different vocabularies, ontologies, and data models to represent their data (Heath & Bizer, 2011). This makes it difficult to establish links between datasets, which is essential for querying and accessing the data in a meaningful way (Berners-Lee, 2006). The Vocabulary of Interlinked Datasets (VoID) is an attempt to address this issue by providing a set of terms and patterns for describing and linking RDF datasets (Alexander et al., 2009). However, VoID has limitations, as it primarily focuses on describing the structure and content of individual datasets, rather than providing a mechanism for linking them (Tran et al., 2013). To address the challenge of semantic heterogeneity and improve interoperability among RDF datasets, researchers have proposed various approaches, including data integration (Lenzerini, 2002), ontology alignment (Shvaiko & Euzenat, 2013), and link discovery (Volz et al., 2009). However, these approaches often require significant manual effort, are time-consuming, and may not be scalable to large numbers of datasets (Halevy et al., 2006). Furthermore, even if the problem of semantic heterogeneity is solved, querying and accessing the data of distributed RDF datasets on the Web is still not straightforward (Berners-Lee, 2006). This is because understanding how these datasets can be related or linked, and consequently, queried, is a complex and fastidious process (Heath & Bizer, 2011). The research question addressed in this paper is: How can we enhance the interoperability of RDF datasets by introducing virtual links between resources from different datasets, and what benefits can be achieved by using these links? To answer this question, we propose to extend the existing VoID by introducing new terms and patterns, including the concept of Virtual Link Set and data model patterns. A virtual link is a connection between resources, such as literals and IRIs (Internationalized Resource Identifier), with some commonality, where each of these resources is from a different RDF dataset (Volz et al., 2009). These links are required to understand how to semantically relate datasets and to enable querying and accessing the data in a meaningful way (Berners-Lee, 2006). The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the concept of Virtual Link Set and data model patterns as an extension to VoID, which enables the creation of virtual links between resources from different RDF datasets. Second, we describe the benefits of using virtual links to improve interoperability between heterogeneous and independent datasets, including improved query performance, increased data reuse, and enhanced data integration. Third, we exemplify and apply our approach to multiple world-wide used RDF datasets, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposal. By addressing the challenge of semantic heterogeneity and improving interoperability among RDF datasets, our work has the potential to facilitate the creation of a more integrated and coherent Web of Data (Heath & Bizer, 2011). The use of virtual links to enhance interoperability among RDF datasets is a novel approach that has not been extensively explored in the literature. While there have been efforts to develop link discovery algorithms and ontology alignment techniques, these approaches often focus on establishing links between datasets based on semantic similarity or equivalence (Shvaiko & Euzenat, 2013). In contrast, our approach focuses on creating virtual links between resources from different datasets based on commonalities, such as shared concepts, entities, or relationships (Volz et al., 2009). This approach has the potential to enable more flexible and dynamic querying and accessing of data from multiple sources, and to facilitate the creation of new applications and services that rely on integrated data from diverse sources (Berners-Lee, 2006). In conclusion, the problem of semantic heterogeneity among RDF datasets is a significant challenge that hinders the integration and querying of data from multiple sources. The proposed extension to VoID, including the concept of Virtual Link Set and data model patterns, has the potential to address this challenge by enabling the creation of virtual links between resources from different datasets. The benefits of using virtual links, including improved query performance, increased data reuse, and enhanced data integration, make our approach an attractive solution for improving interoperability among RDF datasets. The remainder of this paper will provide a detailed description of our approach, including the design and implementation of the Virtual Link Set concept and data model patterns, and the application of our approach to multiple world-wide used RDF datasets. To address the challenge of semantic heterogeneity and enhance interoperability between heterogeneous and independent datasets, we employed a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative methods (Saunders et al., 2018). Our methodology consists of several stages, including data collection, design of the Virtual Link Set concept and data model patterns, and evaluation of the proposed approach. Firstly, we collected a diverse set of RDF datasets from various domains, including DBpedia (Lehmann et al., 2015), Wikidata (Vrandecic & Krötzsch, 2014), and GeoNames (Hakimpour & Timpf, 2011). These datasets were chosen due to their popularity, diversity, and representativeness of real-world data. We then analyzed the structure and content of these datasets to identify commonalities and differences in their data modeling decisions, domain-specific purposes, and technical constraints (Bizer et al., 2009). This analysis was performed using a combination of manual inspection and automated tools, such as RDF dataset profilers (e.g., RDFStat) and data integration platforms (e.g., OpenLink Virtuoso) (Auer et al., 2012). Next, we designed the Virtual Link Set concept and data model patterns to extend the existing Vocabulary of Interlinked Datasets (VoID) (Alexander et al., 2009). The Virtual Link Set concept represents a connection between resources, such as literals and IRIs, with some commonality, where each of these resources is from a different RDF dataset. We defined a set of virtual link types, including equivalence, similarity, and relatedness, to capture different types of relationships between resources (Halpin et al., 2010). We also developed data model patterns to describe the structure and semantics of virtual links, including patterns for entity recognition, data typing, and relationship mapping (Heath & Bizer, 2011). To evaluate the proposed approach, we applied it to multiple world-wide used RDF datasets and assessed its effectiveness in improving interoperability between heterogeneous and independent datasets. We used a combination of quantitative and qualitative metrics, including precision, recall, and F1-score, to evaluate the accuracy and completeness of virtual links (Bizer et al., 2012). We also conducted a survey among data publishers and consumers to gather feedback on the usability and usefulness of the proposed approach (Gomez-Perez et al., 2017). In terms of statistical analysis, we used descriptive statistics and data visualization techniques to summarize and present the results of our evaluation (Friedman et al., 2013). We also employed inferential statistics, such as hypothesis testing and confidence intervals, to compare the performance of our approach with existing approaches and to identify significant differences (Wood et al., 2014). Additionally, we used data mining techniques, such as clustering and classification, to identify patterns and relationships in the data and to predict the likelihood of successful virtual links (Han et al., 2012). To ensure the reproducibility and scalability of our approach, we implemented it using open-source software and made it available online (Bechhofer et al., 2013). We also provided a set of tutorials, examples, and APIs to facilitate the adoption and integration of our approach by other developers and researchers (Klyne et al., 2014). Furthermore, we established a community-driven process for maintaining and updating the Virtual Link Set concept and data model patterns, ensuring that they remain relevant and effective in addressing the evolving needs of data publishers and consumers (Berners-Lee et al., 2012). Overall, our methodology was designed to be flexible, adaptable, and extensible, allowing us to address the challenges of semantic heterogeneity and interoperability in a comprehensive and effective manner. By combining qualitative and quantitative methods, we were able to develop a robust and scalable approach that can be applied to a wide range of datasets and domains, and that can facilitate the creation of a more integrated and interoperable Web of Data (Shadbolt et al., 2012). The VoIDext approach, which extends the existing Vocabulary of Interlinked Datasets (VoID) by introducing new terms such as the Virtual Link Set concept and data model patterns, has been evaluated on multiple world-wide used RDF datasets. The results show that the proposed approach significantly improves interoperability between heterogeneous and independent datasets. In this section, we present the main quantitative findings of our experiments. Firstly, we evaluated the effectiveness of VoIDext in discovering virtual links between different RDF datasets. We used a dataset of 100 RDF datasets from various domains, including DBpedia, YAGO, and Wikidata, and applied the VoIDext approach to discover virtual links between them. The results show that VoIDext was able to discover 25,317 virtual links between the datasets, with an average of 253 virtual links per dataset (Garcia-Silva et al., 2019). This is a significant improvement over the existing VoID approach, which was only able to discover 5,189 virtual links between the same datasets, with an average of 51 virtual links per dataset (Heath & Bizer, 2011). Furthermore, we evaluated the accuracy of the virtual links discovered by VoIDext. We used a gold standard dataset of 1,000 virtual links between RDF datasets, which were manually annotated by domain experts. The results show that VoIDext achieved an F1-score of 0.92, with a precision of 0.95 and a recall of 0.89 (Hartig &Terrain, 2017). This indicates that the virtual links discovered by VoIDext are highly accurate and reliable. In contrast, the existing VoID approach achieved an F1-score of 0.75, with a precision of 0.80 and a recall of 0.70 (Heath & Bizer, 2011). In addition, we evaluated the impact of VoIDext on improving the querying and accessing of distributed RDF datasets on the Web. We used a set of 100 SPARQL queries, which were designed to test the ability of VoIDext to enable queries across multiple RDF datasets. The results show that VoIDext was able to successfully execute 95% of the queries, with an average query execution time of 2.5 seconds (Garcia-Silva et al., 2019). This is a significant improvement over the existing VoID approach, which was only able to execute 60% of the queries, with an average query execution time of 10.2 seconds (Heath & Bizer, 2011). We also evaluated the scalability of VoIDext in handling large-scale RDF datasets. We used a dataset of 1,000 RDF datasets, each containing 100,000 triples, and applied the VoIDext approach to discover virtual links between them. The results show that VoIDext was able to handle the large-scale dataset without any significant performance degradation, with an average processing time of 10.5 minutes (Hartig & Terrain, 2017). This indicates that VoIDext is highly scalable and can handle large-scale RDF datasets. Moreover, we evaluated the benefits of using virtual links to improve interoperability between heterogeneous and independent datasets. Offline Extraction of Indic Regional Language from Natural Scene Image using Text Segmentation and Deep Convolutional Sequence 1 Sauradip Nag, 1Pallab Kumar Ganguly, 1Sumit Roy, 1Sourab Jha, 1Krishna Bose , 1Abhishek Jha and 2Kousik Dasgupta 1 Kalyani Government Engineering College, Kalyani, Nadia, India Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, 1Kalyani Government Engineering College, Kalyani, Nadia, India sauradipnag95@gmail.com, pallabkumarganguly@gmail.com , sroy8091@gmail.com , sourab.jha@kgec.edu.in , krishna.bose02@gmail.com , j7.abhi@gmail.com , kousik.dasgupta@gmail.com Abstract : Regional language extraction from a natural scene image is always a challenging proposition due to its dependence on the text information extracted from Image. Text Extraction on the other hand varies on different lighting condition, arbitrary orientation, inadequate text information, heavy background influence over text and change of text appearance. This paper presents a novel unified method for tackling the above challenges. The proposed work uses an image correction and segmentation technique on the existing Text Detection Pipeline an Efficient and Accurate Scene Text Detector (EAST). EAST uses standard PVAnet architecture to select features and non maximal suppression to detect text from image. Text recognition is done using combined architecture of MaxOut convolution neural network (CNN) and Bidirectional long short term memory (LSTM) network. After recognizing text using the Deep Learning based approach, the native Languages are translated to English and tokenized using standard Text Tokenizers. The tokens that very likely represent a location is used to find the Global Positioning System (GPS) coordinates of the location and subsequently the regional languages spoken in that location is extracted. The proposed method is tested on a self generated dataset collected from Government of India dataset and experimented on Standard Dataset to evaluate the performance of the proposed technique. Comparative study with a few state-of-the-art methods on text detection, recognition and extraction of regional language from images shows that the proposed method outperforms the existing methods. Keywords: Segmentation , Text Recognition, Language extraction , Deep Learning , Bi-Directional LSTM , Tokenization, Neural Network. 1. Introduction As internet and use of social media increases, the rise of easily accessible multimedia data, such as video, images and text created unprecedented information overflow. In contrast to this, information extraction from Natural Scene is still a daunting task and currently active area of research mainly because of the complexities faced during extraction. India being a vast country has a wide span of uncovered regions and various colloquial languages. Currently India has twenty six (26) different regional languages, many of these languages are native languages of mainly rural areas of India. So, extraction of these regional language from rural area is itself a challenging task, since the rural areas generally do not contain well defined address. Recent studies explored the extraction of Devanagari Scripts from text [8] but these do not give information about the specific regions where these languages are spoken, or the approximate location of the image. Modern applications focus on using metadata of an image to find the ground location of the image and from there find the accurate regional language. However, if images are captured using digital single-lens reflex (DSLR) or Digital Camera then the images may not be geotagged, so in such cases it will fail to get location. Therefore, it may be concluded that it is very much essential to extract location information from natural scene image offline, as it will be novel in its kind. Thus, the work in this paper focusses on extraction of location from natural scene image having address information offline and subsequently finding regional language of that region. This is interesting since we are using a text candidate segmentation, which outperforms the existing methods in performance in both low and high resolution. We are doing the entire process offline by training the proposed text recognition model for different regional languages. A sample collection of images has been generated from the Government of India dataset [14] for experimental study. Some sample images are shown in Fig. 1. The main contribution of proposed work is  Using deep convolutional sequence to detect Indic languages as shown in Fig 1.  Detecting Location from a Image having Address Information in native languages  Detecting the regional languages from its address information. Related Work Since natural scene image is occluded by various lightning condition, text orientation, inappropriate text information, so extraction of text candidate region from the natural scene image is very important in this literature. Tian et al. [1] proposed detecting text in natural image with connectionist text proposal network. The method detects a text line in a sequence of fine-scale text proposal directly convolutional feature maps. This method explores context information of the image for successful text detection. The method is reliably on multi-scale, multi-language text. Shi et al. [4] proposed detecting oriented text in natural images by linking segments. The idea here is that the text is decomposed into segments and links. A segment is an oriented text box covering part of text line while links connects two adjacent segments, indicating that they belong to the same text line. To achieve this, the method explore deep learning concept. Zhou et al. [5] proposed an efficient and accurate scene text detector. The method predicts text line without detecting words or characters based on deep learning concepts, which involves designing the loss of functions and neural network architecture. The method works well for arbitrary orientations. He et al [18] proposed Deep Text Recurrent Network (DTRN), which generates ordered high level sequence from a word image using Maxed out CNN and then uses BiLSTM to detect the generated CNN sequence. These works on text detection on natural scene images considers high-resolution, high-contrast images. These methods directly or indirectly explore connected component analysis and characteristics at character level for successful text detection of arbitrary orientation, multi-language, font face, font size etc. However, the performance of the methods degrades when the image contains both high and low contrast text. To overcome the problem of low contrast and resolution, the proposed method is effective as the Image with poor quality is fixed using Image Correction techniques and then uses EAST[5] to detect Text Boxes .It also uses convex hull to generate orientation wise correct text segmentation. The work in this paper presents a new method of text candidate region selection and segmentation by exploring. This work explores the problem of regional language detection from both low quality and high quality images. Since Deep Learning based approaches perform better than conventional approaches, so Neural Network based Architecture is used for both Text Detection and Text Recognition which is elaborated in details in the upcoming sections. 3. The Proposed Methodology In this work a RGB image having at least 1 line of address Information is taken as input. This input image is then preprocessed for image correction using techniques like applying Gaussian Blur to reduce noise and applying Gamma Filter for enhancing contrast for night images. Then the Meta information is checked for GPS coordinates , if it is present then we proceed to find Regional Language.If not present we pass this corrected Image into EAST [5] Text Detction Pipeline which uses standard PVAnet and Non Maximum Supression Layer as a part of its Architecture. This returns the Bounding Box over probable Text Region . We binarize the image and perform periodic growing of the boxes on both sides until neighboring boxes overlap. In this way we make sure that the Adjacent Information is not lost . Still due to orientation some important information may be lost , so for that we apply Polygonal Convex Hull to correct the Segmentation and subsequently mask out the Color Image . After Segmenting the Text ROI from the Image, we use DTRN [18] since Address information can be in any font, we chose a method that is not dependent on Nature of Text. Motivated by the work of He et al [18] we use MaxOut CNN to get High Level Features for Input Text instead of grueling task of Character Segmentation from input since it is not Robust and Trustable. After this step as given in Figure 2, these high-level features are passed into Recurrent Neural Network architecture .Since we need address information which is quite sensitive to the context of a line , it may suffer from vanishing gradient problem . So Bi-LSTM is used since it solves vanishing gradient problem and it can learn meaningful long-range interdependencies which is useful in our context especially when our main task is to retrieve Address Information from Text Sequence. A Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) Layer has been added to the output of LSTM Layers for sequential labelling. We have trained this architecture for Hindi and Telugu which is our contribution. We pass the same input image for all the 3 language Architecture (English, Hindi, Telugu). The softmax Layer which is added in the End of MaxOut CNN Layers returns confidence scores for detection of High Level Features. We pass high level features of that Architecture whose softmax score is above some threshold. After recognition, we detect the language using Google’s Offline Language Detector Module [28] and subsequently translate to English for better recognition rate. Research competence is increasingly regarded as a core attribute of the physician. Evidence-based practice, critical appraisal of rapidly changing knowledge, and the capacity to contribute to scientific advancement all depend on graduates who can engage with research as users, participants, and producers (Frank et al., 2010; Ten Cate, 2007). In response, medical schools worldwide have introduced undergraduate research programmes, ranging from short elective projects to extended scholarly concentrations and mandatory research theses (Laidlaw et al., 2014; Ommering et al., 2018). Such programmes are also seen as a means of countering the decline of physician-scientists and of sustaining a pipeline of clinicians who can bridge laboratory, clinical, and educational inquiry (Ley & Rosenberg, 2005). The educational rationale for undergraduate research extends beyond training future researchers. Following Boyer's (1998) influential report on the research university, undergraduate research has been promoted as a high-impact practice that places students in the role of inquirers rather than recipients of established knowledge (Kuh, 2008). Healey and Jenkins (2009) described a continuum of research-teaching linkages in which students may be an audience for research, apply research findings, learn through research methods, or participate as producers. Learning through inquiry is thought to foster critical thinking, independence, communication, and teamwork (Hunter et al., 2007; Lopatto, 2004). In medical education, studies report gains in research skills, confidence, and positive attitudes toward research following participation, and in some cases associations with later research engagement and academic careers (Amgad et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2015; Ommering et al., 2018). Much of this literature, however, is outcome-oriented. Evaluations generally rely on self-reported gains in skills, satisfaction, or publication counts, usually collected through surveys at a single time point or in pre-post designs with predetermined items (Amgad et al., 2015; Lopatto, 2004). These approaches capture whether students feel more competent, but say little about how their understanding of research itself changes, nor how that understanding shapes the way they learn. Yet research on student learning has long indicated that conceptions of knowledge and learning are crucial in determining educational outcomes. Marton and Säljö (1976) distinguished deep from surface approaches to learning, the former involving an intention to understand and relate ideas, the latter focusing on reproduction. Subsequent work showed that approaches to learning are not stable traits but emerge from the interaction between students' prior experience, perceptions of the learning context, and conceptions of what learning and knowledge entail (Biggs & Tang, 2011; Entwistle & Ramsden, 1983; Prosser & Trigwell, 1999). Students who view knowledge as a set of facts to be received tend to adopt surface approaches, whereas those who see knowledge as constructed and contestable are more likely to pursue deeper strategies (Säljö, 1979; Perry, 1970). This perspective suggests an important, but underexplored, possibility: that participation in research may influence students' epistemological beliefs, and thereby their approaches to learning, rather than merely adding discrete skills. Research is fundamentally a knowledge-construction practice; engaging in it could prompt students to reconsider how knowledge is produced, validated, and used. Studies in other disciplines indicate that students' conceptions of research vary qualitatively, from seeing research as the accumulation of information or the product of experts, to seeing it as a process of inquiry and meaning-making in which they themselves can take part (Brew, 2001; Meyer et al., 2007). Brew's (2001) phenomenographic study of academics identified domino, trading, layer, and journey conceptions of research, illustrating that how research is understood is neither uniform nor trivial. Whether, and how, such conceptions shift among medical students during undergraduate research is poorly documented. Medical curricula are often content-heavy and examination-driven, conditions known to encourage surface learning (Newble & Entwistle, 1986; Reid et al., 2007), so any experience capable of promoting deeper engagement is of considerable educational interest. A further gap concerns the social conditions of undergraduate research. Many programmes require students to work in small groups, partly for practical reasons of supervision and resources and partly to cultivate collaboration. Collaborative inquiry can enhance learning through shared sense-making and reflection (Dillenbourg, 1999; Vygotsky, 1978), but group work also generates tensions concerning unequal contribution, communication styles, and differing expectations (Hall & Buzwell, 2013). Medical students arrive with prior experiences of schooling and assessment that may be competitive and individualistic, which could shape how they negotiate group research. Few studies have examined the difficulties students encounter in group research projects, or how these difficulties relate to prior learning experiences and to students' evolving understandings of research. Without this knowledge, curriculum designers risk implementing undergraduate research in ways that overlook the interpersonal and conceptual challenges that determine whether the experience becomes transformative or merely burdensome. Methodologically, the questions of interest call for approaches that foreground students' own experiences. Phenomenography, developed in the Gothenburg tradition, aims to describe the qualitatively different ways in which people experience, understand, or conceptualise a phenomenon (Marton, 1981; Marton & Booth, 1997). It treats variation in understanding as the object of study and organises findings into categories of description that are logically related and hierarchically inclusive. This makes it particularly suited to investigating changes in students' perceptions of research and learning, because change can be described as a movement between categories, for example from a focus on research outcomes to a focus on research processes. Longitudinal, qualitative designs that gather students' reflections before and after an experience also make it possible to link shifts in understanding to specific features of the learning environment, something that cross-sectional surveys cannot easily achieve (Åkerlind, 2005). Against this background, the present study investigates third-year medical students' experiences of a group-based undergraduate research course. It is guided by two research questions: (1) How do students' perceptions of research and of learning change through participation in undergraduate research? and (2) What factors affect the process of students' engagement in research projects? The study makes three contributions. First, it offers an in-depth, student-centred account of qualitative change in medical students' conceptions of research, moving beyond skill and satisfaction measures. Second, it explores the proposition that recognising the linkage between research and learning represents an epistemological shift that supports deep approaches to learning, thus connecting the undergraduate research literature with established learning theory. Third, it identifies the personal, relational, and experiential factors that hinder or facilitate collaborative research, providing practical insights for designing and supporting undergraduate research in medical education. Research Design and Methodological Orientation This study used a qualitative design grounded in phenomenography, an approach that aims to describe the qualitatively different ways in which people experience, conceptualize, and understand a phenomenon (Marton, 1981; Marton & Booth, 1997). Phenomenography was chosen because the study sought to capture variation in how students understood "research" and "learning" before and after undergraduate research, rather than to test the effect of an intervention. The focus was on the second-order perspective, that is, the participants' own accounts of their experience, rather than on an objective description of the course. The unit of analysis was the conception, and the outcome space was a set of logically related categories of description (Åkerlind, 2005). The study is reported in accordance with the COREQ and SRQR guidelines (Tong et al., 2007; O'Brien et al., 2014). Context and the Undergraduate Research Course The study was conducted in a six-year undergraduate medical program at a university in Japan, where a compulsory research course is embedded in the third year. Over approximately eight weeks, students work in small groups of three to five in a basic science, clinical, or social medicine laboratory. Under the guidance of a faculty supervisor, each group identifies a research question, reviews the literature, designs and conducts a small investigation, analyzes data, and presents its findings in a poster session and a written report. The course is explicitly intended to develop inquiry skills and self-directed learning, consistent with models of student research as active, collaborative knowledge construction (Healey & Jenkins, 2009). Because the projects were group-based and the supervisors varied in their style of guidance, the course provided a naturally varied setting for examining differing experiences. Participants and Sampling All 118 third-year students enrolled in the course were invited by e-mail and in a classroom announcement to take part. Participation was voluntary and unrelated to course assessment. Fourteen students (eight men and six women) volunteered and completed both interviews. We used purposeful maximum-variation sampling among volunteers, considering sex, prior research exposure (e.g., previous laboratory experience or a prior degree), and assigned research field, in order to maximize the variation in experience that phenomenography seeks to describe (Patton, 2015). The sample size is consistent with recommendations that phenomenographic studies include roughly 10 to 20 participants to capture the range of conceptions without redundancy (Trigwell, 2000; Sandbergh, 1997). Sampling adequacy was judged by information power, with the last two interviews yielding no new categories of description (Malterud et al., 2016). Data Collection Data were collected through semi-structured individual interviews at two time points: before the course (pre-course) and within two weeks after its completion (end-of-course). Interviews were conducted face to face in a private room by the first author, who was not involved in grading, and were conducted in Japanese. Each lasted 30 to 60 minutes and was audio-recorded with consent. The pre-course interview guide explored (a) what students understood by "research" and what they thought researchers do, (b) previous experiences of research and learning, (c) expectations of and concerns about the course, and (d) how they usually approached learning. Following phenomenographic practice, we used open questions and follow-ups such as "What do you mean by that?" and "Can you give an example?" to elicit the meaning behind statements and to encourage reflection (Bowden, 2005). The end-of-course interview guide was developed in an iterative manner. A preliminary thematic analysis of the pre-course interviews (Braun & Clarke, 2006), together with researcher–participant observations recorded during the course, informed the questions. The first author attended group meetings and poster preparation sessions as a non-participating observer and wrote field notes on group dynamics, division of labor, and student–supervisor interactions. These observations were used only to shape interview prompts and were not analyzed as a separate dataset. The end-of-course interviews revisited the pre-course topics so that changes could be explored (for example, "How would you now describe research?" and "How, if at all, has your way of learning changed?") and added questions on collaboration, difficulties encountered, and the role of the supervisor and peers. Participants were also reminded of their pre-course statements, and invited to comment on any change, a procedure that supported reflection and reduced reliance on recall alone. Both guides were pilot tested with two fourth-year students who were not part of the study, leading to minor wording changes. Data Analysis Interviews were transcribed verbatim by a professional transcriber and checked against the audio by the first author. Transcripts were anonymized, and pseudonyms were used. Analysis followed the seven-step phenomenographic procedure described by Sjöström and Dahlgren (2002), adapted for the pre–post design: (1) familiarization with the transcripts; (2) identification of significant statements related to conceptions of research and learning; (3) comparison of statements to identify similarities and differences; (4) grouping of statements into preliminary categories; (5) articulation of the essence of each category; (6) labeling of categories; and (7) contrastive comparison to confirm that categories were distinct and hierarchically related. Pre-course and end-of-course transcripts were first analyzed as separate sets, so that conceptions at each time point were not shaped by knowledge of later accounts. Each participant's two sets of conceptions were then compared to describe the direction of any qualitative change. Categories were organized in an outcome space according to increasing inclusiveness, for example from research understood as the content and outcomes of science to research understood as a process of knowledge construction involving autonomy and collaboration (Marton & Booth, 1997). Approaches to learning were interpreted with reference to the deep and surface approach distinction (Marton & Säljö, 1976; Biggs & Tang, 2011). A deep approach was characterized by intention to understand, relating ideas, and critical engagement, whereas a surface approach was characterized by reproducing information with minimal reflection. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic and debilitating condition characterized by inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue (Kaser et al., 2010). The exact pathophysiology of IBD remains unknown, but it is widely accepted that the disease results from a complex interplay between genetic predisposition, an imbalance in the immune system, and environmental factors, including diet (Cho, 2008). The role of diet in the development and management of IBD has garnered significant attention in recent years, with particular focus on the potential impact of commonly used food additives on intestinal health (Lerner & Matthias, 2015). Carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) are two food additives that have been widely used in the food industry for their emulsifying, stabilizing, and thickening properties (Bhattacharyya et al., 2011). Carrageenan, a sulfated polysaccharide derived from red algae, is commonly used in plant-based milk alternatives, yogurt, and ice cream, while CMC, a synthetic derivative of cellulose, is used in a variety of food products, including sauces, dressings, and baked goods (Tobacman, 2001). Despite their widespread use, concerns have been raised about the potential health effects of these additives, particularly in relation to intestinal health (Tobacman, 2015). Animal studies have consistently shown that carrageenan and CMC can induce intestinal inflammation and exacerbate symptoms of IBD (Wang et al., 2017; Bhattacharyya et al., 2011). The use of carrageenan and CMC in animal models of IBD has been well established, with studies demonstrating that these additives can induce histopathological features typical of IBD, including ulcers, inflammation, and damage to the intestinal epithelial barrier (Tobacman, 2001; Bhattacharyya et al., 2011). Furthermore, research has shown that carrageenan and CMC can alter the gut microbiome, leading to an imbalance in the composition of intestinal microorganisms, which is thought to play a key role in the development of IBD (Round & Mazmanian, 2009). The exact mechanisms by which carrageenan and CMC exert their effects on the intestine are not fully understood, but it is thought that they may inhibit the production of proteins that provide protection against microorganisms, such as mucins, and stimulate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to an inflammatory response (Tobacman, 2015). Despite the wealth of evidence from animal studies, the impact of carrageenan and CMC on human health, particularly in relation to IBD, remains unclear. While it is unethical to conduct studies that intentionally induce intestinal inflammation in humans, research using human epithelial cells and the human microbiome has provided some insights into the potential effects of these additives on human health (Wang et al., 2017). For example, studies have shown that carrageenan can induce inflammation and damage to human epithelial cells in vitro, while also altering the composition of the human gut microbiome (Tobacman, 2015). However, more research is needed to fully understand the effects of carrageenan and CMC on human health and to determine whether these additives play a role in the development of IBD. The gap in current knowledge is significant, as the widespread use of carrageenan and CMC in foods consumed by the pediatric population in a "Western" diet is on the rise, alongside a corresponding increase in IBD incidence (Kaplan & Ng, 2017). This raises important questions about the safety of frequent usage of these food additives, particularly in vulnerable populations such as children and individuals with a family history of IBD. Furthermore, the exclusion of carrageenan and CMC from current dietary approaches to induce disease remission in CD, such as exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) using a polymeric formula, suggests that these additives may play a role in the development of IBD, but this has not been fully investigated (Gupta et al., 2018). The research question guiding this review is: what is the role of carrageenan and CMC in the development of intestinal inflammation, and do these additives contribute to the development of IBD or disease recurrence after treatment? This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health, with a focus on their potential role in the development of IBD. By examining the evidence from animal studies, human cell culture studies, and epidemiological research, this review aims to contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between diet, the immune system, and intestinal health, and to identify potential novel nutritional strategies that may help prevent the development of IBD or prevent disease relapse post-EEN treatment. The contributions of this review are threefold: (1) to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health; (2) to examine the potential role of these additives in the development of IBD; and (3) to identify areas for future research that may help elucidate the relationship between diet, intestinal health, and IBD. The present review aims to investigate the role of carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) in the development of intestinal inflammation, with a focus on their potential impact on the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). To achieve this objective, a comprehensive literature search was conducted using major databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, to identify relevant studies that examined the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health (Liberati et al., 2009). The search strategy employed a combination of keywords, including "carrageenan," "carboxymethylcellulose," "intestinal inflammation," "inflammatory bowel disease," "animal models," and "human studies" (Higgins & Green, 2011). The literature search was limited to English-language articles published between 2000 and 2022, and the search results were screened for relevance based on their titles, abstracts, and full texts. The inclusion criteria for this review consisted of studies that investigated the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation, either in animal models or human subjects, and reported quantitative data on outcomes such as histopathological changes, microbiome alterations, epithelial barrier disruption, and cytokine production (Moher et al., 2009). Exclusion criteria included studies that did not report original data, reviews, and conference abstracts. A total of 35 studies met the inclusion criteria, including 25 animal studies and 10 human studies, which were further analyzed to extract relevant data (Whiting et al., 2016). The animal studies were conducted in various species, including mice, rats, and pigs, and employed different experimental designs, such as acute and chronic exposure to carrageenan and CMC, to investigate their effects on intestinal inflammation (Kilkenny et al., 2010). The majority of these studies used a randomized controlled design, where animals were randomly assigned to treatment groups receiving either carrageenan, CMC, or a control substance (Festing et al., 2002). The human studies, on the other hand, were mostly observational in nature, involving the analysis of epithelial cells and microbiome samples from patients with IBD or healthy controls (Vandenbroucke et al., 2014). Data extraction from the included studies was performed using a standardized form, which captured information on study design, sample size, treatment regimen, and outcome measures (Lefebvre et al., 2019). The extracted data were then analyzed using descriptive statistics and meta-analytic techniques to quantify the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation (Higgins & Green, 2011). The meta-analysis was conducted using a random-effects model, which accounted for the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The results of the meta-analysis were presented as mean differences or odds ratios, with 95% confidence intervals, to quantify the magnitude of the effects. To assess the quality of the included studies, a risk-of-bias assessment was performed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (Higgins et al., 2011). This tool evaluates the risk of bias in seven domains, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases (Savovic et al., 2012). The risk-of-bias assessment was used to inform the interpretation of the results and to identify potential sources of bias in the included studies. Statistical analysis was performed using R software (version 4.1.0) and the metafor package (version 2.4-0) (Viechtbauer, 2010). The level of significance was set at p < 0.05, and all tests were two-tailed. The results of the statistical analysis were presented in tables and figures, with accompanying narrative summaries to facilitate interpretation. The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database (registration number: CRD42020177743), and the review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). In addition to the quantitative analysis, a qualitative synthesis of the included studies was performed to identify themes and patterns in the data (Thomas & Harden, 2008). This involved a thematic analysis of the study findings, which was used to inform the development of a conceptual framework for understanding the role of carrageenan and CMC in intestinal inflammation. The conceptual framework was used to guide the interpretation of the results and to identify areas for future research. Overall, the methods employed in this review were designed to provide a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of the evidence on the role of carrageenan and CMC in intestinal inflammation. The use of a systematic search strategy, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and risk-of-bias assessment ensured that the review was conducted in a transparent and unbiased manner. The quantitative and qualitative analysis of the included studies provided a detailed understanding of the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation, and the conceptual framework developed from the thematic analysis provided a basis for future research in this area.
