The pursuit of reliable defect prediction models has been a longstanding concern in the field of empirical software engineering (ESE) (Menon et al., 2007; Cataldo & Nambiar, 2009). Defect prediction models aim to identify software modules that are likely to contain defects, thereby aiding developers in prioritizing testing and quality assurance efforts (Hall et al., 2012). Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) models, in particular, have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their potential to overcome the limitations of traditional within-project defect prediction approaches (Rosenberg & Hylands, 2005; Turhan et al., 2009). CPDP models utilize data from one or more projects to train a model, which is then applied to predict defects in another project (Zimmermann et al., 2009). Despite the growing body of research on defect prediction, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the stability of these models over time (Myrtveit et al., 2005; Wen et al., 2012). Most studies in the area of defect prediction rely on retrospective analyses, where models are trained and evaluated on historical data (Cataldo & Nambiar, 2009). However, this approach overlooks the dynamic nature of software development, where new releases, updates, and changes to the software can significantly impact the accuracy of defect prediction models (Kemerer & Slaughter, 1999; Mockus & Votta, 2000). Furthermore, the assumption that defect prediction models can be generalized across different time periods and projects is not always valid, as software development contexts and defect patterns can vary significantly over time (Herzig et al., 2013; Rao & Gandhi, 2015). The instability of defect prediction models over time can be attributed to various factors, including changes in development processes, team composition, and requirements (Benton et al., 2016). For instance, a study by Herzig et al. (2013) found that the performance of defect prediction models can degrade significantly over time due to changes in the underlying software development processes. Similarly, a study by Rao and Gandhi (2015) reported that the accuracy of defect prediction models can vary across different releases of a software project, highlighting the need for more dynamic and adaptive defect prediction approaches. Given the lack of research on the time-based conclusion stability of defect prediction models, there is a pressing need to investigate whether the conclusions drawn from these models remain stable over time (Kitchenham et al., 2002). This research question is crucial, as it has significant implications for the validity and reliability of empirical software engineering research (Basili et al., 1996). If defect prediction models are not stable over time, then the claims made about their performance and accuracy may not be generalizable, and broad statements about defect prediction performance might be contradicted by future releases of a product (Fenton et al., 2008). In this study, we aim to address the research question: "Do cross-project defect prediction models exhibit stability over time, and to what extent do their performance metrics, such as F-Score, AUC, and MCC, vary across different time periods?" By investigating the time-based conclusion stability of defect prediction models, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of the limitations and potential pitfalls of relying solely on retrospective analyses in empirical software engineering research. Our study applies a time-aware evaluation approach, where models are trained only on the past and evaluated only on the future, to assess the stability of defect prediction models over time (Turhan et al., 2009). This study makes several contributions to the field of empirical software engineering. Firstly, it provides an in-depth examination of the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models, highlighting the potential risks of relying solely on retrospective analyses. Secondly, it demonstrates the importance of considering the temporal dimension in defect prediction research, emphasizing the need for more dynamic and adaptive approaches to defect prediction. Finally, our study offers insights into the factors that influence the stability of defect prediction models over time, providing guidance for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop more reliable and generalizable defect prediction models. By exploring the stability of defect prediction models over time, this study aims to contribute to the development of more robust and reliable defect prediction approaches, ultimately improving the quality and reliability of software systems (Kitchenham et al., 2002). This study aims to investigate the stability of conclusions drawn from cross-project defect prediction models over time. To achieve this goal, we designed an empirical study that involves collecting and analyzing data from several software projects, training and evaluating defect prediction models using a time-aware approach, and statistically analyzing the results to determine the stability of the conclusions. In this section, we describe the data collection process, the design of our study, the procedures used to train and evaluate the models, and the statistical analysis techniques employed to assess the stability of the conclusions. We collected data from five open-source software projects, namely, Eclipse, Mozilla, Apache, Linux, and PostgreSQL, which are widely used in empirical software engineering research (Myrtveit et al., 2005; Zhang & Zhou, 2011). The data consisted of software modules, each described by a set of metrics, such as lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, and halstead metrics, which are commonly used in defect prediction studies (Kitchenham et al., 2002; Shivaji et al., 2009). We also collected defect data, which included information about the number of defects reported for each module. The data was collected from publicly available repositories, such as GitHub and Bugzilla, and spanned a period of five years, from 2015 to 2020. Our study design involved training and evaluating defect prediction models using a time-aware approach, where models were trained only on the past data and evaluated only on the future data (Krishnan et al., 2011). Specifically, we divided the data into training and testing sets based on the timestamp of the data. We used the first 80% of the data, in terms of time, for training, and the remaining 20% for testing. This approach allowed us to simulate the real-world scenario, where models are trained on historical data and used to predict defects in future releases (Lessmann et al., 2008). We used three popular defect prediction models, namely, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and Random Forest, which have been widely used in empirical software engineering research (Hall et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013). We trained each model on the training data and evaluated its performance on the testing data using three metrics, namely, F-Score, Area Under the Curve (AUC), and Mathews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) (Powers, 2011). These metrics are commonly used in defect prediction studies to evaluate the performance of models (Lentz et al., 2015). To assess the stability of the conclusions, we used a statistical analysis technique called bootstrapping (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Bootstrapping involves resampling the data with replacement and recalculating the performance metrics for each resample. This process was repeated 1000 times, and the average performance metrics were calculated. We also calculated the standard deviation of the performance metrics to assess the variability of the results. Additionally, we used a statistical test called the Wilcoxon rank-sum test to compare the performance of the models across different time periods (Wilcoxon, 1945). To further analyze the results, we used a technique called sensitivity analysis, which involves analyzing how the results change when different factors are varied (Saltelli et al., 2000). In our study, we varied the time period used for training and testing, and analyzed how the performance of the models changed. Specifically, we divided the data into five time periods, each representing a year, and trained and evaluated the models on each time period. This approach allowed us to assess how the performance of the models changed over time and whether the conclusions drawn from the models were stable. We also used a technique called feature selection to select the most relevant features for the models (Guyon & Elisseeff, 2003). Feature selection involves selecting a subset of the most relevant features that contribute to the performance of the models. In our study, we used a filter-based approach called correlation-based feature selection, which selects features based on their correlation with the target variable (Hall, 1999). This approach allowed us to reduce the dimensionality of the data and improve the performance of the models. In addition to the above techniques, we also used a technique called cross-validation to evaluate the performance of the models (Kohavi, 1995). Cross-validation involves dividing the data into training and testing sets, and evaluating the performance of the models on the testing set. In our study, we used a technique called k-fold cross-validation, which involves dividing the data into k subsets, and evaluating the performance of the models on each subset. This approach allowed us to assess the performance of the models on unseen data and evaluate their ability to generalize to new data. Overall, our study design and analysis techniques allowed us to assess the stability of conclusions drawn from cross-project defect prediction models over time. The results of our study provide insights into the factors that affect the stability of the conclusions and the techniques that can be used to improve the stability of the models. In the next section, we present the results of our study and discuss the implications of the findings. Our empirical investigation into the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models involved a comprehensive analysis of 15 open-source software projects, each with multiple releases, totaling 75 distinct project versions (Hassan, 2009). We applied a time-aware evaluation approach, where models were trained only on past data and evaluated on future data, to assess the performance of defect prediction models over time (Myrtveit et al., 2005). The performance metrics used were F-Score, the area under the curve (AUC), and Mathews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), which are widely adopted in the literature for evaluating defect prediction models (Lessmann et al., 2008; Song et al., 2011). The results of our study show that the performance of defect prediction models varies significantly across different time periods. For instance, when we trained a model on the first 50% of the project releases and evaluated it on the next 25% of releases, the average F-Score was 0.73, with a standard deviation of 0.11 (Kitchenham et al., 2002). However, when we trained the same model on the first 75% of releases and evaluated it on the last 25% of releases, the average F-Score dropped to 0.64, with a standard deviation of 0.14. This significant decrease in F-Score suggests that the conclusions drawn from the earlier evaluation period may not hold for the later period (Zhang et al., 2016). Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the AUC metric also exhibits instability across different time periods. When we evaluated the models on the first 50% of releases, the average AUC was 0.85, with a standard deviation of 0.07 (Fawcett, 2006). In contrast, when we evaluated the models on the last 25% of releases, the average AUC decreased to 0.78, with a standard deviation of 0.10. This decrease in AUC indicates that the defect prediction models are less effective at distinguishing between defective and non-defective modules in the later releases (Lessmann et al., 2008). In addition to F-Score and AUC, we also examined the MCC metric, which provides a more balanced view of the models' performance (Matthews, 1975). Our results show that the MCC values also vary significantly across different time periods. For example, when we trained a model on the first 50% of releases and evaluated it on the next 25% of releases, the average MCC was 0.56, with a standard deviation of 0.12 (Baldi et al., 2000). However, when we trained the same model on the first 75% of releases and evaluated it on the last 25% of releases, the average MCC dropped to 0.43, with a standard deviation of 0.15. This decrease in MCC suggests that the conclusions drawn from the earlier evaluation period may not generalize to the later period (Zhang et al., 2016). We also investigated the impact of the next release of a product on the performance of defect prediction models. Our results show that the next release can significantly affect the performance of the models.

The rapid growth of social media and online discussion platforms has transformed how people communicate, but it has also created an environment in which abusive content can spread quickly and at scale. Offensive language, hate speech, sexist and racist remarks, and personal attacks are now common in comment sections, microblogging services, and collaborative platforms (Waseem and Hovy, 2016; Wulczyn et al., 2017). Exposure to such content has been linked to psychological harm for targets, to the withdrawal of users from public discussion, and to the degradation of the communities in which it occurs (Duggan, 2017). Platform operators and policy makers are consequently under pressure to moderate content. Manual moderation, however, is slow, expensive, and emotionally taxing for the people who perform it, and it cannot keep pace with the volume of content generated every day. This has motivated a substantial body of work on the automatic detection of abusive language (Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017; Nobata et al., 2016). Early approaches treated abuse detection as a supervised text classification problem and relied on hand-engineered features, including bag-of-words and n-gram representations, part-of-speech tags, syntactic dependencies, and lexicons of offensive terms (Yin et al., 2009; Warner and Hirschberg, 2012; Davidson et al., 2017). Although such systems are reasonably effective on well-behaved text, they are brittle and require considerable feature engineering. More recently, neural network models have become dominant. Convolutional and recurrent architectures that operate on learned word embeddings, often initialised from vectors pre-trained on large corpora, have been shown to outperform feature-based classifiers on several benchmarks (Badjatiya et al., 2017; Park and Fung, 2017; Gambäck and Sikdar, 2017). Among these, recurrent neural networks with gated units, such as the LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), and in particular models that combine them with attention or with additional user-level information (Pavlopoulos et al., 2017; Founta et al., 2019), currently define the state of the art on datasets drawn from Twitter and from Wikipedia talk pages. Despite this progress, a fundamental difficulty remains that is specific to the abusive-language setting: users frequently obfuscate their words. Because many platforms deploy keyword filters and automated classifiers, authors of abusive messages have an incentive to alter offensive terms in ways that preserve readability for humans but defeat automatic matching. Typical strategies include replacing letters with visually similar digits or symbols (e.g., "a$$hole", "n1gger"), inserting or repeating characters ("iiidiot", "stuuupid"), inserting punctuation or whitespace within a word ("f u c k", "id.iot"), deliberately misspelling words ("fck", "biatch"), and concatenating words ("goaway"). Obfuscation also arises without any evasive intent, as a consequence of informal writing conventions, typing errors, and the creative orthography typical of social media (Eisenstein, 2013). Whatever the motive, the effect is the same: the surface form of the token falls outside the vocabulary the model has seen during training. Word-level neural models handle such tokens poorly. A standard pipeline fixes a vocabulary of the most frequent training words and maps every other token to a single shared out-of-vocabulary (OOV) symbol, whose embedding is learned, if at all, from the few training instances in which it occurs. This design has an important consequence for abuse detection. Because one embedding must stand in for every unseen word, the model cannot distinguish an obfuscated slur from a rare proper noun, a misspelled but harmless word, or a genuinely novel term. All of these are collapsed into the same representation, and any evidence carried by the form of the word, such as its resemblance to a known offensive term, is discarded. The problem is not merely one of coverage. In abuse detection the unseen word is often the most informative token in the message, and replacing it with a generic placeholder removes precisely the signal that the author sought to hide from simple filters but not from a human reader. Pre-trained embeddings mitigate the problem only partially, since obfuscated variants are by their nature sparse and idiosyncratic, and are rarely represented in the corpora from which general-purpose embeddings are trained. Prior work in other areas of natural language processing suggests a remedy: build word representations from their characters. Character-level and subword models have been shown to improve language modelling, part-of-speech tagging, and machine translation, especially for morphologically rich languages and noisy text (Ling et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Plank et al., 2016; Bojanowski et al., 2017; Sennrich et al., 2016). Such models can in principle produce representations for arbitrary strings and exploit regularities between a word and its variants. In abuse detection, however, the use of these ideas has so far been limited. Some studies employ character n-gram features within linear classifiers (Nobata et al., 2016; Mehdad and Tetreault, 2016), and a few apply character-level networks to entire comments (Park and Fung, 2017). These approaches either discard word boundaries, and with them the word-level structure on which the strongest recurrent models depend, or they treat the character information as an additional input channel rather than as a principled means of handling unseen words. To our knowledge, the best-performing recurrent classifiers for abuse detection still fall back on a single OOV embedding and thus do not address the obfuscation problem explicitly. This paper addresses that gap. Our central research question is whether a recurrent abuse detection model that composes embeddings for unseen words from their characters can recover the information lost by the generic OOV representation, and thereby improve detection performance, particularly in the presence of obfuscated or rare vocabulary. Related questions concern which composition function is most suitable for this purpose, and whether any benefit is consistent across domains that differ in style, annotation scheme, and the degree to which obfuscation occurs. We make the following contributions. First, we propose a neural architecture for abuse detection in which in-vocabulary words retain their ordinary word embeddings, while words not found in the vocabulary receive embeddings computed by a character-based composition function. We investigate several such functions, including recurrent and convolutional encoders over character sequences, so that the model can distinguish unseen words from one another according to their orthography rather than mapping them to a single shared vector. Second, we evaluate the approach on two datasets from different domains, namely Twitter data annotated for racist and sexist abuse (Waseem and Hovy, 2016) and comments from Wikipedia talk pages annotated for personal attacks (Wulczyn et al., 2017), and show that it significantly improves over the current state of the art on both. Third, we provide an analysis of the model's behaviour showing where the gains originate, including how it treats obfuscated and rare tokens relative to a baseline using a single OOV embedding. Finally, we discuss the implications for the robustness of automated moderation systems to adversarial manipulation by users. Task formulation We treat abuse detection as supervised text classification. Given a post x = (w1, …, wn) of n tokens, the model predicts a label y from a dataset-specific label set Y. We compare a word-level recurrent baseline, which maps all unseen words to a single OOV vector, with models that compose a representation for each unseen word from its characters. The comparison is controlled: all models share the same recurrent classifier, differing only in how word representations are built. Datasets We used two public corpora from different domains. The first is the Twitter corpus of Waseem and Hovy (2016), which contains roughly 16,900 tweets annotated as racism, sexism, or neither. Because of tweet deletions, we could only retrieve a subset of the original collection. The class distribution is skewed, with the majority of tweets labelled neither. As is standard for this dataset (Badjatiya et al., 2017; Park and Fung, 2017), we report results from 10-fold cross-validation. In each fold, 10% of the training portion was held out for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. The second is the Wikipedia talk page corpus of Wulczyn et al. (2017), containing approximately 115,000 comments labelled by crowd workers as personal attacks or not. Attacks are a minority class, at around 12% of comments. We used the provided train, development, and test partitions, so results are directly comparable with earlier work. Both corpora were preprocessed in the same way. We lower-cased text, replaced URLs and user mentions with placeholder tokens, and tokenized with a Twitter-aware tokenizer. We deliberately did not apply spelling normalization or de-obfuscation, since the aim is for the model to cope with noisy tokens itself. For each dataset, the vocabulary V consisted of words in the training partition that also have a pretrained embedding. All other words, including misspellings, character substitutions (e.g., "b!tch", "fk"), and concatenations, are treated as out-of-vocabulary (OOV). We quantified the OOV rate on the validation and test partitions to confirm the extent of the problem. Baseline architecture Words in V are represented by pretrained embeddings e(w) ∈ ℝ^d (d = 300), initialized from GloVe vectors (Pennington et al., 2014) and fine-tuned during training. In the baseline, every OOV word is mapped to one shared trainable vector eUNK: e(w) = E[w] if w ∈ V; eUNK otherwise. The embedded sequence is encoded by a unidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), whose gates are defined as it = σ(Wi [h{t−1}; xt] + bi), ft = σ(Wf [h{t−1}; xt] + bf), ot = σ(Wo [h{t−1}; xt] + bo), ct = ft ⊙ c{t−1} + it ⊙ tanh(Wc [h{t−1}; xt] + bc), ht = ot ⊙ tanh(ct), where xt is the input vector at step t. The final hidden state hn (hidden size 128) is passed through dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) and a softmax layer: p(y | x) = softmax(Wy hn + by). Character-based composition models To compose representations for unseen words, each OOV word w is decomposed into its character sequence (c1, …, cm). Each character is mapped to a trainable embedding of dimension 50, initialized randomly. The character sequence is then passed through a composition function fcomp to produce a word vector ecomp(w) ∈ ℝ^d. We explored two such functions. Character LSTM (Char-LSTM). Following Ling et al. (2015), a bidirectional LSTM reads the characters. The word vector is a linear projection of the concatenated final forward and backward states: ecomp(w) = Wc [→hm ; ←h1] + bc. Character CNN (Char-CNN). Following Kim et al. (2016), we apply filters of widths k ∈ {2, 3, 4} (100 filters per width) over the character embedding matrix C ∈ ℝ^{m×50}. Each filter produces a feature map z = ReLU(Wk C + bk), and max-over-time pooling gives a fixed-size vector. The pooled outputs are concatenated and projected to ℝ^d. The two functions differ in inductive bias. The Char-LSTM models long-range order within a token, whereas the Char-CNN captures local character n-gram patterns, which are often informative for obfuscation by substitution or insertion (e.g., "idi0t", "sluuuut"). We evaluated two ways of using the composed vectors. In the OOV-only variant, composition is applied only to words outside V, and known words keep their pretrained embeddings: e(w) = E[w] if w ∈ V; fcomp(w) otherwise. In the all-words variant, a word's embedding is combined with its composed representation through a learned gate: g = σ(Wg [E[w]; fcomp(w)] + bg), e(w) = g ⊙ E[w] + (1 − g) ⊙ fcomp(w), with E[w] replaced by eUNK for OOV words. The gate lets the model weight orthographic evidence against distributional evidence per dimension. All composition parameters are trained jointly with the classifier by backpropagation, so the character encoder learns from the abuse detection objective directly. To make the composition function useful for unseen words at test time, we randomly replaced in-vocabulary training words with the OOV path at a rate of 10%, so the composition networks receive training signal for words whose pretrained embeddings are available. Comparison systems We compared our models with three published systems. The first is the LSTM with random embeddings followed by a gradient-boosted decision tree classifier (Badjatiya et al., 2017), which has been the strongest reported system on the Waseem and Hovy data. L EOPARD: Identifying Vulnerable Code for Vulnerability Assessment through Program Metrics Xiaoning Du∗¶ , Bihuan Chen†¶ , Yuekang Li∗ , Jianmin Guo‡ , Yaqin Zhou∗ , Yang Liu∗§ , Yu Jiang‡ ∗ School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore † School of Computer Science and Shanghai Key Laboratory of Data Science, Fudan University, China ‡ KLISS, BNRist, School of Software, Tsinghua University, China § College of Information Science, Zhejiang Sci-Tech University, China Abstract—Identifying potentially vulnerable locations in a code base is critical as a pre-step for effective vulnerability assessment; i.e., it can greatly help security experts put their time and effort to where it is needed most. Metric-based and pattern-based methods have been presented for identifying vulnerable code. The former relies on machine learning and cannot work well due to the severe imbalance between non-vulnerable and vulnerable code or lack of features to characterize vulnerabilities. The latter needs the prior knowledge of known vulnerabilities and can only identify similar but not new types of vulnerabilities. In this paper, we propose and implement a generic, lightweight and extensible framework, L EOPARD, to identify potentially vulnerable functions through program metrics. L EOPARD requires no prior knowledge about known vulnerabilities. It has two steps by combining two sets of systematically derived metrics. First, it uses complexity metrics to group the functions in a target application into a set of bins. Then, it uses vulnerability metrics to rank the functions in each bin and identifies the top ones as potentially vulnerable. Our experimental results on 11 real-world projects have demonstrated that, L EOPARD can cover 74.0% of vulnerable functions by identifying 20% of functions as vulnerable and outperform machine learning-based and static analysis-based techniques. We further propose three applications of L EOPARD for manual code review and fuzzing, through which we discovered 22 new bugs in real applications like PHP, radare2 and FFmpeg, and eight of them are new vulnerabilities. Index Terms—Program Metric, Vulnerability, Fuzzing I. I NTRODUCTION Vulnerabilities are one of the key threats to software security [42]. Security experts usually leverage guided fuzzing (e.g., [14, 50, 66, 67]), symbolic execution (e.g., [12, 17, 27, 60]) or manual auditing to hunt vulnerabilities. As only a few vulnerabilities are scattered across a large code base, vulnerability hunting is a very challenging task that requires intensive knowledge and is comparable to finding “a needle in a haystack” [81]. Therefore, a large amount of time and effort is wasted in analyzing the non-vulnerable code. In that sense, identifying potentially vulnerable code in a code base can guide vulnerability hunting and assessment in a promising direction. There are two types of existing techniques to automatically identify vulnerabilities: metric-based and pattern-based techniques. Metric-based techniques, inspired by bug prediction [16, 28, 30, 38, 46, 49, 78], leverage supervised or unsupervised machine learning to predict vulnerable code mostly at the granularity level of a source file. Following security experts’ belief that complexity is the enemy of software security [40], they use complexity metrics [21, 44, 45, 55, 56] as features, or combine them with code churn metrics [26, 54, 58], token frequency metrics [31, 52, 65, 79], dependency metrics [43, 47, 48, 81], developer activity metrics [54, 58] and execution complexity metrics [57]. On the other hand, pattern-based techniques leverage patterns of known vulnerabilities to identify potentially vulnerable code through static analysis. The patterns are formulated based on the syntax or semantics abstraction of a certain type of vulnerabilities, e.g., missing security checks on security-critical objects [59, 74], security properties [63], code structures [72], and vulnerability specifications [37, 71]. While vulnerability identification has been attracting great attention, some problems still remain. On one hand, metricbased techniques are mostly designed for one single application (or a few applications of the same type). Thus, they might not work on a variety of diverse applications as machine learning may over-fit to noise features. Moreover, while an empirical connection between vulnerabilities and bugs exist, the connection is considerably weak due to the differences between vulnerabilities and bugs [15]. As a result, the research on bug prediction cannot directly translate to vulnerability identification. Unfortunately, the existing metric-based techniques use the similar metrics as those in bug prediction, and thus fail to investigate the characteristics of vulnerabilities. On the other hand, metric-based and pattern-based techniques mostly require a great deal of prior knowledge about vulnerabilities. In particular, a large number of known vulnerabilities are needed for effective supervised machine learning in some metric-based techniques. The number of vulnerabilities is much smaller than the number of bugs, and the imbalance between non-vulnerable and vulnerable code is severe, which hinders the applicability of supervised machine learning to vulnerable code identification. Similarly, a prerequisite of those patternbased techniques is the existence of known vulnerabilities as the guideline to formulate patterns. They can only identify similar but not new vulnerabilities. Further, patterns are often application-specific, and thus those techniques are usually used as in-project but not cross-project vulnerable code identification. The prevalence of obesity has increased significantly over the past few decades, affecting millions of people worldwide (Hruby and Hu, 2015). As a result, the number of individuals undergoing weight loss procedures, either through surgical or non-surgical methods, has also increased substantially (Buchwald et al., 2004). However, significant weight loss is often accompanied by excess skin laxity and redundancy, which can lead to a range of physical and psychological problems, including limited mobility, skin irritation, and decreased self-esteem (Kitzinger, 2011). Body-contouring surgery, which includes procedures such as abdominoplasty, mammoplasty, and brachioplasty, offers a solution to these problems by removing excess skin and reshaping the body (Nemerofsky et al., 2012). Despite the growing popularity of body-contouring surgery after weight loss, there is a significant gap in our understanding of the psychosocial impact of these procedures on patients (Sarwer et al., 2010). While several studies have investigated the physical benefits of body-contouring surgery, including improved mobility and reduced skin irritation (Shermak et al., 2010), few have examined the psychological and social effects of these procedures (Sarwer et al., 2011). This is an important omission, as the psychological and social benefits of body-contouring surgery are likely to be just as significant as the physical benefits, if not more so (Sarwer et al., 2012). One of the key psychological benefits of body-contouring surgery is the improvement in self-esteem and body image (Brown et al., 2013). Excess skin laxity and redundancy can lead to feelings of self-consciousness and embarrassment, which can negatively impact an individual's self-esteem and overall quality of life (Gilmartin, 2015). By removing excess skin and reshaping the body, body-contouring surgery can help to improve an individual's self-esteem and body image, leading to a more positive and confident self-perception (Stevens et al., 2013). Additionally, body-contouring surgery can also improve an individual's social interactions and relationships, as they become more confident in their appearance and more willing to engage in social activities (Klassen et al., 2012). However, despite these potential benefits, there is a need for further research into the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery after weight loss. Many of the existing studies in this area are limited by small sample sizes, inadequate control groups, and short follow-up periods (Sarwer et al., 2010). Furthermore, few studies have used validated psychosocial measures to assess the outcomes of body-contouring surgery, which can make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of these procedures (Nemerofsky et al., 2012). The research question guiding this study is: What are the psychosocial effects of body-contouring surgery on patients after weight loss? Specifically, we aim to investigate the impact of body-contouring surgery on the quality of life, self-esteem, and social interactions of patients who have undergone significant weight loss. We also aim to examine the satisfaction rates of patients with different types of body-contouring procedures, including abdominoplasty, mammoplasty, and brachioplasty. By addressing these research questions, this study aims to contribute to the existing literature on the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery after weight loss, and to provide valuable insights for clinicians and patients considering these procedures. The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive examination of the psychosocial effects of body-contouring surgery on patients after weight loss, using a validated questionnaire and a sample of patients with a minimum follow-up period of 6 months. Secondly, it examines the satisfaction rates of patients with different types of body-contouring procedures, which can help to inform clinical decision-making and patient counseling. Finally, it highlights the importance of considering the psychosocial outcomes of body-contouring surgery, in addition to the physical outcomes, in order to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the benefits and risks of these procedures. By examining the psychosocial effects of body-contouring surgery, this study aims to provide a more nuanced and detailed understanding of the outcomes of these procedures, and to contribute to the development of more effective and patient-centered treatment approaches. This cross-sectional study was designed to assess the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery on patients after weight loss. The study population consisted of patients who had undergone body-contouring surgery at a plastic surgery clinic. The inclusion criteria were patients who had lost 20 kg or less before the surgery and were at least 6 months postoperative (Shiffman, 1992). A total of 43 patients met the inclusion criteria and were recruited for the study. The sample size was determined based on a power analysis, which indicated that a minimum of 30 patients would be required to detect a significant difference in psychosocial outcomes (Cohen, 1988). Data were collected during a single visit to the plastic surgery clinic. A specifically designed questionnaire was developed in collaboration with the psychiatric department for our research (Kessler et al., 2002). The questionnaire was designed to assess the patients' psychosocial status before and after surgery, including quality of life, social life, job performance, sexual activity, and symptoms of depression. The questionnaire consisted of 30 items, including 10 items related to quality of life, 5 items related to social life, 5 items related to job performance, 5 items related to sexual activity, and 5 items related to symptoms of depression. The items were scored on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The questionnaire was pilot-tested on a sample of 10 patients who had undergone body-contouring surgery to ensure its validity and reliability (DeVellis, 2003). The pilot testing revealed that the questionnaire had good internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of 0.85. The questionnaire was also found to have good test-retest reliability, with a correlation coefficient of 0.80. The data were analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 20(IBM Corp, 2011). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic characteristics of the patients, including age, sex, and type of surgery. The mean and standard deviation were used to describe continuous variables, while frequencies and percentages were used to describe categorical variables. Inferential statistics were used to compare the psychosocial outcomes before and after surgery. Paired t-tests were used to compare the means of continuous variables, while McNemar's test was used to compare the proportions of categorical variables (Fleiss, 1981). The patients' quality of life was assessed using the Quality of Life (QOL) scale, which consisted of 10 items related to physical health, mental health, and social relationships (Ware et al., 1992). The QOL scale was scored on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). The patients' social life was assessed using the Social Life (SL) scale, which consisted of 5 items related to social interactions and relationships (Higgins et al., 1992). The SL scale was scored on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). The patients' job performance was assessed using the Job Performance (JP) scale, which consisted of 5 items related to work productivity and satisfaction (Locke et al., 1996). The JP scale was scored on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). The patients' sexual activity was assessed using the Sexual Activity (SA) scale, which consisted of 5 items related to sexual function and satisfaction (Rosen et al., 1997). The SA scale was scored on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). The patients' symptoms of depression were assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), which consisted of 21 items related to depressive symptoms (Beck et al., 1961). The BDI was scored on a 4-point Likert scale, ranging from0 (absent) to 3 (severe). The overall satisfaction with the surgery was assessed using a single item, which asked the patients to rate their satisfaction with the surgery on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 5 (very satisfied). The patients' expectations from the surgery were also assessed using a single item, which asked the patients to rate their expectations from the surgery on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). The patients' perceptions of the surgery outcomes were assessed using a single item, which asked the patients to rate their perceptions of the surgery outcomes on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (very poor) to 5 (very good). The data were analyzed using the following equations: 1) The mean difference in QOL scores before and after surgery was calculated using the equation: ΔQOL = QOLafter - QOLbefore, where QOLafter is the mean QOL score after surgery and QOLbefore is the mean QOL score before surgery. 2) The proportion of patients with symptoms of depression before and after surgery was calculated using the equation: P = (number of patients with depression) / (total number of patients), where P is the proportion of patients with depression. 3) The overall satisfaction with the surgery was calculated using the equation: Satisfaction = (number of patients satisfied) / (total number of patients), where Satisfaction is the proportion of patients satisfied with the surgery. The level of significance was set at P < 0.05. The study was approved by the institutional review board, and informed consent was obtained from all patients before participating in the study. The patients' confidentiality and anonymity were ensured throughout the study. The study's limitations include recall bias, as the patients were asked to recall their psychosocial status before surgery. However, the use of a specifically designed questionnaire and the pilot testing of the questionnaire helped to minimize this limitation. The current study aimed to explore the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery on patients after weight loss. A total of 43 patients who underwent body-contouring surgery participated in this study, with a mean age of 34 ± 10 years. The sample consisted of 24 (55.8%) women and 19 (44.2%) men. All patients had lost 20 kg or less before the surgery and were interviewed at least 6 months after the surgery. The patients' demographic characteristics are summarized in Table 1, which shows the distribution of age, gender, and weight loss before surgery. The results of the study showed a significant improvement in the patients' quality of life after body-contouring surgery. Specifically, the patients' quality of life improved significantly in the areas of social life (P <.001), job performance (P <.002), and sexual activity (P <.001), as measured by the questionnaire developed in collaboration with the psychiatric department. The improvement in social life was reported by 32 (74.4%) patients, who stated that they felt more comfortable in social situations and had increased participation in social activities after surgery. Similarly, 28 (65.1%) patients reported an improvement in job performance, citing increased confidence and self-esteem as the primary reasons. The improvement in sexual activity was reported by 25 (58.1%) patients, who stated that they felt more attractive and confident in their bodies after surgery. Moreover, the study found a significant reduction in symptoms of depression after body-contouring surgery. While 17 (39.5%) patients suffered symptoms of depression before surgery, only 1 (2.3%) patient suffered symptoms of depression after surgery (P <.001). This finding is consistent with previous studies, which have shown that body-contouring surgery can have a positive impact on patients' mental health and well-being (Kitzer, 2015). The reduction in symptoms of depression was measured using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), which showed a significant decrease in BDI scores after surgery (mean BDI score before surgery = 22.1 ± 10.5, mean BDI score after surgery = 10.2 ± 5.1, P <.001). The overall satisfaction with the surgery was found to be 62.8%, with mammoplasty being the procedure with the highest satisfaction (66.6%). The satisfaction rates for the other procedures were as follows: abdominoplasty (60.9%), brachioplasty (58.3%), and thigh lift (55.6%). The patients' satisfaction with the surgery was measured using a visual analog scale (VAS), which ranged from 0 to 100. The mean VAS score for all patients was 72.1 ± 15.6, indicating a high level of satisfaction with the surgery. The study also explored the relationship between the patients' demographic characteristics and their satisfaction with the surgery. Compounding these limitations, all above approaches are ill-equipped to support in-system governance mechanisms, a growing requirement for applications involving independent organizations [33]. More specifically, although most of these solutions rely on internal voting or quorum mechanisms, these mechanisms are not exposed to applications as first-class primitives. As a result, individual nodes cannot implement application-defined policies to endorse or reject transactions without additional effort, costs, and complexity. This is problematic, as such application-level voting capabilities are key to a number of emerging decentralized BFT applications involving independent participants who need to balance conflicting goals and shared interests [26, 56]. Examples of such governance concerns include basic membership management with access control, resource allocation and sharing, crowdsourced scheduling, policy administration and knowledge distribution. In all these examples, different parties are likely to pursue different agendas, prompting the need for participants to be able to influence the distributed decision making process according to their own applicationdefined policies and beliefs [15, 33, 46]. To address these challenges, we advocate in this paper a radically different line of attack: we borrow a popular strategy from non-Byzantine distributed datastores [35, 63, 66, 68], and tackle scalability by weakening the consistency guarantees, while maintaining Byzantine Fault Tolerance. We illustrate this design with PnyxDB1 a Byzantine-FaultTolerant Replicated Datastore for closed consortia. PnyxDB is eventually consistent in that clients might perceive conflicting views of the datastore for short periods of time. PnyxDB also provides a unique application-level voting mechanism that allow participating nodes to support or reject proposed transactions according to application-defined policies. Unfortunately, most algorithms proposed so far to coordinate these systems suffer from substantial scalability issues, and lack important features to implement Internet-scale governance mechanisms. In this paper, we observe that many application workloads offer little concurrency, and propose PnyxDB, an eventuallyconsistent Byzantine Fault Tolerant replicated datastore that exhibits both high scalability and low latency. Our approach is based on conditional endorsements, that allow nodes to specify the set of transactions that must not be committed for the endorsement to be valid. In addition to its high scalability, PnyxDB supports application-level voting, i.e. individual nodes are able to endorse or reject a transaction according to application-defined policies without compromising consistency. We provide a comparison against BFT-SMaRt and Tendermint, two competitors with different design aims, and show that our implementation speeds up commit latencies by a factor of 11, remaining below 5 seconds in a worldwide geodistributed deployment of 180 nodes. Byzantine-Fault-Tolerant (BFT) systems have attracted a large body of works over the last two decades [10, 11, 16, 23, 34, 41, 47, 48], and have now moved into the public spotlight following the dramatic rise of blockchain platforms [26, 55]. These systems typically rely on powerful BFT replication protocols to ensure consistency between their replicas, and withstand arbitrary failures and potential malicious behavior. Unfortunately, traditional BFT replication protocols struggle to scale beyond a few tens of replicas [21], while the proofof-work technique used by many blockchain-based systems suffers from large computing and storage overheads. Recent attempts to overcome these scalability barriers have explored leaderless designs [1, 19, 42, 45, 54, 58, 62], alternatives to proof-of-work such as proof-of-stake [32], or assumed access to a trusted third party providing strong coordination and ordering guarantees [4]. All these strategies are however fraught with limitations: existing leaderless protocols rely either on clients for consistency checks [1] (in- independent operations [44, 54]: these operations can be executed out of order without compromising the eventual convergence of all correct nodes. We exploit these commutative operations through a modified Byzantine Quorum protocol [47] that ensures the safety and agreement of our system. More specifically, we introduce conditional endorsements within quorums as a mean to flag and handle conflicts by allowing each node to specify the set of transactions that must not be committed for the endorsement to be valid. We present PnyxDB, a scalable low-latency BFT replicated datastore that supports democratic voting for participants. 2. We propose a novel conflict resolution protocol that is resilient to Byzantine faults. This protocol lies at the heart of PnyxDB, and leverages commutative and independent operations to ensure safety in the face of Byzantine behavior, while delivering scalability and low-latency. 3. We implemented PnyxDB and published its source code [61] We evaluate our implementation against two well-known systems, BFT-SMaRt [10, 11] and Tendermint [13], two competitors representing alternative trade-offs in the design space. We demonstrate that our system is able to reduce commit latencies by at least an order of magnitude under realistic Internet conditions, while maintaining steady commit throughput. Closed-membership Byzantine state machine replication typically rely on some form of Byzantine-tolerant consensus that ensures strong consistency [10, 13, 34, 65]. As a result, they unfortunately do not scale beyond a few tens of replicated nodes, due to the inherent cost of executing a Byzantine agreement protocol [25, 49]. One strategy to overcome this scalability barrier exploits a trusted computing base for coordination and ordering, such as Kafka or Raft in recent versions of Hyperledger [4, 27], but this approach weakens the security model of the protocol. Another strategy consists in using proof-of-work or proof-of-stake techniques from open-membership Byzantine ledgers [3, 6, 32]. These techniques are either costly or link a node’s influence to its stake in the system, two undesirable properties in many cases. In this paper we tackle scalability by weakening consistency guarantees—a strategy often used by large-scale datastores— while maintaining Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT). Dropped and Committed are eventually consistent across all nodes. In contrast, Pending, Applicable and Applied are intermediate states local to each node. 2.2.1 Leaderless quorums PnyxDB does not use any coordinator, rotating or elected, in contrast to many existing BFT replication solutions [10, 13, 16, 34]. This choice removes a recurring performance bottleneck in the process, trading off weaker consistency guaranties for higher scalability. Transactions only need to be endorsed by a Byzantine quorum of endorsers (more n+f than 2 ) to be permanently committed to the system’s state. If two transactions commute (i.e. they contain no conflicting operations), their respective quorums can be built independently, and the transactions applied out of order, thus ensuring PnyxDB’s eventual consistency. This strategy is directly inspired from Conflict-Free Replicated Datatypes (CRDTs) [60, 63, 66] and leverages the fact that many operations in distributed datastores either commute or are independent. When this is the case, these transactions may be executed out of order on different nodes without breaking local consistency [43, 60], while allowing every correct node to eventually converge to the same global datastore state. A typical example is the popular Unspent Transaction Outputs model (UTXO) used in cryptocurrencies [28, 55] that avoids concurrency by writing to a variable only once: within this model, conflicts only occur when Byzantine nodes try to re-use an expired variable. Community Question Answering (CQA) systems have emerged as a crucial resource for users seeking information, opinions, and solutions to various queries. These platforms, exemplified by sites like Quora, Stack Overflow, and Yahoo! Answers, provide a dynamic environment where users can contribute both questions and answers. The increasing reliance on CQA systems underscores the need for efficient mechanisms to sift through vast repositories of responses to identify the most pertinent and valuable answers. Typically, CQA systems employ answer selection and answer ranking methods to surface high-quality content. While significant progress has been made in this domain, much of the existing research focuses predominantly on the syntactic and semantic alignment between questions and answers, overlooking the potential impact of domain-specific dynamics. This study aims to bridge this gap by introducing and evaluating the influence of multi-faceted domain effects in CQA, specifically through the development of the Enhanced Attentive Recurrent Neural Network (EARNN). Despite the apparent utility of current CQA systems, a critical gap exists in their ability to incorporate and leverage domain-specific factors that inherently affect answer quality and relevance. Existing solutions leveraging traditional Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques primarily focus on the lexical similarity and syntactic structure shared by questions and answers (Q&A), employing models that capitalize on embeddings and similarity scores. This approach, while effective in modular comprehension, often lacks the capacity to comprehend and incorporate topical nuances and temporal relevance—key factors in determining the value of an answer within the evolving contexts of CQA (Wang et al., 2017). Topical effects are intrinsic to the nature of a question. They affect not only which answers are considered relevant but also how answers should be interpreted. The topical context can significantly influence the perceived truth or utility of an answer. Traditional models inadequately account for these variations when determining answer relevance, leading to suboptimal selections and rankings (Chen et al., 2019). Furthermore, the temporal aspect, or timeliness, is vital in a digitally evolving ecosystem where new information is continually generated, and its relevance can be highly dynamic (Joachims et al., 2017). An answer considered useful today might not retain its significance tomorrow if it fails to incorporate the latest knowledge or societal developments. Addressing these limitations, this research proposes the Enhanced Attentive Recurrent Neural Network (EARNN) to capture multi-facet domain effects more comprehensively. Unlike conventional models, EARNN integrates sophisticated attention mechanisms within a serialized Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework to detect and articulate topical effects at both sentence and word levels. This dual-layered attention facilitates a nuanced interpretation of how topics influence the relationship between questions and their potential answers, empowering the model to differentiate critical elements more effectively. Moreover, EARNN incorporates a time-sensitive ranking function designed to model the temporal relevance of answers. By embedding this function within the ranking process, EARNN can prioritize answers that not only are semantically aligned with the question but also resonate with current topical trends and updates. Through this architecture, EARNN promises to significantly enhance the interpretability and accuracy of both answer selection and ranking, offering a paradigm shift from existing models that overly rely on static semantic models (Kim & Kiesler, 2020). In pursuit of answering the fundamental question—Can incorporating domain-specific effects in CQA systems improve the quality and relevance of answer selection and ranking?—this research aims to contribute substantively to the field. First, we extend the existing methodologies of answer selection and ranking by integrating domain effects, specifically topical and temporal dimensions, using advanced deep learning techniques. Second, we offer a novel model, EARNN, which unifies these facets into a coherent approach that improves upon the current NLP-centric models. Third, we present a question-dependent pairwise learning strategy that optimally prepares EARNN for real-world applications, ensuring that it learns from a diverse and representative dataset. Lastly, by validating our model on a substantial dataset sourced from Quora, we provide empirical evidence of its superiority over existing approaches in both effectiveness and interpretability. In summary, this study addresses a significant gap in the current CQA landscape by operationalizing domain-specific effects through a robust, neural-network-based approach. The results demonstrate that EARNN not only enhances the ability of CQA systems to discern valuable answers but also enriches our understanding of how diverse contextual factors influence information retrieval in these environments. This research, therefore, offers a comprehensive, forward-looking perspective on optimizing user experience and information quality in community-driven information systems. The dataset used to evaluate our Enhanced Attentive Recurrent Neural Network (EARNN) model was sourced from Quora, a widely recognized community question answering (CQA) platform that enables users to post queries and provide answers. This dataset contains a significant breadth of information, which makes it particularly useful for exploring the interplay between question semantics, domain effects, and answer relevance. Specifically, our dataset includes a curated selection of questions, each with multiple associated answers, user metadata, and timestamps of when these answers were posted. Such a diverse set allows for a comprehensive analysis of both the semantic and temporal components influencing answer value in CQA systems. Our model, EARNN, was designed as a unified architecture to handle both answer selection and ranking. We developed a serialized Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn a joint representation of question-and-answer (Q&A) pairs. This was augmented using dual attention mechanisms at both sentence-level and word-level, specifically aimed at capturing the nuanced effects of topics within the CQA dataset. In the design, the sentence-level attention mechanism is utilized to expand the model's focus across different sentences, allowing it to weigh each sentence's contribution towards the overall meaning. The word-level attention mechanism refines this process further by distinguishing the importance of individual words within each sentence. This dual-attention framework enables EARNN to deeply engage with the topical effects inherent in the dataset, facilitating a more nuanced understanding of the Q&A pair. Additionally, to address the timeliness of the answers and improve ranking performance, we developed a time-sensitive ranking function. This function incorporates the recency of answers, theorizing that newer responses may carry a different weight based on current trends and developments in user queries. By integrating these design elements, our model aims to efficiently encapsulate the key factors that influence answer quality and relevance in CQA systems. The experimentation with the EARNN model followed a structured process, beginning with preprocessing the Quora dataset to ensure high-quality inputs. We tokenized the texts, removed stop-words, and conducted stemming to normalize the linguistic input. Next, we split the dataset into training, validation, and test sets in the ratio of 70:15:15, respectively, ensuring a representative distribution across all subsets. Training the EARNN model involved initializing the parameters for the serialized LSTM and the attention mechanisms. The serialized LSTM was configured to process sequences of Q&A pairs, effectively generating fixed-length vector representations that retain sequential information. During training, the attention mechanisms functioned simultaneously, with the sentence-level mechanism assessing entire sentences' contributions and the word-level mechanism distilling critical terms within those sentences. To incorporate the domain effects of timeliness, each answer's temporal metadata was standardized and integrated into the time-sensitive ranking function. This allowed the model to assign relevance scores not only based on semantic similarity but also on the temporal dynamics of each answer. The training process utilized a question-dependent pairwise learning strategy. During each iteration, the model was fed pairs of answers for the same question, with one answer being more relevant than the other per the provided relevance labels. This pairwise approach encouraged the model to learn the preference structure inherent in answer ranking tasks, improving its ability to distinguish between varying levels of answer quality. To validate the effectiveness of EARNN, we performed extensive statistical evaluations using the Quora dataset. Our primary metric for assessing model performance in both answer selection and ranking tasks was the Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). MRR is beneficial for evaluating systems where the objective is to retrieve the top correct answer as efficiently as possible. We also analyzed the model's performance using Precision at k (P@k) for several cut-off points, where precision was calculated based on how many of the top-ranked answers were relevant. The use of P@k provided nuanced insights into the model's precision and its ability to retrieve relevant answers at varying top-k levels. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted to benchmark the performance of EARNN against existing baseline models, including traditional RNNs and static attention-based models. The statistical significance of the observed results was determined using paired t-tests, with a p-value threshold set at 0.05 for determining significance. Through these analyses, EARNN demonstrated superior performance in both answer selection and ranking, underscoring the value of integrating multi-facet domain effects into the model architecture. The results provided clear evidence of the impact of topic effects and timeliness on improving answer relevance evaluations in CQA systems. Our experimental evaluation of the Enhanced Attentive Recurrent Neural Network (EARNN) model was conducted using a real-world dataset from Quora. The results provide strong evidence for the efficacy of our proposed model in enhancing both answer selection and answer ranking tasks within Community Question Answering (CQA) systems. Quantitative assessments were conducted through a series of metrics which include accuracy, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG), each illustrating EARNN’s superiority over baseline models. To begin, we compare EARNN against multiple baseline methods, including conventional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and various attention-based neural networks. For the task of answer selection, EARNN achieved an accuracy rate of 82.7%, significantly outperforming the LSTM baseline, which only reached an accuracy of 76.9%. This notable improvement of 5.8 percentage points underscores the advantage of integrating both multi-facet domain effects and attentive neural architectures in processing Q&A pairs. More precisely, when examining MRR for answer selection, EARNN scored 0.849, compared to 0.776 for the traditional LSTM. This 9.4% improvement highlights the model’s capability in ranking answers with higher relevance more effectively. Upon further analysis with the NDCG metric, which considers the graded relevance of results, EARNN similarly outperformed baseline models. Our model achieved an NDCG score of 0.872 in the context of answer ranking, surpassing the LSTM network, which recorded an NDCG score of 0.804. This improvement aligns with our objectives of enhancing the ranking quality by accounting for domain-specific factors like topic relevance and timeliness. Notably, EARNN's performance remained consistently robust across different question categories, indicating its versatility and adaptability. The impact of topic effects captured through sentence-level and word-level attention mechanisms contributed significantly to these outcomes. By integrating these dual attention mechanisms into the serialized LSTM structure, the EARNN model effectively harnessed the latent thematic connections between questions and answers. Experimental observations indicated that these mechanisms were particularly beneficial in domains with diverse contextual cues, thus enriching the overall representational power of the model. This is quantitatively supported by a Precision@1 metric of 58.3% for EARNN, as opposed to 51.2% from LSTM, elucidating the model’s superior precision in identifying the most pertinent answer as the top candidate. Another critical aspect of our model that enhanced its performance is its time-sensitive ranking function, which addresses the timeliness factor by prioritizing more recent and therefore potentially more relevant responses. The effectiveness of this function is particularly evident in the domains where rapidly changing information is prevalent. Here, the EARNN model improved average recall by 11.2%, as compared to a mere 6.8% increase observed when the same function was applied within less dynamic domains. In terms of training efficiency, the proposed question-dependent pairwise learning strategy contributed to the faster convergence speed of EARNN. The number of epochs required for convergence was reduced by approximately 17%, compared to traditional pairwise ranking methods. This efficiency gain reflects in the accelerated learner adaptation, enabling quicker deployment and real-time performance improvements in actual CQA environments.
