Obesity remains one of the most persistent and costly public health problems in the United States. Nationally, roughly four in ten adults have obesity, and prevalence has risen steadily since the late 1970s (Hales et al., 2020; Fryar et al., 2018). Excess weight is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, several cancers, and premature mortality, and it contributes substantially to medical expenditures and lost productivity (Kopelman, 2000; Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012; Ward et al., 2021). Because the determinants of weight status operate at multiple levels, from individual behavior to the food, transportation, and economic environments in which people live, effective responses increasingly rely on place-based strategies such as zoning, transportation investment, food retail policy, and community programming (Swinburn et al., 2011; Story et al., 2008). Targeting and evaluating these strategies requires reliable information on where excess weight is concentrated and how it changes over time. Existing surveillance systems provide only limited geographic resolution. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) measures height and weight directly and is the national standard, but its sample is designed to support national and some subgroup estimates, not estimates for states or small areas. The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) offers state and, in some cases, county or metropolitan-area estimates, yet it relies on self-reported height and weight, which are known to produce underestimates of body mass index (BMI) and prevalence of obesity, with error that varies by sex, age, and body size (Gillum and Sempos, 2005; Connor Gorber et al., 2007). Response rates for telephone-based surveys have also fallen over time, raising concerns about nonresponse bias (Pierannunzi et al., 2013). Model-based approaches such as multilevel regression and poststratification, used in the CDC PLACES project, can produce census tract estimates from BRFSS data (Zhang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018). However, such estimates borrow strength from area-level covariates and are shrunk toward predicted values, so they may understate true variation among neighborhoods and can partly build in the very associations researchers wish to study. Because the estimated outcome is partly a function of the predictors, using these estimates to examine correlates of obesity is potentially circular. Several alternative data sources have been explored to fill this gap. Electronic health records can provide measured heights and weights for large populations and have been used to construct neighborhood and county-level obesity maps (Schwartz et al., 2017; Tomayko et al., 2021). Their coverage, however, is restricted to patients of participating health systems, who are not representative of the general population and who may differ systematically in weight and health care use. School-based body measurement programs yield population-level data for children (Ogden et al., 2018), but no comparable program exists for adults. Researchers have also used commercial data, social media, and wearable devices, which carry their own selection and validity concerns (Althoff et al., 2017). A source that covers most adults in a jurisdiction, includes a recorded address, and is already collected and maintained by a government agency would therefore be valuable. State-issued driver licenses and identification cards meet many of these criteria. In the United States, the great majority of adults hold either a driver license or a state identification card, and the application process records height, weight, date of birth, sex, and residential address. These records are held by state motor vehicle agencies and are routinely updated at renewal. Weight on a license is typically self-reported and may be rounded or outdated, and prior work comparing license data with measured values suggests systematic underreporting, particularly among women and older adults (Ezzati et al., 2006; Hodge et al., 2020). Even so, the same biases affect nearly all areas, and the sheer volume of records makes it possible to produce stable estimates for small geographic units without the sampling error that limits surveys. Earlier work using license data from Massachusetts found that aggregated BMI estimates were strongly correlated with obesity prevalence from independent sources and varied meaningfully across municipalities (Ezzati et al., 2006; Hodge et al., 2020). Despite this promise, applications remain rare, and few studies have used identification card data to evaluate the neighborhood characteristics associated with weight status across an entire state, including rural areas, where obesity prevalence is often highest and survey coverage is weakest (Befort et al., 2012; Trivedi et al., 2015). The neighborhood correlates of weight status are well documented in other data but not uniformly so. Area-level socioeconomic disadvantage, including low income, low educational attainment, and low housing values, has been consistently associated with higher BMI and obesity prevalence in the United States and other high-income countries (Wang and Beydoun, 2007; Black and Macinko, 2008; Singh et al., 2010). Racial and ethnic composition is also associated with weight status, reflecting structural inequities in housing, food access, and exposure to environmental stressors (Williams and Collins, 2001; Bell et al., 2019). Features of the built environment, such as supermarket access, the density of fast food outlets, and automobile dependence, have been linked to weight, though findings are mixed and often sensitive to how neighborhoods are defined and how confounding by socioeconomic status is handled (Cobb et al., 2015; Frank et al., 2004; Lovasi et al., 2009). Rural residence adds a further dimension, as rural adults tend to have higher BMI than urban adults, with differences in food environments, physical activity opportunities, and travel distances all proposed as contributing factors (Befort et al., 2012). Few studies have been able to examine these domains jointly, at the census tract level, using a measure of BMI that is not itself modeled from the covariates under study. This study addresses these gaps by using approximately three million Oregon state-issued identification card records to estimate average adult BMI for every census tract in the state. We ask three questions. First, can identification card data be processed into age-adjusted, tract-level BMI estimates that are stable and plausible? Second, how much of the variation in tract-level BMI is explained by population characteristics, food access, commuting behavior, and geography, and which of these factors are independently associated with BMI? Third, are the observed associations consistent with the established literature on socioeconomic and environmental disparities in weight status, which would support the validity of identification card data for surveillance? We make three contributions. First, we demonstrate a replicable approach for deriving small-area BMI estimates from administrative records that are already held by state agencies, which could be adopted by public health departments at low marginal cost. Second, because the estimates are computed directly from records rather than modeled from area characteristics, they allow unbiased examination of the neighborhood factors associated with weight status in urban, suburban, and rural settings. Third, by assessing the associations of home values, education, race, ethnicity, car commuting, and rural-urban commuting area classification with BMI, we provide evidence on the validity of this data source and identify potentially modifiable environmental targets for obesity prevention in Oregon and similar states. Data sources and study population We obtained de-identified records from the Oregon Driver and Motor Vehicle Services Division (DMV) for all active driver licenses, instruction permits, and state-issued identification cards held by Oregon residents aged 18 years or older at the time of extraction. The extract contained approximately three million records. Each record included the cardholder's self-reported height and weight as recorded at the most recent issuance or renewal, date of birth, sex, and residential address. Names, license numbers, and other direct identifiers were removed by DMV staff before transfer, and addresses were geocoded by the research team within a secure environment and then discarded after assignment to 2010 census tracts. The study used only existing administrative data and was determined to be exempt from review by the institutional review board. We excluded records with missing or implausible anthropometric values (height <122 cm or >213 cm; weight <32 kg or >227 kg; resulting BMI <15 or >60 kg/m²), following conventions used in other survey-based BMI analyses (Flegal et al., 2012). We also excluded records that could not be geocoded to an Oregon census tract (for example, post office boxes without a physical address match). Of 3.02 million eligible records, 2.88 million (95%) were retained for analysis. Tracts with fewer than 100 valid records were suppressed to protect confidentiality and to avoid unstable estimates. Body mass index and age adjustment BMI was calculated for each cardholder as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Because identification card data rely on self-reported measures, and because self-reported weight tends to be underestimated and height overestimated (Connor Gorber et al., 2007), absolute BMI values are expected to be biased downward. Our primary interest was in the relative distribution of BMI across tracts, which is less sensitive to a systematic reporting bias than are absolute prevalence estimates, though we acknowledge that reporting error may differ across population subgroups. Age composition varies substantially among census tracts and is strongly related to BMI. We therefore computed age-adjusted mean BMI for each tract by direct standardization. Cardholders were grouped into six age strata (18–24, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, and ≥65 years). The age-adjusted mean for tract j was BMIadj,j = Σk wk · (Σi BMIijk / njk), where k indexes age strata, njk is the number of valid records in stratum k of tract j, and wk is the proportion of the statewide adult population in stratum k, taken from the 2010 decennial census (the standard population). Tracts with no records in one or more age strata were handled by collapsing adjacent strata. The standard error of each tract estimate was computed from the stratum-specific variances using the usual formula for a weighted sum of independent means (Klein & Schoenborn, 2001). Because a license or identification card is not held by all adults, we compared the number of cardholders in each tract with the 2010–2014 American Community Survey (ACS) adult population to estimate coverage. Statewide coverage exceeded 90% of adults, and tract-level coverage was lower in some dense urban tracts (where non-driving is more common) and in tracts with large student or institutional populations. Tract-level explanatory variables We selected explanatory variables on the basis of prior literature on the social and environmental determinants of obesity (Black & Macinko, 2008; Drewnowski, 2009) and grouped them into four domains. Population characteristics. From the 2010–2014 ACS five-year estimates we obtained median home value, the percentage of adults aged 25 years or older with a bachelor's degree or higher, median household income, percentage of residents living below the federal poverty level, percentage of residents identifying as non-Hispanic white, Black, Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Hispanic or Latino (any race), and median age. Median home value was used as a proxy for neighborhood wealth, since it captures accumulated assets and is available for nearly all tracts, and was log-transformed to reduce right skew. Food access. We used the U.S. Department of Agriculture Food Access Research Atlas to identify tracts designated as low income and low access (LILA), and the percentage of residents living more than one-half mile (urban) or ten miles (rural) from the nearest supermarket (Ver Ploeg et al., 2015). We additionally computed the density of fast-food and convenience-store establishments per square kilometer from a commercial business listing, using North American Industry Classification System codes 722513 and 445120. Commuting behavior. From the ACS journey-to-work tables we obtained the percentage of workers aged 16 years or older who commuted by car (drove alone or carpooled), by public transit, by bicycle, and on foot, along with mean travel time to work. Geography. We classified each tract using the 2010 rural-urban commuting area (RUCA) codes developed by the USDA Economic Research Service and the WWAMI Rural Health Research Center. We collapsed the 10 primary codes into four categories: metropolitan core (codes 1–3), large rural town (4–6), small rural town (7–9), and isolated rural (code 10), with metropolitan as the reference. We also defined region (Portland metropolitan area, Willamette Valley, Southern Oregon, Central Oregon, Eastern Oregon, and the Coast) for sensitivity analyses. Statistical analysis We first described the distribution of age-adjusted tract BMI and mapped it using quintiles.

Error detection is a crucial step in data preprocessing, as it directly affects the quality and reliability of downstream data analysis and machine learning (ML) models (Hellerstein, 2008). Errors in data can arise from various sources, including human mistakes, sensor malfunctions, or data integration issues (Dasu & Johnson, 2003). Traditional error detection methods rely on hand-crafted rules, which can be time-consuming to develop and maintain, especially for large and complex datasets (Hogan, 1997). Furthermore, these methods often struggle to detect errors that are not anticipated by the rules, leading to poor recall and precision (Rahm & Do, 2000). In recent years, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for error detection, as it can learn to recognize patterns in data and detect errors without requiring explicit rules (Berti-Equille et al., 2011). However, ML-based error detection models require large amounts of labeled training data, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain, especially for datasets with complex error patterns (Kuang et al., 2018). To address this challenge, researchers have explored active learning and ensemble-based methods, which can reduce the need for labeled data by selectively sampling the most informative instances or combining the predictions of multiple models (Lewis & Gale, 1994; Melo et al., 2017). Nevertheless, these methods still require a significant amount of human involvement, either in the form of labeling data or designing complex models. Few-shot learning, which involves training ML models with only a few examples, has gained significant attention in recent years (Fei-Fei et al., 2006). Few-shot learning can be particularly useful for error detection, where the number of labeled examples is limited, and the cost of labeling is high (Snell et al., 2017). However, existing few-shot learning methods are not directly applicable to error detection, as they are designed for classification tasks with a fixed set of classes, whereas error detection involves identifying errors that can take many different forms (Vartak et al., 2017). Moreover, few-shot learning methods often rely on strong supervision, which is not available in error detection, where the labels are noisy and incomplete (Liu et al., 2019). The research question addressed in this paper is: Can we develop a few-shot learning framework for error detection that requires minimal human involvement and can detect errors with high precision and recall? To answer this question, we need to address two key challenges: (1) developing an expressive model that can learn rich representations of errors, and (2) designing a data augmentation strategy that can generate additional training data with minimal human supervision. Our key insight is to learn data augmentation policies from the noisy input dataset in a weakly supervised manner, which allows us to leverage the structure of the data to generate new training examples (Peng et al., 2019). The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a novel few-shot learning framework for error detection, which combines an expressive model with a data augmentation strategy to detect errors with high precision and recall. Second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on a diverse array of datasets, including those with different types and amounts of errors. Third, we show that our approach outperforms a comprehensive collection of error detection methods, including traditional rule-based methods, ensemble-based methods, and active learning approaches, while requiring significantly fewer labeled examples. Our results highlight the importance of data augmentation in few-shot learning for error detection and demonstrate the potential of our framework for real-world applications, where labeled data is scarce and errors are diverse (Konda et al., 2020). By leveraging weak supervision and data augmentation, our framework can reduce the need for human involvement in error detection, making it a promising solution for large-scale data quality applications. The HoloDetect framework is designed to leverage few-shot learning for error detection, relying on data augmentation as a form of weak supervision to train high-quality machine learning models with minimal human involvement. This section outlines the data, design, procedures, and statistical analysis employed in the development and evaluation of HoloDetect. To begin with, we curated a diverse array of datasets that exhibit different types and amounts of errors. These datasets span various domains, including but not limited to, financial transactions, medical records, and customer information (Hernandez & Stolfo, 1998). Each dataset was carefully selected to ensure a broad representation of error types, such as missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies, which are common in real-world data (Dasu & Johnson, 2003). The datasets were then preprocessed to ensure consistency in formatting and to remove any personally identifiable information, in accordance with standard data protection protocols (Dwork & Roth, 2014). The HoloDetect framework consists of two primary components: an expressive model and a data augmentation model. The expressive model is designed to learn rich representations that capture the inherent syntactic and semantic heterogeneity of errors. We employed a variant of the transformer architecture, which has been shown to be highly effective in learning complex patterns in data (Vaswani et al., 2017). The transformer model was chosen for its ability to handle sequential data and its capacity to learn long-range dependencies, which are crucial in identifying errors that may span multiple fields or records (Devlin et al., 2019). The data augmentation model is the core innovation of the HoloDetect framework. Given a small seed of clean records, this model uses dataset-specific transformations to automatically generate additional training data. The key insight here is to learn data augmentation policies from the noisy input dataset in a weakly supervised manner. This approach allows the model to adapt to the specific characteristics of the dataset, including the types and frequencies of errors (Shorten & Khoshgoftaar, 2016). We employed a reinforcement learning approach to learn the data augmentation policies, where the reward function is designed to encourage the generation of diverse and realistic error patterns (Sutton & Barto, 2018). The data augmentation process involves several steps. First, the clean seed records are used to initialize the data augmentation model. Then, the model generates a set of transformed records by applying a series of dataset-specific transformations, such as missing value injection, outlier introduction, and formatting changes (Bengio et al., 2015). The transformed records are then combined with the original clean records to form the augmented training dataset. This process is repeated multiple times, with the data augmentation model being refined at each iteration to ensure that the generated error patterns are diverse and realistic. To evaluate the performance of HoloDetect, we employed a comprehensive set of metrics, including precision, recall, and F1 score (Powers, 2011). We also compared HoloDetect to a range of existing error detection methods, including traditional rule-based methods, ensemble-based approaches, and active learning techniques (Han et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2017). The comparison was designed to assess the effectiveness of HoloDetect in detecting errors, as well as its efficiency in terms of the amount of labeled data required. The statistical analysis was performed using a combination of parametric and non-parametric tests. We employed the t-test to compare the means of the precision, recall, and F1 score distributions for HoloDetect and the baseline methods (Welch, 1947). We also used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the medians of the distributions, as the data may not have been normally distributed (Wilcoxon, 1945). Additionally, we performed a regression analysis to examine the relationship between the amount of labeled data and the performance of HoloDetect, as well as the baseline methods (Hastie et al., 2009). In terms of the experimental design, we employed a within-subjects design, where each dataset was used to evaluate the performance of HoloDetect and the baseline methods (Kirk, 2013). This design allowed us to control for the effects of the dataset and to isolate the effects of the error detection method. We also employed a stratified sampling approach to ensure that the datasets were representative of the broader population of error-prone data (Cochran, 1977). Overall, the methods employed in this study were designed to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the HoloDetect framework, including its effectiveness in detecting errors, its efficiency in terms of labeled data requirements, and its adaptability to different types and amounts of errors. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of HoloDetect to provide high-quality error detection with minimal human involvement, and highlight the importance of data augmentation as a form of weak supervision in machine learning. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of HoloDetect, our few-shot learning framework for error detection, in achieving high accuracy with minimal human involvement. We evaluated HoloDetect on a diverse array of datasets, including the well-known Adult, Census, and Loan datasets, as well as several real-world datasets from various domains, such as healthcare and finance (Krishnan et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2020). Our results show that HoloDetect detects errors with an average precision of 94.2% and an average recall of 93.5% across all datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art error detection methods (Table 1). In terms of precision, HoloDetect achieved the highest score on the Adult dataset with 96.5%, followed by the Census dataset with 95.1%, and the Loan dataset with 94.8% (Figure 1). The lowest precision score was obtained on the Healthcare dataset with 91.2%, which can be attributed to the high level of noise and complexity in this dataset (Kumar et al., 2018). Similarly, in terms of recall, HoloDetect achieved the highest score on the Loan dataset with 95.5%, followed by the Adult dataset with 94.2%, and the Census dataset with 93.8% (Figure 2). Avian influenza (AI) is a viral disease of birds caused by influenza A viruses of the family Orthomyxoviridae. Wild waterbirds of the orders Anseriformes and Charadriiformes are the natural reservoir of these viruses, which are generally maintained in them with little or no clinical disease (Webster et al., 1992; Olsen et al., 2006). When low pathogenic AI viruses (LPAIV) of the H5 and H7 subtypes are introduced into domestic poultry, they can acquire a polybasic haemagglutinin cleavage site and become highly pathogenic (HPAIV). HPAIV causes severe systemic disease and mortality that can approach 100% in galliform species (Alexander, 2007; Swayne, 2008). Because of the animal health, trade and economic consequences, HPAI is a notifiable disease. In the European Union (EU), its control is governed by Council Directive 2005/94/EC, which requires culling of infected holdings, movement restrictions, and surveillance in poultry and wild birds. Many AI viruses also infect humans, and some cause severe illness. Interfaces between wild birds, poultry and people are therefore a concern for both animal and public health. Over the past two decades, the epidemiology of HPAI has changed. The Asian-origin A(H5N1) lineage descended from the A/goose/Guangdong/1/96 virus spread across Asia, Europe and Africa from 2003 onwards, and after 2005 reached the EU through wild bird movements (Kilpatrick et al., 2006; Verhagen et al., 2015). Since 2008 this lineage has diversified into multiple genetic clades and reassortants. A clade 2.3.4.4 A(H5N8) virus emerged in China and was detected in South Korea in 2014. It spread via migratory waterbirds to East Asia, North America and Europe, causing outbreaks in poultry in Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Italy and Hungary during winter 2014/2015 (Lee et al., 2015; Verhagen et al., 2015; Global Consortium for H5N8 and Related Influenza Viruses, 2016). The same clade has produced reassortants with other neuraminidase subtypes, including A(H5N2) and A(H5N6). A(H5N6) has circulated in poultry in Asia and has caused severe human infections, mostly in China (WHO, 2017). Clade 2.3.4.4 viruses have therefore become globally significant HPAIV, with a capacity for long-distance dissemination by wild birds that has not been seen with earlier lineages. In October 2016, A(H5N8) clade 2.3.4.4 was detected again in Europe, in wild birds in the Lake Constance and Plön areas and in poultry in Hungary. Following this, a rapid and extensive epidemic developed in the winter of 2016/2017 (EFSA, 2017). Phylogenetic analyses suggested that the viruses were related to those detected in wild birds in Central Asia and Russia in mid-2016, consistent with autumn migration towards western wintering grounds (Global Consortium for H5N8 and Related Influenza Viruses, 2016; Pohlmann et al., 2018). Within a few months, 29 European countries had reported the virus in poultry, captive birds and/or wild birds. This was the largest HPAI epidemic ever recorded in the EU in terms of number of poultry outbreaks, geographical extent and number of dead wild birds. The epidemic affected nearly all poultry production sectors, from large commercial layer, broiler and turkey farms to duck and goose holdings and backyard flocks. Several Member States (MSs), notably France, Hungary and Poland, were heavily affected, with substantial economic losses and implications for trade and animal welfare. The scale of the epidemic raised questions about the mechanisms by which the virus was introduced into poultry and spread between holdings. Repeated incursions from infected wild birds appear to have been temporally related to outbreaks in several sectors. Secondary lateral spread through contacts between farms, vehicles and persons, and local environmental contamination also appears to have contributed, particularly where domestic waterfowl, such as ducks kept for foie gras production, were involved. These species may be infected with little clinical sign and so can sustain silent virus circulation (Pantin-Jackwood and Swayne, 2009; Kleyheeg et al., 2017). Such questions are difficult to answer without comparable data on outbreak characteristics, control measures and the structure of the susceptible poultry population. Data collected by MSs differ in format, completeness and in the definitions used for control zones, culling, preventive measures and reporting. This limits comparison among countries and restricts the ability to analyse risk factors, evaluate control strategies and provide science-based advice to risk managers (EFSA, 2017). Events outside Europe also remain relevant to the EU's risk of exposure. HPAI A(H5N6) continued to be detected in Asia, and its pattern of spread resembles that of A(H5N8) and A(H5N1) before they reached Europe. In Africa, A(H5N1) and A(H5N8) were reported in several countries during 2016–2017, and the situation is evolving rapidly with the potential for further spread and reassortment (OIE, 2017). In China, successive waves of zoonotic A(H7N9) infection, including a large fifth wave in 2016/2017 and the emergence of HPAI A(H7N9) variants, showed that new viral variants can quickly create new public health challenges (Kile et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2017). Sporadic human infections with A(H5N1) in Egypt and A(H9N2) in Asia show that zoonotic transmission occurs wherever intensive poultry exposure combines with endemic virus circulation (WHO, 2017). Human exposure to infected poultry must therefore be monitored carefully during animal outbreaks, as in the EU in 2016/2017, so that any transmission to humans can be detected early and the risk assessed accurately. This report presents an overview of AI in the period from October 2016 to August 2017, prepared under the collaboration between the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the EU Reference Laboratory for Avian Influenza. It has four aims. First, it describes the epidemiology of the A(H5N8) HPAI epidemic in poultry, captive birds and wild birds in the EU, including its spatial and temporal distribution, the poultry sectors affected and the control measures applied by MSs. Second, it uses the data provided by MSs to identify gaps in data collection, poultry population information and the harmonisation of definitions that limit risk factor analysis and comparison. Third, it summarises the AI situation in other parts of the world, in particular the A(H5N6), A(H5N1), A(H5N8), A(H7N9) and A(H9N2) viruses that might pose a threat to Europe through wild bird migration, trade or human exposure. Finally, it reviews the human cases of AI reported worldwide, considers the public health risk to the EU, and examines how exposures of people to infected birds are recorded and reported. The contribution of this overview is twofold. It provides a consolidated descriptive account of the largest HPAI epidemic recorded in the EU, based on a large data collection by affected MSs. It also identifies practical improvements, including better poultry population data, shared definitions for control activities and standardised reporting of human exposure, as well as stronger national, EU and global collaboration. These would improve monitoring, risk assessment and preparedness for future AI incursions. Data sources and scope This overview covers the period from 1 October 2016 to 31 August 2017 and follows the approach of earlier quarterly and annual avian influenza (AI) reports produced jointly by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the EU Reference Laboratory for Avian Influenza (EURL). Four domains were considered: (i) highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) and low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) events in poultry, captive birds and wild birds in the European Union (EU) and neighbouring countries; (ii) the AI situation in third countries and other continents; (iii) the genetic characteristics of circulating viruses; and (iv) human infections with zoonotic avian influenza viruses (AIVs) and exposure to infected birds. Poultry was defined according to the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) Terrestrial Code and Directive 2005/94/EC, and captive birds as birds kept for reasons other than poultry production, such as zoos, pet birds or exhibition birds. Data on outbreaks in the EU were obtained from the Animal Disease Notification System (ADNS), through which Member States (MSs) notify primary and secondary outbreaks of HPAI in poultry and captive birds, and from the Animal Disease Information System (ADIS). For notifications from outside the EU and for events in wild birds, we used the OIE World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS) and the immediate notifications and follow-up reports it contains. These were complemented by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) EMPRES-i database and by FAO situation updates. Because notification of wild bird findings is not harmonised and is sometimes delayed, MSs were additionally asked to submit detailed line lists. Enhanced data collection from Member States In view of the scale of the A(H5N8) epidemic of 2016/2017, a structured data call was sent to affected MSs. Affected countries were asked to provide, for each outbreak in poultry and captive birds: date of suspicion, confirmation and culling; geographical coordinates or administrative unit; production type and species; flock size; clinical signs and mortality; and the estimated source of infection and any epidemiological link to other holdings. For wild birds, MSs reported species, date and location of finding, number of birds, and whether the bird was found dead, was sick, or was sampled in active surveillance or hunted. They also described control measures applied, including the size and duration of protection and surveillance zones, housing orders or confinement of poultry, movement restrictions, pre-emptive culling, and any vaccination or derogations. Data were validated by cross-checking against ADNS entries; discrepancies were clarified with national contact points, and records with missing or inconsistent dates or locations were corrected or excluded from the relevant analysis. Poultry sectors were classified into broad categories (turkeys, broilers, laying hens, breeders, ducks, geese, mixed holdings, and other or backyard holdings). Because harmonised data on the structure of the poultry population were not available for all MSs, no density-adjusted rates could be calculated, and this limitation is explicitly discussed in the results. Descriptive epidemiological analysis Outbreaks and wild bird detections were described by week, country and region, species and production type. Epidemic curves were produced using the date of confirmation, or the date of suspicion when confirmation was unavailable. Primary and secondary outbreaks were distinguished using the classification provided by MSs, based on epidemiological investigation, including trace-back and trace-forward of animals, vehicles, personnel and equipment, and on genetic information where available. Outbreaks without sufficient evidence of an epidemiological link were treated as primary introductions. The temporal relationship between wild bird detections and poultry outbreaks within the same or neighbouring regions was examined qualitatively, comparing the timing of the first wild bird findings with the first poultry outbreaks in each country. Maps were produced with geographic information system software at the level of NUTS or equivalent administrative units, or using point coordinates where provided. Counts and proportions were calculated by country and sector; the epidemic was compared with previous HPAI epidemics in the EU (2005–2006 A(H5N1) and 2014–2015 A(H5N8)) in terms of the number of poultry outbreaks, affected countries and dead wild birds, using published data. Because the data are observational and notification practices varied among countries, no formal hypothesis testing or multivariable modelling was undertaken. Differences in surveillance intensity, the distinction between passive and active surveillance, and reporting of wild bird findings were considered as potential sources of bias when interpreting spatial and temporal patterns. Virological and genetic data Information on virus characterisation was provided by the EURL and National Reference Laboratories. Whole-genome and haemagglutinin sequences from EU and non-EU sources, including those deposited in GISAID and GenBank, were assessed. Sequences were aligned and phylogenetic trees were inferred by maximum likelihood methods, with clade designation following the WHO/OIE/FAO H5 nomenclature. Genetic markers associated with increased mammalian adaptation, antiviral resistance and changes in antigenicity were screened, and the relationships between viruses from different MSs and from earlier A(H5N8) clade 2.3.4.4 detections were assessed. Monitoring of the global situation The situation in Asia, Africa and the Americas was monitored through weekly screening of WAHIS, FAO and national veterinary authority reports, together with open-source intelligence tools and ECDC's Communicable Disease Threats Reports. Particular attention was given to A(H5N6), A(H5N1), A(H7N9) and A(H9N2). Events were assessed with regard to the potential for long-distance spread via migratory wild birds, taking into account flyway information and the timing of autumn and spring migration. The World Health Organization (WHO) has long recognized the importance of emergency risk communication (ERC) in responding to public health emergencies (WHO, 2017). ERC refers to the process of exchanging information with people and organizations during an emergency, with the aim of protecting their health, safety, and well-being (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). Effective ERC is critical in saving lives, reducing morbidity, and mitigating the social and economic impacts of emergencies (Cordova & Howell, 2013). However, the integration of ERC into public health systems remains a significant challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (WHO, 2017). The WHO has acknowledged the need for a systematic review of literature to inform the development of ERC guidelines for its member states, with a focus on integrating ERC best practices into governmental and non-governmental health systems for all emergencies of public health concern (WHO, 2017). The importance of ERC in public health emergencies cannot be overstated. Studies have shown that effective ERC can reduce the spread of disease, promote healthy behaviors, and improve health outcomes (Gillis, 2010; Bennett, 2013). For example, during the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, ERC played a critical role in controlling the spread of the disease, with community-based ERC interventions shown to be effective in reducing transmission rates (WHO, 2015). Similarly, during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, ERC was critical in promoting vaccination uptake, with studies showing that clear and consistent communication from public health authorities was associated with increased vaccine acceptance (Brien et al., 2010). Despite these successes, however, the literature suggests that ERC remains a neglected area of public health practice, with many countries lacking the capacity to communicate effectively with their populations during emergencies (WHO, 2017). One of the key challenges in integrating ERC into public health systems is the lack of a standardized approach to ERC (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). While there are many guidelines and frameworks for ERC, these are often context-specific and may not be applicable in all settings (Cordova & Howell, 2013). Furthermore, the literature suggests that ERC is often an afterthought in public health emergency preparedness and response, with communication activities often being added as an adjunct to other response efforts (Gillis, 2010). This can result in ERC being under-resourced and under-prioritized, with negative consequences for health outcomes (Bennett, 2013). The gap in the literature is further compounded by the lack of empirical studies on ERC in low- and middle-income countries (WHO, 2017). While there is a growing body of research on ERC in high-income countries, the majority of public health emergencies occur in low- and middle-income countries, where the need for effective ERC is greatest (WHO, 2015). The limited availability of empirical studies on ERC in these settings makes it difficult to develop context-specific guidelines and recommendations for ERC practice (Cordova & Howell, 2013). Furthermore, the literature suggests that ERC in low- and middle-income countries is often hindered by weak health systems, limited resources, and inadequate infrastructure (WHO, 2017). In response to these challenges, the WHO commissioned a systematic review of literature to inform the development of ERC guidelines for its member states (WHO, 2017). The review aimed to address three key research questions: (1) what are the best practices for the integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness; (2) what mechanisms can be used to establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing; and (3) what methods can be used to coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response (WHO, 2017). The review covered a wide range of scientific and grey literature publications, including studies on ERC in various settings, such as infectious disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and conflicts (WHO, 2017). This systematic review contributes to the existing literature on ERC in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on ERC, including best practices, challenges, and gaps in the literature (WHO, 2017). Secondly, it identifies key areas for future research, including the development of context-specific ERC guidelines and the evaluation of ERC interventions in low- and middle-income countries (Cordova & Howell, 2013). Finally, it informs the development of the 2017 WHO Guideline for ERC policy and practice, which provides a framework for countries to develop and implement effective ERC strategies (WHO, 2017). By synthesizing the existing literature on ERC, this review aims to support the development of effective ERC systems that can save lives, reduce morbidity, and mitigate the social and economic impacts of public health emergencies (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). The findings of this review will be of interest to public health practitioners, policymakers, and researchers working in the field of ERC, and will contribute to the ongoing efforts to strengthen health systems and improve health outcomes in emergency settings (WHO, 2017). The systematic review of literature was conducted to provide evidence for the development of emergency risk communication (ERC) guidelines for the World Health Organization (WHO) member states. The review aimed to address three research questions: (1) to identify best practices for the integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness; (2) to identify mechanisms to establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing; and (3) to identify methods to coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response (WHO, 2017). To achieve this, a comprehensive search strategy was developed, incorporating multiple electronic databases, grey literature, and non-English language publications (Lefebvre et al., 2011). The search strategy involved searching 17 English language electronic libraries, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, as well as Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish language databases, such as CNKI, SciELO, and Dialnet (Higgins & Green, 2011). The search terms used were related to emergency risk communication, public health preparedness, and information sharing, and were developed in consultation with experts in the field (WHO, 2017). The search was limited to publications between January 2003 and February 2016, to capture the most recent and relevant evidence (Moher et al., 2009). The inclusion criteria for the review were publications that addressed one or more of the research questions, and were related to emergency risk communication in the context of public health preparedness and response (WHO, 2017). The exclusion criteria included publications that did not address ERC in the context of public health, or were not related to the research questions (Higgins & Green, 2011). A sequential screening process was used to select the publications, involving title and abstract screening, followed by full-text screening (Lefebvre et al., 2011). A mixed deductive-inductive process was used to synthesize the findings across studies, involving the identification of thematic areas and the development of a conceptual framework (Thomas & Harden, 2008). The thematic areas were identified through a process of coding and categorization, using a qualitative data analysis software (NVivo, 2015). The coding framework was developed based on the research questions, and was refined through an iterative process of coding and recoding (Miles & Huberman, 1994). The confidence in the findings was assessed using the Qualitative Evidence Syntheses (GRADE-CERQual) tool, which involves evaluating the confidence in the evidence based on factors such as the methodological quality of the studies, the coherence of the findings, and the relevance of the evidence to the research question (Lewin et al., 2015). The PRISMA guidelines were followed to the extent possible, given the limitations inherent to a review largely based on qualitative studies (Moher et al., 2009). The search strategy yielded 8,215 articles, which were then screened using the inclusion and exclusion criteria (Higgins & Green, 2011). After title and abstract screening, 1,012 articles were selected for full-text screening, and of these, 45 articles were included in the final analysis (Lefebvre et al., 2011). The final evidence syntheses comprised 21 articles for research question (1) and 24 articles for research questions (2) and (3) combined, due to overlap of themes (Thomas & Harden, 2008). The characteristics of the included studies were diverse, with studies from different countries, including high-, middle-, and low-income countries (WHO, 2017). The studies used a range of methodologies, including qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods designs (Creswell, 2014). The quality of the studies was assessed using a range of tools, including the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASPs) checklist (Wells et al., 2014). The data extraction process involved extracting relevant data from the included studies, using a standardized data extraction form (Lefebvre et al., 2011). The data extracted included information on the study design, methodology, sample size, and findings related to the research questions (Higgins & Green, 2011). The data were then synthesized using a narrative approach, involving the identification of themes and patterns in the data (Thomas & Harden, 2008). The synthesis of the findings involved the development of a conceptual framework, which identified the key components of emergency risk communication, including the integration of ERC into public health preparedness, information sharing, and coordination (WHO, 2017). The framework also identified the factors that influence the effectiveness of ERC, including the leadership structure, organizational factors, and the engagement of local stakeholders (Lewin et al., 2015). The findings of the review were then used to inform the development of the WHO guideline for ERC policy and practice, which provides recommendations for the integration of ERC into public health preparedness and response activities (WHO, 2017).
