Arabic is spoken by more than 400 million people and is the liturgical language of nearly two billion Muslims, and it has one of the longest continuous written records of any living language (Versteegh, 2014). Its earliest extended attestations, the Qur'anic text and pre-Islamic poetry, date to the sixth and seventh centuries CE. Since then it has been used for scripture, law, philosophy, science, historiography, belles-lettres, and, in the modern period, journalism and digital communication. Over this span the language has been shaped by conquest and migration, by contact with Persian, Turkish, Aramaic, and European languages, by the codification efforts of medieval grammarians, and by nineteenth- and twentieth-century modernization (Owens, 2006; Holes, 2004). Despite this record, the history of written Arabic is still described mostly in broad qualitative terms. The standard account distinguishes Classical Arabic, the codified literary language of the early Islamic centuries, from Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), the written and formal register that emerged with the Nahḍa (the Arabic cultural revival) and the rise of the modern press (Badawi, 1973; Versteegh, 2014). Intermediate stages are often invoked, including Post-Classical or Middle Arabic, but their boundaries and linguistic content are contested (Lentin, 2008; Owens, 2006). The picture is complicated by diglossia, the coexistence of a prestigious written standard with unwritten colloquial varieties (Ferguson, 1959). Because many writers deviated from the standard, either unintentionally or by choice, texts mix registers in ways that resist simple classification. Most evidence for these accounts comes from close reading of selected manuscripts, authors, or genres. Such analyses are valuable, but they are small in scale and may not generalize across the full range of the written record. They also depend on the analyst's prior assumptions about where period boundaries lie. Computational methods could test such claims at scale. Diachronic corpora and statistical methods have transformed the study of English, German, French, and other languages. Examples include large-scale analyses of lexical change in digitized books (Michel et al., 2011), distributional models of semantic shift (Hamilton et al., 2016; Kutuzov et al., 2018), and data-driven approaches to periodization (Gries & Hilpert, 2008; Tahmasebi et al., 2021). The Arabic NLP community has built a substantial infrastructure of its own, including morphological analyzers and disambiguators (Habash, 2010; Pasha et al., 2014), open toolkits (Obeid et al., 2020), pretrained language models (Antoun et al., 2020; Inoue et al., 2021), and dialectal resources (Bouamor et al., 2018). Corpora such as Arabic Gigaword (Parker et al., 2011), ArTenTen (Arts et al., 2014), and the King Saud University Corpus of Classical Arabic (Alrabiah et al., 2013) have supported much of this work. However, this effort has concentrated almost entirely on contemporary written Arabic, namely news and web text in MSA, and on the spoken dialects (Zaghouani, 2017). Where historical text has been used, it has usually been treated as a single "Classical" block, often to evaluate the transfer of tools built for MSA (Belinkov et al., 2016). To our knowledge, no existing resource or study treats the Arabic written record as a continuous diachronic object spanning the full 1400 years of its history. The raw material for such a study exists. Large-scale digitization by library projects, volunteer initiatives, and OCR pipelines has produced collections of premodern Arabic texts, such as the OpenITI corpus (Nigst et al., 2020) and the Shamela digital library, as well as contemporary archives. These collections were assembled for retrieval and philological use rather than linguistic analysis, and they pose several problems for a quantitative history of the language. Their metadata are inconsistent, and dates of authorship are often approximate or uncertain. Texts contain OCR and transcription errors, editorial apparatus, and modern commentary interleaved with the historical text. Perhaps most importantly, Arabic scholarly culture relied heavily on quotation, paraphrase, compilation, and commentary, so a large share of the text in any collection is reused from earlier works (Romanov, 2017). If left unaddressed, reuse would bias frequency-based analyses by attributing the language of an early author to the later authors who quote them. Reuse also makes the apparent linguistic character of a period depend on how much its authors copied from earlier ones. Finally, standard Arabic NLP tools are trained on modern data, and their behavior on earlier stages of the language is poorly understood. This paper addresses these gaps. Our central research question is whether the large-scale statistical structure of the written Arabic record, observed without imposing a prior chronology, matches the periodizations proposed by traditional scholarship, and whether it points to further divisions that manual analysis has not identified. We pursue this question in three steps: building a corpus suitable for diachronic analysis, processing it with existing Arabic NLP tools while accounting for their limitations, and applying quantitative methods that infer period structure from the data themselves. We make the following contributions. 1. A large-scale historical corpus of written Arabic. We assemble and release a corpus of approximately 1.2 billion words from roughly 9,000 works, spanning the seventh to the twenty-first century. We harmonize and verify metadata and assign each work to a date or date range. We also document the corpus's composition by century and genre, including its uneven coverage, which is dense for the ninth to eleventh centuries and the twentieth century and sparser elsewhere. We discuss how such unevenness affects inference. 2. Cleaning, processing, and text-reuse identification. We describe a pipeline that removes non-textual and editorial material and normalizes orthographic variation. It applies morphological analysis and lemmatization with existing Arabic NLP tools, and we evaluate how well these tools perform on historical text. We also present a method for detecting reused passages at scale, and we find that a substantial minority of the corpus, roughly one fifth of all tokens, consists of text that also appears in earlier works. Removing or down-weighting this material changes the estimated temporal profiles of many linguistic features, so we treat reuse as a first-order confound in diachronic studies of Arabic. 3. A novel automatic periodization algorithm. We introduce a method that segments the timeline into contiguous periods by maximizing the internal homogeneity of linguistic features within each segment while accounting for corpus size and reuse. Unlike earlier approaches that rely on pre-specified boundaries, it recovers boundaries from the data and quantifies the stability of each boundary under resampling. 4. An empirical account of the history of written Arabic. Our analyses recover the established division between Classical Arabic and MSA, and they place the transition in the nineteenth century, consistent with the traditional association with the Nahḍa. They also reproduce several finer divisions proposed in the literature. In addition, they suggest that the Classical period itself may be divisible into several stages of development, which we characterize through lexical, morphological, and syntactic features. Taken together, these contributions provide both a resource and a methodology for the quantitative study of Arabic historical linguistics, and they offer a template for similar work on other languages with long textual traditions. The remainder of the paper describes the corpus and its processing, presents the periodization method, reports our findings, and discusses their implications and limitations. Corpus compilation We assembled the corpus from three sources chosen to cover the 1400 years of written Arabic with the fewest gaps. For the pre-modern period (7th–19th centuries CE), we used the OpenITI release (Nigst et al., 2020), a collection of digitized Arabic-script books in a lightly annotated markup format, supplemented by texts from the Shamela and Shia Online Library repositories. For the modern period, we used news and periodical text from the Arabic Gigaword (Parker et al., 2011) and the OSIAN corpus (Zeroual et al., 2019), together with a 2022 Arabic Wikipedia dump. Early materials, including the Qur'an and a set of 118 pre-Islamic and early Islamic poetry collections, were added from the Quranic Arabic Corpus (Dukes & Habash, 2010) and from OpenITI. The resulting collection comprised 11,742 documents and approximately 3.4 billion raw tokens. Each document was assigned a date. For pre-modern books we used the author's death year in the Hijri calendar, which is standard in Arabic bibliographic practice and in OpenITI's URI scheme, and converted it to the Gregorian calendar using the tabular civil conversion. Death years are an imperfect proxy for composition date, since authors may have written decades earlier. We therefore treat all dates as having an uncertainty of roughly ±25 years and perform every analysis on bins of at least 50 years. For modern sources, we used the publication year. Documents with undeterminable dates (n = 412) were excluded. Because the modern portion vastly exceeds the pre-modern portion, the corpus was divided into 50-year bins up to 1900 and 10-year bins thereafter, and we subsampled each bin to a maximum of 20 million tokens for all comparative analyses, so that frequency-based measures were not driven by differences in size. Cleaning and normalization Digitized texts contain OCR errors, editorial apparatus, and markup that can distort linguistic analysis. We removed OpenITI markup, page and volume headers, editorial footnotes, tables of contents, and isnād-annotation tags, using regular expressions and OpenITI's structural tags. We then applied the following normalization steps: Unicode NFKC normalization; removal of tatweel (kashida); removal of diacritics, except in experiments that explicitly used them; conversion of Persian and Urdu character variants to Arabic equivalents; and replacement of Arabic-Indic digits with ASCII digits. Non-Arabic passages were detected by script and removed when a paragraph contained over 50% non-Arabic characters. Paragraphs shorter than 5 tokens were discarded. To estimate residual noise, we manually annotated a random sample of 2,000 paragraphs, stratified by period, and marked any paragraph containing OCR corruption or non-linguistic material. The estimated proportion of problematic paragraphs fell from 9.8% before cleaning to 2.1% after. Tokens were then flagged as out-of-vocabulary if they were not analyzable by the CAMeL Tools morphological analyzer (Obeid et al., 2020). Documents in which more than 30% of tokens were unanalyzable were removed (n = 631), as were exact duplicates identified by hashing normalized text (n = 288). The final corpus contained 10,411 documents and 2.9 billion tokens. Linguistic processing Texts were sentence-segmented using punctuation and, in the largely unpunctuated pre-modern texts, a length-based fallback that breaks at conjunctions after 60 tokens. Tokenization, lemmatization, and part-of-speech tagging were carried out with CAMeL Tools, using the MSA disambiguator for all periods and the Classical Arabic model (Inoue et al., 2022) for pre-1800 texts. We compared the two models on a gold-standard sample of 3,000 tokens per period (Pasha et al., 2014; Habash et al., 2022). Lemma accuracy for the Classical model remained above 93% for texts up to 1500 CE but declined to 88% for texts from 1500 to 1800, a bias we considered in interpreting later results. In addition, we ran Farasa (Abdelali et al., 2016) for segmentation as a robustness check. Detection of reused text Arabic literature is characterized by extensive quotation, copying, and paraphrase, so reused passages could inflate similarities between periods or authors. We identified reuse with the passim algorithm (Smith et al., 2014), which indexes word n-grams, clusters candidate document pairs, and aligns them using Smith–Waterman local alignment. Following Vesanto et al. (2017), who applied passim to OpenITI, we used 25-token n-grams, a minimum alignment length of 50 tokens, and a minimum match proportion of 0.5 in an alignment window. Pairs of documents with the same author were ignored. The quality of the detection was assessed on 500 randomly selected alignments, each checked by two annotators; precision was 0.96 (Cohen's κ = 0.88 between annotators). Aligned passages were marked, and unless otherwise stated, all downstream analyses were run on both the full corpus and a version in which reused passages were removed from the later text in each alignment, so that every shared passage was kept only in its earliest occurrence. Feature representations For periodization, each time bin was represented by several feature sets. These were (i) the relative frequencies of the 5,000 most frequent lemmas in the corpus; (ii) the relative frequencies of the 300 most frequent function words and clitics; (iii) the distribution of part-of-speech trigrams; and (iv) the distribution of character

English Language Learners (ELLs) are among the fastest growing segments of the school-age population in the United States. They made up roughly one in ten public school students, more than five million children, in the most recent national counts (National Center for Education Statistics, 2022). The majority are enrolled in elementary grades, where foundational knowledge and attitudes toward science are formed. Yet ELLs have not attained the same academic success as their English-proficient peers. Results from the National Assessment of Educational Progress consistently show large gaps between ELLs and non-ELLs in science, and these gaps persist across grade levels and student cohorts. Such disparities limit ELLs' access to advanced coursework and STEM pathways and ultimately restrict their participation in a society increasingly shaped by science and technology (Lee, 2005; Lee, Quinn, & Valdés, 2013). In response to these concerns, science educators and policy documents have urged teachers to adopt inquiry approaches to instruction. Inquiry-based teaching engages students in posing questions, planning investigations, collecting and interpreting evidence, and constructing explanations, rather than receiving information passively (National Research Council [NRC], 2000). Contemporary standards, including A Framework for K–12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards, place these practices at the center of science learning (NGSS Lead States, 2013; NRC, 2012). Proponents argue that inquiry is especially well suited to ELLs. Hands-on investigation provides concrete, multimodal experiences that make abstract ideas comprehensible. Collaborative discourse creates authentic reasons to use language, and open-ended tasks can draw on the cultural and linguistic resources students bring to class (Rosebery, Ogonowski, DiSchino, & Warren, 2010; Stoddart, Pinal, Latzke, & Canaday, 2002). From this perspective, science and language are learned together, with scientific practice serving as a context for language development (Lemke, 1990; Hakuta, Santos, & Fang, 2013). The evidence that inquiry improves outcomes for students in general is substantial but not unqualified. Syntheses of the literature suggest that inquiry-based instruction can yield positive effects on science achievement, particularly when students are actively engaged in investigation and when teachers guide the process (Furtak, Seidel, Iverson, & Briggs, 2012; Minner, Levy, & Century, 2010). Meta-analytic work on discovery-based learning likewise shows benefits when students receive scaffolding, feedback, or worked examples, but not when instruction is unguided (Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, & Tenenbaum, 2011). The broader debate over minimally guided instruction has argued that inquiry places heavy demands on working memory and may disadvantage novice learners (Kirschner, Sweller, & Clark, 2006). Others have countered that well-scaffolded inquiry supports learners in managing complexity (Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, & Chinn, 2007). These syntheses, however, draw primarily on samples of students who are proficient in the language of instruction, and they rarely disaggregate results by language status. For ELLs, the question is more complicated. The same features that make inquiry attractive may also create obstacles. Inquiry lessons often depend on extended oral discussion, interpretation of ambiguous data, and the production of written explanations and arguments. These tasks require command of the academic language of science, which is distinct from the conversational fluency that students typically acquire first (Cummins, 2000; Janzen, 2008). Where language support is weak, ELLs may participate less in group work and struggle to follow investigative procedures, and as a result may gain less from inquiry than their English-proficient classmates (Lee, 2005). Where teachers integrate language scaffolds such as visuals, sentence frames, native-language support, and explicit vocabulary instruction, inquiry may narrow gaps (Cuevas, Lee, Hart, & Deaktor, 2005; Lee, Maerten-Rivera, Penfield, LeRoy, & Secada, 2008; Settlage, Madsen, & Rustad, 2005). Thus, whether inquiry is effective for ELLs, and under what conditions, is an empirical question that theory alone cannot settle. Despite a growing body of intervention studies, systematic evidence on this question is limited. Existing reviews of science education for ELLs have been largely narrative and have emphasized conceptual frameworks, research agendas, and promising practices over quantification of effects (Janzen, 2008; Lee, 2005). Individual studies vary widely in design, duration, outcome measures, and the degree of language support embedded in instruction, and many involve small samples within a single school or district. As a result, it remains unclear whether the reported benefits of inquiry are consistent across studies, whether they are comparable in magnitude to those found for non-ELLs, and which features of instruction or context account for variation. Without such evidence, calls to implement inquiry with ELLs rest on theoretical appeal and the extrapolation of findings from other populations, rather than on a cumulative empirical base. The present study addresses this gap through a meta-analytic review of research on inquiry instruction and the science achievement of ELLs in elementary school. We focus on the elementary grades for two reasons. First, early schooling is when science identities and foundational concepts develop, and when language support is most readily integrated into instruction. Second, the elementary literature offers a sufficiently large set of studies with comparable outcomes for quantitative synthesis. Specifically, we ask three questions: (1) What is the overall effect of inquiry instruction, relative to direct or traditional instruction, on the science achievement of ELLs? (2) Does the effect of inquiry differ for ELLs and non-ELLs when both groups are studied under comparable conditions? (3) Which contextual, instructional, and methodological factors moderate these effects? This review makes three contributions. First, it provides the first quantitative estimate of the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for elementary ELLs, converting a scattered set of studies into a cumulative evidence base. Second, by comparing ELLs and non-ELLs, it tests whether inquiry is equally beneficial across language backgrounds or whether it may unintentionally widen existing gaps, a distinction with direct implications for equity-oriented reform. Third, by examining moderators such as language support, intervention characteristics, and study design, it identifies the conditions under which inquiry is most likely to benefit ELLs. In doing so, the review aims to inform teachers, curriculum developers, and policymakers who are implementing inquiry-oriented standards, and to guide researchers toward the questions that remain unresolved. Method Literature Search This meta-analysis followed the reporting guidelines of the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009) and the procedures for research synthesis outlined by Cooper (2010). We searched ERIC, PsycINFO, Education Source, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global for reports published between January 2000 and December 2019. The start date reflects the period after the publication of Inquiry and the National Science Education Standards (National Research Council, 2000), which popularized inquiry-based reform in U.S. classrooms. Search strings combined three concept clusters using Boolean operators. The first covered the population (e.g., "English language learner," "English learner," "limited English proficient," "emergent bilingual," "bilingual," "ESL," "ESOL"). The second covered the intervention (e.g., "inquiry," "hands-on," "discovery learning," "problem-based," "project-based," "investigation," "5E"). The third covered the outcome (e.g., "science achievement," "science learning," "science content knowledge," "science performance"). To reduce publication bias, we also hand-searched key journals (e.g., Journal of Research in Science Teaching, Science Education, TESOL Quarterly), examined reference lists of relevant reviews, and screened conference proceedings and technical reports. Inclusion Criteria Studies were eligible if they (a) enrolled students in kindergarten through Grade 6; (b) identified a sample or subsample of ELLs, whether through state classification, home-language surveys, or English proficiency assessments; (c) compared an inquiry-based science intervention with a comparison condition characterized as direct, traditional, or teacher-centered instruction; (d) used an experimental or quasi-experimental design with a comparison group, including pretest–posttest control group designs; (e) reported a quantitative measure of science achievement (e.g., content knowledge tests, standardized science assessments, or performance tasks); and (f) provided data sufficient to compute an effect size. We defined inquiry instruction following the National Research Council (2000) and Minner et al. (2010) as instruction in which students engage with scientific questions, give priority to evidence, formulate explanations from evidence, connect explanations to scientific knowledge, and communicate and justify their findings. Studies of activity-based instruction that lacked these features, such as cookbook laboratory exercises with predetermined outcomes, were excluded. Studies were also excluded if ELL results were aggregated with those of other subgroups so that they could not be isolated, if outcomes were limited to attitudes or language proficiency, or if the report was a duplicate of data published elsewhere. The final sample comprised 26 articles. Screening and Coding Procedures Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, and then full texts, against the inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached. Using a structured coding protocol, the same reviewers independently coded each eligible study for (a) publication characteristics (year, publication type); (b) sample characteristics (grade level, ELL sample size, home language, English proficiency level); (c) intervention characteristics (inquiry level, following Schwab's [1962] distinction among structured, guided, and open inquiry; duration in weeks; teacher professional development; and the presence of explicit language supports such as sentence frames, vocabulary instruction, bilingual instruction, or home-language use); (d) design characteristics (random assignment versus quasi-experimental, unit of assignment, and attrition); and (e) outcome characteristics (researcher-developed versus standardized measures, and science domain). Interrater agreement was calculated as Cohen's kappa for categorical codes and as intraclass correlations for continuous codes. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus and, where necessary, by consulting the original reports. Study Quality Methodological quality was appraised using criteria adapted from the What Works Clearinghouse standards (WWC, 2020), including baseline equivalence, differential attrition, and the reliability of outcome measures. Studies were coded as high or lower quality. Quality was examined as a moderator and used in sensitivity analyses rather than as an exclusion criterion, so that the evidence base could be characterized broadly. Effect Size Computation The standardized mean difference was the primary effect size metric. For each comparison, we computed Hedges' g, which applies a small-sample correction to Cohen's d (Hedges, 1981; Hedges & Olkin, 1985). Two types of effects were computed. The first was the main effect of inquiry versus direct instruction for ELLs, calculated from posttest means and standard deviations, or from t, F, or exact p values when descriptive statistics were unavailable (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). For quasi-experimental designs with pretest data, we calculated the difference between groups in pre-to-post change and divided it by the pooled pretest standard deviation, following Morris (2008), to adjust for baseline nonequivalence. The second was the differential effect for studies that reported outcomes for both ELLs and non-ELLs, defined as the difference between the effect size for non-ELLs and that for ELLs within the same study, with variance equal to the sum of the two sampling variances. Positive values indicated greater benefit for non-ELLs. When studies randomized classrooms or schools but analyzed individual students, we adjusted standard errors for clustering using an assumed intraclass correlation of .20 (Hedges, 2007; Hedges & Hedberg, 2007). Statistical Analysis Many studies contributed multiple effect sizes because they reported several outcomes, multiple ELL subgroups, or several treatment conditions, which violates the assumption of independence. We therefore used robust variance estimation (RVE) with correlated-effects weights (Hedges et al., 2010), which yields valid inference without requiring knowledge of the covariance structure among effect sizes within studies. We assumed a within-study correlation of ρ = .80 and tested sensitivity to values from 0 to 1 (Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014). Because the number of studies was modest, we applied the small-sample correction of Tipton (2015), and we report degrees of freedom for all tests. Models were estimated in R using the robumeta (Fisher & Tipton, 2015) and metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010) packages. Random-effects models were fitted because we expected true effects to vary across studies owing to differences in populations, implementations, and measures (Borenstein et al., 2009). Overall mean effects are reported with 95% confidence intervals and interpreted using Cohen's (1988) benchmarks, with the caveat that such benchmarks are less informative than contextual comparisons in education research (Kraft, 2020). Heterogeneity was assessed with the Q statistic, τ², and I² (Higgins et al., 2003). To explain heterogeneity, we conducted moderator analyses using meta-regression within the RVE framework. Categorical moderators included inquiry level, presence of language supports, research design, outcome type, grade band (K–2 versus 3–6), and publication status. Continuous moderators included intervention duration and the percentage of ELLs in the sample. Moderators were first examined individually, and then entered into

An amount of ≥ 105 bacteria per ml of freshly voided urine and the absence of typical symptoms of urinary tract infection (UTI) is referred to as asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) [1, 2]. The reported prevalence rates in pregnancy range from 2 to 15 % [3–6]. Generally a benign condition in most adults, in pregnant women ASB has been associated with an increased risk of complications, especially upper UTIs (pyelonephritis) and preterm birth [7–9]. While pyelonephritis normally requires hospitalisation and sometimes leads to severe complications such as sepsis and respiratory problems [10], preterm birth is the main contributor to infant morbidity and mortality. Most clinical practice guidelines therefore recommend screening for and antibiotic treatment of ASB in pregnancy [1, 2, 11, 12]. In most health care systems a screening programme for ASB in pregnancy has long been part of routine maternal care [13]. These recommendations are based on data published in the 1960s to 1980s and summarised in an update of a Cochrane Review on the antibiotic treatment of ASB in August 2015 [14]. Our systematic review had an extended scope comprising three objectives: firstly, to assess the patient-relevant benefits and harms of screening for ASB versus no screening; secondly, to compare the benefits and harms of different screening strategies; and thirdly, in case no reliable evidence on the overarching screening question was identified, to determine the benefits and harms of treatment of ASB. This systematic review is an update of a health technology assessment report of the benefits and harms of screening for ASB in pregnancy conducted by the German Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (Institut für Qualität und Wirtschaftlichkeit im Gesundheitswesen, IQWiG). The full (German-language) protocol and report [15], as well as an English-language executive summary, are available on the Institute’s website [16]. Both the preliminary protocol and the preliminary report underwent public commenting procedures. IQWiG’s responsibilities and methodological approach are described in its methods paper [15]. Only previously published studies were used, so there was no requirement for ethical review and consent. Primary studies and secondary publications were searched for in MEDLINE (1946 to January 2016) and EMBASE (1974 to January 2016) via Ovid, and in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (January 2016). The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, the Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects, and the Health Technology Assessment Database were screened to identify systematic reviews. Reference lists of retrieved systematic reviews were searched by hand. In addition, web-based clinical trial registries were screened (ClinicalTrials.gov, International Clinical Trials Registry Platform Search Portal, and the EU Clinical Trials Register). The search strategy included bibliographic index terms on bacteriuria and pregnancy. The complete search strategy, which was developed by one information specialist and checked by another, is presented in Additional file 1. We also screened publications cited in comments addressed to the Federal Joint Committee, the decision-making body in the German statutory healthcare system and IQWiG’s main commissioning body. In addition, persons and parties who had submitted written comments on the preliminary report were asked to provide any additional relevant studies. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts of retrieved citations to identify potentially eligible primary and secondary publications. The full texts of these articles were obtained and independently evaluated by the same two reviewers applying the full set of inclusion and exclusion criteria. All documents retrieved from non-bibliographic sources were also screened for eligibility or relevant information on studies. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs). If insufficient evidence was available from RCTs, we also planned to include non-randomised interventional prospective trials (referred to as controlled clinical trials: CCTs). As no CCTs were identified, no further details of the respective risk-of-bias assessment planned are provided here. If the risk of bias on the study level was rated as “high”, the risk of bias on the outcome level was generally also regarded as “high”. The risk of bias for each outcome was assessed by determining the adequacy of the following quality criteria: blinding of outcome assessors, application of the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle, and selective outcome reporting. We performed a synthesis and analysis of information by means of the methods described below and presented a summarising evaluation. Results of outcomes retrieved from individual studies were described comparatively. For the statistical analysis, we planned to primarily use results from the ITT analysis as reported. If not provided, we calculated the required estimates of location and dispersion. We reported the treatment effects as ORs (including 95 % CIs) for binary data and planned to report mean differences (including 95 % CIs) for continuous data. We planned to assess potential heterogeneity of effect sizes by means of the I2 statistic and a statistical heterogeneity test [18]; if relevant heterogeneity was shown (p < 0.2), we planned to calculate pooled estimates only in justified exceptional cases. As meta-analyses were not feasible, we assessed the results of the individual studies. We performed sensitivity analyses to explore the potential impact of missing data. Andreas Kipf∗ , Harald Lang∗ , Varun Pandey∗ , Raul Alexandru Persa∗ , Peter Boncz† , Thomas Neumann∗ , Alfons Kemper∗ ∗ Technical University of Munich Abstract—Geospatial joins are a core building block of connected mobility applications. An especially challenging problem are joins between streaming points and static polygons. Since points are not known beforehand, they cannot be indexed. Nevertheless, points need to be mapped to polygons with low latencies to enable real-time feedback. We present an adaptive geospatial join that uses true hit filtering to avoid expensive geometric computations in most cases. Our technique uses a quadtree-based hierarchical grid to approximate polygons and stores these approximations in a specialized radix tree. We emphasize on an approximate version of our algorithm that guarantees a user-defined precision. The exact version of our algorithm can adapt to the expected point distribution by refining the index. We optimized our implementation for modern hardware architectures with wide SIMD vector processing units, including Intel’s brand new Knights Landing. Overall, our approach can perform up to two orders of magnitude faster than existing techniques. Fig. 1: We adaptively compute a fine-grained (true hit) filter that identifies most or even all join partners. We can treat candidate hits as true hits while guaranteeing a user-defined precision. The arrow width reflects the amount of data passing through each of the respective paths. I. I NTRODUCTION Connected mobility companies need to process vast amounts of location data in near real-time to run their businesses. For instance, Uber needs to join locations of passenger requests with a set of predefined polygons to display available products (e.g., Uber X) and to enable dynamic pricing1 . Another example are traffic use cases where the positions of vehicles need to be joined with street segments to enable real-time traffic control. With a future of connected (and possibly selfdriving) cars and drones, high-performance geospatial joins will become a key feature for increasingly demanding applications. While geospatial joins have been studied for decades, many of them optimize for I/O operations, which is an important performance factor for disk-based systems. With the large main-memory capacities of modern hardware, however, it is for the first time possible to maintain fine-grained index structures purely in main memory. We propose an adaptive geospatial join that addresses workloads with streaming points and static polygons. Our approach is optimized for modern hardware with large high-bandwidth memory and our implementation fully utilizes many-core processors and their Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) units. 1 https://eng.uber.com/go-geofence/ Figure 1 illustrates our approach. We make use of true hit filtering proposed by [1]. The authors of this work used maximum enclosed rectangles and circles as progressive approximations of single polygons. In contrast, we use an adaptive grid represented by a specialized radix tree, Adaptive Cell Trie (ACT), to not only index single polygons but entire sets of polygons. There are systems (e.g., Oracle Spatial [2] and Spark Magellan2 ) that have used the idea of true hit filtering. We take this idea one step further and leverage the large mainmemory capacities available in modern hardware to maximize the likelihood of true hits. We increase this likelihood by training the index using historical data points. In summary, we transform the traditionally computeintensive problem of geospatial joins into a memory-intensive one. Our approach results in speedups of up to two orders of magnitude compared to state-of-the-art standalone libraries and geospatial database systems. Our contributions include: • An adaptive geospatial join that uses hierarchical grids combined with radix indexing techniques to identify most join partners in the filter phase. An approximate version of this approach that guarantees a user-defined precision. • An optimization of this technique for Intel’s latest Xeon Phi, named Knights Landing (KNL). • II. BACKGROUND Unless stated otherwise, we follow the semantics of the ST Covers join predicate supported by PostGIS and Oracle Spatial. ST Covers evaluates whether one geospatial object (e.g., a polygon) covers another (e.g., a point). Points on the edges or vertices of a polygon are considered to be within the polygon. Other predicates, such as ST Intersects, are not explicitly addressed in this paper but can be implemented with similar techniques. Our geospatial join uses several building blocks: PIP: A point-in-polygon (PIP) test determines whether a point lies within a polygon. Typically such a test is performed using complex geometric operations, such as the ray tracing algorithm which involves drawing a line from the query point to a point that is known to be outside of the polygon and counting the number of edges that the line crosses. If the line crosses an odd number of edges, the query point lies within the polygon. The runtime complexity of this algorithm is O(n) with n being the number of edges. While there are many conceptual optimizations to the PIP test, this operation remains computationally expensive since it processes real numbers (e.g., latitude/longitude coordinates) and thus involves floating point arithmetics. In geospatial joins, this test should thus be avoided whenever possible. Space-filling curves: Geographical coordinates can either be indexed using multi-dimensional data structures, such as R-trees, or they can be linearized and indexed using onedimensional data structures, such as B-trees or tries. Linearization methods include the Hilbert space-filling curve and the Z curve. Our approach relies on discretization and linearization but does not depend on a concrete space-filling curve. For our approach to work, the cell enumeration must only fulfill the property that children cells share a common prefix with their parent cell. Google S2: We use the Google S2 library3 that provides primitives that our approach builds upon. These primitives include a PIP test algorithm and adaptive grid approximations of polygons. In general, S2 offers many features for processing geospatial data in both discrete and non-discrete space. To transform coordinates from the non-discrete space (the latitude/longitude coordinate system) into the discrete space, S2 maps points on earth onto a surrounding unit cube. Then it recursively subdivides each of the six faces of the cube in a quadtree fashion and enumerates the cells using the Hilbert space-filling curve. The enumerated cells are 64 bit integers, called cell ids, that uniquely identify a cell. The three most significant bits represent one of the six faces of the cube. The following zero to 30 bit pairs identify the quadtree cell. The 3 http://code.google.com/archive/p/s2-geometry-library/ Fig. 3: A covering and an interior covering of a polygon next bit is always set and is used to identify the level of a cell. The remaining bits (if any) are set to zero. The smallest cells use all 64 bits. Figure 2 illustrates the hierarchical decomposition of a cube face and shows how many bits the corresponding cell ids require depending on their level. The colored bits encode the levels. The cell ids in the example share a common prefix with their ancestors up to the colored bit. For example, c0 is an ancestor of c1 and c2 (i.e., c0 fully contains c1 and c2 ). A containment relationship between cells can thus be efficiently computed using bitwise operations. As mentioned above, S2 offers methods for approximating polygons. Figure 3a shows a covering of a polygon. A covering is a collection of cells (possibly at different levels) fully covering a polygon. Figure 3b shows an interior covering. As the name suggests, an interior covering approximates the interior of a polygon. All cells of an interior covering (interior cells) are completely contained within the polygon. When a point lies in an interior cell, we know that it also lies within the polygon. Both types of coverings can be utilized to speed up PIP tests. To allow for an efficient search, S2 stores the cell ids of a covering in a sorted vector. Besides sorting the cell id vector, it allows for normalizing the covering. A normalized covering neither contains conflicting nor duplicate cells. A conflict between two cells exists, if one cell contains the other. Only when the covering is normalized, cell containment checks can be efficiently (O(log n)) implemented using a binary search on the sorted vector. The normalization of an covering does not lead to a precision loss. III. G EOSPATIAL J OIN With our approach, we address geospatial joins between streaming points and static polygons. An example of such a workload is mapping Uber or DriveNow cars and passenger requests to predefined zones for allocation purposes. A. Overview Our geospatial join takes a set of simple polygons, builds an index, and probes points against the index. The high level idea is to index adaptive grid approximations of the polygons in a highly-efficient and specialized radix tree. In contrast to techniques that first reduce the number of polygons using an index, e.g., an R-tree on the polygons’ minimum bounding rectangles (MBRs), and then refine candidates using geometric operations, our approach implements true hit filtering [1] and identifies most or even all join partners in the filter phase. Given a memory budget and a precision bound, we adapt our index to satisfy these constraints while maximizing probe performance. Our algorithm consists of five phases: Build logical index: We compute coverings and interior coverings of all polygons and merge them to form a logical index. Build physical index: Then we build a physical index on the cells of the logical index. Training: When our approximate approach cannot guarantee a user-defined precision without exceeding a specified memory budget, we use an exact approach and train the index with historical data points to increase probe performance. Popular areas that expect more hits are approximated using a finergrained grid than less popular areas. Probe index: In this phase, we probe the points against the physical index. An index probe can either return a false hit or a list of hits, where each hit can either be a true hit or a candidate hit. Refine candidates: Finally, we perform exact geometric computations for all candidate hits4 . We use the S2 library to compute coverings and interior coverings. Note that our technique does not rely on S2. In fact, any other adaptive grid index would work as well. We then merge the individual coverings to create a logical index, before we build a physical index. Note that the first two phases can be performed in one step, i.e., the individual coverings can be computed and merged while inserting their cells into the index. In our approach, the probe (filter) phase is the performance critical part. We therefore highly parallelize this phase using thread- and instruction-level parallelism to accelerate lookups in the physical index. In the refinement phase, we use S2’s PIP test, which implements the ray tracing algorithm (cf., [3] for performance numbers). 4 Often, this phase can be skipped. In fact, it is only required if exact results The overall strategy of our technique is to minimize the number of (expensive) refinements. We can decrease the number of refinements by using a more fine-grained index. Since we make use of true hit filtering, a precise index allows us to identify most join partners during the filter phase. We can always omit the refinement phase when approximate results are sufficient. The error of such an approximate algorithm is bound by the length of the diagonal of the largest covering cell, which we choose to be sufficiently small. Our geospatial join takes two parameters: (i) a memory budget that must not be exceeded and (ii) an applicationdependent precision5 that must be guaranteed. We first try using the approximate approach by refining the index until we can guarantee the user-defined precision bound. This involves replacing covering cells with their children cells until the largest covering cell is sufficiently small (i.e., its diagonal is less than the precision bound). It might occur that we exhaust the memory budget during this procedure. In that case, we use the exact approach and train the index until we have used the entire memory budget. Training the index reduces the likelihood for expensive geometric operations. We evaluate these two approaches in Section V. In summary, we trade memory consumption with precision (approximate approach)

Now more than ever, the potential and actual benefits of open data sharing are being debated in the pages of premier scientific journals, funding agency communications, scientific meetings, and workshops1–3. Throughout these discussions an array of potential benefits are acknowledged, ranging from increased transparency of research and reproducibility of findings to decreased redundancy of effort and the generation of large-scale data repositories that can be used to achieve more appropriate sample sizes for analyses. Equally important, data sharing is commonly described as a means of facilitating collaboration across the broader scientific community. Despite its potential, for many, the benefits of data sharing are more theoretical than practical2,4. The reality is that data sharing is relatively limited in many disciplines and little information on its outcomes exists5. In the absence of clear demonstrations of data sharing’s impact, debates on the topic are dominated by formidable—albeit hypothetical—downsides. Common concerns include loss of competitive advantage (especially for junior investigators)6, fear of being scooped with one’s own data, scientifically unsound uses of the data, and concerns that high-impact journals will not accept manuscripts that report findings generated by secondary analysis of open data sets. To assess the tangible benefits of open data sharing, we provide a bibliometric analysis of a large brain image data-sharing initiative. The brain imaging community is a particularly valuable target for examination, as its challenges are representative of those commonly encountered in biomedical research. The high costs and workforce demands required to capture primary data limit the ability of individual labs to generate properly powered sample sizes. These obstacles are amplified when addressing more challenging (e.g., developing, aging, and clinical) populations or attempting biomarker discovery—both prerequisites for achieving clinically useful applications. Inspired by the momentum of molecular genetics, the first functional neuroimaging data-sharing initiative was launched in 20007, though it encountered logistical challenges (e.g., lack of standardization for task-based fMRI methods) and vigorous social resistance. Since then, a range of initiatives for sharing brain imaging data have emerged (e.g., OASIS8, ADNI9, Human Connectome Project10, and OpenfMRI11). While some open data sharing initiatives work to aggregate and share previously collected data sets, others explicitly generate large-scale data resources for the purpose of sharing. The present work focuses on the International Neuroimaging Data-sharing Initiative (INDI)12, as it uniquely embodies both of these models of sharing. The bibliometric measures we have employed could be easily applied to other initiatives in future work. Another distinctive aspect of INDI is its reliance on the formation of grassroots consortia as a primary vehicle for achieving its goal of aggregating and sharing previously collected data. Self-initiated and organized by scientists in the community, these consortia aggregate and share independently collected data from sites around the world. Examples of INDI-based consortia include the 1000 Functional Connectomes Project (FCP; n = 1414, released in December 2009)13, the ADHD-200 (n = 874, released in March 2010)14, the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE; n = 1112, released in August 2012)15, and the Consortium for Reliability and Reproducibility (CoRR; n = 1629, released in June 2014)16. In the present work, we use the grassroots consortium component of the INDI model to examine the relative benefits of open data sharing versus “pay to play” models, in which only those who give data can benefit from sharing. To examine the benefits of data resources explicitly generated for the purposes of sharing, we use INDI’s Nathan Kline Institute-Rockland Sample (NKI-RS) initiatives, a combination of large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal multimodal imaging samples of brain development, maturation, and aging (ages 6.0–85.0)17,18 (initial release in October 2010; quarterly releases ongoing, current n = 1000+). INDI efforts have been lauded by funding agencies, journal editors, and members of the imaging community. However, such subjective recognition does not quantify research impact. Drawing from the field of bibliometrics, we carried out a range of citation analyses19 to quantify the impact of INDI data sets on the brain imaging and broader scientific literatures. Our bibliometric analyses demonstrate the positive impact of openly shared data in the neuroimaging literature. In particular, they highlight the ability of openly shared data to invite the participation of scientists from a broad range of disciplines, to increase the scale of sample sizes, and to yield publications in moderate-to-high-impact journals with a frequency comparable to that of non-shared data. A keyword-based search identified 1541 possible INDI-related publications as of March 22, 2017 of which 913 were determined to have used data from INDI. Figure 1a provides a non-cumulative breakdown of the 913 publications by year and initiative, revealing steady yearly increases in shared data use. Author affiliations for the 913 publications using INDI data spanned 50 countries across 6 continents, with peak affiliation densities in the United States (48.5%), China (10.7%), Germany (6.5%), and the United Kingdom (6.0%) (see http://fcon1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/bibliometrics/map/map.html for the world map of author affiliations generated using the Google Maps JavaScript API V3). The overwhelming majority of publications were either peer-reviewed journal articles (n = 739; 81%) or preprints (n = 65; 7%); scholarly theses had a substantial presence as well (n = 58 [33 doctoral; 19 master’s; 4 bachelor’s; 2 unspecified]), demonstrating the value of shared data for trainees and early career investigators (see Fig. 1b). As expected given the brain imaging focus of the INDI consortia, the largest proportion (45.7%) of publications were in journals focused on general neuroscience, neurology, psychiatry, and psychology. The evolution of healthcare delivery models over recent decades has significantly expanded the role of pharmacists in ambulatory care settings, marking a shift from traditional roles focused primarily on dispensing medications to involving pharmacists in direct patient care and collaborative healthcare teams. This expansion aligns with broader healthcare objectives, aiming to improve patient outcomes, manage costs, and enhance the overall accessibility of healthcare services (Smith & Wheeler, 2019). Given these developments, the integration of clinical pharmacy services into ambulatory care settings is increasingly recognized as a crucial component in achieving these objectives (Anderson et al., 2020). Amidst this changing landscape, the proliferation of colleges of pharmacy in the United States further compounds the necessity for an expansion of ambulatory care practice sites capable of supporting comprehensive pharmacy practice education. As academic responsibilities grow alongside clinical demands, pharmacy practice faculty are often tasked with identifying and establishing new clinical practice sites—a challenge that requires strategic planning and robust support systems (Johnson & Lee, 2021). Despite the apparent need to develop such sites, many potential practice settings lack a precedent for clinical pharmacy services, necessitating innovative approaches to site development and collaboration with healthcare administrators and other stakeholders (Nelson et al., 2020). The gap in current literature suggests that guidance on how to successfully establish new ambulatory care practice sites from the ground up is limited, particularly advice tailored for pharmacy practice faculty who are instrumental in establishing these sites. Most existing resources focus on the operational aspects of established sites rather than the foundational aspects required for new site development (Brown & White, 2018). This gap highlights the need for a comprehensive framework that can be readily adapted by clinical faculty to assess and initiate practice sites that will not only fulfill academic roles but also contribute substantively to patient care and health system efficiency. In response to this need, this article addresses the research question: What are the essential components and strategies for pharmacy practice faculty to successfully establish new ambulatory care practice sites that are devoid of existing clinical pharmacy services, ensuring they provide adequate resources and support? In addressing this question, the manuscript aims to provide a structured approach for faculty members to evaluate potential sites and make informed decisions that align with both educational and clinical care objectives. It also seeks to identify best practices in engaging stakeholders, leveraging institutional resources, and ensuring sustainable site development through continuous evaluation and adaptation. The contributions of this study are manifold. First, it synthesizes existing knowledge on establishing ambulatory care practice sites from diverse healthcare and educational settings, providing novel insights tailored specifically for pharmacy faculty. This synthesis is crucial given that pharmacy practice often intersects with multiple facets of healthcare delivery and education, necessitating a multidimensional approach to site development (Harris et al., 2021). Second, the study offers practical recommendations to address common challenges encountered in new site development, such as gaining administrative support, securing funding, and establishing interprofessional collaborations. A key focus of this manuscript is the pre-establishment phase, which involves comprehensive groundwork crucial for the success of the practice site. This includes developing a coherent vision for the scope and impact of pharmacist services, articulating this vision to relevant stakeholders, and creating a compelling narrative that supports the unique value pharmacists bring to the healthcare team (Miller & Roberts, 2019). Furthermore, the article discusses the importance of assessing the physical and logistical requirements of a potential site, including infrastructure needs, technological support, and workflow integration. Additionally, it considers essential interpersonal elements, such as establishing relationships with key personnel and aligning site goals with the institution's strategic objectives, which are all critical to gaining buy-in from decision-makers (Collins et al., 2018). By addressing these considerations, this study endeavors to empower pharmacy practice faculty with tools to advocate effectively for resource allocation and institutional support—elements that are pivotal in transitioning theoretical concepts into functional, sustainable practice sites. Scholarly contributions also include a framework for ongoing site evaluation and adaptation, highlighting the need for continuous feedback mechanisms and performance assessments in achieving long-term success and scalability (Taylor & Gupta, 2020). In summary, this manuscript contributes to closing the knowledge gap concerning the establishment of new ambulatory care sites by providing pharmacy practice faculty with a practical, evidence-based template for embarking on site development, which is sensitive to the unique challenges and opportunities present in settings without established clinical pharmacy services. This is incumbent upon the active and innovative participation of pharmacy faculty, who are uniquely positioned at the nexus of education, practice, and research. This study employed a mixed-methods design to investigate the establishment of new ambulatory care practice sites by pharmacy practice faculty. The objective was to identify and develop effective strategies to create and sustain these sites in locations where clinical pharmacy services have not been historically utilized. The study consisted of two main components: a quantitative survey and a series of qualitative interviews, both designed to gather comprehensive data about the needs and experiences of pharmacy practice faculty involved in setting up new sites. The quantitative component involved the development and distribution of a structured survey targeting pharmacy practice faculty across various colleges of pharmacy. The survey aimed to capture data regarding faculty experiences and perceptions of the key factors necessary for establishing successful practice sites. It included sections on pre-work requirements, resource assessment, stakeholder engagement, service marketing, implementation processes, and evaluation strategies. Data collection for the survey was conducted over a six-month period from March 2022 to September 2022. Participants were recruited using a stratified random sampling method to ensure diversity across geographic regions, types of institutions (public vs. private), and years of faculty experience. The survey was disseminated online through a secure survey platform, ensuring anonymity and confidentiality of all participants. A total of 500 pharmacy practice faculty members were invited to participate, with a response rate of 60% achieved, yielding 300 completed surveys. In parallel, qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews. This component aimed to gain deeper insights into the challenges and facilitators identified through the survey and to explore the nuanced experiences of faculty members at varying stages of practice site development. Participants for the interviews were selected from the survey respondents who indicated willingness to participate in follow-up research and were purposefully sampled to reflect a wide range of experiences and contexts. A total of 30 in-depth interviews were conducted, each lasting approximately 60 minutes. The interviews were audio-recorded with participant consent and subsequently transcribed verbatim for analysis. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS software (Version 27). Descriptive statistics were computed to summarize demographic information and survey responses. Factors associated with successful site establishment were evaluated using multiple regression analyses, controlling for potential confounding variables such as years of experience and institutional support. Additionally, chi-square tests were employed to examine categorical relationships between institutional characteristics and reported outcomes. The qualitative interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis, following the approach outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006). This involved a six-phase process: familiarization with the data, generating initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and producing the report. NVivo software (Version 12) facilitated coding and theme development. Regular team meetings were held to discuss emerging themes and ensure analytical rigor through triangulation and consensus-building. To enhance the credibility and reliability of the qualitative findings, member checking was conducted. Participants were provided with a summary of the preliminary themes and invited to offer feedback, which was then incorporated into the final analysis. Efforts to ensure methodological rigor included maintaining an audit trail, utilizing multiple coders to cross-verify themes, and continuously reflecting on researcher biases through memo writing. The integration of quantitative and qualitative findings was performed through a process of iterative comparison and triangulation, aimed at enhancing the overall understanding of the phenomena under investigation. This holistic approach allowed for the identification of both broad trends and specific contextual factors influencing the success of new ambulatory care practice sites. In summary, this mixed-methods study combined quantitative surveys and qualitative interviews to provide a comprehensive examination of the processes and factors involved in establishing new ambulatory care practice sites by pharmacy practice faculty. This methodological approach enabled the generation of robust data, capturing both the breadth and depth of faculty experiences across different contexts, thereby contributing valuable insights into best practices for promoting clinical pharmacy services in novel settings. The establishment of a new ambulatory care practice site was evaluated at a large urban healthcare facility, which had previously not integrated clinical pharmacy services into its ambulatory care framework. The quantitative assessment focused on three primary outcomes: patient acceptance of pharmacy services, the impact of pharmacy interventions on clinical outcomes, and the integration of the site into the educational framework for pharmacy students. Patient acceptance of pharmacy services was measured by capturing the utilization rates of the offered pharmacy services and the satisfaction levels of patients who participated in the study. Over a 12-month period, the number of patients seen by the pharmacy practice faculty increased from zero at baseline to 480 at the end of the study (p < 0.001). This count translated to an average of 40 patients per month. Patient satisfaction was gauged through a standardized survey distributed at the six-month and twelve-month marks, yielding response rates of 78% and 75%, respectively. The satisfaction survey revealed a high level of approval with a mean score of 4.6 out of 5, with higher scores indicating greater satisfaction (SD = 0.5). The dimensions of satisfaction that scored notably high included the pharmacist's communication skills (mean = 4.8), perceived expertise (mean = 4.7), and accessibility (mean = 4.6). Pharmacy interventions played a significant role in improving selected clinical outcomes, which was evidenced by comparing patient groups receiving pharmacist services to those who did not. Among diabetic patients (n = 150), the average reduction in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) was 1.3%, from a baseline mean of 9.1% to 7.8% over twelve months (p < 0.01). Similarly, in a cohort of patients with hypertension (n = 120), systolic blood pressure decreased on average by 12 mmHg, from 145 mmHg to 133 mmHg (p < 0.05). These results underscore the pharmacist's role in managing chronic conditions and improving health outcomes. Furthermore, the medication adherence rates improved significantly, as measured through patients' self-reports and pharmacy refill records, with adherence levels rising from 68% at baseline to 92% after 12 months of pharmacy intervention (p < 0.05). The integration of the site into the educational framework involved evaluating the number of pharmacy students trained in the ambulatory care setting and the perceived competency acquisition among these students. In the initial year, 24 pharmacy students rotated through the site, each completing a five-week experiential rotation. Pre- and post-rotation self-assessments showed a marked improvement in students' self-perceived competence in clinical skills, with mean scores rising from 3.1 to 4.4 on a 5-point Likert scale (p < 0.01). Specific competencies, such as conducting medication therapy management and communicating effectively with healthcare professionals, demonstrated the most improvement, with mean score increases of 1.3 and 1.5 points, respectively. Students reported a significant enhancement in their ability to apply clinical knowledge in a practical setting, substantiated by a 95% approval rating for the ambulatory care rotation's impact on their professional development. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are widely recognized as essential tools for synthesizing evidence from multiple studies to inform decision-making in various fields, including healthcare, education, and social sciences (Higgins & Green, 2011). These reviews involve the identification, evaluation, and synthesis of all relevant studies on a specific research question, using clearly defined methods to minimize bias (Moher et al., 2009). However, the process of conducting systematic reviews can be complex, particularly when dealing with multiple data sources for individual trials. A single trial may be reported in multiple sources, such as journal articles, conference abstracts, and study protocols, which can lead to differences in the reported results, methods, and conclusions (Egger et al., 2003). The use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews is not a new phenomenon, but it has become increasingly common with the growing number of studies being published and the ease of access to various sources of information (Song et al., 2010). For example, a study may be reported in a journal article, a conference abstract, and a clinical trial registry, each providing different levels of detail and potentially conflicting information (Zarin et al., 2011). The selection of which sources to use can significantly influence the results of systematic reviews, and therefore, it is essential to develop practical guidance on how to handle multiple data sources (Gøtzsche & Hróbjartsson, 2010). Despite the importance of this issue, there is a lack of clear guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Previous studies have highlighted the potential problems associated with using multiple data sources, including inconsistencies in reporting, selective reporting, and publication bias (Dwan et al., 2013). However, these studies have not provided comprehensive guidance on how to address these issues in practice. The current guidelines for systematic reviews, such as the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) statement, provide some guidance on reporting, but do not specifically address the issue of multiple data sources (Moher et al., 2009). The Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was designed to investigate the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews and to develop practical guidance for reviewers (personal communication). The study involved a comprehensive review of the literature, as well as a survey of systematic review authors and a case study of a sample of systematic reviews. The results of the MUDS study highlighted the complexity of the issue and the need for clear guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews. The study found that the selection of sources can influence the results of systematic reviews, and that reviewers often lack clear protocols for handling multiple data sources (unpublished data). The research question addressed in this paper is: How can systematic reviewers use multiple data sources in a way that minimizes bias and ensures the accuracy and reliability of the results? This question is critical because the use of multiple data sources can introduce bias and errors into systematic reviews, which can have significant consequences for decision-making (Ioannidis, 2005). By developing practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources, we aim to reduce the risk of bias and errors in systematic reviews and to improve the quality of the evidence synthesized. The contributions of this paper are several. First, we provide a comprehensive review of the literature on the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews, highlighting the potential problems and challenges associated with this issue. Second, we present the results of the MUDS study, which provides new insights into the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews. Third, we develop practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews, based on the results of the MUDS study and the literature review. This guidance includes recommendations on how to specify which sources to use, how to link individual trials with multiple sources, how to extract trial characteristics from multiple sources, and how to prespecify outcomes and results to examine in the review and meta-analysis. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the conduct of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and provide recommendations for future research in this area. In terms of the theoretical framework underlying our research, we draw on the concept of "research waste," which refers to the waste of resources, time, and effort in conducting research that is not useful or relevant (Chalmers & Glasziou, 2009). We argue that the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews can contribute to research waste, and that clear guidance on how to use these sources can help to reduce this waste. We also draw on the concept of "evidence-based medicine," which emphasizes the importance of using the best available evidence to inform decision-making (Sackett et al., 1996). By developing practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources, we aim to improve the quality of the evidence synthesized in systematic reviews, and to promote evidence-based decision-making. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the issue of multiple data sources in systematic reviews, and presents practical guidance on how to use these sources in a way that minimizes bias and ensures the accuracy and reliability of the results. The guidance presented in this paper has the potential to improve the quality of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and to promote evidence-based decision-making in a range of fields. The Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was designed to investigate the impact of using multiple data sources on the results of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The study used a combination of empirical research and expert consensus to develop practical guidance for reviewers. We drew on our experience in the MUDS study, as well as evidence from previous studies (e.g., Higgins et al., 2011; Lefebvre et al., 2019), to inform our approach. In this section, we describe the data, design, procedures, and statistical analysis used in the MUDS study. The MUDS study included a total of 50 systematic reviews, each with multiple data sources. We identified these reviews through a comprehensive search of major databases, including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library (see Equation 1 for the search strategy). We included reviews that reported on the use of multiple data sources, such as journal articles, conference abstracts, and clinical trial registries. We excluded reviews that only used a single data source or did not report on the use of multiple sources. Search strategy: (1) (systematic review OR meta-analysis) AND (multiple data sources OR multiple reports OR duplicate publication) We used a standardized data extraction form to collect information from each review, including the number and type of data sources used, the number of trials included, and the outcomes reported. We also extracted information on the methods used to link individual trials with multiple sources, such as contacting study authors or using a modified PRISMA flowchart (Moher et al., 2009). Two reviewers independently extracted data from each review, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. To link individual trials with multiple sources, we used a modified version of the PRISMA flowchart (Moher et al., 2009). This involved creating a flowchart for each review, with separate branches for each data source. We then used this flowchart to document the selection of trials and sources, and to identify any discrepancies between sources. For example, if a trial was reported in two journal articles and a conference abstract, we would create a separate branch for each source and document the information extracted from each source. We also prespecified a protocol for extracting trial characteristics from multiple sources. This involved identifying the most reliable source for each trial characteristic, such as the primary outcome or sample size. If there were discrepancies between sources, we contacted the study authors to resolve the differences if possible. We used a standardized form to document the extraction process, including any discrepancies or uncertainties. To examine the impact of using multiple data sources on the results of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, we used a combination of descriptive and inferential statistics. We calculated the frequency and percentage of reviews that used multiple data sources, and the types of sources used. We also calculated the mean and standard deviation of the number of trials included in each review, and the number of outcomes reported. To examine the relationship between the use of multiple data sources and the results of the review, we used regression analysis (Equation 2). Regression equation: Y = β0 + β1X + ε Where Y is the outcome of interest (e.g., the effect size), X is the number of data sources used, β0 is the intercept, β1 is the slope, and ε is the error term. We also used sensitivity analysis to examine the robustness of our findings to different data sources and analytical approaches. This involved repeating the analysis using different subsets of the data, such as only including reviews that used a specific type of data source (e.g., journal articles). We also used funnel plots and Egger's test to examine the presence of publication bias (Egger et al., 1997). Overall, our study provides practical guidance for using multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. By specifying which sources to use, linking individual trials with multiple sources, following a prespecified protocol for extracting trial characteristics, prespecifying outcomes and results, identifying which data sources were included in the review, and sharing the data used in the review, reviewers can reduce bias and research waste, and increase the accuracy and reliability of their findings. In our investigation of the Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study, we observed that the inclusion of multiple data sources significantly impacted the results of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Specifically, we found that 75% of trials (95% CI: 67-82%) had data available from more than one source, with a median of 3 sources per trial (IQR: 2-5) (Higgins et al., 2011). This multiplicity of sources necessitated the development of a systematic approach to selecting and synthesizing data, as outlined in our protocol (Moher et al., 2009). We applied our methodological framework to a subset of 50 trials, randomly selected from the MUDS study database, and observed that the use of multiple sources resulted in a 25% increase (95% CI: 15-35%) in the number of trials with complete outcome data (Sutton et al., 2000). Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the sources used to inform the review influenced the estimated treatment effects, with a median difference of 10% (IQR: 5-20%) in the odds ratios (ORs) obtained from different sources (Deeks et al., 2008). This highlights the importance of carefully considering the sources used in a systematic review, as also noted by others (Liberati et al., 2009). To illustrate the impact of source selection on the results of meta-analyses, we conducted a series of sensitivity analyses using different combinations of sources (Thompson et al., 2001). Our findings indicated that the choice of sources used in the review could alter the conclusions drawn from the meta-analysis, with a change in the direction of the treatment effect observed in 15% (95% CI: 8-25%) of the analyses (Egger et al., 1997). For example, when we restricted our analysis to only journal articles, the pooled OR was 1.25 (95% CI: 1.05-1.49), whereas the inclusion of conference abstracts resulted in a pooled OR of 1.15 (95% CI: 0.95-1.39) (Borenstein et al., 2009). In addition to examining the impact of source selection on the results of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, we also investigated the feasibility of implementing our proposed methodology in practice. We surveyed 20 systematic review authors and found that 80% (95% CI: 64-96%) reported using multiple data sources in their reviews, although only 40% (95% CI: 22-58%) documented their source selection methods (PRISMA, 2009). Encouragingly, 90% (95% CI: 74-100%) of respondents indicated a willingness to adopt our proposed methods for handling multiple data sources in future reviews (Guyatt et al., 2011).
