The central purpose of science is to explain ( Purtill, 1970). However, who is that explanation for, and how is this explanation communicated once it has been deduced? Scientific research is typically communicated via papers in journals, but whilst to an insider (i.e. a scientist in that field) these papers and journals represent an efficient and effective way of communicating research, to an outsider (i.e. a member of the general public) what they represent and report on may not be at all clear ( Meadows, 1985), and in many instances they may be written with a lexical density that makes them inaccessible to a lay reader ( Halliday & Martin, 2003). Almost all journals require the authors to provide a word-limited abstract as part of the submission process, and whilst the specifics of these abstracts will vary from journal to journal, their purpose effectively remains the same, with Johnson (1995, pp. 28) defining them as “a concise representation of a document’s contents to enable the reader to determine its relevance to specific information.” If the central purpose of science were indeed to explain, is the central purpose of an abstract therefore a summary of that explanation? Swales (1990) considers a scientific abstract to be a ‘rite of passage’ for gaining entry into the scientific community, and that in order to do so the writer needs to demonstrate an “increasing mastery of the academic dialect” ( Orasan, 2001, pp. 2). Andrade (2011, pp. 172) notes that “for the vast majority of readers, the paper does not exist beyond its abstract,” with the majority of researchers using the abstract to determine if the scientific study is relevant to them and worthy of a further investment of their time in reading it in its entirety. As noted by Fletcher (1988), the creation of an abstract is often also an extremely important process for clarifying the narrative of the scientific study in the mind of the author(s) themselves. Hartley (2003) also found that structured abstracts (i.e. those split into subheadings of: Background, Aims, Methods, Results, and Conclusions, or their equivalents) were found to be more informative and also provide greater clarity than their unstructured counterparts. Whilst the exact format and structure of the abstract will be determined by the journal in which the article is to be published, the purpose of writing an abstract should be to extract and summarize ( Alexandrov & Hennerici, 2006), with the primary objective to not only provide information, but also to convince the reader to finish the remainder of the paper, which in some instances will involve paying for the privilege ( Koopman, 1997). Orasan (2001) also observed that many authors of scientific papers do not consider the abstract to be particularly important, arguing that in many cases it is written as a necessity just before the paper is submitted. Is it therefore the case, that rather than being an effective and economical method of communicating the research, that the abstract instead represents a rushed précis of the research findings, with an even higher lexical density than that of the main body of the text? If so, then are they useful to anyone who might consider themselves, or indeed be considered an outsider? And if non-experts are unable to fully grasp the summary of the explanation, then what hope do they have of being able to fully understand the research and its potential relevance to them? Cross & Oppenheim (2006) also notes that there is probably little formal training in abstract writing, which is why in some instances there may be a lack of clarity in the abstracts that are produced in scientific journal articles. Climate change research is a subject which has potential relevance on a global scale, however Rudiak-Gould (2014) found that whilst members of the general public receive information about climate change through the first-hand experience of its effects on their environment, it is still absolutely necessary to effectively communicate the science to them as well. This is because as well as the difficulty in objectively observing long-term trends, there are other issues in their day-to-day lives that the general public must concern themselves with as well. In their study Rudiak-Gould (2014) worked with the Marshall Island’s indigenous population, the Majuro people, where more pressing concerns than long-term sea-level rise were short-term anxieties related to e.g. fluctuations in the cost of rice. This argument is relevant in other communities, where issues such as job security, energy prices and mortgage rates might well take precedence over concerns relating to climate change. In other words, it is not simply enough to assume that people will take notice of their changing environments and act upon them; instead there needs to be an intervention in terms of the effective communication of what is happening, the consequences of this, and what can be done in order to mitigate the effects. Effective science communication should “facilitate conversations with the public that recognize, respect, and incorporate differences in knowledge, values, perspectives, and goals.” ( Nisbet & Scheufele, 2009, pp. 1767). The accurate communication of scientific research is also vital so that the general public are aware of the consensus in terms of scientific understanding, and researchers should not forget the ‘moral dimension’ and sense of responsibility in terms of communicating their findings to others ( Tickell, 2002). This is particularly prominent for studies discussing the anthropogenic nature of climate change, with John et al. (2013) finding that over 97% of climate change papers published between 1991 and 2011 agreed that climate change is a human-caused phenomenon. However, this is not always the way that this argument is presented, which is why it is absolutely vital that scientists endeavour to make their research as transparent and accessible as possible. It has also been shown that the polarization over the validity of climate change science is reduced when information content is communicated alongside a consideration for cultural meanings ( Kahan et al., 2015). Can scientific articles take into account these cultural values, thereby acting as an effective way of communicating information? Likewise, if journals are to act as an effectual conduit between scientists and the general public, then how can abstracts be constructed so as to appeal to the widest possible audience whilst still conveying useful and meaningful information, and is there a medium that can be exploited in order to ease this transition? The former United States Poet Laureate Robert Pinsky writes that ( Pinsky, 2009, pp. 46): “Poetry mediates, on a particular and immensely valuable level between the inner consciousness of the individual reader and the outer world of other people.” Similarly, the English romantic-era poet Percy Bysshe Shelley noted that “poetry lifts the veil from the hidden beauty of the world” ( Shelley, 1888). Could poetry therefore be the medium with which to help encapsulate non-expert audiences with research findings? Science and poetry have much in common, both in terms of their use of metaphor and their embodiment of process (see e.g. Illingworth, 2016), and as the American poet Robert Kelly noted in his poem ‘Science’ ( Kelly, 2007): Science explains nothingbut holds all togetheras many things as it can countscience is a basketnot a religion he saida cat as big as a catthe moon the size of the moonscience is the same as poetryonly it uses the wrong words. Could poetry therefore help scientists to choose their words more carefully, thereby helping them to avoid the academic dialect that so often ostracizes the non-expert? There is in fact a historical precedent for science being written in poetic verse, most famously evidenced by the works of Erasmus Darwin (1798). However, rather than an entire journal article penned in poetic verse, might instead their abstracts be written in this style, and in doing so might they then appeal to a wider audience, be more readily understood, and potentially encourage the reader to investigate the topic further? If poetry is to be used to help better communicate scientific abstracts to the general public however, it is first of all important to establish if this form of communique is still useful to the experts in the field. In other words, if poetic verse were to be accepted as a suitable abstract style, then would this still be accessible and informative to other scientists? It is the purpose of this study to determine if this new format means that the abstract is still a useful commodity to the ‘insiders.’ This paper is organised as follows: the methodology used in this study is described, followed by a presentation and discussion of the results from this study. Finally, some perspectives on this work are outlined, discussing what the results imply for future work and for the scientific abstract in general. In order to assess the suitability of using poetry in scientific abstracts, a survey was conducted in which two different groups of participants were given an abstract relating to a scientific paper, before being asked questions based on this abstract. One of the groups of participants was given the original scientific abstract, whilst the second group were given a poem that was written about the scientific study. Apart from this the two surveys were identical, and the survey was conducted using the free online survey builder ‘Typeform’ ( www.typeform.com), comprising of nine questions delivered with a mixed-method approach. Of these nine questions, five of them asked for demographic information, whilst the remaining four were all related to the abstract itself, asking the participants to sum up in their own words what they thought that the research was about, and also asking them to mark the abstract out of ten (zero being the least) for how accessible and interesting they found the abstract, as well as how likely they were to go and find out more about this research as a result of reading the abstract. A copy of the questionnaire can be found in the Supplementary Materials section of this article, and the non-demographic questions are given below (please note that the numbering of these questions is different to how they appeared in the survey): Q1 How accessible did you find the abstract? (mark from 0 to 10, with 0 being the least)Q2 How interesting did you find the abstract? (mark from 0 to 10, with 0 being the least)Q3 As a result of reading the abstract, how likely are you to go and find out more about this research? (mark from 0 to 10, with 0 being the least)Q4 After reading the abstract, what do you think that this research is about? (open-ended) The choice of the abstract and poem themselves was important, as it was necessary to choose an abstract that was well written so as not to bias the results of the study, it was also important to choose a topic that would be of potential relevance to non-experts. As discussed in the introduction, research concerning climate change demands to be communicated, because of its global relevance and the potential societal consequences of its findings. Ideally then, the scientific study in question would be related to climate change, and would have a well-written abstract. It is also important to consider the issue of transformation, and how this potentially affects the goal of the abstract. As discussed above, the primary objective of the abstract is to both provide information and also to convince the reader to finish the remainder of the paper. The nature of the poem means that it is more likely to be thought of as a popular piece of science writing rather than a professional piece of science writing, as is the case for the original abstract. As such, care must be taken to ensure that in the transformation from prose into poetry, the primary objective does not also fully transform into that of purely establishing the novelty of the topic ( Rowan, 1989). Information hiding is the practice of concealing the existence of a piece of information, or its association with a particular carrier, so that only intended parties can detect or recover it. Its best-known branches are steganography, which hides a secret message inside innocuous-looking data, and digital watermarking, which embeds information in a host object for purposes such as copyright protection and tracing (Cox et al., 2007; Fridrich, 2009). Since Simmons' (1984) formulation of the prisoners' problem, steganography has been modelled as covert communication between two parties through a channel monitored by a warden. Security is then defined by the warden's inability to distinguish cover objects from stego objects (Cachin, 1998). Under this model, research has concentrated on embedding secret data into a cover object, such as an image, audio clip, video, or text, while keeping statistical and perceptual distortion small. Practical progress ranges from early least-significant-bit and transform-domain methods (Provos and Honeyman, 2003; Westfeld, 2001) to content-adaptive schemes based on distortion minimisation and syndrome-trellis codes (Filler et al., 2011), with steganalysis advancing in parallel through rich feature models and machine learning (Fridrich and Kodovský, 2012). Beyond multimedia files, the information hiding community has extended the notion of carrier to communication systems. Network steganography and covert channels hide data in protocol fields, packet timing, or traffic patterns (Zielińska et al., 2014; Mazurczyk et al., 2016; Wendzel et al., 2015). More recently, online social networks (OSNs) have been used as covert media. Researchers have shown that user-generated content on public platforms can carry censorship-resistant messages (Burnett et al., 2010), that social-network structure and activity can support covert botnet command and control (Nagaraja et al., 2011; Pantic and Husain, 2015), and that images and text posted on social media can be turned into stego carriers. These developments reflect a general trend: as digital life moves to large, open, high-volume platforms, such platforms offer both new opportunities for concealment and new difficulties for detection. Despite this diversity, almost all existing approaches share one structural assumption: a cover exists. The cover may be selected from a database, modified in place, synthesised from the message, or, in so-called coverless approaches, chosen or retrieved because its natural features already map to message bits (Zhou et al., 2015). Generative methods using neural networks (Hayes and Danezis, 2017) also produce a concrete cover-like object that carries the payload. In every case the hidden information is attached to a bounded object or message stream that the warden can, in principle, isolate and test. This assumption shapes both attack and defence. Steganalysis is typically framed as a binary classification problem on individual objects, or as pooled analysis over a batch of objects from one source (Ker, 2006). Even when real-world conditions are acknowledged, such as unknown cover sources, mismatched training data, and the sheer volume of traffic, the detection target remains a set of identifiable objects (Ker et al., 2013). This assumption leaves a gap. Contemporary digital environments consist of vast numbers of human and automated agents continuously performing actions: posting, replying, liking, following, retweeting, tagging, and joining groups. The fact that certain actions occurred, with certain attributes (who, when, what type, in what order, toward which targets), is itself observable by anyone with access to the platform. Such activity patterns can encode information without requiring any single content object to be modified or even to be unusual. To our knowledge, the literature has not treated this observable activity space as the carrier in a general, systematic framework. Existing OSN-based schemes typically either embed data in the content of posts or in the traffic and behaviour of a specific malware-like structure, and they do not generalise to a design in which an arbitrary set of entities and activities in an arbitrary digital world encodes the message. Consequently, we lack both a unifying model and an understanding of the security implications when the cover effectively becomes the entire observable digital world. This paper addresses the following research question: can information be hidden not in a chosen or generated cover object, but in the very fact that particular digital activities, with particular attributes, were carried out in particular ways by selected human and computer entities in a receiver-observable digital world, and what does this imply for applications and for detection? Answering it requires specifying how a message can be mapped onto activity patterns, how a receiver can observe and decode them, how the sender and receiver share the necessary secret (for example, the selected entities, activity types, and mapping rules), and how such a scheme behaves with respect to security notions that were developed for object-based covers. We make the following contributions. First, we propose a general framework for information hiding in digital activities. In it, the sender and receiver agree on a digital world (for example, one or several OSNs), a set of entities within it (such as accounts), and a family of activities and attributes through which the message is expressed. The traditional notion of cover nearly disappears: the whole selected digital world, together with the activity it contains, plays the role of the cover. Second, we discuss application areas in both security and non-security settings. For steganography, the framework offers a channel that does not require producing a suspicious stego object. For non-security uses, such as gaming (for instance, treasure-hunt or puzzle designs where clues are carried by activity patterns), it offers a new interaction medium. Third, we analyse the implications for steganalysis. Because there is no isolated object to inspect, we argue that detection would require monitoring and analysing the whole digital world constantly and in real time, a task likely to be more complex, less effective, and less efficient than existing object-based steganalysis, and one calling for fundamentally new techniques. Fourth, we present a proof-of-concept system, implemented as a mobile app built on Twitter activities, showing that the framework can be realised in a real platform. We also outline ongoing work on a hybrid system that spans several online social networks. The rest of this paper is organised as follows: we first formalise the framework and its components, then describe the Twitter-based implementation, and finally discuss security considerations, applications, and directions for future work. Framework formalization. We model the selected digital world as a tuple W = (E, A, T, O), where E = {e1, …, en} is a set of human or computer entities (here, online social network accounts), A is a set of activity types (posting, reposting, liking, following, replying), T is a discrete sequence of time slots, and O is the observation function that determines which activities a receiver can see. An activity is a tuple a = (e, α, v, t), where e is the acting entity, α is the activity type, v is a vector of attributes (e.g., target account, hashtag, text length, or media presence), and t is the slot in which it occurred. The sender and receiver share a secret key K and a public specification of W. The hidden message is carried by the fact that a particular ordered set of activities occurred, not by the content of any cover object. This follows the prisoners' problem setting (Simmons, 1984) and the usual requirement that security rest on the key rather than on secrecy of the scheme (Kerckhoffs, 1883; Cachin, 1998). Because every activity in W is a potential carrier, no cover is chosen or modified. Message preparation. The plaintext is compressed and encrypted with AES-256 in counter mode, using a subkey derived from K by HMAC-SHA256 (Bellare et al., 1996). A short header with message length and sequence number is prepended. The result is protected with a Reed–Solomon code (Reed & Solomon, 1960) over GF(2^8), which tolerates the missing or spurious activities expected on a public platform, where unrelated users act concurrently, posts may be deleted, and rate limits may delay actions. The coded stream is split into symbols of b bits. Codebook and embedding. A key-seeded pseudorandom generator, built from HMAC-SHA256 in counter mode, produces for each slot t a codebook Ct. This is an injective map from the 2^b symbol values to distinct activity tuples drawn from the permitted set. Because the codebook changes with t, repeated symbols do not yield repeated activity patterns. To embed symbol st, the sender performs the activity Ct(st). Decoding is the inverse lookup. The activity choice also determines how many bits each slot carries: if an slot offers m distinguishable tuples, its nominal capacity is log₂ m bits. Embedding capacity therefore grows with the number of controlled accounts, the activity types used, and the attribute resolution. Additional key-derived rules decide which accounts act and when, so that the volume and timing of activity per account stay close to that account's historical behavior. This is meant to reduce statistical deviation from benign activity, in line with the aim of avoiding distributional differences between cover and stego behavior (Cachin, 1998; Hopper et al., 2002). Synchronization and reception. The receiver knows K, the start time, and the slot length. It polls the public timelines and relationship lists of the accounts in E through the platform's REST API at an interval shorter than the slot length, and records each observed activity with its timestamp. For each slot, observed activities are compared with Ct. Matches yield candidate symbols. Activities that match no codeword are treated as background noise and discarded. If several codewords are observed in one slot, the receiver takes the one that also satisfies the header and a message authentication tag. Slots with no match are marked as erasures, which Reed–Solomon decoding handles more efficiently than random errors. After the symbol stream is reassembled, it is decoded, decrypted, and checked for integrity. Proof-of-concept implementation. The prototype is a mobile app with sender and receiver modes. The sender mode authenticates through OAuth to a set of Twitter accounts that we own and operate. It schedules activities in a background service according to the codebook. Activity types are original posts with controlled attributes (hashtag from a key-derived list, tweet-length bin, presence of a link), reposts of designated accounts, likes, and follows or unfollows. The receiver mode uses read-only API access. All keys remain in the device's secure storage. Cryptographic operations use the platform's standard libraries. To reduce risk to the platform and other users, request rates stay within documented limits, and only accounts created for the experiment are used as carriers. Experimental design. We ran controlled experiments with n ∈ {5, 10, 20} experimental accounts, b ∈ {2, 4, 6} bits per slot, and slot lengths of 1, 5, and 15 minutes. For each factor combination, random messages of 32, 64, and 128 bytes were transmitted in 30 independent trials, with the sender and receiver on separate devices and networks. A subset of accounts also followed and interacted with a pool of unrelated public accounts, so that the receiver would see realistic background activity. We also injected synthetic perturbations (deleted posts and suspended polling windows) to test robustness. The primary outcomes were: (i) message recovery rate, the proportion of trials with exact plaintext recovery; (ii) symbol error and erasure rates before error correction; (iii) effective embedding rate in bits per hour, after coding overhead; and (iv) end-to-end latency from the first embedded activity to successful decoding. Detectability analysis. Since the framework implies that a steganalyst must monitor the whole world W, we evaluated detectability under a simplified adversary with access to the same public API. Baseline behavioral profiles were obtained from the pre-experiment activity histories of the same accounts and, where permitted by the platform's terms, from a sample of comparable public accounts. For each account we computed features such as per-hour activity counts by type, inter-activity time distributions, hashtag frequencies, and the entropy of interaction targets. We compared stego and baseline periods using Kullback–Leibler divergence and two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (Cover & Thomas, 2006). The number of individuals forcibly displaced from their homelands has reached unprecedented levels, with over 25 million refugees worldwide, approximately half of whom are children (UNHCR, 2020). Refugee children often experience significant trauma and stress prior to, during, and after their displacement, which can have long-lasting effects on their emotional and psychological wellbeing (Fazel et al., 2012). The resettlement process can be particularly challenging for these children, as they must navigate a new culture, language, and education system while dealing with the aftermath of their displacement (Betancourt et al., 2012). Schools can play a vital role in supporting the resettlement and emotional wellbeing of refugee children (Taylor & Sidhu, 2012), yet the body of research examining the specific school environmental factors that support the mental health and acculturation of refugee children is limited and methodologically heterogeneous (Sayed et al., 2018). Research has consistently shown that refugee children face significant challenges in their daily lives, including social isolation, cultural and linguistic barriers, and stigma (Hodes et al., 2018). These challenges can lead to poor academic performance, social difficulties, and mental health problems, including anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Fazel et al., 2012). Moreover, the experiences of refugee children in schools can have a profound impact on their long-term outcomes, including their educational attainment, career prospects, and overall wellbeing (Beiser, 2009). Therefore, it is essential to identify the specific school factors that support the emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes of refugee children, and to develop evidence-based strategies for promoting their mental health and acculturation. Despite the critical importance of this issue, the existing literature on school factors related to the emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes of refugee children is characterized by several key limitations. First, many studies have focused on the individual-level factors that influence the mental health and acculturation of refugee children, such as their personal experiences of trauma and stress, rather than the school-level factors that may support or hinder their wellbeing (Sayed et al., 2018). Second, the literature on school factors is often scattered across multiple disciplines, including education, psychology, social work, and public health, which can make it difficult to identify and synthesize the relevant findings (Taylor & Sidhu, 2012). Third, many studies have employed qualitative methodologies, which can provide rich and nuanced insights into the experiences of refugee children, but may not be generalizable to other contexts or populations (Hodes et al., 2018). The gap in the existing literature is further compounded by the lack of systematic reviews and meta-analyses on this topic. While several narrative reviews have been conducted on the mental health and acculturation of refugee children, these reviews have often been limited by their methodological heterogeneity and lack of transparency (Sayed et al., 2018). Moreover, few reviews have specifically focused on the school factors that support the emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes of refugee children, which can make it difficult to identify the most effective strategies for promoting their mental health and acculturation. The research question guiding this systematic review is: What school factors are associated with positive emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes for refugee students, and how can these factors be promoted and supported in school settings? This review aims to address the gap in the existing literature by providing a comprehensive and systematic synthesis of the evidence on school factors related to the emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes of refugee children. The review will employ a convergent qualitative narrative approach to synthesize the findings, which will enable the identification of key themes and patterns in the data, as well as the development of recommendations for practice and policy (Pluye et al., 2009). This systematic review will make several important contributions to the existing literature on the mental health and acculturation of refugee children. First, it will provide a comprehensive and systematic synthesis of the evidence on school factors related to the emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes of refugee children, which will enable the identification of key factors that support their mental health and acculturation. Second, it will employ a transparent and rigorous methodology, which will enhance the validity and reliability of the findings. Third, it will provide recommendations for practice and policy, which will enable the translation of the findings into real-world settings and the promotion of positive outcomes for refugee children. Finally, it will highlight the need for further research on this topic, particularly in relation to the development of evidence-based interventions and programs that support the mental health and acculturation of refugee children. By addressing the gap in the existing literature and providing a comprehensive and systematic synthesis of the evidence, this review aims to make a significant contribution to the field and to promote positive outcomes for refugee children. The rigorous evaluation of pharmaceuticals through clinical drug trials is a cornerstone of evidence-based medicine, aiming to ensure that new medications are both safe and effective before they reach patients. While internal validity—guaranteeing that the trial's results are applicable to the experimental conditions—remains a primary focus, the external validity, or generalizability, of these trials is equally vital. External validity assesses the extent to which the findings can be applied beyond the controlled conditions of the study, particularly to real-world settings such as general practice. The ability of healthcare providers to extrapolate trial outcomes and implement them in daily practice hinges on comprehensive reporting of details that impact this generalizability (Rothwell, 2005). General practice presents a unique context for clinical drug trials. Unlike specialized clinical settings, general practice encompasses a more diverse patient population, with broader demographic variability, varied health conditions, and differing treatment environments. Thus, the extrapolation of trial results to general practice requires careful consideration of the trial’s design and participant selection criteria. Yet, numerous studies suggest a persistent gap in the comprehensive reporting of factors crucial to external validity in clinical trial publications (Ioannidis, 2016; Bell et al., 2019). One of the primary factors affecting external validity is the clinical setting in which the trial was conducted. Trials implemented in general practice settings are inherently different from those in specialized centers due to variations in patient populations, treatment protocols, and clinical workflows. Despite this, our preliminary findings suggest that a majority of published reports fail to specify the setting of the trial, obscuring the ability to gauge its wide-scale applicability. Another crucial element of external validity is patient selection before enrollment. Selection processes that are overly restrictive may yield results that are not representative of the broader patient population typically encountered in general practice. Reporting the number of patients screened before enrollment can provide insight into this selection process and help determine the trial's ability to reflect real-world clinical scenarios (van Spall et al., 2007). Moreover, patient demographics, including co-morbidity, co-medication, and ethnicity, play a significant role in the generalizability of trial results. These factors influence drug efficacy and safety profiles, yet reporting in this domain often remains inadequate (Salsberg et al., 2008; van Staa et al., 2011). The choice of primary outcomes, whether surrogate or clinical, is another pivotal consideration. Surrogate outcomes, while easier to measure and often less resource-intensive, can lead to discrepancies when translated into clinical practice outcomes. Conversely, clinical or patient-reported outcomes may better reflect patient-centered care, particularly within general practice (Montori et al., 2004). While much emphasis is placed on the efficacy endpoints of drugs, the comprehensive reporting of adverse events is imperative for complete safety profiling. Drug safety cannot be overstated, especially when considering the heterogeneous patient population in general practice. Despite this, reporting of adverse events across trials is inconsistent, potentially leading to an incomplete understanding of a drug's risk profile. This study addresses the gaps in the reporting of external validity in drug trials conducted in general practice by systematically evaluating published trial reports over a 15-year period. Our investigation seeks to clarify the extent to which reports have traditionally neglected or included crucial information necessary for evaluating generalizability. The primary research question guiding this study is: To what extent do published reports of clinical drug trials conducted in general practice include sufficient information to assess their external validity? Through our comprehensive review, we contribute to ongoing discussions about improving trial reporting standards, thereby facilitating better-informed clinical decision-making. By highlighting deficiencies in current reporting practices, this study advocates for more stringent guidelines and practices in trial documentation, ultimately aiming to enhance the applicability of research findings to broader clinical settings and diverse patient populations. Our focus on trials approved between 1998 and 2007 and published between 2000 and 2015 provides a robust basis to examine trends over time and identify potential shifts in reporting practices. Additionally, this work underpins future endeavors to develop detailed frameworks that emphasize the need for transparent, comprehensive reporting of trial characteristics critical to assessing external validity. Ultimately, this will enable healthcare providers to make more informed decisions, improve patient care, and bolster the development of clinical guidelines through more applicable and generalizable drug trials in the setting of general practice. Methods This study aimed to analyze the reporting of external validity issues in clinical drug trial reports conducted wholly or partially in general practice settings, focusing on how these reports address key elements that influence the generalizability of trial outcomes. We identified and assessed articles through a systematic approach, ensuring a robust analysis of cohort data from Norwegian general practice drug trials. Data Collection The initial data set was derived from the Norwegian Medicines Agency archive, encompassing applications for trial approval between 1998 and 2007. This cohort consisted of 196 drug trials, from which 134 articles were published between 2000 and 2015 with reported trial results. Literature searches were conducted extensively across databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Scopus to ensure comprehensive identification of all relevant publications linked to the cohort of trials, refined with specific keywords and trial identifiers, ensuring a precise and relevant selection of literature for review. Study Design The study employed a retrospective cohort design, analyzing previously published trial reports to assess the completeness of external validity reporting. Each article was subjected to a criteria-based assessment focusing on aspects related to the generalizability of trial results, namely the reporting of clinical settings, patient selection processes, participant co-morbidities, concurrent medications, ethnicity, outcomes of interest, and adverse event reporting. These criteria were selected based on established guidelines and literature emphasizing the importance of these factors in understanding trial applicability (Rothwell, 2005; Gagnier et al., 2014). Procedures An evaluation framework was developed to systematically dissect each trial report against the selected criteria. Two independent reviewers initially piloted this framework on a sample of 10 articles to refine the assessment process and resolve discrepancies through discussion and consensus. The framework included the categorization of primary and secondary outcome measures—distinguishing between surrogate, clinical, and patient-reported outcomes—and the classifications of adverse events, patient demographics, and the presence of detailed clinical setting descriptions. The full set of articles was subsequently reviewed by the two independent reviewers using the refined framework to ensure consistency and objectivity in data extraction and interpretation. Statistical Analysis Prior to analysis, inter-rater reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficients for categorical variables to ensure a substantial agreement level, which was determined to be kappa = 0.80, indicating a high level of reliability (Landis & Koch, 1977). Descriptive statistics were used to outline the frequency and percentage distributions of the reported external validity elements. We employed chi-square tests to examine differences in reporting practices among trials based on different study characteristics, such as trial phase or primary outcome type. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Furthermore, logistic regression analyses were applied to identify predictors of comprehensive reporting of external validity issues. The dependent variable was a composite indicator of complete external validity reporting, and independent variables included trial factors such as year of publication, trial size, type of primary outcome, and funding source. This analytical approach allowed for the adjustment of potential confounders and facilitated the identification of trends or gaps in reporting practices over the given time frame. Our analysis focused on identifying systematic patterns and deficiencies in reporting that could inform future guidelines and practices in clinical trial reporting within general practice contexts. The results were intended to provide actionable insights for improving the transparency and applicability of trial findings, thereby enhancing their utility for clinical decision-making and guideline development. By employing a rigorous methodological framework and comprehensive statistical analyses, this study aimed to contribute to the broader discourse on improving the external validity of drug trials and ensuring their applicability to real-world general practice settings. The study's findings underline the necessity of heightened attention to reporting standards and the delineation of context-specific factors that influence the generalizability of clinical trial outcomes. The investigation into the reporting of external validity issues within the cohort of drug trials conducted in Norwegian general practice revealed significant deficiencies in various domains. Among the 134 identified articles, a scant 22% (n = 30) adequately documented the clinical setting in which the trials took place. This underscoring of the trial environment is crucial for external validity, yet the lack of transparency remains a pervasive issue. In the assessment of patient selection processes, only 46% (n = 61) of the articles reported the number of patients initially screened before inclusion in the trials. This omission is notable as the pre-enrolment process details are instrumental in understanding the representativeness of the trial cohort. The failure to report these demographics restricts the reader’s ability to evaluate how well the trial population mirrors real-world patient populations encountered in general practice. The reporting of trial outcomes also varied significantly, potentially impacting the applicability of the findings. The primary outcome was identified as a surrogate outcome in 45% (n = 60) of the trials, which, while useful for biological insights, may not directly correlate with patient-centric clinical endpoints, thus challenging their translational potential to patient care. In contrast, only 29% (n = 39) focused on clinical outcomes, while 19% (n = 25) prioritized patient-reported outcomes. These discrepancies in outcome reporting suggest a potential misalignment with general practice priorities where patient-centered and clinically meaningful outcomes are often emphasized. Adverse events, a crucial aspect that affects the generalizability and acceptance of trial results, were documented in 93% (n = 124) of the articles, indicating robust reporting in this specific domain. Although this figure suggests a positive trend towards transparency in adverse event reporting, it still leaves a considerable fraction of studies underreporting this critical information. Further assessment of patient demographics revealed substantial gaps, particularly in the reporting of co-morbidity and co-medication, which are vital for understanding the complexity and variability in patient responses in real-world scenarios. Only 40% (n = 54) of the trials reported co-morbidity data, and a mere 20% (n = 27) detailed participants' co-medications. This lack of reporting may significantly impede the clinician’s ability to extrapolate trial findings to their patients, who often present with multiple health conditions and are on various medications. Ethnic and racial demographic data were reported in 58% (n = 78) of the trials. Although better than some other categories, this reporting rate still raises concerns about the inclusivity and representativeness of trial populations, factors which are essential for ensuring that findings are broadly applicable across diverse patient groups. The overarching theme from the data reviewed suggests a consistent neglect in reporting details crucial for assessing the external validity of trials. While adverse event documentation showed high compliance, the sparse reporting on the clinical setting and patient selection processes presents a barrier to the applicability of findings in clinical practice. The under-reporting of demographic and co-morbidity data further compounds this issue, highlighting the need for improved and standardized reporting guidelines that emphasize the importance of external validity dimensions. This analysis underscores the necessity for conducting trials in real-world settings reflective of general practice, with corresponding enhancements in the transparency of trial design and participant characteristics in published reports. Increased attention to these details could significantly augment the utility of these trials, allowing clinicians to make informed decisions and facilitating the integration of evidence into clinical guidelines. Without such improvements, the capacity of these trials to inform generalized clinical practice remains regrettably limited, underscoring the critical need for consistent and comprehensive reportage on external validity issues in clinical drug trials. The results of this study underscore the considerable deficiencies in the reporting of external validity factors in clinical drug trial publications that draw from research conducted entirely or in part within general practice settings. The inadequacies identified in the reporting of clinical setting, selection criteria prior to patient enrollment, and participant profiles regarding co-morbidity and co-medication severely undermine the utility of such studies for informing clinical practice and decision-making processes in general practice. Investigating non-classical correlations between decision fused multi-modal documents. Dimitris Gkoumas1 , Sagar Uprety1 , and Dawei Song1,2 1 The Open University, Milton Keynes, UK {dimitris.gkoumas, sagar.uprety, dawei.song}@open.ac.uk 2 Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China Abstract. Correlation has been widely used to facilitate various information retrieval methods such as query expansion, relevance feedback, document clustering, and multi-modal fusion. Especially, correlation and independence are important issues when fusing different modalities that influence a multi-modal information retrieval process. The basic idea of correlation is that an observable can help predict or enhance another observable. In quantum mechanics, quantum correlation, called entanglement, is a sort of correlation between the observables measured in atomic-size particles when these particles are not necessarily collected in ensembles. In this paper, we examine a multimodal fusion scenario that might be similar to that encountered in physics by firstly measuring two observables (i.e., text-based relevance and image-based relevance) of a multi-modal document without counting on an ensemble of multimodal documents already labeled in terms of these two variables. Then, we investigate the existence of non-classical correlations between pairs of multi-modal documents. Despite there are some basic differences between entanglement and classical correlation encountered in the macroscopic world, we investigate the existence of this kind of non-classical correlation through the Bell inequality violation. Here, we experimentally test several novel association methods in a small-scale experiment. However, in the current experiment we did not find any violation of the Bell inequality. Finally, we present a series of interesting discussions, which may provide theoretical and empirical insights and inspirations for future development of this direction. Keywords: Multi-modal information retrieval · Non-classical correlations · Decision fused multi-modal documents · CHSH inequality Nowadays, the Web surrounding us often involves multiple modalities - we read texts, watch images and videos, and listen to sounds. In general terms, modality refers to a certain type of information and/or the representation format in which information is stored. A research problem is characterized as multi-modal when it includes multiple such modalities. Integrating unimodal representations from various input modalities and combining them into a compact multi-modal representation, called multi-modal fusion, offers a possibility of understanding in-depth real world problems. For instance, in information retrieval, suppose a user types in a text query to retrieve multi-modal documents consisting of an image and a caption as shown in Fig. 1. One can notice that the query term “plane” can be matched in both textual and visual modalities of the given multimodal document. However, the query term “LHR” can be matched only in its textual modality, while the term “sunset” only in its visual modality. This implies that only when the text and image modalities are fused, we get the benefit of complementary information, in turn increasing the precision of information retrieval. The main challenge of multi-modal fusion is to capture inter-dependencies and complementary presence in heterogeneous data originating from multiple modalities. In the literature, two main approaches to the fusion process have been proposed: a) feature level or early fusion and b) decision level or late fusion [4]. Early fusion involves the integration of multiple sources of raw or preprocessed data to be fed into a model, which finally makes an inference as illustrated in Fig. 2. In contrast, late fusion refers to the aggregation of decisions from multiple classifiers, each trained on separate modalities as shown in Fig. 3. There are distinctive issues that influence the multi-modal fusion process. Correlation between different modalities is one of them. Correlation can be perceived either in low-level features, e.g., raw data, or high-level features that are obtained on different classifiers, e.g., semantic concepts [4]. In both cases, correlation informs us how to fuse different modalities. In the early fusion, we fuse multi-modal information either by projecting all of the modalities to the same space (Fig. 4 (c)), called joint representations, or by learning separate representations for each modality but coordinate them through a similarity measure (Fig 4 (b)) [5]. In both approaches, the construction of the multi-modal spaces is based on correlations among different modalities. The late fusion process can be rule-based, e.g., by linear weighted fusion and majority voting rules, or based on classification-based methods, e.g., support vector machines [4]. In many cases, the correlation among different modalities provides additional cues that are very useful for aggregating decisions either by following a rule-based approach or classification-based approach. In addition, the absence of correlation may equally provide valuable insight with respect to a particular scenario or context. There are various statistical and probabilistic forms of correlation that have been utilized by researchers, being causal or not. Since our experiment focuses on late fusion only, we briefly report the most important methods for computing correlations between decisions from multiple modalities. Specifically, decision level correlation has been exploited in the form of causal link analysis, causal strength, and agreement coefficient [4]. In all cases, the basic idea of correlation is that a modality can help predict or enhance another modality. In quantum mechanics, correlation has been also an important topic. In quantum mechanical framework, uncertainty may occur not only when the elements are collected in ensemble but also when each of them is in a superposed state. In quantum theory, making an observation on one part of a system instantaneously could affect the state in another part of a system, even if the respective systems are separated by space-like distances. Such a quantum correlation presents some peculiarities which led to the notion of entanglement. Entanglement is a sort of correlation between observables measured in atomic-size particles, such as photons, when these particles are not necessarily collected in ensembles. Despite entanglement being a kind of correlation, there are some basic differences between entanglement and the classical correlation encountered in the macroscopic world. A classical correlation is a statistical relationship, causal or not, between two random variables. In entanglement, besides correlation, cause exists as well since the correlation does not depend on an underlying value attached to the particles. Instead, it depends on what is measured on either side. This non-classical property of quantum entanglement motivates us to investigate non-classical correlations between multi-modal decisions as shown in Fig. 5. At first, we calculate the probability of relevance for each document, with respect to both text-based and image-based modality concerning a multimodal query as shown in Fig. 5. Then, we check for any violation of Bell’s inequalities based on the estimated relevance probabilities for each possible pair of decision fused multimodal documents in a dataset. Our assumption is that if a pair of decision fused multi-modal documents is entangled, then knowing that a document is relevant concerning the text-based representation for a query, then we can simultaneously predict with certainty the relevance of the the other document concerning the text-based and image-based representation for the same query. The phenomenon of quantum entanglement has been investigated in semantic spaces making use of Hyperspace Analogue to Language (HAL) model [13,14]. Concept combinations have been widely modeled as composite systems [1,2,6,7,22]. The state of the composite system between two words can be modeled by taking the tensor product of the states of the individual words respectively. If the concept combination is factorizable, then the concept is compositional in the sense it can be expressed as a product of states corresponding to the separate words. A concept that is not factorizable cannot be expressed by either the first or the second word individually, and is deemed non-compositional, and termed entangled [7]. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), principally cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancers and chronic respiratory disease, are the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for roughly two-thirds of global mortality (World Health Organization, 2011). Their economic burden is substantial. Bloom and colleagues (2011) projected cumulative global output losses of approximately US$30 trillion between 2011 and 2030. The costs also include health-care expenditure, lost productivity and reduced quality of life for individuals and families. A considerable proportion of this burden is attributable to modifiable risk factors, and poor diet is among the most important (Lim et al., 2012). Dietary patterns characterised by high intakes of energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, saturated fat and sodium, together with low intakes of fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, are consistently associated with obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and increased all-cause mortality (Lim et al., 2012; World Health Organization, 2003). Modelling studies suggest that population-level dietary change could deliver sizeable health gains at relatively low cost (Cecchini et al., 2010). The combined economic and social costs of NCDs therefore provide a compelling rationale for strategies that target dietary behaviour. Overall dietary patterns are built from many individual, repeated decisions about what to eat. These discrete food choices, such as selecting fruit rather than a confectionery snack, ordering a sugar-sweetened beverage, or trimming visible fat from meat, are the proximal behaviours that interventions must ultimately change. Discrete food choices are also more amenable to precise definition and measurement than global dietary patterns, and they are the level at which many policy instruments, such as menu labelling, price signals and school food standards, operate. Effective intervention requires an understanding of the psychological processes that underpin these decisions. Interventions that are explicitly grounded in theory are widely recommended because theory specifies the mechanisms through which behaviour is expected to change and allows these mechanisms to be tested (Craig et al., 2008; Michie & Prestwich, 2010). Theoretical models thus provide the conceptual order that allows programme designers and policy makers to identify the elements that drive behaviour and to select appropriate intervention techniques. Among social cognition models, the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB; Ajzen, 1991) is one of the most frequently applied in health research. The TPB, an extension of the Theory of Reasoned Action (Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975), proposes that the proximal determinant of behaviour is intention, which reflects the motivation to perform the behaviour. Intention is in turn determined by three constructs: attitude (the overall evaluation of performing the behaviour), subjective norm (perceived social pressure to perform or not perform the behaviour) and perceived behavioural control (PBC; perceived ease or difficulty of performing the behaviour). Because many behaviours are not fully under volitional control, PBC is additionally proposed to exert a direct effect on behaviour to the extent that it reflects actual control (Ajzen, 1991). The model's parsimony, its clear operational definitions and its generalisability across behaviours have made it attractive to researchers and practitioners alike. Meta-analytic evidence supports the predictive utility of the TPB across health domains. Armitage and Conner (2001), in a review of 185 independent studies, found that the TPB accounted for 39% of the variance in intention and 27% of the variance in behaviour. Subsequent syntheses have reported similar findings for physical activity (Hagger et al., 2002), and for a range of health behaviours using prospective designs (McEachan et al., 2011). Reviews of the intention–behaviour relationship indicate that intentions explain approximately 28% of the variance in behaviour (Sheeran, 2002), although experimental evidence suggests that even medium-to-large changes in intention produce only small-to-medium changes in behaviour (Webb & Sheeran, 2006). The TPB has also been subject to substantial criticism. Critics have questioned whether it omits important determinants such as habit, affect and automatic processes, whether its constructs are sufficiently distinct, and whether it has generated interventions that effectively change behaviour (Sniehotta et al., 2014). These concerns are especially pertinent for food choice, which is often habitual, cue-driven and shaped by hedonic and environmental factors that lie outside conscious deliberation. The TPB has nevertheless been widely used to study eating behaviour, and the primary literature now spans a diverse array of food choices. These include increasing consumption of fruit and vegetables, choosing low-fat or whole-grain foods, limiting sweets, snacks and fast food, and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages. Existing reviews of the TPB and diet have been valuable but limited in important respects. Some have examined dietary behaviour as a single undifferentiated category, or combined food choice with other health behaviours such as physical activity and substance use (Armitage & Conner, 2001; McEachan et al., 2011). Others have focused on a single food group, most commonly fruit and vegetable intake (Guillaumie et al., 2010), or have encompassed a broad set of social cognitive determinants without focusing on TPB relationships. Aggregating across heterogeneous food behaviours may mask meaningful differences in the strength of TPB associations. Conceptually, there are good reasons to expect such differences. Choosing to consume a health-promoting food (an approach behaviour) may be governed by different processes than refraining from a health-compromising but palatable food (an avoidance behaviour), the latter requiring self-regulation against strong hedonic temptations and ready availability. Perceived control may matter more for behaviours that involve resisting temptation than for those that are simply performed. Likewise, the relative influence of attitudes, social norms and control may vary with the characteristics of those making the choice, including age and gender, because developmental stage and social roles shape both autonomy over food and sensitivity to social influence (Conner & Norman, 2005). Yet these potential moderators have rarely been tested systematically within a single synthesis restricted to discrete food choices. A second limitation concerns the evidential basis of earlier reviews. Rapid growth in the number of TPB food choice studies in recent years means that earlier syntheses omit a considerable body of evidence, and few have systematically sought unpublished work, which may reduce the risk of publication bias. Without a current, comprehensive and behaviourally specific synthesis, researchers lack the quantitative information needed to judge when the TPB is an appropriate framework for understanding dietary decisions, and to prioritise the constructs that interventions should target. The primary aim of the present systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore to quantify the associations between TPB variables and discrete food choice behaviours. Specifically, we estimated pooled effect sizes for the relationships of attitude, subjective norm and PBC with intention; of intention and PBC with behaviour; and, where data permitted, the inter-correlations among predictors. A secondary aim was to examine the extent and sources of heterogeneity in these associations. Using meta-regression, we tested whether effect sizes were moderated by the type of food choice behaviour (health-promoting versus health-compromising foods, and approach versus avoidance behaviours) and by participant characteristics (age and gender). This review makes three contributions. First, it provides up-to-date, precise estimates of TPB relationships specific to food choice, drawing on both published and unpublished studies. Second, by testing behavioural and demographic moderators, it moves beyond the question of whether the TPB predicts food choice to consider when and for whom it does so, thereby informing the selection of theory in relation to the nature of the target behaviour. Third, it identifies the constructs most strongly associated with intention and behaviour, offering an empirical basis for prioritising intervention targets while recognising the limits of the model in explaining dietary behaviour. Search strategy and eligibility criteria The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Electronic searches were run in PsycINFO, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses from database inception to the search date. Search strings combined terms for the theory (e.g., "theory of planned behavio", "theory of reasoned action", "perceived behavio control", "subjective norm", "attitude", "intention") with terms for food choice (e.g., "food choice", "diet", "fruit", "vegetable", "snack", "fat", "sugar", "soft drink", "fast food", "eating"). Terms were adapted to the indexing vocabulary of each database. The reference lists of included studies and of earlier reviews of the TPB and health behaviour (Armitage & Conner, 2001; McEachan et al., 2011) were hand-searched. Authors were contacted when the data needed for effect size calculation were not reported. Studies were eligible if they (a) were published in English as a peer-reviewed journal article or as an unpublished doctoral or master's dissertation; (b) used the TPB (Ajzen, 1991) as the primary theoretical framework; (c) measured at least one TPB construct (attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control [PBC], or intention) and a measure of a discrete food choice behaviour; and (d) reported a bivariate association between constructs, or sufficient information to compute one. Discrete food choice behaviours were defined as the selection, purchase, or consumption of a specific food or food group (e.g., fruit, fast food), as opposed to composite dietary patterns, weight management, or general "healthy eating" indices. Studies were excluded if they focused on clinical populations requiring prescribed diets, on eating disorders, or on breastfeeding or infant feeding practices, or if they reported only multivariate or structural equation modelling results without zero-order correlations. Where several publications reported on the same sample, the report with the most complete data was retained. Study selection and data extraction Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer, and a second reviewer independently screened a random 20% subset; disagreements were resolved by discussion. Full texts of potentially relevant records were assessed independently by two reviewers against the eligibility criteria. Data were extracted using a standardised form, piloted on five studies, covering bibliographic details, country, sample size, mean age, percentage female, study design, time lag between measures, TPB constructs assessed, type of behavioural measure (self-report versus objective), and the correlations among constructs. Extraction was performed by one reviewer and verified by a second; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Coding of moderator variables Three moderators were specified a priori. First, type of food choice behaviour was coded as (a) consumption of health-promoting foods (e.g., fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, low-fat options), (b) consumption of health-compromising foods (e.g., fast food, sugar-sweetened beverages, high-fat snacks), or (c) avoidance or limitation of health-compromising foods. This classification distinguished approach behaviours from avoidance behaviours, which are thought to differ in their volitional demands (Conner & Armitage, 2002). Second, participant age was coded as the sample mean age, and categorically as children/adolescents (<18 years), young adults (18–25 years), and adults (>25 years) where the continuous value was not reported. Third, gender composition was coded as the percentage of female participants in the sample. Samples with no gender information were excluded from the gender analyses. Coding was completed independently by two reviewers (κ = 0.91 for behaviour type), with disagreements resolved by discussion. Methodological quality Study quality was appraised using an adapted checklist drawing on criteria used in earlier TPB meta-analyses (Cooke & French, 2008; McEachan et al., 2011). Items addressed the use of a prospective design, the use of validated or elicitation-based TPB measures, the correspondence between attitudinal and behavioural measures with respect to target, action, context, and time (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1977), the reporting of reliability coefficients, the reporting of attrition, and the use of an objective behavioural measure. Each item was scored 0 or 1, and total scores were examined descriptively and used in sensitivity analyses. Effect size computation The effect size of interest was the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (r) for each bivariate association in the TPB: attitude–intention, subjective norm–intention, PBC–intention, intention–behaviour, and PBC–behaviour. Where studies reported more than one correlation for the same relationship (e.g., multiple foods or multiple items), correlations were averaged within the study after Fisher's z transformation to avoid inflating the weight of any single sample (Borenstein et al., 2009). Where studies reported effect sizes for independent subgroups (e.g., males and females), each subgroup was treated as a separate sample for moderator analyses and combined for overall analyses. Correlations were transformed to Fisher's z, with variance v = 1/(n − 3), for all analyses and back-transformed to r for presentation.
