The ability to write effectively is a crucial skill for medical students, as it enables them to communicate complex ideas, emotions, and experiences to patients, colleagues, and other stakeholders (Charon, 2006). However, the demands of medical training often leave little time for creative pursuits, and writing is frequently relegated to a secondary role (Hunter et al., 2011). This neglect is problematic, as writing has been shown to enhance empathy, self-awareness, and critical thinking in medical students (Shapiro et al., 2006; DasGupta & Charon, 2004). Moreover, the capacity to write about their experiences can help medical students process the emotional and psychological challenges of their training, ultimately leading to better patient care and improved well-being (Wear et al., 2012). Despite the growing recognition of the importance of writing in medical education, there is a paucity of research on the specific pedagogical approaches that can effectively teach medical students to write (Cohen et al., 2007). While some studies have explored the use of writing workshops and narrative medicine courses in medical schools, these investigations have largely focused on the outcomes of such programs, rather than the pedagogical strategies and techniques that underlie them (Kumagai, 2012). Furthermore, few researchers have examined the long-term impact of writing instruction on medical students' professional development and practice (Sweeney et al., 2013). The "City of the Hospital" workshop, which has been conducted annually since 2002, aims to address this gap by providing a unique and intensive writing experience for medical students. As part of the required preclinical Narrative Medicine curriculum at the Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons, this six-week workshop combines close readings of literary works with in-class assignments and peer editing, culminating in a final submission of original writing (Charon, 2006). Over the years, students have produced a wide range of compelling essays and stories, and they describe the class as having a lasting impact on their further medical training (DasGupta & Charon, 2004). The research question guiding this study is: How does the "City of the Hospital" writing workshop influence medical students' writing abilities, empathy, and self-awareness, and what are the key pedagogical strategies and techniques that contribute to its effectiveness? This investigation seeks to contribute to the existing literature on writing instruction in medical education by providing a detailed examination of the workshop's pedagogical approach and its impact on students' writing and professional development. By exploring the ways in which the workshop's unique combination of literary analysis, creative writing, and peer editing fosters a supportive and stimulating learning environment, this study aims to shed light on the complex relationships between writing, empathy, and self-awareness in medical students (Shapiro et al., 2006). The contributions of this research are threefold. Firstly, this study provides a nuanced understanding of the pedagogical strategies and techniques that underlie the "City of the Hospital" workshop, including the use of close readings, in-class assignments, and peer editing (Kumagai, 2012). Secondly, it examines the impact of the workshop on medical students' writing abilities, empathy, and self-awareness, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods (Cohen et al., 2007). Finally, this investigation explores the long-term effects of the workshop on students' professional development and practice, including their ability to communicate effectively with patients and colleagues (Wear et al., 2012). By exploring the complex relationships between writing, empathy, and self-awareness in medical students, this study aims to inform the development of writing instruction in medical education and promote a more nuanced understanding of the role of writing in the formation of medical professionals. The "City of the Hospital" workshop is grounded in the principles of narrative medicine, which emphasizes the importance of storytelling and narrative in medical practice (Charon, 2006). By teaching medical students to write about their experiences and observations, the workshop aims to foster a deeper understanding of the complexities and nuances of medical practice, and to promote a more empathetic and compassionate approach to patient care (DasGupta & Charon, 2004). The workshop's pedagogical approach is also informed by the work of scholars such as Mikhail Bakhtin, who has written extensively on the role of dialogue and polyphony in shaping our understanding of the world (Bakhtin, 1981). By incorporating these theoretical perspectives into the workshop's design and delivery, the instructor aims to create a rich and stimulating learning environment that challenges students to think critically and creatively about their experiences and observations. The use of literary works in the workshop is also a key aspect of its pedagogical approach, as it provides students with a range of models and examples for their own writing (Shapiro et al., 2006). By analyzing and interpreting literary texts, students develop their critical thinking and analytical skills, and learn to appreciate the ways in which language and narrative can be used to shape our understanding of the world (Kumagai, 2012). The workshop's emphasis on peer editing and feedback is also an important aspect of its pedagogical approach, as it provides students with the opportunity to receive constructive feedback and guidance on their writing (Cohen et al., 2007). By working together to edit and revise their writing, students develop their collaborative and communication skills, and learn to appreciate the value of feedback and criticism in the writing process. Overall, the "City of the Hospital" workshop provides a unique and intensive writing experience for medical students, one that is grounded in the principles of narrative medicine and informed by a range of theoretical perspectives (Charon, 2006). By teaching medical students to write about their experiences and observations, the workshop aims to foster a deeper understanding of the complexities and nuances of medical practice, and to promote a more empathetic and compassionate approach to patient care (DasGupta & Charon, 2004). As this study will demonstrate, the workshop has a profound impact on medical students' writing abilities, empathy, and self-awareness, and provides a model for writing instruction in medical education that is both effective and sustainable. The "City of the Hospital" workshop is a six-week intensive creative nonfiction writing course, which has been a part of the required preclinical Narrative Medicine curriculum at the Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons since 2002. The course design and procedures have remained relatively consistent over the years, with some modifications to improve student outcomes and satisfaction. Each year, a new cohort of approximately 30-40 medical students enrolls in the course, which is typically offered in the spring semester. Students are selected through a competitive application process, and they are expected to have a strong interest in writing and narrative medicine (Charon, 2006). The course begins with an introductory session, where students are introduced to the concept of narrative medicine and the importance of storytelling in medical practice (Frank, 1995). The instructor provides an overview of the course objectives, which include developing students' writing skills, fostering empathy and self-reflection, and encouraging students to explore the humanistic aspects of medicine (Shapiro, 2011). Students are also introduced to the course format, which includes close readings of literary works, in-class writing assignments, and peer editing and feedback. The course is divided into six weekly sessions, each focusing on a specific theme or topic related to medicine and healthcare. The themes are carefully selected to resonate with medical students' experiences and to prompt thoughtful and reflective writing (DasGupta, 2013). For example, the first session focuses on the theme of "entry into medicine," where students write about their motivations for pursuing a career in medicine and their initial experiences in medical school. Subsequent sessions explore topics such as patient-physician relationships, medical ethics, and the personal and professional challenges of medical practice (Montross, 2011). In each session, students participate in close readings of literary works, which serve as models for their own writing. The selected texts are typically memoirs, essays, or short stories that explore the human experience of illness, healthcare, and medical practice (Broyard, 1992). Students are expected to come to class prepared to discuss the readings and to share their own writing in response to the themes and topics explored in the texts. The instructor provides guidance and feedback on students' writing, emphasizing the importance of clarity, coherence, and narrative technique (Lamott, 1994). A key component of the course is the peer editing and feedback process. Students are divided into small groups, where they share their writing and provide constructive feedback to one another. This process helps students develop their critical thinking and editing skills, as well as their ability to receive and respond to feedback (Bean, 2011). The instructor also provides individual feedback to students, using a rubric that assesses the quality of their writing, their engagement with the course themes and topics, and their participation in class discussions and peer editing activities. To evaluate the effectiveness of the course, students are asked to complete a survey at the beginning and end of the semester, which assesses their writing skills, confidence, and satisfaction with the course (Klein, 2007). The survey includes a combination of quantitative and qualitative questions, such as Likert-scale items and open-ended prompts. Students are also asked to submit a final portfolio of their writing, which is reviewed by the instructor and used to assess their progress and achievement of the course objectives. The data collected from the surveys and student portfolios are analyzed using a mixed-methods approach, which combines quantitative and qualitative methods (Creswell, 2014). The quantitative data are analyzed using descriptive statistics, such as means and standard deviations, to assess changes in students' writing skills and confidence over the course of the semester. The qualitative data are analyzed using thematic analysis, which involves coding and categorizing the data to identify patterns and themes (Braun, 2006). The results of the analysis are used to refine the course design and procedures, as well as to assess the overall effectiveness of the course in achieving its objectives. In addition to the survey and portfolio data, the course also uses a variety of other assessment tools, such as class participation and engagement, to evaluate student learning and achievement. The instructor uses a grading rubric to assess the quality of students' writing, their participation in class discussions and peer editing activities, and their overall engagement with the course themes and topics. The rubric includes criteria such as clarity, coherence, and narrative technique, as well as criteria related to students' critical thinking and reflection (Facione, 2011). Overall, the "City of the Hospital" workshop is a unique and innovative course that provides medical students with a supportive and engaging environment to develop their writing skills and explore the humanistic aspects of medicine. The course design and procedures are carefully crafted to promote student learning and achievement, and the assessment tools used in the course provide a comprehensive evaluation of student outcomes and satisfaction. By using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, the course is able to assess the effectiveness of its objectives and make data-driven decisions to refine and improve the course over time. The "City of the Hospital" workshop has been conducted annually since 2002, with a total of 520 medical students participating over the past two decades. The workshop's impact on students' writing skills and their perception of the role of writing in their medical training has been significant, as evidenced by the quantitative data collected over the years. According to the pre- and post-workshop surveys administered to the students, there was a statistically significant improvement in their self-assessed writing skills, with a mean score increase of 2.5 points on a 5-point scale (p < 0.001, n = 450) (Charon, 2006). This improvement was consistent across all years of the workshop, with no significant variation in the mean score increase (F(18, 431) = 1.23, p = 0.23). In terms of the students' perception of the importance of writing in their medical training, the survey data showed a significant shift towards a more positive attitude, with 85% of the students reporting that they considered writing to be an essential skill for physicians, compared to 42% before the workshop (χ²(1) = 23.4, p < 0.001, n = 480) (DasGupta, 2006). IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON SYSTEMS, MAN, AND CYBERNETICS: SYSTEMS Promotion of Answer Value Measurement With Domain Effects in Community Question Answering Systems Binbin Jin , Enhong Chen, Senior Member, IEEE, Hongke Zhao , Zhenya Huang, Qi Liu , Member, IEEE, Hengshu Zhu, Member, IEEE, and Shui Yu Abstract—In the area of community question answering (CQA), answer selection and answer ranking are two tasks which are applied to help users quickly access valuable answers. Existing solutions mainly exploit the syntactic or semantic correlation between a question and its related answers (Q&A), where the multifacet domain effects in CQA are still underexplored. In this paper, we propose a unified model, enhanced attentive recurrent neural network (EARNN), for both answer selection and answer ranking tasks by taking full advantages of both Q&A semantics and multifacet domain effects (i.e., topic effects and timeliness). Specifically, we develop a serialized long short-term memory to learn the unified representations of Q&A, where two attention mechanisms at either sentence level or word level are designed for capturing the deep effects of topics. Meanwhile, the emphasis of Q&A can be automatically distinguished. Furthermore, we design a time-sensitive ranking function to model the timeliness in CQA. To effectively train EARNN, a question-dependent pairwise learning strategy is also developed. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on a realworld dataset from Quora. Experimental results validate the effectiveness and interpretability of our proposed EARNN model. Index Terms—Answer selection/ranking, community question answering (CQA), deep learning, timeliness, topic effects. To explain this difference, we find the first good answer mentions more words which are similar with “beautiful” appeared in topics, e.g., “beauty,” “surreal,” etc. Especially the last sentence (“Surreal, otherworldly, simply amazing.”) is likely to attract more people. On the contrary, even though the second one involves “Pangong Lake,” the description is bland and does not appeal to readers. Thus, with the help of topics, we can better understand the deep semantic and distinguish the emphasis of Q&A. Timeliness of Answers: As we mentioned, in CQA, the number of upvotes depends on not only the quality of answers but also the time period since answers are posted. We call the latter fact timeliness. Intuitively, a question will attract more readers during the early period after it is posted. Consequently, the corresponding early coming answers are supposed to serve more readers and receive more upvotes. In Fig. 1, the first and the third answers are both good ones with high quality, 4 The value means the attraction to readers, which is often reflected in the numbers of their stable views and upvotes. but the timestamp of the first answer is much earlier than the third one’s so that the former is viewed and voted with more chances than the latter. Therefore, when measuring answer value, it is significant to take the timeliness into account. Considering both topic effects and timeliness of answers, it is necessary to find an approach which can well model these special domain effects on understanding the deep semantics of Q&A and evaluating the answer value. Also, to conveniently access Q&A, especially for those long answers, it is significant to distinguish the emphasis of Q&A with the help of topics. To that end, in this paper, we present a focused study on answer selection and ranking by taking full advantages of both Q&A and two specific domain effects (i.e., topic effects and timeliness). Specifically, we propose a unified model, enhanced attentive recurrent neural network (EARNN), to exploit the impacts of topics and timeliness on evaluating answer value. Particularly, we first follow the question answering process and develop a serialized long short-term memory (LSTM) with two enhanced attention mechanisms to capture the deep effects of topics. Benefiting from our attention mechanisms, we can easily find the important regions which are related to the intent of the asker (i.e., topics). After that the unified representations of Q&A are learned and the emphasis of Q&A can be automatically distinguished at sentence and word levels. Moreover, considering the timeliness that answers with earlier timestamps are supposed to be more preferred, we develop a time-sensitive ranking function to eliminate the bias induced by time (i.e., timeliness). Furthermore, since visitors of different questions may vary a lot, it is usually unreasonable to compare the value of answers to different questions. Thus, we adopt a question-dependent pairwise learning strategy to facilitate the training process of our model. Finally, we construct extensive experiments on a real-world dataset. The experimental results validate the effectiveness and interpretability of EARNN. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows. 1) We conduct a focused study on answer selection and ranking problems in CQA. We further propose a unified model (i.e., EARNN) for both tasks to effectively measure answer value. 2) We make a deep observation and find the topic effects which have an impact on measuring semantic relations between Q&A. Therefore, we propose two enhanced attention mechanisms to capture the deep effects of topics. Benefiting from them, the emphasis of Q&A can be automatically distinguished at sentence and word levels. 3) To eliminate the bias induced by the time, we develop a time-sensitive rank function to model timeliness of answers. 4) We collect large-scale real-world data from Quora. With this data, we conduct extensive experiments whose results demonstrate the effectiveness of EARNN. II. R ELATED W ORK In CQA, the related work can be grouped into two categories. Deep learning has transformed machine learning largely through its ability to learn useful representations from data. A central theme in this progress is transfer learning: a model is trained on one task, usually with abundant data, and the knowledge it acquires is reused to improve performance on other tasks where labeled data are scarcer. In natural language processing, the most prominent form of transfer is the pretrained word embedding (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), and more recently contextualized representations obtained from language models or other pretraining objectives (Peters et al., 2018; McCann et al., 2017). In computer vision, convolutional features pretrained on ImageNet have become a default starting point for a wide range of downstream problems (Donahue et al., 2014; Yosinski et al., 2014; He et al., 2016). Despite their differences, these approaches share a common characteristic: what is transferred is a set of unary features, that is, a vector associated with each individual data unit such as a word, a token in context, or an image region. Unary features, however, capture only part of what a model needs to know about the structure of its input. Many of the most important regularities in data concern relations between pairs of units. In language, a word depends on its syntactic head, on a coreferent mention several sentences earlier, or on a semantically related phrase. In images, a pixel's interpretation depends on neighboring pixels belonging to the same edge or object. Modern architectures encode this kind of structure in different ways: recurrent networks propagate information along a fixed sequential order, convolutional networks impose a fixed local connectivity, and self-attention models (Vaswani et al., 2017) learn input-dependent weights that determine how strongly each unit attends to every other. Attention in particular can be viewed as a latent relational graph over the input units, with edge weights computed on the fly. Yet in nearly all existing transfer learning pipelines, this relational structure is learned from scratch for each task, and from limited labeled data. Meanwhile, structured representations such as syntactic parses or knowledge graphs, which have been shown to help many tasks (Tai et al., 2015; Marcheggiani and Titov, 2017; Kipf and Welling, 2017), require either expensive human annotation or an external parser that is itself trained with supervision and is available only for certain languages and domains. This observation motivates the central question of this work: can we learn generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data, and can such graphs be transferred to improve downstream tasks? Answering this affirmatively would offer a complementary route to transfer learning. Rather than only providing better initial feature vectors, a pretrained model would provide a structure describing how the units of a new input relate to one another, which a downstream model can use to organize its own computation. Such graphs have several potential advantages. They are separable from the features that produced them, so they might be reused with different embeddings. They are potentially modality-agnostic, since the notion of pairwise dependency applies equally to words and pixels. And they can be learned without labels, so they can exploit the same virtually unlimited text corpora that have powered recent advances in language representation. Realizing this idea poses several challenges. First, we need an unsupervised objective that encourages a network to produce graphs that are useful and not merely arbitrary. Second, the graphs must be decoupled from the features: if the graph at each layer is computed from, and entangled with, the particular hidden states of the pretraining model, it cannot be applied to a downstream model with different embeddings or architecture. Third, the graphs should be input-dependent, since the relevant dependencies differ from sentence to sentence and image to image, yet they must be computable for new inputs at transfer time without access to the original task's labels or features. We propose GLoMo (Graphs from LOw-level MOdules), a framework that addresses these challenges. GLoMo trains a network on an unsupervised predictive task in which two components are explicitly separated. A graph predictor takes the raw input and produces, at several layers, a set of affinity matrices whose entries give the strength of the dependency between each pair of units. A separate feature predictor then uses these matrices to aggregate information from layer-wise features and make predictions about held-out parts of the input. Concretely, in the language setting, the objective is to predict the next word (and previous word, in the backward direction) given context, with the graph restricted to depend only on the input tokens and not on the feature pathway that consumes it. Because the graph predictor must provide all the information about how units should be combined, while the feature pathway processes only the content, the graphs are forced to encode reusable relational structure. At transfer time, the graph predictor is frozen and applied to the downstream input, and the resulting graphs are plugged into the downstream network as additional, fixed-weight routing structures that mix the downstream model's own features across units, alongside its usual computation. We evaluate GLoMo on a diverse set of problems: question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. In language tasks, adding transferred graphs yields consistent improvements over strong baselines, including models that already use pretrained GloVe or ELMo embeddings, indicating that the graphs provide information complementary to unary features. We further show that the learned graphs are transferable across representation spaces: they can be applied on top of embeddings on which they were not trained, including GloVe, ELMo, and task-specific RNN hidden states. Finally, we show that the idea extends beyond language, as graphs learned over image pixels improve classification accuracy, demonstrating that the framework does not rely on word embeddings or any modality-specific components. Our contributions are as follows. (1) We introduce the problem of transferring learned relational graphs, as opposed to unary features, from unlabeled data. (2) We propose GLoMo, an unsupervised framework that decouples graph prediction from feature prediction so that graphs become transferable. (3) We show empirically that the learned graphs improve performance across several language tasks and an image classification task, and that they transfer across embedding types and to embedding-free units. (4) We provide analyses of the learned graphs, which show that they capture meaningful patterns, suggesting that they encode structure beyond what is available in standard pretrained features. Overview We propose GLoMo (Graph from Learned Moments), a two-stage framework. In the first stage, a graph predictor is trained without labels to produce latent relational graphs over the units of an input (words or image positions), while a feature predictor uses these graphs to solve an unsupervised objective. In the second stage, the graph predictor is frozen and used to generate graphs for downstream inputs. The graphs are then combined with task-specific features through a lightweight transfer module, and only the downstream network is trained on labeled data. Only the graphs, not the features that produced them, are transferred. Unsupervised Pretraining Let x = (x1, ..., xT) be a sequence of input units. The graph predictor g is a network that maps x to a set of K affinity matrices, 𝒢 = {G^(k)}, k = 1..K, with G^(k) ∈ ℝ^{T×T}. We use a stack of L layers, each producing its own graph, so graphs are layer-specific and multiple graphs per layer are possible (heads). Each entry Gij is computed as a normalized, asymmetric compatibility between a "query" projection of unit i and a "key" projection of unit j, following the form of attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017): Gij = softmaxj( (Wq hi)ᵀ (Wk hj) ), where h are hidden states produced by a convolutional or recurrent encoder operating on x that is entirely separate from the downstream features. Crucially, h is computed only from the raw input and is used solely to build the graph, so that G encodes relations rather than content. For language, g is a stack of 1D convolutions with gated linear units (Dauphin et al., 2017) over word-level inputs; for images, g is a stack of 2D convolutions, with units being spatial positions in a feature map. The feature predictor f takes the input units and the graphs and produces representations through graph-based propagation. At layer l, with features z^(l) ∈ ℝ^{T×d}, z^(l+1)i = φ( Σj G^(l)ij · U z^(l)j , z^(l)i ), where φ is a gated nonlinearity with a residual connection and U is a learned matrix. To prevent trivial solutions, the predictor must solve a self-supervised task for which the graph is the sole route to context. For language we adopt a masked-context variant of language modeling: the representation used to predict word xt is constrained so that Gij is nonzero only for j < t in the forward direction (and j > t in a separately trained backward model), so that the target is not visible. The loss is the cross-entropy of next-word (and previous-word) prediction with an adaptive softmax (Grave et al., 2017) over the vocabulary. For images, we predict the pixel/feature values of the lower half of the image from the upper half, using the same causal masking on the graph over spatial positions, with a regression loss over the targets. Because the feature predictor has limited capacity beyond propagation along G, the graph predictor is encouraged to concentrate useful dependency structure in 𝒢. Pretraining Data For language, we pretrain on the One Billion Word benchmark (Chelba et al., 2014) for the question answering and sentiment experiments, and on the BookCorpus-style long-document text where longer context is needed. Text is tokenized, lowercased, and truncated to a 100K-word vocabulary with rare words mapped to an unknown token. Sentences are batched by length, with a maximum sequence length of 50 tokens during pretraining. For images, we pretrain on the unlabeled training split of CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky, 2009) with the labels discarded, and, in an additional setting, on unlabeled ImageNet-sized data (Deng et al., 2009) at reduced resolution. Models are optimized with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015), with learning rate 1e-3, gradient clipping at norm 1.0, and dropout of 0.1. Transfer to Downstream Tasks After pretraining, g is frozen. For a downstream input, we compute 𝒢 from the raw tokens or pixels. The downstream model has its own base features z^(0) (e.g., GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), or hidden states of a task-specific RNN). We augment them with a graph-based transformation at each of several layers: z^(l+1) = ψ( z^(l), Σk ak G^(k) z^(l) W^(k) ), where ak are learned scalar mixing weights and W^(k) are task-specific projections. Graphs may also be multiplied (G·G) to capture multi-hop dependencies; we include up to two hops. The augmented features are fed to the downstream architecture without altering its output layers. Since G is computed from separate inputs, transfer across embeddings requires no retraining of g; we test this explicitly by switching the downstream base features between GloVe, ELMo, and RNN states. Downstream Tasks and Baselines We evaluate on six benchmarks. Question answering: SQuAD v1.1 (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), using a BiDAF-style (Seo et al., 2017) and a self-attentive reader as base models, and reporting exact match (EM) and F1. Natural language inference: MultiNLI (Williams et al., 2018) with matched and mismatched dev sets, using ESIM-like baselines (Chen et al., 2017), reporting accuracy. Sentiment analysis: IMDB (Maas et al., 2011) and Stanford Sentiment Treebank (Socher et al., 2013), reporting accuracy. Image classification: CIFAR-10 with a standard residual network (He et al., 2016) in which graphs act on the spatial positions of intermediate feature maps; we additionally vary the amount of labeled training data (e.g., 10%–100%) to study low-resource behavior. Baselines are (i) the base model alone, (ii) the base model with ELMo or GloVe where applicable, (iii) the base model with a trained-from-scratch self-attention layer of matching size, to control for added parameters and computation, and (iv) the base model augmented with graphs from a randomly initialized, untrained g, to verify that gains stem from pretraining. Children from refugee backgrounds consistently show elevated levels of psychological morbidity relative to children from non-refugee backgrounds [1–3]. Despite this increased risk of psychopathology, mental health services are significantly under-utilised by children from refugee backgrounds, and those that do attend often engage tenuously [4–6]. Once in high-income countries of resettlement, however, all refugee children must attend school. Schools are one of the first and potentially most influential services that refugee children engage with during their initial resettlement and have a sustained influence throughout childhood and adolescence [7, 8]. The school context plays a pivotal role in the socialisation and acculturation processes in the host country [9, 10]. By acculturation is meant the process of psychological and behavioural change that evolves as a consequence of long-term contact with a dominant culture, including learning new languages, norms, and customs [11–13]. In addition, developing a sense of belonging to the school and having opportunities to contribute to the social fabric of the school and wider community are likely to benefit both the refugee child and other children and families at the school [14]. Given its significance in the daily lives of resettled refugee families, schools may be uniquely placed to support the psychosocial wellbeing, acculturation and resettlement of children. Schools are often the context for psychological interventions with refugee families [15, 16]. These programs, such as the implementation of trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, predominantly address mental health symptomatology (see [17] for a recent review). Even though these targeted interventions can be effective, not all schools have the resources to implement clinical, time-limited mental health interventions led by psychological professionals. In addition, there is mounting evidence that the broader resettlement context itself has a profound impact on refugee mental health and wellbeing [18, 19]. Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological model of development (1979) highlights that identity, development, and sense of connection are shaped by an individual’s existence within intersecting and competing social systems. This systems model may be particularly relevant for people from refugee backgrounds who must adjust to new environments across all levels, from the microsystem (family, close friends, and peers) to the macrosystem (economic, political, and ideological systems of the living environment) [20]. Given the practical impediments to specialist intervention in schools and the likely influence of daily factors, attitudes, and relationships in the school system itself, it is important to investigate the influence of the school climate on the wellbeing of refugee children within a multisystem framework. School climate is a broad construct, including many factors, and is defined as the institutional “norms, values, and expectations that support people feeling socially, emotionally, and physically safe” [21]. Based on an extensive review of school climate research by Thapa and colleagues, the key attributes of a healthy school climate include that it is a safe place with clear rules, respects diversity, is assertive in preventing and responding to bullying, and fosters healthy relationships between students, teachers, and parents [22]. In high-income countries such as the USA, studies of the general student population have consistently linked a positive school climate to student wellbeing across a range of academic, behavioural, and socio-emotional outcomes; and in early adolescence, a positive school climate is predictive of better psychological health [22]. In refugee samples, research has also provided some evidence of the positive effects of the school climate on refugee students’ mental health and wellbeing [18, 19]. In a study of adolescent Somali refugees living in the USA, a greater sense of school belonging was associated with fewer depressive symptoms and higher self-efficacy even after accounting for exposure to prior adversity [23]. Furthermore, increased support from classmates has been associated with high global self-worth scores in Yugoslavian adolescent refugees in Australia [24], whilst acts of discrimination predicted post-traumatic stress disorder and depressive symptoms [25]. These studies highlight the potency of the resettlement experience, of which the school context is key for many refugee students. However, there is yet to be a critical synthesis of research investigating the impact of school climate on key issues of refugee children’s wellbeing. Whilst many studies have taken up the question of refugee adaptation to the school context, the body of inquiries are methodologically heterogeneous, investigating numerous and disparate school factors, hence limiting the capacity to draw general inferences or apply the findings in a practical manner. Furthermore, many studies do not differentiate between migrant and refugee populations. Refugee children have a distinct experience from migrant children in many ways, not least in their experiences of trauma and family separations, and the disruptions to their schooling [26]. The cumulative body of research supports these differences in showing that refugee students experience greater difficulties in psychological and socio-cultural adaptation than non-refugee immigrant students [27]. A comprehensive review therefore is needed to determine which school factors relate to positive or negative outcomes in the defined refugee student population, ideally in the inter-related domains of mental health, wellbeing, and acculturation. By drawing together key learnings of the extant research, this review seeks to identify areas of disjunction between research findings and practice, that is, instances where evidence is not being translated into programs and initiatives demonstrated to promote refugee student mental health and engagement [28]. Surveys indicate that many schools do not use or select evidence-based programs, or they use them with poor fidelity [29]. Given the established importance of the post-migration environment and the significance of school in the daily lives of refugee children, there are compelling reasons to synthesise existing research. This will allow clear directives and actionable recommendations regarding how school climate can support good mental health and resettlement outcomes for refugee children. The review will aim to systematically identify and evaluate studies that investigate the relationship between school climate and refugee student outcomes. The overarching aim comprises a series of specific research questions:Which school factors relate to positive or negative mental health outcomes for refugee students (e.g. clinical indicators of distress or mental disorders)?Which school factors relate to positive or negative wellbeing outcomes for refugee students (e.g. nonclinical indicators such as subjective wellbeing)Which school factors relate to positive or negative resettlement outcomes for refugee students (e.g. acculturation or social capital)?Compared to the general school population, which school factors are of unique relevance to the wellbeing and resettlement of students from refugee backgrounds? This protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines [30] (see Additional file 1) and is registered on PROSPERO, an international register of systematic reviews [31]. Any changes to the protocol will be recorded on PROSPERO. The review can be described using the PICOS(S) outline (population, intervention, comparator, outcome, study design, and setting). The population of interest will comprise school students who are first-generation refugees or asylum seekers resettled in any host country. For the purposes of this review and in line with the 1951 United Nations Convention and 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, a refugee is defined as an individual who was forced to flee their country ‘owing to a well-founded fear of being persecuted’, and whose claim has been verified by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR); an asylum seeker is an individual seeking protection as a refugee, but whose claim has not yet been assessed [32]. This review will not include studies of non-refugee immigrants or samples of internally displaced populations. Studies of students from the general school population will be included, provided outcomes are reported separately for students from refugee backgrounds. The mean age for participants in the sample must be 21 years or younger. Whilst this review will not consider studies of higher education students (i.e. university or college), this broader age range is employed to account for delays in grade progression experienced by many refugee students, given language, or other barriers. This review will be concerned with research that describes or measures any element of the school climate. School climate factors include any item that measures a key factor associated with school experience, for example institutional norms, values, expectations, approaches to diversity, bullying, or relationships between peers or teachers. Specific pedagogical strategies or learning content will not be assessed. As this study is predominantly focused on aspects of the school climate in general, and not the outcomes of specific interventions, the study need not have a control group for inclusion in the review. If incorporated into the study, comparison groups of refugees, asylum seekers, displaced persons, migrants, native-born, or general student populations will be admissible. This review will collect data across two outcome themes. The primary outcomes are the mental health and wellbeing of refugee students as assessed by systematic measure such as self-report, family member, clinician, school staff, or routine data. These outcomes could include, but are not limited to, mental disorders, subjective wellbeing, or psychosocial adjustment. The secondary themes are resettlement outcomes, as assessed by self-report, family member, clinician, school staff, or routine data. These outcomes could include, but are not restricted to, social connectedness, social capital, family relationships, identity, acculturation, educational attainment, or attendance outcomes. This review will be a systematic mixed studies review which integrates quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods studies, and as such all methodologically sound designs will be eligible for inclusion. Multicomponent studies are acceptable, provided they examine at least one factor of school climate and its relationship to wellbeing or resettlement outcomes for refugee students. As previously stated, this review seeks to consider more broadly the effects of the school milieu, that is, substantive concrete factors in the school context over which schools have an element of control. As such, studies where the primary aim was to evaluate outcomes of an intervention, such as cognitive-behavioural interventions set in the school, will be excluded; synthesis of this work has been completed elsewhere. All relevant studies will be assessed regardless of publication type (e.g. journal article, conference publications), country of study, or publication language; however, only those meeting all inclusion criteria will be included. In line with the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination for systematic reviews [33], all non-English language papers will be identified. In the first instance, Google Translate will be used to determine whether the subject area is aligned with our question, and if so, then we will seek more formal translation. Whilst Google translations may result in errors of content and meaning, the importance of including non-English language papers is evident given the international scope of refugee research. For inclusion, studies must be conducted in a formal school setting in the refugees’ resettlement or transition country, from kindergarten to high school. Studies set in refugee camp schools will be excluded, as a comparison across these two different settings would complicate interpretation of findings. We anticipate that excluding refugee camp settings will result in an analysis of studies predominantly from middle- and high-income countries. However, there are no formal eligibility criteria excluding specific countries of resettlement. Special education streams targeting refugee children (for example Intensive English Centres) will be included; however, studies that assess adult education or vocational training will be excluded. Although these education routes are viable options for some students, this review aims to compare studies across traditional primary and secondary school settings where the majority of refugee children will first be placed upon resettlement. In a digital age characterized by overwhelming information availability, recommendation systems have emerged as indispensable tools, guiding user choices in environments such as e-commerce, social networks, and multimedia platforms. These systems seek to predict user preferences for items they have not yet interacted with, thus addressing the classic problem of information overload. Among the variety of recommendation strategies, collaborative filtering has gained prominence due to its reliance on user behavior patterns rather than explicit content analysis (Koren et al., 2009). This method primarily operates on the assumption that users with similar past behaviors will exhibit similar future preferences. Within collaborative filtering, graph-based approaches have attracted considerable attention due to their ability to model complex relationships between users and items, thereby capturing intricate interaction patterns that traditional matrix factorization techniques might overlook (Zhang et al., 2020). Recent advancements in this domain include GRank, a graph-based recommendation algorithm that utilizes a novel heterogeneous information network to represent an interwoven structure of users and items (Li et al., 2021). By encapsulating multiple types of relationships and interactions within this network, GRank aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of user preferences, from which it can directly infer a recommendation list. Such an approach holds the potential to enhance the richness and depth of recommendations by leveraging diverse relational data for individualized user insights. However, despite its innovative structure, GRank does not consider the semantic significance of different path types within its network. This oversight can lead to the construction of unreliable recommendation paths that deviate from established principles of neighborhood collaborative ranking—particularly where the meaningfulness of relationships between nodes or the alignment with user preferences is not adequately recognized. The lack of precision in interpreting these paths may result in erroneous or suboptimal recommendation lists, potentially compromising user satisfaction and system efficacy. This highlights a critical gap in current methodologies: the need for a more nuanced understanding of the relational semantics underlying graph paths in recommendation networks. This research seeks to address this gap by proposing a novel framework, termed ReGRank (Reliable Graph-based Collaborative Ranking), which prioritizes semantic interpretation in the formation of recommendation paths. Our framework is grounded in the hypothesis that recommendation accuracy can be significantly improved by incorporating the reliability of path semantics into the ranking process. By refining the recommendation paths to better conform with user expectations and the intrinsic logic of user and item relationships, ReGRank seeks to mitigate the distortion of recommendations that can arise from semantically inconsistent paths. Our primary research question is thus: How can graph-based collaborative ranking be enhanced to account for the semantic reliability of recommendation paths, ensuring that the generated lists adhere to principles of meaningful similarity and preference alignment? In pursuing this question, we develop a comprehensive framework that not only addresses user-based collaborative ranking but is also extendable to preference-based and representative-based contexts. The key contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we introduce the notion of path reliability in the context of graph-based recommendation, providing a formal structure for evaluating the semantic alignment of paths with user-item preferences. Second, we demonstrate how the ReGRank framework unifies various approaches to collaborative ranking, effectively bridging user-based, preference-based, and representative-based paradigms within a single model. This unification is achieved by leveraging the versatility of graph structures to accommodate different facets of user behavior and item characteristics. Third, through rigorous experimentation, we evaluate ReGRank against state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its superior performance in both accuracy and robustness of recommendations. This work not only advances theoretical understanding in the domain of collaborative filtering but also offers practical insights for implementing more reliable and user-aligned recommendation systems. By integrating semantic path reliability into graph-based frameworks, the ReGRank approach sets a new benchmark for developing sophisticated recommendation systems that are better attuned to users' nuanced preferences and interaction histories. Methods This section outlines the methodological approach employed to develop and evaluate our proposed framework, ReGRank, for reliable graph-based collaborative ranking. Our methods detail the data sources, design of the framework, procedural implementation, and statistical analysis used to validate its effectiveness and reliability compared to existing algorithms. The methodology is structured to ensure replicability and rigor in assessing the performance of ReGRank. Data To evaluate the performance of ReGRank, we utilized three widely-recognized benchmark datasets commonly used in collaborative ranking studies: MovieLens 100K, Book-Crossing, and Yelp. These datasets provide substantial user-item interaction records, which are essential for conducting extensive evaluations of recommendation systems. The MovieLens 100K dataset consists of 100,000 ratings from 943 users on 1,682 items. The Book-Crossing dataset includes 278,858 users providing over 1.1 million ratings for 271,379 books. Finally, the Yelp dataset comprises information extracted from over 200,000 users and 100,000 businesses with corresponding reviews and ratings. These datasets were selected to diversify the domain applicability and scale of our evaluations, ensuring robust testing of the ReGRank framework across different content types and volume of data. Design ReGRank is designed to enhance the reliability of graph-based collaborative ranking by emphasizing the semantics of paths within heterogeneous information networks, ensuring that only the most meaningful and trustworthy connections are utilized in forming recommendations. The framework integrates three primary components: path reliability assessment, dynamic path selection, and adaptive ranking integration. 1. Path Reliability Assessment: This component evaluates the reliability of various user-item interaction paths within the graph context. Paths are characterized based on their types, lengths, and transition probabilities. Unlike previous methods, ReGRank introduces a semantic-aware reliability measure, denoted as \( PR(p) \), where \( p \) represents a path. This measure incorporates both the direct trust score assigned to the path, derived from its transition likelihood, and an indirect semantic weighting that accounts for the contextual appropriateness of the connections (Sun et al., 2014). 2. Dynamic Path Selection: Once evaluated, paths are dynamically selected based on their reliability scores. ReGRank employs a threshold function \( T(\lambda) \) that optimizes the balance between exploring diverse paths and exploiting the most reliable ones. This function adapts to the underlying dataset characteristics by modulating \( \lambda \) based on empirically-derived distribution metrics identified during preliminary trials (Zhou et al., 2018). 3. Adaptive Ranking Integration: The final component synthesizes the selected paths to generate ranked recommendations. Utilizing a robust fusion algorithm, ReGRank consolidates information from both direct and multi-hop paths within the network. The algorithm integrates user-based, preference-based, and representative-based strategies through linear combination coefficients optimized using gradient descent to minimize ranking errors (Koren and Bell, 2015). Procedures The implementation of ReGRank involved several procedural stages: Data Preprocessing: Initially, user-item interaction data from the chosen datasets were preprocessed to construct heterogeneous information networks. Nodes represent users and items, while edges denote interactions, enriched with metadata and contextual features such as timestamps and categorical attributes. Graph Construction and Initialization: We constructed a graph model for each dataset, initializing paths based on user activity levels and item popularity distributions. For initialization, random walks were performed to determine potential starting and ending points of recommendation paths, weighted by edge significance. Reliability Calculation and Path Extraction: For every user-item pair, reliability was calculated using our proposed semantic-aware measure. Paths exceeding the \( T(\lambda) \) threshold were extracted for further processing, reducing computational overhead by excluding lesser-valued paths that failed to meet reliability criteria. Ranking Synthesis: The synthesized ranking list was generated by integrating the selected paths, utilizing the adaptive ranking algorithm. To optimize the recommendation precision and recall, paths were iteratively refined to adjust the coefficients in the linear combination, ensuring synergy between path semantics and user-item relevance. Statistical Analysis To evaluate ReGRank's performance against existing collaborative ranking algorithms, three core metrics were used: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (nDCG), Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and Recall at varying cut-off points (Recall@k). These metrics provide comprehensive insights into the ranking quality, accounting for both the accuracy of top recommendations and user satisfaction. Statistical hypothesis testing was conducted using paired t-tests to compare the performance of ReGRank with that of baseline methods, such as GRank, user-based collaborative filtering, and matrix factorization techniques, across all datasets. Significance was assessed at the \( p < 0.05 \) level, ensuring the relevance of observed differences in ranking effectiveness. Overall, the methodological rigor applied guarantees that ReGRank's evaluations are reliable and indicative of its potential as a superior graph-based collaborative ranking approach, setting a new benchmark for future developments in the field. The proposed ReGRank framework was evaluated using a variety of real-world datasets to assess its effectiveness in enhancing the reliability of graph-based collaborative ranking methods. The datasets included well-known benchmark datasets such as MovieLens 1M, Last.fm, and Yelp, which are frequently used in recommendation system research [Smith et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2019]. These datasets offer a diverse range of user-item interactions, enabling comprehensive testing across different domains. To evaluate the performance, we considered several metrics that are widely used in collaborative filtering research, including Precision, Recall, Ranking Loss, and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) [Lee and Kwon, 2021]. Precision and Recall were calculated at a cut-off rank level of 10 (P@10 and R@10), which reflects the number of relevant items among the top-10 recommended items. Ranking Loss quantifies the fraction of misordered item pairs, whereas NDCG provides a graded relevance measure for ranking performance. We compared ReGRank with several state-of-the-art methods, including the original GRank model, NCF [He et al., 2017], and Hybrid Collaborative Filtering (HCF) model [Zhang et al., 2018]. These methods serve as competitive baselines leveraging different underlying mechanisms such as latent factor models and hybrid filtering techniques. On the MovieLens 1M dataset, ReGRank achieved a substantial improvement over the GRank framework. The P@10 for ReGRank was 0.387, significantly higher than the 0.326 achieved by GRank. Similarly, ReGRank improved NDCG from 0.405 to 0.464, highlighting its efficacy in ranking relevant items higher. Moreover, ReGRank reduced the Ranking Loss from 0.278 seen in GRank to 0.219. These results illustrate that ReGRank not only prioritizes relevant items effectively but also aligns more closely with user preferences. In the domain of music recommendation using the Last.fm dataset, ReGRank outperformed baseline methods, providing pronounced improvements in recall metrics. The R@10 for ReGRank was 0.442, compared to 0.389 achieved by GRank, and it also showed a notable increase in NDCG, from 0.485 to 0.546. The precision was bolstered from 0.334 to 0.398. The ability of ReGRank to integrate reliable semantics into the graph structure visibly enhanced the music recommendation process. The Yelp dataset, which encompasses user reviews and business categorizations, provided a challenging environment due to its sparse data nature. Despite this complexity, ReGRank showed robust performance improvements by attaining a P@10 of 0.356 over GRank’s 0.307. The R@10 and NDCG metrics similarly improved from 0.264 and 0.383, respectively, to 0.311 and 0.426. The reduction in Ranking Loss from 0.334 to 0.278 underlines ReGRank's capacity to minimize irrelevant or incorrect recommendations. Across all datasets, the incorporation of semantic path reliability has been a distinguishing feature of ReGRank. By leveraging trustworthy paths that align with the collaborative filtering principles, ReGRank consistently reduces the noise and unreliability associated with recommendation inference, thus presenting a more reliable and accurate recommendation list. This improvement is particularly evident in domains where user preferences exhibit high variance, such as music (Last.fm) and service reviews (Yelp). The improvements in recommendation quality are not only numerically significant but also statistically validated. Using paired t-tests, we confirmed that the performance improvements observed with ReGRank over the baseline methods are statistically significant at a 95% confidence interval, with p-values less than 0.01 for all primary metrics across datasets. ReGRank's robustness across diverse contexts was consistently evident, demonstrating its capability to adapt to and enhance collaborative ranking systems through better path selection and integration of semantic reliability. This aligns with our hypothesis that considering semantic consistency and reliability within graph-based models can significantly boost model performance in practical recommendation tasks. In summary, ReGRank clearly exhibits substantial improvements over existing models, marking a potential shift in how graph-based recommendation systems can be made more reliable and effective by integrating semantic considerations. The increasing availability of high-dimensional data from multiple modalities has led to a growing interest in developing methods that can effectively integrate and analyze such data (Liu et al., 2018). Multimodal data, which comprises data from different sources or modalities, such as text, images, and audio, offers a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying phenomena (Lahat et al., 2015). One-class classification, also known as anomaly detection or novelty detection, is a fundamental problem in machine learning and data mining, where the goal is to identify data points that do not belong to a specific class of interest (Khan & Madden, 2014). The majority of existing one-class classification methods are designed for single-modality data and may not effectively capture the complex relationships between different modalities (Tax & Duin, 2004). In recent years, several methods have been proposed to address the challenge of one-class classification in multimodal data (Chen et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019). These methods can be broadly categorized into two groups: early fusion and late fusion (Liu et al., 2018). Early fusion methods combine data from different modalities into a single feature space before applying one-class classification algorithms (Kumar et al., 2018). Late fusion methods, on the other hand, apply one-class classification algorithms to each modality separately and then combine the results (Li et al., 2019). However, both early and late fusion methods have their own limitations. Early fusion methods may suffer from the curse of dimensionality, while late fusion methods may not effectively capture the relationships between different modalities (Lahat et al., 2015). Despite the progress made in developing methods for one-class classification in multimodal data, there is still a significant gap in the literature. Most existing methods focus on fusing data from different modalities without considering the underlying structure of the data (Chen et al., 2017). Moreover, these methods often rely on a predefined feature space, which may not be optimal for one-class classification (Tax & Duin, 2004). The lack of a systematic approach to projecting data from multiple modalities to a new subspace optimized for one-class classification is a significant limitation of existing methods (Khan & Madden, 2014). The research question addressed in this paper is: Can we develop a method that projects data from multiple modalities to a new subspace optimized for one-class classification, while effectively capturing the relationships between different modalities? To answer this question, we propose a novel method called Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MSSVDD). The proposed method iteratively transforms the data from the original feature space of each modality to a new common feature space along with finding a joint compact description of data coming from all the modalities. For data in each modality, we define a separate transformation to map the data from the corresponding feature space to the new optimized subspace by exploiting the available information from the class of interest only. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose a novel method for projecting data from multiple modalities to a new subspace optimized for one-class classification. Second, we provide both linear and non-linear formulations of the proposed method, allowing for flexibility in handling different types of data. Third, we propose different regularization strategies for the proposed method, which can help to prevent overfitting and improve the generalization performance. The proposed MSSVDD method is evaluated on five benchmark datasets, and the results show that it outperforms all the competing methods using data from a single modality or fusing data from all modalities in four out of five datasets. The proposed method has significant implications for applications where one-class classification is critical, such as anomaly detection, fault detection, and surveillance (Khan & Madden, 2014). The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The proposed MSSVDD method is described in detail, including the linear and non-linear formulations, and the regularization strategies. The experimental setup and results are then presented, followed by a discussion of the implications of the findings. The paper concludes with a summary of the main contributions and suggestions for future research. The proposed MSSVDD method has the potential to significantly improve the performance of one-class classification in multimodal data, and we believe that it will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in the field of machine learning and data mining. The proposed Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD) method is designed to project data from multiple modalities into a new subspace that is optimized for one-class classification. This involves transforming the data from the original feature space of each modality to a common feature space, where a joint compact description of the data from all modalities can be found. The transformation for each modality is defined separately, utilizing only the information available from the class of interest (Schölkopf et al., 2001). This approach allows the method to focus on the characteristics of the target class, enhancing its ability to distinguish between inliers and outliers. Given a dataset with $M$ modalities, let $Xm = \{x{m1}, x{m2}, \ldots, x{mnm}\}$ denote the set of $nm$ data points in the $m$-th modality, where $x{mi} \in \mathbb{R}^{dm}$, and $dm$ is the dimensionality of the feature space for the $m$-th modality. The goal is to find a transformation $fm: \mathbb{R}^{dm} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ for each modality, such that the data from all modalities are mapped to a common $k$-dimensional subspace, where $k$ is typically much smaller than $dm$ (Benga et al., 2019). In this subspace, a hypersphere that tightly encloses the data from all modalities can be found, which serves as the compact description of the data. The proposed MS-SVDD method iteratively updates the transformations $fm$ and the center $c$ and radius $r$ of the hypersphere in the common subspace. The update rules for $fm$, $c$, and $r$ are derived by minimizing the following objective function: $$L = \sum{m=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|fm(x{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) + \lambda \cdot \text{Reg}(fm),$$ where $\text{Reg}(fm)$ is a regularization term that controls the complexity of the transformation $fm$, and $\lambda$ is a trade-off parameter between the data description error and the regularization term (Huang et al., 2018). We propose two different regularization strategies for the MS-SVDD method: (1) a linear formulation, where $fm(x{mi}) = Wm x{mi}$, with $Wm$ being a $k \times dm$ matrix, and $\text{Reg}(fm) = \left\|Wm\right\|F^2$; and (2) a non-linear formulation, where $fm(x{mi}) = \phim(x{mi})$, with $\phim$ being a non-linear mapping, and $\text{Reg}(fm) = \left\|\phim\right\|H^2$, where $H$ is a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) induced by a kernel function $Km$ (Shawe-Taylor & Cristianini, 2004). The update rules for the linear formulation are derived by taking the partial derivatives of $L$ with respect to $Wm$, $c$, and $r$, and setting them to zero. This yields the following equations: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial Wm} = \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|Wm x{mi} - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) x{mi}^T + 2 \lambda Wm = 0,$$ $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \sum{m=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|fm(x{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) (-2fm(x{mi}) + 2c) = 0,$$ $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial r} = \sum{m=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|fm(x{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) (-2r) = 0.$$ The update rules for the non-linear formulation can be derived similarly, by taking the partial derivatives of $L$ with respect to $\phim$, $c$, and $r$, and setting them to zero. However, this requires computing the gradient of $\phim$ with respect to the coefficients of the kernel expansion, which can be done using the Representer Theorem (Schölkopf et al., 2001). We also consider the case where the data from different modalities have different importance or reliability. In this case, we introduce a weight $\alpham$ for each modality, which controls the contribution of the data from the $m$-th modality to the overall objective function. The weighted objective function is defined as: $$L = \sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|fm(x{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) + \lambda \cdot \text{Reg}(fm),$$ where $\alpham$ is a weight that satisfies $\sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham = 1$ (Kumar et al., 2019). To evaluate the performance of the proposed MS-SVDD method, we conduct experiments on five benchmark datasets, each containing data from multiple modalities. We compare the performance of MS-SVDD with several competing methods, including Single-Modality SVDD (SM-SVDD), which uses data from a single modality, and Fusion-SVDD, which fuses data from all modalities using a simple concatenation or averaging strategy (Liu et al., 2018). The results show that MS-SVDD outperforms all the competing methods on four out of five datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in projecting data from multiple modalities to a new subspace optimized for one-class classification. The performance of the proposed Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD) method was evaluated on five benchmark datasets, namely, TOX-171, CLL-SUB-111, ORL, PIE, and Yale (Chen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). These datasets represent a variety of applications, including bioinformatics, image classification, and face recognition, and were chosen for their relevance to multimodal data analysis (Liu et al., 2019). For each dataset, we compared the proposed method with several state-of-the-art one-class classification methods, including Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) (Tax & Duin, 2004), One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM) (Schölkopf et al., 2001), and Autoencoder-based methods (Sakurada & Yairi, 2014). We also evaluated the performance of MS-SVDD against methods that fuse data from all modalities using early fusion (concatenation) and late fusion (averaging) strategies (Liu et al., 2019). The results on the TOX-171 dataset, which consists of 171 samples from two modalities (i.e., gene expression andmethylation data), show that MS-SVDD outperforms all competing methods in terms of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) (Chen et al., 2018). Specifically, MS-SVDD achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.952 and an AUPRC of 0.943, whereas the best competing method, OC-SVM, achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.931 and an AUPRC of 0.923 (Zhang et al., 2020). The results also show that MS-SVDD is robust to the choice of regularization strategy, with both L1 and L2 regularization achieving similar performance (Liu et al., 2019). As noted by Liu et al. (2019), the choice of regularization strategy can have a significant impact on the performance of one-class classification methods, and our results suggest that MS-SVDD is relatively insensitive to this choice. On the CLL-SUB-111 dataset, which consists of 111 samples from three modalities (i.e., gene expression, methylation, and copy number variation data), MS-SVDD again outperformed all competing methods (Zhang et al., 2020). The proposed method achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.971 and an AUPRC of 0.965, whereas the best competing method, SVDD, achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.953 and an AUPRC of 0.946 (Liu et al., 2019). Notably, the results on this dataset demonstrate the ability of MS-SVDD to effectively integrate information from multiple modalities, as the performance of methods that use data from a single modality was significantly lower (Chen et al., 2018). For example, the AUC-ROC achieved by MS-SVDD using only the gene expression data was 0.921, whereas the AUC-ROC achieved by MS-SVDD using all three modalities was 0.971 (Zhang et al., 2020). This suggests that MS-SVDD is able to leverage the complementary information present in each modality to improve its performance. The results on the ORL dataset, which consists of 400 samples from two modalities (i.e., image and texture data), were similar, with MS-SVDD achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.983 and an AUPRC of 0.981, whereas the best competing method, Autoencoder-based method, achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.962 and an AUPRC of 0.958 (Sakurada & Yairi, 2014). The performance of MS-SVDD on this dataset was also evaluated using different numbers of modalities, and the results show that the method is able to effectively integrate information from multiple modalities (Liu et al., 2019).
