Speech is produced by a coordinated sequence of movements of the articulators, including the lips, jaw, tongue, velum, and larynx. These movements continuously reshape the vocal tract, the airway extending from the glottis to the lips. By modulating airflow and creating different resonant cavities, the time-varying vocal tract shape determines the acoustic properties of the speech signal (Fant, 1970; Stevens, 1998). Vocal tract configurations therefore carry rich information about the underlying speech production mechanism, and understanding the mapping between vocal tract geometry and acoustics remains a central problem in speech science, with implications for phonetics, speech technology, clinical assessment, and the study of language variation (Narayanan et al., 2014; Lingala et al., 2016). Progress on this problem has depended on instrumentation for observing articulation. Electromagnetic articulography, ultrasound, X-ray microbeam, and video of the face each provide partial views, capturing flesh-point trajectories, the tongue surface, or the external lips (Whalen et al., 2005; Stone, 2005). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is attractive because it is non-invasive, involves no ionizing radiation, and provides a view of the entire vocal tract, including regions such as the pharynx and velum that are hard to reach by other modalities. Advances in fast acquisition and reconstruction have made real-time MRI (rtMRI) of speech practical, with frame rates sufficient to capture dynamic articulation in the midsagittal plane during natural, continuous speech (Narayanan et al., 2004; Bresch et al., 2008; Lingala et al., 2016). Large rtMRI corpora, such as the USC-TIMIT database and related multi-speaker collections, now allow quantitative study of articulation across many speakers (Narayanan et al., 2014). Most computational work on rtMRI speech data has relied on hand-designed or semi-automatic representations of the vocal tract. These include air–tissue boundary segmentation, cross-distance functions along the vocal tract midline, and region-of-interest time series that capture constriction formation at the lips, tongue tip, tongue body, and velum (Kim et al., 2014; Bresch & Narayanan, 2009; Proctor et al., 2010). Such representations are interpretable and have supported insights into coarticulation, compensatory articulation, and the composition of articulatory gestures (Browman & Goldstein, 1992). However, they require segmentation or parameterization pipelines that may be sensitive to image quality and speaker anatomy, and they may discard information that is not captured by the chosen parameters. A complementary strategy is to learn representations directly from the image sequences, letting the data determine which spatial and temporal features are informative about the speech sounds being produced. Deep learning provides tools for this strategy. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn hierarchical visual features and have achieved strong results in image recognition (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015; He et al., 2016). For video, the challenge is to also model temporal dynamics. Approaches include 3D convolutions (Ji et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2015), two-stream networks combining appearance and motion (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014), and architectures that couple per-frame CNN features with recurrent networks such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) are a prominent example of the last family: a CNN extracts deep visual features from each frame, and a recurrent layer integrates them over time, making the model deep in both space and time (Donahue et al., 2015). Such models have been successful in action recognition, video description, and other sequence-learning tasks, and have also been applied to visual speech recognition from lip images (Assael et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2017). Applying them to rtMRI of the full vocal tract is a natural extension, but one that has received comparatively little systematic attention. There is a gap in the existing literature. Studies of automatic recognition from articulatory data have mostly used point-tracking measurements or lip-region video, or have used articulatory features as auxiliary inputs to acoustic recognizers (King et al., 2007; Hueber et al., 2010). Work that learns directly from the full midsagittal rtMRI video to identify speech content is limited, and it is not well understood how standard video-classification architectures behave on this kind of data. Vocal tract videos differ from the natural-scene videos for which these architectures were designed. The images are grayscale, the spatial layout is highly constrained and consistent across frames, and the discriminative information lies in subtle, spatially localized constrictions and their timing rather than in large-scale object motion or scene context. Moreover, the sequences of interest, such as vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) utterances, are short and the relevant dynamics are brief and coarticulated, so assumptions about the value of long temporal context or of pretrained appearance features may not carry over. It is therefore unclear whether design choices that benefit generic video and sequence classification, including network depth, recurrent configuration, and sequence length, transfer to speech. This paper takes a step towards automatic mapping of vocal tract shape geometry to speech acoustics by addressing a closely related question: can speech content be identified directly from the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in rtMRI, using video action recognition techniques? We focus on identifying VCV sequences, which isolate consonant articulation in a controlled vowel context and are a standard probe of coarticulation and articulatory dynamics. We ask how LRCN-style models perform on this task, how their performance depends on parameter settings such as the CNN and recurrent components, and whether the behavior observed differs from that known for generic video or sequence classification. The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we formulate speech identification from rtMRI as a video classification problem and apply LRCN models that combine deep CNN feature extraction with recurrent sequence modeling to 2D rtMRI of VCV utterances from 17 speakers. Second, we conduct a comparative evaluation of this class of models under various parameter settings and for several classification tasks, providing an empirical characterization of what matters for this data. Third, we report that model behavior in speech classification differs markedly from that in generic sequence or video classification tasks, which suggests that architectures and training practices developed for natural video should be adapted for articulatory imaging. Together, these findings inform the design of data-driven models linking vocal tract dynamics and speech, and they provide a baseline for future work on acoustic mapping from articulation. Data We used a database of two-dimensional real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rtMRI) of the midsagittal vocal tract acquired from 17 native speakers of American English during the production of vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences. Image acquisition followed the established protocol for rtMRI of speech production (Narayanan et al., 2004; Narayanan et al., 2014). Participants lay supine in a scanner. A fast spiral gradient-echo sequence with a flexible receiver coil placed around the head and neck was used to image a single midsagittal slice that covered the lips, tongue, velum, larynx, and pharyngeal wall. The reconstructed image sequences had a temporal resolution of approximately 20–25 frames per second and a spatial resolution of a few millimeters per pixel. Reconstructed frames were stored as grayscale video. Audio was recorded simultaneously through a noise-cancelling optical microphone and denoised (Bresch et al., 2006), so the acoustic signal could be used to segment utterances. Audio was used only for segmentation and was not an input to any classifier. Each speaker produced a set of VCV tokens with a symmetric vowel context, in which the same vowel precedes and follows the consonant. The inventory crossed a set of English consonants spanning stops, nasals, fricatives, and approximants with the corner vowels /a/, /i/, and /u/. Each token was repeated several times in a carrier-free, isolated manner. Individual tokens were cut from the continuous recording using the acoustic signal. Each clip began shortly before the onset of the first vowel and ended shortly after the offset of the second vowel, and we manually checked the boundaries. Tokens with visible motion artifacts, incomplete articulations, or acquisition failures were discarded. Each remaining clip was labeled with its VCV identity, and by derivation with its consonant and with its vowel context. Preprocessing Frames were cropped to a fixed region of interest around the vocal tract, resized to 224 × 224 pixels by bilinear interpolation, and replicated across three channels so that ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks could be used directly (Deng et al., 2009). Intensities were normalized per speaker, by subtracting that speaker's mean and dividing by that speaker's standard deviation. This reduces inter-speaker differences in coil sensitivity and overall brightness. Because the number of frames varied across tokens with speaking rate, every clip was converted to a fixed length of T frames. Clips longer than T were uniformly subsampled, and shorter clips were padded by repeating the last frame. We treated T as a design parameter (see below). No horizontal flipping was applied, since the sagittal view has a fixed anatomical orientation. Training-time augmentation consisted of small random translations and rotations (±5°), small brightness and contrast jitter, and mild temporal jitter of the sampled frame indices, applied identically to all frames of a clip. Model architecture The main model was a Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Network (LRCN; Donahue et al., 2015). A convolutional network processes each frame independently and yields a fixed-length feature vector. The sequence of feature vectors is passed to a recurrent network, whose outputs are mapped to class probabilities. We used VGG-16 (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015) as the main visual feature extractor and took the activations of its penultimate fully connected layer. ResNet-style backbones (He et al., 2016) and a small CNN trained from scratch were used as alternatives. The temporal component was a long short-term memory (LSTM) network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), which we compared with a gated recurrent unit variant (Cho et al., 2014). The final hidden state, or alternatively the mean of the outputs across time steps, was fed to a softmax layer. Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) was applied before the recurrent and output layers. To place the LRCN results in context, we trained three reference models on the same splits: (i) a frame-wise CNN whose per-frame predictions were averaged over the clip, which ignores temporal order; (ii) a late-fusion CNN that concatenates features over time (Karpathy et al., 2014); and (iii) a 3D convolutional network that learns joint spatiotemporal filters (Tran et al., 2015). Comparing these tests whether explicit sequence modeling helps beyond what is captured by static vocal tract shape. Experimental design We defined three classification tasks. In the VCV identification task, the model predicted the full VCV label, so the consonant and the vowel context had to be inferred together. In the consonant classification task, clips from all vowel contexts were pooled and labeled only by the consonant, which required invariance to the surrounding vowel. In the vowel classification task, clips were labeled by vowel context regardless of consonant. For each task we varied several parameters, one at a time around a default configuration. The parameters were: (a) clip length T, from short clips of about 10 frames to longer clips of about 30 frames; (b) the number of LSTM units (64, 128, 256) and layers (1 or 2); (c) the CNN backbone; (d) initialization, either ImageNet-pretrained weights with the convolutional layers frozen, pretrained weights fine-tuned end to end, or random initialization; and (e) unidirectional versus bidirectional recurrence. We also ran a comparison with the label set restricted to consonants grouped by manner of articulation, to examine whether errors concentrate within articulatory classes. Training and evaluation protocol To estimate generalization to unseen speakers, we used speaker-independent evaluation. The 17 speakers were partitioned into folds for cross-validation, so that all tokens from a speaker were in the test set of exactly one fold. In each fold, a subset of the remaining speakers (about 10%) was held out as a validation set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection, and no test speaker data influenced model selection. For comparison we also ran a speaker-dependent condition in which tokens from every speaker were split across training and test sets by repetition, to quantify the gap caused by inter-speaker variability in vocal tract anatomy. Scientific workflows play a critical role in the computational and data-driven sciences, where they facilitate the automation and management of complex data analysis processes, often integrating multiple software tools and computational steps into a coherent pipeline (Gil et al., 2007). These workflows are crucial in a diverse array of fields, from bioinformatics and astronomy to climate science and physics, due to their ability to manage large data sets and perform reproducible scientific analyses (Deelman et al., 2009). One of the compelling features of scientific workflow systems is their capacity to capture provenance information that documents the execution trace of the workflow (Chelliah et al., 2014). This execution trace is pivotal since it not only records the computation steps executed during a workflow run but also details the inputs consumed and the outputs produced at each step, forming a comprehensive provenance record that underpins lineage determination, reproducibility, and data trustworthiness (Groth et al., 2012). The execution trace data captured by workflow systems provides the raw information necessary for determining lineage relationships among data items. Lineage, in this context, refers to the ancestry of specific data products in the workflow output, tracing back to the inputs and intermediate data that contributed to their derivation (Bowers et al., 2008). Understanding lineage is fundamental for a variety of applications, including error tracking, debugging, and answering provenance queries that might ask, “Which inputs were instrumental in producing this specific output?” (Zhao et al., 2014). However, the accurate inference of such lineage relationships necessitates detailed knowledge of the data dependencies within each computation step of the workflow; that is, how exactly outputs are functionally dependent on various inputs. Despite the importance of capturing detailed data dependencies within workflows, many scientific workflow systems operate under a simplifying assumption: that all outputs of a workflow step depend on all of its inputs. While this assumption ensures that no potential dependencies are overlooked, it can result in lineage inferences that are overly broad, leading to “false positives” where outputs are incorrectly assumed to depend on irrelevant inputs (Cruz et al., 2009). To address this deficiency, precise annotations of input-output dependencies are necessary, thus allowing for the refinement of lineage inferences. Existing methodologies in lineage computation often lack a granularity of specificity that can distinguish between varying dependency relationships (Freire et al., 2008). This gap in the precise annotation of dependencies represents a significant challenge in the domain of scientific workflows, given that incorrect or oversimplified dependency assumptions can degrade the utility of provenance information. In our preceding work, we introduced a framework for the annotation of dependency relationships that extends beyond conventional representations by allowing users to specify fine-grained dependencies at the schema level (Bowers et al., 2012). These annotations detail precisely which portions of the input data are responsible for which outputs, thus enhancing the accuracy of lineage inferences. Building on our previous annotation framework, this paper addresses a critical gap: ensuring the consistency and completeness of dependency annotations across a workflow’s specification. Unresolved in prior research, this issue involves the challenge of reasoning about the mutual compatibility and completeness of a set of given annotations. Specifically, inconsistencies in annotations can arise when different parts of a workflow specify contradictory or incomplete dependency information, leading to either unsatisfied provenance queries or erroneous inference details. Thus, our research seeks to answer: How can a reasoning framework be developed to verify the consistency of schema-level data-dependency annotations and to infer missing annotations? To address this research question, this paper introduces a formal reasoning framework designed to validate and extend dependency annotations within scientific workflows. The contributions of our research are manifold. First, we present a systematic approach to ensuring that annotations on a workflow specification are coherent, thereby avoiding contradictory or incomplete dependency specifications. This framework is capable of performing logical inference to extrapolate a complete set of annotations from partial annotations, which is particularly beneficial in scenarios where exhaustive manual annotation is impractical, thus streamlining the workflow development process. Our second contribution lies in the practical implementation of this reasoning framework using answer-set programming (ASP), a form of declarative programming ideal for tackling problems involving complex logical relationships (Eiter et al., 2009). This ASP-based implementation demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of our theoretical framework in real-world workflows, providing a tool that enhances the usability and robustness of scientific workflow systems by ensuring their annotation mechanisms are both complete and consistent. In summary, the validation and inference of schema-level dependency annotations represent a necessary advance in the field of scientific workflows, offering a path to more accurate and reliable provenance records. By ensuring annotations are consistent and complete, our framework paves the way for enhanced data lineage tracing, thereby facilitating more precise provenance analysis and, ultimately, improving the integrity of scientific research outputs derived through complex computational workflows. In this section, we detail the methods employed to explore the validation and inference of schema-level workflow data-dependency annotations within scientific workflow systems. Our approach is divided into several interrelated components, including the data collection and preparation, the design of our reasoning framework, the implementation using answer-set programming, and the statistical analysis employed for validation. Data Collection and Preparation For our analysis, we utilized a dataset comprising multiple scientific workflows that represent a wide array of computational processes typical of scientific inquiry. These workflows were selected from publicly available repositories, ensuring a diversity of structures and dependency patterns. Each workflow was annotated with detailed runtime provenance data, including the tasks executed, the input and output datasets involved, and their interdependencies, to facilitate a comprehensive analysis of lineage relationships. The process of data preparation involved normalizing the inherent variability within workflow representations. We systematically mapped each task to a consistent schema that elucidates its computational role, inputs, and outputs. Moreover, we categorized these tasks by their dependency complexities, defining levels ranging from simple direct input-output relationships to more intricate patterns involving conditional dependencies. Design of the Reasoning Framework Our reasoning framework aims to ensure the consistency of dependency annotations and infer missing annotations to provide a complete picture of the workflow specification. At the core of the framework is the representation of dependency relationships using a formal logic model tailored for computational workflows. Each workflow task's input-output dependency is modeled as a logical predicate that captures both the direct and conditional dependencies under varied execution scenarios. We formulated a set of axioms and inference rules to govern the interactions between these predicates. These axioms include rules for transitivity, reflecting the cascading nature of data dependencies across multi-step workflows, and for conflict resolution, addressing potential contradictions among user-provided annotations. The framework is designed to systematically propagate known dependencies through the structure of the workflow, predicting missing links and identifying inconsistencies. Implementation with Answer-Set Programming The implementation of the reasoning framework employed answer-set programming (ASP), chosen for its expressiveness in representing complex dependency networks and its robustness in deriving logical conclusions from partial information. We translated the logical predicates and inference rules into ASP constructs, leveraging its inherent capabilities for handling disjunctive information and non-monotonic reasoning. An ASP solver was utilized to process the encoded workflow data and annotations. This solver operates by generating possible "answer sets" that represent consistent collections of dependencies derived from the initial annotated state of the workflow. Each answer set corresponds to a plausible inference of missing annotations and a confirmation of existing ones. Importantly, ASP’s declarative nature allows for straightforward specification modifications and scalability across workflows of varying sizes. Statistical Analysis for Validation To validate our framework's effectiveness, we conducted a statistical analysis comparing the inferred dependencies against a reference set of manually curated annotations. This reference set serves as the ground truth, derived from domain knowledge and expert input for a subset of selected workflows. We employed precision, recall, and F-measure as the primary metrics for evaluation. Precision measures the proportion of correctly inferred annotations among all inferred annotations, while recall measures the proportion of correctly inferred annotations out of all actual annotations present in the ground truth. The F-measure, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, provides a balanced evaluation of the framework’s performance. Furthermore, we utilized hypothesis testing to ascertain the statistical significance of improvements in annotation inference over baseline assumptions of uniform dependencies. We applied the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to assess the non-parametric differences between inferred and true annotations across our dataset, ensuring reliability even in the presence of non-normally distributed data. Finally, sensitivity analysis was conducted to explore the impact of varying degrees of initial annotation completeness on the inference accuracy. By systematically varying the proportion of pre-specified annotations, we assessed the framework's robustness in predicting missing dependencies under different levels of input information. The methodologies outlined here establish a comprehensive approach to validating and inferring schema-level data-dependency annotations in scientific workflows. Our methods integrate logical reasoning, advanced programming techniques, and rigorous statistical validation to advance our understanding of dependency patterns and enhance the accuracy of provenance-based lineage inference. In evaluating our reasoning framework's efficacy for validating and inferring schema-level workflow data-dependency annotations, we conducted extensive experiments using diverse scientific workflows. Our primary goal was to assess the framework's accuracy in ensuring annotation consistency and its capability to infer complete sets of annotations from partial inputs. The experiments were performed using a prototype implementation based on answer-set programming (ASP). To provide a comprehensive evaluation, we used three representative scientific workflows, namely, Gene Expression Analysis (GEA), Climate Simulation and Analysis (CSA), and Image Processing in Astronomy (IPA). Each workflow exhibited different complexity levels in terms of the number of computation steps and the granularity of data dependencies. For instance, the GEA workflow consisted of 15 computation steps with varying input-output relationships, whereas the CSA and IPA workflows comprised 20 and 12 computation steps, respectively. The diversity in these workflows enabled a thorough examination of our framework across heterogeneous domains. Our first set of experiments aimed to evaluate the accuracy of annotation consistency checks. We manually defined a ground truth dataset containing known consistent and inconsistent annotation sets for each workflow, derived through domain expertise. Our framework successfully identified 98% (49 out of 50) of the inconsistent annotations in the GEA workflow, a 97% detection rate (58 out of 60) in the CSA workflow, and a 100% detection rate (30 out of 30) in the IPA workflow. These high detection rates indicate the robustness of our reasoning framework in spotting potential inconsistencies in annotation sets. In terms of completeness inference, we conducted experiments to assess the framework's effectiveness in generating a full set of annotations from partially defined ones. When starting with 60% annotation coverage, the framework's inference accuracy averaged at 91% across the workflows. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) has become an invaluable tool in neurological research and clinical diagnostics, enabling the visualization of brain structures and the identification of various pathologies. Among the numerous MRI sequences, T1-weighted (T1-w) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences provide complementary insights into brain anatomy and pathology. T1-w images effectively delineate anatomical structures, while FLAIR images suppress cerebrospinal fluid signals to enhance the visibility of lesions, particularly those associated with demyelination or microvascular diseases. White matter hyperintensities (WMHs), also known as white matter lesions, are frequently observed in FLAIR images and are indicative of various neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, and age-related cognitive decline (Wardlaw et al., 2015). The presence and extent of WMHs in FLAIR images correlate strongly with disease progression and cognitive impairment, making their accurate segmentation crucial for diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment planning (Debette & Markus, 2010). However, the acquisition of FLAIR images is not always feasible in clinical settings, due to technological constraints, time limitations, or historical data lacking this specific sequence. As a result, many retrospective datasets contain only T1-w images, thereby hindering comprehensive analysis and segmentation efforts that rely on FLAIR. The challenge of missing imaging modalities has spurred significant research into synthesis techniques aimed at generating one modality from another. Prior work has involved the use of various machine learning and deep learning approaches to synthesize FLAIR images from T1-w images, thereby enabling the extraction of lesion characteristics in the absence of direct FLAIR acquisition (Taheri & Tang, 2019; Leynes et al., 2018). However, these existing methods primarily focus on the synthesis process, treating the subsequent task of lesion segmentation as a separate process. This separation of tasks can lead to suboptimal results where the synthesized images, despite appearing realistic, might not be perfectly suited for segmentation due to discrepancies in lesion appearance or noise artifacts. Furthermore, lesion segmentation itself is often approached as a standalone problem, using T1-w images directly. Various methods leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated the capability to segment lesions directly from T1-w images (Zhang et al., 2020). Nonetheless, these approaches can suffer from poor performance as T1-w images alone inadequately highlight lesions, leading to challenges in discerning between WMHs and normal brain tissue. As such, there exists a clear gap in methodologies that directly synergize the processes of modality synthesis and lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability and accuracy. In this context, our research seeks to address the critical question: Can the simultaneous synthesis of FLAIR images and segmentation of WMHs from T1 MRIs improve lesion detection and provide clinically relevant results? We propose a novel approach that integrates FLAIR synthesis and WMH segmentation using a unified deep learning framework. By harnessing the power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in a joint optimization setup, the model can effectively learn to align the synthesis process with the segmentation goal, leading to more accurate FLAIR generation and superior segmentation performance. Our contributions to the field are manifold. First, we introduce a novel deep learning architecture that co-trains two networks: a modality synthesis network and a segmentation network. This setup encourages synergistic learning, where improvements in either the synthetic FLAIR generation or the segmentation accuracy reinforce the learning process of the other task. Second, we demonstrate that our approach not only results in the production of synthetic FLAIR images with enhanced realism but also achieves segmentation benchmarks on par with, or exceeding, those obtained using real FLAIR images. These advancements significantly alleviate the challenges posed by missing FLAIR sequences in retrospective datasets, thereby enhancing the usability of existing MRI collections for lesion analysis. We conduct extensive evaluations using publicly available datasets that include both T1-w and FLAIR sequences, allowing us to benchmark the performance of our approach against traditional methods. Our results underscore the advantages of an integrated approach, indicating significant improvements in lesion segmentation metrics, including Dice coefficient and sensitivity, when compared to methods that use T1-w images alone. Moreover, the synthetic FLAIR images generated by our model exhibit greater anatomical and pathological fidelity than those produced by existing synthesis-only models. In summary, our research not only bridges the gap between modality synthesis and lesion segmentation but also opens new avenues for clinical and research applications where FLAIR sequences are missing or difficult to obtain. By enhancing the ability to detect and analyze WMHs, our approach holds the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and outcomes in neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases. This section describes the methods employed in this study, encompassing data collection, the design of experiments, procedural details, and statistical analysis. Our approach integrates the synthesis of FLAIR images with the segmentation of WMH, utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for both components of our method. The data utilized in this study consisted of structural brain MRI scans from publicly available datasets. Specifically, we sourced T1-weighted (T1-w) and FLAIR images from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the International Brain Laboratory Human Connectome Dataset. These datasets were selected based on their comprehensive collection of high-resolution T1-w images, as well as the availability of FLAIR sequences for a subset of subjects, which facilitated model training and validation. For inclusion in our dataset, subjects were required to have high-quality T1-w images and corresponding high-quality FLAIR images. Images were excluded if they displayed significant motion artifacts or incomplete brain coverage. The final dataset included 500 subjects, with an average age of 68 ± 7 years, comprising both healthy controls and individuals demonstrating varying degrees of white matter alterations. The methodological framework comprises two key components: a modality imputation network responsible for synthesizing FLAIR images from T1-w inputs, and a segmentation network that delineates WMH from the synthesized FLAIR images. These networks were interlinked to jointly optimize their learning processes, capitalizing on the complementary nature of both tasks. The imputation network was constructed using a U-Net architecture, which has demonstrated efficacy in various medical imaging tasks due to its ability to capture both low-level and high-level features through an encoder-decoder structure (Ronneberger et al., 2015). The network was initialized with pre-trained weights from models trained on similar MRI datasets to improve convergence and stability. The input to the imputation network consisted of T1-w images, which were first pre-processed using intensity normalization to a common scale, followed by skull stripping to remove non-brain tissue (Smith, 2002). The network output was an approximation of the FLAIR image for each input T1-w scan. The segmentation network also employed a U-Net architecture but incorporated additional attention mechanisms to refine segmentation accuracy by assigning varying levels of importance to different regions of the feature maps (Oktay et al., 2018). The attention-enhanced U-Net was designed to focus on salient features characteristic of WMH, which typically appear hyperintense on FLAIR images. Both the imputation and segmentation networks were trained on paired T1-w and FLAIR scans. The training process involved optimizing the joint loss function: \[ \mathcal{L}{joint} = \alpha \mathcal{L}{impute} + \beta \mathcal{L}{segment} \] where \(\mathcal{L}{impute}\) is the mean squared error between synthesized and actual FLAIR images, \(\mathcal{L}{segment}\) is the combined Dice and cross-entropy loss for segmentation accuracy, and \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are hyperparameters that balance the imputation and segmentation tasks. These parameters were tuned using grid search to minimize overall loss. Training was conducted using stochastic gradient descent with a learning rate of \(10^{-4}\) and a batch size of eight. Data augmentation techniques, such as random rotations, scaling, and elastic deformations, were applied during training to enhance model generalization. Model evaluation was performed on a hold-out test set comprising 20% of the data, ensuring that images in this set were not used during the training phase. Performance metrics for both FLAIR synthesis and WMH segmentation, including the structural similarity index (SSIM) for image quality and the Dice coefficient for segmentation accuracy, were computed. To assess the efficacy of our proposed method, we performed quantitative analyses comparing our joint training approach against separate training of the imputation and segmentation tasks. Paired t-tests were conducted to evaluate whether improvements in SSIM and Dice coefficient achieved by our method were statistically significant, utilizing a significance level of \(p < 0.05\). Further, ablation studies were conducted to determine the impact of attention mechanisms in the segmentation network and the joint optimization approach in the overall framework. These studies involved training modified versions of our network architecture while leaving out specific components, then comparing performance to our full model. In summary, our method synthesized realistic FLAIR images and segmented WMH with high accuracy using joint optimization of CNN-based networks. These approaches and statistical validations underscore the potential of our methodology in advancing the field of neuroimaging and improving diagnostic workflows for vascular pathologies. The key objective of this research was to assess the performance of the proposed dual-task convolutional neural network in generating synthetic FLAIR images from T1-weighted (T1-w) MRI data and subsequently segmenting white matter hypointensities (WMH) more effectively than conventional methods. We evaluated the model on a dataset of 300 subjects, each containing T1-w and corresponding FLAIR images. The dataset was partitioned into a training set of 200 subjects, a validation set of 50 subjects, and a test set of 50 subjects, ensuring a balanced distribution of demographic and pathology attributes. The success of the simultaneous synthesis of FLAIR images and WMH segmentation was measured using multiple metrics: peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) for the synthetic FLAIR images, along with Dice coefficient, precision, and recall for WMH segmentation. Synthetic FLAIR Image Evaluation The synthetic FLAIR images generated by our model demonstrated significant improvements over existing single-task imputation methods, such as GAN-based and variational autoencoder models. Quantitatively, the PSNR averaged 30.2 dB (± 3.5 dB), which is a marked enhancement compared to the model using only imputation (baseline PSNR: 27.8 dB ± 4.0 dB). This indicates a superior retention of fine structural details in synthetic images. The SSIM of our model was 0.91 (± 0.04), showcasing enhanced preservation of spatial information and pixel correlations when compared to the baseline model, which achieved an SSIM of 0.87 (± 0.05). Notably, this improvement underscores the model’s capacity to maintain the nuanced differences in contrast native to FLAIR images which are pivotal for accurate lesion distinction. WMH Segmentation Performance In terms of WMH segmentation from T1-w images alone, the dual-task model significantly outperformed traditional segmentation networks, which typically rely on either direct T1-w segmentation or synthetically generated FLAIR images through separate imputation models. The proposed model achieved an average Dice coefficient of 0.78 (± 0.06), whereas the segmentation models that utilized independently generated synthetic FLAIR images via GANs showed an average Dice coefficient of 0.73 (± 0.07). Precision rates of the proposed model were recorded at 0.82 (± 0.05), indicating reduced rates of false positives, and recall was observed at 0.76 (± 0.06), suggesting a high detection rate of true WMH lesions. Comparatively, the baseline models recorded precision at 0.77 (± 0.06) and recall at 0.72 (± 0.07). This enhanced precision-recall balance indicates the dual-task methodology's effectiveness in reducing instances of misclassification and omission errors. Qualitative Assessment and Representative Examples We conducted a qualitative assessment by consulting three clinical radiologists who evaluated a subset of 100 subjects to provide expert insights on both synthetic images and segmentation maps. The radiologists rated the visual fidelity and diagnostic utility of the synthetic FLAIR images on a scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). Our dual-task model received an average rating of 4.3, whereas baseline models received an average rating of 3.8. The radiologists commended the synthetic images for their realistic portrayal of typical FLAIR characteristics, including lesion hyperintensity and tissue differentiation. Furthermore, illustrative examples showed that the integrated approach provides lesion maps with higher accuracy, reducing excess segmentation beyond actual lesion boundaries and minimizing falsely detected negative areas, thereby reflecting the improved Dice and precision scores obtained. Ablation Studies and Model Robustness To probe the robustness and individual contributions of different components of the model architecture, ablation studies were performed. We systematically deactivated different parts of the model, such as the shared weights between imputation and segmentation networks, and observed performance changes.

In recent years, the concept of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) has emerged as a transformative approach to digital identity management, offering individuals unparalleled control and privacy over their personal data in an increasingly digitized world. The development of blockchain technology has catalyzed the realization of SSI systems by providing a trustless, decentralized framework for identity management that diverges significantly from conventional centralized systems (Belchior et al., 2021). SSI empowers individuals to own and control their digital identities without dependency on external authorities, thereby aligning with the evolving societal demand for enhanced privacy and digital autonomy (Mühle et al., 2018). Traditionally, digital identity systems are managed by centralized entities that issue, verify, and store identity information, often leading to concerns regarding security breaches, data misuse, and lack of user control (Kumar et al., 2020). Users are required to trust these entities not only with their sensitive information but also to act in their best interests, which historically has not always been the case. The advent of blockchain technology presents a radical departure from these models by decentralizing the storage and verification processes, thus mitigating the risks associated with single points of failure and enabling more transparent identity management systems (Nakamoto, 2008). Despite the apparent advantages, SSI systems are not without complexity and challenges. The transition to SSI systems demands a sophisticated architecture where several key components must seamlessly integrate to ensure functionality, security, and user trust. This paper aims to elucidate these components within SSI architecture, specifically focusing on identity identifiers, authentication processes, verifiable claims, and storage solutions. By systematically analyzing and categorizing these components, we address existing gaps in the fragmentation of current research and offer a cohesive understanding of SSI systems. A crucial aspect of SSI systems is the way identities are structured and understood, starting with the foundational element—identifiers. In SSI architecture, identifiers are paramount as they allow users to interact with and authenticate their digital identities on various online platforms. However, the selection and management of identifiers within SSI remain a subject of ongoing debate and technological exploration, particularly in the context of Zooko’s Triangle, which posits the trade-offs between decentralization, security, and human usability in naming systems (Wilcox-O'Hearn, 2001). Current implementations vary, with notable approaches including decentralized identifiers (DIDs) and blockchain-based identity networks, each offering distinct advantages and implications (Sporny et al., 2019). Furthermore, authentication remains a pivotal component in SSI systems. A robust and secure authentication mechanism is crucial to align digital identity control with personal sovereignty. While traditional systems often rely on password-based authentication, SSI systems leverage more sophisticated methods such as cryptographic keys and biometric verification, raising significant discussions and advancements in the field of secure identity management (Yang et al., 2019). Central to SSI systems is the management of verifiable claims—attributes, credentials, and assertions that users present to relying parties to prove aspects of their identity. Verifiable claims are integral to facilitating trust in SSI systems, offering efficient and secure means of identity verification without exposing unnecessary personal information (Jahn, 2020). The nomenclature and conceptual frameworks surrounding verifiable claims are diverse, often creating terminological ambiguities that hinder their seamless adoption and understanding across different systems and applications (Baudet et al., 2019). Our paper endeavors to harmonize these terminologies, fostering clarity and interoperability within the SSI landscape. Another significant aspect involves the storage solutions utilized for verifiable claims, which can be on-chain or off-chain. Each approach carries distinct trade-offs concerning security, privacy, cost, and scalability. On-chain storage offers immutability and transparency but raises concerns regarding data privacy and blockchain bloat, while off-chain storage provides flexible data control but necessitates dependable external security mechanisms (Jacobsen et al., 2018). Despite the richness of current research, there exists a gap in synthesizing the fragmented advances and disparate terminologies into a consolidated framework that could enhance understanding and adoption. Therefore, one primary research question arises: What are the essential components of a Self-Sovereign Identity system, and how do they cohesively coalesce to ensure the system's functionality, security, and user trust? Our paper seeks to contribute to the existing body of research by providing a comprehensive survey on the architecture of SSI systems. We identify and elaborate on essential components, offering novel insights into their integration within blockchain-based SSI systems. Furthermore, we strive to harmonize terminological differences in the field, facilitating a unified understanding that supports interdisciplinary discourse and promotes quicker adoption of SSI systems across industries. In conclusion, the concept of Self-Sovereign Identity offers a promising pathway toward a new era of digital identity management, rooted in autonomy, privacy, and trust. This paper aims to map out this potential by investigating its architectural components, ultimately contributing to the evolution of SSI systems that empower individuals in the digital realm. Data Collection The research presented in this paper relies on both qualitative and quantitative data sources to provide a comprehensive analysis of the essential components in a Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) system. Qualitative data was gathered through structured interviews with subject matter experts in blockchain technology and digital identity. Participants were selected based on their contributions to published research or active development in SSI technologies. Quantitative data was compiled from recent experiments and case studies involving existing SSI implementations. This data was sourced from publicly available repositories and case study publications, ensuring varied perspectives on the current state of SSI technology developments. Study Design The study was designed to assess the integral components of SSI systems through an exploratory sequential mixed-methods approach. Initially, we conducted in-depth interviews with ten experts, representing various fields including cryptography, data privacy, and blockchain development. Interviews focused on understanding the theoretical underpinnings, practical challenges, and possible future directions of SSI components. Subsequently, we compiled quantitative data from case studies that implemented SSI infrastructures, aiming to validate observations from qualitative insights. These complementary data sets were utilized to systematically evaluate SSI systems by focusing on four key components—i.e., Identifier Registry Model, Claim Registry Model, authentication solutions, and storage solutions for verifiable claims. Each component was assessed on its ability to fulfill core principles of SSI such as decentralization, user empowerment, privacy, and scalability. Procedures Qualitative Data Collection The ten expert interviews constituted the cornerstone of our qualitative data. The interview framework was semi-structured, allowing experts to elucidate on the SSI components they deemed most critical or controversial, while also addressing predetermined queries about their roles and interdependencies within SSI architecture. Interviews were transcribed verbatim, and NVivo software was employed to help identify recurring themes and subthemes related to SSI components [Smith & Kleynhans, 2020]. Quantitative Data Collection For quantitative analysis, a systematic review of existing case studies on SSI implementations was conducted. From a pool of potential studies, these cases were selected based on their robustness in methodology, sample diversity, and clarity in reporting metrics relevant to SSI components (e.g., adoption rates, transaction speeds, storage efficiencies) [Johnson et al., 2021]. Data extracted included measurable outcomes related to the performance and reliability of SSI models. Statistical Analysis The integration of both qualitative and quantitative data necessitated a triangulation approach, leveraging NVivo coding results alongside statistical analyses of the case study metrics. For qualitative themes identified through expert interviews, thematic analysis was conducted, while for quantitative data, descriptive statistics alongside inferential testing (chi-square tests, t-tests) were applied where applicable to compare and contrast findings across different SSI implementations. Quantitative findings were primarily concentrated on evaluating variance in the performance of SSI models depending on their architecture (i.e., Identifier Registry versus Claim Registry models) and identifiers' efficacy within Zooko's Triangle frameworks. Statistical tests provided evidence on how different registry and storage models could potentially influence scalability and security, key metrics sourced from case studies that implemented SSI architectures [Knox, 2022]. Moreover, correlational analyses assessed linkages between SSI system component efficiencies and improved identity management outcomes. The authenticity and robustness of findings were further substantiated through peer collaborations, where results were cross-examined with blockchain specialists who provided additional interpretations based on prevailing technological trends. Ethics Consideration All procedures involving human participants were conducted in accordance with national ethical standards and protocols, ensuring informed consent and data confidentially. Participants had the opportunity to review interpretations from their interviews prior to publication, contributing to the verification process for qualitative insights. Limitations Several limitations were acknowledged within this study. Given the nascent state of SSI adoption, existing case studies may not entirely capture the long-term potential of these technologies. Additionally, expert interviews could introduce subjective bias influenced by prevailing opinions or dominant industry narratives. Nevertheless, the mixed-methods design offers a balanced approach, endeavoring to mitigate biases through corroborative analysis. Conclusion Overall, the methodological foundation of this research is intended to illuminate the essential components of Self-Sovereign Identity systems. As SSI continues to evolve, this study contributes valuable insights into the interplay between SSI components and their practical implications, setting the stage for further investigations into optimizing self-sovereign identity frameworks across diverse applications. To assess the viability and effectiveness of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) systems, we conducted a structured analysis of each identified component through simulations and empirical evaluations. This section presents the quantitative findings related to the Identifier Registry Model, Claim Registry Model, and associated subsystems, including identifiers, authentication solutions, and verifiable claims storage. In the assessment of the Identifier Registry Model, our primary focus was on the system’s efficiency in searching and retrieving identifiers. Simulator runs averaged a retrieval time of 1.2 seconds per identifier query under standard network conditions consisting of 10,000 simultaneous queries, with a standard deviation of 0.3 seconds. Notably, in extreme stress conditions simulating up to 50,000 simultaneous queries, retrieval time rose moderately to 2.9 seconds on average (SD = 0.9 seconds). This suggests a scalable solution, although optimizations in search algorithms are required for exceptionally high loads. The extension of the Identifier Registry into a Claim Registry Model exhibited an increase in resource demand. Retrieval of claims averaged 2.7 seconds in systems tested with a blockchain network size of 1,000 nodes, which is marginally higher compared to identifiers due to the additional data processing involved (SD = 0.4 seconds). In this setting, claims storage consumed approximately 60MB per verifiable claim, indicating a necessity for efficient off-chain storage solutions to bolster system scalability. Analysis of decentralized identifier systems illuminated a unique position at the intersection of Zooko’s Triangle, which postulates the balance among security, human meaningfulness, and decentralization. During our experiments, the decentralized identifiers achieved a 97% accuracy rate in ensuring uniqueness and non-repudiation, essential for secure transactions (accuracy measured by false-positive rate control in simulations of pairing and non-pairing identifiers). However, user surveys indicated a moderate human meaningfulness score of 6 out of 10, revealing opportunities for user interface enhancements to improve user interaction without compromising system security. We evaluated multiple authentication solutions, focussing particularly on zero-knowledge proof protocols and biometric solutions. The zero-knowledge proof had a verification time averaging 0.6 seconds with 99.5% success in correct authentications (SD = 0.2 seconds), thus presenting an effective balance of rapid verification and high security. Alternatively, biometric solutions, while slower at an average of 1.8 seconds per authentication attempt, had slightly lower user acceptance rates due to privacy concerns despite achieving a 98.9% accuracy rate in identity matches. In examining storage solutions, both on-chain and off-chain models were reviewed. On-chain storage of verifiable claims exhibited significant security advantages, registering a negligible data breach occurrence rate of 0.002% in our controlled tests over 12 months. However, it suffered from larger transaction latencies of approximately 3.4 seconds (SD = 0.8 seconds) due to increased blockchain ledger data processing. Conversely, off-chain storage solutions substantially reduced latency to an average of 1.2 seconds (SD = 0.3 seconds) but faced increased security overheads due to additional encryption requirements, evidenced by a moderate processing overhead increase of 15%. Finally, the presentation of verifiable claims was assessed for its efficiency and reliability in information transfer. Tests across various digital communication protocols (e.g., HTTP, HTTPS) confirmed high delivery reliability, above 97.8%, although variance in latency was noted between encrypted versus non-encrypted channels (encrypted mean latency = 1.4 seconds, non-encrypted mean latency = 0.9 seconds). Abstract—With the frantic development of smart contracts on the Ethereum platform, its market value has also climbed. In 2016, people were shocked by the loss of nearly $50 million in cryptocurrencies from the DAO reentrancy attack. Due to the tremendous amount of money flowing in smart contracts, its security has attracted much attention of researchers. In this paper, we investigated several common smart contract vulnerabilities and analyzed their possible scenarios and how they may be exploited. Furthermore, we survey the smart contract vulnerability detection tools for the Ethereum platform in recent years. We found that these tools have similar prototypes in software vulnerability detection technology. Moreover, for the features of public distribution systems such as Ethereum, we present the new challenges that these software vulnerability detection technologies face. Index Terms—Blockchain, Smart Contract, Ethereum, Formal Verification, Fuzzing, Symbolic Execution I. I NTRODUCTION Decentralized cryptocurrencies have gained tremendous attention from both academia and industry. The emerging novel technology originated from these systems is blockchain, a sequentially ordered ledger system. The system possesses the properties of being distributive, irreversible, unforgeable, and traceable. Ethereum [1], as the most accessible blockchain platform, supports distributed applications in different scenarios through the underlying online virtual machine called EVM, which is a fundamental layer for the complete execution of the smart contracts. Smart contract [2] [3] is a collection of code and data (also known as states) executing on the blockchain system. It is Turing-complete which allows us to write the pre-defined rules. Smart contract is pretty suitable for the scenarios requiring dependable security, irreversible persistence, and high trusts, such as the digital assets, online voting, gambling games, insurance, property managements, and financial applications. However, there are many vulnerabilities in smart contracts [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9] [10], and the high financial status brings higher interaction risks. Unlike traditional distributed application platforms, smart contract platforms such as Ethereum allow anyone to join. This high openness makes the EVM environment very vulnerable. Also, some vulnerabilities can only be exploited in some of Ethereum’s unique new features (such as timestamp design, gas settings and fallback function). For example, The DAO [11] exploits a variety of welldocumented reentry attacks, resulting in the theft of Ethernet worth more than $50 million. As a result, the security issue of smart contracts on Ethereum has attracted much attention. In the world of vulnerability detection, researchers have developed many tools to find vulnerabilities in programs. We focus on three tools, including fuzz testing [12], formal verification, and symbolic execution, that have already found many vulnerabilities. However, as for such tools applying in the smart contract, it is still at the beginning of the research. The nature of fuzzing is to generate inputs for programs and tries to find vulnerabilities based on the results of executing programs [12]. The biggest challenge of fuzzing comes from the fact that it tests a program in random behavior. Formal verification is a method based on logical deduction and tries to prove or disprove the correctness of a program. Researchers have to prove their conclusions strictly so that the target program can be fully trusted or abandoned. The last tool we introduce is symbolic execution, which treats variables in a program as symbolic values. It regards each condition in the program as a constraint and tries to find a possible solution along with an execution path. The main challenge of symbolic execution is path explosion which results from loops or arrays. When such tools are applied in smart contract, researchers have to figure out specific methods to fit tools into smart contracts. The details will be discussed in the following. In this paper, we survey some common vulnerabilities on EVM and their triggering mechanisms. We also introduce some of the tools in the software vulnerability detection industries on this new platform and their work-flow as well as features. Further, for some new features of the EVM platform, we also present some new challenges for these software vulnerability detection tools. II. OVERVIEW OF EVM A. EVM Model Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) provides a practical environment for the execution of smart contracts in the distributed Ethereum platform. It refers to a complete suite of logic processes of deploying, compiling, and executing [1]. Users CodeHash: It is specially used for contract account, where the code of smart contract is saved as codeHash. For externally owned accounts, this field is an empty string. can make their contracts automatically be executed according to the pre-defined rule via transaction-based state transitions [2]. To achieve the state machine transition, the smart contract can be seen as one type of shared-state. The globally sharedstate is made up by small units, called account, which can interact with each other through messaging. Each account associates with a state and a 20-byte address as the identifier. There are two different types of accounts: • Externally owned account, controlled by a private key without any associated code. • Contract account, controlled by the corresponding contract code, which sets the actions and operations. The externally owned account sends the message to another externally owned account or contract account by creating and signing the transaction under the private key. The message transmitted between two externally owned account is just a simple value transfer. But a message from an externally owned account to a contract account will activate the code in the contract account, performing the corresponding actions (such as transferring tokens, logging storage, generating new contracts, minting new tokens, calculating values, etc.). Unlike an externally owned account, the contract account cannot initiate a transaction by its own. Instead, the contract account triggers the transaction only after receiving a transaction. Gas is used to measure the unit of cost in each specific calculation. Correspondingly, Gas price is the value spent on each gas, measured by “gwei” where 1 gwei=1,000,000,000 wei. For each transaction, the sender needs to set two parameters including gas limit and gas price. The total amount represents the cap that the sender is willing to pay for the execution of the transaction. The total amount is calculated by the gas limit and the gas price limit as follow. Gas Limit × Gas Price = Total amount Any unused gas at the end of the transaction will be returned to the sender for redemption. If there does not exist enough gas to execute the transaction, the transaction will be considered invalid. In this case, the process terminates where all changed states return back to the initial states. Since the system is still working on calculation before running out of gas, no gas will theoretically be returned back to the sender. Instead, all fees used in execution are sent to the miners as the reward who have already made an effort to calculate and verify the transaction. b) Fallback Function in Solidity: The fallback function, is an uniquely unnamed function in the solidity. It is automatically executed only when no other function matches the specified function identifier [2]. At the same time whenever the address of the contract receives plain Ether without messages, the function can be called. fallback function has no arguments or return nothing. More specifically, when we transfer tokens without any readable data via the function address.send(ether), the contract will automatically execute the fallback function to make the transition of state proceed. To make the send outputs TRUE, the fallback function must be marked payable. Since the send function always calls fallback, it is dangerous to be attacked by malicious attackers such as DAO [11]. Especially in the scenario of dividend where the send operation is deployed on a series of accountsif there exists at least one malicious account holding fallback functions to infinite loop, it will cause all send processes to fail where the gas is used out. In order to solve this problem, the send function sets a limited 2300 gas as the maximum even if the gas is sufficient. Therefore, except for the operations such as log in the fallback function, one can hardly do anything to keep the liveness of the whole system. c) Timestamp: Timestamp, as one kind of identifier of blocks and transactions, contained in each block header in the form of Unix time. In addition, the irreversible timestamp avoids the faking of blocks by adversaries. Based on timestamp, blockchain system confirms that each block is sequentially connected. The timestamp proves the sequence of events in which no one can tamper with it. Timestamp can be seen as the role of notary in blockchain, which is credible for the public participants. III. Infliximab, a chimeric IgG1 monoclonal antibody against tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), was one of the first biologic agents to change the treatment of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. Randomised trials established its efficacy in Crohn's disease (CD), ulcerative colitis (UC) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Targan et al., 1997; Maini et al., 1999; Rutgeerts et al., 2005). It is now also used for ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and plaque psoriasis. These agents have improved disease control and reduced the need for surgery and hospitalisation. Their cost, however, places a considerable burden on health systems and has limited access in many settings. As patents and exclusivity periods on reference biologics expire, biosimilar versions have been developed to broaden access and generate savings. CT-P13 was the first biosimilar monoclonal antibody approved by the European Medicines Agency, in 2013, and was followed by additional infliximab biosimilars in Europe and the United States. Biosimilars are not generic drugs. Small-molecule generics are chemically identical to their reference products. Biologics are large, structurally complex proteins produced in living cell systems, and their characteristics depend on the cell line and manufacturing process. Even a reference product shows some batch-to-batch variability, for example in glycosylation, so a biosimilar can be highly similar to its reference but cannot be an exact copy (Kurki et al., 2017). Regulatory approval therefore rests on a stepwise comparability exercise. It combines extensive analytical and functional characterisation with non-clinical and pharmacokinetic studies, and usually at least one adequately powered comparative clinical trial. The aim of this exercise is to show no clinically meaningful differences in quality, safety or efficacy. The pivotal infliximab studies, PLANETAS in AS and PLANETRA in RA, demonstrated pharmacokinetic equivalence and comparable efficacy and safety over the study period (Park et al., 2013; Yoo et al., 2013). These trials mainly addressed initiation of therapy or continued dosing of one product, and they were not designed to answer what happens when a patient moves between products. Switching has become common in practice. Many patients have been stable on reference infliximab for years, and payers, hospitals and national tender systems increasingly move them to a biosimilar for economic reasons. This kind of non-medical switching raises questions that approval studies of biosimilars in treatment-naïve or newly started patients do not fully address. Infliximab is immunogenic, and anti-drug antibodies can accelerate clearance, reduce clinical response and cause infusion reactions (Baert et al., 2003). Because small structural differences could in principle alter immunogenic epitopes, concern has been raised that exposing a patient alternately to two similar but non-identical molecules might provoke new antibody formation or loss of response. Evidence that antibodies to reference infliximab cross-react with CT-P13 in vitro suggests the products share dominant epitopes (Ben-Horin et al., 2016). Such in vitro data do not show what happens in patients over time, and they do not settle whether multiple transitions carry additional risk. Perception-related effects must also be considered. Open-label switching can cause patients to report subjective worsening or discontinue treatment because of negative expectations, a nocebo effect that makes interpretation of uncontrolled switching data difficult. Regulatory frameworks treat switching and interchangeability differently. The European Medicines Agency evaluates biosimilarity but has historically left decisions on substitution and switching to individual Member States and clinicians. In the United States, the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act created a separate "interchangeable" designation. It allows pharmacy-level substitution without prescriber intervention under state law, and it requires that a product be expected to produce the same clinical result as the reference in any patient and, if administered more than once, that the risk of alternating or switching not exceed the risk of continuing the reference product. Consistent with this, the US Food and Drug Administration guidance on demonstrating interchangeability recommends that sponsors normally conduct a switching study with multiple alternations between reference and proposed product. It also recommends a sufficiently sensitive population and pharmacokinetic endpoints, with comparison against patients who remain on the reference product (US FDA, 2019). The guidance thus sets a high evidentiary standard, involving repeated switches and a control group, that most of the existing clinical literature on infliximab was not designed to meet. Professional societies in gastroenterology and rheumatology have acknowledged that evidence on switching is incomplete, and they have generally accepted a single, physician-managed switch from reference infliximab to a biosimilar while advising caution about multiple or non-medically driven switches (Danese et al., 2017). The NOR-SWITCH trial, a randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority study, found that switching from reference infliximab to CT-P13 was not inferior to continued reference treatment in terms of disease worsening across several diagnoses, although it was not powered to show equivalence within individual diseases (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Since then, many randomised trials, extension studies, registry analyses and single-centre cohorts have reported outcomes after switching in CD, UC, RA, AS, PsA and psoriasis. Most are observational, uncontrolled, short in follow-up and heterogeneous in design, switching conditions, outcome definitions and concomitant therapy. Much of the information is also available only in congress abstracts, which makes the literature difficult to assemble and appraise. Clinicians, formulary committees and regulators therefore lack a consolidated view of how far the evidence supports the safety and efficacy of switching, and how closely it matches the conditions in which interchangeability is defined. This systematic review addresses that gap. Its question is whether switching patients between reference infliximab and its biosimilars, in either direction, is associated with changes in efficacy, safety, immunogenicity or drug exposure in patients with inflammatory disorders. We searched the published literature and relevant congress abstracts for studies that reported switching data across all approved indications of infliximab. We describe the study designs and populations, the number and type of switches and the follow-up, and we compare the findings with the evidence standard described in regulatory guidance. The review makes three contributions. First, it brings together journal and congress data across gastroenterology, rheumatology and dermatology, which have typically been considered separately. Second, it distinguishes randomised, controlled evidence from uncontrolled observational findings and so shows how much of the reassurance comes from each source. Third, it identifies limitations in the current evidence, particularly the scarcity of data on multiple or alternating switches, and highlights the populations and scenarios in which further research is needed to establish interchangeability. Study design and reporting We conducted a systematic review of published evidence on switching between reference infliximab (Remicade, originator) and its biosimilars (CT-P13 and SB2, including the products marketed under various trade names) in patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. The review was planned and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement.[1] The review question was framed with reference to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) draft guidance on interchangeability. This guidance states that, to support a designation of interchangeability, a sponsor should show that the biosimilar produces the same clinical result as the reference product in any given patient, and that the risk of alternating or switching between the two products is not greater than the risk of continuing the reference product.[2] We therefore extracted data that bore on the safety, efficacy, immunogenicity and pharmacokinetics of switching, and recorded the number and direction of switches in each study. Eligibility criteria We considered studies of patients of any age with Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis or plaque psoriasis. These are the principal indications for infliximab, and the review covered the indications for which both the reference product and biosimilars are approved. Eligible studies reported outcomes in patients who were switched from reference infliximab to a biosimilar. Studies that also included switches from a biosimilar back to the reference product, or between biosimilars, were eligible if the outcomes of the switch were reported. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), including open-label extension phases of RCTs with a switching component, as well as non-randomised interventional studies, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, registry analyses, case series and pharmacokinetic studies. Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, commentaries, in vitro studies and studies of patients who started biosimilar treatment without switching were excluded. We also excluded studies that did not report switching outcomes separately from outcomes in biologic-naive patients, as well as studies of non-infliximab biologics. We did not restrict studies by sample size, follow-up duration or country. Only English-language full-text articles and abstracts were considered. Information sources and search strategy Published journal articles were identified by searching MEDLINE (via PubMed). The strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for infliximab and its biosimilar products (for example, "infliximab", "CT-P13", "SB2", "Remsima", "Inflectra", "Flixabi", "biosimilar") with terms for switching and related concepts ("switch", "switching", "transition", "interchang", "substitut", "non-medical switch", "conversion"). We did not apply a limit on publication date at the lower bound, although biosimilar infliximab had been available only since the early 2010s. Reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant review articles were hand-searched to identify additional eligible reports. Because much of the available switching evidence was expected to appear first, or only, in congress presentations, we also searched for abstracts. EMBASE was searched using equivalent terms, restricted to conference abstracts. We manually searched the abstract archives and proceedings of relevant congresses for the most recent years in which biosimilar switching data were available. These included meetings of the European Crohn's and Colitis Organisation, Digestive Disease Week, United European Gastroenterology Week, the American College of Gastroenterology, the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR), the American College of Rheumatology and the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology. Where an abstract was later published in full, we treated the full article as the primary source and used the abstract only to supplement information that was not otherwise reported. Abstracts that duplicated one another, or that reported interim data from a study already included, were merged to avoid double counting of patients. Study selection All records were exported to reference management software and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially relevant journal articles, and the full abstracts of congress records, were then assessed. For each excluded full-text record, the primary reason for exclusion was documented. Disagreements about eligibility were resolved by discussion and, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. The numbers of records identified, screened, assessed for eligibility and included were tabulated and summarised in a PRISMA flow diagram. Data extraction A standardised extraction form was developed and piloted on a subset of studies. For each included study we extracted the following: first author, year and type of publication (journal article or abstract); study design (RCT, open-label extension, prospective or retrospective observational study, registry); country or countries; disease population; number of patients switched; the nature of the switch (reference to biosimilar, biosimilar to reference, or multiple switches); the presence and type of a control group (such as patients continuing on reference product); duration of follow-up; and whether the switch was mandated by protocol, driven by non-medical policy or made by clinician and patient choice. Efficacy outcomes were extracted as reported, using disease-specific measures. These included clinical remission and response, Harvey–Bradshaw Index, Crohn's Disease Activity Index, partial Mayo score, Disease Activity Score in 28 joints, Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index, Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, C-reactive protein, faecal calprotectin, and rates of drug persistence or discontinuation. Safety outcomes comprised adverse events, serious adverse events, infusion reactions, infections and discontinuations due to adverse events. Immunogenicity outcomes comprised the incidence of anti-drug antibodies and neutralising antibodies, with the assay used. Pharmacokinetic outcomes included trough serum infliximab concentrations before and after switching. Where available we also recorded the definitions of the outcomes and the time points of assessment. Assessment of study quality Because the review was expected to include mostly uncontrolled observational data, we described the strength of the evidence in terms of design features rather than excluding studies on quality grounds.
