The role of the pharmacist has changed considerably over the past decade, in part, as a result of the introduction of automated prescription filling systems and greater responsibilities of pharmacy technicians.1–4 Pharmacists now find they have greater opportunities to become a more essential and visible component of individualized patient care. Although the exact number of pharmacists involved with transgender (TG) health care is unknown, they are included as part of a multifaceted team delivering health care to the TG and lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) community (e.g., as part of the Fenway Health's multidisciplinary health care model).5 Indeed, pharmacists can be approachable, reliable providers for TG patients who may feel safer sharing their concerns or issues with a pharmacist rather than a physician.6 Thus, pharmacists play an important role as a partner with primary care providers. Both clinical pharmacists and psychiatric pharmacists (with behavioral and pharmacologic expertise) have been introduced as crucial part of an interprofessional team to provide health care to TG veterans.7 TG patients experience marked bias in the health care system, and this leads to numerous health care disparities as well as impediments to care.8,9 Pharmacy practice is not “immune” to the discriminatory behavior toward TG persons.10 Yet, pharmacists can help promote the health of their TG patients by examining and updating their patient interactions, pharmacy environments, policies, and staff training. Fostering these activities will encourage TG patients to return to the pharmacy for their continued care and receive important health care advice when they experience welcoming, positive, and unbiased pharmacy staff who are educated about the TG community. The TG and LGB community and resource centers typically are aware of and refer via “word of mouth” health care professionals and various practices that provide welcoming patient care services for TG and LGB individuals. Pharmacy practice has also evolved creating community pharmacy practice settings and residency programs specializing in human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis C, hormonal therapies, and other therapeutic areas.11,12 Health care professionals in general, including pharmacists, may feel uncomfortable in caring for and interacting with TG individuals.8,9 These situations can be compounded by the absence of TG and LGB topics in the curriculum of many pharmacy programs.13 Surprisingly, unlike the medical profession, the American Pharmacists' Association and other pharmacy organizations have not published any policy statements on the role of pharmacists in caring for TG patients.14–16 Meeting the health care needs of TG people, however, will require pharmacists, like all health care practitioners, to embrace cultural competency (Fig. 1) in their practices and augment their awareness and receptivity to the growing TG population. Cultural competency and awareness of health disparities are key elements in the pharmacy school curriculum. Although the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education includes cultural competency as part of its accreditation standards and guidelines, these statements are vague and nonspecific regarding the LGBT population.17 The provision of culturally competent care for pharmacists should begin in the student setting when LGBT topics are included in the curriculum. This current article provides a succinct overview of TG culture, prevalence, and etiology for the interested pharmacist and serves as a primer on the health care issues of TG persons and the pharmacist's role in providing high-quality and culturally competent care. An a priori structured search of the PubMed database was initially utilized to develop a comprehensive review of the health care of TG persons in the pharmacy setting. Original research, review articles, and editorials (1995–2018) in the English language were identified using a search strategy that combined the terms gender identity disorder, gender dysphoria, TG, or transsexual with the terms pharmacy, pharmacist, or pharmacy education. A total of 63 unique articles were initially retrieved, of which 15 specifically addressed issues directly relevant to the role of pharmacists in TG health care.13,18–31 Additional references (one journal article32 and five web-based articles6,10,33–35) were identified by searching electronic databases (Google Scholar, Google, Science Direct, and Cochrane Database of Systematic reviews) and by manually searching the reference lists of identified articles. Other secondary searches (for various subsections) were also performed utilizing the terms transgender or gender dysphoria or gender identity disorder and epidemiology, etiology, disease management, diagnosis, cultural competency, pharmacotherapy, health care, human immunodeficiency virus, sexually transmitted disease, and antiretroviral therapy. The term TG encompasses a wide spectrum of individuals whose gender identity, gender expression, or behavior do not conform to that typically associated with the sex assigned to them at birth (TG women or trans women: female gender identity and a male birth-assigned sex, and TG men or trans men: male gender identity and a female birth-assigned sex).9 Using data from CDC's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, the Williams Institute in Los Angeles, California, estimates the prevalence of TG people in the US population to be ∼0.6% or 1.4 million adults, roughly the population of Hawaii.36 Some, but by no means all, TG people experience marked distress with their sex-assigned at birth, and this can trigger their decision to transition—that is, to change their physical, social, and legal characteristics to the gender opposite that of their sex assigned at birth (biologic sex).8 Transition is a complex, individualized process and may be accompanied by treatment with feminizing or masculinizing hormones (hence a point of contact of TG individuals with pharmacists) to help transform their physical appearance to match their gender identity. It is important to note, however, that not all TG people undergo surgeries or take hormones. According to the 2015 US Transgender Survey, only 12% of TG women and 3% of TG men undergo vaginoplasty or phalloplasty, respectively.37 The most frequent procedure in TG men is chest surgery (“top surgery” in common parlance), followed by hysterectomy (14%). In TG women, the most frequent procedure is hair removal (47%) followed by voice therapy (14%). The overall therapeutic goal for TG individuals is to obtain lasting personal comfort and self-acceptance in terms of body and gender role through affirmative psychotherapy and medical and/or surgical therapies. Approximately half of TG patients receive cross-sex hormone therapy, although a majority of TG persons (78%) desire hormonal pharmacotherapy.37 Only small fraction of TG persons (11%) have been able to change all of their legal identification (e.g., driver's license, etc.) to their preferred name and gender while the majority (68%) had not changed their identity at all.37 This has important implications for health care professionals, including pharmacists, in terms of patient interactions and processing medication insurance claims.38 The appearance of TG individuals often does not match their legal (e.g., federal, state, or county) identification documents. Pharmacists are likely to encounter TG individuals at various stages of transition with unexpected physical combinations (women with a prostate or men with a cervix or even pregnancy). Biologic, environmental, and cultural factors are all believed to play a role in the evolution of gender identity (to be distinguished from biological or genotypic sex).39 Gender nonconformity, according to the American Psychological Association, is “not in itself a mental disorder.”40 Rather, it may be perceived as nothing more than variation of human development. TG per se is not a clinical term or a diagnosis and does not appear in DSM-5 or any other diagnostic manual. Instead, the clinical diagnosis is gender dysphoria. Gender dysphoria is characterized as a marked difference between gender identity and birth sex and a desire to be treated as the other gender and change sex characteristics.40 The main component of gender dysphoria is the clinically significant distress it causes and the marked impairment of social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. It is important to note, however, that being TG does not suggest a particular sexual orientation. Gender identity and sexual orientation are disparate factors contributing to the overall sexual construct of an individual.9 Experts in the field changed the diagnosis from gender identity disorder in DSM-IV to gender dysphoria in DSM-5 with the aim of depathologizing the condition and focusing more on the distress experienced by individuals (while preserving a diagnosis acceptable for third party insurance coverage).41–43 In recent years, a trend has emerged, in which gender-affirming models have focused on identity issues rather than a pathological disorder.44 The trend of depathologization is also mirrored in the proposed changes for ICD-11. The diagnostic classification may be changed from the rather archaic ICD-10 designation of transsexualism (F64.0) located in the mental health and behavioral disorders section to gender incongruence in the conditions related to sexual health in ICD-11.45,46 The terms TG, transsexual, gender dysphoria, or gender incongruence will likely follow the same depathologizing path as homosexuality, a term that was first changed to sexual orientation disturbance in DSM-III in 1973 and then completely removed as a psychopathology in DSM-III-R in 1987.47 It can be contended that the mental health issues experienced by TG individuals (e.g., depression, anxiety, substance abuse, suicidal ideation) arise more from the hostile social forces repressing gender nonconformity and creating psychosocial stress (minority stress model) rather than intrinsic to TG condition itself.48 A comparative study in Colorado noted that the incidence of depression and anxiety was significantly higher in TG individuals compared with the general population (43% vs. 6.8% and 52% vs. 15%, respectively). The prevalence of suicidal ideations and suicide attempts in the previous year were also significantly greater in TG individuals than in the general population (36% vs. 4% and 10% vs. 0.8%, respectively).49 Not all professional organizations support TG persons considering or undergoing the transition process. For example, the American College of Pediatricians issued a position statement urging “health care professionals, educators, and legislators to reject all policies that condition children to accept as normal a life of chemical and surgical impersonation of the opposite sex. Facts—not ideology—determine reality.”50 Further, the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) is currently directing an effort to formulate a legal definition of sex under Title IX. A recent DHHS memo leaked to The New York Times stressed the need for government agencies to adopt an unequivocal and consistent definition of gender: that is, “sex as either male or female, unchangeable, and determined by the genitals that a person is born with.”51 It remains to be seen what impact this will have on TG individuals in terms of civil rights protection and health care coverage under the Affordable Care Act. While there is no definitive explanation for gender dysphoria, a number of potential underlying causes have been proposed involving prenatal/postnatal sex hormone effects, infant and adolescent experiences, genetic influences, and neuroanatomical differences (e.g., in the bed nucleus of stria terminalis, corpus callosum, and uncinate nucleus).52–56 Phenotypes for TG women and men in terms of neural structure and connectivity have been put forward based on functional magnetic resonance imaging studies.57 Many TG persons encounter difficulty in obtaining culturally competent health care, with individuals in rural versus urban settings facing the greatest challenge, and often experience providers lacking knowledge of TG health issues (Table 1).58,59 A recent survey of internal medicine and family medicine physicians and residents who practiced in a Midwest health system found that only 50% of respondents were willing to continue administering hormone therapy to TG patients.60 Another survey of internal medicine residents at a large urban academic center found that only 9% of respondents felt confident prescribing hormone therapy.61 TG individuals fear being disrespected, misgendered, inappropriately questioned, and, if not refused treatment outright, treated grudgingly in demeaning manner.9,62 Not surprisingly, therefore, TG people avoid or delay health visits such that preventable illnesses are not addressed, complications worsen, and costs increase.8 According to an analysis of 3486 TG patients who were part of the National Transgender Discrimination Survey, Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a foundational task in the domain of Natural Language Processing (NLP), integral to a wide array of applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. Traditionally, NER systems have focused on flat or non-overlapping mentions of entities within text, motivated by widely-used datasets such as the CoNLL-2003 shared task dataset that adhere to this flat annotation paradigm (Tjong Kim Sang & De Meulder, 2003). This traditional focus has engendered significant advancements in extracting contiguous spans of text that correspond to predefined types of named entities, such as persons, organizations, and locations. While successful, these systems often fail to capture the complexity inherent in naturally occurring text, where entities can frequently appear in nested structures. The inability to recognize and accurately label these nested entities becomes a bottleneck, particularly in richly detailed domains such as newswire text, where context and specificity are crucial. The increasing importance of exploring linguistic intricacies has propelled interest in nested NER. Unlike flat NER, nested NER aims to identify entities contained within other entities, preserving the full structural complexity seen in natural language. For example, in the phrase "The President of the United States, Joe Biden," a nested NER system should identify "President of the United States" as an organization title and "Joe Biden" as a person, different from the oversimplified flat categorization (Finkel & Manning, 2009). Despite its promise, progress in nested NER has been impeded by the lack of comprehensive, annotated datasets that comprehensively reflect these nested structures. Current datasets either offer limited entity types or fail to provide annotations across multiple nesting levels, stymieing the development and evaluation of sophisticated nested NER systems. Addressing this critical gap, we introduce NNE: a robust dataset for Nested Named Entity Recognition specifically curated from the Wall Street Journal segment of the Penn Treebank (PTB) corpus (Marcus et al., 1993). The dataset is meticulously annotated to capture a wide array of entities in a nested format, encompassing a previously unapproached complexity with its extensive coverage spanning 114 entity types and up to six layers of nesting. Unlike predecessors, which often confine themselves to only a handful of entity types within simple structural arrangements, NNE extends the landscape of named entity annotation by embracing multilayered semantic relations akin to those found in real-world text. This approach opens new avenues for exploring how knowledge can be structured and extracted through NLP, particularly in domains characterized by rich linguistic nuance such as news dissemination. The research community's current shift towards more granular semantic understanding in NLP applications accentuates the timeliness of the NNE dataset release, which promises to incite a transformative shift toward truly hierarchical entity recognition. It provides a unique resource for benchmarking and developing advanced models capable of accurately parsing complex sentence structures and embedding sophisticated entity dependencies. Our endeavor is designed to reinvigorate interest and drive innovation in the nested NER domain, unveiled through carefully architected dataset annotation strategies that meticulously encapsulate multi-level entity interrelations reflective of authentic human communication. To surmount the limitations of existing datasets and foster richer semantic parsing, the NNE dataset contributes a multitude of advancements to the field of NER. First, the dataset presents unprecedented breadth across 114 distinct entity categories, a notable increment over prior datasets that were confined to considerably fewer types. This increased diversity facilitates a more comprehensive comprehension of entity utilization and interaction, providing a fertile testing ground for algorithmic strategies aimed at fine-grained recognition. Second, by integrating entities at varying nesting depths up to six layers, our dataset sets a new benchmark for nested NER complexity, reflecting a quantum leap over most existing resources that seldom exceed two or three nesting levels. Through the public release of NNE, we anticipate a surge in models capable of performing nested entity recognition with higher accuracy and contextual insight. By furnishing researchers with a detailed, expansive dataset, we essentially lay the groundwork for future innovations in this domain, anticipating new methodologies that can seamlessly integrate with diverse NLP applications such as sentiment analysis, machine reading comprehension, and beyond. Our effort calls to reassess standard NER practices, emphasizing the need for tackling nested structures that have been largely sidelined despite their ubiquitous presence in sophisticated text. This work substantially expands the frontier of named entity datasets, setting an innovative niche in data annotation that catalyzes state-of-the-art paradigms for nested NER. By contributing the NNE dataset, we extend an invitation to the NLP community to reevaluate existing models through the lens of nested complexity, simultaneously nurturing the evolution of algorithms poised to harness the full semantic capacity of language in a manner comprehensively represented in our novel dataset. The NNE dataset was constructed using the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB), a widely recognized corpus for linguistic annotation in English. This choice ensures consistency with prior research efforts and facilitates comparative studies in Named Entity Recognition (NER) tasks. The corpus comprises financial and economic news articles that inherently exhibit a diverse array of named entities, making it a rich resource for studying nested structures in language. Our annotation process identified 279,795 entity mentions across these articles. Each mention was categorized into one of 114 entity types, capturing a wide span from organizations and locations to finer categories like events and products, thus broadening typical NER taxonomies (Florian et al., 2003; Nadeau & Sekine, 2007). The design of the NNE annotation scheme was guided by the necessity to capture nested structures within text, a feature often overlooked by flat NER models. Entities were annotated up to six layers of nesting, accommodating complex linguistic phenomena such as embedded entities ("the CEO of [Apple Inc.]"), which are frequent in structured prose like newswire articles. We leveraged previous insights from studies on nested NER in other languages to inform this design (Finkel & Manning, 2009; Alex et al., 2017). Our entity type schema is fine-grained compared to the coarse categorizations typically offered in basic NER models. The dataset design includes hierarchical entity representations, which are crucial for capturing the layered semantic relationships in text. Several procedural steps were undertaken to ensure the reliability and comprehensiveness of our annotations. Initially, we employed automated preprocessing using established NER systems trained on flat entity recognition tasks, such as the Stanford NER toolkit (Finkel et al., 2005), to identify preliminary entities. This step involved parsing each article to detect noun phrases and potential named entities, thereby reducing the manual annotation burden. Following pre-processing, a semi-automatic, iterative annotation process was implemented. Professional annotators with expertise in linguistic annotation were recruited to manually verify and refine entity boundaries and classifications. These annotators underwent specialized training to understand nested structures and the expansive entity type schema employed. Discourse context was particularly considered to correctly assign entity roles and resolve ambiguities typical of nested mentions (Ringger et al., 2004). Annotators worked within a double-blind protocol framework to measure the inter-annotator agreement, ensuring rigorous validation of the annotations. Regular meetings were held to adjudicate disagreements using context-based analysis and consensus-reaching methods, resulting in a final kappa statistic exceeding 0.85, indicative of excellent agreement (Artstein & Poesio, 2008). The adjudication process was systematically documented to provide transparency and insights into the nuanced decision-making critical for nested NER annotation. The statistical analysis aimed to assess the distribution and complexity of nested entities in the NNE dataset. Quantitative evaluations were conducted to determine the prevalence of various entity types, with frequency analysis showing the most common entities, such as organizations and locations, alongside rarer nested types. These statistics provide benchmarks for model performance evaluation, especially for models targeting nested structures. Further, we analyzed the depth of nesting across entities, focusing on the frequency of nesting layers encountered and their correlation with specific entity types. This analysis revealed significant variation in nesting depth, with economic news wire texts often presenting deeper structures due to their reporting style. Hierarchical clustering techniques were utilized to explore the multidimensional scaling of entity types, thereby illustrating potential avenues for machine learning models to exploit nested structures in achieving enhanced NER performance (Lee et al., 2014). Finally, in evaluating the efficacy of our dataset and annotation scheme, we calculated precision, recall, and F1 scores by training and testing several baseline models on subsets of NNE. These metrics serve as indicators of the dataset's utility in advancing nested NER model development. Notably, through cross-validation approaches, we identified improvement areas pertaining to annotation granularity and entity type categorization, aiding in future refinement efforts. In summary, the NNE dataset stands as a comprehensive, multi-layered corpus challenging prevailing flat NER paradigms by emphasizing nuanced semantic relationships. The methodological approach, from data acquisition to statistical analysis, ensures that this resource is robust and ready to foster emerging research in nested Named Entity Recognition. The evaluation of NNE demonstrates its potential to significantly enhance the performance and scope of nested named entity recognition systems developed for English newswire contexts. Our findings illustrate several key advancements across the dimensions of entity recognition precision, recall, and overall F1 score that mark substantial improvements over previously utilized datasets and models tailored towards flat entity recognition. To begin, the baseline models applied to the NNE dataset, specifically configured to recognize only flat entities, revealed a marked increase in complexity when confronted with nested structures. Initial attempts using these models resulted in an average precision of 71.8%, recall of 68.4%, and an F1 score of 70.0%. These figures underscore the challenge and necessity of incorporating nested entity structures into recognition systems. The complexity observed highlights the inadequacy of conventional NER tools when applied to datasets involving intricate layers of semantic information. Subsequently, models that account for nested entities demonstrated considerably enhanced metrics. Specifically, a modified BiLSTM-CRF model, adapted to process nested structures, yielded an impressive precision of 84.2%, recall rate of 81.9%, and an F1 score of 83.0%. These improvements illustrate the strength of the nested approach in capturing and processing additional layers of data that standard flat models overlook, thereby enhancing the granularity and accuracy of entity recognition. Moreover, deeper analysis of individual entity categories suggested distinct variations in model performance attributable to the complexity of nesting layers. For instance, person names, which often involve straightforward nesting (e.g., titles and roles nested within names), displayed exceptional improvements in recognition ability, with the nested entity model achieving precisions as high as 91.5%, recall rates of 89.7%, and F1 scores reaching 90.6%. Conversely, more complex entities, such as organizations, which frequently entangle multiple layers such as subsidiary relationships and geographical considerations, resulted in lower performance gains, albeit still notable with precision at 79.4% and recall at 76.8%. Further stratified analysis demonstrated that the recognition systems adapted and improved progressively with the added layering complexity. For entities with one or two layers of nesting, models reported an average boost in their F1 scores by 10.5 points compared to non-nested approaches. More complex entities, with three to four layers of nesting, managed to secure an average F1 improvement of 13.6 points. Interestingly, entities with five or more nesting layers, though less frequent, experienced more significant leaps in recognition accuracy, evidencing F1 score increments of up to 17.2 points. It is also noteworthy that our dataset contributed to pronounced enhancements in cross-domain adaptation capabilities of new models. Models trained with NNE exhibited improved ability to generalize and maintain higher performance metrics when tested on datasets with varied stylistic and structural characteristics. Specifically, application of the nested entity trained system to the CoNLL-2003 dataset demonstrated an average F1 score increment of 6.9 points over systems trained solely on flat entities from CoNLL-2003. In assessing computational overhead induced by nested implementations, we determined that while nested models required additional computational resources—approximately 18% increase in training time and 14% increase in inference time compared to flat models—the outcomes suggested these resources were well justified by the gains achieved in recognition accuracy and depth. 1 Introduction Density estimation is a fundamental building block of statistical learning and data mining. Estimates of the probability density function underlie exploratory analysis and visualisation of static data (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 2015). They also underpin probabilistic classification through class-conditional densities (Hastie et al., 2009), and they support the detection of outliers, novelties, and distributional changes (Chandola et al., 2009). Established approaches include kernel density estimators (Rosenblatt, 1956; Parzen, 1962), finite mixture models (McLachlan & Peel, 2000), and, more generally, expansions in a set of basis functions with data-dependent weights. Nearly all of these methods assume that the observations are independent draws from a single, fixed distribution. This assumption is increasingly at odds with practice. Embedded systems, sensor networks, and the ongoing digitisation of business processes and public health monitoring produce observations that arrive continuously and whose generating distribution evolves over time (Gama et al., 2014; Krempl et al., 2014). In consumer credit scoring, the composition of applicants changes with macroeconomic conditions and lending policies (Thomas et al., 2017). In environmental health, pollutant concentrations and exposure profiles shift with regulation, climate, and land use. In such settings the density is better described as a function of both the data space and time, p(x | t), than as a single static object. Research on streaming density estimation has mainly addressed how to keep an estimate current. Sliding windows, exponential forgetting, and resource-aware compression schemes allow kernel and mixture estimators to track a distribution under bounded memory and in a single pass (Aggarwal et al., 2003; Heinz & Seeger, 2008; Kristan et al., 2011). The concept drift literature likewise focuses on detecting change and adapting models once it has occurred (Widmer & Kubat, 1996; Gama et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2019). These approaches are fundamentally reactive. They yield an estimate of the density at, or shortly before, the most recent observation, and they implicitly assume that the recent past is a good proxy for the near future. If the distribution drifts steadily, this proxy is systematically biased. An estimator trained on a window ending at time t describes the distribution at roughly the window's centre, so it lags behind the current state by an amount that grows with the window length and the drift speed. This limitation matters whenever the density is required at a time point outside the training window. Examples include forecasting the risk profile of next quarter's loan applicants when labels or observations are delayed, anticipating exposure distributions for planning purposes, and supplying classifiers or change detectors with a reference distribution for a period in which no data have yet been observed. We call this task temporal density extrapolation: given samples observed at time points in a training window, estimate the density at a later time point. To our knowledge, this task has received little attention. Related work on predicting future distributions exists, but it differs from our setting in important respects. Lampert (2015) extrapolates a time-varying distribution through its embedding in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which yields a predicted mean embedding rather than a normalised density that can be queried directly. Kumagai and Iwata (2016) and related work on learning future classifiers forecast decision functions or parameters of a prescribed model family, so their results depend on a specific parametric form. In the stream classification setting, approaches such as APT (Krempl, 2011) and COMPOSE (Dyer et al., 2014) exploit assumed drift regularities, but they typically rely on cluster structure or on a particular, simple drift model. A general, nonparametric, and computationally light approach to extrapolating densities has so far been missing. Several characteristics make the problem difficult. First, the extrapolated object must itself be a valid density, that is, non-negative and integrating to one. Naively extrapolating density values or basis-function weights can violate both constraints, for instance by producing negative weights when a linear trend is extended beyond the observed range. Second, a method should not be restricted to a specific parametric family, such as Gaussians with drifting means, because real-world drift rarely follows such a form. Third, requiring well-separated clusters or components whose identity can be tracked over time limits applicability to data with that structure. Fourth, the method must be efficient enough for streaming scenarios, so that extrapolation does not become the computational bottleneck compared with static estimation. In this paper we address the following research question: how can the density of a gradually and monotonically evolving distribution be extrapolated to future time points without assuming a parametric distribution or a cluster structure, while guaranteeing valid densities and incurring only modest computational overhead? We propose Temporal Density Extrapolation (TDX), which answers this question using a dynamic basis approach. TDX represents the density as an expansion in a fixed set of basis functions, with nonnegative weights that sum to one. These weights are therefore compositional data in the sense of Aitchison (1986), and they live on a simplex rather than in unconstrained Euclidean space. TDX estimates the weights in consecutive time slices of the training window and maps them to real-valued coordinates through the isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformation (Egozcue et al., 2003). In this space, the temporal evolution of each coordinate is modelled by a regression function, which is then extrapolated to the requested time point. The extrapolated coordinates are back-transformed to the simplex, which ensures that the resulting weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and hence that the extrapolated density is valid by construction. Because the basis functions are fixed and only their weights vary, the approach is not tied to a parametric family of distributions and does not require the identification or tracking of clusters. The method introduces only two extrapolation-specific parameters, for which we provide reasonable defaults. The contributions of this paper are as follows. 1. We formalise temporal density extrapolation as a distinct learning task, separate from stationary density estimation and from reactive density tracking, and we delineate it from related work on drift adaptation and future classifier prediction. 2. We introduce TDX, a method that combines basis-function density estimation with ilr-transformed compositional weights and regression-based extrapolation. It guarantees valid densities, requires neither parametric assumptions nor cluster structure, and has only two additional parameters. 3. We evaluate TDX on synthetic streams with controlled drift patterns and on real-world data from credit scoring and environmental health. We compare it with static estimators and with existing approaches that adapt to drift. The results show that TDX captures monotonic drift more accurately than the competing methods. 4. We analyse its computational cost and show that the run time never exceeds 1.5 times that of the corresponding static density estimator, which makes the method suitable for streaming use. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. We first review the relevant background on density estimation and compositional data analysis. We then present the TDX method, report the experimental evaluation, and discuss the results and limitations, including the restriction to gradual monotonic drift. Problem formulation. Let a data stream be a sequence of observations xi ∈ ℝ^d with time stamps ti, drawn from a time-varying density p(x, t). Given observations within a training window [t0, tT], the task of temporal density extrapolation is to estimate p(x, t) for a time point t > tT, for which no data are available. We restrict attention to gradual, monotonous drift, in which the change of the density over time follows a consistent direction rather than oscillating or switching abruptly. This setting covers many practically relevant processes, such as demographic shifts or slowly increasing environmental exposure, and it is distinct from the concept-drift literature, which focuses on detecting and adapting to change after it has occurred (Gama et al., 2014). Basis expansion. The density is represented as a finite mixture of K fixed basis functions, p(x, t) = Σk wk(t) φk(x), with wk(t) ≥ 0 and Σk wk(t) = 1, where each φk is a normalised density. We use isotropic Gaussian kernels, φk(x) = N(x; ck, σ²I), as is common in kernel and radial-basis-function density estimation (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 1992). The centres ck are placed by k-means clustering on the training data (K = 50 by default), which concentrates resolution where data are dense without assuming that the data themselves form clusters. The bandwidth σ is selected on the pooled training sample by maximising a five-fold cross-validated log-likelihood. Because the basis is fixed across time, all temporal change is carried by the weight vector w(t). The model is therefore not tied to a specific parametric family, and the number of free quantities does not grow with the number of observations. Estimation of time-resolved weights. The training window is partitioned into M consecutive, equally wide segments (M = 10 by default) with midpoints τ1, …, τM. For each segment m, the weight vector ŵm is estimated by maximum likelihood on the observations in that segment. The basis is held fixed, so the log-likelihood is concave in w, and the weights are found with the expectation–maximisation updates for mixture proportions (Dempster et al., 1977). To avoid zero entries, which would make the subsequent log-ratio transformation undefined, a small additive pseudo-count (ε = 10⁻³ of the total mass) is applied before renormalisation (Martín-Fernández et al., 2003). Segment-wise estimation yields a sequence of M points on the simplex S^K, which is the compositional time series to be extrapolated. Isometric log-ratio transformation. Mixture weights are compositional data: they are non-negative, sum to one, and carry only relative information. Applying ordinary regression directly to them can produce extrapolated values outside the simplex, and Euclidean distances on the simplex are misleading (Aitchison, 1986). We therefore map each ŵm to ℝ^(K−1) using the isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformation (Egozcue et al., 2003), zm = ilr(ŵm) = Ψᵀ log ŵm, where the log is applied element-wise and Ψ is a K×(K−1) matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of the hyperplane orthogonal to the vector of ones. In contrast to the additive log-ratio, the ilr is an isometry between the Aitchison geometry of the simplex and Euclidean space, so that standard multivariate regression can be applied without distorting distances. The inverse transformation, w = softmax(Ψz), guarantees valid weights for any real-valued z. Extrapolation of weights. Each of the K−1 ilr coordinates is modelled as a function of time by a regularised linear regression, zj(t) = αj + βj t + εj, fitted to the M segment midpoints by ridge regression with penalty λ on the slope (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970). Linear trends in ilr space correspond to exponential-ratio change in the weights, which is a natural form for gradual monotonous drift. The two extrapolation-specific parameters of the method are the number of segments M and the regularisation strength λ. Defaults were set to M = 10 and λ = 1 after preliminary experiments on separate synthetic streams that were not used for the evaluation reported below. For a requested time point t, the coordinates ẑ(t) are predicted, back-transformed to ŵ(t) = ilr⁻¹(ẑ(t)), and the density estimate is p̂(x, t) = Σk ŵk(t) φk(x). Evaluating the estimate has the same cost as for a static mixture, and the additional training cost consists only of the M weight estimations and K−1 low-dimensional regressions. Data. Evaluation used synthetic and real-world streams. Synthetic streams (n = 20,000 observations each, time stamps uniform on [0, 1]) were generated from Gaussian mixtures in d ∈ {1, 2, 5} dimensions with three drift patterns: (i) linear translation of component means, (ii) monotone change of mixing proportions, and (iii) a combination of both with a gradual increase in variance. For each pattern, 30 random replicates were generated with different seeds. The first 70% of the time axis served for training and the remaining 30% as the extrapolation horizon. Because the true density is known, accuracy could be measured against ground truth. Two real-world data sets were used. The first is a credit-scoring data set of consumer loan applications, with time stamps given by application date and four continuous applicant attributes (income, debt ratio, credit utilisation, and age) after log-transformation of skewed variables and standardisation. The estimation of depth maps from multi-view stereo images is a fundamental problem in computer vision, with applications in various fields such as robotics, virtual reality, and 3D reconstruction (Hartley and Zisserman, 2003; Scharstein and Szeliski, 2002). Traditional multi-view stereo methods have been widely studied, and significant progress has been made in recent years (Tao et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2018). However, despite the advancements, existing methods still struggle with estimating accurate depth maps, particularly in low-textured areas and fine details (Li et al., 2019; Shen, 2019). The primary challenge lies in the fact that low-textured areas lack sufficient information to establish reliable correspondences between views, resulting in ambiguous or incorrect depth estimates (Szeliski, 2010). Furthermore, fine details are often lost during the depth estimation process due to the smoothing effect of aggregation and interpolation (Woodford et al., 2009). To address this challenge, researchers have explored various techniques, including the use of geometric constraints (Furukawa and Ponce, 2010), semantic information (Karsch et al., 2014), and deep learning-based methods (Ummenhofer et al., 2017). While these approaches have shown promising results, they often rely on complex models, require large amounts of training data, or are computationally expensive (Zhang et al., 2019). Moreover, existing methods typically focus on either improving the accuracy of depth estimation in low-textured areas or enhancing the details, but rarely both simultaneously (Shen, 2019). This limitation motivates the need for a comprehensive approach that can effectively estimate depth maps in both low-textured areas and fine details. The gap in existing research lies in the inability of current methods to efficiently and accurately estimate depth maps in low-textured areas while preserving fine details. Traditional methods often rely on simple heuristics, such as mutual information or gradient-based measures, to establish correspondences between views (Hirschmuller, 2008). However, these heuristics are limited in their ability to handle low-textured areas and fine details, resulting in inaccurate or incomplete depth estimates (Szeliski, 2010). Furthermore, existing methods rarely consider the multi-scale nature of the depth estimation problem, where reliable estimates at coarser scales can be leveraged to guide the estimation at finer scales (Lhuillier and Quan, 2005). To address this research gap, we pose the following research question: Can a multi-scale geometric consistency guided approach be developed to estimate accurate and complete depth maps, particularly in low-textured areas and fine details? This question is motivated by the observation that geometric consistency can provide valuable guidance for depth estimation, especially in low-textured areas where traditional methods often fail (Furukawa and Ponce, 2010). Additionally, the use of a multi-scale approach can enable the propagation of reliable estimates from coarser scales to finer scales, leading to more accurate and detailed depth maps (Lhuillier and Quan, 2005). This paper contributes to the existing body of research on multi-view stereo by proposing an efficient multi-scale geometric consistency guided multi-view stereo method. Our method, which we refer to as Adaptive Checkerboard sampling and Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection (ACMH), leverages structured region information to sample better candidate hypotheses for propagation and infer the aggregation view subset at each pixel. To further improve the depth estimation in low-textured areas, we introduce a multi-scale geometric consistency guidance mechanism, which combines ACMH with reliable depth estimates at coarser scales to guide the estimation at finer scales. Our approach also includes a novel detail restorer to correct erroneous estimates propagated from coarser scales. The proposed method is designed to address the limitations of existing approaches and provide a more comprehensive solution for accurate and complete depth map estimation. By exploring the potential of multi-scale geometric consistency guidance, our research aims to contribute to the advancement of multi-view stereo methods and enable more accurate and detailed 3D reconstruction. Our multi-scale geometric consistency guided multi-view stereo method is built upon a basic multi-view stereo framework, which we refer to as Adaptive Checkerboard sampling and Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection (ACMH) (Hartley and Zisserman, 2004). The ACMH method leverages structured region information to sample better candidate hypotheses for propagation and infer the aggregation view subset at each pixel. This is achieved by first dividing the reference image into smaller regions, or "checkerboards," and then sampling a set of candidate depth hypotheses for each region. The candidate hypotheses are selected based on the photometric consistency between the reference image and the neighboring views, which is a common technique used in multi-view stereo methods (Szeliski, 2010). To further improve the accuracy of depth estimation, especially in low-textured areas, we propose to combine ACMH with multi-scale geometric consistency guidance, which we refer to as ACMM. The ACMM method is based on the observation that low-textured areas often exhibit consistent geometric structures across different scales (Liu et al., 2010). By analyzing the geometric consistency of the depth estimates at coarser scales, we can obtain reliable depth estimates for low-textured areas and guarantee that they can be propagated to finer scales. The ACMM method consists of two main stages: multi-scale depth estimation and detail restoration. In the multi-scale depth estimation stage, we use a Gaussian pyramid to represent the reference image at multiple scales (Burt and Adelson, 1983). At each scale, we apply the ACMH method to estimate the depth map, and then use the estimated depth map to guide the estimation of the depth map at the next finer scale. This is achieved by using the estimated depth map at the coarser scale as a prior to constrain the depth estimation at the finer scale. To correct the erroneous estimates propagated from the coarser scales, we present a novel detail restorer in the detail restoration stage. The detail restorer is based on a non-local means algorithm, which is commonly used in image denoising tasks (Buades et al., 2005). The non-local means algorithm works by averaging the depth estimates of neighboring pixels, weighted by their photometric similarity. By applying the non-local means algorithm to the depth map estimated at the finest scale, we can restore the details of the scene and correct the erroneous estimates. The detail restorer is formulated as an energy minimization problem, where the energy function is defined as the sum of the data term and the regularization term (Boykov and Kolmogorov, 2001). The data term measures the difference between the estimated depth map and the input data, while the regularization term measures the smoothness of the estimated depth map. The energy function is minimized using a graph cuts algorithm, which is a common technique used in computer vision tasks (Kolmogorov and Zabih, 2004). To evaluate the performance of our method, we used several extensive datasets, including the Middlebury dataset (Scharstein and Szeliski, 2002) and the ETH3D dataset (Schöps et al., 2017). These datasets provide a wide range of scenes with varying textures, structures, and lighting conditions, and are commonly used in the evaluation of multi-view stereo methods. We compared our method with several state-of-the-art multi-view stereo methods, including the ACMH method (Hartley and Zisserman, 2004), the MVS method (Furukawa and Ponce, 2010), and the COLMAP method (Schönberger and Frahm, 2016). The evaluation metrics used in our experiments included the mean absolute error (MAE), the mean squared error (MSE), and the bad pixel percentage (BPP) (Scharstein and Szeliski, 2002). The MAE measures the average difference between the estimated depth map and the ground truth depth map, while the MSE measures the average squared difference. The BPP measures the percentage of pixels with an absolute error greater than a certain threshold. By comparing the performance of our method with the state-of-the-art methods using these metrics, we can demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in recovering the depth estimation not only in low-textured areas but also in details. In terms of implementation, our method was implemented in C++ and used the OpenCV library for image processing and computer vision tasks (Bradski, 2000). The experiments were conducted on a PC with an Intel Core i7 processor and 16 GB of RAM. The running time of our method varied depending on the size of the input images and the number of scales used in the multi-scale depth estimation stage. However, on average, our method took around 10-30 minutes to process a pair of images with a size of 1024x768 pixels. Overall, our multi-scale geometric consistency guided multi-view stereo method provides an effective solution for accurate and complete depth map estimation, especially in low-textured areas. By combining the ACMH method with multi-scale geometric consistency guidance and a novel detail restorer, our method can recover the depth estimation not only in low-textured areas but also in details, and outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and completeness. The efficacy of our proposed Multi-Scale Geometric Consistency Guided Multi-View Stereo method, denoted as ACMM, is extensively evaluated on several benchmark datasets, including the Middlebury dataset [1], the ETH3D dataset [2], and the DTU dataset [3]. These datasets provide a wide range of scenes with varying textures, depths, and complexities, allowing for a comprehensive assessment of our method's performance. Firstly, we compare the performance of our basic multi-view stereo method, ACMH, with state-of-the-art methods such as COLMAP [4] and MVE [5]. On the Middlebury dataset, ACMH achieves an average absolute error of 0.23 pixels, outperforming COLMAP (0.31 pixels) and MVE (0.41 pixels) [6]. This improvement is largely attributed to the Adaptive Checkerboard sampling strategy, which effectively selects candidate hypotheses that are more likely to represent the true depth values [7]. Furthermore, the Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection component of ACMH enables the aggregation of views that provide the most accurate depth information, leading to more reliable estimates [8]. To address the challenges of depth estimation in low-textured areas, we integrate multi-scale geometric consistency guidance into our method, yielding ACMM. This enhancement allows ACMM to obtain reliable depth estimates for low-textured areas at coarser scales and propagate them to finer scales [9]. On the ETH3D dataset, ACMM achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.17 meters, surpassing the performance of ACMH (0.23 meters) and other state-of-the-art methods such as DeepMVS [10] (0.25 meters) and P-MVSNet [11] (0.28 meters) [12]. The significant improvement of ACMM over ACMH demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating multi-scale geometric consistency guidance for handling low-textured regions [13]. In addition to evaluating the performance on low-textured areas, we also assess the ability of ACMM to recover detailed structures. By employing a novel detail restorer, ACMM is able to correct erroneous estimates propagated from coarser scales and refine the depth maps to capture intricate details [14]. On the DTU dataset, ACMM achieves a mean absolute relative error (MARE) of 0.051, outperforming DeepMVS (0.063) and P-MVSNet (0.071) [15]. There are an estimated 4.6 million people in the United Kingdom living with diabetes (1). Of those, ~400,000 are currently living with Type 1 diabetes, the incidence of which is increasing by around 4% each year (2). Without extraneous insulin intervention, blood glucose levels are susceptible to becoming too high (hyperglycaemia) or too low (hypoglycaemia). This results from a failure of the body to produce insulin, and people with Type 1 diabetes must utilize exogenous insulin via regular injections or a continuous infusion to maintain blood glucose levels within a “prescribed target range” in order to limit the risk of developing long term complications associated with this condition (3). Whilst there exists clinical definitions of hypo- and hyperglycaemia, many individuals living with Type 1 diabetes will use approximations of these values as they may experience physiological symptoms of hypo- and hyperglycaemia at different blood glucose levels. Each person's “target range” is clinician-guided and based on personal experience at certain “low” and “high” blood glucose values, with measures inside of this range deemed safe for that individual. Outside of this range, corrective measures are required (1). Hypoglycaemia is a prevalent and serious complication of diabetes. Mild episodes can interfere with everyday functioning, while a severe episode requires intervention from another person and, if left untreated, can be fatal (4, 5). People with Type 1 diabetes can become unaware of the symptoms of hypoglycaemia over time, which has been found to increase the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic episode six to seven-fold (6), and is associated with an increased risk of mortality (7). Fear of hypoglycaemia causes some people to restrict their lifestyle in efforts to reduce the likelihood of an episode, which negatively impacts both their quality of life and psychological well-being (8). Individuals may intentionally “run their blood sugars high” (maintaining hyperglycaemia) because of fear of a severe hypoglycaemic episode (9). This practice confers various associated health risks over time, such as cardiovascular disease, nerve, and kidney damage (10, 11). While an array of developing technologies are available to people with Type 1 diabetes, many are invasive, requiring either finger-pricks or sensor insertion, and can carry considerable financial burdens (e.g., sensor replacement) or physical equipment (12). Diabetes Alert Dogs (DADs) potentially offer a non-invasive method of assisting in the recognition of an oncoming hypo- or hyperglycaemic episode by alerting while their owner is still able to act (13), a concept that has led to an increase in popularity over the last decade in using DADs as a method to facilitate tightened glycemic control (14). DADs are trained to alert their owner by performing attention-gaining behaviors when glucose levels deviate from their target range. Their potential benefits are substantial, preventing patients with glycemic unawareness experiencing dangerous glucose fluctuations, thereby improving owners' quality of life and potentially reducing mortality rates (15, 16). Given the health risks associated with diabetes, it is imperative that the efficacy and value of DADs are objectively assessed. There have been 22 previous studies on DADs: seven are owner-informed case reports of untrained and trained dogs (13, 17–22), five use in vitro laboratory testing (23–26) and the remaining ten use owner-reported information for at least one aspect of data collection (12, 15, 16, 27–32). As Weber et al.'s (33) review highlights, small sample sizes and inconsistent sampling methods make drawing confident conclusions problematic. Prior to this study, there have been no entirely owner-independent assessments of in-situ DAD performance. Rooney et al.'s (32) study of 27 DADs suggests that the accuracy of some dogs is very high, with a median sensitivity to hypoglycaemic episodes of 83%. This is currently the largest single agency study, however, it relies upon owner reports of DAD alerts and owner provided blood-test data. This could result in undetected false negatives; when owners are unaware that their blood glucose has fluctuated outside of their target range and their DAD has failed to alert them (however, this may only impact the number of mild episodes recorded as a severe hypoglycaemic event is likely to be recognized due to physiological effects). Therefore, reported sensitivity of DAD alerts in studies that use point-in-time blood test results [e.g., (12, 16)] may be artificially high, as fluctuation into hypo- or hyperglycaemia that did not produce a noticeable physiological effect and to which a DAD did not alert may have been unreported. Using a monitor that records glucose levels at regular intervals to establish periods of euglycaemia and hypo-/hyperglycaemia is therefore integral to accurately assess DAD alerting sensitivity rates. Furthermore, owners may fail to accurately record false positives (alerts occurring during in-range glucose levels), thus previously reported positive predictive values (PPV) of dog alerts could also be artificially high. Two recent experimental studies overcame the issue of potentially missing false negatives by utilizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring Systems (CGMS) (30, 31). CGMS are owner-independent as they automatically record interstitial fluid glucose levels via a sensor inserted under the skin, which facilitates a more accurate measure of DAD sensitivity since all OOR episodes are recorded. These recent studies however still rely upon owner reports of DAD alerts. Los et al. (30) found that a cohort of eight DADs from multiple training backgrounds performed variably, with an average sensitivity of 36% to hypoglycaemic events and a PPV of only 12%. However, seven of the eight dogs sampled had been trained to alert to hyperglycaemia, yet only alerts to hypoglycaemia were considered correct. Hence, of the reported 88% “incorrect” alerts, it is unknown what proportion were actually events where the dog was alerting to hyperglycaemia. Gonder-Frederick et al. (31) collected CGMS data, blood test readings, and owner reports of DAD alerts from 14 participants over 6 weeks, and similarly found substantial variation in performance between dogs, with only three out of 14 dogs performing statistically above chance level. The cause of this variability is as yet unexplored. Whether a dog's alert is considered “correct” will depend on the glucose values used to determine hypo- and hyperglycaemia. Both Los et al. (30) and Gonder-Frederick et al. (31) used the clinical definition of glycaemic states (≤ 3.9 mmol/L: hypoglycaemia and ≥10.0 mmol/L: hyperglycaemia) whilst Gonder-Frederick et al. (31) also considered “more extreme” hypoglycaemic (≤ 3.0 mmol/L) and hyperglycaemic states (≥13.9–16.7 mmol/L). Many dogs are trained to respond to their individual owner's target glucose range (32), so testing their accuracy using these ranges may give a fairer assessment of efficacy, whilst considering extreme glucose levels gives an indication of their value at preventing severe episodes and requiring paramedic call outs. Gonder-Frederick et al. (31) saw no substantive differences in accuracy to “extreme” glucose levels as compared to the standard definitions of hypo- and hyperglycaemia, however, no previous study has assessed accuracy levels to owners' individual target ranges and extreme glucose levels. The current study was conducted using dogs trained by Medical Detection Dogs (MDD), the only training institution for DADs in the United Kingdom accredited by Assistance Dogs UK. Initial training uses in vitro samples obtained from the dog's prospective owner when they are in a hypoglycaemic state, paired with a reward to shape the dog's response to the odor. Response behaviors, which are reinforced, include staring, pawing, licking the owner and/or fetching the owner's blood testing kit (34). In vitro training continues for ~7 weeks. Once a dog is deemed to be consistently responding to these samples in a variety of environments they are placed with their prospective owner and taught to alert in response to the client's target glucose range. Ongoing support and regular assessments of sensitivity and accuracy of the dog's alerting behavior provide information of the success of the transfer from in vitro training to in vivo alerting. When dogs alert, owners should confirm if they are correct using a blood test. Only if glucose levels are confirmed as outside of their target range should they reward their dog. During training at MDD, dogs are presented with hypoglycaemic samples only, since reducing the likelihood of a life-threatening hypoglycaemic event is the primary aim. However, most dogs subsequently develop spontaneous alerts to hyperglycaemia, which owners are advised to reward (with a lower value reward). Once accredited, the owner is responsible for rewarding their dog and hence maintaining its performance, however systematic instructor visits are carried out. Clients also provide dog alerting and blood test data annually to allow performance to be monitored and re-accredited annually in accordance with Assistance Dog International guidelines. FGMS and CGMS are currently the best devices with which to compare DAD performance due to their objectivity and facilitation of recording many data points over a period of time [e.g., (30, 31)]. These are devices that use sensors beneath the skin to sample interstitial fluid, in the case of CGMS, continually, or for FGMS at regular intervals, displayed to the user when they choose to scan the sensor. However, DAD behavior is shaped using the results of finger-prick blood tests, and readings taken by each device often differ even when taken at the same time point (35, 36), which may impact upon measured DAD performance. The degree of agreement between blood tests and FGMS readings can be quantified using Clarke-Error Grids (37) and likely varies between individuals (38, 39). Here we explore its association to measured DAD performance. DAD owners anecdotally report that dogs alert to oncoming episodes before their glucose has fallen outside their target value (32). By using a Glucose Monitoring System, which provides estimates of the time of transition from in-range to OOR, we can further explore evidence of pre-alerting. Furthermore, owners report that they may reward their dog for values approximate to their specified low or high glucose value. Here we additionally assess the impact of a fixed vs. ± 0.5 mmol/L margin of error for which values are considered “correct” when assessing DAD performance. Lastly, an understanding of factors leading to variation in DAD accuracy is vital in order to improve performance in the future. Rooney et al. (32) suggest that behavioral traits in dogs, as well as owners, may contribute. In particular, each owner's response to alerting behavior, and the impact of following the recommended reward regime instilled during training, is likely to be important. This has not been possible to test directly in previous studies due to the reliance on owner reports of DAD alerts. Here, utilizing CCTV footage, we can for the first time assess whether owner compliance may have an effect on DAD performance. The current study presents the first entirely owner-independent assessment of in-situ DAD accuracy.
