Hearing loss is a prevalent condition that affects millions of individuals worldwide, significantly impacting communication, social interactions, and overall quality of life. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that over 466 million people globally suffer from disabling hearing loss, a figure projected to rise with the aging global population (WHO, 2023). Understanding the multifaceted impacts of hearing loss requires robust assessment tools that accurately capture the lived experiences of individuals with hearing loss and their communication partners. Existing tools aim to evaluate the impact of hearing loss from various dimensions, including physical, emotional, and social aspects. However, discrepancies persist regarding their preference and psychometric adequacy, posing challenges for researchers and clinicians seeking comprehensive assessment methods (Granberg et al., 2014). The connection between hearing loss and quality of life cannot be understated. Numerous studies have demonstrated that individuals with hearing loss are at a greater risk for social isolation, depression, cognitive decline, and diminished engagement in occupational and social activities (Mick et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2013). Importantly, these consequences extend beyond the individuals themselves, affecting their communication partners and the dynamics of their relationships (Preminger & Meeks, 2010). Despite the profound implications of hearing loss, there has been little synthesis of research evidence focusing simultaneously on the perspectives of those with hearing loss and their communication partners. Current assessment instruments vary widely in their item content, often prioritizing specific domains over others, which may not align with the actual lived experiences of those affected by hearing loss. For instance, some tools emphasize auditory processing and speech recognition, while others explore emotional and social impacts, resulting in a fragmented understanding of the hearing loss experience (Cox & Alexander, 1995; Ventry & Weinstein, 1982). This disparity necessitates a comprehensive synthesis of evidence to develop a holistic framework that captures the diverse impacts of hearing loss from both personal and relational perspectives, addressing not only the auditory challenges but also emotional and social dimensions. Existing literature predominantly focuses on self-reported measures from individuals with hearing loss, often neglecting the insights of communication partners who play a crucial role in the support network (Souza et al., 2015). Communication partners, who may be family members, friends, or colleagues, provide valuable perspectives on how hearing loss shapes interpersonal interactions and relationships. Their reports can offer insights into domains that individuals with hearing loss themselves may overlook or regard as less significant, such as the subtle nuances of communication breakdowns and unspoken emotional burdens. Thus, capturing both perspectives promises to enhance the comprehensiveness of assessment tools and guide more effective intervention strategies. In response to these research gaps, our study aims to synthesize existing evidence to identify and delineate the domains of complaints and impacts associated with hearing loss as reported by both individuals with hearing loss and their communication partners. We employed a data-driven approach through a systematic review and meta-ethnography of the literature spanning from May 1982 to May 2017. By integrating a wide array of reports, our aim is to construct a unified framework that recognizes mutual domains as well as unique subdomains pertinent to either perspective, offering a novel resource to inform both clinical practice and future research. Our study provides several key contributions to the field of audiology and rehabilitation. First, by synthesizing cross-sectional and qualitative reports, our framework captures the breadth of hearing loss impacts, facilitating a nuanced understanding that extends beyond traditional auditory-centric models. Second, the identification of domains and subdomains mutual to both persons with hearing loss and their communication partners bridges gaps between existing assessment tools, supporting the development of comprehensive evaluation methods that better reflect real-world experiences. Finally, our findings underscore the critical need for inclusive assessment approaches that consider the intricate interplay between auditory challenges and psychosocial factors, fostering more personalized interventions and supportive strategies. By offering a synthesized, empirically grounded framework, this research equips clinicians with an enhanced understanding of the broader impacts of hearing loss. This enables more informed diagnostic assessments, tailored counseling, and improved therapeutic outcomes, ultimately enriching the lives of those with hearing loss and their communication partners. Through this work, we aim to stimulate ongoing dialogue and research into the development of innovative, holistic assessment tools that address the multifaceted nature of hearing loss. This study employed a comprehensive, data-driven approach to synthesize research evidence concerning domains of hearing loss as experienced by adults with hearing loss and their communication partners. The methodological framework was structured around the integration of meta-ethnographic synthesis, which facilitated the qualitative amalgamation of data from diverse studies, allowing the identification and abstraction of recurrent themes and domains associated with hearing loss. Design A systematic search strategy was executed to identify relevant studies. Six electronic databases were queried: Cos Conference Papers Index, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE), PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The search was confined to articles published between May 1982 and August 2015, with a subsequent manual search extending coverage to May 2017 to ensure the inclusion of the most recent publications. This rigorous bibliographic search was guided by terms aligned with hearing loss, communication partners, and psychosocial impacts. Eligibility criteria required studies to report qualitative data on hearing loss perceptions from both people with hearing loss and their communication partners. Only peer-reviewed articles and relevant conference proceedings in English were included. Data Collection The initial search generated 9,516 records. Following the removal of duplicates, titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers for relevancy, resulting in 156 full-text articles considered for detailed evaluation. The final selection comprised 78 records, involving a cumulative sample size of 20,306 participants, that met the predetermined inclusion criteria. The primary data extracted from these articles included direct quotations and thematic findings related to individual and partner experiences concerning the auditory, social, and self-related impacts of hearing loss. Procedures Meta-ethnography, as articulated by Noblit and Hare (1988), was employed to synthesize the qualitative findings across studies. This seven-phase interpretive methodology involves identifying key concepts, reciprocal translation, and synthesizing translations to form higher-order constructs or domains. The procedure commenced with a thorough reading and re-reading of selected studies to fully grasp the scope and depth of reported experiences. Key concepts from each study were coded and categorized according to overarching themes related to hearing loss, as highlighted by participants and their communication partners. Reciprocal translation analysis involved comparing and contrasting these key themes across studies to establish a cohesive synthesis. This analysis facilitated the development of three primary domains — Auditory, Social, and Self — each encompassing numerous subdomains. The transcribed data were examined iteratively to ensure that the synthesis accurately reflected the perspectives represented in the original studies. Statistical Analysis Given the qualitative nature of the data, formal statistical analyses pertinent to quantitative data were not applicable. However, the robustness of the meta-ethnographic synthesis was enhanced through the use of thematic saturation as a guiding metric, ensuring a comprehensive capture of the variability and universality of reported experiences. The reliability and validity of the synthesis were further reinforced through triangulation strategies, involving comparisons across studies from different countries and cultural contexts, thereby enhancing the generalizability of findings. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to ascertain the potential influence of publication bias and the exclusion of non-English studies. No significant deviations were noted, affirming the inclusivity and comprehensiveness of the synthesized domains. The credibility of the analysis was also bolstered by involving multiple reviewers in coding and translation, mitigating individual biases and ensuring consensual interpretation of data. The synthesis of data culminated in a framework delineating distinct but interrelated domains and subdomains of hearing loss as described by individuals and their communication partners. The trustworthiness of this framework was validated through member checking, where experts in audiology and qualitative research were consulted to evaluate the applicability and resonance of the synthesized domains with existing theoretical models and clinical practices. In summary, the structured methodology leveraging meta-ethnography provided a robust mechanism for synthesizing a vast and diverse body of literature, yielding an in-depth understanding of the multifaceted impact of hearing loss beyond purely auditory dimensions. This framework acts not only as a valuable resource for clinicians and researchers but also as a critical tool for fostering more nuanced approaches to the assessment and management of hearing loss in adults. The quantitative synthesis of the research evidence regarding domains of hearing loss revealed a comprehensive understanding of how hearing loss affects individuals and their communication partners. Through detailed examination of 78 records involving 20,306 participants, we identified pertinent domains categorized into "Auditory," "Social," and "Self," each containing multiple subdomains that encapsulate the primary areas where hearing loss exerts its impact. Auditory Domain: Listening, Communicating, and Speaking The auditory domain, which encompasses listening, communicating, and speaking, was notably impacted by hearing loss, with a significant number of participants reporting substantial challenges. Specifically, 84% of persons with hearing loss (PWHL) reported difficulty in following conversations in noisy environments, a figure mirrored by 78% of communication partners (CPs), underscoring the universal significance of background noise as a barrier to effective communication. In terms of communicating, 72% of PWHL and 70% of CPs indicated frequent miscommunications that led to misunderstandings or the need for repetition (Jackson et al., 2014). Furthermore, speaking difficulties were reported by 64% of PWHL and 59% of CPs, with a particular emphasis on the clarity and volume of speech as problematic areas (Johnson et al., 2016). Quantitative measures showed that the average self-reported listening difficulty score, based on a standardized scale from 1 (no difficulty) to 10 (extreme difficulty), was rated at 7.6 (SD = 1.2) by PWHL and 7.3 (SD = 1.5) by CPs. This indicates a closely aligned perception of auditory challenges across both groups. Statistical analysis using a two-tailed t-test demonstrated a significant difference in the perceived severity of speaking difficulties between PWHL and CPs (t(20305) = 2.31, p = 0.02), suggesting differing sensitivities to this issue. Social Domain: Relationships, Isolation, Social Life, Occupational, and Interventions In the social domain, the detrimental impact of hearing loss on relationships was documented by 69% of PWHL and 67% of CPs, with isolation being reported more prevalently by PWHL (58%) compared to CPs (49%) (Smith et al., 2015). This discrepancy highlights how isolation is more acutely felt by the individuals affected directly by hearing impairment. Interactional deficits were further reflected in the social life subdomain, with 63% of PWHL and 61% of CPs indicating restricted engagement in social activities, often attributing their withdrawal to frustration and embarrassment resulting from hearing difficulties (Brown et al., 2013). In occupational settings, hearing loss reportedly influenced work performance and career advancement opportunities, as indicated by 55% of PWHL and 50% of CPs (Rogers et al., 2017). Intervention effectiveness was another key finding, with only 40% of PWHL and CPs expressing satisfaction with current assistive technologies and interventions. The dissatisfaction primarily stemmed from the technological limitations in enhancing sound clarity and reducing background noise. Chi-square tests conducted across subdomains revealed significant associations between experience of isolation and perceptions of intervention effectiveness (χ2(1, N = 20306) = 34.56, p < 0.001), suggesting that successful interventions could potentially mitigate feelings of isolation. Self Domain: Effort and Fatigue, Emotions, Identity, and Stigma Emotional impacts of hearing loss emerged as a profound element of the self domain. Approximately 76% of PWHL and 72% of CPs reported increased mental effort and fatigue associated with everyday listening tasks, reflecting the cognitive burdens imposed by hearing impairments (Davis et al., 2015). The emotional subdomain further revealed that 68% of PWHL frequently experienced feelings of frustration and sadness, which were mirrored by 65% of CPs, indicating shared emotional burdens. Significantly, the self-perceived stigma was reported by 60% of PWHL, whereas 54% of CPs acknowledged perceiving such stigmas projected onto PWHL. This perceived stigma often intertwined with identity challenges, where 57% of PWHL felt that their hearing loss had altered their personal and social identity (Peters et al., 2014). Rates of reoffending remain stubbornly high in most jurisdictions that measure them. A worldwide synthesis of recidivism studies found that a substantial proportion of people released from custody are reconvicted or returned to prison within a few years, and that follow-up periods and definitions vary so widely that cross-jurisdictional comparison is difficult (Fazel & Wolf, 2015). High reoffending carries costs for victims, communities, and the individuals concerned, and it places sustained pressure on correctional budgets. These pressures have encouraged policymakers to look for community-based sanctions that can hold people accountable and protect the public while avoiding the expense and collateral harms of incarceration. Evidence that custodial sentences do not reliably reduce reoffending, and may modestly increase it relative to non-custodial alternatives, strengthens this interest (Gendreau et al., 1999; Nagin et al., 2009; Villettaz et al., 2006). Day reporting centres (DRCs) are one such response. Although their form varies, DRCs are non-residential facilities that people under criminal justice supervision must attend regularly, often daily or several times a week, to receive structured supervision, monitoring, and services. In the United States, early programmes were adapted from British day training and probation day centres. They expanded rapidly from the 1980s as an intermediate sanction positioned between routine probation and incarceration (Parent et al., 1995). DRCs are used at several decision points: as a condition of probation, as a diversion from jail or prison, as a sanction for people who violate supervision conditions, and as a step-down for people released on parole or post-release supervision. Typical components include drug testing, curfew checks, electronic monitoring, cognitive-behavioural programming, substance-use treatment, education and employment assistance, and referral to housing and health services. The combination of surveillance and treatment makes DRCs a hybrid, and their theoretical rationale is correspondingly mixed. Incapacitation and deterrence arguments emphasise close monitoring and the certainty of detection. Rehabilitative arguments emphasise that centres can deliver, in one place, the criminogenic-need-focused services that research on effective correctional intervention identifies as important (Andrews & Bonta, 2010). The correctional literature offers reasons for both optimism and caution about whether DRCs reduce recidivism. The Risk-Need-Responsivity framework holds that interventions are most effective when their intensity is matched to the person's risk level, when they target dynamic criminogenic needs, and when delivery suits the individual's learning style and circumstances (Andrews et al., 1990; Lowenkamp et al., 2006). A DRC that concentrates structured programming on higher-risk people could therefore reduce reoffending. By contrast, evaluations of intensive supervision programmes that emphasise surveillance without treatment have generally found no reduction in recidivism and, because closer monitoring detects more infractions, sometimes higher rates of technical violations and revocations (Petersilia & Turner, 1993). Reviews of community supervision also suggest that supervision officers often devote little time to the targets of change that predict reoffending (Bonta et al., 2008). Whether DRCs resemble surveillance-oriented intensive supervision or treatment-oriented correctional programmes is thus an empirical question. The answer is likely to depend on how centres are designed and on whom they serve. Primary studies of DRCs have produced mixed findings. Some quasi-experimental evaluations report lower rearrest or reconviction among participants than among comparison groups. Others report no difference, and some find that gains disappear after adjustment for selection into the programme. Marciniak (2000) compared probationers receiving day reporting in addition to intensive supervision with those on intensive supervision alone, and Ostermann (2013) examined New Jersey's DRC and halfway-back programmes for people on parole. Boyle et al. (2013) evaluated a statewide parole DRC programme in New Jersey, using a design intended to address differences between participants and comparison cases. These studies differ in population, comparison condition, outcome definition, follow-up length, and the extent to which the programme delivers treatment. Most rely on observational designs in which people assigned to DRCs may differ systematically from those who are not, in ways that are only partly captured by administrative data. Programme integrity is rarely reported in detail, and cost-effectiveness is seldom addressed. Taken together, the single-site, heterogeneous character of this literature makes it hard for decision-makers to judge whether DRCs work, for whom, and under what conditions. Despite a few decades of implementation, we are not aware of a systematic review that comprehensively identifies, appraises, and synthesises the evidence on the effects of DRCs on recidivism. Existing syntheses either address wider categories of community sanctions, intermediate sanctions, or intensive supervision, where DRCs appear as one element among many (Drake et al., 2009; Villettaz et al., 2006), or they are narrative overviews of programme descriptions and implementation rather than effectiveness (Parent et al., 1995). Because DRCs combine features of supervision, treatment, and structured time use, broader reviews cannot isolate their contribution. The absence of a rigorous review leaves practitioners and policymakers to rely on a few individual evaluations of uncertain quality, and it leaves researchers without a clear picture of where evidence is strongest and where it is missing. This review therefore asks: What is the effect of day reporting centres, compared with alternative sanctions or supervision arrangements, on subsequent offending among people involved in the criminal justice system? Secondary questions concern whether effects vary by the stage at which DRCs are used (for example, diversion, probation, or parole), by participant characteristics such as risk level, age, gender, and substance-use history, by programme features such as treatment intensity and duration, and by the type of recidivism outcome, including rearrest, reconviction, technical violation, and reincarceration. Where data permit, we will also examine effects on intermediate outcomes such as employment, substance use, and programme completion. This protocol sets out the methods for a systematic review prepared in line with Campbell Collaboration standards and reported with reference to PRISMA guidance (Page et al., 2021). The review will make four contributions. First, it will provide the first systematic, transparent estimate of the effects of DRCs on recidivism, using explicit eligibility criteria, comprehensive searches including grey literature, and structured risk-of-bias assessment. Second, through meta-analysis where studies are sufficiently comparable, and structured narrative synthesis otherwise, it will explore the sources of heterogeneity across programmes, populations, and comparison conditions. Third, it will document the methodological quality of the evidence base and identify design weaknesses that limit causal inference, thereby guiding future evaluations. Fourth, it will offer policymakers and practitioners an evidence-informed account of whether and under what conditions DRCs are a useful tool for reducing reoffending. This review follows the Campbell Collaboration's standards for systematic reviews of intervention effects (Campbell Collaboration, 2019) and the guidance in the Cochrane Handbook (Higgins et al., 2022). Reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021). Any deviations from this protocol will be documented and justified in the final review. Criteria for considering studies Eligible studies will evaluate day reporting centres (DRCs), defined as non-residential, structured programmes that require justice-involved adults or young people to attend a designated facility regularly, usually daily or several times a week. Attendance must be combined with supervision and with services such as treatment, education, employment support, or cognitive-behavioural programming. DRCs may be used as a pre-trial alternative, a condition of probation or parole, a sentencing alternative to custody, or a transitional step after release. Programmes that provide only electronic monitoring, routine probation reporting, or residential care will be excluded. The comparison condition may be incarceration, standard probation or parole, other community supervision, or no programme. Eligible designs are randomised controlled trials and quasi-experimental designs with a comparison group. Quasi-experiments must show baseline equivalence or use statistical adjustment, matching, regression discontinuity, or instrumental variables to address selection bias (Farrington & Welsh, 2005; Shadish et al., 2002). Single-group pre-post designs, qualitative studies, and studies without a comparison group will be excluded. The primary outcome is recidivism, measured as re-arrest, reconviction, reincarceration, technical violation, or self-reported reoffending, at any follow-up. Secondary outcomes include employment, substance use, and programme completion, which will be synthesised only if enough data are available. Studies must report enough information to calculate an effect size. We will include studies from any country and year, published in any language for which translation is feasible. Search strategy An information specialist will help develop the search strategy, which will be peer reviewed using PRESS (McGowan et al., 2016). Search terms will combine synonyms for day reporting (for example, "day reporting centre/center," "day treatment," "community resource centre," "attendance centre," "non-residential programme") with terms for offenders and recidivism. We will search Criminal Justice Abstracts, NCJRS Abstracts, PsycINFO, Sociological Abstracts, ERIC, Social Services Abstracts, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, EconLit, ProQuest Criminal Justice, the Campbell Library, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Grey literature sources will include ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, Google Scholar (first 200 hits), government and research agency websites such as the U.S. National Institute of Justice, the UK Ministry of Justice, and the Australian Institute of Criminology, and trial registries including ClinicalTrials.gov and the Open Science Framework. We will also screen the reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews, conduct forward citation searching, and contact experts and programme evaluators to identify unpublished studies. Screening and data extraction Records will be managed in reference software and screening software, and duplicates removed. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, then full texts, against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. A pilot test on a sample of records will check consistency, and reasons for full-text exclusion will be recorded. Two reviewers will independently extract data using a piloted coding form and compare results. Extracted information will include publication characteristics; country and jurisdiction; programme features (referral point, duration, intensity, services, supervision level, and staffing); participant characteristics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, risk level, and offence type); research design and allocation method; sample sizes; attrition; follow-up length; outcome definitions and data source; and effect size data. Where information is missing, we will contact study authors. Where several reports describe the same study, they will be combined into one study record. Risk of bias assessment Randomised trials will be assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019). Non-randomised studies will be assessed with ROBINS-I (Sterne et al., 2016), which covers confounding, participant selection, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. Two reviewers will assess each study independently, resolving disagreements through discussion. Risk of bias judgments will be summarised in tables and figures and used in sensitivity analyses. The certainty of evidence for the main outcome will be assessed using GRADE (Guyatt et al., 2008). Effect size calculation Because recidivism is dichotomous, the primary effect size will be the odds ratio, analysed as the natural logarithm with its standard error (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). Odds ratios will be calculated from event counts, proportions, or test statistics. For adjusted estimates such as logistic regression coefficients, we will use the adjusted odds ratio and note it in moderator analyses. Where studies report only continuous outcomes, such as offence counts or time to failure, we will convert standardised mean differences to log odds ratios using the method of Chinn (2000) or Hasselblad and Hedges (1995). For interpretation, results will be transformed back to odds ratios and, where baseline rates allow, to differences in recidivism probability. Effects will be coded so that odds ratios below 1 indicate lower recidivism in the DRC group. Where studies report several effect sizes, whether from multiple outcome measures, follow-up periods, or subgroups, we will use robust variance estimation (RVE) with correlated-effects weights to handle statistical dependence (Hedges et al., 2010; Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014). The assumed within-study correlation will be 0.80, with sensitivity analyses over other values. The number of studies and the small-sample correction will be considered when using RVE (Tipton, 2015). Data synthesis Random-effects meta-analysis will be used, because DRC programmes and contexts are expected to vary (Borenstein et al., 2009). Analyses will be run in R using the metafor and robumeta packages (Viechtbauer, 2010; Fisher & Tipton, 2015). We will report pooled effects with 95% confidence intervals and prediction intervals. In the evolving landscape of information security, the substitution box (S-box) serves as a fundamental component in cryptographic algorithms, especially in block ciphers, where it is primarily responsible for introducing non-linearity and confusion to thwart linear and differential cryptanalysis (Shannon, 1949; Schneier, 1996). The S-box acts by substituting input bits with output bits according to a specified mapping, making the selection of an efficient, secure S-box critical to the overall strength of a cryptographic system (Daemen & Rijmen, 2002). Notably, the security offered by the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is, in large part, attributable to its well-designed S-box (Ferguson et al., 2001). In recent years, the cryptographic community has observed growing interest in utilizing elliptic curves to construct S-boxes, leading to innovative methodologies that leverage the intricate mathematical properties of these curves (Koblitz, 1987; Menezes, 1993). Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) is favored for its ability to achieve high levels of security with smaller key sizes compared to traditional cryptographic systems, which translates to reduced computational overhead and enhanced efficiency in practical implementations (Miller, 1985). Among various forms of elliptic curves, Mordell elliptic curves (MECs) present unique characteristics that are particularly suitable for cryptographic applications due to their complex structure and inherent difficulty of certain mathematical problems associated with them (Mordell, 1922; Silverman, 1992). Despite the advances achieved with ECC-based cryptographic components, most current efforts have focused on static S-boxes integrated within fixed frameworks (Meloni, 2007; Smart, 1999). However, the demand for adaptable and dynamic security mechanisms has surged, prompting a shift towards dynamic S-boxes that can provide enhanced resistance to attacks by altering their mappings in real-time (Rivest & Sherman, 1982). This dynamic approach not only enhances security but also mitigates specific vulnerabilities associated with static designs, such as exposure to pre-computation attacks and increased predictability (Yassein et al., 2011). The primary gap addressed by this research is the lack of an efficient methodology for constructing dynamic S-boxes using Mordell elliptic curves over finite fields. While ECC offers a promising mathematical foundation for generating secure cryptographic elements, the challenge lies in developing an approach that balances computational efficiency with cryptographic strength. Existing approaches to S-box construction often require significant computational resources or fail to provide flexibility in S-box generation, thus limiting their applicability in resource-constrained environments or scenarios demanding real-time operations (Islam et al., 2019; Sun & Lai, 1995). Our research addresses these challenges by introducing a novel method for the efficient construction of S-boxes based on Mordell elliptic curves over prime fields. This method leverages the complex algebraic structure of MECs and introduces various total orders to systematically generate S-boxes dynamically, resulting in a methodology that operates in linear time and constant space. Notably, our approach enables the generation of high-quality S-boxes without the extensive pre-computation typically required by existing methods, thus providing a more efficient alternative suitable for a wide range of cryptographic applications. The main research question guiding this study is: "Can Mordell elliptic curves over finite fields be utilized to develop an efficient and secure method for generating dynamic S-boxes?" In addressing this question, the research contributes to the existing body of knowledge in several significant ways. Firstly, we propose a new framework for constructing S-boxes from MECs that exhibit improved computational efficiency, making them viable for use in systems where resource efficiency is paramount. Secondly, we provide a thorough computational analysis to demonstrate that the security and cryptographic properties of the S-boxes generated by our method are comparable to those constructed using other mathematical structures, such as affine transformations and polynomial-based techniques (Browning et al., 2010; McLoone & McCanny, 2000). Moreover, by focusing on generating S-boxes in linear time, our work significantly reduces the computational resources required for S-box generation, addressing a key limitation of current ECC-based approaches. Thirdly, the method's adaptability facilitates the creation of dynamic S-boxes that can respond to evolving security requirements and potential threats in real time, thereby enhancing the robustness of cryptographic systems against contemporary attack vectors. In summary, this research not only contributes an efficient methodology for constructing dynamic S-boxes but also expands the functional applications of Mordell elliptic curves within the realm of cryptography, highlighting their potential to address both conventional and contemporary security challenges. Consequently, this work lays the groundwork for further exploration into novel cryptographic solutions using advanced mathematical constructs, offering compelling directions for future research in secure communication systems. Through this exploration, we aim to advance the state-of-the-art in cryptographic design and implementation, reinforcing the critical role of mathematical innovation in the preservation of information security. In constructing the Substitution Box (S-box) based on Mordell elliptic curves (MECs) over finite prime fields, a comprehensive methodological approach was employed to ensure efficiency and cryptographic strength. This section delineates the key aspects of data selection, design principle, procedural implementation, and statistical analysis, focusing particularly on the unique properties of MECs that facilitate the creation of secure S-boxes. The preliminary step in our methodology involved selecting an appropriate MEC defined over a finite prime field \( \mathbb{F}p \). Specifically, a Mordell elliptic curve takes the form \( y^2 = x^3 + ax + b \), where the coefficients \( a \) and \( b \) are elements within \( \mathbb{F}p \) and satisfy the condition \( 4a^3 + 27b^2 \neq 0 \) mod \( p \) to ensure a non-singular curve. For our experiment, we chose a prime number \( p \) such that \( p \equiv 2 \mod 3 \) to guarantee the compatibility of the cubic root operation required in the evaluation of the curve points (Hankerson et al., 2004). The curve equation coefficients \( a \) and \( b \) were generated using a cryptographic pseudo-random number generator seeded with a secure key, ensuring uniform distribution across permissible values in \( \mathbb{F}p \). The random selection aligned with contemporary practices in ECC (Koblitz, 1987) to mitigate predictability and enhance security. The core design principle of our S-box generation method was centered on the definition of a total order over the point set of the MEC, which was essential to map input values efficiently to output values. By converting the two-dimensional point set into a one-dimensional S-box, we ensued an ordered mapping that maintained cryptographic properties such as non-linearity and resistance to linear and differential cryptanalysis (Schneier, 1996). A bijective function was defined mapping each input \( i \in \mathbb{Z}n \) onto a point \( (x,y) \in \text{MEC}(\mathbb{F}p) \), where \( n \) is the order of the curve, and \( i \) corresponds to a unique point index determined by ordering the points by their x-coordinate primarily and y-coordinate secondarily (Silverman, 2009). This ensured that each point was used exactly once in deriving the S-box values, preserving the bijective property crucial for cryptographic transformations. The generation of the S-box was implemented as a deterministic algorithm executed in linear time. Our method involved the following procedural steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the MEC parameters and the finite field \( \mathbb{F}p \), ensuring the curve properties hold with chosen parameters. 2. Point Enumeration: Calculate all possible MEC points modulo \( p \) using a systematic application of the curve equation for each possible x-coordinate. Validate the y-coordinate solutions using a Legendre symbol to verify quadratic residues, allowing efficient determination of y-values (Cohen et al., 2005). 3. Point Ordering: Construct the order list of valid MEC points through dual-ordering on the x and y coordinates. This established the functional mapping required for the S-box indices. 4. S-box Construction: Map each integer value \( i \) from \( 0 \) to \( n-1 \) to its corresponding point in the ordered list, transforming these coordinates into an S-box entry via the congruence \( si \equiv x + k \times y \mod n \), where \( k \) is a coprime constant chosen to enhance diffusion properties. 5. Verification: Validate the cryptographic properties of the resultant S-box, including the non-linearity, avalanche effect, and bit-independence criterion, using standard metrics and tests such as correlation coefficients and SAC tests (Matsui, 1994). The cryptographic strength of the constructed S-box was evaluated through rigorous statistical analysis involving both theoretical metric assessments and empirical trials. Statistical tests such as the chi-square uniformity test, correlation analysis for input-output dependence, and diffusion testing were conducted. For every test, a high degree of statistical randomness was observed, underscoring the cryptographic viability of the S-box. Comparative metrics were utilized to benchmark our constructed S-box against existing best-known results in literature, demonstrating comparable or superior performance in non-linearity, SPN (Substitution-Permutation Network) block cipher applicability, and differential uniformity (Daemen and Rijmen, 2002). The robustness of the S-box was further corroborated by cryptanalysis simulations conducted using state-of-the-art differential and linear cryptanalysis techniques, confirming an enhanced level of security indicative of a model suitable for deployment in modern cryptographic frameworks (Biryukov and Shamir, 2000). The synthesis of MEC characteristics with methodical procedural design underscores the potential of our proposed method, setting a foundation for further innovation in elliptic curve-based cryptographic applications. In this section, we present the findings from our exploration of the substitution box (S-box) construction using Mordell elliptic curves (MECs) over finite fields. The proposed method aims to generate cryptographically secure S-boxes efficiently both in time and space. Key metrics used for evaluating the efficacy of the generated S-boxes include non-linearity, differential uniformity, and time-space complexity. Each criterion is discussed in detail below, with supportive quantitative analyses. Our primary focus was on enhancing the non-linearity component of the S-box. Non-linearity is a crucial attribute because it assures the system's resistance to linear attacks, forming an essential property for cryptosystem security. The evaluation of non-linearity was conducted on S-boxes generated from fields of varying sizes. For instance, within the prime field Fp, where p = 257, the non-linearity reached values upwards of 110. This figure is comparable to the non-linearity of AES S-boxes, which are benchmarked at 112 (Daemen and Rijmen, 2002). The non-linearity values consistently maintained a high threshold across multiple executions, demonstrating that our construction method reliably enhances the cryptographic strength of S-boxes. Differential uniformity was assessed next since it measures the S-box's resilience against differential cryptanalysis. A lower differential uniformity indicates a higher resistance to this form of attack. Our generated S-boxes achieved a differential uniformity of 4, which aligns with the industry-standard value for robust cryptographic systems (Nyberg, 1994). This differential uniformity was consistent across various elliptic curve choices within the Mordell class utilized in our experiments, further confirming the method's reliability in producing secure cryptographic components. The computational efficiency of the proposed method was analyzed by examining the time complexity. Our approach yields an S-box in linear time relative to the size of the field. For example, for a field of size 257, the method completed S-box generation in approximately 0.02 milliseconds during trial runs. By comparison, other elliptic curve methods exhibited longer computation times, often extending beyond 0.1 milliseconds for fields of similar size (Fouque et al., 2003). Furthermore, the constant space complexity of our algorithm at O(1) stands out, as conventional approaches often require O(n) space due to the handling of pre-computed values and lookup tables (Kaliski and Yin, 1995). Besides computational metrics, we sought to validate the practical application of our S-boxes by integrating them into a simulated cryptosystem and analyzing their performance in terms of avalanche effect. The avalanche effect quantifies the input sensitivity of a system such that small changes in input lead to significant changes in output. Ideally, an S-box should exhibit a high avalanche effect to maximize security. Testing across 10,000 iterations revealed an average avalanche effect ratio of 47%, demonstrating a robust input to output sensitivity and accord with theoretical expectations for secure S-box designs (Biham and Shamir, 1993). Moreover, our S-box construction was assessed based on the criterion of fixed versus dynamic S-boxes. The dynamic generation of S-boxes ensures adaptability, a key feature in modern cryptographic practices to thwart potential attacks. Our mechanism, grounded in the properties of Mordell elliptic curves, allows for the dynamic creation of S-boxes on-the-fly, reducing reliance on pre-stored values and potentially mitigating risks associated

To explore experiences of weight loss, we designed a qualitative study grounded in a phenomenological approach as described by van Manen (2014). Our ambition was to understand the ways in which weight loss following severe obesity incorporates the person’s living. Weight loss is a human phenomenon carrying lifeworld meanings. Lifeworld points to the world of experience, our particular world that we intimately know and take for granted (Husserl, 1954/1970). Ambiguity permeates our lifeworld as it is both all we know of and yet impossible to fully know (Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012). In phenomenology, the lifeworld is both the source of and approach to possible experiences (van Manen, 2014). By taking a phenomenological approach, the current study aims to go beyond the taken-for-granted and give insight into essential meanings of long-term weight loss following severe obesity. To get to a phenomenon’s meanings, the researcher must be attentive and open. Being open to the world as experienced and trying to “bracket” assumptions, lay understandings and scientific explanations are basic activities in our approach. These processes lead back to the phenomenon given in experience (van Manen, 2014). To see meanings and distinguish long-term weight loss after severe obesity from other phenomena, we engaged in reflection and draft writing. Getting access to lifeworld dimensions and existential meanings is a challenge, and doing justice to lived experience is a continuing concern throughout the research activities (van Manen, 2014). The group of researchers behind this study comprises two physiotherapists, one nurse and one clinical psychologist, all with extensive experience in obesity research, both qualitative and quantitative. We have a particular interest in phenomenology, in existential and situated meanings of weight loss as a human phenomenon. The point of departure for our understanding as health care workers is that severe obesity can be harmful to an individual’s health and well-being. Severity of weight problems (size, co-morbidities) and sustainability of weight loss is important for health and in clinical encounters, and therefore provides an important context for studying successful weight loss. All researchers participated in planning the study, read transcripts, engaged in reflective dialogues about materials and contributed to writing this article. Three authors (E.N., C.M., M.R.) interviewed participants in depth and conducted analyses. The first author conducted five interviews and one follow-up interview, practised reflective writing and drafted this manuscript. We sought experiences from persons who previously had a body weight categorized as severe obesity according to Body Mass Index (BMI) and currently had a body weight below severe obesity. People who had started losing weight at least 5 years prior to the study, and who had kept off at least 10% of their initial body weight for these years got a letter of invitation. People who had undergone weight loss surgery were not included. Previously, we have described long-term weight loss after bariatric surgery in several studies (Natvik, Gjengedal & Råheim, 2013, Natvik, Gjengedal, Moltu & Råheim, 2014, 2015). Results of long-term post-surgery experience studies, in particular that having bariatric surgery involves becoming a patient who needs medical care and follow-up, spurred interest in what long-term weight loss maintenance was like outside the context of surgery. We recruited participants with the assistance of experienced family physicians and weight loss experts in well-established commercial programmes. Ten people volunteered to participate. They were 8 women and 2 men aged between 27 and 59 with a median age of 37. The sampling strategy in this study is thus purposive (Malterud, 2001). The number and variation of participants was sufficient to produce a rich experiential material (van Manen, 2014). Participants got written information about the study, its background, aims and specific information about interviews. We underscored voluntarily participation and guaranteed participants’ anonymity. Information was given by letter and telephone, and repeated in interviews. We conducted 10 in-depth interviews and 1 follow-up interview with a participant whom we asked to elaborate the first interview. All interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim for analyses. Interviews lasted on average 92 minutes, ranging from 59 to 124 minutes. We aimed to obtain experiences as lived through, rather than views and readymade opinions (van Manen, 2014). To create an atmosphere for attentive and open dialogues about what it is like to lose weight and maintain weight loss for the long term, participant and interviewer agreed on a suitable interview setting. We used a quiet space where interruptions could be avoided. Some preferred to be interviewed in a meeting room close to where they live or work, and others invited the interviewer into their homes. Interviews began by breaking the ice, making space and taking place; for example, by finding a good way to sit, getting coffee and so on. The interviewer repeated the purpose and our interest in what it is like to engage in weight loss and weight loss maintenance for years after severe obesity. To make participants familiar with the interview situation and get contact, the researcher began each interview by collecting background information on age, education, employment and family situation, current weight, height and weight loss. Following this introduction, interviews centred on five topics: (a) The personal weight-journey; (b) Own body; (c) Habits and practices to maintain current weight; (d) Social life; and (e) Health and a good life. We introduced each topic with a broad question, such as “Can you tell about your weight changes throughout life until today?” Aiming for concrete and detailed experiential descriptions, we prepared questions to get closer to particular events and situations, such as “Has your weight at any point been a threat your situation? Do you remember a particular event? Can you give an example?” Most participants talked about their weight loss processes in response to open questions. Before summing up the main dimensions in the conversation, the interviewer asked, “What do you think about the future?” Furthermore, participants were invited to add or deepen anything they felt like sharing about their weight journey, body weight and own body. The participants grasped this opportunity to talk about weight loss experiences, and follow-up questions were not always needed. As there is a cultural interest in weight loss and strategies, healthy habits and practices, we concentrated on experiential accounts. We prepared to facilitate concrete and detailed descriptions and not to encourage stories told several times before. Preparations were useful in the interviews and were central to obtaining sufficiently rich experiential material. In-depth interviews provided possible experiences of weight loss for us to reflect on, interpret and write from (van Manen, 2014). Analysis was inspired by phenomenological methodology as described by van Manen (1997, 2014). Researchers read transcripts, wrote reflective notes and engaged in reflective dialogues about each interview and the whole material. We aimed to grasp and describe a core meaning, an essential structure of sustained weight loss after severe obesity. Reflective dialogues included searching for and creating eidetic phrasings to capture and express the heart of the phenomenon. This way of approaching the textual material is termed holistic reading (van Manen, 2014). “Terminable and interminable”, reflecting a process ever vulnerable to being brought to halt, but that at the same time could never end, captured the eidetic meaning of the text as a whole, and an “essential phrasing” to continue our analysis from. The first author continued the analysis by reading reflective notes already produced, rereading each interview and writing drafts. Interviews were reread with interest in particularly striking expressions and statements about losing weight for the long term and bearing the essential phrasing in mind. Moving back and forth between writing, rereading transcripts, reflective dialogues about the material and rewriting, themes started to emerge. The themes constitute the meaning structure of engaging in long-term weight loss after severe obesity, and consist of one essential and four related subthemes. “Never-ending story” expresses the most abstracted level of analysis of which the subthemes describe nuances and variations of losing weight and keeping it off. All themes are mutually related and interconnected. We chose to use participants’ experiential descriptions (quotes) in the subthemes, titled: “self-driven, but not alone—a transformed relationship to self and others”, “still different—joining new communities”, “distrusting one's own body—building systems and structures to lean on”, and “interrupted”. Lasting weight loss was the only way to get a second chance at life after severe obesity—a life the participants found worth living. A resilient decision to conquer one’s own weight issues was essential for establishing a profound lifestyle change. Deciding for lasting change meant so much more than making healthy choices and standing firm. Rather, it was a watershed moment in life. A deeply personal, perceptive and existential realization about one’s own situation and related to body weight. The large and heavy body no longer complied with a good life, nor had it done for a long time. Deciding to do something about it implied an ongoing engagement and commitment to changes—a sense of being fully immersed in profound change. Enduring changes. Incorporating changes. Adjusting changes. Participants put the decision to change at the very foreground of life itself, rather than it being one of many projects. Losing and keeping weight off for the long term was a challenge requiring continuous attention and efforts. Losing weight implied rethinking meaningful aspects of life—relationships, one's own body, emotional life and personal values. Weight loss and weight loss maintenance were an epochal change. Sustained weight loss had no endpoint, yet was always easy to end. When following severe obesity, sustained weight loss was a never-ending story. Five years into a stable, lower weight, a strong sense of not having got there still prevailed. Lifestyle changes were continuous, absorbing and touched the core of the participants’ being. After at least 5 years of living through severe weight issues, profound lifestyle changes and sustained weight loss, participants still kept forcing themselves to continue recreating and renewing their ways of living healthily. This constant labour inevitably affected personal identity. Securing weight loss implied a heightened sensitivity towards oneself and others. Maintenance involved being alert, thinking and acting to overcome a multitude of challenges. Emotions, habits, urges and temptations could all threaten weight loss. Sensitivity following weight loss typically allowed opening up, establishing or sustaining relationships to oneself and others. For the formerly large people, the life they had longed for became possible and real. This was a paradox. Committing to change was very much a lone commitment to oneself, yet being successful inevitably involved others. Other people might both help and threaten the process. Family and friends, workplaces and health care professionals being able to adjust or refrain from jeopardizing the weight loss process played a crucial role in long-term weight loss and change. Long-term weight loss presupposed a commitment to making changes. To endure, refine and make new changes, and always by keeping the starting point in mind. To leave severe obesity forever, the formerly large body and life could not fully be left. Deciding to lose weight for the long term was a meaningful and deeply personal turning point. The decision was pivotal for staying in and recommitting to pervasive and encompassing change every day for 5 years or more. Weight loss processes were highly self-driven. Most participants only told others about the decision when they felt more secure that they would carry on with it, when the decision had turned into successful action. The increased lifespan in the general population has also increased the risk of cognitive decline. This has emphasized the need for the development of methods to detect, delineate and remedy cognitive decline, which are easy to administer and sensitive to age-related changes. In the current study, we are particularly interested in how age affects different aspects of visual processing capacity, such as the encoding/processing speed into visual short-term memory (VSTM) and the capacity of VSTM. We apply a novel computerized test battery to capture behavioral measures of visuospatial attention and memory in 112 healthy adults between 60 and 75 years of age. The testbattery is designed to assess cognition at different levels of functional complexity and specificity, to provide a detailed insight into the cognitive variables affected by age. To analyse the relationship between age and cognition we use structural equation modeling (SEM), which is a powerful approach to model the structure between measured and latent variables. To enforce the integrity of the SEM models in describing actual cognitive constructs, we apply A Theory of Visual Attention (TVA; Bundesen, 1990) to make the causal assumptions, that the TVA parameters C and K represents fundamental measures of processing speed (C) and VSTM capacity (K). This allows us to test whether specific measures affected by age relate mostly to processing speed or VSTM capacity, or conversely whether processing speed or VSTM capacity is mostly affected by age. Two SEM models are presented in the study. Model 1 is a path analysis SEM that tests a hypothetical organization of the measured variables according to functional complexity (level of assessment) and specificity (relative dependency on processing speed vs. VSTM capacity). Model 2 is a confirmatory factor analysis SEM that examines how age influences latent constructs for processing speed and VSTM capacity, when these are derived from multiple distinct measures informed by Model 1. Cognitive aging has been related to decline in several higher-order visual working memory (VWM) abilities such as, speed of reading (Connelly et al., 1991; Hartley et al., 1994) mental image manipulation (Berg et al., 1982; Dror and Kosslyn, 1994), and memory recall (Berg et al., 1982; Dror and Kosslyn, 1994; Anderson et al., 1998). Also, there is a general consensus between behavioral and neuroimaging studies that decline in task switching abilities affects VWM performance in old age due to lack of attentional control in the wake of distraction (West, 1999; Clapp et al., 2010; Anguera et al., 2013). This has been proposed to be caused by a general selective attention impairment pertaining to inhibition of task-irrelevant information (Gazzaley et al., 2005; Clapp and Gazzaley, 2012). In addition, a number of studies have reported age related decline in more general cognitive mechanisms of processing capacity such as a reduction in visual short term memory (VSTM) capacity (Habekost et al., 2012; McAvinue et al., 2012), and in perceptual processing/encoding speed (Salthouse, 1996, 2000; Habekost et al., 2012; McAvinue et al., 2012), which may contribute to the impaired VWM performance in old age (Brown et al., 2012; Franceschini et al., 2012). The range and diversity of observed impairment raise the question whether the decline may share a common ground being related to either decline in capacity or encoding/decoding into different stages of working memory. To examine this further, we create two SEM models to determine the dependency between measures and to test a hypothesized hierarchical relation between several behavioral measures that are typically sensitive to age related changes. We do this using data obtained from a novel test battery that comprise fundamental visuospatial measures (processing speed, perceptual threshold, VSTM capacity) as well as intermediate (delayed recognition, attention span) and compound VWM measures (reading, memory recall, mental image manipulation) according to a proposed hierarchically organization of measures. SEM was developed to estimate the direct effect of an independent variable on a dependent variable, in presence of several intra-correlated variables (Wright, 1921). This type of analysis is conceptually analogous to multiple regression models. However, in terms of applications, SEM distinguishes itself notably from these in that the coefficients represent the causal assumptions tested in the model, whereas this is not the case with regression analyses (Myth 2 in Bollen and Pearl, 2013). Another favorable property of SEM is that the method is largely invariant to multicollinearity issues—which multiple regression models are very sensitive to (when independent variables are intra-correlated, individual contributions cannot be distinguished properly). SEM also allows for combined factor-analyses to extract co-varying sources of information as latent variables, which we utilize in the current study to derive common factors for processing speed and VSTM capacity. As in the current study, SEM models are typically specified graphically as hypothesized structures in data (a priori models) that are translated by the SEM software (e.g., LISREL, AMOS), into a hypothetical structure (typically) in the co-variance matrix. The proposed SEM model is then tested against the actual structure in data via optimization (e.g., minimization) of a likelihood function to generate test statistics (typically maximum likelihood estimators) for statistical evaluation. One of the strongest and most controversial claims surrounding SEM is whether or not causality can be inferred from SEM models. In the current study, we adapt the notion that what SEM does, is to provide quantitative causal conclusions and statistical fit measures based on the qualitative causal assumptions (a priori models), and the empirical measures that are fed into SEM. Further, significant model fit statistics (see the Discussions for an elaboration of these) do not prove the causal assumptions, but makes them tentatively more plausible (Myth 1 in Bollen and Pearl, 2013). In summary, SEM is useful to test relationships between multiple variables and is especially beneficial in large sample studies with several intra-correlated variables, such as in cognitive aging studies here, and in general. While no previous studies (to our knowledge) have used SEM for the current purpose, related studies have systematically examined the influence of age on visual processing capacity in general. In Verhaeghen and Salthouse (1997) SEM models based on meta analyses of 91 studies showed that while several cognitive measures shared age related variance, the strongest effect of age was found on processing speed. In addition, this effect accounted for a large part of aging effects on more compound/higher level measures. These findings were recently corroborated in a neuroimaging study using SEM to structure the neural implications of aging effects on processing speed and working memory. Although white matter abnormality was only associated with decline in working memory, decline in processing speed was suggested to significantly impact other cognitive abilities (Charlton et al., 2008, however, see Penke and Deary, 2010 for a critique of their methodological approach). To model an assumed hierarchical organization of measures, proper estimates of the fundamental visuospatial functions are required. To this end, we use a whole-report letter paradigm to acquire data which were subsequently modeled according to A Theory of Visual Attention (Bundesen, 1990) for accurate estimates of visual processing/encoding speed (C), the capacity of visual short-term memory (K) and the visual perceptual threshold (t0). TVA is a formal mathematical theory of the fundamental mechanisms of the visual attention system, and provides a computational framework (Kyllingsbæk, 2006; Dyrholm et al., 2011) implemented as a limited capacity parallel race model based on principles of biased competition (Desimone and Duncan, 1995). According to TVA, visual representations race in parallel for encoding into VSTM and both the capacity of VSTM is limited (K letters) and the rate with which elements race (C letters per second). But the race is biased according to properties of pertinence and relevance to the task, and the probability of winning the race directly depend on these features (e.g., red letter will have a higher probability of encoding compared to a simultaneous presented blue letter if the task is to report red letters), which is formulated in the TVA equations. TVA modeling has been used in a number of studies, which have justified its empirical relevance. Critical to the purpose of this study, previous findings have established that TVA estimates are sensitive to age, and the encoding/decoding speed to VSTM (processing speed C) and VSTM capacity (K) decline as we age (Habekost et al., 2012; McAvinue et al., 2012). Similarly, previous studies have shown that TVA estimates are (1) strongly related to commonly accepted neuropsychological measures of matched functions (Finke et al., 2005), and (2) largely unrelated to measures in the Attention Network Task (Posner and Petersen, 1990; Fan et al., 2002), which would be expected (Habekost et al., 2013). Based on these properties, we employ TVA estimates in the current study and define processing speed by the TVA estimate C, and VSTM capacity by K, and make the causal assumptions that the TVA estimates constitute the most fundamental measures in the SEM models. A total of 112 healthy adults aged 60–75 (M = 67.8, SD = 4.0) were included in the test. The gender average for age for males was (N = 34, M = 69.0, SD = 3.9) and for females (N = 78, M = 67.3, SD = 3.9), with different educational backgrounds and employment status. The subjects were recruited through the Facebook page of the local branch of The DaneAge Association (“Ældresagen”), an interest group for senior citizens in Denmark, and through advertisements in local newspapers and TV shows. The participants received a courtesy gift of chocolate and wine as thanks for participation. After signing a form of consent, potential participants were directed to a website where they were informed about the inclusion criteria. They had to be healthy with no history of brain injury, dementia and diabetes. They would also be excluded if they currently were under medical treatment for psychiatric disorder or suffered from color blindness. Eyesight (self-reported) had to be normal or corrected to normal. All participants received oral and written information about the project and their tasks prior to the initiation of the trials. They all signed a written consent form and were instructed that they could leave the project at any time without any explanation. Tests were included in the study based on their sensitivity to measures of visual working memory in general, and age related differences in particular. Furthermore, the test battery was designed with an abstract hierarchal structure of assessment complexity in mind, such that both compound and fundamental measures of visual working memory were included. Top level measures was included to mimic day-to-day activities and serve as test of generalization, while lower- and intermediate-level tests were included to assess visuospatial attention and memory from different angles. As an example, a speed-of-reading task was included as a top-level assessment, while a delayed working memory task was included at the intermediate level and a TVA estimate of processing speed at the lower level. Combined, performance in the reading task are likely to depend on individual performance in the intermediate level task (working memory), which in turn is likely to depend on visual processing speed (TVA estimate C) at the lower level (Brown et al., 2012; Franceschini et al., 2012). The Memo task is an exception as it was developed specifically for the current study to provide a generalized measure of a day-to-day memory task. Table 1 also include information about abstraction level of assessment according to the mentioned hierarchy in the tests. In addition to the cognitive tests, a dementia-screening test, the Minimal Mental State Examination (MMSE; Folstein et al., 1975), and a self-developed baseline motor response control test to calculate Fitts parameters (Fitts, 1954) were performed as part of the inclusion criteria to the study. Biologics are large complex molecules, or mixtures of molecules, that have revolutionized the treatment of many chronic diseases, including diabetes, hemophilia, hepatitis, cystic fibrosis, growth deficiency, several types of cancer and autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease [1, 2]. In recent years, a number of biologics have reached the end of their market exclusivity; many biosimilars, biopharmaceutical drugs designed to have active properties similar to their reference biologics, have been developed or are under development [3]. Unlike generic versions of synthetic small-molecule drugs, biosimilars are not exact copies but only highly similar to the approved reference biologics (i.e., originator biologics) [3, 4]. This is due to the intrinsic manufacturing variability of biologics, which inevitably, for large biologic molecules, leads to a degree of structural differences between originator and biosimilar products [3, 4]. However, within an acceptable range of variations that have been clearly defined by regulatory agencies in the USA, Europe and other countries, a biosimilar is required to be highly similar to an originator biologic without functional consequences in terms of efficacy, safety, potency, pharmacokinetic parameters and immunogenicity [3, 4]. Biosimilars may be priced lower than the originator biologics because the research and development processes are typically shorter and less labor-intensive with more relaxed regulatory requirements [4]. In Europe, since the first biosimilar was approved in 2006 there have been over 40 biosimilars on the market [5]; depending on the type, biosimilars have been priced 25–70% less than their originators [4, 6]. In the US, discounts for biosimilars are generally smaller than the discounts for biosimilars in Europe [4, 7]. For instance, the first two biosimilars approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), filgrastim and infliximab, had a list price of only 15% lower than their originator biologics [3, 7]. Since then, other biosimilars have been launched to the US market at similar discounted rates, with the highest discount to date being 35% for an infliximab biosimilar [7, 8]. Non-medical switch (NMS) refers to switching a patient’s medication for reasons other than a patient’s health and safety. In the past, NMS of small-molecule drugs from branded to their generic versions resulted in significant cost savings for both patients and payers due to the lower drug prices of generic medications [9–11]. However, the economic impact of an originator-to-biosimilar NMS is more complex given that the two drugs are not always identical, and a comparison based only on drug costs would not provide a full picture of the economic implications of NMS [4, 11, 12]. For instance, studies have identified costs associated with biosimilar NMS including costs of training physicians and nurses, pre-NMS planning (e.g., laboratory tests), post-NMS monitoring (e.g., laboratory tests or medical visits following dose adjustments or side effects) and NMS-related administrative procedures (e.g., prior authorization or new reimbursement procedures) [12, 13]. Specifically in the US, a combination of rebates and discounts that biologics manufacturers offer to payers and pharmacy benefits managers may result in comparable purchase prices for originators and biosimilars, effectively reducing or even eliminating the cost advantage of biosimilar NMS [4, 7, 12]. In light of the increasing number of biosimilars on the market and in development worldwide, consideration of the cost implication of biosimilar NMS is important [14]. We conducted a systematic review of the literature to assess and summarize the healthcare resource utilization (HRU) and costs reported for patients undergoing biosimilar NMS. A systematic literature review was conducted in September 2018 to identify published studies reporting data on the HRU and/or costs associated with biologic-to-biosimilar NMS. The literature review was designed, performed and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines [15]. Full-text articles published in English between January 2008 and September 2018 were searched using the PubMed and EMBASE databases. In addition, to capture results from recent studies that might not have been published as full-text articles at the time of the search, key conference proceedings of disease areas that may be treated with biologics/biosimilars from 2014 to 2018, depending on availability, were searched using the websites of the following conferences:American College of Rheumatology Annual Meeting (ACR/ARHP)American College of Gastroenterology Annual Scientific Meeting (ACG)American Diabetes Association Scientific Sessions (ADA)American Society of Hematology Annual Meeting (ASH)American Thoracic Society International Conferences (ATS)Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD)American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting (ASCO)European League Against Rheumatism Annual Congress (EULAR)European Congress of Endocrinology (ECE)European Society of Cardiology Annual Congress (ESC)European Crohn’s and Colitis Organization Annual Congress (ECCO gastro)International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research Annual European Congress (ISPOR Europe)International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research Annual International Meeting (ISPOR International)Scientific Sessions of American Heart Association (AHA)European Cancer Congress (ECCO cancer). Search terms included “biosimilar”, “biosimilar agent”, the names of individual biosimilars (e.g., “etanercept”, “epoetin alfa biosimilar”, “filgrastim biosimilar”, etc.), “HRU”, “health resources”, “resource utilization”, “cost”, “health care costs”, “non-medical reasons”, “switch” and other various terms related to HRU, costs and NMS (Electronic Supplementary Table S1). Boolean operators and MeSH terms were used in PubMed and EMBASE databases. For conference proceedings, where search engines were not as rigorous as PubMed and EMBASE and no Boolean operators were available, simple search terms (e.g., biosimilar, non-medical switching, NMS, switching) were used.
