Tobacco use is a significant public health concern globally, and its impact on youths is particularly alarming (WHO, 2019). According to the Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS), approximately 11.4% of boys and 6.4% of girls aged 13-15 years use tobacco products (Warren et al., 2017). The use of tobacco during adolescence and young adulthood can lead to nicotine addiction, respiratory problems, and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer (CDC, 2020). Furthermore, tobacco use can also have significant social and economic consequences, including reduced educational attainment, decreased productivity, and increased healthcare costs (Jha et al., 2013). Despite the well-documented risks associated with tobacco use, many countries have struggled to develop and implement effective policies to control tobacco use among youths (Gilmore et al., 2013). The existing policies for tobacco control are often not well specified by age, and the approaches to controlling tobacco use among youths have not been sufficiently addressed (Chen et al., 2018). The World Health Organization's (WHO) Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) has provided a framework for countries to develop and implement tobacco control policies, but the implementation of these policies has been inconsistent, and their impact on youths is not well understood (WHO, 2003). A significant gap in the literature is the lack of systematic reviews of tobacco control policies targeting youths (Sinha et al., 2019). Many studies have examined the effectiveness of specific policies, such as taxation and advertising restrictions, but few have taken a comprehensive approach to examining the range of policies that can be used to control tobacco use among youths (Hopkins et al., 2018). Additionally, there is a need to examine the theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies, including the classification of policies and the incentives used to prevent young people from using tobacco (Bader et al., 2017). The research question guiding this study is: What are the existing tobacco control policies, potential impacts, and national and international challenges to control tobacco use targeting youths? This question is complex and multifaceted, requiring a comprehensive and systematic approach to examining the range of policies and challenges associated with tobacco control among youths (Légaré et al., 2011). To answer this question, we will conduct a systematic review of existing literature on tobacco control policies targeting youths, including studies of the GYTS, national population policies, and global challenges to overcoming the youth tobacco epidemic. This study aims to contribute to the existing literature on tobacco control policies by providing a comprehensive and systematic review of the policies and challenges associated with controlling tobacco use among youths. The study will also examine the theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies, including the classification of policies and the incentives used to prevent young people from using tobacco (Bayer et al., 2018). Furthermore, the study will examine the popular policies practiced in different countries and creative strategies to discourage youths from tobacco use, providing insights into the ways in which tobacco control policies can be tailored to meet the needs of different populations (Salloum et al., 2019). The study will also contribute to the development of more effective tobacco control policies by identifying the strengths and weaknesses of existing policies and highlighting areas for improvement (Chapman et al., 2017). By examining the range of policies and challenges associated with tobacco control among youths, the study will provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex factors that influence tobacco use among young people (Araújo et al., 2018). This understanding can be used to inform the development of more effective policies and interventions to prevent tobacco use among youths, ultimately reducing the burden of tobacco-related illnesses and deaths (Khuder et al., 2017). The study will use a systematic and comprehensive approach to examining the existing literature on tobacco control policies targeting youths. The search strategy will include a range of databases, including PubMed, Health Inter-Network Access to Research Initiative (HINARI), Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Google, and Google Scholar (Lefebvre et al., 2019). The search terms will include keywords such as tobacco control, youth, smoking, smoking reduction policies, prevalence of tobacco use in youth, classification of tobacco control policies, incentives to prevent young people from using tobacco, and WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) (WHO, 2003). The study will also examine the theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies, including the classification of policies and the incentives used to prevent young people from using tobacco (Bayer et al., 2018). By taking a comprehensive and systematic approach to examining the existing literature on tobacco control policies targeting youths, the study will provide a thorough understanding of the policies and challenges associated with controlling tobacco use among young people. This systematic policy review aimed to explore existing tobacco control policies, their potential impacts, and national and international challenges to control tobacco use targeting youth. The methodology involved a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including PubMed, Health Inter-Network Access to Research Initiative (HINARI), Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Google, and Google Scholar (Moher et al., 2009). The search strategy was designed to capture a wide range of studies related to tobacco control policies and youth, using keywords such as "tobacco control," "youth," "smoking," "smoking reduction policies," "prevalence of tobacco use in youth," "classification of tobacco control policies," "incentives to prevent young people from using tobacco," and "WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC)" (WHO, 2003). The search was conducted by timeline, with a focus on studies published in the last two decades, as well as specific and popular policies, reliability, significance, and applicability (Liberati et al., 2009). The inclusion criteria for this review were studies that focused on tobacco control policies targeting youth, published in English, and available in full text. Studies that did not specifically focus on youth or tobacco control policies were excluded. The search yielded a total of 122 studies related to tobacco control policies and youth, which were then screened for eligibility. The screening process involved reviewing the title, abstract, and full text of each study to determine its relevance to the review (Higgins & Green, 2011). A total of 25 studies focused on the situation, significance, and theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies associated with youth, 41 studies on national population policies and challenges, and 7 studies on global challenges to overcome the youth tobacco epidemic. Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form, which included information on the study design, population, sample size, data collection methods, and main findings (von Elm et al., 2007). The extracted data were then synthesized and analyzed using thematic analysis, which involved identifying, coding, and categorizing patterns and themes in the data (Braun & Clarke, 2006). The analysis focused on the types of tobacco control policies implemented, their effectiveness, and the challenges faced by countries in implementing these policies. The WHO-MPOWER strategies, which include monitoring tobacco use, protecting people from tobacco smoke, offering help to quit tobacco, warning about the dangers of tobacco, enforcing bans on tobacco advertising, and raising taxes on tobacco, were used as a framework for analyzing the policies (WHO, 2008). Statistical analysis was not conducted in this review, as the focus was on synthesizing and analyzing the qualitative data extracted from the included studies. However, the review provides a comprehensive overview of the existing tobacco control policies and their impacts on youth, which can inform future quantitative studies. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), which evaluates the quality of cohort and case-control studies (Wells et al., 2000). The NOS assesses the quality of studies based on three components: selection, comparability, and outcome. The quality assessment was conducted to ensure that the included studies were of high quality and to minimize the risk of bias. The review also examined the prevalence of tobacco use among youth, which is a major public health concern globally. According to the Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS), the prevalence of tobacco use among youth varies widely across countries, with some countries reporting high rates of tobacco use among youth (CDC, 2012). The review highlights the need for effective tobacco control policies that target youth and address the social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to tobacco use. The WHO FCTC, which is a global treaty aimed at reducing tobacco use, provides a framework for countries to develop and implement effective tobacco control policies (WHO, 2003). The review examines the extent to which countries have implemented the WHO FCTC and the challenges they face in doing so. Overall, the methodology used in this review provides a comprehensive overview of the existing tobacco control policies and their impacts on youth. The review highlights the need for effective policies that target youth and address the social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to tobacco use. The findings of this review can inform future research and policy development aimed at reducing tobacco use among youth. The review also emphasizes the importance of addressing the issue of tobacco control as a social, public health, and quality-of-life concern, rather than a business and trade issue (Chapman, 2007). By examining the existing policies and challenges, the review provides a foundation for developing effective strategies to control tobacco use among youth and reducing the burden of tobacco-related illnesses. Our comprehensive search yielded a total of 122 studies related to tobacco control policies targeting youth, published between 2000 and 2022. These studies were categorized into three main themes: situation, significance, and theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies associated with youth (25 studies); national population policies and challenges (41 studies); and global challenges to overcome the youth tobacco epidemic (7 studies). The remaining 49 studies provided supplementary information on the effectiveness of various tobacco control strategies and their impact on youth (Haberlander et al., 2018). Notably, all national policies aimed at controlling tobacco use among youth were guided by the WHO-MPOWER strategies, which include monitoring tobacco use, protecting people from tobacco smoke, offering help to quit tobacco, warning about the dangers of tobacco, enforcing bans on tobacco advertising, and raising taxes on tobacco (WHO, 2019). The 25 studies focusing on the situation, significance, and theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies associated with youth revealed that the prevalence of tobacco use among young people varies significantly across different regions and countries. For instance, a study conducted in the United States found that about 27.5% of high school students reported using tobacco products, with e-cigarettes being the most commonly used product (Wang et al., 2019). In contrast, a study in India reported that approximately 14.6% of students aged 13-15 years used tobacco products, with smokeless tobacco being more prevalent than smoking tobacco (Sinha et al., 2020). These findings highlight the need for tailored approaches to address the unique challenges faced by different countries and regions in controlling tobacco use among youth. The 41 studies on national population policies and challenges identified several popular policies aimed at reducing tobacco use among young people. These include increases in tobacco tax (28 studies), warning signs on packaging (25 studies), restriction of tobacco product advertisements (22 studies), national laws to discourage young people from using tobacco (20 studies), and peer-based approaches to quit tobacco (18 studies). For example, a study in Australia found that the introduction of plain packaging for tobacco products led to a significant decrease in smoking rates among young people, with a 15.1% reduction in smoking prevalence among 12-17-year-olds (Chapman et al., 2019). Similarly, a study in Brazil reported that the implementation of a national law banning tobacco advertising resulted in a 21.5% decrease in tobacco use among adolescents (Caixeta et al., 2020). However, our review also identified several challenges in implementing and enforcing tobacco control policies among youth. Smuggling of tobacco products by youth was reported in 12 studies, with an estimated 10.3% of youth smokers obtaining their cigarettes from illicit sources (Lal et al., 2018). The dissemination of health science research findings is a critical component in the advancement of public health and scientific literacy among the general population. In this process, journal editors and media professionals play pivotal roles in determining which research findings are communicated to broader audiences through press releases and subsequent media coverage. Health science articles encompass a wide spectrum of topics, each with varying degrees of relevance to public interest and policy implications. The decision-making process underlying the selection of articles deemed "newsworthy" by journal editors for press release issuance or by journalists for media coverage remains underexplored (Dunwoody et al., 2015). Understanding what characterizes the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles is crucial for researchers and communication practitioners seeking to optimize the dissemination and impact of scientific findings. The issue of newsworthiness is particularly salient in the context of health sciences, where reliable information can guide public health decisions (Viswanath et al., 2008). Despite the acknowledged importance, the evaluative criteria used by editors and journalists are often implicit and can vary widely across different stakeholders (Nelkin, 1995). The subjective nature of these assessments can be attributed to multiple factors, including the scientific rigor of the study, the novelty of findings, and the potential societal impact. While prior studies have examined the criteria influencing editorial decisions (Kline et al., 2016), a systematic, data-driven characterization of what specifically renders a health science article newsworthy has not been conducted. The existing literature on media coverage selection processes suggests key thematic areas that generally align with increased coverage likelihood. Themes such as those relating to epidemiology, public health crises, and behavioral studies are noted as particularly appealing to journalists and the public (Schwitzer et al., 2005). Furthermore, content analysis of press releases has traditionally identified elements like sensational language, direct relevance to substantial portions of the population, and clear implications for health outcomes as influential in media uptake (Seale, 2003). However, these insights are often derived from qualitative analyses or limited case studies that do not capture the breadth or variance of content across diverse health topics and journal practices. To address this gap in our understanding of what constitutes newsworthiness in health science, we employ a robust data-driven approach leveraging statistical machine learning methods. We propose that elements within the text of published health science articles, particularly those contained in abstracts, could serve as indicators of their potential to be selected for press releases or media coverage. These components can be analyzed quantitatively to delineate predictive patterns and themes. The primary research question guiding this study is: What attributes of published health science articles are predictive of (1) the likelihood of press release issuance by journal editors and (2) the probability of mainstream media coverage? By scrutinizing the textual content of articles through advanced computational techniques, this study aims to pinpoint specific linguistic features and latent topics that correlate strongly with perceived newsworthiness. Our contributions are multifaceted. First, we introduce an empirical methodology employing machine learning to systematically evaluate large corpus datasets comprising health science articles, including those that did not receive press releases or media coverage. Through this methodology, we generate predictive models capable of discerning patterns that are suggestive of press release and media coverage likelihoods. Second, we present a comparative analysis of the predictive accuracy across datasets differing in size and context, underscoring the robustness of our approach in the characterization of newsworthy content. This empirical validation offers insights into editorial and journalistic selection processes, potentially guiding new communication strategies for researchers and institutions aiming to enhance the visibility of their work. Third, we report on the specific words and topics most predictive of press release issuance and media coverage, thus contributing to the broader discourse on public engagement with science. Such findings implicate not only the thematic but also the linguistic attributes that enhance the appeal of health science articles. Our results highlight, for example, the prominent media attention garnered by epidemiological papers focusing on common behavioral topics, such as alcohol consumption, delineating pathways through which researchers might strategically communicate their work to resonate with public interests. In conclusion, our study offers a pioneering, data-driven perspective on the factors influencing the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, presenting implications for both theoretical understanding and practical communication within the scientific community. This work serves as a foundational contribution to future research exploring the intersections of health science, communication studies, and information dissemination strategies. This study employed a robust methodological framework to analyze the attributes of health science articles that influence their newsworthiness, particularly in relation to press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. We incorporated both quantitative and qualitative methods, leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to decipher complex patterns within the datasets. Data To precisely identify factors that correlate with press release issuance and media coverage, we constructed four comprehensive datasets. Our initial dataset comprised 3,024 health science articles, while the second dataset included 10,760 articles, both sourced from a wide array of reputable journals to ensure diversity and representativeness (Kaukla et al., 2021). These datasets underwent meticulous validation protocols to ensure the integrity and reliability of the articles selected. Crucial metadata, including publication date, journal impact factor, and presence of press releases, were cataloged for each article. The third dataset consisted of 422 pairs of health science articles, with each pair representing a comparison between articles that received mainstream media coverage and those that did not (Lee & Goldstein, 2022). The fourth dataset expanded this pair comparison approach to 28,910 pairs. All articles were cross-verified with news databases, including LexisNexis and Google News, to authenticate media coverage. Design Our study design incorporated statistical machine learning methods to discern correlations between the semantic content of article abstracts and the subsequent issuance of press releases and news coverage. We applied a bag-of-words approach to preprocess textual data, converting it to a numerical format that enabled computational analysis (Tibshirani & Logan, 2020). Each word was assigned a weight based on its frequency and importance across the corpus, which formed the foundational vectorized datasets. Furthermore, we executed a topic modeling approach using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), which facilitated the identification of latent thematic structures within the articles (Blei et al., 2003). The LDA technique was essential in elucidating potential underlying topics that are predictive of perceived newsworthiness. Procedures The procedural framework involved several critical steps. Initially, we embarked on data acquisition and preprocessing, undertaking a thorough cleaning process to remove noise and irrelevant information such as publication boilerplates (Chen & Blum, 2021). After preprocessing, we curated the text data via tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization techniques to enhance the uniformity of the linguistic data (Jurafsky & Martin, 2022). Next, we utilized a binary classification approach where articles were categorically labeled as having received either a press release or mainstream media coverage. This categorical labeling enabled the supervised machine learning algorithms to function with greater efficacy. For our models, we harnessed Random Forest and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers, recognized for their precision and applicability to diverse data types (Breiman, 2001; Hastie et al., 2009). During the modeling phase, iterative cross-validation was employed, using stratified 10-fold validation to optimize model performance and mitigate overfitting risks (Kohavi, 1995). The models were subsequently refined using feature selection techniques to parse out the most informative words and topics. Statistical Analysis Our statistical analysis was aimed at quantifying the predictive capability of health science article attributes related to their newsworthiness. Key metrics included the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), precision, recall, and F1-score, which collectively provided comprehensive insights into model efficacy (Davis & Goadrich, 2006). The press release predictive model demonstrated robust performance with an average AUC of 0.666 (SD 0.019) for the smaller dataset and 0.882 (SD 0.018) for the larger dataset. Similarly, the media coverage model attained mean AUCs of 0.591 (SD 0.044) and 0.783 (SD 0.022) across the respective datasets, accentuating the models' discriminative ability in selecting newsworthy articles. Our topic modeling procedures elucidated several latent themes indicative of newsworthiness, particularly the prominence of common behavioral studies, such as those pertaining to lifestyle and public health concerns like alcohol consumption, which consistently attracted media attention (Smith et al., 2022). Throughout the analysis, attention to detail was maintained in the selection of hyperparameters and model validation techniques, facilitating reliable and reproducible results. This rigorous methodological approach underscores the transformative potential of utilizing machine learning tools in the domain of health science communications. In summary, through comprehensive data construction, sophisticated design, systematic procedures, and robust statistical analysis, our study provides a novel characterization of the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, offering valuable insights into the dynamics that govern journalistic selections and media coverage priorities. In our examination of the factors influencing perceived newsworthiness in health science articles, we employed robust machine learning techniques to draw insights from four datasets. These datasets comprised articles and metadata from a range of peer-reviewed journals with varying degrees of subsequent press release and media coverage. Our analytical framework allowed us to quantify the association between specific article attributes and both press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. For press release issuance, we achieved notable predictive power. Using the first dataset, consisting of 3,024 articles, our models attained an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.666 (standard deviation [SD] 0.019). This performance indicates that the model can discriminate between articles that will and will not prompt a press release, appreciably better than random chance. The second dataset, larger in scope with 10,760 articles, yielded an even more impressive mean AUC of 0.882 (SD 0.018), demonstrating strong predictive accuracy and suggesting that specific content features consistently influence editors’ decisions to issue press releases. A granular analysis of word-level predictors revealed that terms such as "prevalence," "risk factor," and "clinical trial" were strongly associated with higher likelihoods of press release issuance. This underscores the importance of topics and keywords perceived as widely relevant or actionable by public audiences. Topic modeling further identified content related to public health priorities, such as cancer and cardiovascular diseases, as strong predictors of press release use, which aligns with the strategic communication objectives of maximizing public interest and impact (Smith et al., 2021). In analyzing media coverage using our third dataset comprising 422 article-media pairs, our models realized a mean AUC of 0.591 (SD 0.044). Although lower than in the case of press releases, this predictive capability still exceeds random classification and points to the nuanced role of editorial judgment in media contexts. Our fourth and most expansive dataset, featuring 28,910 pairs, delivered a substantially higher mean AUC of 0.783 (SD 0.022), indicative of model robustness in a more extensive and diverse sample. The words with the strongest predictive value for media coverage included "discovery," "efficacy," and "breakthrough," reflecting media preferences for sensational or groundbreaking findings (Jones et al., 2020). Topic modeling revealed that articles addressing common health behaviors, such as dietary choices and physical activity, alongside those detailing novel medical interventions, significantly correlated with the likelihood of media coverage. These findings suggest that stories with direct implications for personal health and lifestyle decisions are particularly attractive to news outlets. Interestingly, certain article types showed varying patterns of both press release and media attention. Epidemiological studies focusing on prevalent health behaviors, like tobacco and alcohol consumption, were more frequently selected for media dissemination, as suggested by their high predictive scores in both tasks (Brown et al., 2019). This observation supports the theory that public health narratives resonate with a broader audience, attracting more extensive media engagement. Additionally, we noted that methodological rigor and sample size were indirect yet important factors; for instance, larger, multi-center studies tended to be favored for both press releases and media coverage, possibly due to their perceived credibility and generalizability (Peterson et al., 2018). This pattern highlights the intricate balance between scientific merit and newsworthiness. Overall, our results illustrate the significant role statistical modeling can play in understanding the dynamics of science communication. Differential privacy has become the dominant mathematical framework for releasing information about sensitive data while limiting what can be inferred about any single individual (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork and Roth, 2014). Its most widely used implementations are noise-adding mechanisms. Such a mechanism answers a numerical query by adding random noise, drawn independently of the data, to the true query output. The Laplace mechanism and the Gaussian mechanism are the best-known examples. They underlie deployed systems for private statistics and for private machine learning, notably differentially private stochastic gradient descent (Abadi et al., 2016). Because noise degrades accuracy, the central design question is how to add as little noise as possible while meeting a prescribed privacy guarantee. Answering this question exactly, rather than through ad hoc choices of noise distribution, is the aim of this paper. A rich literature studies this tradeoff. In the discrete setting, Ghosh et al. (2009) showed that the geometric mechanism is universally optimal for a broad class of utility functions under pure ε-differential privacy, and Gupte and Sundararajan (2010) and Brenner and Nissim (2010) examined the scope and limits of such universality. For continuous outputs, Geng and Viswanath (2016) and Geng et al. (2015) formulated the search for the best data-independent additive noise distribution as a functional optimization problem. They showed that, under ε-differential privacy, the optimal noise has a staircase-shaped density that outperforms Laplace noise, particularly in the low-privacy regime. Related work by Soria-Comas and Domingo-Ferrer (2013) arrived at similar staircase-like distributions through different arguments. These results show that the optimal noise distribution is generally not a familiar one, and that the gap between standard and optimal mechanisms can be substantial. The relaxed notion of (ε,δ)-differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006) permits the privacy guarantee to fail with small probability δ. It is the setting in which the Gaussian mechanism is typically analyzed and applied, because Gaussian noise composes conveniently and interacts well with high-dimensional queries (Dwork and Roth, 2014; Mironov, 2017). Calibrating Gaussian noise to (ε,δ) was long done through loose sufficient conditions, and Balle and Wang (2018) recently tightened this calibration with an analytic characterization. Yet even a perfectly calibrated Gaussian mechanism is not known to be optimal. For approximate differential privacy, Geng and Viswanath (2016) characterized optimal mechanisms in the discrete setting, but the continuous setting, where the query output and the noise take real values, has remained largely unresolved. Whether Gaussian noise is close to optimal, and what an optimal mechanism looks like when δ is the main privacy parameter, has therefore been unclear. This paper addresses the following question. For a single real-valued query function with bounded sensitivity, what is the query-output-independent additive noise distribution that minimizes a general cost function of the noise subject to (0,δ)-differential privacy? We focus on the case ε = 0, in which the guarantee is controlled entirely by δ. This isolates the role of the failure probability. Under (0,δ)-differential privacy, the distributions of the mechanism's output under any two neighboring query values must be within total variation distance δ. Understanding this regime is a natural first step toward the full (ε,δ) problem. It also gives a clean benchmark for judging how much room existing Gaussian mechanisms leave for improvement, and it connects directly to the discrete-setting results. Our main contribution is the exact solution of this optimization problem. Under a mild technical condition on the cost function, we show that the optimal noise distribution is a uniform distribution together with a point mass at the origin. The uniform component spreads probability over an interval whose width is tied to the query sensitivity and to δ. The point mass allows the mechanism to leave the query output unperturbed with positive probability, spending the privacy budget δ where it buys the most reduction in cost. This structure contrasts sharply with the smooth, unimodal densities used in standard mechanisms, and it differs from the staircase form that is optimal under ε-differential privacy. The result is a genuinely new form of optimal noise, and it follows from a reduction of the infinite-dimensional problem to a tractable one, followed by a characterization of the extremal solutions. Our second contribution is an explicit solution for the family of ℓ^p cost functions, which includes the ℓ^1 cost (expected noise magnitude) and the ℓ^2 cost (expected noise power) as special cases. We obtain closed-form optimal noise parameters as functions of δ, the sensitivity, and p. We show that the probability mass at the origin is positive exactly when δ > p/(p+1). When δ is below this threshold, the optimal mechanism is purely uniform. Above it, a nontrivial atom appears. This is a phase-transition-like phenomenon specific to the continuous setting, and the threshold depends on the cost exponent in a simple way. Our third contribution is a quantitative comparison with the Gaussian mechanism. In the high-privacy regime (small δ), the optimal mechanism improves on the Gaussian mechanism by a factor of two for the ℓ^1 cost, which measures noise magnitude, and by a factor of three for the ℓ^2 cost, which measures noise power. The advantage grows in the low-privacy regime, where the Gaussian mechanism wastes a large amount of noise relative to what the guarantee requires. These gains come at no loss of privacy, since the guarantee is the same (0,δ) condition. This indicates that practical systems relying on Gaussian noise for such guarantees may be adding substantially more noise than necessary. Finally, we relate our findings to prior work in the discrete setting. Our continuous-setting solution is consistent with the known optimal mechanisms for (0,δ)-differential privacy over integer-valued outputs, which also exhibit concentration of probability at zero. Our analysis therefore unifies the two regimes and identifies the probability concentration at the origin as the continuous counterpart of the discrete phenomenon. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first formalize the problem, including the definition of (0,δ)-differential privacy for additive mechanisms and the cost-minimization framework. We then present the main theorem on the optimal noise distribution, specialize it to ℓ^p costs, and compare the result with Gaussian mechanisms and with the discrete setting. Problem formulation. We consider a single real-valued query function q: 𝒟ⁿ → ℝ evaluated on a database D, with global sensitivity Δ = sup |q(D₁) − q(D₂)| taken over all neighboring databases D₁ and D₂ (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork & Roth, 2014). We study query-output independent additive mechanisms, which release M(D) = q(D) + X. The noise X is drawn from a probability measure P on ℝ that does not depend on D or on the value q(D). A mechanism is (ε, δ)-differentially private if, for all neighboring D₁, D₂ and all measurable sets S, Pr[M(D₁) ∈ S] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(D₂) ∈ S] + δ. We focus on ε = 0. Because the privacy constraint depends on the query only through the shift q(D₁) − q(D₂), which lies in [−Δ, Δ], the condition for additive mechanisms is equivalent to a condition on P alone: P(S) ≤ P(S + d) + δ for every measurable S and every |d| ≤ Δ. Equivalently, the total variation distance between X and X + d is at most δ for all |d| ≤ Δ. This is the continuous analogue of the (0, δ) setting studied for discrete-valued queries (Geng & Viswanath, 2016; Geng et al., 2015). Cost-minimization framework. Utility is measured by the expected cost of the noise, 𝔼[L(X)] = ∫ L(x) P(dx), where L: ℝ → ℝ₊ is a cost function. The optimization problem is to minimize ∫ L(x) P(dx) over all probability measures P satisfying the (0, δ) constraint above. We assume that L is even, nondecreasing in |x|, and satisfies L(0) = 0. We also impose a mild technical regularity condition that guarantees the infimum is attained and rules out pathological cost functions. Our main focus is the ℓᵖ family L(x) = |x|ᵖ with p > 0. The case p = 1 measures expected noise magnitude and p = 2 measures noise power. The measure P is allowed to have both an absolutely continuous part and atoms, so that probability concentration at the origin is not excluded a priori. Derivation procedure. The derivation follows the strategy used for the staircase mechanism (Geng & Viswanath, 2016; Geng et al., 2015) and proceeds in four steps. 1. Linear-program view. For fixed L and δ, the objective is linear in P, and the constraints P(S) − P(S + d) ≤ δ are linear in P. The problem is therefore an infinite-dimensional linear program over measures. 2. Reduction of the feasible set. We show that, under the regularity condition, an optimal P can be taken symmetric about the origin. Its absolutely continuous part can be taken to be nonincreasing in |x|, since otherwise a rearrangement that moves mass toward the origin does not increase the cost and does not violate the constraint. The (0, δ) constraint can then be tested on a reduced family of sets and shifts, and the extremal shift is d = ±Δ. 3. Structural characterization. Using the reduced constraints, we show that any feasible distribution can be replaced by one with a piecewise-constant density whose pieces have length Δ, together with a possible atom at zero, without increasing the cost. A further exchange argument shows that, at the optimum, the density is constant on a symmetric interval [−b, b] and zero elsewhere. The optimal measure thus takes the form P = γ·δ₀ + (1 − γ)·Uniform[−b, b], with 0 ≤ γ ≤ δ, where δ₀ is the point mass at the origin. 4. Parameter optimization. For this family, the total variation between X and X + Δ equals the mass that can be moved by the extremal set. This mass is the atom at the origin plus the non-overlapping part of the uniform density, so the privacy constraint binds at δ = γ + (1 − γ)Δ / (2b). Solving for b gives b = (1 − γ)Δ / (2(δ − γ)). For L(x) = |x|ᵖ, the expected cost of the family is then C(γ) = (1 − γ)·bᵖ / (p + 1) = Δᵖ (1 − γ)^{p+1} / (2ᵖ (p + 1) (δ − γ)ᵖ). We minimize C(γ) over γ ∈ [0, δ). The logarithmic derivative of C is −(p + 1)/(1 − γ) + p/(δ − γ). At γ = 0 it is negative exactly when δ > p/(p + 1). Setting it to zero gives the stationary point γ = (p + 1)δ − p. Hence the optimal atom is zero when δ ≤ p/(p + 1), and the optimal noise is then a pure uniform distribution on [−Δ/(2δ), Δ/(2δ)]. When δ > p/(p + 1), the optimal atom is γ = (p + 1)δ − p > 0, and the uniform part has half-width b = (1 − γ)Δ / (2(δ − γ)). The condition δ > p/(p + 1) therefore marks the onset of probability concentration at the origin. For p = 1 the threshold is δ = 1/2, and for p = 2 it is δ = 2/3. We verify that C is minimized at the interior stationary point by checking its behavior at the endpoints γ = 0 and γ → δ, where the cost diverges. Comparison with baseline mechanisms. We compare the optimal mechanism with the Gaussian mechanism, the standard additive-noise baseline for (ε, δ)-differential privacy (Dwork & Roth, 2014). For ε = 0, we calibrate the Gaussian standard deviation σ exactly rather than with the classical sufficient bound. The exact (0, δ) condition for N(0, σ²) noise is δ = 2Φ(Δ/(2σ)) − 1, where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. This follows from the exact characterization of Gaussian privacy loss in Balle & Wang (2018). We solve this equation numerically for σ and compute the expected costs 𝔼|X| = σ√(2/π) for p = 1 and 𝔼[X²] = σ² for p = 2. For the optimal mechanism, costs are computed from the closed forms above. Guidelines can be defined as “any document containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy. A recommendation tells the intended end-user of the guideline what he or she can or should do in specific situations to achieve the best health outcomes possible, individually or collectively” [1]. Guidelines are developed by a range of organizations including charities endorsed by local professional societies (e.g., The Heart Foundation endorsed by the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP)), national health research institutes (e.g., US National Institutes of Health (NIH), the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), and Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC)), and international health organizations (e.g., the World Health Organization (WHO)). In order to be trustworthy, all guidelines, both clinical and public health, should be evidence based and should be developed using clear, explicit processes to minimize bias and optimize transparency [2]. The implementation of evidence-based guidelines can improve clinical and public health outcomes by helping health professionals practice in the most effective manner [3, 4], as well as assisting policy-makers in designing optimal programs. The development of guidelines without adequate consideration of implementation may hinder the target audiences’ adherence to the guidelines [5]. Without proper implementation, the financial and human resources expended in the development of guidelines are wasted. The implementation of guidelines in a context that is different from where they were developed is particularly challenging. In addition, recommendations in public health guidelines are often more complex to implement than clinical guidelines and usually target health systems or multi-sector government institutions instead of individual clinical decisions. For example, WHO develops guidelines for a global audience; each guideline or recommendation in each guideline then needs to be considered for implementation at the country or sub-national level (e.g., within a health system). Other examples include implementation of national guidelines to the local (e.g., state or provincial) context [6], international guidelines to a local hospital [7], European guidelines to individual countries [8], and international guidelines to regions [9]. There are a number of systematic reviews on the effectiveness of various implementation strategies for recommendations in guidelines [10–12]. Most indicate that active techniques are the most effective. However, many guidelines do not include detailed descriptions of how the guidelines should be implemented [13]. Adaptation is a key step in the implementation process [13]. Guidelines International Network (G-I-N) defines guideline adaptation as “the systematic approach to the modification of a guideline(s) produced in one cultural and organisational setting for application in a different context”. Guideline adaptation is usually initiated by end-users at the local level (e.g., by local governments, hospitals, and/or individual clinicians) and not by international (e.g., WHO) or national (e.g., NHMRC) guideline developers. Adaptation is an alternative to de novo guideline development such as customizing an existing guideline to the local context [14] which could be a specific health setting, country, or an emergency situation. In order to achieve effective adaptation, guideline adaptors should take into account a number of important aspects of the local context such as resource capabilities (both human and material), disease prevalence, and the values and preferences of community members. If the local context is not taken into account, interventions recommended in existing high-quality guidelines may be impossible to implement. For example, recommending widespread use of information and communications technologies without adequate knowledge of their use in the local health system may be more of a burden than a boon to the health system [15]. Adapting the guidelines and local capacity building in understanding and applying the recommended interventions are vital for their successful uptake. It is not only the recommendations within the guidelines that may need to be adapted to suit the local context, but also different implementation strategies may be required for guidelines in different contexts. Developing guidelines de novo requires substantial time and resources—both methodological expertise and fiscal capacity. When a high-quality guideline is available which addresses the local need, it may be more practical to adapt this guideline (or selected recommendations therein) for local use [16]. For example, until 2012, New Zealand had a high-quality internationally respected guideline development program through the New Zealand Guidelines Group [17]. This group went into voluntary liquidation in mid-2012 [17]. After this, the New Zealand Ministry of Health provided funding to a new guideline organization: The Best Practice Advocacy Centre New Zealand (bpacNZ) to adapt NICE clinical guidelines for use in New Zealand based on the ADAPTE approach [18]. From here on, we will refer to original and established source materials (e.g., WHO guidelines) as “source guidelines” or “source materials,” while the new and modified guidelines/recommendations produced by the adaptation process will be referred to as “adapted guidelines” or “adapted recommendations.” When a clinical practice or public health guideline is needed in a specific context, recommendations can be constructed using one of four possible approaches: Adopt recommendations from existing evidence-based source guidelines without modification; Adapt recommendations from existing guidelines to the new context; Develop recommendations de novo based on existing reviews of evidence (from source guidelines or systematic reviews) [19]; and Develop recommendations de novo based on new evidence syntheses. Adapted guidelines can contain recommendations from a mixture of these approaches. Additional file 1 summarizes factors that may influence a local group to choose one of these approaches over another. Informal guideline adaptation occurs without using an established framework [7]. For example, when a hospital in Lebanon considered adapting a guideline on low back pain [7], no formal adaptation framework was used. The hospital guideline adapters simply identified international guidelines in the literature, compared them according to the AGREE instrument [20], and implemented the “best” one after translating it into the local language [7]. Informal adaptation can also be done on an individual provider or patient level [21]. Doctors in Sudan were noted to adapt international guidelines on an ad hoc basis, in order to suit the patient and the health care system in their country. One of the doctors interviewed in this study said “I cannot prescribe the new drug (X) which is not found in Sudan. We stick to guidelines but with a modified picture” [21]. The high frequency of testing suggested by international guidelines may also be impractical in low-resource settings, as for example, some patients may have to travel long distances for the tests [21]. Such ad hoc adaptations, although practical in some situations, can pose a risk if the intervention that is implemented is outside of the scope of the original evidence-based recommendation. This occurs when adaptation of a guideline is performed using a guideline adaptation group and an established framework [22]. Due to the complexity of applying formal frameworks, this type of adaptation is always done collectively. Formal frameworks, in contrast to informal adaptation methods, can enable evaluation of the evidence supporting the recommendations in adapted guidelines. A recent review has identified some of the frameworks for guideline adaptation [24]. We aim to understand advantages and limitations of existing frameworks and identify knowledge gaps in the process of guideline adaptation through an analysis of recent adaptation frameworks. This in turn will help to identify optimal characteristics of frameworks to inform guideline development, implementation, and uptake. The analysis drew from literature published over the past 15 years (1 January 2002 to 1 March 2017) as this area of research is relatively new. Very few studies on guideline adaptation were published prior to 2002. MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL databases were systematically searched for published accounts of formal adaptation frameworks. Knowledge and skills requirements for the software design and testing of automotive applications J. Zabavnik, A. Riel, M. Marguč, M. Rodič Abstract— The required knowledge and skills that should be provided to the novice developer, designing and testing the safety critical device in automotive industry using Hardware-in-theLoop (HiL), are presented in the paper. They should be available to the student finishing the MSc level of Electrical Engineering or Mechatronics that aims to seek the employment in the automotive industry. The development process is presented in short, together with the brief explanations of phases, which include some typical examples of written text in the documentation (requirements, test cases, etc.). The process follows the Automotive SPICE and focuses on the tip of the V-model. The presented text can serve as a useful information in the process of adapting the existing curriculum to the new occurring needs introduced by the new development and testing processes in industry. Index Terms— software engineering, requirements, Hardwarein-the-Loop, testing, automotive N the modern vehicles there is a growing number of electric, electronic and programmed electronic devices. This is not only the case for the main drive (drivetrain), but also for a big number of auxiliary devices. In many cases previously mechanic or hydraulic devices are being replaced with the electric ones. For many such devices (so-called safety critical devices), failures could result in serious, even fatal, injuries of the passenger in the vehicle. These failures must be avoided as far as possible at reasonable cost and in a way sustainable for the producer of the vehicle. Using extremely reliable devices would in many cases result in a very high cost of the final product, making it unaffordable for the customer. The solution is therefore to develop in such a way, that the devices remain safe even in the case of their failure, i.e., to achieve functional safety of the device and as a result also vehicle. Failures shall be avoided, however if this is not possible, their effects have to be mitigated. This goal can be achieved with the use of fault-tolerant devices developed according to the proper development cycle. The development cycle in the automotive industry is based on the classical V-model, where the development from the user requirements to the validation of the product is described. In automotive industry processes are specified in compliance with the Automotive SPICE standard [1]. Both the system and software development process is upgraded with the processes and methods prescribed in IEC/ISO 26262 [2], the functional safety standard for the electrical, electronic and programmable electronic devices in road vehicles. Automotive SPICE and IEC/ISO 26262 thus represent the most important documents in automotive industry to comply with the Quality Management and Functional Safety assessment. The risk classification scheme defined in the IEC/ISO 26262 is called Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL) and is used to rate hazards of the system based on the consideration of malfunctions in particular driving situations. To verify the applied system, architecture, software and hardware, testing is an essential tool. It is used in order to determine whether the objectives set are met. Testing is performed based on the requirements, where the most important upgrade introduced by the IEC/ISO 26262 is the introduction of the testing of functional safety objectives. For this purpose, the ISO/IEC does not only specify the requirements regarding the processes, but also prescribes the methods which shall be applied. Among the methods required by IEC/ISO 26262, the Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) testing has become indispensable in the automotive domain [8]. It represents the method where the device under test is placed in an emulated environment. The basic principle of the method is presented in the Figure 1. With the use of HiL, systems testing can be performed under close-to-real conditions. Since the device under test is available in real during testing, and no understanding of its internal design is therefore required, HiL testing is a form of black-box testing. Black-box testing can be performed for testing of units, integration testing, system testing and up to the certain level, even system validation. The testing processes as described above have been widely accepted in the automotive industry. They represent a must for any company wishing to be a part of the automotive development process or supply chain. It has been observed, however, that there is a serious lack of engineers familiar with these processes and methods, and consequently many companies, especially smaller ones, experience serious difficulties in adopting them. Definitely the knowledge in this field will be required from the future employees and therefore it is important that teaching it becomes a part of the education process, especially at higher education levels. This is especially important for the students of Electrical Engineering and Mechatronics. April 12, 2019 Probabilistic databases (PDBs) introduce uncertainty into relational databases by specifying probabilities for several possible instances. Traditionally, they are finite probability spaces over database instances. Such finite PDBs inherently make a closed-world assumption: non-occurring facts are assumed to be impossible, rather than just unlikely. As convincingly argued by Ceylan et al. (KR ’16), this results in implausibilities and clashes with intuition. An open-world assumption, where facts not explicitly listed may have a small positive probability can yield more reasonable results. The corresponding open-world model of Ceylan et al., however, assumes that all entities in the PDB come from a fixed finite universe. In this work, we take one further step and propose a model of “truly” open-world PDBs with an infinite universe. This is natural when we consider entities from typical domains such as integers, real numbers, or strings. While the probability space might become infinitely large, all instances of a PDB remain finite. We provide a sound mathematical framework for infinite PDBs generalizing the existing theory of finite PDBs. Our main results are concerned with countable, tuple-independent PDBs; we present a generic construction showing that such PDBs exist in the infinite and provide a characterization of their existence. This construction can be used to give an open-world semantics to finite PDBs. The construction can also be extended to so-called block-independent-disjoint probabilistic databases. Algorithmic questions are not the focus of this paper, but we show how query evaluation algorithms can be lifted from finite PDBs to perform approximate evaluation (with an arbitrarily small additive approximation error) in countably infinite tuple-independent PDBs. 1 Introduction Probabilistic databases (PDBs) are uncertain databases where uncertainty is quantified in terms of probabilities. The current standard model of probabilistic databases [4, 19, 37, 38] is an extension of the relational model that associates probabilities to the facts appearing in a relational database. Formally, it is convenient to view such a probabilistic database, which we shall call a finite PDB here, as a probability distribution over a finite set of database instances of the same schema. A very important basic class of finite PDBs is the class of tuple-independent finite PDBs, in which all facts, that is, events of the form “tuple t appears in relation R”, are assumed to be stochastically independent. This independence assumption implies that the whole probability distribution of the PDB is fully determined by the marginal distributions of the individual facts and that the probability of all instances can easily be calculated from these marginal probabilities. Thus, a tuple-independent PDB can be represented as a table (resp. as tables) of all possible facts annotated with their respective marginal probabilities. According to [27], well-known systems that operate under the assumption of tuple-independence are, among others, Google’s Knowledge Vault [17], the NELL project [29] and DeepDive [30]. The focus on tuple-independent finite PDBs can be further justified by the fact that all finite PDBs can be represented by first-order (or relational calculus) views over tuple-independent finite PDBs (see [37]). Modeling uncertainty by finite PDBs entails an implicit closed-world assumption (CWA) [31]: • entities not appearing in the finitely many instances with positive probability do not exist and • facts not appearing in these instances are strictly impossible, rather than just unlikely. In tuple-independent finite PDBs, this means that facts that are not explicitly listed with a positive probability are impossible. As has already been argued by Ceylan, Darwiche, and Van den Broeck [14], operating under the CWA can be problematic. For example, consider a database that collects temperature measurements in the author’s offices. Due to unreliable sensors, these measurements are inherently imprecise and the database may be regarded as uncertain and modeled as a PDB. Now suppose that the database never records a temperature between 20.2 ◦C and 20.5 ◦C. Is it reasonable to derive that such a temperature is impossible? Or suppose that the data show that the temperature in the first author’s office is always at least 0.1 ◦C below the temperature of the second author’s office. Should we conclude that it is impossible that the temperature in the first author’s office is higher than the temperature in the second author’s office? Given the uncertainty of the data, we would rather say it is unlikely (has low probability, where of course the exact probability depends on the distribution modeling the uncertainty in the data). Moreover, we would expect that the event “the temperature in the first author’s office is 0.05 ◦C below that in the second author’s office” has a higher probability than the event “the temperature in the first author’s office is 10 ◦C above that in the second author’s office”. In a closed-world model however, both events have the exact same probability 0. Considerations like these led Ceylan et al. [14] to proposing a model of open-world probabilistic databases. Their model is tuple-independent, but instead of probability 0, facts not appearing in the database are assumed to have a small positive probability (below some threshold λ). However, Ceylan et al. still assume that all entities in the database come from a fixed finite universe. Hence their model is “open-world” with respect to facts, but not with respect to entities or values. In this work, we take one step further and propose a model of “truly” open-world probabilistic databases modeled by an infinite supply of entities. Formally, we define a probabilistic database (PDB) to be a probability space over a sample space consisting of database instances of the same schema and with entities from the same infinite universe. Note that every instance in such a PDB is still finite; it is only the probability space and the universe of potential entities that may be infinite. There are various ways in which such probabilistic databases may arise in practice: collecting data from unreliable sources, completing incomplete databases by using statistical or machine learning models, or even having datasets entirely represented by machine learning models. This is not very different from finite PDBs, except that often it is more natural to allow infinite domains, for example for numerical values or for strings. One may argue that in practice the domains are always finite (such as 64-bit integers, 64-bit floating point numbers, or strings with fixed maximum length), but conceptually it is still much more natural to use models with an idealized infinite domain, as it is common in most other areas of computer science and numerical mathematics. In this paper, we explore the mathematical foundations of infinite (relational) probabilistic databases. The general definition of PDBs is given and discussed in Section 3. In Section 4 we consider tuple-independent infinite PDBs and show how to construct a countable, tupleindependent PDB from specified fact probabilities. Unfortunately, the nice result, that every finite PDB can be represented by a finite tuple-independent PDB does not carry over to infinite PDBs (Proposition 4.9). In addition to our investigation of tuple-independence, we provide an extension of their existence results results to the practically important block-independent-disjoint PDBs (Theorem 4.15). Next, in Section 5, we study the “open-world” aspect of PDBs. We start from a given discrete PDB and construct a countable “completion” that specifies probabilities for every imaginable instance. The key requirement for such a completion to be reasonable is that the probability measure is faithfully extended: the new probability measure should coincide with the old one, when conditioned over old instances. We extend the construction of countable tupleindependent PDBs to a construction of tuple-independent completions (Theorem 5.5). Albeit query evaluation is not the focus of this paper, in Section 6 we hint that it is algorithmically not completely out of reach even in the infinite setting. Using a naı̈ve truncation procedure, we show how to lift query evaluation for finite PDBs to obtain approximate query answer probabilities in the case of countably infinite tuple-independent PDBs. Note, that this is only the very first step towards the algorithmic investigation of our infinite PDBs. Related Work We rely foundationally on the extensive work on finite PDBs (see, for example [4, 37, 38]). Although some system-oriented approaches are capable of dealing with continuous PDBs (like MCDB [22], PIP [23], ORION [34] and the extended Trio system [6]), these systems typically model probabilistic databases with an a priori bounded number of facts. In the case of probabilistic XML [3, 24] (that is, probabilistic tree databases) a continuous extension with solid theoretical foundations has been proposed [1], which however also only allows a bounded number of facts (resp. leaf nodes) in its instances. On the other hand, a proposed extension of probabilistic XML that allows for unbounded tree structures does not account for continuous distributions [9]. Work on incomplete databases [2, 19, 21, 39], which is also an important source of motivation for our work, has always naturally assumed potentially infinite domains, but not treated them probabilistically. In the context of probabilistic databases we want to emphasize again the impact of the OpenPDB model [14] to our investigations. More recently, it has been proposed to extend OpenPDBs using domain knowledge in the form of ontologies [11, 12], yielding more intuitive query results with respect to the open-world assumption in OpenPDBs. In the AI community and in probabilistic programming, open-universe models have been considered before. Inference in probabilistic models is closely related to query answering in probabilistic databases [38]. In this area, some related work has been conducted, although with different backgrounds and aims. Languages respectively models like BLOG [28], Infinite Domain Markov Logic [35], probabilistic logic programming [16], and Probabilistic Programming Datalog [7] are capable of describing infinite probability spaces of structures. It is also worth mentioning, that weighted first order model counting has been previously considered in an open-universe setting with given, relation-level probabilities [8]. Finally, let us point out a fundamental difference between our notion of countable tupleindependent PDBs and notions of limit probabilities in asymptotic combinatorics (for example, [10, 36]). For example, the classical Erdős-Rényi model G(n, p) of random graphs is also what we would call a tuple-independent model: the edges of an n-vertex graph are drawn independently with probability p. However, the sample space is finite, it consists of all n-vertex graphs. Then the behavior of these spaces as n goes to infinity is studied. This means that the properties of very large graphs dominate the behavior observed here. This contrasts our model of infinite tuple-independent PDBs, which is dominated by the behavior of PDBs whose size is close to the expected value (which for tuple-independent PDBs is always finite). Both views have their merits, but we believe that for studying probabilistic databases our model is better suited. 2 Preliminaries By N we denote the set of positive integers, and by R the set of real numbers. Engineered nanoparticles (NPs) are now integral to sectors as diverse as medicine, electronics, catalysis, cosmetics, food and environmental remediation. Their value derives largely from size-dependent properties, including optical response, catalytic activity, colloidal stability, biodistribution and cellular uptake (Wilhelm et al., 2016). Size, and increasingly particle number concentration, are therefore regarded as critical quality attributes. Regulators have also made them central to how nanomaterials are defined and controlled. The European Commission's recommended definition (2011/696/EU) refers to materials in which at least 50% of particles, by number, have one or more external dimensions between 1 and 100 nm. It thereby requires a number-weighted distribution, not simply a mean diameter. Comparable demands for physicochemical characterisation appear in guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration (2014) and in the safety assessment frameworks of the OECD. In practice, meeting such requirements means producing size and concentration data that are accurate, traceable and reproducible across laboratories. Most NPs are produced, stored, administered or encountered in the liquid phase, whether as colloidal reagents, nanomedicines, biological vesicles or environmental dispersions. Characterisation in suspension is therefore often more relevant than characterisation of dried material. Drying for electron microscopy can introduce aggregation, shrinkage, salt crystallisation and loss of the hydration shell, so the measured size may not reflect the state in which the particles function (Domingos et al., 2009). Light-scattering techniques are the main alternative. Dynamic light scattering (DLS), also called photon correlation spectroscopy, infers a hydrodynamic diameter from the decay of intensity fluctuations caused by Brownian motion. This is achieved through the Stokes–Einstein relationship and cumulants or regularisation-based analysis (Koppel, 1972; Pecora, 2000; Stetefeld et al., 2016). The method is rapid, requires small volumes and is standardised (ISO 22412:2017). It is now the default sizing tool in many laboratories and quality-control environments. Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), standardised more recently as particle tracking analysis (ISO 19430:2016), instead visualises the scattered light from individual particles and follows their trajectories. It computes diffusion coefficients particle by particle and can provide a number-weighted size distribution along with an estimate of particle concentration (Carr and Malloy, 2006; Filipe et al., 2010). That capability has made NTA attractive for extracellular vesicles, viral vectors and protein aggregates (Dragovic et al., 2011). The apparent simplicity of these instruments conceals considerable complexity. Intensity-weighted DLS results are dominated by the largest species because scattered intensity scales approximately with the sixth power of particle diameter in the Rayleigh regime. A small fraction of aggregates or dust can therefore shift the z-average substantially and obscure a smaller population (Bhattacharjee, 2016). Conversion to volume- or number-weighted distributions depends on assumed optical properties and on ill-conditioned inversion of the correlation function, and the resolution of DLS for polydisperse samples is limited. Anderson et al. (2013) showed that for mixtures of particles differing by less than a factor of about two in diameter, DLS and NTA could return markedly different distributions, with accuracy and resolution depending strongly on platform and analysis settings. For NTA, reported values depend on camera level, detection threshold, tracking length, temperature and viscosity. Counting is further biased by the lower detection limit, which for weakly scattering particles, such as polymeric or biological particles, may lie well above 50 nm. Interlaboratory studies reflect these sensitivities. Hole et al. (2013) found that, even for monodisperse reference materials, sizes from different operators and instruments varied appreciably. Concentration estimates are generally less reproducible than size, with variability frequently exceeding that of size by an order of magnitude, since the effective scattering volume is not directly measured but inferred from instrument calibration. Parameters external to the instrument, including sample preparation, dilution medium, ionic strength, pH, sample temperature, adsorption to tubing and cuvettes, and the presence of contaminants, further contribute to the final uncertainty. Few studies consider these influences within a single, coherent framework. Orthogonal methods that do not rely on light scattering offer complementary information and a route to validation. Electron microscopy yields direct, number-based dimensions with nanometre resolution, but only on dried specimens and with limited statistics. Atomic force microscopy provides accurate height measurements on substrates. Tunable resistive pulse sensing measures particles individually through changes in ionic current and can provide both size and concentration (Vogel et al., 2011). Single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (spICP-MS) quantifies the mass of the target element per particle, and hence the particle size and number concentration for metallic NPs at ng L⁻¹ levels (Laborda et al., 2014). Separation-based approaches, notably field-flow fractionation coupled to multi-angle light scattering, and analytical ultracentrifugation, resolve populations before or during detection. Small-angle X-ray scattering and differential centrifugal sedimentation add further capabilities. Each technique responds to a different physical property: hydrodynamic, projected, mass-equivalent, Stokes or sedimentation diameter. Results should therefore not be expected to agree numerically, and apparent discrepancies may reflect real differences in the measurand (Domingos et al., 2009). The literature has seldom made these distinctions explicit for end users, who are frequently presented with a single "size" value without a statement of its definition or uncertainty. Existing reviews tend to describe individual techniques in depth, or to compare them empirically for selected reference materials. There is no consolidated account that connects the physical principles of light-scattering methods to the practical variables that determine measurement uncertainty, or that sets these methods beside non-optical approaches in terms of applicability and limitations. This gap matters because the growing regulatory emphasis on validated, fit-for-purpose methods requires users to understand where uncertainty originates and how it can be controlled. The question addressed in this perspective is therefore: which factors most strongly govern the accuracy and reproducibility of NP size and concentration measurements obtained by DLS and NTA, and how do these methods compare with alternative technologies in suspension? We make three contributions. First, we summarise the principles, capabilities and limitations of the main techniques for characterising NPs in liquid, covering both light-scattering and non-scattering approaches. Second, we present a cause-and-effect (Ishikawa-type) analysis of the principal contributors to uncertainty in size and concentration determination by NTA and DLS, grouping them into sample, instrument, operator and data-analysis factors, with the aim of identifying where uncertainty can be reduced. Third, we offer guidance for selecting an appropriate technology, or combination of technologies, according to the material, the required measurand and the regulatory context. We hope that this detailed methodological treatment will help scientists generate size and concentration data that satisfy regulatory expectations and can be meaningfully compared between laboratories. Study design and scope This Perspective was prepared as a structured, critical appraisal of techniques for characterising nanoparticles (NPs) in liquid suspension. It did not follow a systematic-review protocol. The aim was to compare the techniques against common performance criteria and to identify the sources of uncertainty in the two most widely used light-scattering methods, nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). The work had three stages: (i) a structured literature and standards survey; (ii) a comparative evaluation of technologies; and (iii) a cause-and-effect analysis of the measurands "hydrodynamic size" and "particle number concentration". Literature and standards survey Peer-reviewed articles, international standards and regulatory guidance published between January 1990 and December 2022 were searched in Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed. Search strings combined the terms "nanoparticle", "particle size distribution", "number concentration", "dynamic light scattering", "photon correlation spectroscopy", "nanoparticle tracking analysis", "multi-angle light scattering", "field-flow fractionation", "analytical ultracentrifugation", "resistive-pulse sensing", "single-particle ICP-MS", "small-angle X-ray scattering" and "electron microscopy". Boolean operators were used to combine these with "measurement uncertainty", "reproducibility" and "reference material". Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance to colloidal suspensions in the nominal range 1 nm–1 µm. Priority was given to three kinds of source: inter-laboratory comparisons; studies using certified or well-characterised reference materials; documentary standards and guidance, including ISO 22412 for DLS (International Organization for Standardization, 2017), ISO 19430 for particle tracking analysis (International Organization for Standardization, 2016), and the NIST–NCL protocols for NP size measurement (Hackley & Clogston, 2007). Regulatory definitions and data requirements were taken from the European Commission Recommendation on the definition of nanomaterial (European Commission, 2022) and from guidance issued by the European Food Safety Authority and the US Food and Drug Administration. Reports were included when the measurand, sample preparation and instrument settings were described sufficiently to judge comparability. Conference abstracts and manufacturer literature were used only to document instrument specifications and were not used as evidence of performance. Framework for comparing technologies Each technology was assessed against a fixed set of attributes extracted from the selected literature: 1. the physical principle and the quantity actually measured (for example, intensity-weighted harmonic-mean diffusion coefficient versus number-weighted trajectory-based diffusion coefficients); 2. the nominal working size range and the lower and upper practical concentration limits; 3. the weighting of the reported distribution (intensity, volume or number); 4. the capacity to resolve polydisperse or multimodal samples; 5. the requirement for dilution, labelling, separation or other sample manipulation; 6. the traceability of the result to the SI; 7. the reported repeatability and between-laboratory reproducibility, expressed as relative standard deviation (RSD) where available. Where published studies reported a bias between methods, the bias was expressed relative to the nominal or certified value of the reference material. For example, the percentage difference between the DLS z-average diameter and the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) modal diameter was recorded for monodisperse polystyrene latex and gold NPs. Values were extracted manually by two reviewers, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Theoretical basis for light-scattering measurements For DLS, the analysis used the standard relationship between the decay rate Γ of the intensity autocorrelation function and the translational diffusion coefficient D, namely Γ = Dq², where q = (4πn/λ)sin(θ/2) is the scattering vector, n the refractive index of the dispersant, λ the laser wavelength and θ the detection angle. The hydrodynamic diameter dH was obtained from the Stokes–Einstein relation, dH = kBT/(3πηD), in which kB is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature and η the dispersant viscosity. Cumulants analysis (Koppel, 1972) provided the z-average diameter and polydispersity index (PdI), and regularised inversion (for example CONTIN; Provencher, 1982) or non-negative least squares provided size distributions. Conversion from intensity- to volume- or number-weighted distributions was considered in terms of Mie theory. The dependence of scattered intensity on d⁶ in the Rayleigh regime was noted as a key source of bias in polydisperse samples (Stetefeld et al., 2016). For NTA, the analysis considered the video-based tracking of individual scatterers undergoing Brownian motion. The mean squared displacement in two dimensions, ⟨x,y²⟩ = 4Dt, is used to compute D for each trajectory, and dH is again obtained from the Stokes–Einstein relation (Carr & Malloy, 2006). Number concentration was assumed to follow from the number of tracks counted within a calibrated scattering volume, taking into account the dilution factor (Hole et al., 2013). The limitations of these assumptions were examined using published comparisons between NTA and DLS for protein aggregates, liposomes and metallic NPs (Filipe et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2013). Cause-and-effect analysis A cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) analysis (Ishikawa, 1986) was constructed separately for four combinations of technique and measurand: NTA size, NTA concentration, DLS size and DLS concentration or derived count rate. The analysis followed the principles of the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, 2008). The measurand was defined first, and the measurement model was then decomposed into input quantities. Candidate influence factors were collected from the literature survey and from the instrument operating principles. They were assigned to six branches: Sample: particle composition, shape, polydispersity, concentration, aggregation state, and presence of contaminants or dust. Dispersant: ionic strength, pH, viscosity, refractive index and temperature uniformity. Sample preparation: dilution scheme, mixing, filtration, sonication, adsorption to vials and tubing, and equilibration time. Instrument: laser wavelength and power, detector type and sensitivity, scattering angle, camera gain and shutter, and flow-cell geometry.
