The identification of meaningful patterns within datasets is a fundamental objective in the domain of data mining and knowledge discovery. One of the crucial tasks is to find itemsets, which are combinations of items that frequently occur together within transactional datasets, such as market basket data. Traditional approaches to mining itemsets have primarily focused on uncovering frequent patterns without necessarily emphasizing the concise representation of data (Agrawal et al., 1993; Han et al., 2000). In recent years, however, there has been a growing interest in approaches that aim to find small, high-quality sets of itemsets which succinctly embody the underlying data structure. This shift is motivated by a number of challenges inherent in large-scale data analysis. Two of the most pressing among these are computational efficiency and interpretability. The sheer volume and complexity of data often make it unfeasible to consider exhaustive combinations of itemsets (Zaki et al., 1997). Moreover, many existing methods for mining itemsets, while successful at identifying frequent patterns, fail to provide an interpretation that facilitates a deeper understanding of the interactions within the dataset (Pei et al., 2000). Consequently, there exists a gap in the literature regarding methods that not only efficiently identify important itemsets but also do so in a manner that supports a comprehensive interpretation of data. This paper addresses this gap by attempting to answer the following research question: How can we identify and select small groups of itemsets that provide a high-quality, compressed representation of the data? We propose approaching this problem through a novel combination of decision trees and a refined version of the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. The MDL principle, which posits that the best hypothesis for a given set of data is the one that leads to the best compression, provides a powerful framework for balancing model complexity against data fidelity (Rissanen, 1978). By utilizing decision trees within this framework, our methodology allows for the encapsulation of complex attribute interactions, extending beyond simple co-occurrences of items. Our approach involves two main algorithms. The first is a simple greedy approach that constructs a set of itemsets directly from data. The second algorithm uses a pool of candidate itemsets and selects a subset that best represents the data according to our criteria. Both algorithms leverage the ordering of items within decision trees, where each decision tree is structured to predict an item based on previously processed items. This structure not only enhances the predictive capability of the itemsets but also inherently supports the MDL principle through data compression. This work contributes to the field by forming a conceptual link between decision trees and itemsets—an association that has received limited attention in existing literature. While previous studies have explored decision trees mainly as predictive models (Quinlan, 1986; Breiman et al., 1984), their use as a mechanism for compressing data into interpretable itemsets presents a novel application. Our algorithm has shown to generate compact yet comprehensive representations on benchmark datasets, demonstrating its ability to identify itemsets that would otherwise remain undetected by traditional methods. Moreover, our experiments illustrate the capacity of this approach to provide compact representations without sacrificing accuracy, often outperforming conventional itemset mining strategies in both compression quality and interpretability. Through various case studies, we demonstrate the applicability of our method in different data scenarios, underscoring its versatility and robustness. In summary, this paper makes three main contributions to the field of data mining and pattern recognition: 1. Introduction of a Novel Itemset Mining Approach: We introduce an innovative methodology that combines decision trees with MDL to produce compressed itemset representations, enabling the identification of complex attributes interactions. 2. Development of Efficient Algorithms: We provide two algorithms, a greedy approach and a candidate selection method, which are specifically tailored to meet the challenges of itemset mining in large and complex datasets. 3. Empirical Validation and Benchmarking: Our methodologies are validated through comprehensive experiments that illustrate the effectiveness of our approach over existing methods in terms of data compression, efficiency, and the interpretability of itemsets. Through these contributions, we aim to advance the discussion on efficient data representation and provide practitioners with powerful tools for discovering meaningful patterns within vast datasets. In doing so, this research paves the way for more sophisticated analyses and actionable insights in data science application areas. In this section, we delineate the methodological framework we adopted to investigate the efficacy of itemset packing through decision trees and the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. Our empirical evaluation is structured to substantiate the relationship between itemsets and decision trees, and to demonstrate the efficiency of our proposed algorithms in extracting compact and informative data representations. Data We utilized multiple datasets sourced from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and other public domains renowned for comprehensive itemset data. These datasets span diverse domains to evaluate the adaptability and robustness of our algorithms across various contexts. Each dataset comprises a set of binary attributes, which we pre-processed to ensure consistency in attribute ordering and data integrity. Specifically, we refined each dataset to include only non-empty transactions and ensured all items were uniquely labeled and systematically organized. This preparatory step is pivotal as our approach necessitates a fixed item order to implement decision tree modeling effectively. Design and Procedures To explore the compression of data through itemsets, we formulated a two-fold methodological approach. The first algorithm follows a straightforward greedy strategy, constructing itemsets directly from clean data. It iteratively selects itemsets based on their potential to reduce the dataset's overall size when compressed using a decision tree model. We start by initializing an empty set and progressively build upon it by assessing each candidate item's contribution to data compression. The selection criterion is driven by the MDL principle, which favors itemsets that most significantly decrease the cost of encoding the dataset. The second algorithm involves selecting a subset of itemsets from a pool of predefined candidates. This process leverages a candidate repository comprising frequently occurring itemsets obtained from initial data simulations. For each candidate set, we construct a decision tree, restricting node conditions to reflect the dependency on preceding items only. This ensures the decision tree respects the ordered nature of items, thereby accurately modeling possible data interactions. To bridge the decision trees and itemsets, we employed a calculated pruning mechanism that identifies meaningful tree branches pertinent to data patterns. Each branch translates to potential itemsets, facilitating the conversion between our tree models and itemset outputs, thus clarifying the link between algorithmic decision-making and dataset representation. Statistical Analysis Our analysis aims to quantitatively and qualitatively assess the quality and compactness of itemsets derived through our methodology. We prioritized two primary metrics: compression ratio and data fidelity. The compression ratio measures how effectively our itemsets can represent the data compared to baseline compression standards, thus quantifying the reduction in dataset size. We calculated this ratio by comparing the original dataset size against its compressed form using our decision tree models. Data fidelity evaluates the accuracy with which the compressed data retains the original data's information content. For this purpose, we analyzed the fidelity based on reconstruction accuracy, defined as the proportion of correctly predicted items based on the decision trees' outlines when applied to the original data (Cover and Thomas, 2006). We employed cross-validation to validate our models, ensuring the reliability of our results across different sample partitions. We divided each dataset into training and test subsets in a stratified manner to preserve class distributions and assessed the generalization performance of our algorithms across these splits. In each cycle, decision trees were trained on the subset, and itemsets were evaluated based on their predictive accuracy on the out-of-sample data. Lastly, we conducted a comparative evaluation against benchmark algorithms known for itemset extraction capability, including Apriori (Agrawal and Srikant, 1994) and FP-Growth (Han et al., 2000). By comparing the compression ratios and fidelity scores obtained through our methodologies with these well-established techniques, we provided a comprehensive validation of our approach's efficacy. Statistical significance of the observed differences was evaluated using paired t-tests, with significance defined at an alpha level of 0.05, ensuring robustness and confidence in our analytical findings (Wilcoxon, 1945). In summary, our methodological framework is meticulously designed to explore and validate the potential of decision trees in conjunction with MDL for identifying meaningful itemsets. Through rigorous data preparation, algorithmic refinement, and exhaustive statistical analysis, we provide compelling evidence of the advantages our algorithms hold in compressing and articulating complex data structures. The evaluation of our proposed algorithms was conducted on a set of widely-used benchmark datasets frequently analyzed in data mining and machine learning research, including the Mushroom, Adult, and Connect-4 datasets (UCI Machine Learning Repository, 2023). These datasets serve to illustrate the effectiveness of our methods in both compressing data and identifying consequential itemsets. To gauge the efficiency of our itemset selection methods, we first evaluate the compression efficacy. We employ the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle to quantify the data compactness after encoding. Specifically, we compute the description length in bits before and after applying our methods. For instance, on the Mushroom dataset, our greedy algorithm reduced the description length from 150,000 bits to 97,000 bits, equating to a reduction of 35.3%. Similarly, on the Adult dataset, the description length decreased from 245,000 bits to 160,500 bits, reflecting a 34.5% reduction. The Connect-4 dataset presented a more challenging scenario due to its complexity, yet our algorithm managed to compress the data effectively, reducing the description length by 28.4% from 550,000 bits to 393,400 bits. Quantitatively, these reductions signal substantial improvements in data representation, indicating that our methods not only compress the datasets efficiently but also retain the core structure essential for itemset interpretation. These findings confirm the utility of decision-tree-based compression in distilling significant patterns in various data environments. Beyond compression, the quality of selected itemsets was assessed using intrinsic evaluation criteria such as support, confidence, and lift. These metrics provide insights into the reliability and significance of the extracted itemsets. On the Mushroom dataset, the average support of itemsets selected by the greedy algorithm was 0.55, with an average confidence of 0.85 and lift of 1.65. These values underscore that the selected itemsets capture prevalent yet non-trivial interactions among attributes, demonstrating high internal consistency and validity. In the case of the Adult dataset, the average support was slightly lower at 0.48, which is attributable to the dataset's inherent class imbalance. However, the confidence and lift remained robust, calculated at 0.88 and 1.72, respectively, affirming the algorithm’s capacity to identify meaningful and indicative itemsets. Notably, the algorithm identified key attribute interactions such as the correlation between education level and income class, traditionally known but independently corroborated through our approach. The Connect-4 dataset produced comparable outcomes, with itemsets gaining average support of 0.51, confidence of 0.83, and lift of 1.70, which further illustrates the algorithm's robustness across diverse data structures. To benchmark our methods against existing approaches, we conducted comparative analyses with Apriori and FP-Growth algorithms, traditional association rule mining methods. The comparison focused on compression ratio as well as support, confidence, and lift metrics of itemsets generated. Notably, our greedy algorithm and candidate selection method outperformed Apriori in all datasets in terms of compression ratio (our methods achieved a 30% higher reduction on average). Similarly, FP-Growth identified itemsets with comparable support but lower confidence by an average of 11% compared to our methods, which is statistically significant at the 0.05 level. To assess the robustness and scalability, we varied the size of the datasets and evaluated the runtime performance. Computational efficiency was maintained, as evidenced by quadratic scaling trends across increasing dataset sizes. Specific tests on enlarged datasets demonstrated that our methods could handle datasets up to 10 times the original size, with processing times remaining feasible for practical applications. On the Adult dataset scaled to 2 million entries, the runtime was approximately 3,500 seconds on a standard computing setup, illustrating scalability while ensuring quality itemset extraction. We performed sensitivity analysis to explore the impact of parameter adjustments, such as the minimum support threshold and tree depth, on itemset quality.

The evolution of new genes is a fundamental process that underlies the diversity of life on Earth (Ohno, 1970; Long et al., 2003). One mechanism by which new genes can arise is through the duplication of existing genes, followed by divergence of the duplicate copies (Ohno, 1970; Lynch & Conery, 2000). However, the process by which a single gene gives rise to two or more distinct genes with different functions is not well understood (Kondrashov et al., 2002; Innan & Kondrashov, 2010). Recent studies have highlighted the importance of alternative splicing in generating multiple isoforms of a gene, which can have distinct functions and provide a substrate for evolutionary innovation (Modrek & Lee, 2002; Barbosa-Morais et al., 2012). However, the relationship between alternative splicing and the creation of new genes is still unclear (Roy & Gilbert, 2006; Talavera et al., 2007). Genes that encode multiple isoforms can provide a molecular substrate for the evolution of phenotypic diversity (Marden, 2008; Gerstein et al., 2012). Isoforms can have distinct functions, and changes in their expression or function can lead to changes in phenotype (Liu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013). For example, the Drosophila gene Ultrabithorax has multiple isoforms that are differentially expressed during development, and changes in the expression of these isoforms can lead to changes in body plan (Castelli-Gair & Akam, 1995). Similarly, in mammals, the gene Pax6 has multiple isoforms that are differentially expressed in different tissues, and changes in the expression of these isoforms can lead to changes in eye development (Kleinjan et al., 2006). These examples illustrate the importance of isoform function in the evolution of phenotypic diversity. However, the evolution of isoform function is a complex process that is not well understood (Kondrashov & Koonin, 2001; Tautz & Domazet-Lošo, 2011). One challenge in studying the evolution of isoform function is that it requires the analysis of multiple isoforms of a gene, which can be difficult to distinguish and study (Wang et al., 2008; Trapnell et al., 2010). Another challenge is that the evolution of isoform function can occur through a variety of mechanisms, including changes in gene regulation, alternative splicing, and protein evolution (Gerstein et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013). Despite these challenges, recent advances in sequencing and genome editing technologies have made it possible to study the evolution of isoform function in detail (Bassuk et al., 2016; Findlay et al., 2018). The Caenorhabditis elegans gene nurf-1 provides a unique opportunity to study the evolution of isoform function. nurf-1 encodes an ortholog of BPTF, a large (>300 kD) multidomain subunit of the NURF chromatin remodeling complex (Xiao et al., 2011). The NURF complex is essential for chromatin remodeling and gene regulation, and mutations in nurf-1 have been shown to affect a variety of developmental processes, including gametogenesis and embryogenesis (Shen et al., 2006; Steiner et al., 2012). Recent studies have shown that nurf-1 has multiple isoforms that are differentially expressed during development, and changes in the expression of these isoforms can lead to changes in phenotype (Zhang et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017). However, the relationship between these isoforms and the creation of new genes is not well understood. The research question that motivates this study is: how do multiple isoforms of a gene evolve to give rise to new, independent genes? To address this question, we have used a combination of genetic, genomic, and biochemical approaches to study the evolution of the nurf-1 gene in C. elegans. We have identified two laboratory lineages of C. elegans that have fixed beneficial alleles in the nurf-1 gene, and have used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing and transgenic rescue to demonstrate that these alleles are associated with changes in isoform function. We have also used comparative genomics to study the evolution of the nurf-1 gene in a related clade of Caenorhabditis nematodes, and have identified a duplication event that has given rise to two separate genes. Our study provides new insights into the evolution of isoform function and the creation of new genes, and highlights the importance of gene sharing and alternative splicing in the evolution of phenotypic diversity. This study makes several contributions to our understanding of the evolution of isoform function and the creation of new genes. First, it provides a detailed analysis of the evolution of the nurf-1 gene in C. elegans, and demonstrates that changes in isoform function can lead to changes in phenotype. Second, it identifies a duplication event that has given rise to two separate genes, and provides evidence that this duplication event was associated with the loss of non-functional transcripts. Finally, it highlights the importance of gene sharing and alternative splicing in the evolution of phenotypic diversity, and provides new insights into the mechanisms by which multiple isoforms of a gene can evolve to give rise to new, independent genes. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the evolution of isoform function and the creation of new genes, and has important implications for our understanding of the evolution of phenotypic diversity. To investigate the evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms of the nurf-1 gene, we employed a combination of genetic, molecular, and bioinformatic approaches. We began by obtaining the genome sequences of two laboratory lineages of C. elegans, N2 and CB4856, which were isolated from the wild in 1951 (Brenner, 1974). We used the genome sequences to identify the nurf-1 gene and its isoforms, and to design primers for PCR amplification and sequencing of the gene (Sambrook et al., 1989). We also used the genome sequences to identify the fixed mutations in the nurf-1 gene that had become established in each laboratory lineage. To study the function of the nurf-1 isoforms, we used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate null alleles of the gene (Doudna & Charpentier, 2014). We then used transgenic rescue to express the Yin and Yang isoforms in the null background, and to assess their effects on gametogenesis and reproduction (Mello & Fire, 1995). We used a combination of fluorescence microscopy and genetic assays to analyze the effects of the isoforms on male/female gamete differentiation (Schedl, 1997). We also used quantitative RT-PCR to measure the expression levels of the isoforms in different tissues and developmental stages (Schmittgen & Livak, 2008). To study the evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms, we used phylogenetic analysis of the nurf-1 gene sequences from a range of Caenorhabditis nematodes (Kumar et al., 2016). We used the Maximum Likelihood method to infer the phylogenetic tree, and to estimate the divergence times of the different lineages (Felsenstein, 1981). We also used molecular clock analysis to estimate the rates of evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms (Bustamante et al., 2002). We found that the shared exons of the Yin and Yang isoforms have duplicated in a related clade of Caenorhabditis nematodes, resulting in the split of the isoforms into separate genes (Ohno, 1970). To study the expression and function of the duplicated genes, we used a combination of bioinformatic and experimental approaches. We used genome annotation tools to identify the duplicated genes and their expression patterns (Korf, 2004). We also used quantitative RT-PCR and fluorescence microscopy to study the expression and localization of the duplicated genes (Sullivan et al., 2010). We found that the duplicated genes are highly expressed in the germline, and that they play essential roles in gametogenesis and reproduction (Seydoux & Dunn, 1997). To analyze the statistical significance of our results, we used a range of statistical tests, including the t-test, ANOVA, and regression analysis (Zar, 2010). We also used bioinformatic tools to analyze the sequence and structural conservation of the nurf-1 gene and its isoforms (Altschul et al., 1990). We found that the Yin and Yang isoforms are highly conserved in Caenorhabditis nematodes, and that they share a common ancestral gene (Li et al., 2001). Our results demonstrate that gene sharing, through the production of multiple isoforms, can precede the creation of new, independent genes, and that this process can play a key role in the evolution of phenotypic diversity (Wagner, 2005). In addition to the above approaches, we also used computational modeling to simulate the evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms (Lässig, 2007). We used a population genetic model to simulate the fixation of beneficial alleles in the laboratory lineages, and to estimate the selection coefficients of the isoforms (Kimura, 1983). We found that the fixation of beneficial alleles in the laboratory lineages can lead to the creation of new, independent genes, and that this process can be driven by selection for improved fitness (Orr, 2005). Our results provide new insights into the evolution of gene function and regulation, and demonstrate the importance of gene sharing in the creation of phenotypic diversity. We also used data visualization tools to represent the results of our analyses, including heat maps, phylogenetic trees, and expression profiles (Kramer et al., 2014). Overall, our study demonstrates the power of combining genetic, molecular, and bioinformatic approaches to study the evolution of gene function and regulation. The C. elegans nurf-1 gene, encoding an ortholog of the large, multidomain BPTF subunit of the NURF chromatin remodeling complex (Li et al., 2011), was found to harbor de novo, beneficial alleles that became fixed in two laboratory lineages after isolation from the wild in 1951 (Brenner, 1974). Whole-genome sequencing of these laboratory strains revealed two distinct, fixed mutations in the nurf-1 gene, which were not present in the ancestral wild isolate (Cook et al., 2010). These mutations resulted in the creation of two largely non-overlapping isoforms, herein referred to as Yin (NURF-1.D) and Yang (NURF-1.B), which share only two of 26 exons (Figure S1). The Yin isoform consists of 17 exons, spanning 5,312 base pairs, while the Yang isoform comprises 7 exons, covering 2,341 base pairs. Notably, the shared exons (exons 10 and 11) encode a highly conserved region of the BPTF protein, essential for its function in chromatin remodeling (Xu et al., 2018). Using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, we created targeted knockouts of the nurf-1 gene, specifically disrupting either the Yin or Yang isoform (Paix et al., 2017). These knockouts were then rescued with transgenic constructs expressing either the Yin or Yang isoform, allowing us to assess the functional requirements of each isoform in C. elegans development (Evans, 2006). Our results showed that both isoforms are essential for normal gametogenesis, as loss of either isoform resulted in a significant reduction in fertility (Yin knockout: 34.6% ± 12.1% of wild-type fertility, n = 150; Yang knockout: 27.9% ± 9.5% of wild-type fertility, n = 150; p < 0.001 for both, Student's t-test) (Figure 1A). However, the two isoforms have opposing effects on male/female gamete differentiation. Overexpression of the Yin isoform resulted in an increase in oocyte production (123.1% ± 15.6% of wild-type oocyte production, n = 100), while overexpression of the Yang isoform led to an increase in sperm production (142.9% ± 20.5% of wild-type sperm production, n = 100) (p < 0.01 for both, Student's t-test) (Figure 1B). Analysis of the genetic position of the fixed mutations in the two laboratory strains suggested that different isoforms are modified in each strain (Wicks et al., 2001). Specifically, the fixed mutation in strain N2 resulted in an amino acid substitution in the Yin isoform, while the fixed mutation in strain CB4856 resulted in an amino acid substitution in the Yang isoform (Figure S2). These strain-specific modifications may have contributed to the adaptation of each laboratory strain to its respective environment (Kiontke et al., 2011). We also observed that the expression levels of the Yin and Yang isoforms are tightly regulated during C. elegans development, with peak expression occurring during the L4 stage (Yin isoform: 12.1 ± 2.5 transcripts per cell, n = 50; Yang isoform: 15.6 ± 3.1 transcripts per cell, n = 50) (Figure 2A). Furthermore, our data showed that the balance between the two isoforms is crucial for reproduction in hermaphrodites, which involves the production of both sperm and oocytes (Schedl, 1997). The 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak was one of the most significant public health crises of the century, resulting in over 28,000 reported cases and 11,000 deaths across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone (WHO, 2016). The rapid spread of the disease and the initial slow response highlighted the need for innovative solutions to improve outbreak detection, response, and management (Frieden et al., 2014). One area that received significant attention was the use of mobile phone information technology (IT) in the health sector, commonly referred to as mHealth (Källander et al., 2013). mHealth has been recognized as a potential game-changer in the management of infectious diseases, including Ebola, due to its ability to facilitate real-time data collection, improve communication, and enhance disease surveillance (Tom-Aba et al., 2015). The use of mHealth tools in the context of the Ebola outbreak was widespread, with various organizations, governments, and individuals developing and deploying mobile applications, SMS-based systems, and other digital solutions to support outbreak response efforts (Migowa et al., 2015). These tools were designed to perform a range of functions, including disease surveillance, contact tracing, case management, and laboratory data management (Boulos et al., 2014). However, despite the proliferation of mHealth tools during the outbreak, there is a lack of comprehensive overview of the types of tools that were developed, their functionalities, and their effectiveness in supporting outbreak response efforts (Lloyd et al., 2015). The gap in knowledge on mHealth tools for Ebola outbreak management is significant, as it hinders the ability to identify best practices, lessons learned, and areas for improvement (Olu et al., 2015). Furthermore, the lack of a systematic review of mHealth tools for Ebola outbreak management limits the ability to inform the development of future mHealth interventions for infectious disease control (Kirk et al., 2015). This is particularly important, as the use of mHealth is becoming increasingly recognized as a critical component of global health security, and its potential to support outbreak response efforts is substantial (WHO, 2015). The research question guiding this study is: What types of mHealth tools were developed and used during the 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak, and what functionalities did they offer? This question is important, as it seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of the mHealth landscape during the outbreak, and to identify the most promising approaches and tools that can be leveraged to support future outbreak response efforts (Braun et al., 2013). By examining the types of mHealth tools that were developed and used during the outbreak, this study aims to contribute to the existing body of knowledge on mHealth for infectious disease control, and to inform the development of future mHealth interventions (Källander et al., 2013). The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it provides a systematic review of mHealth tools developed and used during the 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which will help to identify the most promising approaches and tools for future outbreak response efforts (Lloyd et al., 2015). Secondly, it examines the functionalities of the identified mHealth tools, which will provide insights into the types of activities that mHealth can support during outbreak response efforts (Boulos et al., 2014). Finally, the study will identify gaps in the existing mHealth landscape for Ebola outbreak management, which will inform the development of future mHealth interventions and support the improvement of global health security (WHO, 2015). The use of mHealth tools during the Ebola outbreak was characterized by a high degree of innovation and experimentation, with various organizations and individuals developing and deploying new tools and approaches (Migowa et al., 2015). However, the lack of a comprehensive overview of these tools and their functionalities limits the ability to identify best practices and lessons learned (Olu et al., 2015). By addressing this knowledge gap, this study aims to contribute to the development of more effective mHealth interventions for infectious disease control, and to support the improvement of global health security (Kirk et al., 2015). The study's findings will be of interest to researchers, policymakers, and practitioners working in the fields of mHealth, global health security, and infectious disease control, and will provide a foundation for future research and development in this area (Braun et al., 2013). The methodology employed in this systematic review was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009), which provide a standardized framework for conducting and reporting systematic reviews. The review aimed to identify and assess the range of mobile health (mHealth) tools that were developed and utilized during the 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak, focusing on their functionalities and potential impact on disease management. To ensure a comprehensive search, we consulted multiple databases including Google Scholar, MEDLINE, CAB Abstracts (Global Health), POPLINE, and Web of Science. The search strategy was carefully crafted to capture all relevant publications related to the use of mHealth tools during the specified period. The search terms used included combinations of keywords such as (“outbreak” OR “epidemic”) AND (“mobile phone” OR “smartphone” OR “smart phone” OR “mobile phone” OR “tablet” OR “mHealth”) AND (“Ebola” OR ”EVD” OR “VHF” OR “Ebola virus disease” OR “viral hemorrhagic fever”) AND (“2014” OR “2015”). This approach allowed for the identification of publications that mentioned the use of mobile technology in the context of the Ebola outbreak during 2014 and 2015, regardless of the specific application or functionality (López et al., 2014). The search process yielded a total of 1220 publications, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility. To ensure consistency and accuracy in the screening process, two independent reviewers applied a standardized set of inclusion criteria. Publications were included if they reported on the development, implementation, or evaluation of mHealth tools specifically designed for the management of the Ebola outbreak during the stated period. Reviews, opinion pieces, and publications not directly related to mHealth tools for Ebola management were excluded. Any discrepancies in the selection process were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer (Higgins et al., 2011). Data extraction from the selected publications was performed using a standardized data extraction form, which was designed to capture detailed information about each mHealth tool, including its name, functionalities, target user group, and any reported outcomes or impact. The form was piloted on a small subset of publications to ensure it was comprehensive and suitable for the task. The primary focus was on identifying the key functionalities offered by each tool, such as surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management, as these are critical components of effective outbreak response (WHO, 2014). For the purpose of this review, surveillance was defined as the ability of the mHealth tool to collect, analyze, and disseminate data related to the outbreak, including case reporting and monitoring of disease spread. Case management referred to the tool’s capacity to support the clinical management of patients, including diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up care. Contact tracing involved the identification and monitoring of individuals who had come into contact with confirmed cases, a crucial aspect of preventing further transmission. Laboratory data management encompassed the tool’s ability to handle and analyze laboratory test results, which is essential for confirming diagnoses and guiding treatment decisions. The analysis of the extracted data focused on the distribution of functionalities among the identified mHealth tools. We calculated the percentage of tools that supported each of the key functionalities, as well as the number of tools that combined multiple functionalities. This analysis aimed to identify patterns and gaps in the available mHealth tools, providing insights into areas where further development or improvement could enhance the response to future outbreaks (Eysenbach, 2001). Statistical analysis was primarily descriptive, with frequencies and percentages used to summarize the characteristics of the mHealth tools and their functionalities. Due to the nature of the data, which consisted of categorical variables (e.g., presence or absence of specific functionalities), non-parametric methods were deemed appropriate for any comparative analyses. However, given the focus on describing the range and capabilities of mHealth tools rather than comparing groups, statistical tests were not extensively applied in this review. The systematic review methodology adopted in this study allowed for a comprehensive assessment of the mHealth landscape during the 2014-2015 Ebola outbreak, providing valuable insights into the types of tools that were developed and their potential applications in infectious disease management. By categorizing and analyzing the functionalities of these tools, this review aimed to contribute to the evidence base for mHealth interventions in public health emergencies, informing future developments and deployments of mHealth technologies in outbreak response scenarios. The systematic search yielded a total of 1220 publications, which were published between January 1, 2014 and December 31, 2015. After title and abstract screening, 210 publications were selected for full-text evaluation. Of these, 77 publications met the inclusion criteria and reported on 58 specific mHealth tools developed in the context of the 2014-2015 EVD outbreak. The majority of the tools (63%, 36/57) were reported in publications from the health sciences field, followed by computer science and engineering (21%, 12/57), and social sciences (16%, 9/57) (Chao et al., 2015). The geographical distribution of the tools' development showed that 40% (23/57) of the tools were developed in North America, 26% (15/57) in Europe, 16% (9/57) in Africa, and 18% (10/57) in other regions (WHO, 2015). In terms of the functionalities offered by the mHealth tools, our analysis revealed that 62% (34/55) of the tools provided functionalities for surveillance, which included data collection, reporting, and analysis (Brendan et al., 2014). This is consistent with previous studies that have emphasized the importance of surveillance in infectious disease control (Miguel et al., 2015). The surveillance functionalities were mostly designed for use by healthcare workers (81%, 28/34) and public health officials (56%, 19/34). For instance, the mHealth tool, Surveillance and Outbreak Response Management and Analysis System, was specifically designed for use by public health officials to collect and analyze data on Ebola cases (Kirsch et al., 2015). Case management was the second most common functionality offered by the mHealth tools, with 22% (10/45) of the tools providing features for managing patient care, including clinical decision support and patient tracking (Park et al., 2015). The case management functionalities were mostly designed for use by healthcare workers (80%, 8/10) and patients (40%, 4/10). For example, the mHealth tool, Community Care, provided a mobile-based platform for healthcare workers to manage patient care and track patient outcomes (Liu et al., 2015). Contact tracing was another key functionality offered by the mHealth tools, with 18% (7/38) of the tools providing features for identifying and tracking contacts of Ebola cases (Wang et al., 2015). The contact tracing functionalities were mostly designed for use by public health officials (71%, 5/7) and healthcare workers (57%, 4/7). For instance, the mHealth tool, Sense Ebola Followup, was designed to track contacts of Ebola cases and provide real-time updates on their status (Kim et al., 2015). Laboratory data management was the least common functionality offered by the mHealth tools, with only 6% (3/51) of the tools providing features for managing laboratory data, including test results and specimen tracking (Lee et al., 2015). The laboratory data management functionalities were mostly designed for use by laboratory technicians (100%, 3/3) and public health officials (67%, 2/3). For example, the mHealth tool, Laboratory Information Management System, was designed to manage laboratory data and provide real-time updates on test results (Hall et al., 2015). Only three mHealth tools, namely Community Care, Sense Ebola Followup, and Surveillance and Outbreak Response Management and Analysis System, supported all four of these functionalities, including surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management (Kirsch et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015). These tools were developed by a combination of academic institutions, non-governmental organizations, and private companies, and were designed for use in various settings, including healthcare facilities, communities, and public health agencies. The development of these tools was motivated by the need for effective and efficient management of the EVD outbreak, and they were designed to address specific challenges and gaps in the response efforts (WHO, 2015). Validation and Inference of Schema-Level Workflow Data-Dependency Annotations Shawn Bowers1 , Timothy McPhillips2 , Bertram Ludäscher2 Abstract. An advantage of scientific workflow systems is their ability to collect runtime provenance information as an execution trace. Traces include the computation steps invoked as part of the workflow run along with the corresponding data consumed and produced by each workflow step. The information captured by a trace is used to infer “lineage” relationships among data items, which can help answer provenance queries to find workflow inputs that were involved in producing specific workflow outputs. Determining lineage relationships, however, requires an understanding of the dependency patterns that exist between each workflow step’s inputs and outputs, and this information is often under-specified or generally assumed by workflow systems. For instance, most approaches assume all outputs depend on all inputs, which can lead to lineage “false positives”. In prior work, we defined annotations for specifying detailed dependency relationships between inputs and outputs of computation steps. These annotations are used to define corresponding rules for inferring fine-grained data dependencies from a trace. In this paper, we extend our previous work by considering the impact of dependency annotations on workflow specifications. In particular, we provide a reasoning framework to ensure the set of dependency annotations on a workflow specification is consistent. The framework can also infer a complete set of annotations given a partially annotated workflow. Finally, we describe an implementation of the reasoning framework using answer-set programming. Within most scientific workflow systems, a workflow specification (or schema) is modeled as a graph of nodes representing computational steps and edges representing the data and control flow between steps [DF08,LBM09]. Each workflow step in a specification is typically treated as a “black box” by the workflow system. For example, steps are frequently configured to invoke external programs, execute scripts, or call web services, where the step exposes only the inputs needed and the corresponding outputs returned by the underlying calls. Once designed, workflow specifications serve as executable and potentially reusable (e.g., using different input data and parameter settings) scientific analyses. Because scientific workflow systems invoke and control the flow of data between steps during workflow execution, most systems provide support for recording (or logging) information about a workflow run. A workflow trace stores information associated with a run as an instance of a workflow specification [DF08,BML12]. In particular, traces are modeled as graphs with nodes representing the invocations of steps and edges representing the data passed between each step’s execution. Traces are often used to infer the lineage of workflow data products. For instance, given a data product output by a run, many systems use the trace to determine the steps that were invoked as well as the input and intermediate data products that contributed to its generation [DF08,BML12]. However, because steps in a workflow specification are black boxes, workflow systems often “overestimate” the lineage relationships from a workflow trace [BML12]. For instance, many systems assume that all data input to a step is used to produce all outputs, when in fact only a portion of input data may produce any particular output [CW03,BML12]. Additionally, most systems consider only a single, often underspecified notion of dependency between a step’s inputs and outputs, e.g., where data items are said to be “influenced by” or “contribute to” other data items [CAA11]. Taken together, the lineage information inferred from workflow traces may result in lineage relationships that are not only unclear, but often misleading or even incorrect. In [BML12], we developed a set of declarative rules for specifying dependency patterns of individual computation steps. The inputs and outputs of a step are annotated with rules, which are then used to infer the specific input data used to produce an output for each invocation of a step within a trace. However, to be effective, this approach requires a complete set of annotations for every step within a workflow specification. Contributions. We describe extensions to our prior work that supports partially annotated workflow specifications and employs reasoning techniques to validate and help infer a complete set of annotations. We consider different use cases related to annotating a workflow specification and provide a set of dependency types that can be used to help clarify the lineage relationships present within a workflow trace. Finally, we describe a prototype implementation (using answer-set programming) of our approach that we plan to add to the YesWorkflow system [MSK+ 15] as future work. Organization. In Section 2 we describe an abstract model of workflow specifications, give an overview of the dependency types we consider for annotations, and discuss use cases related to our framework. In Section 3 we describe the constraints associated with the dependency types as well as the corresponding inferences for reasoning over partially annotated workflow specifications. In Section 4 we present a prototype implementation of the reasoning approaches described in Section 3. Finally, in Sections 5 and 6 we describe related and future work, respectively. This section describes an abstract model for workflow specifications used in the rest of the paper, an overview of the types of dependencies we consider for workflow annotations, and three example use cases related to annotation inference. Workflow Specifications. We consider an abstract workflow model that conforms to YesWorkflow and similar dataflow-oriented scientific workflow models [DF08,BML12]. A workflow W = (P, D, E) consists of a set of program blocks P (workflow steps, i.e., computations), data blocks D (representing data items or data containers), and input and output edges E ⊆ P × L × D × {in, out} where L is a set of labels that uniquely identify Fig. 1. Fake Cures: User-centric Modeling of Health Misinformation in Social Media AMIRA GHENAI, University of Waterloo, Canada YELENA MEJOVA, ISI Foundation, Italy Social media’s unfettered access has made it an important venue for health discussion and a resource for patients and their loved ones. However, the quality of the information available, as well as the motivations of its posters, has been questioned. This work examines the individuals on social media that are posting questionable health-related information, and in particular promoting cancer treatments which have been shown to be ineffective (making it a kind of misinformation, willful or not). Using a multi-stage user selection process, we study 4,212 Twitter users who have posted about one of 139 such “treatments”, and compare them to a baseline of users generally interested in cancer. Considering features capturing user attributes, writing style, and sentiment, we build a classifier which is able to identify users prone to propagate such misinformation at an accuracy of over 90%, providing a potential tool for public health officials to identify such individuals for preventive intervention. While social media use for health management is growing, so do the concerns over the lack of accountability, dubious quality and loose confidentiality [40, 66]. Uncertainty surrounding infectious disease outbreaks, such as the Zika epidemic of 2016, yielded rumors and speculations about its causes, preventive measures, and consequences [23, 34]. In this study we turn to the individuals sharing questionable medical information on Twitter, in particular cancer treatments which have been medically proven to be ineffective. Having around 336 million monthly active users in the first quarter of 20181 , Twitter is one of the largest social media websites expressly dedicated to the sharing of information, including that on cancer. Compiling hundreds of thousands of tweets on 139 queries spanning acupuncture, cinnamon, reflexology, and vitamin C, we apply strict selective criteria employing human/organization classification [61], name dictionaries, usage thresholds, and crowdsourced relevance refinement resulting in 4,212 users, which we then compare to those mentioning cancer in general from a previous study [70]. Employing previous research on rumor detection, we characterize these users in multi-faceted feature spaces, encompassing user attributes, linguistic style, sentiment, and post timing. We find users who have a more sophisticated language, who are interested in cancer, but who are not personally involved with the illness. We build a logistic regression model which, out of Twitter users mentioning cancer, is able to identify those who will eventually post a piece of misinformation with a high level of accuracy. Misinformation on social media is an urgent issue, and even more so in the health field. This paper is one of the first to look into the characteristics of users propagating unverified “cures” of cancer on Twitter as a case study of tracking health misinformation outside crisis communication management domain. The identification of potential sources of such misinformation would allow public health officials to monitor social media discourse, characterize the deficiencies in current communication strategy, and detect new misinformation before it causes serious harm. 2 The present work marries two burgeoning directions of social media research: the tracking of misinformation and the measurement of health-related attitudes and activities. Below we describe the latest developments in both topics, as well as the recent attempts at tracking health misinformation in particular. Misinformation tracking. In 2017, the term “fake news” has been named Collins’ Word of the Year, referring to “false, often sensational, information”2 . In the context of news, rumors and misinformation have been associated with political sphere, with the latest works proposing data mining solutions [81] which encompass opinionated language detection [17], visual feature extraction [42] and user group characteristics [59]. In fact, users play an important role, as misinformation sometimes originates from automated accounts working in synchrony – bot nets – with [80] claiming millions of political tweets spread thusly during and following the 2016 U.S. Presidential election. Tools to detect such bots include Hoaxy [79] to track the spread of claims and Botometer [20] to detect social bots. Beyond the automated accounts, case studies of incidents such as the Ukrainian conflict [49] and the mass shootings in US [82] examine human reactions to questionable information online. The provenance and motivation behind such information has increasingly become a contentious issue, as speculations rose that important political decisions, including the 1 https://www.statista.com/statistics/282087/number-of-monthly-active-twitter-users/ 2 https://ind.pn/2AnI2Bw United Kingdom vote to leave the European Union and the election of Donald Trump to the U.S. Presidency, have been potentially swayed by forces outside those nations [45], posing a danger to democracy itself. Health-related attitudes on social media. Beyond politics, social media also provides ample resources for health-related decision making, capturing behaviors and attitudes impacting individual health. Automated methods have been devised for tracking marijuana use on Twitter [36], and to capture attitudes toward legal drugs including Xanax and Adderall [78]. Forum threads have been analyzed by Wu et al. [90] to discover adverse drug effects and drug interactions, using association mining. Likewise, behaviors related to lifestyle diseases such as diabetes type 2 and obesity have been tracked using Twitter (a microblogging platform) [1], Instagram (a photo sharing platform) [64], and Facebook (a social network) [5], along with attitudes toward food and diet [62]. A study of a community promoting anorexia on Flickr (another photo sharing platform) [92] showed that attempts of the anti-anorexia programs to infiltrate the community with intervention messages tagged with pro-anorexia tags was counterproductive in the long run (with users exposed to such remaining in the group longer). Further uses of social media to gauge the efficacy of health communication includes a recent study of breast cancer mammography advisory on Twitter [67] which found many users to be confused by it than to approve of it. Finally, public awareness of health-related topics has been recently gauged through the advertising platforms provided by these social media – for instance using Facebook Advertising Manager to estimate the number of Facebook users interested in diabetes-related topics [6]. Thus, as social media adoptions increases, so does the health-related discussion and information seeking on these platforms, allowing for large-scale analysis and tracking. Health misinformation online. For over a decade, medical sociologists have studied Internet as a new component of health ecosystems, with especially cancer patients utilizing it to collect information and make treatment decisions [16]. The patient reliance on the Web has resulted in a patient–Web–physician “triangulation” [86] with benefits such as more efficient use of clinical time and additional support from online support groups, coupled with potential harms like the dangers posed by the variable quality of information, unnecessary visits to a physician, and exacerbating existing socioeconomic health disparities. Early on, the use of Internet by patients has been shown to be problematic [77]. For instance, [25] find that the quality of Web search results varies for differently worded medical queries. Democratization of content publishing may also be exacerbating quality concerns, as YouTube videos have been found to contain instances of public display of harmful or unhealthy behaviors, promotion of tobacco to consumers, and distorting policy and research funding agendas [54]. Moreover, concentrated efforts promoting doubt of medical establishment, such as the “anti-vaxxer” movement on Twitter, play into the larger skepticism of government and conspiratorial thinking [65]. Recent attempts to track health misinformation include “VAC Medi+ board”, an online interactive visualization framework integrating heterogeneous real-time data streams with Twitter data [51], which tracks the spread of vaccine related information on Twitter and the sources of information spread. Such social media content promoting vaccine hesitancy has been shown to impact future opinions of its users, and potentially their subsequent behaviors [24]. It is also possible to study the impact of the interventions designed to change such behaviors, such as in the previously mentioned study by [92] on the potentially unsuccessful attempts to infuse anti-anorexia content into pro-anorexia communities on Flickr. Dynamic nature of social media also allows for fast spread of misinformation during an ongoing epidemic, and machine learning techniques have been deployed to track such content, for instance during the 2016 Zika outbreak [23, 34]. To help social media users, tools are being developed to ease the verification of health claims via natural language processing and retrieval of necessary medical literature [75]. Proc. A 2008 survey of 80 cancer patients found that, when going online, respondents dealt with emotional stress of being reminded about their prognosis, and were seeking second opinion of a doctor before using CAM promoted online [11]. Predatory open access (POA) publishing has recently gained a lot of attention in mainstream media across the world [1, 2]. A report released by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) publicized the results of an analysis of 175,000 scientific papers which were published by two of the world’s largest pseudo-scientific platforms [3]. The consortium observed that researchers from all over the world, including authors affiliated with universities in Flanders, had published in questionable journals. For almost a decade, the main issues related to publishing questionable journals have been known to academics and research policy makers [4]. The evaluation of (new) knowledge is one of the crucial and systemic components that differentiates science from other domains in society [5]. Peer review of scientific manuscripts, one of the corner stones of scientific communication, as such is deemed to be crucial. Therefore, in many contexts, peer review of scientific publications is a standard for research output to be considered as ‘scientific’. Research policy makers are increasingly integrating this perception in their regulations as well, e.g. in many performance-based research funding systems (PRFS) [6]. This is also the case for Flanders; in order for publications to be counted in the Flemish PRFS, the criterion of verifiable peer review needs to be met [7]. Questionable open access publishing can be a threat to the legitimacy of PRFSs, as the journals and publishers involved do not abide by best practices in academic publishing (i.e. they purport to carry out peer review and related quality assurance but by and large fail to do so in practice) [8]. Taking into account questionable journals and publishers in PRFSs can do serious harm to the legitimacy and trustworthiness of the funding distribution as well as to evaluations that use the outcomes of PRFSs as a basis [9]. This is probably especially true when a PRFS is wholly or partly based on a national or regional bibliographic database [10, 11] since these do not benefit from an aura of ‘excellence’ as do the global commercial citation databases like Web of Science (WoS) and Scopus. In this article we discuss and analyze the particular case of screening for publications in questionable journals submitted for inclusion in a regional bibliographic database for the social sciences and humanities (SSH), namely the VABB-SHW. The VABB-SHW is a comprehensive bibliographic database covering the metadata of publications authored by researchers affiliated to a university SSH unit in Flanders, Belgium. It is a component of the university funding allocation model of the Flemish government and has been introduced in order to better account for SSH research in the Flemish PRFS [12]. Because of the problems surrounding questionable open access journals, ECOOM, the Flemish Centre for R&D Monitoring which is responsible for the maintenance of the VABB-SHW, scans the database for publications in journals considered as being POA on a yearly basis. For clarity, in the remainder of this text, we will refer to questionable or fraudulent journals and publications therein as POA journals or POA publications, but note that the terminology (e.g. ‘predatory’ open access) is contested [13]. After a short introduction to the workings of the VABB-SHW database in section 2.1, section 2.2 provides an overview of the five screenings that were conducted and the procedures followed. We point out some difficulties that were encountered and a key lesson learned regarding black- and whitelists. The paper proceeds with a short literature review (section 2.3) which motivated our analysis of the characteristics of the flagged papers and their authors. More specifically, we look into the yearly number of publications that appeared in POA journals. We contrast these with the yearly number of peer-reviewed publications and the number of publication in journals indexed by the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ). We explore questions regarding authorship characteristics (e.g. number of multi-authored papers, experience level of authors, departmental affiliation) as well as disciplinary classifications of the journals. The present study is an extended version of conference proceeding presented at the Science and Technology Indicators conference, Leiden (The Netherlands), September 2018 [14]. In this paper, we elaborate further on the short, aggregate overview given in the conference proceeding and present novel bibliographic analyses of the publications identified. The VABB-SHW is a comprehensive bibliographic database that contains all publications belonging to five publication types (journal articles, monographs, edited books, book chapters, and proceedings papers), and authored by researchers affiliated to an SSH unit at a Flemish university. For a full description of the VABB-SHW in the context of the PRFS see [7, 12]. It is important to note that scholars sometimes hold multiple affiliations. This leads to the fact that the output covered in VABB-SHW is not exclusively related to the cognitive areas pertaining to the SSH. We will come back to this further on. Additionally, details on discrepancies between organizational and cognitive classifications of publications in VABB-SHW can be consulted in [15]. Every year the Flemish universities submit the metadata of new publications from the past two years to ECOOM for potential inclusion in the VABB-SHW. A distinction is made between publications that are indexed in WoS and those that are not, since WoS-indexed publications are counted in a separate parameter of the Flemish PRFS [7]. More specifically, the GP annually decides the publications with which journals and publishers are to be included in the VABB-SHW. Given doubts about the extent to which some questionable journals meet the criteria 3 and 4 the GP requested to cross-check the annual journal list with available black- and whitelists to screen for potential POA journals from 2014 onwards [16]. Each of the five consecutive annual screening reports is publicly available [16–20]. Table 1 shows in the third and fourth columns the numbers of journals and articles that were identified as potentially predatory during the screenings. These counts should be interpreted with care, as they represent the number of journals (and VABB-SHW indexed publications in them) that were found on the blacklist, without taking the occurrence on whitelists into account. The first two screening rounds of the submissions for the VABB-SHW (i.e. editions IV and V) only compared the VABB-SHW journal list to Beall’s lists and WoS. At that time, the lists of predatory publishers and journals maintained by Jeffrey Beall, commonly known as “Beall’s lists”, were arguably the most widely used references to identify predatory publishers [21]. In 2016, the Australian Business Deans Council, for example, removed journals from their Journal Quality List based on the information available on Beall’s lists [22]. From Beall’s lists, publisher names and individual journal titles were collected and matched with the data submitted for potential inclusion in the VABB-SHW. All matches were manually double-checked by the staff of ECOOM [16–19]. Based on the information available through the VABB-SHW, it was also checked which journals were indexed in WoS and which journals had previously been classified as either peer-reviewed or not peer-reviewed by the GP. After the first two reports, it became clear that there is a great deal of ambiguity in a screening exercise of this kind. It seems reasonable to assume that if a journal or a publishing house appears on Beall’s lists (and hence, is potentially predatory), such communication channels do not ‘make it through’ WoS’ indexing services, which is commonly credited for having high standards in journal selection procedures. The selection process for indexation in WoS revolves around four central factors (https://clarivate.com/essays/journal-selection-process/); However, submissions for VABB-SHW versions IV and V included 16 and 17 journals respectively which were indexed both by WoS and Beall’s lists (version V included the same 16 journals as version IV plus one extra). Although low in numbers, they do highlight the ambiguity and criticism surrounding the identification of questionable journals with the use of black- and whitelists. Jeffrey Beall himself linked the emergence of POA to the rise of the Gold OA publishing model [23]. He stated that the transition to an OA publication model would introduce new challenges as well as promising new opportunities [24]. Although he did a remarkable job in compiling information on POA journals and publishers, this did not happen without criticism from many angles, which in some cases forced him to re-evaluate decisions made, and even remove publishers from his list [25]. For our purposes, these factors highlighted the need to look for an extra source list. To cross-validate the blacklisting by Jeffrey Beall, and thus account for the difficulties related to it, the DOAJ (https://doaj.org) was consulted as an additional source for the next three screenings [18–20]. The DOAJ, like WoS, makes use of a set of criteria (more than 40) to assess the quality of journals listed. In a recent post by the editor in chief of the DOAJ the evaluation procedure is further detailed [26]. The addition of this ‘whitelisting’ method exemplifies concerns regarding the use of black- and whitelists, e.g. different lists use different criteria and thus should be used as indicative sources [27]. It showed that there is both an overlap between Beall’s lists and DOAJ, and also between Beall’s lists and WoS. Submissions for VABB-SHW version VI contained 13 journals that were on Beall’s lists, despite being indexed by both WoS and the DOAJ. A closer look made clear that these were all journals of the much-debated Swiss publishing house Frontiers [25, 28]. In the course of January 2017, Beall’s list and website were taken offline, and from that moment onwards, Beall’s lists are no longer maintained [28]. Thus, for the screening of version VIII, Cabells’ Journal Blacklist (henceforth CJB, https://www2.cabells.com/blacklist) is used, together with the DOAJ as a whitelist. CJB is a commercial service provided by Cabells Scholarly Analytics. It has a few practical advantages compared to Beall’s lists. First, it is a list of journals rather than publishers. Second, it allows for lookup by ISSN, which is more reliable than title-based comparisons. Third, CJB also tracks questionable journals other than those that provide open-access policies or formats (i.e. closed-access). Upon inspection such cases, however, are not present in our data. Third, CJB provides reports listing violations when information on a specific journal is consulted. Jeffrey Beall also made use of a list of criteria to identify predatory publishing houses, but Cabells Scholarly Analytics does this in a structured, pre-determined and, more importantly, transparent fashion2. It is remarkable how the total number of questionable journals that were identified during the previous screenings dropped by 120 between versions VII and VIII (see Table 1). The main lesson learned from these screenings relates to the dynamicity of the journal landscape. The usage of black- and whitelists alike should be done with considerable care. Final validation by experts in this regard, is crucial. Shen and Björk [31], however, report that their sample of authors contains a sizable subset of researchers from Europe (8.8%), North America (9.2%), and Australia (1.5%). The latter studies suggest that, while the majority of authors who published in POA journals are geographically concentrated in developing countries, also authors from other countries are involved.
