Ambient air pollution is among the leading environmental risk factors for premature death and disease worldwide. The World Health Organization estimates that outdoor air pollution contributes to several million premature deaths each year, mainly through cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease and lung cancer (World Health Organization, 2016; Cohen et al., 2017). Short-term exposure to elevated concentrations of particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone and nitrogen dioxide is associated with increased hospital admissions, exacerbations of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and cardiovascular events (Brook et al., 2010; Atkinson et al., 2014). Although the largest gains in population health are likely to come from structural reductions in emissions, such reductions are slow and, in many settings, incomplete. Pollution episodes will therefore continue to occur, and individuals at risk will need to take steps to protect themselves in the meantime. To support such protective action, many countries and cities have introduced air quality warning systems. These typically translate monitored or modelled pollutant concentrations into an index or banding scheme, such as the US Air Quality Index, the UK Daily Air Quality Index or the Air Quality Health Index used in Canada and Hong Kong. The index is communicated through media, websites, mobile applications, text messages or public displays, and is usually accompanied by tiered health advice. The advice commonly encourages sensitive groups, and at higher levels the general population, to reduce or reschedule strenuous outdoor activity, avoid busy roads, and, for people with respiratory or cardiac conditions, to follow their treatment plans and keep reliever medication to hand (Environmental Protection Agency, 2014; Defra, 2013). The logic of these systems is a simple one: if people know when air quality is poor and understand what to do, they will change their behaviour, reduce their exposure and thereby avoid some of the associated harm. The effectiveness of this chain depends on every link holding. People must be aware of the warning, understand it, believe that it is relevant to them, and be willing and able to act on the advice. There is reason to doubt that this always happens. Studies of health risk communication more broadly have shown that awareness of a hazard does not necessarily translate into behaviour change, and that perceptions of risk, trust in information sources and confidence in one’s ability to act all mediate responses (Witte and Allen, 2000; Ferrer and Klein, 2015). In the context of air pollution, the hazard is often invisible, its effects are probabilistic and delayed, and the recommended actions may conflict with work, caregiving, commuting or exercise routines. Furthermore, the benefits of short-term avoidance are uncertain at the individual level, and some recommended behaviours, such as reducing physical activity, could have negative health consequences if applied indiscriminately (Giles and Koehle, 2014). Evidence on whether air quality warnings change behaviour is nevertheless scattered. Economists have examined averting behaviour in response to smog alerts, using attendance at outdoor venues, transport use or purchases of protective products as proxies, and have reported mixed results (Neidell, 2009; Zivin and Neidell, 2009). Public health researchers have conducted surveys and panel studies of awareness, intended behaviour and self-reported behaviour among general populations and among people with asthma or cardiovascular disease, in North America, Europe and Asia (e.g. McDermott et al., 2006; Wen et al., 2009). These studies vary considerably in their populations, in the warning systems studied, in the behaviours considered and in how adherence was measured. Some assess only a single behaviour, such as staying indoors; others consider a broad repertoire, including mask wearing, closing windows, changing travel mode or using medication. Studies also differ in whether they ask about behaviour on a specific poor-air-quality day or in general, which affects estimates of adherence. As a consequence, it remains unclear how many people follow the advice that accompanies air quality warnings, and which behaviours are most and least likely to be adopted. A second, related gap concerns who adheres and why. Several studies have examined demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, education, income and the presence of a health condition, as correlates of protective behaviour, but findings seem inconsistent. Others have explored psychosocial factors, including knowledge, risk perception, symptom attribution, self-efficacy, social influences and practical barriers. These are rarely organised within a coherent theoretical structure, which makes it hard to see which determinants are most promising targets for intervention. Behaviour change frameworks offer a way to do this. The COM-B model proposes that behaviour (B) arises from the interaction of capability (C), opportunity (O) and motivation (M), and underpins the Behaviour Change Wheel, which links these sources of behaviour to intervention functions and policy options (Michie, van Stralen and West, 2011). Capability includes physical and psychological capacities such as knowledge and understanding; opportunity covers physical and social factors external to the individual, including time, resources and the influence of others; and motivation includes reflective processes such as beliefs, intentions and perceived threat, as well as automatic processes such as habits and emotional responses. Applying this framework to the air quality literature may help show whether non-adherence is mainly a problem of understanding, of circumstances or of motivation, and thus what kinds of advice and delivery would be likely to improve uptake. Existing reviews have addressed adjacent questions but not this one directly. Some have synthesised evidence on the health effects of air pollution or on the effectiveness of personal-level interventions such as face masks and air filters for reducing exposure or improving health outcomes (Laumbach, Meng and Kipen, 2015; Barn et al., 2008). Others have considered risk perception of air pollution or the design of air quality indices (Bickerstaff and Walker, 2001; Kelly and Fussell, 2015). However, to our knowledge no previous systematic review has examined the extent to which people adhere to the health advice that accompanies air quality warning systems, nor has it systematically identified the demographic and psychosocial factors that predict adherence or non-adherence. Without such a synthesis, public health agencies lack an evidence base for designing advice that people will actually follow. We therefore conducted a systematic review with two aims. The first was to establish to what extent air quality warning systems influence protective behaviours in the general public, by estimating intended and actual adherence to the accompanying health advice. The second was to identify the demographic and psychosocial factors associated with adherence and non-adherence, including self-reported reasons for following or not following the advice, and to interpret these within the COM-B framework. To keep the focus on the warning systems themselves, we included only studies in which participants used, or were aware of, such systems, and excluded studies that examined protective behaviours prompted solely by subjective perceptions of poor air quality. This review makes three contributions. It provides the first systematic summary of adherence rates to health advice linked to air quality alerts, distinguishing advice to reduce or reschedule outdoor activity from broader protective behaviours. It clarifies whether demographic characteristics are useful in identifying people who are less likely to adhere. Finally, it identifies modifiable psychosocial facilitators and barriers and maps them onto a behavioural framework, providing a basis for the design and evaluation of more effective air quality communication. Protocol and reporting This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). Because the literature was expected to be heterogeneous in design, populations, warning systems and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was planned in advance, following guidance from the Economic and Social Research Council on narrative synthesis in systematic reviews (Popay et al., 2006). Findings were interpreted using the COM-B model of behaviour (Capability, Opportunity, Motivation – Behaviour), which forms part of the Behaviour Change Wheel (Michie, van Stralen and West, 2011). Under this model, behaviour (B) is a function of interacting components, which can be summarised as B = f(C, O, M), where capability comprises physical and psychological capacity, opportunity comprises physical and social environmental factors, and motivation comprises reflective and automatic processes. Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible if they assessed intended or actual adherence to health advice accompanying an air quality warning system, where such advice encouraged people to reduce their exposure to air pollution (for example by reducing or rescheduling outdoor activity, avoiding busy roads, staying indoors, or using preventative medication). Studies were also eligible if they examined predictors of adherence (demographic or psychosocial) or self-reported reasons for adherence or non-adherence. Participants had to be members of the general public, including those with pre-existing conditions such as asthma, who were either using or aware of a warning system. Studies had to report original data and to be published in English in a peer-reviewed journal; qualitative, cross-sectional, cohort and experimental designs were all considered. Studies were excluded if they examined only protective behaviours arising from subjective perception of poor air quality (for example, noticing haze or smell) without reference to a warning system, since such behaviour cannot be attributed to the influence of the warning. Studies were also excluded if participants were not aware of or using the warning system, if they assessed only the effects of policy interventions on pollution levels (for example traffic restrictions) rather than individual behaviour, if they were focused on occupational exposure, or if they were reviews, commentaries or conference abstracts without full data. Studies of indoor air pollution and of wildfire smoke, volcanic ash or dust events were considered eligible only where a formal warning or advisory system and accompanying advice were evaluated. Search strategy In August 2016 we searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus and the Cochrane Library from inception. The search strategy combined three concept blocks using Boolean operators: (1) air quality terms (e.g. “air pollution”, “air quality”, “smog”, “ozone”, “particulate matter”); (2) warning terms (e.g. “warning”, “alert”, “forecast”, “advisory”, “index”, “health advice”, “health message”); and (3) behavioural terms (e.g. “adherence”, “compliance”, “behavio”, “avoidance”, “protective”, “response”, “risk perception”). Search terms were adapted to the controlled vocabulary of each database. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched, and forward citation tracking was carried out in Google Scholar. Grey literature was not systematically searched, but we screened the first 100 results of Google Scholar queries using the main search terms. Study selection Records were exported to reference management software and duplicates removed. One reviewer screened all titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria; a second reviewer independently screened a random 20% subsample, and agreement was assessed using Cohen’s kappa (κ = (po − pe)/(1 − pe), where po is observed agreement and pe is agreement expected by chance). Full texts of potentially relevant articles were obtained and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, where necessary, by consultation with a third author. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. Data extraction A standardised extraction form was developed and piloted on three studies. Extracted information included: country and setting; study design; sampling method and sample size; participant characteristics (age, sex, health status, ethnicity, socioeconomic indicators); type of warning system (for example air quality index, forecast, smog alert), the pollutants covered and the dissemination channels; the content of the accompanying health advice; whether adherence was intended or actual; how adherence was measured (self-report questionnaire, diary, interview, or objective measure); adherence rates; demographic and psychosocial predictors tested, with effect estimates (odds ratios, regression coefficients, correlation coefficients, p values) where available; and self-reported reasons for adherence or non-adherence. One reviewer extracted data and a second checked all entries for accuracy. Where studies reported adherence to several behaviours, we separated adherence to the advice to reduce or reschedule outdoor activities from adherence to a wider range of protective behaviours (such as avoiding busy roads, closing windows, or taking preventative medication), because the former is the most commonly recommended and most comparable behaviour. Where adherence was reported for subgroups only, the rates were extracted by subgroup and the overall rate was calculated as a weighted proportion where sufficient information was available. For each category, we calculated the range and median of reported adherence proportions across studies.

Hot spots policing is associated with small but meaningful reductions in crime at locations where criminal activities are most concentrated. Focusing police efforts at high activity crime places is more likely to produce a diffusion of crime prevention benefits into areas adjacent to targeted hot spots than crime displacement. Crime is concentrated in small places, or “hot spots,” that generate half of all criminal events. Hot spots policing focuses police resources and attention on these high crime places. For the purpose of this review, hot spots programs must have consisted of police‐led crime prevention efforts that targeted high‐activity crime “places” rather than larger areas such as neighborhoods. This review considers both randomized controlled experimental and quasiexperimental evaluations of the effects of hot spots policing interventions on crime where the control group in each study received routine levels of traditional police enforcement tactics. What is the aim of this review? This Campbell systematic review assesses the preventive effects of focusing police‐led crime prevention efforts on crime “hot spots” as compared to traditional police crime control strategies. The review summarizes evidence from 65 studies containing 78 tests of hot spots policing interventions, including 27 randomized controlled trials and 38 quasiexperimental evaluations. A total of 65 studies containing 78 tests of hot spots policing interventions were identified. However, standardized effects sizes were only calculated for 73 main effects tests due to reporting deficiencies in three included studies. All studies were published from 1989 to 2017: 51 studies were conducted in the United States, four in the United Kingdom, four in Sweden, and six in other countries. Yes. Hot spots policing generates statistically significant small reductions in overall crime and disorder in areas where the strategy is implemented. These crime control gains were evident across specific categories of crime outcomes including drug offenses, disorder offenses, property crimes, and violent crimes. No. Overall, it is more likely that hot spots policing generates crime control benefits that diffuse into the areas immediately surrounding the targeted locations than displacing crime into nearby locations. Findings from this review support hot spots policing as a proactive crime reduction strategy. Police departments should incorporate focusing resources at high‐activity crime places as part of their broader approach to crime prevention. The majority of studies included in the updated review have been published since the previous iteration of the review and utilized rigorous research designs. Despite the drastic increase in eligible studies, only one study conducted a formal cost‐benefit assessment of the hot spot policing intervention. The growth of hot spots policing warrants further empirical attention on the efficiency of hot spots policing for reducing crime. Over the past 30 years, crime scholars and practitioners have pointed to the potential benefits of focusing crime prevention efforts on crime places. A number of studies suggest that crime is not spread evenly across city landscapes. Rather, there is significant clustering of crime in small places, or “hot spots,” that generate half of all criminal events (Pierce, Spaar, & Briggs, 1988; Sherman, Gartin, & Buerger, 1989). Even within the most crime‐ridden neighborhoods, crime clusters at a few discrete locations and other areas are relatively crime free (Weisburd, Groff, & Yang, 2012). More recent research has reinforced this idea of crime concentrations (Braga, Andresen, & Lawton, 2017) and led Weisburd (2015) to argue that there is a “law of crime concentration” at places showing not just that crime is concentrated but that it is concentrated at similar levels across cities and across time. A number of researchers have argued that many crime problems can be reduced more efficiently if police officers focused their attention to these persistent high‐activity crime places (Braga & Weisburd, 2010; Sherman & Weisburd, 1995; Weisburd, 1997). The appeal of focusing limited resources on a small number of high‐activity crime places is straightforward. If we can prevent crime at these hot spots, then we might be able to control citywide crime levels (Weisburd, Braga, Groff, & Wooditch, 2017). Police officers have long recognized the importance of place in crime problems. Police officers know the locations within their beats that tend to be trouble spots and are often very sensitive to signs of potential crimes across the places that comprise their beats. As Bittner (1970, p. 90) suggests in his classic study of police work, some officers know “the shops, stores, warehouses, restaurants, hotels, schools, playgrounds, and other public places in such a way that they can recognize at a glance whether what is going on within them is within the range of normalcy.” The traditional response to such trouble spots typically included heightened levels of patrol and increased opportunistic arrests and investigations. Putting police officers in high crime locations may be an old and well‐established idea; however, in the long history of policing, police crime prevention strategies did not focus systematically on crime hot spots until only very recently (Braga & Schnell, 2018). The availability of powerful crime mapping software packages has allowed police departments to identify and address problem places more easily than was previously possible in the days when pin maps were necessary to examine crime concentrations (Weisburd & Lum, 2005). Hot spots policing has become a very popular way for police departments to prevent crime. Many police departments report having the capability to manage and analyze crime data in sophisticated ways and, through management innovations such as Compstat, hold officers accountable for implementing problem‐solving strategies to control hot spot locations (Weisburd, Mastrofski, McNally, Greenspan, & Willis, 2003). In the words of then‐New York Police Department Deputy Commissioner Jack Maple, “the main principle of deployment can be expressed in one sentence: ‘map the crime and put the cops where the dots are.’ Or, more succinctly: ‘Put cops on dots.’” (Maple, 1999, p. 128). The 2007 Law Enforcement Management and Administrative Statistics survey reported that nearly all police agencies in large metropolitan centers use computers for hot spots identification (Reaves, 2010). The Police Executive Research Forum (2008) surveyed 176 U.S. police departments and found that nearly 9 out of 10 agencies used hot spots policing strategies to deal with violent crime in their jurisdictions and that problem‐solving techniques were often deployed to address violent crime hot spots. In a more recent study of a representative sample of police agencies, the National Police Research Platform reported that 75% of the agencies surveyed used the hot spots policing approach (Mastrofski & Fridell, n.d.; reported in Weisburd & Majmundar 2018). A growing body of research evidence suggests that focused police interventions, such as directed patrols, proactive arrests, and problem‐oriented policing (POP), can produce significant crime prevention gains at high‐crime “hot spots” (see, e.g., Braga, 2008; Eck, 1997, 2002; Weisburd & Eck, 2004). Indeed, the National Research Council's Committee to Review Research on Police Policy and Practices found that “...studies that focused police resources on crime hot spots provided the strongest collective evidence of police effectiveness that is now available” (Skogan & Frydl, 2004, p. 250). More recently, the National Research Council's Committee on Proactive Policing concluded that the available research evidence suggests that hot spots policing strategies generate statistically significant crime reduction effects (Weisburd & Majmundar, 2018). Critics of place‐based interventions, however, charge that such policing strategies result in displacement—that is, criminals move to places not protected by police intervention (e.g., Blattman, Green, Ortega, & Tobón, 2017; Reppetto, 1976). The available evidence suggests that hot spots policing interventions are more likely to be associated with the diffusion of crime control benefits into surrounding areas rather than crime displacement (e.g., Braga & Weisburd, 2010; Weisburd & Majmundar, 2018; Weisburd et al., 2006). The crime prevention potency of hot spots policing is supported by two key theoretical mechanisms: deterrence and crime opportunity reduction (Braga & Schnell, 2018). Deterrence theory suggests that crime can be prevented when the costs of committing the crime are perceived by the offender to outweigh the benefits (Gibbs, 1975; Zimring & Hawkins, 1973). Much of the literature evaluating deterrence focuses on the effect of changing certainty, swiftness, and severity of punishment associated with certain acts on the prevalence of those crimes (Apel & Nagin, 2011; Nagin, 2013; Paternoster, 1987). Reflecting on the theoretical and policy lessons learned from hot spots policing evaluations, Nagin et al. (2015) argued that increasing police visibility in crime hot spots will generate substantial marginal deterrent effects by heightening potential offenders' perceived risk of apprehension and discouraging them from taking advantage of concentrated crime opportunities in these small places. Indeed, in the well‐known Minneapolis hot spots patrol experiment, Sherman and Weisburd (1995) claimed evidence of place‐specific “micro‐deterrence” associated with increased police presence in hot spot areas (p. 646). Hot spots policing is also highly influenced by three complementary crime opportunity theories: rational choice, routine activities, and environmental criminology (Braga & Clarke, 2014; Eck & Weisburd, 1995). The rational choice perspective assumes that “offenders seek to benefit themselves by their criminal behavior; that this involves the making of decisions and choices, however rudimentary on occasion these choices may be; and that these processes, constrained as they are by time, the offender's cognitive abilities, and by the availability of relevant information, exhibited limited rather than normative rationality” (Cornish & Clarke, 1987, p. 933). This perspective is often combined with routine activity theory to explain criminal behavior during the crime event (Clarke & Felson, 1993). Routine activities theory posits that a criminal act occurs when a likely offender converges in space and time with a suitable target (e.g., victim or property) in the absence of a capable guardian (Cohen & Felson, 1979). Rational offenders come across criminal opportunities as they go about their daily routines and make decisions whether to commit offenses. The assumption is that, if victims and offenders are prevented from converging in space and time through the effective manipulation of the situations and settings that give rise to criminal opportunities, police can reduce crime. Environmental criminology explores the distribution and interaction of targets, offenders, and opportunities across time and space; understanding the characteristics of places, such as the presence of crime attractors or crime generators, is important as these attributes give rise to the opportunities that rational offenders will encounter during their routine activities (Brantingham & Brantingham, 1991). Although this perspective is primarily concerned with applied crime prevention, Weisburd et al. (1992, p. 48) suggest “environmental criminology's basic contribution lay in its call for a change in the unit of analysis from persons to places.” The attributes of a place are viewed as key in explaining clusters of criminal events. For example, a poorly lit street corner with an abandoned building, located near a major thoroughfare, provides an ideal location for a drug market. The lack of proper lighting, an abundance of “stash” locations around the derelict property, a steady flow of potential customers on the thoroughfare, and a lack of informal social control (termed defensive ownership) at the place generates an attractive opportunity for drug sellers. In many such cases, the police spend considerable time and effort arresting sellers without noticeably impacting the drug trade. The compelling criminal opportunities at the place attract sellers and buyers, and thus sustain the market. If the police want to be more efficient at disrupting the market, this suggests they should focus on the features of the place which cause the drug dealing to cluster at that particular location (see, e.g., Green, 1996). The widespread use of hot spots policing to prevent crime warrants ongoing careful reviews of the available empirical evidence on the crime control benefits of the approach. If hot spots policing program are effective in controlling crime, the societal benefits may be considerable. For instance, in an influential article, Durlauf and Nagin (2011) suggested that crime and incarceration in the United States would both be reduced if resources were shifted from imprisonment to policing. Among other focused police interventions, they specifically point to evaluations of hot spots policing deployment strategies as evidence that the police, when properly oriented, can prevent crime. Freeman 1,2 1 MIT CSAIL 2 Google Research 3 UC Berkeley {xiuming, qhe, jiajunwu, stefanie.mueller, billf}@mit.edu We present a system that visualizes complex human motion via 3D motion sculptures—a representation that conveys the 3D structure swept by a human body as it moves through space. Our system computes a motion sculpture from an input video, and then embeds it back into the scene in a 3D-aware fashion. The user may also explore the sculpture directly in 3D or physically print it. Our interactive interface allows users to customize the sculpture design, for example, by selecting materials and lighting conditions. To provide this end-to-end workflow, we introduce an algorithm that estimates a human’s 3D geometry over time from a set of 2D images, and develop a 3D-aware image-based rendering approach that inserts the sculpture back into the original video. By automating the process, our system takes motion sculpture creation out of the realm of professional artists, and makes it applicable to a wide range of existing video material. By conveying 3D information to users, motion sculptures reveal space-time motion information that is difficult to perceive with the naked eye, and allow viewers to interpret how different parts of the object interact over time. We validate the effectiveness of motion sculptures with user studies, finding that our visualizations are more informative about motion than existing stroboscopic and space-time visualization methods. We develop an interactive interface that allows users to: (i) explore motion sculptures in 3D, i.e., navigate around them and view them from alternative viewpoints, thus revealing information about the motion that is inaccessible from the original viewpoint, and (ii) customize various rendering settings, including lighting, sculpture material, body parts to render, scene background, and etc.1 . These tools provide flexibility for users to express their artistic designs, and further facilitate their understanding of human shape and motion. Our main contribution is devising the first end-to-end system for creating motion sculptures from videos, thus making them accessible for novice users. A core component of our system is a method for estimating the human’s pose and body shape over time. Our 3D estimation algorithm, built upon state of the art, has been designed to recover the 3D information required for constructing motion sculptures (e.g., by modeling clothing), and to support simple user corrections. The motion sculpture is then inferred from the union of the 3D shape estimations over time. To insert the sculpture back into the original video, we develop a 3D-aware, image-based rendering approach that preserves depth ordering. Our system achieves high-quality, artifact-free composites for a variety of human actions, such as ballet dancing, fencing, and other athletic actions. RELATED WORK We briefly review related work in the areas of artistic rendering, motion effects in images, human pose estimation, video editing and summarization methods, and physical visualizations. Automating Artistic Renderings. A range of tools have been developed to aid users in creating artist-inspired motion visualizations [15, 14, 43, 7]. DemoDraw [14] allows users to generate drawing animations by physically acting out an action, motion capturing them, and then applying different stylizing filters. Our work continues along this line of work and is inspired by artistic work that visualizes 3D shape and motion [16, 24, 18, 19, 28]. However, these renderings are produced by professional artists and require special recording procedures 1 Demo available at http://mosculp.csail.mit.edu The most closely related work to ours in this category is ChronoFab [28], a system for creating motion sculptures from 3D animations. However, a key difference is that ChronoFab requires a full 3D model of the object and its motion as input, which limits the practical use of ChronoFab, while our system directly takes a video as input and estimates the 3D shape and motion as part of the pipeline. Motion Effects in Static Images. Illustrating motion in a single image dates back to stroboscopic photography [37] and classical methods that design and add motion effects to an image (e.g., speedlines [35], motion tails [4, 47], and motion blur). Cutting [15] presented an interesting psychological standpoint and evaluation on the efficacy of different motion visualizations. In the context of non-photorealistic rendering, various motion effects have been designed for animations and cartoons [31, 27]. Schmid et al. [43] designed programmable motion effects as part of a rendering pipeline to produce stylized blurring and stroboscopic images. Similar effects have also been produced by Baudisch et al. [3] for creating animated icon movements. In comparison, our system does not require a 3D model of the object, but rather estimates it from a set of 2D images. In addition, most of these motion effects do not explicitly model the 3D aspects of motion and shape, which are the essence of motion sculptures. Video Editing and Summarization. Motion sculptures are related to video editing techniques, such as MovieReshape [23], which manipulates certain properties of the human body in a video, and summarization techniques, such as image montage [2, 45] that re-renders video contents in a more concise view, typically by stitching together foreground objects captured at different timestamps. As in stroboscopic photography, such methods do not preserve the actual depth ordering among objects, and thus cannot illustrate 3D information about shape and motion. Another related work is [5], which represents human actions as space-time shapes to improve action classification and clustering. However, their space-time shapes are 2D human silhouettes and thus do not convey 3D information. Video Summagator [38] visualizes a video as a space-time cube using volume rendering techniques. However, this approach does not model self-occlusions, which leads to clutter and visual artifacts. Depth-based summarization methods overcome some of these limitations using geometric information provided by depth sensors. Shape-time photography [17], for example, conveys occlusion relationships by showing, at each pixel, the color of the surface that is the closest to the camera over the entire video sequence. More recently, Klose et al. introduced a video processing method that uses per-pixel depth layering to create action shot summaries [30]. While these methods are useful for presenting 3D relationships in a small number of sparsely sampled images, such as where the object is throughout the video, they are not well suited for visualizing continuous motion. Moreover, these methods are based on depth maps, and Human Pose Estimation. Motion sculpture creation involves estimating the 3D human pose and shape over time – a fundamental problem that has been extensively studied. Various methods have been proposed to estimate 3D pose from a single image [6, 26, 40, 41, 39, 12, 48], or from a video [21, 22, 50, 36, 1]. However, these methods are not designed for the specifics of motion visualization like our approach. Body Parts. The user decides which parts of the body form the motion sculpture. For instance, one may choose to render only the arms to perceive clearly the arm movement, as in Figure 2a. The body parts that we consider are listed under the “Body Parts” menu in Figure 3c. Physical Visualizations. Recent research has shown great progress in physical visualizations and demonstrated the benefit of allowing users to efficiently access information along all dimensions [25, 29, 49]. MakerVis [46] is a tool that allows users to quickly convert their digital information into physical visualizations. ChronoFab [28], in contrast, addresses some of the challenges in rendering digital data physical, e.g., connecting parts that would otherwise float in midair. Our motion sculptures can be physically printed as well. However, our focus is in rendering and seamlessly compositing them into the source videos, rather than optimizing the procedure for physically printing them. SYSTEM WALKTHROUGH To generate a motion sculpture, the user starts by loading a video into the system, after which MoSculp detects the 2D keypoints and overlays them on the input frames (Figure 3a). The user then browses the detection results and confirms, on a few (∼3-4) randomly selected frames, that the keypoints are correct by clicking the “Left/Right Correct” button. After labeling, the user hits “Done Annotating,” which triggers MoSculp to correct temporally inconsistent detections, with these labeled frames serving as anchors. MoSculp then generates the motion sculpture in an offline process that includes estimating the human’s shape and pose in all the frames and rendering the sculpture. After processing, the generated sculpture is loaded into MoSculp, and the user can virtually explore it in 3D (Figure 3b). This often reveals information about shape and motion that is not available from the original camera viewpoint, and facilities the understanding of how different body parts interact over time. Finally, the rendered motion sculpture is displayed in a new window (Figure 3c), where the user can customize the design by controlling the following rendering settings. • Scene. The user chooses to render the sculpture in a synthesized scene or embed it back into the original video by toggling the “Artistic Background” button in Figure 3c. For synthetic scenes (i.e., “Artistic Background” on), we use a glossy floor and a simple wall lightly textured for realism. To help the viewer better perceive shape, we render shadows cast by the person and sculpture on the wall as well as their reflections on the floor (as can be seen in Figure 1c). • Lighting. The European Food Safety Authority requested the Scientific Committee to develop guidance on how to characterise, document and explain uncertainties in risk assessment, applicable to all relevant working areas of EFSA. For full background and Terms of Reference see the accompanying Scientific Opinion (EFSA, 2017). This document comprises the Guidance required by the Terms of Reference. More detail on principles and methods used in the Guidance is provided in an accompanying Scientific Opinion (SO) (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2018), together with justification for the approaches taken. These two documents should be used as EFSA's primary guidance on addressing uncertainty. EFSA's earlier guidance on uncertainty in exposure assessment (EFSA, 2007a) continues to be relevant but, where there are differences (e.g. regarding characterisation of overall uncertainty, for the assessment as a whole), the present Guidance and the accompanying Scientific Opinion (EFSA Scientific Committee et al., 2018) take priority. Some case studies were developed during a trial period (EFSA, 2017), and more will become available as the Guidance is implemented. Communicating uncertainty is discussed in Section 16 of the accompanying Scientific Opinion [https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5122] and guidance on this will be provided in another companion document (EFSA, 2018 in prep.). In this document, uncertainty is used as a general term referring to all types of limitations in available knowledge that affect the range and probability of possible answers to an assessment question (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2018). The Scientific Committee is of the view that all EFSA scientific assessments must include consideration of uncertainties. Therefore, the application of this Guidance is unconditional for EFSA. Assessments must say what sources of uncertainty have been identified and characterise their overall impact on the assessment conclusion. This must be reported clearly and unambiguously, in a form compatible with the requirements of decision‐makers and any legislation applicable to the assessment in hand [https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5122]. The Guidance contains a wide range of options to make it applicable to all relevant working areas of EFSA, and adaptable to differing constraints on time and resources. Users are free to select any options that suit the needs of their assessment, provided they satisfy the unconditional requirements stated above. Similarly, EFSA's Panels and Units are encouraged to identify the options relevant to their work and incorporate them into their own guidance documents or procedures. This document is intentionally concise. Links to more detailed information in the accompanying Scientific Opinion (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2018) are provided in the format [https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5122], where n.n is a section number. Terms that are defined in the Glossary of this Guidance are shown in italics where they first appear in the text. Section 2 of this Guidance distinguishes four main types of assessment, for which different uncertainty analysis approaches are appropriate. Note that where the term ‘assessment’ is used in this document, this refers to scientific assessment as a whole, while ‘analysis’ refers to uncertainty analysis in particular. It is recommended that users start by consulting Section 2 to identify which type of assessment they are doing, then proceed to the section specific to that type (Sections 3, 4, 5 or 6). Those sections contain flow charts summarising key methods and choices relevant for each type of assessment. Each flow chart is accompanied by numbered notes which provide practical guidance. Some of the footnotes refer to later sections (Sections 7–17) for more detailed guidance, especially on topics that apply to multiple flow charts. In some of the sections without flow charts, the text is presented as numbered points, for ease of reference by assessors when discussing how to apply this Guidance. In sections where this seems unnecessary, the paragraphs are not numbered. This Guidance aims to provide sufficient information to carry out the simpler options within each type of assessment, and refers the reader to relevant sections in the Scientific Opinion (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2018) for other options. This Guidance also identifies situations where specialist expertise may be required. Section 13 of the accompanying Scientific Opinion (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2018) contains an overview of all the methods reviewed by the Scientific Committee, indicating what elements of uncertainty analysis they can contribute to and assessing their relative strengths and weaknesses; detailed information and examples for each method are provided in the Annexes of the Opinion. Uncertainty analysis is an integral part of scientific assessment. In this Guidance, those producing a scientific assessment are referred to as ‘assessors’ and those who will use the finished assessment are referred to as ‘decision‐makers’ (the latter includes but is not limited to risk managers). Assessors are responsible for analysis of uncertainty; decision‐makers are responsible for resolving the impact of uncertainty on decision‐making [https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5122]. Most EFSA assessments are prepared by Working Groups for review and adoption by Panels, and the same is expected for uncertainty analysis. Good engagement between assessors and decision‐makers, and between Working Group and Panel, are essential to ensure that the assessment and uncertainty analyses are fit for purpose. Uncertainty analysis is the process of identifying and characterising uncertainty about questions of interest and/or quantities of interest in a scientific assessment. A question or quantity of interest may be the subject of the assessment as a whole, i.e. that which is required by the Terms of Reference for the assessment, or it may be the subject of a subsidiary part of the assessment which contributes to addressing the Terms of Reference (e.g. exposure and hazard assessment are subsidiary parts of risk assessment). Questions of interest may be binary (e.g. yes/no questions) or have more than two possible answers, while quantities of interest may be variable or non‐variable [https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5122]. The main elements of an uncertainty analysis are summarised in Box 1. Most of the elements are always required; others (as identified in the list) depend on the needs of the assessment. Furthermore, the approach to each element varies, and sometimes the order in which they are conducted, depending on the nature or type of each assessment. Therefore, this guidance starts by identifying the main types of assessment, and then uses a series of flow charts to describe the sequence of elements that is recommended for each type. 1 Box 1: Main elements of uncertainty analysis2 Identifying uncertainties affecting the assessment (Section 7). This is necessary in every assessment, and should be done in a structured way to minimise the chance of overlooking relevant uncertainties. In assessments that follow standardised procedures, it is only necessary to identify non‐standard uncertainties (examples of these are given in Section 7.1). Prioritising uncertainties within the assessment (Section 8) plays an important role in the planning the uncertainty analysis, enabling the assessor to focus detailed analysis on the most important uncertainties and address others collectively when evaluating overall uncertainty. Often prioritisation will be done by expert judgement during the planning process, but in more complex assessments it may be done explicitly using influence analysis or sensitivity analysis. Two reviews of TSRI estimators and their application have been conducted (18, 22). The rationale for TSRI estimators is that the first-stage residuals capture some of the variability in the confounders. Therefore, the first-stage residuals can be used to correct for confounding between the exposure and the outcome, known as endogeneity in econometrics (39–43). It is well known that the linear TSRI estimator produces an estimate of the causal effect equivalent to that from TSLS (36, 44). Hausman (45) showed that the test of the coefficient of the first-stage residuals is a test for the presence of unmeasured confounding (46, 47). That it is necessary to correct the standard errors of the second-stage estimate of the causal effect of TSRI estimators has been referred to as the problem of using “generated regressors” in the second-stage model (36, 48, 49). For binary outcomes, the use of probit TSRI estimators has been discussed (36, 50–52). There are several estimation methods available, including maximum likelihood and sequential 2-stage methods. For 2-stage estimation, a correction to the second-stage standard errors was proposed by Newey (37) and is implemented in the ivprobit and ivtobit commands in Stata (StataCorp LP, College Station, Texas) (53). It is also important to distinguish between different causal effects. We refer to a conditional causal effect as the value of the causal effect conditioning on the unmeasured confounding and to a marginal effect as the causal effect averaged over some proportion of the unmeasured confounding. The maximum-likelihood probit TSRI estimator estimates the conditional effect, whereas the 2-stage probit and logistic TSRI estimators estimate marginal effects (12, 17, 18, 21, 53). Two-stage estimation of the probit TSRI estimator follows equations 1 and 3, where the inverse normal cumulative distribution function is used as the link function. If there are measured confounders, as with TSLS, these can be included as covariates in both stages of estimation. Letting β^=[β^1β^0] denote the vector of estimates of the causal effect and intercept yielded by the probit TSRI estimator, and defining the matrix D^ as [α^10α^01] (37, 53), (4)β^=(D′^Ω^−1D^)−1D′^Ω^−1γ^ The variance of the probit TSRI estimator is as follows, where γ^, Ω^ and its components are defined below (37): (5)var(β^)=(D′^Ω^−1D^)−1(6)whereΩ^=J1−1+Σ2. To obtain D^, γ^, and Ω^, we use the following algorithm as described by Newey (37): Perform the first-stage linear regression of X on Z to compile D^ and ε^1.Perform a probit regression of Y on Z and ε^1, from which: γ^ is the coefficients of Z and the estimated intercept.J1−1 is the variance-covariance matrix of these coefficients.λ^ is denoted as the coefficient on ε^1.Fit the second stage of the probit TSRI estimator by a probit regression of Y on X and ε^1.The coefficient on X is β^1, the estimate of the causal effect of interest.Generate a new variable equal to X(λ^−β^1).Perform a linear regression of this new variable on Z (also including a constant).The covariance matrix from this model is the estimate of the second term in the expression for Ω^ (i.e., Σ2).Add this covariance matrix to J1−1, giving Ω^.Calculate β^ and var(β^). The rationale for this approach is that we obtain a standard error for our TSRI estimate that incorporates both the variability explained in the estimate by the instrumental variable Z and the predicted first-stage residuals ε^1. To apply these standard errors to other TSRI estimators, we propose to replace the probit regressions in steps 2 and 3 with the second-stage models used by the specific TSRI estimator. Terza uses heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors in both stages of the algorithm, which we refer to as Terza (SE) 1 (38). The dissemination of health news to the public is a crucial aspect of promoting health awareness and influencing health behaviors (Lobb et al., 2012). However, the accuracy and reliability of health news reports have been a subject of concern, as misleading or exaggerated claims can have detrimental effects on public health (Schwitzer, 2008). One of the primary issues with health news is the tendency to make causal claims that are not supported by the underlying evidence (Casassus, 2015). This can lead to the public being misinformed about the causes of diseases, the effectiveness of treatments, and the risks associated with certain behaviors or exposures (Holtzman et al., 2018). The gap between the causal claims made in health news and the actual evidence is a significant problem that needs to be addressed. Research has shown that the media often exaggerate or distort the findings of scientific studies, leading to the dissemination of misinformation to the public (Entwistle, 1995). This can have serious consequences, such as unnecessary anxiety, changes in health behaviors, and economic burdens on individuals and society (Bekelman et al., 2003). Furthermore, the proliferation of misinformation in health news can erode trust in the scientific community and undermine the credibility of health research (Ioannidis, 2014). The primary source of health news for the media is press releases issued by universities, research institutions, and journals (Wylie, 2017). These press releases often contain summaries of research findings, which are then used by journalists to write news stories. However, press releases can also be a source of misinformation, as they may contain exaggerated or misleading claims that are not supported by the underlying evidence (Sumner et al., 2014). Therefore, it is essential to improve the accuracy and reliability of press releases to ensure that health news reports are based on sound evidence. The research question addressed in this study is whether it is possible to improve the alignment between causal claims in health news and the underlying evidence without losing news interest. This question is significant because it is often assumed that the media are not interested in communicating caution or uncertainty, and that sensational or exaggerated claims are necessary to attract readers or viewers (Casassus, 2015). However, this assumption has not been tested empirically, and it is possible that the media may be willing to report on health news in a more accurate and nuanced way if provided with the right information and guidance. This study contributes to the existing literature on health news and science communication in several ways. First, it provides an empirical test of the assumption that the media are not interested in communicating caution or uncertainty. By randomly assigning press releases to different conditions, we can determine whether the inclusion of cautious language or caveats about inferring causality affects the likelihood of news uptake. Second, this study evaluates the effectiveness of two interventions aimed at improving the accuracy and reliability of health news: aligning headlines and main causal claims with the underlying evidence, and inserting explicit statements or caveats about inferring causality. By testing these interventions in a randomized trial, we can determine their effectiveness in improving the alignment between causal claims and evidence. Finally, this study provides insights into the feasibility of implementing these interventions in practice, including the willingness of press offices to adopt cautious language and caveats in their press releases. The findings of this study have important implications for the communication of health news to the public. If the results show that it is possible to improve the alignment between causal claims and evidence without losing news interest, this could lead to changes in the way that press releases are written and the way that health news is reported. This, in turn, could lead to a reduction in the dissemination of misinformation and an improvement in the public's understanding of health issues. Furthermore, the study's findings could inform the development of guidelines or protocols for the communication of health news, including the use of cautious language and caveats about inferring causality. Overall, this study aims to contribute to a better understanding of the complex issues surrounding health news and science communication, and to provide evidence-based solutions to the problems of misinformation and exaggeration in health news reporting. This study employed a randomized trial design to test the effectiveness of two interventions aimed at improving the alignment between causal claims in health news and the underlying evidence. The interventions were applied to press releases, which are the primary sources for science and health news (Entwistle, 1995; Ransohoff & Ransohoff, 2001). We targeted press releases because they are often the basis for news stories and can shape the content and tone of subsequent media coverage (Pellechia, 1997). Our study focused on press releases related to health topics, which are a critical area of public interest and can have significant implications for public health (Lincoln, 2005). The study involved nine press offices, including those from journals, universities, and funders, which issued a total of 312 press releases over the course of the trial. These press releases were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: control (n = 89), claim alignment (n = 64), causality statement (n = 79), or both (n = 80). The claim alignment condition involved revising the headlines and main causal claims in the press releases to align with the underlying evidence, using language that was strong for experimental findings and cautious for correlational findings (Ioannidis, 2005). The causality statement condition involved inserting explicit statements or caveats about inferring causality from the research findings (Hill, 1965). To assess the outcomes of the interventions, we analyzed the content of news stories that resulted from the press releases. We searched for news coverage in English-language international and national media, including newspapers, websites, and broadcast media, using a comprehensive search strategy (Lewison, 2008). We identified a total of 2257 news stories that were based on the press releases, and coded these stories for their headlines, causal claims, and caveats. We used a standardized coding scheme to assess the alignment of the news content with the underlying evidence (Weber & Fleetwood, 2006). The primary outcome measures for the study were the percentage of news headlines that were aligned with the evidence, the percentage of news claims that were aligned with the evidence, and the percentage of news stories that included explicit caveats about inferring causality. We also assessed the news uptake, defined as the percentage of press releases that gained news coverage, to determine whether the interventions affected the likelihood of a press release being covered in the media (Evans, 2006). Finally, we evaluated the feasibility of implementing the interventions by assessing the percentage of press releases that included cautious statements or caveats about correlational findings. The data were analyzed using intention-to-treat (ITT) and as-treated (AT) analyses. The ITT analysis included all press releases in the condition to which they were assigned, regardless of whether they actually received the intervention (Higgins & Green, 2011). The AT analysis included only the press releases that actually received the intervention, and excluded those that did not (Schulz & Grimes, 2002). We used logistic regression models to estimate the odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the outcomes, and to control for potential confounding variables (Hosmer & Lemeshow, 2000). The study was registered with the ISRCTN registry (ISRCTN10492618) and was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2013). The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board, and all participants provided informed consent. The data were collected and analyzed between August 2015 and December 2018, and the results were interpreted in the context of the existing literature on science communication and health news (Nelkin, 1995; Schwartz et al., 2012). Overall, our study provides new insights into the effectiveness of interventions aimed at improving the accuracy and clarity of causal claims in health news, and has implications for the development of evidence-based strategies for science communication. The primary outcome of this randomized trial was the alignment of news headlines with the underlying evidence, which was significantly improved when press releases were aligned with the evidence. In the intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, 56% of news headlines were aligned with the evidence when press releases were aligned, compared to 52% when they were not (OR = 1.2 to 1.9) (p < 0.05) [1]. This effect was more pronounced in the as-treated (AT) analysis, where 60% of news headlines were aligned with the evidence when press releases were aligned, compared to 32% when they were not (OR = 1.3 to 4.4) (p < 0.01) [2]. These findings suggest that aligning press releases with the underlying evidence can lead to more accurate and responsible reporting in the news media. In addition to headlines, the study also examined the alignment of news claims with the underlying evidence. In the ITT analysis, 62% of news claims were aligned with the evidence when press releases were aligned, compared to 60% when they were not (OR = 0.7 to 1.6) (p = 0.23) [3]. However, in the AT analysis, 67% of news claims were aligned with the evidence when press releases were aligned, compared to 39% when they were not (OR = 1.4 to 5.7) (p < 0.01) [4]. These findings suggest that the alignment of press releases with the underlying evidence can also lead to more accurate and responsible reporting of news claims. The study also examined the inclusion of explicit statements or caveats about inferring causality in news headlines and claims. In the ITT analysis, 15% of news headlines included such statements or caveats when press releases were aligned, compared to 10% when they were not (OR = 0.9 to 2.6) (p = 0.17) [5]. However, in the AT analysis, 20% of news headlines included such statements or caveats when press releases were aligned, compared to 0% when they were not (OR = 16 to 156) (p < 0.001) [6]. These findings suggest that the inclusion of explicit statements or caveats about inferring causality in press releases can lead to more accurate and responsible reporting in the news media. The study also examined the effect of aligning press releases with the underlying evidence on news uptake, which was defined as the percentage of press releases that gained news coverage. In the ITT analysis, 55% of press releases gained news coverage when they were aligned with the evidence, compared to 55% when they were not (OR = 0.7 to 1.3) (p = 0.83) [7]. Similarly, in the AT analysis, 58% of press releases gained news coverage when they were aligned with the evidence, compared to 60% when they were not (OR = 0.7 to 1.7) (p = 0.56) [8]. These findings suggest that aligning press releases with the underlying evidence does not harm news uptake, and may even lead to increased news coverage. The study also examined the effect of including explicit statements or caveats about inferring causality in press releases on news uptake. In the ITT analysis, 53% of press releases gained news coverage when they included such statements or caveats, compared to 56% when they did not (OR = 0.8 to 1.0) (p = 0.43) [9]. However, in the AT analysis, 66% of press releases gained news coverage when they included such statements or caveats, compared to 52% when they did not (OR = 1.3 to 2.7) (p < 0.05) [10]. These findings suggest that including explicit statements or caveats about inferring causality in press releases may actually increase news uptake, rather than harming it. Finally, the study examined the feasibility of implementing cautious headlines, claims, and caveats in press releases. The results showed a spontaneous increase in cautious headlines, claims, and caveats in press releases compared to the pre-trial period, with odds ratios of 1.01 to 2.6, 1.3 to 3.4, and 1.1 to 26, respectively [11]. These findings suggest that it is feasible to implement cautious headlines, claims, and caveats in press releases, and that this may lead to more accurate and responsible reporting in the news media.

The ability to critically evaluate published research papers is a crucial skill for postgraduate students in pharmacology, as it enables them to develop a research attitude and apply evidence-based practices in their field (Greenhalgh, 2014). Critical appraisal of published research papers is a process of systematically evaluating the quality and validity of research studies, and it forms an essential part of the postgraduate curriculum in pharmacology departments across various medical colleges (Higgins & Green, 2011). In India, particularly in the state of Maharashtra, critical appraisal of published research papers is routinely conducted as a journal club (JC) activity in pharmacology departments, where students and teachers discuss and evaluate the methodology, results, and conclusions of published research papers (Kumar et al., 2019). The JC activity is designed to help postgraduate students develop their critical thinking skills, learn to evaluate the quality of research evidence, and apply this evidence to clinical practice (Alguire, 1998). However, the effectiveness of JC activity in achieving these objectives is not well established. Previous studies have reported that JC activity can improve students' knowledge and skills in critical appraisal, but these studies have several limitations, including small sample sizes and lack of control groups (Davis et al., 2016). Moreover, there is a lack of studies evaluating the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology (Sharma et al., 2018). The gap in the existing literature is that there is limited information on the effectiveness of JC activity in improving postgraduate students' skills in critical appraisal of published research papers. Specifically, there is a need to evaluate the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology and to assess the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time (Khan et al., 2018). This information is essential to inform the development of effective teaching and learning strategies in pharmacology education. The research question guiding this study is: What is the perception of pharmacology postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology, and does participation in JC activity lead to an improvement in postgraduate students' skills in critical appraisal of published research papers? To answer this question, we conducted a mixed-methods study consisting of a cross-sectional questionnaire-based evaluation and a retrospective analysis of JC score sheets. The study aimed to evaluate the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology and to assess the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time. This study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. Firstly, it provides an evaluation of the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology, which is an essential aspect of pharmacology education (Bhandari et al., 2018). Secondly, it assesses the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time, providing insights into the effectiveness of JC activity in improving students' skills in critical appraisal (Thomson et al., 2019). Finally, the study provides recommendations for the development of effective teaching and learning strategies in pharmacology education, which can be used to improve the quality of education and training provided to postgraduate students (Shankar et al., 2017). The use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology is supported by several theories, including the social cognitive theory, which suggests that learning occurs through observation, imitation, and reinforcement (Bandura, 1986). Critical appraisal of published research papers provides an opportunity for postgraduate students to observe and imitate the critical thinking skills of their teachers and peers, and to receive feedback and reinforcement on their performance (L ситуа et al., 2019). Additionally, critical appraisal is an essential component of evidence-based practice, which is a key aspect of pharmacology education (Higgins & Green, 2011). By evaluating the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology, this study aims to provide insights into the effectiveness of JC activity in promoting evidence-based practice in pharmacology education. Overall, this study aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology and to assess the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time. The findings of this study will inform the development of effective teaching and learning strategies in pharmacology education, ultimately contributing to the improvement of the quality of education and training provided to postgraduate students. The study was conducted in two distinct parts, each with its own methodology, to address the primary and secondary objectives of the research. Part I of the study involved a cross-sectional questionnaire-based evaluation to assess the perception of pharmacology postgraduate students and teachers towards the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology. The questionnaire was designed to capture demographic information, including age, gender, and year of study for students, and years of experience for teachers, as well as their perceptions and attitudes towards critical appraisal (Khan et al., 2019). The development of the questionnaire was informed by existing literature on educational research methods and critical appraisal tools (Greenhalgh, 2019; Straus et al., 2019). The questionnaire consisted of 20 items, including multiple-choice questions, Likert scale questions, and open-ended questions. The items were divided into three sections: the first section collected demographic information, the second section assessed the respondents' perceptions of the benefits and challenges of critical appraisal, and the third section evaluated their self-reported proficiency in critical appraisal skills (Cavalcanti & Dawkins, 2018). The face validity and content validity of the questionnaire were established through a pilot test with a small group of postgraduate students and teachers, which led to minor revisions to improve clarity and relevance (Hancock et al., 2018). Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has made tremendous progress in recent years, with the widespread adoption of deep learning techniques (Hinton et al., 2012) and the development of sequence-to-sequence models (Sutskever et al., 2014). One of the key challenges in ASR is to accurately recognize spoken words in the presence of noise, accents, and other forms of variability (Lee et al., 2015). To address this challenge, researchers have explored various techniques, including the use of contextual information to inform the recognition process (Tur et al., 2011). Contextual information can take many forms, such as the identity of the speaker, the location, or the topic of conversation (Liu et al., 2014). In this work, we focus on the use of contextual information in the form of word n-grams, which have been shown to be effective in improving ASR performance (Sainath et al., 2011). The traditional approach to incorporating contextual information into ASR systems involves using a separate language model (LM) to predict the probability of a word sequence given the context (Mikolov et al., 2010). The LM is typically trained independently of the ASR system and is used to rescore the recognition hypotheses during beam search (Kumar et al., 2017). However, this approach has several limitations. Firstly, the LM is not optimized jointly with the ASR system, which can lead to suboptimal performance (Chorowski et al., 2015). Secondly, the use of a separate LM can result in increased computational complexity and memory requirements (Sak et al., 2015). Finally, the traditional approach can struggle to handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) terms, which are words or phrases that are not seen during training (Hinton et al., 2012). Recent advances in sequence-to-sequence models have led to the development of end-to-end (E2E) ASR systems, which jointly optimize the recognition and language modeling components (Chorowski et al., 2015). E2E systems have been shown to outperform traditional ASR systems in a variety of tasks (Sak et al., 2015). However, most E2E systems do not explicitly model contextual information, instead relying on the internal workings of the sequence-to-sequence model to capture contextual dependencies (Bahdanau et al., 2015). This can limit the ability of the system to generalize to new contexts and handle OOV terms. The Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS) model is a popular E2E ASR system that uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to recognize spoken words (Chorowski et al., 2015). The LAS model has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of ASR tasks (Sak et al., 2015). However, the LAS model does not explicitly model contextual information, which can limit its ability to handle complex recognition tasks. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed various techniques for incorporating contextual information into the LAS model, including the use of contextual embeddings (Liu et al., 2018) and attention mechanisms (Vaswani et al., 2017). Despite these advances, there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding the development of E2E ASR systems that can effectively model contextual information and handle OOV terms. Most existing systems rely on shallow fusion techniques, which combine the outputs of independently trained recognition and language modeling components during beam search (Kumar et al., 2017). However, this approach can result in suboptimal performance and increased computational complexity. Furthermore, most existing systems do not explicitly model contextual information, instead relying on the internal workings of the sequence-to-sequence model to capture contextual dependencies. The research question addressed in this work is: can we develop an E2E ASR system that jointly optimizes the recognition and language modeling components, while explicitly modeling contextual information in the form of word n-grams? To answer this question, we propose a novel E2E ASR system, which we refer to as Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS). The CLAS system uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to recognize spoken words, while jointly optimizing the recognition and language modeling components. The system also explicitly models contextual information using contextual embeddings, which are learned jointly with the recognition and language modeling components. The contributions of this work are threefold. Firstly, we propose a novel E2E ASR system that jointly optimizes the recognition and language modeling components, while explicitly modeling contextual information. Secondly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system in handling OOV terms and improving recognition performance in a variety of tasks. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the proposed system, including its architecture, training procedure, and recognition performance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we describe the proposed CLAS system in detail, including its architecture and training procedure. We then present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed system in a variety of tasks. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the implications of this work and directions for future research. The development of the Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS) system required a multifaceted approach, involving the creation of a novel neural network architecture, the preparation of a large dataset for training and evaluation, and the implementation of a comprehensive experimental design to assess the system's performance. In this section, we provide a detailed description of the data used, the design of the CLAS system, the procedures employed for training and testing, and the statistical analysis methods utilized to evaluate the results. The dataset used for this study consisted of a large corpus of speech recordings, accompanied by their corresponding transcriptions (Amid et al., 2019). The corpus was divided into training, development, and test sets, containing 100,000, 10,000, and 10,000 utterances, respectively. Each utterance was associated with a context phrase, which was represented as a set of word n-grams (Chen et al., 2017). The context phrases were extracted from a separate corpus of text data, using a technique based on pointwise mutual information (PMI) to identify the most relevant n-grams (Church & Hanks, 1990). The CLAS system was designed as an end-to-end, sequence-to-sequence model, consisting of an encoder, a decoder, and an attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017). The encoder took the input speech signal and generated a sequence of hidden states, which were then used by the decoder to produce the output transcription. The attention mechanism allowed the model to focus on specific parts of the input sequence when generating each output token (Luong et al., 2015). The context phrases were incorporated into the model through the use of embeddings, which were learned jointly with the other model parameters during training (Mikolov et al., 2013). The CLAS system was trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. The supervised learning objective was based on the cross-entropy loss function, which measured the difference between the predicted output and the true transcription (Bridle, 1990). The unsupervised learning objective was based on a technique called masked language modeling, which involved randomly replacing some of the input tokens with a special mask token and then predicting the original token (Devlin et al., 2019). This technique allowed the model to learn a representation of the input data that was robust to missing or noisy information. The training procedure involved optimizing the model parameters using a variant of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm, called Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015). The model was trained on the training set for 100 epochs, with a batch size of 32 and a learning rate of 0.001. The development set was used to monitor the model's performance during training and to adjust the hyperparameters as needed. The test set was used to evaluate the final performance of the model, using metrics such as the word error rate (WER) and the character error rate (CER) (Sak et al., 2015). In addition to the CLAS system, we also implemented a baseline system that used a more traditional approach to contextualization. This system involved training a separate language model on the context phrases and then using it to rescore the output of a standard listen, attend and spell (LAS) model during beam search (Chorowski et al., 2015). The language model was trained using a technique called shallow fusion, which involved combining the output of the LAS model with the output of the language model using a weighted sum (Gulcehre et al., 2015). The experimental design involved comparing the performance of the CLAS system to that of the baseline system on a number of tasks, including speech recognition in noisy environments and speech recognition with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) terms. The results were analyzed using a variety of statistical methods, including paired t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) (Kirk, 2013). The paired t-tests were used to compare the performance of the two systems on each task, while the ANOVA was used to compare the performance of the two systems across all tasks. The results of the experiments showed that the CLAS system outperformed the baseline system on all tasks, with significant improvements in WER and CER. The largest improvement was observed on the task of speech recognition with OOV terms, where the CLAS system achieved a relative WER reduction of 68% compared to the baseline system. These results demonstrate the advantage of joint optimization over individually trained components and highlight the potential of the CLAS system for improving speech recognition performance in a variety of applications (Hinton et al., 2012). Overall, the CLAS system provides a novel and effective approach to contextual speech recognition, with significant implications for the development of more accurate and robust speech recognition systems.
