The ability to learn effective representations of data without relying on explicit supervision is a long-standing goal in the field of machine learning (Bengio et al., 2013). Self-supervised learning, which involves training models on pretext tasks that do not require labeled data, has emerged as a promising approach to achieving this goal (Doersch et al., 2015; Noroozi & Favaro, 2016). One of the key challenges in self-supervised learning is designing pretext tasks that encourage the model to learn representations that capture high-level, abstract features of the data, rather than simply memorizing low-level details (Kolesnikov et al., 2019). In recent years, a number of approaches have been proposed that involve maximizing mutual information between different views or transformations of the data (Hjelm et al., 2018; Bachman et al., 2019). These approaches are based on the idea that by maximizing mutual information between different views, the model is forced to capture information about high-level factors that are shared across views, rather than simply learning to recognize specific low-level features. One of the key insights underlying these approaches is that mutual information can be used as a proxy for the presence of high-level, abstract features in the data (Bell & Sejnowski, 1995). By maximizing mutual information between different views, the model is encouraged to learn representations that capture these high-level features, rather than simply memorizing low-level details. For example, in the context of image recognition, maximizing mutual information between different views of an image (e.g., different crops or rotations) can encourage the model to learn representations that capture the presence of objects or textures, rather than simply recognizing specific pixel patterns (Gidaris et al., 2018). Similarly, in the context of natural language processing, maximizing mutual information between different views of a sentence (e.g., different paraphrases or translations) can encourage the model to learn representations that capture the semantic meaning of the sentence, rather than simply recognizing specific word patterns (Conneau et al., 2019). Despite the promise of these approaches, there are still a number of challenges and limitations that must be addressed. One of the key challenges is designing pretext tasks that are effective at capturing high-level, abstract features of the data, while also being computationally efficient and scalable to large datasets (Kolesnikov et al., 2019). Another challenge is evaluating the quality of the learned representations, and determining whether they are effective at capturing the high-level features of interest (Bengio et al., 2013). Finally, there is a need for more research on the theoretical foundations of self-supervised learning, and the conditions under which maximizing mutual information between different views can be expected to produce effective representations (Bell & Sejnowski, 1995). In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a new approach to self-supervised representation learning based on maximizing mutual information between features extracted from multiple views of a shared context. Our approach is based on the idea that by producing multiple views of a local spatio-temporal context, and maximizing mutual information between the features extracted from these views, we can encourage the model to learn representations that capture high-level, abstract features of the data. For example, in the context of image recognition, we can produce multiple views of an image by applying different data augmentations (e.g., cropping, rotating, or color jittering), and then maximize mutual information between the features extracted from these views. This can encourage the model to learn representations that capture the presence of objects or textures, rather than simply recognizing specific pixel patterns. Our research question is: Can maximizing mutual information between features extracted from multiple views of a shared context produce effective representations of data, without relying on explicit supervision? We hypothesize that by maximizing mutual information between different views, we can encourage the model to learn representations that capture high-level, abstract features of the data, rather than simply memorizing low-level details. We evaluate our approach on a number of benchmark datasets, including ImageNet, and demonstrate that our model learns representations that significantly outperform prior methods on the tasks we consider. Most notably, using self-supervised learning, our model learns representations which achieve 68.1% accuracy on ImageNet using standard linear evaluation, beating prior results by over 12% and concurrent results by 7%. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose a new approach to self-supervised representation learning based on maximizing mutual information between features extracted from multiple views of a shared context. Second, we develop a model that learns image representations that significantly outperform prior methods on the tasks we consider. Finally, we demonstrate that our model can be extended to use mixture-based representations, and that segmentation behavior emerges as a natural side-effect. Our code is available online, and we hope that it will provide a useful starting point for future research in this area. Overall, our approach provides a new and effective way to learn representations of data without relying on explicit supervision, and has the potential to be applied to a wide range of applications, including image recognition, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. By maximizing mutual information between features extracted from these views, we can learn representations that capture this shared information, which is essential for downstream tasks such as image classification and segmentation. To produce multiple views of a shared context, we employ data augmentation techniques, which have been widely used in self-supervised learning (Chen et al., 2020; He et al., 2020). Specifically, we apply a set of random transformations to the input image, including random cropping, color jittering, and Gaussian blurring. These transformations are designed to preserve the high-level factors of the image while altering the low-level details, thereby creating multiple views of the same context. The shared encoder is a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a ResNet-50 backbone (He et al., 2016), which has been widely used in image classification tasks. The view-specific projection heads are simple neural networks with two fully connected layers, which are used to map the extracted features to a lower-dimensional space. To maximize mutual information between the features extracted from multiple views, we use a contrastive loss function, which has been shown to be effective in self-supervised learning (Chen et al., 2020; Oord et al., 2018). Specifically, we use the infoNCE loss function (Oord et al., 2018), which measures the mutual information between two random variables by contrasting positive pairs (i.e., pairs of features extracted from the same view) with negative pairs (i.e., pairs of features extracted from different views). The infoNCE loss function is defined as: L = -E[log(exp(sim(z, z+)) / (exp(sim(z, z+)) + Σexp(sim(z, z-)))] where z and z+ are the features extracted from the same view, z- are the features extracted from different views, and sim is a similarity function, such as cosine similarity or L2 distance. The automotive industry has undergone significant transformations in recent years, driven by the increasing demand for safety, efficiency, and connectivity in vehicles (Broy et al., 2019). One of the key factors contributing to this transformation is the growing use of software-intensive systems, which has led to a rise in the complexity of automotive applications (Kopetz, 2011). As a result, the development and testing of these systems have become critical components of the automotive industry, requiring specialized knowledge and skills (ISO/IEC26262, 2018). The use of Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) testing, in particular, has become a widely accepted practice in the industry, allowing for the simulation of real-world scenarios and the testing of complex systems in a controlled environment (Sasena et al., 2017). Despite the growing importance of software design and testing in the automotive industry, there is a significant gap in the existing literature regarding the knowledge and skills required for novice developers to effectively design and test safety-critical devices using HiL testing (Schultz, 2017). While there are various studies that focus on the development and testing of automotive applications, few of them provide a comprehensive overview of the knowledge and skills required for novice developers to succeed in this field (Broy et al., 2019). Furthermore, the existing curricula for Electrical Engineering and Mechatronics programs often do not provide sufficient coverage of the specific knowledge and skills required for the development and testing of automotive applications, leaving many graduates unprepared for the demands of the industry (Kopetz, 2011). The development process for automotive applications typically follows the Automotive SPICE (Software Process Improvement and Capability dEtermination) framework, which provides a set of guidelines and best practices for the development and testing of safety-critical systems (Automotive SPICE, 2019). The V-model is a key component of this framework, providing a graphical representation of the development process and highlighting the importance of testing and validation at each stage (ISO/IEC 26262, 2018). However, the tip of the V-model, which focuses on the integration and testing of individual components, is often where novice developers struggle the most, due to the complexity of the systems and the need for specialized knowledge and skills (Sasena et al., 2017). In order to address this gap, it is essential to identify the specific knowledge and skills required for novice developers to design and test safety-critical devices in the automotive industry using HiL testing. This requires an understanding of the development process, including the various phases and activities involved, as well as the specific tools and techniques used in the industry (Broy et al., 2019). Additionally, it is necessary to consider the specific challenges and requirements of the automotive industry, including the need for safety, reliability, and efficiency, and the importance of meeting regulatory requirements and industry standards (ISO/IEC 26262, 2018). The research question guiding this study is: What are the specific knowledge and skills required for novice developers to design and test safety-critical devices in the automotive industry using HiL testing, and how can these be incorporated into existing curricula for Electrical Engineering and Mechatronics programs? This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the knowledge and skills required for novice developers to succeed in this field, and to identify the key challenges and requirements of the automotive industry. By addressing this research question, this study contributes to the existing literature on software design and testing in the automotive industry, and provides a valuable resource for educators and industry professionals seeking to develop the next generation of automotive engineers. The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the knowledge and skills required for novice developers to design and test safety-critical devices in the automotive industry using HiL testing. Secondly, it identifies the key challenges and requirements of the automotive industry, including the need for safety, reliability, and efficiency, and the importance of meeting regulatory requirements and industry standards. Finally, it provides a framework for incorporating these knowledge and skills into existing curricula for Electrical Engineering and Mechatronics programs, thereby helping to address the gap between industry requirements and academic preparation. By providing a clear understanding of the knowledge and skills required for novice developers to succeed in this field, this study aims to contribute to the development of a new generation of automotive engineers who are equipped to meet the demands of the industry. The research methodology employed in this study is based on a comprehensive review of existing literature and industry practices in the field of automotive software design and testing. The study focuses on the knowledge and skills required for novice developers to design and test safety-critical devices in the automotive industry using Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) testing. Soft biometric traits such as sex, age, ethnicity, and eye colour describe a person coarsely but are useful in practice. They are not distinctive enough to identify an individual on their own, but they can narrow a search space, complement primary biometric modalities, and support applications where explicit identification is unnecessary or undesirable (Jain, Dass, & Nandakumar, 2004; Dantcheva, Elia, & Ross, 2016). Among these traits, sex is one of the most widely studied, with uses in indexing large biometric databases, demographic analysis, human–computer interaction, and forensic investigation. Predicting sex from a person's appearance is commonly called "gender classification" in the literature. We use the term sex-prediction because the quantity inferred from biometric data is a biological attribute rather than a social identity (Bobeldyk & Ross, 2016). The face is the most intuitive source for such predictions, and deep learning has made face-based sex classification highly accurate under favourable conditions. In many real scenarios, however, the full face is not available. Surgical masks, scarves, helmets, and extreme poses or viewing angles can all hide the lower facial region. Under these conditions the periocular region, which covers the eye, eyelids, eyelashes, eyebrows, and surrounding skin, is an attractive alternative. It remains visible when the rest of the face is occluded, it can be captured by a wide range of sensors, and it combines shape, texture, and colour information that is useful for recognition (Park, Ross, & Jain, 2009; Alonso-Fernandez & Bigun, 2016). Periocular images also arise naturally from iris acquisition in the near-infrared (NIR) spectrum and from visible wavelength (VW) imaging with smartphones and other consumer devices. Early work showed that the periocular region contains information about sex. Merkow, Jou, and Savvides (2010) reported accuracies of roughly 85% from periocular crops of web-collected face images using hand-crafted features. Dong and Woodard (2011) showed that eyebrow shape alone carries a discriminative signal. For NIR iris and ocular images, Thomas et al. (2007) and Lagree and Bowyer (2011) predicted sex from texture descriptors, with accuracies typically between 60% and 80%. More recent studies have applied convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and obtained better results. Tapia and Aravena (2018) obtained high accuracy from NIR iris images, and Bobeldyk and Ross (2016, 2018) examined which ocular regions contribute most to sex-prediction and how covariates influence it. Rattani, Reddy, and Derakhshani (2018) extended the problem to smartphone-based VW ocular images and reported competitive accuracies with deep architectures. Taken together, these studies suggest that sex can be inferred from the periocular region with a reasonable degree of reliability. The reported figures, however, need to be interpreted with care. First, most studies train and test on a single database, and often on a single sensor. In such protocols images in the training and test partitions share acquisition conditions such as illumination, resolution, optics, and sensor noise. In several cases they also share subjects or sessions. A classifier can then exploit sensor-specific or session-specific cues instead of sex-related structure, which inflates performance. The concern is more than theoretical. Kuehlkamp, Becker, and Bowyer (2017) showed that apparent sex-related information in iris images can be partly attributed to cosmetics such as mascara, and that accuracy drops substantially once this confound is removed. It is also well documented that biometric algorithms trained on one sensor often degrade when evaluated on another, which is the cross-sensor problem studied extensively in iris and periocular recognition (Alonso-Fernandez, Raja, Busch, & Bigun, 2019). If sex-prediction is to be deployed on periocular images whose origin is unknown, accuracy estimated under same-sensor conditions is an optimistic upper bound. Second, NIR and VW periocular images are almost always treated separately. The two spectra differ in the visual information they offer. NIR imaging suppresses melanin-related pigmentation and emphasises structural texture, whereas VW images contain colour, pigmentation, and cosmetic cues. Whether sex-related patterns learned in one spectrum transfer to the other, and whether a single model can handle both, is largely unexplored. This question matters for heterogeneous deployments, for example when a model trained on NIR iris-capture databases is applied to selfie-type VW images, or the reverse. Third, the methodological details of prior studies make results hard to compare. They differ in image size, in how the periocular region is cropped, in architecture, in partitioning protocol, and in whether subjects are disjoint across training and test sets. Few studies test the generalisation of a single model across many databases with a consistent protocol, and the effect of fusing heterogeneous sources into one training set has received little attention. These gaps lead to the central research question of this paper: How accurately can the sex of a subject be predicted from periocular images when the sensor and the spectrum of the test images are unknown at training time? We split this into three subquestions. (i) What accuracy can be expected when training and testing are performed on disjoint sensors within the same spectrum (NIR–NIR and VW–VW)? (ii) How well does a model generalise across spectra, that is, when trained on NIR data and tested on VW data, and vice versa? (iii) Can a single model trained on a multi-spectral collection perform comparably to spectrum-specific models? To answer these questions, we train CNNs on fused sets composed of several NIR and VW periocular databases acquired with different sensors, and we evaluate them under protocols that keep the test sensor out of training. This design reflects a more realistic setting in which the origin of an image is not known beforehand. It also discourages the network from using sensor-specific artefacts as shortcuts, since a model trained on a heterogeneous mixture cannot rely on any single sensor's signature. The contributions of this work are as follows: 1. A cross-sensor evaluation within each spectrum. Using leave-one-database-out protocols, we estimate sex-prediction accuracy for unseen sensors in NIR and VW imagery. The average accuracy is approximately 85% in both cases, which is a more cautious figure than those often reported for single-database experiments. 2. A cross-spectral evaluation. We quantify the transferability of learned sex-related features between NIR and VW images. The average classification accuracy is about 82%, only a few points below the within-spectrum case, which suggests that a substantial portion of the discriminative information is spectrum-independent. 3. A multi-spectral model. We show that a single CNN trained on combined NIR and VW data attains an average accuracy of 83%. It can therefore be used when the spectrum of the input is not known, at a modest cost in accuracy relative to specialised models. 4. A consistent, reproducible protocol. We apply the same preprocessing, periocular cropping, network configurations, and partitioning rules across all databases, so that differences in performance can be attributed to the acquisition scenario rather than to differences in experimental design. Overall, the findings give a more realistic estimate of how feasible it is to predict a subject's sex from the periocular region. They also indicate where current approaches are likely to fail when applied to unconstrained data. The results are relevant to both the design of soft-biometric systems and the discussion of privacy, since the ease with which sex can be inferred from periocular images captured without a subject's explicit intent has implications for how such data are stored and shared (Mirjalili & Ross, 2017). Databases. Experiments were conducted on publicly available periocular and iris databases covering two spectra and several acquisition sensors. The near-infrared (NIR) set comprised BioSec (Fierrez et al., 2007), CASIA-Iris-Thousand (CASIA, 2010), IITD-Iris (Kumar and Passi, 2010), and ND-CrossSensor (Connaughton et al., 2013). The visible-wavelength (VW) set comprised UBIPr (Padole and Proença, 2012), MICHE-I (De Marsico et al., 2015), and CSIP (Santos et al., 2015). Sex labels were taken from the metadata distributed with each database, and subjects without reliable labels were excluded. Because the labels are binary (male or female), we refer to the task as sex-prediction. After filtering, the NIR set contained approximately 41,000 images from 1,650 subjects and the VW set approximately 22,000 images from 940 subjects. The proportion of female subjects ranged from 29% to 47% across databases. Databases differ in resolution, illumination, stand-off distance, and subject demographics, so a sensor-specific model may exploit dataset-specific artefacts rather than sex-related periocular characteristics (Torralba and Efros, 2011). The cross-database protocols below were designed to expose and control this effect. Preprocessing. Eye regions were localised with a landmark detector (Kazemi and Sullivan, 2014) for VW images. For NIR images, we used the pupil and iris boundaries from a Hough-transform-based segmentation (Masek and Kovesi, 2003) with manual verification of a random 5% subset. A periocular region of interest was cropped around the eye centre with a width of 6.0 times the iris radius and a height of 4.5 times the iris radius. This included eyebrow, eyelids, and surrounding skin and avoided hair and facial context. Right-eye images were mirrored horizontally so that all samples had the same canonical orientation. Crops were resized to 224 × 224 pixels by bicubic interpolation. NIR images were replicated across three channels, and VW images were kept in RGB. Pixel intensities were normalised with the ImageNet channel statistics used for pretraining (Deng et al., 2009). Images for which landmark detection or segmentation failed (3.1% of all samples) were discarded. Network architecture and training. We used ResNet-50 (He et al., 2016) and DenseNet-121 (Huang et al., 2017) as feature extractors. Both were initialised with ImageNet weights and fine-tuned end to end. The original classification layer was replaced by global average pooling, a dropout layer (rate 0.5), and a two-unit softmax layer. Models were optimised with stochastic gradient descent with momentum 0.9, an initial learning rate of 10⁻³ decayed by a factor of 10 when validation loss plateaued for five epochs, a batch size of 64, and weight decay of 5 × 10⁻⁴. Training ran for at most 60 epochs with early stopping (patience 10) on validation loss. The loss was cross-entropy. To reduce the effect of class imbalance, each training epoch used class-balanced mini-batches drawn by oversampling the minority class. Data augmentation consisted of random rotations (±10°), random scaling (0.9–1.1), random translations (up to 5% of image size), brightness and contrast jitter (±20%), and Gaussian blur (σ ≤ 1.5), applied on the fly. Horizontal flipping was not used for augmentation because mirroring was already applied for canonicalisation. All experiments were implemented in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) and repeated with five random seeds, and results are reported as means over seeds. Experimental protocols. To approximate the realistic case in which the capture device is unknown, models were trained on fused sets of multiple databases and evaluated on a database that was entirely excluded from training. Three scenarios were defined. Cross-sensor, within spectrum. For each spectrum, we applied a leave-one-database-out protocol. A model was trained on the union of all other databases of the same spectrum and tested on the held-out database. With four NIR and three VW databases, this gave seven train–test configurations. Training data were split 80/20 into training and validation partitions at subject level. Cross-spectrum. Models were trained on the union of all NIR databases and tested on each VW database, and vice versa. Neither the sensor nor the spectrum of the test data was seen during training. Domain adaptation and spectrum-specific normalisation were deliberately not used, so that the evaluation reflects the transferability of learned features alone. Multi-spectral. Models were trained on the union of NIR and VW databases, excluding one database that served as the test set. This was repeated for all seven databases. The aim was to determine whether exposure to both spectra yields a more general representation than spectrum-specific training. Subject-disjoint partitions were enforced in all scenarios, so that no subject's images, including those of the contralateral eye, appeared in both training and testing. Within a database, left and right eyes of the same subject were always assigned to the same partition. Training sets were capped at a fixed number of images per subject (20) to prevent subjects with many samples from dominating. Profiled community search. In this paper, we study profiled community search (PCS), which aims to find profiled communities, or PC’s, for a profiled graph. To obtain high-quality communities, we use structure cohesiveness and profile cohesiveness to constrain PC’s. We adopt widely used metric minimum degree [8, 25– 29] to measure the structure cohesiveness. Note that in PCS problem, the minimum degree matric can be replaced by other useful matrics, e.g., k -truss [10] and k -clique [22], to fit in other possible application scenarios. In a profiled graph, each vertex is associated with a P-tree. To measure the profile cohesiveness, we fully utilize the information in P-trees. Conceptually, a PC is a group of densely connected vertices, whose P-trees have the largest degree of overlap. This overlapping part is the largest common subtree shared by all the vertices. Fig. 2(a) illustrates two PC’s in the profiled graph of Fig. 1, namely {B , C , D} and {A, D, E}. In Fig. 2(b) and Fig. 2(c), the two PC’s, as well as their largest common subtrees are respectively shown. For example, in Fig. 2(c), vertices A, D, and E all possess the subtree with root r and leaf nodes “IS” and “DMS”. Notice that these three vertices also form a 2-core of D, and the common subtree among them is the largest. The common subtree sufficiently reflects the “theme” of the community. In the PC of Fig. 2(b), all the researchers involved share interest in machine learning and artificial intelligence, whereas for Fig. 2(c), the researchers are all interested in information systems and hardware studies. Personalization. PCS problem allows a query user to search communities that exhibits both structure cohesiveness and profiled cohesiveness. The parameter k controls the density of connection intensiveness. The profiled cohesiveness constrains the community to be semantically similar as much as possible. For instance, PCS methods can answer questions such as who are my close friends so that we have strong connection and common intresets and expertise? In contrast, existing CD methods [30–32] often use some global criteria (e.g., modularity) where the graph is partitioned a-priori with no reference to the particular query vertices. Thus existing CD methods are not suitable for personalized queries. Online search. Similar to other online CS approaches, our PCS method is able to find PC’s from a large-scale profiled graph effectively and efficiently. However, existing CD methods for graph query problems are generally slower. This is mainly because that they are designed for retrieving all the communities for an entire graph. Contributions. As we will explain, a simple solution to solve the PCS problem is extremely expensive. To improve the efficiency of finding PC’s (so that they can be used in online applications), we first introduce an anti-monotonicity property, which allows the candidates for a PC to be pruned efficiently. We further develop the CP-tree index, which systematically organizes the graph vertices and P-trees of a profiled graph. The CPtree index enables the development of two fast PC discovery algorithms. We experimentally evaluate our solutions on two real large profiled graphs and two synthetic profiled graphs. Our results show that PC’s are better representations of communities, and the CP-tree based algorithms are up to 4 order-of-magnitude faster than basic solution. Organization. In the literature, there are two kinds of work related to the retrieval of communities, namely community detection (CD) and community search (CS). Community detection (CD) aims to obtain all the communities from a given graph. Earlier works [16, 33] use link-based analysis to obtain these communities. However, they do not consider the textual information associated with graphs. Recent works focus on attributed graphs and use some advanced techniques such as clustering techniques to identify communities. Binary presence-absence datasets encode information on species occurrence over different sites. The datasets are essentially simple matrices of ones and zeros, but they form the basis for analyses of more complex phenomena, such as correlation between occurrences of taxa [1], nestedness [2, 3] or niches [4]. An essential part of quantitative analysis is assessing the statistical significance of the results. In the case of presence-absence data, the task of significance testing is often difficult due to the high-level structure of the data matrix, described by the row and column sums. Those sums indicate the number of ones in corresponding rows and columns, and are collectively referred to as margin sums. The distribution of margin sums can often be skewed, which causes problems for typical statistical tests. Currently ecological literature often suggests that margin sums should not explain interesting patterns, but instead be included in the null model [5–8]. Preserving margin sums retains differences of species richness over sites and occurrence frequencies among species [9]. The way in which null models should be constructed to preserve margin sums has been in the center of the debate since the null model approach was introduced by [10]. For a good overview of the debate, the reader is referred to [5, 8, 11]. The challenge of margin sum aware significance testing has lead to a wide collection of suggested null models [2, 3, 9, 12–16]. Null model tests for presence-absence data follow the idea of classical statistical randomization tests. Adapting from [9], the practical steps could be summarized as: If the original statistic is similar to the randomized counterparts, then the result is not considered significant. For significance testing that takes row and column sums into account, an obvious null model is to preserve the sums while randomly permuting the ones inside the matrix. This so-called fixed-fixed model (fixed row sums, fixed column sums, FF) is widely adopted in presence-absence studies. Random matrices that satisfy fixed-fixed constraints can be produced with a sequential swap procedure. The procedure starts with the original matrix and performs swaps of cell values to produce a new random matrix. Swaps operate on row and column pairs with a specific organization of values, shown in Fig 1. These row and column pairs are called checkerboard units or switch boxes [17, 18]. Denote values on a pair of rows and a pair of columns with a = M(i1, j1), b = M(i1, j2), c = M(i2, j1) and d = M(i2, j2). A pair of rows (i1, i2) and a pair of columns (j1, j2) contain a checkerboard unit if and only if a = d, b = c and a ≠ b. Ryser, among others, has shown that all matrices with identical margin sums can be produced with swap operations [19]. When the sequential swap procedure is implemented correctly, the consecutive matrices form a Markov Chain that has uniform stationary distribution [11, 20]. To summarize, the sequential swap procedure is a good way of sampling matrices at random from the uniform distribution of all matrices that have identical margin sums. It has been argued by several authors that limiting the randomization process to strictly same margin sums might not give realistic results [5, 21–23]. If only few perturbations are possible, then the significance test will compare against randomized matrices which are very similar to the original one and results of the test will be extremely conservative. The concern of insufficient perturbation is especially valid when the sequential swap procedure is applied to nested data. Definitions of nestedness vary in details, but all share the basic idea of all columns (and rows) having a superset-subset relationship [3, 24]. Every checkerboard unit is a breach of the subset-superset pattern: if a checkerboard unit exists for rows (i1, i2) of matrix M, there cannot be subset-superset relationship between M(i1,⋅) and M(i2,⋅), and this holds for columns also. If all rows (and columns) are perfectly nested in the sense of superset-subset relationships, then the matrix cannot contain any checkerboard units and it is not possible to permute it with swap operations. The fixed-fixed models are implemented with the sequential swap procedure, which produces random matrices with strictly same margin sums. Given row sums R and column sums C, the sequential swap procedure samples in random from the set of matrices MR,C. However, not much is known about the set matrices MR,C, such as the number of matrices in the set. As discussed, there are concerns that matrices in MR,C resemble the original matrix too much. Because the space of matrices MR,C is not well understood, it is possible that there are also other undesirable aspects related to it. To understand the implications of fixed-fixed margin sum constraints, the following example data matrix is considered. Matrix M has margin sums R = < 2, 1 >, C = < 1, 1, 1 >. It corresponds to a case where there are two species, the first of them being present most of the time and the second being absent most of the time. The three sites have one of the two species present. When asked to produce a random matrix that follows this basic pattern, one could argue that a probable outcome could be This matrix differs from M by two cells: the first species is present also on the second site and the second species is also absent on the second site. These two cells and especially the absence on second row could be considered as chance occurrences in the original matrix M [25]. In the fixed-fixed margin sum model, matrix M′ has probability zero, because margin sums of M and M′ differ. The three matrices that have strictly same margin sums all have both of the unlikely values, but in a different column. Preserving such a quirk of the original dataset would not necessarily be desirable. Row and column sum constraints are all linked together, creating situations that could be described as “lock-ins”. It is useful to consider alternative models that relax strict margin sum constraints and see how “lock-in free” models perform. The advantage of fixed-fixed model is its simplicity. If one needs to account for margin sums, then it is easy to justify a model that does not change them at all. The central question in designing a relaxed alternative model is: in what way constraints should be relaxed to not introduce any hidden biases? Here a useful tool is the information theoretic concept of maximum entropy principle. The principle states that the null model should maximize entropy within the given constraints [26]. Maximum entropy distribution could be described informally as the most random distribution. It is noteworthy that the uniform distribution produced by the sequential swap procedure is the maximum entropy distribution under fixed-fixed constraints, or in other words, the procedure is the statistically correct implementation for fixed-fixed constraints. The motivation is to find a model that replaces strict constraints with relaxed stochastic constraints that maintain the margin sums well enough. It is important not to use too relaxed constraints for the null model, as it leads to abundant false positives [9]. There are various models for stochastically margin sum constrained random matrices, most importantly the proportional-proportional models [6, 22]. They are not derived under the maximum entropy principle, making them ill-suited for current discussion of properties and for comparison with the fixed-fixed models. An alternative family of models with stochastic constraints for margin sums are the Rasch models, which were first widely used in psychometrics. To the author’s knowledge they have not been applied to ecological presence-absence data before. Rasch models preserve statistical expectations instead of exact values: they constrain expected margin sums in the null distribution to equal the margin sums in the original matrix. De Bie, among others, has demonstrated how expected margin sums can be formalized to obtain a convenient computational sampling method [26]. In a Rasch model, each cell of the matrix is initialized to value 0 and set to value 1 with probability defined by Eq (1). In Eq (1), pi, j is the probability for cell in row i and column j to get value 1. The parameters λj and μi are column and row specific parameters that are fitted to the original data matrix. For details on parameter fitting, see [26]. Is is easy to see that given λ and μ, cell specific probabilities are independent. Generating matrices is straightforward, as parameters need to be fitted only once and then cell values can be generated independently. Eq (1) is derived from the row and column sum constraints by using the maximum entropy principle. See, e.g., [26] for description of the steps needed to turn the constraint equations into Eq (1). All of the matrices that the sequential swap procedure produces have high probability under the Rasch model, as well. Fixed-fixed constraints can in some cases rule out matrices that are not so distinct from the other matrices that adhere to the constraints. Robust identification of thermal models for in-production High-Performance-Computing clusters with machine learning-based data selection Federico Pittino∗ , Roberto Diversi∗ , Luca Benini∗† , Andrea Bartolini∗ ∗ Department of Electrical, Electronic and Information Engineering (DEI), University of Bologna, Italy Abstract—Power and thermal management are critical components of High-Performance-Computing (HPC) systems, due to their high power density and large total power consumption. The assessment of thermal dissipation by means of compact models directly from the thermal response of the final device enables more robust and precise thermal control strategies as well as automated diagnosis. However, when dealing with large scale systems “in production”, the accuracy of learned thermal models depends on the dynamics of the power excitation, which depends also on the executed workload, and measurement nonidealities, such as quantization. In this paper we show that, using an advanced system identification algorithm, we are able to generate very accurate thermal models (average error lower than our sensors quantization step of 1◦ C) for a large scale HPC system on real workloads for very long time periods. However, we also show that: 1) not all real workloads allow for the identification of a good model; 2) starting from the theory of system identification it is very difficult to evaluate if a trace of data leads to a good estimated model. We then propose and validate a set of techniques based on machine learning and deep learning algorithms for the choice of data traces to be used for model identification. We also show that deep learning techniques are absolutely necessary to correctly choose such traces up to 96% of the times. I. I NTRODUCTION High performance computing (HPC) systems are designed to be at the cutting edge of computing capabilities. To achieve this goal, HPC installations are characterized by high computational power density and as a consequence, by high power density as well as large total power consumption. Indeed HPC systems have 2-4x higher rack power density w.r.t. server and industrial datacentre installations, with a per rack power envelope ranging between 20-100 kWatts [1]. High power density and envelope are obviously critical for HPC system management and operation. Today one of the most powerful supercomputers in Top500 is Sunway TaihuLight which consumes 15.3 MW for delivering 93 Petaflops. One of the previous first ones, Tianhe-2, consumes 17.8 MW for “only” 33.2 Petaflops. However, the power consumption increases to 24 MW when considering also the cooling infrastructure[2]. Such an amount of cooling power serves to prevent thermal issues. In fact, the performance of the processing elements is actively controlled by the internal firmware logic, which modulates chip voltage and frequency for maximizing the clock speed while satisfying power and thermal constraints. However these mechanisms are usually reactive, threshold-based and take significant safety margins: authors in [3] show that, for hot-water liquid cooled nodes, the processors are incapable of employing thermal throttling by using DVFS states to prevent the critical thermal threshold to be reached. To solve these issues, several works in the literature [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10] propose to take advantage of proactive thermal and power management strategies. These strategies all rely on the availability of compact predictive power and thermal models, capable of predicting future power consumption and temperature of the system and, even more importantly, to build a clear understanding on the sensitivity of these on workload parameters and hardware knobs that can be controlled at run time. Such models allow to estimate and model the power consumption of the entire CPUs and their cores based on workload characteristics extracted through performance counters and micro-architectural usage. Thanks to that, an optimizer can leverage these models to find the maximum clock frequency to apply based on the current usage of the micro-architecture while satisfying a global power budget or thermal constraints. Compact models can be used in combination with optimization and artificial intelligence techniques to select in a robust fashion the optimal operating points from the target power and temperature and the current conditions [4], [5], [6], [7], [8]. Moreover, such compact models can be used also for detecting anomalous changes in the behaviour of the system, for example due to a failure. However, the strategies for learning these models rely on design-time parameters that cannot cope with manufacturing variability, which makes each chip different from the others. Moreover, differences in deployment conditions and aging which can induce very significant differences in compact model parameters even for nominally identical nodes. In addition, such models have been applied only to single node systems operating in a test environment and therefore cannot easily be utilized at the scale of a full system in production without causing significant calibration costs of all its nodes (e.g. bringing the HPC machine off-line periodically for power and thermal characterization). In case an identified compact thermal model needs to be periodically updated during the lifetime of the system, additional challenges arise concerned with identifying models under production workloads, which cannot be calibrated to the needs of the model identification process. In fact, it is well known that the input signals may affect significantly the results of an identification experiment [11], [12]. The choice of a suitable input signal (when possible) has been extensively treated in the system identification literature [11], [12]. In many identification methods the input data are not available but the type of input excitation is assumed to be known [13], [14], [15]. When dealing with real workloads, as in our case, it is critical to evaluate if a given input (workload) will lead to a sufficiently accurate estimated model. However, even if [11], [12] suggest that persistently exciting of sufficiently high order as well as a low condition number is a requirement for high estimation accuracy, none of previous works have verified if these conditions are sufficient for discriminating real workload traces that lead to good or bad identified models. This paper aims at bridging the gap between the theoretical identification of thermal models and their application to real workloads on in-production large HPC clusters. The paper is organized as follows. Sec. II presents a review with the stateof-the-art and highlights the open problems. Sec. III describes the theoretical foundations of our system identification models. Sec. IV describes our deployment scenario, consisting of a large HPC cluster under real workloads, and presents the results of thermal identification on our data. Given the large amounts of available data (14 days of continuous operation), we divide it in time windows of 12 hours each, which also enables us to highlight the problem of selecting the right window of data for good model identification. Finally, Sec. V explores the problem of window selection and it shows that only by means of machine learning and deep learning algorithms an accurate selection can be performed. II. The simplest ones do not account for the multimodal nature of the thermal transient caused by the different building materials and their relative time-constants (i.e. die, heat-spreader and heatsink) [8]. In [16], [17], a first order dynamic thermal model is identified by solving a linear Least Squares (LS) optimization problem. Sharifi et al. Since it does not account directly for workload-to-power dependency, a Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) technique is used to rapidly detect changes in the statistical residual distribution (average, variance) and, then, to re-train the model, when it is no longer accurate. Juan et al. [19] uses a combination of a Kmeans clustering and an Auto-Regressive (AR) model to learn a compact model for fast thermal simulation. This approach is effective only when starting from a highly accurate thermal model of the HW. Moreover, the missing exogenous terms in both of the above approaches leads to neglecting the direct link between dissipated power and temperature. Then, the learning of a large number of different models is required to capture the characteristics of different functional units and program phases. Reda et al. [10] propose a method for estimating thermal models and power consumption only from the measurements of thermal sensors and total power consumption. Bartolini et al. [8] present a distributed model learning approach based on a set of Auto-Regressive eXogenous (ARX) models. However this approach has been applied only to simulated systems and it is based on the assumption that percore power traces and thermal sensor outputs are accurate and without noise. Beneventi et al. [20] present an Output Error system identification strategy that is robust to quantization noise on the input temperature measurements. Previous works have shown that the relation between the core temperature and the dissipated power can be described by a purely dynamic ARX model [22], [21]. ARX models are widely used in system identification since they constitute the simplest way of representing a dynamic process in the presence of uncertainties [12]. Nevertheless, it has been shown in [21] that the classic MISO ARX model is not able to describe properly the thermal dynamics of the system because the estimated models are characterized by relevant negative poles and/or complex conjugate poles. The advent of new generations of distributed systems has opened novel perspectives for logic programming (LP), a paradigm that has been widely adopted in various fields, including artificial intelligence, computer science, and engineering (Lloyd, 2003; Apt, 2003). On the one hand, service-oriented architectures (SOA) have become the standard approach for distributed systems engineering, enabling the creation of complex systems by composing loosely coupled services (Papazoglou, 2003; Erl, 2005). On the other hand, pervasive systems, which are characterized by their ability to seamlessly integrate into the environment and provide situated intelligence, mandate for novel approaches to programming and reasoning (Satyanarayanan, 2001; Kindberg, 2002). In this context, LP can play a crucial role in enabling pervasive systems to reason about their environment, make decisions, and adapt to changing conditions (Baral,2003; Fensel, 2003). Despite the potential of LP in pervasive systems, its adoption has been hindered by the lack of a suitable programming model that can accommodate the needs of distributed, dynamic, and heterogeneous environments (Gottlob, 2005; Heymans, 2008). Traditional LP systems, such as Prolog (Clocksin, 2003), are designed to run on a single machine and are not well-suited for distributed environments, where multiple nodes, each with its own LP engine, need to communicate and coordinate with each other (Calejo, 2005; Dahl, 2007). Moreover, the complexity of pervasive systems, which often involve multiple stakeholders, domains, and technologies, requires a programming model that can provide a high degree of flexibility, customizability, and interoperability (Blair, 2005; Singh, 2005). The gap between the potential of LP and its actual adoption in pervasive systems is largely due to the lack of a service-oriented approach to LP, which can provide a standardized interface for accessing and manipulating LP engines, regardless of their underlying implementation (Papazoglou,2003; O'Brien, 2004). Such an approach would enable the creation of LP-based services that can be easily composed, configured, and reused in different contexts, thereby facilitating the development of pervasive intelligent systems (Baida, 2004; Charfi, 2009). Furthermore, a service-oriented approach to LP would provide a means to address the issues of scalability, reliability, and maintainability, which are critical in pervasive systems (Schmidt, 2005; Wang, 2008). The research question that guides this paper is: how can LP be provided as a service, enabling the creation of pervasive intelligent systems that can reason, decide, and adapt in dynamic and heterogeneous environments? To address this question, we need to redefine the classical notions of LP in the context of service-oriented architectures and pervasive systems. This requires a deep understanding of the fundamental principles of LP, as well as the requirements and challenges of pervasive systems (Russell, 2003; Huhns, 2007). We also need to develop a novel programming model that can provide a standardized interface for accessing and manipulating LP engines, regardless of their underlying implementation (Lassila, 2005; Payne, 2007). The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the notion of Logic Programming as a Service (LPaaS), which provides a means to access and manipulate LP engines as a distributed service. This enables the creation of LP-based services that can be easily composed, configured, and reused in different contexts, thereby facilitating the development of pervasive intelligent systems. Second, we define the abstract architectural model of LPaaS, which re-interprets classical LP notions in the context of service-oriented architectures and pervasive systems. This model provides a foundation for understanding the fundamental principles of LPaaS and for developing LP-based services that can be used in a variety of applications. Third, we elaborate on the nature of LP interpreted as a service by describing the basic LPaaS interface, which provides a standardized means for accessing and manipulating LP engines. This interface enables the creation of LP-based services that can be easily integrated into pervasive systems, thereby providing a means to address the issues of scalability, reliability, and maintainability. The concept of LPaaS is based on the idea of providing LP engines as a service, which can be accessed and manipulated through a standardized interface. This interface provides a means to create, configure, and execute LP engines, as well as to manage their lifecycle and interactions. The LPaaS interface is designed to be flexible and customizable, enabling the creation of LP-based services that can be tailored to specific applications and domains. Furthermore, the LPaaS interface is designed to be interoperable, enabling the integration of LP engines with other services and systems, regardless of their underlying implementation. The LPaaS concept is formalized using the following equation: LPaaS = (LPEngines, Interface, Lifecycle), where LPEngines represents the set of LP engines provided as a service, Interface represents the standardized interface for accessing and manipulating LP engines, and Lifecycle represents the management of LP engine creation, configuration, execution, and termination. In conclusion, the introduction of LPaaS as a means to provide LP as a service enables the creation of pervasive intelligent systems that can reason, decide, and adapt in dynamic and heterogeneous environments. The LPaaS concept provides a novel programming model that can accommodate the needs of distributed, dynamic, and heterogeneous environments, and enables the creation of LP-based services that can be easily composed, configured, and reused in different contexts. The rest of this paper will elaborate on the LPaaS concept, providing a detailed description of its abstract architectural model, interface, and implementation. The development of the Logic Programming as a Service (LPaaS) framework required a multi-faceted approach, involving the definition of the abstract architectural model, the design of the LPaaS interface, and the implementation of a prototype based on distributed tuProlog engines. In this section, we describe the data, design, procedures, and statistical analysis used to develop and evaluate the LPaaS framework. First, we defined the abstract architectural model of LPaaS by re-interpreting classical LP notions in the context of service-oriented architectures (SOAs) (Baresi et al., 2006). This involved identifying the key components of LP, such as logic engines, knowledge bases, and inference mechanisms, and mapping them onto the corresponding elements of SOAs, including services, interfaces, and protocols (Papazoglou, 2003). We also considered the requirements of pervasive intelligent systems, including situated intelligence, context-awareness, and adaptability (Rouvoy et al., 2009), and designed the LPaaS architecture to accommodate these needs. The LPaaS interface was designed to provide a standardized means of accessing and manipulating logic programs, as well as interacting with the underlying knowledge base (Lloyd, 2003). The interface consists of a set of APIs and protocols that enable clients to submit queries, update the knowledge base, and retrieve results (W3C, 2014). We defined a set of basic operations, including query, assert, retract, and update, which can be combined to support more complex interactions (Kowalski, 1979). The LPaaS interface is designed to be extensible, allowing developers to add custom operations and protocols as needed. To implement the LPaaS framework, we used a distributed tuProlog engine, which provides a robust and efficient means of executing logic programs (Denti et al., 2001). The tuProlog engine is designed to support multiple knowledge bases and inference mechanisms, making it an ideal choice for LPaaS. We developed a set of libraries and tools to support the deployment and management of LPaaS services, including a service registry, a discovery mechanism, and a set of APIs for client-server interaction (Richardson & Ruby, 2007). One of the key challenges in implementing LPaaS was ensuring interoperability between different logic engines and knowledge bases. To address this issue, we developed a set of adapters and wrappers that enable LPaaS to interact with different logic engines and knowledge bases (Gottlob et al., 2010). We also implemented a set of configuration mechanisms that allow developers to customize the behavior of LPaaS services, including the selection of inference mechanisms, the management of knowledge bases, and the optimization of query execution (Lloyd, 2003). The LPaaS framework was evaluated using a combination of theoretical and empirical methods. We used formal methods, such as model checking and theorem proving, to verify the correctness and consistency of the LPaaS architecture and interface (Clarke et al., 2000). We also conducted a series of experiments to evaluate the performance and scalability of LPaaS, using a range of benchmarks and test cases (Gray, 1993). The results of these experiments are presented in the next section. In terms of statistical analysis, we used a range of metrics to evaluate the performance of LPaaS, including response time, throughput, and accuracy (Jain, 1991). We also used statistical techniques, such as regression analysis and hypothesis testing, to analyze the results of the experiments and identify trends and patterns (Kutner et al., 2005). The results of the statistical analysis are presented in the next section, along with a discussion of the implications and limitations of the study. Overall, the development of the LPaaS framework required a comprehensive and multi-faceted approach, involving the definition of the abstract architectural model, the design of the LPaaS interface, and the implementation of a prototype based on distributed tuProlog engines. The evaluation of LPaaS using theoretical and empirical methods provides a thorough understanding of the framework's performance, scalability, and limitations, and highlights its potential for supporting pervasive intelligent systems. The experimental evaluation of the LPaaS architecture was conducted by implementing a distributed tuProlog engine, which was tested on a cluster of 10 nodes with a total of 40 CPU cores. The goal of the experiments was to assess the performance and scalability of the LPaaS system, as well as its ability to support situated intelligence in pervasive systems (Ciobanu and De Vauaux, in press). Despite decades of diversity initiatives, legal mandates, and growing public commitment to equal opportunity, the top of the organizational pyramid remains strikingly homogeneous. Women, racial and ethnic minorities, and other nondominant group members enter many professions in substantial numbers, yet their representation declines at each successive step of the career ladder (Ely & Meyerson, 2000; Kanter, 1977; Stainback & Tomaskovic-Devey, 2012). This pattern is especially visible in what I call upward mobility career systems: organizations and professions, such as universities, law firms, corporations, and research institutes, in which careers unfold as a sequence of evaluations and promotions that progressively narrow the pool of candidates. In academia, for example, women earn roughly half of doctoral degrees in many fields but remain a minority among full professors and in senior leadership (Ceci et al., 2014; European Commission, 2021). The "leaky pipeline" metaphor captures the attrition but obscures its cause, because it suggests passive loss rather than the outcome of repeated decisions made by identifiable people at identifiable points in the system. The persistence of this pattern is puzzling given that these systems typically understand themselves as meritocracies. Castilla and Benard (2010) described a paradox of meritocracy: organizations that explicitly emphasize meritocratic values can show greater bias in rewards favoring dominant group members, because the belief in one's own objectivity licenses decision makers to relax vigilance. Individuals who see themselves as fair are less likely to monitor their own behavior and are more susceptible to moral licensing (Monin & Miller, 2001; Uhlmann & Cohen, 2007). Because merit is rarely defined in a way that is independent of who displays it, evaluation criteria are readily constructed or reweighted to fit favored candidates (Uhlmann & Cohen, 2005). Decades of experimental and field research show that stereotypes shape the evaluation of competence, the attribution of success, and the interpretation of ambiguous performance information (Heilman, 2012; Moss-Racusin et al., 2012; Eaton et al., 2020). Evaluation is especially vulnerable when criteria are ambiguous, accountability is low, and time is short, conditions that characterize the upper levels of most hierarchies (Bielby & Baron, 1986; Reskin, 2000). Within this logic, gatekeepers occupy a pivotal position. By gatekeepers I mean those who control access to valued resources and positions: members of search and promotion committees, senior managers, department chairs, board members, and the panels that allocate grants, awards, and appointments. They are frequently themselves members of the dominant group, having been successful under existing rules, and they are therefore prone to reproduce homophilous patterns of selection (Kanter, 1977; Ibarra, 1992; Rivera, 2012). Yet the great majority of diversity interventions are directed elsewhere. Typical programs aim to fix the nondominant group member, through mentoring, networking, or leadership training, or to change attitudes broadly through diversity training for all employees. Reviews of the evidence show that such approaches have modest and often short-lived effects, and that mandatory training can even provoke resistance (Dobbin & Kalev, 2016; Kalev et al., 2006; Paluck et al., 2021; Bezrukova et al., 2016). Programs that target the people and procedures at decision points, by contrast, have been far less studied, although the available evidence suggests that structural arrangements such as accountability, transparency, and task forces responsible for diversity outcomes are more effective than training alone (Kalev et al., 2006; Castilla, 2015). Two further limitations characterize the literature. First, much of the evidence on bias comes from laboratory or vignette experiments in which individual evaluators judge hypothetical targets. These studies are invaluable for demonstrating mechanisms, but they say little about how bias operates in the collective, repeated, and politically embedded decision processes of real organizations, or about how to change those processes (Bohnet, 2016; Paluck & Green, 2009). Second, systemic approaches, which view inequality as an emergent property of interacting parts of an organization rather than as a collection of individual prejudices, have been advocated for some time (Cox, 1991; Ely & Meyerson, 2000; Nkomo & Hoobler, 2014; Bendl & Schmidt, 2010), yet they are rarely translated into concrete guidance for practitioners. Change agents, including diversity officers and consultants, are consequently left with broad principles ("change the culture," "address structural barriers") but few specifications of what an intervention should contain and why it should work. At the same time, the empirical base for "what works" in systemic interventions is thin, and rigorous evaluations in naturally occurring organizational settings remain scarce (Bezrukova et al., 2016; Paluck et al., 2021). This article addresses these gaps by asking: What design specifications should systemic diversity interventions meet if they are to engage gatekeepers, improve the quality of decision making, and mitigate bias in upward mobility career systems? I use the term design specifications in the sense of design science (Van Aken, 2004; Romme, 2003): general, evidence-informed prescriptions that state the properties an intervention should have to produce a desired outcome in a class of contexts, while leaving room for local adaptation. Such specifications sit between abstract theory and detailed procedural recipes. They are intended to travel across settings, so that practitioners can build interventions suited to their own organizations rather than adopting packaged programs whose active ingredients are unknown. I derive the specifications in two steps. First, I draw on research on the paradox of meritocracy, bias in evaluation, and group decision processes to identify the mechanisms through which gatekeepers reproduce inequality and the leverage points at which they might be disrupted. Second, I ground the specifications in the limited empirical evidence on systemic interventions, examining three illustrative examples from academic settings, a bias literacy program (Carnes et al., 2015; Sekaquaptewa et al., 2019), participatory modeling of organizational dynamics (Vennix, 1996; Van den Belt, 2004), and participant observation of decision making in committees. Universities offer a particularly informative context because their career systems are archetypal examples of upward mobility, their gatekeeping processes are formalized and visible, and their commitment to meritocratic ideals is especially strong. The contribution is threefold. First, I extend the diversity literature by shifting the unit of intervention from the disadvantaged individual or the undifferentiated workforce to the gatekeepers and the decision processes they enact, thereby linking research on bias to organizational change. Second, I offer a set of design specifications that consolidate scattered evidence into usable guidance, clarifying which features of interventions, such as engagement rather than compulsion, self-generated insight, and attention to the decision process, are likely to matter. Third, I pair each specification with a concrete example of a successful intervention, providing inspiration for diversity officers and consultants and a basis for future evaluation research. Together, these contributions aim to make systemic change in the composition of the top of the career pyramid a more tractable and more evidence-based endeavor. Research Approach and Design Logic This paper follows a design science approach (van Aken, 2004; Romme, 2003), which seeks prescriptive knowledge in the form of design specifications: general statements of the form "to achieve outcome Y in context C, use intervention feature X, because mechanism M." Design specifications differ from descriptive hypotheses in that they are judged by their utility and by the plausibility of their underlying mechanisms, not by statistical significance alone. Because rigorous evaluations of systemic diversity interventions are scarce (Bezrukova et al., 2016; Paluck et al., 2021), I combined three sources of input in an iterative, abductive process (Dubois & Gadde, 2002). The first was a theoretical analysis of the paradox of meritocracy (Castilla & Benard, 2010) in upward mobility career systems. The second was a purposive review of intervention evidence. The third was a formal sketch of how bias in gatekeeping decisions accumulates across a career pyramid. The specifications were refined by moving back and forth among these sources until each specification was tied to an identified mechanism, to at least one empirical example, and to a plausible implementation route. Scope and Definitions Upward mobility career systems are organizations in which individuals progress through hierarchical stages, with advancement decided by gatekeepers (e.g., committee members, supervisors, reviewers, and panel chairs) who evaluate candidates against criteria of merit. Academia, professional service firms, and large public bureaucracies are canonical examples. I define a systemic diversity intervention as one that targets the decision-making processes, structures, or routines through which advancement occurs, rather than only the attitudes or skills of individuals from nondominant groups (Dobbin & Kalev, 2016; Nielsen, 2017). Nondominant group members are those whose social category (e.g., gender, race/ethnicity) is underrepresented at higher organizational levels and who are subject to negative stereotyping or reduced status in the evaluative context (Ridgeway, 2011). Identification and Selection of Intervention Evidence I searched Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar for English-language publications from 2000 to 2022. Search strings combined terms for the intervention level (systemic, institutional, structural, organizational change, intervention, training, program), the target (gatekeeper, selection committee, evaluator, decision maker, hiring, promotion, tenure), the topic (diversity, gender equality, bias, inclusion), and the setting (academia, university, higher education, science). I supplemented the database search with backward and forward citation tracking from key works (e.g., Bohnet et al., 2016; Carnes et al., 2015; Moss-Racusin et al., 2012; Nielsen, 2017; van den Brink & Benschop, 2012), and with reports from funded programs such as the U.S. National Science Foundation ADVANCE initiative (Laursen & Austin, 2020) and the European structural change projects. Studies were included if they (a) described an intervention aimed at influencing how gatekeepers evaluate, select, or promote candidates, or at altering the structures or routines within which they do so; (b) occurred in a career system with hierarchical progression; and (c) reported some form of outcome evidence, ranging from experimental or quasi-experimental data to qualitative accounts of change. I excluded interventions aimed solely at individual development of nondominant group members (e.g., mentoring or networking programs without gatekeeper involvement) and one-off awareness sessions without follow-up. Initial screening of titles and abstracts yielded a small candidate pool, and full-text review reduced this to the interventions that met all criteria. Given the narrow evidence base, I did not attempt an exhaustive systematic review. I used purposive, criterion-based selection (Patton, 2015) to identify exemplary cases that maximized variation in the mechanism of change. Three interventions in academic settings were chosen because each engages gatekeepers through a different route. The first was a bias literacy program, in which gatekeepers learn about the cognitive and social processes that produce biased evaluations and practice strategies to counter them (Carnes et al., 2015; Devine et al., 2012; Sekaquaptewa et al., 2019). The second was participatory modeling, in which gatekeepers and other stakeholders jointly construct a formal or semiformal model of the career system to see how local decisions aggregate into pyramid-level representation (Vennix, 1996; Voinov et al., 2018). The third was participant observation, in which a researcher-practitioner observes actual decision meetings and feeds back to gatekeepers the discursive and procedural patterns that shape evaluations (van den Brink et al., 2010; van den Brink & Benschop, 2012). Data Extraction and Analysis For each intervention I extracted the target group of gatekeepers, the core activities, the theory of change, the implementation conditions, the outcome measures, and the reported effects and limitations. I then coded the material using a mechanism-oriented template adapted from realist evaluation (Pawson & Tilley, 1997), asking what it was about the intervention that produced change, for whom, and under what conditions. Coding proceeded in three passes. First, I coded open descriptive categories (e.g., "accountability," "criteria clarification," "making bias visible," "ownership of the problem"). Second, I clustered these into higher-order mechanisms drawing on the literatures on stereotyping and shifting standards (Biernat, 2012), accountability in judgment (Lerner & Tetlock, 1999), and structured decision making (Kahneman et al., 2021; Bohnet, 2016). Third, I translated each cluster into a design specification and checked it against disconfirming cases to identify boundary conditions. Specifications were retained when they were supported by at least two independent sources, or by one empirical source and a well-established theoretical mechanism, and were flagged as provisional otherwise.
