Universities are increasingly expected to act as engines of innovation and economic renewal, as well as centres of teaching and scholarship. The "entrepreneurial university" thesis holds that the academy has undergone a second academic revolution in which the capitalisation of knowledge has become an institutional mission alongside research and teaching (Etzkowitz, 2003; Etzkowitz et al., 2000). Related accounts of "academic capitalism" describe how declining public funding and rising competition have pushed institutions and individual scholars toward market-like behaviours in pursuit of resources (Slaughter & Leslie, 1997). Much of the resulting literature concerns the commercialisation of research through patenting, licensing and spin-off formation (Shane, 2004; Perkmann et al., 2013). Far less attention has been paid to a more basic question: to what extent are academics themselves entrepreneurial in disposition, and does that disposition help them to produce more research? This question matters because research productivity is central to the careers of individual academics and to the competitiveness of universities and national systems. Productivity is associated with a range of individual and organisational factors, including gender, career stage, collaboration networks, institutional resources and workload (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005; Hesli & Lee, 2011). Dispositional and behavioural characteristics of the researcher have received comparatively little systematic attention. In the broader management literature, entrepreneurial orientation (EO) is a well-established construct for capturing the strategic posture of an actor through innovativeness, proactiveness and risk-taking (Miller, 1983; Covin & Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Meta-analytic evidence shows a positive association between EO and performance in firms (Rauch et al., 2009), and the construct has been extended to the individual level, where it describes a person's propensity to pursue opportunities, act ahead of events and tolerate uncertainty (Bolton & Lane, 2012). Whether it also explains variation in scholarly output among academics remains largely untested. There are reasons to expect both a positive relationship and a more equivocal one. On the one hand, academic research involves opportunity identification, resource mobilisation and the acceptance of uncertain returns, all of which are characteristic of entrepreneurial behaviour. Academics who proactively seek out funding, collaborators and publication outlets, and who accept the risk of rejection or failure, may accumulate more output over time. On the other hand, some schools of thought in the philosophy and sociology of science suggest that research is conducted within "paradigms," or circumscribed areas of study with shared assumptions, methods and problem sets (Kuhn, 1962). Within such boundaries, much "normal science" consists of incremental puzzle-solving, and journals and peer reviewers may reward conformity as much as novelty (Azoulay et al., 2011). If so, the innovativeness dimension of EO may not be a reliable predictor of productivity, and some research may not be inherently innovative at all. Whether the dimensions of EO matter equally, or whether only some translate into output, is therefore an empirical question that existing theory does not settle. A second and related gap concerns the adoption of novel technological methods in the research process. Digital platforms have created new ways of financing and conducting inquiry. Crowdfunding allows researchers to solicit small contributions from large numbers of backers (Mollick, 2014; Belleflamme et al., 2014), while crowdsourced R&D and open innovation approaches allow problems to be distributed to external solvers (Lakhani et al., 2013; Afuah & Tucci, 2012). These approaches may be especially relevant where traditional funding is scarce. Yet little is known about how willing academics are to adopt them, or whether a technological propensity of this kind is associated with higher output. Treating such a propensity as a distinct but complementary construct to EO allows us to separate a general entrepreneurial posture from the specific readiness to use new tools for resourcing and conducting research. These issues are especially pertinent in developing-country contexts. South African universities operate under considerable resource constraints, including limited public funding relative to enrolment growth, heavy teaching loads and a need to redress historical inequities, while simultaneously facing strong performance incentives. The national research subsidy system rewards accredited publication output, and institutions in turn pressure staff to publish (Cloete et al., 2015). In this environment, academics who can mobilise alternative resources and act proactively may have a distinct advantage. Conversely, if unconventional financing and research methods are underutilised, this may signal untapped opportunities for a sector that cannot rely on increases in conventional funding. Research from such settings is also valuable because the entrepreneurship and higher education literatures have been dominated by evidence from advanced economies with very different funding and incentive structures. Against this background, this study addresses two research questions. First, to what extent are academics entrepreneurial, and is a higher self-reported level of EO, and of each of its constituent dimensions, associated with higher research productivity? Second, is a greater propensity to apply novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, associated with higher productivity, and how prevalent is the use of such methods? To answer these questions, we conducted a survey of academics at a large South African university using a comprehensive purposive sampling process, which yielded 292 usable responses. We estimated the relationships using ordinary least squares regression and assessed the robustness of the findings with bootstrapped standard errors and negative binomial regression, which is appropriate for the count-based and over-dispersed nature of publication output (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013). The study makes three contributions. First, it extends entrepreneurship theory to a setting in which it has seldom been applied, demonstrating that EO, a construct developed to explain firm behaviour, can be meaningfully measured among individual scholars and linked to a core academic outcome. In doing so, it responds to calls for closer synthesis between educational and entrepreneurship theory and for greater attention to the micro-foundations of the entrepreneurial university (Fini et al., 2018). Second, by disaggregating EO into its dimensions, the study contributes to the debate on whether innovativeness, in particular, is rewarded in paradigm-bound academic work. Our findings suggest that, although individuals with higher endowments of EO may be more productive, innovativeness is not significantly related to productivity, which complicates simple narratives that equate scholarly success with novelty. Third, the study provides some of the first evidence on the technological propensity of academics to use crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, indicating that these methods may be underutilised. For university leaders and policymakers in resource-constrained systems, this has practical implications for the design of research support, training and incentive structures. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. We first develop the theoretical background and hypotheses, then describe the data, measures and estimation strategy. We then present the results and robustness tests, and conclude by discussing the implications, limitations and directions for future research. Research design and sampling The study employed a cross-sectional, quantitative survey design, appropriate for estimating associations between individual-level dispositions and self-reported performance outcomes in a defined population (Creswell & Creswell, 2018). Data were collected from academic staff at a large, research-intensive public university in South Africa. This setting is analytically useful because it combines formal research-output incentives, through the national Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET) subsidy system, with the resource constraints typical of developing-country higher education. A comprehensive purposive sampling procedure was applied. The sampling frame comprised all permanent and fixed-term academics, from lecturer to full professor, who were affiliated with a faculty or school and held a formal research mandate. Staff in purely administrative, support or short-term teaching-only contracts were excluded, as were postdoctoral fellows, whose research mandates differ structurally. Purposive selection was preferred to probability sampling because the construct of interest, research productivity, is meaningful only for individuals with an opportunity to conduct research (Etikan et al., 2016). Within this boundary, an effort was made to include every eligible academic across all faculties to maximise disciplinary variation. After deduplication and verification against the institutional staff directory, 1,214 eligible individuals were identified. Each was invited by personalised e-mail to complete an online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform. Two reminders were sent at ten-day intervals. A total of 317 questionnaires were returned. Twenty-five were excluded because of substantial missing data (more than 20% of items) or straight-lining, leaving 292 usable responses (an effective response rate of 24.1%). This rate is comparable to those reported in other surveys of academic staff (Baruch & Holtom, 2008). To assess non-response bias, early respondents (first quartile) were compared with late respondents (last quartile) on all focal variables, following Armstrong and Overton (1977). No significant differences were found (all p > 0.10). The sample was also compared with institutional staff records for rank and faculty, and the distributions did not differ materially. A sensitivity analysis showed that a sample of 292 gave over 0.95 power to detect a medium effect (f² = 0.15) in a regression with up to 15 predictors at α = 0.05 (Cohen, 1988). It also exceeded the minimum of 50 + 8k observations suggested by Green (1991). Measures Dependent variable. Academic research productivity was measured as the number of DHET-accredited research output units that respondents reported for the preceding three calendar years. These units include articles in accredited journals, books, book chapters and peer-reviewed conference proceedings, and are fractionalised by authorship share. A three-year window was used to smooth annual volatility in publication outcomes (Abramo et al., 2011). Self-reports were verified, where respondents consented, against the institutional research-office repository for a random subsample of 40 respondents. The correlation between the two sources was high (r = 0.93). Entrepreneurial orientation. EO was measured using the nine-item scale of Covin and Slevin (1989), adapted from the firm level to the individual-academic level in line with Bolton and Lane (2012). The scale operationalises the three classical dimensions identified by Miller (1983): innovativeness, proactiveness and risk-taking. Respondents indicated agreement on a seven-point Likert scale. Example items were rewritten to reflect research behaviour, for example "I favour novel research questions over well-established lines of enquiry" (innovativeness) and "I typically initiate research collaborations rather than respond to others" (proactiveness). Dimension scores were computed as item means, and an overall EO score was computed as the mean of all items (Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Technological propensity. The propensity to apply novel technological methods was measured using a five-item scale developed for this study, informed by technology-readiness research (Parasuraman, 2000) and the literature on open and crowdsourced innovation (Howe, 2006; Mollick, 2014). Items captured the extent to which respondents had used, or would consider using, crowdfunding to finance research, crowdsourced R&D or citizen-science data collection, online collaborative platforms, and open-data repositories. Responses were captured on a seven-point scale. Exploratory factor analysis (principal axis factoring, oblique rotation) of the items indicated a single factor (Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin = 0.81; Bartlett's test χ² significant at p < 0.001), with an eigenvalue of 3.04 explaining 60.8% of the variance. Two items on crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D specifically were also analysed separately because of their theoretical salience. Control variables. Controls were selected for their established associations with research output (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005). They comprised age (years), gender (female = 1), academic rank (ordinal, 1 to 5), possession of a doctorate (yes = 1), years in academia, average weekly teaching hours, receipt of external research funding in the review period (yes = 1), and broad disciplinary cluster (natural sciences and engineering, health sciences, humanities and social sciences, and economic and management sciences), which was dummy-coded. Reliability, validity and common-method bias Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha (Cronbach, 1951) and composite reliability. All scales exceeded the conventional threshold of 0.70 (Nunnally, 1978): overall EO α = 0.84, innovativeness α = 0.77, proactiveness α = 0.79, risk-taking α = 0.73 and technological propensity α = 0.86. Convergent validity was supported by average variance extracted values above 0.50 for all constructs, and discriminant validity was established using the Fornell and Larcker (1981) criterion. Because the independent and dependent variables were self-reported by a single source, common-method bias was evaluated following Podsakoff et al. (2003). In 1782, Jan Ingen-Housz, in Vienna, sent a hastily written paper to the President of the Royal Society of London, Joseph Banks, ‘trust[ing] upon your friendly sentiments for me, that you will get it re[a]d’ at a meeting.1 Seventy-five years later, James David Forbes, in Edinburgh, described himself as waiting in ‘inuendo and suspense’ to learn what had really been argued at a recent meeting of the Society.2 In both cases, men of science from distant cities were avidly interested in the meetings of the Royal Society: Ingen-Housz wanted his research read at the meeting, and Forbes wished to know in detail what had happened. Their interest is a clear indication of the important role of the meetings of the Society to eighteenth- and nineteenth-century science. We suggest that this is an opportune moment to reconsider the functions of learned society meetings. Scholars of scientific societies, correspondence networks, salons and conversazioni have shown how, at various times, these were all valuable means of communicating natural knowledge among scholars and other audiences.3 We are interested, here, in the interplay between meetings and publication; and, particularly, in the role of society meetings during a period in which journals were an established but not yet dominant form of academic communication.4 At the Royal Society, and organizations like it, research was ‘made public’ long before actually being ‘published’ in print in the Society's transactions or memoirs. Mario Biagioli has examined this space between ‘making public’ and ‘publication’ from the perspective of priority and ownership, leading him to refer to it as a ‘phase of heightened vulnerability’ for authors.5 But the implications are broader-ranging than this suggests. First, the meetings opened up a range of possibilities for the public and quasi-public discussion, dissemination and refinement of natural knowledge long before the printed Transactions appeared. Second, any analysis of the selection and editorial processes of scientific knowledge needs to start with those who were involved in organizing the meetings, not editors and referees. Processes of discussion and comment began prior to publication, inside and outside the Society, running parallel to and sometimes feeding into the process of publication. Third, the relationship between meetings and publications was not static: over time learned societies changed their procedures, and the book trade (and thus the context and competition) changed around them. In this article, we focus on the Royal Society between 1752 and 1892. Printed journals were part of a complex ecosystem of ways of making research public, and enabling subsequent discussion, conversation, comment and revision. 1752 marks the Royal Society's assumption of management of the Philosophical Transactions, and the official requirement that all research communicated to the Society be presented first at a meeting, and only later considered for publication in the Transactions.6 Despite increasing internal pressure to reform and external pressure from new and competing modes of scientific print, Society meetings retained their primacy throughout this period. In 1892, however, a new set of standing orders formally acknowledged that, due to the press of papers submitted and the limited time available in meetings, papers could be considered for publication even if all that was read of them in the meetings was the title.7 Our aim is not simply to point out that learned society meetings have been significant means of communicating scientific knowledge. Rather, we investigate how such meetings functioned, and how they related to print publication, in an age when the variety of forms of print publication was increasing, and certain forms of print were becoming essential to scholarly reputation-building. We will start by explaining how the relationship between the Royal Society's meetings and publications changed over the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. We next discuss two case studies: Jan Ingen-Housz's experiences in the 1780s illustrate how meetings were organized and papers shaped by the power of the Society's officers, and demonstrate the importance of personal influence and connections; while James David Forbes's frustration in the 1850s, as he waited for details of John Tyndall's paper on glaciers, enables us to illustrate the range of public and quasi-public discussion that arose after the meeting and before publication.8 We will then consider the challenges created by this mixed ecosystem of meetings and publications, and the ongoing usefulness of Royal Society meetings despite growing competition from new forms of print. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of these historical perspectives for current discussions of the ‘ends’ of the scientific journal. The weekly London meeting had been the irreducible element of the Society's activity since its foundation in 1660. As conceived by the founding Charters and Statutes, meetings were intended as sites of natural-philosophical experiment and discussion.9 This twin emphasis, and the experiments shown at meetings in the 1660s and 1670s by Robert Hooke, Christopher Wren, Robert Boyle and Denis Papin, among others, are well known.10 The gleanings of natural-philosophical news, letters, books and discoveries from beyond London, which made up much of the early Philosophical Transactions, represented a secondary activity in the eyes of the Society, as one of us has argued elsewhere.11 By the early 1750s the situation had changed. Experiment had disappeared from meetings altogether, and discussion had waned. Meetings were given over instead to the reading of ‘papers’—research communiqués authored by Fellows and non-Fellows of the Society. A selection of these would be published by the editor of Transactions (by custom the Society's Secretary, but operating outside its oversight). The tenuous seventeenth-century link between what was published in Transactions and what went on in Society meetings became much stronger during the first half of the eighteenth century, and the official takeover of the periodical by the Society in 1752 made the relationship absolute.12 Editorial control was transferred from a succession of single individuals to a Committee of Papers: a reorganization that was intended to shield the Society, collectively and individually, from the imputation of negligence, nepotism or malpractice, but which also had the effect of marking each paper published with an institutional stamp of approval. From 1832, one or more Fellows was also asked to report in writing on papers being considered for publication in Transactions; but the Committee of Papers remained the ultimate decision-making body. Transactions usually appeared in biannual parts, so that most individual papers appeared in print many months after they had first been communicated. In this arrangement, every paper read to the Society was to be considered for publication; equally, no paper was to be considered for publication without being read to the Society. Only Fellows could communicate research to a meeting, though they could do so on behalf of others. This was the most obvious form of gatekeeping, which clearly favoured those with personal connections to the Fellowship: friendship and family connection were established routes for getting the attention of the President or Secretary, and thus bringing a paper to the attention of the Society. Even after the sheer volume of incoming papers enforced changes to the standing orders in the 1890s, the rule about communicators remained in force. The Society's claim to print the materials communicated to its meetings was an expression of ownership, and is discernible at many levels, from the Society's record-keeping practices to its public relations. Tracing its ramifications reveals both the complexities of particular cases and broad changes in the commercial, social, professional and organizational contexts of British science as well as the Society's own practices and priorities. There were, for example, several instances in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries when the Society was dismayed to learn of papers approved for publication in Transactions finding their way into print in other venues, including London newspapers and the new commercial scientific journals.13 The greater uptake and circulation of ‘separate copies’—later known as offprints—by authors had increased the danger of a Transactions paper being anticipated in print. By the nineteenth century, their circulation through an author's correspondence networks had become a thoroughly established aspect of the ways in which new scientific research spread; but the Society printed a warning on the cover asking recipients to do their best to ‘prevent them from being reprinted till one Month after the publication’ of Transactions itself.14 This was all the more necessary because of a fundamental change in the landscape of scientific print: the multiplication of increasingly reputable sites for the publication of scientific work. As well as commercial monthly magazines devoted to the sciences, there were the publications of the new learned societies and a variety of daily, weekly and monthly periodicals that sometimes reported scientific news.15 Some of these sites offered alternative routes to publication that did not entail the built-in delay between communication and publication associated with Transactions; and others provided routes for some of the content of Society meetings to circulate before publication of Transactions. One way to obviate the threat of being scooped in this way was for the Society to create its own, more rapidly appearing source of news. From 1831 it began publishing abstracts of all papers read at recent meetings, effectively redoubling the link between meetings and papers.16 Known as Proceedings, this periodical marks the Society's acceptance that there was a need for information about what went on in the Society to circulate before (and beyond) Transactions. The Society's publication of meeting reports helped drive another important change in the meetings–papers relationship. As we will see, the selection and ordering of material for meetings was not subject to collective control or Society oversight, but was left to the judgement of the President and Secretaries. This important power was widely understood and potentially manipulable, and Society officers were accused of abusing it at different times throughout the period in view. Once it became the case that having a paper accepted for reading at a meeting virtually guaranteed publication, even if only in brief form in Proceedings, there was correspondingly more at stake in the initial screening process, from both the author's and the institution's point of view. New standing orders of 1892 publicly articulated for the first time the criteria that would be used for choosing papers for meetings (papers which ‘the author is prepared to illustrate by experiments, diagrams &c., or which is likely to give rise to discussion’); but in doing so, the Society, also for the first time, relaxed the condition that tied publication to meetings.17 Henceforth a subset of papers accepted for publication would be read at a meeting, rather than a subset of the papers read at the meeting being published. It was, we suggest, a critical symbolic moment, representing a tacit acknowledgement of the subordination of meetings and the primacy of print publication. Royal Society meetings in the 1780s were regimented affairs—in contrast to the noisy, slovenly chaos described by John Hill in one of his series of satires on the Society from the early 1750s. Hill's writings are frequently supposed to have helped spur the Society to assume formal editorial control of Transactions.18 The orderly conduct of meetings in the latter part of the eighteenth century is often ascribed to the personal style of Joseph Banks (President from 1778 to 1820).19 One of Banks's early initiatives as President was to move Society meetings to later in the evening—to 6 p.m. from 8 p.m.—and to limit them to an hour's duration.20 Among other things, this permitted members of the Royal Society Club, and their guests, to dine together ahead of the meeting.21 The slightly pressurized running of Society meetings under Banks was therefore partly a function of the limited time available in the meetings themselves, coupled with the fact that the Society only met between the beginning of November and the end of June (so that a paper communicated towards the end of June might have to wait until the following November to be read aloud). The officers had to make choices about which papers to prioritize, how much time to spend on any given communication, and how much of it to read out. Some papers were split between meetings, and others read in abstract rather than in full.22 This power of sequencing, cutting and

The PubMed database contains the most comprehensive listing of articles in the life sciences. At the time of our writing, PubMed contained more than 25 million articles; because each of these articles, on average, has more than one author, it includes more than 70 million authorships [1]. If one could trace individuals over time, it would allow researchers to explore a variety of questions relevant to the science of science policy: Do life scientists benefit from cross-institutional or international collaboration? How do careers unfold in the publication record? Do men and women differ in their publication trajectories? The difficulty in answering these questions comes in trying to determine whether authorships on two or more different articles represent the same individual or different people. Numerous problems arise in trying to connect individuals across articles. Many different people may have the same name, and the names and affiliations of an individual sometimes change over time. Articles may also list only authors’ initials instead of their full first names. To overcome these complications, researchers have typically relied on some form of manual matching, using either a survey of scientists or curricula vitae (CVs) gathered from the Internet as a means of associating articles with authors [2]. Although these approaches ensure high levels of accuracy, they also come at a high cost. Most notably, they require a very large investment in labor to collect and code the relevant data. More recently, registries, such as Google Scholar, ORCID, and Thomson Reuters’ ResearcherID, have offered lower cost alternatives to the manual collection of data. Through the active participation of researchers identifying their own publications, these registries offer a source of highly accurate and easily accessible disambiguation of authorships for large numbers of authors. But both of these approaches have a common downside. They introduce selection bias into the sampling—not all scientists post their CVs online and registries cover only a small proportion of the population of researchers [3, 4]. These selection issues likely also introduce a form of survivor bias into samples, as those who remain in academia are more likely to organize and post their personal publication records to databases and on websites. Automated methods for author name disambiguation can potentially avoid these shortcomings [5, 6, 7, 8]. These methods typically estimate the similarity between pairs of publications that have listed authors with identical last names using information beyond the name itself. For example, if two articles list authors with the same name and the same affiliation, the likelihood that those two articles reference the same person increases substantially. Some examples of the information that has been found to assist with disambiguation would include coauthor information [9], citation patterns [10], and combinations of features, such as author affiliations and journal names [5, 11]. To associate a set of articles with a particular individual, these automated methods typically rely on some form of supervised or unsupervised machine learning, where the machine learns how to weight the various pieces of information and where to impose cutoffs in assigning a pair either to the same or to two different authors [12, 13]. These automated disambiguation techniques have been applied to several forms of documents, from the authors of articles and conference proceedings [14, 15] to the inventors of patents [16]. For PubMed articles, the Author-ity database [5, 17] represents the most recent and most comprehensive attempt at author disambiguation in the life sciences available to researchers. The online version of the PubMed database also includes its own disambiguation [4]. But the codes underlying that disambiguation do not appear on any of the pages that a researcher could access. One can only use this disambiguation in the process of manual searches by author name. It therefore cannot associate a list of articles with authors and it does not even seem a practical solution to finding all of the publications associated with a large list of researchers. Author-ity provides alphanumeric Author IDs (henceforth referred to as Author-ity IDs) that aim to identify individual scientists across publications and over time. Author-ity IDs have the potential to offer correct (precise) and complete (recall) enumeration of individuals’ publication histories in the bibliographic database. Evaluations of the Author-ity mapping using a variety of techniques suggests that it rarely assigns articles by a single individual to more than one Author-ity ID [5]. But evaluations of the extent to which it assigns the same Author-ity ID to two individuals have been limited to manual tests in small samples [5]. One ideally would want to assess the accuracy of the Author-ity IDs against another set of author identifications known to have few if any errors. We developed such an assessment by using the Principal Investigator IDs (PI IDs) assigned by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to the scientists that it funds through grants. Because applicants establish a unique PI ID when they first apply and then must use that PI ID across all grant applications—with failure to do so punishable by disqualification and potentially by federal law—these PI IDs have extremely high fidelity. We match PI IDs to Author-ity IDs based on individuals’ publication histories that can be unambiguously determined via a unique publication identifier—PubMed Identifier (PMID)—common to both the NIH ExPORTER database and the PubMed database. Using data on 36,987 scientists and 355,921 articles, our matching provides additional evidence on the precision and recall associated with Author-ity IDs available for PubMed. Our results suggest that, at least within the United States, researchers could proceed with confidence treating Author-ity IDs as an accurate disambiguation of author names in the life sciences. PubMed is a free resource maintained by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) at the U.S. National Library of Medicine. It comprises citations for biomedical literature from MEDLINE, life science journals, and online books. It associates each publication with a unique PMID that we use to connect PubMed with the NIH ExPORTER database [1]. Because the PubMed database entries for many journals only include initials and surnames for authors, we use the Author-ity database, developed by the Torvik Research Group at the University of Illinois to match authors across publications [5, 17]. The Author-ity database uses a variety of information about the authors and the publications to determine whether two or more instances of the same name (or of highly similar names) on different papers actually represent the same person. In determining unique Author IDs, the algorithm incorporates information on shared title words, journal names, coauthors, medical subject headings, publication language, affiliations, email addresses, and author name features (middle initial, suffix, and name prevalence). Author-ity contains and disambiguates all names on all papers included in PubMed as of September 2008 [5, 17], when the Torvik Research Group last updated its database. Its developers have already subjected their mapping to substantial verification, particularly with regard to whether it incorrectly assigns the same individual to more than one Author-ity ID. Most notably, assuming that the ISI Web of Science correctly disambiguates researchers, they calculated that their mapping associated 98.2% of the 2,313 most highly cited biomedical researchers with a single Author-ity ID. They also found that 98% of articles associated with a unique grant identifier in PubMed (not necessarily from the NIH) had at least one common Author-ity ID across the articles. We essentially refine their grant approach, which they refer to as the “CRISP gold standard” by using the NIH PI IDs to ensure that these grants relate to the same verified individual researcher. We also expanded the evaluation criteria using this approach to examine the extent to which the mapping assigned more than one person to a single Author-ity ID. NIH ExPORTER provides access to data files that include information on research projects funded by the NIH, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), as well as publications and patents citing support from these projects. For our analysis, we focus on NIH-funded research, which accounts for approximately 94% of all grant records in our download of the database from January 26, 2016 [18]. The NIH ExPORTER database contains a unique PI ID for each scientist who received NIH funding between 1985 and 2015 (see Fig 1 for an illustration). We focused our analysis on the 25 years between 1985 and 2009, given that the Author-ity IDs only cover articles that had appeared in PubMed by late 2008. One can associate a specific principal investigator to journal articles in PubMed through the database’s PI-article link, which identifies both the PI and the journal article through unique identifiers (e.g., PI ID “2792918” and the PMID “16544205”). Of note, PI IDs remain constant from project to project and from year to year [19]. We matched the bibliographies for NIH-funded scientists that received their first R01s during the years 1985-2009 using STATA [20]. Focusing on first R01 recipients has at least three advantages for the purposes of our evaluation. First, it provides a large set of scientists. Out of 136 distinct grant mechanisms included in our download of the NIH ExPORTER database, R01 grants are the most common. Out of 246,215 recorded grant numbers (1985-2009), the R01 mechanism accounts for 41.25%. For comparison, the second most frequent mechanism (F32) accounts for only 7.94%. Second, because the NIH awards these grants to productive scientists [21], the typical scientist in the database has multiple publications, providing more information on which to evaluate the accuracy and coverage of the Author-ity IDs. Third, focusing on PIs who received their first R01 (as opposed to renewed R01s) increases the likelihood of being able to associate at least one publication with each grant. Using the set of 45,439 first R01 recipients, our Author-ity ID evaluation process involved three steps, depicted in Fig 2. We identified the grant number associated with the first R01 for each PI ID. This identification used data contained in the Projects table of the NIH ExPORTER. Of the 45,439 PI IDs, 99.87% (45,381 PIs) are associated with a unique R01 grant number. As the NIH may award an R01 to a team that includes more than one PI, we used last names and initials to determine whether this fact might account for the 18 non-unique mappings. In 17 of 18 discrepant cases, the grant appears to have more than one PI. We dropped all 17 because they could lead to an ambiguous credit allocation. One duplicate grant number resulted from an erroneous assignment of two distinct NIH PI IDs to the same individual. Step 1 resulted in 45,381 unique matches of PI IDs to grant numbers. We matched the unique grant numbers to articles acknowledging support by the grant, as recorded in the NIH ExPORTER Links table. By construction, this matching only identifies articles published after the receipt of the R01 grant. We are able to match 41,708 of the grants to at least one article (91.91%). We examined the distribution of the fiscal years in which the 3,673 “unproductive” grants had been awarded and found that their numbers diminish over time (S1 Fig). This evolution appears consistent with the idea that the NIH has become more conservative over time in its awarding of grants, usually requiring detailed preliminary data to indicate a high likelihood of research success [22]. Public health emergencies, whether they arise from infectious disease outbreaks, natural disasters, chemical or radiological releases, or conflict-related crises, are as much communication events as they are medical or logistical ones. The way authorities and responders share information with affected populations, partners, and the media can determine whether protective behaviors are adopted, whether trust in institutions is preserved, and ultimately whether lives are saved (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). Emergency risk communication (ERC) is the real-time exchange of information, advice, and opinions between experts, officials, and the people who face a threat to their survival, health, or economic or social well-being (WHO, 2017). It differs from routine health communication and from crisis communication in the corporate sense because it must function under conditions of uncertainty, time pressure, high public emotion, and rapidly evolving evidence. It also requires the participation of communities, not only the dissemination of messages to them. The past two decades have supplied repeated reminders of what is at stake. The severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) outbreak of 2003, the 2009 influenza A(H1N1) pandemic, the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic in West Africa, and the emergence of Zika virus in 2015–2016 each exposed weaknesses in how risk information was produced, coordinated, and delivered. Post-event evaluations of these responses commonly identified communication shortcomings, including delayed or contradictory messages, unclear spokesperson roles, poor coordination among agencies, limited engagement with communities, and legal or bureaucratic barriers to the release of information (Fineberg, 2014; Gostin & Friedman, 2015). These shortcomings were not simply failures of message design. They reflected a deeper problem: ERC was often treated as a peripheral activity, activated late and staffed ad hoc, rather than as a core function embedded in the architecture of emergency preparedness and response. International instruments have recognized this problem. The International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) oblige States Parties to develop, strengthen, and maintain core capacities for surveillance and response, and the associated monitoring framework identifies risk communication as one of those capacities (WHO, 2005). The post-Ebola reviews of the IHR and of WHO's own performance reinforced the call for stronger risk communication capacity at national and international levels (WHO, 2016). Yet WHO's earlier guidance, notably the 2005 Outbreak Communication Guidelines, predated much of the experience and evidence generated over the following decade and was oriented principally toward outbreaks. Member states needed updated, evidence-informed guidance that covered all emergencies of public health concern and that spoke not only to how messages should be crafted but also to how ERC should be organized, governed, and coordinated within complex response systems. Two aspects of this organizational challenge are especially difficult. The first is integration: placing ERC within national and international public health preparedness, planning, and response structures so that communication is considered in decisions from the outset, has authority and resources, and is linked to operations rather than appended to them. Models such as the incident command system and the Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication framework developed by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention offer templates for this kind of integration (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005), but how well they transfer across political, legal, and cultural settings is not well established. The second is coordination: ensuring that agencies at different levels of government, across sectors, and across jurisdictions share information and align their public messages. Emergencies rarely respect administrative boundaries, and multiple responders, including ministries of health, civil protection, local authorities, international organizations, nongovernmental organizations, and the private sector, inevitably speak to the same publics. Inconsistent messaging can erode credibility and encourage rumor, while uncoordinated information flows can leave local actors without the data they need to act (Rubin et al., 2009; Vaughan & Tinker, 2009). Despite substantial professional attention to these issues, the evidence base on integration and coordination is fragmented. Much of what is known comes from after-action reports, case studies, expert commentary, exercises, and qualitative evaluations rather than from experimental or comparative designs. This literature is dispersed across public health, emergency management, communication, political science, and disaster research, and across scientific and grey sources, making it difficult for policymakers to identify what is known, how reliable it is, and in what contexts it applies. Existing reviews of risk and crisis communication have focused largely on message content, channels, and audience behavior, and comparatively little synthesis has addressed the system-level questions of how ERC is embedded in and coordinated across response organizations. Moreover, evidence from low- and middle-income countries, where health systems are most strained and emergencies are frequently most severe, has been underrepresented in the published record. To address these gaps, WHO commissioned a series of systematic reviews to inform its 2017 Guideline for Emergency Risk Communication policy and practice. This paper reports the review that examined the system-level dimensions of ERC. It addresses three questions: (1) what are the best practices for integrating ERC into national and international public health preparedness and response; (2) what mechanisms establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and cross-jurisdictional information sharing; and (3) what methods coordinate risk communication activities among responding agencies across organizations and levels of response. The review makes several contributions. First, it provides a structured synthesis of scientific and grey literature published between 2003 and 2016, drawing on multiple languages and databases, to capture experience from the period following SARS through the Zika response. Second, it applies a mixed deductive-inductive thematic approach and assesses confidence in the findings using GRADE-CERQual, offering transparency about the strength of the evidence that underpins guideline recommendations, a practice still uncommon in communication-related guidance. Third, it identifies the organizational, legal, and leadership factors that facilitate or impede integration, as well as the networks, task forces, and stakeholder engagement mechanisms that support coordination. Finally, by documenting the scarcity of empirical studies, particularly from low- and middle-income countries, it sets out a research agenda and argues for complementing systematic evidence with case studies across WHO regions to understand what evidence is needed in practice. Design and Reporting Framework We conducted a systematic review with qualitative evidence synthesis to inform the World Health Organization (WHO) guideline on emergency risk communication (ERC). The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) as far as possible. Strict adherence was limited because the evidence base consisted largely of qualitative, descriptive, and grey literature that does not fit the PRISMA template. The review was structured around three questions set by the WHO Guideline Development Group: (1) What are the best practices for integrating ERC into national and international public health preparedness and response? (2) What mechanisms establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing? (3) What methods coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response? The WHO handbook for guideline development (WHO, 2014) shaped the protocol, and the review team agreed the protocol with WHO before screening began. Eligibility Criteria Eligible publications were scientific and grey literature published between January 2003 and February 2016. The start date reflects the period after the 2001 anthrax attacks and the 2003 SARS outbreak, which prompted extensive reform of public health communication systems. We included studies of any design (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods) as well as case reports, after-action reviews, program evaluations, and policy documents, provided they described or evaluated the integration of ERC into public health emergency systems, information-sharing mechanisms, or coordination of communication activities. The setting could be any emergency of public health concern, including infectious disease outbreaks, natural disasters, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear events, and humanitarian crises. Eligible populations were governmental and non-governmental organizations and personnel involved in emergency preparedness and response at local, national, or international levels. We excluded publications that addressed only communication with the public (such as message design or audience reception) without an organizational or systems component. We also excluded opinion pieces lacking a description of practice or experience, and publications outside the date range. Articles in English, Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish were eligible. Search Strategy A search strategy was developed with a medical librarian, using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for emergency or disaster contexts, risk or crisis communication, and organizational integration, coordination, or information sharing. Searches covered 17 English-language electronic libraries, including biomedical, social science, and public administration databases, plus Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish-language databases to broaden geographic and linguistic coverage. Grey literature was identified through targeted searches of websites of national public health agencies, ministries of health, WHO regional offices, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, and other humanitarian and academic organizations. We also searched Google and Google Scholar, screened reference lists of included documents, and consulted topic experts for additional sources. Searches were run in February 2016, and results were pooled and deduplicated in reference management software. Study Selection Screening proceeded sequentially: title review, abstract review, and full-text review. At each stage, two reviewers independently assessed records against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were settled by discussion or, when necessary, by a third reviewer. Records that could not be judged from the title or abstract advanced to the next stage. Full-text exclusions were documented with reasons. Because the questions overlapped substantially, literature for question (2) and question (3) was screened together and ultimately synthesized jointly, while literature for question (1) was synthesized separately. Data Extraction and Quality Appraisal A standardized form was piloted on a subset of articles and refined. Extracted information included bibliographic details, country and WHO region, income classification, type of emergency, level of response (local, subnational, national, international), study design and methods, organizations involved, ERC integration or coordination mechanisms described, reported facilitators and barriers, outcomes, and recommendations. One reviewer extracted data and a second verified the entries for accuracy and completeness. Study quality was appraised with instruments suited to each design. Qualitative studies were assessed with the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative checklist (CASP, 2013). Quantitative and mixed-methods studies were assessed with criteria suited to the design, and descriptive reports, case studies, and grey literature were judged on clarity of aims, transparency of methods, relevance of context, and plausibility of conclusions. Appraisal results informed the assessment of confidence in findings, and no study was excluded because of low quality, since the aim was to describe the available evidence comprehensively. Evidence Synthesis Because the included material was heterogeneous in design, setting, and outcomes, meta-analysis was not feasible, and we used narrative thematic synthesis. We applied a mixed deductive–inductive approach (Thomas & Harden, 2008). Initial deductive categories were drawn from the WHO questions and from ERC frameworks, such as the functions of leadership, planning, coordination, training, and information sharing. The reviewers then coded the text of each article line by line and allowed additional themes to emerge inductively. Codes were grouped into descriptive themes and then compared across studies, settings, and levels of response to identify convergent and divergent findings, as well as contextual influences. Two reviewers coded independently on a subset of articles, compared the resulting coding frameworks, and reconciled differences until they agreed on a final thematic structure. Findings were tabulated by theme, with supporting studies and contexts listed. Assessment of Confidence in the Findings Confidence in each synthesized finding was assessed with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research (GRADE-CERQual) approach (Lewin et al., 2015). Four components were judged for each finding: methodological limitations of the contributing studies, relevance of the evidence to the review question and context, coherence between the data and the finding, and adequacy of the data supporting it, in terms of richness and quantity. Each component was rated as having no or minor, moderate, or serious concerns, and an overall rating of high, moderate, low, or very low confidence was assigned. Two reviewers made the assessments independently and resolved disagreements by consensus. Results were summarized in evidence profiles and provided to the WHO Guideline Development Group to support its deliberations. Statistical Analysis No quantitative pooling or inferential statistical testing was performed, as the included studies were predominantly qualitative or descriptive and varied widely in outcomes. Descriptive counts and proportions were used to summarize the screening flow,

Contemporary veterinary graduates enter a profession in which technical competence is necessary but not sufficient. Veterinarians are routinely asked to navigate disagreements about animal welfare, euthanasia, the use of animals in research and production, breed-related disease, and the competing interests of animals, owners, employers, and society. These issues are often emotive, morally complex, and politically charged, and members of the public and the profession can hold sharply divergent views about them (Fraser, 2008; Mellor, 2016). Accreditation bodies and professional organizations accordingly expect graduates to be able to identify ethical problems, reason about them systematically, and engage respectfully with people who disagree (Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, 2020; American Veterinary Medical Association, 2019). Developing these capacities requires structured opportunities to practice discussing contested topics, yet such opportunities are not simple to create within crowded curricula and diverse student cohorts. Educators have long recognized that discussion-based and cooperative learning strategies can promote deeper engagement with controversial material. Cooperative learning, in which students work interdependently and are accountable for their own and others' contributions, is associated with improved achievement, higher-order thinking, and more positive attitudes toward peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009; Slavin, 2014). Exposure to alternative perspectives can also prompt cognitive conflict, which in turn encourages students to re-examine and refine their reasoning (Piaget, 1985; Johnson et al., 2000). Structured academic controversy, role-play, and debate are therefore commonly used to teach ethics, sustainability, and other socially contested subjects (Oros, 2007; Kennedy, 2007). However, classroom discussion of polarizing issues carries risks. Students may be reluctant to speak when they fear judgment, social exclusion, or conflict with peers or instructors, and dominant voices can crowd out quieter ones (Hess, 2009; Hand & Levinson, 2012). Such reluctance may be amplified in professional programs where students are already managing performance pressure, emotional exposure to animal suffering, and concerns about how their views will be perceived by future colleagues. One established approach to structured, whole-class discussion is the human continuum exercise (HCE). In this activity, students are presented with a stimulus statement or question and asked to position themselves physically along a line between two poles, such as strong agreement and strong disagreement. They then explain their reasoning to nearby peers and to those at other points on the line, and may move as their views change. The HCE makes the distribution of opinion visible, demonstrates that positions are rarely binary, and requires each student to commit to a stance before discussion begins. These features support active learning, opinion formation, and perspective-taking, and the exercise has been used at both secondary and tertiary levels in disciplines including science, health professions, and ethics education (Kagan & Kagan, 2009; Kolb, 2014). Nonetheless, the HCE has practical and psychological limitations. It requires physical space and synchronous attendance, which restricts its use in large, distributed, or online cohorts. Because students' positions are publicly visible to peers and teachers, those who hold minority or uncertain views may feel exposed, and may move toward perceived majority positions rather than express their own (Noelle-Neumann, 1974; Asch, 1956). Time constraints may also limit the depth with which individual students can articulate their reasoning. Digital technologies offer potential means of addressing such constraints. Online discussion environments can extend participation beyond the classroom, give students time to consider and compose responses, and reduce some social cues that inhibit contribution (Suler, 2004; Hrastinski, 2008). Anonymity or pseudonymity can encourage candor, particularly for sensitive subjects, and can lessen the effect of status differences among participants (Diakopoulos & Naaman, 2011; Peddle et al., 2016). At the same time, online discussion is not uniformly beneficial. Anonymity can enable incivility, asynchronous forums often suffer from low participation and superficial exchanges, and generic platforms rarely scaffold the specific cognitive moves that make discussion educationally productive, such as taking a position, justifying it, and responding to counterarguments (Gao et al., 2013; Wise & Chiu, 2011). Existing tools for online debate or polling typically either aggregate opinions without prompting dialogue, or provide open-ended discussion boards without a clear structure for committing to and revising a position. There is therefore a gap between established, pedagogically grounded discussion exercises such as the HCE and the digital tools available to deliver them in flexible, supportive, and scalable ways. This gap is particularly salient for veterinary education. Veterinary curricula increasingly include ethics, welfare, and professional communication, but students often report discomfort when discussing controversial issues, and educators have limited evidence-based tools for creating safe spaces in which differing views can be expressed (Magalhães-Sant'Ana et al., 2014; Batchelor & McKeegan, 2012). Moreover, the expansion of online and blended delivery, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has intensified the need for activities that preserve the interactive and reflective qualities of face-to-face teaching in virtual settings (Hodges et al., 2020). Evidence is needed on whether an online adaptation of the HCE can retain the strengths of the original while mitigating its social risks. This paper addresses that need by describing the design of the virtual human continuum (VHC), an online platform that reproduces the core structure of the HCE. Students respond to a stimulus question by placing themselves on a continuum, provide a rationale for their position, view the reasoning of others, and engage with differing viewpoints in a virtual environment. We also report a first evaluation of the tool with first-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine students at the University of Sydney. The study was guided by the following research question: to what extent do students perceive the VHC as providing a non-threatening environment in which they can express their views, learn how others form arguments, and consider alternative opinions on emotive and challenging issues? The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a transparent description of an innovative educational tool and the pedagogical principles underlying its design, enabling other educators to adapt or replicate it. Second, it offers empirical data on student perceptions of the platform, including comfort in expressing views relative to face-to-face discussion. Third, it contributes to the broader literature on technology-supported dialogue by showing how an established cooperative learning exercise can be translated into an online format that supports engagement with potentially polarizing topics in professional education. Study Design and Context This study used a descriptive, cross-sectional design to document the development of the virtual human continuum (VHC) and to evaluate student perceptions of it following a single classroom trial. The work was conceived as an educational design and evaluation project, drawing on principles of design-based research in which a tool is created, implemented in an authentic setting, and refined using user feedback (Anderson & Shattuck, 2012). The pedagogical basis was the human continuum exercise (HCE), a cooperative learning strategy in which students physically position themselves along a line between two opposing statements in response to a stimulus question, and then explain or defend their position to peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). The VHC was designed to reproduce this exercise in an online environment. Platform Development The VHC was developed in collaboration with the university's educational technology staff. Design requirements were identified from the first author's experience of delivering the face-to-face HCE and from the literature on online discussion, which emphasises anonymity, low barriers to participation, and clear structure as features that support open dialogue on sensitive topics (Suler, 2004). The platform was required to: (a) present a stimulus statement or question with a response scale anchored by "strongly disagree" and "strongly agree"; (b) allow each participant to place a marker on the continuum; (c) require participants to provide a written justification for their position; (d) display the distribution of all positions and rationales to the group; and (e) permit participants to revise their position after reading others' contributions. Participants were identified by pseudonym within the activity, so that peers could not attribute positions to individuals, although instructors could access identifying information for administrative purposes. The platform was built as a web-based application accessible through standard browsers on laptops, tablets, and smartphones, and was integrated with the university's learning management system for authentication. Prototype versions were tested by teaching staff and two student volunteers not involved in the evaluation, and minor changes to the interface and instructions were made before implementation. Participants and Setting Participants were first-year students enrolled in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program at the University of Sydney, Australia. The activity was embedded in a scheduled unit of study addressing professional and ethical issues in animal-related practice. All students in the cohort (N = approximately 40) were invited to take part in the VHC session and to complete an optional, anonymous evaluation survey. Thirty-eight students completed the survey. Because the cohort was small and participation was voluntary, the sample was one of convenience, and the design did not include a comparison group. Procedure The session was delivered during a timetabled class. Students first received a short introduction to the purpose of the exercise, the ground rules for respectful discussion, and a demonstration of the platform. Three stimulus statements concerning ethically contentious issues relevant to veterinary practice and animal use were then presented sequentially. The topics were selected because they were likely to elicit divergent views and emotional responses, consistent with the definition of potentially polarising issues as those on which reasonable people hold strongly differing values (Hess, 2009). For each statement, students (i) placed themselves on the continuum and wrote a brief rationale, (ii) viewed the distribution of positions and the anonymised rationales of their peers, (iii) took part in a facilitated whole-class discussion in which selected comments were explored, and (iv) were given the opportunity to adjust their position and record any change. Facilitators were academic staff experienced in teaching ethics. They did not express personal views on the topics and intervened only to maintain respectful conduct or to prompt deeper reasoning. At the end of the session, students were given a link to the evaluation questionnaire and encouraged to complete it immediately, while the experience was fresh. The survey remained open for one week, and one reminder was provided in class. Data Collection Instrument Student perceptions were collected using a short online questionnaire developed by the research team for this evaluation. Items were generated from the intended pedagogical aims of the VHC and from prior literature on the benefits of structured classroom debate and online discussion, including exposure to diverse perspectives, development of argumentation skills, and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999; Kennedy, 2007). The questionnaire comprised statements rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Key items asked whether the VHC (1) provided a non-threatening environment for discussing emotive and challenging issues; (2) provided an opportunity to see how other people form their ideas; (3) made students think about how to express their ideas and construct arguments; (4) left students feeling more comfortable expressing their views than in face-to-face discussion; and (5) encouraged students to consider other opinions. Additional items addressed usability, and open-text fields invited general comments. Content validity was checked informally by two colleagues in veterinary education, and the wording was refined for clarity. No formal psychometric validation was undertaken, which is acknowledged as a limitation. Ethical Considerations The project was approved by the University of Sydney Human Research Ethics Committee. Participation in the survey was voluntary and anonymous, and no identifying information was collected. Students were provided with an information statement explaining the purpose of the study, and completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied consent. Declining to participate had no bearing on assessment or progression. Because the topics could be distressing, students were reminded of available university counselling services, and they could leave the activity at any time. Data Analysis Survey responses were exported from the online survey tool to a spreadsheet and checked for completeness. Given the descriptive aims and small sample, analysis was limited to descriptive statistics. For each item, the frequency and percentage of respondents selecting each response category were calculated. Responses of "agree" and "strongly agree" were combined to report overall agreement, a common approach for summarising ordinal attitudinal data (Sullivan & Artino, 2013).
