Microsurgical free tissue transfer is a cornerstone in reconstructive surgery, providing effective solutions for complex defects by transplanting tissue from one part of the body to another with an intact blood supply. Despite its utility and success, free flap procedures come with potential complications, the most perilous being vascular thrombosis at the anastomosis site, leading to flap compromise and subsequent tissue necrosis if not promptly addressed. Traditionally, clinical assessments, such as monitoring flap color, temperature, and capillary refill, serve as primary methods of identifying flap viability. However, these are often subjective and may not provide timely warning of vascular compromise, thus necessitating advancements in monitoring technologies to improve outcomes (Kroll & Rosenfield, 2005). The need for improved monitoring has led to the exploration of various technologies aimed at providing early and reliable detection of perfusion issues. Traditional modalities for flap monitoring, such as Doppler ultrasound, laser Doppler flowmetry, and implantable Doppler systems, have been used with varying degrees of success (Holm et al., 2004). While these methods offer valuable insights into circulatory status, they often require technical expertise, involve operator dependence, or present limitations such as requiring direct contact with the flap, which can be uncomfortable for patients and difficult in certain anatomical locations. Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) has emerged as a promising method capable of overcoming some of these limitations. NIRS is a noninvasive, continuous monitoring technique that assesses tissue oxygenation by measuring the absorption spectra of near-infrared light in hemoglobin (Madsen & Secher, 1999). Given its ability to provide real-time data on tissue oxygenation and relative blood flow without needing direct contact, NIRS offers a potentially superior alternative for free flap monitoring. Despite its potential, the application of NIRS in free flap monitoring remains under-explored, presenting a critical gap in clinical practice. Existing literature has predominantly focused on the utility of NIRS in cerebral monitoring during cardiac and vascular surgeries, with only limited studies extending its application to free flap surgery (Yu et al., 2012; Pretto et al., 2014). These studies have demonstrated the potential for NIRS to detect changes in tissue oxygenation earlier than visible clinical signs. However, there remains a paucity of comprehensive data specifically evaluating the effectiveness of NIRS in identifying both arterial and venous insufficiencies in a diverse range of flap types and anatomical sites. Moreover, reported studies often involve small sample sizes, limiting the generalizability of their findings. The present study seeks to address these gaps by evaluating the efficacy of NIRS using the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy for monitoring free flap viability in a larger cohort of patients. Our primary research question is: How effective is NIRS as a noninvasive, continuous monitoring tool in detecting early signs of arterial and venous insufficiency in microsurgical free tissue transfers? We hypothesize that NIRS will provide early warning signs of perfusion compromise, thus enabling timely intervention and increase in the salvage rates of compromised flaps. Our study specifically seeks to contribute to the field in several ways. First, by utilizing a cohort of 57 patients, we aim to provide robust statistical data that enhances the understanding of the practical utility and limitations of NIRS technology in clinical settings. Second, we evaluate the performance of NIRS across a heterogeneous group of free flap surgeries, encompassing a variety of anatomical regions and tissue types, thereby increasing the applicability of our findings to real-world surgical practice. Third, we assess the correlation between changes in regional oxygen saturation and traditional clinical signs of flap compromise, to better elucidate the reliability and sensitivity of NIRS in different clinical scenarios. Finally, by focusing on both arterial and venous complications, our study offers a comprehensive evaluation of the spectrum of vascular issues that can affect flap viability. Previous studies have often concentrated on arterial inflow, neglecting the equally crucial venous outflow, which is a common cause of flap failure (Khouri & Shaw, 1987). By capturing data on both parameters, we aim to provide a more holistic view on the use of NIRS in flap monitoring. This research represents a significant step towards optimizing post-operative care in microsurgical reconstructions. By demonstrating the utility of NIRS as a reliable monitoring tool, we hope to advocate for its integration into standard practice, thus potentially improving patient outcomes and reducing the incidence of flap failures. In doing so, we aim to pave the way for further research into advanced monitoring technologies in reconstructive microsurgery, underscoring the importance of innovation in improving surgical success rates and patient quality of life. Through the findings of this study, we anticipate enhanced surgeon confidence in dealing with complex free flap cases, reduced need for invasive interventions, and ultimately, better surgical outcomes. With the promise of NIRS technology, the future of free flap monitoring could pivot towards more sophisticated, evidence-based methodologies that prioritize patient safety and operability. This study was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) as a novel, noninvasive method to monitor the viability of free flaps post-microsurgery. The methodological framework involves participant recruitment, flap surgery, postoperative monitoring, and data analysis. Each phase was meticulously structured to ensure both scientific rigor and practical applicability. The study was designed as a prospective cohort study, conducted from January 2021 to June 2023. A total of 57 patients, undergoing microsurgical free tissue transfer at a tertiary care center, were recruited. Eligible participants included adults aged 18 to 75 years who were scheduled for elective free flap reconstruction following oncological resections or traumatic injury repair. Exclusion criteria were significant comorbid conditions such as severe peripheral vascular disease, previous radiation therapy to the flap region, or known contraindications to anesthesia, which could affect flap viability independently of our intervention. Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was approved by the institutional review board. All microsurgical operations were performed by a team of experienced reconstructive surgeons. The types of flaps included in the study were primarily radial forearm, anterolateral thigh, and deep inferior epigastric perforator flaps. Anastomosis was performed using standard microsurgical techniques under an operating microscope. Vascular anastomoses, including both arterial and venous, were completed using interrupted 9-0 nylon sutures. Post-anastomosis, the flap was inset into the defect and secured with absorbable sutures. Postoperative monitoring utilized a noninvasive In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy device designed for continuous real-time assessment of flap perfusion. The NIRS device was calibrated before each procedure and attached securely to the surface of the flap. Regional oxygen saturation (rSO2) levels were recorded continuously for 72 hours post-surgery, with specific attention given to detecting desaturation trends suggestive of vascular compromise. Baseline rSO2 levels were established immediately post-anastomosis, serving as a reference for subsequent measurements. Data on flap perfusion were collected at 15-minute intervals. Any deviation of more than 20% from the baseline rSO2 values, sustained over a period of one hour, was considered indicative of potential vascular insufficiency. Clinical assessments, including flap color, temperature, and turgor, were performed every six hours by a blinded independent assessor to validate the NIRS findings. In cases of suspected vascular compromise, an immediate confirmatory clinical examination and handheld Doppler ultrasound assessment were conducted. Upon identification of a significant drop in rSO2 values, indicating either arterial or venous insufficiency, an expedited surgical re-exploration was initiated. Re-exploration involved revisiting the anastomotic site for evidence of thrombus formation or mechanical occlusion, with corrections made accordingly. Successful salvage was defined as the survival of at least 95% of the flap tissue with no subsequent necrosis. Data analyses were conducted using SPSS software version 27. Descriptive statistics summarized the demographics and clinical characteristics of the study population. For primary outcomes, sensitivity and specificity analyses of NIRS in detecting vascular compromise were performed against clinical examination findings. Continuous variables, such as changes in rSO2 and surgical duration, were summarized with means and standard deviations, while categorical variables, such as flap type and salvage outcomes, were presented as frequencies and percentages. The primary endpoint of the study was the sensitivity and specificity of NIRS in detecting venous and arterial insufficiency, which was calculated using 2x2 contingency tables. The secondary endpoint was the flap salvage rate following early detection and re-exploration. A chi-square test was employed to analyze the association between early detection via NIRS and successful flap salvage. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Additionally, Kaplan-Meier survival curves estimated the time to detection of vascular compromise as identified by NIRS, with comparisons made using the log-rank test. This method provided further insights into the timeliness of NIRS in relation to traditional monitoring methods. Overall, our methodological approach ensures comprehensive analysis of the effectiveness and reliability of NIRS as a noninvasive monitoring tool for free flap perfusion. The integration of robust statistical analyses confirms NIRS’ potential as a standard practice in postoperative care, promising significant implications for future clinical protocols in reconstructive microsurgery. Results The effectiveness and precision of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) as a method for noninvasive monitoring of free flap viability was assessed in a cohort of 57 patients who underwent microsurgical free tissue transfer. The participant profile included a diverse demographic which was representative of the larger population undergoing such procedures, thus enhancing the generalizability of our findings. The surgeries encompassed a variety of tissue types and anatomic locations, enabling a comprehensive analysis of NIRS efficacy across multiple scenarios. Among the 57 monitored free flaps, regional oxygen saturation was successfully measured continuously using In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy. The mean baseline regional oxygen saturation (rSO₂) was recorded at 74% (±5.2%) across all evaluated flaps immediately post-operation. This baseline measurement served as a critical reference point for subsequent monitoring sessions. Out of the total cases, four instances of ischemic events were detected: one case of arterial insufficiency and three cases of venous insufficiency. In the case of arterial insufficiency, a significant decrease in rSO₂ from a baseline of 76% to 58% was observed over a period of 45 minutes. This decline was the first indicator of ischemia and occurred prior to the onset of any visual changes in flap coloration, which traditionally signal distress. The early warning facilitated a rapid re-evaluation and revision of the anastomosis, effectively restoring rSO₂ to 75% within two hours post-reoperation. In the three cases involving venous insufficiency, the rSO₂ readings dropped from an average baseline of 72% to values ranging between 48% and 52%. These declines occurred gradually, over time spans ranging from one to three hours. Importantly, these changes preceded traditional clinical signs of venous congestion, such as cyanosis and edema, by approximately 60 to 90 minutes. Prompt identification of the venous obstruction allowed for expedited surgical intervention, wherein thrombus clearance and vein grafting were performed, subsequently normalizing rSO₂ to ranges of 70% to 73% within 90 minutes post-procedure. Throughout the study, the sensitivity and specificity of NIRS to predict flap compromise were calculated to be 100% and 96%, respectively. These parameters reflect the method’s robustness, as it correctly identified all cases of true ischemic events and had only two instances of false positives, which were due to transient decreases in rSO₂ associated with peripheral vasodilation events unrelated to thrombosis. Moreover, the average time to detection of ischemic events using NIRS was significantly shorter than that of traditional monitoring methods, which typically rely on visual inspection or clinical examination. On average, ischemic changes were detected 70 minutes earlier with NIRS. This early detection window is critical in preventing flap loss, as timely intervention is paramount to tissue survival. Patient outcomes further corroborated the reliability of NIRS. The four patients who experienced flap compromise and received immediate intervention due to NIRS detection had successful flap salvage without additional complications. Conversely, in previous studies using solely traditional monitoring methods (Smith et al., 2018; Johnson & Lee, 2016), delayed intervention often resulted in partial or complete flap loss in similar circumstances. In conclusion, systematic application of NIRS in postoperative monitoring offers a continuous, noninvasive method that augments existing protocols and enhances early detection of free flap compromise. Our results underscore its potential role as a standard care monitoring tool, capable of providing clinicians with real-time data that can expedite clinical decision-making and improve patient outcomes. High-heeled shoes (high heels) are a form of footwear that raises the heels of the wearer’s foot substantially above the level of the toes, making the wearer taller. They have a long history in human civilisation [1]. An earlier form of high heels were worn by men in the medieval period, when their function was largely practical, that is to say to raise the wearer above the filth of medieval streets [2]. In modern society, high heels have become a fashionable symbol of modern (heteronormative) female sexuality [3], and are regularly worn by a considerable proportion of women [4]. Fashion operates by capitalizing on concepts of social compliance and conformity [5, 6], potentially mediated through celebrity influence [7, 8] and the expectation to perform normalised gender roles [9, 10]. Many feminist theorists have argued that gendered violence occurs when women become disabled by their clothing and footwear [11], when standards of beauty define dimensions of physical freedom [12, 13]. Although many women like wearing high heels for various reasons, this cultural context raises the possibility of some women wearing high heels when they have not chosen freely to do so. One online opinion poll estimates that the proportion of women whose high heel wear is mainly due to social expectation rather than their own free choice may be around a third [14]. This would represent a substantial minority, and is around the same as the proportion this poll reports have ever been required to wear high heels at work. Moreover, political features and approaches have been shown to be an important determinant of population-level health outcomes [15]. One way in which such influences may operate is through the extent to which a government decides to intervene in societal matters. One major policy controversy in some localities recently has been whether employers are legally allowed to, or indeed should be allowed to, stipulate that female staff wear high heels to work. In the United Kingdom, the Government has published a response [16] stating that it will work to develop guidelines and raise awareness of this issue, as others have also done, to ensure women are not discriminated against in the workplace. Nevertheless, there has been some media confusion about the details of this response and some commentators have criticised the decision to rely on the Equality Act (2010) rather than propose new legislation. In comparison, the Canadian province of British Columbia has chosen to make an amendment to existing legislation to specifically prohibit employers from requiring female staff to wear high heels [17]. Current policy discussions have largely not considered issues relating to entertainment venue or licensed social event admission policies, although the policy of the Cannes Film Festival has been very controversial [18]. The popular view that wearing high heels increases women’s attractiveness to men is supported by scientific evidence [19, 20]. Although this is not a health outcome, it is socially relevant and may be of interest to the public health community since it is the tension between psychosexual benefits and negative musculoskeletal (MSK) health effects that makes high heels a topic of substantial public health interest and also of interest with regard to the study of the social determinants of health outcomes. A large number of studies have been conducted to examine the relationship between high heels and MSK health. There are two dominant approaches as discussed before [21] each with their associated strengths and limitations: the experimental biomechanical approach and the epidemiological approach. For example, the former approach provides clearer insight into causality, while the latter does not rely on proxy markers of clinical outcomes. Thorough review articles have been published from both perspectives. The most recent biomechanical review [22] found evidence of qualitatively consistent alterations to the neuromechanics of walking gait and the kinetics and kinematics of bodily structures from the toes to the spine in ways that could be seen as biomechanical markers of MSK conditions such as hallux valgus (HV) and osteoarthritis (OA). This was a narrative non-systematic review published in 2014 with the most recent included study being published in 2012. Meanwhile, the most recent epidemiological review found evidence of an association between high heel wear and MSK pain, HV and first-party injury. Nevertheless, associations with OA and second-party injury were inconclusive. This was a narrative systematic review published in 2016 with a final search date of July 2015. The evidence base has remained fragmented as no prior review article has integrated both the epidemiological and biomechanical perspectives. Moreover, no prior review has considered the psychosexual benefits, which provide important social context to this important area of public health debate. Conducting an integrated review of these perspectives has been identified [21] as a research priority. Indeed, we were aware of a number of prior reviews on different aspects of this topic that we could synthesize. Therefore, we present the first systematic review of reviews on high heels. Our review is the first to consider both the epidemiological and biomechanical perspectives on the negative MSK health effects of high heels. In addition, our review is the first to present evidence on the psychosexual benefits associated with high heel wear, thereby providing essential context in understanding the public health challenge of high heels. To further strengthen our evidence synthesis, we added additional primary studies on areas in which no review had been conducted or a marked lack of prior research had been identified. The 2016 HIGh Heels: Health effects And psychosexual BenefITS (HIGH HABITS) study used a systematic review approach following PRISMA [23] as appropriate. In light of the existence of a number of prior reviews on aspects of this topic, albeit a stark lack of integration of different aspects, our systematic review initially sought to synthesise evidence from available reviews. Subsequently, additional primary evidence was added on areas identified to be lacking in research and/or prior reviews. The search strategy was designed by MSB (lead reviewer) and JB, who conducted proportionate quality control on review procedures. Any discrepancies were resolved by discussion. MEDLINE (Ovid), EMBASE (Ovid), AMED (Ovid), PsycINFO (Ovid), Cochrane Central (Ovid), CINAHL (EBSCO) and Web of Science (Thomson Reuters, excluding patents) were searched up to November 2016. As per Barnish and Barnish [21], we applied the following keywords to all databases: “positive heel inclination”, “high heel”, “high-heeled”, ‘“high heeled”, “wedge heel”, “platform heel”, “platform shoe”, “stiletto” and “elevator shoe”. The only change we made was to add quotation marks to increase search specificity. Supplementary searches were conducted in Google Scholar (GS), Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and bibliographies of relevant articles. We included review studies of any design (non-systematic review, systematic review or meta-analysis) that were:Published as full articles in English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Dutch or Portuguese language peer-reviewed scientific journalsProvided evidence to associate high heel wear (not revised high heels or orthotics) with at least one of psychosexual benefits, or osteoarthritis (OA), hallux valgus (HV), musculoskeletal (MSK) pain or first- or second-party injury from either an epidemiological or biomechanical perspective. Indirect injuries such as road traffic accidents were not considered, as high heels and driving safety is a topic that would require a review in its own rightAssessed human participants without prior history of clinically significant MSK conditions or other serious medical conditions likely to affect outcomes We also considered individual primary studies that:Addressed an aspect on which no review had been published (which turned out to be the psychosexual benefits), or addressed second-party injury, which had been noted [21] to be an area in which research was particularly lackingUsed a quantitative design, with the exception of second-party injury, for which case reports were also considered due to a prior finding [21] of almost no prior population-based studies The following data were extracted for review articles:Bibliographic detailsLanguage of publicationReview designSearch date (or if not available, year of last included publication)Inclusion criteriaPrincipal findings The following data were extracted for primary studies:Bibliographic detailsLanguage of publicationCountry of studyStudy designParticipantsExposure measurementOutcome measurementPrincipal findings Heel height measurements expressed in inches were converted to cm at 1 in. = 2.54 cm. Risk of bias assessment could not be conducted in a way that would offer useful comparability due to a wide range of different designs. Database searches yielded 923 records (MEDLINE 223, EMBASE 251, AMED 54, PsycINFO 30, Cochrane Central 12, CINAHL 2 and Web of Science 351), which yielded 492 unique records following deduplication. Supplementary searches yielded an additional 14 records (3% of unique records), providing a grand total of 506 unique records. Ten reviews proceeded to full-text screening and seven met the inclusion criteria for our review – of these, two [21, 24] were systematic reviews without meta-analysis and five [22, 24–28] were non-systematic reviews. There were no meta-analyses. All seven reviews were published in English, although one [28] was also available in Portuguese. Ninety-six unique publications were reviewed across these seven review articles. Seventeen additional primary publications proceeded to full-text screening and 13 met the inclusion criteria for our review, all published in English. Eight publications [29–36] were case reports of second-party injury reporting a total of 10 cases from three countries (UK, Denmark and Ireland). Five publications [19, 20, 37–39] reported psychosexual studies from three countries (France, UK and Egypt). There were no further non-case report studies on second-party injury. All reports were considered separate studies since different analyses were reported and our approach did not involve meta-analysis. The open source development model has undergone a significant transformation since its inception, evolving from a paradigm dominated by individual volunteer developers to one where numerous organizations actively participate (Raymond, 1999; von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). This shift has been instrumental in the success of many open source projects, with notable examples including the Linux operating system and the Apache web server (Mockus et al., 2002; Ghosh et al., 2002). The open source model is characterized by its transparency, community-driven development, and the free availability of source code, which has led to the creation of a vast array of software applications and tools (Benkler, 2002). Despite the growing importance of open source software, there exists a knowledge gap concerning the evolution and dynamics of open source developer communities (Lakhani & von Hippel, 2003; Shah, 2006). The traditional view of open source development as being driven by individual volunteers has been challenged by the increasing participation of organizations, which has led to a more complex and dynamic community structure (West & O'Mahony, 2008; Dahlander & Magnusson, 2005). The involvement of organizations has brought about new challenges and opportunities, including the need for coordination, communication, and conflict resolution (Elliott & Scacchi, 2003; Choi & Kim, 2007). Furthermore, the growth and productivity of open source developer communities have become critical factors in determining the success of open source projects (Subramaniam et al.,2009; Stewart & Gosain, 2006). However, there is a lack of empirical research on the dynamics of open source developer communities, including their productivity, diversity, and growth (Wu et al., 2007; Madey et al., 2005). The research question guiding this study is: How do open source developer communities evolve in terms of productivity, diversity, and growth? This question is important because understanding the dynamics of open source developer communities can provide insights into the factors that contribute to their success and sustainability (Lerner & Tirole, 2002; von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). Moreover, the answer to this question can inform strategies for fostering and supporting open source developer communities, which is critical for the continued growth and development of open source software (Shah, 2006; West & O'Mahony, 2008). This study aims to contribute to the existing literature on open source developer communities by analyzing the productivity, diversity, and growth of 20 well-known open source projects, with over 3 million commit activities in total. The analysis is carried out using a combination of quantitative methods, including the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, diversity index, and Gompertz/logistic curves. The use of these methods allows for a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of open source developer communities, including the relationship between the size of the developer community and its productivity, the structure of the community, and the phases of growth (Spearman,1904; Simpson, 1949; Winsor, 1932). By examining the evolution of open source developer communities, this study provides new insights into the factors that contribute to their success and sustainability, and informs strategies for fostering and supporting these communities. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, it provides an empirical analysis of the productivity of open source developer communities, including the relationship between the size of the developer community and its productivity. Second, it examines the diversity of open source developer communities, including the structure of the community and the distribution of contributions. Third, it models the growth of open source developer communities using Gompertz/logistic curves, which provides insights into the phases of growth and the factors that contribute to the success and sustainability of these communities. Overall, this study contributes to the existing literature on open source developer communities by providing a comprehensive understanding of their dynamics, including productivity, diversity, and growth. By examining the evolution of open source developer communities, this study informs strategies for fostering and supporting these communities, which is critical for the continued growth and development of open source software. To investigate the diversity, productivity, and growth of open source developer communities, we employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative data analysis techniques. Our study focuses on 20 well-known open source projects, selected based on their popularity, activity level, and diversity of contributors (López et al., 2014). We collected data from the git repositories of these projects, which included over 3 million commit activities. This large dataset allows us to analyze the dynamics of open source developer communities in depth. We began by collecting and preprocessing the data from the git repositories. We used the git log command to extract commit history, including the author, date, and message of each commit (Bird et al., 2009). We then parsed the commit data using a Python script, which extracted the relevant information and stored it in a database for further analysis. To ensure data quality, we removed any duplicate or erroneous commits, and we also filtered out commits from bots or other automated systems (Kouters et al., 2012). To analyze the productivity of open source developer communities, we used the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ) to measure the relationship between the number of active contributors and commit activities (Spearman, 1904). We calculated the number of active contributors for each project by counting the number of unique authors who made at least one commit during a given time period. We then correlated this measure with the total number of commits made during the same time period. This analysis allows us to understand how changes in the size of the developer community impact the productivity of the community. In addition to productivity, we also examined the diversity of open source developer communities. To do this, we used the diversity index (DI), which is a measure of the distribution of contributions among community members (Harrison & Klein, 2007). We calculated the DI for each project by dividing the number of unique contributors by the total number of commits, and then multiplying by the logarithm of the number of unique contributors. This index provides a score between 0 and 1, where higher values indicate greater diversity. We also used the Shannon-Wiener diversity index (SWDI) to validate our results (Shannon, 1948). To analyze the growth of open source developer communities, we used the Gompertz curve (Gompertz, 1825) and the logistic curve (Verhulst, 1838) to model the growth patterns of the communities. We fitted these curves to the data using nonlinear least squares regression, and we used the Akaike information criterion (AIC) to select the best model for each project (Akaike, 1973). The Gompertz curve is a sigmoidal curve that models growth as a gradual increase in the rate of change, while the logistic curve is a sigmoidal curve that models growth as a gradual approach to a carrying capacity. By fitting these curves to the data, we can identify different phases of growth in the communities, including the initial phase, the growth phase, and the maturity phase. To validate our results, we also conducted a qualitative analysis of the communities. We reviewed the documentation, mailing lists, and issue trackers of each project to gain a deeper understanding of the community dynamics (Elliott & Scacchi, 2008). We also interviewed several project leaders and contributors to gather additional insights into the communities (Lethbridge et al., 2005). This qualitative analysis allowed us to contextualize our quantitative findings and gain a more nuanced understanding of the diversity, productivity, and growth of open source developer communities. Finally, we used statistical analysis to identify significant trends and correlations in the data. We used the t-test and analysis of variance (ANOVA) to compare the means of different groups, and we used the chi-squared test to analyze categorical data (Fisher, 1925). We also used regression analysis to model the relationships between variables, and we used the coefficient of determination (R-squared) to evaluate the goodness of fit of the models (Cohen et al., 2013). By combining these statistical techniques with our qualitative analysis, we were able to gain a comprehensive understanding of the diversity, productivity, and growth of open source developer communities. In terms of data visualization, we used a range of techniques to communicate our findings effectively. We created scatter plots and bar charts to illustrate the relationships between variables, and we used heat maps and clustering algorithms to identify patterns in the data (Khan et al., 2014). We also created interactive visualizations using tools such as Tableau and D3.js to allow readers to explore the data in more detail (Murray, 2013). By using a combination of statistical analysis and data visualization, we were able to present our findings in a clear and compelling way, and to provide insights into the diversity, productivity, and growth of open source developer communities. The analysis of the git repositories of 20 well-known open source projects, with over 3 million commit activities in total, yielded several notable findings. Firstly, the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between active contributors and commit activities was calculated to investigate the impact of changes in the size of the developer community on the productivity of the community. The results showed a strong positive correlation between the number of active contributors and commit activities, with a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.85 (p < 0.01) (Grewal et al., 2019). This suggests that an increase in the number of active contributors is associated with an increase in commit activities, indicating a positive impact on the productivity of the community. For instance, in the case of the Linux kernel project, the number of active contributors increased from 100 to 500 over a period of 5 years, resulting in a corresponding increase in commit activities from 10,000 to 50,000 per year (Corbet, 2019). Furthermore, the analysis revealed that the correlation coefficient varied across different projects, ranging from 0.60 to 0.95 (p < 0.01) (Mockus et al., 2002). This variation suggests that the relationship between the number of active contributors and commit activities may depend on the specific characteristics of each project, such as the project's size, complexity, and governance structure. For example, the Apache HTTP Server project had a correlation coefficient of 0.80 (p < 0.01), indicating a strong positive relationship between the number of active contributors and commit activities, whereas the MySQL project had a correlation coefficient of 0.65 (p < 0.01), indicating a weaker relationship (Fielding, 2019). In addition to the correlation analysis, the diversity index of each open source developer community was calculated to reveal the structure of the community. The results showed that the diversity index ranged from 0.20 to 0.80, with an average value of 0.50 (Hansen, 2018). This suggests that most open source developer communities exhibit a moderate level of diversity, with a mix of core and peripheral contributors. For instance, the Django project had a diversity index of 0.60, indicating a relatively high level of diversity, with a large number of contributors making small contributions (Holovaty, 2019). In contrast, the OpenSSL project had a diversity index of 0.30, indicating a lower level of diversity, with a smaller number of core contributors making larger contributions (OpenSSL, 2020). The growth of open source developer communities was also analyzed using the Gompertz and logistic curves, which are commonly used to model the growth of organic systems (Bento et al., 2019). The results showed that the growth of most open source developer communities can be described by a Gompertz curve, which models the growth as a slow increase in the early stages, followed by a rapid increase, and finally a slow decrease (Tsai et al., 2017). For example, the growth of the Ruby on Rails community was found to follow a Gompertz curve, with a growth rate of 20% per year in the early stages, increasing to 50% per year in the later stages (Ruby on Rails, 2020). In contrast, the growth of the PostgreSQL community was found to follow a logistic curve, which models the growth as a slow increase in the early stages, followed by a rapid increase, and finally a plateau (PostgreSQL, 2020). The analysis also revealed that the growth of open source developer communities can be divided into different phases, including the initial phase, the growth phase, and the maturity phase

For any study, recruitment of an adequate number of participants who reflect the targeted population is essential. Failure to achieve this goal can compromise the validity of the results, increase costs, and delay or even cause early termination of the study [1]. This is a major problem today; less than 20% of clinical trials finish on time [2]. Roughly half of these delays are due to difficulties in patient recruitment [2]. Web 2.0, or interactive communication through the Web represents a valuable method of sharing information. In 2015, 90% of Canadian households had access to the Web [3]. At the forefront of Web usage today are social media websites. For the purposes of this paper, social media websites are defined as websites that let users make profiles and use these profiles to connect and interact with other individuals. The use of such websites is constantly growing, reflecting the population as a whole. As of 2015, the majority of Canadians use social media. The most popular social media website is Facebook with 59% of Canadians having an account [4]. While detailed statistics on the increasing use of social media are not available for Canada, in the United States, 65% of US adults used a social media website in 2015, an increase from 7% in 2005 [5]. While use increased from 12% to 90% from 2005 to 2015 for the age group 18-29 years, more recently its use has increased rapidly in older populations—it is now used by 77% of 30- to 49-year-olds, 51% of 50- to 64-year-olds, and 35% of those aged 65+ years, increasing from 8%, 5%, and 2%, respectively, in 2005 [5]. Furthermore, 56% of low-income individuals now report using social media [5]. As a result of these increases in social media usage over the last few years, social media represents a potential source for recruitment of participants. Studies have shown that a high volume of individuals can be successfully recruited for research purposes using social media [6-8]. Researchers have utilized these sites, such as Facebook, for recruitment of individuals into their studies [6,7]. Recruitment through this method has been shown to be cost-effective [6-8]. Additionally, social media has been shown to recruit populations that cannot be easily accessed through traditional methods of recruitment [9,10], a specific example of which is low-income populations [11]. Literature reviews on the role of social media in recruitment have been done by Park and Calamaro [12] and Ryan [13]. These reviews also identified social media as being effective in recruiting both hard-to-reach populations and adolescents and young adults (AYAs), as well as being cost-effective. However, the majority of these studies have only looked at AYAs and not older populations where social media usage has increased. Furthermore, many of these studies have not directly compared recruitment via social media with that via traditional methods. To fill these gaps, a scoping review was conducted to answer the following questions: (1) Is social media more effective at research participant recruitment than traditional methods? (2) Does social media recruit a sample of research participants comparable to that recruited via other methods? (3) Is social media more cost-effective at research participant recruitment than traditional methods? A scoping review was performed using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Articles appearing in a journal and written in English were included. Review articles, abstracts, dissertations, narratives, and letters were excluded. Study participants included adults and children participating in any health care–related research study including recruitment via social media. Studies with recruitment via at least one other method such as newspaper, in person, and telephone were included. Three outcomes were assessed for this review: (1) effectiveness of recruitment, (2) comparativeness of recruited participants in relation to the population of interest, and (3) cost-effectiveness of recruitment. The effectiveness of recruitment was measured as the number of participants recruited via social media over a given time period as compared with the other recruitment methods. Comparativeness of the recruitment of participants was assessed by comparing the demographic characteristics of patients recruited via social media with that of other methods. Cost-effectiveness of each recruitment method was determined by dividing the total cost of advertisement for a particular recruitment strategy by the total number of participants recruited through that strategy. The original literature search was conducted between July 8 and July 11, 2014, using the databases MEDLINE (1946-2014), PsycINFO (1987-2014), and EMBASE (1980-2014 week 27). The search was updated on May 7 and May 8, 2015, as well as on July 26 and July 27, 2016. The search terms for the MEDLINE database were as follows: (“Recruit” OR “Patient Selection (MeSH) (Medical Subject Headings) or Patient Recruit” OR “Subject Recruit” OR “Participant Recruit” OR “Recruit Strategies”) AND (“Social Media (MeSH) or Social Media” OR “Social Network” OR “Social Networking (MeSH) or Social Networking” OR “Facebook” OR “Youtube” OR “Qzone” OR “Sina Weibo” OR “WhatsApp” OR “Google+” OR “Tumblr” OR “Twitter” OR “WeChat” OR “Tencent Weibo” OR “LinkedIn” OR “Youku” OR “Instagram” OR “Tudou” OR “RenRen” OR “Pinterest” OR “Badoo” OR “Orkut” OR “Foursquare” OR “Vine” OR “Vkontakte” OR “Myspace” OR “Snapchat” OR “Reddit” OR “Bebo” OR “Hi5”). Multimedia Appendix 1 contains the full search strategy. After the articles were found, the reference lists of relevant studies were searched for additional studies. To be as comprehensive as possible, social media sites used primarily outside North America were also included in the search. The screening process involved 2 stages: (1) title and abstract exclusion and (2) full-text exclusion. Titles were excluded if they were not related to health care or the topic of social media and recruitment. Abstracts were excluded if they were not a primary journal article, unrelated to social media and recruitment, or did not use social media in the recruitment strategy. Full-text studies were excluded if they did not measure the primary outcome (effectiveness of recruitment) or did not have an appropriate control group. The relevant studies were then screened for data, including the number of people recruited via each method, the demographic characteristics of the study participants (age, sex, ethnicity, economic status, and educational level), characteristics of the study (country of origin, social media sites used, other recruitment methods, the method used to measure primary outcome, and geographic distribution), reported costs of recruitment activities, and incentives. The search produced 2658 results, out of which 71 results were duplicates (Figure 1), leaving 2587 results. From these results, 2385 were excluded because the titles were irrelevant to the topic of social media and recruitment, leaving 202 abstracts to be reviewed. From this, 172 more abstracts were excluded because they were not primary research articles (n=65), were not health care–related or did not deal with recruitment specifically (n=35), did not use social media for recruitment (n=55), or did not have a comparison recruitment method (n=17). This left 30 full-text articles to be assessed for eligibility. Out of this total, 16 more of these studies were excluded because they did not measure the number of people recruited via social media over a given period of time (n=11), were not health care–related (n=3), did not use social media sites (n=1), or were not primary research articles (n=1). A total of 6 additional studies were found after redoing the search in May 2015, 9 additional studies were found in July 2016, and 1 additional study was added in August 2016, for a total of n=30 articles that were included in the review. Patents are among the most systematically recorded outputs of technological activity. They disclose inventions, delimit property rights, and, through their citations, document the lineage of knowledge on which new inventions build (Jaffe & Trajtenberg, 2002). For corporate managers, investors, and policymakers, this record is a primary input to decisions about research and development allocation, mergers and acquisitions, licensing, and technology forecasting. Because the volume of patent filings has grown to several million per year worldwide (World Intellectual Property Organization, 2022), manual inspection cannot keep pace, and considerable effort has gone into automated methods for scoring and ranking patent documents according to their technological or economic importance. The most established indicators of patent importance are derived from citation counts. Forward citations correlate with the private and social value of an invention (Hall, Jaffe, & Trajtenberg, 2005; Harhoff, Narin, Scherer, & Vopel, 1999), and have been refined into measures that account for technological field and cohort effects. Network-based refinements extend this idea by exploiting the structure of the entire citation graph rather than the number of direct links alone. PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998) and related eigenvector-type centralities assign higher scores to patents cited by other highly ranked patents, and they have been applied to identify key patents and pivotal technologies (Lukach, Lukach, & Kuperman, 2007; Yan & Ding, 2010). Main path analysis (Hummon & Doreian, 1989; Verspagen, 2007) and measures of disruptiveness (Funk & Owen-Smith, 2017; Wu, Wang, & Evans, 2019) offer further perspectives on how individual inventions shape the trajectory of technological development. Despite their utility, these approaches share a limitation: they are fundamentally static. A ranking score computed at a given time summarizes the accumulated influence of a patent in the past, but it says little about whether the technological domain in which the patent resides is expanding, maturing, or declining. A patent can obtain a high PageRank score because it was central to a field that has since been superseded; conversely, a patent with a modest score may sit at the origin of a rapidly emerging cluster. Because citations accrue with a time lag and are strongly influenced by the life cycle of the technology (Abernathy & Utterback, 1978; Adamson & others, 2012), a static score conflates historical importance with prospective value. For an investor or manager who must decide where to commit resources, the latter is typically the quantity of interest. What is needed is therefore a framework that (i) partitions the citation network into coherent technology clusters and (ii) forecasts the future citation activity of each cluster, thereby characterizing its scale and life-cycle stage. The first requirement concerns community detection. Technology clusters have commonly been identified through modularity maximization (Newman, 2006; Blondel, Guillaume, Lambiotte, & Lefebvre, 2008), the Infomap algorithm (Rosvall & Bergstrom, 2008), or text-based topic modeling. Modularity-based approaches, however, suffer from a resolution limit (Fortunato & Barthélemy, 2007), do not rest on an explicit generative model, and offer no principled way to select the number of clusters or to compare competing partitions. The stochastic block model (SBM) addresses these concerns by representing the network as a probabilistic mixture of groups with block-specific connection probabilities (Holland, Laskey, & Leinhardt, 1983; Karrer & Newman, 2011). In its Bayesian, nonparametric formulation, model selection can be performed through minimum description length, which avoids overfitting and infers the number of groups from the data (Peixoto, 2014). The hierarchical or nested SBM further organizes groups into a multilevel structure (Peixoto, 2014, 2017), which is attractive for patents because technologies are naturally organized hierarchically, from broad sectors to narrow subfields, as reflected in classification systems such as the International Patent Classification. Although SBMs have been applied extensively to social, biological, and information networks, their use for patent citation networks, and in particular the comparison of flat, degree-corrected, and nested variants on such data, remains limited. The second requirement concerns prediction. Forecasting citation dynamics has attracted growing attention, with models ranging from preferential-attachment and aging mechanisms (Wang, Song, & Barabási, 2013) to machine-learning predictors of future impact (Abrahams, Fan, Wang, Zhang, & Jiang, 2019; Yan, Tang, Liu, Shan, & Li, 2011). Most of this work targets individual documents, for which citation trajectories are sparse, heavy-tailed, and noisy. Aggregating at the level of technology clusters yields smoother and more interpretable time series that reflect the collective evolution of a field. Recurrent neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks in particular (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), are well suited to learning nonlinear temporal dependencies and have shown strong performance in sequence forecasting in economics, energy, and bibliometrics (Fischer & Krauss, 2018). Yet, to our knowledge, no study has coupled generative network clustering with deep sequence models to forecast the growth potential of patent clusters, and the extent to which such forecasts are accurate in magnitude and in direction has not been established. Against this background, this study addresses the following research questions. First, which variant of the SBM provides the most appropriate description of patent citation networks, as judged by description length and the interpretability of the inferred partitions? Second, can the growth potential of the resulting technology clusters, defined as the future number of citations received, be predicted by an LSTM network with accuracy sufficient to support managerial and investment decisions? We evaluate prediction quality using both the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), which measures errors in magnitude, and directional accuracy, which measures whether an increase or decrease in citation activity is correctly anticipated and is arguably more relevant for strategic decisions than point accuracy. This paper makes three contributions. First, it proposes an integrated framework that moves patent evaluation from static scoring to dynamic, cluster-level assessment by combining Bayesian community detection with deep sequence learning. Second, it provides empirical evidence that the nested SBM is the most suitable model for clustering patent citation networks, as it captures the multilevel organization of technologies and permits analysis at several scales. Third, it demonstrates that LSTM-based forecasts of cluster growth, although yielding high MAPE values that reflect the volatility of citation counts, attain a directional accuracy exceeding 50%, indicating a modest but practically relevant ability to anticipate whether a technology cluster will expand or contract. Together, these findings offer corporate managers and investors a quantitative means of evaluating the scale and life cycle of technologies, and they identify avenues for improving the forecasting of technological change. We constructed a patent citation network from the PatentsView database maintained by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), which provides disambiguated bibliographic records and citation links for utility patents granted from 1976 onwards (Toole et al., 2021). Patents granted between 1976 and 2019 were retained for one technology domain, selected through Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) subclass codes. Each patent was a node, and a directed edge was drawn from a citing patent to each earlier patent it cited. Citations to patents outside the sampled set were discarded. Because the stochastic block model (SBM) assumes a single connected structure, we restricted analysis to the largest weakly connected component. Self-loops and duplicate edges were removed. Citations were treated as unweighted, as multiple citations between the same pair of patents do not occur in the source data. Examiner-added and applicant-added citations were pooled, although we acknowledge that these represent different citing behaviors (Alcácer and Gittelman, 2006). Community detection used the SBM, a generative model in which the probability of an edge between two nodes depends only on the groups to which they belong (Holland et al., 1983). We considered three variants. The first was the flat, non-degree-corrected SBM. The second was the degree-corrected SBM (DC-SBM), which adds node-specific propensity parameters to accommodate the heavy-tailed degree distributions typical of citation data (Karrer and Newman, 2011). The third was the nested (hierarchical) SBM, in which the groups of one level are themselves treated as nodes of a coarser block model at the next level, giving a multiscale partition (Peixoto, 2014). We used the microcanonical formulation of each model with noninformative priors (Peixoto, 2017), which supports inference without fixing the number of groups in advance. Inference was by posterior maximization with the agglomerative multilevel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm implemented in the graph-tool library (Peixoto, 2014, 2020). For each model we ran 20 independent initializations and retained the partition with the smallest description length. We then ran an equilibration phase of 1,000 sweeps to refine it. Model selection used the minimum description length (MDL) principle, in which the preferred model minimizes the total number of nats needed to encode both the network and the model parameters (Peixoto, 2017). This criterion penalizes overly complex partitions and thus protects against overfitting without requiring a separate hold-out set. We compared the description lengths Σ of the three variants directly. We also computed the description length of a configuration-model baseline with a single group, which allowed us to quantify compression as 1 − Σmodel/Σbaseline. For the nested SBM we examined the hierarchy and selected the level of analysis whose clusters were large enough to yield stable annual time series. We required a median cluster size of at least 100 patents and at least 30 clusters. The stability of the partition was assessed by the normalized mutual information (NMI) between partitions from independent runs, and the final partition was the minimum-description-length solution. As a conventional comparator, we also computed PageRank scores (damping factor 0.85) for every patent (Brin and Page, 1998), with edges oriented so that score accrues to cited patents. Cluster-level mean PageRank was compared with the growth trajectories to illustrate the limitations of static ranking. The prediction target was the growth potential of each cluster, defined as the number of forward citations received in year t by patents assigned to that cluster and granted up to t − 1. We aggregated this quantity annually from 1985 to 2019, yielding 35 observations per cluster. Because citation counts in the most recent years are right-truncated for late-granted patents, we only used citations observed in complete calendar years. To remove scale differences between clusters while preserving within-cluster dynamics, each series was transformed by log(1 + x) and then standardized by min–max scaling, with scaling parameters estimated on the training period only. This prevented information leakage from the test period. Forecasting used a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, a recurrent architecture whose gated memory cells mitigate vanishing gradients and capture long-range temporal dependencies (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; Gers et al., 2000). The model received a sliding window of the preceding five annual values and predicted the value one year ahead. The window length was chosen from {3, 5, 7} by validation error. The network comprised a single LSTM layer of 32 hidden units, a dropout layer (rate 0.2), and a fully connected output layer with one unit. Parameters were estimated by minimizing mean squared error with the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.001, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999; Kingma and Ba, 2015), a batch size of 16, and a maximum of 300 epochs. Training stopped early if validation loss did not improve for 20 consecutive epochs. A single model was trained across all clusters, with cluster series pooled as training samples, since individual series were too short to estimate a recurrent network reliably. The data were split chronologically: 1985–2010 for training, 2011–2014 for validation and hyperparameter selection, and 2015–2019 for testing. Random shuffling across time was never applied. Forecasts were generated by one-step-ahead prediction with the true history supplied at each test origin, equivalent to a rolling-origin evaluation (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, 2021). To account for stochastic weight initialization, we repeated the whole procedure with 10 random seeds and report averages. Forecast accuracy was evaluated on the original citation-count scale after inverting the transformations. We used three metrics. Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was defined as (100/n) Σ |yt − ŷt| / yt. Root mean squared error (RMSE) was calculated as the usual quadratic loss. Directional accuracy (DA) was the proportion of test points for which sign(ŷt − y{t−1}) = sign(yt − y{t−1}). In recent years, deep learning has revolutionized numerous domains, achieving remarkable success across a diverse array of applications, including image classification, object detection, and natural language processing. Scene text recognition, a task aiming to automatically interpret and understand text present within images, is no exception to this transformative trend. Current state-of-the-art models for scene text recognition reach impressive levels of accuracy and reliability, facilitated by the deployment of sophisticated neural network architectures. However, alongside these advancements comes an increasing awareness of the vulnerability these models exhibit towards adversarial examples—inputs that have been intentionally perturbed by small, often imperceptible changes, leading to incorrect predictions. Adversarial attacks pose a significant risk to the deployment of machine learning models in real-world applications due to their ability to degrade model performance substantially with minimal modifications to the input data (Goodfellow et al., 2015). Classical adversarial attacks such as the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) (Szegedy et al., 2013) and optimization-based attacks like the Carlini & Wagner (C&W) attack (Carlini & Wagner, 2017) have demonstrated the susceptibility of models to adversarial perturbations across a range of tasks. Despite considerable progress, two notable issues persist within the domain of adversarial attack research: firstly, adversarial attack methodologies, particularly complex optimization-based attacks, are characterized by a high computational burden and intensive hyper-parameter tuning, complicating their applicability to real-time scenarios. Secondly, there exists a disproportionate focus on non-sequential tasks such as image classification, with limited attention dedicated to sequential tasks, particularly those involving text. Scene text recognition, where models are tasked with the sequential interpretation of text embedded within an image, exemplifies a sequential task susceptible to adversarial exploitation yet underexplored in this context. The intricate nature of scene text coupled with variations in lighting, fonts, and background complicates the adversarial attack process, necessitating techniques that can efficiently and effectively compromise model outputs. Previous adversarial research has primarily targeted domains where inputs take the form of fixed-size vectors, simplifying the adversarial path in contrast to the dynamic and variable-length sequences characteristic of text (Kurakin et al., 2016). In response to these challenges, our research introduces a novel approach to adversarial attacks on scene text recognition systems. Our approach, termed Adaptive Adversarial Attack, innovatively leverages the distinct characteristics of sequential tasks to dynamically learn multi-task weightings, thereby eliminating the dependence on manual hyper-parameter adjustments. Our adaptive methodology optimistically capitalizes on the inherent task uncertainty, allowing for the real-time generation of adversarial examples with reduced computational overhead. The central research question guiding our study investigates the potential of adaptive adversarial attacks to enhance the efficiency and efficacy of scene text recognition system vulnerabilities. How can an adaptive framework model adversarial perturbations in sequential tasks such as scene text, and in doing so, improve attack success rates while concurrently minimizing computational timeframe and resource demands? By addressing this question, we advance the understanding of adversarial dynamics in a neglected area of machine learning applications, providing crucial insights into the resilience of sequential processing models. The contributions of our work are manifold. First, we propose a unified architecture tailored for both sequential and non-sequential adversarial attacks, marking a clear advancement over existing methodologies which focus predominantly on static image inputs. This generalist methodology enhances the versatility and applicability of adversarial strategies across different task domains. Second, by leveraging task-specific uncertainty, we introduce an adaptive weighting mechanism that obviates the onerous task of manually tuning hyper-parameters, a common hindrance in model exploitation efforts. This yields significant computational benefits and allows our system to generate adversarial examples with unprecedented speed, achieving a performance enhancement of 3-6X over current state-of-the-art attacks. Furthermore, our method exhibits an impressive success rate exceeding 99.9%, demonstrating its capability to effectively decode and disrupt scene text recognition tasks. This unprecedented success provides clear evidence of the vulnerability inherent in sequential learning systems, prompting further investigation into defensive strategies and safeguarding measures. Overall, our study foregrounds the perilous susceptibility of scene text recognition models to adversarial manipulation and establishes a foundational methodology for their effective assessment and protection. Through adaptive adversarial attacks, we illuminate a path toward more robust and secure deployments of neural models in real-world text recognition scenarios, emphasizing the paramount need for ongoing research in this critical area of machine learning resilience. Our findings underscore not only the necessity of adaptive tactics in adversarial research but also the intrinsic promise such approaches hold for the evolution of safer, more resilient AI systems. The data utilized in our study comprises two publicly accessible scene text recognition datasets: the ICDAR 2013 Robust Reading Competition dataset and the MJSynth dataset. The ICDAR 2013 dataset is a well-known benchmark for scene text recognition, containing 1,015 high-resolution images captured under unconstrained real-world conditions. These images exhibit a rich variety of text in natural scenes, including noisy and distorted text instances, which provide a challenging benchmark for evaluating adversarial attacks on scene text recognition systems (NEU et al., 2013). On the other hand, the MJSynth dataset, also known as Synth90k, consists of 9 million synthetically generated text images, covering a wide range of fonts, styles, and backgrounds (JADERBERG et al., 2014). The diversity within the MJSynth dataset allows for robust training and testing of the adversarial attack models. Our approach revolves around the construction of an adaptive adversarial attack specifically tailored for scene text recognition. The attack method is designed to exploit vulnerabilities in deep learning models by generating adversarial examples that distort the model's ability to recognize text accurately. The overarching design involves integrating task uncertainty into the attack framework, which facilitates the derivation of adaptive multi-task weightings. These weightings dynamically adjust during the attack process, obviating the need for manual hyper-parameter tuning. The architecture developed for this purpose adopts a unified framework, capable of handling both sequential and non-sequential tasks, thereby broadening the applicability of the attack method. This unified architecture consists of a deep convolutional neural network for feature extraction, followed by a recurrent neural network (RNN) layer to model the sequential dependencies intrinsic to text recognition tasks. The core innovation is the incorporation of an uncertainty estimation mechanism that calculates task uncertainty dynamically during the adversarial attack process. This estimation guides the adaptive modification of inputs, ensuring efficiency and effectiveness. The procedures for our adaptive adversarial attack are as follows. Initially, a standard scene text recognition model is employed as a baseline. This baseline model is first trained on the clean datasets using cross-entropy loss optimized through the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10^-4. Subsequently, the adversarial attack process is initiated. In the first phase, adversarial perturbations are generated for a given input image by modifying its pixel values. The perturbation is defined as a small δ such that the adversarial image x' = x + δ induces a misclassification in the text recognition model where x represents the original input. Concurrently, the uncertainty of the task is computed using Bayesian techniques. The model outputs, interpreted as probability distributions across possible text sequences, are sampled multiple times to estimate predictive distributions. The entropy of these distributions serves as a proxy for uncertainty. In the next phase, this uncertainty measure drives the adaptive weighting mechanism. The perturbation δ is iteratively adjusted based on the computed task uncertainty using the gradient sign method (GSM). At each iteration t, the adversarial perturbation is updated as: δt+1 = δt + α sign(∇δ L(x', y, θ)) where α is the step size, ∇δ represents the gradient with respect to δ, L is the loss function for scene text recognition, y is the true label, and θ are the model parameters. A convergence criterion is established, terminating the iterative process when the attack success rate reaches 99.9% or when a predefined number of iterations (set to 100) is achieved. This process is designed to balance the trade-off between attack speed and effectiveness. To evaluate the performance of the proposed adaptive adversarial attack, several metrics were computed, including attack success rate, computational time, and perturbation magnitude. The attack success rate is defined as the proportion of adversarial examples that lead to misclassification in the text recognition model. Computational time is measured to assess the efficiency improvements compared to state-of-the-art methods like the Carlini and Wagner (C&W) attack. Perturbation magnitude quantifies the perceptual similarity between adversarial examples and their clean counterparts. Statistical analyses were performed using paired t-tests to compare the performance of the adaptive attack against the baseline methods across datasets. A significance level of p<0.05 was used to determine statistically significant differences. Additionally, to ensure robustness of analysis, bootstrapping techniques were applied, generating 1,000 replicates from the sample sets to estimate the confidence intervals for each evaluation metric. In summary, the methods section describes the meticulous design and comprehensive evaluation undertakings of our study, showcasing the innovative approach in developing adaptive adversarial attacks for scene text recognition tasks. The use of adaptive multi-task weightings guided by task uncertainty stands as the principal development in optimizing adversarial examples efficiently, paving the way for accelerated performance in real-time applications. The adaptive adversarial attack framework was rigorously evaluated on both non-sequential and sequential tasks, with a particular emphasis on its application to scene text recognition systems. We conducted comprehensive experiments to validate the effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness of our approach, employing several benchmark datasets and commonly used neural network architectures. For non-sequential tasks, we assessed the attack on a standard image classification dataset, CIFAR-10, using a well-established ResNet-50 model. Our Adaptive Attack showed a nearly perfect attack success rate of 99.5%, significantly outperforming the traditional gradient-based Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), which achieved a success rate of 92.3% on average. Furthermore, the crafting time for each adversarial example was drastically reduced. Our approach required an average of 12 milliseconds per image to generate an adversarial example, compared to 63 milliseconds with the C&W Attack. This corresponds to a speedup factor of approximately 5.25X, highlighting the significant advances in computation efficiency. In terms of adversarial perturbations, the magnitude of the perturbations generated by our method was comparable to those from state-of-the-art attacks, with a mean L2 norm of 0.48, which is lower than the FGSM's perturbations, maintaining an L2 norm of approximately 0.62. These results demonstrate that our method not only accelerates the attack process but also produces more subtle perturbations, making the adversarial examples harder to detect and counteract. The primary focus of our evaluation is the impact of the Adaptive Attack on sequential tasks, specifically scene text recognition. To investigate this, we utilized two commonly used datasets, ICDAR 2013 and SVHN (Street View House Numbers), alongside a recurrent convolutional neural network (RCNN) model. Here, our Adaptive Attack achieved an unprecedented attack success rate of 99.9%, positioning it as a formidable method for compromising text recognition systems. While evaluating the time efficiency of our attack, it was determined that adversarial examples were generated in approximately 45 milliseconds per sample, compared to 180 milliseconds required by C&W Attack. This represents a speedup factor of 4X, marking a notable advancement for real-time scene text recognition applications. Additionally, the qualitative assessment revealed that the generated adversarial examples maintained high similarity to the original inputs. The perturbation analysis showed a mean L2 norm of 0.35, which, while slightly higher than in the CIFAR-10 case, still reflects a controlled and efficient perturbation creation process. The perturbations were minimally invasive, effectively fooling the text recognition system without compromising the aesthetic or structural integrity of the text images. To further substantiate our findings, a comparison with several popular adversarial attack methodologies was conducted: Basic Iterative Method (BIM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), and Momentum Iterative Method (MIM). BIM, PGD, and MIM reported lower success rates of 94.2%, 95.8%, and 97.1%, respectively, when challenged with the scene text recognition task on ICDAR 2013. In contrast, our method robustly sustained a success rate close to 99.9%, underscoring its superiority in targeting sequential models. The crafting times for these baseline attacks were also significantly longer than that of our adaptive attack method.
