The idea that the loss of one sense is offset by the enhancement of others is deeply rooted in popular culture and has a long history in philosophy and early psychology. Blind individuals are often assumed to have a "sharper" sense of smell, touch, or hearing that helps them navigate a world designed primarily for the sighted. In the olfactory domain, such beliefs are reinforced by anecdotal reports from blind people themselves, who often say they rely on smell to recognize people, locate places, and evaluate food and objects (Wakefield, Homewood, & Taylor, 2004). Olfaction is an especially interesting case because it is a chemical sense with a comparatively weak link to the visual system in everyday behavior, yet it is closely tied to cognition, emotion, and memory (Herz & Engen, 1996). If sensory loss triggers compensatory adaptations, olfaction is a plausible candidate. The theoretical basis for such expectations lies in the neuroplasticity literature. In congenitally and early blind individuals, the occipital cortex is not simply silent; it is recruited for a range of non-visual functions, including Braille reading, auditory localization, speech comprehension, and verbal memory (Sadato et al., 1996; Röder et al., 2002; Amedi et al., 2003; Bedny, 2017). Behavioral studies often report superior performance in blind people on pitch discrimination, sound localization, and tactile acuity, although the findings are not uniform and depend on task demands and the age at which vision was lost (Collignon, Voss, Lassonde, & Lepore, 2009; Wan, Wood, Reutens, & Wilson, 2010). Neuroimaging has also suggested that olfactory stimulation may engage regions beyond the classical olfactory network in blind individuals. Kupers and colleagues (2011), for example, reported activation of occipital areas during odor processing, and Araneda et al. (2016) reported structural and functional differences in olfactory-related regions in early blind participants. Such results indicate that cross-modal reorganization could, in principle, have consequences for olfactory perception. The behavioral evidence, however, is far less consistent. Olfactory function is generally considered to comprise several partly separable components (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997). Lower-level, sensory-driven abilities include the detection threshold, defined as the lowest concentration at which an odorant can be perceived, and odor discrimination, which requires distinguishing between different odorants. Higher-order abilities involve cognitive and linguistic processes and include cued odor identification, in which participants choose a label from a set of alternatives, and free odor identification, in which participants name an odor without help. Performance on the latter tasks depends heavily on semantic memory, verbal ability, and attention, in addition to sensory sensitivity (Cain, 1979; Larsson, 1997). A plausible possibility is that blindness could selectively affect some of these components but not others, for example by improving higher-order processing through increased attention to olfactory cues, without altering peripheral sensitivity. Empirical findings do not clearly support either a general or a selective enhancement. Several studies have found lower olfactory thresholds in blind than in sighted participants (Cuevas, Plaza, Rombaux, De Volder, & Renier, 2009; Beaulieu-Lefebvre, Schneider, Kupers, & Ptito, 2011), whereas others have found no difference (Smith, Doty, Burlingame, & McKeown, 1993; Rosenbluth, Grossman, & Kaitz, 2000) or even poorer performance in blind individuals (Wakefield et al., 2004). Studies of odor discrimination show a similar pattern: some report an advantage for blind participants (Cuevas et al., 2009), and others report equivalent performance (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska, Sorokowski, & Karwowski, 2013). The picture for identification is also mixed. Some investigations have shown superior free or cued identification in blind participants (Murphy & Cain, 1986; Rosenbluth et al., 2000; Cuevas et al., 2009), while others have found no group differences (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska et al., 2013). Heterogeneity in methods may partly explain these discrepancies. Studies differ in the psychophysical procedure used (e.g., staircase methods vs. forced-choice batteries), the odorants tested, the criteria for sample selection, and the way blindness is characterized. Moreover, many studies have small samples, which limits statistical power and increases the probability that observed effects, whether positive or null, are unreliable (Button et al., 2013). Participant characteristics are a further source of uncertainty. Olfactory function declines with age and differs between women and men, with women often outperforming men on several olfactory measures (Doty & Cameron, 2009; Sorokowska et al., 2017). If the age or sex composition of blind and sighted samples differs, or if these factors moderate the effects of sensory deprivation, estimates of group differences could be distorted. Most important, the timing of vision loss may be critical. Plasticity is thought to be greatest during sensitive periods of development, so early or congenitally blind individuals might show larger compensatory effects than those who lose their sight later in life (Voss, Lepore, Gougoux, & Zatorre, 2010; Collignon et al., 2009). Yet studies of olfaction have often combined early and late blind participants, or have not reported onset in sufficient detail, making it difficult to determine whether the timing of blindness matters. Narrative reviews have summarized parts of this literature (Sorokowska, 2016; Kupers & Ptito, 2014), and they generally conclude that evidence of superior olfaction in blindness is equivocal. Narrative approaches, however, are vulnerable to selective citation and cannot quantify the magnitude or consistency of effects, nor assess whether the published record is distorted by selective reporting. Publication bias is a particular concern in this field: an intriguing and intuitively appealing finding of superior performance in blind people may be more likely to be published than a null result, which would inflate the apparent evidence for compensation (Rothstein, Sutton, & Borenstein, 2005). Meta-analytic methods allow the combination of effect sizes across studies, the examination of heterogeneity, the testing of moderators, and the application of procedures that detect and adjust for small-study effects (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Duval & Tweedie, 2000). To our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively synthesized the evidence on olfactory abilities in blind individuals across the full range of olfactory functions. The present work therefore provides a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing blind and sighted individuals on four outcomes: odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. Our primary question was whether blindness is associated with better olfactory performance, and whether any such effect differs between sensory-driven tasks (threshold, discrimination) and higher-order tasks (identification). Because publication bias could influence these estimates, we explicitly assessed and corrected for it. In addition, we conducted exploratory moderator analyses to test whether participants' age, the proportion of women in the samples, and the onset of blindness (early vs. late) explain variability in effect sizes across studies. This work contributes in three ways. First, it offers the first comprehensive quantitative estimate of olfactory performance in blindness, replacing impressionistic summaries with effect sizes and confidence intervals. Second, it examines whether the published literature supports the notion of compensatory plasticity in olfaction once bias is taken into account. Third, it identifies methodological gaps, such as small samples and inconsistent reporting, that can guide the design of future research on sensory compensation. Protocol and reporting standards The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher, Liberati, Tetzlaff, & Altman, 2009) and followed recommendations for meta-analysis in the behavioral sciences (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Cooper, Hedges, & Valentine, 2009). The inclusion criteria, outcomes, and the analytic strategy for the primary analyses were specified before data extraction. The analyses of moderators were exploratory. Literature search Relevant articles were identified through a computerized search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and PsycINFO, supplemented by Google Scholar. The search combined terms related to blindness (blind, visual impairment, visual deprivation, visually impaired, anophthalmi, early blind, late blind, congenital blind) with terms related to olfaction (olfact, smell, odor, odour, chemosens, threshold, discrimination, identification). No restrictions on publication year were imposed, and the search covered records from database inception until the date of the final search. We also screened the reference lists of all eligible articles and of relevant narrative reviews, and we searched for conference abstracts and unpublished dissertations to reduce the risk of missing unpublished data. When essential statistics were missing, corresponding authors were contacted by e-mail. Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they (a) compared a group of blind participants with a group of sighted controls, (b) assessed at least one of four olfactory outcomes (odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, or free odor identification), (c) used human participants, and (d) reported data sufficient to calculate an effect size (means and standard deviations, t or F statistics, exact p values with sample sizes, or equivalent). Blindness was defined as congenital or acquired total blindness or severe visual impairment, as described by the original authors. Studies were excluded if they lacked a sighted control group, if participants had additional conditions known to affect olfaction (e.g., neurodegenerative disease, Kallmann syndrome, head trauma, or chronic rhinosinusitis), if the data were reported only for subjective ratings of odor properties (e.g., intensity, pleasantness) or for olfactory-related tasks that did not map onto the four outcomes, or if the data duplicated those of another included study. Where a sample was reported in more than one article, only the most complete report was retained. Studies in languages other than English were considered if they could be translated. Outcome definitions Odor threshold tasks estimated the lowest concentration at which an odorant (typically n-butanol or phenylethyl alcohol) could be detected, usually through a staircase, forced-choice procedure (e.g., Sniffin' Sticks). Discrimination tasks required participants to identify the odd item among three odorants presented in a triangle test. Cued identification required selection of the correct label from a list of alternatives (typically four), whereas free identification required participants to name the odor without any response options. Because threshold is generally considered a sensory-driven function and identification a higher-order function dependent on semantic and mnemonic processes (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997), the four outcomes were analyzed separately. Where studies reported more than one measure within an outcome (e.g., several odorants or subtests), we averaged them to obtain one effect size per study and comparison. When separate early-blind and late-blind groups were compared with the same sighted group, the shared control group was handled as described below. Study selection and data extraction Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third author. Data were extracted independently by two coders using a standardized form, which recorded: authors and year, country, sample size per group, mean age, proportion of women, onset of blindness (early/congenital vs. late), olfactory test used, and the statistics necessary to compute effect sizes. Inter-coder agreement was high (Cohen's κ > .90 for categorical variables) and discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Studies were classified as early blind when blindness was congenital or began in early childhood (typically before the age of 5 years, or as defined by the authors), and as late blind otherwise. Effect size computation The effect size was the standardized mean difference, Hedges' g, with positive values indicating better performance in blind than in sighted participants. For threshold tasks, in which lower scores reflect higher sensitivity (in studies reporting concentration), the sign was reversed accordingly. For each study, d = (Mblind − Msighted) / SDpooled, with SDpooled = √[((n₁ − 1)SD₁² + (n₂ − 1)SD₂²) / (n₁ + n₂ − 2)], and the small-sample correction g = d × [1 − 3 / (4(n₁ + n₂) − 9)]. The sampling variance was vg = (n₁ + n₂)/(n₁n₂) + g² / (2(n₁ + n₂)) multiplied by the squared correction factor. When only t or F values were reported, they were converted to d using standard formulas (Borenstein et al., 2009). For nonparametric tests, we converted exact p values or z statistics to equivalent effect sizes. When a study contained two blind subgroups compared with one control group, we combined the subgroups into one group (computing pooled means and standard deviations) for the main analyses and treated them separately only in the onset moderator analysis, where the shared control group's sample size was divided between the comparisons to avoid

As part of the Medical Library Association (MLA) Nursing and Allied Health Resources Section (NAHRS) project to map the literature of allied health [1], Haaland published a dental hygiene mapping study in 1999 [2] to identify core journals in dental hygiene and determine indexing coverage for these journal titles. In light of changes in the dental hygiene profession and the amount of time passed since the original mapping study, it is prudent to update and reassess the dental hygiene literature to provide useful information for both librarians and dental hygiene professionals. As noted in Haaland’s article [2], dental hygienists work with dentists to provide services that “include dental prophylaxis, radiography, application of medications, and provision of dental education at chairside and in the community” [3]. While this definition still describes a large portion of the profession, it does not encompass all of the roles currently played by dental hygienists, who also work in academia, industry, public health, and research [4]. In addition, when the original mapping study was published, only 212 accredited US dental hygiene programs were in place, whereas there are now 330 programs with 21 graduate programs. Most programs grant an associate degree, others lead to a bachelor’s degree, and some offer master’s degrees in dental hygiene or dental therapy [5, 6]. In 2013, dental hygiene celebrated 100 years as a profession. Research articles in dental hygiene began appearing in the 1940s, and in the 1960s, dental hygienists began to engage in dental research projects, usually as associates or administrators rather than principal investigators. The first conference on dental hygiene research was held in 1982 [7]. The National Center for Dental Hygiene Research (established in 1993 and now known as the National Center for Dental Hygiene Research & Practice) updated its research agenda twice: in 2007 and 2016 [8]. Of note, in its 2016 research agenda, the American Dental Hygiene Association stated, “[t]he goal of increasing dental hygienists’ participation in research is to grow beyond reliance on research originating from other disciplines and, instead, build upon existing research so the knowledge base can emerge from within dental hygiene itself” [9]. Another driver of this increased research emphasis was the 2016 Revised Standards for Clinical Dental Practice, which stated that dental hygienists should “[a]ccess and utilize current, valid, and reliable evidence in clinical decision-making through analyzing and interpreting the literature and other resources” [10]. A current mapping study would support such research endeavors and shed light on changes that have shaped applicable literature during the last two decades. Thus, the purpose of this study is, like the original study [2], to identify core journals in the field of dental hygiene and determine the extent of indexing coverage for these journal titles. Its findings could reveal whether the field of dental hygiene is expanding due to increased intellectual contributions and can aid librarians in deciding which journals to collect and which databases to teach and aid dental hygienists in deciding where to submit their manuscripts for publication. This study used the mapping protocol outlined by NAHRS, as updated in December 2017 [1]. Using EndNote Basic, the author entered cited references from a three-year sample of core dental hygiene source journals from 2015–2017 into Excel 2016 and then sorted and analyzed the references. Two source journals from the 1999 mapping study [2], the Journal of Dental Hygiene and Probe (now called Canadian Journal of Dental Hygiene), were reused. The third source journal used in Haaland’s study, Journal of Practical Hygiene, is no longer published. After consulting with and interviewing the director and faculty of a dental hygiene program, Dimensions of Dental Hygiene was selected as a replacement, as it is a widely read journal covering practical issues. All three journals are North American–based titles. References from each journal article that were published from 2015–2017 in the three source journals were collected. Letters to the editor, editorials, supplementary issues, and brief news items were omitted. Each reference was given a unique identifier and categorized as one of five formats: journal (print or online), book (print or online), government publication (US or foreign, print or online), Internet source (not otherwise categorized as journal, book, or government publication), or miscellaneous (e.g., software, videos, dissertations, conference abstracts). The year of publication of each reference was noted. For journal citations, the cited journal name was recorded as the current or most recent title. The National Library of Medicine (NLM) catalog was used to track title changes. Spreadsheets of references from each journal were sorted by format and publication year. References from journal titles were listed in order from the most frequently cited to the least frequently cited. The list of journal titles was separated into three zones, each containing about a third of the total cited journal references. According to the NAHRS mapping protocol, these zones correspond roughly to the highly productive, moderately productive, and minimally productive journals in the field [1]. Data were then analyzed using Bradford’s Law of Scattering, which predicts that, in a given discipline, a small number of journals publishes a substantial portion of the literature, with the rest being widely scattered across titles. The number of Zone 1 journals multiplied by n equals the number of Zone 2 journals, and the number of Zone 3 journals is predicted to be n2 × the total number of journals in Zone 1 [10]. The indexing coverage of the cited journals in CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE was recorded. Coverage was determined from 2018 online title lists that database producers published and recorded as “yes,” “no,” or “selective.” A total of 10,901 cited references were recorded: 78.4% were journal articles, 8.4% were Internet sources, 6.5% were government documents, 5.1% were books, and 1.6% were miscellaneous (Table 1). Notably, over half of the references (n=6,299) came from Dimensions of Dental Hygiene. Over half (64.8%) of the cited journal articles and most of the cited Internet sources (90.1%) and government publications (85.6%) were published in 2007–2017 (Table 2). Zone 1 contained 11 journals that accounted for 33.5% of the cited references (Table 3). All Zone 1 journals were well-established titles, including 7 dental journals, 3 dental hygiene journals, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Zone 2 contained 108 journals and included a mixture of dental or oral health journals (61%) and non-dental journals (39%) such as JAMA, the New England Journal of Medicine, the American Journal of Public Health, MMWR, Academic Medicine, and the Journal of Allied Health. Compared with the 1999 mapping study [2], these results reflect a 13% increase in the citation of non-dental journals. According to Bradford’s Law of Scattering, the n for this study was 9.8 (108 journals in Zone 2/11 journals in Zone 1), meaning that the number of Zone 3 journals should be 1,056 (9.82 × 11). However, there were 1,556 journals in Zone 3, which was larger than predicted and might be attributed to the growing utilization of online-only journals. CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE indexed most of the resources in all three zones, but no single database indexed all of the resources (Table 4). EMBASE had slightly better coverage of Zone 1 and Zone 2 resources than MEDLINE, followed by CINAHL Complete. The most striking finding was the sheer volume of work that has been produced since the 1999 dental hygiene mapping study was performed. Previously, a small core of only 5 titles constituted Zone 1, which has now grown to 11 titles. In 1999, Zone 2 comprised 42 journals, which number has grown to 108. The total number of journals referenced has grown more than 4-fold from 389 to 1,675. Citation patterns may have been skewed by the fact that over half the citations came from Dimensions of Dental Hygiene, a journal that is highly practice oriented. The increased number of journal titles cited may be due to the use of web search engines, such as Google Scholar, for scholarly research. However, the 2 time periods are not strictly comparable due to the greater number of source articles (426 versus 149) and the larger number of citations (10,901 versus 2,632) in the present study. Bradford’s Law of Scattering, a unifying feature of NAHRS mapping studies, is described as “most valuable to librarians who are faced with the cost-benefit considerations of additional journal coverage” [11]. Based on Bradford’s classic, Documentation [12], this law postulates that journals in a discipline can be divided into three zones, each containing one-third of the references cited by writers in that discipline. Its utility for librarians lies in the assumption that Zone 1 contains a small number of core journals, which could be considered a library’s “must have” titles. Zone 2 is a larger number of “nice to have” journals, and Zone 3 contains an even larger number of titles to which one need not subscribe but which one may be asked to obtain. Because 78.4% of citations came from journals and one-third of these came from 11 core journals, the notion of “core” journals still seems viable. Traditional refereed journals have retained their preeminent place in dental hygiene research. In fact, the percentage of journal article citations increased from 69.5% of total cited references in the 1999 study [2] to 78.4% in the present study. Moreover, the same 5 journals occupied the top spots in both the 1999 and the present study, albeit in different order: Journal of Dental Hygiene, Journal of the American Dental Association, Journal of Periodontology, Journal of Dental Education, and Journal of Clinical Periodontology. All Zone 1 journals were refereed, and all but Dimensions of Dental Hygiene are subscription-based and might be less accessible to dental hygienists outside an academic setting. Two journal titles that began in 2003 now appear in Zone 1: Dimensions of Dental Hygiene, a refereed, practice-oriented title freely available on the web, and the International Journal of Dental Hygiene, a more research-oriented journal. Another interesting addition to Zone 1 is the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, which began in the 1990s and was cited ninety-one times. In all, Zone 1 contained seven dental titles, three dental hygiene titles, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. The Zone 1 journal list provides a good answer to the frequently asked question, “What are the ‘top’ journals in my field to which I should submit my manuscript?” A key development in dental hygiene research from 1999 to 2018 was the growth of the World Wide Web. In 1995, CompuServe and America Online began marketing dial-up access to end users [13], but most research literature was still used in print format. The 1999 mapping study [2] did not even mention the web or evidence-based practice. The present study, like other recent mapping studies, considers a fifth format type, “Internet sources,” which accounted for 8.1% of citations. A more accurate designation for this format type might be “Internet sources, not otherwise specified,” as most journal articles and government publications, and many books are now consulted online. One might expect the cited references in the present study to be more current than in the 1999 study [2], as online publishing allows quicker access, but this was not the case for journal articles. Interestingly, in the present study, only 64.8% of articles cited were published in the previous 10 years, compared with 71.1% in 1999 [2]. Perhaps researchers are partially switching to Internet sites or government publications for current information. Most Internet sources (72.1%) and government documents (71.8%) were 5 years old or less when they were cited. Conversely, historical sources were conspicuously absent from this sample. In both the 1999 study [2] and the present study, there was little use of materials that were older than 25 years. Only 3.8% of citations in 1999 [2] and 6.2% in the present study were more than 25 years old. Book citations, including both print and electronic books, shrank from 18.1% of total citations in 1999 [2] to 5.1% in the present study. This might be because researchers now browse the web for information that used to be found in books. Items

Undergraduate research has been increasingly recognized as a transformative pedagogical tool in higher education, particularly within the realm of medical education (Lopatto, 2007). Historically, research training was reserved for postgraduate students; however, recent shifts in educational paradigms emphasize the integration of research experiences at the undergraduate level to cultivate critical thinking, foster intellectual curiosity, and promote a deeper understanding of scientific inquiry (Hunter, Laursen, & Seymour, 2007). This shift in focus is aligned with a broader educational agenda aimed at preparing students to navigate complex, interdisciplinary issues they are likely to encounter in their professional careers (Healey & Jenkins, 2009). The inclusion of research components in undergraduate curricula is argued to have a range of benefits. Notably, it bridges the often-perceived gap between theory and practice, fostering a learning environment where students extend their knowledge beyond textbook theory to practical, context-driven applications (Russell, Hancock, & McCullough, 2007). Undergraduate research experiences (UREs) have been linked not only to the enhancement of academic skills but also to the development of personal and professional attributes such as resilience, leadership, and collaboration (Thiry, Weston, Laursen, & Hunter, 2012). Moreover, it has been demonstrated that participation in research at the undergraduate level is positively correlated with students' aspirations for further studies and careers within the scientific domain (Eagan et al., 2013). Despite these acknowledged benefits, the process by which students' perceptions of research and their approaches to learning transform through undergraduate research remains underexplored. While existing literature suggests that UREs can engender a more robust understanding of research processes (Bauer & Bennett, 2003), little is known about how these experiences concretely shape students' cognitive and epistemological views toward research and learning (Seymour, Hunter, Laursen, & Deantoni, 2004). In particular, the transformative learning perspectives of medical students engaged in research, who are often balancing demanding curricula with research activities, requires further investigation. An initial review of the literature indicates a gap in understanding how undergraduate research experiences particularly influence medical students. This demographic, with its unique educational journey and ultimate goal of becoming healthcare professionals, presents a distinct model for evaluating the impacts of UREs. Addressing the question of how medical students' perceptions of research and their learning approaches evolve over the course of participation in research projects could have significant implications for medical education curriculum design and pedagogical strategies. This study seeks to fill this gap by exploring the transformative experiences of third-year medical students engaged in undergraduate research. By employing a phenomenographic approach, this research delves into students' subjective perceptions and experiences, offering a rich, nuanced understanding of how engaging in research can shape their academic and professional trajectories. The research is guided by the following central research question: How do students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research? The contribution of this study is twofold. Firstly, it provides empirical insights into the cognitive changes that occur within medical students as they engage with research activities, thereby contributing to the broader discourse on the role of undergraduate research in higher education. Secondly, it identifies key factors that influence these changes, such as prior learning experiences, interpersonal communication preferences, and group dynamics, offering practical guidance for institutions looking to optimize their undergraduate research programs. By addressing these gaps, this study extends the understanding of undergraduate research as an educational practice and its broader implications for medical education. It argues for the intentional design of research opportunities that do not merely augment current medical curricula but transform how students engage with their learning environments. Insights drawn from this research can support educators and curriculum designers in crafting experiences that not only promote high-impact learning but also foster an enduring appreciation for scientific inquiry among future medical professionals. Ultimately, this research underscores the potential of undergraduate research experiences to effectuate meaningful educational reforms, illustrating how comprehensive engagement with research can redefine both the acquisition and application of knowledge within medical education. This positions undergraduate research not as an ancillary aspect of learning, but as a pivotal component in shaping innovative, research-oriented healthcare practitioners equipped to contribute to the dynamic landscape of medicine. This study employed a qualitative research design using a phenomenographic approach to explore and understand the variations in third-year medical students' perceptions of research and their approaches to learning throughout their participation in an undergraduate research project. Phenomenography was selected as the methodological framework because of its focus on the qualitative mapping of different ways in which individuals experience, conceptualize, understand, and perceive various phenomena (Marton, 1981). In this context, the phenomenon under investigation was the undergraduate research experience itself. The study sample consisted of 14 third-year medical students from a large university in the United States. These students were purposively selected based on their enrollment in a compulsory research methods course embedded within the medical curriculum. This course mandated participation in a semester-long research project, providing a suitable context for exploring changes in perceptions and approaches to learning. All participants provided informed consent prior to data collection, were assured of anonymity, and were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any point without penalty. Demographically, the participants varied in terms of gender, age, and prior research experience, offering a diverse array of perspectives on the research phenomenon. Data were collected using semi-structured individual interviews conducted both at the beginning and at the end of the research course. The pre-course interviews aimed to establish a baseline understanding of the students' initial perceptions of research and their approaches to learning. The open-ended interview questions focused on students' definitions and conceptions of research, their previous experiences, and their expectations for the upcoming research project. Sample questions included: "How would you define research?" and "What are your expectations for conducting research this semester?" The post-course interviews, conducted after the completion of the research project, aimed to capture any shifts in perceptions and learning approaches. These interviews built upon the themes identified in the pre-course responses. Questions were refined based on ongoing thematic analysis of pre-course data and observations during the research process. End-of-course questions included: "How has your perception of research changed after completing the project?" and "In what ways did participating in the research project influence your learning process?" Each interview lasted approximately 45 to 60 minutes and was audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim for subsequent analysis. Simultaneously, researcher-participant observations were carried out during select collaborative work sessions and presentations. These observations provided rich contextual data and allowed for methodological triangulation in understanding the interactions and challenges experienced by students in their research activities (Cohen et al., 2018). Data were analyzed using thematic analysis as outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006), with an emphasis on capturing the qualitative variation in participants' experiences. The analysis followed a structured yet iterative process, beginning with familiarization through repeated readings of the transcripts. Initial codes were generated inductively, capturing salient features of the data that aligned with the study's objectives. Codes were organized into potential themes that were then reviewed and refined to ensure consistency across the data and alignment with the phenomenographic focus on variation in experience (Åkerlind, 2012). Particular attention was given to identifying categories of description, representing qualitatively different ways of understanding the research process. These categories were validated through member-checking, allowing participants to provide feedback on the interpretations derived from their interview data. Furthermore, recurrent themes were mapped to highlight patterns of change in students' perceptions and approaches to learning from pre-course to post-course. Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the university where the study was conducted. Given the reflective nature of the interviews, participants were encouraged to consider the influence of their own biases and experiences on the research process. An emphasis on reflexivity was maintained throughout the study, with the principal researcher engaging in ongoing critical reflection to mitigate potential bias and ensure that the students' voices were authentically represented. While the phenomenographic approach provides deep insights into the students’ experiences, it is important to acknowledge that the findings may not be generalizable beyond the specific context and population studied. The relatively small sample size allowed for an in-depth exploration of individual experiences but does not permit broader generalizations. Nonetheless, the findings offer valuable implications for understanding the role of undergraduate research in medical education and contribute to the ongoing discourse on pedagogical strategies within this field. Phenomenology’s intentional focus on variation acknowledges the richness and complexity of student experiences, serving to inform evidence-based improvements in educational practice. The results of this study reveal significant transformations in students' perceptions of research and their approaches to learning following their engagement in undergraduate research projects. This section presents the key findings from both the pre-course and end-of-course interviews, highlighting the qualitative changes in perceptions and approaches among the 14 third-year medical students who participated in this study. At the outset of the course, we identified that a majority of the participants (71%, n=10) held a conventional understanding of research, primarily associating it with the scientific method and the production of new knowledge through hypothesis testing and experimental validation. This initial perception was largely outcome-focused, with students emphasizing the importance of generating tangible and publishable results. Several students openly admitted to seeing research as a distant and clinical endeavor, one that is primarily the domain of experienced scientists and academics, rather than a component of their personal education pathway. As the course progressed, however, we noted a marked shift in students' perceptions. By the end of the course, 86% of the students (n=12) began to redefine research as an engaging and iterative process, emphasizing its role in fostering critical thinking and problem-solving skills. For instance, a notable segment of students (64%, n=9) pointed to the autonomy involved in the research process, appreciating the opportunity to formulate their questions and design the methodology. This transition reflects a movement from a narrow view of research as a solitary task toward a more holistic appreciation of research as an inclusive and dynamic process (Biggs & Tang, 2011). Another significant theme, which emerged through qualitative coding of end-of-course interviews, was the recognition of collaboration and teamwork as intrinsic elements of the research process. Initially, only 29% of students (n=4) acknowledged the importance of collaborative work in research settings. However, post-course data showed that 93% (n=13) valued the experience of working in diverse research teams, highlighting that interpersonal interactions were crucial for fostering innovation and a deeper understanding of complex problems (Vygotsky, 1978). The ability to articulate ideas, synthesize multiple perspectives, and negotiate research directions in their teams was seen as transformative in their understanding and practice of research. Moreover, the end-of-course reflections indicated a notable epistemological shift in the students' approaches to learning, with 79% (n=11) expressing a preference for a deep approach to learning, as opposed to a surface or strategic approach noted in pre-course interviews (Marton & Säljö, 1976). This was evidenced by students actively seeking to understand underlying principles and relationships, rather than merely memorizing facts for exams. They demonstrated increased engagement with course materials and a greater propensity to integrate and apply theoretical knowledge in practical, research-related contexts. This shift underscores the beneficial impact of research experiences in promoting meaningful and contextually relevant learning (Entwistle, 2009). Despite these positive changes, the results also indicated challenges faced by students, which can be understood through the lens of prior learning experiences and cultural factors. In the turn of the millennium after over four decades of intensive research in the genetics of cancer, an important paradigm shift has occurred, in which instrumental for the development of the disease is not only the link between cumulative instability of key genes and the rise of aberrant cell cycle control, but also the orchestration of a heterogeneous cell-based stromal network supportive of tumor invasion and metastasis. This switch in focus has led to the elucidation of the composition of this microenvironmental niche and of the interaction dynamics of its multiple cellular and extracellular components. Concomitant have been the emergence of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) process as a key cellular mechanism in tumorigenesis, as well as the important discovery that stem cells of mesenchymal origin (mesenchymal stem cells (MSC)) can home towards tumor sites. The latter has formed the basis of an exciting new anti-cancer strategy, namely cancer cytotherapy, in which allogeneic MSC can be used to specifically target and deregulate the local tumor microenvironment, as an answer to modern oncology’s desperate need for a promising alternative to the current gold-standard therapy of combined chemotherapy (Additional file 1: Figure S1). Towards this end, various MSC populations have been recruited in different experimental setups in dozens of in vitro and in vivo preclinical studies. Unfortunately, until recently, MSC-based cancer cytotherapy has to a large extent failed to deliver its initial promise of a high-end translational oncology option. In their vast majority, the 500 or more clinical trials employing the use of MSC take advantage of the immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, and tissue regenerative properties of these cells for treating, for example, autoimmune diseases, graft rejection and osteochondral degeneration, without, until very recently, any significant data on the anti-cancer efficacy of MSC in humans. The problem of translating experimental MSC-based cancer cytotherapy work into successful human clinical trials is multi-faceted. In the case where MSC are engineered to overexpress molecules with anti-cancer properties, tumor suppression is achieved with relatively high efficiency and reproducibility in the majority of experimental protocols applied. Nevertheless, genetic engineering of cells not only adds extra costly and time-consuming manipulation steps in vitro, but also raises safety concerns since it usually relies on the use of viral vectors that introduce instability and chances of mutation at the genome integration sites of the host. On the other hand, the use of naïve, unmodified stem cells, although more straightforward, is hampered by contradictory findings, largely driven by the immense biological variability inherent to cell-based products and therapies (compared to traditional pharmaceuticals), as well as by multi-parameter variability relating to the methods, processes and manipulation steps mediating transformation of lab findings to clinical-grade products. With a mortality rate of nearly 60% for the over 14 million people diagnosed with cancer yearly worldwide, it is imperative that any novel therapeutic regime should be optimized to its full potential. Obviously, experimental cancer cytotherapy is at a nodal point, where the critical mass of information accumulated by the series of studies performed over the last two decades needs to be thoroughly revised, carefully analyzed, and properly evaluated in the context of immunobiology of the tumor microenvironment. With the first-in-human clinical trials assessing genetically modified MSC in gastrointestinal and lung cancer settings only very recently and more to follow, this task has become an essential one more than ever before [1]. More specifically, in order for the field to move forward, any new experimental attempt should be built upon (a) a clear understanding of the interactions between components of the local tumor environment during its progression from benign stromal tissue to a niche tuned to support growth, invasion, and metastasis of malignant cells and (b) careful experimental design that minimizes unnecessary duplication of work as well as the emergence of technical heterogeneity. With all the above in mind, we present here a systematic review of the advances in the MSC-based cancer cytotherapy field from its inception onwards, including the state-of-the art of the biology and relationship between the effectors (MSC populations) and targets (tumor niche components) implicated (discussed in the section “MSC and the tumor microenvironment—attributes and inter-relationship in the context of cancer cytotherapy”). Amalgamated in this review is a meta-analysis of the related bibliography, which was carefully designed and implemented in such a way to allow the extraction and decoding of the overwhelming number of experimental data presented therein and, hence enable the identification of commonalities and differences between studies, the dissection of emerging trends and patterns in reported findings, and possibly highlight any significant omissions or weaknesses in experimental design (presented in the “Methodology of the meta-analysis” and “Overview and discussion of the meta-analysis’ main findings” sections). Finally, in the concluding part (“Conclusions” section) of this review, an effort is made to both present the main findings as concise summary points in the context of state-of-the-art knowledge, which potentially can serve as a guide map, aiding the adoption of optimal conditions for the development of more efficient, translational cytotherapy protocols with extended clinical relevance. Cells within the tumor parenchyma are not self-sustaining entities, but develop in a symbiotic manner by interacting via paracrine and juxtacrine signaling with the surrounding stroma. The stromal microenvironment is the non-neoplastic compartment of tumors and comprises a dynamic and highly heterogeneous network of tumor vasculature (including pericytes), infiltrating inflammatory and immune cells, extracellular matrix (ECM), (myo) fibroblastic cells (also known as tumor-associated fibroblasts (TAFs)), mesenchymal stromal/stem cells, and sometimes adipocytes [2], as well as reactive stroma [3]. Most if not all solid tumors have some degree of tumor stroma, and the presence of reactive stroma is often an indicator of poor prognosis [4]. Communication between cellular components of the tumor microenvironment is achieved through cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and inflammatory and matrix remodeling enzymes that contribute to the malignant properties of the cells. Among the immune cells that infiltrate the tumor stroma and are present within the tumor microenvironment, selective T and B lymphocyte populations favor or suppress tumor growth and their detection has been associated with subsequent clinical outcomes [5–7]. Tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) and neutrophils (TAN) are usually pro-tumorigenic. TAMs participate actively in metastasis, being thus implicated in poor prognosis [8], while TANs enhance angiogenesis and immune suppression [9, 10]. Perivascular stromal cells, known as pericytes, are another essential component of the tumor stroma that secures vasculature maintenance by providing structural support to blood vessels [11]. Although pericytes are present within normal blood vessels, tumor vessels are characterized by excess pericyte coverage that contributes to their abnormal physiology. Fibroblastic stromal cells within the tumor stroma, known as TAFs, have been linked to several processes that promote cancer metastasis and growth, including angiogenesis [12], EMT [13], and progressive genetic instability [14, 15]. TAFs exert their tumor-promoting actions through secretion of growth factors, cytokines, chemokines, structural protein components, and metabolites that act upon tumor cells [2]. Additionally, fibroblastic stromal cells can deregulate antitumor immune responses, as exemplified by experiments demonstrating that allogeneic murine tumor cells, when co-injected with fibroblastic stromal cells, can engraft across immunologic barriers [16]. Together, these studies suggest that tissue-specific fibroblasts are influential players in the progression of metastatic cancer and, at first glance, appear to benefit tumor growth and decrease overall patient survival. However, there is mounting experimental evidence that healthy tumor microenvironments suppress tumor growth, and it is only after acquisition of tumor-like genetic lesions that fibroblasts appear to promote tumor progression [14, 17, 18]. ECM is another key regulator of tumor development and progression by providing both a structural scaffold for the tumor stroma and also active soluble factors including growth and angiogenic factors, cytokines, and chemokines that regulate tumor behavior. During tumor development, the ECM is usually disorganized and collagen deposition as well as cross-linking with other matrix proteins such as elastins, laminins, or fibronectin has been associated with cancer invasion and metastasis [19]. Among the ECM-secreted growth factors, TGF-β is known to promote EMT in cancer cells, thus increasing local and distant invasive potential [20]. ΕΜΤ is the process by which epithelial cells reduce the expression or function of proteins that promote cell-cell and cell-basement-membrane adhesion and thus obtain a mesenchymal-like phenotype. Except for the regulation of metastatic properties, the EMT has been also associated with acquired drug resistance [21]. Furthermore, high expression of EMT-induced markers (vimentin, α-smooth muscle actin (a-SMA), N-cadherin, cadherin 11, SpArC, laminin and fascin) with simultaneous low expression of E-cadherin has been associated with poor prognosis in patients with breast cancer [22]. Stem cells possess a unique capacity of self-renewal, differentiation into multiple cell types and in vivo tissue repopulation [23]. These functions are triggered by signals that impel a stem cell to undergo either symmetric or asymmetric divisions [24]. Based on their ability to give rise to one or more different cell lineages, stem cells are characterized as totipotent (able to give rise to all cells constituting the developing embryo), pluripotent (e.g., isolated embryonic stem cells (ESC) that can differentiate into cells of all three germ layers), multipotent (capacity for differentiation towards most cell lineages), and unipotent (mono-specific differentiation). Mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) are multipotent stem cells that upon stimulation give rise to most body cell types including those of muscle, bone, fat, and cartilage lineages [25]. MSC were originally isolated from bone marrow (BM) aspirates; nevertheless, they can be isolated from many types of adult and fetal tissues using similar methodologies [26]. Adipose tissue (AT) provides a particularly abundant and accessible source, although many other adult tissue sites can also be utilized including kidney, skin, and the parathyroid gland [27]. In another study, it has also been suggested that a small population of MSC circulates within the peripheral blood and is highly mobilized during hypoxia [28]. MSC or MSC-like cells have been isolated from fetal tissues as well, including skin, cord blood (-CB), umbilical cord (-UC), and placenta [29]. Regardless of their origin, these MSC share similar defining characteristics including plastic adherence, cell surface marker expression (negative for hematopoietic markers CD34, CD35/positive for core markers CD29, CD44, CD73, CD90, CD105), and at least a tri-lineage differentiation potential (towards fat, bone, cartilage) under certain conditions [26]. The native functions are thought to include wound healing and support of hematopoiesis. More interestingly, when engrafted at sites of injury, MSC differentiate into connective tissue elements, support vasculogenesis, and secrete cytokines and growth factors that facilitate healing and tissue regeneration. In addition, due to their complex immunomodulatory properties, MSC can counteract inflammation, suppress host immune responses, and prevent fibrosis [30]. As a consequence of their diverse properties, MSC have been extensively utilized in the last decade in therapeutic applications such as tissue repair and regeneration, as well as autoimmune disease [31]. For example, the immunosuppressive effects of MSC have been used for therapy of graft-vs.-host disease (first MSC biologic drug). Another common feature of MSC is that they are able to localize to sites of hematopoiesis, inflammation, or injury as well as to solid tumors, by a mechanism characterized as homing. Tumor tropism distinguishes MSC from other mesenchymal cells, such as differentiated fibroblasts [32]. This homing ability of MSC to injured sites and their interaction with the local microenvironment has encouraged investigation into the possibility of using these cells, either unmodified or as gene or even drug delivery vehicles for targeted cytotherapy, most notably cancer treatment [33, 34]. Interestingly, it has also been shown that co-injection of MSC promotes growth of various tumors in vivo, possibly due to the immunosuppressive effects that help cancer cells escape immunosurveillance [16, 35]. Tumor tropism of MSC and the dynamic interaction between MSC and the tumor microenvironment, due to their complexity as well as their significance for cancer therapy, require a deeper understanding and merit further investigation and hence are discussed in more detail in the following sections of this review. Homing is the process by which cells migrate to, and engraft in, the tissue in which they can exert local functional effects. It is well established that MSC are recruited to sites of injury to support tissue repair, stem cell homeostasis, and immunomodulation. Tumors

Aphasia is one of the most common and disabling consequences of left-hemisphere stroke, affecting roughly a third of stroke survivors and persisting into the chronic phase in a substantial proportion of them (Engelter et al., 2006; Flowers et al., 2016). It is not a unitary disorder. Patients differ in which components of language are affected (e.g., phonology, semantics, syntax, fluency), in how severely, and in the extent to which domain-general cognitive abilities such as short-term memory and executive function are also compromised (Butler et al., 2014; Fridriksson et al., 2018; Lacey et al., 2017). Classical taxonomies (Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction, anomic aphasia and so on) capture some of this heterogeneity but are poorly suited to the graded, multidimensional profiles seen in real patients, and many individuals are unclassifiable or shift between categories over time (Kertesz & Poole, 1974; Wilson et al., 2018). Data-driven approaches have therefore been used to derive the underlying dimensions of impairment directly from patients' performance on extensive behavioural batteries. Principal component analysis (PCA) and related methods have consistently identified a small number of latent factors, typically reflecting phonological, semantic, fluency/speech production and cognitive-executive abilities, which together explain most of the variance in aphasic performance (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015; Ingram et al., 2020). These factors have, in turn, been related to lesion location and white-matter damage, providing a more graded and mechanistically interpretable account of brain–behaviour relationships than aphasia syndromes (Halai et al., 2017; Kümmerer et al., 2013; Schumacher et al., 2019). Alongside these impairment scores, the paraphasias that patients produce are central to the clinical description of aphasia. Errors in picture naming, in particular, are used to characterise the nature of the underlying disorder: semantic paraphasias (e.g., "dog" for cat) are typically taken to indicate disrupted semantic representation or lexical selection, phonological paraphasias and neologisms (e.g., "cap" or "tat" for cat) to indicate disrupted phonological retrieval or encoding, and omissions, circumlocutions and dysfluent attempts to reflect other failures of retrieval or articulation (Dell et al., 1997; Schwartz et al., 2006; Kohn & Goodglass, 1985). Error types are explicitly included in the diagnostic criteria and classification of aphasia and form the basis of influential computational models, such as the interactive two-step model, in which the relative proportions of semantic and phonological errors are used to estimate the integrity of semantic-lexical and lexical-phonological mappings (Dell et al., 1997; Foygel & Dell, 2000; Schwartz et al., 2006). Lesion-symptom mapping studies of naming errors have reported that semantic errors are associated with damage to anterior temporal and middle temporal regions, whereas phonological errors are linked to damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus and the underlying arcuate fasciculus (Schwartz et al., 2009; Walker et al., 2011; Mirman et al., 2015; Halai et al., 2017; Pillay et al., 2017). Despite this, the field has largely treated language impairments and paraphasias as separate topics. Most studies of the neural basis of aphasia have focused on scores summarising deficits, whereas studies of paraphasias have often been conducted in isolation, with little reference to the patients' broader language-cognitive profile. This separation is problematic for several reasons. First, the relationship between impairments and errors is unlikely to be one-to-one. Semantic errors, for example, may arise not only from degraded semantic knowledge but also from impaired phonological retrieval, reduced executive control over competing alternatives, or limited speech output (Mirman et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 2006; Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006). Similarly, omissions may reflect failures at multiple processing stages and are often excluded from analyses or considered uninformative. Second, previous studies of errors have typically examined a restricted subset of error categories, commonly semantic and phonological, or have collapsed errors into experimenter-defined composite scores or ratios. Such approaches presuppose a particular theoretical account, ignore the co-occurrence structure of the full range of errors patients produce, and may obscure the relationship between less-studied categories (e.g., circumlocutions, mixed errors, dysfluent responses) and underlying deficits. Third, because errors and impairment scores are rarely modelled together, the lesion correlates reported for each are difficult to relate, and it remains unclear whether error-based and deficit-based analyses converge on the same neural substrates or capture partially distinct aspects of the aphasic syndrome. An integrated, data-driven framework is needed to address these issues. Such a framework should (i) derive the structure of paraphasias empirically, from the pattern of co-occurrence across a broad set of error types, rather than imposing a theory-driven selection or combination; (ii) align this error structure with the patients' multidimensional language and cognitive profile within a single model; and (iii) relate the resulting fused dimensions to lesion data, so that errors, deficits and neural correlates can be considered simultaneously, that is, "triangulated". Dimension-reduction techniques such as PCA are well suited to this purpose, as they identify orthogonal latent factors, permit the examination of cross-loadings (and thus many-to-many mappings between errors and impairments), and produce continuous factor scores that can be used in lesion-symptom mapping without the need for arbitrary categorisation (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015). In the present study, we applied this approach to a cohort of individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia who completed an extensive language and cognitive battery and a picture-naming task in which responses were coded into fifteen error types. In the first step, we used PCA to establish the pattern of co-occurrence among these error types. In the second step, we entered the resulting error components, together with the patients' scores from the neuropsychological battery, into an omnibus PCA to generate fused impairment-paraphasia factors. In the third step, we mapped these factors onto the patients' structural lesion profiles to identify their neural correlates. We asked three questions: (1) what are the latent dimensions underlying naming errors when all error types are considered together; (2) how do these dimensions map onto language and cognitive impairments, and which relationships are one-to-one versus distributed across multiple factors; and (3) which lesion correlates are associated with the fused factors, and do they converge with the existing literature? This study makes three contributions. Methodologically, it offers a unified, theory-agnostic model that avoids selective focus on particular errors or experimenter-derived composites. Empirically, it clarifies the complex relationships between specific error types and underlying deficits, including those for omissions and circumlocutions that have been comparatively neglected. Neurally, it tests whether the lesion correlates of these combined factors align with established regions implicated in phonology, semantics and speech production, thereby providing a more complete characterisation of post-stroke aphasia. Participants We analysed behavioural and neuroimaging data from a cohort of patients with chronic post-stroke aphasia recruited from community stroke groups and clinical services (cf. Halai et al., 2017; Butler et al., 2014). Inclusion criteria were: a left-hemisphere middle cerebral artery infarct at least one year before testing; premorbid right-handedness and native English fluency; no history of other neurological or psychiatric disorder; and no contraindication to MRI. Patients were included if they had a clinical diagnosis of aphasia confirmed by the Western Aphasia Battery-Revised (WAB-R; Kertesz, 2007) and had completed both the picture-naming task and the extended language-cognitive battery described below. Patients gave written informed consent, with supported-consent procedures for those with comprehension difficulties, and the study was approved by the local National Health Service research ethics committee. The sample comprised 70 patients (age and demographic details are given in the Results). Neuropsychological assessment Each patient completed a detailed battery spanning language and cognition, following the approach used in earlier data-driven studies of aphasia (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015). Phonological processing was assessed with tasks of auditory discrimination (e.g., same-different judgement of minimal pairs from PALPA; Kay et al., 1992), repetition of words and nonwords, and phoneme segmentation and blending. Semantic processing was assessed with the 64-item Cambridge Semantic Battery (Bozeat et al., 2000), including spoken word-to-picture matching, picture-based and written-word-based semantic association tests (Camel and Cactus Test), and category fluency. Phonological working memory was indexed by digit span (forward and backward) and word and nonword span tasks. Executive-cognitive function was assessed with Raven’s Coloured Progressive Matrices (Raven, 1962), a brief test of visuospatial and attention function, and a test of nonverbal reasoning. Speech production and fluency were quantified from the WAB-R spoken-output subscales and from connected speech elicited by the Cinderella story-telling task (Saffran et al., 1989), from which we derived the number of words, number of utterances and speech rate per minute (collectively termed “speech quanta”). Reading and writing tasks were also administered but are not analysed here. All scores were converted to percentage correct, or to the appropriate continuous measure, and entered into analyses in a consistent direction such that higher values indicated better performance, except for the error-based variables described below. Picture naming and error coding Picture naming was assessed with the 60-item Object and Action Naming Battery (Druks & Masterson, 2000), with items presented one at a time on a computer screen and patients allowed ample time to respond. Responses were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The first complete response (or, where explicitly self-corrected, the final response) was coded by trained raters who were blind to lesion data. Each response was classified into one of fifteen mutually exclusive categories adapted from existing taxonomies (Dell et al., 1997; Schwartz et al., 2006; Kümmerer et al., 2013): correct; omission or “don’t know”; semantic paraphasia (same category or associate); circumlocution; mixed semantic-phonological error; formal paraphasia (real-word phonological error); phonological paraphasia (nonword with substantial target overlap); neologism (nonword with little overlap); unrelated word; visual error; perseveration; phonemic cue-dependent response; dysfluent response (stuttering, effortful or abandoned attempts, or repeated fragments); description of function or gesture; and a residual “other” category. Two raters independently coded 25% of responses (Cohen’s κ = 0.87), with disagreements resolved by consensus before one rater coded the remainder. For each patient, the number of responses in each category was expressed as a proportion of total trials, giving fifteen error-rate variables. The correct category was excluded from the error analysis, as it is the complement of the total error set. Neuroimaging acquisition and lesion identification Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired on a 3.0T Philips Achieva scanner with an eight-element SENSE head coil (voxel size 1 × 1 × 1 mm³). Lesions were identified using an automated, patient-specific approach (Seghier et al., 2008): images were normalised to MNI space using a modified unified segmentation-normalisation procedure in SPM, with an additional tissue class for abnormal tissue, and fuzzy-clustering outliers relative to a healthy control sample were thresholded to give binary lesion maps. The maps were checked and, where necessary, manually corrected by an expert neurologist. Lesion volume was calculated for each patient and used as a covariate in lesion analyses. Statistical analysis Step 1: Principal component analysis of paraphasias. To characterise the co-occurrence of errors without selecting a subset of error types or imposing experimenter-defined groupings, the fifteen error-rate variables were entered into a PCA with varimax rotation. Because error proportions are skewed and zero-inflated, variables were examined for distributional properties and, where appropriate, transformed prior to analysis. Sampling adequacy was assessed with the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure and Bartlett’s test of sphericity. The number of components was determined by the Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1) in conjunction with inspection of the scree plot and parallel analysis (Horn, 1965). The PCA decomposes the standardised data matrix X (patients × variables) as X = TPᵀ + E, where T contains the component scores, P the loadings, and E the residual. Rotated loadings with absolute value ≥ 0.4 were used for interpretation. Component scores for each patient were saved for subsequent analysis. Step 2: Omnibus PCA fusing impairments and errors. To align error patterns with underlying deficits, the five paraphasia component scores were combined with the patients’ scores from the neuropsychological battery in a second PCA. The human vocal tract is a dynamic and complex system that plays a crucial role in generating distinguishable speech sounds. The shape and configuration of the vocal tract, including the position and movement of the lips, tongue, and jaw, modulate the airflow and create different resonant cavities, resulting in the production of diverse speech sounds (Johnson, 2003). Understanding the relationship between vocal tract configurations and speech production is essential for developing effective speech recognition systems, as well as for improving our knowledge of the underlying mechanisms of speech production (Stevens, 2000). Recent advances in real-time magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have enabled researchers to non-invasively capture the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the vocal tract's role in speech production (Narayanan et al., 2011). The vocal tract's shape and configuration contain abundant information that can be utilized to better understand the underlying speech production mechanism. Studies have shown that the vocal tract's geometry and dynamics can be used to identify different speech sounds, such as vowels and consonants (Story, 2007). For example, the shape of the vocal tract during the production of a vowel sound can be used to distinguish between different vowel categories (Fujimura, 1975). Furthermore, research has demonstrated that the vocal tract's dynamics, including the movement and velocity of the articulators, can provide valuable information for speech recognition (Ostry et al., 1997). However, the majority of these studies have focused on the analysis of static vocal tract configurations, and the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production remains poorly understood (Mitra et al., 2010). The development of automatic speech recognition systems that can effectively map vocal tract shape geometry to acoustics is a long-standing goal in the field of speech processing (Lee et al., 2013). Traditional speech recognition systems rely on acoustic features, such as mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), to recognize speech sounds (Davis et al., 1980). However, these systems often struggle to recognize speech in noisy environments or when the speaker has a strong accent (Liu et al., 2015). The use of vocal tract geometry and dynamics offers a promising alternative to traditional acoustic features, as it can provide more robust and speaker-independent representations of speech sounds (Guenther et al., 2006). Despite the potential benefits of using vocal tract geometry and dynamics for speech recognition, there are several challenges that must be addressed. One of the primary challenges is the development of effective algorithms for analyzing and recognizing the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract (Kim et al., 2012). Traditional computer vision techniques, such as those used for object recognition, are not well-suited for analyzing the dynamic and complex movements of the vocal tract (Wang et al., 2013). Recently, deep learning-based approaches, such as Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) models, have shown great promise for analyzing and recognizing complex sequential data, including videos and speech signals (Donahue et al., 2015). The research question that this paper aims to address is: Can effective video action recognition techniques, such as LRCN models, be used to identify different vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences from dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in real-time MRI data? To answer this question, we will employ a database consisting of 2D real-time MRI of vocal tract shaping during VCV utterances by 17 speakers. The use of real-time MRI data provides a unique opportunity to analyze the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production, and the application of LRCN models offers a promising approach for recognizing the complex sequential patterns in this data. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of LRCN models for analyzing and recognizing the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production. Secondly, we show that the use of vocal tract geometry and dynamics can provide more robust and speaker-independent representations of speech sounds compared to traditional acoustic features. Finally, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of LRCN models for speech recognition tasks, including a comparison of different parameter settings and classification tasks. The results of this study have significant implications for the development of automatic speech recognition systems, and highlight the potential benefits of using vocal tract geometry and dynamics for speech recognition. The primary objective of this study was to investigate the feasibility of employing Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) models for automatic speech identification from vocal tract shape dynamics in real-time MRI. To achieve this, we utilized a database consisting of 2D real-time MRI scans of vocal tract shaping during vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) utterances by 17 speakers (Kim et al., 2017). The database was collected using a real-time MRI scanner with a frame rate of 23.19 frames per second, resulting in a total of 10,000 frames per speaker (Narayanan et al., 2011). Each speaker uttered a set of 20 different VCV sequences, with each sequence repeated five times, yielding a total of 100 utterances per speaker. The data was pre-processed to extract the vocal tract contours from each frame, which were then used to create a sequence of binary masks representing the vocal tract shape dynamics (Wang et al., 2018). These binary masks were used as input to the LRCN model, which consisted of a convolutional neural network (CNN) based deep hierarchical visual feature extractor and a recurrent network (RN) (Donahue et al., 2015). The CNN was designed to extract spatial features from each frame, while the RN was used to model the temporal relationships between frames (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). The LRCN model was trained using a leave-one-speaker-out cross-validation approach, where the data from 16 speakers was used for training and the data from the remaining speaker was used for testing (Kohavi, 1995). This approach was repeated for each speaker, resulting in 17 different models, each trained on a different subset of the data. The performance of each model was evaluated using a set of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score (Sokolova & Lapalme, 2009). The hyperparameters of the LRCN model, including the number of convolutional layers, the number of recurrent layers, and the learning rate, were optimized using a grid search approach (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012). To investigate the effect of different parameter settings on the performance of the LRCN model, we conducted a series of experiments with varying numbers of convolutional and recurrent layers (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). The results showed that increasing the number of convolutional layers improved the performance of the model, but at the cost of increased computational complexity (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). On the other hand, increasing the number of recurrent layers improved the performance of the model, but only up to a certain point, beyond which the performance began to degrade (Pascanu et al., 2013). In addition to the LRCN model, we also investigated the performance of other video action recognition techniques, including the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) (Karpathy et al., 2014). The results showed that the LRCN model outperformed both the CNN and RNN models, demonstrating the importance of modeling both spatial and temporal relationships in vocal tract shape dynamics (Ng et al., 2015). Furthermore, we compared the performance of the LRCN model with other state-of-the-art models, including the Two-Stream Convolutional Neural Network (Two-Stream CNN) and the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network (Feichtenhofer et al., 2016; Graves et al., 2013). The results showed that the LRCN model achieved comparable performance to these state-of-the-art models, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling vocal tract shape dynamics. The statistical analysis of the results was performed using a paired t-test to compare the performance of the LRCN model with other models (Dietterich, 1998). The results showed that the LRCN model significantly outperformed the other models, with a p-value of less than 0.01. Additionally, we used a confusion matrix to analyze the errors made by the LRCN model, which showed that the majority of errors occurred between similar VCV sequences (Stehman, 1997). This suggests that the LRCN model was able to capture the underlying patterns in the vocal tract shape dynamics, but struggled to distinguish between similar sequences. To further investigate the performance of the LRCN model, we conducted a series of experiments with different types of noise added to the input data (Vincent et al., 2010). The results showed that the LRCN model was robust to small amounts of noise, but its performance degraded significantly with increasing levels of noise. This suggests that the LRCN model is sensitive to the quality of the input data and requires high-quality data to achieve optimal performance. Furthermore, we investigated the effect of different frame rates on the performance of the LRCN model, which showed that increasing the frame rate improved the performance of the model, but at the cost of increased computational complexity (Chen et al., 2018).
