The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) epidemic continues to disproportionately affect certain populations, with men who have sex with men (MSM) and other marginalized groups bearing a significant burden of the disease (Baral et al., 2014). In many African nations, the prevalence of HIV among MSM is substantially higher than among the general population, with some studies suggesting that MSM are up to 10 times more likely to be living with HIV (Beyrer et al., 2011). This disparity is often attributed to a combination of factors, including limited access to healthcare services, social stigma, and discriminatory laws and policies (Garcia et al., 2016). In particular, laws that penalize same-sex intercourse contribute to a cycle of stigma, homonegativity, and discrimination, which can dissuade individuals from seeking treatment and healthcare providers from offering it (Altman et al., 2012). In many African countries, anti-homosexuality laws are a major obstacle to effective HIV prevention and treatment efforts (Eba, 2017). These laws, which criminalize same-sex relationships and often carry severe penalties, can lead to a climate of fear and intimidation, making it difficult for individuals to access healthcare services or disclose their sexual behavior to healthcare providers (Kawachi et al., 2017). Furthermore, anti-homosexuality laws can also limit the ability of healthcare providers to offer targeted HIV prevention and treatment services to MSM, as they may be reluctant to provide services that are perceived as promoting or condoning same-sex behavior (Percy et al., 2017). The US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) is a major international initiative aimed at reducing the burden of HIV in developing countries, including many African nations (PEPFAR, 2020). Since its inception, PEPFAR has provided billions of dollars in funding for HIV prevention and treatment programs, and has played a significant role in reducing the global HIV epidemic (Institute of Medicine, 2013). However, despite its successes, PEPFAR has faced criticism for its approach to addressing the needs of marginalized populations, including MSM (Amon et al., 2014). In particular, it has been argued that PEPFAR has not done enough to address the root causes of stigma and discrimination, including anti-homosexuality laws, which perpetuate the HIV epidemic among MSM (Kriel, 2017). A significant gap in the existing literature is the lack of analysis on the role of PEPFAR in addressing anti-homosexuality laws and related stigma in African countries (Gupta et al., 2018). While there have been numerous studies on the impact of PEPFAR on HIV prevention and treatment outcomes, few have examined the program's response to the specific challenges faced by MSM in Africa (Haberer et al., 2017). Furthermore, there is a need for a more nuanced understanding of how PEPFAR's policies and practices have addressed the intersection of HIV, stigma, and human rights in the region (Smith et al., 2019). This study aims to address this gap by analyzing the ways in which PEPFAR has addressed anti-homosexuality laws and related stigma in African countries. Specifically, the research question guiding this study is: What role has PEPFAR played in addressing the criminalization of homosexuality in African nations, and how have its policies and practices contributed to reducing stigma and promoting human rights for MSM? By examining PEPFAR's approach to addressing anti-homosexuality laws and related stigma, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between HIV, human rights, and international development programs. The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive analysis of PEPFAR's policies and practices related to anti-homosexuality laws and stigma in African countries, highlighting both successes and challenges (Collins et al., 2018). Secondly, it sheds light on the ways in which international development programs can contribute to promoting human rights and reducing stigma for marginalized populations, including MSM (Stahlman et al., 2019). Finally, it offers recommendations for how PEPFAR and other international development programs can better address the intersection of HIV, human rights, and stigma in African countries, with a focus on promoting more effective and sustainable responses to the HIV epidemic (Dworkin et al., 2018). By examining the role of PEPFAR in addressing anti-homosexuality laws and related stigma, this study aims to inform more effective and sustainable responses to the HIV epidemic in African countries, and to promote greater awareness and understanding of the complex relationships between HIV, human rights, and international development programs. This study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis techniques to examine the relationship between anti-homosexual legislation and HIV-related stigma in African nations, with a specific focus on the role of the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) program. The research design involved a comprehensive review of existing literature, policy documents, and datasets related to PEPFAR's operations in Africa, as well as an in-depth analysis of the legal frameworks governing homosexuality in African countries (Altman et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2015). We identified 21 African countries that received significant PEPFAR funding, aimed at reducing the HIV epidemic, and assessed the homosexuality laws in these countries. This assessment was based on data from reputable sources, including the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association (ILGA) and the Human Rights Watch, which provide detailed information on laws and policies related to sexual orientation and gender identity worldwide (ILGA, 2020; Human Rights Watch, 2020). To gather data on PEPFAR's policies and practices related to reducing stigma and addressing the criminalization of homosexuality, we examined PEPFAR Policy Framework agreements, also known as Partnership Frameworks, which are documents outlining the strategic plans and commitments between the US government and partner countries (PEPFAR, 2020). These agreements typically include provisions aimed at reducing stigma and discrimination against people living with HIV and key populations at higher risk of infection, such as men who have sex with men (MSM) and sex workers (SW) (Kurth et al., 2013). We analyzed 14 Partnership Framework agreements associated with the 16 PEPFAR-funded countries in Africa that have laws characterized as harsh in relation to homosexuality. This analysis involved a systematic review of the agreements to identify any language or provisions that explicitly address the decriminalization of homosexuality or the reduction of penalties on individuals who engage in homosexual behavior. The qualitative analysis of the Partnership Framework agreements and other PEPFAR documents, such as country operational plans and progress reports, was conducted using a thematic analysis approach (Braun & Clarke, 2006). This involved coding and categorizing the data to identify patterns and themes related to PEPFAR's response to anti-homosexuality laws and its efforts to reduce stigma and discrimination against key populations. The coding framework was developed based on the research objectives and included themes such as "stigma reduction," "homosexuality laws," "key populations," and "human rights" (Vitoria et al., 2017). The analysis was conducted by two independent reviewers to ensure inter-rater reliability and consistency in the coding process. In addition to the qualitative analysis, we also conducted a quantitative analysis of the PEPFAR funding data to examine the relationship between PEPFAR funding levels and the presence of harsh anti-homosexuality laws in African countries. This analysis involved descriptive statistics and correlation analysis to identify any patterns or associations between PEPFAR funding and the legal environment related to homosexuality (Mukherjee et al., 2017). The data on PEPFAR funding were obtained from the PEPFAR website and included information on the annual funding allocations to each country from 2004 to 2020. The analysis was conducted using statistical software, and the results were interpreted in the context of the research objectives and the qualitative findings. To ensure the validity and reliability of the findings, we employed several strategies, including data triangulation, which involved combining multiple data sources and methods to confirm the results (Denzin, 2012). We also conducted a thorough review of the literature to contextualize the findings and provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex issues surrounding anti-homosexuality laws, HIV-related stigma, and PEPFAR's response in African nations. The study's limitations were acknowledged, and the findings were interpreted in light of these limitations, which included the potential for bias in the data sources and the complexity of the issues being studied (Beyrer et al., 2011). Overall, the mixed-methods approach and the comprehensive analysis of the data provided a rich and nuanced understanding of the role of PEPFAR in addressing anti-homosexuality laws and HIV-related stigma in African nations. The analysis of the PEPFAR Policy Framework agreements revealed that while most of the agreements included provisions aimed at reducing stigma and discrimination, none of them explicitly addressed the decriminalization of homosexuality or the reduction of penalties on individuals who engage in homosexual behavior. This finding suggests that PEPFAR has missed opportunities to explicitly address the role of the criminalization of homosexuality in fueling stigmatizing attitudes and hindering the response to the HIV epidemic in African nations (Amon et al., 2012). The quantitative analysis of the PEPFAR funding data revealed a pattern of higher funding allocations to countries with harsh anti-homosexuality laws, which may indicate a lack of consideration for the legal environment related to homosexuality in PEPFAR's funding decisions (Bingham et al., 2018). These findings have significant implications for PEPFAR's programming and policy development, highlighting the need for a more explicit and comprehensive approach to addressing anti-homosexuality laws and HIV-related stigma in African nations. In conclusion, the methods employed in this study provided a comprehensive understanding of the complex issues surrounding anti-homosexuality laws, HIV-related stigma, and PEPFAR's response in African nations. The mixed-methods approach and the analysis of the PEPFAR Policy Framework agreements and funding data revealed significant findings that highlight the need for PEPFAR to explicitly address the role of the criminalization of homosexuality in fueling stigmatizing attitudes and hindering the response to the HIV epidemic. The study's findings have implications for PEPFAR's programming and policy development, and they underscore the importance of considering the legal environment related to homosexuality in PEPFAR's funding decisions and strategic planning. These laws not only criminalize same-sex intercourse but also perpetuate a cycle of stigma, homonegativity, and discrimination, making it challenging for gay men and other men who have sex with men (MSM) to access HIV prevention and treatment services (Smith et al., 2015). Among the top eight PEPFAR-funded countries in Africa, seven had harsh anti-homosexuality laws, including Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Democratic Republic of Congo, and South Africa (PEPFAR, 2020). The presence of these laws is a significant concern, as they can drive the HIV epidemic underground, making it difficult to reach key populations with effective prevention and treatment interventions (Beyrer et al., 2011). We examined the PEPFAR Policy Framework agreements associated with these countries and found that most (14 out of 16) of the African 'Partnership Framework' (PEPFAR) policy agreements between African governments and the US State Department call for stigma reduction (87.5%) (PEPFAR, 2019). The failure to address the root causes of stigma, including the criminalization of homosexuality, may undermine the effectiveness of PEPFAR's efforts to reduce stigma and promote HIV prevention and treatment (Auerbach et al., 2011). Introduction Anaemia, characterized by a deficiency in the number or quality of red blood cells, is a prevalent health challenge that disproportionately affects children across the globe, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. It manifests primarily as fatigue, lethargy, and impaired cognitive function, severely impacting children's overall health and academic performance. The etiology of anaemia in children is frequently multifactorial, involving nutritional deficiencies, genetic disorders, and infectious diseases, with iron deficiency being the most common cause (World Health Organization, 2020). Iron is a critical micronutrient necessary for cognitive development, influencing neurotransmitter function, myelination, and brain energy metabolism (Beard, 2003). Despite the growing body of literature around anaemia's impact on health outcomes, there remains limited evidence from South Africa specifically examining its effects on cognitive and psychomotor development in school-aged children. In the context of South Africa's educational landscape, where disparities in educational attainment are starkly aligned with socioeconomic status, understanding the factors influencing cognitive development and school performance is paramount (van der Berg, 2008). The prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency in South African children has been reported to be significant, yet there is sparse literature directly correlating these deficiencies with academic achievement (Labadarios et al., 2011). This gap represents a missed opportunity for targeted interventions that can mitigate education and health inequities in disadvantaged communities. Prior international studies have underscored the detrimental effects of iron deficiency on children's cognitive and psychomotor skills (Lozoff et al., 2006). Specifically, iron deficiency in early childhood has been linked to long-term deficits in mental and motor development as well as behavioral problems. Such findings stress the critical need for early detection and management of anaemia to prevent the potential adverse impacts on educational outcomes (Grantham-McGregor and Ani, 2001). However, there is a paucity of data from South African contexts that adequately explores this phenomenon and provides a foundation for culturally relevant and pragmatic interventions. Our study aimed to address this research gap by examining the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency among school-aged children in a peri-urban disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, and investigating their associations with psychomotor development and school performance. This research is significant for several reasons. Firstly, it builds upon existing knowledge, providing context-specific insights that align with the challenges faced by South African children. Such insights are crucial for informing policy and program development aimed at improving child health and educational outcomes in similar settings across the region. Furthermore, the study contributes to the literature by using a multidimensional approach to investigate the associations between anaemia and school performance. This approach encompasses clinical assessments, biochemical evaluations, and qualitative insights from caregivers and educators, offering a holistic picture of the potential impacts of iron deficiency on child development. By elucidating the relationships between these variables, this study provides empirical evidence necessary to advocate for the integration of health interventions into educational policies. The research questions guiding this study are: (1) What is the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency in the sample of school-aged children from KwaZulu-Natal? (2) How are these health conditions associated with psychomotor development and school performance? Through answering these questions, this study aims to unearth actionable insights that can propel both local and broader educational and health agendas. In sum, while prior research has explored the associations between anaemia, iron deficiency, and cognitive outcomes, the evidence specific to the South African context, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, remains scarce. This study not only seeks to bridge this gap but also aims to provide a framework for future research that can support the implementation of effective health and educational interventions. The findings of this investigation have the potential to inform strategies to prevent anaemia and related complications, ultimately contributing to improved educational achievement and broader societal progress. Data, Design, Procedures, Statistical Analysis The present study employed a cross-sectional design to explore the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency, and their respective impacts on cognitive development and school performance among school-aged children in a peri-urban community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The study was conducted over a six-month period, from January to June 2022, using a sample size of 184 children, aged 6 to 8 years. The target population was selected from two primary schools situated in the specified community, chosen for their accessibility and representation of the broader demographic of rural and peri-urban South African schools. The study was approved by the institutional review board and adhered to ethical standards for research involving minors, including obtaining informed consent from parents or guardians and assent from the children involved. Data Collection The study utilized a multi-faceted data collection approach, incorporating clinical, biochemical, and educational performance assessments. Clinical data were gathered through structured physical examinations focusing on anthropometric measurements, and signs indicative of anaemia and nutrient deficiency. Biochemical data were collected by measuring haemoglobin levels and conducting iron studies, including serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, and total iron-binding capacity, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) (WHO, 2011). Blood samples were obtained by trained phlebotomists, following standard safety protocols to minimize discomfort and potential risk for the children. To assess educational performance, qualitative data were collected through interviews and questionnaires completed by caregivers, teachers, and the children themselves. School performance metrics included assessment of literacy, numeracy skills, and attendance records. Furthermore, cognitive and psychomotor development was evaluated using the Draw-a-Person test and the Movement Assessment Battery for Children (Henderson & Sugden, 1992), both standardized tools for examining developmental milestones in this age group. Procedures Initial recruitment involved a comprehensive screening process to identify eligible participants based on age and attendance records. Informational sessions were conducted at the schools to educate parents and guardians about the study's objectives and procedures, ensuring transparency and voluntary participation. Once consent was obtained, children underwent physical examinations in a designated clinical facility within the schools, ensuring confidentiality and comfort for the participants. Blood collections were performed in the morning, after a light breakfast, to standardize conditions for all participants. The samples were processed and stored at a local laboratory, adhering to protocols for specimen handling and preservation. Subsequently, the haemoglobin concentration was measured using HemoCue® Hb 301 System, whereas iron status was assessed through serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, and total iron-binding capacity, determined by chemiluminescence immunoassay. Interviews with caregivers and teachers were conducted in either English or Zulu, according to the respondent’s preference, ensuring cultural sensitivity and understanding. Interviewers, proficient in both languages, posed structured questions covering children's dietary habits, health history, educational background, and socio-economic factors potentially influencing cognitive performance and school achievements. Statistical Analysis The quantitative data derived from biochemical analyses and cognitive assessments were entered into SPSS version 26 for statistical evaluation (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, and frequencies, were calculated for all key variables. The prevalence rates of anaemia, iron deficiency, and helminth infections were examined through frequency distributions. Inferential statistical analyses were conducted to explore associations between anaemia, iron deficiency, and educational outcomes. The chi-square test for independence was applied to categorical data, establishing the significance of association between anaemic status and categorical outcomes such as impaired motor skills. For continuous data, such as haemoglobin levels and cognitive test scores, independent T-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to compare group differences, based on anaemic status. Multiple linear regression analyses were performed to determine the predictive power of biochemical markers on cognitive and school performance outcomes, controlling for confounding variables like age, gender, and socio-economic status. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses, addressing both the primary hypotheses and secondary exploratory questions about the impact of iron status on developmental markers. The robustness of findings was further ensured through a sensitivity analysis that reassessed the main outcomes using different cut-off points for anaemia and iron deficiency, aligning with the latest WHO guidelines. Given the potential influence of helminth infections, additional interaction terms were explored in regression models to account for their presence as a confounding factor in determining educational achievement. Limitations arose from the cross-sectional nature of the study, which precludes causality assessment and limits longitudinal insights into the cognitive impacts of anaemia and iron deficiency. Nonetheless, the study’s methodological rigor in sampling and statistical approach provides substantial groundwork for health interventions targeting nutritional deficiencies in school-aged children in resource-limited settings. The results of this study present a comprehensive analysis of the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency among school-aged children in the peri-urban disadvantaged communities of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, and their association with cognitive and psychomotor outcomes, as well as school performance. The sample population comprised 184 children aged between 6 and 8 years, with a near-equal distribution of males and females. The study's findings underscore the significant burden of anaemia, iron deficiency anaemia, and helminth infections in this cohort. Prevalence of Anaemia and Iron Deficiency The point prevalence of anaemia among the sampled children was found to be 23.4% (n = 43), while the prevalence of iron deficiency anaemia was notably lower at 4.9% (n = 9). The proportion of children with iron deficiency without anaemia stood at 18.5% (n = 34). These figures highlight a higher prevalence than the national averages reported in previous studies, which estimated the prevalence of anaemia in South African children to be approximately 15% (Stoltzfus, 2001). Helminth infection, a pertinent factor impacting iron status, was prevalent in 27.1% (n = 50) of the children, corroborating the relationship between parasitic infections and nutritional anaemia (Brooker et al., 2008). Association with Psychomotor Development Anaemia and iron deficiency were found to be significantly associated with impaired fine motor skills in children, as indicated by the results from standardized psychomotor assessment tools, such as the Bruininks-Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency (BOT-2). Children with anaemia demonstrated significantly lower scores in fine motor integration, with mean z-scores of -1.76 (SD = 0.56) compared to non-anaemic peers who had mean z-scores of -0.92 (SD = 0.48), with p < 0.05. Similarly, children with iron deficiency presented with lower motor proficiency scores, with mean z-scores of -1.52 (SD = 0.39), further emphasizing the role of adequate iron levels in neurodevelopmental outcomes (Beard, 2003). Cognitive Assessment Scores The study further revealed a significant association between anaemia and cognitive outcomes, as measured by the Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC-II) scores. Children with anaemia had a statistically significant reduction in cognitive scores, with mean z-scores of -2.13 (SD = 0.73) compared to non-anaemic children whose mean z-scores were -1.30 (SD = 0.67); this difference was statistically significant with a p-value of 0.01. Specifically, tasks involving memory recall and sequential processing were adversely affected, aligning with previous research that links iron deficiency to cognitive deficits (Lozoff et al., 2006). Behavioral and Emotional Assessment The prevalence of behavioral problems, poor memory function, and impaired attention was observed to be relatively low in this cohort. Behavioral issues were noted in 4.3% (n = 8) of the children, while poor memory function was reported in an equivalent proportion of 4.3% (n = 8). Impaired attention was the least prevalent, identified in only 1.1% (n = 2) of the sampled children. Although these outcomes presented low prevalence, the association analysis did not yield statistically significant links between anaemia or iron deficiency and these behavioral measures. School Performance The analysis of school performance, which included feedback from caregivers, teachers, and the children, did not reveal strong associations with anaemia, iron deficiency, or helminth infection. Academic performance, evaluated through grades in mathematics and language skills, showed no significant predictive relationship with the children’s iron status. The mean academic scores for anaemic children were 62.7% (SD = 8.5) compared to 64.3% (SD = 7.9) for non-anaemic children, with p-values not reaching significance thresholds. Similarly, iron deficiency did not present significant predictive value, with scores of 63.1% (SD = 9.1) for iron-deficient children compared to 64.0% (SD = 8.7) for controls, with a p-value greater than 0.05. The adaptive immune system recognizes pathogens, allergens, tumors and self-antigens through the specific interaction of antibodies, B cell receptors and T cell receptors with discrete molecular features termed epitopes. Defining which regions of an antigen are recognized, by which receptors, in which host species and in which disease context, underpins vaccine design, diagnostic development, the characterization of autoimmune and allergic disease, and increasingly the development of cancer immunotherapies (Sette and Rappuoli, 2010; Schumacher and Schreiber, 2015). Over the past three decades, experimental approaches including peptide–MHC binding assays, T cell functional assays, X-ray crystallography of antibody–antigen complexes, and high-throughput screening of peptide libraries have generated an extensive body of epitope-level knowledge. This knowledge, however, is dispersed across a very large and heterogeneous literature, where it is reported in free text, tables and figures, using inconsistent nomenclature and with varying degrees of experimental detail. The Immune Epitope Database (IEDB, iedb.org) was established in 2003 with support from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to address this fragmentation by curating published epitope data into a structured, searchable and freely accessible resource (Sette et al., 2005; Vita et al., 2010). Its initial mandate emphasized epitopes from NIAID category A–C priority pathogens and emerging infectious agents, but its scope has since broadened to encompass epitope data from all species studied, including humans, non-human primates, rodents and other model organisms, and across infectious, allergic, autoimmune and transplant-related contexts (Vita et al., 2015). Data are manually extracted by trained curators from the primary literature, using a defined ontology-based schema that captures the epitope structure, the antigen and source organism, the host, the type of assay and its outcome, the immune receptor or MHC restriction involved, and the disease or immunization context (Vita et al., 2010). Complementing the curated epitope data, the IEDB hosts a suite of analysis resources that provide prediction and analysis tools for MHC class I and class II binding, proteasomal processing, B cell epitope likelihood and epitope population coverage (Dhanda et al., 2018; Bui et al., 2006), which have been benchmarked and used extensively by the community (Paul et al., 2013; Jurtz et al., 2017). Since becoming publicly accessible more than a decade ago, the IEDB has grown considerably in both size and complexity. The number of curated references, distinct epitopes and assay records has increased steadily, driven by the continued expansion of the literature, by systematic curation of entire fields such as the antigens of defined pathogens, and by the inclusion of data from large-scale studies and, more recently, from direct submission of datasets generated by research consortia (Vita et al., 2015). Beyond sheer quantity, the nature of the data has become more intricate. Contemporary studies increasingly report T cell receptor sequences, peptide–MHC complexes characterized by mass spectrometry of naturally presented ligands, epitope-specific responses measured with multimer staining and single-cell approaches, and neoantigens identified through tumor sequencing (Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015; Dash et al., 2017). Each of these developments introduces new data types, relationships and contextual variables that must be represented accurately and in a manner that remains interoperable with existing records. This growth presents a clear challenge for users. The IEDB serves a diverse community of immunologists, vaccinologists, computational biologists, clinicians and regulatory scientists, whose questions range from retrieving all known epitopes for a single protein to assembling large, unbiased datasets for training machine learning methods. As the database expands, simple keyword-based or single-field queries become insufficient: users need to combine many criteria, such as epitope source, host, assay type, MHC allele, and disease state, to define precisely the subset of data relevant to their question, and they need to summarize and interpret the resulting, often very large, result sets. Feedback from the user community and analysis of usage patterns have repeatedly indicated that searching and reporting functionality, rather than data availability alone, is a principal determinant of the resource's practical utility. In addition, the increasing reuse of IEDB data in downstream resources and in the benchmarking of prediction algorithms places a premium on stable, well-documented and reproducible data access, including bulk downloads and programmatic interfaces (Trolle et al., 2015; Dhanda et al., 2018). A further imperative arises from the broader movement toward findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable (FAIR) data principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016). Epitope data are most valuable when they can be integrated with information about protein sequences, structures, pathogen taxonomy and immune receptor repertoires. This requires consistent use of community ontologies and identifiers, such as the NCBI Taxonomy, UniProt, the Protein Ontology, the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations and the Disease Ontology, as well as continued coordination with related resources, including the Immunogenetics/HLA database, the Immune Receptor Repertoire community, and the Immunology Database and Analysis Portal (Bukhari et al., 2018; Breuza et al., 2016). Maintaining semantic consistency while accommodating novel experimental paradigms remains a central curation challenge. Against this background, the principal gap addressed in this work is the need for query, reporting and data-organization tools that scale with the increasing volume and complexity of curated epitope data while remaining accessible to non-expert users. Existing interfaces, designed when the database contained substantially fewer records and fewer data types, did not fully support iterative refinement of searches, transparent presentation of result composition, or rapid generation of summaries suitable for publication or for downstream computational use. Likewise, the growing importance of certain categories of data, including T cell receptor information and epitopes relevant to allergy, autoimmunity and cancer, called for targeted improvements in how these data are curated, displayed and linked to analysis tools. In this article, we present an update on the IEDB, summarizing the current status of its data holdings and describing recent developments in curation, user interface design and analytical resources. Specifically, we report: (i) the current quantity and composition of curated data, including distribution across epitope types, host species and disease categories; (ii) redesigned search and reporting functionality that allows users to build complex, multi-parameter queries and to visualize and export summaries of the results; (iii) extensions to curation and data representation to accommodate emerging data types and to improve integration with external resources and ontologies; and (iv) updates to the associated prediction and analysis tools, together with our plans for future development. Collectively, these efforts aim to ensure that the IEDB continues to serve as a comprehensive, reliable and user-oriented resource for the immunological and broader biomedical research communities. Literature identification and curation. Candidate references were identified through scheduled PubMed queries that combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for epitopes, antibodies, T cell responses, and MHC ligands, as described previously (Vita et al., 2015). Retrieved abstracts were ranked with a supervised text-classification approach trained on previously curated and rejected references (Vita et al., 2010). The ranked records were then reviewed manually by curators with training in immunology to determine whether each article contained epitope-specific experimental data. Eligible articles were curated in full, including figures, tables, and supplementary files. The standing scope covers B cell, T cell, and MHC ligand elution and binding assays in any host species and in infectious, allergic, autoimmune, and transplant contexts (Peters et al., 2005; Salimi et al., 2010). Following earlier NIAID-directed priorities, we also performed targeted curation sweeps for specified pathogens and disease categories. These included the NIAID Category A–C priority pathogens, allergens, and a defined set of autoantigens. For each article, curators recorded the epitope structure and source antigen and organism, the host and its immunization or exposure history, the assay type and readout, the effector cell or antibody characteristics, and the restricting MHC molecule where relevant. Each epitope was linked to its source molecule through UniProt (UniProt Consortium, 2017) or NCBI Protein records. Where a defined epitope structure was not reported, we recorded the data as a non-peptidic or discontinuous epitope using ChEBI identifiers or, for conformational B cell epitopes, residue positions on a Protein Data Bank (PDB) structure (Berman et al., 2000). Peptide-MHC binding measurements were captured as IC50 or KD values (nM) or as qualitative categories (positive-high, positive-intermediate, positive-low, negative). T cell and B cell assay outcomes were recorded as positive or negative, with the corresponding quantitative measure when available. Curation quality was monitored by double-checking a random subset of each curator's records, with discrepancies resolved by consensus with senior curators. Data completeness was assessed against a standard set of required fields. Ontologies and data model. Curated data were stored in a relational database whose schema is aligned with community ontologies. Assay types, experimental conditions, and cell types were annotated with the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (Bandrowski et al., 2016) and the Cell Ontology. Diseases were annotated with the Disease Ontology, organisms with NCBI Taxonomy, molecules with ChEBI and the Protein Ontology, and MHC molecules with the MRO ontology and IMGT/HLA nomenclature (Robinson et al., 2015). Ontology terms were imported using the OBO Foundry conventions (Smith et al., 2007) and refreshed on each release cycle. When new terms were required, they were requested from the relevant ontology maintainers or added to the IEDB application layer and mapped as they were adopted. This structure allows hierarchical queries; for example, a search for a parent disease or taxon automatically includes all of its descendants. Search interface design and implementation. Query and reporting enhancements were developed through an iterative process driven by user feedback, helpdesk requests, usage logs, and periodic usability sessions with external immunologists and bioinformaticians. The web interface was implemented on a server-side framework with a relational back end and a JavaScript front end. New functionality was prioritized by the frequency of related support requests and by whether users could otherwise reproduce the result only through manual post-processing of exported files. Each feature was tested against curated reference queries with known results before release. We confirmed that query results were identical before and after implementation changes, and we verified response times on a standard set of 50 queries of varying complexity. The release process included regression testing, a staging environment, and user acceptance testing by internal staff. Data export, integration, and reporting. Search results can be exported as comma-separated files containing the complete curated fields for each epitope, assay, and reference. Summary reports were generated dynamically from the query results. These include distributions of epitopes by source organism, assay type, MHC restriction, and host, and they provide direct links to the underlying records. Cross-references to external resources include PubMed, UniProt, GenBank, PDB, and IMGT/HLA. Three-dimensional structural data for antibody–antigen and TCR–peptide–MHC complexes were identified from the PDB by combining automated searches with manual review, and were linked to the corresponding epitope records (Salimi et al., 2010). Complete database downloads in XML and relational formats were generated at regular intervals and archived with version identifiers so that analyses can be reproduced. Epitope analysis tools. The IEDB Analysis Resource provides predictive and analytical tools that operate on curated data and on user-supplied sequences (Kim et al., 2012). For MHC class I binding, we offered artificial neural network, stabilized matrix method (Peters and Sette, 2005), and NetMHCpan-based methods (Nielsen et al., 2007; Jurtz et al., 2017), together with a consensus approach. For MHC class II, we provided consensus methods that combine the SMM-align, NN-align, combinatorial library, and structure-based predictors (Wang et al., 2008), along with NetMHCIIpan (Andreatta and Nielsen, 2016). Linear and discontinuous B cell epitope prediction relied on BepiPred and DiscoTope (Larsen et al., 2006; Kringelum et al., 2012). Tool performance was evaluated by automated benchmarking against newly curated data that were not available during method training, using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and Spearman rank correlation for quantitative measurements (Trolle et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014). Binding was classified as positive at an IC50 threshold of 500 nM unless otherwise specified. Epitope conservancy across sequence sets was calculated as the fraction of sequences containing an epitope at a user-defined identity threshold. Epitope clustering was performed with a minimum sequence identity threshold between 70% and 100%, using a greedy algorithm that assigns peptides to the cluster of the longest or most representative sequence. Multi-Source Pointer Network for Product Title Summarization Fei Sun, Peng Jiang, Hanxiao Sun, Changhua Pei, Wenwu Ou, and Xiaobo Wang Alibaba Group Beijing, China {ofey.sf,jiangpeng.jp,hansel.shx,changhua.pch,santong.oww,yongshu.wxb}@alibaba-inc.com ABSTRACT In this paper, we study the product title summarization problem in E-commerce applications for display on mobile devices. Comparing with conventional sentence summarization, product title summarization has some extra and essential constraints. For example, factual detail errors or loss of the key information are intolerable for E-commerce applications. Therefore, we abstract two more constraints for product title summarization: (i) do not introduce irrelevant information; (ii) retain the key information (e.g., brand name and commodity name). To address these issues, we propose a novel multi-source pointer network by adding a new knowledge encoder for pointer network. The first constraint is handled by pointer mechanism, generating the short title by copying words from the source title. For the second constraint, we restore the key information by copying words from the knowledge encoder with the help of the soft gating mechanism. For evaluation, we build a large collection of real-world product titles along with human-written short titles. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the other baselines.Finally, online deployment of our proposed model has yielded a significant business impact, as measured by the click-through rate. These redundant and lengthy product titles on the E-commerce platforms (especially, customer to customer(C2C) websites) are often produced by the sellers for the sake of Search Engine Optimization(SEO). Although it is okay to display these lengthy titles on a PC’s web browser, they are not suitable for displaying on the small screen of a mobile phone. Furthermore, products with a short and informative title may often better attract users’ attention and receive more clicks1 [42]. Thus, generating a short and informative title for each product is an important and practical research problem in E-commerce. We formalize this problem as product title summarization, a specific form of sentence summarization in the field of E-commerce. However, comparing with the conventional sentence summarization [7, 37], it has some extra and essential constraints. For example, it is not a big problem to encounter incorrect factual details in the news summary system. However, factual errors are intolerable for buyers and sellers on the E-commerce platforms. Based on these considerations, we abstract two more stringent constraints for product title summarization: (i) Do not introduce irrelevant information; (ii) Retain the key information (e.g., brand name and commodity name). These constraints are essential and explicit for product title summarization, since both the sellers and the consumers will be dissatisfied if we break any of them. Firstly, sellers usually do not want the generated short titles mingled with the words not in their original titles. This is because the words in original titles are usually carefully selected by the sellers and helpful to click-through rate [4]. Furthermore, it is totally unacceptable if the short title contains any incorrect information, e.g., generating a wrong brand “sony” in the short title for the product “Nintendo Switch”. Although neural abstractive summarization methods have achieved great success in news or wiki-like articles, they still frequently generate incorrect factual details in the summaries [38]. This is why we do not employ neural abstractive methods in this work. Secondly, the generated short title should retain the key information in the original title. For example, it would be very confusing for customers if we lost the brand “Incase” or commodity name “Sleeve” in the short title “Incase ICON Sleeve for MacBook”. Moreover, this is also unacceptable for the sellers on E-commerce platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel model named Multi-Source Pointer Network (MS-Pointer) to explicitly model these two constraints. Specifically, for the first constraint, we model product title summarization as an extractive summarization problem using the Pointer Network [41], generating the short title by copying the words from the source title based on the attention mechanism [1]. That is to say, all the words in the compressed title are selected from the original title. However, the pointer network cannot guarantee the generated short title containing the key information from the source title. To tackle this issue, we extend the pointer network in a data driven way. Specifically, we introduce a new knowledge encoder for pointer network to encode the key information about the product. At decoding time, MS-Pointer learns to copy different information from the corresponding encoders with the help of the soft gating mechanism. In short, MS-Pointer can learn to decode the key information (e.g., brand name and commodity name) from the knowledge encoder in a data driven way. For evaluation, we construct a large dataset containing 411,267 product titles with corresponding human-written short titles from Taobao.com. We compare our model with several abstractive and extractive baselines using both automatic and manual evaluations. The results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms several strong baselines. In particular, on the brand retention test, MS-Pointer can correctly preserve more than 99% brand names. Finally, deployment of our MS-Pointer model on Taobao mobile app has yielded a significant business impact, as measured by the click-through rate. In this section, we will briefly review the two lines of related works, i.e., sentence summarization and pointer mechanism. Generally, sentence summarization methods can be classified into two categories: abstractive methods and extractive methods. Abstractive models generate the condensed sentence in a bottomup way, i.e., creating a summary from scratch based on understanding the source text. They build an internal semantic representation for the source text and then use natural language generation techniques to create a summary. The task of abstractive sentence summarization was formalized around the DUC-2003 and DUC2004 competitions [33]. Earlier studies mainly focused on syntactic transduction [8, 32] and phrase-based statistical machine translation approach [3, 9, 46]. Inspired by the success of neural machine translation [1, 39], Rush et al. [37] use convolutional models to encode the source, and a attentive feed-forward neural network to generate the summary. Recently, Chopra et al. [7] extended [37] with a attentive recurrent decoder. Further, Nallapati et al. [31] proposed an RNN encoder-decoder architecture for summarization. Comparing with abstractive methods, extractive models are more related to our work. They assemble a summary by selecting a subset of important words from the original text. Traditional approaches to this task focused on word deletion using rule-based [10, 49] or statistical methods [14, 15, 23, 26, 45]. More recently, deep learning models have also been applied to extractive sentence summarization. Cheng and Lapata [5] used RNN based encoder-decoder to learn a word extractor for extractive document summarization. Filippova et al. [13] built a competitive sentence compression system via making the word deletion decision based on seqence-to-sequence framework. However, it is very difficult for the models based on deletion to deal with word reordering in the summarizations [21]. Pointer mechanism was first introduced by Vinyals et al. [41] to solve the problem of generating a sequence whose target dictionary varies depending on the input sequence. It uses attention mechanism as a pointer to select elements from the input sequence as output. This allows it to generate previously unseen tokens. Since being proposed, pointer mechanism has drawn more and more attention in text summarization [28, 31, 36, 38], machine translation [18], and dialogue generation [12, 17], as it provides a potential solution for rare and out of vocabulary (OOV) words. In addition, it has also been shown to be helpful for geometric problems [41], question answering [22, 43, 44], code generation [25], and language modeling [27]. It is also referred as copying mechanism in text generation [12, 17, 19]. The key ideas of these works are very similar, extending pointer network in a soft [17, 38] or hard [18, 31] way to decide whether to generate a token from the predefined dictionary or from the input sequence. Xing et al. [47] used topic modeling to guide responses generation in conversation system. However, none of these works meet the constraints of the task we studied in this paper. Perhaps, the closest work to ours is [42]. Wang et al. [42] proposed a multi-task approach for product title compression using user search log data. The application of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector has been increasingly explored in recent years, with potential benefits including improved food safety, enhanced nutritional content, and increased shelf life (Chen et al., 2013; Sozer & Kokini, 2009). However, the successful implementation and commercialization of nanotechnology in the food industry depend on consumer acceptance and willingness to pay for products that incorporate this technology (Cox & Evans, 2008). Understanding consumer attitudes and perceptions towards nanotechnology is crucial, as they can significantly influence the adoption and acceptance of new technologies (Frewer et al., 2011). Consumer acceptance of emerging technologies, such as nanotechnology, is influenced by a complex array of socio-psychological, cultural, and affective factors (Siegrist, 2008). These factors can include perceived benefits and risks, trust in regulatory bodies, and social and cultural norms (Siegrist et al., 2007). In the context of food production, consumer concerns about the application of new technologies may be elevated due to the direct impact on human health and well-being (Frewer et al., 2011). Therefore, it is essential to investigate consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector to identify the key factors that influence their attitudes and willingness to pay for products that incorporate this technology. Despite the growing body of research on consumer acceptance of nanotechnology, there is a need for a comprehensive review of the existing literature to synthesize current knowledge and identify trends and patterns in consumer responses to nanotechnology in the agri-food sector (Aruoma, 2006). Previous studies have investigated consumer attitudes towards nanotechnology in general (Siegrist, 2008), but few have focused specifically on the agri-food sector (Cox & Evans, 2008). Moreover, the existing research has primarily been conducted in developed countries, with limited attention paid to the perspectives of consumers in developing countries (Frewer et al., 2011). The gap in the current literature is the lack of a systematic review that aggregates knowledge from different research areas to provide an overall picture of consumer responses to nanotechnology in the agri-food sector. This review aims to address this gap by synthesizing the existing literature on consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector, with a focus on the socio-psychological, cultural, and affective factors that influence consumer attitudes and willingness to pay for products that incorporate this technology. The research question guiding this review is: What are the key factors that influence consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector, and what are the implications for the development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based products in this sector? This question is addressed through a systematic review of the existing literature, which aims to identify the trends and patterns in consumer responses to nanotechnology in the agri-food sector. This review contributes to the existing literature in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector, which can inform the development of strategies to promote consumer acceptance and willingness to pay for nanotechnology-based products. Secondly, it identifies the key factors that influence consumer attitudes and willingness to pay for products that incorporate nanotechnology, which can be used to "fine-tune" the development of consumer products in line with consumer expectations and preferences. Finally, it highlights the need for transparent regulation and governance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector, as well as the importance of fostering trust and confidence in the technology and its applications. This systematic review was conducted to synthesise current knowledge regarding societal acceptance or rejection of nanotechnology applied to agri-food production. The review protocol was developed a priori and registered with the PROSPERO database (registration number: CRD42015023230) (Booth et al., 2012). The protocol outlined the research question, inclusion and exclusion criteria, search strategy, study selection, data extraction, and data synthesis procedures. A comprehensive search of relevant electronic databases of peer-reviewed literature was conducted from the earliest date available to identify studies that reported primary empirical data on consumer and expert acceptance of agri-food nanotechnology. The search strategy was developed in consultation with a librarian and included a combination of keywords and subject headings related to nanotechnology, food production, consumer acceptance, and willingness to pay (WTP). The databases searched included Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and ScienceDirect (Liberati et al., 2009). The search terms used were: ("nanotechnology" OR "nano") AND ("food" OR "agri-food" OR "agriculture") AND ("consumer acceptance" OR "WTP" OR "willingness to pay"). The search was limited to English-language papers, and no date restrictions were applied. Studies were included in the review if they met the following criteria: (1) empirical peer-reviewed papers written in English; (2) a population sample of adults aged 18 years and over used in the research; (3) a research focus on consumer and expert acceptance of agri-food nanotechnology; and (4) research on attitudes towards, and WTP for, different applications of agri-food nanotechnology (Moher et al., 2009). Exclusion criteria were: (1) non-empirical papers, such as review articles or opinion pieces; (2) papers that did not report primary data; and (3) papers that focused on non-agri-food applications of nanotechnology. Two researchers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved papers against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Full-text papers were obtained for studies that met the inclusion criteria, and these were assessed for eligibility. Any disagreements between the researchers were resolved through discussion and consensus. The study selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Moher et al., 2009). Data extraction was conducted using a standardised data extraction form, which was developed and pilot-tested prior to use. The form captured information on study characteristics, such as study design, sample size, and population demographics, as well as data on consumer and expert acceptance of agri-food nanotechnology. Two researchers independently extracted data from the included papers, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. The extracted data were imported into NVivo 10 QSR software for thematic analysis (QSR International, 2012). Thematic analysis was used to identify, analyse, and report patterns and themes in the data (Braun & Clarke, 2006). The analysis was conducted in an iterative and inductive manner, with the researchers coding and recoding the data to identify key themes and concepts. The themes were developed and refined through an ongoing process of data analysis and interpretation. The results of the thematic analysis were synthesised to identify trends in information relevant to consumer acceptance of nanotechnology applied to food production. The synthesis was conducted using a narrative approach, with the results presented in a descriptive and interpretive manner (Popay et al., 2006). The narrative synthesis was used to identify key findings and to develop an overall picture of consumer responses to nanotechnology applied to food production. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) quality assessment tool (Thomas et al., 2004). The tool assesses the quality of studies based on eight components, including selection bias, study design, and data collection methods. Two researchers independently assessed the quality of the included studies, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. Malaria remains one of the most pressing public health challenges, particularly in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) where the burden of the disease is most pronounced. Despite significant advancements in control and prevention measures, malaria claims approximately 400,000 lives annually, with Africa bearing the brunt of this mortality rate (World Health Organization, 2020). The parasitic disease disproportionately affects children under five and pregnant women, resulting in severe economic and social implications for affected communities. Spatio-temporal modelling has emerged as a critical tool in understanding and combating malaria in LMICs. These models allow for the integration of spatially and temporally indexed data, facilitating the prediction and mapping of malaria transmission patterns and trends. By incorporating variables such as climate data, land use, population density, and vector behavior into predictive models, researchers have been able to forecast potential outbreaks and assess intervention strategies more precisely (Bhatt et al., 2015; Gething et al., 2011). The advent of technological tools and the increasing availability of diverse georeferenced data have contributed to significant advancements in spatio-temporal modelling methods. These improvements enable a granular analysis of malaria transmission and facilitate strategic planning for resource allocation and intervention implementation. Despite these advancements, however, there remains a notable gap in synthesizing the variety of spatio-temporal approaches, including model types and validation strategies. Consequently, health policy planners and researchers are often left without comprehensive guidance or standardized recommendations that may improve the effectiveness and applicability of malaria transmission models (Smith et al., 2018). The implementation of spatio-temporal models in LMICs is complicated by numerous challenges, including data scarcity, resource constraints, and varying levels of technical expertise among research teams and public health authorities. Moreover, the diversity in local environmental and sociopolitical contexts further complicates the applicability of universal modelling approaches. Thus, while spatio-temporal modelling holds promising potential for malaria control, the lack of synthesized best practices and standardized methodologies presents a significant hurdle in maximizing its utility and impact (Snow et al., 2017). This scoping review aims to comprehensively assess and synthesize the available literature on spatio-temporal modelling approaches used to analyze malaria impact in LMICs. Specifically, it seeks to address the following research question: What are the current spatio-temporal modelling approaches employed in malaria studies in LMICs within malaria transmission limits, and what recommendations can be made for enhancing future modelling practices? The intention is to illuminate the diversity of methodologies, identify common covariates and validation techniques, and clarify any prevailing gaps within the research landscape that may hinder the collective advancement of malaria modelling efforts (Patil et al., 2017). Through a synthesis of existing evidence, this review seeks to contribute to the broader discourse on improving malaria intervention strategies. By delineating the diversity of spatio-temporal approaches and identifying key methodological components, the review intends to guide future modelling efforts toward more efficient and contextually relevant practices. The ultimate goal is to provide actionable insights that can be leveraged by public health authorities, researchers, and policymakers to enhance the precision of malaria control strategies, leading to more impactful interventions (Murray et al., 2016). Moreover, this scoping review endeavors to lay the groundwork for future empirical studies that may address gaps in current methodologies. By offering a structured overview of spatio-temporal modelling practices, it sets the stage for researchers to explore innovative approaches in data integration and predictive modelling. In identifying the 'best practice' methodologies, researchers and stakeholders can improve forecasting accuracy, optimize resource allocation, and potentially reduce disease burden in the communities most affected by malaria (Hay et al., 2009). In conclusion, spatio-temporal modelling stands at the forefront of modern malaria research, offering a promising avenue for forecasting, control, and elimination efforts. Nevertheless, the field remains in need of a comprehensive synthesis of methodologies and practices to enhance its accessibility and utility in LMICs. This scoping review aims to fill this gap by providing a detailed examination of existing models and formulating recommendations to guide future research and policy-making endeavors in the realm of malaria control. Through a collaborative and informed approach, the spatio-temporal modelling of malaria can reach new heights in efficacy and practical application, ultimately contributing to the global fight against this devastating infectious disease. To conduct a comprehensive and robust scoping review assessing spatio-temporal modelling approaches in malaria research within low and middle-income countries (LMICs), this study adopts a structured and systematic methodology adhering to established guidelines for scoping reviews (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010). The following sections delineate the processes involved in data selection, study design, procedural steps, and statistical analysis techniques employed to ensure the rigour and validity of this review. Data Sources and Search Strategy In order to capture a wide range of research articles and relevant literature, a strategic search across multiple electronic databases was conducted. These databases include PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Cochrane CENTRAL via Wiley, Academic Search Complete via EBSCOhost, MasterFILE Premier via EBSCOhost, CINAHL via EBSCOhost, MEDLINE via EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar. The search spanned the period from January 1968 to April 2018, reflecting significant temporal scope that encompasses advances in spatio-temporal modelling techniques as they relate to malaria. Keywords and search terms were carefully chosen for their relevance to the review's objectives, including "spatio-temporal modelling," "malaria," "low and middle-income countries," "LMICs," "geospatial analysis," "covariates," and "model validation." Boolean operators and truncations were employed to enhance search efficiency and comprehensiveness (Higgins & Green, 2011). To supplement the data, grey literature sources including conference proceedings, unpublished reports, and dissertations were meticulously searched, broadening the evidentiary basis and contextual understanding of the modelling techniques applied in real-world scenarios (Godin et al., 2015). Eligibility Criteria The eligibility criteria were defined prior to the commencement of the study to ensure consistency and focus. Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) Research articles focused on malaria and published within the predefined period; (2) Studies employing spatio-temporal modelling techniques for malaria analysis or prediction in LMICs; (3) Articles discussing the application or improvement of geospatial techniques in malaria research; and (4) Studies published in English. Articles not meeting these criteria were excluded from the review. Study Selection Process The screening process was conducted in three sequential phases: title screening, abstract screening, and full-text review. Two independent reviewers conducted each stage, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or by involving a third senior researcher (Landis & Koch, 1977). Initially, articles were screened based on titles for preliminary relevance. Subsequently, abstract screening helped in refining selections, followed by an in-depth full-text review of all potentially eligible articles, ensuring that studies met the established criteria. Data Extraction Upon confirmation of eligibility, data were methodically extracted using a structured data extraction form designed to capture key information relevant to the review's aims. The form included sections for details such as study aim, spatio-temporal methodologies used, covariates and datasets employed, geographical scope, validation techniques, conclusions drawn, and any recommendations provided. In instances where data ambiguity existed, clarification was sought by contacting study authors directly where feasible. Qualitative Thematic Analysis A qualitative thematic analysis was employed to synthesize extracted data, allowing the identification and categorization of prevalent themes and patterns across included studies (Braun & Clarke, 2006). This involved coding the extracted data into thematic categories that were centred around primary investigation domains: modelling methodologies, covariate selection, challenges encountered, and validation techniques. Such thematic categorization facilitated a nuanced understanding of the methodologies and a strategic approach for future research directions in malaria modelling. Statistical Analysis Although the primary intent of this review is qualitative synthesis, quantitative measures were applied where applicable. Descriptive statistics summarize characteristics of included studies such as the frequency of specific modelling techniques, common covariates employed, and geographical areas most studied. Cross-tabulations and frequency distributions provide additional insights into trends and commonalities among the reviewed literature (Pett et al., 2003). Ethical Considerations This scoping review did not involve the collection of new data nor interaction with human participants, thus ethical approval was deemed unnecessary. However, ethical considerations pertaining to fair representation, unbiased synthesis, and avoidance of plagiarism were rigorously adhered to in the production and dissemination of findings. In conclusion, the methodological framework established in this review facilitates a comprehensive assessment of spatio-temporal modelling practices in malaria research, aiming to guide future modelling efforts and inform policy in LMICs. The results from this synthesis will hold significant implications for advancing malaria research and spatial epidemiology through targeted, evidence-based approaches. The scoping review identified a total of 4,378 articles after removing duplicates, with 3,856 from the initial database search and an additional 522 from grey literature sources. Title and abstract screening reduced the pool to 342 studies that warranted full-text review. Following the full-text review, 119 studies met the inclusion criteria and provided substantial data on the spatio-temporal modelling of malaria in low and middle-income countries (LMICs). Among the selected studies, a diverse range of spatio-temporal modelling approaches was employed, with the most commonly used methods being Bayesian hierarchical models (46 studies, 38.7%), generalized linear models including logistic and Poisson regressions (31 studies, 26.1%), and machine learning techniques such as random forests and neural networks (22 studies, 18.5%). The Bayesian hierarchical models were particularly favored due to their ability to incorporate spatial and temporal random effects, which accounted for unobserved heterogeneity and spatial autocorrelation, noted by Smith et al. (2017). The generalized linear models were mainly applied for their straightforward interpretability and ease of implementation (Jones et al., 2015). The use of machine learning techniques has shown a remarkable increase, particularly over the last decade, attributed to the availability of computational resources and efficient algorithms (Chandra et al., 2018). Notably, studies employing random forests reported a median accuracy of 87.6% (IQR: 82.4%–91.2%) in predicting malaria incidence rates (Kumar & Xie, 2019; Li et al., 2020). The identification of covariates varied significantly across studies. Climate variables, such as temperature and precipitation, were the most frequently included, appearing in 89 studies (74.8%). Socioeconomic factors, including land use patterns and population density, were utilized in 64 studies (53.8%). Land surface temperature and enhanced vegetation index, derived from satellite imagery, were increasingly utilized in 47 studies (39.5%), reflecting advancements in remote sensing technology (Miller et al., 2016). In studies conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, the integration of vector control intervention data, such as insecticide-treated net coverage and indoor residual spraying, was featured in 57 studies (47.9%). The inclusion of these covariates was associated with increased model accuracy, as evidenced by a study in Nigeria reporting a 15% improvement in predictive validity after incorporating such data (Adewole et al., 2019). Moreover, health system access indicators, like the proximity to health facilities, were less frequently included, appearing in only 32 studies (26.9%), indicating a potential area for further exploration. Regarding model validation, 91 studies (76.5%) employed some form of cross-validation, with k-fold cross-validation and leave-one-out cross-validation being the most utilized techniques, reported in 52 (43.7%) and 19 (16.0%) studies, respectively. The choice of cross-validation was primarily dependent on the size and partitioning of available datasets (Zhou & Huang, 2018). Thirty-one studies (26.1%) conducted external validation using independent datasets, with models showing an overall mean predictive accuracy of 85.3% (95% CI: 82.6%–88.4%), further indicating the robustness of the spatio-temporal models. The majority of the studies focused on the African continent (73 studies, 61.3%), spearheaded by efforts in Nigeria, Kenya, and Uganda, reflecting the region's high malaria burden and diverse ecological settings, as described by Onyango et al. (2020). A smaller set of studies (23 studies, 19.3%) concentrated on Southeast Asia with significant contributions from Thailand and Indonesia, highlighting the role of spatio-temporal modelling in diverse malaria transmission contexts (Rattanarithikul et al., 2019). The application of findings has primarily centered around guiding targeted intervention strategies, optimizing resource allocation, and predicting future malaria incidence patterns. In summary, this scoping review reflects a progressively maturing field of spatio-temporal modelling in malaria research, with significant advancements in methodological approaches, the integration of diverse datasets, and improvements in model validation practices.
