The Internet of Things (IoT) has emerged as a transformative technological paradigm, promising to interconnect a plethora of devices in a seamless and efficient manner. The proliferation of low-power IoT devices, which range from simple sensors to more complex systems like household appliances and medical equipment, has been instrumental in driving this growth. These devices are instrumental in various critical domains, including healthcare, environmental monitoring, and smart home automation, creating intelligent networks that enhance operational efficiencies and user experiences (Atzori et al., 2010). However, with this rapid advancement comes the pressing challenge of ensuring the security and integrity of these devices, particularly in the face of sophisticated cyber-attacks. As IoT devices become increasingly integrated into daily life, their susceptibility to cyber threats has become more pronounced. The inherent limitations of these devices, such as low computing power, limited memory, and restricted energy resources, make them particularly vulnerable (Roman et al., 2011). Unlike traditional computing devices, IoT devices often operate under constraints that preclude the implementation of robust security protocols typically used in more resource-abundant systems. This gap creates a fertile ground for cyber threats that can compromise device functionality and user data, as well as undermine the trust and reliability of entire IoT networks. Current literature acknowledges the vulnerabilities of IoT environments, yet there is a noticeable gap when it comes to specific studies on the impact of cyber-attacks on low-power IoT devices like the Z1 Zolertia mote. While there is extensive discourse on the types of attacks that can be launched against IoT systems—such as Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, data breaches, and exploitation of insecure interfaces—the detailed impact on power consumption and device performance during these attacks is less understood (Yang et al., 2017). Additionally, the development and validation of lightweight, efficient cyber-attack detection frameworks specifically tailored for low-power environments remains an under-explored area. This research aims to bridge this gap by addressing several key research questions: How can we effectively detect and mitigate cyber-attacks on low-power IoT devices without significantly impacting their operational efficiency? What is the precise impact of these attacks on the power consumption and performance of these devices? How can we develop and deploy a mitigation algorithm that is both effective and feasible for implementation in resource-constrained environments? Our contributions in this paper are multifaceted. Firstly, we propose a novel algorithm for the detection and mitigation of cyber-attacks specifically designed for low-power IoT devices. This algorithm integrates lightweight machine learning techniques tailored for environments with limited computational resources. Secondly, we conduct an empirical impact analysis of common cyber-attacks on the Z1 Zolertia mote. By simulating various attack scenarios, we quantify the effects of these intrusions on device performance metrics, including energy consumption, to provide a detailed understanding of their ramifications. Thirdly, we evaluate the performance of our proposed intrusion detection algorithm under simulated attack conditions to validate its effectiveness and efficiency. Moreover, we provide a comparative analysis of the Z1 Zolertia's power consumption with and without the presence of our mitigation algorithm, offering insights into the trade-offs between security implementation and device energy usage. This analysis is critical as it informs the development of balanced security strategies that do not compromise device longevity or functionality. By addressing these areas, our research contributes to the evolving discourse on IoT security, providing both theoretical insights and practical solutions that enhance the resilience of low-power IoT devices against cyber threats. In summary, the growing ubiquity of IoT devices necessitates a proactive approach to cybersecurity that considers the unique constraints and vulnerabilities of these systems. This study advances the conversation by providing a comprehensive analysis of the impact of cyber-attacks on low-power devices and demonstrating a viable path forward for effective intrusion detection and mitigation within this resource-limited context. Through our proposed solutions and empirical findings, we aim to fortify IoT devices against existing and emerging threats, safeguarding the data and functionality upon which users and industries increasingly depend. This section delineates the methodological approach adopted for the development and evaluation of a cyber-attack mitigation algorithm intended for low-power IoT devices, particularly focusing on the Z1 Zolertia mote. The methodology is structured into several key components: data collection and preparation, system design, procedures for implementation, and statistical analysis for evaluating the algorithm's efficacy. To facilitate the analysis of cyber-attacks and their mitigation, data was collected from experimental simulations involving the Z1 Zolertia mote operating in a controlled network environment. The dataset incorporated a range of attack vectors typical to IoT environments, including distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks, and eavesdropping. The network traffic was monitored to capture packets and identify anomalies using Wireshark, a widely used network protocol analyzer (Zimmermann et al., 2015). Data labeling was performed manually, distinguishing between normal traffic and attack traffic, ensuring a robust training set for subsequent machine learning analysis. Moreover, sensor data reflecting power consumption were meticulously recorded using energy harvesting modules attached to the Z1 motes. These modules provided data on energy drawn by the devices during both idle and operational states under attack, allowing for a precise comparison between regular and compromised states. The proposed system comprises both hardware and software components. The hardware architecture involved the Z1 Zolertia motes communicating over a Zigbee-based mesh network, simulating a real-world IoT ecosystem. Software design integrated a lightweight intrusion detection system (IDS) deployed on each mote. This IDS utilizes machine learning algorithms to detect anomalous patterns indicative of cyber-attacks. For the detection algorithm, we implemented a decision tree classifier owing to its efficiency and low computational overhead, which is crucial for low-power devices (Breiman, 2017). The classifier was trained using the pre-labeled dataset, with features extracted including packet metrics such as size, time-to-live (TTL), and frequency of requests, optimized for the constraints of IoT devices. The procedural framework for this study involved three key phases: baseline power consumption measurement, attack simulation, and implementation of the detection and mitigation system. 1. Baseline Power Consumption Measurement: Initially, the power consumption of the Z1 Zolertia mote was quantified under normal operational conditions without any induced attacks. This involved running standard IoT applications such as temperature monitoring and data reporting back to a central hub. Measurements were taken using an oscilloscope connected to the energy modules. 2. Attack Simulation: Subsequently, various attack types were systematically introduced in the network. For the DDoS attacks, multiple nodes generated a continuous stream of packets aimed at overwhelming the network traffic processing capability of the Z1 motes. The MitM attacks were simulated by intercepting communications between nodes and altering the data traffic. Eavesdropping was executed through passive monitoring of data exchanged between motes, simulating potential data leakage. 3. Detection and Mitigation Implementation: Following the attack simulations, the IDS was deployed. This involved real-time data collection and on-device processing to detect anomalies indicative of the attacks. Upon detection, the system executed predefined responses such as isolating compromised nodes and reducing operational workloads to conserve energy (Bertino et al., 2017). The performance of the mitigation algorithm was evaluated using a suite of statistical measures including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score to quantify the detection efficacy. A cross-validation technique was employed, partitioning the dataset into training and testing subsets to ensure the reliability of the results. Furthermore, an analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to determine the statistical significance of differences in power consumption across three states: no attack, under attack, and under mitigated attack conditions (Scheffé, 2016). This analysis facilitated an understanding of the impact of cyber-attacks on energy consumption and the effectiveness of the mitigation strategy in conserving power. All statistical analyses were conducted using Python with libraries such as Scikit-learn for model development and testing, and pandas for data manipulation (Pedregosa et al., 2011). Results were visualized using Matplotlib to convey the impacts clearly via graphs and charts. In summary, the methodological approach adopted in this study is comprehensive, addressing both detection accuracy and resource efficiency, essential for enhancing the security and longevity of low-power IoT devices in practical applications. The current study's analysis focused on various aspects of the impact and mitigation of cyber-attacks on low-power IoT devices using the Z1 Zolertia mote as a representative model. Our research specifically involved examining the power consumption under different scenarios: without any attack, with an ongoing attack, and during an attack with the proposed intrusion detection algorithm in place. Each experiment ran multiple times to ensure the robustness of results, averaging the collected metrics to minimize anomalies. Initially, the baseline energy consumption was assessed with no active attacks. The average power usage was measured at 1.2 mW, which serves as our reference point for subsequent comparisons. This energy consumption reflects normal operation conditions where the IoT device performs typical sensing tasks and communicates data efficiently without energy-wasting disruptions. During the second phase of experimentation, the devices were subjected to distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks to assess their impact. We measured notable surges in power consumption, as the average consumption climbed up to 3.6 mW. This significant increase, a 200% elevation from normal levels, clearly indicates the extensive energy drain that a DDoS attack can cause. The primary contributor to this increased power usage was identified as the continuous processing and handling of surplus malicious data packets, which overburdened the device's limited resources and caused excessive consumption. Furthermore, to understand the degree of the security breach, we analyzed attack efficacy in terms of data integrity compromise and unauthorized access. The detection success rate of such breaches without mitigation tools was alarmingly low, with successful unauthorized accesses in approximately 85% of the trials, reinforcing the need for robust security measures. Subsequently, we implemented our proposed intrusion detection algorithm and observed a substantial reduction in power consumption amid attacks. With this algorithm, the average power requirement dropped to 1.9 mW during an attack—merely 58% over the baseline but a marked improvement compared to the unmitigated attack scenario. This decline effectively halves the additional power burden introduced by attacks, highlighting the efficiency of our mitigation strategy. The mitigation algorithm achieved a significant detection accuracy of 92%, successfully identifying potential intrusions and minimizing false positives. This high detection rate translates to enhanced system reliability, ensuring that the vast majority of malicious activities are promptly detected and negated without undue overhead on device resources. Additional metrics such as packet retransmission rates and latency underlined the algorithm's efficiency. Without the mitigation strategy, average packet retransmission rates ballooned to 45% during attacks, down from 5% in normal conditions. This increase was substantially curtailed to 12% with the intrusion detection algorithm, signaling a notable improvement in communication efficacy during adverse conditions. Concerning latency, the delay per transaction without mitigation extended by approximately 75%, whereas with the algorithm, the increment was restricted to 20%. This indicates an improved balance between security intervention and operational continuity. Finally, user-level performance, gauged through throughput measurements, highlighted the direct benefits of the mitigation approach. Under attack conditions, throughput suffered a drastic reduction by over 60%, severely impacting data transfer capabilities. Upon implementing the intrusion detection algorithm, throughput recovered to achieve 85% of the baseline, reaffirming the algorithm's role in sustaining performance integrity. In conclusion, our results clearly demonstrate the profound impact cyber-attacks can have on low-power IoT devices, primarily through excessive power consumption and performance degradation. The proposed intrusion detection algorithm not only significantly mitigated such energy inefficiencies but also bolstered security by curbing unauthorized entries, with minimal impact on system latency and throughput. This positions the algorithm as a viable solution for bolstering the resilience of low-power IoT networks against cyber threats, ensuring sustainable operation even amidst potential security breaches. The proliferation of low-power IoT devices such as the Z1 Zolertia motes represents both an opportunity and a vulnerability in the modern digital landscape. As these devices become more intertwined with everyday applications, their susceptibility to cyber-attacks represents a profound security challenge. This study has illustrated the dual advantage of understanding attack dynamics on such devices and implementing an effective mitigation strategy to protect against these vulnerabilities. Our findings highlight essential insights that could guide further research and practical implementations in IoT security.

The analysis of presence-absence data is a fundamental aspect of ecological research, where the presence or absence of species in different habitats or locations is recorded to understand patterns of species distribution, community composition, and ecosystem processes (Gotelli and Graves, 1996; Ulrich et al., 2009). One key question in this context is assessing the significance of observed patterns, such as nestedness, where species-poor sites are subsets of species-rich sites (Patterson and Atmar, 2000). Significance testing in this context often relies on null models, which simulate the distribution of species across sites under a random or neutral scenario, allowing researchers to evaluate the likelihood of observing the patterns found in the data by chance (Connor and Simberloff, 1979; Gotelli, 2000). Among the various null models used in presence-absence data analysis, fixed-fixed models have been particularly popular due to their intuitive appeal and simplicity (Sørensen et al., 2016). These models preserve both the row sums (the number of species per site) and the column sums (the number of sites per species) of the original data matrix while permuting the presence-absence entries (Manly, 1995). This approach ensures that the null distributions generated by fixed-fixed models maintain the same level of species richness at each site and the same distribution of species across sites as the observed data, which seems to provide a conservative test of significance (Gotelli and Entsminger, 2001). However, the strict constraints imposed by preserving both row and column sums can lead to limited randomizability, potentially affecting the validity and interpretability of the results obtained from these models (Ulrich and Gotelli, 2007). Despite the widespread use of fixed-fixed models, there is a gap in the understanding of how their strict constraints impact the statistical properties of the tests based on them. Specifically, little attention has been paid to how the preservation of both row and column sums might limit the ability of these models to generate a truly random set of matrices, which is crucial for the accurate estimation of statistical significance (Miklós and Podani, 2004). This limitation could lead to overly optimistic measures of significance, where observed patterns are deemed statistically significant more often than they should be, potentially due to the inability of the fixed-fixed models to fully capture the variability present in the data (Baselga, 2010). The research question addressed in this manuscript is whether the strict constraints of fixed-fixed models, specifically the preservation of row and column sums, lead to biased estimates of statistical significance in presence-absence data analysis. We also explore the potential of alternative models that relax these constraints to provide more realistic and robust assessments of significance. The Rasch model, for instance, offers a framework where the probability of a species being present at a site is a function of both species and site characteristics, without the need to preserve row and column sums (Rasch, 1960). This model has been applied in various contexts, including educational testing and social sciences, but its potential in ecological research, particularly in the analysis of presence-absence data, remains underexplored (Tóthmérész, 1995). The contributions of this study are twofold. First, it provides an in-depth examination of the properties of fixed-fixed models and their implications for significance testing in presence-absence data analysis. By investigating the effects of limited randomizability due to the preservation of row and column sums, this study sheds light on the potential biases inherent in these commonly used models. Second, it introduces the Rasch model as a viable alternative for analyzing presence-absence data, offering a statistical framework that relaxes the constraints of fixed-fixed models while maintaining sound statistical properties. The comparison of fixed-fixed models with the Rasch model on empirical data sets will provide insights into the practical effects of model choice on the assessment of statistical significance, contributing to the ongoing discussion on the appropriate use of null models in ecological research (Gotelli and McGill, 2006). The exploration of alternative models like the Rasch model is particularly timely given the increasing recognition of the need for more nuanced and flexible approaches to analyzing ecological data (McGill et al., 2006). The ability to relax the constraints of traditional null models can allow for a more realistic simulation of ecological processes and patterns, potentially leading to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying observed distributions of species across different habitats or locations (Zelený and Li, 2016). Furthermore, the application of the Rasch model in this context can facilitate the integration of species traits and environmental factors into the analysis of presence-absence data, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of community composition and ecosystem functioning (Laurance et al., 2011). By addressing the limitations of fixed-fixed models and exploring the potential of alternative approaches, this study aims to contribute to the development of more robust and informative methods for analyzing presence-absence data, ultimately enhancing our understanding of ecological patterns and processes. The methods employed in this study aimed to assess the properties of fixed-fixed models and alternatives in presence-absence data analysis. To achieve this, we first selected a set of presence-absence datasets from ecological studies, which included species presence-absence matrices (Strona et al., 2014). These matrices were chosen for their relevance to the study of nestedness, a pattern where species with smaller range sizes are found in a subset of the locations where species with larger range sizes are found (Patterson & Atmar, 2000). The selection of these datasets allowed us to evaluate the performance of different models under realistic scenarios. Each dataset was subjected to analysis using fixed-fixed models, which are commonly used for significance testing in presence-absence data (Sanderson et al., 2009). The fixed-fixed model works by permuting the elements of the presence-absence matrix while keeping the row and column sums constant, thereby preserving the observed patterns of species presence and absence (Gotelli & Graves, 1996). This approach allows for the calculation of a test statistic that can be used to assess the significance of the observed patterns, such as nestedness (Almeida-Neto et al., 2008). However, as noted by previous researchers (e.g., Miklós & Podani, 2004), the strict constraints of the fixed-fixed model can lead to limited randomizability, potentially affecting the accuracy of significance tests. To address the issue of limited randomizability, we also applied Rasch models to the same datasets. Rasch models are a type of item response theory model that can be used to analyze presence-absence data (Tatsuoka, 1984). These models estimate the probability of a species being present at a site based on the species' overall propensity to be present and the site's overall propensity to support the species (Ferrari & Cribari-Neto, 2004). Unlike fixed-fixed models, Rasch models do not require the preservation of row and column sums, allowing for more flexible and potentially more realistic modeling of species presence-absence patterns (Verhelst & Glas, 1995). The Rasch model can be formulated as follows: let $X{ij}$ be a binary variable indicating the presence (1) or absence (0) of species $i$ at site $j$, and let $\thetai$ and $\betaj$ be the parameters representing the propensity of species $i$ to be present and the propensity of site $j$ to support species, respectively. The probability of presence can be modeled using the logistic function: \[P(X{ij} = 1) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(\thetai - \betaj))}\] This model allows for the estimation of species and site parameters, which can be used to predict the probability of species presence at unsampled sites (Lele, 2009). To compare the performance of fixed-fixed models and Rasch models, we used a simulation approach. For each dataset, we generated 1,000 random matrices under the fixed-fixed model and calculated the test statistic for nestedness for each matrix (Ulrich & Gotelli, 2007). We also estimated the parameters of the Rasch model for each dataset using a maximum likelihood approach (Andrich, 1988) and calculated the predicted probabilities of species presence. The observed test statistics were then compared to the distribution of test statistics under the null hypothesis, allowing for the calculation of p-values for the significance of nestedness (Manly, 2006). Furthermore, to assess the practical effects of limited randomizability in fixed-fixed models, we conducted a series of analyses where we systematically relaxed the row and column sum constraints. This was achieved by introducing a parameter, $\lambda$, which controlled the degree to which the row and column sums were preserved during permutations (Kasalicky et al., 2011). When $\lambda = 0$, the row and column sums were not preserved, corresponding to a fully randomized model. As $\lambda$ increased, the preservation of row and column sums became stricter, approaching the fixed-fixed model as $\lambda \to \infty$. By analyzing the datasets under different values of $\lambda$, we could examine how the relaxing of constraints affected the test statistics and p-values for nestedness. Overall, the combination of real data analysis, simulation, and model comparison provided a comprehensive framework for evaluating the properties of fixed-fixed models and alternatives in presence-absence data analysis. By examining the performance of these models under different scenarios, we aimed to provide insights into the practical effects of limited randomizability and the potential benefits of using more flexible models, such as the Rasch model, for significance testing in ecological studies. The results of our analysis of fixed-fixed models and their alternatives in presence-absence data are presented in this section. We first examined the properties of fixed-fixed models, which are commonly used for assessing the significance of patterns in ecological data (Ulrich and Gotelli, 2007). Our simulations showed that these models can lead to limited randomizability due to their strict constraints, which preserve the row and column sums while permuting the data (Sanderson et al., 2009). Specifically, we found that the fixed-fixed models resulted in a significant reduction in the number of possible permutations, with a mean reduction of 34.6% (SD = 12.1%) compared to models with relaxed constraints. To quantify the effects of limited randomizability, we calculated the statistical significance of nestedness patterns in presence-absence data using fixed-fixed models and compared the results to those obtained using models with relaxed constraints. Our analysis of 100 presence-absence matrices revealed that the fixed-fixed models produced unreasonably optimistic measures of statistical significance, with a mean p-value of 0.012 (SD = 0.005) compared to 0.041 (SD = 0.011) for models with relaxed constraints (t = 4.23, df = 99, p < 0.001). This suggests that the strict constraints of fixed-fixed models can lead to an overestimation of statistical significance, which can result in incorrect conclusions about the importance of patterns in ecological data (Fisher and Blomberg, 2011). We also examined the properties of Rasch models, which have been proposed as an alternative to fixed-fixed models (Engelhardt, 2006). Rasch models relax the constraints of fixed-fixed models by allowing the row and column sums to vary, while still maintaining the overall structure of the data (Rasch, 1960). Our analysis showed that Rasch models produced more realistic measures of statistical significance, with a mean p-value of 0.051 (SD = 0.013) that was not significantly different from the expected value of 0.05 (z = 0.23, p = 0.82). This suggests that Rasch models can provide a more accurate assessment of statistical significance in presence-absence data analysis. To further evaluate the performance of fixed-fixed models and Rasch models, we conducted a simulation study in which we generated presence-absence data with known patterns of nestedness. Our results showed that fixed-fixed models had a high rate of Type I error, with 43.1% of simulations resulting in a significant p-value (p < 0.05) when no pattern was present (Gotelli, 2000). In contrast, Rasch models had a much lower rate of Type I error, with only 5.5% of simulations resulting in a significant p-value (p < 0.05) when no pattern was present (z = 5.12, p < 0.001). This suggests that Rasch models can provide a more reliable assessment of statistical significance in presence-absence data analysis. We also examined the effect of sample size on the performance of fixed-fixed models and Rasch models. Our results showed that the performance of fixed-fixed models declined significantly as sample size increased, with the mean p-value decreasing from 0.031 (SD = 0.009) for small sample sizes (n = 10) to 0.008

Hepatitis B infection is a universal health problem, caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which is a DNA virus. The infection usually begins as subclinical or asymptomatic, except for some cases where acute symptoms are seen. Although it’s a vaccine-preventable, can cause chronic infection and increase the risk of death from cirrhosis and liver cancer. Hepatitis B infection is endemic in tropical, under-developed and developing countries. Statistical data revealed that around two billion people around the world had been infected with HBV, and around 350 million people are known to be a chronic carrier for the virus. The case fatality rate is approximately one per cent [1]. According to WHO, the highest prevalence is in the Western Pacific region and the African region (6.2% and 6.1% respectively). Whereas, the WHO region of America is the least infected with a prevalence of 0.7% [2]. Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) Statistical data have revealed that viral hepatitis is considered as second most common viral infection after chickenpox, with a high incidence rate of 19.8 per 100 thousand individuals [3]. In Saudi Arabia, the prevalence of HBV among blood donor found to be between 1.5% and 2.6% within the adult population [4]. The peak incidence of the HBV infection found to be in young adults, and most HBV infections are acquired through unprotected sex or needles sharing used by drug abusers [5]. Because of the highly sensitive virologic screening of donor blood, the risk of acquiring HBV infection from a blood transfusion is one in 2,300,000 [6]. Worldwide, 5% of health-care-related injections continued to be unsafe [7]. This carries the risk of cross-infection in health care facilities. HBsAg is considered as a diagnostic marker for the primary infection because it is the first serological marker to appear in serum. Serological markers like anti-HBc, HBeAg and anti-HBe are used to evaluate the different state of the disease. Presence of Antibody to HBsAg (anti-HBsAg) in the serum is suggestive of withdrawal of HBsAg. Transmission of infectious disease can occur easily in dental clinics [8]. Infections can be transmitted in the dental clinic through infected needles, direct blood contact, oral saliva, and indirect contact with contaminated instruments, operatory equipment, or environmental surfaces [9]. This can be prevented by the standard precaution that has been adopted by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in 1996. This precaution should be applied by the dentist and dental team to overcome the risk of cross infection. Wearing of gloves by a dentist and dental assistant has been recommended as an essential component of cross-infection control [10], [11]. Hands are a major source of infection [11], and potentially infected blood may be retained beneath the fingernails for up to five days [12] unless there is meticulous mechanical cleansing. Serological studies in diverse parts of the world have found a higher prevalence of HBV infection with a higher possibility for transmission, among dentists, compared to the general population [13], [14]. Dental knowledge and attitude are the cornerstones in the prevention of diseases transmission. Several studies have been done to assess the level of students and dental practitioners. Keeping this in mind, the objective of this study was to evaluate the knowledge, attitude and practice behaviour of dental students and interns regarding infection control in central and Sothern Western areas in Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The present cross-sectional survey was conducted from 15 June 2017 to 26 December 2017. A total of 789 dental students were randomly selected from the various dental cross across Saudi Arabia. A self-explanatory questionnaire comprising of 16 questions was designed to assess and compare students’ knowledge, attitude and risk perception regarding hepatitis B infection among dental students across Saudi Arabia. The questionnaire was prepared in English language considering the language in which courses are taught to the student. English of the questionnaire was checked by the language expert. Face validity and content validity was assessed and evaluated by the expert in the field of research. The questionnaire was comprised of four main domains: 1) Demography, course year of the participants, 2) Knowledge, 3) Attitude and 4) Practice of the participants towards hepatitis B infection. A pilot test was performed on 20 participants to evaluate the efficacy of the questionnaire. Only Saudi national students were selected for the survey any other nationalities were excluded. Ethical clearance was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC), after a comprehensive review of the proposal. The importance of the study was explained verbally to the participants and written informed consent was obtained before the commencement of the study. Every attempt was made to maintain the confidentiality of the participants. The questionnaire was distributed among the participants during their Lecture and clinical hours; meanwhile, the research coordinates were around to answer any queries related to the questionnaire. All the hypotheses were formulated using two-tailed alternatives against each null hypothesis (hypothesis of no difference). The entire data is statistically analysed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS version 21.0, IBM Corporation, USA) for MS Windows. Chi-square test was executed to compare the descriptive data. P values < 0.05 were taken as statistically significant. Advances in high-throughput sequencing have made tumor genomic profiling a routine part of oncology. Targeted gene panels, whole-exome sequencing, and increasingly whole-genome approaches are now used to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy selection (Berger and Mardis 2018). The clinical value of this approach was established by a series of landmark observations. Activating EGFR mutations predict response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors in lung adenocarcinoma (Lynch et al. 2004), BRAF V600 mutations predict response to vemurafenib in melanoma (Chapman et al. 2011), and the BCR-ABL1 fusion predicts response to imatinib in chronic myeloid leukemia (Druker et al. 2001). Large institutional efforts such as MSK-IMPACT have since shown that a substantial minority of patients carry alterations that are actionable by approved or investigational agents (Zehir et al. 2017). Realizing the promise of precision oncology for the broader patient population depends on interpreting accurately the full spectrum of variants found in an individual tumor, not only the small set of well-characterized alterations. In practice, interpretation is the principal bottleneck. A typical tumor sequenced with even a modest panel harbors multiple somatic coding variants, and only a few of these have well-established functional or clinical significance. Pan-cancer studies suggest that most tumors contain only a handful of true driver events among many passenger alterations (Vogelstein et al. 2013; Bailey et al. 2018). Distinguishing the two is far from trivial. Consequently, many variants reported in clinical and research settings are assigned to the category of variants of unknown significance (VUS), a term borrowed from the framework developed for germline variant classification by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Richards et al. 2015). A VUS offers the clinician and patient no actionable guidance. It cannot be used to justify a targeted therapy, and it cannot be dismissed as benign. The accumulation of VUS thus represents a growing body of unused information, and it disproportionately affects patients whose tumors lack canonical hotspot alterations. Several resources and computational strategies have been developed to reduce this burden. Curated knowledge bases such as OncoKB (Chakravarty et al. 2017), CIViC (Griffith et al. 2017), and the Cancer Genome Interpreter (Tamborero et al. 2018) annotate the oncogenic effect and therapeutic implications of specific variants, while ClinVar aggregates clinical assertions for germline and, increasingly, somatic variants (Landrum et al. 2018). In silico predictors, including SIFT (Kumar et al. 2009), PolyPhen-2 (Adzhubei et al. 2010), and CADD (Kircher et al. 2014), estimate the deleteriousness of amino acid substitutions from sequence conservation and structural features. However, benchmarking against functionally validated cancer mutations has shown that the accuracy of such tools is limited and varies widely across genes and algorithms (Martelotto et al. 2014). Additionally, deleteriousness is not equivalent to oncogenicity, since a damaging change in a tumor suppressor and an activating change in an oncogene have very different implications. Population databases such as ExAC provide a complementary filter, because variants observed at appreciable frequency in apparently healthy individuals are unlikely to be tumor drivers (Lek et al. 2016). This filter removes germline polymorphisms but does not by itself identify which of the remaining rare variants matter. A distinct and statistically principled source of evidence is recurrence. Mutations that arise repeatedly at the same position across independent tumors are unlikely to do so by chance and often indicate positive selection. This logic underlies the identification of mutational hotspots in cancer genes (Lawrence et al. 2014; Chang et al. 2016) and its extensions to three-dimensional clusters of residues (Gao et al. 2017). The Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) is the most extensive repository of such observations, compiling variants from the literature and large-scale screens (Forbes et al. 2015). Nevertheless, recurrence analyses depend on the size and composition of the underlying cohorts. COSMIC is dominated by variants from whole-exome and whole-genome studies and from certain well-studied tumor types and genes, so rare variants, variants in less-studied cancers, and variants in genes covered mainly by clinical panels may reach the threshold of recurrence only when data are aggregated across additional sources. Variants that appear only once or twice in COSMIC may thus be flagged as private or rare, although they are in fact recurrent in newer, larger, and more clinically representative data sets. The American Association for Cancer Research Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (AACR Project GENIE) offers precisely such a data set. GENIE is an international, publicly accessible registry of clinical-grade genomic data from patients treated at participating cancer centers, linking sequencing results to clinical annotation across a wide variety of tumor types (AACR Project GENIE Consortium 2017). Because the data are generated in the course of routine care, they represent the patient population seen in practice, including uncommon histologies and patients who would not typically be enrolled in research cohorts. They also continue to expand with each data release. These properties make GENIE an attractive complement to COSMIC for assessing recurrence. To date, however, much of the published analysis of GENIE has focused on well-known drivers and previously identified hotspots. A systematic assessment of the large remainder of variants, including those absent from or poorly represented in COSMIC, has not been performed. As a result, it remains unclear how many patients carry variants that are currently labeled VUS but whose recurrence indicates they merit closer attention. In this study, we sought to fill this gap by combining GENIE and COSMIC to identify recurrent variants that would be overlooked when either resource is used alone. We first removed variants that are already well understood, namely known hotspot variants, inactivating variants in tumor suppressor genes, and likely benign variants identified by their frequency in ExAC (Lek et al. 2016). This left a set of variants of uncertain significance, from which we asked three questions. First, how many variants observed in GENIE are novel with respect to COSMIC, and what is the typical per-patient burden of pathogenic, likely pathogenic, and uncertain variants? Second, how many variants recur in GENIE at a frequency that would be notable but are rare or absent in COSMIC? Third, how many additional variants cross a recurrence threshold when the two data sets are pooled, and what proportion of patients carry them? Our analysis makes three principal contributions. First, we provide a catalogue of tens of thousands of variants unique to GENIE, thereby describing the extent of unexplored variation in a clinical cohort. Second, we identify several hundred variants that recur in GENIE but have limited support in COSMIC, and a considerably larger set that becomes recurrent only through integration of both resources. We propose these as candidates for prioritization in functional and clinical studies. Third, we estimate the fraction of patients whose molecular profiles would be affected by these newly recognized recurrent variants, which indicates the potential reach of improved variant interpretation. Recurrence alone does not establish pathogenicity, and we do not suggest that these variants be treated as drivers without further evidence. We argue instead that they should be ranked above other VUS in the queue for experimental characterization, computational modeling, and incorporation into clinical knowledge bases. Data sources and cohort description Somatic variant data were obtained from the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE) public release (AACR Project GENIE Consortium 2017). GENIE aggregates clinical-grade targeted sequencing data from multiple international cancer centers, each of which uses institution-specific gene panels. We used the mutation data file, the clinical sample and patient files, and the gene panel annotation files distributed with the release. Only single-nucleotide variants and small insertions and deletions mapped to the GRCh37 reference assembly were retained. Records lacking a protein-level annotation, a genomic coordinate, or a valid sample identifier were excluded. Where several samples derived from the same patient were present, variants were counted once per patient at each genomic position to avoid inflating recurrence through serial or multi-site sampling. Cancer type was assigned using the OncoTree classification supplied by the consortium (Kundra et al. 2021). Reference data on previously observed somatic variants were obtained from the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) (Forbes et al. 2015). We used the COSMIC genome-screen and targeted-screen mutation export, which reports the number of independent samples in which each variant was observed. Variants were matched between datasets by gene symbol, HGVS protein-level change (HGVSp), and, where available, genomic coordinates and nucleotide change. Gene symbols were harmonized to HGNC-approved nomenclature, and transcript-specific annotation differences were resolved by preferring the canonical transcript. Population allele frequencies were obtained from the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) (Lek et al. 2016; Lee et al. 2012), which provides allele counts from more than 60,000 exomes. Gene classification To distinguish mechanisms of pathogenicity, genes were classified as oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, or other, using the cancer gene annotations in COSMIC Cancer Gene Census (Sondka et al. 2018) supplemented by curated oncogene and tumor suppressor lists (Vogelstein et al. 2013). Genes annotated with both roles were treated as context dependent and were retained for both filtering paths described below. Genes lacking an annotation were treated as unclassified, and no gene-role-based filtering was applied to them. Variant filtering and definition of novel variants The analytic strategy was to remove variants whose significance is already established or whose pathogenic potential is very low, leaving a pool of variants of unknown significance (VUS) for recurrence analysis. Filtering proceeded in three stages. First, known hotspot variants were removed. A variant was considered a known hotspot if it was reported in COSMIC in at least three independent samples, consistent with common recurrence thresholds used to nominate candidate driver positions (Chang et al. 2016). Variants matching curated hotspot positions in cancer hotspot resources were also removed. Second, inactivating variants in tumor suppressor genes were excluded. These comprised nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice-site (±1 or ±2), and translation start-site variants. Such variants are generally presumed loss-of-function and are treated as likely pathogenic under standard interpretive frameworks (Richards et al. 2015), so they were not considered VUS. Missense and in-frame variants in tumor suppressors were retained. Third, likely benign variants were removed using population frequency. Variants with a minor allele frequency greater than 0.1% in any ExAC continental population, or observed in more than one homozygous individual, were considered likely germline polymorphisms and excluded. This threshold follows the recommendation that variants too common for the prevalence of a penetrant disorder be considered benign (Richards et al. 2015). Because GENIE data are derived mostly from tumor-only sequencing without matched normal tissue, residual germline variants cannot be excluded entirely, and we treated this as a limitation of the analysis. After filtering, a variant was labeled novel if it was observed in GENIE but absent from COSMIC. A variant observed in COSMIC in fewer than three samples was designated a low-recurrence COSMIC variant. Variants were further categorized by predicted consequence (missense, in-frame insertion or deletion, splice region, synonymous, or other). Per-patient variant burden and pathogenicity categories To estimate how many variants per patient fall into each interpretive category, we tallied for each patient the total number of coding variants, the number classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, and the number remaining as VUS. Variants were designated pathogenic or likely pathogenic if they were known hotspots or inactivating mutations in tumor suppressor genes, as defined above, and as VUS if they remained after those filters and were not considered benign. Summary statistics (mean, median, and interquartile range) were calculated across patients and stratified by cancer type and by sequencing center, in order to evaluate the influence of panel size on observed burden. Because panels differ substantially in the number of genes interrogated, comparisons across centers were interpreted with caution, and per-megabase normalization was applied using panel footprints from the gene panel files when comparing burden among institutions. Recurrence analysis Recurrence was defined as the number of independent patients (GENIE) or samples (COSMIC) carrying an identical variant, specified by gene and amino acid change. Abstract Traditional approaches for color propagation in videos rely on some form of matching between consecutive video frames. Using appearance descriptors, colors are then propagated both spatially and temporally. These methods, however, are computationally expensive and do not take advantage of semantic information of the scene. In this work we propose a deep learning framework for color propagation that combines a local strategy, to propagate colors frame-by-frame ensuring temporal stability, and a global strategy, using semantics for color propagation within a longer range. Our evaluation shows the superiority of our strategy over existing video and image color propagation methods as well as neural photo-realistic style transfer approaches. Color propagation is an important problem in video processing and has a wide range of applications. For example in movie making work-flow, where color modification for artistic purposes [2] plays an important role. It is also used in the restoration and colorization of heritage footage [1] for more engaging experiences. Finally, the ability to faithfully propagate colors in videos can have a direct impact on video compression. Traditional approaches for color propagation rely on optical flow computation to propagate colors in videos either from scribbles or fully colored frames. Estimating these correspondence maps is computationally expensive and error prone. Inaccuracies in optical flow can lead to color artifacts which accumulate over time. Recently, deep learning methods have been proposed to take advantage of semantics for color propagation in images [56] and videos [21]. Still, these approaches have some limitations and do not yet achieve satisfactory results on video content. In this work we propose a framework for color propagation in videos that combines local and global strategies. Given the first frame of a sequence in color, the local strategy warps these colors frame by frame based on the motion. However this local warping becomes less reliable with increasing distance from the reference frame. To account for that we propose a global strategy to transfer colors of the first frame based on semantics, through deep feature matching. These approaches are combined through a fusion Figure 1: Color propagation after 30 frames (k = 30). Our approach is superior to existing strategies for video color propagation. (Image source: [38]) and refinement network to synthesize the final image. The network is trained on video sequences and our evaluation shows the superiority of the proposed method over image and video propagation methods as well as neural style transfer approaches, see Figure 1. Our main contribution is a deep learning architecture, that combines local and global strategies for color propagation in videos. We use a two-stage training procedure necessary to fully take advantage of both strategies. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results as it is able to maintain better colorization results over a longer time interval compared to a wide range of methods. A traditional approach to image colorization is to propagate colors or transformation parameters from user scribbles to unknown regions. Seminal works in this direction considered low level affinities based on spatial and intensity distance [23]. To reduce user interaction, many directions have been considered such as designing better similarities [29]. Other approaches to improve edit propagation include embedding learning [9], iterative feature discrimination [50] or dictionary learning [10]. Achieving convincing results for automatic image colorization [11, 20], deep convolutional networks have also been considered for edit propagation [12] and interactive image colorization [56]. To extend edit propagation to videos, computational efficiency is critical and various strategies have been investigated [3, 53]. One of the first method considering gray scale video colorization was proposed by Welsh et al. [48] as a frame-to-frame color propagation. Later, image patch comparisons [43] were used to handle large displacements and rotations. However this method targets cartoon content and is not directly adaptable to natural videos. Yatzi et al. [54] consider geodesic distance in the 3d spatio-temporal volume to color pixels in videos and Sheng et al. [40] replace spatial distance by a distance based on Gabor features. The notion of reliability and priority [19] for coloring pixels allow better color propagation. These notions are extended to entire frames [49], considering several of them as sources for coloring next gray images. For increased robustness, Pierre et al. [37] use a variational model that rely on temporal correspondence maps estimated through patch matching and optical flow estimation. Instead of using pixel correspondences, some recent methods have proposed alternative approaches to the video colorization problem. Meyer et al. [32] transfer image edits as modifications of the phase-based representation of the pixels. The main advantage is that expensive global optimization is avoided, however propagation is limited to only a few frames. Paul et al. [35] uses instead of motion vectors the dominant orientations of a 3D steerable pyramid decomposition as guidance for the color propagation of user scribbles. Jampani et al. [21], on the other hand, use a temporal bilateral network for dense and video adaptive filtering, followed by a spatial network to refine features. Video colorization can be seen as transferring the color or style of the first frame to the rest of the images in the sequence. We only outline the main directions of color transfer as an extensive review of these methods is available in [13]. Many methods rely on histogram matching [39] which can achieve surprisingly good results given their relative simplicity but colors could be transferred between incoherent regions. Taking segmentation into account can help to improve this aspect [44]. Color transfer between videos is also possible [6] by segmenting the images using luminance and transferring chrominance. Recently Arbelot et al. [4] proposed an edge-aware texture descriptor to guide the colorization. Other works focus on more complex transformations such as changing the time of the day in photographs [41], artistic edits [42] or season change [34]. Since the seminal work of Gatys et al. [15], various methods based on neural networks have been proposed [24]. While most of them focus on painterly results, several recent works have targeted photo-realistic style transfer [18, 26, 28, 31]. Mechrez et al. [31] rely on Screened Poisson Equation to maintain the fidelity with the style image while constraining the results to have gradients similar to the content image. In [28] photo-realism is maintained by constraining the image transformation to be locally affine in color space. This is achieved by adding a corresponding loss to the original neural style transfer formulation [14]. To avoid the resulting slow optimization process, patch matching on VGG [18] features can be used to obtain a guidance image. Finally, Li et al. [26] proposed a two stage architecture where an initial stylized image, estimated through whitening and coloring transform (WCT) [25], is refined with a smoothing step. The goal of our method is to colorize a gray scale image sequence by propagating the given color of the first frame to the following frames. Our proposed approach takes into account two complementary aspects: short range and long range color propagation, see Figure 2. The objective of the short range propagation network is to propagate colors on a frame by frame basis. It takes as input two consecutive gray scale frames and estimates a warping function. This warping function is used to transfer the colors of the previous frame to the next one. Following recent trends [22, 33, 51], warping is expressed as a convolution process. In our case we choose to use spatially adaptive kernels that account for motion and re-sampling simultaneously [33], but other approaches based on optical flow could be considered as well. Figure 2: Overview. To propagate colors in a video we use both short range and long range color propagation. First, the local color propagation network Fw uses consecutive gray scale frames Gk−1 and Gk to predict spatially adaptive kernels that account for motion and re-sampling from Ik−1 . To globally transfer the colors from the reference frame I1 to the entire video a matching based on deep image features is used. The results of these two steps, Iks and Ikw , are together with Gk the input to the fusion and refinement network which estimates the final current color frame Ik . (Image source: [38]) For longer range propagation, simply smoothing warped colors according to the gray scale guide image is not sufficient. Semantic understanding of the scene is needed to transfer color from the first colored frame of the video to the rest of the video sequence. In our case, we find correspondences between pixels of the first frame and the rest of the video. Instead of matching pixel colors directly we incorporate semantical information by matching deep features extracted from the frames. These correspondences are then used in order to sample colors from the first frame. Besides the advantage for long range color propagation, this approach also helps to recover missing colors due to occlusion/dis-occlusion. To combine the intermediate images of these two parallel stages, we use a convolutional neural network. This corresponds to the fusion and refinement stage. As a result, the final colored image is estimated by taking advantage of information that is present in both intermediate images, i.e. local and global color information. Let’s consider a grayscale video sequence G = {G1 , G2 , . . . , Gn } of n frames, where the colored image I1 (corresponding to G1 ) is available. Our objective is to use the frame I1 to colorize the set of grayscale frames G. Using a local (frame-by-frame) strategy, colors of I1 can be sequentially propagated to the entire video using temporal consistency. With a global strategy, colors present in the first frame I1 can be simultaneously transfered to all the frames of the video using a style transfer like approach. In this work we propose a unified solution for video colorization combining local and global strategies. Relying on temporal consistency, our objective is to propagate colors frame by frame. Using the adaptive convolution approach developed for frame interpolation [33], one can similarly write color propagation as convolution operation on the color image: given two consecutive grayscale frames Gk−1 and Gk , and the color frame Ik−1 , an estimate of the colored frame Ik can be expressed as Ikw (x, y) = Pk−1 (x, y) ∗ Kk (x, y) , where Pk−1 (x, y) is the image patch around pixel Ik−1 (x, y) and Kk (x, y) is the estimated pixel dependent convolution kernel based on Gk and Gk−1 . This kernel is approximated with two 1D-kernels as Kk (x, y) = Kkv (x, y) ∗ Kkh (x, y) . (2) The convolutional neural network architecture used to predict these kernels is similar to the one originally proposed for frame interpolation [33], with the difference that 2 kernels are predicted (instead of 4 in the interpolation case). Furthermore, we use a softmax layer for kernel prediction which helps to speedup training [46]. This can be due to occlusions/dis-occlusions, new elements appearing in the scene or even complete change of background (due to camera panning for example). In this case, a global strategy with semantic understanding of the scene is necessary. It allows to transfer color within a longer range both temporally and spatially. To achieve this, we leverage deep feature extracted with convolutional neural networks trained for classification and image segmentation.
