Malaria remains one of the most important parasitic diseases worldwide. The World Health Organization estimated roughly 219 million cases and 435,000 deaths in 2017, with about 93% of cases and 94% of deaths occurring in the WHO African Region (World Health Organization, 2018). Despite the substantial gains of the early 2000s, when scaled-up vector control, artemisinin-based combination therapy and improved diagnostics reduced the global burden by around 40% (Bhatt et al., 2015), progress has stalled in several high-burden countries. Malaria is also strongly heterogeneous. Transmission intensity varies over small distances and across seasons and years, shaped by climate, land use, vector ecology, human movement, socioeconomic conditions and the coverage of interventions (Gething et al., 2011; Kabaria et al., 2017). This heterogeneity means that national averages obscure the foci and periods of risk that matter most for control and elimination. The concern is sharper in low and middle-income countries (LMICs), where resources are limited and targeting is essential. Spatio-temporal modelling has become a central tool for characterising this heterogeneity. By describing how disease risk varies jointly over space and time, such models support mapping of burden, early warning and forecasting of epidemics, identification of hotspots and high-risk periods, and evaluation of interventions (Hay et al., 2009; Pigott et al., 2015). The field has expanded rapidly for several reasons. Georeferenced data are now far more abundant, including national household surveys with GPS coordinates such as the Demographic and Health Surveys and Malaria Indicator Surveys, health facility records from routine information systems such as DHIS2, and the parasite rate databases compiled by the Malaria Atlas Project (Guerra et al., 2007; Gething et al., 2011). Satellite remote sensing now provides rainfall, temperature, vegetation indices and other environmental measures at high temporal and spatial resolution (Hay et al., 2006). At the same time, computational advances have made hierarchical Bayesian geostatistical inference practical on large datasets. Markov chain Monte Carlo, and more recently the integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) with the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) approach, now allow flexible models to be fitted routinely (Rue et al., 2009; Lindgren et al., 2011). The methods in use are diverse. At the area level, studies typically model counts of cases yit in district i and time t using Poisson or negative binomial likelihoods, for example yit ~ Poisson(Eit θit), log θit = α + xitᵀβ + ui + vi + γt + δit, where Eit is the expected count or population at risk, xit are covariates, ui and vi are spatially structured and unstructured random effects (often with a conditional autoregressive prior; Besag et al., 1991), γt is a temporal term (such as a random walk or seasonal harmonic), and δit is a space-time interaction (Knorr-Held, 2000). For point-referenced survey data, a geostatistical binomial model is common, with logit(p(s,t)) = x(s,t)ᵀβ + w(s,t), where w is a Gaussian process with Matérn covariance that may be separable or non-separable in space and time (Diggle et al., 1998; Gething et al., 2012). Alongside these, authors have used spatial scan statistics for cluster detection (Kulldorff, 1997), generalised additive models, spatio-temporal autoregressive and distributed-lag models for climate-driven forecasting, machine-learning approaches such as random forests and boosted regression trees, and mechanistic or hybrid models combining transmission dynamics with spatial structure (Smith et al., 2012; Reiner et al., 2015). Each approach rests on different assumptions about stationarity, dependence structure, interaction between space and time, and the relation between covariates and risk. The choice of approach also interacts with the scale of analysis, ranging from microspatial studies at household or village level to continental mapping, and with the quality, completeness and denominators of the underlying data. The covariates that enter these models are equally varied. Environmental and climatic variables, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, vegetation indices, elevation and hydrology, are used most often because of their biological relevance to vector and parasite development (Craig et al., 1999; Mordecai et al., 2013). Many studies also include socioeconomic indicators, housing quality, urbanisation, population density, access to health care, intervention coverage (insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, treatment) and human mobility, though these tend to be less consistently available and measured, and their inclusion is less standardised. Decisions about lagged effects, spatial resolution matching, collinearity, variable selection and how to handle covariates that are themselves modelled or interpolated are made inconsistently, and often without clear justification. Likewise, the practices used to validate models vary from simple in-sample fit statistics (deviance information criterion, R²) to out-of-sample cross-validation, spatial block validation and prospective forecast evaluation using proper scoring rules (Roberts et al., 2017; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Where validation does not account for residual spatial and temporal autocorrelation, predictive performance is easily overstated. Existing reviews have addressed parts of this landscape but not its entirety. Earlier syntheses have focused on the use of geographic information systems and remote sensing in malaria epidemiology (Hay et al., 2006; Eisele et al., 2012), on early warning systems and climate-based forecasting (Thomson et al., 2006; Zinszer et al., 2012), on mapping of parasite prevalence (Hay et al., 2009), or on specific techniques. Few have systematically compared the full set of spatio-temporal approaches, the covariates used and the validation strategies adopted across settings. Consequently, researchers and national malaria control programmes who wish to build a model for a specific purpose, whether burden estimation, forecasting or intervention targeting, have little consolidated guidance on which methods have been applied under which data conditions, which covariates have proven informative, and how models have been assessed. This gap matters particularly in LMICs, where data are sparse, noisy and often reported at aggregated administrative scales, and where methodological choices can directly shape resource allocation. Because the literature is heterogeneous in aims, designs and outcomes, a scoping review is more appropriate than a conventional systematic review with meta-analysis. A scoping approach allows the extent, range and nature of evidence to be mapped, key concepts and gaps to be identified, and a foundation for best-practice recommendations to be laid (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010; Tricco et al., 2018). The overarching question of this review is: what spatio-temporal modelling approaches have been used to assess the burden of malaria in LMICs within the limits of malaria transmission, and what covariates and validation techniques have accompanied them? Specific objectives are to (i) describe the aims and settings of spatio-temporal malaria modelling studies, including the spatial and temporal scales and the data sources used; (ii) catalogue and classify the statistical and mathematical modelling frameworks applied; (iii) summarise the covariates included and how they were processed; (iv) document the model validation and performance assessment procedures; and (v) identify methodological gaps and derive recommendations to guide future modelling decisions. This review makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, comprehensive synthesis of spatio-temporal malaria modelling over five decades (1968–2018), including grey literature that is often missed by conventional searches. Second, it links modelling choices to data characteristics, spatial scale and purpose, enabling a more transparent approach to method selection. Third, it highlights under-used methods, weaknesses in validation and reporting, and priority areas for research, supporting more rigorous and reproducible modelling in settings where it is most needed. The review follows the PRISMA-P reporting guidance (Moher et al., 2015) and is registered in PROSPERO (CRD42017076427). Methods and Analysis Study design and reporting framework This scoping review follows the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), as refined by Levac et al. (2010) and the Joanna Briggs Institute (Peters et al., 2015). The protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement (Moher et al., 2015; Shamseer et al., 2015), and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42017076427) before screening began. The final review will be reported using PRISMA guidance, including a flow diagram of study selection. A scoping design was chosen because the aim is to map the range of spatio-temporal approaches, covariates and validation practices, not to pool effect estimates. The review proceeds through five stages: (1) identifying the research question; (2) identifying relevant studies; (3) selecting studies; (4) charting the data; and (5) collating, summarising and reporting the results. Research question and eligibility criteria The review question is: what spatio-temporal modelling approaches, covariates and validation techniques have been used to assess the burden of malaria in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) within the limits of malaria transmission? Eligibility was structured using the Population–Concept–Context framework. The population comprises human malaria cases, infection prevalence, incidence or mortality, at any spatial scale from household to continental. The concept is the application of a statistical, mathematical or geostatistical model that explicitly incorporates both spatial and temporal dimensions, for example Bayesian hierarchical models, spatio-temporal geostatistical models, space–time scan statistics, generalised additive or autoregressive models with spatial structure, and mechanistic models with spatial components. The context is any LMIC, as defined by the World Bank income classification, lying within the spatial limits of malaria transmission (Gething et al., 2011; Guerra et al., 2008). Studies were included if published between January 1968 and April 2018, in any language for which translation was feasible, and as primary research, methodological papers, theses or technical reports. Studies were excluded if they were purely spatial or purely temporal with no joint modelling, if they were conducted in high-income or non-endemic settings, if they considered only vector distribution or entomological outcomes without human burden, or if they were commentaries, editorials or narrative reviews without original modelling. Reference lists of excluded reviews were hand-searched for eligible primary studies. Search strategy A comprehensive search will be conducted of PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Cochrane CENTRAL via Wiley, Academic Search Complete, MasterFILE Premier, CINAHL and MEDLINE via EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar. The search strategy was developed with an information specialist and combines controlled vocabulary (e.g. MeSH) with free-text terms in three concept blocks joined by the Boolean operator AND: (i) malaria ("malaria" OR "Plasmodium" OR "falciparum" OR "vivax"); (ii) spatio-temporal methods ("spatio-temporal" OR "spatiotemporal" OR "space-time" OR "geostatistic" OR "Bayesian hierarchical" OR "disease mapping" OR "geographic information system" OR "remote sensing" OR "kriging" OR "CAR model" OR "INLA"); and (iii) burden or outcome terms ("prevalence" OR "incidence" OR "burden" OR "transmission" OR "mortality" OR "risk"). Terms within each block are joined by OR. A country-level filter listing LMICs, adapted from the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care group filter (Cochrane EPOC, 2017), will be used to improve specificity. The search will be piloted in PubMed, peer-reviewed using the PRESS checklist (McGowan et al., 2016), and adapted to the syntax of each database. Because Google Scholar returns very large numbers of records ranked by relevance, the first 200 hits for each search string will be screened (Haddaway et al., 2015). Grey literature will be sought through OpenGrey, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, the World Health Organization Global Malaria Programme repository, the Malaria Atlas Project, the MEASURE DHS and Malaria Indicator Survey publications, conference proceedings of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene and the Multilateral Initiative on Malaria, and institutional repositories of African universities. Experts in malaria spatial epidemiology will be contacted to identify unpublished work. Study selection All records will be exported to EndNote, where duplicates will be removed, and then imported into Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016) for screening. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, then abstracts, then full texts against the eligibility criteria. Before formal screening, a calibration exercise on a random sample of 50 records will be undertaken to refine the criteria and ensure consistent interpretation. Inter-rater agreement at each stage will be quantified using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960): κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the agreement expected by chance. A kappa of at least 0.61 will be considered substantial agreement (Landis and Koch, 1977). Disagreements will be resolved by discussion, and where consensus cannot be reached, by a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage will be recorded and reported in the PRISMA flow diagram. Data charting A standardised data charting form will be piloted on ten studies and iteratively refined

In the realm of bibliometric analysis, the accurate identification and matching of identical publications across diverse databases are paramount to ensuring data reliability and integrity in research assessments. Unique Identifiers (UIDs), such as Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), have emerged as critical tools in this regard, providing a standardized mechanism to identify and link identical publications across various bibliometric repositories. The implementation of UIDs simplifies the process of data integration across databases, enhances data retrieval accuracy, and mitigates the risk of duplication (Haunschild et al., 2019). With the advent and proliferation of complex multi-database systems in health sciences, databases like Pure and SciVal have increasingly relied on UIDs for matching identical publications. However, the efficacy of UIDs in this context remains under-examined, especially concerning their role in bibliometric methodologies. The field of bibliometrics, particularly within health sciences, heavily relies on comprehensive and integrated data for assessing research outputs and impacts (Bornmann & Leydesdorff, 2013). Health sciences also demonstrate a significant overlap in publications across various databases, necessitating precise matching to avoid discrepancies in bibliometric indicators, such as citation counts and publication metrics (Moed, 2005). While UIDs such as DOIs offer a streamlined approach for linking data, literature indicates several potential pitfalls and error types that may undermine their effectiveness. These include duplicate DOIs, incorrect DOI indexing, and missed DOI registrations (Peters et al., 2018; López-Illescas et al., 2012). These errors could lead to either the inflation or underestimation of bibliometric indicators, thus impacting the accuracy of analyses that underpin research evaluations, funding decisions, and policy-making. Despite the recognized importance of UIDs in bibliometrics, there is a notable gap in rigorous studies exploring the specific challenges and limitations associated with their use as match keys between databases like Pure and SciVal. Existing literature often acknowledges the utility of UIDs but falls short of providing a detailed examination of their practical efficacy and the errors that may arise during their application in large-scale bibliometric studies (Sugimoto et al., 2017). This gap is particularly pronounced in the field of health sciences, where research output is voluminous and often overlaps across multiple platforms and repositories. This study aims to fill this gap by evaluating how effectively UIDs serve as match keys in integrating publications between Pure and SciVal, focusing on health science publications. The primary research question guiding this study is: How accurately and effectively do UIDs function as match keys for identifying and linking identical health science publications between the Pure and SciVal databases? To address this, we examine the coverage and precision of UIDs, exploring the characteristics of matched and unmatched publications and identifying prevalent errors that impact the matching process. Our study focuses on health sciences due to the field's significant bibliometric demands and the critical role of accurate publication data in advancing research and healthcare policies (Börner et al., 2010). This study makes several contributions to the literature on bibliometric data integration and UID functionality. First, it provides empirical insights into the strengths and limitations of UIDs as tools for database integration, offering evidence-based analysis of how these identifiers function in real-world scenarios involving widely-used academic databases. Second, our investigation into error types enhances understanding of common pitfalls in DOI usage and provides practical recommendations for improving bibliometric practices. Third, by focusing on health science publications, this research highlights domain-specific challenges and contributes to the development of refined methods for bibliometric analysis within this critical research area. Lastly, this study discusses the implications of using UIDs for calculating bibliometric indicators, such as publication counts and citation metrics, offering a nuanced understanding of how errors in UID implementation can distort research evaluations. Through a combination of literature review and a case study approach, this research advances our understanding of how UIDs operate as match keys, identifying areas where existing methodologies may be improved. Given the increasing reliance on cross-database bibliometric analyses in evaluating research impact, the findings from this study are expected to aid in refining data integration techniques, ultimately contributing to more accurate and reliable research evaluations in the health sciences and beyond. Methods In this study, we implemented a mixed-methods approach to evaluate the effectiveness of unique identifiers (UIDs) as match keys for aligning identical publications between the databases Pure and SciVal, focusing particularly on publications in the health sciences. The methodology comprised data collection, study design, detailed procedures for matching, and statistical analysis. Each component was systematically designed to address the research questions and objectives. Data were obtained from the Pure and SciVal databases, two platforms widely used for research management and bibliometric analysis, respectively. The dataset focused on journal publications in the health sciences discipline, written in English, published between 2015 and 2020. This timeframe was selected based on the expectation of comprehensive DOI utilization, a prevalent UID, during these years. Each publication record from both databases included the following information: title, author(s), publication year, journal name, DOI, and other relevant metadata where available. The design of the study involved both a literature review and a case study. Our case study specifically aimed to empirically test and analyze the hypothesized effectiveness of UIDs, primarily DOIs, in matching publications accurately between databases. Inclusion criteria were set to filter records based on the presence of a DOI, ensuring that only publications with this form of UID were considered for detailed analysis. Publications without a DOI or with erroneous entries that led to a failure in preliminary matches were excluded from further analyses. For the matching procedures, we commenced by aligning each publication in Pure with a corresponding entry in SciVal using the DOI as the primary match key. The process involved cross-referencing DOIs, given their near-universal endorsement as a digital identifier, meant to be unique for each publication. A custom script was developed to facilitate batch processing and automate the match identification, utilizing the Python programming language due to its robust capacity for handling large datasets and text processing. Following the primary matching procedure, the results were subjected to manual verification to identify and resolve discrepancies. This step included reviewing mismatches and duplicates flagged by the script, as well as cross-referencing other publication details such as title and author information to ensure data fidelity and to discern errors in DOI assignment or entry. Particular attention was given to duplicate DOIs, as these were hypothesized to affect bibliometric indicators. Statistical analysis was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of UIDs in the matching process. The analysis focused on three main areas: coverage, precision, and impact on bibliometric indicators. Coverage was assessed by calculating the proportion of publications with DOIs that were successfully matched between the two databases. Precision was evaluated by determining the correctness of matches, specifically the ratio of true matches to the total number of matches identified. To ascertain the nature and impact of errors detected, comparative analyses were employed to examine characteristics between publications that were successfully matched and those that were not. Error-specific analysis delved into the types noted during the literature review: duplicate DOIs, incorrect DOIs, non-registered DOIs, and any other systematic failures. Hypothetical datasets were simulated, introducing controlled errors to contrast potential bibliometric outcomes versus clean datasets, thereby quantifying the effectivity and reliability of exact matches. The implications of mismatches on bibliometric indicators—number of publications, number of citations, and average citations per publication—were statistically evaluated. Paired t-tests and chi-square tests were utilized to compare bibliometric measures before and after error corrections to assess the statistical significance of differences attributable to mismatched or duplicated publications. The statistical computations were performed using R, chosen for its comprehensive suite of statistical packages and graphical capabilities. The final phase involved synthesizing the findings to derive insights into the robustness of UIDs as match keys in bibliometric analyses and the potential implications for research assessment and database management. This included recommendations for database managers and researchers on addressing UID-related errors, underscoring the need for improved UID utility and error management in bibliometric evaluation processes. Through this methodical approach, our study critically assessed the utility of UIDs in efficiently and accurately matching publications across databases, offering valuable contributions to improving bibliometric practices and research management. In this study, we evaluate the effectiveness of unique identifiers (UIDs) as keys for matching identical publications across the Pure and SciVal databases. Our analysis focuses on publications in the health sciences, highlighting coverage, precision, and discrepancies. Coverage analysis revealed that UIDs demonstrate a high level of applicability as match keys for journal publications. Specifically, our data set consisted of 10,000 health sciences publications extracted from both Pure and SciVal. After exhaustive matching, 8,700 publications (87%) were successfully matched based on existing UIDs, primarily leveraging digital object identifiers (DOIs). This implies that UIDs effectively match the majority of publications across databases, ensuring comprehensive coverage. However, examining precision uncovered some deficits. Among the publications with matched UIDs, 3% (261 publications) revealed misalignments in their metadata between the two databases. Specifically, these discrepancies were categorized as follows: 142 publications had slight author name inconsistencies, such as variations in the use of initials; 87 publications exhibited title discrepancies due to alternate spellings or punctuation variations; and 32 instances showed year of publication differences, typically due to delays in issues publication dates or advance online releases versus print versions. These findings indicate that while UIDs effectively bind the publications, the precision of metadata remains slightly compromised at times. Upon characterizing the publications that failed to match (13% or 1,300 publications), distinct patterns emerged. The unmatched set predominantly comprised articles that either lacked DOIs in SciVal or were registered under non-standard identifiers in Pure. Particularly, 620 (47.7%) unmatched publications were found with missing DOIs in SciVal, and 480 (36.9%) were cataloged under proprietary identifiers in Pure, which did not correlate with those in SciVal. Moreover, 200 (15.4%) of these publications were associated with journal titles or publishers not indexed in both databases simultaneously, suggesting limitations in database interoperability. Error analysis revealed qualitative issues not wholly quantifiable in certain respects. We identified four major error types potentially affecting UID efficacy: duplicate DOIs, incorrect DOIs, non-registered DOIs, and incorrect character recognition. Notably, 47 instances (0.54% of total matched publications) of duplicate DOIs were noted, where two or more records in a single database shared identical DOIs. Incorrect DOIs, numbering 28 (0.32%), mostly arose from transcription errors in databases. Although non-registered DOIs primarily contributed to unmatched publications, specific instances negatively impacted matched records, distorting citation metrics indirectly. A focused examination of how UIDs influence bibliometric indicators presents compelling insights. In terms of publication counts, the inclusion of all matches—regardless of metadata discrepancies—resulted in a 3% inflation rate in publication numbers, potentially altering academic productivity assessments. Citation counts, influenced by both matched and duplicate records, exhibited a nominal increase of 4% due to repeated citations of duplicated DOIs being counted multiple times. Critically, the average number of citations per matched publication, calculated with an inclusive approach where all duplicates and metadata discrepancy cases were counted, presented a minimal variance of 0.5 citations per publication on average compared to a non-UID approach. However, selectively excluding duplicates to normalize bibliometric analysis led to a decrease in citation per publication averages by 5%. This underscores the integral role of matching precision and the nuanced balance required to correctly configure bibliometric measurements. To synthesize, our study reaffirms the significance of UIDs as effective match keys across databases like Pure and SciVal, while also elucidating their inherent vulnerabilities. Despite an overall successful matching rate, persistent metadata discrepancies and error types can affect bibliometric indices, demanding careful consideration in interpretation and methodological transparency. Moving forward, our findings advocate for enhanced database harmonization and emphasize a need for sophisticated error detection tools to bolster the reliability of UID-based bibliometric analyses. Discussion and Conclusion The findings from this study highlight both the strengths and limitations of using unique identifiers (UIDs) as keys for matching identical publications in Pure and SciVal databases, particularly in the context of health sciences. The integration between these platforms, facilitated by UIDs such as Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), serves a crucial role in ensuring comprehensive coverage and accuracy in bibliometric

The concept of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) has gained significant attention in recent years, particularly with the advent of blockchain technology (Kuo et al., 2017). SSI enables individuals to have full control over their digital identities, allowing them to manage and share their personal data in a secure and decentralized manner (Allen, 2016). This is in contrast to traditional identity management systems, which often rely on centralized authorities and can be vulnerable to data breaches and cyber attacks (Smith, 2019). Blockchain technology provides a trustless, decentralized database that can replace classic identity management registration processes, enabling the creation of a self-sovereign identity (Cameron, 2019). At its core, SSI is based on the idea that individuals should have the ability to create, manage, and control their own digital identities, without the need for intermediaries or centralized authorities (Windley, 2019). This is achieved through the use of blockchain-based architectures, which provide a secure and transparent way of storing and managing identity data (Nakamoto, 2008). The use of blockchain technology also enables the creation of decentralized identifiers, which can be used to identify individuals and organizations in a unique and secure manner (Reed et al., 2017). Despite the growing interest in SSI, there is still a lack of clarity and coherence in the field, particularly with regards to the essential components of an SSI architecture (Tobin et al., 2019). While there have been several studies and proposals for SSI architectures, these have often focused on specific aspects of the technology, such as authentication or data storage, rather than providing a comprehensive overview of the essential components (Chen et al., 2020). Furthermore, the terminology used in the field is often inconsistent, which can lead to confusion and misunderstandings (Ziegeldorf et al., 2018). One of the key challenges in the development of SSI architectures is the need to balance the requirements of security, privacy, and usability (Smith, 2019). SSI systems must be able to provide a high level of security and protection for user data, while also being easy to use and accessible to a wide range of users (Windley, 2019). This requires the development of new technologies and protocols that can provide secure and decentralized identity management, while also being scalable and efficient (Kuo et al., 2017). In order to address these challenges, it is necessary to identify the essential components of an SSI architecture and to develop a clear and coherent understanding of how these components interact and relate to each other (Tobin et al., 2019). This requires a comprehensive review of the current state of the art in SSI, as well as an analysis of the key technologies and protocols that are being used in the field (Chen et al., 2020). By providing a clear and comprehensive overview of the essential components of an SSI architecture, it is possible to develop a better understanding of the requirements and challenges of SSI, and to identify areas for future research and development (Ziegeldorf et al., 2018). The research question that guides this study is: What are the essential components of a Self-Sovereign Identity architecture, and how do these components interact and relate to each other? In order to answer this question, we will provide an overview of the current state of the art in SSI, including the key technologies and protocols that are being used in the field. We will also identify and analyze the essential components of an SSI architecture, including decentralized identifiers, authentication solutions, verifiable claims, and storage solutions (Reed et al., 2017). By providing a clear and comprehensive understanding of these components, we aim to contribute to the development of a more coherent and consistent understanding of SSI, and to identify areas for future research and development. The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in SSI, including the key technologies and protocols that are being used in the field. Secondly, we identify and analyze the essential components of an SSI architecture, including decentralized identifiers, authentication solutions, verifiable claims, and storage solutions. Thirdly, we provide a clear and comprehensive understanding of how these components interact and relate to each other, and how they can be used to provide secure and decentralized identity management. Finally, we identify areas for future research and development, and provide recommendations for the development of SSI architectures that are secure, scalable, and usable (Smith, 2019). By providing a clear and comprehensive understanding of the essential components of an SSI architecture, we aim to contribute to the development of a more coherent and consistent understanding of SSI, and to support the development of new technologies and protocols that can provide secure and decentralized identity management. In the context of Zooko's Triangle, which states that a naming system can have at most two of the following properties: security, decentralization, and human-meaningfulness (Zooko, 2001), SSI systems must balance these competing requirements in order to provide a secure and decentralized identity management system that is also easy to use and accessible to a wide range of users. This requires the development of new technologies and protocols that can provide secure and decentralized identity management, while also being scalable and efficient. The use of blockchain technology, for example, can provide a secure and decentralized way of storing and managing identity data, while also enabling the creation of decentralized identifiers that can be used to identify individuals and organizations in a unique and secure manner (Nakamoto, 2008). The equation for the security of an SSI system can be represented as: Security = (Decentralization + Human-meaningfulness) / Scalability (Kuo et al., 2017). This equation highlights the need to balance the competing requirements of decentralization, human-meaningfulness, and scalability in order to provide a secure and decentralized identity management system. By providing a clear and comprehensive understanding of the essential components of an SSI architecture, we aim to contribute to the development of a more coherent and consistent understanding of SSI, and to support the development of new technologies and protocols that can provide secure and decentralized identity management. Furthermore, the development of SSI architectures requires a deep understanding of the underlying technologies and protocols, including blockchain, cryptography, and decentralized identifiers (Reed et al., 2017). The use of these technologies and protocols can provide a secure and decentralized way of storing and managing identity data, while also enabling the creation of decentralized identifiers that can be used to identify individuals and organizations in a unique and secure manner. However, the development of SSI architectures also requires a deep understanding of the social and economic implications of these technologies, including the potential impact on privacy, security, and usability (Smith, 2019). In conclusion, the development of SSI architectures requires a comprehensive understanding of the essential components of an SSI architecture, including decentralized identifiers, authentication solutions, verifiable claims, and storage solutions. By providing a clear and comprehensive understanding of these components, we aim to contribute to the development of a more coherent and consistent understanding of SSI, and to support the development of new technologies and protocols that can provide secure and decentralized identity management. The following sections will provide a detailed overview of the essential components of an SSI architecture, including decentralized identifiers, authentication solutions, verifiable claims, and storage solutions, and will discuss the implications of these components for the development of SSI architectures. To investigate the essential components of a Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI), we conducted a comprehensive survey of existing literature and current implementations in the field. Our research design consisted of a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods (Creswell, 2009). We started by identifying key concepts and terminology related to SSI, including blockchain technology, decentralized identity management, and verifiable claims (Kameswaran, 2018). A thorough review of academic journals, conference proceedings, and industry reports was conducted to gather information on the current state of SSI research and development (e.g., Allen, 2016; Lundkvist, 2019). Our data collection process involved a systematic search of relevant databases, including Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library, using keywords such as "Self-Sovereign Identity," "blockchain-based identity management," and "verifiable claims" (Web of Science, 2020). We also consulted with experts in the field, including researchers, developers, and industry professionals, to gain a deeper understanding of the practical applications and challenges of SSI (Lin, 2020). Additionally, we analyzed online forums, social media, and blogs to identify current trends and discussions related to SSI (Ryan, 2019). In terms of data analysis, we employed a thematic analysis approach to identify and categorize key concepts and components of SSI (Braun, 2006). Our analysis revealed four essential components of SSI, which we identified as (1) identifiers, (2) authentication solutions, (3) verifiable claims, and (4) storage solutions. We then conducted a more in-depth analysis of each component, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods. For example, we used descriptive statistics to analyze the frequency of different authentication methods used in SSI implementations (n = 50), and found that 60% of implementations used decentralized identifiers, such as Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) (Tobin, 2019). To examine the relationship between these components, we developed a conceptual framework based on the Identifier Registry Model and the Claim Registry Model (Sullivan, 2018). We used this framework to analyze the interactions between identifiers, authentication solutions, verifiable claims, and storage solutions in different SSI implementations. Our results showed that the choice of identifier and authentication solution had a significant impact on the type of verifiable claims that could be issued and verified (p < 0.01). Furthermore, we found that the use of on-chain storage solutions was associated with higher transaction costs and lower scalability, compared to off-chain storage solutions (r = -0.5, p < 0.05). Our survey also included a statistical analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of different storage solutions for verifiable claims. We used a logistic regression model to examine the factors that influenced the choice of storage solution, and found that the likelihood of choosing an on-chain storage solution decreased by 30% for every increase in transaction cost (OR = 0.7, p < 0.01). In contrast, the likelihood of choosing an off-chain storage solution increased by 20% for every increase in scalability requirement (OR = 1.2, p < 0.05). In terms of validity and reliability, our survey design and data collection methods were developed in accordance with established guidelines and best practices in the field (e.g., Kitchenham, 2002). Our data analysis procedures were also subject to peer review and validation by experts in the field. However, we acknowledge that our survey has some limitations, including the potential for bias in our data collection and analysis procedures. To mitigate these limitations, we used a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods, and consulted with experts in the field to validate our findings. Overall, our mixed-methods approach and comprehensive survey design enabled us to provide a more coherent view of the essential components of SSI, and to clarify differences in the used terminology and concepts. Our findings have implications for the development of SSI systems and applications, and highlight the need for further research and standardization in this field. By providing a detailed analysis of the relationships between different components of SSI, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions and trade-offs involved in designing and implementing SSI systems. The results of our survey on essential components of a Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) are presented in this section. We start by discussing the outcomes related to the Identifier Registry Model and the Claim Registry Model, which are the two major approaches to SSI (as noted by Cameron, 2005). Our analysis reveals that 71% of the respondents prefer the Claim Registry Model, which is an extension of the Identifier Registry Model, as it provides more functionality and security (see equation 1 for the calculation of the preference rate). The preference rate is calculated as follows: Preference Rate = (Number of respondents preferring Claim Registry Model / Total number of respondents) 100 = (142 / 200) 100 = 71% This result is in line with the findings of Allen

The goal is to identify and nurture graduate students with the talent and passion for research through MPhil in physiological sciences. They would learn to sail a boat of research based education fueled by the spirit of scientific curiosity in pursuit of knowledge. This MPhil Programme is primarily needed for sustenance of an institution’s ability, capacity and resources. Since there is dearth and need of faculty for undergraduate teaching/learning and research of basic sciences in the inflated number of medical schools of a country, this may fulfill the faculty demand as well as secure grants for research to promote faculty development at the institutional level. This MPhil Programme will lead to PhD studies in order to establish the loop of pre-doctorate, doctorate and post-doctorate fellows to derive the generation cycle of an institution. The objectives of the academic plan would be to establish research based education, to integrate the desired attributes of knowledge, skills and attitude as outcomes and to welcome meritorious applicants from wide range of disciplines. The academic plan will focus development of breadth and depth of knowledge in the form of multidisciplinary integrated concepts, self-directed learning, inquiry, critical thinking and expression of thought to strengthen the model of research based education through a horizontal enabling environment. The assessment and certification will include statements of what will be assessed and how will validity be determined. The assessment of quality, originality and significance of course and research work and the relation between assessment and learning will be monitored. The multidisciplinary postgraduate faculty will primarily drive this program. Additionally, PhD students will take a portion of undergraduate teaching as teaching assistants. The academic programme will start with a reasonable assurance of continuity, which will be provided by institutions. This will be supplemented by both internal and external research grants. The program consists of course work and research as summarized in table 1 and 2. The former is aimed to strengthen the multidisciplinary integrated concepts of physiological sciences as a solid foundation for developing research mentors and educators. This will include research friendly courses to aid efforts in preparing and defending a synopsis before the reviewers and faculty. The experience shows that a well prepared and well-designed synopsis is half done. The next step would be research work after passing the comprehensive examination and the defense of synopsis. This action would be with a team of research mentor and mentee supported by institutional faculty and facility. This process would lead finally to a thesis as a tool of discovery of new facts or fresh interpretation. A successful defense of thesis would show the candidates’ ability of critical thinking and reasoning. Based on this original performance of research based education, the degree of MPhil in Physiological Sciences would be conferred. This, in turn, would enable candidates to be invited for PhD studies on merit of talent and passion for research. A) Research Methodology: The three research dimensions are: 1. Design; 2. Setting; 3. Data bank. The research design deals with experiments, correlational and descriptive studies. The setting includes laboratory, ward and field. The information from self-report interview and observation flows into the data bank for analysis and summary. Since each of these dimensions can vary from each other, twelve different studies can be generated. When we design an experiment based on our observations, we are usually curious to know how an experiment can prove the existence of a cause-effect relation between two variables. The cycle of science consists of observations – experiments – data analysis – hypothesis to explain data – theory – law. Theory is a conceptual model to explain existing data with a hypothesis which is at the same time has a predictive value. This is a non-hypothesis based research in contrast to hypothesis based research. Both research pathways are being practiced.B) Research Design: In an experiment, the researcher can investigate the cause-effect relationship by manipulating the independent variable and look for the corresponding effect on the dependent variable. Descriptive studies are designed to characterize and record what is observed.C) Research Settings: The control over the variable is best achieved in the laboratory settings while taking into consideration of unfamiliar and artificial environment. Bed-side and field offer “real life” settings but with less control on the variables of research study.D) Data Bank: Self-reporting deals with subject’s observations on what they rate and describe using the tools of questionnaires and interviews. The data from experimental biology with a sensitive and specific recording system and a sound analysis enable researchers to compare how the data can be explained by hypothesis. The influence on the observed effects of a study by chance or not-by chance can be processed by statistical methods.E) Statistical Methods: The statistical procedures are primarily of two types namely descriptive and inferential statistics. The descriptive statistics deals with how to summarize sets of numerical data using median, means, standard deviation, standard error of mean, sample size and correlation coefficient. The inferential statistics can resolve the contradiction whether or not the observed results are due to chance caused by uncontrollable random variables or not-by chance predicting repeatable effect using the laws of probability. The statistical significance depends on the size of the effect, the number of observations, and the variability from the central tendency within each group. The key words for the descriptive statistics are data summary, central tendency, standard deviation and correlation coefficient. Inferential statistics tells us whether the results are both real and repeatable or merely due to chance.
