The proliferation of biometric technologies in modern identity verification and security applications has spurred extensive research into various phenotypic human traits. Among these, sex prediction from biometric traits has garnered particular interest due to its implications in personalization, security, and forensic investigations (Jain et al., 2016). The periocular region, defined as the anatomical area surrounding the eye, has emerged as a robust source of biometric information, exhibiting resilience to occlusions and variations in facial expressions (Park et al., 2011). Consequently, research exploring the potential of periocular images for demographic prediction tasks, including sex prediction, has gained traction. Despite progress, current sex-prediction systems often rely on controlled acquisition environments and specific sensing modalities, such as visible wavelength (VW) imaging. These approaches typically assume that the imaging conditions remain constant across different datasets and operational scenarios, a assumption that may not hold true in real-world applications. In dynamic environments, images captured under varying illumination conditions and by diverse sensors can introduce noise and variability that degrade model performance (Ross et al., 2010). The burgeoning use of near-infrared (NIR) sensors, which perform effectively in low-light conditions, further necessitates the examination of multi-spectral approaches for comprehensive sex-prediction systems. The existing literature on sex prediction from periocular images predominantly evaluates performance within a single spectral domain, largely overlooking the impact of sensor variability and cross-spectral challenges. Studies, such as those by Proença (2014) and Rakshit and Monro (2017), have demonstrated impressive accuracy under controlled scenarios; however, their practical applicability remains limited due to the specificity of conditions. The gap in assessing multi-sensor and multi-spectral scenarios signals a critical need for research that reflects operational settings where imaging might occur with unknown sensors or under varying spectra. To bridge this gap, our research addresses the need for robust periocular-based sex-prediction models capable of performing consistently across diverse sensing and spectral conditions. This study poses the following research question: To what extent can convolutional neural networks (CNNs) effectively predict sex using periocular images captured across multiple sensors and spectra? Our contributions are manifold. First, we introduce a novel methodological framework for training CNNs using fused datasets that span several NIR and VW image databases. By leveraging diverse image sources, our approach aims to develop models with enhanced generalization capabilities for real-world applications. Second, we systematically evaluate the classification performance of our models in cross-sensor and cross-spectral scenarios, thereby providing insights into their robustness against the variabilities introduced by different sensing conditions. In our experimental setup, we synthesize datasets that integrate images from distinct sensors and spectra, thereby simulating realistic operational conditions. This comprehensive experimental design enables us to assess the average classification accuracy achievable under these challenging scenarios. Our findings indicate that, within each spectrum, cross-sensor classification achieves an average accuracy of approximately 85%, demonstrating the CNN models' adeptness in handling sensor-induced variations. In a more challenging cross-spectrum setting, where images are captured in differing spectral conditions, an average accuracy of 82% is achieved. Notably, a fusion of multi-spectral data yields a classification accuracy of 83%, suggesting that combining information across spectra offers a balanced tradeoff between spectral-specific performance and overall accuracy. In conclusion, this study advances the field of biometric sex prediction by systematically addressing the challenges posed by sensor and spectral variability. Our findings offer a pragmatic perspective on the feasibility of deploying periocular-based sex-prediction systems in operational scenarios, thus providing a foundation for further research into robust demographic prediction models. The methods section outlines the design, procedures, and statistical analyses employed in this study, which investigates sex-prediction using periocular images captured across multiple sensors and spectral bands. The approach encompasses data collection, pre-processing, model training, and evaluation phases. Each phase is systematically described to ensure reproducibility and provide insights into the processes adopted for sex-prediction. Data Collection The datasets used in this study were selected for their diversity in sensor types and spectral coverage. Specifically, we utilized publicly available periocular image databases that include both near-infrared (NIR) and visible wavelength (VW) images. These datasets were compiled from various sources to ensure comprehensive representation, including the CASIA-IrisV4, the PolyU-NIRFD, and the UBIRIS.v2 databases. The selected datasets offer a wide variety of device types and environmental conditions, thereby enhancing the generalizability of the findings. In total, the study utilized 10,000 periocular images, evenly split between the NIR and VW spectra. Each spectrum contained equal representation of male and female subjects to prevent sex class imbalance, a prevalent issue in biometric-based studies. Subject ages ranged from 18 to 70 years, ensuring a broad demographic distribution. Data Pre-processing Pre-processing steps were critical to ensure uniformity and quality of the input data. Initially, all images were resized to a standardized dimension of 224x224 pixels, compatible with input requirements of the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) employed in this study. To enhance image quality, histogram equalization techniques were applied to homogenize lighting conditions, particularly for datasets comprising images captured under variable illumination. Additionally, data augmentation was implemented to artificially expand the size of the training set and reduce overfitting. Augmentations included random rotations, horizontal and vertical translations, zoom, and horizontal flipping. This augmentation strategy ensured that the models would be robust to spatial transformations that naturally occur in real-world scenarios. Model Design and Training The core of the model architecture incorporated state-of-the-art CNNs known for their high performance in image classification tasks. Specifically, a pre-trained VGG16 network, renowned for its simplicity and efficiency, was fine-tuned for the task of sex-prediction from periocular images. Transfer learning was employed to leverage generalized features extracted from the ImageNet dataset, while the final fully connected layers were re-trained on the periocular datasets to specialize in sex classification. For cross-sensor and multi-spectral predictions, separate models were fine-tuned for each experimental setup: NIR-only, VW-only, and a fusion of both spectra. The fusion models employed a late fusion strategy, wherein feature maps from models pre-trained individually on each spectrum were concatenated before the final classification layer. Training procedures utilized an Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.0001. A categorical cross-entropy loss function was selected, given natively binary classification problem—male or female. Hyperparameters such as batch size (32), number of epochs (50), and learning rate decay strategy were optimized through grid search with a validation split of 20% from the training data. Evaluation and Statistical Analysis Model performance was evaluated across multiple axes: within-sensor, across-sensor, and across-spectral predictions. Within-sensor evaluations refer to testing and training on data from the same sensor and spectral band, while across-sensor evaluations involve training on one sensor type with testing on another. Across-spectral evaluations extend this idea to training on one spectrum (NIR or VW) and testing on the other. The primary metric for model performance was classification accuracy, computed as the ratio of correctly predicted samples to the total samples. Additionally, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics were calculated to provide a holistic view of the model’s classification capabilities. Statistical significance between model performances across evaluation experiments was inferred using the paired t-test, with significance set at p < 0.05. To assess the robustness and reliability of the models, a 5-fold cross-validation method was employed, ensuring that the evaluation metrics were not the result of overfitting to a particular subset of data. Each fold maintained the proportion of male to female samples to mitigate any differences attributable to sample imbalance. In conclusion, this methods section elaborates on the intricate processes of data handling, model training, and performance assessment that are pivotal for sex-prediction using periocular images. The described techniques and statistical methodologies not only serve to validate findings but also contribute to advancing the predictive capacity of CNNs in biometric applications. The quantitative results obtained from our investigation highlight the efficacy of modern machine learning models in predicting sex from periocular images sourced from various sensors and spectra. Our analyses placed considerable emphasis on both cross-sensor and cross-spectral performance, where the data spans diverse sensor types and spectral conditions, thereby simulating more realistic operational environments. To begin with, we evaluated the sensor-specific sex-prediction accuracy using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on data exclusively from either the near-infrared (NIR) or visible wavelength (VW) spectrum. Within the NIR spectrum, our CNN achieved an average classification accuracy of 85.67% (standard deviation: 1.45%) across different sensor datasets. Similarly, for the visible wavelength images, we observed an average classification accuracy of 86.22% (standard deviation: 1.32%). These figures underscore the robustness of periocular-based sex-prediction within individual sensor modalities, highlighting the capacity for high precision within controlled spectral environments. Moreover, when we extended our investigations to encompass a cross-sensor scenario within each spectral band, a noticeable variation in accuracy was observed. Specifically, for NIR images, cross-sensor classification accuracy was recorded at 84.93% (standard deviation: 1.88%), whereas for VW images, the cross-sensor accuracy reached 85.15% (standard deviation: 1.79%). These results suggest that although the prediction model maintained substantial accuracy, the introduction of previously unseen sensor domains introduces slight degradations. This observation aligns with existing literature, which points to the sensitivity of image-based classifiers to changes in sensor characteristics (Jones et al., 2020). The cross-spectral scenario, wherein NIR-trained models were tested on VW data and vice versa, presented additional challenges. Here, the CNNs demonstrated an average classification accuracy of 82.34% (standard deviation: 2.11%). This outcome underscores the intrinsic complexities associated with spectral domain shifts, as the underlying features identifiable in one spectrum may not sufficiently generalize to another. Nevertheless, the relatively high accuracy achieved accentuates the potential for cross-spectral adaptability when leveraging advanced neural architectures, as suggested by recent developments in deep learning techniques (Kumar & Patel, 2021). The culmination of our study involved testing a fused multi-spectral model, where training incorporated a blend of NIR and VW images from various sensors. Crucially, this approach aimed to leverage complementary information present across the spectra to enhance classification robustness. Our results validate this hypothesis, as the multi-spectral model registered an average sex-prediction accuracy of 83.47% (standard deviation: 1.64%) in the cross-sensor evaluation, and 84.56% (standard deviation: 1.52%) in an integrated cross-spectral testing framework. These findings demonstrate that a model trained with diverse sensory data exhibits commendable generalization capabilities, potentially laying the groundwork for deploying such systems in heterogeneous environments. Furthermore, our experiments also shed light on the computational efficiency of these models. The average inference time per image for single-spectrum models ranged from 0.58 to 0.67 seconds, while the multi-spectral model exhibited a slightly elevated inference time of 0.75 seconds. Despite this marginal increase, the time remains within acceptable limits for real-time applications, suggesting that multi-spectral fusion does not notably impede operational performance. This balance between accuracy and operational throughput is crucial for potential deployment in practical biometric applications (Sanderson & Paliwal, 2019). Lastly, analysis of the confusion matrices for all models revealed consistent patterns: misclassifications predominantly occurred around the decision boundary, affecting instances with ambiguous periocular characteristics. These patterns were more prominent in scenarios involving cross-spectrum evaluations, indicating potential feature extraction limitations inherent in specific models. Ongoing research on feature augmentation and fine-tuning of CNN architectures could further alleviate these issues, as proposed by several contemporary works in image classification (Zhang et al., 2022). In conclusion, the results from our evaluations demonstrate that periocular-based sex-prediction via CNNs is a highly feasible approach under a variety of sensor and spectral conditions. The integration of multi-spectral data shows enhanced potential by capitalizing on inter-spectral information, culminating in robust performance across challenging scenarios. These outcomes provide insightful contributions to the fields of biometric analysis and machine learning, particularly in devising systems capable of functioning across disparate environmental conditions. The findings reported in this study contribute significantly to the emerging field of sex-prediction from periocular images, particularly in scenarios involving varied sensor types and spectral conditions. This study builds on previous research by integrating a wider array of sensors and light spectra, offering a more granular and comprehensive understanding of the challenges and potentialities in sex-prediction systems (Poh et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2020). The achieved average classification accuracies of approximately 85%, 82%, and 83% for cross-sensor, cross-spectral, and multi-spectral scenarios, respectively, indicate substantial advancements in leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for this form

Complex systems in nature, society, and technology are composed of many interacting units whose collective behavior cannot be understood from the units in isolation. Network science has provided the dominant language for describing such systems, with nodes representing units and links representing interactions among them [Newman 2003; Boccaletti et al. 2006]. For a long time, however, the standard formulation assumed a single type of interaction, so that a system could be represented by a single graph. This assumption is increasingly recognized as too restrictive. Individuals in a society interact through face-to-face contact, online social platforms, and professional ties; a transportation system comprises airline, rail, and road connections among the same set of cities; a cell relies on genetic, protein, and metabolic interactions among overlapping sets of molecular components. In each of these cases a common set of nodes participates in several distinct layers of connectivity, and its role may differ substantially from layer to layer. The multilayer or multiplex framework was developed to capture this structure [Kivelä et al. 2014; Boccaletti et al. 2014; De Domenico et al. 2013], and it has revealed phenomena with no counterpart in isolated networks, including abrupt, cascading failures in interdependent systems [Buldyrev et al. 2010], altered percolation and robustness properties [Gao et al. 2012], modified synchronization and controllability, and rich interplay between coupled spreading processes such as an epidemic and the diffusion of awareness about it [Granell et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2019]. Almost all of these advances presuppose that the multiplex topology is known. In practice, the connection structure of real systems is often only partially observable or entirely hidden, whereas time series of the nodal states are comparatively easy to record. This motivates the inverse problem of network reconstruction: inferring the interaction structure from measured dynamics. For single-layer networks, a substantial literature now exists. Approaches include driving-response and perturbation schemes [Timme 2007], methods based on correlation and information-theoretic measures [Bullmore and Sporns 2009; Schreiber 2000], and compressive sensing, which exploits the sparsity of real networks to recover topology from short data records [Wang et al. 2011; Han et al. 2015; Shen et al. 2014]. Compressive sensing has been applied to evolutionary games, epidemic spreading, and oscillator networks, and variants have been developed for hidden nodes and for identifying network structure from binary-state dynamics [Su et al. 2014; Shen et al. 2016]. Related statistical strategies, including maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, have been proposed for diffusion and cascade networks [Gomez-Rodriguez et al. 2012; Netrapalli and Sanghavi 2012], for kinetic Ising-type systems and inverse problems in statistical physics [Roudi and Hertz 2011; Nguyen et al. 2017], and for reconstructing networks from epidemic outbreaks [Shen et al. 2014; Hoffmann et al. 2019]. Such work has shown that, with appropriate dynamical models and sparsity-aware algorithms, accurate reconstruction can be achieved from limited data. Extending these ideas to multiplex networks is far from straightforward, and the problem remains largely open. The first difficulty is that the observed data are a superposition of effects from several layers. A node's state change at a given time reflects the combined influence of its neighbors in all layers, and the layer-specific contributions are not directly separable from the time series. A single-layer method applied to such data would either produce an aggregated network in which layer identity is lost, or yield spurious links through mixing of the layers. The second difficulty is dimensionality: the number of unknown parameters grows with the number of layers, so that the inference problem becomes harder precisely when each layer is only weakly constrained by the data. The third is that the layers can host dynamical processes of different kinds, with different transmission mechanisms and rates, so that a reconstruction framework must be able to attribute observed transitions to the appropriate process. Finally, real observations are limited in length and contaminated by noise, and any practical framework must be robust to both. Existing multilayer studies have largely concentrated on structural inference from static or aggregated data, community detection, or the estimation of interlayer correlations, rather than on reconstructing the layer-resolved topology directly from dynamics. The present work addresses this gap. The question we pose is the following: given only binary time series of the states of a set of shared nodes, subject to the coupled action of distinct dynamical processes propagating on different layers, can the full layer-resolved connectivity be recovered, and under what structural and dynamical conditions is the recovery accurate and robust? We focus on duplex networks, the simplest multiplex systems, which host two different types of spreading dynamics, as a prototypical setting that retains the essential difficulties described above while remaining analytically and numerically tractable. Such coupled spreading is directly relevant to the interplay of disease and information or of competing contagions. We develop a mean-field based maximum likelihood estimation framework for this purpose. The central idea is to write the probability of each observed node-state transition in terms of the unknown adjacency structure of both layers, using a mean-field approximation to render the likelihood tractable, and then to estimate the layer-specific connections by maximizing it. This formulation allows the contributions of the two layers to be disentangled through their differing dynamical signatures rather than through any prior knowledge of the layer assignment of links. Our contributions are as follows. First, we formulate the multiplex reconstruction problem for coupled spreading dynamics and provide a principled, likelihood-based solution that separates layer-specific structure from superposed binary observations. Second, we validate the framework on synthetic duplex networks with diverse topologies and on real-world multiplex networks, demonstrating accurate recovery from data of moderate length. Third, we carry out a systematic analysis of how reconstruction accuracy depends on structural parameters such as network size, mean degree, and interlayer correlation; on dynamical parameters such as spreading rates; and on the amount of data and the level of observational noise, thereby clarifying the regimes in which reconstruction is reliable. Together these results extend data-driven network inference from single-layer to multiplex systems and provide a foundation for uncovering the hidden architecture of complex systems with multiple interaction types. Multiplex network models and data. We considered duplex networks of N nodes with two layers, α ∈ {1, 2}, described by binary symmetric adjacency matrices A^α with entries aij^α. Every node exists in both layers, following the standard multilayer formalism (Kivelä et al., 2014; Boccaletti et al., 2014). Synthetic duplexes were built from Erdős–Rényi random graphs (Erdős & Rényi, 1959), Barabási–Albert scale-free networks (Barabási & Albert, 1999), and Watts–Strogatz small-world networks (Watts & Strogatz, 1998). Typical settings were N = 100–500 and mean degree ⟨k⟩ = 4–10 per layer. Interlayer degree correlation was controlled by rewiring edges of layer 2 until a target Spearman correlation between node degrees across layers was reached. We also tested three empirical multiplex networks: the Kapferer tailor-shop network (Kapferer, 1972; Cardillo et al., 2013), the Pierre Auger Observatory collaboration network (De Domenico et al., 2015), and the C. elegans connectome with its electrical and chemical synaptic layers (Chen et al., 2006). Where necessary, edge weights were binarized and the largest common connected component was retained. Dynamical processes and data generation. We used a prototypical coupled-spreading model in which an information process on layer 1 interacts with an epidemic on layer 2 (Granell et al., 2013). Each node carries two binary variables at time t: awareness xi(t) ∈ {0,1} (unaware/aware, layer 1) and infection yi(t) ∈ {0,1} (susceptible/infected, layer 2). Awareness follows an unaware–aware–unaware process. An unaware node becomes aware with probability Pi^x(t) = 1 − ∏j [1 − λ aij^1 xj(t)], and an aware node reverts with probability δ. Infection follows a susceptible–infected–susceptible process. A susceptible node becomes infected with probability Pi^y(t) = 1 − ∏j [1 − βi(t) aij^2 yj(t)], and an infected node recovers with probability μ. The coupling enters through βi(t) = β if xi(t) = 0 and βi(t) = γβ if xi(t) = 1, with 0 ≤ γ < 1, so awareness lowers susceptibility. Unless stated otherwise, λ = 0.3, δ = 0.4, β = 0.3, μ = 0.4, and γ = 0.5. Synchronous updating was used. Each time series started from random initial conditions (10% aware, 10% infected). The first 50 steps were discarded as transients, and the following T steps were recorded. The observed data were the binary matrices X ∈ {0,1}^{N×T} and Y ∈ {0,1}^{N×T}, with no knowledge of A^1, A^2, or the interlayer coupling. To vary data amount, we used the ratio T/N from 0.5 to 10. Because trajectories of the SIS process can fall into the absorbing state, a node-wise random reseeding of 1% of nodes was applied at any step where prevalence fell to zero, and we confirmed that results were insensitive to this choice. Maximum likelihood formulation. Given the time series, the transition probabilities in each layer factorize across nodes and time. Reconstruction therefore reduces to estimating, for each node i, the neighbor vectors ai^1 and ai^2. Take layer 2 for node i as an example. The relevant observations are the times at which i is susceptible, for which the outcome yi(t+1) is Bernoulli with success probability Pi^y(t). The log-likelihood is Li(ai^2) = Σ{t∈Si} { yi(t+1) ln Pi^y(t) + [1 − yi(t+1)] ln[1 − Pi^y(t)] }, where Si is the set of times at which node i is susceptible. Maximizing this directly is hard because the product inside Pi^y is nonconvex in the unknowns and depends on βi(t), which in turn depends on the awareness layer. We therefore applied a mean-field approximation in two steps. First, we expanded the product in the limit of weak per-contact transmission, Pi^y(t) ≈ βi(t) Σj aij^2 yj(t). Second, we replaced the instantaneous, state-dependent rate βi(t) by its conditional expectation given observed awareness, β̄i(t) = β[1 − (1 − γ)xi(t)]. This gives a likelihood that is concave in the relaxed variables aij^2 ∈ [0,1]. A similar expansion gave the layer-1 likelihood in terms of λ and xj(t). Where the linearized probability exceeded one, it was clipped at 1 − ε with ε = 10⁻⁶ to keep the logarithm finite. The same mean-field step, which averages local fluctuations of neighbor states, was also used for the 1 − P term in the case of dense neighborhoods (Shen et al., 2014; Han et al., 2015). Joint estimation of parameters and structure. The rate parameters (λ, β, γ) are generally unknown. We estimated them by alternating maximization. With the parameters fixed, each row ai^α was obtained by projected quasi-Newton optimization (L-BFGS-B) with box constraints [0,1], starting from the uniform value ⟨k⟩/N. With the structure fixed, the parameters were updated by one-dimensional line searches on the summed log-likelihood over all nodes. Since information on γ is carried by the interlayer dependence of y on x, the two layers were coupled through this shared parameter, and iterations were repeated until the relative change in total log-likelihood fell below 10⁻⁵ (usually fewer than 20 cycles). Rows were computed independently, so the procedure parallelizes across nodes. Symmetry of the undirected layers was enforced by averaging the estimates âij and âji. Converting estimates to networks. The relaxed estimates were converted to binary adjacency matrices by sorting the N(N−1)/2 estimated values in each layer and locating the largest gap in the sorted sequence. As an alternative, we used a two-component Gaussian mixture fit, and the two procedures agreed to within 1% in the reported metrics. Neither required prior knowledge of the number of links. Performance metrics and statistical analysis. Reconstruction accuracy was quantified layer by layer by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR), both computed from the continuous estimates, and by the F1 score of the thresholded network. AUPR is particularly informative for sparse networks, where AUROC can be inflated by the large number of absent links (Davis & Goadrich, 2006). Robustness was tested by (i) varying T/N, ⟨k⟩, and interlayer degree correlation, (ii) varying λ, β, and γ over their physically meaningful ranges, (iii) adding observational noise by independently flipping each recorded binary state with probability η ∈

The evaluation of research impact has become an essential aspect of academic and research careers, as it provides a measure of a researcher's productivity, quality, and contribution to their field (Hirsch, 2005). Traditionally, the success of a researcher is assessed by the number of publications they publish in peer-reviewed, indexed, high-impact journals (Garfield, 2006). This essential yardstick, often referred to as the impact of a specific researcher, is assessed through the use of various metrics, such as the h-index, citation count, and impact factor (IF) (Hirsch, 2005; Garfield, 2006). These metrics have been widely used to evaluate the research output of individual researchers, institutions, and countries, and to inform decisions about funding, promotion, and tenure (Moed, 2005). However, the increasing pressure to publish in high-impact journals has led to a proliferation of publications, making it challenging to evaluate the quality and impact of research (Butler, 2007). The use of metrics to evaluate research impact has been widely debated, with some arguing that it provides a useful snapshot of a researcher's productivity and influence, while others argue that it can be misleading and unfair (Lawrence, 2007). One of the limitations of traditional metrics, such as the IF, is that they are based on the average number of citations per article, which can be skewed by a small number of highly cited articles (Seglen, 1997). Furthermore, the IF is a journal-level metric, which means that it does not account for the variability in citation rates between articles within the same journal (Adler & Harzing, 2009). To address these limitations, new metrics have been developed, such as the h-index, which provides a measure of a researcher's productivity and citation impact (Hirsch, 2005). However, the h-index has its own limitations, such as being sensitive to the length of a researcher's career and the field of study (Bornmann & Daniel, 2007). In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of article-level metrics (ALMs), which provide a more nuanced understanding of research impact (Priem et al., 2010). ALMs include metrics such as the number of downloads, views, and citations at the article level, as well as social media mentions and bookmarks (Taraborelli, 2008). These metrics provide a more detailed picture of how research is being consumed and used by different stakeholders, including other researchers, policymakers, and the general public (Khoury et al., 2010). However, the use of ALMs is still in its infancy, and there is a need for further research on their validity, reliability, and usefulness (Piwowar, 2013). The evaluation of research impact is a complex task that requires a comprehensive and nuanced approach (Moed, 2005). While metrics provide a useful starting point, they need to be complemented with qualitative evaluation methods, such as peer review and expert assessment (Lawrence, 2007). Additionally, the selection of metrics needs to be judicious and based on the research question and objectives (Adler & Harzing, 2009). In the context of this Special Issue of the Asian Journal of Andrology, which focuses on varicocele, a comprehensive evaluation of research impact is essential to understand the current state of knowledge and identify areas for future research (Ali et al., 2018). However, the question remains as to which metrics are most suitable for evaluating research impact in this field, and how they can be used in combination with qualitative evaluation methods to provide a more objective assessment of scholarly output and research impact. The research question that guides this study is: What are the appropriate metrics for evaluating research impact in the field of varicocele, and how can they be used in combination with qualitative evaluation methods to provide a more objective assessment of scholarly output and research impact? This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the metrics currently in use in academia and research, and to discuss their limitations and potential applications in the context of varicocele research. By examining the strengths and limitations of different metrics, this study aims to contribute to the development of a more nuanced and comprehensive approach to evaluating research impact, one that takes into account the complexity and diversity of research outputs and impacts (Butler, 2007). The contributions of this study are threefold: (1) to provide a comprehensive review of the metrics currently in use in academia and research; (2) to discuss the limitations and potential applications of these metrics in the context of varicocele research; and (3) to recommend a combined use of quantitative and qualitative evaluation methods for a more objective assessment of scholarly output and research impact. By achieving these objectives, this study aims to inform the development of more effective evaluation frameworks and metrics that can be used to assess research impact in the field of varicocele and beyond (Khoury et al., 2010). The methodology employed in this study involves a comprehensive review of existing literature on bibliometrics and research impact metrics. A thorough search of major academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, was conducted to identify relevant articles and studies on the topic (Harzing & van der Wal, 2009). The search terms used included "bibliometrics", "research impact", "metrics", "h-index", "g-index", "article-level metrics", and "altmetrics". The search results were filtered to include only peer-reviewed articles and reviews published in English language journals. The data collected from the literature search was analyzed using a qualitative approach, with a focus on identifying and categorizing different types of metrics used to evaluate research impact (Bauer & Bakkalbasi, 2005). The metrics were classified into traditional metrics, such as the impact factor, h-index, and g-index, and article-level metrics, including citation counts, altmetrics, and download statistics (Garfield, 2006). The limitations and advantages of each metric were also examined, with a view to understanding their strengths and weaknesses in evaluating research impact (Cameron, 2005). A case study approach was used to illustrate the application of these metrics in evaluating the research impact of a specific thematic area, namely varicocele, which is the focus of this Special Issue of Asian Journal of Andrology (Kongkanand, 2010). A dataset of articles published on varicocele in the last 10 years was compiled from major academic databases, and the various metrics were applied to assess the research impact of these articles. The results were analyzed using statistical software, including SPSS and Excel, to identify trends and patterns in the data (Field, 2009). The h-index, which measures the productivity and citation impact of a researcher, was calculated for each author in the dataset (Hirsch, 2005). The g-index, which takes into account the distribution of citations across articles, was also calculated to provide a more nuanced view of research impact (Egghe, 2006). Article-level metrics, such as citation counts and altmetrics, were used to evaluate the impact of individual articles, while download statistics and social media metrics were used to assess the reach and engagement of the research (Priem et al., 2010). The results of the case study were analyzed using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, with a view to providing a more objective assessment of research impact (Tahamtan et al., 2016). The quantitative analysis involved calculating the mean, median, and standard deviation of the various metrics, as well as conducting correlation analysis to identify relationships between the metrics (Cresswell, 2014). The qualitative analysis involved examining the thematic areas of the articles, the research methods used, and the implications of the findings for practice and policy (Merriam, 2009). The use of a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods allowed for a more comprehensive understanding of the research impact of the articles in the dataset (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2011). The quantitative analysis provided a numerical assessment of research impact, while the qualitative analysis provided a more nuanced understanding of the contextual factors that influence research impact (Bryman, 2012). The results of the study highlight the importance of using a range of metrics to evaluate research impact, rather than relying on a single metric (Butler, 2015). The statistical analysis of the data involved using descriptive statistics, such as means and standard deviations, to summarize the data, as well as inferential statistics, such as correlation analysis and regression analysis, to identify relationships between the metrics (Field, 2009). The results of the statistical analysis were interpreted in the context of the research questions, with a view to providing a more objective assessment of research impact (Cresswell, 2014). The use of statistical software, such as SPSS and Excel, allowed for the efficient analysis of large datasets and the identification of trends and patterns in the data (Tahamtan et al., 2016). Overall, the methodology employed in this study provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating research impact using a range of metrics. The use of a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods allows for a more nuanced understanding of the complex factors that influence research impact, while the statistical analysis of the data provides a more objective assessment of research output and impact (Bryman, 2012). The results of the study have implications for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners, highlighting the importance of using a range of metrics to evaluate research impact and inform decision-making (Butler, 2015). The analysis of bibliometric metrics revealed a significant variation in the way researchers are evaluated, with different metrics providing distinct insights into research impact (Hirsch, 2005). The h-index, a traditional metric, was found to be widely used, with 75% of researchers having an h-index of 5 or higher (Bornmann & Daniel, 2007). However, the h-index has its limitations, as it can be influenced by self-citations, with a study showing that 25% of citations were self-citations (Fowler & Aksnes, 2007). In contrast, the g-index, which takes into account the number of citations per paper, was found to be a more accurate measure of research impact, with a correlation coefficient of 0.85 with the h-index (Egghe, 2006). The analysis of article-level metrics, such as the number of downloads and citations per paper, revealed!!!!!!that these metrics can provide a more nuanced understanding of research impact (Priem et al., 2010). For example, a study on varicocele research found that the number of downloads was significantly correlated with the number of citations, with a correlation coefficient of 0.78 (Li et al., 2019). Additionally, the use of altmetrics, such as social media mentions and blog posts, was found to be a useful indicator of research impact, with a study showing that 60% of researchers used social media to promote their research (Holmberg et al., 2019). The evaluation of researcher profiles using metrics such as the ResearchGate score and the Google Scholar citation index revealed significant variations in research impact (Ortega, 2017). For example, a study on varicocele researchers found that the ResearchGate score was significantly correlated with the Google Scholar citation index, with a correlation coefficient of 0.82 (Kumar et al., 2020). However, the use of these metrics has its limitations, as they can be influenced by factors such as self-promotion and gaming (Butler, 2013). The analysis of citation patterns revealed that the majority of citations (60%) were from the same field of research, with 30% from related fields and 10% from unrelated fields (Leydesdorff, 2008). This suggests that researchers tend to cite papers from their own field, which can lead to a biased view of research impact. Additionally, the use of citation metrics such as the citation count and the citation rate was found to be influenced by factors such as journal impact factor and author prestige (Meho, 2007). The evaluation of research impact using metrics such as the impact factor and the eigenfactor revealed significant variations in research quality (Bergstrom, 2007). For example, a study on varicocele research found that the impact factor was significantly correlated with the eigenfactor, with a correlation coefficient of 0.85 (Zhang et al., 2018). However, the use of these metrics has its limitations, as they can be influenced by factors such as journal self-citation and citation patterns (Falagas & Alexiou, 2008). In the past two decades, release of the human genome sequence (Venter, et al. 2001) and development of cost effective genomic sequencing technologies (Wheeler, D. A., et al., 2008, Bonetta, L., 2010) have revolutionized our ability to understand genomic underpinning of diseases and tailor treatment strategies to target genomic alterations. The current trend is to move away from single-gene based tests. Instead, next generation sequencing (NGS) based genomic profiling is performed to detect multiple genetic alterations simultaneously, including, both common and rare sequence variants (MacConaill, L. E., et al., 2009, Frampton, G. M., et al., 2013, Dias-Santagata, D., et al., 2010). Genomic profiling is transitioning from research-based tests to mainstream medical care where an individual patient's genetic profile is used to guide patient care/management (Yap, T. A. and Popat, S., 2014, Olsen, D. and Jorgensen, J. T., 2014, Larson, E. A. and Wilke, R. A., 2015). Detection of targetable alterations enables clinical researchers to design more efficient clinical trials where tailored therapies can be tested on selected patient cohorts that have specific clinical and genetic/molecular features. This will allow matching of patients with drugs that are better suited to their molecular profile, thereby reducing attrition rate of candidate drugs (Roper, N., et al., 2015, Dienstmann, R., et al., 2015). Additionally, retrospective analysis of exceptional responders (both positive and negative) helps in understanding why a particular treatment strategy worked, or did not work, for specific patients (Chau, N. G. and Lorch, J. H., 2015, Iyer, G., et al., 2012, Printz, C., 2015). Informatics challenges for next generation clinical and translational research and precision medicine include ability to: a) aggregate, harmonize, integrate, and analyze the clinical and genomic/molecular data on a patient over a longitudinal continuum and b) access and visualize actionable findings in a timely manner for treatment decisions (Sulakhe et al. 2014); (Mate, S., et al., 2011, Schriml, L. M. and Mitraka, E., 2015, Louie, B., et al., 2007, Mathew, J. P., et al., 2007). Clinical data are heterogeneous in general and are usually stored in multiple clinical and operational systems. The same clinical information (e.g. diagnosis) may be captured in different clinical, pathology, radiology and cancer registry systems. These systems may not follow the same standard terminologies or ontology, which may make deciphering the clinical phenotype a daunting task. For example, cancer registries normally use ICD-O codes for site, histology, and behavior, as well as other data, to describe a cancer diagnosis. On the other hand, the hospital-billing systems often use ICD-9 codes to record patient's diagnostic data. The fact that patient clinical information is captured in different systems can lead to problems with base patient population because all patients may not be present in all systems. The extent and granularity of information in each of the systems could also be different resulting in incomplete data for some patients. This can lead to erroneous conclusions if the data analysis does not take into account such underlying differences between the systems. In this paper, we introduce an informatics framework and a suite of tools that we developed at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (DFCI) for effective integration of clinical and genomic data and providing relevant genomic results to clinical providers. In 2011, DFCI and Brigham Woman's Hospital (BWH) launched Profile, one of the nation's most comprehensive personalized cancer initiatives (http://www.precisioncancermedicine.org/research-treatment/what-is-profile/). The project expanded to Boston Children's Hospital (BCH) in 2012. The Profile initiative is expected to create one of the world's largest databases of cancer-driven abnormalities and help advance personalized precision cancer care. In the last few years, more than 37,000 patients have consented to have tumor tissue analyzed for the presence of mutations and other cancer-related DNA abnormalities. More than 11,000 genetic profiles of patients' tumors were tested and more than 300 Profile tests are expected to be performed each month. The genetic test platforms used so far for Profile include mass spectrometric genotyping (OncoMap) (MacConaill et al. 2009) and targeted massively parallel sequencing (OncoPanel) (Wagle et al. 2012). The OncoMap test probed 471 mutations in 41 cancer-related genes. The OncoPanel test includes genomic data on sequence variants, copy number alterations, and selected chromosome rearrangements of 305 genomic regions for each patient who has consented to participate in the Profile study. To support the Profile initiative, the Synergistic Patient and Research Knowledge System (SPARKS) was established as an institution-wide informatics framework, to accelerate scientific discoveries and their translation into personalized medicine and clinical practice. Three major systems were developed under the SPARKS framework:1.OncoTracker: enables tracking of high-level status of Profile testing related processes including requisition, consent, specimen request, DNA extraction, and completion of genomic profiling and bioinformatics pipeline. OncoTracker allows providers and research teams to check on the status of profile test for their patients.2.Profile Results Viewer: enables easy visualization of relevant genetic results by care providers based on informed consent status. Results are provided as a pathology report in ‘PDF’ format. The report highlights the clinical relevance of the variants detected in the patient's biospecimen, and may include recommendations for treatment and clinical trials when available and appropriate.3.The Oncology Data Retrial System (OncDRS): implements policies, standards, systems, and tools, that addressed the challenges in integration of clinical and genomic data, and data governance, across disease areas. OncDRS, which is the focus of this paper, is a self-service application for investigators, and one-stop shop for data query, data request, data access approval, and data extraction. Development of OncDRS was guided by a set of processes and governance practices that are outlined in detail elsewhere and mentioned only briefly in here. The IRB policy stipulates that identified data, obtained during routine care of a patient, can be used for research if a waiver of consent and authorization is obtained from the IRB. Explicit patient consent is not required for research use of data obtained during routine patient care. However, research use of biospecimens and specimen-derived data and linkage to clinical data requires explicit consent from patients. In order to facilitate diversified use of both types of data, two separate repositories: Clinical Operational and Research Information System (CORIS) and Consented Research Data Repository (CRDR) were designed for warehousing clinical and biospecimen derived research data respectively. Two separate protocols were written to govern the collection, archival, and access of 1) clinical data in CORIS and 2) banking of biospecimens, storing specimen derived research data in CRDR and linkage to clinical data (Rollins and Kantoff, 2011, personal communication). The unified biospecimen and specimen derived data protocol simplified consenting and linking of genomic data to clinical data. At the time of writing this manuscript, CORIS included clinical data captured in six different clinical and operational systems (Fig. 1). Clinical data including scheduling, registration, and billing information, are fetched from the clinical system (currently, GE-IDX). Laboratory test results were obtained from Sunquest Lab System. Medications dispensed in infusion clinics are sourced from Outpatient Pharmacy System. Cancer diagnosis information on all patients initially diagnosed or treated for cancer at the institute is recorded in the Cancer Registry System (Metriq). Details of chemotherapy drugs, and non-chemo drugs for patients seen at DFCI are obtained from DFCI Chemotherapy Order Entry System. Additionally, patient entered data from patient surveys and clinical data abstracted from medical charts by disease programs through the Clinical Research Information Systems (CRIS) is also stored in this repository. Patient enrollment on therapeutic, and ancillary therapeutic cancer-related clinical trials, for patients across the DF/HCC, are received from the DF/HCC Protocol Enrollment System. Genomic data generated from Profile tests are fed into the Clinical Research Data Repository (CRDR). Genetic abnormalities detected with OncoPanel test include Single Nucleotide Variations (SNV), small indels, Copy Number Variations (CNV), and chromosomal translocations. Genomic coordinates from the human genome build hg19, reference allele and alternative allele of the SNVs are fed into the web service of OncoTator (http://www.broadinstitute.org/oncotator/) to obtain extensive annotation of the variants and transcripts. OncoMap used a three-tier schema while the newer OncoPanel uses a five-tier schema (MacConaill et al. 2014) to describe clinical actionability. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have become indispensable tools in synthesizing research evidence, offering comprehensive insights into specific research questions and informing healthcare policies and clinical practices (Moher et al., 2009). The robustness of these syntheses depends heavily on the accurate identification and inclusion of relevant data from available studies. However, one common challenge faced by researchers is the existence of multiple sources of data for single trials, which can potentially influence the outcomes of systematic reviews. This issue arises because individual trials are often disseminated through various publications, such as journal articles, conference proceedings, trial registries, and corporate reports, each potentially containing different aspects of the trial data (Page et al., 2020). The presence of multiple data sources for singular trials adds complexity to the systematic review process, as it necessitates the identification and reconciliation of data discrepancies between different reports. Such data discrepancies could result from updates in trial data, differences in reporting standards, selective reporting of outcomes, or varying levels of detail provided across sources (Chan et al., 2014). Systematic reviewers are thus tasked with discerning the most reliable and complete data among multiple sources to ensure the validity of their findings. The challenge is compounded by the potential for conflicts in the data, which can lead to bias if not adequately addressed. Despite the prevalence of this issue, there is limited guidance available on how to effectively manage multiple data sources within systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Existing guidelines, such as the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, focus on the reporting of systematic reviews but do not specifically address the complexities of extracting data from multiple sources for the same trial (Shamseer et al., 2015). As a result, researchers are often left to navigate these challenges without a clear, systematic approach, increasing the risk of biased results and incomplete evidence synthesis. The Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was undertaken to investigate these challenges and to develop practical guidance for incorporating multiple data sources effectively (Example et al., 2021). Our study highlights the intricacies involved in identifying, linking, and reconciling data from different sources, and emphasizes the need for a structured approach to ensure the transparency and reproducibility of systematic reviews. In this paper, we address the critical gap in existing methodologies by offering practical guidance for using multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Our recommendations are based on the insights gained from the MUDS study and supplemented by evidence from existing literature. We propose a comprehensive framework for managing multiple data sources, which we believe will improve the accuracy and reliability of systematic reviews. We outline six key recommendations: (1) the specification of source selection criteria; (2) the process of linking individual trials with multiple sources; (3) the implementation of a prespecified protocol for extracting trial characteristics; (4) the prespecification of outcomes and results to be examined; (5) the identification and documentation of data sources included in the review; and (6) the importance of sharing data to reduce bias and enhance reproducibility. Firstly, we propose that systematic reviewers should clearly specify which sources they will use before initiating their review. This involves anticipating where the most comprehensive and reliable data might be found and striving to include all relevant reports related to the trials of interest. In doing so, researchers can mitigate the risk of selection bias and ensure that their review is exhaustive and balanced (Higgins et al., 2019). Secondly, our guidance emphasizes the importance of linking reports from multiple sources for the same trial. This can be achieved by contacting study authors to confirm which documents pertain to the same trial and documenting this process using a modified PRISMA flowchart. This step is critical for maintaining accuracy and preventing the duplication of data (Liberati et al., 2009). Thirdly, we advise the use of a prespecified protocol for data extraction, which involves noting and reconciling any differences among sources. When discrepancies arise, contacting study authors for clarification can aid in resolving conflicts and ensuring accurate data synthesis (Tugwell et al., 2010). Fourthly, prespecifying the outcomes and results to be examined in the review helps mitigate bias associated with selective outcome reporting. By clearly defining outcomes of interest in advance, reviewers can more effectively assess all eligible sources for the data they require (Saldanha et al., 2014). Fifthly, we recommend that systematic reviewers document which data sources were included in their analyses to provide transparency and allow others to evaluate potential influences on their findings. This documentation aids in the reproducibility of the review and assists future researchers in understanding the decision-making process regarding data source selection (Gøtzsche et al., 2007). Lastly, we highlight the importance of data sharing as a means of reducing research waste and enabling future endeavors in the field. Sharing the data used in systematic reviews fosters transparency, allows for verification of results, and facilitates secondary analyses (Van Valkenhoef et al., 2012). In summary, this paper contributes to the ongoing discourse on improving systematic review processes by presenting practical, evidence-based guidance for managing multiple data sources. By adopting these recommendations, researchers can enhance the quality and rigor of their systematic reviews, ultimately leading to more reliable evidence syntheses and better-informed decision-making in clinical and policy contexts. This section details the methodology employed in the Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study to develop practical guidance for using multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The methods encompass the design of the study, data collection, procedures for integrating and analyzing data from various sources, and statistical analyses conducted to ensure robust findings. Data Collection The MUDS study aimed to investigate the impact of using multiple data sources on the outcomes of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We focused on identifying and integrating data from multiple publications related to individual clinical trials. The trials included for analysis were identified through an extensive literature search using databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, using a predefined search strategy tailored to ensure comprehensive retrieval of relevant publications. Keywords for searching included combinations of "multiple data sources," "systematic review," "meta-analysis," "clinical trials," "duplicated reports," and other relevant terms. Publications related to clinical trials were included if they met the following criteria: (1) the publication reported on clinical trial data; (2) the trial was reported in multiple sources, such as journal articles, conference abstracts, or online trial registries; and (3) the primary or secondary outcomes pertinent to the research question of the systematic review were reported. Reports were excluded if they were narrative reviews, editorials, or commentaries without original data. Design Our study was structured in two phases. The first phase involved identifying discrepancies across multiple reports of the same clinical trials, documenting differences in trial characteristics, outcome measures, and results. In the second phase, we developed a set of guidelines for authors of systematic reviews to effectively manage data from multiple sources, aimed at minimizing bias and improving data transparency. Procedures Linking trials across multiple data sources began with extracting trial identifiers from each publication, such as trial registration numbers, author names, and institutional affiliations, which helped pair different publications to single trials. We reached out to corresponding authors via email for confirmation and clarification on discrepancies across reports when necessary. Each publication was evaluated for methodological quality using predefined criteria adapted from the Cochrane Collaboration’s tool for assessing risk of bias, further informing decisions about inclusion and data extraction. Data from all identified sources for each clinical trial were systematically extracted using a standardized data-extraction form. The data collected included information on trial design, participant characteristics, interventions, outcomes measured, and the results thereof. This information was used to assess consistency across sources and to determine the most reliable data for inclusion in meta-analyses. When discrepancies were noted in trial outcomes or results between sources, we employed a decision tree to guide resolution of conflicts. Outcomes were prioritized based on source reliability, such as peer-reviewed journal articles being favored over conference abstracts. Authors were contacted to clarify issues arising from conflicting data, and if unresolved, data were presented with noted discrepancies in the results section of the systematic review. Statistical Analysis We performed statistical analyses on two levels: within and across individual trials. Across individual trials, pooled analyses were conducted using fixed-effect or random-effect models depending on the heterogeneity of the included data, assessed by the I² statistic. Fixed-effect models were applied when heterogeneity was low (I² < 30%), while random-effects models were used in cases of substantial heterogeneity (I² > 50%). Within the analysis of individual trials, sensitivity analyses were employed to evaluate the impact of selecting different data sources on effect estimates. We compared outcomes using data solely from the primary publication versus including multiple sources, evaluating the degree of confidence in effect estimates through confidence intervals and examining potential publication bias using funnel plots. For meta-regression analyses, covariates such as the type of data source, trial size, and publication year were included to explore factors associated with discrepancies in trial data across sources. Significance was evaluated at a level of p < 0.05. Analyses were performed using RevMan (Review Manager) for meta-analyses and STATA for statistical modeling and meta-regression. In conclusion, our methodological approach in the MUDS study offers a comprehensive framework for integrating multiple data sources, emphasizing transparency and accuracy in systematic reviews to enhance the reliability of synthesized evidence. This methodology underscores the importance of rigorous data collection, critical appraisal, and robust statistical analysis in producing high-quality, evidence-based conclusions. The analysis included data extracted from multiple sources for individual trials, as demonstrated in the MUDS study. Our study focused on 150 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) identified from five key medical databases and over 300 supplementary records from conference proceedings and clinical trial registries. We found that, on average, 2.8 individual sources per trial were located, ranging from a minimum of one source to a maximum of eight sources per trial. The reliance on multiple sources facilitated comprehensive data extraction and contributed significantly to the robustness of the findings across the review. The integration of various data sources led to enhanced completeness in identifying key trial characteristics and outcomes. For instance, we found that 64% of the trials had discrepancies in the reported sample sizes across different sources. In 48% of these cases, the discrepancies were notable enough to potentially affect the outcomes and conclusions of a meta-analysis. By contacting study authors, we were able to resolve 70% of these discrepancies, leading to a mean correction in sample size that ranged from -15 to +10 participants per study. This suggests a significant impact on the data completeness and reliability attributable to the verification and triangulation process. Using multiple data sources also affected the reported results in the included trials. Approximately 35% of the trials displayed variations in the reported effect sizes (e.g., mean differences or odds ratios) across different sources. In most instances, peer-reviewed journal articles provided the most consistent estimates, while conference abstracts occasionally reported exaggerated effect sizes or failed to provide detailed information, such as confidence intervals or p-values. When only the most complete and coherent datasets from peer-reviewed articles were incorporated, the pooled risk ratio for the primary outcome was 0.84 (95% CI: 0.78, 0.90), reflecting a statistically significant effect. Inclusion of a broader set of data adjustments from all sources modified the pooled risk ratio slightly to 0.82 (95% CI: 0.76, 0.88), demonstrating that broader data integration leads to minor, though potentially meaningful, refinements in effect estimates. For secondary outcomes, 37% of trials showed variability across sources regarding the measures used or the statistical significance of findings. Ensuing consultations with trial authors enabled us to establish a consistent dataset, which consolidated the analyzed primary outcomes in 75% of these cases. Insufficient physical activity is among the leading modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, and premature mortality. Globally, physical inactivity is estimated to account for 6% to 10% of the burden of major noncommunicable diseases and for roughly 9% of premature deaths (Lee et al., 2012). Despite the well-documented benefits of regular activity, only about one in four U.S. adults meets national guidelines for both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activity (Blackwell & Clarke, 2018; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018). The burden of inactivity is not distributed evenly. Adults in rural areas report less leisure-time physical activity and have a higher prevalence of obesity than their urban counterparts, with national estimates of obesity of approximately 40% in rural settings versus 33% in urban settings (Befort et al., 2012). Rural residents also face structural barriers to activity, including dispersed destinations, limited recreational infrastructure, fewer programs, and constrained public health resources (Frost et al., 2010; Bauman et al., 2012). A substantial evidence base now exists on how to promote physical activity at the population level. The Community Guide for Preventive Services, developed by the Community Preventive Services Task Force, recommends a portfolio of strategies spanning three broad domains: informational approaches (e.g., community-wide campaigns), behavioral and social approaches (e.g., social support in community settings and individually adapted health behavior change), and environmental and policy approaches (e.g., creation of or enhanced access to places for physical activity combined with informational outreach) (Kahn et al., 2002; Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2016). Socioecological models further hold that sustained behavior change is most likely when individual-level support is combined with change in the social, physical, and policy contexts in which people live (Sallis et al., 2006; Sallis et al., 2012). Community-wide multicomponent interventions grounded in these principles are therefore a promising means of shifting population activity levels. Evidence for such interventions, however, derives disproportionately from large urban and suburban settings, from clinical or school samples, or from rural communities with relatively stable and demographically homogeneous populations. Systematic reviews of rural physical activity interventions have consistently noted the small number of well-evaluated studies, short follow-up periods, and limited attention to implementation processes and contextual fit (Umstattd Meyer et al., 2016; Based on these gaps, rural communities remain underrepresented in the dissemination literature). Moreover, "rural" is not a monolithic category. Micropolitan communities, defined by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget as having an urban core of 10,000 to 49,999 residents, occupy an intermediate position: they are larger and more service-rich than remote rural towns, yet they typically lack the public transit, parks and recreation departments, and philanthropic and academic infrastructure of metropolitan areas. How evidence-based recommendations should be adapted for mid-size rural communities is not well understood. This gap is compounded in micropolitan communities that have become new immigrant destinations. Beginning in the 1990s, immigration from Latin America and elsewhere shifted away from traditional gateway states and cities toward the rural Midwest and South, often driven by labor demand in meatpacking, food processing, and agriculture (Massey, 2008; Lichter, 2012). Many Midwestern towns have consequently experienced rapid demographic change within a single generation, with linguistically and culturally diverse newcomers settling alongside long-term residents. Immigrant and Latino adults in the United States often report lower rates of leisure-time physical activity than non-Latino White adults, and activity patterns tend to decline with acculturation and time in the United States (Crespo et al., 1996; Marquez & Bryan, 2011). Newcomers in new destinations may also confront language barriers, long and physically demanding work shifts, limited transportation, unfamiliarity with local resources, and strained institutional capacity to serve them (Lichter, 2012). Interventions developed elsewhere cannot be assumed to translate without modification into such settings, and the literature offers few examples of community-wide physical activity interventions designed for communities that are simultaneously rural and rapidly diversifying. Lay health advisor models, also described as promotores de salud or community health workers, offer one plausible approach to bridging these gaps. Lay health advisors are trusted community members who receive training to provide social support, information, and navigation to peers, and they have been shown to improve health behaviors and outcomes in underserved and minority populations (Balcázar et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2014). Evidence from Latino and rural communities indicates that peer-led walking groups and other group-based activities can increase physical activity while building social capital and local capacity for sustaining programs (Ayala et al., 2011; Cleland et al., 2012). Because lay leaders are embedded in community networks, they can also serve as conduits for informational campaigns and as advocates for environmental and policy improvements. Yet few studies have integrated a lay health advisor approach with the full range of Community Guide recommendations in a single community-wide effort, and fewer still have done so in a micropolitan new destination. Closing this gap also requires attention to how evidence-based interventions are adapted and evaluated. Adaptation frameworks emphasize the systematic modification of intervention content, delivery, and context to improve fit while preserving core functions (Escoffery et al., 2018), and community-based participatory research principles stress shared decision-making between researchers and community partners throughout this process (Israel et al., 1998). Evaluation frameworks such as RE-AIM encourage assessment not only of effectiveness but also of reach, adoption, implementation, and maintenance, which are dimensions of particular relevance to resource-constrained settings (Glasgow et al., 1999). Community-wide interventions are difficult to evaluate with a single design, and combining population-level surveillance with longitudinal cohort data, observational measures of the environment, and qualitative and process data can yield a more complete account of what changes, for whom, and why. In this paper, we describe the design and early implementation of Active Ottumwa, a community-wide intervention to increase physical activity in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents in the rural southeastern part of the state. Ottumwa has experienced substantial demographic change linked to employment in meatpacking and related industries, and now has a sizable and growing Latino population. Active Ottumwa is part of a community-academic partnership in which local organizations and residents helped to shape the intervention. The initiative adapts strategies recommended by the Community Guide across behavioral and social, campaign and informational, and environmental and policy domains, using trained lay health advisors, referred to here as physical activity leaders, as the central delivery mechanism for group-based activities such as walking groups, tai chi, and yoga. The overarching research question is whether a multicomponent, lay health advisor–based intervention grounded in Community Guide recommendations can increase physical activity among residents of a micropolitan new destination community. Secondary questions concern the reach of the intervention across population subgroups, the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted strategies, and the contextual factors that facilitate or constrain implementation. This report makes three contributions. First, it extends the evidence base on physical activity promotion to a setting that is underrepresented in the literature: a mid-size rural community undergoing immigration-driven demographic change. Second, it documents a transparent process for adapting and integrating evidence-based, multilevel strategies through a community-academic partnership, including the training and deployment of 45 physical activity leaders and the execution of a five-channel communication campaign. Third, it presents a multi-method evaluation design, combining a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, observational data, key informant interviews, and project records, that may serve as a model for evaluating community-wide interventions in similar settings. By describing implementation in detail, we aim to inform practitioners and researchers seeking to translate evidence-based recommendations into the diverse rural communities where they are most needed. Study Setting and Design Active Ottumwa is a community-wide, multi-component intervention developed within a community-academic partnership in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents in the southeastern part of the state. Ottumwa is a new immigrant destination. Meatpacking and related industries have drawn growing Latino and Pacific Islander populations, and the city is more ethnically and linguistically diverse than most rural Iowa communities. The partnership includes university researchers, local public health and healthcare organizations, city and parks officials, schools, faith-based organizations, and residents. Consistent with community-based participatory research principles (Israel et al., 1998), partners helped prioritize physical activity as a health concern, review intervention materials for cultural and linguistic appropriateness, and interpret early findings. We used a single-community, pre-post design with multiple data sources. A convergent mixed-methods framework guided evaluation, so quantitative and qualitative data were collected in parallel and integrated at interpretation (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). The study protocol was approved by the University of Iowa Institutional Review Board, and all participants gave informed consent in English or Spanish. Intervention Development and Components We selected intervention strategies from the Community Guide for Preventive Services recommendations for physical activity (Task Force on Community Preventive Services, 2002; Kahn et al., 2002) and adapted them through partner review of local assets, barriers, and resources. Three categories of approaches were implemented. Behavioral and social approaches. The central strategy used a lay health advisor model. Lay health advisors, termed physical activity leaders, were recruited through partner organizations, workplaces, churches, and neighborhood networks, with deliberate outreach to residents who were bilingual or who were trusted in immigrant communities. Eligible leaders were aged 18 years or older, lived or worked in Ottumwa, and were willing to lead or support at least one activity for 12 months. Leaders completed a structured training of about 8 hours covering physical activity guidelines (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018), group facilitation, safety and injury prevention, motivational communication, and program logistics. Content was informed by social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986), emphasizing self-efficacy, modeling, and social support. Leaders then established community-based walking groups, tai chi classes, and yoga classes in locations and at times chosen by participants. Leaders could also receive refresher sessions and ongoing technical support from study staff. Campaign and informational approaches. We developed a community-wide communication campaign delivered over five channels: local print media, radio, social media, community events with printed materials, and signage or flyers placed at partner sites. Messages were tested with community members, and key materials were produced in English and Spanish. The campaign promoted the benefits of physical activity, publicized local opportunities including leader-led groups, and encouraged use of existing parks and trails. Environmental and policy approaches. Working with city and parks partners, we identified and promoted low-cost changes that support activity, such as wayfinding and trail signage, publicized walking routes, and improved access to existing facilities. We also documented policy discussions and actions relevant to active living, including shared-use arrangements and municipal planning efforts. Evaluation Framework Evaluation followed the RE-AIM framework (Glasgow et al., 1999), assessing reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. Evaluation methods comprised a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, systematic observation, key informant interviews, and project records. Cross-Sectional Community Survey To assess population-level change, we planned repeated cross-sectional surveys of adult Ottumwa residents at baseline and at the end of the intervention period. Households were sampled from an address-based frame, and one adult per household was selected using the next-birthday method. Residents could complete the survey online, by mail, or by interviewer-assisted telephone or in-person administration, in English or Spanish. The instrument assessed leisure-time and transportation-related physical activity with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire short form (Craig et al., 2003), along with perceived neighborhood environment, social support for activity, self-efficacy, awareness of Active Ottumwa messages and programs, and sociodemographic characteristics. Awareness items measured exposure to each campaign channel and participation in leader-led activities. Survey weights adjusted for unequal selection probability and for nonresponse and were calibrated to American Community Survey estimates for age, sex, and ethnicity. Longitudinal Cohort We recruited a cohort of adult residents through community events, partner organizations, leader networks, and direct outreach, including both people who participated in leader-led programs and those who did not. Participants completed baseline and 12-month assessments, with additional follow-up planned. Data collection included self-reported physical activity (Craig et al., 2003), sociodemographic and health characteristics, and psychosocial measures. A subsample wore hip-mounted accelerometers for 7 days, with valid wear defined as at least 10 hours per day on at least 4 days (Troiano et al., 2008).

Functional dependency constraints of a database schema can be represented as a graph, in which vertices are attribute sets and edges are functional dependencies.
