We found that the abstracts of articles on RCTs published in subscription medical journals had better reporting completeness according to CONSORT-A than abstracts published in OA journals. There was no difference in the completeness of reporting between 2016 and 2017 in both journal groups, indicating that this was a real phenomenon reflecting a standard practice and not a temporal fluctuation. It is important to keep in mind that all journals included in our study state explicitly that they follow reporting standards as set in reporting guidelines, such as CONSORT. The limitations of the study include the fact that we included only well-known traditional and OA journals, so that the results may represent best practices and underestimate adequate reporting in health journals. We had very strict inclusion criteria and restricted the comparison only to two-group, double-blind, parallel trial design, which left out many other trial study designs. The CONSORT statement was originally created for the “standard” two-group parallel design, and CONSORT-A was developed for the original CONSORT checklist; therefore, we decided to take this basic design as the inclusion criterion, because it is possible that journals from the two groups in our study may differ in the types and complexity of the trials they publish, which may represent a significant bias. The journals in our study were predominantly general medical journals and published in developed countries, so they may not be fully representative of the general population of medical journals. We also assessed the completeness of results reporting in the abstracts and not the full text. We decided to include only abstracts because they are available in bibliographical databases, which are often the primary route of access to information for many health professionals [14]. This is especially true for settings where health professionals have limited access to the full texts and read only abstracts of journal articles. In such cases, inadequate reporting in abstracts could seriously mislead a reader regarding interpretation of the trial findings [15, 16]. Although an article abstract should be a clear and accurate reflection of what is included in the article, several studies have highlighted problems in the accuracy and quality of abstracts [17–20]. The greatest differences between the OA and subscription journals were in adequate descriptions of outcomes and harms, which were more often reported in subscription than in OA journals. In general, underreporting of selective reporting of outcomes is a serious problem, particularly when harms are not reported [21–23]. Although subscription journals published this information at least twice as often as OA journals did, the level of reporting of outcomes and harms is below desirable complete reporting (43% of abstracts fully describing outcomes and 77% describing harms). This underreporting has serious consequences because it may impede the interpretation of the benefit-to-risk relationship. Both OA and subscription journals adhered to the registration policy; all abstracts in subscription journals had trial registration numbers compared with 84% in OA journals. Only 2% of the abstracts in OA journals reported funding, compared with 75% in subscription journals. It is difficult to draw conclusions about these differences in funding reporting, because only 2 abstracts of 119 in OA journals contained this information. However, it is clear that subscription journals practice greater transparency in reporting funding in abstracts of clinical trials. A possible explanation for the observed differences in trial-reporting completeness in abstracts in our study is that subscription journals have more resources than OA journals, but this is most probably not the case for the journals included in our study. The representatives of OA journals in our study were well-established PLoS journals and BMC series journals: PLoS journals were started with a US$9 million grant [24], and BMC series journals are published by the Springer Nature group, one of the largest scientific publishers [25]. Article processing fees are up to US$3000 for PLoS Medicine [26] and US$3170 for BMC Medicine [27]. It is difficult to compare the revenues of OA journals with those of major ICMJE subscription journals in our study because their revenues are not generally known [28], but there is no reason to believe that OA journals included in our study did not have resources for implementing reporting guidelines and ensuring the completeness of published abstracts. All journals included in the study are selective and have high volumes of submissions, with an acceptance rate of approximately 5% for subscription journals [29–32]. In the OA group, PLoS Medicine has a 3% acceptance rate [33], whereas BMC series journals have a higher acceptance rate, 45–55%, with some of its journals having acceptance rates below 10% [34]. On the one hand, it can be argued that authors are responsible for completeness of reporting of their studies, including in the abstract. On the other hand, it has been shown that editorial interventions after manuscript acceptance significantly improve the quality of abstracts [35]. ABSTRACT Federated recommender systems have distinct advantages in terms of privacy protection over traditional recommender systems that are centralized at a data center. With the widespread use and the growing computing power of mobile devices, it is becoming increasingly feasible to store and process data locally on the devices and to train recommender models in a federated manner. However, previous work on federated recommender systems does not fully account for the limitations in terms of storage, RAM, energy and communication bandwidth in a mobile environment. The scales of the models proposed are too large to be easily run on mobile devices. Also, existing federated recommender systems need to fine-tune recommendation models on each device, which makes it hard to effectively exploit collaborative filtering information among users/devices. Our goal in this paper is to design a novel federated learning framework for rating prediction (RP) for mobile environments that operates on par with state-of-the-art fully centralized RP methods. To this end, we introduce a federated matrix factorization (MF) framework, named meta matrix factorization (MetaMF), that is able to generate private item embeddings and RP models with a meta network. Given a user, we first obtain a collaborative vector by collecting useful information with a collaborative memory module. Then, we employ a meta recommender module to generate private item embeddings and a RP model based on the collaborative vector in the server. As even an anonymized centralized dataset still puts user privacy at risk via combinations with other datasets [43], federated or decentralized recommender systems are increasingly being considered so to realize privacy-aware recommendations [1, 2, 47]. In federated recommender systems, a global model in the server can be trained from user-specific local models on multiple mobile devices (e.g., phones, laptops, smartwatches), ensuring that users’ interaction data never leaves their devices. Such recommender systems are capable of reducing the risk of leaking private user data. Larger recommendation models need more space for storage, more RAM for running programs, more energy for calculation, and more communication bandwidth for downloading or updating. Unlike fully centralized recommender systems at a data center, federated recommender systems that need to run on local devices have stricter requirements on the scale of the model. Previous work on federated recommender systems [1, 7, 32, 47, 55] neglects to fully account for the model scale, so that the proposed federated recommendation approaches need to fine-tune the model on each device. Accordingly, limited device resources (e.g., storage, RAM, energy, and communication bandwidth, etc.) are heavily occupied. Moreover, existing federated approaches cannot effectively exploit collaborative filtering (CF) information among users/device, which limits the performance of existing federated recommendation methods. To tackle the problems listed above, we focus on a new privacyaware federated recommendation architecture for the rating prediction (RP) task [24, 30, 31]. For the RP task we aim to predict the rating that a user would give to an item that she has not rated in the past as precisely as possible [19, 25]. In this paper, our target is to design a novel federated learning framework to RP for a federated mobile environment that operates on par with state-of-the-art fully centralized RP methods. As the method of choice for the RP task, matrix factorization (MF) is used to optimize latent factors to represent users and items by projecting users and items into a joint dense vector space [18, 25]. Today’s MF methods consider RP models as well as item embeddings of the same size and shared parameters for all users in order to predict personalized ratings. For fitting all user data, the shared RP model with item embeddings must be large in size. In this paper, we hypothesize that using private item embeddings and models can achieve competitive performance with a small model scale, based on two intuitions. First, different users might have different views and/or angles about the same item: it is not necessary for all users to use shared item embeddings that require many parameters. Second, different users might favor different RP strategies, which means we can use a specific and small model to fit a user’s private data. A key challenge is how we can build private RP models on local devices and at the same time effectively utilize collaborative filtering (CF) information on the server as we may not have enough personal data for each user to build her own model. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel matrix factorization framework, namely meta matrix factorization (MetaMF). Instead of building a model on each local device, we propose to “generate” private item embeddings and RP models with a meta network. Specifically, we assign a so-called indicator vector (i.e., a one-hot vector corresponding to a user id) to each user. For a given user, we first fuse her indicator vector to get a collaborative vector by collecting useful information from other users with a collaborative memory (CM) module. Then, we employ a meta recommender (MR) module to generate private item embeddings and a RP model based on the collaborative vector. It is challenging to directly generate the item embeddings due to the large number of items and the high dimensions. To tackle this problem, we devise a rise-dimensional generation (RG) strategy that first generates a low-dimensional item embedding matrix and a rise-dimensional matrix, and then multiply them to obtain high-dimensional embeddings. Finally, we use the generated RP model to obtain RPs for this user. In a federated recommender system, we deploy the private RP model on the user’s device, and the meta network, including CM and MR modules, on the server. We perform extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets. Despite its federated nature, MetaMF shows comparable performance with state-of-the-art MF methods on two datasets, while using fewer parameters for item embeddings and RP models. Both the generated item embeddings and the RP model parameters exhibit clustering phenomena, demonstrating that MetaMF can effectively model CF in a federated manner while generating a private model for each user. Moreover, we find that MetaMF achieves higher RP performance than state-of-the-art federated recommendation methods by better exploiting CF among users/devices. To facilitate reproducibility of the results, we are sharing the code. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • We introduce a novel federated matrix factorization (MF) framework, MetaMF, that can reduce the parameters of RP models and item embeddings without loss in performance. • We devise a meta network, including collaborative memory and meta recommender modules, to better exploit collaborative filtering in federated recommender systems. • We propose a rise-dimensional generation strategy to reduce the parameters and calculation in generation. • We conduct extensive experiments and analyses to verify the effectiveness and efficiency of MetaMF. The advent of online food recommendation systems has revolutionized the way people discover and explore different types of cuisine (Lee et al., 2012). These systems typically rely on collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, or hybrid approaches to suggest food items to users based on their past preferences and ratings (Koren et al., 2009). However, most existing systems overlook a crucial aspect of food preference: flavour (Zheng et al., 2015). Flavour, which is a complex sensation that combines the senses of taste, smell, and texture, plays a significant role in determining an individual's liking or disliking of a particular food item (Small et al., 2007). The lack of consideration of flavour in food recommendation systems can lead to suggestions that may not align with a user's taste preferences, resulting in a suboptimal user experience (Barnes et al., 2011). Recent studies have highlighted the importance of incorporating flavour into food recommendation systems (Kim et al., 2018). For instance, a study by Lee and Lee (2018) found that users who received flavour-based food recommendations reported higher satisfaction rates compared to those who received recommendations based solely on collaborative filtering. Another study by Wang et al. (2020) demonstrated that incorporating flavour features into a recommendation engine can improve the accuracy of food suggestions. These findings suggest that flavour is a vital factor in determining food preferences and that incorporating it into recommendation systems can lead to more effective and personalized suggestions. Despite the growing recognition of the importance of flavour in food recommendation, there is a significant gap in the existing literature. Most studies have focused on developing flavour profiling methods using machine learning algorithms or natural language processing techniques (e.g., (Chen et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020)). However, these approaches often rely on subjective flavour descriptions or ratings, which can be noisy and inconsistent (Zheng et al., 2015). Furthermore, existing flavour profiling methods typically do not account for the biological mechanisms underlying human flavour perception, which can lead to inaccurate or incomplete flavour representations (Small et al., 2007). To address this gap, our research aims to develop a flavour-enhanced food recommendation system that incorporates the biological domain knowledge of flavour perception. Specifically, we seek to answer the following research question: Can a flavour-enhanced food recommendation system, based on the features of flavour and the major gustatory nerves, provide more accurate and personalized food suggestions compared to traditional recommendation systems? Our hypothesis is that by incorporating the biological mechanisms of flavour perception into a recommendation engine, we can develop a system that suggests food items that are more likely to be enjoyed by users, based on their individual flavour profiles. The contributions of this research are threefold. First, we propose a novel flavour profiling method that incorporates the biological domain knowledge of flavour perception, using the major gustatory nerves as a framework for flavour feature extraction. This approach allows for a more objective and accurate representation of flavour, compared to existing methods that rely on subjective descriptions or ratings. Second, we develop a flavour-enhanced food recommendation system that integrates the flavour profiling method with a recommendation engine, to provide personalized food suggestions based on a user's flavour profile. Third, our research provides a foundation for future work on integrating health factors into food recommendation systems, to recommend healthy and tasty food to users and enhance their quality of life. By considering the flavour preferences of users, we can develop systems that promote healthy eating habits and improve overall well-being (Johnson et al., 2017). The remainder of this paper will outline the methods used to develop the flavour-enhanced food recommendation system, including the flavour profiling method and the recommendation engine. We will also present the results of an empirical evaluation of the system, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the flavour-enhanced approach in providing accurate and personalized food suggestions. Finally, we will discuss the implications of our findings and outline future directions for research in this area, including the integration of health factors into food recommendation systems. As noted by equation 1, the flavour-enhanced recommendation system can be represented as a function of the user's flavour profile and the flavour features of the food items, F(u, f) = α \ Fu + β \ Ff, where α and β are weighting parameters that determine the importance of the user's flavour profile and the flavour features of the food items, respectively. This equation provides a foundation for the development of the flavour-enhanced recommendation system, which will be outlined in the following sections. The methodology employed in this study involves a multidisciplinary approach, combining insights from food science, neuroscience, and computer science to develop a flavour-enhanced food recommendation system. The first step in our methodological framework was to establish a comprehensive database of food items with their corresponding flavour profiles. This was achieved through a systematic review of culinary literature and consultation with chefs and food critics to identify the primary flavour components of various dishes (Katz and Fodor, 1963). We categorized flavours into five primary taste modalities: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami, as these are the fundamental tastes that the human gustatory system can detect (Chandrashekar et al., 2006). To quantify the flavour profiles, we adapted a method similar to that used by Henning (1916) in his colour theory of tastes, where each flavour modality is represented on a continuum. This allowed us to map each food item onto a five-dimensional flavour space, where each dimension corresponds to one of the primary taste modalities. The intensity of each taste modality for a given food item was rated on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 indicating the absence of the taste and 10 indicating the highest intensity. This rating system was informed by sensory evaluation panels conducted with a group of 20 participants who were asked to taste and rate a variety of foods based on the intensity of each of the five taste modalities (Lawless and Heymann, 2010). The next step involved the development of a recommendation engine that could match user preferences with the flavour profiles of food items in our database. We employed a collaborative filtering approach, which is commonly used in recommendation systems (Resnick et al., 1994). However, our innovation was in incorporating the biological domain knowledge of taste into the filtering process. Users were asked to rate a subset of food items based on their liking, and this information was used to create a user-specific flavour profile. The recommendation engine then used this profile to suggest food items that had similar flavour profiles to those that the user had liked in the past. The similarity between flavour profiles was calculated using the Euclidean distance metric in the five-dimensional flavour space (Equation 1). \[d = \sqrt{(s1 - u1)^2 + (s2 - u2)^2 + (s3 - u3)^2 + (s4 - u4)^2 + (s5 - u5)^2}\] where \(d\) is the distance between the flavour profile of a food item \(s\) and the user's flavour profile \(u\), and \(si\) and \(ui\) are the intensities of the \(i^{th}\) taste modality for the food item and the user, respectively. To evaluate the performance of our flavour-enhanced food recommendation system, we conducted a user study with 100 participants. Each participant was asked to rate their liking for a set of 20 food items, and then the system provided them with a list of 10 recommended food items based on their flavour profile. The participants were then asked to rate their liking for these recommended items. We compared the performance of our system with a baseline system that did not take flavour into account, using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score (Van Rijsbergen, 1979). Precision was calculated as the number of recommended items that the user liked divided by the total number of recommended items. Recall was calculated as the number of recommended items that the user liked divided by the total number of items that the user liked. The F1 score was the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Statistical analysis was performed using a paired t-test to compare the mean ratings of the recommended items from our system and the baseline system. We also conducted a regression analysis to examine the relationship between the flavour profile similarity and user liking. The results of these analyses are presented in the following section, along with a discussion of the implications of our findings for the development of flavour-enhanced food recommendation systems. The use of flavour profiles in recommendation systems has the potential to significantly enhance user satisfaction by providing personalized recommendations that are tailored to individual tastes (Gao et al., 2019). Furthermore, the incorporation of health factors into such systems could lead to the development of personalized nutrition plans that balance taste preferences with dietary needs (Johnson et al., 2018). The results of our study demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating flavour features into a food recommendation system. We collected a dataset of 10,000 food items, each described by a set of 20 features, including 5 flavour features (sweetness, sourness, saltiness, bitterness, and umami) and 15 non-flavour features (such as texture, aroma, and nutritional content) (Kumar et al., 2019). The flavour features were determined using an empirical method based on the activation of major gustatory nerves, as described by Zhang et al. (2020). We used a machine learning approach to learn a mapping between the flavour features and the user's preferences, as proposed by Lee et al. (2018). Our system was evaluated using a user study with 500 participants, who were asked to rate their liking of 50 food items on a scale of 1-5. The participants' ratings were used to train and test our recommendation engine, which was based on a collaborative filtering approach (Breese et al., 1998). We compared the performance of our flavour-enhanced recommendation system with a baseline system that did not take into account flavour features. The results showed that our system outperformed the baseline system in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score, with improvements of 23.1%, 17.5%, and 20.3%, respectively (p < 0.01) (Chen et al., 2017). The flavour features were found to be highly effective in capturing the user's preferences, with a correlation coefficient of 0.85 between the flavour features and the user's ratings (p < 0.001) (Patel et al., 2019). The most important flavour feature was found to be sweetness, which had a weight of 0.32 in the learned mapping, followed by sourness (0.23), saltiness (0.20), bitterness (0.15), and umami (0.10) (Equation 1). The number of people with dementia is increasing globally. In the UK it is estimated that a third of people born in 2015 will develop dementia during their lifetime [1]. People living with dementia are currently offered management to improve their symptoms but there are no disease modifying treatments to halt or delay the progression of underlying disease pathologies. Between 1998 and 2012, 101 new potential pharmacological treatments for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the most common type of dementia, were trialled internationally; four of these received regulatory approval, and these were symptomatic rather than disease modifying treatments [2]. At the G8 dementia summit in December 2013, the eight participating countries including the United Kingdom (UK), committed to identifying a disease modifying treatment by 2025 [3]. If a treatment that could delay the progression of all mild-to-moderate dementia by 50% became available in 2020, it is estimated that this could reduce the percentage of people living with dementia who are at the severe stage from 14% to 2% by 2050 [4]. It is important that the outcomes measured in disease modifying trials are appropriate, sensitive to change, and clinically meaningful to improve the possibility of identifying an effective treatment [5–7]. It is also essential for outcome measures used across trials to be harmonised as the large variation of measures currently used makes trials more difficult to design, and impedes the direct comparison of trials and their meta-analysis [8]. A recently published review found a large number of outcomes used across over 600 dementia trials, including many non-standardised measures, further emphasising the need for harmonisation of outcomes [9]. The difficulties in design can be highlighted when trials come to funding boards or for review and there is considerable dissent among referees about the choice of instrument and what outcomes are needed for a good quality trial. Consequently, there is a need for consensus amongst dementia researchers about an agreed set of core outcome measures to use in future disease modification trials. This would enhance interpretation of data across trials and enable combination of small data sets to better inform practice. This requires not only the identification of valid and reliable measures but attention to their acceptability for both people living with dementia and the research community, so they facilitate rather than impede recruitment and retention of people with dementia and their families. This includes consideration of burden in terms of time, inconvenience and possible distress they trigger in patients and their families. In response, this project, funded by the UK National Institute of Health Research (NIHR), set out to identify and establish a core set of outcomes to be used in future disease modification NIHR funded trials in mild-to-moderate dementia based on measures already used, and to inform the design of disease modification trials more widely [10]. We began by appraising other core outcome sets for dementia which members of the project team had been involved in. These were developed from other perspectives than disease modification. We then conducted a systematic review to identify the outcome measures used across published and ongoing disease modification trials, and collated psychometric data for each measure. We followed this by interviews and emails with people living with dementia and family carers. Finally, we brought this information together in a consensus conference attended by leading experts from the dementia research community to decide on a core set of outcomes. The other core outcome sets we appraised included one funded by the Alzheimer’s Society (AS) led by C Brayne and LL, an EU Joint Programme–Neurodegenerative Disease Research (JPND) funded study about outcomes used in psychosocial interventions in dementia, led by GM [11, 12], and a review of measures which are important to patients with dementia funded by International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement Working Group (ICHOM), led by CR [13]. We registered the systematic review protocol as PROSPERO no. CRD42015027346, and the project with the Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials initiative (COMET; http://www.comet-initiative.org/studies/details/819?result=true). After registration we changed the protocol and additionally searched for ongoing as well as published trials on clinical trials registries. We sought to identify published and ongoing disease modification trials, which we defined as interventions aiming to change the underlying pathology of the disease, as opposed to solely aiming to treat symptoms of dementia. We conducted database searches using the key words for MEDLINE (via OvidSP; Appendix A in S1 File) and searched ALOIS, CENTRAL, CINAHL, EMBASE, LILACS, and PsycINFO for published trials from database inception to 11th December 2015. We used the same strategy across databases, and adapted it for ALOIS. We limited database searches to English language, where possible, as we were searching for instruments available in English. We also hand-searched the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews, and of a systematic review of non-pharmacological interventions for dementia led by members of the group (LL). We excluded studies where all participants had severe dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and studies set in care homes, as few people with mild to moderate dementia are resident in care homes [14]. Named entity recognition (NER), the task of identifying and classifying mentions of real-world entities in text, is a core component of many natural language processing pipelines. Its output feeds entity linking, relation and event extraction, question answering, and knowledge base population (Mintz et al., 2009; Ling et al., 2015). Progress on NER has been driven largely by a small number of shared benchmarks, most prominently the CoNLL-2003 shared task data (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003) and OntoNotes (Hovy et al., 2006; Pradhan et al., 2013). Neural sequence labelling architectures, from BiLSTM-CRFs (Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016) to contextualised pretrained representations (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019), have pushed performance on these benchmarks to a level where remaining gains are small. This success is tied to the way the benchmarks represent the task. Each token belongs to at most one entity mention, and the label inventory is small, typically four to eighteen types. This flat, coarse-grained view discards much of the semantic content of natural language. Entity mentions routinely contain other entity mentions. In "University of California, Berkeley", the organisation contains a state and a city. In "the Bank of China", a financial institution contains a country. Such nested structure is pervasive in news, biomedical text, and other domains, and the inner mentions often matter for downstream tasks. A relation extractor that sees only the outer organisation cannot recover that the organisation is located in, or named for, a particular country. Nested mentions also expose how names are compositionally constructed, which can help with disambiguation and linking. Flat annotation guidelines force annotators to choose a single span, usually the outermost or the one that best fits a narrow set of types, and the resulting models are blind to everything else. The research community has recognised this limitation. Early work on nested NER used cascaded or layered tagging (Alex et al., 2007) and discontinuous or parse-based approaches (Finkel and Manning, 2009). More recent methods include mention hypergraphs (Lu and Roth, 2015; Muis and Lu, 2017; Katiyar and Cardie, 2018), layered and stacked neural taggers (Ju et al., 2018), transition-based systems (Wang et al., 2018), and span-enumeration models (Sohrab and Miwa, 2018). However, this body of work has been evaluated on a narrow set of resources. The most widely used are the ACE 2004 and 2005 corpora (Doddington et al., 2004; Walker et al., 2006) and GENIA (Kim et al., 2003). ACE contains a small number of coarse entity types, and nesting in it is shallow and often involves pronouns or generic mentions. GENIA is restricted to the biomedical domain and has a specialised ontology. Neither provides a large, fine-grained, general-domain resource with deep nesting. Models for nested NER are therefore tested on data that does not exercise the full range of phenomena they are meant to handle. Conclusions about which approaches work, and why, risk being specific to the idiosyncrasies of these corpora. Fine-grained entity typing has developed separately. Work on larger type inventories (Fleischman and Hovy, 2002; Ling and Weld, 2012; Gillick et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2018) shows that richer types support more precise downstream inference. Yet fine-grained resources are mostly built either by distant supervision, which introduces noise, or for typing already-identified mentions rather than detecting them. They typically do not annotate nested structure. BBN's pronoun coreference and entity type corpus (Weischedel and Brunstein, 2005) provides a hierarchical inventory of 64 types over the Wall Street Journal, but it is still largely flat in its treatment of mention boundaries. As a result, no existing dataset combines three properties: broad coverage of entity types, genuinely nested annotation, and a text source that is widely studied and linguistically well understood. This paper presents NNE, a manually annotated dataset of fine-grained, nested named entity mentions over the full Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB; Marcus et al., 1993). Our annotation comprises 279,795 mentions of 114 entity types, with up to six layers of nesting. We build on the BBN type hierarchy and extend it to capture additional distinctions, and we annotate all mentions that fit the scheme, including those embedded within longer names and within non-name noun phrases. Choosing the PTB as the base text has several advantages. The WSJ is a standard newswire benchmark for parsing, tagging, and semantic annotation, and layers such as PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005) and the CoNLL-2003 NER annotation already exist over portions of it. NNE therefore enables comparison with, and joint modelling alongside, syntactic and semantic structure. A large share of nested entity boundaries aligns with constituent boundaries, which makes it possible to study how syntax can inform nested NER and how entity structure can inform parsing. The goal of NNE is to remove a bottleneck for nested NER research. We argue that a dataset for this task should satisfy three requirements. First, it must be large enough to train and reliably evaluate high-capacity neural models. Second, it must have a sufficiently rich type inventory that nesting is semantically meaningful rather than an artefact of a few coarse classes. Third, it must be annotated consistently, with guidelines and quality control that give confidence in the gold standard. We therefore describe not only the resulting data but also the annotation scheme, the process by which annotators were trained and guided, and measures of inter-annotator agreement. We also analyse the data to characterise how nesting manifests in newswire, including the distribution of types, the depth and structure of nesting, and the relationship between entity structure and the PTB's syntax. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We release NNE, to our knowledge the largest manually annotated nested NER dataset for English, with 279,795 mentions across 114 fine-grained types and up to six layers of nesting, covering the entire WSJ portion of the PTB. 2. We describe the annotation scheme and process, including type definitions, handling of ambiguous cases, and agreement statistics, so that the resource can be understood, extended, and replicated. 3. We provide a quantitative analysis of the nesting and type distributions and of how the annotation relates to the underlying syntactic structure. 4. We provide standard training, development, and test splits and evaluation of existing nested NER approaches as baselines, to indicate how much difficulty remains once data scale, type granularity, and nesting depth are increased. We hope that the public release of NNE will encourage the development of new techniques for nested and fine-grained NER and will support research on how entity structure interacts with syntax, linking, and other downstream applications. Corpus selection and preprocessing We annotated the complete Wall Street Journal (WSJ) portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB; Marcus et al., 1993), covering sections 00–24. The PTB is the most heavily annotated English newswire resource, with part-of-speech tags, constituency structure, and (through later projects) semantic role and coreference layers. Annotating it lets nested entity structure be studied alongside existing syntactic and semantic information. We kept the PTB tokenization so that mention boundaries align with the treebank. Annotators saw each sentence in its original document order and could see neighboring sentences, which let them resolve ambiguous types (for example, a company name versus its product). We did not use gold parse trees to restrict candidate spans. Mentions were free to cross constituent boundaries wherever the text required. Annotation scheme Our type inventory began with the BBN Pronoun Coreference and Entity Type Corpus (Weischedel and Brunstein, 2005), which was already annotated over the same WSJ text. We extended it with ideas from the Extended Named Entity Hierarchy (Sekine et al., 2002), the ACE guidelines (Doddington et al., 2004), and the GENIA ontology (Kim et al., 2003). We then ran several rounds of pilot annotation on held-out documents, adding, merging, or splitting types whenever annotators disagreed systematically or found that frequent phenomena had no suitable label. The final scheme has 114 types organized in a three-level hierarchy. Top-level categories include person, organization, geopolitical entity, location, facility, event, product, work of art, law, language, and several numeric and temporal families (e.g., monetary values, percentages, dates, times, cardinal and ordinal numbers, and measurements). Fine-grained subtypes encode distinctions such as the kind of organization (corporation, government body, educational institution) or the kind of numeric expression. Annotators always chose the most specific applicable type, so the hierarchy can be collapsed to coarser labels when needed. Guidelines defined a mention as a contiguous token span that refers to an entity of one of the scheme's types. Names, numeric expressions, and temporal expressions were annotated, whereas pronouns and generic common-noun phrases were not. Nesting was permitted to arbitrary depth under one structural constraint. Any two mentions must be either disjoint or strictly nested, so partially overlapping spans are not allowed. Identical spans with different types were permitted only for a small set of documented cases of genuine type ambiguity, such as metonymic uses. Where a mention contained others, annotators labeled every inner mention independently. For instance, a company name contains a person name, and a date range contains two dates. Annotators were instructed to label inner mentions even when the surface form was the same as an outer mention's component, and to treat possessives, appositions, and coordinations according to explicit rules in the guidelines. For coordinated structures with shared modifiers, annotators marked each conjunct as its own mention. They did not use discontinuous spans, which keeps the annotation compatible with standard span-based and tree-structured models. Annotation procedure The annotation team consisted of trained annotators with linguistics backgrounds, who received a guideline document and supervised practice before working on the main corpus. We built a browser-based interface for efficient span selection and hierarchical type assignment. It supports keyboard shortcuts, type search over the hierarchy, and visual display of nested mentions so that annotators can verify structure at a glance. To reduce effort and improve consistency, the tool pre-populated candidate annotations from the existing BBN labels where these were compatible with our scheme, and annotators then corrected, extended, and re-typed them. BBN annotation is flat and uses a different type set, so it served only as a starting point. Every sentence received full manual review, and annotators were encouraged to flag uncertain cases rather than guess. Annotation proceeded in batches by PTB section. After each batch, a senior annotator reviewed a sample and all flagged items, and recurring problems were resolved through guideline revisions and group discussion. When a guideline changed, earlier batches were searched for affected patterns, using type and string queries over the existing annotations, and corrected. In a final consistency pass, we ran automatic checks to catch structural errors and implausible labelings. These checks looked for partially overlapping spans, mentions whose boundaries split a token, inner mentions of a type not licensed inside a given outer type, and strings that received different labels in different places without a contextual reason. Flagged items were manually adjudicated. Quality assessment We measured inter-annotator agreement on a subset of documents that were annotated independently by multiple annotators from scratch, without pre-populated labels. Because the number of mentions per sentence is unbounded and there is no natural notion of negative items, chance-corrected coefficients such as Cohen's kappa are poorly defined for this task. Following Hripcsak and Rothschild (2005), we instead treated one annotator's labels as the reference and computed precision, recall, and F1 for the other, which is equivalent to pairwise F1 agreement. A mention counted as matching only if its start, end, and type were all identical. We report agreement at three granularities: unlabeled span match, match at the top level of the hierarchy, and match at the full fine-grained type. This separates disagreements about where mentions are from disagreements about what they are. We also compared agreement at different nesting depths to see whether inner mentions are harder to annotate than outermost ones, and we examined confusion between types to find systematically ambiguous distinctions. The rapid growth and increasing complexity of network protocols, exemplified by the widespread adoption of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, necessitate advanced methodologies for protocol interpretation and analysis. Network protocols like TLS are foundational to secure communications on the Internet, as they provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication between communicating entities. Traditionally, the understanding and analysis of such protocols have required considerable manual effort and domain expertise to characterize their abstract behavioral models. Such expertise-driven approaches, while often effective, are neither scalable nor adaptable to the evolving dynamics and intricacies of modern protocols. Abstraction in protocol analysis involves simplifying the complex interactions inherent in communication protocols to a manageable representation without sacrificing significant meaning or functionality. The current paradigm largely depends on manual abstraction, wherein experts curate models based on their understanding of protocol operations. However, this process is labor-intensive and susceptible to human error, bias, and the inability to keep pace with rapidly evolving network landscapes and threats. As such, there exists a critical gap in automating this abstraction process to streamline scalability, reliability, and adaptability in protocol analysis. This paper addresses the automation of protocol abstraction by introducing a novel framework based on weakly-supervised clustering. Weak supervision refers to machine learning paradigms wherein the model is guided with limited labeled data, relying primarily on predominantly unlabeled datasets (Zhou, 2018). Such an approach is particularly suited for the analysis of network protocols, where comprehensive labeled datasets are rare, costly to produce, and may quickly become obsolete due to protocol evolution. By leveraging a small amount of side-information, weakly-supervised clustering holds promise in reducing the reliance on exhaustive expert supervision while maintaining the fidelity of abstraction. The research question driving this inquiry is: Can a weakly-supervised clustering algorithm produce an effective abstraction for the TLS protocol, comparable to a manually constructed reference abstraction with limited side-information? This inquiry is motivated by the need to balance between precision in abstraction and the pragmatic limitations of manual model construction. Our hypothesis is that with a foundational framework, enriched by minimal but strategic human inputs, the model can successfully form meaningful abstractions that are congruent with those designed by experts. In addressing this question, the present study makes several contributions to the field: 1. Automation of Abstraction in Protocol Analysis: We introduce a novel application of weakly-supervised clustering to derive representative abstractions of network protocols. This approach systematically reduces dependency on expert-generated models, offering a scalable alternative to traditional abstract modeling methods. 2. Efficient Learning from Limited Labeled Data: Our methodology leverages weak supervision to infer abstraction, demonstrating that meaningful protocol abstractions can be achieved with minimal labeled examples. This efficiency circumvents the data intensity requirement commonly associated with supervised learning approaches, providing a cost-effective solution. 3. Empirical Validation Using the TLS Protocol: The study's methodology is validated through its application to the TLS protocol, a benchmark for secure communication protocols. Our results evidence the robustness of the proposed approach by achieving abstractions that closely align with manually constructed reference models. 4. Potential for Generalization: While the focus of this paper is on TLS, the principles underlying our approach are not protocol-specific. This adaptability positions our framework as a potential universal solution for automatic abstraction across varied protocols, pending further analysis and testing. Addressing automated abstraction through the lens of weak supervision offers significant advancements in system modeling and security analysis. It equips analysts with tools that are not only efficient and scalable but also adaptable to the continually changing ecosystem of network protocols. Ultimately, our contribution lies in bridging the gap between manual expertise-dependent models and fully automated solutions, offering a balanced approach that retains the nuances of protocol interaction while streamlining the abstraction process. The significance of this work is underscored by the pressing need for more robust and scalable methods amid the incessant emergence of new protocol specifications and network demands. As the landscape of digital communication continues to expand, the methodologies posited in this paper provide a foundation for further research and development, fostering an era of more intelligent, autonomous protocol analysis. With a solid grounding in both theoretical rationale and empirical evaluation, this approach lays the cornerstone for subsequent innovation in protocol abstraction and analysis, promoting enhanced understanding and responsiveness in cybersecurity infrastructures. In summary, the paper sets forth a transformative method in the domain of network protocol analysis, augmenting the capabilities of analysts to engage with complex, evolving systems in a more efficient, accurate, and sustainable manner. In this section, we delineate the methodological framework employed in the automatic clustering of network protocol messages using a weakly supervised clustering approach. This includes a comprehensive discussion on the data acquisition and preprocessing stages, the clustering algorithm's design, the experimental procedures for the clustering process, and the statistical analysis performed to evaluate our results. The primary data used in this study comprises network traffic captures containing messages exchanged during TLS sessions. This dataset was prepared by capturing packets from a variety of popular web services employing TLS, ensuring a broad representation of protocol behavior. The network traces were captured in packet capture (PCAP) format and subsequently parsed using a specialized library capable of extracting application-layer protocol units (ALPUs) from the raw packets. Preprocessing of the data was needed to convert these ALPUs into a format suitable for clustering. Each ALPU was first sanitized to remove noise and identify meaningful byte sequences. These sequences were then represented in a feature space that captures essential properties relevant for clustering, such as message length, common byte patterns, and structural layout frequently observed in TLS messages. The core of our methodology is the application of weakly supervised clustering. Unlike fully unsupervised approaches, our method leverages a sophisticated semi-supervised algorithm that can incorporate limited a priori knowledge in the form of side information, used here as a small set of labeled samples. These labels, provided by domain experts, serve as guidance to the clustering process, thereby improving the quality of the resultant message abstraction. For this study, we selected the Constrained k-means algorithm (Wagstaff et al., 2001) due to its proven efficacy in incorporating instance-level constraints in clustering tasks. The algorithm was extended to work efficiently on large-scale network protocol data by employing a mini-batch approach, allowing it to process massive quantities of message data without significant computational overhead. This design choice ensures scalability, which is vital when dealing with network captures that can encompass millions of messages. The clustering procedure begins with the initialization phase where the labeled examples are used to determine initial cluster centroids. These centroids are strategically positioned within the feature space as indicated by the similarity of the labeled instances to their corresponding known categories. This initialization reduces the potential for cluster drift during the iterative phases of k-means clustering. During the iteration phase, the algorithm assigns each unlabeled message to its nearest cluster centroid while respecting the constraints derived from the labeled examples. These constraints ensure that similar messages as defined by the side-information are grouped together, facilitating the learning of semantic message abstractions. A crucial step in the procedure is the periodic refinement of cluster boundaries, which is achieved through a feedback mechanism that evaluates cluster quality based on the internal cohesion and external separation metrics. Messages that appear on the boundary between clusters are reevaluated more frequently to ensure they are not incorrectly classified due to noise or feature overlap. The clustering process is iterated until convergence, defined as the point at which changes in cluster assignments fall below a pre-set threshold over multiple iterations or a maximum number of iterations is reached. To gauge the effectiveness of the clustering method, a comprehensive comparison with a manually constructed reference abstraction was conducted. The key metrics used for this evaluation include Precision, Recall, and the F1 Score, which together offer a robust measure of the clustering accuracy concerning the established reference. Additionally, an Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) was employed to measure the degree of similarity between the clustering result and the reference abstraction, adjusting for chance groupings. We conducted a paired comparison test to statistically determine the significance of improvements observed in the weakly supervised method over a baseline unsupervised clustering approach. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was chosen due to its suitability for assessing matched pairs, making it ideal for comparing clustering results across different trials with paired samples. Finally, sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate how variations in the amount and quality of side information influenced clustering performance. This involved systematic alteration of labeled examples in terms of quantity and representativeness, with results indicating a marked improvement in clustering accuracy even with minimal side information input. In summary, through meticulous data preparation, informed clustering design, structured experimental procedures, and rigorous statistical validation, the proposed method demonstrates a potent capability for generating accurate and meaningful abstractions of network protocol communications, specifically within the TLS protocol domain. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed weakly-supervised clustering method for automatic abstraction of the TLS protocol, we conducted a series of experiments comparing the algorithm-generated abstractions with a manually constructed reference abstraction. The experiments were designed to quantitatively assess the vocabulary size reduction, abstraction accuracy, and overall fidelity between automated and manual abstractions. The dataset used for experimentation consisted of 10,000 TLS network packet samples, from which excerpts were selected to simulate real-world messaging patterns associated with the protocol. The manually constructed reference abstraction was formulated by domain experts who reduced the vocabulary size from the initial 5,000 distinct symbols in raw communication to 150 abstract symbols. This abstraction served as the baseline against which the weakly-supervised clustering results were compared. In the first set of experiments, the weakly-supervised clustering approach achieved a vocabulary size reduction from 5,000 to 155 abstract symbols. This reduction represents a substantial compression factor of approximately 96.9%, which is nearly identical to the 97% achieved by the reference abstraction. This similarity in compression factors is an early indicator that the clustering approach effectively synthesizes the abstraction process typically performed by experts. To investigate abstraction accuracy, a total of 500 labeled examples were employed as side-information to guide the clustering process. These labeled examples were strategically selected to cover a diverse set of TLS packet scenarios to ensure comprehensive representation. The automated abstraction was subsequently tested against 1,000 unseen packet samples not included in the labeling step. The automated abstractions demonstrated an accuracy of 98.7% in matching the reference abstraction labels on these unseen samples, a nearly perfect alignment. Furthermore, the automated system correctly identified and abstracted unique and less frequent communication patterns with an accuracy of 97%, showing robustness across varying packet types. One of the critical metrics assessed was the semantic fidelity between the automatically-generated abstractions and the reference. Using semantic similarity scoring, the average fidelity score of automated abstractions was determined to be 0.95 out of 1.0, indicative of high congruity in preserving the semantic essence of the original communications. This scoring incorporated comparisons regarding contextual appropriateness and maintenance of protocol characteristics post-abstraction. The experiments also assessed computational efficiency gains in the abstraction process. The weakly-supervised clustering method reduced computational time for abstraction formulation by over 70% compared to domain expert-driven manual abstraction. On average, the clustering method required 2.5 hours to process the complete dataset and generate abstractions, whereas manual abstraction necessitated approximately 8.5 hours of expert input. This efficiency in computational processing time introduces significant potential for scalability when applying the method to larger datasets or additional network protocols. Additionally, sensitivity analyses were conducted to determine the impact of varying the number of labeled examples used as side-information. The results illustrated that abstraction accuracy maintained an increasing trend with a higher number of labeled examples, plateauing at around 100 labeled examples with accuracy enhancement rates diminishing subsequently. This signifies that while the inclusion of labeled examples is critical to achieving high abstraction accuracy, optimal performance is attainable with relatively minimal side-information input, emphasizing efficiency and practicality in deployment scenarios. Over the last few years, we have seen growth of grassroots movements to increase access to scholarly products, such as articles, code, data, and educational resources (e.g., [1–5]). We have also seen a rise in the number of government and private funders mandating open access and open data [6,7] and the emergence of the Open Research Funders Group (http://www.orfg.org). These initiatives have been key in raising awareness and acceptance of open scholarship. However, despite these advances, I believe we have hit a wall that is impeding widespread adoption. While increasing numbers of academics may ideologically support sharing their work, many are concerned with how these practices will affect their career prospects and advancement [8–13]. Academic institutions are one of the primary influencers affecting how faculty perceive open scholarship and how willing they are to engage in certain practices [8, 13, 14]. Faculty often cite a lack of institutional support for open access, especially in evaluations, as one reason they are reluctant to publish in these journals [11]. Moreover, faculty express fear that open scholarship practices, especially those that fall outside the traditionally rewarded research products, will not only not be rewarded but may even hurt their evaluations. For example, one respondent of a 2011 survey of medical faculty [15] wrote, Faculty understandably pay attention to what institutions value and where evaluation committees place the most weight to decide where to invest the most personal effort. As a University of Idaho faculty member wrote in response to a 2013 survey [11], A 2015 survey in the United Kingdom found that academics are increasingly tailoring their scholarly production and publication decisions to fit institutional evaluation criteria [16]. Thus, I believe universities are in a unique position to support open scholarship and break through some of the barriers to widespread adoption. This support could come in many forms, including recognition of open access and open data in promotion and tenure evaluations, small grants to support the development of open educational resources, and redirecting existing funds from proprietary software to support creation and training in open source solutions. Simple actions could demonstrate that universities value sharing, thereby changing faculty behavior. Such support could, in turn, have benefits for institutions, such as increased funding, visibility, and recruiting power. Most importantly, the sharing of scholarly outputs could help universities meet their stated missions to create and disseminate knowledge for broader public good. There is no one unanimously accepted definition of open scholarship; the debate continues as to what the minimum requirements and best practices are for different types of open content [17]. Some of the earliest and perhaps most well-accepted international open standards are the Budapest Open Access Initiative (2002) [18], the Bethesda Statement (2003) [19], and the Berlin Declaration (2003) [20]—all of which deal with open access to articles. At the time these declarations were written, they were revolutionary, and their original language still guides open scholarship efforts today. However, research has rapidly changed over the last 10–15 years, and projects are now producing much more than just articles, including large amounts of data, different types of digital media, electronic notebooks, and complex software. In recent years, open science has emerged as an umbrella term to refer to open access, open data, open notebooks, open source, or any other aspect of our work as researchers that can be shared [21, 22]. International standards for these products have emerged, including the Open Source Definition (2007) [23] for openly licensed software and the Panton Principles for open data (2010) [24]. More recently, there has been recognition that “open science” may not be as inclusive a term as we might like [25], and some have opted instead to refer to “open research” to include disciplines like the humanities [26, 27]. I will use the even broader term “open scholarship” to encompass sharing of research and nonresearch products, such as those arising from educational and outreach activities [28, 29]. I see inclusivity as crucial to the success of open scholarship as a social movement. While open scholarship can encompass all of the aforementioned practices, academics do not have to engage in all of these to contribute. Openness can be considered a continuum of practices [6]. Researchers can start with simple actions, like self-archiving free copies of their articles, and work their way up to sharing code, data, or notebooks. Educators can begin by sharing electronic copies of their class notes and work their way up to the creation of open textbooks or interactive online materials. It is important we welcome people at whatever level of sharing with which they are comfortable. For this to work, it is in turn important that universities have ways of recognizing diverse scholarly products and different types of sharing. But with all the different standards, how are universities to determine what counts as open scholarship? I propose that universities take guidance from perhaps the simplest and all-encompassing international standard, the Open Definition from Open Knowledge, which states, "Open means anyone can freely access, use, modify, and share for any purpose" [30]. This definition can be applied to any educational or research product, allowing universities to set a clear baseline. Colleges, schools, and departments could then set more specific standards to fit disciplinary needs. A comprehensive discussion of the benefits of open scholarship is beyond the scope of this paper (see instead [6, 31, 32]). Here, I focus on just a few ways sharing can transform research and education, falling largely into the democratic (“equal access for all”) and pragmatic (“sharing improves research and education”) schools of thought [22]. In each section, I begin by outlining some of the democratic and pragmatic benefits of open scholarship, then describe how I see such practices also benefiting universities and fitting in well with institutional missions. While many of the societal benefits of open scholarship have sometimes been considered to be at odds with the interests of institutions, I argue there are several points of intersection at which what is good for the public may also be good for the university. In my opinion, many universities have drifted away from their stated missions of knowledge dissemination, community engagement, and public good. Open scholarship provides an opportunity for universities to return to these core values. In 2010, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) committed to the creation of Inclusive Knowledge Societies [33]: Currently, our societies are far from inclusive. All over the world, people lack access to scientific information (Fig 1). A study by Laakso and Björk reported that only 17% of 1.6 million articles published in 2011 were available without a subscription [34]. Studies up to 2012 [35] and 2015 [10] put the estimate around 22%–24%, although this number is likely to vary with discipline. A new study by Piwowar et al. estimates that, overall, 28% of the academic literature is free to access online, and although that number is growing, it was only 45% as of 2015 [36]. A study by the World Health Organization demonstrates the scope of the problem [37]: Just recently, it was announced that scientists in Germany, Peru [38], and Taiwan are losing access to Elsevier journals, in part because of increasing subscription fees [39]. Rising costs have also made textbooks unaffordable, negatively impacting education [40, 41]. As Nicole Allen, Director of Open Education for the Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition (SPARC), has said, "Students can’t learn from materials they can’t afford" [42]. A lack of access can impede learning and slow discoveries. Science itself could suffer, too, losing valuable perspectives when many researchers can't participate in their rapidly evolving fields. Open scholarship democratizes access to information by making research available to all, regardless of financial resources—a necessary, though not sufficient, step in creating a true "knowledge democracy" [43]. Removing financial barriers helps those in low- and middle-income countries keep up to speed with their fields, potentially increasing their participation and the diversity of perspectives in research. (Improved access is a necessary condition but should not be seen as the magic bullet that will resolve all inequalities [44]. Much more than access to information is required to increase participation in research, including improved infrastructure and better funding for research in these countries [45]. These are not easy problems to solve, but they should not be ignored.) In addition, when research is open, participation is not limited to academics. The fast-growing area of citizen science is a testament to what can be achieved when we encourage contributions from outside the academy [46]. In sum, open scholarship allows us to create Inclusive Knowledge Societies [33], which I would argue should be one goal, if not the goal, of universities. Universities are by nature exclusionary—there are limited spots and often only those with the highest grades and test scores are accepted. In the 1940s, people began referring to academic institutions as ivory towers, where an elite few engaged in intellectual pursuits, largely "disengaged" from the concerns or needs of the public [47]. If anything, the perception of universities as ivory towers has only grown over the last decades, as competition for student and faculty positions increases, leaving many more on the outside. As Shapin writes, "Today, almost no one has anything good to say about the Ivory Tower and specifically about the university in its supposed Ivory Tower mode" [47]. How can institutions move away from this negative image and become more inclusionary? Increasing acceptance rates is not feasible for economic and infrastructure reasons. However, universities can allow everyone access to the knowledge created inside their walls. Open educational resources (OERs) are a prime example of openness increasing inclusion [48, 49] and are especially important for increasing access to education in developing countries [50, 51]. When universities make lecture notes, exams, and textbooks openly available online, even those who cannot attend in person can benefit from what the institution has to offer. In fact, 20%–50% of surveyed visitors to open courseware (OCW) websites identify as "self learners" [52]. Educators also benefit from OCW sites, making up around a quarter of visitors from regions like Latin America, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East and North Africa [53]. As an educator in Mexico, I use open textbooks available through projects like OpenStax (https://openstax.org), run by Rice University, because I know my students cannot afford expensive textbooks but still need access to quality information to learn. The recent growth of massive online open courses (MOOCs) [54], particularly large-scale, free course initiatives by prestigious United States universities (e.g., edX, https://www.edx.org, run by Harvard and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology), is one indication that institutions are recognizing their exclusionary nature as a problem and trying to improve access to education by lowering financial and presential barriers. While this can be seen as positive, it is also important to not lose sight of the goal to increase inclusion. The issue is not just access but also participation [45]: who is creating knowledge, and how do their experiences influence and inherently bias educational content? If the majority of OERs are produced by prestigious US universities, it represents another form of exclusion and reinforces the problem of Western perspectives (and the English language) dominating educational content [44, 50, 52]. Resource-rich universities in Canada, the US, and Europe should look for ways to support, raise visibility, and increase the use of OERs from other countries with diverse global perspectives to facilitate a "true knowledge exchange" [44]. An example of an OER project from Africa is the Science Education Exchange for Sustainable Development (SeeSD; https://www.seesd.org), based in Senegal, which is designing open resources to improve access to education and participation in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). SeeSD is also developing a MOOC-style online learning platform called Afreecademy (http://afreecademy.org). Examples from South Asia and Southeast Asia, respectively, include Sakshat from India (http://www.sakshat.ac.in) and the Vietnam Open Educational Resources program (http://www.voer.edu.vn). More on OER projects in Asia can be found in [55]. An example from Latin America comes from the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), where I work. UNAM does not have

Using a UAS to visually navigate a rescue USV to victims can help responders during marine mass casualty events. First responders lack the manpower to effectively address marine mass casualty events during which it is not uncommon to have 80 victims in the water at the same time. While rescue USVs can help, teleoperation is problematic due to the lack of depth perception when USV is far away and the manpower requirements, and global positioning system (GPS) waypoint navigation is not precise enough as exact GPS coordinates of the victims are unknown and victims might drift with waves and currents. A UAS can visually navigate the USV to the victims by using visual feedback eliminating the need for teleoperation or GPS-based navigation as was shown in our previous work presented in Dufek et al. (2017), Karnan et al. (2017), Xiao et al. (2017), and Dufek and Murphy (2018). Such a heterogeneous multi-robot team of a UAS and a USV is illustrated in Figure 1. Visual navigation requires visual pose estimation of the USV which can be generalized to visual pose estimation of any fast moving object using UAS leading to the following problem statement: Visually estimate the pose of a fast maneuvering object using moving UAS, relative to UAS's image frame of reference, in an outdoor environment from an oblique view angle at large distances in real-time. In this article, a USV is taken as an instance of this object. The solution must satisfy working environment requirements, vehicular requirements, physical settings requirements, and desired output requirements. The working environment requirements are that the solution must work in an outdoor water environment where the rescues are being performed. Vehicular requirements are that the solution must work for moving UAS and moving USV. Small inexpensive UAS that would be used in rescue application (e.g., DJI Inspire 1) can move at speeds of up to 22 m s−1. Rescue- USVs (e.g., EMILY) can move at speeds of up to 22 m s−1 and make abrupt maneuvers with turn rate of up to 180 ° s−1. The physical settings requirements are that the solution must work at a large distance between UAS and USV and at an oblique view angle. The radius of marine mass casualty event rescue operations is typically 180 m. This distance causes the spatial resolution of the USV to be very low as illustrated in Figure 2 implicating that fiducial markers encoding full pose (e.g., AprilTag) would not be visible. The UAS might be operated above shore while USV is in the water causing the oblique view angle of up to 85° from nadir. The desired output requirements are that the output should be full pose (both position and orientation) and it should be updated in real-time (at least 5 Hz) to enable the visual navigation. While it might be beneficial to use multiple UAS as well as to estimate the pose of multiple objects simultaneously, for the sake of simplicity, it is assumed in this paper that there is only a single UAS and it is estimating the pose of a single object. The contributions of this article are addressing a problem of how can a moving small UAS visually estimate the position and orientation of a fast maneuvering object, relative to UAS's image frame of reference, in an outdoor environment from an oblique view angle at large distances in real-time, that previous work failed to fully address, analyzing this problem on an example of a life-saving USV, proposing a method satisfying all the introduced requirements, and comparing two algorithms for solving this problem. First, this work addresses a problem defined above that none of the 58 reviewed studies fully covered. Second, it presents an analysis of this problem and justifies why some approaches would not work. Third, it presents a hue-based visual pose estimation method consisting of two algorithms for visual position estimation and four techniques for visual orientation estimation. Fourth, it compares two algorithms, thresholding and histogramming, for visual position estimation combined with one technique for orientation estimation in four physical experiments. The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses related work in visual pose estimation of an object from UAS and identifies gaps and opportunities in research, most notably the lack of solution satisfying all the requirements discussed above. Section 3 presents two algorithms for position estimation (thresholding and histogramming) and four shape analysis techniques for orientation estimation. Section 4 details implementation of those algorithms on a laptop using C++ and OpenCV and describes platforms used for the implementation. Section 5 introduces experimental methodology to determine pose estimation error relative to manually annotated ground truth and presents results from four physical trials comparing thresholding and histogramming. Section 6 discusses reasons histogramming algorithm is better than thresholding (it can better model the object under local illumination conditions), points out problems with the proposed algorithms (particularly large orientation estimation error, necessity of tuning, and low robustness to significant illumination changes), examines how the experiments could have been improved (most notably testing for robustness in addition to precision), and indicates machine learning would be suitable to explore for future work. Finally, section 7 summarizes the article. Fifty-eight studies from the robotics and computer vision scientific literature were reviewed. While all the eight requirements introduced in section 1 were partially addressed by those studies, none satisfied all the requirements combined. The studies were classified to seven categories depending on what was the object for which the visual pose estimation using UAS was done: UGV (27 studies), car (9 studies), person (7 studies), landing platform (7 studies), standalone fiducial marker (3 studies), another UAS (2 studies), and other objects (3 studies). There were no studies on visual pose estimation of USV from UAS. All the categories except UGV category were limited in scope to only those studies where the visual pose estimation was done outdoors. Each study was evaluated using eight criteria to validate if the particular study satisfied the requirements introduced in section 1. To validate the working environment requirements, one criterion was evaluated: (1) Were the experiments performed indoors or outdoors? To validate the vehicular requirements, two criteria were evaluated: (1) Was the UAS static or moving? (2) Was the object static or moving? To validate physical settings requirements, three criteria were evaluated: (1) Was the distance between UAS and the object short or long (distance is considered short for the purpose of this review if less than or equal 30 m)? (2) Was a fiducial marker used or not? (3) Was the view from UAS nadir or oblique? To validate desired output requirements, two criteria were evaluated: (1) Was just a position estimated or full pose (both position and orientation)? (2) Was the output generated real-time (i.e., updating at least at 5 Hz)? Table 1 lists all the studies and for each, it shows which criteria were satisfied.
