Cohen4†, Ruslan Salakhutdinov1 , Yann LeCun23 ∗ Equal contribution 1 2 Carnegie Mellon University, New York University, 3 Facebook AI Research, 4 Google, Inc. {zhiliny,bdhingra,rsalakhu}@cs.cmu.edu {jakezhao,yann}@cs.nyu.com, kaiminghe@fb.com, wcohen@google.com Abstract Modern deep transfer learning approaches have mainly focused on learning generic feature vectors from one task that are transferable to other tasks, such as word embeddings in language and pretrained convolutional features in vision. However, these approaches usually transfer unary features and largely ignore more structured graphical representations. This work explores the possibility of learning generic latent relational graphs that capture dependencies between pairs of data units (e.g., words or pixels) from large-scale unlabeled data and transferring the graphs to downstream tasks. Our proposed transfer learning framework improves performance on various tasks including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. We also show that the learned graphs are generic enough to be transferred to different embeddings on which the graphs have not been trained (including GloVe embeddings, ELMo embeddings, and task-specific RNN hidden units), or embedding-free units such as image pixels. Recent advances in deep learning have largely relied on building blocks such as convolutional networks (CNNs) [19] and recurrent networks (RNNs) [14] augmented with attention mechanisms [1]. While possessing high representational capacity, these architectures primarily operate on grid-like or sequential structures due to their built-in “innate priors”. As a result, CNNs and RNNs largely rely on high expressiveness to model complex structural phenomena, compensating the fact that they do not explicitly leverage structural, graphical representations. This paradigm has led to a standardized norm in transfer learning and pretraining—fitting an expressive function on a large dataset with or without supervision, and then applying the function to downstream task data for feature extraction. Notable examples include pretrained ImageNet features [13] and pretrained word embeddings [24, 29]. In contrast, a variety of real-world data exhibit much richer relational graph structures than the simple grid-like or sequential structures. This is also emphasized by a parallel work [3]. For example in the language domain, linguists use parse trees to represent syntactic dependency between words; information retrieval systems exploit knowledge graphs to reflect entity relations; and coreference resolution is devised to connect different expressions of the same entity. As such, these exemplified structures are universally present in almost any natural language data regardless of the target tasks, which suggests the possibility of transfer across tasks. These observations also generalize to other domains such as vision, where modeling the relations between pixels is proven useful [28, 50, 44]. † Figure 1: Traditional transfer learning versus our new transfer learning framework. Instead of transferring features, we transfer the graphs output by a network. The graphs are multiplied by task-specific features (e.g. embeddings or hidden states) to produce structure-aware features. One obstacle remaining, however, is that many of the universal structures are essentially humancurated and expensive to acquire on a large scale, while automatically-induced structures are mostly limited to one task [17, 42, 44]. In this paper, we attempt to address two challenges: 1) to break away from the standardized norm of feature-based deep transfer learning2 , and 2) to learn versatile structures in the data with a data-driven approach. In particular, we are interested in learning transferable latent relational graphs, where the nodes of a latent graph are the input units, e.g., all the words in a sentence. The task of latent relational graph learning is to learn an affinity matrix where the weights (possibly zero) capture the dependencies between any pair of input units. To achieve the above goals, we propose a novel framework of unsupervised latent graph learning called GLoMo (Graphs from LOw-level unit MOdeling). Specifically, we train a neural network from large-scale unlabeled data to output latent graphs, and transfer the network to extract graph structures on downstream tasks to augment their training. This approach allows us to separate the features that represent the semantic meaning of each unit and the graphs that reflect how the units may interact. Ideally, the graphs capture task-independent structures underlying the data, and thus become applicable to different sets of features. Figure 1 highlights the difference between traditional feature-based transfer learning and our new framework. Experimental results show that GLoMo improves performance on various language tasks including question answering, natural language inference, and sentiment analysis. We also demonstrate that the learned graphs are generic enough to work with various sets of features on which the graphs have not been trained, including GloVe embeddings [29], ELMo embeddings [30], and taskspecific RNN states. We also identify key factors of learning successful generic graphs: decoupling graphs and features, hierarchical graph representations, sparsity, unit-level objectives, and sequence prediction. To demonstrate the generality of our framework, we further show improved results on image classification by applying GLoMo to model the relational dependencies between the pixels. We propose a framework for unsupervised latent graph learning. Given a one-dimensional input x = (x1 , · · · , xT ), where each xt denotes an input unit at position t and T is the length of the sequence, the goal of latent graph learning is to learn a (T × T ) affinity matrix G such that each entry Gij captures the dependency between the unit xi and the unit xj . The affinity matrix is asymmetric, representing a directed weighted graph. In particular, in this work we consider the case where each column of the affinity matrix sums to one, for computational convenience. In the following text, with a little abuse of notation, we use G to denote a set of affinity matrices. We use the terms “affinity matrices” and “graphs” interchangeably. During the unsupervised learning phase, our framework trains two networks, a graph predictor network g and a feature predictor network f . Given the input x, our graph predictor g produces a 2 Throughout the paper, we use “feature” to refer to unary feature representations, and use “graph” to refer to structural, graphical representations. set of graphs G = g(x). The graphs G are represented as a 3-d tensor in RL×T ×T , where L is the number of layers that produce graphs. Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy, characterized by the presence of a significant number of bacteria in the urine without signs or symptoms of a urinary tract infection, has been subject to medical scrutiny due to its potential implications for maternal and fetal health. It is estimated that ASB occurs in 2% to 10% of pregnant women (Macejko et al., 2007). Historically, the detection and treatment of ASB during pregnancy have been a routine part of antenatal care in many developed countries, primarily due to concerns that untreated ASB can progress to symptomatic urinary tract infections (UTIs), including pyelonephritis, and may be associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm labor and low birth weight (Smaill, 2001; Nicolle, 2015). In the mid-20th century, studies suggested that the antibiotic treatment of ASB in pregnant women could significantly reduce the incidence of pyelonephritis and potentially mitigate some of these risks (Kass, 1960; Sweet, 1977). As a result, clinical practice guidelines in Europe and North America have historically endorsed routine screening and treatment of ASB in pregnancy as a standard preventive measure (PHE, 2011; ACOG, 2008). However, the foundational studies that have underpinned these recommendations primarily date back to the 1950s through the 1980s. A great deal has changed in the fields of microbiology, pharmacotherapy, and obstetric care since that time, prompting a re-evaluation of these guidelines. New insights into antibiotic resistance, more stringent data evaluation techniques, and a lessened reliance on broad-spectrum antibiotics due to their associated risks necessitate that we re-examine the validity of these historical findings under contemporary clinical contexts (Gupta et al., 2011; Nicolle, 2015). Additionally, the routine use of antibiotics is not without potential harms. The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria presents a significant public health challenge, exacerbated by unnecessary antibiotic use (Ventola, 2015). Meanwhile, the side effects and potential consequences of antibiotic exposure to both the mother and developing fetus during pregnancy warrant careful consideration (Shmuely et al., 2007). The balance between benefitting the individual and contributing to broader public health concerns presents a complex dilemma, emphasizing the urgency of assessing the current evidence and updating clinical guidelines appropriately. Despite the historical emphasis on treating ASB, recent literature casts doubt on whether this intervention's benefits outweigh the potential harms, especially given the notable improvements in maternal and neonatal care over the decades. Modern trials often confront ethical and practical challenges, such as the ethical dilemma of withholding treatment in placebo-controlled settings and variability in study designs, contributing to a lack of uniformity in research findings. Additionally, the decreased incidence of pyelonephritis and perinatal complications in high-resource settings today compared to those from decades earlier has further complicated the assessment of ASB's clinical significance in pregnancy (Nicolle, 2015; Smaill & Vazquez, 2015). In light of these considerations, the primary research question we aim to address in this systematic review is whether routine screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy confer more benefits than harms. Critically, this requires examining not only the effectiveness of screening and treatment but also comparing different screening strategies or approaches, where data are available. Given the scarcity of recent comprehensive studies directly addressing this fundamental issue, we are also compelled to explore the direct outcomes of treating ASB, particularly using newer classes of antibiotics and current protocols. This systematic review contributes to the existing body of knowledge by providing a current synthesis of available data on ASB screening and treatment during pregnancy, assessing the methodological quality of included studies, and evaluating the applicability of old data to modern clinical practice. In doing so, this review seeks to illuminate gaps in the literature and offer guidance for future research agendas aimed at optimizing prenatal care strategies. Furthermore, our study considers the broader implications of treatment strategies in the context of public health and antibiotic stewardship. By evaluating the relative risks and benefits of current screening and treatment practices, our findings aim to inform evidence-based policy and clinical guidelines, ultimately improving maternal and neonatal health outcomes while addressing resistance patterns and antibiotic usage more effectively. In summary, despite longstanding clinical guidelines endorsing the treatment of ASB in pregnant women, we recognize the critical need for a contemporary evaluation of these interventions. This systematic review endeavors to provide a robust analysis to determine the current evidence's quality, relevance, and implications on modern praxis in prenatal care. Through this approach, we strive to contribute valuable insights that inform clinical guidelines and support optimal health outcomes for both mothers and their infants. Methods In this systematic review, we followed a rigorous methodological framework to assess the benefits and harms of screening and treatment for asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnant women. Our research aimed to evaluate the patient-relevant outcomes of screening versus no screening for ASB, compare different screening strategies, and, in the absence of reliable evidence for the primary screening question, scrutinize the effects of treating ASB. Data Sources and Search Strategy We conducted a comprehensive search in several bibliographic databases, including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and CINAHL, up to February 2016. The search strategy was developed with the assistance of a librarian specializing in systematic reviews to ensure inclusivity and precision. We also explored trial registries, such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, to capture ongoing or unpublished trials. The grey literature was reviewed via sources like OpenGrey and conference proceedings to identify potentially overlooked studies. Our search terms incorporated variations and combinations of "asymptomatic bacteriuria," "screening," "pregnancy," "urinary tract infection," and "antibiotic treatment," along with Boolean operators to expand or narrow the search scope appropriately. No language restrictions were applied. The full search strategy, including specific database and keyword combinations, is available as supplementary material online. Study Selection Eligibility criteria for inclusion were predefined. We targeted randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective non-randomized trials examining pregnant women screened for ASB. to reflect contemporary health care contexts. For studies comparing antibiotics to either placebo or no treatment, we included trials explicitly evaluating the outcomes of pyelonephritis, lower urinary tract infection, and preterm labor. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts, discarding studies that were obviously irrelevant. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were retrieved and assessed for inclusion. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment We developed a standardized data extraction form that captured study characteristics, including design, population, interventions, comparators, outcomes, and results. Quality assessment of included studies was independently performed by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for RCTs, which evaluates seven domains: sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, and other potential biases. For non-randomized studies, we used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, which assesses selection, comparability, and outcomes. Discrepancies in data extraction or quality assessment were discussed, and consensus was reached with input from an expert in methodology when needed. We contacted authors for clarification on ambiguous or missing data whenever possible. Data Synthesis and Statistical Analysis Given the heterogeneity in study designs and outcomes across the included trials, a quantitative synthesis using meta-analysis was deemed inappropriate; thus, a qualitative synthesis approach was employed. We analyzed and compared the effects of antibiotic treatment on the incidence of pyelonephritis, lower UTI, and preterm delivery. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were extracted from the original studies or calculated using the data provided. In presenting our findings, we prioritized reporting dichotomous outcomes. Results from older studies were contextualized against the backdrop of modern clinical practices and medical advancements. We adopted the Peto odds ratio method for studies that reported rare events, as it is generally more valid when there are low event rates. Qualitative synthesis involved comparing findings from different studies and narratively summarizing the evidence, focusing specifically on studies' applicability to current health care settings. The GRADE approach was used to rate the quality of evidence for each outcome, rating evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. Our analysis included a critical appraisal of the applicability of older evidence to contemporary medical practices, given changes in pathogen resistance, antibiotic availability, and updated clinical guidelines. Due consideration was given to the impact of early study termination and low event rates on the robustness of recent findings. Through meticulous methodology, this systematic review endeavored to deliver an evidence-based elucidation of the contemporary necessity and impact of screening and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy. Results Our systematic review, conducted to evaluate the benefits and harms associated with the screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnant women, yielded a comprehensive analysis of the available literature. Our primary aim was to assess the impact of routine screening for ASB as compared to no screening, and secondarily to compare the efficacy of varying screening strategies. However, the absence of eligible studies made it imperative to focus on the treatment aspect of ASB where we found limited but insightful evidence. Upon initial screening of numerous bibliographic databases and trial registries, our search did not identify any randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or prospective non-randomised trials that directly assessed the outcomes of screening versus no screening for ASB in pregnant populations. Similarly, no studies provided comparative results of different screening strategies. This lack of direct evidence highlights a critical gap in research and is suggestive of the need for rigorous clinical trials to definitively address these questions. Despite the absence of screening data, we identified four RCTs that compared the outcomes of antibiotic treatment against no treatment or placebo in 454 pregnant women diagnosed with ASB. These studies provided some insight into the treatment pathways and their implications. Two studies, originating from the 1960s, demonstrated statistically significant reductions in the occurrence of pyelonephritis and lower urinary tract infections (UTIs) in pregnant women treated with antibiotics. Specifically, one of these studies reported an odds ratio (OR) of 0.21 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.07–0.59) for the occurrence of pyelonephritis, indicating a substantial decrease in risk. Similarly, the OR for lower UTIs was observed at 0.10 (95% CI, 0.03–0.35), suggesting that antibiotic treatment could significantly prevent the progression from ASB to symptomatic UTI conditions (Author et al., 196X; Researcher et al., 196X). Contrastingly, a more recent study, deemed of higher methodological quality, presented results that differed markedly from its predecessors. This particular trial did not observe a statistically significant difference in pyelonephritis rates, which were 0% in the treatment group versus 2.2% in the placebo group (OR = 0.37, 95% CI, 0.01–9.25, p = 0.515). Furthermore, the incidence of lower UTIs was 10% for the antibiotic group compared to 18% for placebo, yielding a Peto odds ratio (POR) of 0.53 (95% CI, 0.16–1.79, p = 0.357), which did not reach statistical significance (Smith et al., 20XX). It is crucial to note that this study was concluded prematurely due to a very low number of primary outcome events. The primary composite outcome included preterm delivery and pyelonephritis, adding a layer of complexity to the interpretation of its findings. The heterogeneity in results between the older and contemporary studies could be attributed to several factors, including advancements in healthcare practices, antibiotic resistance patterns, and study design quality. The older studies, while suggestive of benefits in treating ASB, have been scrutinized for methodological shortcomings such as inadequate allocation concealment, lack of blinding, and smaller sample sizes, which could have contributed to an overestimation of the treatment effect. These limitations, coupled with changing demographic and microbial resistance profiles, put into question the applicability of these historical findings to current clinical practices. Additionally, none of the included studies specifically assessed the potential harms associated with antibiotic treatment in pregnant women, revealing another significant gap in the literature. While antibiotics are generally prescribed with a favorable risk-benefit ratio, the potential for adverse effects, including the development of antibiotic resistance, the impact on maternal and fetal health, and alterations in the microbiome, remain areas requiring thorough investigation. In recent decades, the disclosure of adverse events (AEs) related to health care interventions has become a focal point for clinicians, researchers, and policymakers alike. Adverse events, defined as any unfavorable and unintended sign, symptom, or disease temporally associated with the use of a medical intervention, are critical to evaluating the risk-benefit profile of therapies (Ioannidis et al., 2010). Understanding the full spectrum of adverse events is essential for patient safety, informed consent, and the refinement of clinical guidelines. However, accumulating evidence suggests that the reporting of adverse events in the published medical literature may be incomplete, potentially leading to skewed perceptions of safety and efficacy (Dwan et al., 2008; Golder et al., 2016). The relative underreporting of adverse events in published sources compared to unpublished documents has been a topic of ongoing concern. Several studies have highlighted substantial discrepancies between the adverse event data presented in published trial reports and those available in clinical study reports, regulatory submissions, or other nonpublicly available repositories (Smyth et al., 2011; Prayle et al., 2012). These discrepancies can distort systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which often form the foundation for clinical guidelines and decision-making processes (Song et al., 2010). Research in this area reveals that adverse events are systematically underreported or selectively reported in published literature. Many factors contribute to this phenomenon, including publication bias, where studies with negative or unfavorable results are less likely to be published, and selective outcome reporting, where certain outcomes are reported based on their statistical significance or perceived importance (Chan et al., 2004; Turner et al., 2008). These biases compromise the ability to synthesize comprehensive and accurate evidence for assessing the risks associated with medical interventions. Despite these insights, the extent to which adverse event information is underreported, and the resultant impact on meta-analytical estimates, remain inadequately quantified. Earlier investigations have predominantly focused on qualitative assessments or have addressed a limited spectrum of interventions and adverse events (Zhao et al., 2016). Consequently, there exists a critical gap in the literature regarding the systematic evaluation of adverse event reporting practices and their implications for evidence synthesis and clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, the current systematic review aims to quantify the underreporting of adverse events in published clinical trials as compared to other nonpublished sources. Specifically, this review seeks to determine the proportion of adverse event data reported in published literature versus unpublished documents and to evaluate how this underreporting influences the outcomes of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of adverse events. This study contributes to the existing body of literature by providing a comprehensive assessment of the differences in adverse event reporting between published and unpublished sources, through an extensive analysis of published and nonpublished documentation related to clinical trials. By examining methodological evaluations and exploiting diverse data sources, our review extends beyond mere recognition of publication biases and provides quantifiable evidence of the disparities in adverse event reporting. A robust aspect of this investigation is its reliance on a wide array of data sources, including established medical databases such as MEDLINE and Embase, augmented by handsearching and expert consultations, to ensure a comprehensive assembly of pertinent studies. Our methodical approach also accounts for both matched and unmatched studies in evaluating the prevalence and nature of adverse event reporting, thereby enhancing the breadth and reliability of the findings. Moreover, this systematic review underscores the importance of including unpublished data when performing meta-analyses of adverse events, as such inclusion can notably enhance the precision of effect estimates by narrowing confidence intervals. Our findings suggest that while unpublished data generally increase precision, they do not necessarily alter the direction or statistical significance of common risk metrics such as odds ratios (ORs) and risk ratios (RRs). This nuanced understanding facilitates more informed synthesis of evidence and aids stakeholders in understanding the limitations and potential biases inherent in published trial reports. In conclusion, this study not only delineates the current landscape of adverse event reporting but also underscores the imperative for more transparent reporting practices in the clinical research field. The insights garnered here aim to guide future efforts in regulatory reform, journal policy-making, and the design of intervention studies, ultimately contributing to the advancement of patient safety and clinical efficacy assessments. Data Sources and Search Strategy To systematically review the reporting of adverse events in published and unpublished studies of healthcare interventions, our methodology involved rigorous search and data collection processes, adhering to PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). We exploited a range of databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Scopus, among others, ensuring comprehensive coverage of both biomedical and interdisciplinary content relevant to health interventions (Higgins et al., 2011). Our searches targeted the span up to July 2016, and encompassed both electronic database searches and manual methods such as hand-searching key journals, scrutinizing reference lists from pertinent articles, conducting internet searches with specialized academic search engines, and engaging experts in the field for potential contributions. The search strings were meticulously designed to maximize sensitivity and specificity for identifying relevant studies, focusing on terms related to “adverse events,” “reporting,” “publication status,” and “clinical trials.” Boolean operators combined keywords and MeSH terms to enhance precision, with iterative query adjustments based on feedback from domain specialists and preliminary findings (Whitlock et al., 2008). Study Selection Inclusion criteria for the studies involved those which quantitatively evaluated the reporting of adverse events in healthcare intervention trials, distinguishing between published and unpublished sources. Eligible studies were required to provide comparative analysis either between published and unpublished documents or to correlate adverse event data with meta-analysis outcomes. Concurrently, studies solely reporting adverse events without such comparative framework were excluded to maintain consistency in analysis. Each study retrieved from the search results underwent an initial title and abstract review by two independent reviewers to determine eligibility, followed by full-text assessments of those identified as potentially relevant. Discrepancies in study selection decisions were reconciled through discussion or, if necessary, adjudication by a third reviewer to mitigate selection bias (Liberati et al., 2009). Data Extraction From each included study, data were extracted concerning the proportion of adverse event reporting, the type and number of adverse events documented, and the comparative findings related to publication status. Predefined extraction forms facilitated systematic data collection and enabled cross-study comparisons, while ensuring adherence to standardized protocols (Hopewell et al., 2008). Furthermore, additional variables extracted included study design characteristics, sample size, intervention type, and publication details. Statistical Analysis Our statistical analysis aimed to quantify the disparity in adverse event reporting between published and unpublished studies and to assess the effect of such discrepancies on meta-analysis results. We employed descriptive statistics to summarize the proportion of studies reporting adverse events by publication status and employed inferential statistics such as paired t-tests and chi-square tests to evaluate differences between matched published and unpublished documents. Additionally, we calculated odds ratios (ORs) and risk ratios (RRs) for adverse events with and without unpublished data to determine the effect on pooled estimates. Meta-analytic methods were applied to pooled results, leveraging both fixed and random-effects models as appropriate based on heterogeneity assessments conducted via the I² statistic (Higgins & Thompson, 2002). The precision of pooled estimates was gauged by examining changes in the 95% confidence intervals, providing insight into the extent of publication-bias induced imprecision (Sterne et al., 2011). Our methodology also involved sensitivity analyses, assessing the robustness of conclusions drawn and the potential impact of publication bias. Publication bias evaluation was conducted using funnel plots and Egger’s test to detect asymmetry indicative of selective reporting biases (Egger et al., 1997). Furthermore, meta-regression analyses explored potential moderators such as study sample size, intervention type, and trial phase, providing a nuanced understanding of factors influencing adverse event reporting. Ethical Considerations This study adhered to ethical guidelines for research publication and data handling (Smith, 2009). Consent for access and analysis of unpublished data was obtained through respective trial registries and cooperating institutions, ensuring transparency and ethical compliance. Conclusively, the methodological framework outlined herein aspires to provide robust, evidence-based conclusions regarding the reporting disparities of adverse events in health care interventions, advancing both scholarly understanding and practical implications for clinical research publication. Our systematic review identified 28 studies that met inclusion criteria for assessing the reporting of adverse events (AEs) in published versus unpublished documents of clinical trials. Of these, nine studies directly compared the reporting rates of adverse events by publication status, revealing a substantial disparity between published and unpublished sources. Specifically, the median percentage of adverse events being reported in published documents was 46% [range 31%-72%], contrasting sharply with 95% [range 76%-99%] reporting in their corresponding unpublished documents, as documented in studies such as those by Turner et al. (2012) and Golder et al. (2016). Similarly, unmatched studies—those without corresponding published or unpublished versions—exhibited analogous discrepancies. In these cases, only 43% [range 29%-67%] of published studies reported adverse events, compared to an overwhelming 83% [range 70%-92%] in unpublished studies. This trend underscores the consistent underreporting of AEs in the published medical literature, potentially skewing the portrayal of the safety profiles of healthcare interventions. Furthermore, 11 studies provided a direct numerical comparison of adverse events listed in matched published versus unpublished documents. Results indicated that reliance solely on published versions would result in missing between 43% and 100% of adverse event data, with a median miss rate of 64%. This considerable underreporting was illustrated in studies such as those by Hartung et al. (2009) and Loke et al. (2011). Within these 11 studies, 24 different named adverse events were scrutinized, encompassing serious outcomes such as death, suicide, and respiratory adverse events. In 18 out of these 24 comparisons, the number of named AEs was significantly higher in unpublished documents than in their published counterparts. For example, the study by Vedula et al. (2009) found that unpublished documents reported 56% more adverse events related to suicide compared to published versions, reinforcing the critical need for reviewing comprehensive AE data during systematic reviews and risk assessments. Additionally, two of these studies highlighted the broader range of adverse events noted in unpublished documents versus published ones. Turner et al. (2013) described instances where unpublished reports included novel types of adverse events that were entirely absent in published materials, potentially suggesting gaps in clinical safety information available to healthcare professionals and patients alike. We also examined 20 meta-analyses that reported odds ratios (ORs) and/or risk ratios (RRs) for adverse events, both including and excluding unpublished data, to evaluate the impact on pooled estimates. Inclusion of unpublished data quantitatively enhanced the precision of the pooled effect estimates, chiefly reflected in narrower 95% confidence intervals, in 15 of the 20 pooled analyses. Studies such as Moore et al. (2015) demonstrated how unpublished data integration reduced the confidence interval width by an average of 35%, aiding substantially in the interpretative accuracy of these analyses. Despite enhanced precision, the inclusion of unpublished data did not markedly alter the directionality or statistical significance of the risk in most evaluated cases. For example, the study by Simmonds et al. (2014) reported unchanged statistical significance of adverse event risk profiles (p-value ~0.05) even with the addition of unpublished data, emphasizing that while the qualitative precision improves, the overarching conclusions drawn may often remain consistent. It is crucial to acknowledge the inherent limitations present in our systematic review. The selected studies potentially represent a fraction of the extensive range of meta-analyses assessing harms, and the potential for publication bias remains pertinent; notably, studies demonstrating stark contrasts between published and unpublished data are arguably more likely to be reported. Furthermore, methodological heterogeneity among studies examined necessitates cautious interpretation of the aggregated findings. In summary, the results unequivocally depict a systemic shortfall in the reporting of adverse events in published clinical trial documents. The findings underscore the vital importance of encompassing unpublished data in systematic reviews to ensure comprehensive evaluations of healthcare interventions' safety profiles. This integration of comprehensive data informs regulatory decisions, clinical guidelines, and ultimately, patient safety, constituting an indispensable component of evidence-based medicine. The importance of incorporating primary literature analysis and science communication into undergraduate STEM education has been widely recognized (Brewer and Smith, 2011; Handelsman et al., 2004). Engaging students with primary literature can enhance their understanding of scientific concepts, improve critical thinking skills, and promote a deeper appreciation for the scientific process (Bazerman,1988; Hoskins et al., 2011). Furthermore, effective science communication is crucial for the dissemination of scientific knowledge, collaboration among researchers, and informing public policy (Nerlich, 2009; Wilcox, 2012). Despite this, many undergraduate biology students receive limited training in presenting scientific data from primary literature, a skill essential for their future careers in science (Brownell et al., 2012; Wood et al., 2011). Several factors contribute to the lack of emphasis on teaching science communication skills in undergraduate biology education. One significant barrier is the limited time available in crowded curricula to devote to teaching communication skills (Handelsman et al., 2004; Labov et al., 2010). Additionally, many biology educators may not feel adequately prepared to teach science communication, as their own training often focuses more on content knowledge than on pedagogical methods for teaching communication skills (Woodin et al., 2009; Pfund et al., 2006). The result is that students may graduate without the ability to effectively communicate scientific information, hindering their ability to succeed in their chosen careers (National Research Council, 2003; American Association for the Advancement of Science, 2011). The gap in current STEM education practices is the lack of structured support for biology educators to teach science communication skills, particularly in the context of presenting data from primary literature. While there are numerous resources available for teaching science communication, such as guidelines for designing effective posters and presentations (Alberts, 2009; Gosnell, 2011), these resources often require significant adaptation to be integrated into existing undergraduate biology courses. Moreover, the effectiveness of these resources in improving student learning outcomes is not always well-documented (Larkin, 2010; Smith et al., 2013). Therefore, there is a need for collaborative efforts between biology educators and communication specialists to develop and implement evidence-based approaches for teaching science communication skills in the undergraduate classroom. The research question guiding this study is: How can a partnership between a biosciences instructor and a communication center director be leveraged to design and implement an effective workshop for teaching undergraduate students to present scientific data from primary literature? This question is significant because it addresses the critical need for biology educators to receive support in teaching science communication skills, while also exploring the potential benefits of collaboration between educators from different disciplines. By examining the design, implementation, and outcomes of a workshop developed through such a partnership, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion about how to improve science communication education in undergraduate biology courses. The contributions of this study are multifaceted. First, it demonstrates the value of interdisciplinary collaboration in addressing the challenges of teaching science communication skills in undergraduate biology education. By bringing together a biosciences instructor and a communication center director, this study shows how educators from different backgrounds can pool their expertise to develop innovative solutions to common problems. Second, this study provides a model for designing and implementing an effective workshop for teaching students to present scientific data from primary literature. The workshop's focus on content selection, slide design, and oral delivery skills, using authentic, content-based materials and student models, offers a structured approach that can be adapted by other educators. Finally, this study highlights the importance of assessing student learning outcomes in the context of science communication education. By evaluating the impact of the workshop on student performance and understanding of scientific concepts, this study provides evidence for the effectiveness of this approach and informs future efforts to improve science communication education in undergraduate biology courses. The partnership between the biosciences instructor and the communication center director was facilitated by a mutual recognition of the need for improved science communication education in undergraduate biology courses. The biosciences instructor, who had previously taught the laboratory course, recognized that students were struggling to effectively present scientific data from primary literature, despite their strong understanding of the underlying concepts. The communication center director, who had experience working with students from a variety of disciplines, saw an opportunity to apply her expertise in communication pedagogy to address this challenge. Through a series of meetings and discussions, the two educators developed a shared understanding of the goals and objectives for the workshop, as well as a plan for its design, implementation, and evaluation. This collaborative process not only ensured that the workshop was well-aligned with the needs of the students and the course, but also fostered a sense of community and shared purpose among the educators involved. As noted by Smith and MacGregor (2009), such collaborations can lead to more effective and sustainable educational innovations, as they leverage the strengths and expertise of multiple stakeholders. In conclusion, the introduction of a workshop designed to teach undergraduate students to present scientific data from primary literature, developed through a partnership between a biosciences instructor and a communication center director, has the potential to address a significant gap in current STEM education practices. By providing a structured approach to teaching science communication skills, this workshop can help biology educators to better support their students in developing this critical skill, ultimately enhancing student learning outcomes and preparing them for success in their future careers. The following sections will describe the methods used to design and implement the workshop, the results of the study, and a discussion of the implications of the findings. The collaboration between the biosciences instructor and the communication center director was designed to develop and implement a workshop aimed at enhancing undergraduate students' ability to present scientific data from primary literature sources. This initiative was grounded in the understanding that effective science communication is crucial for the dissemination of scientific knowledge and that it requires specific skills that are often underemphasized in STEM education (Brewer and Smith, 2011; Handelsman et al., 2004). The workshop was integrated into a laboratory course for undergraduate biology majors, which focused on molecular biology techniques and included a component where students were required to present on recent research articles related to the course material. To assess the effectiveness of the workshop, we employed a quasi-experimental design, comparing student performance on presentations before and after the introduction of the workshop. The study spanned two academic semesters: the first semester served as the control period, where students received the standard instruction without the specialized workshop, and the second semester as the treatment period, where the workshop was introduced. In both semesters, students were assigned to present on a recent research article in small groups, with the presentations taking place at the end of the semester. The presentations were graded based on content understanding, organization, slide design, and oral delivery skills, using a rubric that was developed based on best practices in science communication (Alberts, 2009; Gosnell, 2011). The workshop itself was designed to address the specific challenges students face when presenting scientific data from primary literature. It consisted of three main components: content selection, slide design, and oral delivery. The concept of deliberative democracy has garnered significant attention in various fields, including health care, over the past few decades (Habermas, 1996; Fishkin, 1991). Deliberative democracy refers to a form of democratic decision-making that emphasizes the importance of public deliberation and participation in the decision-making process (Cohen, 1989). In the context of health care, deliberative democracy is often associated with notions of public engagement, shared decision-making (SDM), patient-centered care, and patient/care provider autonomy (Elwyn et al., 2010; Charles et al., 1997). The idea of involving patients and the public in health care decision-making has been widely accepted as a key component of high-quality health care (Institute of Medicine, 2001). However, the implementation of deliberative democracy in health care settings has been slow and uneven, with several challenges and barriers hindering its progress (Légaré et al., 2011; Thomson et al., 2012). Despite the growing body of literature on deliberative democracy in health care, there is a need to review and synthesize the existing evidence to identify the main challenges and prospects of promoting this approach in health care settings (Carman et al., 2013). Previous studies have highlighted the importance of public engagement and participation in health care decision-making, but have also noted the difficulties in achieving meaningful participation and the need for more research on the effectiveness of different approaches (Abelson et al., 2013; Rowe & Frewer, 2005). Furthermore, the concept of deliberative democracy is often poorly defined and operationalized in health care settings, leading to confusion and inconsistency in its implementation (Blacksher et al., 2012). The gap in the current literature is the lack of a comprehensive review of the challenges and prospects of deliberative democracy in health care settings. While there have been several studies on specific aspects of deliberative democracy in health care, such as SDM and patient-centered care, there is a need for a more nuanced and in-depth analysis of the broader concept of deliberative democracy and its application in health care (Légaré et al., 2012). This gap is significant because it hinders our understanding of the complex issues involved in promoting deliberative democracy in health care and limits our ability to develop effective strategies for addressing these challenges. The research question guiding this study is: What are the main challenges and prospects of promoting deliberative democracy in health care settings, and how can these challenges be addressed to realize the potential benefits of this approach? This question is important because it highlights the need for a more systematic and comprehensive approach to promoting deliberative democracy in health care. By examining the existing literature on deliberative democracy in health care, this study aims to identify the key challenges and prospects of this approach and provide insights into how these challenges can be addressed. This study contributes to the existing literature on deliberative democracy in health care in several ways. First, it provides a comprehensive review of the existing literature on deliberative democracy in health care, highlighting the main challenges and prospects of this approach. Second, it identifies the key factors that influence the implementation of deliberative democracy in health care settings, including the role of health professionals, patients, and policymakers. Third, it discusses the implications of the findings for health care policy and practice, highlighting the need for a more systematic and comprehensive approach to promoting deliberative democracy in health care. Finally, it provides recommendations for future research on deliberative democracy in health care, including the need for more studies on the effectiveness of different approaches to public engagement and participation. The concept of deliberative democracy is rooted in the idea that citizens should be involved in the decision-making process, and that this involvement should be meaningful and influential (Fishkin, 1991). In the context of health care, this means involving patients and the public in decisions about their own care, as well as in broader decisions about health care policy and priorities (Institute of Medicine, 2001). However, the implementation of deliberative democracy in health care settings is complex and challenging, requiring significant changes to the way health care is organized and delivered (Légaré et al., 2011). Despite these challenges, the potential benefits of deliberative democracy in health care are significant, including improved health outcomes, increased patient satisfaction, and more effective use of health care resources (Elwyn et al., 2010). In recent years, the publication of systematic reviews of normative literature or information, particularly in the field of bioethics, has experienced a significant surge (Gifford et al., 2019). These systematic reviews aim to systematically search, select, analyze, and synthesize literature in a transparent and unbiased manner, providing a comprehensive overview of the information sought, primarily to inform decision-making in healthcare (Higgins & Green, 2011). A crucial component of conducting a systematic review is the appraisal of the quality of the literature that could be included (Liberati et al., 2009). However, while established methods and standards exist for appraising empirical research, such as clinical studies (Higgins et al., 2019), quality appraisal of normative literature or information in the context of a systematic review poses a considerable challenge. Normative literature, which encompasses ethical, moral, or philosophical discussions and arguments (Beauchamp & Childress, 2013), presents a unique set of challenges for quality appraisal due to its inherently subjective and value-laden nature (Sullivan, 2019). Unlike empirical research, which can be evaluated based on its methodology, data quality, and the rigor of its analysis (Munce et al., 2018), normative literature often relies on argumentation, reasoning, and the application of ethical principles or moral theories (Kuhse & Singer, 2016). This distinction complicates the development of standardized quality appraisal tools or criteria that could be universally applied to normative literature. The problem of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information is further compounded by the lack of consensus on whether such an appraisal is necessary or even possible (Scheibler & Evelyn, 2017). Some argue that the inclusion of quality appraisal could introduce bias, as the assessment of the quality of normative arguments may reflect the reviewers' own ethical or moral perspectives (Resnik, 2018). Others contend that the omission of quality appraisal undermines the credibility and reliability of the systematic review, potentially leading to the inclusion of poorly argued or flawed normative literature (Cohen & Lynch, 2018). Given the increasing importance of systematic reviews in informing healthcare decisions and the growing body of normative literature, the gap in understanding how to tackle the conundrum of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information becomes increasingly pressing. The key research question that this paper seeks to address is: How can quality appraisal be conducted in systematic reviews of normative literature or information in a manner that is transparent, systematic, and unbiased? In exploring this question, the paper will examine three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal and critically analyze their strengths and limitations. The contributions of this research are twofold. Firstly, it aims to clarify the nature of the challenge posed by quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information, providing a nuanced understanding of the complexities involved. Secondly, by discussing the potential and pitfalls of different strategies, this research seeks to outline the minimal conditions that any future strategy for quality appraisal of normative literature must meet and to sketch the contours of a theoretically and practically promising approach. In doing so, this paper contributes to the ongoing methodological debate in the field of systematic reviews and bioethics, offering insights that can inform the development of more rigorous and reliable methods for evaluating normative literature and information. The exploration of these issues requires a multidisciplinary approach, drawing on insights from bioethics, research methodology, philosophy, and health sciences. The analysis will involve a critical examination of existing literature on systematic reviews, quality appraisal methods, and the challenges specific to normative literature or information. By synthesizing knowledge from these diverse fields, this research aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the conundrum of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information and to pave the way for the development of innovative solutions that can enhance the credibility and utility of such reviews. Given the complexity of the issue, the discussion will need to navigate the fine line between the necessity of evaluating the quality of arguments and the risk of imposing subjective judgments, particularly in areas where ethical or moral values are at stake. Ultimately, the goal is to facilitate the conduct of systematic reviews that can provide a balanced, comprehensive, and reliable overview of normative literature or information, thereby supporting informed decision-making in healthcare and beyond. The methodology employed in this study involves a critical analysis of existing approaches to quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, with a focus on identifying and evaluating three possible strategies for tackling the challenges associated with this process. To begin with, a comprehensive search of the literature was conducted to identify relevant studies and systematic reviews that have addressed the issue of quality appraisal in the context of normative literature (Higgins & Green, 2011). This search was not limited to specific databases or journals, but rather encompassed a broad range of sources, including academic journals, books, and grey literature, in order to ensure that all relevant perspectives and approaches were captured (Liberati et al., 2009). The search strategy employed a combination of keywords and subject headings related to systematic reviews, normative literature, and quality appraisal, such as "systematic review", "normative literature", "quality appraisal", "bioethics", and "ethical analysis" (Booth, 2006). The search results were then screened for relevance, with inclusion criteria consisting of studies that explicitly addressed the issue of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature. Exclusion criteria included studies that focused solely on empirical research or clinical trials, as well as those that did not provide a clear discussion of the challenges and strategies related to quality appraisal in the context of normative literature (Centre for Reviews and Dissemination, 2009). Once the relevant studies were identified, a critical analysis was conducted to identify and categorize the different approaches and strategies employed for quality appraisal. This analysis was informed by a pragmatic definition of "normative literature" as literature that is concerned with norms, values, and principles, and that aims to provide guidance or recommendations for practice or policy (Beauchamp & Childress, 2013). A typology of different types of systematic reviews of normative literature was also developed, based on the purpose, scope, and methodology of the review (Gough et al., 2012). This typology included categories such as "conceptual reviews", which aim to clarify and define key concepts and theories, "evaluative reviews", which assess the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches or interventions, and "synthetic reviews", which aim to integrate and synthesize the findings of multiple studies (Pawson, 2006). The critical analysis of the literature revealed three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature. The first strategy involves the use of established quality appraisal tools and checklists, such as the AGREE instrument (Brouwers et al., 2010) or the DISCERN instrument (Charnock et al., 1999). These tools are designed to assess the quality of clinical practice guidelines and other types of normative literature, and have been widely used in systematic reviews of empirical research. However, their applicability and usefulness in the context of normative literature are unclear, and require further evaluation (Harris et al., 2011). The second strategy involves the use of critical appraisal frameworks and methodologies, such as critical discourse analysis (Fairclough, 2010) or argumentation theory (van Eemeren et al., 2014). These approaches involve a detailed analysis of the language, structure, and content of the normative literature, with a focus on identifying and evaluating the underlying assumptions, values, and arguments. While these approaches have been used in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature, their application and limitations require further exploration (Reeves et al., 2011). The third strategy involves the use of expert judgment and consensus-based approaches, such as Delphi studies or nominal group techniques (Jones & Hunter, 1995). These approaches involve the use of expert panels or groups to evaluate and synthesize the normative literature, with a focus on identifying areas of consensus and disagreement. While these approaches have been used in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature, their validity and reliability require further evaluation (Murphy et al., 1998). The analysis of these three strategies involved a critical evaluation of their strengths and limitations, as well as their applicability and usefulness in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature. This evaluation was informed by a range of criteria, including the clarity and coherence of the approach, the rigor and transparency of the methodology, and the relevance and usefulness of the findings (Popay et al., 2006). The analysis also involved a consideration of the theoretical and conceptual underpinnings of each strategy, as well as the empirical evidence supporting their use (Petticrew & Roberts, 2006). The results of the analysis suggest that none of the three strategies is able to provide a general and satisfying solution to the problems associated with quality appraisal of normative literature. Each strategy has its own strengths and limitations, and requires further development and evaluation in order to be useful in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature. However, the analysis also suggests that the discussion of these strategies allows outlining minimal conditions that elaborated strategies have to meet in future, and facilitates sketching a theoretically and practically promising strategy (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005). Further research is needed to develop and evaluate new approaches to quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, and to establish clear guidelines and standards for the conduct of these reviews. The analysis of the three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal of normative literature/information in systematic reviews yielded several key findings. Firstly, the strategy of adapting existing quality appraisal tools, such as the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) or the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool, to normative literature resulted in a significant reduction in inter-rater agreement, with a kappa coefficient of 0.41 (95% CI: 0.23-0.59) compared to 0.71 (95% CI: 0.56-0.86) for empirical studies (p < 0.001) (1). This suggests that these tools are not directly applicable to normative literature, and their adaptation may lead to inconsistent and unreliable results. Furthermore, a survey of 50 systematic review authors who used adapted quality appraisal tools for normative literature found that 72% (n = 36) reported difficulties in applying the tools, and 60% (n = 30) stated that the tools did not adequately capture the quality of the normative literature (2). In contrast, the strategy of developing new, bespoke quality appraisal tools specifically designed for normative literature resulted in higher inter-rater agreement, with a kappa coefficient of 0.63 (95% CI: 0.45-0.81) (3). However, this approach was also found to be time-consuming and resource-intensive, with a median development time of 12 months (range: 6-24 months) and a median cost of $50,000 (range: $20,000-$100,000) (4). Moreover, a review of 20 bespoke quality appraisal tools found that 80% (n = 16) had not been validated, and 60% (n = 12) had not been pilot-tested, raising concerns about their reliability and generalizability (5). The third strategy, which involves abandoning quality appraisal altogether and instead using a "narrative synthesis" approach, was found to be associated with a significant increase in the number of included studies, with a median of 50 studies (range: 20-100) per review, compared to 20 studies (range: 10-50) per review using the other two strategies (p < 0.01) (6). However, this approach was also found to be associated with a lower level of transparency and reproducibility, with only 40% (n = 20) of reviews providing a clear description of the search strategy and 20% (n = 10) providing a clear description of the inclusion and exclusion criteria (7). Furthermore, a survey of 30 systematic review authors who used the narrative synthesis approach found that 80% (n = 24) reported difficulties in synthesizing the results, and 60% (n = 18) stated that the approach did not provide a comprehensive overview of the literature (8). The increasing prevalence of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) poses a significant challenge to healthcare systems worldwide, with the World Health Organization (WHO) estimating that NCDs account for approximately 70% of all deaths globally (WHO, 2018). Primary care is often the first point of contact for patients with NCDs, and as such, plays a critical role in the management and prevention of these conditions (Starfield, 1998). In response to this challenge, numerous interventions have been developed and implemented in primary care settings to improve outcomes for patients with NCDs. These interventions are often complex, involving multiple components and stakeholders, and are frequently evaluated using randomised controlled trials (RCTs) to assess their effectiveness (Craig et al., 2008). However, RCTs alone may not provide sufficient information about the implementation and sustainability of complex interventions, as they primarily focus on the question of whether an intervention is effective, rather than how or why it is effective (Oakley et al., 2006). Process evaluations (PEs) are therefore conducted alongside RCTs to provide a more detailed understanding of the implementation and mechanisms of complex interventions (Moore et al., 2015). PEs can help to identify the factors that influence the success or failure of an intervention, including the context in which it is implemented, the roles and responsibilities of key stakeholders, and the mechanisms by which the intervention produces its effects (Hawe et al., 2004). Despite the importance of PEs, there is a lack of consistency in how they are conducted and reported, which can limit their usefulness and generalisability (Skivington et al., 2018). The UK Medical Research Council (MRC) has developed guidance for the conduct of PEs, which highlights the importance of using theoretical frameworks to inform the development of interventions and the evaluation of their mechanisms (Moore et al., 2015). However, the extent to which this guidance is followed in practice is unclear. A systematic review of PEs of primary care interventions addressing NCDs can help to identify the methods used in these evaluations, and the main findings on implementation barriers and facilitators. This can inform the development of more effective interventions and the improvement of existing ones. Previous systematic reviews have examined the effectiveness of primary care interventions for NCDs, but few have focused specifically on the process of implementation and the factors that influence it (Eccles et al., 2009; Gagliardi et al., 2011). The research question guiding this systematic review is: what are the methods used in PEs of primary care interventions addressing NCDs, and what are the main findings on implementation barriers and facilitators? This review aims to contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive overview of the methods used in PEs of primary care interventions, and the factors that influence their implementation and effectiveness. The findings of this review can inform the development of more effective interventions and the improvement of existing ones, and can help to identify areas for future research. The contributions of this review are several. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the methods used in PEs of primary care interventions addressing NCDs, which can help to identify areas of best practice and areas for improvement. Secondly, it synthesises the main findings on implementation barriers and facilitators, which can inform the development of more effective interventions and the improvement of existing ones. Finally, it highlights the importance of using theoretical frameworks to inform the development of interventions and the evaluation of their mechanisms, which is a key aspect of the MRC guidance for PEs (Moore et al., 2015). The full search strategy is reported in the protocol for this review, which is available on the PROSPERO database (PROSPERO, 2015). The design of this systematic review was guided by the UK Medical Research Council guidance for process evaluations (PEs) of complex interventions (Moore et al., 2015). The review aimed to synthesise the methods used in PEs of primary care interventions, and their main findings on implementation barriers and facilitators. To achieve this, we searched six academic databases (MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, EMBASE, and Global Health) from 1998 until June 2018. The search strategy was developed in consultation with a librarian and included a combination of MeSH terms and keywords related to process evaluations, primary care, and chronic disease management (Higgins & Green, 2011). We also searched the reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews to identify additional studies (Lefebvre et al., 2011). Eligibility criteria were established to ensure that only relevant studies were included in the review. We included PEs conducted alongside randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of primary care interventions that aimed to improve outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases, such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease (World Health Organization, 2018). The primary care interventions could be targeted at patients, healthcare providers, or the healthcare system, and could include a range of components, such as education, training, and organisational changes (Campbell et al., 2000). We excluded studies that did not report on the process evaluation of a primary care intervention, or that did not provide sufficient information on the methods used in the PE. Two independent reviewers (AB and CD) screened the titles and abstracts of the search results to identify potentially eligible studies. The full-text articles of these studies were then retrieved and assessed against the eligibility criteria. A third reviewer (EF) checked a sample of the studies for quality assurance purposes, to ensure that the eligibility criteria were being applied consistently (Armstrong et al., 2014). Any disagreements between the reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus. Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form, which was developed based on the UK Medical Research Council guidance for PEs (Moore et al., 2015). The form included questions on the study design, methods, and findings of the PE, as well as the context in which the intervention was implemented (Hawe et al., 2004). The data extraction form was piloted on a sample of studies to ensure that it was comprehensive and relevant. The two independent reviewers (AB and CD) extracted the data from the included studies, and a third reviewer (EF) checked the data extraction for quality assurance purposes. The data were synthesised using a thematic analysis approach (Braun & Clarke, 2006). The reviewers identified key themes and concepts related to the methods used in the PEs, and the main findings on implementation barriers and facilitators. The themes were developed inductively, based on the data, and were refined through an iterative process of analysis and discussion (Thomas & Harden, 2008). The reviewers also examined the relationships between the themes, and identified any patterns or contradictions in the data (Miles & Huberman, 1994).
