Abstract. We present new operational semantics for serverless computing that model the event-driven relationships between serverless functions, as well as their interaction with platforms services such as databases and object stores. These semantics precisely encapsulate how control transfers between functions, both directly and through reads and writes to platform services. We use these semantics to define the notion of the service call graph for serverless applications that captures program flows through functions and services. Finally, we construct service call graphs for eight serverless JavaScript applications, using a prototype of our call graph construction algorithm, and we evaluate their accuracy. Keywords: serverless computing, formal semantics, call graph Serverless computing is a programming model where code executes on-demand in a shared network of pre-configured computing resources [26]. By pooling resources and managing the execution platform, serverless platform providers are able to offer highly elastic scaling by balancing workloads across multiple physical servers [32]. This distribution across physical servers is made possible through the use of containers that bundle serverless code with a virtual execution environment. Serverless providers can dynamically scale the number of instances of a serverless application by creating multiple containers. To facilitate this approach, serverless application code is organized into stateless serverless functions that execute in response to events. As a consequence, serverless computing heavily favors microservice architectures; serverless functions pass messages and subscribe to notifications from other platform services to complete tasks cooperatively [34]. The advantages of this platform have led to the rapid adoption of commercial serverless platforms by developers in industry [12]. However, the serverless model also presents new challenges. In particular, previous research has cited a lack of tooling for development and debugging of serverless applications [36]. Without access to these tools, developers may struggle to trace executions, measure performance, and verify the security of programs they write. While significant progress has been made toward answering these questions for traditional programs using program analysis, this analysis has not yet been significantly extended to work in the serverless domain. Recent surveys of the state of serverless computing have suggested that static analysis can help address these challenges [22]. Existing abstractions for serverless computing emphasize unique features of the environment where serverless functions are executed [20,15]. However, these abstractions do not consider effects of transmitting data to other services and functions. Data transmitted in this fashion is commonly replicated to new executions of serverless functions that spawn in response to a change in state on their associated service. Without operational semantics that capture this behavior, program analysis cannot construct a precise call graph and cannot soundly reason about dataflow between parts of a serverless application. The lack of semantics to describe these event triggers also serves as a barrier to more advanced reasoning about data privacy, application correctness, and resource usage. To address this gap, we propose new operational semantics for event-driven serverless computation. These semantics describe how writes and reads to platform services create inter-function control transfer in serverless applications. Our semantics formalize the most common platform services including object stores, databases, notifications, queues and stateless services. We then define a new approach to call graph construction for serverless applications that uses these semantics to augment call graphs with information about relationships between serverless functions and platform services. We introduce the notion of the service call graph, which extends the classical call graph to include new nodes. These new nodes represent the platform services written to or read by application code to produce control flow that spans multiple disconnected parts of a program. By tracing control flow through reads and writes to services, individual serverless functions become a single unified application with additional context describing what data may flow to later functions in a call chain. We make the following contributions: – We formulate new operational semantics for the execution of serverless programs. These semantics precisely model interactions with platform services, including event triggers that causes additional functions to execute. – We extend the traditional notion of a call graph with new types of nodes and edges that represent event-driven behavior on serverless platforms. These new nodes and edges capture the inter-function control and state transfer represented in our operational semantics. – We design and implement an algorithm for constructing call graphs of serverless programs. We evaluate the accuracy of our approach by presenting metrics on the call graphs produced by a prototype implementation of our algorithm against serverless programs collected from GitHub. We focus on applications written in Javascript for the AWS Lambda platform [9]; we choose Javascript as it is the most common language for AWS Lambda programs. Related Work. The semantics we define for the lifecycle of a single serverless function are closely related to those used in a recent formalization of serverless computing [20]. That work focused on modeling low-level behavior of serverless systems. Such models are useful for capturing behavior such as program non-determinism that can arise from reading state from previous executions of serverless functions. Our semantics start from this model to describe initiating requests, language-agnostic computation steps, and generated responses. However, the semantics defined in [20] do not capture inter-function communication and program flows that span multiple serverless functions. Specifically, these semantics limit data persistence to a locking transactional key-value store. Our semantics introduce several new state domains that model the behavior of these services. More importantly, the previous semantics also lack a conceptualization of serverless events, which initiate execution of a serverless function when state is manipulated on a data storage service. We model these interactions by extending the semantics with a new collection of event semantics that capture state transfer between serverless components. Dynamic analysis has also been previously explored as a tool for reasoning about the behavior of serverless applications. Specifically, this line of research has developed systems to visualize program structure [24,25], track the flow of sensitive information [1], and measure resource costs [35]. These systems instrument new tools that modify or extend serverless platforms with runtime logging and label checking that enable them to make partial judgments about security given their partial view of current system state. By contrast, we are interested in formalizing serverless behavior so that such analyses may be performed statically without requiring application deployment or execution. The service call graph shares some features of message flow graphs for distributed event-based systems that communicate through publish-subscribe middleware [16]. The publish-subscribe model is related to the serverless notification systems, however, retrieval of data from databases and object stores cannot be succinctly captured in publish-subscribe semantics. Our work considers not only notification-based communication, but also messages that pass through other channels available to serverless applications. In preliminary work [30], we introduced the notion of a service call graph for serverless applications. In this paper, we formalize the call graph definition in terms of our new operational semantics. Further, we design and implement a call graph construction algorithm and present experimental results on eight real-world serverless applications. Outline. The remainder of this paper is organized into the following sections. Section 2 defines the serverless computing model, then Section 3 maps this model onto a set of operational semantics that formalize serverless computation. Section 4 presents our a serverless call graph construction. We evaluate the accuracy of call graph construction in Section 5, and present conclude in Section 6. Serverless computing is a new programming model that allows developers to execute modules of code in a distributed setting without specifying the physical servers where this code will run. The most common implementation of serverless computing is the Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) model. In this model, an application is decomposed into a collection of serverless functions. Most platforms provision resources for serverless functions by deploying virtual containers to execute function code [14]. These containers provide a minimal operating system, including a language interpreter specified by the function runtime. Since these containers can be quickly created and destroyed on-demand, serverless platforms are able to reuse the same physical hardware to service multiple functions, even from different users. Additionally, many serverless platforms are optimized to allow the container of a frequently-called function to remain provisioned. A warm start occurs when a function is invoked from a reused container. Warm starts eliminate the latency associated with waiting for new containers to initialize during a cold start, but create a risk of stale memory allocations from previous invocations of the function affecting program behavior. Serverless functions interact with one another either via direct invocation or via services that expose interfaces for data storage and messaging. Below, we present the set of common services provided by serverless platforms, followed by a description of the methods by which larger serverless applications can be constructed from functions and services. 2.1 Services and functions interact in two main ways: 1) functions write data to services through the use of platform-provided libraries, and 2) functions receive data from services, either as part of an explicit read using those same libraries, or as inputs assigned to the parameters of a function when it is initially invoked. We define five broad categories of services. Object stores. Object stores persist unstructured data in buckets. Each item uploaded to a bucket is identified by a unique key. This key can be used to retrieve the item for reading. Object stores are commonly used as a replacement for a filesystem in serverless applications. Examples of object store services include Amazon Simple Storage Service [6], Google Cloud Storage [19], and Azure Blob Storage [28]. Databases. Databases store semi-structured data in one or more tables. Unlike object stores, databases provide advanced APIs for retrieving data based on queries. This category includes both relational databases such as Amazon Aurora [2] and Azure Cosmos DB [29], as well as column-store NoSQL databases such as DynamoDB [3]. Notifications. Notification services expose a collection of named topics, which may be organized into a hierarchy for granular filtering. When a serverless function publishes data under a topic, all functions that subscribe to that topic or a parent topic are invoked and receive a copy of the data. Commercially available notification services include Amazon Simple Notification Service [7], Google Cloud Pub/Sub [18], and Firebase Cloud Messaging [17]. Queues. Queues allow for intermediate storage of data that requires further processing. Serverless functions can be configured to execute when a queue receives new items. Queues either invoke serverless functions immediately when Fig. 1. In the call graph at left, we see that GET and POST API gateway events in the top left of the call graph trigger the app-dev-uploader serverless function. This function then writes to the ORIGINALS S3 bucket, which in turn triggers the app-dev-rotate serverless function. This function reads from its triggering bucket then writes to a ROTATED bucket. The process repeats for two more image processing functions before the final image is uploaded to THUMBS. data is added to the queue, or batch several queued items in an array to be processed by a single invocation of a serverless function. Example serverless queues include the Amazon Simple Queue Service [8] and Amazon Kinesis Streams [4]. Stateless Services. Stateless services perform data processing on-demand for serverless applications and store the results in another service. Often, stateless services implement common but computationally expensive tasks, such as image identification or speech parsing through services such as Amazon Rekognition [5]. 2.2 There are three main ways that functions are composed into larger applications in serverless platforms. Direct Invocation. Direct invocation is the simplest method of invoking successor serverless functions. A serverless function may directly invoke another serverless function by passing the identifier of the successor function into a library call that interacts with the serverless platform. Composition Frameworks. Most serverless platforms also implement frameworks for directly composing services and functions. These frameworks, such as Amazon StepFunctions [10] and OpenWhisk Composer [11], provide a declarative syntax for composing serverless functions and supported services. In addition to declaring the relationship between functions

GILE: A Generalized Input-Label Embedding for Text Classification Nikolaos Pappas James Henderson Idiap Research Institute, Martigny 1920, Switzerland {nikolaos.pappas,james.henderson@idiap.ch} Neural text classification models typically treat output labels as categorical variables which lack description and semantics. This forces their parametrization to be dependent on the label set size, and, hence, they are unable to scale to large label sets and generalize to unseen ones. Existing joint input-label text models overcome these issues by exploiting label descriptions, but they are unable to capture complex label relationships, have rigid parametrization, and their gains on unseen labels happen often at the expense of weak performance on the labels seen during training. In this paper, we propose a new input-label model which generalizes over previous such models, addresses their limitations, and does not compromise performance on seen labels. The model consists of a joint non-linear inputlabel embedding with controllable capacity and a joint-space-dependent classification unit which is trained with cross-entropy loss to optimize classification performance. We evaluate models on full-resource and low- or zero-resource text classification of multilingual news and biomedical text with a large label set. Our model outperforms monolingual and multilingual models which do not leverage label semantics and previous joint input-label space models in both scenarios. Text classification is a fundamental NLP task with numerous real-world applications such as topic recognition (Tang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016), sentiment analysis (Pang and Lee, 2005; Yang et al., 2016), and question answering (Chen et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2015). Classification also appears as a sub task for sequence prediction tasks such as neural machine translation (Cho et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015), and summarization (Rush et al., 2015). Despite the numerous studies, existing models are trained on a fixed label set using k-hot vectors and, therefore, treat target labels as mere atomic symbols without any particular structure to the space of labels, ignoring potential linguistic knowledge about the words used to describe the output labels. Given that semantic representations of words have been shown to be useful for representing the input, it is reasonable to expect that they are going to be useful for representing the labels as well. Previous work has leveraged knowledge from the label texts through a joint input-label space, initially for image classification (Weston et al., 2011; Mensink et al., 2012; Frome et al., 2013; Socher et al., 2013). Such models generalize to labels both seen and unseen during training, and scale well on very large label sets. However, as we explain in Section 2, existing input-label models for text (Yazdani and Henderson, 2015; Nam et al., 2016) have the following limitations: (i) their embedding does not capture complex label relationships due to its bilinear form, (ii) their output layer parametrization is rigid because it depends on the dimensionality of the encoded text and labels, and, (iii) they are outperformed on seen labels by classification baselines trained with cross-entropy loss (Frome et al., 2013; Socher et al., 2013). In this paper, we propose a new joint input-label model which generalizes over previous such models, addresses their limitations, and does not compromise performance on seen labels (see Figure 1). The proposed model is comprised of a joint non-linear input-label embedding with controllable capacity and a joint-space-dependent classification unit which is trained with cross-entropy loss to optimize classification performance.1 The need for capturing complex label relationships is addressed by two non-linear transformations which have the same target joint space dimension1 ality. The parametrization of the output layer is not constrained by the dimensionality of the input or label encoding, but is instead flexible with a capacity which can be easily controlled by choosing the dimensionality of the joint space. Training is performed with cross-entropy loss, which is a suitable surrogate loss for classification problems, as opposed to a ranking loss such as WARP loss (Weston et al., 2010) which is more suitable for ranking problems. Evaluation is performed on full-resource and low- or zero-resource scenarios of two text classification tasks, namely on biomedical semantic indexing (Nam et al., 2016) and on multilingual news classification (Pappas and Popescu-Belis, 2017) against several competitive baselines. In both scenarios, we provide a comprehensive ablation analysis which highlights the importance of each model component and the difference with previous embedding formulations when using the same type of architecture and loss function. Our main contributions are the following: (i) We identify key theoretical and practical limitations of existing joint input-label models. (ii) We propose a novel joint input-label embedding with flexible parametrization which generalizes over the previous such models and addresses their limitations. (iii) We provide empirical evidence of the superiority of our model over monolingual and multilingual models which ignore label semantics, and over previous joint input-label models on both seen and unseen labels. Introduction Biologic drugs have revolutionized the treatment landscape for a variety of chronic inflammatory diseases, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis (Dörner & Kay, 2015). Among these biologic agents, infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody that targets tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), has emerged as a critical therapeutic option due to its efficacy in reducing inflammation and modifying disease progression (Tracey et al., 2008). However, the high cost of biologic therapies like infliximab poses significant challenges to healthcare systems and restricts patient access (Blackstone & Fuhr, 2007). In response to these issues, biosimilar versions of biologic drugs have been developed and introduced to the market to provide more cost-effective alternatives (Mulcahy et al., 2018). Biosimilars are designed to be highly similar to their corresponding reference products with no clinically meaningful differences in terms of safety, purity, and potency (European Medicines Agency, 2017). However, unlike generic drugs for small molecules, biosimilars are not identical replicas of their reference biologics due to inherent variabilities in their manufacturing processes (McCamish & Woollett, 2011). As such, thorough comparative studies are essential to establish biosimilarity and to evaluate the interchangeability between reference products and their biosimilar counterparts. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires evidence from switching studies to confirm that biosimilars remain equivalent to the reference product after a patient is switched back and forth between products multiple times (FDA, 2019). The potential to switch between reference infliximab and its biosimilars holds great promise for improving the accessibility and affordability of biologic therapies. However, healthcare providers and patients express concerns about the safety, efficacy, and immunogenic potential when switching from an originator biologic to a biosimilar or vice versa (Calvo et al., 2018). Immunogenicity, which refers to the ability to provoke an immune response, is of particular concern as it can impact clinical outcomes by reducing drug efficacy or causing adverse reactions (Moots et al., 2017). Thus, understanding the implications of switching is vital for optimizing treatment strategies and ensuring patient safety. Despite these concerns, the literature on switching between reference infliximab and its biosimilars is still in its infancy, presenting an opportunity for further research. Existing studies have primarily focused on single switches from reference to biosimilar infliximab with limited data on multiple switching scenarios, which are equally plausible in real-world clinical settings (Buer & Jørgensen, 2020). Furthermore, many studies are observational in nature and lack the rigorous control necessary to account for confounding factors and causation (Cohen et al., 2018). Although a few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted, the scope of patient populations and disease conditions examined remains restricted. Given these limitations, significant gaps remain in our understanding of the long-term effects of switching, especially beyond just single transitions. Important questions also linger about the consistency of safety and efficacy outcomes across different inflammatory diseases and patient sub-populations (e.g., pediatric versus adult patients, or those with varying disease severities) (Yazici et al., 2019). These considerations call for a comprehensive evaluation of available data, as well as the identification of areas where further research is most needed. The present systematic review aims to address these gaps by investigating the evidence on the efficacy and safety of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab in inflammatory disorders. By synthesizing data from both controlled and uncontrolled studies, as well as from congress abstracts where new findings are often first reported, we seek to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge. Our objectives are to discern patterns, highlight consistencies or discrepancies in findings, and recommend directions for future research that can resolve uncertainties about multiple switches. Given the current global healthcare context, with rising demands for cost containment and improved patient access to high-quality medications, the implications of these findings are potentially substantial. Understanding the interchangeability of biosimilar and reference infliximab could aid in formulating policies that maximize the therapeutic and economic benefits of biosimilars. Our review contributes to the discourse by providing evidence-based insights that can inform clinical practice, patient decision-making, and policy development regarding the integration of biosimilars into treatment protocols. Overall, this study seeks to fill the critical gaps in biosimilar research by focusing on switching efficacy and safety, thereby contributing new knowledge that is essential for advancing the acceptance and utilization of biosimilars worldwide. This systematic review was designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of switching patients between reference and biosimilar infliximab in treating various inflammatory disorders, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis. The study sought to identify and analyze both observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that have addressed this subject. Our methodological approach adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to ensure rigor and transparency in the review process. A comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify relevant literature. The primary sources were the MEDLINE and EMBASE databases, chosen for their extensive biomedical repositories. The search included terms related to "infliximab," "biosimilar," "switching," "Crohn's disease," "ulcerative colitis," "rheumatoid arthritis," "ankylosing spondylitis," "psoriatic arthritis," and "plaque psoriasis," among others. Boolean operators were applied to combine different keywords effectively. The search was limited to articles published up until October 2023 to include the most recent data. Additionally, congress abstracts were manually searched from relevant rheumatology and gastroenterology congresses to capture any unpublished or ongoing studies that could supplement our findings. The initial search yielded 113 journal articles and 149 abstracts. After de-duplication, titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers (initials for reviewers). Studies were included if they reported data on at least one switch between reference and biosimilar infliximab in humans and assessed either efficacy or safety outcomes. Exclusion criteria encompassed non-English language articles, case reports, editorials, and studies exclusively involving pediatric populations. A total of 70 studies met the inclusion criteria for the final analysis, comprising 64 observational studies and six randomized controlled trials. Discrepancies in study selection were resolved through discussion and consensus with a third reviewer (initials for third reviewer). Key data from the included studies were extracted using a standardized data extraction form. Extracted information included study design, patient demographics, sample size, inflammatory condition, switch protocol, duration of follow-up, primary and secondary outcomes, and adverse events. Where available, data on the number of switches and comparators were also collected. The quality of included observational studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, which evaluates selection, comparability, and outcome assessment. For the included RCTs, the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool was employed, assessing domains such as selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, and reporting bias. Studies were classified as having a low, moderate, or high risk of bias based on these assessments. Given the heterogeneity in study designs, patient populations, and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was chosen to summarize the evidence rather than a quantitative meta-analysis. Exploratory data synthesis was conducted to identify common themes in efficacy and safety outcomes following infliximab switching. Descriptive statistics were utilized for patient demographics and study characteristics. Where data permitted, efficacy outcomes were analyzed in terms of disease activity indices, such as the Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) and the Disease Activity Score in 28 Joints (DAS28) for rheumatoid arthritis. Safety outcomes were documented as frequency and types of adverse events, including infusion-related reactions and immunogenicity. Publication bias was assessed qualitatively due to the limitations of conducting funnel plots with the diverse and mostly observational data. A sensitivity analysis was performed, wherein studies classified with a high risk of bias were separately analyzed to gauge their influence on the overall conclusions. Ethical approval was not required for this systematic review as it involved synthesizing existing data. Nevertheless, the ethical standards of the included studies, where reported, were considered during the quality assessment phase to ensure that the conclusions drawn are based on ethically sound research. In synthesizing the current evidence on the efficacy and safety of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab, our methodology highlights the need for high-quality, controlled studies to determine the clinical implications of multiple switches across diverse patient populations. This systematic review is expected to assist clinicians in understanding the current landscape of infliximab biosimilar use and inform future research directions in this evolving field. Among these, six studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and the remainder comprised uncontrolled observational studies. The primary outcomes assessed across these studies included clinical efficacy, safety, immunogenicity, and pharmacokinetics. In the RCTs, the sample sizes ranged from 100 to 250 participants, with an average follow-up period of 52 weeks. In a study conducted by Smolen et al. (2018), involving 210 patients with rheumatoid arthritis, the switch from reference infliximab to its biosimilar resulted in an equivalent clinical response as measured by the American College of Rheumatology 20 (ACR20) response criteria. At the end of 48 weeks, 72% of patients in the reference group and 70% in the biosimilar group achieved an ACR20 response, demonstrating non-inferiority (p=0.85). Another RCT, involving 150 patients with ankylosing spondylitis, found no significant difference in the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society 20 (ASAS20) response rates between the groups that continued with the reference product (77%) and those that switched to the biosimilar (74%) after one year of treatment (Jones et al., 2019, p=0.72). Similarly, a study by Patel et al. (2020) that included 130 patients with ulcerative colitis reported no statistically significant differences in the rates of clinical remission between the reference and biosimilar groups, with remission rates of 65% and 64%, respectively, after switching (p=0.78). Observational studies, although lacking the rigorous design of RCTs, provided a larger dataset for assessing real-world outcomes of switching. A cohort study by Garcia et al. (2020) included 300 patients with Crohn's disease who underwent a switch to a biosimilar infliximab. The study reported that 80% of patients maintained clinical remission over a 12-month period, a figure comparable to historical data for reference infliximab. The rates of adverse events were also similar, occurring in 18% of patients who switched compared to 16% in those who remained on the originator, as referenced in prior studies. In terms of safety, the incidence of adverse events was comparable across the reference and biosimilar groups. The study by Tan et al. (2021) focused on immunogenicity and found no significant increase in anti-drug antibody (ADA) formation following a switch. The incidence of ADA was reported at 12% in the reference group and 14% in the biosimilar group, with a p-value of 0.30, indicating no statistical difference in immunogenic response. Additionally, infusion-related reactions were low across both groups, at 5% and 6%, respectively, and were manageable with standard premedication protocols. Pharmacokinetic analyses confirmed bioequivalence between the biosimilar and reference infliximab following a switch, as demonstrated in a study involving 186 patients across multiple inflammatory conditions, including psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis (Lee et al., 2019). No significant deviations were noted in serum trough levels or drug clearance rates after switching, preserving the therapeutic concentrations necessary for efficacy. Furthermore, subgroup analyses were performed to assess whether disease-specific factors influenced the outcomes of switching. In patients with plaque psoriasis, the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) scores remained stable after the switch, with 75% of patients maintaining a PASI 75 response at 24 weeks (Liu et al., 2021). For those with psoriatic arthritis, 68% achieved a Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) remission at follow-up, aligning with prior performance outcomes of the reference product (Brown et al., 2020). However, the majority of these findings stem from single-switch scenarios. The advent of social media has transformed the way we communicate, interact, and disseminate information (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010). In the context of academic publishing, social media has emerged as a vital tool for promoting research, increasing visibility, and enhancing the impact of scholarly work (Eysenbach, 2011). Many journals, including Circulation, have taken to social media platforms such as Facebook and Twitter to promote their articles, engage with readers, and foster a community of scholars (Groves, 2012). However, despite the growing importance of social media in academic publishing, there is limited evidence on its effectiveness in increasing the dissemination and uptake of research (Terrell, 2016). Previous studies have explored the impact of social media on various aspects of academic publishing, including article downloads, citations, and altmetrics (Thelwall et al., 2013; Bowman, 2015). For instance, a study published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research found that social media promotion was associated with increased article views and downloads (Shuai et al., 2012). Another study published in the journal PLOS ONE found that tweets about articles were associated with increased citations (Eysenbach, 2011). However, these studies have several limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of control groups, and limited generalizability (Terrell, 2016). A prior randomized controlled trial of social media exposure at Circulation found that social media did not increase 30-day page views (Lovett, 2015). This study was one of the first to use a randomized controlled design to evaluate the impact of social media on article page views. However, the authors noted that the intensity of the social media intervention may have been insufficient, which could have contributed to the null findings (Lovett, 2015). Specifically, the study used a relatively small base of followers and did not employ paid advertising or other strategies to increase the reach and engagement of social media posts (Lovett, 2015). Therefore, it is uncertain whether a more intensive social media strategy would be effective in increasing article page views. The research question guiding this study is: Does a more intensive social media strategy, including a larger base of followers, paid advertising, and increased posting frequency, increase 30-day page views of original research articles? This study aims to address the gap in the literature by using a randomized controlled design to evaluate the impact of a more intensive social media strategy on article page views. The study's findings will contribute to our understanding of the effectiveness of social media in promoting academic research and inform the development of social media strategies for journals and academic publishers. This study makes several contributions to the literature. First, it uses a randomized controlled design, which is considered the gold standard for evaluating the effectiveness of interventions (Higgins & Green, 2011). This design allows for the control of confounding variables and the establishment of causality between the social media intervention and article page views. Second, the study uses a more intensive social media strategy, including a larger base of followers, paid advertising, and increased posting frequency, which addresses the limitations of previous studies (Terrell, 2016). Third, the study evaluates the impact of social media on article page views over a 30-day period, which provides insight into the short-term effects of social media promotion (Shuai et al., 2012). Furthermore, this study's findings will have practical implications for journals and academic publishers seeking to promote their research through social media. By evaluating the effectiveness of a more intensive social media strategy, this study will provide evidence-based guidance on the use of social media in academic publishing. Additionally, the study's findings will inform the development of social media strategies for journals and academic publishers, including the use of paid advertising, posting frequency, and engagement strategies (Groves, 2012). Overall, this study aims to contribute to our understanding of the role of social media in promoting academic research and to inform the development of effective social media strategies for journals and academic publishers. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) was designed to evaluate the effect of increased intensity of social media exposure on the 30-day page views of original research articles published in Circulation. The study protocol was developed in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement (Moher et al., 2010). The trial was registered with the appropriate regulatory bodies, and the protocol was approved by the institutional review board. The study population consisted of original research articles published in Circulation between January 2015 and September 2015. Articles were eligible for inclusion if they were published online and had a corresponding author with a valid email address. Articles were excluded if they were published as part of a special issue or had a prior social media promotion. A total of 152 articles were randomized to either the social media arm or the control arm. The social media exposure consisted of Facebook and Twitter posts on the journal's accounts. To increase social media intensity, a larger base of followers was built using advertising and organic growth, and posts were presented in triplicate and boosted on Facebook and retweeted on Twitter. The social media posts included a brief summary of the article, a link to the article, and relevant hashtags. The control arm consisted of no social media exposure. The primary outcome was 30-day page views, which was defined as the number of times an article was viewed on the Circulation website within 30 days of publication. The outcome was measured using Google Analytics (Google, Inc., Mountain View, CA), which provides accurate and reliable metrics on website traffic (Sullivan, 2015). The secondary outcomes included the number of tweets, retweets, and likes on Twitter, as well as the number of Facebook likes and shares. The study used a randomized controlled design, where articles were randomly assigned to either the social media arm or the control arm using a computer-generated randomization sequence (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC). The randomization was stratified by article type (e.g., clinical trials, basic science) to ensure balance between the two arms. The allocation was concealed using sealed envelopes, and the researchers were blinded to the allocation until the data analysis stage. The sample size was calculated based on the results of a prior study (Kim et al., 2014), which reported a mean difference in 30-day page views of 100 between the social media arm and the control arm. Assuming a standard deviation of 200, a sample size of 152 articles (76 per arm) was required to detect a statistically significant difference with 80% power and a two-sided alpha level of 0.05. The data analysis was conducted using SAS software (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC). The primary outcome was analyzed using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which is a non-parametric test that is suitable for skewed data (Higgins, 2004). The test was used to compare the median 30-day page views between the social media arm and the control arm. The secondary outcomes were analyzed using descriptive statistics, such as means and standard deviations. Stopping rules were established a priori to ensure the trial was stopped if the intervention was found to be futile. The rules were based on the primary outcome, and the trial was stopped if the probability of detecting a statistically significant difference was less than 20% (Friedman et al., 1998). The trial was stopped on September 26, 2015, after 50% of the manuscripts had been randomized and had 30-day follow-up. Interactions between the treatment and covariates, such as article type, geographic location of the corresponding author, and whether the manuscript had an editorial, were evaluated using logistic regression models (Hosmer et al., 2013). The models were used to estimate the odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for each interaction term. The results were interpreted in the context of the study objectives and the results of prior studies (Eysenbach, 2011; OPERA, 2015). In conclusion, the methods used in this study were designed to evaluate the effect of increased intensity of social media exposure on the 30-day page views of original research articles published in Circulation. The study used a randomized controlled design, a clear primary outcome, and a robust data analysis plan to ensure the results were reliable and generalizable. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of social media promotion in increasing article views and engagement. A total of 152 manuscripts were randomized, with 74 manuscripts assigned to receive social media exposure and 78 manuscripts assigned to the control arm (Demer et al., 2016). The intervention and control arms were similar in terms of article type, with 45 (60.8%) and 48 (61.5%) original research articles, respectively (P=0.85), suggesting that the randomization process was successful in achieving balance between the two groups (Friedman et al., 2015). The geographic location of the corresponding author was also similar between the two groups, with 42 (56.8%) manuscripts from North America in the social media arm and 45 (57.7%) in the control arm (P=0.33), indicating that the results are generalizable across different regions (Ioannidis, 2005). Furthermore, the presence of an editorial accompanying the manuscript was also balanced between the two groups, with 23 (31.1%) manuscripts having an editorial in the social media arm and 24 (30.8%) in the control arm (P=0.80), suggesting that the editorial status did not influence the outcome (Lee et al., 2013). The primary outcome of interest was the 30-day page views, which was measured for all randomized manuscripts. The median number of 30-day page views was 499.5 in the social media arm and 450.5 in the control arm, indicating a slight increase in page views for the social media arm, but this difference was not statistically significant (P=0.38) (DeMets, 2006). This finding suggests that the increased intensity of social media intervention did not result in a significant increase in 30-day page views, consistent with the results of a previous study (Kurtz et al., 2012). To further explore the relationship between social media exposure and 30-day page views, we performed subgroup analyses to examine potential interactions between treatment and manuscript characteristics. We found no statistically significant interactions of treatment by manuscript type (P=0.86), suggesting that the effect of social media exposure on 30-day page views was consistent across different types of manuscripts (Blargen et al., 2017). Similarly, there were no significant interactions by corresponding author (P=0.35), trimester of publication date (P=0.34), or editorial status (P=0.79), indicating that these factors did not modify the effect of social media exposure on 30-day page views (Chen et al., 2018). The lack of significant interactions suggests that the increased intensity of social media intervention had a consistent effect across different subgroups, but this effect was not sufficient to result in a significant increase in 30-day page views (Demer et al., 2016). The results of this study are consistent with those of a previous study, which found that social media exposure did not increase 30-day page views (Kurtz et al., 2012). The findings of this study have implications for the use of social media as a tool to increase the dissemination and uptake of research findings, and suggest that alternative strategies may be needed to achieve this goal (Stewart et al., 2019). These findings have implications for the use of social media in the dissemination of research findings and suggest that alternative strategies may be needed to increase the uptake of research articles (Ioannidis, 2005).
